Cakkhusotādīnanti cakkhusotādīnaṃ aṅgānaṃ. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “sabbaṅgapaccaṅga”nti, sabbaaṅgapaccaṅgavantanti attho. Pasādo nāma natthīti imināva bhāvajīvitindriyānampi abhāvo vuttoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Rucivasenāti icchāvasena. Aññampīti bhagavatā kariyamānato aññampi kiriyaṃ karoti. Ayañcettha buddhānubhāvo. Yadi sāvakanimmitesu nānappakāratā natthi, “sace pana nānāvaṇṇe kātukāmo hotī”tiādi yaṃ heṭṭhā vuttaṃ, taṃ kathanti? Taṃ tathā tathā parikammaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhahantassa te te vaṇṇavayādivisesā parikammānurūpaṃ ijjhantīti katvā vuttaṃ. Idha pana yathādhiṭṭhite nimmitarūpe sace sāvako “ime visesā hontū”ti [M 2.0034] icchati, na ijjhati, buddhānaṃ pana ijjhatīti ayamattho dassitoti na koci virodho.

‘Of the eye, ear, etc.’ (Cakkhusotādīnaṃ) means of the limbs such as the eye and ear. For indeed, it is said, ‘complete with all major and minor limbs’ (sabbaṅgapaccaṅgaṃ); the meaning is ‘possessing all major and minor limbs.’ By this very phrase, ‘there is no sensitivity’ (pasādo nāma natthi), the absence of the materiality of sex and the life faculty is also stated; thus it should be understood. ‘According to inclination’ (rucivasena) means by the power of wish. ‘And other’ (aññampi) means he performs another action different from the action being performed by the Blessed One. And this, herein, is the power of a Buddha. If there is no variety in the forms created by disciples, then how is that which was stated before—‘But if he wishes to create various colors,’ and so on—to be understood? That was stated because, for one who makes a determination after having performed the preliminary work in such and such a way, those respective distinctions of color, age, and so on, are accomplished in accordance with the preliminary work. Here, however, in a created form that has been determined, if a disciple wishes, ‘Let these distinctions be,’ it is not accomplished; but for the Buddhas, it is accomplished. Thus, this meaning is shown, so there is no contradiction.

Idāni yāni tāni “yāva brahmalokāpi kāyena vasaṃ vattetī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.10) pāḷiyā atthadassanavasena vibhattāni “dūrepi santike adhiṭṭhātī”tiādīni cuddasa pāṭihāriyāni[V 2.0033], tattha sikhāppattaṃ kāyena vasavattanapāṭihāriyaṃ dassetuṃ “ettha cā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha yanti kiriyāparāmasanaṃ, tena “rūpaṃ passatī”ti ettha yadetaṃ rūpadassanaṃ, “saddaṃ suṇātī”ti ettha yadetaṃ saddasavanaṃ, “cittaṃ pajānātī”ti ettha yadetaṃ cittajānananti evaṃ dibbacakkhusotacetopariyañāṇakattukaṃ dassanasavanajānanakiriyaṃ parāmasatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ito paresu santiṭṭhatītiādīsupi eseva nayo. Yampissāti yampi assa. Yogino adhiṭṭhānanti sambandho. Yañca khoti ettha kho-saddo avadhāraṇattho, visesattho vā, tena ayamevettha kāyena vasavattanapāṭihāriyesu ukkaṭṭhataranti dīpeti. Kasmā? “Ayaṃ nu kho iddhimā, ayaṃ nu kho nimmito”ti ekaccassa brahmuno āsaṅkuppādanato. Yadaggena cetaṃ adhiṭṭhitaṃ visesato manomayanti vuccati, tadaggena ukkaṭṭhataranti veditabbaṃ. Tenāha “ettāvatā kāyena vasaṃ vatteti nāmā”ti. Yadi evaṃ kasmā idha sesāni gahitānīti āha “sesaṃ…pe… vutta”nti.

Now, regarding those fourteen marvels—such as ‘he resolves upon what is far as near’—which are explained by way of showing the meaning of the Pāli text ‘he wields mastery with the body even up to the Brahma-world,’ in order to show the marvel of wielding mastery with the body, which is the peak among them, the passage beginning with ‘Here also…’ is introduced. Therein, ‘yanti’ is a reference to action. By that, it should be understood that it refers to the action of seeing, hearing, and knowing—which has the divine eye, divine ear, and knowledge of others’ minds as its agent—in such cases as ‘whatever is this seeing of form’ in the phrase ‘he sees form’; ‘whatever is this hearing of sound’ in the phrase ‘he hears sound’; and ‘whatever is this knowing of mind’ in the phrase ‘he knows mind’. This same method applies also in the following passages, such as ‘santiṭṭhati’. ‘Yampissāti’ is ‘yampi assa’. The connection is ‘and whatever resolve of this yogī’. Here, in ‘yañca kho’, the particle ‘kho’ has the meaning of emphasis or, alternatively, specification. By that, it indicates that this very marvel is more excellent among these marvels of wielding mastery with the body. Why? Because it arouses doubt for a certain Brahmā, thus: ‘Is this one the powerful one, or is this one the created one?’ And by which factor this resolved form is especially called 'mind-made', by that factor it should be known as more excellent. Therefore, he said: ‘To this extent, it is called “wielding mastery with the body”.’ If so, why are the remaining marvels included here? To this, he said: ‘The rest… and so on… is stated.’

398. Idaṃ nānākaraṇanti kāmamimāpi dve iddhiyo adhiṭṭhānavaseneva ijjhanti, tathāpi idaṃ idāni vuccamānaṃ imāsaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ viseso. Pakativaṇṇaṃ vijahitvāti attano pakatirūpaṃ vijahitvā apanetvā, paresaṃ adassetvāti attho. Kumārakavaṇṇanti kumārakasaṇṭhānaṃ. Dassetīti tathā vikubbanto attani dasseti. Nāgavaṇṇaṃ vātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Hatthimpi dassetīti attānampi hatthiṃ katvā dasseti, bahiddhāpi hatthiṃ dasseti. Etadatthameva hi idha “hatthivaṇṇaṃ vā dassetī”ti avatvā “hatthimpi dassetī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.13) vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana keci bahiddhā hatthiādidassanavacanaṃ “pakativaṇṇaṃ vijahitvā”ti vacanena vikubbaniddhibhāvena virujjhatīti vadanti, tadayuttaṃ. Kasmā? Pakativaṇṇavijahanaṃ nāma attano pakatirūpassa aññesaṃ adassanaṃ, na sabbena sabbaṃ tassa nirodhanaṃ. Evaṃ sati attānaṃ adassetvā bahiddhā hatthiṃ dassento “pakativaṇṇaṃ vijahitvā hatthiṃ dassetī”ti [M 2.0035] vuccamāne ko ettha virodho, attanā pana hatthivaṇṇo hutvā bahiddhāpi hatthiṃ dassante vattabbameva natthi. Tenevāha “bahiddhāpi hatthiādidassanavasena vutta”nti. Evañca katvā vikubbaniddhibhāvena ca na koci virodho.

398. ‘This is the differentiation’ (idaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ): although these two psychic powers are indeed accomplished by the power of resolve alone, still, what is now being stated is the differentiating distinction between them. ‘Having abandoned one’s natural appearance’ (pakativaṇṇaṃ vijahitvā) means having given up and removed one’s own natural form, so that others do not see it—this is the meaning. ‘The appearance of a boy’ (kumārakavaṇṇaṃ) means the form of a young boy. ‘Manifests’ (dasseti) means that, transforming in such a way, one displays it in oneself. The same principle applies to ‘the appearance of a serpent,’ and so on. ‘Manifests an elephant as well’ (hatthimpi dasseti) means one makes oneself into an elephant and displays it, and one also displays an elephant externally. It is for this very reason that here, instead of saying, ‘manifests the appearance of an elephant’ (hatthivaṇṇaṃ vā dasseti), it is said, ‘manifests an elephant as well.’ As for what some say, that the statement about displaying an external elephant or the like contradicts the statement ‘having abandoned one’s natural appearance’ and the nature of transformative psychic power, that is incorrect. Why? ‘Abandoning one’s natural appearance’ means that one’s own natural form is not seen by others; it is not the complete and utter cessation of that form. This being the case, when one, without showing oneself, displays an elephant externally, what contradiction is there when it is said, ‘having abandoned one’s natural appearance, one manifests an elephant’? Furthermore, when one has personally assumed the appearance of an elephant and also displays an elephant externally, there is nothing at all to be said against it. For that reason, it was said, ‘It is stated in terms of displaying an external elephant, etc.’ And in this way, there is no contradiction with the nature of transformative psychic power.

Pāḷiyañca kumārakavaṇṇaṃ vātiādīsu aniyamattho vā-saddo vutto. Tesu ekekasseva karaṇadassanatthaṃ. Hatthimpītiādīsu pana hatthiādīnaṃ bahūnaṃ ekajjhaṃ kātabbābhāvadassanatthaṃ samuccayattho pi-saddo vutto. Tena “hatthimpi dassetī”tiādīsu dutiye vuttanayeneva attho gahetabbo.

In the Pāli text, in phrases such as ‘kumārakavaṇṇaṃ vā,’ the word ‘vā’ is stated with the meaning of indeterminacy, for the purpose of showing the performance of each one of these individually. However, in phrases such as ‘hatthimpi,’ the word ‘pi’ is stated with the meaning of aggregation, for the purpose of showing that many things, such as elephants, can be created simultaneously. Therefore, in passages such as ‘hatthimpi dasseti,’ the meaning should be understood according to the method stated in the second instance.

Iddhimato [V 2.0034] attano kumārakākārena paresaṃ dassanaṃ kumārakavaṇṇanimmānaṃ, na ettha kiñci apubbaṃ pathavīādivatthu nipphādīyatīti kasiṇaniyamena payojanābhāvato “pathavīkasiṇādīsu aññatarārammaṇato”ti vuttaṃ. Satipi vā vatthunipphādane yathārahaṃ taṃ pathavīkasiṇādivaseneva ijjhatīti evampettha kasiṇaniyamena payojanaṃ nattheva. Kumārakavaṇṇañhi dassentena nīlavaṇṇaṃ vā dassetabbaṃ siyā, pītādīsu aññataravaṇṇaṃ vā. Tathā sati nīlādikasiṇāni samāpajjitabbānīti āpannova kasiṇaniyamo. Eseva nayo sesesupi. Evamadhiṭṭhite yadeke pathavīkasiṇavasena “ekopi hutvā bahudhā hotī”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.238; ma. ni. 1.147; saṃ. ni. 5.842; paṭi. ma. 3.10) bhāvoti evaṃ pavattena kasiṇaniddesena idha vikubbaniddhiniddese “pathavīkasiṇādīsu aññatarārammaṇato”tiādivacanassa virodhaṃ āsaṅkanti, so anokāsovāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nimminitabbabhāvena attanā icchitoti attano kumārakavaṇṇo, na pana attano daharakāle kumārakavaṇṇoti. Nāgādivaṇṇesupi ayaṃ nayo byāpī evāti yadeke “nāgādinimmāne na yujjati viyā”ti vadanti, tadapohataṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

For one endowed with psychic power, the manifestation of oneself to others in the form of a young boy is the creation of the form of a young boy. Here, nothing unprecedented, no object like earth, etc., is produced. Therefore, because there is no purpose served by a fixed rule regarding kasiṇas, it is said, 'from any one of the objects such as the earth-kasiṇa, etc.' Or alternatively, even if the production of an object were to occur, it would be accomplished appropriately only by the power of the earth-kasiṇa, etc.; thus, even in this case, there is indeed no purpose served by a fixed rule regarding kasiṇas. For when manifesting the form of a young boy, one might have to display a blue color or some other color such as yellow, etc. In that case, the blue-kasiṇa, etc., would have to be entered into; thus, the fixed rule of the kasiṇa would indeed apply. The same method applies to the remaining cases as well. When it is thus determined, that some suspect a contradiction between the statement that occurs in the exposition of the kasiṇa by means of the earth-kasiṇa, 'having been one, he becomes many,' etc., and the statement here in the exposition of the power of transformation, 'from any one of the objects such as the earth-kasiṇa, etc.'—that suspicion should be seen as baseless. 'One's own form of a young boy' means a form desired by oneself as something to be created; it is not, however, the form of a young boy from one's own youth. This method is indeed applicable also to the forms of nāgas, etc. Therefore, that some say, 'It seems unsuitable in the creation of nāgas, etc.'—that should be seen as refuted.

Bahiddhāpīti pi-saddena ajjhattaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Ayañhettha attho – hatthimpi dassetītiādi ajjhattaṃ, bahiddhāpi hatthiādidassanavasena vuttaṃ, na “kumārakavaṇṇaṃ vā”tiādi viya ajjhattameva kumārakavaṇṇādīnaṃ dassanavasenāti. Yaṃ ettha vattabbaṃ adhiṭṭhānavidhānaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

By the word 'pi' in 'bahiddhāpi,' it includes 'internally.' For herein this is the meaning: 'showing an elephant,' etc., is stated by way of showing an elephant, etc., both internally and externally; it is not like 'or the form of a young boy,' etc., which is stated only by way of showing the form of a young boy, etc., internally. Whatever method of determination should be stated here, that has already been stated previously.

399. Kāyanti [M 2.0036] attano karajakāyaṃ. Vuttanayenevāti “ayaṃ kāyo susiro hotū”ti parikammaṃ katvā puna “pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāyā”ti imaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayānusāramāha. Aññaṃ kāyanti yaṃ manomayaṃ kāyaṃ nimminitukāmo, taṃ. Muñjamhāti muñjatiṇato. Īsikanti tassa kaṇḍaṃ. Kosiyāti asikosato. Karaṇḍāyāti peḷāya, nimmokatoti ca vadanti. Abbāhatīti uddharati. Pavāheyyāti ākaḍḍheyya.

399. By 'kāyaṃ' is meant one's own physical body. By 'vuttanayena' (in the manner stated) is meant this, in accordance with the method stated previously: having performed the preliminary practice, 'May this body become hollow,' and again, having entered and emerged from the base jhāna. By 'aññaṃ kāyaṃ' (another body) is meant that mind-made body which one wishes to create. By 'muñjamhā' is meant from muñja grass. By 'īsikaṃ' is meant its stalk. By 'kosiyā' is meant from a scabbard. By 'karaṇḍā' is meant from a basket; and they also say, 'from a sloughed-off skin.' 'Abbāhati' means 'extracts.' 'Pavāheyya' means 'would pull out.'

Iddhividhaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the kinds of psychic power is finished.

Iti dvādasamaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus ends the commentary on the twelfth chapter.

13. Abhiññāniddesavaṇṇanā

13. Commentary on the Exposition of the Higher Knowledges

Dibbasotadhātukathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Divine-Ear Element

400. Tatthāti [M 2.0037][V 2.0035] dibbasotadhātuyā niddese. Abhiññāpāḷiyā hi niddesamukhena abhiññānaṃ nibbattanavidhi vidhīyati. Abhiññāsīsenettha abhiññāpāḷi vuttā. Tenāha “tato parāsu ca tīsu abhiññāsū”ti. Tato parāsūti ca satthuno desanākkamaṃ, attano ca uddesakkamaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na paṭipattikkamaṃ. Na hi paṭipajjantā imināva kamena paṭipajjanti. Sabbatthāti dibbasotadhātupāḷiyaṃ, sesābhiññāpāḷiyañcāti sabbattha. Tatrāti vākyopaññāse nipātamattaṃ, tatra vā yathāvuttapāṭhe. Dibbasadisattāti dibbe bhavāti dibbā, devānaṃ sotadhātu, tāya dibbāya sadisattā. Idāni taṃ dibbasadisataṃ vibhāvetuṃ “devānaṃ hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sucaritakammanibbattāti saddhābahulatāvisuddhadiṭṭhitānisaṃsadassāvitādisampattiyā suṭṭhu caritattā sucaritena devūpapattijanakena puññakammena nibbattā. Pittasemharuhirādīhīti ādi-saddena vātarogādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Apalibuddhāti anupaddutā. Pittādīhi anupaddutattā, kammassa ca uḷāratāya upakkilesavimutti veditabbā. Upakkilesadosarahitaṃ hi kammaṃ tiṇādidosarahitaṃ viya sassaṃ uḷāraphalaṃ anupakkiliṭṭhaṃ hoti. Kāraṇūpacārena cassa phalaṃ tathā voharīyati, yathā “sukkaṃ sukkavipāka”nti (dī. ni. 3.312; ma. ni. 2.81; a. ni. 4.233). Dūrepīti pi-saddena sukhumassāpi ārammaṇassa sampaṭicchanasamatthataṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Pasādasotadhātūti catumahābhūtānaṃ pasādalakkhaṇā sotadhātu.

400. ‘Therein’ refers to the exposition of the divine ear element. For in the Abhiññā Pāḷi, the method of producing the higher knowledges is laid down by way of exposition. Here, the Abhiññā Pāḷi is referred to by the heading of ‘Abhiññā’. Therefore, he said, ‘and thereafter in the three higher knowledges.’ ‘Then thereafter’ is said with reference to the Teacher’s order of teaching and his own order of exposition, not the order of practice. For those who practice do not necessarily practice in this very order. ‘Everywhere’ means in the Pāḷi on the divine ear element and in the Pāḷi on the remaining higher knowledges. ‘Therein’ is merely a particle for introducing a sentence, or ‘there’ refers to the passage as stated. ‘Like the divine’ means divine because it exists in the divine realm; this refers to the ear-element of the gods, being similar to that divine element. Now, to explain that likeness to the divine, ‘For the gods…’ and so on is said. Therein, ‘produced by kamma of good conduct’ means produced by meritorious kamma that generates rebirth among the gods, which is called ‘good conduct’ because it was well-practiced through the accomplishment of such things as abundance of faith, purity of view, and seeing the benefits. By ‘bile, phlegm, blood, etc.,’ the word ‘etc.’ includes disorders of wind and the like. ‘Unafflicted’ means unmolested. Because it is unmolested by bile and the like, and because of the greatness of the kamma, it should be understood as freedom from defilements. For kamma free from the defect of defilements, like a crop free from the defect of weeds, has an abundant, undefiled result. And, by way of causal designation, its result is spoken of thus, as in ‘wholesome kamma has a wholesome result.’ In ‘even from afar,’ the particle ‘pi’ includes the ability to apprehend even a subtle object. ‘The sensitive ear-element’ is the ear-element that has the characteristic of clarity of the four great elements.

Vīriyārambhavaseneva ijjhanato sabbāpi kusalabhāvanā vīriyabhāvanā, padhānasaṅkhārasamannāgatā vā iddhipādabhāvanāpi visesato vīriyabhāvanā, tassā ānubhāvena nibbattā vīriyabhāvanābalanibbattā. Ñāṇamayā sotadhātu ñāṇasotadhātu. Tādisāyevāti upakkilesavimuttatāya, dūrepi sukhumassapi ārammaṇassa sampaṭicchanasamatthatāya ca taṃsadisā eva[V 2.0036]. Dibbavihāravasena paṭiladdhattāti dibbavihārasaṅkhātānaṃ catunnaṃ bhūmīnaṃ vasena paṭiladdhattā, iminā kāraṇavasenassā dibbabhāvamāha. Yaṃ cettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Dibbavihārasannissitattāti [M 2.0038] aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgamena ukkaṃsagataṃ pādakajjhānasaṅkhātaṃ dibbavihāraṃ sannissāya pavattattā, dibbavihārapariyāpannaṃ vā attanā sampayuttaṃ rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānaṃ nissayapaccayabhūtaṃ sannissitattāti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Savanaṭṭhenāti saddagahaṇaṭṭhena. Yāthāvato hi saddūpaladdhi saddasabhāvāvabodho savanaṃ. Santesupi aññesu sabhāvadhāraṇādīsu dhātuatthesu attasuññatāsandassanatthā satthu dhātudesanāti āha “nijjīvaṭṭhena cā”ti. Sotadhātukiccaṃ saddasampaṭicchanaṃ, saddasanniṭṭhānapaccayatā ca.

Since all wholesome development succeeds by the power of the initiation of effort alone, it is the development of effort. Or, the development of the bases of psychic power, which is endowed with the factor of striving, is especially the development of effort. Born through its power, it is produced by the strength of the development of effort. The knowledge-made ear-element is the knowledge-ear-element. It is similar precisely in being free from defilements and in the ability to receive even subtle objects from afar. 'Because it is attained through divine abidings' means because it is attained by means of the four planes called divine abidings; by this reason, its divine nature is stated. Whatever needs to be said here has already been stated below. 'Dependent on divine abidings' means because it operates relying on the divine abiding, which is the base jhāna attained to excellence, endowed with eight factors, or because it relies on the fourth jhāna of the form sphere, which is included in divine abidings, associated with itself, and serves as a supporting condition—this meaning should be understood in this way. 'In the sense of hearing' means in the sense of grasping sound. For the apprehension of sound as it truly is, the understanding of the nature of sound, is hearing. Even though there are other meanings of 'element', such as bearing its intrinsic nature, the Teacher's exposition of the elements is for the purpose of showing the emptiness of self; thus he said, 'and in the sense of being lifeless.' The function of the ear-element is the reception of sound and serving as a condition for the determination of sound.

Ñāṇassa parisuddhi upakkilesavigamenevāti āha “nirupakkilesāyā”ti. Mānusikā manussa santakā, maṃsasotadhātu, dibbavidūrādivisayaggahaṇasaṅkhātena attano kiccavisesena atikkantaṃ mānusikaṃ etāyāti atikkantamānusikā. Tenāha “manussūpacāraṃ atikkamitvā saddasavanenā”ti. Tattha manussūpacāranti manussehi upacaritabbaṭṭhānaṃ, pakatiyā sotadvārena gahetabbaṃ visayanti adhippāyo. Tenāha “saddasavanenā”ti. Dibbeti devalokapariyāpanne. Te pana visesato devānaṃ kathā saddā hontīti āha “devānaṃ sadde”ti. Manussānaṃ eteti mānusā, te mānuse. Evaṃ devamanussasaddānaṃyeva gahitattā vuttaṃ “padesapariyādāna”nti, ekadesaggahaṇanti attho. Sadehasannissitā attano sarīre sannissitā. Nippadesapariyādānaṃ ṭhānabhedaggahaṇamukhena saviññāṇakādibhedabhinnassa saddassa anavasesena saṅgaṇhanato.

The purity of knowledge is only by the removal of defilements; therefore, it is said, 'for the undefiled.' 'Human' means what belongs to humans: the flesh-ear-element. That which surpasses the human element by its own special function—described as the grasping of objects such as divine and very distant sounds—is 'surpassing the human.' Therefore, it is said, 'by hearing sound, having surpassed the human sphere.' Therein, 'human sphere' means the place to be frequented by humans; the intention is the object to be grasped by the ear-door by nature. Therefore, it is said, 'by hearing sound.' 'Divine' means those included in the deva-world. And those, specifically, are the sounds of the devas' conversation; therefore, it is said, 'the sounds of devas.' 'These belong to humans,' thus they are 'human'; those human sounds. Thus, because only the sounds of devas and humans are grasped, it is called 'partial grasping,' which means the grasping of a portion. 'Residing in one's own body' means residing in one's own body. 'Complete grasping' is so called because of the grasping without remainder—by means of grasping the distinction of location—of sound differentiated by divisions such as animate and so forth.

Ayaṃ dibbasotadhātu. Parikammasamādhicittenāti parikammabhūtāveṇikasamādhicittena, dibbasotañāṇassa parikammavasena pavattakkhaṇikasamādhinā samāhitacittenāti attho. Parikammasamādhi nāma dibbasotadhātuyā upacārāvatthātipi vadanti. Sā pana nānāvajjanavasena vuttāti daṭṭhabbā. Sabboḷārikasaddadassanatthaṃ sīhādīnaṃ saddo paṭhamaṃ gahito. Tiyojanamatthakepi kira kesarasīhassa sīhanādasaddo suyyati. Ādi-saddena meghasaddabyagghasaddādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Ettha ca yathā oḷārikasaddāvajjanaṃ yāvadeva sukhumasaddāvajjanūpāyadassanatthaṃ, tathā saddaggahaṇabhāvanābalena sukhumatarasaddaggahaṇasaṃsiddhito.

This is the divine-ear element. 'With a mind of preliminary concentration' means with a mind of unique concentration that has become preliminary work, and with a mind concentrated by momentary concentration that has arisen by way of preliminary work for the divine-ear-knowledge—this is the meaning. Preliminary concentration is also said to be the access-stage of the divine-ear-element. But this should be understood as stated in terms of various advertings. For the purpose of showing the grossest sound, the sound of lions and so forth is first taken. It is said that even at a distance of three yojanas, the roaring sound of a maned lion is heard. By the word 'etcetera,' the inclusion of sounds such as the sound of thunder, the sound of tigers, and so forth should be understood. And here, just as the adverting to gross sounds is only for the purpose of showing the means for adverting to subtle sounds, so too is it because of the successful accomplishment of grasping even subtler sounds through the power of the development of grasping sound.

Evaṃ [M 2.0039] āsannasaddaggahaṇānusārena dūradūratarasaddaggahaṇampi samijjhatīti dassetuṃ “puratthimāya [V 2.0037] disāyā”tiādinā disāsambandhavasena saddānaṃ manasikāravidhi āraddho. Tattha saddanimittanti ñāṇuppattihetubhāvato saddo eva saddanimittaṃ, yo vā yathāvutto upādāyupādāya labbhamāno saddānaṃ oḷārikasukhumākāro, taṃ saddanimittaṃ. Tenevāha “saddānaṃ saddanimitta”nti. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “oḷārikānampi sukhumānampi saddānaṃ saddanimittaṃ manasi kātabba”nti, taṃ oḷārikasukhumasammatesupi oḷārikasukhumasabbhāvadassanatthaṃ. Tañca sabbaṃ sukhume ñāṇaparicayadassanatthaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Saddanimittassa apaccuppannasabhāvattā “saddova saddanimitta”nti ayameva pakkho ñāyāgatoti keci, taṃ na oḷārikasukhumānaṃ saddānaṃ vaṇṇārammaṇena ñāṇena nīlapītādivaṇṇānaṃ viya tattheva gahetabbato. Oḷārikasukhumabhāvo cettha saddanimittanti adhippetanti. Tassāti yathāvuttena vidhinā paṭipajjantassa yogino. Te saddāti ye sabboḷārikato pabhuti āvajjantassa anukkamena sukhumasukhumā saddā āvajjitā, te. Pākatikacittassāpīti pādakajjhānasamāpajjanato pubbe pavattacittassāpi. Parikammasamādhicittassāti dibbasotadhātuyā uppādanatthaṃ pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhitassa saddaṃ ārabbha parikammakaraṇavasena pavattakkhaṇikasamādhicittassa. Pubbepi ñāṇena parimadditattā ativiya pākaṭā hontīti sambandho.

To demonstrate that in this way, by following the method of grasping a nearby sound, the grasping of a distant and a more distant sound also succeeds, the method of attending to sounds in relation to the directions—beginning with 'from the eastern direction'—is set forth. Therein, the sound-sign is the sound itself, because it is the cause for the arising of knowledge; or, it is that coarse and subtle aspect of sounds which is obtained by repeatedly grasping them as described—that is the sound-sign. For that very reason, he said, 'the sound-sign of sounds.' Again, as for what was said—'the sound-sign of sounds, both coarse and subtle, should be attended to'—that is for the purpose of showing the actual existence of coarseness and subtlety even in sounds that are considered coarse and subtle. And all that should be understood as being for the purpose of showing the familiarity of knowledge with the subtle. Some say that because the sound-sign does not have a present nature, this very position, 'sound itself is the sound-sign,' is the logical one. But that is not so, because coarse and subtle sounds are to be grasped in that very way, just as colors such as blue and yellow are grasped by knowledge that has color as its object. And here, coarseness and subtlety are intended as the sound-sign. 'His' refers to the yogī who practices by the method as described. 'Those sounds' are those sounds which, beginning from the very coarsest, are adverted to successively by one who is adverting, becoming increasingly subtle. 'Even for the natural mind' means even for the mind that has arisen before entering the base jhāna. 'For the mind of preliminary concentration' refers to the momentary concentration mind of one who, having entered the base jhāna for the purpose of producing the divine ear element and then emerged, has a mind that arises by way of performing preliminary work, taking sound as its object. The connection is that because they were also previously refined by knowledge, they become extremely manifest.

Tesu saddesūti ye parikammassa visayadassanatthaṃ bahū saddā vuttā, tesu saddesu. Aññataranti yatthassa parikammakaraṇavasena abhiṇhaṃ manasikāro pavatto, taṃ ekaṃ saddaṃ. Tato paranti tato appanuppattito paraṃ. Tasmiṃ soteti tasmiṃ ñāṇasote. Patito hotīti dibbasotadhātu antogadhā hoti appanācittassa uppattito pabhuti dibbasotañāṇalābhī nāma hoti, na dānissa tadatthaṃ bhāvanābhiyogo icchitabboti attho. Tanti dibbasotadhātuṃ. Thāmajātanti jātathāmaṃ daḷhabhāvappattaṃ. Vaḍḍhetabbaṃ pādakajjhānārammaṇaṃ. Kinti kittakanti āha “etthantare saddaṃ suṇāmīti ekaṅgulamattaṃ paricchinditvā”ti. Pādakajjhānassa hi ārammaṇabhūtaṃ kasiṇanimittaṃ “ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ pharatū”ti manasi karitvā pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjantassa kasiṇanimittaṃ tattakaṃ ṭhānaṃ pharitvā tiṭṭhati[M 2.0040]. So samāpattito vuṭṭhāya tattha gate sadde āvajjati, subhāvitabhāvanattā tattha aññataraṃ saddaṃ ārabbha uppannāvajjanānantaraṃ cattāri, pañca vā javanāni uppajjanti. Tesu pacchimaṃ iddhicittaṃ, itarassa punapi pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitabbameva. Tato eva hi pādakajjhānārammaṇena phuṭṭhokāsabbhantaragatepi sadde suṇātiyevāti sāsaṅkaṃ vadati. Ekaṅguladvaṅgulādiggahaṇañcettha sukhumasaddāpekkhāya kataṃ.

“Among those sounds” refers to those many sounds that have been mentioned for the purpose of showing the object of the preliminary work. “A certain one” means that one sound to which his attention has been frequently directed by way of preparatory practice. “After that” means after the arising of absorption. “With that ear” means with that stream of knowledge. “He has fallen into” means the divine ear-element is included. From the arising of the absorption consciousness onward, he is called one who has obtained the divine ear-knowledge, and from then on, no further effort in cultivation for that purpose is to be desired for him—this is the meaning. “That” refers to the divine ear-element. “Become strong” means having become strong and attained a state of firmness. The object of the base jhāna is to be extended. How? And to what extent? To this, it is said, “Having defined the space as, ‘I hear the sound within this one fingerbreadth.’” For, when one enters the base jhāna after mentally determining regarding the kasiṇa-nimitta that is its object, ‘Let it pervade this much space,’ the kasiṇa-nimitta pervades that much space and remains. Having emerged from that attainment, he attends to the sounds that have occurred there. Due to the well-developed cultivation, immediately after the adverting has arisen taking a certain sound there as its object, four or five impulsions arise. Among these, the last is the mind of psychic power; for another person, the base jhāna must be entered again. For this very reason, the author states with reservation, “he surely hears even the sounds that have occurred within the space pervaded by the object of the base jhāna.” And here, the measurement of one fingerbreadth, two fingerbreadths, and so on, is made with respect to subtle sounds.

Evaṃ [V 2.0038] suṇantovāti evaṃ paricchinditvā paricchinditvā savanena vasīkatābhiñño hutvā yathāvajjite sadde suṇanto eva. Pāṭiyekkanti ekajjhaṃ pavattamānepi te sadde paccekaṃ vatthubhedena vavatthapetukāmatāya sati.

“Hearing thus” means that having thus discerned again and again and become skilled in the supernormal knowledge through listening, he hears the sounds as they are attended to. “One by one” means when there is a desire to distinguish those sounds individually by their distinct bases, even when they occur simultaneously.

Dibbasotadhātukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Divine Ear-Element is concluded.

Cetopariyañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Knowledge of Penetrating Others’ Minds

401. Pariyātīti sarāgādivibhāgena paricchijja jānāti. Tenāha “paricchindatīti attho”ti. Yesañhi dhātūnaṃ gati attho, buddhipi tesaṃ attho. “Parasattāna”nti ettha para-saddo aññatthoti āha “attānaṃ ṭhapetvā sesasattāna”nti, yathā hi yo paro na hoti, so attā. Yo attā na hoti, so paroti. Sattānanti cettha rūpādīsu sattāti sattā. Tassā pana paññattiyā saviññāṇakasantāne niruḷhattā nicchandarāgāpi sattātveva vuccanti, bhūtapubbagatiyā vā. “Pu”nti narakaṃ, tattha galanti papatantīti puggalā, pāpakārino. Itarepi saṃsāre saṃsārino taṃsabhāvānātivattanato puggalātveva vuccanti. Taṃtaṃsattanikāyassa vā tattha tattha upapattiyā pūraṇato, aniccatāvasena galanato ca puggalāti neruttā.

401. “Pariyāti” means one knows by distinguishing through categories such as “with lust” and so forth. Therefore, it is said, “The meaning is ‘discerns.’” For, of those verbal roots which have the meaning of “going” (gati), they also have the meaning of “knowing” (buddhi). In the phrase “parasattānaṃ” (of other beings), the word “para” means “other”; therefore, it is said, “excluding oneself, the remaining beings,” just as whoever is not “other” is oneself, and whoever is not oneself is “other.” And in the phrase “sattānaṃ” (of beings), because they are attached (sattā) to forms and so forth, they are called “sattā” (beings). However, because that designation is established in a conscious continuum, even those without desire and lust are called “beings,” or by way of what has been before. “Pu” refers to hell; because they fall (galanti) and plunge there, they are called “puggalā” (persons), the evildoers. Others too, wandering in saṃsāra, are called “puggalā” because they do not transcend that nature. Alternatively, etymologists say they are called “puggalā” because of the filling (pūraṇa) of various groups of beings by rebirth in various places, and because of the falling away (galana) by way of impermanence.

Etañhīti ettha hi-saddo hetuattho. Yasmā “etaṃ cetopariyañāṇaṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇavasena ijjhatī”ti taṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ, etassa cetopariyañāṇassa uppādane parikammaṃ, tasmā tena cetopariyañāṇaṃ uppādetukāmena adhigatadibbacakkhuñāṇena bhikkhunāti evaṃ yojanā kātabbā[M 2.0041]. Hadayarūpanti na hadayavatthu, atha kho hadayamaṃsapesi. Yaṃ bahi kamalamakuḷasaṇṭhānaṃ, anto kosātakīphalasadisanti vuccati, tañhi nissāya dāni vuccamānaṃ lohitaṃ tiṭṭhati. Hadayavatthu pana imaṃ lohitaṃ nissāya pavattatīti. Kathaṃ pana dibbacakkhunā lohitassa vaṇṇadassanena arūpaṃ cittaṃ pariyesatīti āha “yadā hī”tiādi. Kathaṃ pana somanassasahagatādicittavuttiyā kammajassa lohitassa vividhavaṇṇabhāvāpattīti? Ko vā evamāha “kammajameva taṃ lohita”nti catusantatirūpassāpi tattha labbhamānattā. Tenevāha “idaṃ rūpaṃ somanassindriyasamuṭṭhāna”ntiādi. Evampi yaṃ tattha acittajaṃ, tassa yathāvuttavaṇṇabhedena [V 2.0039] na bhavitabbanti? Bhavitabbaṃ, sesatisantatirūpānaṃ tadanuvattanato. Yathā hi gamanādīsu cittajarūpāni utukammāhārasamuṭṭhānarūpehi anuvattīyanti, aññathā kāyassa desantaruppattiyeva na siyā, evamidhāpi cittajarūpaṃ sesatisantatirūpāni anuvattamānāni pavattanti. Pasādakodhavelāsu cakkhussa vaṇṇabhedāpattiyeva ca tadatthassa nidassanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

In “Etañhi,” the particle “hi” has the meaning of a reason. Because “this knowledge of others’ minds is accomplished by means of the divine eye knowledge,” that divine eye knowledge is the preliminary action for the arising of this knowledge of others’ minds. Therefore, the connection should be made thus: “by a monk who has attained divine eye knowledge and wishes to produce the knowledge of others’ minds.” “Heart-form” does not refer to the heart-base, but rather to the flesh of the heart. It is said that externally it is like a lotus bud and internally similar to a kosātakī fruit; the blood now being spoken of depends on this. The heart-base, however, functions depending on this blood. But how does one search for the formless mind by observing the color of blood with the divine eye? To this, it is said, “For when…” and so on. And how does the blood produced by kamma assume various colors in accordance with mental states such as joy and so forth? Who would say, “That blood is solely produced by kamma,” when the four continuities of material phenomena are also present there? Hence, it is stated, “This form arises from the joy faculty,” and so on. Even so, one might object that for that which is not mind-produced there, there should not be the aforementioned variations in color. It must, due to the conformity of the remaining three continuities of material phenomena. For just as in actions like walking, material forms arising from temperature, kamma, and nutriment conform to the mind-produced material forms—otherwise, the body’s movement to another place would not occur—so too here, the remaining three continuities of material phenomena proceed in conformity with the mind-produced material form. Moreover, the variations in the eye’s color during moments of clarity or anger should be seen as illustrating this point.

Pariyesantenāti paṭhamaṃ tāva anumānato ñāṇaṃ pesetvā gavesantena. Cetopariyañāṇañhi uppādetukāmena yoginā heṭṭhā vuttanayena rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānaṃ aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ abhinīhārakkhamaṃ katvā dibbacakkhuñāṇassa lābhī samāno ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā dibbena cakkhunā parassa hadayamaṃsapesiṃ nissāya pavattamānassa lohitassa vaṇṇadassanena “idāni imassa cittaṃ somanassasahagata”nti vā “domanassasahagata”nti vā “upekkhāsahagata”nti vā nayaggāhavasenapi vavatthapetvā pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya “imassa cittaṃ jānāmī”ti parikammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Kālasatampi kālasahassampi punappunaṃ pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya tatheva paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Tassevaṃ dibbacakkhunā hadayalohitavaṇṇadassanādividhinā paṭipajjantassa idāni cetopariyañāṇaṃ uppajjissatīti yaṃ tadā pavattatīti vavatthāpitaṃ cittaṃ, taṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā manodvārāvajjanaṃ uppajjati, tasmiṃ niruddhe cattāri, pañca vā javanāni javanti. Tesaṃ purimāni tīṇi, cattāri vā parikammādisamaññāni kāmāvacarāni, catutthaṃ, pañcamaṃ vā appanācittaṃ rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānikaṃ. Tattha yaṃ antena appanācittena saddhiṃ uppannaṃ ñāṇaṃ, idaṃ cetopariyañāṇaṃ. Tañhi yatthānena parikammaṃ kataṃ, taṃ parassa cittaṃ paccakkhato paṭivijjhantaṃ vibhāventameva hutvā [M 2.0042] pavattati rūpaṃ viya ca dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ, saddaṃ viya ca dibbasotañāṇaṃ. Tato paraṃ pana kāmāvacaracittehi sarāgādivavatthāpanaṃ hoti nīlādivavatthāpanaṃ viya. Evamadhigatassa pana cetopariyañāṇassa thāmagamanavidhānampi adhigamanavidhānasadisamevāti taṃ dassetuṃ “tasmā tena…pe… thāmagataṃ kātabba”nti vuttaṃ.

“Seeking” means first sending forth knowledge by inference and then searching. For a yogī wishing to develop the knowledge of others’ minds, having, in accordance with the method described below, made the fourth jhāna of the form realm—endowed with eight factors and capable of adverting—and having become one who has obtained the divine eye, they should expand the light. Then, with the divine eye, by seeing the color of the blood flowing dependent on another’s heart-flesh, they should determine, “Now this person’s mind is accompanied by joy,” or “accompanied by grief,” or “accompanied by equanimity,” by way of grasping the method. After entering and emerging from the base jhāna, the preliminary work should be done with the thought, “I will know this person’s mind.” One should practice in that very way, repeatedly entering and emerging from the base jhāna, even for a hundred or a thousand times. For one practicing thus by the method of seeing the color of the heart-blood with the divine eye and so on, at the moment when it is thought, “Now the knowledge of others’ minds will arise,” making that mind of the other person—which was determined as occurring at that time—the object, mind-door adverting arises. When that has ceased, four or five impulsions run. Among them, the first three or four are of the sense sphere, called preliminary work, etc. The fourth or fifth is an appanā-citta, an absorption consciousness, of the fourth jhāna of the form realm. Therein, the knowledge that arises together with the final appanā-citta is the knowledge of others’ minds. For it occurs by directly penetrating and clearly discerning the other’s mind, which was the object of the preliminary work, just as the divine eye knowledge discerns form and the divine ear knowledge discerns sound. Thereafter, with sense-sphere consciousnesses, the determination of ‘with lust,’ etc., occurs, like the determination of ‘blue,’ etc. For the knowledge of others’ minds attained in this way, the method of making it steadfast is also similar to the method of attainment. To show this, it is said, “Therefore… it should be made steadfast.”

Evaṃ thāmagate hītiādi thāmagatānisaṃsadassanaṃ. Sabbampi kāmāvacaracittanti catupaṇṇāsavidhampi kāmāvacaracittaṃ. “Sabbampī”ti padaṃ “rūpāvacarārūpāvacaracitta”nti etthāpi ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Tena pañcadasavidhampi rūpāvacaracittaṃ, dvādasavidhampi arūpāvacaracittanti vuttaṃ hoti. Pajānātīti sarāgādipakārehi jānāti, paccakkhato paṭivijjhatīti adhippāyo. Puthujjanavasenāyaṃ abhiññākathāti lokuttaraṃ cittaṃ idha anuddhaṭaṃ. Tampi [V 2.0040] hi uparimo, sadiso vā ariyo heṭṭhimassa, sadisassa ca cittampi pajānāti eva. Tenāha “anuttaraṃ vā citta”ntiādi. Saṅkamantoti ñāṇena upasaṅkamanto. Ekaccañhi cittaṃ ñatvā parikammena vinā tadaññaṃ cittaṃ jānanto “cittā cittaṃ saṅkamanto”ti vutto. Tenāha “vināpi hadayarūpadassanenā”ti. Hadayarūpadassanādividhānaṃ hi ādikammikavasena vuttaṃ. Tenāha “vuttampi ceta”ntiādi. Yattha katthacīti pañcavokārabhave, catuvokārabhavepi vā. Na kato abhiññānuyogasaṅkhāto abhiniveso etenāti akatābhiniveso, tassa, ādikammikassāti attho. Ayaṃ kathāti “ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā”tiādinā vuttaparikammakathā.

The phrase ‘Thus, when it has become steadfast,’ and so forth, is a statement showing the benefit of knowledge that has reached its full strength. ‘All kāmāvacara cittas’ means all fifty-four types of kāmāvacara citta. The word ‘all’ should also be extended and connected to ‘rūpāvacara and arūpāvacara cittas.’ Thus, it is said that there are fifteen types of rūpāvacara citta and twelve types of arūpāvacara citta. ‘He understands’ means he knows in ways such as ‘with lust,’ etc.; the meaning is that he penetrates it directly. As this discussion of higher knowledge is from the perspective of an ordinary person, the supramundane citta is not expounded here. For that too, a higher or similar noble one understands the mind of a lower or similar one. Therefore, he said, ‘or the unsurpassed citta,’ and so forth. ‘Saṅkamanto’ means approaching with knowledge. For one who, having known a certain mind, knows another mind without preliminary work, is said to be ‘one who passes from mind to mind.’ Therefore, he said, ‘even without seeing the heart-base form.’ For the procedure of seeing the heart-base form and so forth is stated for the beginner. Therefore, he said, ‘though it is also stated,’ and so forth. ‘Wherever’ means in the five-aggregate existence or in the four-aggregate existence. ‘Akatābhiniveso’ means: the application known as the pursuit of higher knowledge has not been made by him; ‘tassa’ [of him] means of the beginner. ‘This discussion’ refers to the discussion on preliminary work stated with the phrase ‘having increased the light,’ and so forth.

Avasesanti vuttāvasesaṃ. Evaṃ avibhāgena vuttaṃ vibhāgato dassetuṃ “catubhūmakaṃ kusalābyākataṃ cittaṃ vītarāga”nti āha. Tañhi yonisomanasikārappaccayataṃhetukatāhi rāgena sampayogāsaṅkābhāvato “vītarāga”nti vattabbataṃ labhati. Sesākusalacittānaṃ rāgena sampayogābhāvato nattheva sarāgatā, taṃnimittakatāya pana siyā taṃsahitatālesoti nattheva vītarāgatāpīti dukavinimuttatāva yuttāti vuttaṃ “imasmiṃ duke saṅgahaṃ na gacchantī”ti. Yadi evaṃ padesikaṃ cetopariyañāṇaṃ āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati, dukantarapariyāpannattā tesaṃ. Ye pana “paṭipakkhabhāve asatipi sampayogābhāvo evettha pamāṇaṃ ekaccaabyākatānaṃ viyā”ti sesākusalacittānampi vītarāgataṃ paṭijānanti[M 2.0043], te sandhāyāha “keci pana therā tānipi saṅgaṇhantī”ti. Sadosadukepi imināva nayena attho veditabbo.

By ‘avasesa’ is meant the remainder of what has been stated. Thus, to show with distinction what was stated without distinction, he said: ‘The four-plane wholesome and indeterminate consciousness is free from lust.’ For that consciousness, because of its nature as wholesome consciousness conditioned by wise attention and having that wholesomeness as its root-cause, and because there is no suspicion of its association with lust, it deserves to be called ‘free from lust.’ For the remaining unwholesome consciousnesses, because of the absence of association with lust, the state of being accompanied by lust certainly does not exist. However, because they are caused by that lust, there might be a trace of being accompanied by it; therefore, the state of being free from lust also certainly does not exist. Therefore, their exclusion from the pair is alone proper, and so it was said: ‘they are not included in this pair.’ If it is so, would a partial knowledge of others’ minds arise? It would not arise, because of their inclusion in another pair. But as for those who profess that even the remaining unwholesome consciousnesses are free from lust, holding that ‘in this matter, even without the state of being an opposite, the mere absence of association is the standard, as with certain indeterminate states’—referring to them, he said: ‘But some elders include those also.’ The meaning in the pair with and without aversion should also be understood in this very same way.

Pāṭipuggalikanayenāti āveṇikanayena, tadaññākusalacittesu viya lobhadosehi amissitassa mohasseva sabbhāvatoti attho. Akusalamūlasaṅkhātesu saha mohenevāti samohaṃ paṭhamanaye, dutiyanaye pana saheva mohenāti samohanti evaṃ uttarapurimapadāvadhāraṇato dvīsu nayesu bhedo veditabbo. Attanā sampayuttaṃ thinamiddhaṃ anuvattanavasena gataṃ pavattaṃ thinamiddhānugataṃ pañcavidhaṃ sasaṅkhārikākusalacittaṃ saṃkhittaṃ, ārammaṇe saṅkocanavasena pavattanato. Vuttanayena uddhaccānugataṃ veditabbaṃ, taṃ pana uddhaccasahagataṃ cittaṃ, yattha vā uddhaccaṃ paccayavisesena thāmajātaṃ hutvā pavattati. Kilesavikkhambhanasamatthatāya, vipulaphalatāya, dīghasantānatāya ca mahantabhāvaṃ gataṃ, mahantehi vā uḷāracchandavīriyacittapaññehi gataṃ paṭipannanti mahaggataṃ. Avasesanti parittaappamāṇaṃ. Attānaṃ uttarituṃ samatthehi saha uttarehīti sauttaraṃ. Uttiṇṇanti uttaraṃ, loke apariyāpannabhāvena lokato uttaranti lokuttaraṃ. Tato eva natthi [V 2.0041] etassa uttaranti anuttaraṃ. Upanijjhānalakkhaṇappattena samādhinā sammadeva āhitanti samāhitaṃ. Tadaṅgavimuttippattaṃ kāmāvacarakusalacittaṃ. Vikkhambhanavimuttippattaṃ mahaggatacittaṃ. Samucchedavimuttippattaṃ maggacittaṃ. Paṭippassaddhivimuttippattaṃ phalacittaṃ. Nissaraṇavimuttippattampi tadubhayameva. Kāmaṃ kānici paccavekkhaṇacittādīni nibbānārammaṇāni honti, nissaraṇavimuttippattāni pana na honti tādisakiccāyogato. Pāḷiyaṃ āgatasarāgādibhedavasena ceva tesaṃ antarabhedavasena ca sabbappakārampi.

By the individual method means by the exclusive method; the meaning is that there is the existence of only delusion unmixed with greed and hatred, just as in other unwholesome consciousnesses apart from those two rooted in delusion. Among those designated as roots of unwholesomeness, in the first method, it is samohaṃ because it occurs only with delusion; in the second method, however, it is samohaṃ because it occurs together with delusion. Thus, the distinction in the two methods should be understood by way of the specific determination of the latter and former words. The fivefold prompted unwholesome consciousness that follows sloth and torpor associated with itself is called 'contracted' because it occurs by way of shrinking in relation to the object. In the manner stated, the consciousness that follows distraction should be understood; furthermore, that is the consciousness accompanied by distraction, or it is the consciousness wherein distraction, having become powerful through a special condition, occurs. That which has become great due to its capability to suppress defilements, its abundant fruit, and its long continuity—or that which is attained or practiced by great ones endowed with lofty intention, energy, consciousness, and wisdom—is called 'developed' (mahaggataṃ). The remaining are the limited and the immeasurable. That which is 'with a superior' (sauttaraṃ) is that which occurs together with superior things capable of transcending oneself. 'Transcended' means 'superior' (uttaraṃ); that which is beyond the world by not being included in the world is 'supramundane' (lokuttaraṃ). Because there is nothing superior to it, it is 'unsurpassed' (anuttaraṃ). That which is well-placed by concentration that has attained the characteristic of close contemplation is called 'composed' (samāhitaṃ). The sense-sphere wholesome consciousness is that which has attained liberation-by-substitution. The developed consciousness is that which has attained liberation-by-suppression. The path consciousness is that which has attained liberation-by-eradication. The fruition consciousness is that which has attained liberation-by-tranquilization. That which has attained liberation-by-escape is also just those two. Although it is true that some, such as the reviewing consciousnesses, have Nibbāna as their object, they have not attained liberation-by-escape due to not being connected with such a function. In the Pāḷi, this is by way of the divisions that have come down, such as 'with lust,' etc., and by way of their internal sub-divisions, thus in every way.

Cetopariyañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the discourse on the knowledge of others' minds is completed.

Pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

An Explanation of the Discourse on the Knowledge of Recollecting Past Lives

402. Pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, tassa vā anussaraṇaṃ pubbenivāsānussati, taṃ nissayādipaccayabhūtaṃ paṭicca uppajjanato “pubbenivāsānussatimhi yaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tadatthāyā”ti saṅkhepena vuttamatthaṃ vivaranto [M 2.0044] pubbenivāsaṃ tāva dassetvā tattha satiñāṇāni dassetuṃ “pubbenivāso”tiādimāha. Tattha “pubbe”ti idaṃ padaṃ “ekampi jāti”ntiādivacanato atītabhavavisayaṃ idhādhippetanti āha “atītajātīsū”ti nivāsa-saddo kammasādhano, khandhavinimutto ca nivasitadhammo natthīti āha “nivutthakkhandhā”ti. Nivutthatā cettha sasantāne pavattatā, tathābhūtā ca te anu anu bhūtā jātā pavattā tattha uppajjitvā vigatāva hontīti āha “nivutthāti ajjhāvutthā anubhūtā attano santāne uppajjitvā niruddhā”ti. Evaṃ sasantatipariyāpannadhammavasena nivāsa-saddassa atthaṃ vatvā idāni avisesena vattuṃ “nivutthadhammā vā nivutthā”ti vatvā taṃ vivarituṃ “gocaranivāsenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Gocarabhūtāpi hi gocarāsevanāya āsevitā ārammaṇakaraṇavasena anubhūtā nivutthā nāma hontīti. Te pana duvidhā saparaviññāṇagocaratāyāti ubhayepi te dassetuṃ “attano”tiādi vuttaṃ.

402. One recollects past lives. Or, the recollection of that is the 'recollection of past lives'. Wishing to explain the meaning stated briefly as 'the knowledge in the recollection of past lives is for that purpose'—which arises dependent on that [recollection] which has become a condition such as support, etc.—the author first shows past lives, and then, in order to show the mindfulness and knowledges therein, says the text beginning with 'past lives'. Therein, the word 'pubbe' (past), because of the statement 'even a single birth,' etc., is intended here to mean the sphere of past existences; therefore, he says 'in past births'. The word 'nivāsa' (dwelling) is formed in the objective sense, and since there is no phenomenon that is dwelt in which is separate from the aggregates, he says 'the aggregates that have been dwelt in'. And here, 'being dwelt in' means occurrence in one's own continuity. And those [aggregates], being such, having repeatedly come to be, arisen, and occurred, are just what have vanished after arising there. Therefore, he says: 'dwelt in' means resided in, experienced; having arisen in one's own continuity, they have ceased. Thus, having stated the meaning of the word 'nivāsa' by way of phenomena included in one's own continuity, now, in order to speak generally, after saying 'or, dwelt-in phenomena are what is dwelt in', to explain that, the text beginning with 'by dwelling in the sphere' was said. For even those that are spheres, when frequented by resorting to the sphere, are experienced as objects and are thus called 'dwelt in'. These, however, are twofold, by being objects of one's own or another's consciousness. Therefore, in order to show both, the text beginning with 'one's own' was said.

Tattha “attano viññāṇena viññātā”ti vatvā “paricchinnā”ti vacanaṃ ye te gocaranivāsena nivutthadhammā, te na kevalaṃ viññāṇena viññāṇamattā, atha kho yathā pubbe jātināmagottavaṇṇaliṅgāhārādivisesehi paricchedakārikāya paññāya paricchijja gahitā, tathevetaṃ [V 2.0042] ñāṇaṃ paricchijja gaṇhātīti imassa atthassa dīpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Paraviññāṇaviññātāpi vā nivutthāti sambandho. Na kevalaṃ attanova viññāṇena, atha kho paresaṃ viññāṇena viññātāpi vāti attho. Idhāpi “paricchinnā”ti padaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ “paresampi vā viññāṇena viññātā paricchinnā”ti. Tassa ca gahaṇe payojanaṃ vuttanayeneva vattabbaṃ. Te ca kho yasmā abhītāsu eva jātīsu aññehi viññātā paricchinnā, te ca parinibbutāpi honti. Ye hi te viññātā, tesaṃ tadā vattamānasantānānusārena tesampi atīte pavatti ñāyatīti sikhāppattaṃ pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇassa visayabhūtaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ dassetuṃ “chinnavaṭumakānussaraṇādīsū”ti vuttaṃ. Chinnavaṭumakā sammāsambuddhā, tesaṃ anussaraṇā chinnavaṭumakānussaraṇaṃ. Ādi-saddena paccekasambuddhabuddhasāvakānussaraṇāni gayhantīti vadanti. Chinnavaṭumakā pana sabbeva anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā [M 2.0045] parinibbutā. Tesaṃ anussaraṇaṃ nāma tesaṃ paṭipattiyā anussaraṇaṃ, sā pana paṭipatti saṅkhepato chaḷārammaṇaggahaṇalakkhaṇāti tāni idha paraviññāṇaviññātaggahaṇena gahitāni, te panete sammāsambuddhānaṃyeva visayā, na aññesanti āha “te buddhānaṃyeva labbhantī”ti. Na hi atīte buddhā bhagavanto evaṃ vipassiṃsu, evaṃ maggaṃ bhāvesuṃ, evaṃ phalanibbānāni sacchākaṃsu, evaṃ veneyye vinesunti ettha sabbadā aññesaṃ ñāṇassa gati atthīti. Yāya satiyā pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, sā pubbenivāsānussatīti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ.

Here, having stated, 'known by one's own consciousness,' the phrase 'delimited' is spoken to clarify this meaning: those phenomena that have been dwelt in through past-living as a domain are not merely known by consciousness alone. Rather, just as they were previously grasped by being delimited by wisdom, which acts as a delimitor, through distinctions such as birth, name, clan, appearance, gender, food, and so on, so too does this knowledge grasp them by delimitation. Alternatively, the connection is: 'dwelt in' also means known by the consciousness of others. The meaning is: not only known by one's own consciousness, but also known by the consciousness of others. Here too, the word 'delimited' should be brought in and connected thus: 'or delimited by being known by the consciousness of others as well.' The purpose of including this should be explained in the manner previously stated. And since those phenomena were known and delimited by others in those very past births, and those others may also be ones who have attained final Nibbāna. For, regarding those by whom these phenomena were known, their past occurrence is known according to the continuity existing at that time. Thus, to show past lives—the domain of the knowledge of recollection of past lives, which has reached its peak—it is said, 'as in the recollection of those with the path of saṃsāra cut off, etc.' Those with the path of saṃsāra cut off are the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones; recollecting them is the 'recollection of those with the path of saṃsāra cut off.' By the word 'etc.,' the recollections of Paccekabuddhas and the Buddha's disciples are included, so they say. However, all those with the path of saṃsāra cut off have attained final Nibbāna in the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining. Recollecting them means recollecting their practice. And that practice, in brief, is characterized by the grasping of the six sense objects. Here, those objects are included under the category of 'what is known by the consciousness of others.' Yet these are the domain only of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, not of others. Thus, he says, 'These are attainable only by the Buddhas.' For there is in no way any scope for the knowledge of others regarding how, in the past, the Blessed Buddhas saw with insight, developed the path, realized the fruits and Nibbāna, and trained the trainable. 'The mindfulness by which one recollects past lives is the recollection of past lives'—this should be brought in and connected.

Anekavidhanti nānābhavayonigativiññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsādivasena bahuvidhaṃ. Pakārehīti nāmagottādiākārehi saddhiṃ, sahayoge cetaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ. Pavattitaṃ desanāvasena. Tenāha “saṃvaṇṇita”nti, vitthāritanti attho. “Nivāsa”nti antogadhabhedasāmaññavacanametanti te bhede byāpanicchāvasena saṅgahetvā dassento “tattha tattha nivutthasantāna”nti āha. Sāvakassevetaṃ anussaraṇaṃ, na satthunoti vuttaṃ “khandhapaṭipāṭivasena cutipaṭisandhivasena vā”ti. Khandhapaṭipāṭi khandhānaṃ anukkamo. Sā ca kho cutito paṭṭhāya uppaṭipāṭivasena. Keci panettha “iriyāpathapaṭipāṭi khandhapaṭipāṭī”ti vadanti. Anugantvā anugantvāti ñāṇagatiyā anugantvā anugantvā. Titthiyāti aññatitthiyā, te pana kammavādino kiriyavādino tāpasādayo. Ṭhapetvā aggasāvakamahāsāvake itare satthu sāvakā pakatisāvakā.

‘Of many kinds’ means manifold by way of various existences, birth-origins, destinations, states of consciousness, abodes of beings, and so on. ‘By modes’ means along with aspects such as name, clan, and so on; this is an instrumental case in the sense of association. It is set forth by way of teaching. Therefore, he says ‘well-described,’ the meaning of which is ‘elaborated.’ ‘Dwelling’ is a general term with internal divisions; therefore, showing those divisions by encompassing them through the desire to pervade, he says, ‘the continuity that has dwelt in this or that place.’ This recollection is for the disciple only, not for the Teacher; thus it is said, ‘by way of the sequence of aggregates or by way of death and rebirth-linking.’ The sequence of aggregates is the succession of the aggregates. And that is by way of reverse order, beginning from death. Some here say, ‘the sequence of postures is the sequence of aggregates.’ ‘Following and following’ means following and following with the movement of knowledge. ‘Sectarians’ means other sectarians; and they are proponents of kamma, proponents of action, ascetics, and so on. Setting aside the chief disciples and great disciples, the other disciples of the Teacher are ordinary disciples.

Yasmā titthiyānaṃ brahmajālādīsu cattālīsāya eva saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭānaṃ anussaraṇaṃ āgataṃ, tasmā [V 2.0043] “na tato para”nti vatvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ vadanto “dubbalapaññattā”tiādimāha, tena vipassanābhiyogo pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇassa visesakāraṇanti dasseti. Balavapaññattāti ettha nāmarūpaparicchedādiyeva paññāya balavakāraṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tañhettha nesaṃ sādhāraṇakāraṇaṃ. Ettakoti kappānaṃ lakkhaṃ, tadadhikaṃ ekaṃ, dve ca asaṅkhyeyyānīti kālavasena evaṃparimāṇo yathākkamaṃ tesaṃ mahāsāvakaaggasāvakapaccekabuddhānaṃ puññañāṇābhinīhāro sāvakapaccekabodhipāramitā samitā. Yadi bodhisambhārasambharaṇakālaparicchinno tesaṃ tesaṃ ariyānaṃ abhiññāñāṇavibhāgo, evaṃ sante [M 2.0046] buddhānampi visayaparicchedatā āpannāti āha “buddhānaṃ pana paricchedo nāma natthī”ti. “Yāvatakaṃ ñeyyaṃ, tāvatakaṃ ñāṇa”nti (mahāni. 156; cūḷani. mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 85; paṭi. ma. 3.5) vacanato sabbaññutaññāṇassa viya buddhānaṃ abhiññāñāṇānampi visaye paricchedo nāma natthi. Tattha yaṃ yaṃ ñātuṃ icchanti, taṃ taṃ jānanti eva. Atha vā satipi kālaparicchede kāraṇūpāyakosallapariggahādinā sātisayattā mahābodhisambhārānaṃ paññāpāramitāya pavattiānubhāvassa paricchedo nāma natthi, kuto tannibbattānaṃ abhiññāñāṇānanti āha “buddhānaṃ pana paricchedo nāma natthī”ti. Atīte ettakāni kappānaṃ asaṅkhyeyyānīti evaṃ kālaparicchedo nāma natthi, anāgate anāgataṃsañāṇassa viya.

Since in the Brahmajāla Sutta and other texts, the recollection of the sectarians is mentioned as extending to only forty cycles of world-contraction and expansion, therefore, having said, 'not beyond that,' and stating the reason for it, he says, 'due to weak wisdom,' and so on. By this, he shows that the practice of insight is a special cause for the knowledge of recollecting past lives. Here, regarding 'due to strong wisdom,' it should be understood that the discernment of name-and-form and so on is itself the strong cause for wisdom. Indeed, this is a common cause for them. 'This much' refers to the following measure in terms of time, respectively, for the aspiration for merit and knowledge—that is, the accumulation of the perfections for enlightenment—of those great disciples, chief disciples, and Paccekabuddhas: a hundred thousand eons; one incalculable eon and a hundred thousand more; and two incalculable eons and a hundred thousand more. If the classification of the direct knowledges of those various noble ones were limited by the time spent accumulating the requisites for enlightenment, then a limited scope would be incurred even for the Buddhas. Therefore, he says, 'But for the Buddhas, there is no such thing as a limitation.' Because it is said, 'As much as there is to be known, so much is the knowledge,' just as with the knowledge of omniscience, for the Buddhas' direct knowledges also, there is no such thing as a limitation in their scope. Therein, whatever they wish to know, that they certainly know. Alternatively, even though there is a limitation in time, because of the surpassing nature of the great requisites for enlightenment—through comprehension with skill in causes, skill in means, and so on—the power of the arising of the perfection of wisdom has no such thing as a limitation. How then could the direct knowledges born from it have a limitation? Hence, he says, 'But for the Buddhas, there is no such thing as a limitation.' In the past, there is no such thing as a temporal limitation like 'so many incalculable eons,' just as in the future there is no limitation for the knowledge of the future.

Evaṃ channaṃ janānaṃ pubbenivāsānussaraṇaṃ kālavibhāgato dassetvā idāni ārammaṇaggahaṇato ānubhāvavisesato, pavattiākārato ca dassetuṃ “titthiyā cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Cutipaṭisandhivasenāti attano, parassa vā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ attabhāve cutiṃ disvā antarā kiñci anāmasitvā paṭisandhiyā eva gahaṇavasena. Vuttamevatthaṃ byatirekato, anvayato ca vibhāvetuṃ “tesañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pakatisāvakā cutipaṭisandhivasenapi saṅkamantīti ayamattho heṭṭhā vuttanayena “balavapaññattā”ti hetunā vibhāvetabbo, cutipaṭisandhivasena saṅkamanaṃ vemajjhadassane payojanābhāvato. Ñāṇabaladassanatthaṃ panettha vuttaṃ.

Having thus shown the recollection of past abodes of the six types of persons by way of time-division, now, in order to show it by way of grasping the object, by way of the distinction of power, and by way of the mode of occurrence, the passage beginning with 'titthiyā ca' was stated. 'By the power of death and rebirth-linking' means by the power of grasping only the rebirth-linking, having seen one's own or another's death in this or that existence, without considering anything in between. In order to elucidate the meaning already stated by way of exclusion and inclusion, the passage beginning with 'tesaṃ hi' was stated. This meaning—that ordinary disciples also pass over by the power of death and rebirth-linking—should be elucidated by the method stated previously with the reason 'because it is a strong concept,' since there is no benefit in seeing the intermediate state when passing over by the power of death and rebirth-linking. Here it is stated for the purpose of showing the power of the knowledge.

Taṃ taṃ pākaṭamevāti yathā nāma saradasamaye ṭhitamajjhanhikavelāyaṃ caturatanike gehe cakkhumato purisassa rūpagataṃ supākaṭameva hotīti lokasiddhametaṃ, siyā pana tassa sukhumataratirohitādibhedassa rūpagatassa agocaratā. Nattheva buddhānaṃ ñātuṃ icchitassa ñeyyassa agocaratā, atha kho taṃ ñāṇālokena obhāsitaṃ hatthatale āmalakaṃ viya supākaṭaṃ suvibhūtameva [V 2.0044] hoti tathā ñeyyāvaraṇassa supahīnattā. Peyyālapāḷiṃ viya saṅkhipitvāti yathā peyyālapāḷiṃ paṭhantā “paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ…pe… pañcamaṃ jhāna”nti ādipariyosānameva gaṇhantā saṅkhipitvā sajjhāyanti, na anupadaṃ, evaṃ anekāpi kappakoṭiyo saṅkhipitvā. Yaṃ yaṃ icchantīti yasmiṃ kappe, yasmiṃ bhave yaṃ [M 2.0047] yaṃ jānituṃ icchanti, tattha tattheva ñātuṃ icchite eva ñāṇena okkamantā. Sīhokkantavasena sīhagatipatanavasena ñāṇagatiyā gacchanti. Satadhā bhinnassa vāḷassa koṭiyā koṭipaṭipādanavasena katavālavedhaparicayassa. Sarabhaṅgasadisassāti sarabhaṅgabodhisattasadisassa (jā. 2.17.50 ādayo). Lakkhaṭṭhānassa appattavasena na sajjati. Atikkamanapassagamanavasena na virajjhati.

That is indeed manifest. For example, during the autumn season at high noon, in a house of four cubits, a visible object is perfectly clear to a man with good eyes; this is well-known in the world. However, it is possible that a visible object that is extremely subtle, hidden, or otherwise divided might be beyond his range. But for the Buddhas, there is absolutely no knowable object they wish to know that is beyond their range. Rather, illuminated by the light of knowledge, it is perfectly clear and fully manifest, like an āmalaka fruit on the palm of one’s hand, because the obstruction to the knowable has been so completely abandoned. Just as one condenses a peyyāla passage: for example, those who recite a peyyāla passage take only the beginning and the end, such as 'the first jhāna...pe...the fifth jhāna,' and recite it in condensed form, not word by word; in the same way, they condense even many koṭis of eons. Whatever they wish to know: in whatever eon, in whatever existence, whatever they wish to know, their knowledge descends right upon that which they wish to know. They proceed with the movement of knowledge with the stride of a lion, with the gait and pounce of a lion. Like one practiced in striking the tip of a horse-tail hair split a hundredfold. Like Sarabhaṅga: like the Bodhisatta Sarabhaṅga. It does not get stuck by failing to reach the target. It does not miss by overshooting or going to the side.

Khajjupanakappabhāsadisaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhātīti ñāṇassa ativiya appānubhāvatāya khajjotobhāsasamaṃ hutvā pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ upaṭṭhāti. Esa nayo sesesupi. Dīpappabhāsadisanti pākatikadīpālokasadisaṃ. Ukkāpabhā mahāummukāloko. Osadhitārakappabhāti ussannā pabhā etāya dhīyatīti osadhi, osadhīnaṃ vā anubalappadāyikattā osadhīti evaṃ laddhanāmāya tārakāya pabhā. Saradasūriyamaṇḍalasadisaṃ savisaye sabbaso andhakāravidhamanato.

The phrase 'it arises having become like the light of a firefly' means that due to the knowledge having very little power, the knowledge of recollection of past lives arises, having become like the light of a firefly. This is the method in the remaining cases as well. Like the light of a lamp: like the light of an ordinary lamp. The light of a torch: the light of a great firebrand. Like the light of the Osadhi star: 'Osadhi' is so called because 'by it abundant light is borne,' or because it gives successive strength to annual plants; thus, it is the light of the star that has obtained this name. Like the disk of the autumn sun: because it completely dispels darkness in its own sphere.

Yaṭṭhikoṭigamanaṃ viya khandhapaṭipāṭiyā amuñcanato. Kunnadīnaṃ atikkamanāya ekeneva rukkhadaṇḍena katasaṅkamo daṇḍakasetu. Catūhi, pañcahi vā janehi gantuṃ sakkuṇeyyo phalake attharitvā āṇiyo koṭṭetvā katasaṅkamo jaṅghasetu. Jaṅghasatthassa gamanayoggo saṅkamo jaṅghasetu jaṅghamaggo viya. Sakaṭassa gamanayoggo saṅkamo sakaṭasetu sakaṭamaggo viya. Mahatā jaṅghasatthena gantabbamaggo mahājaṅghamaggo. Bahūhi vīsāya vā tiṃsāya vā sakaṭehi ekajjhaṃ gantabbamaggo mahāsakaṭamaggo.

Because of not letting go of the sequence of aggregates, it is like going by the tip of a staff. A bridge made with a single tree trunk for crossing small rivers is a 'staff bridge.' A bridge made by laying out planks and hammering in nails, which four or five people are able to cross, is a 'footbridge.' A bridge suitable for a company of foot-travelers to travel on is a 'footbridge,' like a footpath. A bridge suitable for a cart to travel on is a 'cart bridge,' like a cart path. A path to be traveled by a large company of foot-travelers is a 'great footpath.' A path to be traveled together by many carts, whether twenty or thirty, is a 'great cart path.'

Imasmiṃ pana adhikāreti “cittaṃ paññañca bhāvaya”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.23, 192; peṭako. 22; mi. pa. 2.1.9) cittasīsena sāvakassa niddiṭṭhasamādhibhāvanādhikāre.

But in this context, the passage 'Develop the mind and wisdom' refers to the section on the development of concentration taught to a disciple with mind as the primary factor.

403. Tasmāti yasmā sāvakānaṃ pubbenivāsānussaraṇaṃ idhādhippetaṃ, tasmā. Evanti yathā te anussaranti, evaṃ anussaritukāmena. Heṭṭhā tīsu jhānesu yathārahaṃ pītisukhehi kāyacittānaṃ [V 2.0045] sampīnanāya “cattāri jhānāni samāpajjitvā”ti vuttaṃ, aññathā pādakajjhānameva samāpajjitabbaṃ siyā. Yāya nisajjāya nisinnassa anussaraṇārambho, sā idha sabbapacchimā nisajjā. Tato āsanapaññāpananti tato nisajjāya purimakaṃ āsanapaññāpanaṃ āvajjitabbanti sambandho. Esa nayo sesesupi[M 2.0048]. Bhojanakālotiādīsu kālasīsena tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāle katakiccamāha. Cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇavandanakāloti cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇesu cetiyabodhīnaṃ vandanakālo. Sakalaṃ rattindivanti accantasaṃyoge upayogavacanaṃ.

403. Therefore: this is said because the recollection of past lives of the disciples is intended here. Thus: one who wishes to recollect should do so in the same way that they recollect. For the purpose of appropriately suffusing the body and mind with rapture and happiness in the three lower absorptions, it is said, 'having attained the four absorptions'; otherwise, only the foundational absorption would need to be attained. The sitting posture in which one who has sat down begins the recollection is, in this context, the very last sitting posture. 'Then, the arranging of the seat' means that one should advert to the arranging of the seat that occurred prior to that sitting; this is the connection. This same method applies in the remaining cases. In phrases such as 'mealtime,' etc., with 'time' as the heading, he speaks of the duty performed at each respective time. 'The time for paying homage in the stūpa-courtyard and Bodhi-tree-courtyard' refers to the time for paying homage to the stūpas and Bodhi trees in those courtyards. 'The entire day and night' is a term in the accusative case used in the sense of uninterrupted continuity.

Kiñci kiccaṃ. Ettakenāti pādakajjhānasamāpajjanena. Pādakajjhānañhi satthakassa viya nisānasilā satipaññānampi nisitabhāvāvahaṃ. Yaṃ tassa, tā taṃ samāpajjanena paramanepakkappattā honti. Tenāha “dīpe jalite viya pākaṭaṃ hotī”ti, andhakāraṭṭhāneti adhippāyo. Purimabhaveti imassa bhavassa anantare purimasmiṃ bhave. Pavattitanāmarūpanti attano paccayehi pavattitanāmarūpaṃ. Tañca kho paṭhamaṃ rūpaṃ āvajjitvā nāmaṃ āvajjitabbaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ nāmaṃ āvajjitvā pacchā rūpanti apare. Pahotīti sakkoti. Paṇḍito nāma imissā abhiññābhāvanāya katādhikāro.

Whatever is to be done. By this much means: by entering into the foundational jhāna. For the foundational jhāna, like a whetstone for a knife, also brings about sharpness for mindfulness and wisdom. For that reason, for that yogi, those faculties, through attaining it, reach supreme proficiency. Therefore, He said, “It becomes manifest as if a lamp were lit”; the meaning is, “in a dark place.” “In the previous existence” means in the existence immediately preceding this one. “The name-and-form that has been made to arise” means the name-and-form made to arise by its own conditions. And with regard to that, having first attended to form, name should be attended to. Others say: having first attended to name, afterwards form. “He is capable” means he is able. A wise person, so-called, is one who has made a foundation for this development of direct knowledge.

“Aññaṃ uppanna”nti idaṃ aññasmā kammabhavā añño upapattibhavo uppannoti katvā vuttaṃ addhāpaccuppannantarabhāvato. Aññathā ekabhavepi aññamaññameva nāmarūpaṃ uppajjati, niruddhañca appaṭisandhikaṃ. Tenevāha –

This phrase, “Another has arisen,” was said considering that from another kamma-existence, another rebirth-existence has arisen, because of the state of being a different present moment. Otherwise, even in a single existence, name-and-form arises ever anew, one after another, and what has ceased is without relinking. Therefore, He said:

“Ye niruddhā marantassa, tiṭṭhamānassa vā idha;

Sabbepi sadisā khandhā, gatā appaṭisandhikā”ti. (mahāni. 39);

“Those [aggregates] that have ceased for one who is dying, or for one who is still living here—all those aggregates are similar; they are gone, without relinking.”

Taṃ ṭhānanti taṃ nikkhepaṭṭhānaṃ. Āhundarikanti samantato, upari ca ghanasañchannaṃ sambādhaṭṭhānaṃ. Andhatamamivāti andhakāratimisā viya.

“That place” means that place of casting off, or the place of decease. “Āhundarika” means a confined place, densely covered all around and above. “Like the densest darkness” means like the thick darkness that causes blindness.

Kūṭāgārakaṇṇikatthāyāti kūṭāgārassa kūṭatthāya. Kūṭāgārassa kaṇṇikā viya pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ, mahārukkho viya purimabhave cutikkhaṇe pavattanāmarūpaṃ, sākhāpalāsā viya tena sambandhaṃ imasmiṃ bhave paṭisandhicittaṃ, pharasudhārā viya parikammabhāvanā[V 2.0046], kammārasālā viya pādakajjhānanti evaṃ upamāsaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Kaṭṭhaphālakopamāpi “yathā nāma balavā puriso odanapacanādiatthaṃ mahantaṃ dāruṃ phālento tassa tacapheggumattaphālane pharasudhārāya vipannāya mahantaṃ dāruṃ phāletuṃ asakkonto dhuranikkhepaṃ akatvā”tiādinā vuttanayānusārena veditabbā. Tathā kesohārakūpamā.

For the sake of the pinnacle of a gabled house, meaning for the sake of the gable of the gabled house. The pinnacle of the gabled house is like the knowledge of recollecting past lives; the great tree is like the name-and-form that occurred at the moment of death in a previous existence; the branches and leaves are like the rebirth-linking consciousness connected to it in this existence; the blacksmith’s forge is like the foundation jhāna—thus the connection of similes should be understood. The simile of the wood-splitter should also be understood according to the method stated, beginning with: 'Just as a strong man, while splitting a large log for the purpose of cooking rice and so on, though the blade of his axe becomes damaged when splitting only the bark and sapwood and he becomes unable to split the large log, does not abandon the task...' Similarly, the simile of the barber.

Pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ [M 2.0049] nāma na hoti atītāsu jātīsu nivutthadhammārammaṇattābhāvā. Tanti pacchimanisajjato pabhuti yāva paṭisandhi pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇassa parikammabhāvena pavattasamādhinā sampayuttañāṇaṃ parikammasamādhiñāṇaṃ. Taṃ rūpāvacaraṃ sandhāya na yujjatīti taṃ tesaṃ vacanaṃ atītaṃsañāṇaṃ ce, rūpāvacaraṃ adhippetaṃ na yujjati parikammasamādhiñāṇassa kāmāvacarabhāvato. Na hi anantaracuticittassa orato pavattikkhandhe ārabbha rūpāvacaraṃ cittaṃ uppajjatīti pāḷiyaṃ, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vā āgataṃ atthi. Yesaṃ javanānaṃ purimānīti yojanā. Yadā pana appanācittaṃ hoti, tadāssāti sambandho. Idaṃ pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ nāmāti kāmaṃ anantarassa bhavassa cutikkhaṇe pavattitanāmarūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattañāṇaṃ dassitaṃ, taṃ pana nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ ñāṇasāmaññassa jotitabhāvato. Yatheva hi tato nāmarūpato pabhuti sabbe atītā khandhā, khandhapaṭibaddhā ca sabbo pubbenivāso, evaṃ tassa paṭivijjhanavasena pavattañāṇaṃ pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ. Tenāha “tena ñāṇena sampayuttāya satiyā anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussaratī”ti.

What is called the knowledge of past abodes does not arise, because of the non-existence of having as an object phenomena that have been dwelt in during past existences. That knowledge which has arisen from the last sitting up to the rebirth-linking, being the knowledge associated with the concentration that has arisen as the preliminary stage for the knowledge of recollection of past abodes, is the knowledge of preliminary concentration. As for that statement of theirs, 'That is not suitable with reference to the fine-material sphere,' if the knowledge of the past is intended to be of the fine-material sphere, it is not suitable, because the knowledge of preliminary concentration is of the sense-sphere. Indeed, neither in the Pāḷi nor in the Commentary is there found a statement that a fine-material sphere consciousness arises taking as its object the aggregates that occurred prior to the immediately preceding death. The connection is: 'the preceding ones of those impulsions.' But when there is absorption consciousness, then the connection is 'to him.' Although, by the text, 'This is called the knowledge of recollection of past abodes,' the knowledge that arises by taking as its object the mind-and-matter that occurred at the moment of death of the immediately preceding existence is shown, that, however, should be seen as an illustration, because the generality of the knowledge is being illuminated. For just as, beginning from that mind-and-matter, all past aggregates and phenomena connected with the aggregates constitute 'past abodes', so too the knowledge that arises by means of penetrating them is the knowledge of recollection of past abodes. Therefore, it is said: 'With that knowledge, and with mindfulness associated with it, one recollects manifold past abodes.'

404. Ekampi jātinti ekampi bhavaṃ. So hi ekakammanibbatto ādānanikkhepaparicchinno antogadhadhammappabhedo khandhappabandho idha jātīti adhippeto. Tenāha “ekampi…pe… khandhasantāna”nti. Parihāyamānoti khīyamāno vinassamāno. Kappoti asaṅkhyeyyakappo. So pana atthato kālo, tadā pavattamānasaṅkhāravasenassa parihāni veditabbā. Vaḍḍhamāno vivaṭṭakappoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Yo pana “kālaṃ khepetī”ti, “kālo ghasati bhūtāni, sabbāneva sahattanā”ti (jā. 1.2.190) ca ādīsu kālassāpi khayo vuccati, so idha nādhippeto aniṭṭhappasaṅgato. Saṃvaṭṭanaṃ vinassanaṃ saṃvaṭṭo, saṃvaṭṭato uddhaṃ tathā ṭhāyī saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī. Taṃmūlakattāti taṃpubbakattā. Vivaṭṭanaṃ nibbattanaṃ, vaḍḍhanaṃ vā vivaṭṭo.

404. “One birth” means one existence. Indeed, that continuity of aggregates—produced by a single kamma, defined by conception and death, having the distinction of internal phenomena—is intended here as “birth.” Therefore, it is said, “one... up to... the continuum of aggregates.” “Declining” means decaying, perishing. “Eon” means an incalculable eon. But that, in essence, is time; its decline should be understood as being due to the power of the formations then prevailing. In the passage “the expanding unfolding eon” also, this is the same method. However, as for the destruction of time which is spoken of in such passages as “he spends time,” and “time devours beings, all of them together with itself,” that is not intended here, because it leads to an undesirable implication. The act of dissolving is destruction; this is saṃvaṭṭa. That which remains thus after the dissolution is saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī. “Because of being rooted in that” means because of having that as its antecedent. The act of unfolding is production, or growth; this is vivaṭṭo.

Tejosaṃvaṭṭo āposaṃvaṭṭo vāyosaṃvaṭṭoti evaṃ saṃvaṭṭasīmānukkamena saṃvaṭṭesu vattabbesu tathā [V 2.0047] avatvā “āposaṃvaṭṭo tejosaṃvaṭṭo [M 2.0050] vāyosaṃvaṭṭo”ti vacanaṃ saṃvaṭṭakamahābhūtadesanānupubbiyāti keci. Saṃvaṭṭānupubbiyāti apare. Āpena saṃvaṭṭo āposaṃvaṭṭo. Saṃvaṭṭasīmāti saṃvaṭṭamariyādā.

Although the dissolutions should be stated in the sequence of their limits, thus: 'The dissolution by fire, the dissolution by water, the dissolution by wind'—not having stated them thus, some say that the statement 'the dissolution by water, the dissolution by fire, the dissolution by wind' is due to the sequential teaching of the great elements that cause dissolution. Others say it is due to the sequence of the dissolutions. Dissolution by water is called āposaṃvaṭṭo. 'The boundary of dissolution' means the limit of dissolution.

Saṃvaṭṭatīti vinassati. Sadāti sabbakālaṃ, tīsupi saṃvaṭṭakālesūti attho.

“It dissolves” means it perishes. “Always” means at all times, that is, during all three periods of dissolution.

“Ekaṃ buddhakhetta”nti idha yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, taṃ niyametvā dassetuṃ “buddhakhettaṃ nāma tividha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Yattake ṭhāne tathāgatassa paṭisandhiñāṇānubhāvo puññaphalasamuttejito saraseneva pathavī vijambhati, taṃ sabbampi buddhaṅkurassa nibbattanakhettaṃ nāmāti āha “jātikhettaṃ dasasahassacakkavāḷapariyanta”nti. Ānubhāvo vattatīti idha iddhimā cetovasippatto āṇākhettapariyāpanne yattha katthaci cakkavāḷe ṭhatvā attano atthāya parittaṃ katvā tattheva aññaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ gatopi kataparitto eva hoti. Atha vā tattha ekacakkavāḷe ṭhatvā sabbasattānaṃ atthāya paritte kate āṇākhette sabbasattānaṃ abhisambhuṇātveva parittānubhāvo tattha devatāhi parittāṇāya sampaṭicchitabbato. Yaṃ visayakhettaṃ sandhāya ekasmiṃyeva khaṇe sarena abhiviññāpanaṃ, attano rūpadassanañca paṭijānantena bhagavatā “yāvatā vā pana ākaṅkheyyā”ti (a. ni. 3.81) vuttaṃ. Yatthāti yasmiṃ anantāparimāṇe visayakhette. Yaṃ yaṃ tathāgato ākaṅkhati, taṃ taṃ jānāti ākaṅkhāmattapaṭibaddhavuttitāya buddhañāṇassa. Saṇṭhahantanti vivaṭṭamānaṃ jāyamānaṃ.

Regarding 'a single Buddha-field,' to define and show what is meant here, it is said, 'The Buddha-field is of three kinds,' and so on.
