For indeed, that which arises in those two moments is not called “arising in a single moment together with another’s mind.” And that which arises in the moments of duration and dissolution partly has a present object and partly has a past object. And as for what was said, “having adverted to the mind of a great multitude by way of a mass, thinking, ‘I will know another’s mind,’” here, “great multitude” in meaning is “other numerous individuals”; therefore, the occurrence of advertence should be stated as, “I will know the minds of others.” Or, even if the meaning of “of another” as “of a great multitude” were possible, even so, having adverted to the mind-mass of that multitude or of just a single individual, the penetration of one mind is unsuitable. For indeed, adverting to a mass is not adverting to a part. Therefore, they should not say, “having adverted to the mind of a great multitude,” and so on.

Yaṃ pana te vadanti “yasmā iddhimassa ca parassa ca ekakkhaṇe cittaṃ uppajjatī”ti. Tatthāyaṃ adhippāyo yutto siyā, cetopariyañāṇalābhī parassa cittaṃ ñātukāmo pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya atītādivibhāgaṃ akatvā cittasāmaññena “imassa cittaṃ jānāmi, imassa cittaṃ jānāmī”ti parikammaṃ katvā puna pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya sāmaññeneva cittaṃ āvajjitvā tiṇṇaṃ, catunnaṃ vā parikammānaṃ anantarā cetopariyañāṇena paracittaṃ paṭivijjhati vibhāveti rūpaṃ viya dibbacakkhunā. Tato paraṃ pana kāmāvacaracittehi sarāgādivavatthānaṃ hoti nīlādivavatthānaṃ viya. Tattha dibbacakkhunā diṭṭhahadayavatthurūpassa sattassa abhimukhībhūtassa cittasāmaññena cittaṃ āvajjayamānaṃ āvajjanaṃ abhimukhībhūtaṃ vijjamānaṃ cittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā cittaṃ āvajjeti. Parikammāni ca taṃ taṃ vijjamānaṃ cittaṃ cittasāmaññeneva ārammaṇaṃ katvā cittajānanaparikammāni [V 2.0064] hutvā pavattanti. Cetopariyañāṇaṃ pana vijjamānaṃ cittaṃ paṭivijjhantaṃ vibhāventaṃ tena saha ekakkhaṇe eva uppajjati.

Furthermore, as to what those teachers say, “Because the mind of the one with psychic power and of another person arises in a single moment”—in that statement this meaning would be suitable: a person who has obtained the knowledge of others' minds, wishing to know another's mind, having entered the base jhāna and emerged, without making a division of past, etc., makes the preliminary preparation by the generality of mind, thinking, “I know this person’s mind, I know this person’s mind.” Then, having entered the base jhāna again and emerged, one adverts to the mind by that generality alone. Immediately after three or four preliminary preparations, one penetrates and makes clear another's mind with the knowledge of others' minds, like form with the divine eye. Furthermore, after that, the determination of states such as ‘with lust’ occurs by means of sense-sphere minds, like the determination of colors such as blue. In that case, the advertence, adverting by the generality of mind to the mind of a being whose heart-basis-materiality has been seen with the divine eye and who is present, makes the present, existing mind its object and adverts to it. And the preliminary preparations, having made that existing mind their object by the generality of mind alone, proceed, having become preliminary preparations for knowing the mind. But the knowledge of others' minds, penetrating and making clear the existing mind, arises in one and the same moment together with it.

Tattha yasmā santānassa santānaggahaṇato ekattavasena āvajjanādīni “citta”ntveva pavattāni. Tañca cittameva, yaṃ cetopariyañāṇena vibhāvitaṃ. Tasmā samānākārappavattito na aniṭṭhe maggaphalavīthito aññasmiṃ ṭhāne nānārammaṇatā āvajjanajavanānaṃ hoti. Paccuppannārammaṇañca parikammaṃ paccuppannārammaṇassa cetopariyañāṇassa āsevanapaccayena paccayoti siddhaṃ hoti. Atītattiko ca evaṃ upapanno hoti. Aññathā santatipaccuppanne, addhāpaccuppanne ca “paccuppanna”nti idha vuccamāne atītānāgatānañca paccuppannatā āpajjeyya. Tathā ca sati “paccuppanno dhammo paccuppannassa dhammassa anantarapaccayena paccayo”ti vattabbaṃ siyā, na ca taṃ vuttaṃ. “Atīto dhammo paccuppannassa dhammassa anantarapaccayena paccayo. Purimā purimā atītā khandhā pacchimānaṃ pacchimānaṃ paccuppannānaṃ khandhānaṃ anantara [M 2.0068] …pe… anulomaṃ gotrabhussā”tiādi vacanato (paṭṭhā. 2.18.5) na addhāsantatipaccuppannesveva ca anantarātītā cattāro khandhā atītāti viññāyanti. Na ca abhidhammamātikāyaṃ (dha. sa. tikamātikā 18-19) āgatassa paccuppannapadassa addhāsantatipaccuppannapadatthatā katthaci pāḷiyaṃ vuttā. Tasmā tehi iddhimassa ca parassa ca ekakkhaṇe cittuppattiyā cetopariyañāṇassa paccuppannārammaṇatā vuttā. Yadā pana “yaṃ imassa cittaṃ pavattaṃ, taṃ jānāmi. Yaṃ bhavissati, taṃ jānāmī”ti vā ābhogaṃ katvā pādakajjhānasamāpajjanādīni karoti, tadā āvajjanaparikammāni, cetopariyañāṇañca atītānāgatārammaṇāneva honti āvajjaneneva vibhāgassa katattā.

Therein, because, due to taking the mental continuum as a single thing, minds such as advertence occur only as 'mind,' and that which is discerned by the knowledge of others' minds is also only mind, therefore, due to its occurrence with a similar characteristic, there is no diversity of objects for advertence and impulsion in an undesirable instance, that is, in a cognitive process other than that of path and fruition. And it is established that the preliminary action with a present object is a condition for the knowledge of others' minds with a present object by way of the repetition condition. And the past triad is thus justified. Otherwise, if 'present' were spoken of here as 'continuity-present' and 'duration-present,' then the state of being present would also befall the past and future. And that being so, it would have to be said, 'A present phenomenon is a condition for a present phenomenon by way of the contiguity condition,' but that was not stated. From the statement, 'A past phenomenon is a condition for a present phenomenon by way of the contiguity condition. The preceding, preceding past aggregates are for the succeeding, succeeding present aggregates by way of contiguity... in sequence up to adaptation for the change-of-lineage' (Paṭṭhāna 2.18.5), it is known that the four immediately past aggregates are 'past' even within the duration-present and continuity-present. And nowhere in any Pāḷi text is it stated that the term 'present' which has come in the Abhidhamma Mātikā has the meaning of 'duration-present' and 'continuity-present.' Therefore, by them it is stated that the knowledge of others' minds has a present object through the arising of the mind of the one with psychic power and of the other in a single moment. But when one makes a reflection, 'I know what mind has occurred in this person,' or 'I know what will occur,' and performs the attainment of the base jhāna, etc., then the advertence, preliminary actions, and the knowledge of others' minds have only past and future objects, since the division is made by the advertence itself.

Ye pana “iddhimā parassa cittaṃ jānitukāmo āvajjeti, āvajjanaṃ khaṇapaccuppannaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā teneva saha nirujjhati. Tato cattāri, pañca vā javanāni, yesaṃ pacchimaṃ iddhicittaṃ, sesāni kāmāvacarāni, tesaṃ sabbesampi tadeva niruddhaṃ cittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hoti, na ca tāni nānārammaṇāni honti addhānavasena paccuppannārammaṇattā”ti idaṃ vacanaṃ nissāya “āvajjanajavanānaṃ paccuppannātītārammaṇabhāvepi nānārammaṇatābhāvo viya ekadviticatupañcacittakkhaṇānāgatesupi cittesu āvajjitesu āvajjanajavanānaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ anāgatapaccuppannātītārammaṇabhāvepi nānārammaṇatā na siyā. Tena catupañcacittakkhaṇānāgate āvajjite [V 2.0065] anāgatārammaṇaparikammānantaraṃ khaṇapaccuppannārammaṇaṃ cetopariyañāṇaṃ siddha”nti vadanti. Tesaṃ vādo “anāgatārammaṇo dhammo paccuppannārammaṇassa dhammassa āsevanapaccayena paccayo, paccuppannārammaṇo dhammo atītārammaṇassa dhammassa āsevanapaccayena paccayo”ti imesaṃ pañhānaṃ anuddhaṭattā, gaṇanāya ca “āsevane tīṇī”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.19.39) vuttattā na sijjhati. Na hi kusalakiriyāmahaggataṃ anāsevanaṃ atthīti. Etassa ca vādassa nissayabhāvo āvajjanajavanānaṃ khaṇapaccuppannaniruddhārammaṇatāvacanassa na sijjhati, “yaṃ pavattaṃ, pavattissati cā”ti visesaṃ akatvā gahaṇe āvajjanassa anāgataggahaṇābhāvaṃ, tadabhāvā javanānampi vattamānaggahaṇābhāvañca sandhāyeva tassa vuttattā. Tadā hi bhavaṅgacalanānantaraṃ abhimukhībhūtameva cittaṃ ārabbha āvajjanā pavattatīti jānanacittassapi vattamānārammaṇabhāve āvajjanajānanacittānaṃ sahaṭṭhānadosāpattiyā, rāsiekadesāvajjanapaṭivedhe [M 2.0069] sampattasampattāvajjanajānane ca aniṭṭhe ṭhāne āvajjanajavanānaṃ nānārammaṇabhāvadosāpattiyā ca yaṃ vuttaṃ “khaṇapaccuppannaṃ cittaṃ cetopariyañāṇassa ārammaṇaṃ hotī”ti, taṃ ayuttanti paṭikkhipitvā yathāvuttadosāpattiṃ, kālavasena ca addhāsantatipaccuppannārammaṇattā nānārammaṇatābhāvaṃ disvā āvajjanajavanānaṃ vattamānataṃ niruddhārammaṇabhāvo vuttoti. Tampi vacanaṃ purimavādino nānujāneyyuṃ. Tasmiṃ hi sati “āvajjanā kusalāna”ntiādīsu (paṭṭhā 1.1.417) viya aññapadasaṅgahitassa anantarapaccayavidhānato “paccuppannārammaṇaāvajjanā atītārammaṇānaṃ khandhānaṃ anantarapaccayena paccayo”ti ca vattabbaṃ siyā, na ca vuttanti.

On the other hand, there are those who, relying on this statement: “One with psychic power, wishing to know another's mind, adverts. The advertence, having made a momentarily present object its object, ceases together with it. Then four or five impulsions arise, of which the last is the psychic consciousness, and the rest are sense-sphere consciousnesses. For all of them, that same ceased consciousness is the object, and they do not have different objects because their object is present in terms of duration”—argue as follows: “Just as there is no state of having different objects even when advertence and impulsion have present and past objects, so too, when consciousnesses that are yet to come by one, two, three, four, or five mind-moments are adverted to, there would not be a state of having different objects for advertence and impulsion, even when they have future, present, or past objects, as is possible. Therefore, when a consciousness that is yet to come by four or five mind-moments is adverted to, immediately after the preliminary action which has a future object, the knowledge of others' minds, which has a momentarily present object, is accomplished.” Thus they say. Their view is not established because these questions—“Is a phenomenon with a future object a condition for a phenomenon with a present object by way of the repetition condition? Is a phenomenon with a present object a condition for a phenomenon with a past object by way of the repetition condition?”—have not been brought up, and because in the enumeration it is stated, “In repetition, there are three.” For there is no wholesome, functional, or sublime consciousness that is without the repetition condition. Furthermore, the Aṭṭhakathā statement that advertence and impulsion have as their object that which is momentarily present and has ceased is not established as a basis for this view. This is because that statement was made referring only to the fact that advertence does not grasp a future object—in taking an object without making a distinction such as ‘what has occurred’ and ‘what will occur’—and, due to the absence of that, the fact that impulsions also do not grasp a present object. For at that time, immediately after the vibration of the life-continuum, advertence arises taking as its object the consciousness that has just become manifest. Thus, one rejects as incorrect the statement that “a momentarily present consciousness is the object of the knowledge of others' minds.” This rejection is made because: (1) if the knowing consciousness also had a present object, advertence and the knowing consciousness would incur the fault of co-existence; and (2) in the case of adverting to one part of a collection and penetrating another, or in the case of adverting to and knowing what is just arriving, there would be, in an undesirable situation, the fault of advertence and impulsion having different objects. Having thus rejected that statement, and having seen the incurring of the aforementioned faults, and also seeing that there is no state of having different objects because, by way of time, the object is present in terms of duration (addhā) and continuity (santati), it was stated that the state of advertence and impulsion is one of having as object the present consciousness and that which has ceased from it. Even that statement, the proponents of the earlier view would not approve. For if that were the case, just as in the texts such as “advertence for wholesome states…”, through the ordaining of the contiguity condition for a state that is included by another term, it would also have to be said that “advertence with a present object is a condition for aggregates with a past object by way of the contiguity condition”—but this has not been stated.

Kasmā panevaṃ cetopariyañāṇassa paccuppannārammaṇatā vicāritā, nanu “atīto dhammo paccuppannassa dhammassa, anāgato dhammo paccuppannassa dhammassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.18.2) etesaṃ vibhaṅgesu “atītā khandhā iddhividhañāṇassa cetopariyañāṇassa pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇassa yathākammūpagañāṇassa āvajjanāya ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo, anāgatā khandhā iddhividhañāṇassa cetopariyañāṇassa anāgataṃsañāṇassa āvajjanāya ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti, uppannattike ca “anuppannā khandhā uppādino khandhā iddhividhañāṇassa cetopariyañāṇassa anāgataṃsañāṇassa āvajjanāya ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.17.3) cetopariyañāṇaggahaṇaṃ katvā “paccuppanno dhammo paccuppannassa dhammassā”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.18.3) etassa vibhaṅge “paccuppannā khandhā iddhividhañāṇassa āvajjanāya ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.18.3), uppannattike ca “uppannā khandhā [V 2.0066] iddhividhañāṇassa āvajjanāya ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.17.2) ettakasseva vuttattā paccuppanne citte cetopariyañāṇaṃ nappavattatīti viññāyati. Yadi hi pavatteyya, purimesu viya itaresu ca cetopariyañāṇaggahaṇaṃ kattabbaṃ siyāti? Saccaṃ kattabbaṃ, nayadassanavasena pana taṃ saṃkhittanti aññāya pāḷiyā viññāyati.

But why is the state of the knowledge of penetrating minds having a present object investigated in this way? Is it not understood that, since in the analyses of the questions, “A past dhamma is a condition for a present dhamma…” and so on, the inclusion of the knowledge of penetrating minds is made, stating, “Past aggregates are a condition… for the knowledge of penetrating minds…,” and so on; whereas in the analysis of the question, “A present dhamma is a condition for a present dhamma…,” and in the arisen triad, only this much is stated: “Present aggregates are a condition… for the knowledge of psychic power…” and “Arisen aggregates are a condition… for the knowledge of psychic power…,” therefore the knowledge of penetrating minds does not occur with respect to a present consciousness? For if it were to occur, should not the inclusion of the knowledge of penetrating minds have been made in these latter cases, as in the former cases? Truly, it should have been done. However, it is understood from another Pāḷi text that this is abbreviated for the purpose of showing the method.

“Atītārammaṇo dhammo paccuppannārammaṇassa dhammassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo, anāgatārammaṇo dhammo paccuppannārammaṇassa, paccuppannārammaṇo [M 2.0070] dhammo paccuppannārammaṇassā”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.19.20-22) etesaṃ hi vibhaṅgesu “cetopariyañāṇena atītārammaṇapaccuppannacittasamaṅgissa cittaṃ jānāti, atītārammaṇā paccuppannā khandhā cetopariyañāṇassa āvajjanāya ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo, cetopariyañāṇena anāgatārammaṇapaccuppannacittasamaṅgissa cittaṃ jānāti, anāgatārammaṇā paccuppannā khandhā cetopariyañāṇassa āvajjanāya ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo, cetopariyañāṇena paccuppannārammaṇapaccuppannacittasamaṅgissa cittaṃ jānāti, paccuppannārammaṇā paccuppannā khandhā cetopariyañāṇassa āvajjanāya ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.19.20-22) cetopariyañāṇassa paccuppannārammaṇe pavatti vuttāti. Tenevāyaṃ vicāraṇā katāti veditabbā.

“A phenomenon with a past object is a condition by way of object condition for a phenomenon with a present object; a phenomenon with a future object is a condition by way of object condition for a phenomenon with a present object; a phenomenon with a present object is a condition by way of object condition for a phenomenon with a present object.” For in the analyses of these, it is said: “By means of the knowledge of penetrating minds, one knows the consciousness of one endowed with a present consciousness that has a past object; the present aggregates that have a past object are a condition by way of object condition for the knowledge of penetrating minds and for its advertence. By means of the knowledge of penetrating minds, one knows the consciousness of one endowed with a present consciousness that has a future object; the present aggregates that have a future object are a condition by way of object condition for the knowledge of penetrating minds and for its advertence. By means of the knowledge of penetrating minds, one knows the consciousness of one endowed with a present consciousness that has a present object; the present aggregates that have a present object are a condition by way of object condition for the knowledge of penetrating minds and for its advertence.” Thus, the functioning of the knowledge of penetrating minds regarding a present object is stated. It should be understood that this investigation has been made for this very reason.

417. Tesanti tesu dvīsu ñāṇesūti niddhāraṇe sāmivacanaṃ. Cittameva ārammaṇaṃ cetopariyañāṇattāti adhippāyo. Tenāha “aññaṃ khandhaṃ vā khandhappaṭibaddhaṃ vā na jānātī”ti. Tattha khandhappaṭibaddhaṃ nāmagottādi. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ maggārammaṇanti āha “maggasampayuttacittārammaṇattā pana pariyāyato maggārammaṇanti vutta”nti. Cetanāmattameva ārammaṇaṃ, tathā hi taṃ “yathākammūpagañāṇa”nti vuccatīti adhippāyo. Khandhappaṭibaddhesūti ettha nibbānampi khandhappaṭibaddhameva. Khandhehi visayīkatattāti vadanti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ “atīte buddhā maggaṃ bhāvayiṃsu, phalaṃ sacchākaṃsu, anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyiṃsūti chinnavaṭumakānussaraṇavasena maggaphalanibbānapaccavekkhaṇatopi appamāṇārammaṇa”nti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1421). Tattha maggaphalapaccavekkhaṇāni tāva pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇena maggaphalesu ñāṇesu pavattanti. Nibbānapaccavekkhaṇañca nibbānārammaṇesu appamāṇadhammesu ñāṇesūti maggādipaccavekkhaṇāni pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇassa appamāṇārammaṇataṃ sādhentīti veditabbāni. “Appamāṇā khandhā pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇassa [V 2.0067] ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”icceva (paṭṭhā. 9.12.58) hi vuttaṃ, na vuttaṃ “nibbāna”nti. Tasmā pubbenivāsañāṇena eva maggaphalapaccavekkhaṇakicce vuccamānepi nibbānapaccavekkhaṇatā na sakkā vattuṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana nibbānārammaṇatā nidassitā.

417. The word ‘tesaṃ’ is a genitive case used in the sense of specification, meaning ‘among those two knowledges’. The meaning is that consciousness itself is the object because it is the knowledge of penetrating minds. Therefore, it is said, ‘One does not know another aggregate or what is connected with an aggregate.’ Herein, what is connected with an aggregate refers to name, lineage, and so forth. If so, how is the path an object? It is said, ‘Because its object is the consciousness associated with the path, it is called the path-object in a figurative sense.’ The object is merely volition, for it is called ‘knowledge conforming to deeds’—this is the meaning. Regarding ‘what is connected with aggregates’, here even Nibbāna is connected with aggregates, because it is made an object by the mental aggregates, so they say. Thus, it is said in the Aṭṭhasālinī: ‘Past Buddhas developed the path, realized the fruit, and attained final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without remainder—thus, by way of recollecting those whose round of existence has been severed, the reviewing of the path, fruit, and Nibbāna also has the immeasurable as its object.’ Herein, the reviewing of the path and fruit, for one, occurs when the path and fruit have been known through the knowledge of recollection of past lives. And the reviewing of Nibbāna occurs when the immeasurable phenomena that have Nibbāna as their object have been known. Thus, it should be understood that the reviewing of the path and so forth establishes that the knowledge of recollection of past lives has the immeasurable as its object. For it is said, ‘The immeasurable aggregates are a condition for the knowledge of recollection of past lives by way of the object condition,’ but it is not said, ‘Nibbāna.’ Therefore, even when the function of reviewing the path and fruit is spoken of as being done by the knowledge of recollection of past lives itself, the reviewing of Nibbāna cannot be asserted. However, in the commentary, its having Nibbāna as an object is indicated.

Kusalā [M 2.0071] khandhāti iddhividhapubbenivāsānāgataṃsañāṇāpekkho bahuvacananiddeso, na cetopariyayathākammūpagañāṇāpekkhāti tesaṃ catukkhandhārammaṇabhāvassa asādhakoti ce? Na, aññattha “avitakkavicāramattā khandhā ca vicāro ca cetopariyañāṇassa pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇassa anāgataṃsañāṇassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.6.72), “savitakkasavicārā khandhā ca vitakko ca cetopariyañāṇassa pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇassa anāgataṃsañāṇassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.6.73) ca vuttattā cetopariyañāṇāpekkhāpi bahuvacananiddesoti imassa atthassa siddhito. Evampi yathākammūpagañāṇassa “avitakkavicāramattā khandhā ca vicāro cā”tiādīsu avuttattā catukkhandhārammaṇatā na sijjhatīti? Na, tattha avacanassa aññakāraṇattā. Yathākammūpagañāṇena hi kammasaṃsaṭṭhā cattāro khandhā kammamukhena gayhati. Tañhi yathā cetopariyañāṇaṃ purimaparikammavasena avitakkādivibhāgaṃ, sarāgādivibhāgañca cittaṃ vibhāveti, na evaṃ vibhāgaṃ vibhāveti. Kammavaseneva pana samudāyaṃ vibhāveti, tasmā “avitakkavicāramattā khandhā ca vicāro cā”tiādike vibhāgakaraṇe taṃ na vuttaṃ, na catukkhandhānārammaṇatoti. Idaṃ panassa akāraṇanti keci. Tatthāpi “pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇassa yathākammūpagañāṇassa anāgataṃsañāṇassā”ti paṭhanti eva. Na hi taṃ kusalākusalavibhāgaṃ viya savitakkādivibhāgaṃ kammaṃ vibhāvetuṃ asamatthaṃ. Duccaritasucaritavibhāvanampi hi lobhādialobhādisampayogavibhāgavisesavibhāvanaṃ hotīti.

If it is said: The plural designation 'wholesome aggregates' refers to the knowledge of psychic powers, the recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of future events, but not to the knowledge of others' thoughts or the knowledge of rebirth according to one's deeds; therefore, for these latter two, the state of having the four aggregates as an object is not established? No. Because elsewhere it is stated: 'The aggregates that are without initial thought and only with sustained thought, along with sustained thought, are a condition for the knowledge of others' thoughts, the recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of future events by way of object condition' (Paṭṭhā. 2.6.72), and 'The aggregates that are with initial thought and sustained thought, along with initial thought, are a condition for the knowledge of others' thoughts, the recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of future events by way of object condition' (Paṭṭhā. 2.6.73). Due to this statement, the meaning that the plural designation also refers to the knowledge of others' thoughts is established. Even so, since the knowledge of rebirth according to one's deeds is not mentioned in passages such as 'the aggregates that are without initial thought and only with sustained thought, along with sustained thought,' is the state of having the four aggregates as its object not established? No, because its non-mention there is for another reason. For by the knowledge of rebirth according to one's deeds, the four aggregates associated with kamma are grasped through the principal aspect of kamma. For just as the knowledge of others' thoughts clarifies the mind with its divisions of 'without initial thought,' etc., and 'with lust,' etc., by means of prior preparatory practices, that knowledge does not clarify the division in the same way. Rather, it clarifies the collection solely by way of kamma. Therefore, in making divisions such as in 'the aggregates that are without initial thought and only with sustained thought, along with sustained thought,' it is not mentioned; not because it does not take the four aggregates as its object. Some, however, say this is not the reason. Even there, they do indeed recite: '...for the recollection of past lives, for the knowledge of rebirth according to one's deeds, and for the knowledge of future events.' For that knowledge is not incapable of clarifying kamma with divisions of 'with initial thought,' etc., just as it clarifies the division of wholesome and unwholesome. Indeed, the clarification of misconduct and good conduct is also the clarification of the specific division of association with greed, etc., and non-greed, etc.

“Pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ nāmagottānussaraṇakāle na vattabbārammaṇa”nti ettakameva aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Nāmagottaṃ pana khandhūpanibandho sammutisiddho byañjanattho, na byañjananti. Ayamettha amhākaṃ khantīti ācariyassāyaṃ attano mati. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “na byañjana”nti, tassa samatthanaṃ “byañjanañhī”tiādi.

“The knowledge of recollecting past lives, at the time of recollecting name and clan, has an ineffable object”—only this much was said in the commentary. However, name and clan are bound up with the aggregates, established by convention, and are the meaning of the expression, not the expression itself. “This here is our view”—this is the teacher’s own opinion. As for what was said, “it is not the expression,” the support for that is the text beginning with, “For the expression indeed…”.

419. Kāmāvacare [V 2.0068] nibbattissatīti nibbattikkhandhajānanamāha.

419. With the text, “One will arise in the sense-sphere realm,” he stated the knowledge of the aggregates that are to arise.

420. Etthāti etasmiṃ ajjhattārammaṇattikavasena abhiññāñāṇānaṃ, ārammaṇavicāre. “Ajjhattārammaṇañceva bahiddhārammaṇañcā”ti ekajjhaṃ gahetvā [M 2.0072] yaṃ vuttaṃ porāṇaṭṭhakathāyaṃ, taṃ “kālena…pe… hotiyevā”ti iminā adhippāyena vuttanti attho. Na hi ajjhattabahiddhā nāma visuṃ ekaṃ atthi, nāpi taṃ ekajjhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karīyatīti. Yadi evaṃ tiko eva na pūrati padadvayāsaṅgahitassa tatiyassa atthantarassa abhāvato, na, pakārabhedavisayattā tikaniddesassa. Tathā hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “te eva tippakārepi dhamme”ti vuttaṃ. Te eva ajjhattādivasena tividhepi dhammeti attho. Ettha hi “te eva dhamme”ti avatvā “tippakāre”ti vacanaṃ pakārabhedanibandhanā ayaṃ tikadesanāti dassanatthaṃ. Yathā hi kusalattikādīnaṃ desanā yathārahaṃ dhammānaṃ jātisampayogappahānasikkhābhūmiārammaṇappabhedaniyamakālādibhedanibandhanā, na evamayaṃ jātiādibhedanibandhanā, nāpi sanidassanattikahetudukādidesanā viya sabhāvādibhedanibandhanā, atha kho pakārabhedanibandhanā. Pañceva hi khandhā sasantatipariyāpannataṃ upādāya “ajjhattā”ti vuttā, parasantatipariyāpannataṃ upādāya “bahiddhā”ti, tadubhayaṃ upādāya “ajjhattabahiddhā”ti. Tenāha “anindriyabaddharūpañca nibbānañca ṭhapetvā sabbe dhammā siyā ajjhattā, siyā bahiddhā, siyā ajjhattabahiddhā”ti (dha. sa. 1435). Nanu cettha atthantarābhāvato, pakārantarassa ca anāmaṭṭhattā tatiyo rāsi natthīti? Nayidamevaṃ. Yadipi hi paṭhamapadena asaṅgahitasaṅgaṇhanavasena dutiyapadassa pavattattā sabbepi sabhāvadhammā padadvayeneva pariggahitā, tehi pana visuṃ visuṃ gahitadhamme ekajjhaṃ gahaṇavasena tatiyapadaṃ vuttanti attheva tatiyo rāsi. Na hi samudāyo avayavo hoti, bhinnavatthuke pana dhamme adhiṭṭhānabhedaṃ amuñcitvā ekajjhaṃ gahaṇaṃ na sambhavatīti kālena ajjhattaṃ, kālena bahiddhā jānanakāleti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

420. The word Ettha ('here') refers to this examination of the object of the super-knowledges by way of the triad of internal objects. What was said in the ancient commentary, taking 'both the internal object and the external object' together, was said with this intention: 'at times... it indeed is.' This is the meaning. For there is not a single separate thing called 'internal-and-external', nor can it be taken as a single object. If so, the triad itself is not complete, due to the absence of a different meaning for the third term that is not included by the two terms. No, because the designation of the triad has difference of mode as its domain. Indeed, it is said in the commentary: 'those very same phenomena, which are also of three kinds.' The meaning is: those very same phenomena, which are also threefold by way of 'internal', etc. For here, the statement 'of three kinds', without saying 'those very same phenomena', is for the purpose of showing that this teaching of the triad is based on a difference of mode. For just as the teaching of the wholesome triad, etc., is based on the difference of birth, association, abandonment, training, plane, object, distinction, determination, time, etc., of the respective phenomena, this teaching is not so based on the difference of birth, etc., nor is it based on the difference of intrinsic nature, etc., like the teaching of the triad 'with manifestation', the dyad of roots, etc., but rather, it is based on the difference of mode. For the five aggregates themselves, by reason of being included in one's own continuity, are called 'internal'; by reason of being included in another's continuity, 'external'; and by reason of both, 'internal-and-external'. Therefore, it is said: 'Excluding non-faculty-bound matter and Nibbāna, all phenomena may be internal, may be external, or may be internal-and-external' (Dhs. 1435). Surely, is it not that here there is no third category, due to the absence of a different meaning and because another mode is not considered? It is not so. For although all intrinsic phenomena are indeed included by the two terms alone—because the second term proceeds by way of including what is not included by the first term—nevertheless, the third term is stated by way of taking together the phenomena taken separately by those two. Thus, the third category does indeed exist. For a collection is not a constituent part. However, for phenomena with different bases, taking them together is not possible without abandoning the difference of foundation. Therefore, it should be understood that it is said with reference to 'the time of knowing at times the internal, at times the external'.

Abhiññāniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Higher Knowledges is concluded.

Iti terasamaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus is the Commentary on the Thirteenth Chapter.

14. Khandhaniddesavaṇṇanā

14. Commentary on the Exposition of the Aggregates

Paññākathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on Wisdom

421. Sabbākārenāti [M 2.0073][V 2.0069] upacārākāro, appanākāro, vasībhāvākāro, vitakkādisamatikkamākāro, rūpādīhi virajjanākāro, cuddasadhā cittassa paridamanākāro, pañcavidhaānisaṃsādhigamākāroti evamādinā sabbena bhāvanākārena.

421. As for 'in all aspects': the aspect of access, the aspect of absorption, the aspect of mastery, the aspect of transcending initial thought and so on, the aspect of dispassion towards form and so on, the aspect of taming the mind in fourteen ways, and the aspect of attaining the five kinds of benefits—thus, by every such aspect of development.

Tadanantarāti “cittaṃ pañña”nti evaṃ desanākkamena, paṭipattikkamena ca tassa samādhissa anantarā. Paññā bhāvetabbā samādhibhāvanāya samannāgatena bhikkhunāti sambandho. “Paññañca bhāvaya”nti evaṃ atisaṅkhepadesitattā, gāthāvaṇṇanāyaṃ vā “samādhisilāyaṃ sunisitaṃ vipassanāpaññāsattha”nti evaṃ ativiya saṅkhepena bhāsitattā ayaṃ sā paññāti sabhāvato viññātumpi tāva na sukarā. Bhāvanāvidhānassa pana adassitattā pageva bhāvetuṃ na sukarāti sambandho. Pucchanaṭṭhena pañhā, kammaṃ kiriyā karaṇaṃ, pañhāva kammaṃ pañhākammaṃ, pucchanapayogoti attho.

As for 'immediately after that': immediately after that concentration, both by the order of the teaching and by the order of practice. The connection is: 'Wisdom is to be developed by a bhikkhu who is endowed with the development of concentration.' Because it was taught very concisely as, 'And develop wisdom,' or because it was stated extremely concisely in the explanation of the verse as, 'the weapon of insight-wisdom well-sharpened on the whetstone of concentration,' it is not easy at first even to understand by its intrinsic nature what this wisdom is. Moreover, because the method of development has not been shown, it is all the more not easy to develop it—this is the connection. By the meaning of questioning, it is a 'pañhā' (question). 'Kamma' is action, doing. A question itself is an action, hence 'pañhākamma' (question-action). The meaning is 'the application of questioning'.

Kā paññāti sarūpapucchā. Kenaṭṭhena paññāti kena atthena paññāti vuccati, “paññā”ti padaṃ kaṃ abhidheyyatthaṃ nissāya pavattanti attho. Sā panāyaṃ paññā sabhāvato, kiccato, upaṭṭhānākārato, āsannakāraṇato ca kathaṃ jānitabbāti āha “kānassā lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānānī”ti. Katividhāti pabhedapucchā. Kasmā panettha saṃkilesavodānapucchā na gahitāti? Vuccate – lokuttarāya tāva paññāya nattheva saṃkileso. Asati ca tasmiṃ kuto vodānapucchāti tadubhayaṃ na gahitaṃ. Lokiyāya pana tāni bhāvanāvidhāne eva antogadhānīti katvā visuṃ na gahitāni maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhiantogadhattā[V 2.0070], samādhibhāvanāyaṃ vā vuttanayānusārena veditabbānīti na gahitāni. Paṭipatti nāma diṭṭhānisaṃse eva hotīti āha “paññābhāvanāya ko ānisaṃso”ti.

“What is wisdom?” is a question about its intrinsic nature. “By what reason is it called ‘wisdom’?” The meaning is: depending on what denotable meaning does the term ‘wisdom’ occur? Furthermore, how is this wisdom to be understood in terms of its nature, its function, its manifestation, and its proximate cause? Thus, it is asked, “What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause?” “How many kinds?” is a question about its divisions. Why, herein, is the question about defilement and cleansing not taken up? It is stated: Firstly, for supramundane wisdom, there is no defilement whatsoever. And when that is absent, whence could there be a question about cleansing? For this reason, both are not taken up. As for mundane wisdom, those defilements and cleansings are included within the very method of development because they are encompassed by the purification of knowledge and vision of path and not-path; thinking thus, they are not taken up separately. Or, because they are to be known according to the method stated in the development of concentration, they are not taken up. Practice, indeed, occurs only when the benefit is seen; for this reason, he stated, “What is the benefit of the development of wisdom?”

422. Tatrāti tasmiṃ, tassa vā pañhākammassa. Vissajjananti vivaraṇaṃ. Pucchito hi attho avibhāvitattā nigūḷho muṭṭhiyaṃ kato viya tiṭṭhati, tassa [M 2.0074] vivaraṇaṃ vissajjanaṃ vibhūtabhāvakaraṇato. Kā paññāti kāmañcāyaṃ sarūpapucchā, vibhāgavantānaṃ pana sabhāvavibhāvanaṃ vibhāgadassanamukheneva hotīti vibhāgo tāva anavasesato dassetabbo. Taṃdassanena ca ayamādīnavoti dassetuṃ “paññā bahuvidhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha bahuvidhāti kusalādivasena anekavidhā. Nānappakārāti atthajāpikādibhedena, sutamayañāṇādibhedena ca nānāvidhā. Taṃ sabbanti taṃ anavasesaṃ paññāvibhāgaṃ. Na sādheyyāti vipassanābhāvanāya saddhiṃ maggabhāvanā idha adhippetattho. Tāya hi taṇhājaṭāvijaṭanaṃ, tañca na sādheyya. Anavasesato hi paññāpabhede vissajjiyamāne “ekavidhena ñāṇavatthū”tiādiko (vibha. 751) sabbo ñāṇavatthu vibhaṅge, suttantesu ca tattha tattha āgato paññāpabhedo. Sakalopi vā abhidhammanayo āharitvā vissajjetabbo bhaveyya, tathā ca sati yvāyaṃ idha paññābhāvanāvidhi adhippeto, tassa vissajjanāya okāsova na bhaveyya. Kiñca yvāyaṃ ṭhānāṭhānakammantaravipākantarādivisaye paññāya pavattibhedo, sopi yathārahaṃ saddhiṃ phalāphalabhedena vibhajitvā vissajjetabbo siyā. So ca pana vissajjiyamāno aññadatthu vikkhepāya saṃvatteyya, yathā taṃ avisaye. Tenāha “uttari ca vikkhepāya saṃvatteyyā”ti. Kusalacittasampayuttaṃ vipassanāñāṇanti ettha kusala-ggahaṇena duvidhampi abyākataṃ nivatteti, tathā “atthi saṃkiliṭṭhapaññā”ti evaṃ pavattaṃ micchāvādaṃ paṭisedheti. Vipassanāñāṇa-ggahaṇena sesakusalapaññā.

422. Therein (Tatrāti): in that matter of the question, or of that matter of the question. An 'answer' (vissajjana) means a clarification (vivaraṇa). Indeed, the meaning that is asked, because it has not been made manifest, remains concealed like something held in a clenched fist; its clarification is the 'answer' because it makes it manifest. Although this question, 'What is wisdom?', is a question about its intrinsic nature, for things that have divisions, the explanation of their nature occurs only by means of showing the divisions. Therefore, the division should first be shown completely. And in order to show, 'This is the danger in that showing,' it was said, 'Wisdom is of many kinds,' etc. Therein, 'of many kinds' (bahuvidhā) means it is of many kinds by way of the wholesome, etc. 'Of various types' (nānappakārā) means it is of various kinds by the distinction of wisdom that clarifies the meaning (atthajāpikā), etc., and by the distinction of knowledge based on learning (sutamayañāṇa), etc. 'All that' refers to that complete division of wisdom. 'Would not accomplish': the intended meaning here is the development of the path together with the development of insight. For by that, the disentangling of the tangle of craving occurs, and that would not be accomplished. For if the distinctions of wisdom were answered completely, all the distinctions of wisdom that have come in the Vibhaṅga on the Bases of Knowledge—such as 'the basis of knowledge in one way,' etc.—and in the Suttas here and there, or even the entire Abhidhamma method, would have to be brought forth and answered. That being so, there would be no opportunity at all for answering about this method for the development of wisdom that is intended here. Moreover, whatever distinction there is in the functioning of wisdom in the domain of the possible and the impossible, the diversity of kamma, the diversity of results, and so on—that too would have to be divided and answered appropriately, together with the distinction between what is fruitful and what is not. And that, if it were answered, would only lead to distraction, just as something answered that is not the proper domain. Therefore, it was said: 'And it would lead to further distraction.' In the phrase 'insight knowledge associated with wholesome consciousness,' by the inclusion of 'wholesome,' both kinds of indeterminate wisdom are excluded; likewise, the wrong view that occurs as 'there is defiled wisdom' is refuted. By the inclusion of 'insight knowledge,' the remaining wholesome wisdoms are excluded.

423. Sañjānanavijānanākāravisiṭṭhanti sañjānanākāravijānanākārehi sātisayaṃ. Yato nānappakārato jānanaṃ jānanabhāvo visayaggahaṇākāro. So hi nesaṃ samāno, na sañjānanādiākāro. Pītakantīti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho, tena “lohitakaṃ odātaṃ dīghaṃ rassa”ntiādike saññāya gahetabbākāre saṅgaṇhāti. Sañjānanamattamevāti ettha sañjānanaṃ nāma “nīlaṃ pīta”ntiādikaṃ ārammaṇe vijjamānaṃ vā avijjamānaṃ vā saññānimittaṃ katvā jānanaṃ. Tathā hesā puna sañjānanapaccayanimittakaraṇarasā. Matta-saddena visesanivattiatthena vijānanapajānanākāre nivatteti, eva-saddena kadācipi imissā te visesā [V 2.0071] natthevāti avadhāreti. Tenāha “aniccaṃ dukkha”ntiādi[M 2.0075]. Tattha viññāṇakiccampi kātuṃ asakkontī saññā kuto paññākiccaṃ kareyyāti “lakkhaṇapaṭivedhaṃ pāpetuṃ na sakkoti”cceva vuttaṃ, na vuttaṃ “maggapātubhāva”nti. Ārammaṇe pavattamānaṃ viññāṇaṃ na tattha saññā viya nīlapītādikassa sañjānanavaseneva pavattati, atha kho tattha aññañca visesaṃ jānantameva pavattatīti āha “viññāṇa”ntiādi. Kathaṃ pana viññāṇaṃ lakkhaṇapaṭivedhaṃ pāpetīti? Paññāya dassitamaggena. Lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanāya hi anekavāraṃ lakkhaṇāni paṭivijjhitvā paṭivijjhitvā pavattamānāya paguṇabhāvato paricayavasena ñāṇavippayuttacittenapi vipassanā sambhavati, yathā taṃ paguṇassa ganthassa sajjhāyane ñāyāgatāpi vārā na viññāyanti. Lakkhaṇapaṭivedhanti ca lakkhaṇānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇamattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na paṭivijjhanaṃ. Ussakkitvāti udayabbayañāṇapaṭipāṭiyā āyūhitvā. Maggapātubhāvaṃ pāpetuṃ na sakkoti asambodhasabhāvattā. Vuttanayavasenāti viññāṇe vuttanayavasena ārammaṇañca jānāti, lakkhaṇapaṭivedhañca pāpeti. Attano pana anaññasādhāraṇena ānubhāvena ussakkitvā maggapātubhāvañca pāpeti.

423. 'Distinguished by the modes of recognition and discernment' means: with excellence beyond the modes of recognition and discernment. Because it is thus with excellence, knowing occurs in various ways; the state of knowing is the mode of grasping an object. Indeed, that mode of grasping an object is common to them, but the mode of recognition, etc., is not. In the phrase 'as yellow,' the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'and so on'; by it, one includes the modes to be grasped by perception, such as 'red, white, long, short,' and so on. Here, in the phrase 'mere recognition,' 'recognition' refers to knowing by making a sign for perception—such as 'blue,' 'yellow,' etc.—of what is present or absent in the object. By the word 'matta' (mere), which has the meaning of excluding specifics, it negates the modes of discernment and understanding. By the word 'eva' (only), it determines that for this perception, those specifics never exist. Therefore, he said, 'impermanent, suffering,' and so on. There, since perception is unable to perform even the function of consciousness, how could it perform the function of wisdom? Thus, it is said only that 'it cannot lead to the penetration of characteristics'; it is not said 'to the manifestation of the path.' Consciousness occurring in relation to an object does not proceed there like perception, merely by the power of recognizing 'blue,' 'yellow,' etc. Rather, it proceeds there knowing some other distinction as well. Therefore, he said, 'consciousness,' and so on. But how does consciousness lead to the penetration of characteristics? Through the path shown by wisdom. For, in the case of insight meditation that has characteristics as its object, which proceeds by repeatedly penetrating the characteristics, due to proficiency and familiarity, insight is possible even with a mind dissociated from knowledge—just as, in the recitation of a familiar text, passages that come by rote are not consciously discerned. And 'penetration of characteristics' is said in reference to merely making the characteristics an object, not in reference to penetration itself. 'Having striven' means having exerted oneself by the sequence of the knowledge of arising and passing away. It cannot lead to the manifestation of the path because its nature is non-awakening. The phrase 'according to the stated method' refers to the method stated in the case of consciousness, by which it both knows the object and leads to the penetration of characteristics. But through its own unique power, having exerted itself, it also leads to the manifestation of the path.

Idāni yathāvuttamatthaṃ upamāya patiṭṭhāpetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ajātabuddhīti asañjātabyavahārabuddhi. Upabhogaparibhoganti upabhogaparibhogārahaṃ, upabhogaparibhogavatthūnaṃ paṭilābhayogyanti attho. Chekoti mahāsāro. Kūṭoti kahāpaṇapatirūpako tambakaṃsādimayo. Addhasāroti upaḍḍhagghanako. Iti-saddo ādiattho, tena pādasāra samasāraparopādasārādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Te pakāreti indajālājātipupphādippakāre ceva chekādippakāre ca.

Now, to establish the meaning as stated through a simile, the passage beginning with “Just as…” was spoken. Therein, 'one with undeveloped intellect' means one whose commercial intellect has not yet arisen. 'For enjoyment and use' means that which is worthy of enjoyment and use; the meaning is that which is suitable for obtaining objects of enjoyment and use. 'Genuine' means of great value. 'Counterfeit' means a replica of a coin made of copper, bronze, and so forth. 'Of half-value' means worth half the price. The word 'iti' has the meaning of “and so forth”; by it, the inclusion of coins of quarter-value, full-value, more than quarter-value, and so on, is to be understood. 'Their types' refers to both those with various markings, such as the Indajāla weapon shape and the Jāti flower, and those of various kinds, such as genuine coins and so forth.

Saññā hītiādi upamāsaṃsandanaṃ. Saññā vibhāgaṃ akatvā piṇḍavaseneva ārammaṇassa gahaṇato dārakassa kahāpaṇadassanasadisī vuttā. Tathā hi sā “yathāupaṭṭhitavisayapadaṭṭhānā” vuccati. Viññāṇaṃ ārammaṇe ekaccavisesagahaṇasamatthatāya gāmikapurisassa kahāpaṇadassanasadisaṃ vuttaṃ. Paññā ārammaṇe anavasesavisesāvabodhato heraññikassa kahāpaṇadassanasadisī vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Nānappakārato [M 2.0076] jānana”nti iminā ñeyyadhammā paccekaṃ nānappakārāti tesaṃ yāthāvato avabodho paññāti dasseti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “sabbe dhammā sabbākārena buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇamukhe āpāthamāgacchantī”ti (mahāni. 156; cūḷani. mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 85).

The passage beginning with “Perception indeed…” is a connection with the simile. Perception is said to be like a child’s seeing of coins because it grasps the object as a whole, without making distinctions. Indeed, it is called ‘that which has the object as it is presented for its proximate cause.’ Consciousness is said to be like a villager’s seeing of a coin because of its ability to grasp a certain particular aspect of the object. It should be understood that wisdom is said to be like a money-changer’s seeing of a coin because of its understanding of all particular aspects in the object without remainder. By the phrase “knowing in various ways,” it is shown that knowable things are individually of various kinds; therefore, the understanding of them as they really are is wisdom. For thus it is said: “All phenomena in all their aspects come into the range of the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One.”

Yatthāti [V 2.0072] yasmiṃ cittuppāde. Na tattha ekaṃsena hotīti tasmiṃ cittuppāde paññā ekantena na hoti. Na hi duhetukaahetukacittuppādesu paññā uppajjati. Avinibbhuttāti aviyuttā. Tehīti saññāviññāṇehi. Yathā hi sukhaṃ pītiyā na niyamato aviyuttaṃ, evaṃ saññāviññāṇāni paññāya na niyamato aviyuttāti. Yathā pana pīti sukhena niyamato aviyuttā, evaṃ paññā saññāviññāṇehi niyamato aviyuttā. Tasmā evaṃ avinibbhuttesu imesu tīsu dhammesu tesaṃ vinibbhogo dukkaroti tiṇṇaṃ janānaṃ kahāpaṇadassanaṃ nidassitanti. Tesaṃ duviññeyyanānattataṃyeva vacanantarenapi dassetuṃ “tenāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha rūpadhammesupi tāva nānānadīnaṃ udakassa, nānātelassa vā ekasmiṃ bhājane pakkhipitvā mathitassa “idaṃ asukāya nadiyā udakaṃ, idaṃ asukatela”nti niddhāretvā sarūpato dassanaṃ dukkaraṃ, kimaṅgaṃ pana arūpadhammesūti dassento “yaṃ arūpīnaṃ cittacetasikāna”ntiādimāha.

'Where' means: in which thought-moment. 'Not invariably there' means: in that thought-moment wisdom is not invariably present, for indeed, wisdom does not arise in two-rooted or rootless thought-moments. 'Inseparable' means: not dissociated. 'By them' means: by perception and consciousness. Just as happiness is not invariably associated with joy, so too perception and consciousness are not invariably associated with wisdom. Just as, on the other hand, joy is invariably associated with happiness, so too wisdom is invariably associated with perception and consciousness. Therefore, because these three states are thus inseparable, their distinction is difficult; for this reason, the seeing of a coin by three people was presented as an example. To show their diversity, which is difficult to discern, by another expression as well, the passage beginning with “Therefore, he said,” was spoken. Therein, first, even regarding material phenomena: it is difficult to distinguish and show in its own nature the water of various rivers or various oils, which has been placed in a single vessel and stirred, by specifying, “This is the water of such-and-such a river; this is such-and-such an oil.” How much more so with immaterial phenomena! Showing this, he said, “As to those immaterial states of mind and mental factors…” and so on.

424. Dhammānaṃ sako bhāvo, samāno ca bhāvo dhammasabhāvo. Tattha paṭhamena kakkhaḷaphusanādisalakkhaṇaṃ gahitaṃ, dutiyena aniccadukkhatādisāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ. Tadubhayassa ca yāthāvato paṭivijjhanalakkhaṇā paññāti āha “dhammasabhāvapaṭivedhalakkhaṇā paññā”ti. Ghaṭapaṭādipaṭicchādakassa bāhirandhakārassa dīpālokādi viya yathāvuttadhammasabhāvapaṭicchādakassa mohandhakārassa viddhaṃsanarasā. Uppajjamāno eva hi paññāloko hadayandhakāraṃ vidhamento evaṃ uppajjati, tato eva dhammasabhāvesu asammuyhanākārena paccupatiṭṭhatīti asammohapaccupaṭṭhānā. Kāraṇabhūtā vā sayaṃ phalabhūtaṃ asammohaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetīti evampi asammohapaccupaṭṭhānā. Vipassanāpaññāya idha adhippetattā “samādhi tassā padaṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ. Tathā hi “samāhito yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti suttapadaṃ nibandhanabhāvena āgataṃ (saṃ. ni. 3.5, 99; saṃ. ni. 5.1071; netti. 40; mi. pa. 2.1.14).

424. The own nature of phenomena, and their common nature, is the nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva). Therein, by the first is taken the individual characteristic such as hardness and touching, and by the second, the general characteristic such as impermanence and suffering. Wisdom has the characteristic of penetrating both of these as they really are; thus it is said, 'wisdom has the characteristic of penetrating the nature of phenomena.' Its function is to destroy the darkness of delusion that conceals the aforesaid nature of phenomena, just as the light of a lamp, etc., destroys the external darkness that conceals a pot, a cloth, etc. For indeed, the light of wisdom, as it arises, arises while dispelling the darkness of the heart. For that very reason, it manifests in the manner of non-bewilderment regarding the natures of phenomena; thus, its manifestation is non-bewilderment. Alternatively, being the cause, it itself causes the resultant non-bewilderment to manifest; for this reason also, its manifestation is non-bewilderment. Because insight wisdom is intended here, it is said, 'Concentration is its proximate cause.' Indeed, the Sutta passage, 'One who is concentrated understands as it really is,' is cited as evidence.

Paññāpabhedakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Varieties of Wisdom

425. Dhammasabhāvapaṭivedho [M 2.0077] nāma paññāya āveṇiko sabhāvo, na tenassā koci vibhāgo labbhatīti āha “dhammasabhāvapaṭivedhalakkhaṇena tāva ekavidhā”ti. Lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena loko vuccati vaṭṭaṃ, tappariyāpannatāya loke niyuttā, tattha vā viditāti lokiyā. Tattha apariyāpannatāya lokato uttarā uttiṇṇāti lokuttarā. Lokuttarāpi [V 2.0073] hi maggasampayuttā bhāvetabbā. Vipassanāpariyāyopi tassā labbhatevāti lokuttara-ggahaṇaṃ na virujjhati. Attānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattehi saha āsavehīti sāsavā, ārammaṇakaraṇavasenapi natthi etissā āsavāti anāsavā. Ādi-saddena āsavavippayuttasāsavadukādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Nāmarūpavavatthānavasenāti nāmavavatthānavasena, rūpavavatthānavasena ca. Paṭhamaṃ nibbānadassanato dassanañca, nissayabhāvato sampayuttā dhammā bhavanti ettha, sayampi vā bhavati uppajjati na nibbānaṃ viya apātubhāvanti bhūmi cāti dassanabhūmi, paṭhamamaggo. Sesamaggattayaṃ pana yasmā paṭhamamaggena diṭṭhasmiṃyeva dhamme bhāvanāvasena uppajjati, na adiṭṭhapubbaṃ kiñci passati, tasmā bhāvanā ca yathāvuttenatthena bhūmi cāti bhāvanābhūmi. Tattha paññā dassanabhūmibhāvanābhūmivasena duvidhāti vuttā. Sutādinirapekkhāya cintāya nibbattā cintāmayā. Evaṃ sutamayā, bhāvanāmayā ca. Mayasaddo paccekaṃ sambandhitabbo. Āye vaḍḍhiyaṃ kosallaṃ āyakosallaṃ, apāye avaḍḍhiyaṃ kosallaṃ apāyakosallaṃ, upāye tassa tassa atthassa nibbattikāraṇe kosallaṃ upāyakosallanti visuṃ visuṃ kosallapadaṃ sambandhitabbaṃ. Ajjhattaṃ abhiniveso paṭipajjanaṃ etissāti ajjhattābhinivesā. Evaṃ bahiddhābhinivesā, ubhayābhinivesā ca veditabbā.

425. The penetration of the true nature of phenomena is the unique characteristic of wisdom, and by that characteristic, no distinction can be made in it. Hence, it is said: 'First, it is of one kind by the characteristic of penetrating the true nature of phenomena.' The cycle (vaṭṭa) is called the world (loka) in the sense of breaking up and crumbling away. Those engaged in it are called 'worldly' (lokiyā) because they are included in that cycle, or are known therein. That which, by not being included therein, is beyond and has transcended the world is 'supramundane' (lokuttarā). Indeed, even the supramundane (wisdom) associated with the path is to be developed. The synonymous term 'insight' is also obtained for it, so the inclusion of 'supramundane' is not contradicted. That which occurs together with the cankers that proceed having taken the self as object is 'with cankers' (sāsavā); because for this (wisdom) there are no cankers even by way of making them an object, it is 'cankerless' (anāsavā). By the term 'etc.' (ādi), the inclusion of the pair 'with cankers but dissociated from cankers', and so on, should be understood. 'By way of the determination of name-and-form' means: by way of the determination of name, and by way of the determination of form. Because of seeing Nibbāna for the first time, it is 'vision' (dassana); and because it is a support, associated states exist in it; or, it itself arises, comes to be, and is not a non-manifestation like Nibbāna, it is also a 'plane' (bhūmi); thus, it is the 'plane of vision' (dassanabhūmi), which is the first path. The remaining triad of paths, however, arises by way of development in regard to the very Dhamma seen by the first path, and it does not see anything not seen before. Therefore, it is 'development' (bhāvanā), and for the reason already stated, it is also a 'plane' (bhūmi); thus, it is the 'plane of development' (bhāvanābhūmi). Therein, wisdom is said to be twofold by way of the plane of vision and the plane of development. That which is produced by reflection independent of learning, etc., is 'based on reflection' (cintāmayā). Similarly, 'based on learning' (sutamayā) and 'based on development' (bhāvanāmayā). The suffix 'maya' should be connected with each term individually. Skill in growth or increase is 'skill in growth' (āyakosallaṃ). Skill in non-growth or decline is 'skill in decline' (apāyakosallaṃ). Skill in the cause for producing this or that benefit is 'skill in means' (upāyakosallaṃ); thus the term 'skill' should be connected separately with each. That for which there is the practice of inward adherence is 'having inward adherence' (ajjhattābhinivesā). Similarly, 'having outward adherence' (bahiddhābhinivesā) and 'having adherence to both' (ubhayābhinivesā) should be understood.

426. Lokiyamaggasampayuttāti lokiyakusalacittuppādesu maggasampayuttā, visesato diṭṭhivisuddhiādivisuddhicatukkasaṅgahitamaggasampayuttā. Samudāyesu pavattā samaññā tadekadesesupi vattatīti āha “maggasampayuttā”ti, paccekampi vā sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ maggasamaññāti katvā evaṃ vuttaṃ.

426. "Associated with the mundane path" means associated with the path in mundane wholesome consciousnesses; specifically, associated with the path included in the fourfold purification beginning with the purification of view. The designation, which operates on an aggregate, also operates on its individual parts; therefore, it is said, "associated with the path." Alternatively, it is said thus, having considered that even individually, 'right view' and so on have the designation 'path'.

Dhammanānattābhāvepi [M 2.0078] padatthanānattamattena dukkaravacanaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ “atthato panesā lokiyalokuttarāvā”ti. Āsavavippayuttasāsavadukādīsupi vippayuttatādiggahaṇameva viseso, atthato lokiyalokuttarāva paññāti āha “eseva nayo”ti. Ādi-saddena oghanīyaoghavippayuttaoghanīyādidukānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Paṭhamajjhānikāni cattāri maggacittāni, tathā dutiyādijjhānikāni cāti evaṃ soḷasasu maggacittesu. Vipassanāpaññāya idha adhippetattā mahaggatapaññā na gahitā.

Even though there is no diversity of natures, by the mere diversity in the meaning of words, there is the statement of a different couplet; therefore, it is said, "But in meaning, these are mundane and supramundane." Also in the couplets such as 'dissociated from the cankers' and 'associated with the cankers', the distinction is only the grasping of the state of being dissociated, and so on. In terms of intrinsic meaning, it is only mundane and supramundane wisdom; therefore, it is said, "This is the very method." By the word 'ādi', the inclusion of couplets such as 'pertaining to the floods' and 'dissociated from what pertains to the floods' should be understood. The four path-consciousnesses associated with the first jhāna, and similarly those associated with the second jhāna and so on—thus, in the sixteen path-consciousnesses. Because insight-wisdom is intended here, exalted wisdom is not included.

427. Attano cintāvasenāti tassa tassa anavajjassa atthassa sādhane paropadesena vinā [V 2.0074] attano upāyacintāvaseneva. Sutavasenāti yathāsutassa paropadesassa vasena. Yathā tathā vāti parato upadesaṃ sutvā vā asutvā vā sayameva bhāvanaṃ anuyuñjantassa. “Appanāppattā”ti idaṃ sikhāppattabhāvanāmayaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ, na pana “appanāppattāva bhāvanāmayā”ti.

427. "By the power of one's own thought" means: in accomplishing this or that blameless aim, without instruction from another, only by the power of one's own reflection on the means. "By the power of hearing" means: by the power of another's instruction as it was heard. "In whatever way" means: of one who strives in cultivation by oneself, whether having heard instruction from another or not. This [phrase] "attained absorption" is said in order to show that which consists in cultivation that has reached the peak, but not in order to show that "only that which has attained absorption consists in cultivation."

Yogavihitesūti paññāvihitesu paññāpariṇāmitesu upāyasampāditesu. Kammāyatanesūti ettha kammameva kammāyatanaṃ, kammañca taṃ āyatanañca ājīvānanti vā kammāyatanaṃ. Esa nayo sippāyatanesupi. Tattha duvidhaṃ kammaṃ hīnañca vaḍḍhakīkammādi, ukkaṭṭhañca kasivāṇijādi. Sippampi duvidhaṃ hīnañca naḷakārasippādi, ukkaṭṭhañca muddāgaṇanādi. Vijjāva vijjāṭṭhānaṃ. Taṃ dhammikameva nāgamaṇḍalaparittaphudhamanakamantasadisaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tāni panetāni ekacce paṇḍitā bodhisattasadisā manussānaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ ākaṅkhantā neva aññehi kariyamānāni passanti, na vā katāni uggaṇhanti, na kathentānaṃ suṇanti. Atha kho attano dhammatāya cintāya karonti, paññavantehi attano dhammatāya cintāya katānipi aññehi uggaṇhitvā karontehi katasadisāneva honti.

"Established by effort" refers to those established by wisdom, matured by wisdom, and accomplished through suitable means. In the passage on "fields of action," action itself is a field of action; or, it is action and it is a basis for livelihoods, therefore it is called a field of action. This same method also applies to "fields of craft." Therein, action is twofold: inferior, such as the work of a carpenter, and superior, such as agriculture and trade. Craft is also twofold: inferior, such as the craft of a reed-worker, and superior, such as the art of calculation by hand and accounting. Knowledge itself is the basis of knowledge. It should be understood as only that which is in accordance with the Dhamma, such as the protective spell called Nāgamaṇḍala and mantras muttered with 'phu'. However, some wise people, who are like Bodhisattas, desiring the comfortable living of human beings, neither see these things being performed by others, nor learn them when they have been done, nor listen to those who explain them. Rather, they create them through their own nature and thought. And even those things done by the wise through their own nature and thought, when learned and performed by others, become just like those that were done before.

Kammassakatanti “idaṃ kammaṃ sattānaṃ sakaṃ, idaṃ no saka”nti evaṃ jānanañāṇaṃ. Saccānulomikanti vipassanāñāṇaṃ. Taṃ hi saccapaṭivedhassa anulomanato “saccānulomika”nti vuccati. Idānissa pavattanākāraṃ dassetuṃ “rūpaṃ aniccanti vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha vā-saddena aniyamatthena dukkhānattalakkhaṇānipi [M 2.0079] gahitānevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ nānantariyakabhāvato. Yaṃ hi aniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattāti. Yaṃ evarūpinti yaṃ evaṃ heṭṭhā niddiṭṭhasabhāvaṃ. Anulomikaṃ khantintiādīni paññāvevacanāni. Sā hi heṭṭhā vuttānaṃ kammāyatanādīnaṃ apaccanīkadassanena anulomanato, tathā sattānaṃ hitacariyāya maggasaccassa, paramatthasaccassa, nibbānassa ca avilomanato anulometīti anulomikā. Sabbānipi etāni kāraṇāni khamati daṭṭhuṃ sakkotīti khanti. Passatīti diṭṭhi. Rocetīti ruci. Munātīti muti. Pekkhatīti pekkhā. Te ca kammāyatanādayo dhammā etāya nijjhāyamānā nijjhānaṃ khamantīti dhammanijjhānakhanti. Parato asutvā paṭilabhatīti aññassa upadesavacanaṃ asutvā sayameva cintento paṭilabhati. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ cintāmayā paññā nāma vuccati. Sā panesā abhiññātānaṃ bodhisattānameva uppajjati. Tatthāpi [V 2.0075] saccānulomikañāṇaṃ dvinnaṃyeva bodhisattānaṃ antimabhavikānaṃ, sesapaññā sabbesampi pūritapāramīnaṃ mahāpaññānaṃ uppajjati. Parato sutvā paṭilabhatīti kammāyatanādīni parena kariyamānāni vā katāni vā disvāpi parassa kathayamānassa vacanaṃ sutvāpi ācariyasantike uggahetvāpi paṭiladdhā sabbā parato sutvāva paṭiladdhā nāmāti veditabbā. Samāpannassāti samāpattisamaṅgissa, nidassanamattañcetaṃ. Vipassanāmaggapaññā idha “bhāvanāmayā paññā”ti adhippetā.

The knowledge of ownership of kamma is the knowledge that knows thus: 'This kamma is the own property of beings, this is not their own property.' Knowledge in conformity with the truths refers to insight knowledge. Indeed, because it conforms to the path-knowledge that penetrates the truths, it is called 'knowledge in conformity with the truths'. Now, to show its mode of occurrence, it was said: 'Form is impermanent, or...' and so on. Therein, by the word 'or', which indicates non-exclusivity, the characteristics of suffering and non-self are also included, and this should be understood as being due to their non-intervening nature. Indeed, what is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self. 'Whatever is of such nature' means whatever has the nature previously indicated. 'Conformity', 'endurance', and so on are synonyms for wisdom. Indeed, that wisdom is called 'conformity' (anulomikā) because it conforms by seeing without opposition the previously mentioned fields of action, etc., and also because it is not in opposition to the welfare-practice for beings, to the truth of the path, and to Nibbāna, which is the ultimate truth. It is called 'endurance' (khanti) because it accepts and is able to see all these causes. Because it sees, it is called view (diṭṭhi). Because it approves, it is called liking (ruci). Because it knows, it is called comprehension (muti). Because it observes, it is called contemplation (pekkhā). And those phenomena, the fields of action, etc., being scrutinized by this wisdom, accept the scrutiny; therefore, it is called 'endurance of the scrutiny of phenomena' (dhammanijjhānakhanti). 'One obtains it without hearing from another' means one obtains it by reflecting by oneself, without hearing the instructional words of another. This is called 'wisdom born of reflection' (cintāmayā paññā). Furthermore, this wisdom arises only for renowned Bodhisattas. Even among them, the knowledge in conformity with the truths arises only for the two Bodhisattas in their final existence, while the remaining wisdom arises for all beings of great wisdom who have fulfilled the perfections. 'One obtains it by hearing from another' means that all wisdom obtained by seeing the fields of action, etc., being done or having been done by another, or by hearing the words of another who is speaking, or by learning in the presence of a teacher, should be understood as being named 'obtained by hearing from another'. 'Of one who has attained' means of one endowed with attainment; and this is merely an example. Here, the wisdom of insight and path is intended as 'wisdom born of development' (bhāvanāmayā paññā).

Sāti “parittārammaṇā mahaggatārammaṇā”ti (vibha. 753) vuttapaññā. Lokiyavipassanāti lokiyavipassanāpaññā. Sā lokuttaravipassanāti yā nibbānaṃ ārabbha pavattā appamāṇārammaṇā paññā vuttā, sā lokuttaravipassanāti maggapaññaṃ sandhāyāha. Sā hi saṅkhārānaṃ aniccatādiṃ agaṇhantīpi vipassanākiccapāripūriyā, nibbānassa vā tathalakkhaṇaṃ visesato passatīti vipassanāti vuccati. Gotrabhuñāṇaṃ pana kiñcāpi appamāṇārammaṇaṃ, maggassa pana āvajjanaṭṭhāniyattā na vipassanāvohāraṃ labhati.

That is the wisdom spoken of as 'having a limited object and having a sublime object.' This is mundane insight-wisdom. That which is called supramundane insight is the wisdom which, having arisen by taking Nibbāna as its object, is described as having an immeasurable object; this is said in reference to path-wisdom. For although it does not grasp the impermanence, etc., of formations, it is called 'insight' because of the complete fulfillment of the function of insight, or because it sees in a special way the true characteristic of Nibbāna. However, although change-of-lineage knowledge has an immeasurable object, because it stands in the position of adverting to the path, it does not receive the designation 'insight'.

Ayanti etāya sampattiyoti āyo, vuddhi. Tattha kosallanti tasmiṃ anatthahāniatthuppattilakkhaṇe āye kosallaṃ kusalatā nipuṇatā.

Because accomplishments come by means of it, it is called 'gain' (āyo); it is growth (vuddhi). Therein, skillfulness is skill, competence, and proficiency in that gain which is characterized by the decline of what is disadvantageous and the arising of what is advantageous.

Taṃ [M 2.0080] pana ekantikaṃ āyakosallaṃ pāḷivaseneva dassetuṃ “ime dhamme”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha idaṃ vuccatīti yā imesaṃ akusaladhammānaṃ anuppattipahānesu, kusaladhammānañca uppattiṭṭhitīsu paññā, idaṃ āyakosallaṃ nāmāti vuccati.

Furthermore, to demonstrate that absolute skill in gain by means of the Pāḷi itself, 'these states', etc., was said. Therein, this is said: the wisdom regarding the non-arising and abandoning of these unwholesome states, and the arising and establishing of wholesome states—this is called 'skill in gain'.

Vuddhilakkhaṇā āyato apetattā apāyo, avuddhi. Tattha kosallanti tasmiṃ atthahānianatthuppattilakkhaṇe apāye kosallaṃ kusalatā apāyakosallaṃ. Tampi pāḷivaseneva dassetuṃ “ime dhamme”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha idaṃ vuccatīti yā imesaṃ kusaladhammānaṃ anuppajjananirujjhanesu, akusaladhammānaṃ vā uppattiṭṭhitīsu paññā, idaṃ apāyakosallaṃ nāmāti vuccati. Āyakosallaṃ tāva paññā hotu, apāyakosallaṃ kathaṃ paññā nāma jātāti? Evaṃ maññati “apāyuppādanasamatthatā apāyakosallaṃ nāma siyā”ti, taṃ pana tassa matimattaṃ. Kasmā? Paññavā eva hi “mayhaṃ evaṃ manasi karoto anuppannā kusalā dhammā nuppajjanti, uppannā [V 2.0076] nirujjhanti. Anuppannā akusalā dhammā uppajjanti, uppannā pavaḍḍhantī”ti pajānāti, so evaṃ ñatvā anuppanne akusale na uppādeti, uppanne pajahati. Anuppanne kusale uppādeti, uppanne bhāvanāpāripūriṃ pāpeti. Evaṃ apāyakosallampi paññā evāti.

Because it is devoid of gain, which has the characteristic of growth, it is called decline (apāya), that is, non-growth (avuddhi). Therein, skillfulness (kosallaṃ) in that decline, which is characterized by the decline of benefit and the arising of non-benefit, is skill, competence; this is skill in decline (apāyakosallaṃ). To show that too by means of the Pāḷi itself, “these phenomena,” etc., was said. Therein, it is said thus: whatever wisdom there is concerning the non-arising and cessation of these wholesome phenomena, or the arising and persistence of unwholesome phenomena, this is called skill in decline. Let skill in gain be wisdom for now; how has skill in decline come to be called wisdom? One might think thus: “Skill in decline would be the ability to cause decline.” But that is merely their opinion. Why? Because only a wise person understands thus: “For me, attending in this way, unarisen wholesome phenomena do not arise, and arisen ones cease. Unarisen unwholesome phenomena arise, and arisen ones increase.” That person, having known thus, does not cause unarisen unwholesome phenomena to arise and abandons arisen ones. They cause unarisen wholesome phenomena to arise and bring arisen ones to the fulfillment of development. Thus, skill in decline is also indeed wisdom.

Sabbatthāti sabbesu. Tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānanti sattānaṃ taṃtaṃhitasukhadhammānaṃ. Taṅkhaṇappavattanti accāyike kicce vā bhaye vā uppanne tassa tikicchanatthaṃ tasmiṃyeva khaṇe pavattaṃ. Ṭhānena uppatti etassa atthīti ṭhānuppattikaṃ, ṭhānaso eva uppajjanakaṃ. Tatrupāyāti tatra tatra karaṇīye upāyabhūtā.

Sabbattha means: in all. Tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ means: of the respective phenomena of welfare and happiness of beings. Taṅkhaṇappavattaṃ means: when an urgent matter or danger has arisen, it is that which occurs at that very moment for the purpose of remedying it. Ṭhānuppattikaṃ is so called because for this knowledge, there is arising by way of the occasion (ṭhānena); it is apt to arise from the occasion itself. Tatrupāya means: being a means for whatever should be done in each particular case.

Gahetvāti “idaṃ rūpaṃ, ettakaṃ rūpa”ntiādinā pariggaṇhanavasena gahetvā. Ubhayaṃ gahetvāti “ajjhattaṃ bahiddhā”ti ubhayaṃ anupubbato pariggahetvā. Atha vā “yaṃ kiñci samudayadhammaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhamma”nti ekappahāreneva sabbepi pañcakkhandhe avibhāgena pariggahetvā. Ayaṃ pana tikkhavipassakassa mahāpuññassa bhikkhuno vipassanābhiniveso.

Gahetvā means: having taken by way of comprehending thus: “this is form, this much is form,” and so on. Ubhayaṃ gahetvā means: having comprehended both—that is, internal and external—in sequence. Or alternatively: having comprehended all five aggregates without distinction by a single stroke thus: “whatever has the nature of arising, all that has the nature of ceasing.” This, however, is the application to insight-meditation of a bhikkhu with sharp insight and great wisdom.

428. Dukkhasaccaṃ ārabbhāti dukkhasaccaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā, tappaṭicchādakasammohavidhaṃsanavasena ca pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ dukkhe ñāṇaṃ. Dukkhasamudayaṃ ārabbhāti [M 2.0081] etthāpi eseva nayo. Tathā sesapadadvayepi. Paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ hi catusaccaṃ ārabbha pavattañāṇaṃ nāma, tatiyaṃ pana maggañāṇaṃ, itarasaccāni vipassanāñāṇanti pākaṭameva.

428. “Concerning the truth of suffering” (Dukkhasaccaṃ ārabbha) refers to the knowledge that arises by taking the truth of suffering as its object and by means of destroying the delusion that conceals it; this is “knowledge in suffering” (dukkhe ñāṇaṃ). In the phrase “Concerning the origin of suffering” (Dukkhasamudayaṃ ārabbha), this same method applies. Likewise for the remaining two phrases. Indeed, the knowledge that arises having taken the fourth truth as its object is called reviewing knowledge; however, that concerning the third truth is path-knowledge, and that concerning the other truths is insight-knowledge. This is indeed clear.

“Atthādīsu pabhedagatāni ñāṇānī”ti saṅkhepena vuttamatthaṃ pāḷivaseneva vivarituṃ “vuttañheta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha atthe ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidāti yaṃ atthappabhedassa sallakkhaṇavibhāvanavavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ atthe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ, ayaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā nāma. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Dhammappabhedassa hi sallakkhaṇavibhāvanavavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ dhamme pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā. Niruttippabhedassa sallakkhaṇavibhāvanavavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ niruttābhilāpe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidā. Paṭibhānappabhedassa sallakkhaṇavibhāvanavavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ paṭibhāne pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā. Niruttipaṭibhānappabhedā tabbisayānaṃ atthādīnaṃ paccayuppannatādibhedehi bhinditvā veditabbā.

To explain the meaning stated concisely as “knowledges that have gone to distinction in effect, etc.,” by means of the Pāḷi itself, the passage beginning with “For this was said” was stated. Therein, “knowledge in effect is the analytical knowledge of effect” refers to whatever knowledge has gone to distinction in effect and is capable of marking well, making clear, and defining the distinctions of effect; this is called the analytical knowledge of effect. In the remaining phrases, this same method applies. Indeed, the knowledge that has gone to distinction in cause and is capable of marking well, making clear, and defining the distinctions of cause is the analytical knowledge of cause. The knowledge that has gone to distinction in the utterance of language and is capable of marking well, making clear, and defining the distinctions of language is the analytical knowledge of language. The knowledge that has gone to distinction in perspicuity and is capable of marking well, making clear, and defining the distinctions of perspicuity is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity. The distinctions of language and perspicuity should be known by analyzing their objects—effect, etc.—according to distinctions such as being condition-arisen.

Nibbānampi [V 2.0077] sampāpakahetuanusārena arīyati, adhigammatīti attho. “Yaṃ kiñci paccayasambhūta”nti etena saccahetudhammapaccayākāravāresu āgatāni dukkhādīni gahitāni. Saccapaccayākāravāresu nibbānaṃ, pariyattivāre bhāsitattho, abhidhammabhājanīye vipāko, kiriyā cāti evaṃ pāḷiyaṃ vuttānaṃ eva vasena pañca atthā veditabbā. Dahatīti vidahati, nibbattakahetuādīnaṃ sādhāraṇametaṃ nibbacanaṃ. Tadatthaṃ pana vibhāvetuṃ “pavatteti vā sampāpuṇituṃ vā detī”ti vuttaṃ. Tesu purimo attho maggavajjesu daṭṭhabbo. Bhāsitampi hi avabodhanavasena atthaṃ pavatteti, maggo pana nibbānaṃ pāpetīti tasmiṃ pacchimo attho. Nibbānaṃ hi pattabbo attho, bhāsitattho ñāpetabbo attho, itaro nibbattetabbo atthoti evaṃ tividho hoti.

Nibbāna also is `attha` (effect, goal) because, by following the cause that leads to its attainment, it is realized (`arīyati`, `adhigammati`). By 'whatever is condition-born,' suffering and so on, which are mentioned in the sections on Truth, Cause, Dhamma, and Conditional Relations, are included. Thus, by way of only what is stated in the Pāḷi, five `atthas` (effects) are to be understood: Nibbāna in the sections on Truth and Conditional Relations; the meaning of what is spoken in the section on scripture; and resultant and functional consciousness in the Abhidhamma classification. 'Dahati' means 'vidahati' (arranges, performs); this explanation is common to productive cause and so on. But to clarify its meaning, it is said, 'it sets in motion or enables one to reach.' Among these, the first meaning should be understood in relation to dhammas other than the path. For what is spoken sets meaning in motion by way of making it known, whereas the path leads to Nibbāna; therefore, in regard to the path, the latter meaning should be understood. Indeed, Nibbāna is an effect to be attained, the meaning of what is spoken is an effect to be made known, and the other is an effect to be produced—thus, it is threefold.

“Yo koci phalanibbattako hetū”ti etena saccahetudhammapaccayākāravāresu āgatāni samudayādīni gahitāni, saccapaccayākāravāresu maggo, pariyattivāre bhāsitaṃ, abhidhammabhājanīye kusalākusalanti evaṃ pāḷiyaṃ vuttānaṃ eva vasena pañca dhammā veditabbā. Tattha [M 2.0082] maggo sampāpako, bhāsitaṃ ñāpako, itaraṃ nibbattakoti evaṃ tividho hetu veditabbo. Ettha ca kiriyānaṃ avipākatāya dhammabhāvo na vutto. Yadi evaṃ vipākā na hontīti atthabhāvopi na vattabbo? Na, paccayuppannabhāvato. Evaṃ sati kusalākusalānampi atthabhāvo āpajjatīti ce? Nāyaṃ doso appaṭisiddhattā. Vipākassa pana padhānahetutāya pākaṭabhāvato dhammabhāvo eva tesaṃ vutto. Kiriyānaṃ paccayabhāvato dhammabhāvo āpajjatīti ce? Nāyaṃ doso appaṭisiddhattā. Kammaphalasambandhassa pana hetubhāvassābhāvato dhammabhāvo na vutto. Apica “ayaṃ imassa paccayo, ayaṃ paccayuppanno”ti etaṃ bhedamakatvā kevalaṃ kusalākusale, vipākakiriyādhamme ca paccavekkhantassa dhammatthapaṭisambhidā hontīti tesaṃ atthadhammatā na vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

By the phrase 'any cause that produces a result,' the following are included: the origins (`samudaya`) and so forth, mentioned in the sections on Truth, Cause, Dhamma, and Conditional Relations; the path, in the sections on Truth and Conditional Relations; what is spoken, in the section on scripture (`pariyatti`); and the wholesome and unwholesome, in the Abhidhamma analysis. Thus, five `dhammas` (causes) are to be understood by way of only what is stated in the Pāḷi. Among these, the path is an accomplishing cause, what is spoken is an indicating cause, and the others are producing causes; thus, the cause is to be understood as threefold. And here, the nature as `dhamma` (cause) is not stated for functional consciousness (`kiriyā`) because they do not produce results. If so, should it not be said that the nature as `attha` (effect) is also not stated for resultants, on the grounds that 'they are not causes'? No, because they have the nature of being conditionally arisen. If this is so, does it follow that the nature as `attha` (effect) also applies to wholesome and unwholesome states? This is not a fault, as it is not denied. However, because the resultant is prominent on account of its principal cause, only the nature as `dhamma` (cause) of those [wholesome and unwholesome states] is stated. If it is said that the nature as `dhamma` (cause) applies to functional consciousness because they have the nature of a condition? This is not a fault, as it is not denied. But because of the absence of the nature of a cause in the context of the kamma-result relationship, their nature as `dhamma` (cause) is not stated. Furthermore, it should be understood that their nature as `attha` (effect) and `dhamma` (cause) is not stated because the analytical knowledges of effect and cause arise for one who reflects only on wholesome and unwholesome states, and resultant and functional states, without making the distinction, 'This is a condition for this; this is conditionally arisen.'

Ayameva hi atthoti yvāyaṃ atthadhammānaṃ pañcadhā vibhajanavasena attho vutto, ayameva abhidhamme vibhajitvā dassitoti sambandho.

The connection is this: that very meaning which was stated by way of the fivefold division of effect (`attha`) and cause (`dhamma`) is the very one that is shown analyzed in the Abhidhamma.

“Dhammaniruttābhilāpe”ti ettha dhamma-saddo sabhāvavācakoti katvā āha “sabhāvaniruttī”ti, aviparītaniruttīti attho. Tenāha “abyabhicārī vohāro”ti, tassa tassa atthassa bodhane paṭiniyatasambandho saddavohāroti attho. Tadabhilāpeti tassa sabhāvaniruttisaññitassa [V 2.0078] abyabhicārivohārassa abhilāpane. Sā panāyaṃ sabhāvanirutti māgadhabhāsā. Atthato nāmapaññattīti ācariyā. Apare pana yadi sabhāvanirutti paññattisabhāvā, evaṃ sati paññatti abhilapitabbā, na vacananti āpajjati. Na ca vacanato aññaṃ abhilapitabbaṃ uccāretabbaṃ atthi. Atha phassādivacanehi bodhetabbaṃ abhilapitabbaṃ, evañca sati atthadhammānampi bodhetabbattā tesampi niruttibhāvo āpajjati. Phassoti ca sabhāvanirutti, phassaṃ phassāti na sabhāvaniruttīti dassitovāyamattho. Na ca avacanaṃ evaṃpakāraṃ atthi. Tasmā vacanabhūtāya eva tassā sabhāvaniruttiyā abhilāpe uccāraṇeti attho daṭṭhabbo.

In the phrase 'dhammaniruttābhilāpe', the word 'dhamma' is taken as denoting intrinsic nature (sabhāva), hence it is said 'sabhāvanirutti' (expression of intrinsic nature), meaning a non-deviating expression. Therefore, it is said, 'abyabhicārī vohāro' (non-deviating usage), meaning that the word-usage is fixed in its relation to making known the meaning of each thing. 'Tadabhilāpe' (in the expression of that) means in the expression of that non-deviating usage which is designated as 'sabhāvanirutti'. Moreover, this expression of intrinsic nature is the Māgadha language. According to the teachers, it is a name-concept (nāmapaññatti) in terms of meaning. Others, however, say: if the expression of intrinsic nature were of the nature of a concept, this being so, it would follow that the concept is to be expressed, not the speech. And apart from speech, there is nothing else to be expressed or uttered.
