Alternatively, if that which is to be made known by words such as 'contact' is what is to be expressed, then this being so, since the meaning and the phenomena themselves must also be made known, they too would attain the state of being an expression ('nirutti'). And 'phasso' (contact) is the expression of intrinsic nature, but 'phassaṃ' or 'phassā' is not the expression of intrinsic nature—this meaning has indeed been shown. And non-speech does not have such a nature. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as: in the expression, that is, the utterance, of that very expression of intrinsic nature which is itself speech.

Taṃ sabhāvaniruttisaddaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā paccavekkhantassa tasmiṃ sabhāvaniruttābhilāpe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidā, “evamayaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidā saddārammaṇā [M 2.0083] nāma jātā, na paññattiārammaṇā”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 718) ca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttattā niruttisaddārammaṇāya sotaviññāṇavīthiyā parato manodvāre niruttipaṭisambhidā pavattatīti vadanti. “Niruttipaṭisambhidā paccuppannārammaṇā”ti (vibha. 749) ca vacanasaddaṃ gahetvā pacchā jānanaṃ sandhāya vuttanti. Evaṃ pana aññasmiṃ paccuppannārammaṇe aññaṃ paccuppannārammaṇaṃ vuttanti āpajjati. Yathā pana dibbasotañāṇaṃ manussādisaddabhedanicchayassa paccayabhūtaṃ taṃtaṃsaddavibhāvakaṃ, evaṃ sabhāvāsabhāvaniruttinicchayassa paccayabhūtaṃ paccuppannasabhāvaniruttisaddārammaṇaṃ taṃvibhāvakaṃ ñāṇaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidāti vuccamāne na koci pāḷivirodho. “Taṃ sabhāvaniruttisaddaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā paccavekkhantassā”ti ca “paccuppannasaddārammaṇaṃ paccavekkhaṇaṃ pavattentassā”ti na nasakkā vattuṃ. Tañhi ñāṇaṃ sabhāvaniruttiṃ vibhāventameva taṃtaṃsaddapaccavekkhaṇānantaraṃ taṃtaṃpabhedanicchayahetubhāvato niruttiṃ bhindantaṃ paṭivijjhantameva uppajjatīti pabhedagatampi hotīti.

For one who reviews, having taken as an object that sound of natural expression, the knowledge that has penetrated the distinctions in that utterance of natural expression is the analytical knowledge of language. Furthermore, since it is said in the commentary, “Thus, this analytical knowledge of language arises with sound as its object, not with designations as its object,” they say that the analytical knowledge of language arises at the mind-door after the ear-consciousness process that has the sound of language as its object. And they say that the statement, “The analytical knowledge of language has a present object,” is said with reference to knowing afterwards, having grasped the sound of the utterance. However, in this way, it follows that while there is one present object, another is said to have a present object. Just as the knowledge of the divine ear, being a condition for determining the distinctions in the sounds of humans and so on, makes those respective sounds clear, so too, if it is said that the analytical knowledge of language is the knowledge that has the present sound of natural expression as its object, which is a condition for determining natural and unnatural expressions, and which makes that natural expression clear, there is no contradiction with the Pāḷi. And regarding the phrase, “for one who reviews, having taken that sound of natural expression as an object,” it is not impossible to state its meaning as, “for one who engages in a review that has the present sound as its object.” For that knowledge arises precisely by revealing the natural expression, immediately after reviewing those respective sounds; because it is the cause for determining those respective distinctions, it arises by analyzing and penetrating the expression. Thus, it also becomes knowledge that has penetrated distinctions.

Sabbattha ñāṇanti sabbasmiṃ visaye ñāṇaṃ, sabbampi ñāṇanti adhippāyo. Tenāha “ñāṇārammaṇaṃ ñāṇa”nti. Sabbatthāti vā sabbesu atthādīsu, tīsu, catūsupi vā pavattattā, kusalakiriyābhūtāya paṭibhānapaṭisambhidāya dhammatthabhāvato tīsu eva vā pavattattā “sabbattha ñāṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “yathāvuttesu vā”tiādi. Tattha sagocarakiccādivasenāti sagocarassa, kiccādikassa ca vasena “idaṃ ñāṇaṃ idaṃ nāma ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattaṃ iminā nāma [V 2.0079] kiccenā”ti jānanaṃ. Ādi-saddena lakkhaṇapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānabhūmiādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Tenevāha “imāni ñāṇāni idamatthajotakānī”tiādi.

"Knowledge everywhere" (sabbattha ñāṇaṃ) means knowledge in every sphere; the intention is "all knowledge." Therefore, it is said, "knowledge whose object is knowledge." Or, "everywhere" (sabbattha) is said because it occurs in all, such as meaning (attha), etc., or in three, or in all four; or because the analytical knowledge of discernment (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā), which is a wholesome or functional state, occurs only in three due to its nature being Dhamma and meaning. Therefore, it is said, "or in the aforementioned," etc. Therein, "by means of its own object, function, etc." means the knowing, by means of its own object and its function, etc., thus: "This knowledge, having made such-and-such its object, has occurred with such-and-such a function." By the word "etc." (ādi), the inclusion of characteristic, manifestation, proximate cause, basis, etc., is to be understood. For that very reason, it is said, "These knowledges illuminate this meaning," etc.

429. Pabhedaṃ gacchantīti anekabhedabhinnesu ārammaṇesu tesaṃ yāthāvato taṃtaṃpabhedāvabodhanasamatthataṃ upagacchanti.

429. "They go into distinction" (pabhedaṃ gacchanti) means: in regard to objects differentiated by many distinctions, they attain the ability to understand their respective distinctions as they truly are.

Mahāsāvakānañca asekkhabhūmiyaṃ pabhedaṃ gatāti sāmaññavidhinā dassitamatthaṃ apavādena nivattetuṃ ānandatthera-ggahaṇaṃ kataṃ.

The mentioning of the Elder Ānanda was made in order to refute, by way of an exception, the meaning shown by the general method, which is: "And for the great disciples, they have reached distinction in the non-learner's stage."

Etā paṭisambhidā. Sekkhabhūmiyaṃ pabhedagamanaṃ appavisayaṃ, asekkhabhūmiyaṃ bahuvisayanti āha “adhigamo nāma arahattappattī”ti, sātisayaṃ vā adhigamaṃ sandhāya evaṃ vuttaṃ. Sekkhena pattānampi hi imāsaṃ arahattappattiyā visadabhāvādhigamoti[M 2.0084]. Pubbayogo viya pana arahattappatti arahatopi paṭisambhidāvisadatāya paccayo na na hotīti pañcannampi yathāyogaṃ sekkhāsekkhapaṭisambhidāvisadatāya kāraṇatā yojetabbā. Atthadhammādīnaṃ anavasesasaṅgaṇhanato buddhavacanavisayā eva pariyattiādayo dassitā. Pāḷiyā sajjhāyo pariyāpuṇanaṃ, tadatthasavanaṃ savanaṃ, parito sabbaso ñātuṃ icchā paripucchāti āha “pāḷiaṭṭhakathādīsu gaṇṭhipadaatthapadavinicchayakathā”ti, padatthato, adhippāyato ca duviññeyyaṭṭhānaṃ vitthārato sanniṭṭhānakathāti attho. Yassa hi padassa attho duviññeyyo, taṃ gaṇṭhipadaṃ, yassa adhippāyo duviññeyyo, taṃ atthapadaṃ. Ādi-saddena khandhādipaṭisaṃyutte kathāmagge saṅgaṇhāti. Bhāvanānuyogasahitaṃ gataṃ, paccāgatañca etassa atthīti gatapaccāgatiko, tassa bhāvo, tena gatapaccāgatikabhāvena. Vasanaṭṭhānato yāva gocaragāmo, tato ca yāva vasanaṭṭhānaṃ kammaṭṭhānānuyuttoti attho. Yāva anulomagotrabhusamīpanti saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇamāha. Tañhi tesaṃ samīpappavattaṃ.

These are the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). The penetration in the stage of a learner (sekkhabhūmi) is limited in scope, while in the stage of a non-learner (asekkhabhūmi) it is extensive in scope. Therefore, it is said, “Realization (adhigama) is the attainment of Arahantship.” Alternatively, this was said with reference to a superior realization. Indeed, even for learners who have attained these, the attainment of the state of clarity occurs through the attainment of Arahantship. However, just as prior practice (pubbayoga), the attainment of Arahantship is indeed a condition for the clarity of the analytical knowledges even of an Arahant. Therefore, the causality of all five causes for the clarity of the analytical knowledges of both learners and non-learners should be applied as appropriate. Because they encompass the entirety of meaning (attha), Dhamma, and so on, learning (pariyatti) and the rest are shown to have the word of the Buddha as their domain. Recitation of the Pāḷi is learning (pariyāpuṇana); listening to its meaning is hearing (savana); the wish to know completely and in every way is inquiry (paripucchā). Thus it is said, “the discourse in the Pāḷi, commentaries, and so on, that resolves knotty passages (gaṇṭhipada) and difficult words (atthapada).” The meaning is: it is the conclusive discourse that explains in detail the points that are difficult to understand both in terms of word-meaning (padattha) and in terms of intention (adhippāya). For a passage whose meaning is difficult to understand is a 'knotty passage' (gaṇṭhipada); one whose intention is difficult to understand is a 'difficult word' (atthapada). By the word 'etc.' (ādi-saddena), it includes the lines of discourse connected with the aggregates and so on. 'One who goes and returns' (gatapaccāgatika) is so called because for this person there is going forth and returning accompanied by the practice of meditation; its state is the state of one who goes and returns (gatapaccāgatikabhāva). The meaning is: being devoted to the meditation subject from the dwelling place up to the alms-round village, and from there back to the dwelling place. By the phrase “up to the proximity of conformity and change-of-lineage (anuloma-gotrabhū),” it refers to the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa). For this occurs in their proximity.

Satthesūti anavajjesu sattānaṃ hitasukhāvahesu ganthesu. Tathā sippāyatanesūti etthāpi. Pubbakāle ekasatarājūnaṃ desabhāsā ekasatavohārā. Dhammapade (dha. pa. 1 ādayo) yamakavaggo opammavaggoti vadanti, mūlapaṇṇāse (ma. ni. 1.325 ādayo; 439 ādayo) yamakavaggo opammavaggo evāti apare. Sutapaṭibhānabahulānanti bahussutānaṃ paṭibhānavantānaṃ.

"In sciences" (satthesu), meaning in blameless treatises that bring welfare and happiness to beings. Likewise in this term, "in the fields of crafts" (sippāyatanesu). In ancient times, the regional languages of the one hundred and one kings were the one hundred and one usages. In the Dhammapada, they say that the Yamaka Vagga is the Opamma Vagga; in the Mūlapaṇṇāsa, others say that the Yamaka Vagga is just the Opamma Vagga. "Of those abounding in learning and ready wit" (sutapaṭibhānabahulānaṃ) means of those who are learned (bahussuta) and possess ready wit (paṭibhānavanta).

Sabbānīti [V 2.0080] pubbe vuttāni pañca, pacchā vuttāni aṭṭhapi vā. Sekkhaphalavimokkhapariyosāne bhavā sekkhaphalavimokkhantikā. Ṭhānāṭhānañāṇabalādīni sabbabuddhaguṇesu sakiccato pākaṭatarānīti vuttaṃ “dasa balāni viyā”ti, aññe vā sabbaññutaññāṇādayopi sabbe bhagavato guṇavisesā asekkhaphalavimokkhantikā eva.

"All" (sabbāni) means the five mentioned previously, or also the eight mentioned later. Those that exist at the culmination of the liberation which is the learner's fruit are 'ending in the liberation which is the learner's fruit' (sekkhaphalavimokkhantikā). The powers such as the knowledge of what is possible and impossible are more distinctly evident by their own function among all the qualities of the Buddha; therefore, it is said, "like the ten powers." Or, other special qualities of the Blessed One apart from the ten powers, such as the knowledge of omniscience and so on, are indeed those that culminate in the liberation which is the non-learner's fruit (asekkhaphalavimokkhantikā).

Paññābhūmi-mūla-sarīravavatthānavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Analysis of the Wisdom-Ground, Root, and Body

430. Imāya paññāyāti vipassanāpaññāya. Bhūmi sallakkhaṇādiggahaṇavasena pavattiṭṭhānabhāvato. Ādi-saddena āhārādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Kasmā panete evaṃ bahudhammā bhūmibhāvena gayhanti, nanu khandhādīsu ekenāpi [M 2.0085] atthasiddhi hotīti? Na, tividhasattānuggahatthaṃ khandhādittayaggahaṇaṃ kattabbaṃ, aññathā sabbasādhāraṇo anuggaho na kato siyā. Tividhā hi sattā rūpasammūḷhā arūpasammūḷhā ubhayasammūḷhāti. Tesu ye arūpasammūḷhā, tadatthaṃ khandhānaṃ gahaṇaṃ arūpadhammānaṃ catudhā vibhattattā. Ye rūpasammūḷhā, tadatthaṃ āyatanānaṃ rūpadhammānaṃ addhekādasadhā vibhattattā. Ye pana ubhayasammūḷhā, tadatthaṃ dhātūnaṃ ubhayesampi vibhattattā. Tathā indriyabhedena tikkhindriyā majjhimindriyā mudindriyā, saṃkhittarucī majjhimarucī vitthārarucīti ca tividhā sattā, tesampi atthāya yathākkamaṃ khandhādiggahaṇaṃ katanti yojetabbaṃ. Indriyaggahaṇaṃ pana kāmaṃ ete dhammā issarā viya sahajātadhammesu issariyaṃ ādhipaccaṃ pavattenti, taṃ pana nesaṃ dhammasabhāvasiddhaṃ, na ettha kassaci vasībhāvo “suññā ete avasavattino”ti anattalakkhaṇassa sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ. Taṃ panetaṃ catubbidhampi pavattinivattitadubhayahetuvasena diṭṭhameva upakārāvahaṃ, na aññathāti saccādidvayaṃ gahitaṃ. Ādi-saddena gahitadhammesupi ayaṃ nayo netabbo. Mūlaṃ patiṭṭhābhāvato. Sati hi sīlavisuddhiyaṃ, cittavisuddhiyañca ayaṃ paññā mūlajātā hoti, nāsatīti. Sarīraṃ paribrūhetabbato. Imissā hi paññāya santānavasena pavattamānāya pādapāṇisīsaṭṭhāniyā diṭṭhivisuddhiādikā imā pañca visuddhiyo avayavena samudāyūpalakkhaṇanayena “sarīra”nti veditabbā.

430. "By this wisdom" means by insight-wisdom. "Ground" is so called because it is the state of being a place of occurrence through the discernment of its own characteristic, etc. By the word "etc.", the inclusion of nutriment and so forth should be understood. But why are these many phenomena taken as grounds? Is the purpose not achieved by just one of the aggregates, etc.? No. The grasping of the triad of aggregates, etc., should be done for the benefit of the three kinds of beings; otherwise, the assistance rendered would not be common to all. For beings are of three kinds: those deluded by form, those deluded by the formless, and those deluded by both. Among them, for those deluded by the formless, the aggregates are grasped, because therein formless phenomena are divided in four ways. For those deluded by form, the sense bases are grasped, because therein form phenomena are divided in eleven and a half ways. But for those deluded by both, the elements are grasped, because therein both are divided. Similarly, beings are of three kinds according to the distinction of faculties—those with sharp, medium, and dull faculties—and also according to their preference—those who prefer the concise, the medium, and the detailed. It should be understood that for their benefit too, the grasping of the aggregates, etc., is done respectively. Furthermore, the grasping of the faculties is for the sake of easily grasping the characteristic of not-self. Although it is true that these phenomena, like lords, exercise sovereignty and dominance over co-arisen phenomena, that is accomplished by their intrinsic nature; there is no mastery of anyone herein. Thus it is said: "These are empty, not subject to will." Furthermore, this fourfold group of phenomena is beneficial only when seen in terms of the cause of occurrence, cessation, and both; not otherwise. Therefore, the pair beginning with the Truths is grasped. This same method should be applied also to the phenomena grasped by the word 'etc.'. "Root" is so called because it is the state of being a foundation. For when purification of virtue and purification of mind exist, this wisdom becomes rooted; when they do not, it does not. "Body" is so called because it is to be developed. For, with regard to this wisdom that occurs as a continuum, these five purifications beginning with purification of view—which are in the position of feet, hands, and head—are to be understood as the 'body' by the method of indicating the whole through the part.

431. Pañca khandhāti ettha pañcāti gaṇanaparicchedo, tena na tato heṭṭhā, na uddhanti dasseti. Khandhāti paricchinnadhammanidassanaṃ. Yasmā cettha khandha-saddo rāsaṭṭho “mahāudakakkhandho”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.51; 6.37) viya, tasmā atītādivibhāgabhinnaṃ [V 2.0081] sabbaṃ rūpaṃ rāsivasena buddhiyā ekajjhaṃ gahetvā “rūpameva khandho rūpakkhandho”ti samānādhikaraṇasamāso daṭṭhabbo. “Tīhi khandhehi iṇaṃ dassāmā”tiādīsu viya koṭṭhāsaṭṭhe pana khandha-sadde nibbānassāpi khandhantarabhāvo āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati atītādivibhāgābhāvato. Na hi ekassa niccassa sato nibbānassa atītādivibhāgo atthīti. Paṭhamenatthena rūparāsīti attho, dutiyena rūpakoṭṭhāsoti. Vedanākkhandhotiādīsupi eseva nayo. Kasmā panete khandhā pañceva vuttā iminā eva ca kamenāti? Bhājanabhojanabyañjanabhattakārakabhuñjakavikappadassanato[M 2.0086], yathoḷārikayathāsaṃkilesūpadesato cāti veditabbaṃ. Vivādamūlahetubhāvaṃ saṃsārahetutaṃ, kammahetutañca cintetvā vedanāsaññā saṅkhārakkhandhato nīharitvā visuṃ khandhabhāvena desitā.

431. Herein, in 'the five aggregates,' the word 'five' is a numerical designation, indicating that there is nothing less or more than that. The word 'aggregate' is an indication of demarcated phenomena. In this context, the term 'aggregate' has the meaning of 'mass,' as seen in phrases like “the great mass of water.” Therefore, all form, divided into past, etc., should be understood as a unified mass grasped by wisdom, and thus expressed as “the aggregate of form is simply the form aggregate,” using a compound of apposition. However, in phrases like “We will repay the debt with three portions,” the term 'aggregate' is used in the sense of a portion. Does this imply that Nibbāna is also included as another aggregate? No, it does not, because of the absence of the division into past, etc. Indeed, for Nibbāna, which is one, permanent, and existent, there is no division into past, etc. In the first sense, the meaning is a mass of form; in the second sense, it is a portion of form. The same method applies to the 'aggregate of feeling' and so on. But why are these aggregates specifically stated as five, and in this particular order? It should be understood that this is due to the analogy of a vessel, food, curry, the cook, and the eater, and for the purpose of teaching in order of coarseness and defilement. Considering their state as the root cause of disputes, the cause of saṃsāra, and the cause of kamma, feeling and perception are extracted from the aggregate of formations and taught as distinct aggregates.

Rūpakkhandhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Discourse on the Aggregate of Form

432. Tatthāti tesu pañcasu khandhesu. Yaṃ kiñcīti anavasesapariyādānaṃ. Ruppanalakkhaṇanti atippasaṅganiyamanaṃ. Yaṃ-saddena hi sanipātena kiṃ-saddena ca gahitena aniyamatthatāya atippasaṅge āpanne taṃ ruppanasaddo nivatteti, tena rūpassa anavasesapariggaho kato hoti. Sītādīhīti sītuṇhajighacchāpipāsādīhi. Hetuatthe cetaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ. Ruppanaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etassāti ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ. Dhammo eva dhammajātaṃ. Ruppanañcettha sītādivirodhipaccayasannipāte visadisuppatti. Nanu ca arūpadhammānampi virodhipaccayasamāgame visadisuppatti labbhatīti? Saccaṃ labbhati, na pana vibhūtataraṃ. Vibhūtataraṃ hettha ruppanaṃ adhippetaṃ sītādiggahaṇato. Yadi evaṃ, kathaṃ brahmaloke rūpasamaññā? Tatthāpi taṃsabhāvānativattanato hotiyeva rūpasamaññā, anuggāhakapaccayavasena vā. Virodhipaccayasannipāte yo attano santāne bhinne bhijjamānasseva visadisuppattihetubhāvo, taṃ ruppananti aññe. Imasmiṃ pakkhe rūpayati vikāraṃ āpādetīti rūpaṃ, purimapakkhe pana ruppatīti. Saṅghaṭṭanena vikārāpattiyaṃ ruppanasaddo niruḷhoti keci. Imasmiṃ pakkhe arūpadhammesu rūpasamaññāya pasaṅgo eva natthi saṅghaṭṭanābhāvato. Paṭighāto ruppananti apare. Sabbaṃ taṃ ekato katvāti rāsaṭṭhaṃ hadaye ṭhapetvā vadati.

432. Herein: in these five aggregates. 'Whatever' is a term for complete inclusion. 'Having the characteristic of being afflicted' is a term for restricting over-extension. For, because the meaning taken by the word 'yaṃ' together with the word 'kiṃ' is indeterminate, when over-extension occurs, the word 'ruppana' turns it back. By this, the complete inclusion of form is accomplished. 'By cold, etc.' means by cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and so on. This instrumental expression is used in the sense of cause. 'Having the characteristic of being afflicted' means that which has affliction as its characteristic. And here, 'affliction' is the dissimilar arising that occurs on the conjunction of opposing conditions, such as cold. But is a dissimilar arising not also found in immaterial phenomena when they meet with opposing conditions? Truly, it is found, but it is not as manifest. For here, a more manifest affliction is intended, due to the inclusion of 'cold,' etc. If so, how is there the designation 'form' in the Brahma world? Even there, the designation 'form' certainly exists because that nature is not transcended, or by way of supporting conditions. Others say: on the conjunction of opposing conditions, that which is the cause of a dissimilar arising in one's own continuum as it is breaking, that is 'affliction.' In this view, it is 'form' because it causes alteration; but in the former view, it is 'form' because it is afflicted. Some say the word 'ruppana' is conventionally established as undergoing alteration due to impact. In this view, there is no occasion at all for the designation 'form' to apply to immaterial phenomena, due to the absence of impact. Others say that impingement is 'affliction.' 'Having gathered all this together'—he speaks keeping the sense of 'mass' in mind.

Bhūtopādāyabhedatoti [V 2.0082] ettha tadadhīnavuttitāya bhavati ettha upādāyarūpanti bhūtaṃ. Bhūtāni upādiyateva, na pana sayaṃ tehi, aññehi vā upādīyatīti upādāyaṃ.

Herein, regarding the distinction between primary elements and derived form: It is called a 'primary element' (bhūta) because derived form exists (bhavati) in dependence on it. It is called 'derived' (upādāya) because it (derived form) depends on the primary elements, but it itself is not depended upon by them or by others.

Kāmaṃ catudhātuvavatthāne vacanatthāditopi bhūtāni vibhāvitāneva, sabhāvadhammānaṃ pana lakkhaṇādivibhāvanāti katvā vuttaṃ “lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānāni catudhātuvavatthāne vuttānī”ti. Tattha padaṭṭhānassa avuttattā āha “padaṭṭhānato panā”tiādi. Avacanañca tassa tassatthassa paccayatoti ettha pakārantarena vibhāvitattāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sabbāpīti catassopi dhātuyo. Āposaṅgahitāya tejonupālitāya vāyovitthambhitāya [M 2.0087] eva pathavīdhātuyā pavatti, na aññathāti sā sesabhūtattayapadaṭṭhānā, evamitarāpīti āha “avasesadhātuttayapadaṭṭhānā”ti.

Indeed, in the analysis of the four elements, the primary elements have already been explained by way of terms, meanings, and so on. However, having considered that the explanation of phenomena with intrinsic nature is by way of characteristics, etc., it was said, 'Characteristics, functions, and manifestations are stated in the analysis of the four elements.' There, because the proximate cause was not stated, he said, 'But from the proximate cause...' and so on. And the non-mentioning of it should be understood as being because that meaning has been explained in another way in the phrase 'as a condition'. 'All' means all four elements. The occurrence of the earth element is only when it is held together by the water element, maintained by the fire element, and supported by the air element, and not otherwise. Therefore, it has the remaining three primary elements as its proximate cause. Likewise for the others, thus he said, 'they have the remaining three elements as their proximate causes.'

Catuvīsatividhanti gaṇanaparicchedo balarūpādīnaṃ paṭisedhanattho. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ parato āvi bhavissati. Cakkhatīti cakkhu, viññāṇādhiṭṭhitaṃ rūpaṃ assādentaṃ viya hotīti attho. Cakkhatīti hi ayaṃ cakkhati-saddo “madhuṃ cakkhati, byañjanaṃ cakkhatī”tiādīsu viya assādanattho. Vuttañhetaṃ “cakkhuṃ kho, māgaṇḍiya, rūpārāmaṃ rūparataṃ rūpasamudita”nti (ma. ni. 2.209). Aṭṭhakathāyampi vuccati “rūpesu āviñchanarasa”nti (visuddhi. 2.433; dha. sa. aṭṭha. 600). Satipi sotādīnaṃ saddārammaṇādibhāve niruḷhattā dassane eva cakkhu-saddo pavattati padumādīsu paṅkajādisaddā viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā cakkhatīti viññāṇādhiṭṭhitaṃ samavisamaṃ ācikkhantaṃ viya abhibyattaṃ vadantaṃ viya hotīti attho. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “vibhāveti cā”ti (mahāni. aṭṭha. 13; vibha. aṭṭha. 154) vuttaṃ. Taṃ anekatthattā dhātūnaṃ vibhāvanatthatāpi cakkhati-saddassa sambhavatīti katvā vuttaṃ. Suṇāti etena, viññāṇādhiṭṭhitaṃ sayaṃ vā suṇātīti sotaṃ. Ghāyati etena, sayaṃ vā ghāyatīti ghānaṃ. Rasaggahaṇamūlakattā ajjhoharaṇassa jīvitanimittaṃ āhāraraso jīvitaṃ, tasmiṃ ninnatāya taṃ avhāyatīti jivhā niruttinayena. Kucchitānaṃ sāsavadhammānaṃ āyo uppattiṭṭhānanti kāyo anuttariyahetubhāvaṃ anāgacchantesu kāmarāganidānakammajanitesu, kāmarāgassa ca visesapaccayesu ghānajivhākāyesu kāyassa visesato sāsavapaccayattā. Tena hi phoṭṭhabbasukhaṃ assādentā sattā methunampi sevanti. Kāyindriyavatthukā vā cattāro khandhā balavakāmāsavādihetubhāvato visesena sāsavāti kucchitānaṃ sāsavadhammānaṃ āyoti kāyo vutto. Vaṇṇavikāraṃ āpajjamānaṃ hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ rūpayatīti rūpaṃ, rūpamiva pakāsaṃ karoti saviggahamiva [V 2.0083] dassetīti attho. Anekatthattā vā dhātūnaṃ pakāsanattho eva rūpasaddo daṭṭhabbo. Sappatīti saddo, udāharīyati, sakehi vā paccayehi sappīyati sotaviññeyyabhāvaṃ upanīyatīti attho. Gandhayatīti gandho, attano vatthuṃ sūcayati apākaṭaṃ “idaṃ sugandhaṃ, duggandha”nti pakāseti[M 2.0088], paṭicchannaṃ vā pupphaphalādiṃ “idamettha atthī”ti pesuññaṃ karontaṃ viya hotīti attho. Rasanti taṃ sattāti raso, asādentīti attho.

The twenty-fourfold classification is for the purpose of rejecting strength-form and so on. What needs to be said about this will become clear later. The eye (`cakkhu`) is so called because it savors (`cakkhati`); the meaning is that, being the basis for consciousness, it is as if it savors form. For this word `cakkhati` has the meaning of savoring, as in such phrases as 'he savors honey' or 'he savors curry.' And this was said: 'The eye, Māgaṇḍiya, truly has form as its delight, is fond of form, is overjoyed by form.' In the commentary, too, it is said: 'Its function is to draw in forms.' It should be understood that although the ear and other senses have sound and so on as their objects, due to convention, the word 'eye' is applied only to seeing, just as words like 'mud-born' (`paṅkaja`) are applied to lotuses and so on. Alternatively, `cakkhati` means that, being the basis for consciousness, it is as if it indicates the even and uneven, as if it speaks manifestly. In the commentary, however, it is said, 'And it makes clear.' That was said having considered that, due to the multiple meanings of roots, the meaning of making clear is also possible for the word `cakkhati`. The ear (`sota`) is so called because one hears by means of it, or because, being the basis for consciousness, it hears by itself. The nose (`ghāna`) is so called because one smells by means of it, or because, being the basis for consciousness, it smells by itself. The tongue (`jivhā`) is so called, by way of etymology, because the grasping of taste is the root of consumption, and the taste of food, which is the cause of life, is 'life'; because of its inclination towards that, it 'calls' (`avhāyati`) to it. The body (`kāya`) is so called because it is the source (`āyo`), the place of origin, of contemptible, tainted states. This is because among the nose, tongue, and body—which do not lead to the state of being a cause for the supreme, are generated by kamma originating from sensual desire, and are specific conditions for sensual desire—the body is especially a condition for the taints. For by means of it, beings, savoring the pleasure of the tangible, also engage in sexual intercourse. Alternatively, the four aggregates that have the body-faculty as their physical basis are especially tainted because they are a cause for the strong taints of sensual desire, etc.; therefore, the body is called the 'source' of contemptible, tainted states. Form (`rūpa`) is so called because, undergoing a change of appearance, it reveals (`rūpayati`) the state that has gone to the heart; the meaning is that it makes it manifest as if it were a body, showing it as if it had substance. Alternatively, due to the multiple meanings of roots, the word `rūpa` should be understood as having only the meaning of manifesting. Sound (`sadda`) is so called because it is sounded (`sappati`), that is, it is uttered; or, by its own conditions, it is made to sound (`sappīyati`), meaning it is brought to the state of being cognizable by the ear—this is the meaning. Odor (`gandha`) is so called because it indicates (`gandhayati`); it indicates its own basis, it makes manifest the unapparent, [saying,] 'This is fragrant,' 'This is foul.' Or, it is as if it were informing about a concealed flower, fruit, etc., [saying,] 'This is here'—this is the meaning. Taste (`rasa`) is so called because beings savor (`rasanti`) it; the meaning is that they savor it.

Itthiyāva indriyaṃ itthindriyaṃ, tathā purisindriyaṃ. Jīvanti tena sahajātadhammāti jīvitaṃ, tadeva indriyaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ. Hadayañca taṃ vatthu ca, hadayassa vā manoviññāṇassa vatthu hadayavatthu. Copanakāyabhāvato kāyo ca so adhippāyaviññāpanato viññatti cāti kāyaviññatti. Copanavācābhāvato, adhippāyaviññāpanato ca vacī ca sā viññatti cāti vacīviññatti. Viggahābhāvato na kassati, kasituṃ chindituṃ na sakkā, na vā kāsati dibbatīti akāsaṃ, akāsameva ākāsaṃ, tadeva nissattanijjīvaṭṭhena ākāsadhātu. Rūpassāti nipphannarūpassa. Lahubhāvo lahutā. Sayaṃ anipphannatāya “rūpassā”ti visesitaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Ayaṃ pana viseso – kammani sādhu kammaññaṃ, tassa bhāvo kammaññatā. Paṭhamaṃ, upari ca cayo pavatti upacayo. Pubbāparavasena sambandhā tati pavatti santati. Aniccassa vināsino bhāvo aniccatā. Kabalaṃ karīyatīti kabaḷīkāro. Āharatīti āhāro. Evaṃ tāva upādāyarūpaṃ saddatthato veditabbaṃ.

The faculty of a woman only is the femininity-faculty; likewise, the masculinity-faculty. Life (jīvita) is so called because co-nascent states live by means of it; that very life is the life-faculty (jīvitindriya). The heart-base (hadayavatthu) is the heart and that base, or the base of the heart or of mind-consciousness. Bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti) is so called because it is the body by way of causing movement and it is intimation by way of conveying intention. Verbal intimation (vacīviññatti) is so called because it is speech by way of causing utterance and it is intimation by way of conveying intention. Space (ākāsa) is so called because, due to the absence of substance, it is not plowed (na kassati); it cannot be plowed or cut. Or, it does not shine (na kāsati) or is not apparent (dibbati), hence 'akāsa'; this 'akāsa' itself is 'ākāsa', and that very thing is the space-element (ākāsadhātu) by reason of being non-sentient and non-living. 'Of form' (rūpassa) refers to produced form. Lightness (lahutā) is the state of being light. It is specified as 'of form' because it is unproduced by itself. This method applies to the rest as well. Here, however, is the distinction: what is suitable for action is workability (kammaññaṃ); its state is workability (kammaññatā). First and later, accumulation or occurrence is growth (upacayo). Connection in terms of before and after, and thus continuous occurrence, is continuity (santati). The state of what is impermanent and perishable is impermanence (aniccatā). What is made into a mouthful is a morsel (kabaḷīkāro). That which brings is food (āhāro). Thus far, derived form should be understood according to its literal meaning.

Kamato pana sabbesaṃ rūpadhammānaṃ nissayabhāvena mūlabhūtattā paṭhamaṃ bhūtarūpāni uddiṭṭhāni. Itaresu ajjhattikabhāvena attabhāvasamaññāya mūlabhāvato cakkhādīni pañca ādito uddiṭṭhāni. Tesaṃ visayīnaṃ ime visayāti dassetuṃ rūpādīni cattāri uddiṭṭhāni. Phoṭṭhabbaṃ pana anupādārūpattā, bhūtaggahaṇena gahitattā ca idha na gahitaṃ. Svāyaṃ attabhāvo imehi “itthī”ti vā “puriso”ti vā saṅkhaṃ gacchatīti dassanatthaṃ tadanantaraṃ itthipurisindriyadvayaṃ uddiṭṭhaṃ. “Iminā jīvatī”ti vohāraṃ labbhatīti dassanatthaṃ tato jīvitindriyaṃ. Tassa imaṃ nissāya viññāṇappavattiyaṃ attahitādisiddhīti dassanatthaṃ hadayavatthu. Tassa imāsaṃ vasena sabbe kāyavacīpayogāti dassanatthaṃ viññattidvayaṃ. Imāya rūpakāyassa paricchedo, añjaso cāti dassanatthaṃ ākāsadhātu. Imehissa sukhappavatti, uppattiādayo [V 2.0084] cāti dassanatthaṃ lahutādayo. Sabbo cāyaṃ catusantatirūpasantāno iminā upatthambhīyatīti dassanatthaṃ ante kabaḷīkāro āhāro uddiṭṭhoti veditabbo.

Moreover, in order, the primary material elements were mentioned first because they are the foundation for all material phenomena by being their support. Among the others, the five sensitive material phenomena beginning with the eye were mentioned at the beginning because they are internal and are the foundation for the designation 'personal existence'. To show that these are the objects of those sense-faculties, the four objects beginning with visible form were mentioned. The tangible object, however, is not included here because it is not a derived material phenomenon and is already included with the inclusion of the primary material elements. To show that this personal existence is reckoned as 'woman' or 'man' by means of these faculties, the pair of sex faculties was mentioned immediately after. To show that the conventional expression 'one lives by this' is obtained, the life faculty was then mentioned. To show that for that personal existence, when consciousness arises depending on this, one's own welfare and so forth are accomplished, the heart-base was mentioned. To show that for that personal existence, all bodily and verbal exertions occur by means of these, the two intimations were mentioned. To show that by this element there is the delimitation of the material body and also a passage, the space element was mentioned. To show that by means of these, there is for this personal existence ease of occurrence, origination, and so on, lightness and the others were mentioned. And to show that this entire continuity of matter of fourfold origin is sustained by this, edible food was mentioned at the end; thus it should be understood.

433. Idāni [M 2.0089] yathāuddiṭṭhāni upādārūpāni lakkhaṇādito niddisituṃ “tattha rūpābhighātārahabhūtappasādalakkhaṇa”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu upādārūpesu. Rūpe, rūpassa vā abhighāto rūpābhighāto, taṃ arahatīti rūpābhighātāraho, rūpābhighāto hotu vā mā vā evaṃsabhāvo catunnaṃ bhūtānaṃ pasādo rūpābhighātārahabhūtappasādo, evaṃlakkhaṇaṃ cakkhūti attho. Yasmā paccayantarasahito eva cakkhupasādo rūpābhihananavasena pavattati, na kevalo. Tasmā taṃsabhāvatāva pamāṇaṃ, na rūpābhighātoti dassanatthaṃ rūpābhighātārahatā vuttā yathā vipākārahaṃ kusalākusalanti. Abhighāto ca visayavisayīnaṃ aññamaññaṃ abhimukhībhāvo yogyadesāvaṭṭhānaṃ abhighāto viyāti katvā. So rūpe cakkhussa, rūpassa vā cakkhumhi hoti. Tenāha “yaṃ cakkhu anidassanaṃ sappaṭighaṃ rūpamhi sanidassanamhi sappaṭighamhi paṭihaññi vā”ti, “yamhi cakkhumhi anidassanamhi sappaṭighamhi rūpaṃ sanidassanaṃ sappaṭighaṃ paṭihaññi vā paṭihaññati vā”ti (dha. sa. 597) ca ādi. Paripuṇṇāparipuṇṇāyatanattabhāvanibbattakassa kammassa nidānabhūtā kāmataṇhā, rūpataṇhā ca tadāyatanikabhavapatthanābhāvato daṭṭhukāmatādivohāraṃ arahatīti dutiyanayo sabbattha vutto. Tattha daṭṭhukāmatānidānakammaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ etesanti daṭṭhukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānāni. Evaṃvidhānaṃ bhūtānaṃ pasādo daṭṭhukāmatā…pe… pasādo, evaṃlakkhaṇaṃ cakkhu. Tassa tassa hi bhavassa mūlakāraṇabhūtā taṇhā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ bhave uppajjanārahāyatanavisayāpi nāma hotīti kāmataṇhādīnaṃ daṭṭhukāmatādivohārārahatā vuttā.

433. Now, to explain the derived material phenomena, which were previously indicated, in detail beginning with their characteristics, the text beginning, 'Therein, [the eye] has the characteristic of being the sensitivity of the primary elements capable of being struck by visible form,' and so on, is commenced. Therein, 'therein' refers to among those derived material phenomena. Striking upon visible form, or the striking of visible form, is 'rūpābhighāta'; because it is worthy of that, it is 'rūpābhighātāraha'. The sensitivity of the four primary elements, which has the nature of being capable of being struck by visible form—whether the striking by visible form occurs or does not occur—is 'rūpābhighātārahabhūtappasāda'. The meaning is that the eye has such a characteristic. Because the eye-sensitivity functions by way of being struck by visible form only when accompanied by other conditions, not independently. Therefore, to show that its very nature is the measure, not the striking by visible form, the 'capability of being struck by visible form' is stated, just as wholesome and unwholesome deeds are 'capable of [producing] a result'. And 'striking' (abhighāta), it is held, is like the mutual facing of the object and the faculty, their being situated in a suitable place. That striking is of the eye upon the visible form, or of the visible form upon the eye. Therefore, it is said: 'That eye, which is unmanifest and with impact, was struck by visible form, which is manifest and with impact,' and, 'In that eye, which is unmanifest and with impact, visible form, which is manifest and with impact, was struck or is struck' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 597), and so on. The sensual craving and craving for form, being the cause of kamma that produces an existence with complete or incomplete sense bases, are worthy of the designation 'desire to see' and so on, because of being an aspiration for an existence related to those sense bases; this second method is stated everywhere. Therein, 'daṭṭhukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānāni' means 'those whose origin is kamma caused by the desire to see'. The sensitivity of the primary elements of such a kind is the 'sensitivity... [originating from kamma caused by] the desire to see'. The eye has such a characteristic. For indeed, craving, which is the root cause of this or that existence, is also one that has as its object the sense bases fit to arise in that particular existence; thus, the worthiness of sensual craving and so on for the designation 'desire to see' and so forth is stated.

Daṭṭhukāmatāti hi daṭṭhumicchā, rūpataṇhāti attho. Ettha ca daṭṭhukāmatāya, sesānañca taṃtaṃattabhāvanibbattakakammāyūhanakkhaṇato sati purimanibbattiyaṃ vattabbaṃ natthi, asati pana maggena asamugghātitabhāvoyeva kāraṇanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yato maggena asamucchinnaṃ kāraṇalābhe sati uppajjitvā attano phalassa paccayabhāvūpagamanato vijjamānamevāti uppannatā atthitā pariyāyehi vuccati “ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bhāvento ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bahulīkaronto uppannuppanne [M 2.0090] pāpake akusale dhamme antarāyeva antaradhāpetī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.156), “santaṃ [V 2.0085] vā ajjhattaṃ kāmacchandaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ kāmacchando’ti pajānātī”ti (dī. ni. 2.382; ma. ni. 1.115) ca evamādīsu.

Indeed, 'desire to see' (daṭṭhukāmatā) means the wish to see; that is, craving for forms (rūpataṇhā). And here, regarding the desire to see and the rest, if there is a previous manifestation at the moment of striving for the kamma that produces those respective states of existence, there is nothing to be said. But when it is not present, it should be understood that the cause is simply its not yet being completely eradicated by the path. Because what is not cut off by the path, upon obtaining a condition, arises and becomes a condition for its own result, it is, as existing, spoken of by the modes of 'arisen' and 'present' in such passages as: 'One who develops the noble eightfold path, one who repeatedly cultivates the noble eightfold path, causes arisen evil unwholesome states to disappear right in between' (SN 5.156); and 'When there is sensual desire present within, one understands, "There is sensual desire within me"' (DN 2.382; MN 1.115), and so forth.

Rūpesu puggalassa, viññāṇassa vā āviñchanarasaṃ. Ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ nissayapaccayabhāvato. Daṭṭhukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ yesaṃ bhūtānaṃ pasādo, tevassa āsannakāraṇanti katvā. Ettha ca taṃtaṃattabhāvanipphādakasādhāraṇakammavasena purimaṃ cakkhulakkhaṇaṃ vuttaṃ kāraṇavisesassa anāmaṭṭhattā. “Evarūpaṃ nāma me cakkhu hotū”ti evaṃ nibbattitaāveṇikakammavasena dutiyanti vadanti. Satipi pana pañcannaṃ pasādabhāvasāmaññe savisayāvabhāsanasaṅkhātassa pasādabyāpārassa vasena purimaṃ vuttaṃ. Pasādakāraṇassa satipi kammabhāvasāmaññe, ekatte vā attano kāraṇabhedena bhedadassanavasena dutiyanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sotādīnaṃ lakkhaṇādīsu vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo.

Its function is to attract a person or consciousness towards forms. Its manifestation is the state of being a support, due to its nature as a dependence-condition. Its proximate cause is the elements produced by kamma that is rooted in the desire to see; this is because those very elements, of which it is the clarity, are its immediate cause. And here, the first characteristic of the eye is stated by way of the common kamma that produces those respective states of existence, because a specific cause is not considered. They say the second is by way of the specific kamma produced thus: 'May an eye of such a nature be for me.' However, although there is a commonality in the state of clarity among the five faculties, the first is stated by way of the function of clarity, which is called the illumination of its own object. And although there is a commonality, or even oneness, in kamma as the cause of clarity, the second characteristic should be understood as being shown as distinct through the difference in its own cause. The meaning for the characteristics, etc., of the ear and so on should be understood by the method already stated.

Etthāha – cakkhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ kiṃ ekakammunā uppatti, udāhu nānākammunāti? Ubhayathāpīti porāṇā. Tattha nānākammunā tāva uppattiyaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ visese vattabbaṃ natthi kāraṇassa bhinnattā. Ekakammunā pana uppattiyaṃ kathaṃ nesaṃ visesoti? Kāraṇassa bhinnattā eva. Taṃtaṃbhavapatthanābhūtā hi taṇhā taṃtaṃbhavapariyāpannāyatanābhilāsatāya sayaṃ vicittarūpā upanissayabhāvena taṃtaṃbhavanibbattakakammassa vicittabhedataṃ vidahati. Yato tadāhitavisesaṃ taṃ tathārūpasamatthatāyogenānekarūpāpannaṃ viya anekaṃ visiṭṭhasabhāvaṃ phalaṃ nibbatteti. Na cettha samatthatā samatthabhāvato aññā veditabbā kāraṇavisesena āhitavisesassa visiṭṭhaphalanipphādanayogyatāmattato. Ayañca ekassapi kammassa anekindriyahetutāvisesayogo yuttito, āgamanato ca parato āgamissati. Apica ekasseva kusalacittassa soḷasādivipākacittanibbattihetutā vuccati. Lokepi ekasseva sālibījassa paripuṇṇāparipuṇṇataṇḍulaātaṇḍulaphalanibbattihetutā dissateva, kiṃ vā etāya yutticintāya. Yato kammaphalaṃ cakkhādīni, kammavipāko ca sabbaso buddhānaṃyeva ñāṇassa visayoti.

Herein, it is asked: 'Is the arising of the faculties, such as the eye, by a single kamma, or by various kammas?' The ancients say it can be in both ways. In that regard, when there is an arising from various kammas, there is nothing to be said about the distinction among the faculties, such as the eye, because the causes are different. But when there is an arising from a single kamma, how is there a distinction among them? It is precisely because of the difference of the cause. For craving, which is the aspiration for this or that existence, is itself of a variegated nature due to its desire for the sense-bases pertaining to this or that existence. By serving as a supporting condition, it brings about a variegated distinction in the kamma that produces this or that existence. Therefore, that kamma, having a distinction imparted to it, produces a manifold result with distinct natures through its connection with such a capacity, as if it had attained a manifold nature. And here, capacity should not be understood as something other than the state of being capable, for it is merely the suitability of that which has a distinction imparted by a specific cause to produce a distinct result. And this fact, that even a single kamma is connected with the distinction of being the cause for many faculties, will be shown later both by way of reason and by way of scripture. Furthermore, it is said that a single wholesome consciousness is the cause for the arising of sixteen or more resultant consciousnesses. In the world, too, it is indeed seen that a single rice seed is the cause for producing the results of whole and broken grains, as well as that which is not grain. But what is the use of this line of reasoning? Because the faculties, such as the eye, are the fruit of kamma, and the result of kamma, in all respects, is the domain of the knowledge of the Buddhas alone.

434. Kecīti [M 2.0091] mahāsaṅghikesu ekacce. Tesu hi vasudhammo evaṃ vadati “cakkhumhi tejo adhikaṃ, sote vāyu, ghāne pathavī, jivhāya āpo, kāye sabbepi samā”ti. Cakkhādīsu tejādiadhikatā nāma tannissayabhūtānaṃ tadadhikatāyāti dassento “tejādhikānaṃ bhūtānaṃ [V 2.0086] pasādo cakkhū”tiādimāha. Kāyo sabbesanti ko ettha viseso, nanu tejādiadhikānañca bhūtānaṃ pasādā sabbesaṃyevāti? Saccametaṃ, idaṃ pana “sabbesa”nti vacanaṃ samānānanti imamatthaṃ dīpeti anuvattamānassa ekadesādhikabhāvassa nivāraṇavasena vuttattā. Tejādīnaṃ hi paccekaṃ adhikabhāve viya dvinnaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ vā adhikabhāvepi yathāvuttādhikabhāveneva ekakādivasena labbhamānāya omattatāyapi kāyappasādo na hotīti pākaṭoyamattho. Tasmā catunnampi bhūtānaṃ samabhāvena kāyappasādo hotīti sabbasaddo idha samabhāvadīpako daṭṭhabbo. Tejādīnanti padīpasaṅkhātassa tejassa obhāsarūpena, vāyussa saddena, pathaviyā gandhena, kheḷasaṅkhātassa udakassa rasenāti purimavāde, pacchimavāde ca yathāyogaṃ taṃtaṃbhūtaguṇehi anuggayhabhāvato, rūpādīnaṃ gahaṇe upakāritabbatoti attho. Ālokādisahakārīkāraṇasahitānaṃyeva cakkhādīnaṃ rūpādiavabhāsanasamatthatā, vivarassa ca sotaviññāṇūpanissayabhāvo guṇoti tesaṃ laddhi. Tejādīnaṃ viya pana vivarassa bhūtabhāvābhāvato yathāyoga-ggahaṇaṃ. Atha vā rūpādayo viya vivarampi bhūtaguṇoti parādhippāye tejassa ālokarūpena, ākāsasaṅkhātassa vivarassa saddena, vāyussa gandhena, udakassa rasena, pathaviyā phoṭṭhabbenāti evaṃ yathāyogaṃ taṃtaṃbhūtaguṇehīti yojanā.

434. Some, that is, certain ones among the Mahāsaṅghikas. Among them, Vasudhamma states thus: 'In the eye, fire is predominant; in the ear, wind; in the nose, earth; in the tongue, water; and in the body, all are equal.' To explain that the predominance of fire etc. in the eye and so forth means the predominance of those elements that are their support, he says, 'The clarity of elements where fire is predominant is the eye,' and so on. But what is the distinction in saying 'all are equal' in the body? Is it not true that the clarities, even of elements where fire etc. are predominant, are clarities of all the elements indeed? Indeed, it is so. However, the phrase 'all' here indicates the meaning 'equal,' because it is stated with a view to preventing the partial predominance that would otherwise follow. For, just as in the case of the individual predominance of fire and so on, so too in the case of the predominance of two or three, the body's clarity does not arise even with the deficiency that is consequently found in the remaining element or elements. This meaning is clear. Therefore, the word 'all' here should be understood as indicating equality, meaning that the body's clarity arises from the equal proportion of all four elements. As for 'fire and others', the meaning is this: in both the former and latter theses, because they are supported by their respective elemental qualities as is appropriate—by the light-form of fire (called a lamp), by the sound of wind, by the smell of earth, by the taste of water (called saliva)—and because they are helpful in the apprehension of forms and so forth. Their doctrine is that the eye and other senses have the capacity to illuminate forms and so on only when accompanied by cooperative causes such as light, and that the auditory aperture's being a supporting condition for ear-consciousness is a quality. However, unlike fire etc., since the aperture is not a primary element, the phrase 'as is appropriate' is used. Alternatively, according to the view of others, just as forms and so on are qualities of the elements, the aperture is also a quality of the elements. Thus, the connection is: by the light-form of fire, by the sound of the aperture called space, by the smell of wind, by the taste of water, and by the tangible of earth; this is the meaning of 'by their respective elemental qualities, as is appropriate'.

Rūpādīnaṃ adhikabhāvadassanatoti aggimhi rūpassa pabhassarassa, vāyumhi saddassa sabhāvena suyyamānassa, pathaviyā surabhiādino gandhassa, āpe ca rasassa madhurassāti imesaṃ visesayuttānaṃ dassanato “rūpādayo tesaṃ guṇā”ti paṭhamavādī āhāti. Tasseva “iccheyyāmā”tiādinā uttaramāha. Imināva upāyena dutiyavādinopi niggaho hotīti. Atha vā rūpādivisesaguṇehi tejaākāsapathavīāpavāyūhi cakkhādīni katānīti vadantassa kaṇādassa vādaṃ uddharitvā [M 2.0092] taṃ niggahetuṃ “athāpi vadeyyu”ntiādi vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Āsave upalabbhamānopi gandho pathaviyā āposaṃyuttāya kappāsato visadisāyāti na kappāsagandhassa adhikabhāvāpattīti ce? Na, anabhibhūtattā. Āsave hi udakasaṃyuttā pathavī udakena abhibhūtā, na kappāsapathavīti tassa eva gandhena adhikena bhavitabbaṃ. Uṇhodakasaṃyutto ca aggi upalabbhanīyo mahantoti katvā tassa phasso viya vaṇṇopi pabhassaro upalabbheyyāti uṇhodake vaṇṇato agginā anabhisambandhassa sītodakassa vaṇṇo parihāyetha. Tasmāti etassa ubhayassa abhāvā. Tadabhāvena hi rūpādīnaṃ tejādivisesaguṇatā nivattitā. Tannivattanena “tejādīnaṃ guṇehi rūpādīhi anuggayhabhāvato”ti idaṃ kāraṇaṃ nivattitanti evaṃ [V 2.0087] paramparāya ubhayābhāvo visesaparikappanapahānassa kāraṇaṃ hotīti āha “tasmā pahāyeta”ntiādi. Ekakalāpepi rūparasādayo visadisā, ko pana vādo nānākalāpe cakkhādayo bhūtavisesābhāvepīti dassetuṃ rūparasādinidassanaṃ vuttaṃ.

Because of seeing the state of predominance of form and so on—that is, seeing in fire the radiant form, in wind the sound heard by its own nature, in earth the fragrance such as a pleasant scent, and in water the sweet taste—thus seeing these things endowed with distinctiveness, the first proponent says, 'Form and so on are their qualities.' With 'iccheyyāma,' etc., he states the reply to that very proponent. By this very method, the refutation of the second proponent also occurs. Alternatively, it should be understood that having brought forth the doctrine of the teacher Kaṇāda—who says that the eye and so on are made by the fire, space, earth, water, and wind elements, which possess the distinctive qualities of form and so on—the passage 'athāpi vadeyyuṃ,' etc., was stated in order to refute that doctrine. If it is said: Although a scent is found in liquor, it is of the earth element conjoined with water, which is dissimilar to that from cotton; therefore, the scent of cotton does not attain a state of predominance. No, because of not being overpowered. For in liquor, the earth element conjoined with water is overpowered by water, but the earth element in cotton is not. Therefore, the scent of that very cotton should be predominant. And since the fire element conjoined with hot water is perceived as great, its color, like its touch, should also be perceived as radiant. If that were so, then compared to the color of hot water, the color of cold water, which is not connected with fire, would be diminished. Therefore, due to the absence of both of these, the state of form and so on being the distinctive qualities of fire and so on is refuted. By that refutation, this reason—'because of the state of not being supported by form and so on, which are the qualities of fire and so on'—is refuted. Thus, in sequence, the absence of both becomes the reason for abandoning the assumption of distinctions. Therefore, he says, 'tasmā pahāyeta,' etc. The illustration of form, taste, and so on was stated in order to show this: Even in a single kalāpa, form, taste, and so on are dissimilar; what then needs to be said of the eye and so on in different kalāpas, which are dissimilar even when there is no distinction in the primary elements?

Yadi bhūtaviseso natthi, kiṃ pana cakkhādivisesassa kāraṇanti taṃ dassetuṃ “yaṃ aññamaññassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ekampi kammaṃ pañcāyatanikattabhāvabhavappatthanānipphannaṃ cakkhādivisesahetutāya aññamaññassa asādhāraṇanti ca kammavisesoti ca vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi taṃ yena visesena cakkhussa paccayo, teneva sotassa paccayo hoti indriyantarābhāvappattito. “Paṭisandhikkhaṇe mahaggatā cetanā kaṭattārūpānaṃ kammapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.12.78) vacanena paṭisandhikkhaṇe vijjamānānaṃ sabbesaṃ kaṭattārūpānaṃ ekā cetanā kammapaccayo hotīti viññāyati. Nānācetanāya hi tadā indriyuppattiyaṃ sati parittena ca mahaggatena ca kammunā nibbattitaṃ kaṭattārūpaṃ āpajjeyyāti. Na cekā paṭisandhi anekakammanibbattā hotīti siddhamekena kammena anekindriyuppatti hotīti.

If there is no distinction of the primary elements, what then is the cause of the distinction of the eye and so forth? To explain this, the phrase “which is for one another” and so on was stated. It should be understood that even a single kamma, produced by the craving for an existence possessing five sense-bases, is, on account of being the cause for the distinction of the eye and so forth, said to be 'uncommon to one another' and 'a specific kamma'. For by the same distinction by which it is a condition for the eye, it is not a condition for the ear, because it would attain the state of not being another faculty. By the statement, “At the moment of rebirth-linking, the exalted volition is a condition for kamma-produced materiality by way of kamma-condition,” it is understood that at the moment of rebirth-linking, a single volition is the kamma-condition for all present kamma-produced materiality. For if at that time the arising of the faculties were due to various volitions, it would follow that kamma-produced materiality is produced by both sense-sphere kamma and exalted kamma. And since a single rebirth-linking is not produced by multiple kammas, it is established that a single kamma gives rise to multiple sense faculties.

435. Anallīno nissayo etassāti anallīnanissayo, rūpasaddasaṅkhāto visayo. Gandharasānaṃ nissayā ghānajivhānaṃ nissaye allīyantīti [M 2.0093] te nissayavasena allīnā. Phoṭṭhabbaṃ sayaṃ kāyanissayaallīnaṃ bhūtattā. Aparo nayo – cakkhusotāni appattavisayaggāhakāni sāntare, adhike ca visaye viññāṇuppattihetubhāvato. Sotampi sampattavisayaggāhīti keci. Yadi sotaṃ sampattaggāhi, cittajo saddo sotaviññāṇassa ārammaṇaṃ na siyā. Na hi bahiddhā cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ uppatti atthi. Pāḷiyañca avisesena saddārammaṇassa sotaviññāṇārammaṇabhāvo vutto. Kiñca disādesavavatthānañca saddassa na siyā, attano visayipadesassa eva gahetabbato gandho viya. Tasmā yattha uppanno saddo, tattheva ṭhito. Sace sotapathe āpāthamāgacchati, nanu dūre ṭhitehi rajakādisaddā cirena suyyantīti? Na dūrāsannānaṃ yathāpākaṭe sadde gahaṇavisesato. Yathā hi dūrāsannānaṃ vacanasadde yathāpākaṭe gahaṇavisesato ākāravisesānaṃ aggahaṇaṃ, gahaṇañca hoti, evaṃ rajakādisaddepi āsannassa ādito pabhuti yāva avasānā kamena pākaṭībhūte, dūrassa ca avasāne, majjhe vā piṇḍavasena pavattipākaṭībhūte nicchayaggahaṇānaṃ sotaviññāṇavīthiyā parato pavattānaṃ visesato lahukaṃ suto “cirena suto”ti adhimāno hoti. So pana saddo yattha uppanno, tannissitova attano vijjamānakkhaṇe sotassa āpāthamāgacchati[V 2.0088]. Yadi saddassa bhūtaparamparāya samantato pavatti natthi, kathaṃ paṭighosuppattīti? Dūre ṭhitopi saddo aññattha paṭighosuppattiyā, bhājanādicalanassa ca ayokanto viya ayocalanassa paccayo hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

435. ‘Its support does not cling’ (anallīno nissayo etassa), therefore it is a ‘non-clinging support’ (anallīnanissayo); the object is that which is designated as form and sound. The supports of smell and taste cling to the support of the nose and tongue; therefore, they are ‘clinging’ by way of their support. The tangible object itself clings to the support of the body because it is a primary element. Another method: The eye and ear apprehend objects that have not reached them, because they are the cause for the arising of consciousness with regard to an object that is separated and extensive. Some say the ear also apprehends an object that has reached it. If the ear apprehends an object that has reached it, a sound produced by the mind could not be an object of ear-consciousness. For there is no external arising of phenomena originated by the mind. And in the Pāḷi, the status of a sound-object as an object for ear-consciousness is stated without distinction. Furthermore, there would be no determination of direction and location for sound, since only the location of its subject (the ear-sensitivity) could be apprehended, just as with smell. Therefore, wherever a sound arises, it comes into the range of the ear's path while remaining right there. Are not, then, the sounds of washermen and so on heard by those at a distance only after a long time? No. It is due to the distinction in grasping a sound as it is manifest for those far and near. For just as, with a spoken sound as it is manifest for those far and near, there is, due to the distinction in grasping, the non-grasping and grasping of particular characteristics, so too with the sounds of washermen and so on: for one who is near, when the sound becomes manifest in sequence from beginning to end, and for one who is far, when it becomes manifest at the end or in the middle as a single mass, due to the distinction in the determinative graspings that occur after the ear-consciousness process, the overestimation, ‘It was heard after a long time,’ occurs, although it was heard quickly. However, that sound, wherever it has arisen, dependent on that very basis, comes into the range of the ear at the moment of its own existence. If there is no propagation of sound in all directions through a succession of primary elements, how does an echo arise? It should be understood that a sound, even though located at a distance, is a condition for the arising of an echo elsewhere and for the movement of a vessel and so on, just as a magnet is a condition for the movement of iron.

436. Pubbe lakkhaṇādinā vibhāvitampi cakkhuṃ ṭhitaṭṭhānādito vibhāvetuṃ “cakkhu cetthā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha cakkhu sādhayamānaṃ tiṭṭhatīti sambandho. Ca-kāro byatirekattho, tenassa vuccamānameva visesaṃ joteti. Etthāti etesu yathāniddiṭṭhesu pañcasu upādārūpesu. “Sarīrasaṇṭhānuppattidese”ti etena avasesaṃ kaṇhamaṇḍalaṃ paṭikkhipati. Snehamiva satta akkhipaṭalāni byāpetvā ṭhitāheva attano nissayabhūtāhi catūhi dhātūhi katūpakāraṃ tannissiteheva āyuvaṇṇādīhi anupālitaṃ parivāritaṃ tisantatirūpasamuṭṭhāpakehi utucittāhārehi [M 2.0094] upatthambhiyamānaṃ tiṭṭhati. Sattaakkhipaṭalabyāpanavacaneneva cakkhussa anekakalāpagatabhāvaṃ dasseti. Pamāṇato ūkāsiramattanti ūkāsiramatte padese pavattanato vuttaṃ. Cakkhuviññāṇassa vatthubhāvaṃ nissayabhāvato āvajjanasampaṭicchanādīnaṃ tadārammaṇāvasānānaṃ dvārabhāvaṃ samavasaraṭṭhānato. Taṃ panetaṃ cakkhu adhiṭṭhānabhedato, tatthāpi paccekaṃ anekakalāpagatabhāvato anekampi samānaṃ sāmaññaniddesena āvajjanāya ekattā, ekasmiṃ khaṇe ekasseva ca kiccakarattā ekaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Evampi bahūsu kathamekasseva kiccakarattaṃ. Yaṃ tattha visadaṃ hutvā rūpābhighātārahaṃ, taṃ viññāṇassa nissayo hotīti gahetabbaṃ. Phoṭṭhabbaviseso viya kāyaviññāṇassa ārammaṇabhāve.

436. Although the eye has already been explained in terms of its characteristics and so on, the passage beginning with “the eye is here” is introduced to explain it from the standpoint of its location, etc. Herein, the connection is that the eye abides accomplishing. The particle “ca” has the meaning of distinction; thereby, it illuminates the very distinction being spoken of for it. “Here” refers to these five derived material phenomena as specified. By “in the part of the body where it arises,” it excludes the remaining dark circle. Having pervaded the seven eye-membranes like oil, it abides, having been rendered service by the four elements that are its own basis. It is maintained and surrounded by vitality, complexion, etc., which are dependent on them, and it abides being sustained by temperature, consciousness, and nutriment, which are the producers of the three continuities of material phenomena. By the statement that it pervades the seven eye-membranes, it shows that the eye consists of multiple kalāpas. In size, it is said to be “as large as a louse’s head” because it occurs in a place of that size. It is the basis for eye-consciousness due to its nature as a support, and it is the door for adverting, receiving, etc., which end in registration, due to its nature as a place of convergence. However, this eye, though manifold due to the difference in its bases and because each individually consists of many kalāpas, is spoken of as one by way of a general designation, due to the unity of adverting, and because only one performs its function at a single moment. Even so, how is it to be understood that only one performs the function when there are many? It should be understood that whatever among them is clear and fit for the impact of form is the support for consciousness, just as a particular tangible object is in the state of being an object for body-consciousness.

Manupassatīti ma-kāro padasandhikaro, atha vā manūti macco.

In `manupassati`, the letter `ma` is a euphonic connector; or alternatively, `manū` means a mortal.

Aṅgulivedhakaṃ aṅgulīyakaṃ.

`Aṅgulivedhaka` is a finger-ring.

Visamajjhāsayatāya cakkhu vammikachiddābhiratasappo viya, bilajjhāsayatāya sotaṃ udakabilābhiratakumbhīlo viya, ākāsajjhāsayatāya ghānaṃ ajaṭākāsābhiratapakkhī viya, gāmajjhāsayatāya jivhā gāmābhiratakukkuro viya, upādinnakajjhāsayatāya kāyo āmakasusānābhiratasiṅgālo viya passitabboti dassento “vammi…pe… daṭṭhabbā”ti āha. Visamajjhāsayatā ca cakkhussa visamajjhāsayaṃ viya hotīti katvā vuttā, cakkhumato vā puggalassa [V 2.0089] ajjhāsayavasena cakkhu visamajjhāsayaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Sabbopi ca yathāvutto papañco sotādīsupi yathārahaṃ veditabbo.

Showing that the eye, due to its inclination for what is uneven, should be seen like a snake that delights in an anthill hole; the ear, due to its inclination for a cavity, like a crocodile that delights in a water hole; the nose, due to its inclination for space, like a bird that delights in the unobstructed sky; the tongue, due to its inclination for a village, like a dog that delights in a village; and the body, due to its inclination for the appropriated, like a jackal that delights in a charnel ground for fresh corpses, he said: “An anthill…should be seen.” And the eye’s state of having an uneven inclination is spoken of because it is as if it has an uneven inclination; or, the eye should be seen as having an uneven inclination by way of the disposition of the person who has the eye. This is the method in the remaining cases as well. And all the elaboration as stated should be understood for the ear and so forth, as is appropriate.

437. Cakkhumhi, cakkhussa vā paṭihananaṃ cakkhupaṭihananaṃ, taṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etassāti cakkhupaṭihananalakkhaṇaṃ. Paṭihananañcettha yathāvutto abhighātova. Visayabhāvo ārammaṇapaccayatā. Kāmaṃ sā eva gocaratā, tathāpi visayagocarānaṃ ayaṃ viseso – anaññatthabhāvo, tabbahulacāritā ca cakkhuviññāṇassa. Visayabhāve cassa yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ parato āvi bhavissati. Yattha pana kāyaviññattiādike.

437. Striking in the eye, or of the eye, is eye-striking; that is its characteristic, hence it has the characteristic of eye-striking. And here, striking is just the impact as stated before. The state of being an object is the state of being an object-condition. Indeed, that very state is the state of being a range; nevertheless, this is the distinction between object and range: for eye-consciousness, its 'object' is its state of not arising in relation to another type of object, while its 'range' is its state of frequenting that object. And regarding its state of being an object, what should be said about that will become manifest later. But where, in matter such as bodily intimation and the like...

438. Itthiyā [M 2.0095] bhāvo, “itthī”ti vā bhavati etena cittaṃ, abhidhānañcāti itthibhāvo, taṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etassāti itthibhāvalakkhaṇaṃ. Tato eva “itthī”ti taṃsahitaṃ santānaṃ pakāsentaṃ viya hotīti vuttaṃ “itthīti pakāsanarasa”nti. Vaṭṭaṃsatā avisadahatthapādāditā ca itthiliṅgaṃ. Thanamaṃsāvisadatā, nimmassudāṭhitā, kesabandhanaṃ, vatthaggahaṇañca “itthī”ti sañjānanassa paccayabhāvato itthinimittaṃ. Daharakālepi suppakamusalakādīhi kīḷā, mattikatakkena suttakantanādi ca itthikuttaṃ, itthikiriyāti attho. Avisadaṭṭhānagamanādiko ākāro itthākappo. Aparo nayo – itthīnaṃ muttakaraṇaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ. Sarādhippāyā itthinimittaṃ. Avisadaṭṭhānagamananisajjākhādanabhojanādikā itthikuttaṃ. Itthisaṇṭhānaṃ itthākappo. Imāni ca itthiliṅgādīni yathāsakaṃ kammādinā paccayena uppajjamānānipi yebhuyyena itthindriyasahite eva santāne taṃtadākārāni hutvā uppajjantīti itthindriyaṃ tesaṃ kāraṇanti katvā vuttaṃ “itthiliṅganimittakuttākappānaṃ kāraṇabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāna”nti. Itthiliṅgādīsu eva ca kāraṇabhāvasaṅkhātena adhipatibhāvena tassa indriyatā vuttā, indriyasahite santāne itthiliṅgādiākārarūpapaccayānaṃ aññathā anuppādanato, itthiggahaṇassa ca tesaṃ rūpānaṃ paccayabhāvato.

438. The state of a woman, or that by which the mind and designation “woman” arise, is the state of woman; that is its characteristic, hence it has the characteristic of the state of woman. For that very reason, it is as if it reveals the continuity associated with it as “woman,” hence it is said, “its function is revealing as a woman.” Roundness of shoulders and indistinctness of hands, feet, etc., are the feminine characteristic. Indistinctness of the flesh of the breasts, absence of a beard and canine teeth, the tying of hair, and the manner of wearing garments are the feminine sign because they are a cause for recognizing “a woman.” Even in childhood, playing with small winnowing baskets, small pestles, etc., and spinning thread with a clay spindle, etc., are feminine conduct; this means feminine actions. The manner, such as indistinct standing and moving, is feminine deportment. Another method: The urinary organ of women is the feminine characteristic. Voice and inclinations are the feminine sign. Indistinct standing, moving, sitting, chewing, and eating, etc., are feminine conduct. The feminine form is feminine deportment. And these feminine characteristics, etc., although arising by their respective causes such as kamma, mostly arise in the continuity associated with the female faculty, taking on those particular forms. Therefore, it is said that the female faculty is their cause, as stated: “The female faculty is presented as the cause of the feminine characteristic, sign, conduct, and deportment.” And its faculty-nature is stated in terms of its governing role, reckoned as the cause, precisely in relation to the feminine characteristics, etc., because the forms of feminine characteristics, etc., do not arise otherwise in a continuity associated with the faculty, and because the grasping of femininity is a condition for those forms.

Yasmā pana bhāvadasakepi rūpānaṃ itthindriyaṃ na janakaṃ, nāpi anupālakaṃ, upatthambhakaṃ vā, na ca aññesaṃ kalāparūpānaṃ, tasmā taṃ jīvitindriyaṃ viya sakalāparūpānaṃ, āhāro viya vā kalāpantararūpānañca “indriyaatthiavigatapaccayo”ti pāḷiyaṃ na vuttaṃ. Yasmā ca paccayantarādhīnāni liṅgādīni, tasmā yatthassa ādhipaccaṃ, taṃsadisesu matacittakatarūpesupi taṃsaṇṭhānatā dissati. Esa nayo purisindriyepi. Yaṃ panettha visadisaṃ, taṃ vuttanayānusārena veditabbaṃ[V 2.0090]. Tayidaṃ dvayaṃ yasmā ekasmiṃ santāne saha na pavattati “yassa itthindriyaṃ uppajjati, tassa purisindriyaṃ uppajjatīti? No”tiādi (yama. 3.indriyayamaka.188) vacanato, tasmā ubhatobyañjanakassāpi ekasmiṃ khaṇe ekameva hotīti veditabbaṃ. Ye pana “sarīrekadesavutti bhāvarūpa”nti vadanti, tesampi taṃ micchāti dassetuṃ “tadubhayampi…pe… byāpakamevā”ti vatvā yadi evaṃ kāyappasādena saṅkaro siyāti āsaṅkaṃ nivattento “na ca kāyappasādenā”tiādimāha. Tassattho – yadipi [M 2.0096] sakalasarīrabyāpitāya kāyappasādena aṭṭhitokāse ṭhitanti vattabbataṃ nāpajjati, tena pana bhinnanissayattā ṭhitokāse ṭhitantipi vattabbataṃ nāpajjatīti ayameva cettha nippariyāyakathā. “Rūparasādayo viyā”ti etena samānanissayesupi nāma saṅkaro natthi lakkhaṇabhedato, kimaṅgaṃ pana bhinnanissayasabhāvesūti dasseti.

However, because the female faculty, even in the sex-decad, is neither generative, nor sustaining, nor supportive of forms, nor of the forms in other kalāpas, therefore, unlike the life faculty for all other forms or nutriment for the forms of other kalāpas, it is not stated in the Pāḷi to be an 'indriya, atthi, and avigata condition'. And because the gender characteristics and so forth are dependent on other conditions, that same configuration is seen even in things that resemble it, such as in the forms of a corpse or in paintings and drawings, where this faculty has no dominance. This same principle applies to the male faculty. Whatever is dissimilar here should be understood according to the method already stated. Since this pair does not occur together in a single continuum—according to the statement, “For whom the female faculty arises, does the male faculty arise? No,” and so on (Yama. 3.Indriyayamaka.188)—therefore, it should be understood that even for one with both sexual characteristics, only one single faculty exists in a single moment. As for those who say, “The sex-materiality exists in one part of the body,” to show that their statement is wrong, having said, “Both… are indeed pervasive,” and then to dispel the doubt that, “If so, there would be an intermingling with the body-sensitivity,” he stated, “And not with the body-sensitivity,” and so on. Its meaning is this: Although, due to its pervasiveness throughout the entire body, it cannot be said that the sex-materiality is located in a place where body-sensitivity is not located, yet because it has a different support, it also cannot be said that it is located in the same place where body-sensitivity is located. This very statement is the direct explanation here. By the phrase, “like visible form, taste, etc.,” he shows that even among things with a common support, there is no intermingling due to the difference in their characteristics; what then needs to be said of things that have different supports and natures?

439. Sahajarūpānupālanalakkhaṇanti attanā sahajātarūpānaṃ anupālanalakkhaṇaṃ. Jīvitindriyassa ekantakammajattā sahaja-ggahaṇeneva anupāletabbānampi kammajabhāvo siddhoti kammaja-ggahaṇaṃ na kataṃ. Yathāsakaṃ khaṇamattaṭṭhāyinopi kammajarūpassa pavattihetubhāvena taṃ anupālakaṃ, tasmā sahajarūpānupālanalakkhaṇaṃ. Na hi kammajānaṃ kammaṃyeva ṭhitihetu bhavituṃ arahati āhārajādīnaṃ āhārādi viya. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Taṅkhaṇābhāvato. Tesanti sahajarūpānaṃ. Pavattanaṃ yāpanaṃ. Ṭhapanaṃ ṭhitihetutā. Attanā anupālanavasena yāpetabbāni pavattetabbāni bhūtāni etassa padaṭṭhānanti yāpayitabbabhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Anupālanalakkhaṇādimhīti ādi-saddena pavattanarasādimeva saṅgaṇhāti. Atthikkhaṇeyevāti anupāletabbānaṃ atthikkhaṇeyeva. Asati anupāletabbe uppalādimhi kiṃ udakaṃ anupāleyya. Yadi kammajānaṃ ṭhitihetumantarena ṭhiti na hoti, jīvitindriyassa ko ṭhitihetūti āha “saya”ntiādi. Yadi kammajānaṃ ṭhānaṃ jīvitindriyapaṭibaddhaṃ, atha kasmā sabbakālaṃ na ṭhapetīti āha “na bhaṅgato”tiādi. Tassa tassa anupālanādikassa sādhanato. Taṃ sādhanañca jīvamānatāvisesassa paccayabhāvato. Indriyabaddharūpassa hi matarūpato kammajassa, tadanubandhabhūtassa ca utusamuṭṭhānādito jīvitindriyakato viseso, na kevalaṃ khaṇaṭṭhitiyā eva, pabandhānupacchedassāpi jīvitindriyaṃ kāraṇanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, itarathā āyukkhayato maraṇaṃ na yujjeyyāti.

439. The characteristic of maintaining co-nascent materiality means the characteristic of maintaining material forms co-arisen with itself. Since the life faculty is exclusively kamma-originated, the kamma-originated nature of even those that should be maintained is established by the mere inclusion of 'co-nascent,' so the inclusion of 'kamma-originated' is not made. By being a cause for the continuity of kamma-originated material form—which, for its own part, persists for only a moment—it (the life faculty) maintains it. Therefore, it has the characteristic of maintaining co-nascent material forms. Indeed, kamma alone cannot be the condition for the persistence of kamma-originated forms, just as nutriment, etc., is for nutriment-originated forms, etc. For what reason? Because of its absence at that moment. 'Of those' refers to co-nascent material forms. 'Causing to continue' (pavattana) is sustenance (yāpana). 'Establishing' (ṭhapana) is being a condition for persistence (ṭhitihetutā). Its proximate cause is the primary elements that are to be sustained and made to continue by means of its own maintaining. In the phrase 'the characteristic of maintaining, etc.,' the word 'etc.' includes the function of causing to continue, etc. 'Only at the moment of existence' means only at the moment of existence of those that are to be maintained. When there is no lotus, etc., to be maintained, what would water maintain? If the persistence of kamma-originated forms does not occur without a condition for persistence, what then is the condition for the persistence of the life faculty? To this, he says, 'by itself,' etc. If the persistence of kamma-originated forms depends on the life faculty, then why does it not sustain them at all times? To this, he says, 'not because of disintegration,' etc. This is due to the accomplishment of its respective function of maintaining, etc. And that accomplishment is because it is a condition for the particular state of being alive. Indeed, a distinction is made by the life faculty for faculty-bound material form as compared to dead material form, and for kamma-originated form and its concomitant, temperature-originated form, etc., as compared to other temperature-originated forms, etc. The life faculty should be understood as a cause not only for momentary persistence but also for the non-interruption of the series of kamma-originated material forms; otherwise, death due to the exhaustion of the life-span would not be logical.

440. Manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātūnaṃ nissayalakkhaṇaṃ hadayavatthūti kathametaṃ viññātabbanti? Āgamato, yuttito ca. “Yaṃ rūpaṃ nissāya manodhātu ca manoviññāṇadhātu ca [V 2.0091] pavattanti, taṃ rūpaṃ manodhātuyā ca manoviññāṇadhātuyā ca taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ nissayapaccayena paccayo”ti [M 2.0097] (paṭṭhā. 1.1.8) evamādi āgamo. Yadi evaṃ, kasmā rūpakaṇḍe taṃ na vuttanti? Tattha avacanaṃ aññakāraṇaṃ. Kiṃ pana tanti? Desanābhedo. Yathā hi cakkhuviññāṇādīni ekantato cakkhādinissayāni, na evaṃ manoviññāṇaṃ ekantena hadayavatthunissayaṃ. Nissitavasena ca vatthudukādidesanā pavattā “atthi rūpaṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa vatthu, atthi rūpaṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa na vatthū”tiādinā (dha. sa. 584). Yampi ekantato hadayavatthunissayaṃ, tassa vasena “atthi rūpaṃ manoviññāṇassa vatthū”tiādinā dukādīsu vuccamānesupi na tadanuguṇā ārammaṇadukādayo sambhavanti. Na hi “atthi rūpaṃ manoviññāṇassa ārammaṇaṃ, atthi rūpaṃ na manoviññāṇassa ārammaṇa”nti sakkā vattunti vatthārammaṇadukā bhinnagatikā siyunti ekarasā desanā na bhaveyya. Ekarasañca desanaṃ desetuṃ idha satthu ajjhāsayo. Tasmā tattha hadayavatthu na vuttaṃ, na alabbhamānattāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

440. How is this to be understood: that the heart-base has the characteristic of being a support for the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element? Through scripture and through reasoning. The scripture is as follows: “That material form depending on which the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element proceed, that material form is a condition for the mind-element, for the mind-consciousness-element, and for the states associated with them by way of support condition” (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.8), and so forth. If so, why is that not stated in the section on material form? The non-statement there has another reason. What is that reason? A difference in the teaching. For, just as eye-consciousness, etc., are exclusively dependent on the eye, etc., mind-consciousness is not in the same way exclusively dependent on the heart-base. And the teaching on the dyads of bases, etc., proceeds by way of dependence, with such as: “There is material form that is a base for eye-consciousness; there is material form that is not a base for eye-consciousness” (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 584). And even with respect to that [mind-consciousness] which is exclusively dependent on the heart-base, although it is stated in the dyads, etc., by means of that, with such as: “There is material form that is a base for mind-consciousness,” the corresponding object-dyads, etc., are not possible. For it is not possible to say: “There is material form that is an object of mind-consciousness; there is material form that is not an object of mind-consciousness.” Thus, the base-dyad and the object-dyad would have different courses, and thus the teaching would not be uniform. And here, it is the Teacher’s intention to give a uniform teaching. Therefore, the heart-base is not stated there; it should be understood that this is not because of its unobtainability.

Yutti pana evaṃ veditabbā – nipphannaupādāyarūpanissayaṃ dhātudvayaṃ pañcavokārabhave. Tattha rūpāyatanādīnaṃ, ojāya ca indriyabaddhato bahipi pavattidassanato na taṃnissayatā yujjati, itthipurisindriyānampi tadubhayarahitepi santāne dhātudvayadassanato na taṃnissayatā yujjati, jīvitindriyassāpi aññakiccaṃ vijjatīti na taṃnissayatā yujjati evāti pārisesato hadayavatthu, tesaṃ nissayoti viññāyati. Sakkā hi vattuṃ nipphannaupādāyarūpanissayaṃ dhātudvayaṃ pañcavokārabhave rūpapaṭibaddhavuttibhāvato. Yaṃ yañhi rūpapaṭibaddhavutti, taṃ taṃ nipphannaupādāyarūpanissayaṃ diṭṭhaṃ yathā “cakkhuviññāṇadhātū”ti. “Pañcavokārabhave”ti ca visesanaṃ manoviññāṇadhātuvasena kataṃ. Manodhātu pana catuvokārabhave nattheva. Nanu ca indriyanissayatāyapi sādhanato viruddho hetu āpajjatīti? Na diṭṭhabādhanato. Diṭṭhaṃ hetaṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa viya dhātudvayassa vatthuno mandatikkhādiananuvidhānaṃ. Tathā hissa pāḷiyaṃ indriyapaccayatā na vuttā. Tena tadanuvidhānasaṅkhātā indriyanissayatā bādhīyati. Hotu dhātudvayanissayo hadayavatthu, upādāyarūpañca, etaṃ pana kammasamuṭṭhānaṃ, paṭiniyatakiccaṃ, hadayapadese ṭhitamevāti kathaṃ viññāyatīti? Vuccate – vatthurūpabhāvato kammasamuṭṭhānaṃ cakkhu viya, tato eva [M 2.0098] paṭiniyatakiccaṃ, vatthurūpabhāvatoti ca viññāṇanissayabhāvatoti attho. Aṭṭhiṃ katvā manasi katvā sabbacetasā samannāharitvā kiñci cintentassa hadayassa khijjanato tatthetamavaṭṭhitanti viññāyati. Tāsaññeva dhātūnanti manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātūnaṃyeva[V 2.0092]. Nissayabhāvato upari āropetvā vahantaṃ viya paccupatiṭṭhatīti ubbahanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

Reasoning, however, should be understood thus: In the five-constituent becoming, the two elements depend on produced derived material form. Among these, for the visible-form base and others, and for nutriment, since their occurrence is seen even outside of being bound to the faculties, being their support is not justified. Also, for the female and male faculties, since the two elements are seen even in a continuum devoid of both of them, being their support is not justified. The life faculty also has another function, so being its support is likewise not justified. Thus, by elimination, the heart-base is understood as their support. For it can indeed be said that the two elements in the five-constituent becoming depend on produced derived material form because their functioning is bound to material form. For whatever functions bound to material form is seen to depend on produced derived material form, just as the eye-consciousness-element. And the qualification 'in the five-constituent becoming' is made with reference to the mind-consciousness-element. The mind-element, however, does not exist at all in the four-constituent becoming. But surely, does a contradictory reason not arise from establishing dependence on the faculties? No, because of an observed refutation. For it is observed that the two elements do not conform to the dullness, sharpness, and so on of their base, unlike the eye-consciousness.
