Thus, indeed, its conditionality as a faculty is not stated in the Pāḷi. Therefore, its nature as a support that is a faculty, which is defined as conformity to it, is refuted. Let the heart-base be the support for the two elements, and let it be derived material form; but how is it understood that this is kamma-originated, has a fixed function, and is located only in the heart region? It is said: Because it is a base-material-form, it is kamma-originated, like the eye; and for that very reason, it has a fixed function. And 'because it is a base-material-form' means 'because it is a support for consciousness'. When one makes a firm resolve, pays attention, directs the mind with all one's consciousness, and contemplates something, from the agitation of the heart it is understood that it is located there. 'Of those very elements' means of only the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element. Because of its nature as a support, it manifests as if placing them upon itself and carrying them; thus, its manifestation is that of uplifting. The rest is just as explained previously.

441. Abhikkamo ādi yesaṃ te abhikkamādī. Ādi-saddena paṭikkamasamiñjanapasāraṇaukkhepanaavekkhepanādikā sabbā kiriyā pariggayhati. Tesaṃ abhikkamādīnaṃ pavattakaṃ cittaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ yassā sā abhikkamādippavattakacittasamuṭṭhānā, vāyodhātu. Tassā yaṃ sahajarūpakāyassa thambhanasandhāraṇacalanasaṅkhātaṃ kiccaṃ, tassa sahakārīkāraṇabhūto ākāraviseso kāyaviññatti nāmāti dassento āha “abhikkamādi…pe… kāyaviññattī”ti.

441. Abhikkamādī are those whose beginning is stepping forward. By the word ādi, all actions such as stepping backward, bending, stretching, raising, lowering, and so forth, are included. The wind element is that whose origin is the mind that initiates these actions beginning with stepping forward; hence, it is 'originated by the mind that initiates stepping forward, etc.' To show that a particular mode, which is a cooperative cause for its function of stiffening, supporting, and moving the co-nascent material body, is called 'bodily intimation,' he says: 'Beginning with stepping forward… bodily intimation.'

Kassa pana ākāravikāroti? Sāmatthiyato vāyodhātuadhikānaṃ cittajamahābhūtānaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ sāmatthiyaṃ? Cittajatā, upādāyarūpatā ca. Atha vā vāyodhātuyā ākāravikāro sahaja…pe… paccayoti sambandhitabbaṃ. Yadi evaṃ viññattiyā upādāyarūpabhāvo na yujjati. Na hi upādāyarūpaṃ ekabhūtasannissayaṃ atthi. “Catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāyarūpa”nti hi vuttaṃ, nāyaṃ doso catunnaṃ vikāro catūsu ekassāpi hoti catusādhāraṇadhanaṃ viya. Vāyodhātuadhikatāya ca kalāpassa “vāyodhātuyā”ti vacanaṃ na virujjhati. Evaṃ adhikatā ca sāmatthiyato, na pamāṇato. Aññathā hi avinibbhogavuttitā na yujjeyya. Vāyodhātuyā evāti keci. Tesaṃ matena viññattiyā upādāyarūpatā durupapādā. Na hi ekassa vikāro catunnaṃ hoti. Sā panāyaṃ hatthacalanādīsu phandamānavaṇṇaggahaṇānantaramaviññāyamānantarena manodvārajavanena gayhati. Phandamānavaṇṇavinimutto koci vikāro atthi. Tassa ca taggahaṇānantaraṃ gahaṇaṃ hotīti kathametaṃ viññāyatīti adhippāyaggahaṇato. Na hi viññattivikārarahitesu rukkhacalanādīsu “idamesa kāreti maññe”ti adhippāyaggahaṇaṃ [M 2.0099] diṭṭhaṃ, hatthacalanādīsu pana diṭṭhaṃ. Tasmā phandamānavaṇṇavinimutto koci vikāro atthi adhippāyassa ñāpakoti viññāyati. Ñāpako ca hetu ñāpetabbamatthaṃ sayaṃ gahito eva ñāpeti, na vijjamānatāmattenāti vaṇṇaggahaṇānantaraṃ vikāraggahaṇampi anumānato viññāyati. Tathā hi vadanti –

But of what is this an alteration of mode? It is of the mind-produced great elements in which the wind element predominates, by way of potency. What is that potency? It is being mind-produced and being derived material form. Alternatively, the alteration of mode of the wind element is to be connected as a co-nascent... condition. If so, the status of intimation as derived material form would not be justified. For there is no derived material form dependent on a single great element. It is said, "Derived material form is of the four great elements." This is no fault, for an alteration of the four can also be of any one among the four, like wealth held in common by four. Moreover, the statement "of the wind element" regarding the kalāpa is not contradicted due to the predominance of the wind element. Thus, this predominance is in terms of potency, not in quantity. Otherwise, their inseparable nature would not be justified. Some say it is of the wind element alone. According to their view, the status of intimation as derived material form is difficult to establish. For the alteration of one is not that of the four. Furthermore, this bodily intimation, in movements like that of the hand, is grasped by a mind-door impulsion with an unperceived interval immediately after the apprehension of the flickering form. There is some alteration apart from the flickering form. And how is it known that its apprehension occurs right after the apprehension of that? It is understood through the apprehension of intention. For in movements like the shaking of a tree, where there is no alteration of intimation, no apprehension of intention like "I suppose this one is causing it" is seen, but in movements of the hand, it is seen. Therefore, it is understood that there is some alteration apart from the flickering form, which indicates intention. An indicator, as a cause, reveals the object to be known only when it is itself apprehended, not merely by its existence. Thus, the apprehension of the alteration after the apprehension of the form is also known by inference. As they say:

“Visayattamanāpannā, saddā nevatthabodhakā;

Na sattāmattato atthe, te aññātā pakāsakā”ti.

Sounds, not having become an object, do not convey meaning; unknown, they do not reveal meaning by their mere existence.

Yadi [V 2.0093] vikāraggahaṇameva kāraṇaṃ adhippāyaggahaṇassa, kasmā aggahitasaṅketānaṃ adhippāyaggahaṇaṃ na hotīti? Na kevalaṃ vikāraggahaṇameva adhippāyaggahaṇassa kāraṇaṃ, atha kho purimasiddhasambandhaggahaṇañca imassa upanissayoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Thambhanasandhāraṇacalanāni viññattivikārasahitāya vāyodhātuyā hontīti vuttaṃ. Kiṃ sabbāva vāyodhātū sabbāni tāni karontīti? Nayidamevaṃ. Sattamajavanasambhūtā hi vāyodhātu purimajavanasambhūtā vāyodhātuyo upathambhakapaccaye labhitvā desantaruppattihetubhāvena calayati cittajarūpaṃ, na itarā. Itarā pana santhambhanasandhāraṇamattaṃ karontiyo tassā upakārāya honti. Desantaruppatti eva calananti nimitte ca kattubhāvo samāropitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aññathā dhammānaṃ abyāpāratā, khaṇikatā ca na siyā. Sattahi yugehi ākaḍḍhitabbasakaṭamettha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ nidassitaṃ. Cittajarūpe pana calante taṃsambandhatāya utukammāhārajarūpampi calati nadīsote pakkhittasukkhagomayapiṇḍaṃ viya phandamānavaṇṇaggahaṇānantaraṃ viññattiggahaṇassa vuttattā. Kiṃ calanakarā eva vāyodhātu viññattivikārasahitāti? Nayidamevaṃ, tathā calayitumasakkuṇantiyopi thambhanasandhāraṇamattakarā paṭhamajavanādisambhūtāpi vāyodhātuyo viññattivikārasahitā evāti gahetabbaṃ. Yena disābhāgenāyaṃ abhikkamādiṃ pavattetukāmo, tadabhimukhavikārasabbhāvato. Adhippāyasahabhāvī hi vikāro viññatti. Evañca katvā manodvārāvajjanassāpi viññattisamuṭṭhāpakavacanaṃ suṭṭhu yujjati. Yathāvuttavikāraggahaṇamukhena taṃsamaṅgino adhippāyo viññāyatīti vuttaṃ “adhippāyappakāsanarasā”ti.

If the mere apprehension of alteration is the reason for apprehending intention, why is there no apprehension of intention for those who have not grasped the conventional signs? It is not only the apprehension of alteration that is the reason for apprehending intention; rather, the apprehension of a previously established connection should also be understood as a decisive support for this. It has been said that stiffening, supporting, and moving are performed by the wind element together with the alteration of intimation. Do all wind elements perform all these actions? No, it is not so. For the wind element produced by the seventh javana impulse, having obtained supporting conditions from the wind elements produced by the earlier javana impulses, moves the mind-born materiality by being the cause of arising in another location—not the others. The others, however, merely perform stiffening and supporting, being helpful to it. Arising in another location is itself the movement, and the role of agent is superimposed upon the sign. Otherwise, the non-agency of phenomena and their momentariness would not hold. In the commentary, the example of a cart that must be pulled by seven yokes is shown. When the mind-born materiality moves, due to its connection, the materiality produced by temperature, kamma, and nutriment also moves—like a lump of dry cow dung thrown into a river current—because the apprehension of intimation is stated to occur after the apprehension of the flickering form. Are only the wind elements that cause movement accompanied by the alteration of intimation? No, it is not so; even those wind elements produced by the first javana impulse, etc., which are incapable of moving in that way but merely perform stiffening and supporting, should be understood as being accompanied by the alteration of intimation, because there is an alteration facing the direction in which one wishes to proceed, etc. For the alteration that co-arises with intention is intimation. Thus, the statement that even the mind-door adverting produces intimation is well justified. Through the means of apprehending the alteration as described, the intention of the one who possesses it is understood; hence it is said, 'Its function is to reveal intention.'

Kāyavipphandanassa [M 2.0100] hetubhūtāya vāyodhātuyā vikārabhāvato pariyāyena viññatti kāyavipphandanahetubhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā vuttā. Cittasamuṭṭhānavāyodhātupadaṭṭhānāti ca vāyodhātuyā kiccādhikatāya vuttaṃ. Kāyavipphandanena adhippāyaviññāpanahetuttāti kāyavipphandanena karaṇabhūtena adhippāyassa viññāpanahetubhāvato kāyaviññattīti vuccatīti sambandho. Ayañhettha attho – viññāpetīti viññatti. Kiṃ viññāpeti? Adhippāyaṃ. Kena? Kāyena. Kīdisena? Vipphandamānenāti. Dutiyanaye pana yathāvuttena kāyena viññāyatīti kāyaviññatti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Because the wind element, which is the cause of bodily movement, is a modification, intimation is said, by way of method, to have as its manifestation the state of being the cause of bodily movement. And it is said that its proximate cause is the mind-originated wind element, due to the predominance of the wind element's function. The connection is that it is called 'bodily intimation' (kāyaviññatti) because bodily movement, being the instrument, is the cause of making intention known. This is the meaning here: It makes known, therefore it is 'intimation' (viññatti). What does it make known? Intention. By what? By the body. Of what sort? By a moving one. In the second method, however, it is 'bodily intimation' (kāyaviññatti) because it is known by the body as aforesaid. The rest is as has been explained.

Atthāvabodhanasamattho vacīviseso vacībhedo. Tena vāyuvanappatinadīghosādiṃ nivatteti. Tassa pavattakaṃ cittaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ yassā sā vacībhedappavattakacittasamuṭṭhānā, pathavīdhātu. Tassā yaṃ upādinnasaṅkhātassa [V 2.0094] akkharuppattiṭṭhānassa ghaṭṭanasaññitaṃ kiccaṃ, tassa sahakārīkāraṇabhūto ākāraviseso vacīviññatti nāmāti dassento āha “vacībhe…pe… vacīviññattī”ti.

A particular utterance capable of making meaning understood is vocal expression (vacībheda). By that, it excludes sounds such as those of wind, forest trees, and rivers. The earth element for which the mind that sets that vocal expression in motion is the origin is [the one called] vacībhedappavattakacittasamuṭṭhānā. Showing that a particular mode, which is a co-operating cause of the function of that [earth element]—namely, the function termed 'striking' of the place of origin of letters, which is termed 'appropriated'—is named 'vocal intimation', he said: 'vocal expression...vocal intimation.'

Idāni “kassa pana ākāravikāro”tiādi kāyaviññattiyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso – yathā tattha “phandamānavaṇṇaggahaṇānantara”nti vuttaṃ, evamidha “suyyamānasaddasavanānantara”nti yojetabbaṃ. Idha ca thambhanādīnaṃ abhāvato “sattamajavanasambhūtā”tiādinayo na labbhati. Ghaṭṭanena hi saddhiṃ saddo uppajjati. Ghaṭṭanañca paṭhamajavanādīsupi labbhateva. Ghaṭṭanaṃ paccayavasena bhūtakalāpānaṃ aññamaññaṃ āsannataruppādo. Calanaṃ ekassāpi desantaruppādaparamparatāti ayametesaṃ viseso. Yathā ca vāyodhātuyā calanaṃ kiccaṃ, evaṃ pathavīdhātuyā ghaṭṭanaṃ. Tenevāha “pathavīdhātuyā upādinnaghaṭṭanassa paccayo”ti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Yathā hītiādi kāyavacīviññattīnaṃ anumānavasena gahetabbabhāvavibhāvanaṃ. Yathā hi ussāpetvā baddhagosīsādirūpāni disvā tadanantarappavattāya aviññāyamānantarāya manodvāravīthiyā gosīsādīnaṃ udakasahacārippakārasaññāṇākāraṃ gahetvā udakaggahaṇaṃ hoti, evaṃ vipphandamānasamuccāriyamānavaṇṇasadde gahetvā tadanantarapavattāya aviññāyamānantarāya manodvāravīthiyā purimasiddhasambandhagahaṇūpanissayasahitāya sādhippāyavikāraggahaṇaṃ hoti.

Now, the examination beginning with, “But whose alteration of appearance?” etc., should be understood by the method stated for bodily intimation. This, however, is the difference: just as there it was said, “immediately after apprehending the flickering form,” so here it should be connected as “immediately after hearing the audible sound.” And here, due to the absence of stiffening, etc., the method of “arising from the seventh javana impulse” and so on does not apply. For sound arises together with striking, and striking can indeed occur even during the first javana impulse and so on. Striking, in terms of condition, is the closer arising of material aggregates to each other. Movement is the successive arising in another location of even a single entity—this is their distinction. And just as movement is the function of the air element, so striking is the function of the earth element. Therefore, it is said, “The earth element is the condition for the appropriated striking.” The rest follows the same method as previously explained. The phrase “just as” etc. serves to clarify how bodily and verbal intimation are to be apprehended by inference. For just as, upon seeing shapes like raised and bound cow-heads, and immediately afterward, by the mind-door process that occurs without any intervening cognition, apprehending the characteristic sign of cow-heads etc. as a kind that accompanies water, there is the apprehension of water—so too, upon apprehending the flickering form and the uttered sound, and immediately afterward, by the mind-door process that occurs without any intervening cognition, accompanied by the decisive support of apprehending a previously established connection, there is the apprehension of the alteration with intention.

442. Rūpāni [M 2.0101] paricchindati, sayaṃ vā tehi paricchijjati, rūpānaṃ vā paricchedamattaṃ rūpaparicchedo, taṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etissāti rūpaparicchedalakkhaṇā. Ayaṃ hi ākāsadhātu taṃ taṃ rūpakalāpaṃ paricchindantī viya hoti. Tenāha “rūpapariyantappakāsanarasā”ti. Atthato pana yasmā rūpānaṃ paricchedamattaṃ hutvā gayhati, tasmā vuttaṃ “rūpamariyādapaccupaṭṭhānā”ti. Yasmiṃ kalāpe bhūtānaṃ paricchedo, teheva asamphuṭṭhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā. Vijjamānepi hi kalāpantarabhūtānaṃ kalāpantarabhūtehi samphuṭṭhabhāve taṃtaṃbhūtavivittatā rūpapariyanto ākāsoti yesaṃ so paricchedo, tehi so asamphuṭṭhova. Aññathā paricchinnatā na siyā tesaṃ bhūtānaṃ byāpibhāvāpattito. Abyāpitā hi asamphuṭṭhatā. Tenāha bhagavā “asamphuṭṭhaṃ catūhi mahābhūtehī”ti (dha. sa. 637, 724). Kaṇṇacchiddamukhavivarādivasena ca chiddavivarabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā vā. Yesaṃ rūpānaṃ paricchedo, tattheva tesaṃ paricchedabhāvena labbhatīti vuttaṃ “paricchinnarūpapadaṭṭhānā”ti. “Yāya paricchinnesū”tiādinā ākāsadhātuyā taṃtaṃkalāpānaṃ kalāpantarehi asaṅkarakāraṇataṃ dasseti.

442. It delimits matter, or is itself delimited by them, or is merely the delimitation of matter—this is the delimitation of matter. This is its characteristic; thus, it has the characteristic of delimiting matter. For this space element appears as if delimiting each respective material group. Therefore, he said: “Its function is to reveal the boundary of matter.” In meaning, however, because it is grasped as being merely the delimitation of matter, it is said: “Its manifestation is the boundary of matter.” In whichever material group there is the delimitation of the primary elements, its manifestation is the state of being untouched by those very primary elements. For even when there exists a state of contact of the primary elements of one material group with the primary elements of another, the separateness of each respective primary element—the boundary of matter, which is space—is the delimitation of those elements, and it is untouched by them. Otherwise, there would be no state of being delimited for those primary elements, due to their attaining a state of pervasiveness. For non-pervasiveness is indeed untouchedness. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “Untouched by the four great elements.” Alternatively, by way of ear-holes, mouth-apertures, and so on, its manifestation is the state of being a hole and an aperture. Because for whichever matter there is a delimitation, it is obtained right there as the state of delimitation for that matter, it is said: “Its proximate cause is delimited matter.” With the phrase “By which, in the delimited…” and so on, he shows that the space element is the cause for the non-confusion of each respective material group with other material groups.

443. Adandhatāti [V 2.0095] agarutā. Vinodanaṃ vikkhipanaṃ, apanayananti attho. Athaddhatāti akathinatā. Attano mudubhāveneva sabbakiriyāsu avirodhitā. Mudu hi katthaci na virujjhati. Tīsupi ṭhānesu paṭipakkhe a-kāro dandhatādihetūnaṃ paṭipakkhasamuṭṭhānattā lahutādīnanti keci. Apare pana “sattāpaṭisedhe”ti vadanti. Sarīrena kattabbakiriyānaṃ anukūlatāsaṅkhātakammaññabhāvo lakkhaṇaṃ etissāti sarīrakiriyānukūlakammaññabhāvalakkhaṇā. Akammaññaṃ dubbalaṃ nāma hotīti kammaññatā adubbalabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā vuttā.

443. ‘Adandhatā’ means non-sluggishness. ‘Vinodanaṃ’ means casting away, removing; this is the meaning. ‘Athaddhatā’ means non-stiffness. Due to its own softness, it is unopposed in all actions. Indeed, what is soft does not oppose anything anywhere. In all three instances, some say that the prefix ‘a-’ is in the sense of the opposite, because qualities such as lightness, etc., arise from the opposite of the causes of sluggishness, etc. Others, however, say it is in the sense of ‘negation of existence.’ The state of workability, which is termed suitability for actions to be performed by the body, is its characteristic; thus, it has the characteristic of the state of workability suitable for bodily actions. Because an unworkable thing is called weak, workability is said to have non-weakness as its manifestation.

Lahutādīnaṃ aññamaññāvijahanena duviññeyyanānattatā vuttāti taṃtaṃvikārādhikarūpehi taṃnānattappakāsanatthaṃ “evaṃ santepī”ti vuttaṃ. Dhātukkhobho vātapittasemhapakopo, rasādidhātūnaṃ vā vikārāvatthā. Dvidhā vuttopi atthato pathavīdhātuādīnaṃ dhātūnaṃyeva vikāroti daṭṭhabbo. Paṭipakkhapaccayā sappāyautuāhārāvikkhittacittatā. Te ca taṃtaṃvikārassa visesapaccayabhāvato vuttā, avisesena pana [M 2.0102] sabbe sabbesaṃ paccayā. Yato nesaṃ aññamaññāvijahanaṃ, iddhivaḷañjanādīsu viya vasavattanaṃ maddavappakāro. Suparimadditacammasudhantasuvaṇṇagahaṇañcettha mudukammaññasadisarūpanidassanamattaṃ, na taṃ idha adhippetaṃ mudutākammaññatāsabbhāvato. Na hi anindriyabaddharūpasantāne lahutādīni sambhavanti, indriyabaddhepi rūpabhave na santi dandhattakarādidhātukkhobhābhāvato. Sati hi tādise dhātukkhobhe tappaṭipakkhapaccayasamuṭṭhānāhi lahutādīhi bhavitabbanti keci, taṃ akāraṇaṃ. Na hi vūpasametabbapaccanīkāpekkho tabbirodhidhammasamuppādo, tathā sati sahetukakiriyacittuppādesu kāyalahutādīnaṃ abhāvova siyā. Kasmā pana kammajarūpesu lahutādayo na hontīti? Paccuppannapaccayāpekkhattā. Aññathā sabbadābhāvīhi lahutādīhi bhavitabbaṃ siyāti.

Because of the non-separation of lightness and so on from one another, their distinctness is said to be difficult to discern. Thus, the passage beginning with ‘even so’ is stated to reveal that distinctness by means of their respective forms which are predominant in particular alterations. ‘Disturbance of the elements’ refers to the corruption of wind, bile, and phlegm, or the state of disorder in the elements such as nutritive essence, etc. Though described in two ways, it should be understood in meaning as only the disturbance of the elements beginning with the earth element. The counteracting causes are suitable climate, food, and an undistracted mind. These are stated as specific causes for their respective alterations, but generally, all are causes for all. Since they do not abandon one another, mastery, as in the case of employing psychic power and so on, is a type of pliancy. And here, the mention of well-tanned leather and well-refined gold is merely an illustration of a similar form by way of softness and workability; that is not intended here, because of the non-existence of the qualities of softness and workability in them. For lightness and so on do not arise in a continuum of matter not connected with the sense faculties; and even in a continuum connected with the sense faculties, they do not exist in the form realm, because of the absence of the disturbance of elements that causes sluggishness and so on. Some argue that when such a disturbance of elements exists, lightness and similar qualities must arise from counteracting causes, but this is not a valid reason. For the arising of an opposing phenomenon is not dependent on the adversary that is to be pacified; if it were so, there would only be the absence of bodily lightness and so on in the arising of functional consciousness accompanied by roots. Why then do lightness and similar qualities not arise in kamma-born matter? Because they depend on present conditions. Otherwise, lightness and so on would have to be ever-present.

444. Ādi cayo, īsaṃ vā cayoti ācayo, yathāpaccayaṃ tato tato āgatassa viya cayoti vā ācayo, tadubhayaṃ ekajjhaṃ gahetvā ācayo lakkhaṇaṃ etassāti ācayalakkhaṇo. Rūpassa upacayo paṭhamuppādo, vaḍḍhi ca “upaññattaṃ upasitta”ntiādīsu viya upa-saddassa paṭhamūpariatthassa nidassanato. Pubbantatoti pubbakoṭṭhāsato, anāgatabhāvatoti attho. Uppajjamāne rūpadhamme uppādo anāgatakkhaṇato ummujjāpento viya hotīti vuttaṃ “ummujjāpanaraso”ti. Tathā so “ime rūpadhammā”ti niyyātento viya gayhatīti āha “niyyātanapaccupaṭṭhāno”ti. Paripuṇṇabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānatā “uparicayo upacayo”ti imassa atthassa vasena [V 2.0096] veditabbā. Pavattilakkhaṇāti rūpānaṃ pavattananti lakkhitabbā. Anuppabandhanarasāti pubbāparavasena anu anu pabandhanakiccā. Tato eva anupacchedavasena gahetabbato anupacchedapaccupaṭṭhānā.

444. Ācayo is initial arising, or slight arising. Or, ācayo is an arising as if coming from here and there according to conditions. Taking both these meanings together: accumulation is its characteristic; therefore, it is ācayalakkhaṇo (characterized by accumulation). The upacayo of material phenomena is its initial arising and growth, because in expressions such as “upaññattaṃ upasittaṃ,” the prefix upa- is seen to have the meaning of 'first' and 'above'. Pubbantato means from the prior part, that is, from the state of not yet having come into being. When a material phenomenon is arising, its arising is as if causing it to emerge from the future moment; therefore, it is said to have the function of causing to emerge. Similarly, it is apprehended as if delivering, “These are material phenomena”; therefore, it is said to have the manifestation of delivering. The manifestation of completeness should be understood by way of the meaning of this: “Arising above is upacayo (growth).” Pavattilakkhaṇā should be characterized as the continuous occurrence of produced material phenomena. Anuppabandhanarasā means having the function of continuous connection in succession. Therefore, because it is to be apprehended as being without interruption, it has the manifestation of non-interruption.

Ubhayampīti upacayo santatīti ubhayampi. Jātirūpassevāti rūpuppādasseva adhivacanaṃ. Yadi evaṃ kasmā vibhajja vuttāti āha “ākāranānattato”ti, jātirūpassa pavattiākārabhedatoti attho. Veneyyavasena vibhajjakathane kāraṇaṃ parato āvi bhavissati. Kathaṃ panetaṃ viññātabbaṃ, pavattiākāranānattato jātirūpassa bhedo, na sabhāvatoti[M 2.0103]? Niddesatoti dassento “yasmā panā”tiādimāha. Tattha yo āyatanānanti yo aḍḍhekādasannaṃ rūpāyatanānaṃ ādicayattā “ācayo”ti vutto. So eva upacayo paṭhamuppādabhāvato upa-saddo paṭhamatthoti katvā. Yo pana tattheva uppajjamānānaṃ upari cayattā upacayo, sā eva santati anupabandhavasena uppattibhāvato. Atha vā yo āyatanānaṃ ācayo paṭhamabhāvena upalakkhito uppādo, so pana tattheva uppajjamānānaṃ upari cayattā upacayo, vaḍḍhīti attho. Upacayo vaḍḍhibhāvena upalakkhito uppādo, sā eva santati pabandhākārena uppattibhāvato. Tenāha “aṭṭhakathāyampī”tiādi.

As for 'both' (ubhayampi): it means both growth (upacayo) and continuity (santati). 'Of birth-form' (jātirūpasseva) is a designation for the arising of form. If so, why is it stated separately? To this, it is said, 'Due to the diversity of aspects,' meaning, due to the difference in the mode of occurrence of birth-form. The reason for this separate explanation, according to the disposition of the disciples, will become clear later. Furthermore, how is this to be understood: that the distinction of birth-form is due to the diversity in the mode of occurrence, and not due to its intrinsic nature? Showing that this is to be understood through the detailed exposition (niddesa), he said, 'yasmā pana,' and so on. Therein, 'that of the bases' (yo āyatanānaṃ) refers to that which, due to being the initial accumulation of the eleven and a half form-bases, is called 'accumulation' (ācayo). That very thing is 'growth' (upacayo) because it is the initial arising, taking the prefix upa- to mean 'first'. Furthermore, that which is 'growth' (upacayo) due to the piling up of what arises there, that very thing is 'continuity' (santati) because of its nature of arising in an unbroken succession. Alternatively, that arising which is characterized by being first, called the 'accumulation' (ācayo) of the bases, is 'growth' (upacayo) due to the piling up of what arises there, meaning 'increase' (vaḍḍhi). The arising characterized by the state of increase is 'growth' (upacayo), and that very thing is 'continuity' (santati) because of its nature of arising in the manner of a continuous series. Therefore, he said, 'In the commentary too,' and so on.

Tattha evaṃ kiṃ kathitanti “yo āyatanānaṃ ācayo”tiādinā (dha. sa. 641) niddesena kiṃ atthajātaṃ kathitaṃ hoti? Āyatanena ācayo kathito. Ācayupacayasantatiyo hi nibbattibhāvena ācayo evāti āyatanehi ācayādīnaṃ pakāsitattā tehi ācayo kathito. Āyatanānaṃ ācayādivacaneneva ācayasabhāvāni uppādadhammāni āyatanānīti ācayena taṃpakatikaṃ āyatanaṃ kathitaṃ. Lakkhaṇañhi uppādo, na rūparūpanti.

Therein, what sort of meaning is stated by the detailed exposition beginning with, ‘that which is the accumulation of the bases,’ and so on? By 'base,' 'accumulation' is stated. Indeed, accumulation, growth, and continuity, by way of being an occurrence, are just accumulation. Thus, because accumulation and so on are made known by the bases, 'accumulation' is stated by them. By the very statement of 'accumulation and so on' of the bases, it is shown that the bases are things that arise, having the nature of accumulation. Thus, by 'accumulation,' the base which has that nature is stated. Indeed, arising is a characteristic, not the form-as-form.

Rūpaparipāko rūpadhammānaṃ jiṇṇatā. Upanayanarasāti bhaṅgupanayanakiccā. Sabhāvānapagamepīti kakkhaḷatādisabhāvassa avigamepi. Ṭhitikkhaṇe hi jarā, na ca tadā dhammo sabhāvaṃ vijahati nāma. Navabhāvo uppādāvatthā, tassa apagamabhāvena gayhatīti āha “navabhāvāpagamapaccupaṭṭhānā”ti. “Arūpadhammāna”nti idaṃ tesaṃ jarāya suṭṭhu paṭicchannatāya vuttaṃ. Rūpadhammānampi hi khaṇikajarā paṭicchannā eva, yā avīcijarātipi vuccati. Esa vikāroti khaṇḍiccādivikāramāha. So hi arūpadhammesu na labbhati. Yā avīcijarā nāma, tassāpi [V 2.0097] esa vikāro natthīti sambandhitabbaṃ. Natthi etissā jarāya vīcīti avīcijarā, navabhāvato duviññeyyantarajarāti attho.

The ripening of form is the agedness of material phenomena. Its function is that of leading to dissolution. 'Even in the non-departure of its own nature' means even when there is no departure from its nature, such as the state of hardness. For at the moment of duration there is aging, and at that time a phenomenon is said not to abandon its own nature. Newness is the stage of arising; it is grasped through the state of its departure. Therefore, it is said, 'it has as its manifestation the departure of newness.' The phrase 'of immaterial phenomena' is said because their aging is extremely concealed. Indeed, even of material phenomena, the momentary aging is concealed, which is also called 'uninterrupted aging.' By 'this alteration,' it refers to the alteration of broken teeth and so forth. For that is not found in immaterial phenomena. It should be connected thus: For that which is called uninterrupted aging, this alteration also does not exist. Because for this aging there is no interval (vīci), it is called 'uninterrupted aging' (avīcijarā); the meaning is: aging with an interval that is difficult to discern from the state of newness.

Parito sabbaso “bhijjana”nti lakkhitabbāti paribhedalakkhaṇā. Niccaṃ nāma dhuvaṃ, rūpaṃ pana khaṇabhaṅgitāya yena bhaṅgena na niccanti aniccaṃ, so aniccassa bhāvoti aniccatā. Sā pana yasmā ṭhitippattaṃ rūpaṃ vināsabhāvena [M 2.0104] saṃsīdantī viya hotīti vuttaṃ “saṃsīdanarasā”ti. Yasmā ca sā rūpadhammānaṃ bhaṅgabhāvato khayavayākāreneva gayhati, tasmā vuttaṃ “khayavayapaccupaṭṭhānā”ti.

Because it should be marked as 'breaking' in every way, it has the characteristic of shattering. What is called permanent is stable. But material form, on account of its momentary disintegration, is impermanent by that very disintegration through which it is not permanent; that state of being impermanent is impermanence. And since it is as if it causes material form that has reached the state of duration to sink down with a nature of destruction, it is said to have 'the function of collapsing.' And since it is grasped, from the state of disintegration of material phenomena, only in the mode of decay and vanishing, therefore it is said, 'it has as its manifestation decay and vanishing'.

445. Ojālakkhaṇoti ettha aṅgamaṅgānusārino rasassa sāro upathambhabalakaro bhūtanissito eko viseso ojā. Kabaḷaṃ karīyatīti kabaḷīkāro. Āharīyatīti āhāro, kabaḷaṃ katvā ajjhoharīyatīti attho. Idaṃ pana savatthukaṃ ojaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Bāhiraṃ āhāraṃ paccayaṃ labhitvā eva ajjhattikāhāro rūpaṃ uppādeti, so pana rūpaṃ āharatīti āhāro. Tenāha “rūpāharaṇaraso”ti. Tato eva ojaṭṭhamakarūpuppādanena imassa kāyassa upathambhanapaccupaṭṭhāno. Ojāya rūpāharaṇakiccaṃ bāhirādhīnanti āha “āharitabbavatthupadaṭṭhāno”ti.

445. Here, in this passage, nutriment (ojā) is a certain specific material quality, the essence of the nutritive sap that flows along the major and minor limbs, which produces supporting strength, and is dependent on the primary elements. Because it is made into a morsel, it is called kabaḷīkāra. Because it is brought, it is called āhāra; the meaning is that having been made into a morsel, it is consumed. This, however, is said to show nutriment together with its physical basis. Only having obtained external food as a condition does internal food produce material form. That internal food, however, brings forth material form; therefore, it is called āhāra. For that reason, it is said, 'its function is the bringing forth of material form.' Precisely because of that, through the production of the material octad with nutriment as the eighth, its manifestation for this body is support. The function of nutriment in bringing forth material form is dependent on the external; therefore, it is said, 'its proximate cause is the object to be brought'.

446. Balarūpantiādīsu imasmiṃ kāye balaṃ nāma atthi, sambhavo nāma atthi, rogo nāma atthi, “jāti sañjātī”ti (vibha. 191) vacanato jāti nāma atthi, tehipi catūhi mahābhūtehi vinā abhāvato upādāyarūpehi bhavitabbanti adhippāyo. Ekaccānanti abhayagirivāsīnaṃ. Paṭikkhittanti ettha evaṃ paṭikkhepo veditabbo – middhaṃ rūpameva na hoti nīvaraṇesu desitattā. Yassa hi nīvaraṇesu desanā, taṃ na rūpaṃ yathā kāmacchando. Siyā panetaṃ duvidhaṃ middhaṃ rūpaṃ, arūpañcāti. Tattha yaṃ arūpaṃ, taṃ nīvaraṇesu desitaṃ “na rūpa”nti? Taṃ na, visesavacanābhāvato. Na hi visesetvā middhaṃ nīvaraṇesu desitaṃ, tasmā middhassa duvidhataṃ parikappetvāpi na sakkā nīvaraṇabhāvaṃ nivattetuṃ. Sakkā hi vattuṃ “yaṃ taṃ arūpato aññaṃ middhaṃ parikappitaṃ, tampi nīvaraṇaṃ middhasabhāvattā itaraṃ middhaṃ viyā”ti.

446. In passages such as 'form as strength' (balarūpa), etc., in this body there is what is called strength, there is what is called semen, there is what is called disease, and according to the text 'birth is production,' there is what is called birth. The intention is that since these too do not exist without the four great elements, they must be derivative material forms. 'Of some' (ekaccānaṃ) means of the Abhayagirivāsins. Here, in the passage on 'is rejected' (paṭikkhittaṃ), the rejection should be understood thus: sloth is not material form at all, because it is taught among the hindrances. For whatever is taught among the hindrances, that is not material form, like sensual desire. It might be, however, that sloth is twofold: material and immaterial. Among them, is it that the immaterial sloth is taught among the hindrances, but not the material? That is not so, because there is no differentiating statement. For sloth is not taught among the hindrances by making a distinction. Therefore, even having conceived of the twofold nature of sloth, it is not possible to avert its nature as a hindrance. For it can be said: 'That other sloth which is conceived as different from the immaterial, that too is a hindrance due to its nature as sloth, just like the other sloth.'

Bhavatu [V 2.0098] nīvaraṇaṃ, ko virodhoti ce? Nīvaraṇañca pahātabbaṃ. Pañca nīvaraṇe pahāya “addhā munīsi sambuddho, natthi nīvaraṇā tavā”ti (su. ni. 546) vacanato. Appahātabbañca rūpaṃ “katame dhammā neva dassanena na bhāvanāya pahātabbā? Catūsu bhūmīsu kusalaṃ, catūsu bhūmīsu vipāko, tīsu bhūmīsu kiriyābyākataṃ, rūpañca nibbānañca. Ime dhammā neva dassanena na bhāvanāya pahātabbā”ti [M 2.0105] (dha. sa. 1407) vacanato. Na cettha tadārammaṇakilesappahānaṃ adhippetaṃ “rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ, taṃ pajahathā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.34) viya kāmacchandādīnaṃ tathā pahānassa anadhippetattā. Tasmā na middhaṃ rūpaṃ. Yadi middhassa rūpabhāvaṃ na sampaṭicchatha, kathaṃ bhagavato niddā. Middhañhi “niddāpacalāyikā”tiādinā vibhaṅge vibhattattā niddāti? Na middhaṃ niddā, niddāhetubhāvato pana taṃ “niddā”ti vibhattaṃ yathā itthiliṅgādi. Evampi niddāhetuno middhassa abhāvato kathaṃ bhagavato niddāti? Niddā bhagavato sarīragilāniyā, na middhena. Sā ca natthīti na sakkā vattuṃ “piṭṭhi me āgilāyati, tamahaṃ āyamissāmī”ti (ma. ni. 2.22) vacanato. Na cettha evamavadhāraṇaṃ middhameva niddāhetūti, niddāhetu eva middhanti evamavadhāraṇā. Tasmā aññopi atthi niddāhetu, ko pana soti? Sarīragilāniyā. Tena vuttaṃ “niddā bhagavato sarīragilāniyā, na middhenā”ti.

Let it be a hindrance. What is the contradiction, if you say so? And the hindrance is to be abandoned, because of the saying, “Having abandoned the five hindrances… Truly, you are a sage, fully awakened; there are no hindrances in you” (Sutta Nipāta 546). And material form is not to be abandoned, because of the saying, “Which phenomena are not to be abandoned by seeing or by developing? The wholesome in the four planes, the resultants in the four planes, the functional indeterminate in the three planes, material form, and Nibbāna. These phenomena are not to be abandoned by seeing or by developing” (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1407). And here, the abandonment of defilements that have that object is not intended, as in such statements as, “Monks, material form is not yours, abandon it” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.34), because the abandonment of sensual desire and so on in that way is not intended. Therefore, sloth is not material form. If you do not accept that sloth has the nature of material form, how is there sleep for the Blessed One? For since sloth is analyzed in the Vibhaṅga by such phrases as “sleep, drowsiness,” is it therefore sleep? Sloth is not sleep, but because it is a cause of sleep, it is analyzed as “sleep,” just as with feminine gender and so on. Even so, due to the absence of sloth, which is a cause of sleep, how is there sleep for the Blessed One? Sleep for the Blessed One is due to bodily fatigue, not due to sloth. And it cannot be said that this fatigue does not exist, because of the saying, “My back is tired, I will stretch it” (Majjhima Nikāya 2.22). And here, one should not make the determination that “sloth alone is the cause of sleep”; rather, the determination is that “sloth is only a cause of sleep.” Therefore, there is another cause of sleep. What is that? Bodily fatigue. Hence it was said, “Sleep for the Blessed One is due to bodily fatigue, not due to sloth.”

Niddā ca bhagavato natthīti na sakkā vattuṃ “abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ aggivessana…pe… divā supitā”ti (ma. ni. 1.387) vacanato. Itopi na middhaṃ rūpaṃ sampayogavacanato. Vuttañhi “thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ avijjānīvaraṇena nīvaraṇañceva nīvaraṇasampayuttañcā”tiādi (dha. sa. 1176). Na cettha yathālābhabhavanaṃ? Sakkā paccetuṃ “sakkharakathalikampi macchagumbampi carantampi tiṭṭhantampī”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.249) viya appasiddhatāya rūpabhāvassa. Siddhe hi tassa rūpabhāve sambhavato yathālābhapaccayo yujjeyyāti. Itopi na rūpaṃ middhaṃ āruppesu uppajjanato. Vuttampi cetaṃ “nīvaraṇaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca nīvaraṇo dhammo uppajjati napurejātapaccayā”ti (paṭṭhā. 3.8.8) imassa vibhaṅge “āruppe kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ paṭicca thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ uddhaccanīvaraṇaṃ avijjānīvaraṇaṃ uppajjatī”ti vitthāro. Tasmā “na middhaṃ rūpa”nti yaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu paṭikkhittaṃ, taṃ supaṭikkhittameva.

And that the Blessed One has no sleep—this cannot be said, because of the statement: "I indeed recall, Aggivessana... having slept during the day" (MN 1.387). Also for this reason, sloth is not material form: because it is spoken of in terms of association. For it has been said: "The hindrance of sloth and torpor is both a hindrance and is associated with the hindrance of ignorance," and so on (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1176). And here, it is not possible to accept the principle of 'being in accordance with what is obtained'—as in the cases of 'gravel and potsherds,' 'a shoal of fish,' 'that which is moving,' and 'that which is standing still,' etc. (DN 1.249)—due to the unestablished nature of its being material form. For if its nature as material form were established, then because it would be possible, the acceptance in accordance with what is obtained would be suitable. Also for this reason, sloth is not material form: because it arises in the formless realms. And this was also stated: In the exposition of this question, "Depending on a hindrance-state, does a hindrance-state arise not by the pre-nascence condition?" (Paṭṭhāna 3.8.8), it is elaborated: "In the formless realm, depending on the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness, and the hindrance of ignorance arise." Therefore, the rejection in the commentaries, which concludes, "Sloth is not material form," is indeed a good rejection.

Itaresūti [V 2.0099] balarūpādīsu. Kammasamuṭṭhānassāpi rogassa visabhāgapaccayasamuppanno dhātukkhobho āsannakāraṇaṃ, pageva itarassa. So ca atthato rūpadhammānaṃ vikārāvatthāṭhitibhaṅgakkhaṇesu eva siyāti vuttaṃ “rogarūpaṃ jaratāaniccatāgahaṇena gahitamevā”ti. Upacayasantatigahaṇena gahitamevāti tabbinimuttassa rūpuppādassa abhāvato. Upādāvatthāya [M 2.0106] ca aññā jāti nāma nattheva. Sambhavo kāmadhātuyaṃ ekacciyasattānaṃ indriyaparipākapaccayo āpodhātuyā pavattiākāravisesoti āha “sambhavarūpaṃ āpodhātuggahaṇena gahitamevā”ti. Kāyabalaṃ nāma atthato vāyodhātuyā pavattiākāraviseso tassā vipphārabhāvato. Yato naṃ “pāṇabala”nti vadanti, tenāha “balarūpaṃ vāyodhātuggahaṇena gahitamevā”ti. Kasmā pana nesaṃ ayathākkamato paṭikkhepo katoti? Visuṃ natthīti katvā anupalabbhamānattā anādaradassanatthaṃ, middhapaṭikkhepo vā mahāpañhoti paṭhamaṃ kato. Tadanusārena paṭilomanayena itaresampi abhāvo vuttoti veditabbaṃ.

As for the others, this means in strength-materiality and so on. For a disease arising from kamma also, the disturbance of elements produced by incompatible conditions is the proximate cause; how much more so for another. And that, in essence, can occur only at the moments of the state of alteration, duration, and dissolution of material phenomena. Thus it is said: “The materiality of sickness is already included by the grasping of aging and impermanence.” It is already included by the grasping of accumulation and continuity because of the absence of the arising of materiality apart from them. And apart from the state of arising, there is indeed no other so-called birth. Origin is a particular mode of occurrence of the water element, which is a condition for the maturity of the faculties for some beings in the desire realm; therefore, he said: “The materiality of origin is already included by the grasping of the water element.” So-called bodily strength is, in essence, a particular mode of occurrence of the wind element due to its nature of distension. Since they call it “life-force strength,” therefore he said: “The materiality of strength is already included by the grasping of the wind element.” But why was their rejection made out of order? Because they do not exist separately, and because they are not found separately, it is for the purpose of showing disregard. Or, the rejection of sloth was made first because it is a great problem. It should be understood that, following that, the absence of the others was also stated in reverse order.

“Itī”ti idaṃ “aṭṭhavīsatividha”nti iminā sambandhitabbaṃ, iminā vuttakkamena aṭṭhavīsatividhaṃ hotīti. So ca kho pāḷiyaṃ āgatanayenevāti anūnatā veditabbā. Anadhikabhāvo pana dassito eva.

This word 'iti' (thus) should be connected with 'aṭṭhavīsatividhaṃ' (twenty-eightfold) as follows: 'By this stated sequence, it is twenty-eightfold.' And indeed, that division is just according to the method found in the Pāḷi; thus, its completeness should be understood. Furthermore, its non-excess has already been shown.

447. Sampayuttadhammarāsi hinoti etena patiṭṭhahatīhi hetu, mūlaṭṭhena lobhādiko, alobhādiko ca, tādiso hetu na hotīti nahetu. Nāssa hetu atthīti ahetukaṃ, sahetukapaṭiyogibhāvato hetunā saha na uppajjatīti attho. Ahetukameva hetunā vippayuttatāya hetuvippayuttaṃ. Dhammanānattābhāvepi hi saddatthanānattena veneyyavasena dukantaradesanā hotīti dukapadavasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Paccayādhīnavuttitāya saha paccayenāti sappaccayaṃ. Attano paccayehi loke niyuttaṃ, viditanti vā lokiyaṃ. Ā bhavaggaṃ, ā gotrabhuṃ vā savantīti āsavā, saha āsavehīti sāsavaṃ, āsavehi ālambitabbanti attho. Ādisaddena saṃyojanīyaṃ oghanīyaṃ yoganīyaṃ nīvaraṇīyaṃ saṃkilesikaṃ parāmaṭṭhaṃ acetasikaṃ cittavippayuttaṃ narūpāvacaraṃ naarūpāvacaraṃ naapariyāpannaṃ aniyataṃ aniyyānikaṃ aniccanti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

447. 'Cause' (hetu) is so called because by it the collection of associated states is firmly established. In the sense of a root, greed and the like, and non-greed and the like are also 'causes'. Because such a cause is not, it is 'not a cause' (nahetu). Because it has no cause, it is 'causeless' (ahetukaṃ); because it is the counterpart of that which has a cause, the meaning is that it does not arise together with a cause. The causeless itself, because of being dissociated from a cause, is 'dissociated from a cause' (hetuvippayuttaṃ). For even when there is no diversity of states, a teaching of another couplet occurs due to the diversity of terms and meanings, according to the capacity of those to be trained; therefore, this is also stated by way of a couplet-term. Because its occurrence is dependent on conditions, it is 'with a condition', hence 'conditioned' (sappaccayaṃ). It is appointed in the world by its own conditions, or it is known in the world, thus it is 'worldly' (lokiyaṃ). They flow up to the peak of existence or up to the change-of-lineage; therefore, they are 'taints' (āsavā). 'Together with taints', thus 'with taints' (sāsavaṃ); the meaning is 'that which is taken as an object by the taints'. By the word 'etc.', the inclusion of the following should be understood: that which pertains to the fetters (saṃyojanīyaṃ), that which pertains to the floods (oghanīyaṃ), that which pertains to the yokes (yoganīyaṃ), that which pertains to the hindrances (nīvaraṇīyaṃ), that which pertains to defilements (saṃkilesikaṃ), that which is wrongly grasped (parāmaṭṭhaṃ), non-mental (acetasikaṃ), dissociated from mind (cittavippayuttaṃ), not of the fine-material sphere (narūpāvacaraṃ), not of the immaterial sphere (naarūpāvacaraṃ), not included (naapariyāpannaṃ), indeterminate (aniyataṃ), not leading out (aniyyānikaṃ), and impermanent (aniccaṃ).

Āhito ahaṃ māno etthāti attā, attabhāvo. Taṃ attānaṃ adhikicca uddissa pavattā ajjhattā[V 2.0100], indriyabaddhadhammā, tesu bhavaṃ ajjhattikaṃ, cakkhādi. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana vuttanayena ajjhattameva ajjhattikaṃ yathā venayikoti [M 2.0107] (a. ni. 8.11; pārā. 8) imamatthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “attabhāvaṃ adhikicca pavattattā ajjhattika”nti. Sesaṃ tevīsatividhaṃ. “Tato bāhirattā”ti idaṃ ajjhattikalakkhaṇābhāvato vuttaṃ. Ghaṭṭanavasenāti visayī, visayo ca hutvā saṅghaṭṭanavasena. Sesaṃ soḷasavidhaṃ. Viparītattāti ghaṭṭanavasena agahetabbato. Duppaṭivijjhasabhāvattāti sukhumabhāvena duviññeyyasabhāvattā. Ñāṇassa āsanne na hotīti dūre. Terasa hadayavatthupariyosānāni. Sabhāvenevāti “rūpassa paricchedo, rūpassa vikāro, rūpassa upacayo”tiādinā aggahetvā attano sabhāveneva kakkhaḷattādinā ñāṇena paricchijja gahetabbato. Sesaṃ dasavidhaṃ. Tabbiparītatāyāti sabhāvena apariggahitabbato. Sotādīnampi cakkhuno viya pasannasabhāvattā eva yathāsakaṃ visayaggahaṇapaccayatāti dassento āha “cakkhādi…pe… pasādarūpa”nti. Viparītattāti tabbidhurasabhāvattā. Adhipatiyaṭṭhenāti ettha cakkhādīnaṃ tāva pañcannaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīsu ādhipateyyaṃ tesaṃ paṭumandabhāvānuvattanato, itthipurisindriyadvayassa sakicce jīvitindriyassa sahajarūpānupālane. Tadubhayaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Upādinnattāti gahitattā. Kammanibbattañhi “mametaṃ phalaṃ”nti kammunā gahitaṃ viya hoti apaṭikkhepato.

Because the conceit 'I am' is placed herein, it is called 'attā' (self); it is individual existence (attabhāvo). The dhammas that arise in reference to that self are internal (ajjhattā); they are dhammas connected with the sense faculties. That which occurs among them is internal (ajjhattikaṃ), such as the eye, etc. In the commentary, however, it is explained that the internal is indeed internal, just as in the case of 'venayiko'. With reference to this meaning, it was said: 'Because it arises in reference to individual existence, it is internal.' The remaining are of twenty-three kinds. 'Because of being external to that'—this was said due to the absence of the characteristic of the internal. 'By way of impact' means: by way of collision, having become both the subject (faculty) and the object. The remaining are of sixteen kinds. 'Because of being the opposite' means: because of not being graspable by way of impact. 'Because of having a nature difficult to penetrate' means: due to its subtlety, because of having a nature that is difficult to cognize. 'It is not near to knowledge,' therefore it is 'far.' Thirteen end with the heart-base. 'By its own nature alone' means: because it is to be grasped by knowledge through delimitation by its own nature alone, such as hardness, etc., without grasping it as 'delimitation of materiality, alteration of materiality, accumulation of materiality,' and so forth. The remaining are of ten kinds. 'Because of being the opposite of that' means: because of not being graspable by its own nature. Showing that for the ear, etc., just as for the eye, it is the condition for apprehending its respective object precisely because of its clear nature, he said: 'the eye... etc... sensitive materiality.' 'Because of being the opposite' means: because of having a nature dissimilar to that. 'In the sense of dominance'—herein, firstly, the five faculties (eye, etc.) have dominance over eye-consciousness, etc., because they conform to their sharp or dull nature; the two faculties of femininity and masculinity, in their respective functions; and the life faculty, in sustaining co-nascent materiality. Both of these have been explained previously. 'Because of being clung to' means: because of being grasped. Indeed, karma-produced materiality is as if grasped by karma as 'this is my fruit,' due to non-rejection.

448. Sanidassanakammajādīnaṃ tikānanti sanidassanattikassa, kammajādittikānañca. Oḷāriketi dvādasavidhe oḷārikarūpe. Rūpanti rūpāyatanaṃ. Daṭṭhabbabhāvasaṅkhātena saha nidassanenāti sanidassanaṃ, paṭihananabhāvasaṅkhātena saha paṭighenāti sappaṭighaṃ, sanidassanañca taṃ sappaṭighañcāti sanidassanasappaṭighaṃ. Tattha yassa daṭṭhabbabhāvo atthi, taṃ sanidassanaṃ. Cakkhuviññāṇagocarabhāvova daṭṭhabbabhāvo. Tassa rūpāyatanato anaññattepi aññehi dhammehi rūpāyatanaṃ visesetuṃ aññaṃ viya katvā vuttaṃ “saha nidassanena sanidassana”nti. Dhammabhāvasāmaññena hi ekībhūtesu dhammesu yo nānattakaro viseso, so añño viya katvā upacarituṃ yutto. Evaṃ hi atthavisesāvabodho hotīti. Yo sayaṃ, nissayavasena ca sampattānaṃ, asampattānañca paṭimukhabhāvo aññamaññaṃ patanaṃ, so paṭihananabhāvo, yena byāpārādivikārapaccayantarasahitesu cakkhādīnaṃ [M 2.0108] visayesu vikāruppatti. Sesaṃ ekādasavidhaṃ oḷārikarūpaṃ. Tañhi sanidassanattābhāvato anidassanaṃ, vuttanayeneva sappaṭighaṃ. Ubhayapaṭikkhepena anidassanaappaṭighaṃ. Kammato jātanti ettha yaṃ ekantakammasamuṭṭhānaṃ aṭṭhindriyāni, hadayañcāti navavidhaṃ rūpaṃ, yañca navavidhe catusamuṭṭhāne kammasamuṭṭhānaṃ navavidhameva rūpanti [V 2.0101] evaṃ aṭṭhārasavidhampi kammato uppajjanato kammajaṃ. Yañhi jātañca yañca jāyati yañca jāyissati, taṃ sabbampi “kammaja”nti vuccati yathā duddhanti. Tadaññapaccayajātanti kammato aññapaccayato jātaṃ utucittāhārajaṃ. Nakutocijātanti lakkhaṇarūpamāha. Viññattidvayaṃ, saddo, ākāsadhātu, lahutādittayaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānāni avinibbhogarūpānīti etaṃ pañcadasavidhaṃ rūpaṃ cittajaṃ. Ākāsadhātu, lahutādittayaṃ, āhārasamuṭṭhānāni avinibbhogarūpānīti etaṃ dvādasavidhaṃ rūpaṃ āhārajaṃ. Ettha saddaṃ pakkhipitvā terasavidhaṃ rūpaṃ ututo samuṭṭhitaṃ utujaṃ. Sesaṃ kammajatike vuttanayānusāreneva veditabbaṃ.

448. The triads of the visible, kamma-born, etc., refer to the triad of the visible and the triads of the kamma-born and so forth. Regarding 'gross' (oḷārika), this is in the context of the twelve types of gross matter. By 'form' (rūpa) is meant the form-base. Sanidassana (visible) means: it exists together with visibility (nidassana), which is designated as the state of being seeable. Sappaṭigha (with impact) means: it exists together with impact (paṭigha), which is designated as the state of impinging. Sanidassanasappaṭigha (visible and with impact) means: it is sanidassana and it is sappaṭigha. Herein, whatever has the state of being seeable is 'visible' (sanidassana). The state of being an object for eye-consciousness is precisely the state of being seeable. Although that state of being seeable is not other than the form-base, in order to distinguish the form-base from other phenomena, it is spoken of as if it were something else, thus: 'it is sanidassana because it is together with visibility.' For among phenomena that are unified by the commonality of their nature, a distinction that creates diversity is suitably treated figuratively as if it were something else. In this way, an understanding of a special meaning arises. The state of impinging is that state of confrontation, the falling upon one another, of things that have arrived (are in contact) and have not arrived (are not in contact), either by themselves or by way of a support. By this, an alteration arises in the supports of the eye, etc., when they are accompanied by other conditions which are the alteration of activity and so forth. The remaining eleven types of gross matter are 'invisible' (anidassana) because of the absence of visibility, and 'with impact' (sappaṭigha) in the manner already stated. By the rejection of both, they are 'invisible and without impact' (anidassana-appaṭigha). In the phrase 'born from kamma' (kammato jāta): here, the nine-fold matter that is exclusively kamma-originated—namely, the eight faculties and the heart-base—and also the nine-fold matter that is kamma-originated among that which has four origins; thus, all eighteen types are 'kamma-born' (kammaja) because they arise from kamma. Indeed, whatever has been born, is being born, or will be born—all of it is called 'kamma-born,' just as with the term duddha (milked). 'Born from other conditions' refers to that which is born from a condition other than kamma, namely, that which is born of temperature, consciousness, and nutriment. 'Not born from anything' refers to characteristic-matter. The two intimations, sound, the space element, the triad of lightness, etc., and the consciousness-originated inseparable matter—this fifteen-fold matter is consciousness-born (cittaja). The space element, the triad of lightness, etc., and the nutriment-originated inseparable matter—this twelve-fold matter is nutriment-born (āhāraja). Herein, by including sound, the thirteen-fold matter that has arisen from temperature is temperature-born (utuja). The remainder should be understood according to the method stated in the kamma-born triad.

449. Diṭṭhādicatukkavasena, rūparūpādicatukkavasena, vatthādicatukkavasenāti pāṭekkaṃ catukkasaddo yojetabbo. Yaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ adakkhi yaṃ passati yaṃ dakkhissati yaṃ passeyya, taṃ sabbaṃ diṭṭhaṃ nāma diṭṭhasabhāvānātivattanato yathā duddhanti. Esa nayo sesesupi. Dassanavisayattāti cakkhuviññāṇaviññeyyattā. Savanavisayattāti sotaviññāṇaviññeyyattā. Gandharasaphoṭṭhabbattayanti gandho raso phoṭṭhabbanti etaṃ tayaṃ. Mutaṃ nāma mutvā patvā gahetabbato. Tenāha “sampattaggāhakaindriyavisayattā”ti.

449. The term 'tetrad' should be applied individually: by way of the tetrad of the seen, etc.; by way of the tetrad of rūparūpa, etc.; and by way of the tetrad of the base, etc. Whatever form-base one has seen, is seeing, will see, or might see—all that is called 'diṭṭha' (seen) because it does not transcend the nature of the seen, just as with the term 'duddha' (milk). This same principle applies to the remaining terms. 'Because it is an object of sight' means because it is knowable by eye-consciousness. 'Because it is an object of hearing' means because it is knowable by ear-consciousness. 'The state of being odor, taste, and tangible object' refers to this triad: odor, taste, and tangible object. This is called 'muta' because it is to be grasped by having been contacted. Hence it is said: 'because it is the object of the sense faculties that grasp by attainment.'

Kimidaṃ phoṭṭhabbaṃ nāmāti? Pathavītejovāyodhātuttayaṃ. Kasmā panettha āpodhātu aggahitā, nanu sītatā phusitvā gayhati, sā ca āpodhātūti? Saccaṃ gayhati, na pana sā āpodhātu. Kiñcarahīti? Tejodhātu eva. Mande hi uṇhabhāve sītabuddhi. Na hi sītaṃ nāma koci guṇo atthi, kevalaṃ pana uṇhabhāvassa mandatāya sītatābhimāno. Kathametaṃ viññātabbanti ce? Anavaṭṭhitattā sītabuddhiyā yathā pārāpāre. Tathā hi ghammakāle ātape ṭhitānaṃ chāyaṃ paviṭṭhānaṃ sītabuddhi hoti, tattheva pana pathavīgabbhato uṭṭhitānaṃ uṇhabuddhi. Yadi hi sītatā āpodhātu siyā, ekasmiṃ kalāpe uṇhabhāvena saddhiṃ upalabbheyya, na ca upalabbhati. Tasmā viññāyati na āpodhātu sītatāti[M 2.0109]. Idañca bhūtānaṃ avinibbhogavuttitaṃ icchantānaṃ uttaraṃ, anicchantānampi pana catunnaṃ bhūtānaṃ ekasmiṃ kalāpe kiccadassanena sabhāgavuttitāya sādhitāya uttarameva. Ye pana “vāyodhātuyā lakkhaṇaṃ sītatā”ti vadanti, tesampi idameva uttaraṃ. Yadi hi vāyodhātu sītatā siyā, ekasmiṃ kalāpe uṇhabhāvena saddhiṃ sītatā upalabbheyya, na ca upalabbhati. Tasmā viññāyati na vāyodhātu sītatāti. Yesaṃ pana dravatā āpodhātu, sā ca phusitvā [V 2.0102] gayhatīti dassanaṃ. Te vattabbā “dravabhāvopi phusīyatīti āyasmantānaṃ adhimānamattaṃ saṇṭhānaṃ viyā”ti. Vuttañhetaṃ purātanehi –

What is this called the tangible object? It is the triad of elements: earth, fire, and air. Why is the water element not taken here? Is not coldness grasped by touching, and is not that the water element? It is true that it is grasped, but that is not the water element. What then is it? It is only the fire element. For when the state of heat is weak, there is the perception of cold. Indeed, there is no quality called 'cold'; it is merely a conceit of coldness due to the weakness of the state of heat. If it is asked how this is to be understood, it is by the instability of the perception of cold, as on the near and far banks. For in the hot season, for those who have stood in the sun and entered the shade, there is a perception of cold; but for those who have come up from an underground chamber, in that very same place there is a perception of heat. For if coldness were the water element, it would be found together with heat in a single material group, but it is not so found. Therefore, it is understood that coldness is not the water element. And this is the answer for those who accept the inseparable nature of the primary elements. But even for those who do not accept it, since the common nature of the four primary elements has been established by seeing their function in a single material group, it is indeed the answer. As for those who say, 'Coldness is the characteristic of the air element,' for them too, this very same thing is the answer. For if the air element were coldness, coldness would be found together with heat in a single material group, but it is not so found. Therefore, it is understood that coldness is not the air element. As for those whose view is that fluidity is the water element, and that it is grasped by touching, they should be told: 'Venerable sirs, the notion that the state of fluidity is also touched is merely a conceit on your part, just as it is with shape.' For this was said by the ancients—

“Dravatā sahavuttīni, tīṇi bhūtāni samphusaṃ;

‘Dravataṃ samphusāmī’ti, lokoyamabhimaññati.

Touching the three elements that co-exist with fluidity, this world conceives, 'I touch fluidity.'

“Phusaṃ bhūtāni saṇṭhānaṃ, manasā gaṇhate yathā;

‘Paccakkhato phusāmī’ti, ñātabbā dravatā tathā”ti.

Just as one, while touching the primary elements, grasps shape with the mind, thinking, 'I touch it directly,' so too should fluidity be understood.

Sesanti yathāvuttaṃ rūpādisattavidhaṃ rūpaṃ ṭhapetvā avasiṭṭhaṃ ekavīsatividhaṃ rūpaṃ. Viññāṇassevāti manoviññāṇasseva. Avadhāraṇena rūpāyatanādīnampi manoviññāṇaviññeyyatte niyamābhāvato na viññātarūpatāti saṅkarābhāvaṃ dasseti.

“The remaining” refers to the twenty-one kinds of form that are left after setting aside the seven kinds of form beginning with the form-object, as has been stated. `Viññāṇasseva` means “of mind-consciousness only.” By this limitation, it shows the absence of conflation thus: although the form-base and so on are knowable by mind-consciousness, due to the absence of a fixed rule, they do not have the state of being a known-form.

Nipphannarūpaṃ panettha rūparūpaṃ nāmāti yadettha aṭṭhavīsatividhe rūpe “nipphanna”nti vuttaṃ rūpaṃ, tadeva rūpalakkhaṇayogato rūpaṃ. Ruppanaṃ rūpaṃ, taṃ etassa atthīti yathā arisasoti, rūpaguṇayogato vā yathā nīlaguṇayogato nīlaṃ vatthanti. Svāyaṃ rūpasaddo ruḷhiyā ataṃsabhāvepi pavattatīti aparena rūpasaddena visesetvā vuttaṃ “rūparūpa”nti yathā tilatelaṃ, dukkhadukkhanti (visuddhi. 2.539) ca, ruppanasabhāvaṃ rūpanti attho. Yadi evaṃ, ākāsadhātuādīnaṃ kathaṃ rūpabhāvoti? Nipphannarūpassa paricchedavikāralakkhaṇabhāvato taggatikamevāti “rūpa”ntveva vuccati.

As for `nipphannarūpaṃ...nāma`: among these twenty-eight kinds of form, that form which is called 'produced' (`nipphanna`), that very form is `rūpa` due to its connection with the characteristic of transformation. `Ruppana` is transformation; because this form possesses that, it is called `rūpa`, just as in `arisaso`. Or, it is called `rūpa` due to its connection with the quality of transformation, just as a cloth is called 'blue' due to its connection with the quality of blue. Because this word `rūpa` also occurs by convention even in a state that does not have that nature of transformation, it is distinguished by another word `rūpa` and is called `rūparūpa`, just as in `tilatela` (sesame oil) and `dukkhadukkha` (suffering that is suffering). The meaning is: form which has the nature of transformation. If it is so, how can the space element and so on have the state of form? Because they are the delimitation, modification, and characteristic of produced form, they are of the same nature as that produced form; therefore, they are called just 'rūpa'.

Vasanti ettha cittacetasikā pavattantīti vatthu, cittataṃsampayuttānaṃ ādhārabhūtaṃ rūpaṃ. Taṃ pana chabbidhaṃ. Tattha hadayarūpaṃ vatthu eva manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātūnaṃ nissayabhāvato. Na dvāraṃ aññanissayānaṃ cakkhādi viya. Yathā hi cakkhādīni sampaṭicchanādīnaṃ pavattiyā dvāraṃ honti, na [M 2.0110] evaṃ hadayavatthu. Tena vuttaṃ “yaṃ panettha hadayarūpaṃ nāma, taṃ vatthu, na dvāra”nti. Viññattidvayaṃ dvāraṃ kammadvārabhāvato. Tannissitassa cittuppādassa abhāvato na vatthu. Pasādarūpaṃ vatthu ceva attasannissitassa cakkhuviññāṇādikassa, dvārañca aññanissitassa sampaṭicchanādikassa. Sesaṃ ekavīsatividhaṃ rūpaṃ vuttavipariyāyato neva vatthu na ca dvāraṃ.

Because consciousness and mental factors dwell (`vasanti`) and occur (`pavattanti`) here (`ettha`), it is called a basis (`vatthu`); it is the form that is the support for consciousness and its concomitants. That basis-form, however, is of six kinds. Among them, the heart-form is a basis only, because it is the support for the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element. It is not a door for other consciousnesses that have other supports, like the eye and so on. For just as the eye and so on are a door for the arising of receiving-consciousness and so on, the heart-basis is not so. Therefore it is said: 'That which herein is called heart-form, that is a basis, not a door.' The two intimations are a door because they are a door of kamma. Because of the absence of the arising of consciousness that is dependent on them, they are not a basis. The sensitive form is both a basis for eye-consciousness and so on, which is dependent on itself, and a door for receiving-consciousness and so on, which is dependent on another. The remaining twenty-one kinds of form, by the reverse of what has been stated, are neither a basis nor a door.

450. Ekato [V 2.0103] eva jātaṃ ekajaṃ. Nanu ca ekato eva paccayato paccayuppannassa uppatti natthīti? Saccaṃ natthi, rūpajanakapaccayesu ekatoti ayamettha adhippāyo. Na hi rūpuppatti rūpajanakato aññaṃ paccayaṃ apekkhati. Dvijantiādīsupi eseva nayo. Imesanti imesaṃ pabhedānaṃ vasena. Kammajamevāti kammato eva jātaṃ. Cittajamevāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Cittato ca ututo ca jātanti kālena cittato, kālena ututoti evaṃ cittato ca ututo ca jātaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Taṃ dvijaṃ dvīhi jātanti. Parato dvīsupi eseva nayo. Saddāyatanamevāti ettha yaṃ cittajaṃ saddāyatanaṃ, taṃ saviññattikamevāti eke. Aviññattikopi atthi vitakkavipphārasaddoti porāṇā.

450. That which is born from one cause alone is `ekajaṃ` (singly-born). Is it not so that there is no arising of a conditionally-arisen phenomenon from one cause alone? It is true that there is not. Here, the meaning of 'from one' is 'from one among the conditions that generate materiality.' For the arising of materiality does not depend on a condition other than that which generates materiality. The same principle applies to `dvijaṃ` (twice-born) and so forth. `Imesaṃ` (of these) means by way of these divisions. `Kammajameva` (born from kamma only) means born from kamma alone. In `cittajameva` (born from consciousness only) also, the same principle applies. `Cittato ca ututo ca jātaṃ` (born from consciousness and from temperature) should be understood thus: at one time from consciousness, at another time from temperature; thus, born from consciousness and from temperature. That is `dvijaṃ` (twice-born) because it is born from two. The same principle applies to the subsequent two terms as well. Here, in `saddāyatanameva` (only the sound-base), some say that the sound-base which is born of consciousness is only that which is accompanied by intimation. The ancients say there is also the sound of the diffusion of thought, which is without intimation.

Vitakkavipphārasaddo na sotaviññeyyoti hi evaṃ pavattamahāaṭṭhakathāvādaṃ nissāya cittasamuṭṭhānassa saddassa viññattiyā vināpi uppatti icchitabbā. Na hi viññatti “kāyavācāya viññattī”ti vacanato asotaviññeyyena saddena saha uppajjati, evaṃ sante cittajenāpi saddanavakena bhavitabbaṃ. So ca vādo “saddo ca hoti, na sotaviññeyyo cā”ti viruddhamevetanti maññamānehi saṅgahakārehi paṭikkhitto. Apare pana mahāaṭṭhakathāvādaṃ appaṭikkhipitvā tassa adhippāyaṃ vaṇṇenti. Kathaṃ? “Jivhātālucalanādikaṃ vitakkasamuṭṭhitaṃ viññattisahajameva sukhumasaddaṃ dibbasotena sutvā ādisatī”ti sutte, paṭṭhāne ca oḷārikaṃ saddaṃ sandhāya sotaviññāṇassa ārammaṇapaccayabhāvo vuttoti iminā adhippāyena vitakkavipphārasaddassa asotaviññeyyatā vuttāti. Taṃ catujaṃ. Avasesanti avinibbhogarūpena saddhiṃ ākāsadhātumāha.

Indeed, relying on the established doctrine of the Great Commentary that 'the sound of the diffusion of thought is not cognizable by ear-consciousness,' the arising of sound produced by consciousness, even without intimation, should be accepted. For intimation, according to the saying 'intimation by means of body and speech,' does not arise together with a sound that is not cognizable by ear-consciousness. This being so, even the consciousness-born kalāpa would have to be a sound-nonad. And that doctrine—'there is sound, and it is not cognizable by ear-consciousness'—was rejected by the compilers of the compendium, who considered this to be a contradiction. But other teachers, not rejecting the doctrine of the Great Commentary, explain its meaning. How? In the Sutta it is said: 'Having heard with the divine ear the subtle sound—which is arisen from thought that causes the movement of the tongue, palate, etc., and is accompanied by intimation—one declares it.' And in the Paṭṭhāna, the status of being an object-condition for ear-consciousness is stated with reference to gross sound. With this meaning, the non-cognizability by ear of the sound of the diffusion of thought is stated. That is four-born. By 'the remainder' (avasesa), he speaks of the space element together with the inseparable material phenomena.

Lakkhaṇarūpaṃ [M 2.0111] pana nakutocijātanti kutocipi paccayato na jātaṃ, nāpi sayameva jātaṃ paccayehi vinā sayameva jātassa sabbena sabbaṃ abhāvato. Kathaṃ panetaṃ viññātabbaṃ lakkhaṇarūpaṃ na jāyatīti? Lakkhaṇābhāvato. Uppattimantānaṃ hi rūpāyatanādīnaṃ jātiādīni lakkhaṇāni vijjanti, na evaṃ jātiādīnaṃ. Tasmā viññātabbametaṃ jātiādīni na jāyantīti. Siyā panetaṃ “jātiādīnaṃ jātiādīni lakkhaṇāni vijjantī”ti? Taṃ na, kasmā? Tathā sati anavaṭṭhānāpattito. Yadi hi jātiādīni jātiādimantāni siyuṃ, tānipi jātiādimantāni, tānipi jātiādimantānīti anavaṭṭhānameva āpajjati. Tasmā suṭṭhu vuttaṃ “jātiādīni [V 2.0104] na jāyantī”ti. Tenāha “na hi uppādassa uppādo atthi, uppannassa ca paripākabhedamattaṃ itaradvaya”nti, jarāmaraṇanti attho.

But characteristic materiality is not born from anywhere, that is, it is not born from any condition whatsoever, nor is it born by itself, because that which is born by itself without conditions is utterly non-existent. How then should it be understood that characteristic materiality is not born? Because of the absence of characteristics. For sense bases such as the form-base and so forth, which possess arising, have characteristics such as birth and so forth, but it is not so for birth and so forth themselves. Therefore, it should be understood that birth and so forth are not born. But could it be the case that 'birth and so forth have characteristics such as birth and so forth'? That is not so. Why? Because that would lead to an infinite regress. For if birth and so forth were to possess birth and so forth, then those too would possess birth and so forth, and those in turn would possess birth and so forth, thus leading to an infinite regress. Therefore, it is well said, 'Birth and so forth are not born.' Hence he said, 'For there is no arising of arising, and for that which has arisen, the other two are merely decay and dissolution'—meaning aging and death.

Tattha “uppādo natthī”ti etena uppādassa jarāmaraṇābhāvamāha. Asati uppāde kuto jarāmaraṇanti mattaggahaṇena jarāmaraṇassa uppādābhāvampi. Yadi evaṃ jātiyā kutoci jātatāvacanaṃ kathanti āha “yampī”tiādi. Tattha kiccānubhāvakkhaṇe diṭṭhattāti ye te cittādayo rūpāyatanādīnaṃ rūpānaṃ janakapaccayā, tesaṃ taduppādanaṃ pati anuparatabyāpārānaṃ yo so paccayabhāvūpalakkhaṇīyo kiccānubhāvakkhaṇo, tadā jāyamānānaṃ rūpāyatanādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ vikārabhāvena upalabbhamānataṃ sandhāya veneyyapuggalavasena jātiyā kutoci paccayato jātattaṃ pāḷiyaṃ anuññātaṃ yathā taṃ cittasamuṭṭhānatādi viññattiādīnaṃ. Ayañhettha saṅkhepattho – yehi paccayadhammehi rūpādayo uppajjeyyuṃ, tesaṃ paccayabhāvūpagamanakkhaṇe upalabbhamānā rūpādayo tato pure, pacchā ca anupalabbhamānā tato uppajjantīti viññāyanti, evaṃ jātipi veditabbā. Yadi evaṃ nippariyāyato jātiyā kutoci jātatā siddhā, atha kasmā veneyyapuggalavasenāti vuttanti? Nayidamevaṃ jāyamānadhammavikārabhāvena upalabbhamānattā. Yadi hi dhammo viya upalabbheyya jāti, nippariyāyova tassā kutoci jātabhāvo, na evamupalabbhati, atha kho vikārabhāvena. Tasmā vuttaṃ “veneyyapuggalavasenā”ti.

Herein, by 'there is no arising,' the absence of aging-and-death for arising is stated. If there is no arising, from where would aging-and-death be? By the term 'merely' (matta), the absence of arising for aging-and-death is also stated. If so, how can there be the statement that birth is born from some cause? Therefore, he said the text beginning with 'yampi'. Therein, regarding the phrase 'because it is seen at the moment of the power of the function': with reference to the fact that arising phenomena such as the form-base are found as a state of alteration at that moment of the power of the function—a moment marked by the state of being a condition of those generating conditions (like consciousness, etc., which generate material phenomena such as the form-base) that have unceasing activity in producing them—it is permitted in the Pāḷi, by way of the persons to be trained, that birth is born from some condition, just as the state of being mind-originated, etc., is for intimation, etc. Herein, this is the brief meaning: Material phenomena, etc., that would arise from certain conditional phenomena are found at the moment those conditions arrive at the state of being a condition, but are not found before or after that moment. Thus, they are understood as 'they arise from that.' In the same way, birth also should be understood. If so, the state of birth having been born from some cause is established directly. Then why is it said, 'by way of the persons to be trained'? This is not so, because it is found as a state of alteration of arising phenomena. For if birth were found like an ultimate reality, its state of having been born from some cause would be direct indeed. But it is not found thus; rather, it is found as a state of alteration. Therefore, it was said, 'by way of the persons to be trained'.

Tadā kira sotūnaṃ evaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ “ayaṃ jāti sabbesaṃ dhammānaṃ pabhavo, sayañca na kutoci jāyati yathā taṃ pakativādīnaṃ pakatī”ti, taṃ [M 2.0112] nesaṃ micchāgāhaṃ vidhamento satthā “upacayo santatī”ti dvidhā bhinditvā kutoci paccayato jātañca katvā desesi, na pana jarāmaraṇaṃ paccayadhammānaṃ kiccānubhāvakkhaṇe adassanato. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ “jarāmaraṇaṃ paṭiccasamuppanna”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.20) vuttaṃ? Yasmā paṭiccasamuppannānaṃ dhammānaṃ paripākabhaṅgatāya tesu santesu honti, na asantesu. Na hi ajātaṃ paripaccati, bhijjati vā, tasmā taṃ jātipaccayataṃ sandhāya “jarāmaraṇaṃ paṭiccasamuppanna”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.20) pariyāyena suttesu vuttaṃ. Yo panettha kāmabhavādīsu kammādinā paccayena yonivibhāgato paṭisandhiyaṃ, pavattiyañca rūpadhammānaṃ pavattibhedo vattabbo, so parato paṭiccasamuppādakathāyaṃ āvi bhavissatīti na vuttoti daṭṭhabbo.

At that time, it is said, this thought arose in the listeners: 'This birth is the origin of all phenomena, and it itself is not born from any cause, just like the primordial nature of those who hold the doctrine of primordial nature.' Dispelling that wrong view of theirs, the Teacher, having divided it into two as 'accumulation' and 'continuity,' taught that it is arisen from some cause. However, he did not teach aging-and-death in the same way, because it is not seen at the moment of the power of the function of the conditioning phenomena. If so, how is it said, 'Aging-and-death is dependently arisen'? Because they are of the nature of ripening and breaking up of dependently arisen phenomena, they exist when those phenomena exist, and do not exist when they do not exist. Indeed, what is unborn neither ripens nor breaks up. Therefore, with reference to its having birth as its condition, it is said indirectly in the Suttas, 'Aging-and-death is dependently arisen.' Furthermore, whatever distinction in the arising of material phenomena should be stated here—at the time of rebirth-linking and during the course of existence, according to the division of wombs, conditioned by kamma, etc., in the sensual existences, etc.—that distinction will become clear later in the discourse on dependent origination; therefore, it is not stated here. Thus it should be understood.

Iti rūpakkhandhe vitthārakathāmukhavaṇṇanā.

Thus, the explanation of the introduction to the detailed discourse on the aggregate of materiality.

Viññāṇakkhandhakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Discourse on the Aggregate of Consciousness

451. Yaṃ [V 2.0105] kiñcīti anavasesapariyādānadīpakena padadvayena vedayitassa bahubhedataṃ dassento vuccamānaṃ rāsaṭṭhaṃ ulliṅgeti. Vedayitaṃ ārammaṇarasānubhavanaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etassāti vedayitalakkhaṇaṃ. Sabbaṃ taṃ dhammajātanti adhippāyo, pubbe vā rūpakkhandhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ adhikārato ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Ekato katvāti atītādibhedabhinnaṃ sabbaṃ taṃ buddhiyā ekato katvā. Evañhi rāsaṭṭhassa sambhavo. Nīlādibhedassa ārammaṇassa sañjānanaṃ, “nīlaṃ pītaṃ dīghaṃ rassa”nti (dha. sa. 615) ca ādinā saññuppādavasena jānanaṃ gahaṇaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etassāti sañjānanalakkhaṇaṃ. Abhisaṅkharaṇaṃ āyūhanaṃ byāpārāpatti, abhisandahanaṃ vā, ubhayathāpi cetanāpadhānatāya saṅkhārakkhandhassa evaṃ vuttaṃ “abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇa”nti. Tathā hi suttantabhājanīye saṅkhārakkhandhaṃ vibhajantena bhagavatā “cakkhusamphassajā cetanā”tiādinā (vibha. 21) cetanāva vibhattā. Minitabbavatthuṃ nāḷiyā minamāno puriso viya yena sañjānanākāravisiṭṭhena ākārena visayaṃ gaṇhāti, taṃ ārammaṇūpaladdhisaṅkhātaṃ vijānanaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etassāti vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ. Itare vedanākkhandhādayo suviññeyyā hontīti viññāṇena ekuppādādibhāvato, samānajātiādivibhāgato ca.

451. By the two words 'Whatever it is,' which indicate complete inclusion without remainder, he shows the manifoldness of what is experienced, thereby revealing the meaning of 'aggregate' which is to be spoken of. Its characteristic is the experiencing of the flavor of an object; thus, it has the characteristic of feeling. The meaning is 'all that nature of phenomena'; or, the term stated previously in the discussion on the aggregate of form should be brought in and connected here by way of relevance. 'Having made it one' means having made all that, which is differentiated by distinctions such as past, into one by means of wisdom. For in this way the meaning of 'aggregate' is possible. Its characteristic is the perceiving of an object with distinctions such as blue, and the knowing and grasping by way of the arising of perception, such as 'blue,' 'yellow,' 'long,' 'short,' etc.; thus, it has the characteristic of perception. 'Forming' is accumulating, engaging in activity, or coordinating. In either case, due to the predominance of volition, it is said of the aggregate of formations that it has 'the characteristic of forming.' Indeed, in the Suttanta Analysis, when the Blessed One analyzed the aggregate of formations, he analyzed only volition, by way of 'volition born of eye-contact,' and so on. Like a person measuring a measurable object with a `nāḷi` measure, by whichever mode distinct from the mode of perception it grasps the object, that specific knowing, which is termed 'apprehending the object', is its characteristic; thus, it has the characteristic of consciousness. The other aggregates, beginning with the feeling aggregate, are easily understood because of their state of co-arising, etc., with consciousness, and because of their division into similar classes, etc.

Attanā [M 2.0113] “vijānanalakkhaṇa”nti vuttamatthaṃ suttena samatthetuṃ “yaṃ kiñcī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yathāpaccayaṃ pavattimattametaṃ, yadidaṃ sabhāvadhammoti dassetuṃ “vijānanalakkhaṇa”nti bhāvasādhanavasena vuttaṃ. Dhammasabhāvā vinimutto koci kattā nāma natthīti tasseva kattubhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “vijānātī”ti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ vijānanaṭṭhena viññāṇaṃ, tadeva cintanādiatthena cittaṃ, mananaṭṭhena manoti pariyāyatopi naṃ bodheti. Ettāvatā ca khandhato, bhedato, pariyāyato ca viññāṇaṃ vibhāvitaṃ hoti.

To support with a Sutta the meaning stated by himself as 'having the characteristic of consciousness,' the phrase 'whatever,' etc., was stated. To show that this is merely an occurrence according to conditions—that is, this nature of phenomena—'having the characteristic of consciousness' was stated in the sense of a state (bhāvasādhana). As there is no agent whatsoever apart from the nature of phenomena, to show the agency of that very thing, 'it knows' was stated. He also makes it known through synonyms: that which is consciousness (viññāṇa) in the sense of specifically knowing, that very thing is mind (citta) in the sense of thinking, etc., and it is intellect (mano) in the sense of knowing. And by this much, consciousness comes to be elucidated in terms of aggregate, distinction, and synonym.

Jāyanti ettha visadisāpi sadisākārāti jāti, samānākāro. Sā panāyaṃ jāti kāmaṃ anekavidhā nānappakārā, taṃ idhādhippetameva pana dassento “kusalaṃ, akusalaṃ, abyākatañcā”ti āha. Tattha kusalaṭṭhena kusalaṃ. Koyaṃ kusalaṭṭho nāma? Ārogyaṭṭho anavajjaṭṭho sukhavipākaṭṭho. Ārogyaṭṭhenāpi hi kusalaṃ vuccati “kacci nu bhoto kusala”ntiādīsu (jā. 1.15.146; 2.20.129). Anavajjaṭṭhenāpi “katamo pana, bhante, kusalo kāyasamācāro? Yo kho, mahārāja[V 2.0106], anavajjo kāyasamācāro”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.361). Sukhavipākaṭṭhenāpi “kusalānaṃ, bhikkhave, dhammānaṃ samādānahetū”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.80). Kusalacittañhi rāgādīnaṃ cetasikarogānaṃ avajjasabhāvānaṃ paṭipakkhabhāvato, sukhavipākavipaccanato ca arogaṃ, anavajjaṃ, sukhavipākañcāti.

It is 'class' (jāti) because herein even dissimilar things are born with a similar character; it has a similar character. But although this class is indeed of many kinds and various types, showing only that which is intended here, he said, 'wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.' Therein, 'wholesome' is in the sense of wholesome. What is this 'sense of wholesome'? It is the sense of health, the sense of blamelessness, and the sense of resulting in happiness.
