For 'wholesome' is indeed also said in the sense of health, as in such phrases as, 'Is your honor well?' It is also said in the sense of blamelessness, as in, 'But what, venerable sir, is wholesome bodily conduct? That which, great king, is blameless bodily conduct.' And it is also said in the sense of resulting in happiness, as in, 'On account of undertaking wholesome states, O monks…' Indeed, wholesome consciousness—because it is the opposite of mental diseases such as lust, which have a blameworthy nature, and because it ripens into a happy result—is healthy, blameless, and results in happiness.

Saddatthato pana kucchite pāpadhamme salayati calayati kammeti viddhaṃsetīti kusalaṃ. Kucchitena vā ākārena sayantīti kusā, pāpadhammā, te kuse lunāti chindatīti kusalaṃ. Kucchitānaṃ vā sānato tanukaraṇato ñāṇaṃ kusaṃ nāma, tena lātabbaṃ gahetabbaṃ pavattetabbanti kusalaṃ. Yathā vā kuso ubhayabhāgagataṃ hatthapadesaṃ lunāti, evamidaṃ uppannānuppannavasena ubhayabhāgagataṃ saṃkilesapakkhaṃ lunāti chindati, tasmā kuso viya lunātīti kusalaṃ. Kucchitānaṃ vā sāvajjadhammānaṃ salanato saṃvaraṇato kusalaṃ. Kusaladhammavasena hi akusalā pavattinivāraṇena, appavattibhāvāpādanena ca manacchaṭṭhesu dvāresu appavattiyā saṃvutā pihitā honti. Kucchite vā pāpadhamme salayati kampeti apanetīti kusalaṃ. Kucchitānaṃ vā pāṇātipātādīnaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ [M 2.0114] sānato nisānato tejanato kusā, dosalobhādayo. Dosādīnañhi vasena cetanāya tikkhabhāvappattiyā pāṇātipātādīnaṃ mahāsāvajjatā, te kuse lunāti chindatīti kusalaṃ. Kucchitānaṃ vā sānato antakaraṇato vināsanato kusāni, puññakiriyavasena pavattāni saddhādīni indriyāni, tehi lātabbaṃ pavattetabbanti kusalaṃ. “Ku” iti vā bhūmi vuccati, adhiṭṭhānabhāvena taṃsadisassa attano nissayabhūtassa rūpārūpappabandhassa sampati, āyatiñca anudahanena vināsanato kuṃ siyantīti kusā, rāgādayo, te viya attano nissayassa lavanato chindanato kusalaṃ. Payogasampāditā hi kusaladhammā accantameva rūpārūpadhamme appavattikaraṇena samucchindantīti.

However, in terms of etymology, it shakes, stirs, agitates, and destroys vile, evil qualities; therefore, it is called wholesome (kusala). Or, because evil qualities lie down (sayanti) in a vile manner, they are called 'kusā'; it cuts (lunāti) and severs these 'kusā'; therefore, it is called wholesome (kusala). Or, because the knowledge that thins out (sānato) and makes subtle vile qualities is called 'kusa'; by that knowledge, it is to be obtained (lātabbaṃ), grasped, and brought into being; therefore, it is called wholesome (kusala). Or, just as a kusa blade cuts the hand that has come into contact with both its sides, so too does this cut and sever the faction of defilements that has come into both parts, by way of the arisen and the unarisen. Therefore, because it cuts (lunāti) like a kusa blade, it is called wholesome (kusala). Or, it is wholesome because it blocks (salanato) and restrains vile, blameworthy qualities. For indeed, by the power of wholesome qualities, unwholesome qualities are restrained and closed off from occurring at the six doors with mind as the sixth, both by preventing their arising and by bringing them to a state of non-arising. Or, it shakes, agitates, and removes vile, evil qualities; therefore, it is called wholesome. Or, because they sharpen (sānato) and whet vile evil qualities such as killing living beings, hatred, greed, and so on are called 'kusā'. For indeed, through the power of hatred and so on, by volition attaining a state of sharpness, acts like killing living beings become greatly blameworthy; it cuts (lunāti) and severs these 'kusā'; therefore, it is called wholesome (kusala). Or, because they make an end of (sānato) and destroy vile qualities, the faculties—faith and others—that arise through meritorious action are called 'kusāni'; by them, it is to be obtained (lātabbaṃ) and brought into being; therefore, it is called wholesome (kusala). Or, 'ku' is said to be the earth. Because they destroy the 'ku'—that is, the continuum of materiality and immateriality which is one's own support and is similar to the earth in being a foundation—both in the present and in the future by scorching it, lust and so on are called 'kusā' (from kuṃ siyanti). Like them, because it cuts (lavanato) and severs its own support, it is called wholesome (kusala). For indeed, wholesome qualities, when accomplished through right effort, utterly cut off the phenomena of materiality and immateriality by bringing them to a state of non-arising.

Na kusalanti akusalaṃ, kusalapaṭipakkhanti attho. Na kusalanti hi kusalapaṭikkhepena akusalapadassa avayavabhedena atthe vuccamāne yathā yaṃ dhammajātaṃ na arogaṃ, na anavajjaṃ, na sukhavipākaṃ, na ca kosallasambhūtaṃ, taṃ akusalanti ayamattho dassito hoti, evaṃ yaṃ na kucchitānaṃ salanasabhāvaṃ, na kusānaṃ lavanasabhāvaṃ, na kusena kusehi vā pavattetabbaṃ, na ca kuso viya lavanakaṃ, taṃ akusalaṃ nāmāti ayampi attho dassito hoti. Ettha ca yasmā kusalaṃ akusalassa ujuvipaccanīkabhūtaṃ, yato cetasikarogapaṭipakkhādibhāvato arogādipariyāyenapi [V 2.0107] bodhitaṃ, tasmā akusalaṃ pana kusalassa ujuvipaccanīkabhūtanti vuttaṃ “kusalapaṭipakkhanti attho”ti. Taṃ pana yathākkamaṃ pahāyakapahātabbabhāvenevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Not wholesome, therefore it is unwholesome; the meaning is that it is the opposite of the wholesome. For when, by negating 'wholesome,' the meaning of the word 'unwholesome' is stated by way of its component parts, just as the meaning is shown that whatever class of phenomena is not free from illness, not blameless, not resulting in happiness, and not produced from skillfulness, that is unwholesome, so too is this meaning shown: whatever is not of a nature to shake off contemptible things, not of a nature to cut down contemptible things, not to be brought about by wisdom or by the faculties, and not cutting like kusa grass, that is called unwholesome. And here, because the wholesome is the direct opposite of the unwholesome—since, due to its being the antidote to mental disease and so on, it is also made known by the synonym 'free from illness', etc.—therefore, that the unwholesome is the direct opposite of the wholesome is stated by the words, 'the meaning is the opposite of wholesome.' That, however, should be understood as being in terms of the abandoner and what is to be abandoned, respectively.

Na byākatanti abyākataṃ, kusalākusalabhāvena akathitanti attho. Tattha kusalabhāvo anavajjasukhavipākaṭṭho. Akusalabhāvo sāvajjadukkhavipākaṭṭho, tadubhayabhāvena avuttanti vuttaṃ hoti. Eteneva arogasarogādibhāvena ca avuttatā vaṇṇitāti daṭṭhabbā. Ettha ca “kusalaṃ akusala”nti ca vatvā “abyākata”nti vuttattā kusalākusalabhāveneva avuttatā viññāyati, na pakārantarena. Avuttatā cettha na tathā avattabbatāmattena, atha kho tadubhayavinimuttasabhāvatāya tesaṃ dhammānanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hetaṃ “avipākalakkhaṇa”nti vuccati.

Not declared, therefore it is undeclared; the meaning is: not spoken of in terms of being wholesome or unwholesome. Therein, the state of being wholesome has the characteristic of being blameless and resulting in happiness. The state of being unwholesome has the characteristic of being blameworthy and resulting in suffering. It is said to be unspoken of in terms of both these states. By this very reason, it should be understood that its unstated nature is also described in terms of being free from illness, having illness, and so on. And here, because 'undeclared' is said after having said 'wholesome' and 'unwholesome,' its unstated nature is understood only in terms of being wholesome or unwholesome, not in any other way. And here, this unstated nature is not merely a matter of its being unstatable in that way, but rather, it should be understood, it is because those phenomena are by nature free from both. For so it is said, 'It has the characteristic of being without result.'

452. Bhūmibhedatoti bhavanti ettha dhammāti bhūmi, ṭhānaṃ, avatthā ca. Avatthāpi hi avatthāvantānaṃ pavattiṭṭhānaṃ viya gayhati, evaṃ nesaṃ sukhaggahaṇaṃ hotīti[M 2.0115]. Tattha lokiyā bhūmi ṭhānavaseneva veditabbā, lokuttarā avatthāvasena. Lokiyā vā ṭhānāvatthāvasena, lokuttarā avatthāvaseneva. Kāmāvacaranti ettha vatthukāmo kilesakāmoti dve kāmā. Tesu vatthukāmo visesato pañca kāmaguṇā kāmīyantīti, kilesakāmo taṇhā kāmetīti. Te dvepi sahitā hutvā yattha avacaranti, taṃ kāmāvacaraṃ. Kiṃ pana tanti? Ekādasavidho kāmabhavo. Idaṃ yebhuyyena tattha avacarati pavattatīti kāmāvacaraṃ ekassa avacarasaddassa lopaṃ katvā. Evaṃ rūpārūpāvacarānipi veditabbāni rūpataṇhā rūpaṃ, arūpataṇhā arūpanti katvā. Atha vā kāmataṇhā kāmo uttarapadalopena, avacarati etthāti avacaraṃ, kāmassa avacaraṃ kāmāvacaraṃ. Evaṃ rūpāvacarārūpāvacarānipi veditabbāni. Lokato uttaratīti lokuttaraṃ kusalassa adhippetattā. Itaraṃ pana lokato uttiṇṇanti lokuttaraṃ.

452. “By distinction of plane” (bhūmibhedato): Because phenomena (dhammā) exist (bhavanti) here (ettha), it is called a “plane” (bhūmi), which is a place (ṭhāna) and a state (avatthā). For a state is also taken as the place of occurrence for those things possessing a state, thus making them easy to grasp. Herein, the mundane plane should be understood solely in terms of place, and the supramundane in terms of state. Alternatively, the mundane may be understood in terms of both place and state, while the supramundane is understood solely in terms of state. In “sense-sphere” (kāmāvacara), there are two kinds of sensual pleasure (kāma): sensual pleasure as object (vatthukāma) and sensual pleasure as defilement (kilesakāma). Among these, sensual pleasure as object refers specifically to the five strands of sensual pleasure, because they are desired (kāmīyanti); sensual pleasure as defilement is craving (taṇhā), because it desires (kāmeti). When these two combine and move about in a certain sphere, that is the sense-sphere (kāmāvacaraṃ). And what is that? The elevenfold sense-sphere existence. This [consciousness] for the most part moves about and occurs there; hence it is called 'kāmāvacara', by the elision of one 'avacara' word. Similarly, the form-sphere and formless-sphere should be understood by taking craving for form as 'form' and craving for the formless as 'formless'. Alternatively, 'sensual craving' (kāmataṇhā) becomes 'kāma' by the elision of the latter word. It moves about herein, thus it is a 'sphere of movement' (avacaraṃ); the sphere of movement of sensual pleasure is 'kāmāvacaraṃ'. The form-sphere and formless-sphere should also be understood in this way. It transcends the world, thus it is 'supramundane' (lokuttaraṃ); this is because the wholesome [path consciousness] is intended. The other [fruition consciousness], however, is 'supramundane' because it has transcended the world.

Somanassupekkhāñāṇasaṅkhārabhedatoti ettha somanassupekkhābhedo tāva yutto tesaṃ bhinnasabhāvattā, ñāṇasaṅkhārabhedo pana kathanti? Nāyaṃ doso ñāṇasaṅkhārakato bhedoñāṇasaṅkhārabhedo, so ca tesaṃ bhāvābhāvakatoti katvā. Sobhanaṃ mano, sundaraṃ vā mano etassāti sumano, sumanassa bhāvo somanassaṃ, mānasikasukhā vedanā ruḷhiyā, somanassena uppādato paṭṭhāya yāva bhaṅgā sahagataṃ pavattaṃ saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, sampayuttanti attho. Somanassasahagatatā cassa ārammaṇavasena veditabbā. Iṭṭhārammaṇe hi cittaṃ somanassasahagataṃ hoti. Nanu ca iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ lobhassa vatthu, kathaṃ [V 2.0108] tattha kusalaṃ hotīti? Nayidamekantikaṃ iṭṭhepi ābhogādivasena kusalassa uppajjanato. Yassa hi catusampatticakkasamāyogādivasena yonisova ābhogo hoti, kusalameva ca mayā kattabbanti kusalakaraṇe cittaṃ niyamitaṃ, akusalappavattito ca nivattetvā kusalakaraṇe eva pariṇāmitaṃ, abhiṇhakaraṇavasena ca samudācaritaṃ, tassa iṭṭhepi ārammaṇe alobhādisampayuttameva cittaṃ hoti, na lobhādisampayuttaṃ.

Herein, in the text 'by distinction of joy, equanimity, knowledge, and formations,' the distinction between joy and equanimity is, in the first place, appropriate because of their having distinct natures. But how is the distinction of knowledge and formations appropriate? This is not a fault, for 'the distinction of knowledge and formations' means a distinction made by knowledge and formations, and that, it is held, is made by their presence and absence. 'Sumana' means one with a 'beautiful mind' (sobhanaṃ mano) or a 'good mind' (sundaraṃ mano). The state of a 'sumana' is 'somanassa' (joy). By conventional usage, it is a mentally pleasant feeling. The meaning is that from its arising up to its dissolution, it is accompanied by, has occurred with, is conjoined with, and is associated with joy. And the state of this mind being accompanied by joy should be understood by way of the object. Indeed, the mind is accompanied by joy when there is a desirable object. But is it not so that a desirable object is a basis for greed? How then can a wholesome state arise therein? This is not an absolute rule, because a wholesome state can arise even in a desirable object by way of attention, etc. For one who has proper attention by way of conjunction with the four wheels of accomplishment, etc.; whose mind is fixed on the performance of the wholesome, thinking, 'Only what is wholesome should be done by me'; who, having turned away from the proceeding of the unwholesome, has directed the mind only to the performance of the wholesome; and who has engaged in it through frequent practice—for such a person, even with a desirable object, the mind is associated only with non-greed, etc., and not associated with greed, etc.

Ñāṇena [M 2.0116] samaṃ pakārehi yuttanti ñāṇasampayuttaṃ. Ekuppādādayo eva cettha pakārāti veditabbā. Tattha kammūpapattiindriyaparipākakilesadūrībhāvā ñāṇasampayuttatāya kāraṇaṃ. Yo hi paresaṃ dhammaṃ deseti, anavajjāni sippāyatanakammāyatanavijjaṭṭhānāni sikkhāpetīti evamādikaṃ paññāsaṃvattaniyaṃ karoti, tassa kammūpanissayavasena kusalacittaṃ uppajjamānaṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ hoti. Tathā abyāpajje loke uppannassa upapattiṃ nissāya ñāṇasampayuttaṃ hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ “tassa tattha sukhino dhammapadā plavanti, dandho, bhikkhave, satuppādo, atha kho so satto khippaṃyeva visesabhāgī (a. ni. 4.191) hotī”ti. Tathā paññādasakapattassa indriyaparipākaṃ nissāya kusalaṃ uppajjamānaṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ hoti. Yena pana kilesā vikkhambhitā, tassa kilesadūrībhāvaṃ nissāya ñāṇasampayuttaṃ hoti. Vuttampi cetaṃ “yogā ve jāyate bhūri, ayogā bhūrisaṅkhayo”ti (dha. pa. 282). Attano vā parassa vā samussāhajanitaṃ cittapayogasaṅkhātaṃ saṅkharaṇaṃ saṅkhāro, so etassa natthīti asaṅkhāraṃ. Tena pana saha saṅkhārena pavattatīti sasaṅkhāraṃ. Ñāṇena vippayuttaṃ virahitanti ñāṇavippayuttaṃ. Vippayogoti cettha ñāṇassa abhāvo appavattiyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Upekkhatīti upekkhā, vedayamānāpi ārammaṇaṃ ajjhupekkhati majjhattatākārasaṇṭhitattāti attho. Atha vā upetā sukhadukkhānaṃ aviruddhā ikkhā anubhavananti upekkhā. Atha vā iṭṭhe ca aniṭṭhe ca ārammaṇe pakkhapātābhāvena upapattito yuttito ikkhati anubhavatīti upekkhā, tāya sahagatanti upekkhāsahagataṃ. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

‘Associated with knowledge’ (ñāṇasampayutta) means being connected with knowledge in various modes. Here, simultaneous arising and so on should be understood as the modes. In this context, the reasons for being associated with knowledge are kamma, rebirth, the ripening of faculties, and the distancing of defilements. For one who teaches the Dhamma to others, trains them in blameless arts, crafts, and fields of knowledge, and performs such deeds that lead to wisdom—when wholesome consciousness arises in them by way of kamma as a strong supporting condition, it is associated with knowledge. Similarly, for one reborn in a world free from affliction, consciousness is associated with knowledge, relying on that rebirth. As it is said: “For that happy one, the words of the Dhamma appear clearly. Slow, monks, is the arising of mindfulness, yet that being quickly becomes a partaker of distinction.” Likewise, when wholesome consciousness arises relying on the ripening of faculties in one who has reached the decade of wisdom, it is associated with knowledge. For one by whom defilements are suppressed, consciousness is associated with knowledge, relying on the distancing of defilements. And this is also stated: “Truly, from practice wisdom arises; from non-practice, the destruction of wisdom.” A formation (saṅkhāra) is the prompting, called mental exertion, generated by one's own or another's urging. That for which this is absent is unprompted (asaṅkhāra). That which proceeds with such a formation is prompted (sasaṅkhāra). ‘Dissociated from knowledge’ (ñāṇavippayutta) means disjoined from, or devoid of, knowledge. And here, dissociation should be understood as the very absence or non-occurrence of knowledge. ‘Equanimity’ (upekkhā) is so called because it looks on with equanimity; even while experiencing, it looks upon the object with equanimity because it is established in a state of neutrality—this is the meaning. Alternatively, equanimity (upekkhā) is the suitable seeing or experiencing that is not opposed to pleasure and pain. Or, because of the absence of partiality toward desirable and undesirable objects, it sees and experiences suitably and appropriately; therefore, it is equanimity. That which is accompanied by it is ‘accompanied by equanimity’ (upekkhāsahagata). All the rest is in the same way as explained previously.

Evaṃ aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalacittāni uddisitvā idāni tesaṃ pavattiākāraṃ dassetuṃ “yadā hī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha paṭiggāhakādisampattinti ettha ādi-saddena desakālakalyāṇamittādisampattiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Aññaṃ vā somanassahetunti ettha aññaggahaṇena saddhābahulatā, visuddhadiṭṭhitā, kusalakiriyāya ānisaṃsadassāvitā, somanassapaṭisandhikatā, ekādasa [V 2.0109] pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhāniyā dhammāti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Ādinayappavattanti ettha ādi-saddena na kevalaṃ “atthi yiṭṭha”ntiādīnaṃ (ma. ni. 1.441; 2.95) navannaṃyeva sammādiṭṭhivatthūnaṃ gahaṇaṃ, atha kho dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgaṭṭhāniyādīnampi [M 2.0117] saṅgaho veditabbo. Purakkhatvāti pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā. Tañca kho sahajātapubbaṅgamavasena “manopubbaṅgamā dhammā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 1-2) viya sampayogassa adhippetattā. Asaṃsīdantoti silokamacchariyādivasena puññakiriyāyaṃ saṃsīdaṃ saṅkocaṃ anāpajjanto, tena muttacāgatādiṃ dasseti. Anussāhitoti kenacipi na ussāhito. Sarasato hi puññapaṭipattidassanamidaṃ. Parehīti pana pākaṭussāhanadassanaṃ.

Having thus enumerated the eight wholesome consciousnesses pertaining to the sense-sphere, now, to explain their mode of occurrence, the text beginning with ‘When indeed’ is commenced. Herein, in ‘the suitability of the recipient, etc.,’ the word ‘etc.’ includes the suitability of place, time, good friends, and so on. In ‘or another cause for joy,’ the inclusion of ‘another’ encompasses being rich in faith, having a purified view, seeing the benefits of wholesome deeds, having a joy-accompanied rebirth, the eleven factors that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of joy, and so on. In ‘Occurring in the initial way,’ by the word ‘initial,’ not only are the nine grounds of right view, such as ‘there is what is offered,’ etc., included, but the basis for the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, and so on, should also be understood. ‘Having placed in front’ means having made it a forerunner. And that too, by way of being a co-arisen forerunner, as in ‘Mind is the forerunner of all phenomena,’ etc., because association is intended. ‘Not sinking down’ means not shrinking back in the performance of meritorious acts due to desire for fame, stinginess, etc., thereby showing open-handed generosity and so on. ‘Unurged’ means not urged by anyone, for this shows the spontaneous practice of merit. ‘But by others’ shows evident urging.

Dānādīnīti dānaṃ sīlaṃ yāva diṭṭhijukammanti imāni dānādīni dasa puññāni, dānādīnīti vā dānasīlabhāvanāmayāni itaresampi sattannaṃ etthevantogadhattā. Yattha sayaṃ uppajjanti, taṃ santānaṃ punanti, pujjaṃ bhavaphalaṃ nibbattentīti vā puññāni. Assa puññacetanāsamaṅgino. Amuttacāgatā deyyadhamme sāpekkhacittatā. Ādi-saddena sīlasamādānādīsu anadhimuttatādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tadevāti somanassasahagatādinā sadisatāya vuttaṃ. Sadisampi hi “tadevā”ti voharīyati yathā “sā eva tittirī, tāniyeva osadhānī”ti. Imasmiñhi attheti līnassa cittassa ussāhanapayogasaṅkhāte atthe. Etanti “saṅkhāro”ti etaṃ padaṃ. Pubbapayogassāti puññakiriyāyaṃ saṅkoce jāyamāne tato vivecetvā samussāhanavasena pavattassa cittapayogassa, pubbaggahaṇañcettha tathāpavattapubbābhisaṅkhāravasena so saṅkhāro hotīti katvā vuttaṃ, na tassa saṅkhārassa pubbakālikattā. “Atthi dinna”ntiādi (ma. ni. 1.441; 2.95) nayappavattāya sammādiṭṭhiyā asambhavadassanatthaṃ bāla-ggahaṇaṃ. Saṃsīdanussāhanābhāvadassanatthaṃ sahasā-gahaṇaṃ. Somanassarahitā honti puññaṃ karontāti adhippāyo. Somanassahetūnaṃ abhāvaṃ āgammāti idaṃ nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Majjhattārammaṇatathārūpacetosaṅkhārādayopi hi upekkhāsahagatatāya kāraṇaṃ hontiyevāti.

‘Merit beginning with giving’ (dānādīni) refers to the ten meritorious deeds starting with giving, virtue, and so on, up to straightening of view. Alternatively, ‘merit beginning with giving’ refers to the merit consisting of giving, virtue, and mental development, because the other seven are included right within them. Or, they are called merits (puññāni) because where they themselves arise, they purify that mental continuum, or because they bring forth a venerable result of existence. For one endowed with such meritorious volition: Not giving unreservedly (amuttacāgatā) means having a mind with attachment towards things to be given. The word ‘etc.’ (ādi-saddena) includes lack of resolve, etc., regarding undertaking virtue, etc. ‘That very thing’ (tadeva) is said due to similarity with being accompanied by joy, etc. For indeed, even what is similar is referred to as ‘that very thing,’ as in ‘that very partridge,’ or ‘those very medicines.’ In this matter (imasmiñhi atthe), it is in the sense of applying exertion for a sluggish mind. ‘This’ (etaṃ) refers to the word ‘formation’ (saṅkhāro). Regarding ‘previous effort’ (pubbapayogassa): it refers to the mental exertion that proceeds by way of vigorous effort, having been distinguished from the shrinking that arises in the performance of a meritorious action. And here, the inclusion of ‘previous’ (pubba) is stated because that formation occurs by way of a prior volitional formation that proceeded in such a way, not because that formation is of a previous time. The inclusion of ‘foolish’ (bāla-ggahaṇaṃ) is to show the impossibility of right view that proceeds in the manner of ‘There is what is given,’ etc. The inclusion of `sahasā` (sahasā-gahaṇaṃ) is to show the absence of both sinking down and urging. The meaning is that they are devoid of joy when performing merit. This should be seen as a mere indication, referring to the absence of causes for joy. For indeed, neutral objects, mental formations of such a kind, and so on, are also a cause for being accompanied by equanimity.

Evantiādi nigamanaṃ. Tayidaṃ aṭṭhavidhampi kāmāvacaraṃ kusalacittaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ yāva dhammārammaṇanti chasu ārammaṇesu yaṃ vā taṃ vā ālambitvā upekkhāsahagatāhetukakiriyāmanoviññāṇadhātānantaraṃ kāyadvārādīhi tīhi dvārehi kāyakammādivasena uppajjatīti veditabbaṃ. Tattha [M 2.0118] ñāṇasampayuttāni cattāri yadā tihetukapaṭisandhiṃ uppādenti, tadā soḷasa vipākacittāni [V 2.0110] phalanti. Yadā pana duhetukaṃ, tadā dvādasa tihetukavajjāni. Ahetukaṃ pana paṭisandhiṃ tihetukāni na uppādenteva, duhetukāni pana duhetukapaṭisandhidānakāle dvādasa, ahetukapaṭisandhiṃ dānakāle aṭṭha phalanti. Tihetukā pana paṭisandhi duhetukehi na hotiyeva. “Aṭṭha phalantī”ti cetaṃ paṭisandhiṃ janakakammavasena vuttaṃ. Aññena pana kammunā “sahetukaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ ahetukassa bhavaṅgassa anantarapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 3.1.102) vacanato sahetukampi vipākacittaṃ ahetukapaṭisandhikassa hotiyeva. Imasmiṃ ca pakkhe balavatā paccayena uppannaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ, dubbalena sasaṅkhāranti veditabbaṃ. Ye pana āgamanato ca vipākassa asaṅkhārasasaṅkhārabhāvaṃ icchanti, tesaṃ matena dvādasa, aṭṭha ca phalantīti yojetabbaṃ. Evaṃ tidhā phalaṃ dadantañcetaṃ kāmāvacarasugatiyaṃ upapattiṃ, sugatiduggatīsu bhogasampadañca karoti. Nāgasupaṇṇādīnampi hi yaṃ devabhogasampattisadisaṃ bhogajātaṃ uppajjati, tampi kāmāvacarakusalasseva phalaṃ. Na hi akusalassa iṭṭhaṃ phalaṃ atthīti.

This is the conclusion. This eightfold sense-sphere wholesome consciousness, taking as an object any one whatsoever among the six objects from a form-object up to a mind-object, should be understood to arise either immediately after the equanimity-accompanied, rootless, functional mind-consciousness-element or after the mind-door-adverting consciousness, through the three doors beginning with the body-door, by way of bodily action, etc. Among these, when the four types associated with knowledge produce a three-rooted rebirth-linking, they yield sixteen resultant consciousnesses. But when they produce a two-rooted one, they yield twelve, excluding the three-rooted resultants. The three-rooted types, however, do not produce a rootless rebirth-linking at all; the two-rooted types, however, yield twelve at the time of giving a two-rooted rebirth-linking, and eight at the time of giving a rootless rebirth-linking. A three-rooted rebirth-linking, however, does not occur at all due to the two-rooted types. And this statement, 'they yield eight,' is said with reference to the kamma that generates the rebirth-linking. However, due to another kamma, in accordance with the Paṭṭhāna which states, 'a rooted bhavaṅga is a condition for a rootless bhavaṅga by way of proximity condition' (Paṭṭhāna 3.1.102), even a rooted resultant consciousness certainly occurs for one with a rootless rebirth-linking. And in this case, it should be understood that what arises through a strong condition is unprompted, and what arises through a weak one is prompted. But as for those who hold that the unprompted or prompted nature of a resultant is also due to its originating kamma, according to their view, it should be construed that they yield twelve and eight. Thus, giving its result in three ways, this consciousness produces rebirth in a sense-sphere happy destination, and it produces the accomplishment of wealth in both happy and unhappy destinations. Indeed, whatever collection of possessions similar to the divine accomplishment of wealth arises for nāgas, supaṇṇas, and so on, that too is the result of sense-sphere wholesome kamma alone. For indeed, there is no desirable result for the unwholesome.

Rūpāvacaraṃ panāti pana-saddo visesatthajotako. Tena yathā kāmāvacaraṃ kilesānaṃ tadaṅgappahānamattakaraṃ, na evamidaṃ, idaṃ pana vikkhambhanappahānakaraṃ. Yathā vā taṃ vedanāñāṇasaṅkhārabhedato aṭṭhadhā bhijjati, na evamidaṃ, idaṃ pana tato aññathā vāti vakkhamānaṃ visesaṃ joteti. Taṃ panetaṃ savatthukaṃ, sāsavaṃ, vinīvaraṇañca rūpāvacaranti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Savatthukaṃ evā”ti hi iminā arūpāvacaraṃ nivatteti, “sāsava”nti iminā paṭhamamaggacittaṃ, “vinīvaraṇa”nti iminā paṭighasahitadvayaṃ. Katthaci pañca jhānaṅgāni, katthaci cattāri, katthaci tīṇi, katthaci dve, katthaci aparāni dveti evaṃ jhānaṅgayogabhedato pañcavidhanti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “seyyathida”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā jhānakathāyaṃ (visuddhi. 1.79 ādayo) vuttameva. Tayidaṃ bhāvanāmayameva hutvā vuttanayena pathavīkasiṇādikaṃ ālambitvā yathārahaṃ ñāṇasampayuttakusalānantaraṃ uppajjati, hīnādibhedabhinnaṃ panetaṃ yathākkamaṃ brahmapārisajjādīsu soḷasasupi brahmalokesu upapattinipphādakanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Moreover, concerning the fine-material sphere, the word `pana` illuminates a special meaning. By this, it is shown that whereas sense-sphere wholesome consciousness accomplishes only the momentary abandonment of the defilements, this fine-material sphere consciousness is not so; on the other hand, this accomplishes their abandonment by suppression. Or, whereas that sense-sphere wholesome consciousness is divided eightfold by the distinctions of feeling, knowledge, and volitional formations, this is not so divided; on the other hand, this is divided in another way. Thus, it illuminates the distinction to be stated. Furthermore, this fine-material sphere consciousness should be understood as having a physical basis, being subject to the taints, and being free from the hindrances. For, by the phrase 'having a physical basis,' it excludes the immaterial-sphere consciousness. By the term 'subject to the taints,' it excludes the first path-consciousness. By the phrase 'free from the hindrances,' it excludes the pair of consciousnesses accompanied by aversion. In some instances, there are five jhāna factors; in some, four; in some, three; in some, two; and in some, another two. Thus, to elaborate on the meaning briefly stated—that it is fivefold according to the distinction in the combination of jhāna factors—the passage beginning with 'seyyathidaṃ' is introduced. Therein, whatever is to be said has already been stated below in the discussion on jhāna (Vism I, §79ff.). This, being solely of the nature of mental development, arises after taking as its object the earth kasiṇa, etc., in the manner described, and arises, as is appropriate, immediately after a wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge. Furthermore, it should be understood that this consciousness, differentiated by the distinctions of inferior, etc., in due order, brings about rebirth in the sixteen Brahmā worlds, beginning with the Retinue of Brahmā.

Rūpasaññāsamatikkamādinā [M 2.0119] samadhigantabbaṃ arūpāvacaraṃ. Catunnaṃ arūpānanti upekkhāsamādhisaṅkhātehi catūhi arūpajjhānehi. Karaṇe hi etaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Arūpānaṃ vā yo ārammaṇādikato sampayuttadhammehi yogo yogabhedo, tassa vasena. Vuttappakārenāti heṭṭhā āruppakathāyaṃ [V 2.0111] (visuddhi. 1.275 ādayo) vuttappakārena. Paṭhamanti paṭhamaṃ arūpāvacarakusalacittaṃ. Dutiyatatiyacatutthānīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tānimāni bhāvanāmayāneva hutvā yathānupubbaṃ kasiṇugghāṭimākāsaṃ, paṭhamāruppaviññāṇaṃ, natthibhāvaṃ, ākiñcaññāyatananti imāni ālambitvā upekkhāsahagatañāṇasampayuttakusalānantaraṃ uppajjitvā catūsu arūpībrahmalokesu paṭisandhipavattivipākadāyīni. Sesaṃ panettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Chavisuddhiparamparāya samadhigantabbaṃ lokuttaraṃ. Tattha vattabbaṃ parato āgamissati. Catumaggasampayogatoti sotāpattimaggo yāva arahattamaggoti imehi catūhi ariyamaggehi sampayogato. Catubbidhampi cetaṃ bhāvanāmayameva hutvā nibbānaṃ ālambitvā suññato vimokkho, animitto vimokkho, appaṇihito vimokkhoti nāmena uppajjati, sattabhavādibhavūpapattinivattakanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ekavīsatividhaṃ hoti nātisaṅkhepavitthāranayenāti adhippāyo.

The immaterial-sphere wholesome consciousness is to be attained by transcending perceptions of form, etc. 'Of the four immaterial states' means by the four immaterial jhānas, which are designated as equanimity and concentration. For this is a genitive in the sense of the instrumental. Or, it is by way of the distinction in the connection of the immaterial states with their associated phenomena based on their object, etc. 'In the manner stated' means in the manner explained below in the discussion on the immaterial attainments (Vism I, §275ff.). 'The first' means the first immaterial-sphere wholesome consciousness. The same method applies to the second, third, and fourth. These, being solely of the nature of mental development, arise immediately subsequent to a wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge and accompanied by equanimity, after taking successively as their objects: space from the removal of the kasiṇa, the first immaterial consciousness, the state of nothingness, and the base of nothingness. They yield rebirth-linking and life-continuum resultants in the four immaterial Brahmā worlds. The rest that is to be said here has already been stated below. The supramundane is to be attained through the sequence of the six purifications. What is to be said on that will come later. 'By association with the four paths' means by association with these four noble paths, from the path of stream-entry up to the path of arahantship. And all four kinds, being solely of the nature of mental development, take Nibbāna as their object and arise under the names: the liberation through emptiness, the signless liberation, and the desireless liberation. They should be understood as preventing rebirth in seven existences, etc. The meaning is that it is twenty-onefold according to a method that is neither too brief nor too detailed.

453. Kāmāvacaramevāti ettha nikāyantariyā rūpārūpāvacarampi akusalaṃ icchantīti tesaṃ matinisedhanatthaṃ kāmāvacaraggahaṇaṃ. Mahaggatabhūmiyaṃ uppajjantampi tattha rūpadhātuyaṃ pavattivipākaṃ dentampi ekantena kāmāvacaramevāti dassanatthaṃ avadhāraṇaṃ. Yadi evaṃ, kasmā kāmāvacaramevāti? Tattha kāraṇaṃ vuttameva. Kathaṃ vuttaṃ? “Kāmataṇhā kāmo uttarapadalopato, avacarati etthāti avacaraṃ, kāmassa avacaraṃ kāmāvacara”nti. Ettha hi kāmataṇhāvisayatā “kāmāvacarabhāvassa kāraṇaṃ” vuttā yathā rūpārūpataṇhāvisayatā “rūpārūpāvacarabhāvassa”. Ekaṃsena cetaṃ evaṃ icchitabbaṃ. Aññathā byāpilakkhaṇaṃ na siyā. Yadi hi ālambitabbadhammavasena bhūmivavatthānaṃ kareyya, evaṃ sati anārammaṇānaṃ saṅgaho na siyā. Atha vipākadānavasena, evampi avipākānaṃ saṅgaho na siyā. Tasmā ālambaṇadhammavasena pariyāpannānaṃ sā kātabbā, apariyāpannānaṃ pana lokato uttiṇṇatāya lokuttaratā, uttaritarābhāvato anuttaratā ca veditabbā.

453. Regarding 'only of the sense-sphere': here, the term 'sense-sphere' is included to refute the view of adherents of other schools who hold that there is unwholesome consciousness also in the fine-material and immaterial spheres. The emphasis is to show that even though it arises in the sublime planes and gives resultant-activity in the fine-material element, it is exclusively of the sense-sphere. If so, why is it 'only of the sense-sphere'? The reason for this has already been stated. How was it stated? 'Sensual craving is kāma (by elision of the latter part of the word); it wanders there, thus avacara; the sphere of sensual craving is kāmāvacara.' For here, being the domain of sensual craving is stated as the reason for being of the sense-sphere, just as being the domain of craving for form and the formless is the reason for being of the fine-material and immaterial spheres. And this should be accepted as certain. Otherwise, the characteristic of pervasiveness would not be present. For if one were to establish the planes based on the phenomena to be taken as object, then there would be no inclusion of those without an object. Or if it were based on the giving of resultants, even so there would be no inclusion of those that are not resultants. Therefore, that classification should be made for the included states based on the phenomenon that takes an object. But for the unincluded states, their supramundane nature should be known from their having transcended the world, and their unsurpassed nature from there being nothing higher.

Pariyāpannāti [M 2.0120] ca paricchedakārikāya taṇhāya paricchijja āpannā, gahitāti attho. Nanu cettha kāmataṇhā katamā? Kāmāvacaradhammārammaṇā taṇhā, kāmāvacaradhammā katame? Kāmataṇhāvisayāti itaretarasannissayatādosoti? Nayidamevaṃ avīciādiekaādasokāsaninnatāya kañci taṇhaṃ kāmataṇhābhāvena gahetvā taṃsabhāvāya taṇhāya visayabhāvena [V 2.0112] kāmāvacaradhammānaṃ upalakkhitabbattā. Nikkhepakaṇḍepi (dha. sa. 985 ādayo) “etthāvacarā”ti vacanaṃ avīciparanimmitaparicchinnokāsāya kāmataṇhāya visayabhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttanti gahetabbaṃ. Tadokāsatā ca taṇhāya tanninnatāya veditabbā.

And 'included' (pariyāpanna) means defined and entered into by the craving that defines; the meaning is 'grasped.' Is it not the case that here the flaw of mutual dependence arises: What is sensual craving? Craving that has sense-sphere phenomena as its object. What are sense-sphere phenomena? The domain of sensual craving. This should not be understood thus. For having taken any craving that is inclined towards the eleven planes beginning with Avīci as being 'sensual craving,' the sense-sphere phenomena are to be characterized as the domain of that craving which has such a nature. In the Nikkhepakaṇḍa as well, the statement 'resorting to this' should be taken as said with reference to its being the domain of sensual craving, a domain defined by the space from Avīci and the Paranimmitavasavatti heaven. And that craving's having that domain should be known by its inclination towards it.

Mūlato tividhanti tīṇi akusalamūlāni lobhādīni, tesaṃ vasena taṃsahitampi tividhanti attho. Tāni hi suppatiṭṭhitabhāvakāraṇattā mūlamivāti mūlāni, lobho mūlaṃ etassāti lobhamūlaṃ. Asādhāraṇena niddeso yathā bherisaddo, yavaṅkuroti. Tathā dosamūlaṃ. Moho eva mūlaṃ imassa, nāññanti mohamūlaṃ.

'Threefold by way of root' means that by the power of the three unwholesome roots—greed, etc.—the consciousness associated with them is also threefold; this is the meaning. For they are called roots because, like a root, they are the cause of a firm state. 'Greed is its root,' thus 'rooted in greed.' The designation is by the uncommon factor, as in 'the sound of a drum' or 'a sprout of barley.' Similarly for 'rooted in hatred.' 'Delusion alone is its root, nothing else,' thus 'rooted in delusion.'

Somanassupekkhādiṭṭhigatasaṅkhārabhedatoti somanassupekkhābhedato diṭṭhigatabhedato saṅkhārabhedatoti paccekaṃ bhedasaddo yojetabbo. Yadettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Diṭṭhigatasampayuttanti diṭṭhiyeva diṭṭhigataṃ “gūthagataṃ, muttagata”nti (ma. ni. 2.119; a. ni. 9.11) yathā. Atha vā vipariyesaggāhatāya diṭṭhiyā gatameva, na ettha gantabbavatthu tathā sabhāvanti diṭṭhigataṃ. Tayidaṃ “idameva saccaṃ, moghamañña”nti (ma. ni. 2.187, 202, 203, 427; 3.27-29) abhinivesabhāvato lobheneva saddhiṃ pavattati, na dosena.

'By the distinction of joy, equanimity, view, and volitional formation' means the word 'distinction' should be connected with each term separately: by the distinction of joy and equanimity, by the distinction of view, and by the distinction of volitional formation. Whatever is to be said here follows the method already stated. 'Associated with wrong view': view itself is `diṭṭhigata` (gone to by view), just as in 'gone to excrement' or 'gone to urine'. Alternatively, because of being perversely grasped, it is merely the 'going' of a view; here there is no object to be gone to that has such a nature, and thus it is called `diṭṭhigata`. This wrong view, because of its nature of adherence—'This alone is true, all else is false'—occurs only together with greed, not with hatred.

Yadāhītiādi lobhamūlacittānaṃ pavattiākāradassanaṃ. Micchādiṭṭhinti ucchedadiṭṭhiādimicchādiṭṭhiṃ. Tāya hi vipallatthacittā sattā “etāvako jīvavisayo yāva indriyagocaro”ti paralokaṃ paṭikkhipitvā “natthi kāmesu ādīnavo”ti yathā tathā kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjanti. Ādi-saddena “esa pantho pageva vihito devayāne, yena yanti puttavanto visokā. Taṃ passanti pasavo, pakkhino ca, tena te mātaripi mithunaṃ carantī”tiādinā nayena puttamukhadassanaṃ saggamokkhamaggoti evamādikaṃ micchādiṭṭhiṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

The passage beginning 'For when' shows the mode of occurrence of consciousness rooted in greed. 'Wrong view' means wrong views such as annihilationism. For with minds perverted by that, beings reject the next world, thinking, 'The domain of a living being extends only as far as the range of the senses,' and so they fall into indulgence in sensual pleasures in any way whatsoever, thinking, 'There is no danger in sensual pleasures.' By the word 'etc.' it includes such wrong views as the idea that seeing the face of one's son is the path to heaven and liberation, according to the method of such passages as: 'This path to the divine vehicle has long been laid down, by which those with sons go on free from sorrow. Cattle and birds see it, and thus they have intercourse even with their mothers.'

Kāme [M 2.0121] vāti ettha vā-saddo aniyamattho, tena brāhmaṇānaṃ suvaṇṇaharaṇameva adinnādāne sāvajjaṃ, itaraṃ anavajjaṃ. Garūnaṃ, gunnaṃ, attano, jīvitassa, vivāhassa ca atthāya musāvādo anavajjo, itaro sāvajjo. Garuādīnaṃ atthāya pesuññaharaṇaṃ anavajjaṃ, itaraṃ sāvajjaṃ. Bhāratayuddhasītāharaṇādikathā pāpavūpasamāya hotīti evamādike micchāgāhe saṅgaṇhāti. Diṭṭhamaṅgalādīnīti diṭṭhasutamutamaṅgalāni. Sabhāvatikkhenāti lobhassa, micchābhinivesassa [V 2.0113] vā vasena saraseneva tikhiṇena kurūrena. Mandenāti dandhena atikhiṇena. Tādisaṃ pana attano, parassa vā samussāhanena pavattatīti āha “samussāhitenā”ti. Parabhaṇḍaṃ vā haratīti vā-saddena tathāpavattanakamusāvādādīnampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Kāmānaṃ vā anubhuyyamānānaṃ. Vā-saddena parasantakassa vā ayathādhippetatāya yaṃ laddhaṃ, taṃ gahetabbanti gahaṇādikaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

In 'or in regard to sensual pleasures,' the word 'or' (vā) has the sense of non-restriction. By this, it includes such wrong graspings as that for brahmins, only the taking of gold is blameworthy as theft, while other things are blameless. False speech for the sake of teachers, cattle, oneself, one's life, or marriage is blameless; otherwise it is blameworthy. Slander for the sake of teachers, etc., is blameless; otherwise it is blameworthy. Talk about the Bhārata war, the abduction of Sītā, etc., leads to the calming of evil. 'Auspicious signs seen, etc.' means auspicious signs seen, heard, and cognized. 'With natural sharpness' means by the sharp, cruel power of greed or wrong adherence, by its own nature. 'Slowly' means sluggishly, not sharply. But since such a state occurs through one's own or another's instigation, it is said 'instigated.' In 'or he takes another's property,' by the word 'or,' the inclusion of false speech, etc., that occurs in such a way should be understood. Or 'of sensual pleasures being enjoyed.' By the word 'or,' it includes taking, etc., based on the view that since another's property is not as one desires, whatever is obtained from it should be taken.

Duvidhameva hoti sampayuttadhammavasena bhedābhāvato. Yadi evaṃ, kasmā “domanassasahagataṃ paṭighasampayutta”nti vuttanti? Asādhāraṇadhammehi tassa cittassa upalakkhaṇatthaṃ. Pāṇātipātādīsūti pāṇātipātanādīsu. Ādi-saddena adinnādānamusāvādapesuññapharusasamphappalāpabyāpāde saṅgaṇhāti. Sabhāvatikkhaṃ hutvā pavattamānaṃ cittaṃ asaṅkhārameva hoti, itaraṃ sasaṅkhāranti adhippāyenāha “tikkhamandappavattikāle”ti. Mandaṃ pana hutvā pavattamānaṃ ekaṃsena sasaṅkhāramevāti na sakkā viññātuṃ. Yaṃ sasaṅkhārena sappayogena pavattati, taṃ mandameva hotīti katvā tathāvuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

It is only twofold by way of associated states, due to the absence of distinction. If so, why is it said, 'accompanied by displeasure and associated with aversion'? To distinguish that consciousness by its unshared states. The phrase 'in killing living beings, etc.' refers to killing living beings and so forth. By the word 'etc.,' it includes taking what is not given, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, and ill-will. A mind occurring with inherent sharpness is unprompted, while the other is prompted—with this intention it is said, 'at the time of sharp or slow occurrence.' However, a mind occurring slowly cannot be known for certain to be exclusively prompted. It should be understood that it is stated thus because what occurs with prompting and effort is invariably slow.

Mohekahetukaṃ cittaṃ mūlantaravirahato atimūḷhaṃ, vicikicchuddhaccayogato cañcalañcāti upekkhāsahagatameva hoti, na tassa kadācipi sabhāvatikkhatā atthi. Ārammaṇe hi saṃsappanavasena, vikkhipanavasena ca pavattamānassa cittadvayassa kīdise kicce sabhāvatikkhatāya, ussāhetabbatāya vā bhavitabbaṃ, tasmā na tattha saṅkhārabhedo atthi. Aññesu akusalacittesu labbhamānampi uddhaccaṃ visesato ettheva balavaṃ, tato eva sampayuttadhammesu padhānaṃ hutvā pavattatīti idameva uddhaccena visesetvā vuttaṃ “uddhaccasampayutta”nti. Tathā hi pāḷiyaṃ (dha. sa. 427) idha sarūpato [M 2.0122] uddhaccaṃ āgataṃ, evaṃ asādhāraṇapadhānadhammavasena mohamūlaṃ “vicikicchāsampayuttaṃ, uddhaccasampayutta”nti duvidhaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Asanniṭṭhānaṃ saṃsayo. Vikkhepo avūpasamo, bhantatāti attho.

The consciousness that has the single root of delusion, being devoid of another root, is extremely deluded. Due to its association with doubt and restlessness, it is very agitated, and thus it is accompanied only by equanimity. For it, there is never any inherent sharpness. Indeed, for the two types of consciousness that occur by way of wavering with doubt in the object and by way of distraction, in what kind of function could there be inherent sharpness or the need to be prompted? Therefore, there is no distinction of prompting therein. Although restlessness is found in other unwholesome consciousnesses, it is particularly strong here. For that very reason, it occurs as predominant among its associated states. Thus, this very consciousness is specifically distinguished by restlessness and called 'associated with restlessness.' Indeed, in the Pāḷi text, restlessness is presented here in its own form. Thus, by way of the unshared factor (doubt) and the predominant factor (restlessness), the delusion-rooted consciousness is said to be of two types—'associated with doubt' and 'associated with restlessness'—this should be understood. Indecision is doubt. Distraction is non-tranquility, the state of agitation; this is the meaning.

Tayidaṃ dvādasavidhampi akusalacittaṃ chasu ārammaṇesu yaṃ vā taṃ vā ālambitvā upekkhāsahagatāhetukakiriyāmanoviññāṇadhātānantaraṃ kāyadvārādīhi tīhi dvārehi kāyakammādivasena yathārahaṃ pāṇātipātādikammapathavasena ceva kammavasena ca uppajjatīti veditabbaṃ.

These twelve types of unwholesome consciousness, taking any of the six objects whatsoever, arise immediately after the equanimity-accompanied, rootless, functional mind-consciousness-element. They arise through the three doors, beginning with the body door, appropriately by way of bodily action, etc., and by way of the courses of action such as killing living beings, and also by way of kamma. This should be understood.

Tattha [V 2.0114] ṭhapetvā uddhaccasahagataṃ sesaṃ ekādasavidhampi catūsupi apāyesu paṭisandhiṃ deti, pavattivipākaṃ sugatiyampi. Uddhaccasahagataṃ pana pavattivipākamevāti. Etthāha – kiṃ pana kāraṇaṃ sabbadubbalaṃ vicikicchāsampayuttaṃ paṭisandhiṃ deti, adhimokkhasabbhāvato tato balavantampi uddhaccasahagataṃ na detīti? Dassanena pahātabbesu avuttattā. Idaṃ hi paṭisandhiṃ dentaṃ apāyesu dadeyya, apāyagamanīyañca dassanapahātabbanti tattha vucceyya, na ca vuttaṃ. Tasmā paṭisandhiṃ na deti, pavattivipākadānaṃ panassa na sakkā paṭikkhipituṃ. Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅge “uddhaccasahagate ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā, tassa vipāke ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 730 atthato samānaṃ) vacanato.

Among them, setting aside the consciousness accompanied by restlessness, the remaining eleven types give rebirth-linking in the four woeful states, and also give resultants during the course of existence in a happy destination. The consciousness accompanied by restlessness, however, gives only resultants during the course of existence. Here it is asked: What, then, is the reason that the weakest of all, the consciousness associated with doubt, gives rebirth-linking, while the consciousness accompanied by restlessness, though stronger than it due to the presence of decision, does not? Because of its not being stated among the things to be abandoned by vision. For if this consciousness were to give rebirth-linking, it would do so in the woeful states, and that which leads to the woeful states is to be abandoned by vision; thus it would be stated there. But it was not stated. Therefore, it does not give rebirth-linking. However, its giving of resultants during the course of existence cannot be denied, because of the statement in the Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga: 'Knowledge in a mind accompanied by restlessness is the analytical knowledge of Dhamma; knowledge in its resultant is the analytical knowledge of meaning.'

Apare panāhu – puthujjanassa uppajjamānaṃ uddhaccasahagataṃ dassanappahātabbasahāyasabbhāvato ubhayavipākampi deti, na sekkhassa tadabhāvatoti. Idamettha vicāretabbaṃ, yassa vipākadānaṃ vuttaṃ, kiṃ taṃ bhāvanāya pahātabbaṃ, udāhu noti? Kiñcettha – yadi tāva bhāvanāya pahātabbaṃ, paṭṭhāne bhāvanāya pahātabbassa nānākkhaṇikakammapaccayabhāvo vattabbo siyā. Atha na bhāvanāya pahātabbaṃ, dassanenapahātabbattike “nevadassanenanabhāvanāyapahātabba”miccassa vibhaṅge vattabbaṃ siyā. Yadi tabbiruddhasabhāvatāya tattha na vucceyya, evampi tasmiṃ tike tassa navattabbatā āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati, kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Cittuppādakaṇḍe (dha. sa. 365 ādayo) āgatānaṃ dvādasannaṃ akusalacittuppādānaṃ dvīhi padehi saṅgahitattā vibhajitvā dassetabbassa niyogato kassaci cittuppādassa abhāvā, yathā uppannattike atītādīnaṃ navattabbatā na vuttā, evametassāpi. Atha vā bhāvanāya pahātuṃ asakkuṇeyyassāpi tassa puthujjane vattamānassa [M 2.0123] bhāvanāya pahātabbasabhāvasāmaññato, sāvajjato ca bhāvanāya pahātabbapariyāyo vijjatīti natthi navattabbatāpasaṅgadoso. Nippariyāyena ca na bhāvanāya pahātabbanti tassa vasena nānākkhaṇikakammapaccayabhāvopi na vutto. Dassanapahātabbapaccayassāpi uddhaccasahagatassa sahāyavekallamattameva dassanena kataṃ, na kocipi bhāvo anuppādadhammataṃ tassa āpāditoti ekantena bhāvanāya pahātabbatā vuttā. Atha vā apāyagamanīyabhāvāpekkhaṃ dassanappahātabbavacananti tadabhāvato taṃ vibhajanaṃ vuttanti.

Others, however, say: The consciousness associated with restlessness arising in a worldling, due to the presence of its companion which is to be abandoned by vision, gives both kinds of results (in the course of life and at rebirth-linking); but for a noble disciple in training, due to the absence of that companion, it does not. Herein, this should be investigated: Regarding that consciousness for which the giving of result is stated, is it to be abandoned by development, or is it not? And here, something further should be considered: If, in the first place, it is to be abandoned by development, then in the Paṭṭhāna, the state of being a different-moment kamma-condition for what is to be abandoned by development should be declared. Or if it is not to be abandoned by development, then it should be stated in the analysis of the term 'to be abandoned neither by vision nor by development' within the Triad on what is to be abandoned by vision. If it is not stated there due to its nature being contrary to both, even so, does its unstateability in that triad come about? It does not come about. What is the reason? Because the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses that come in the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness are included by the two terms, and because there is no specific consciousness that must necessarily be shown separately. Just as in the Triad on the Arisen, the unstateability of the past, etc., is not stated, so too for this consciousness. Alternatively, for that consciousness occurring in a worldling, which is indeed unable to be abandoned by development, due to its commonality of nature with what is to be abandoned by development and due to its being faulty, the figurative expression 'to be abandoned by development' exists. Therefore, there is no fault of the consequence of unstateability. And in the primary sense, it is not to be abandoned by development; therefore, on account of it, the state of being a different-moment kamma-condition is also not stated. Even for the consciousness associated with restlessness which has a condition that is to be abandoned by vision, only the mere deficiency of its companion has been effected by vision; no state of it whatsoever has been brought to the nature of non-arising. Therefore, its nature of being abandoned by development is stated definitively. Alternatively, the statement 'to be abandoned by vision' is made in consideration of the state of leading to the plane of misery; therefore, due to the absence of that state, that consciousness is not stated separately.

454. “Viññāṇa”nti padaṃ apekkhitvā “abyākataṃ vipāka”nti ādiko napuṃsakaniddeso, tato eva adhikatābyākatāpekkhāya duvidhanti vuttaṃ. Aññathā rūpanibbānānampi abyākatabhāvato [V 2.0115] taṃ catubbidhanti vattabbaṃ siyā. Vipākassa kāmāvacarādibhāvo kusale vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Ahetukatā sahetukatā viya sampayuttahetuvasena, na nibbattakahetuvasena. Vipākassa hi sahetukatā sahetukakammavasena sijjhamānāpi sampayuttahetuvaseneva vuccati, aññathā ahetukānampi sahetukatā āpajjeyyāti. Kasmā pana sahetukassa ahetuko vipāko hotīti? Tattha kāraṇaṃ vuttameva. Kiñca ārammaṇābhinipātamattesu pañcasu viññāṇesu yathā alobhādisampayogo na sambhavati, evaṃ mandataramandakiccesu sampaṭicchanasantīraṇesūti hetūnaṃ uppattiyā asambhavatopi nesaṃ ahetukatā daṭṭhabbā.

454. With reference to the term 'consciousness' (viññāṇa), the neuter designation such as 'indeterminate' (abyākata) and 'resultant' (vipāka) is made. For that very reason, with reference to the indeterminate state connected with consciousness, it is said to be twofold. Otherwise, since form and Nibbāna are also indeterminate, that indeterminate state should be said to be fourfold. The state of the resultant as being of the sense-sphere, etc., should be understood by the very method explained in the section on the wholesome. The state of being rootless, like the state of being with roots, is to be understood by way of associated roots, not by way of productive roots. Indeed, although the state of a resultant as being with roots is accomplished by way of kamma with roots, it is spoken of only by way of associated roots; otherwise, even rootless resultants would attain the state of being with roots. Why, then, is there a rootless resultant of kamma with roots? The reason for that has already been stated. Moreover, just as in the five consciousnesses, which are merely the falling upon an object, association with non-greed and so forth is not possible, so too in receiving and investigating, which have very weak and weak functions, it is not possible. Thus, also because of the impossibility of the arising of the roots, their state of being rootless should be understood.

Manoviññāṇato uppajjanavisiṭṭhamananakiccānaṃ abhāvato manomattā dhātu manodhātu.

The mind-element is merely mind, due to the absence of the distinct mental functions that arise from mind-consciousness.

Cakkhusannissitaṃ hutvā rūpassa vijānanaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etassāti cakkhusannissitarūpavijānanalakkhaṇaṃ. Tattha cakkhusannissitavacanena rūpārammaṇaṃ aññaṃ viññāṇaṃ nivatteti. Vijānanaggahaṇena cakkhusannissite phassādike nivatteti. Cakkhurūpaggahaṇena nissayato, ārammaṇato ca viññāṇaṃ vibhāveti ubhayādhīnavuttikattā. Yadi hi cakkhu nāma na siyā, andhāpi rūpaṃ passeyyuṃ, na ca passanti. Yadi ca nīlādirūpaṃ nāma na siyā, desādiniyamena na bhavitabbaṃ, attheva ca niyamo, ekantasārammaṇatā ca cittassa vuttāti “ārammaṇena vinā nīlādiābhāsaṃ cittaṃ pavattatī”ti evaṃ [M 2.0124] pavatto vādo micchāvādoti veditabbaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇa”ntiādi (ma. ni. 1.204, 400; 3.421, 425; saṃ. ni. 2.44; 4.60; kathā. 465).

Being dependent on the eye, the cognition of form is its characteristic—thus, it has the characteristic of cognition of form dependent on the eye. Herein, the statement 'dependent on the eye' excludes other consciousness that takes form as its object. The term 'cognition' excludes contact and other factors dependent on the eye. By mentioning the eye and form, it distinguishes consciousness in terms of both basis and object, because its activity depends on both. For if there were no such thing as the eye, even the blind would see forms—but they do not. And if there were no such thing as blue or other forms, there would be no restriction based on location, but such a restriction exists. Furthermore, the mind has been declared to be exclusively with an object. Thus, the statement 'Without an object, the mind manifests the appearance of blue, etc.' is to be understood as a false doctrine. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Dependent on the eye and on forms, eye-consciousness arises,' and so forth.

Kasmā panettha vacanabhedo katoti? Ekampi cakkhu viññāṇassa paccayo hoti, rūpaṃ pana anekameva saṃhatanti imassa visesassa dassanatthaṃ. Kiṃ pana kāraṇaṃ ekampi cakkhu viññāṇassa paccayo hoti, rūpaṃ pana anekamevāti? Paccayabhāvavisesato. Cakkhu hi cakkhuviññāṇassa nissayapurejātaindriyavippayuttapaccayehi paccayo hontaṃ atthibhāveneva hoti, tasmiṃ sati tassa bhāvato, asati abhāvato. Yato taṃ atthiavigatapaccayehissa paccayo hotīti vuccati, taṃnissayatā cassa na ekadesena allīyanavasena icchitabbā arūpabhāvato, atha kho garurājādīsu sissarājapurisādīnaṃ viya tappaṭibaddhavuttitāya. Itare pana paccayā tena [V 2.0116] tena visesena veditabbā. Svāyaṃ paccayabhāvo na ekasmiṃ na sambhavatīti ekampi cakkhu viññāṇassa paccayo hotīti “cakkhuñca paṭiccā”ti ekavacanena niddeso kato.

But why is a difference in number made here? It is for the purpose of showing this distinction: even a single eye is a condition for consciousness, whereas form is a condition only as many combined. What, then, is the reason that even a single eye is a condition for consciousness, while form is only many? It is due to the distinction in the state of being a condition. For the eye, while being a condition for eye-consciousness by means of dependence, pre-nascence, faculty, and dissociation conditions, is so only by its state of presence. For when it is present, that consciousness exists; when it is not present, it does not exist. Because of this, it is said that it is a condition for this consciousness by means of presence and non-disappearance conditions, and its state of dependence should not be understood as clinging in part, due to its [consciousness'] non-corporeal nature. Rather, it is like the dependence of disciples and royal attendants on teachers and kings, by way of having an occurrence bound to them. The other conditions, however, should be understood by their respective distinctions. It is not that this state of being a condition is impossible in a single instance; therefore, because even a single eye is a condition for consciousness, the statement 'dependent on the eye' is made in the singular.

Rūpaṃ pana yadipi cakkhu viya purejātaatthiavigatapaccayehi paccayo hoti puretaraṃ hutvā vijjamānakkhaṇeyeva upakārakattā, tathāpi anekameva saṃhataṃ hutvā paccayo hoti ārammaṇabhāvato. Yañhi paccayadhammaṃ sabhāvabhūtaṃ, parikappitākāramattaṃ vā viññāṇaṃ vibhāventaṃ pavattati, tadaññesañca satipi paccayabhāve so tassa sārammaṇasabhāvatāya yaṃ kiñci anālambitvā pavattituṃ asamatthassa olubbha pavattikāraṇatāya ālambanīyato ārammaṇaṃ nāma. Tassa yasmā yathā tathā sabhāvūpaladdhivasena ārammaṇapaccayalābho, tasmā cakkhuviññāṇaṃ rūpaṃ ārabbha pavattamānaṃ tassa sabhāvaṃ vibhāventameva pavattati. Sā cassa indriyādhīnavuttikassa ārammaṇasabhāvūpaladdhi, na ekadvikalāpagatavaṇṇavasena hoti, nāpi katipayakalāpagatavaṇṇavasena, atha kho ābhogānurūpaṃ āpāthagatavaṇṇavasenāti anekameva rūpaṃ saṃhaccakāritāya viññāṇassa paccayo hotīti dassento bhagavā “rūpe cā”ti bahuvacanena niddisi.

Moreover, although form, like the eye, is a condition by way of pre-nascence, presence, and non-disappearance—because, having arisen earlier, it is of assistance at the very moment of its existence—nevertheless, it is only as many forms combined that it is a condition, because of being an object. For, whatever conditional phenomenon consciousness arises while making clear—be it an intrinsic nature or merely a conceptual form—that phenomenon, even though other conditions are present, is called an 'object'. This is because, for that consciousness which is incapable of arising without taking hold of something due to its nature of having an object, that phenomenon is the cause of its arising by being depended upon and is that which is to be taken hold of. Since for that consciousness, the object-condition is gained by means of apprehending the intrinsic nature in some way or other, therefore, when eye-consciousness arises taking form as its object, it arises only while making clear that intrinsic nature. And for this consciousness, whose occurrence is dependent on the faculty, that apprehension of the object's intrinsic nature does not occur by means of color located in one or two material groups, nor by means of color located in a few material groups; but rather, it occurs by means of color that has come into range in accordance with the mind's turning towards it. Thus, showing that 'It is only many forms that are a condition for consciousness by acting in combination,' the Blessed One indicated with the plural, 'and on forms.'

Yaṃ [M 2.0125] pana “rūpāyatanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.2) vuttaṃ, taṃ kathanti? Tampi yādisaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo hoti, tādisameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kīdisaṃ pana tanti? Samuditanti pākaṭoyamattho. Evañca katvā yadeke vadanti “āyatanasallakkhaṇavasena cakkhuviññāṇādayo sallakkhaṇārammaṇā, na dabbasallakkhaṇavasenā”ti, tampi yuttameva hoti. Na cettha samudāyārammaṇatā āsaṅkitabbā samudāyābhogassevābhāvato. Samuditā pana vaṇṇadhammā ārammaṇapaccayā honti. Kathaṃ pana paccekaṃ asamatthā samuditā ārammaṇā paccayā honti, na hi paccekaṃ daṭṭhuṃ asakkontā andhā samuditā passantīti? Nayidamekantikaṃ visuṃ visuṃ asamatthānaṃ sivikāvahanādīsu samatthatāya dassanato. Kesādīnañca yasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhitānaṃ paccekaṃ vaṇṇaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkā, tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne samuditānaṃ vaṇṇaṃ gahetuṃ sakkāti bhiyyopi tesaṃ saṃhaccakāritā paribyattā. Etena cakkhuviññāṇassa paramāṇurūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ, udāhu taṃsamudāyotiādikā codanā paṭikkhittāti veditabbā. “Sotañca paṭicca sadde cā”tiādīsupi (ma. ni. 1.204, 400; 3.421, 425, 426) eseva [V 2.0117] nayo. Evaṃ ubhayādhīnavuttikatāya cakkhuviññāṇassa nissayato, ārammaṇato ca vibhāvanaṃ kataṃ, evaṃ sotaviññāṇādīsupi yathārahaṃ vattabbaṃ.

Regarding what is said: 'The form-āyatana is a condition for the eye-consciousness-element and its associated mental states by way of the object-condition' (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.2), how is that to be understood? That too is stated referring to just such a form-āyatana as is a condition for eye-consciousness by way of the object-condition. But what kind is that? It is the composite—this meaning is obvious. And for this reason, when some say, 'Eye-consciousness, etc., take an object by way of the characteristic of the āyatana, not by way of the characteristic of the substance,' that too is quite correct. And here, having a composite as an object should not be suspected, because there is simply no adverting to a composite. However, composite color-phenomena are object-conditions. But how can things which are individually incapable be object-conditions when composite? For indeed, blind people, being unable to see individually, do not see even when gathered together. This is not an absolute rule, for the capability of those who are individually incapable is seen in cases such as carrying a palanquin. Moreover, regarding hairs, etc., in a place where the color of them individually cannot be grasped, in that very same place the color of them as a composite can be grasped; thus, their cooperative functioning is even more clearly revealed. By this, it should be understood that the objection—whether the object of eye-consciousness is atomic form or its composite—is refuted. The same method applies also to passages such as, 'Dependent on the ear and sounds...' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.204, 400; 3.421, 425, 426). Thus, the explanation of eye-consciousness has been made in terms of its twofold dependence—from the support and from the object; in the same way, it should be stated appropriately regarding ear-consciousness, etc.

Rūpamattārammaṇarasanti rūpāyatanamattasseva ārammaṇakaraṇarasaṃ. Mattasaddena yathā ārammaṇantaraṃ nivatteti, evaṃ rūpāyatanepi labbhamāne ekacce visese nivatteti. Na hi cakkhuviññāṇaṃ vaṇṇamattato aññaṃ kiñci visesaṃ tattha gahetuṃ sakkoti. Tenāha bhagavā “pañcahi viññāṇehi na kiñci dhammaṃ paṭivijānāti aññatra abhinipātamattā”ti. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ uppajjamānaṃ rūpārammaṇe eva uppajjanato tadabhimukhabhāvena gayhatīti vuttaṃ “rūpābhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāna”nti. Attano anantaraṃ uppajjamānānaṃ arūpadhammānaṃ samanantaravigatā arūpadhammā pavattiokāsadānena anantarasamanantaranatthivigatapaccayehi upakārakā nissayārammaṇadhammā viya āsannakāraṇanti dassento āha “rūpārammaṇāya kiriyamanodhātuyā apagamapadaṭṭhāna”nti. Sotaviññāṇādīsupi vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo.

'Its function is having only form as its object' means it has the function of taking only the form-āyatana as its object. Just as the word 'mere' excludes another object, so too, it excludes certain particulars even within the form-āyatana that is being apprehended. For eye-consciousness cannot grasp any particular there other than mere color. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'With the five consciousnesses, one does not discern any phenomenon apart from mere impinging.' Because eye-consciousness, when arising, arises only in relation to a form object, it is regarded as confronting that object; therefore, it is said, 'its manifestation is the state of confronting form.' To show that immediately ceased immaterial states are a proximate cause for the immaterial states arising immediately after them—just as support and object conditions are—by giving the opportunity for their arising and being helpful through the proximity, contiguity, absence, and disappearance conditions, he said it has 'cessation as its proximate cause for the functional mind-element with a form-object.' The meaning for ear-consciousness and so on should be understood in the very same way that has been stated.

Cakkhuviññāṇādigahitaṃ [M 2.0126] rūpādiārammaṇaṃ tadanantarameva aparipatantaṃ katvā sampaṭicchantī gaṇhantī viya hotīti vuttaṃ “rūpādisampaṭicchanarasā”ti. Tathābhāvena sampaṭicchanabhāvena paccupatiṭṭhatīti tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā.

It takes up the form-object etc. grasped by the eye-consciousness and so on, immediately after them, preventing it from passing away, as if receiving and grasping it; therefore, it is said to have 'the function of receiving form and so on.' It manifests with that nature, the nature of receiving; therefore, its manifestation is that very nature.

Chasu ārammaṇesu kadāci pañcannaṃ, tato vā katipayānaṃ vijānanasabhāvāpi chaḷārammaṇavijānanalakkhaṇā vuttā taṃsabhāvānativattanato, chasveva vā itaresaṃ ārammaṇānaṃ antogadhattā. Santīraṇādikiccāti santīraṇatadārammaṇakiccā vā, santīraṇatadārammaṇapaṭisandhibhavaṅgacutikiccā vāti adhippāyo. “Hadayavatthupadaṭṭhānā”ti idaṃ imāsaṃ dvinnaṃ manoviññāṇadhātūnaṃ ekanteneva hadayavatthusannissayatāya vuttaṃ. Heṭṭhā vuttanayena pana taṃtaṃanantarātītaviññāṇāpagamapadaṭṭhānātipi vattuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Tassā bhedoti tassā vipākamanoviññāṇadhātuyā “duvidhā”ti vuttāya duvidhatāsaṅkhāto bhedo. Ekantamiṭṭhārammaṇeti ekanteneva iṭṭhe ārammaṇe, ativiya iṭṭhārammaṇeti attho. Pañcadvāre ceva javanāvasāne cāti ettha pañcadvāre sampaṭicchanavoṭṭhabbanānaṃ antarāḷaṃ ṭhānaṃ, itaratra javanabhavaṅgānanti evaṃ dviṭhānā hoti. Itarāyapi santīraṇatadārammaṇakāle yathāvuttameva ṭhānaṃ, paṭisandhiādikāle pana cutibhavaṅgānaṃ [V 2.0118] antarāḷaṃ paṭisandhiyā, paṭisandhiāvajjanānaṃ tadārammaṇāvajjanānaṃ javanāvajjanānaṃ voṭṭhabbanāvajjanānañca antarāḷaṃ bhavaṅgassa, tadārammaṇapaṭisandhīnaṃ javanapaṭisandhīnaṃ vā antarāḷaṃ cutiyā ṭhānanti veditabbaṃ.

Although having the nature of cognizing sometimes five of the six objects, or from that a few, they are said to have the characteristic of cognizing the six objects because of not transcending that nature, or because the other objects are included within the six themselves. 'The functions of investigating, etc.' means either the functions of investigating and registering, or the functions of investigating, registering, rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death; this is the intended meaning. This phrase, 'having the heart-base as proximate cause,' is said concerning these two mind-consciousness elements because of their being exclusively dependent on the heart-base. However, according to the method stated previously, it is indeed proper to say also that they have as proximate cause the cessation of the respective immediately preceding consciousness. 'Its division' means the division, designated as twofoldness, of that resultant mind-consciousness element which was said to be 'of two kinds.' 'On an exclusively desirable object' means on an object that is exclusively desirable; the meaning is 'on an extremely desirable object.' Herein, in the phrase 'at the five doors and at the end of impulsion,' at the five doors the place is the interval between receiving and determining; elsewhere, it is between impulsion and life-continuum. Thus, it has two places. For the other element also, at the time of investigating and registering, the place is just as stated. But at the time of rebirth-linking, etc., the interval between death and life-continuum is the place for rebirth-linking; the interval between rebirth-linking and adverting, registering and adverting, impulsion and adverting, and determining and adverting is the place for the life-continuum; and the interval between registering and rebirth-linking, or between impulsion and rebirth-linking, is the place for death. This should be understood.

Chasūti ettha pubbe vuttanayeneva vibhāgo veditabbo. Kāyassa nissayabhūtānaṃ nātiiṭṭhaphoṭṭhabbabhūtānaṃ paṭighaṭṭanānighaṃsassa balavabhāvato kāyaviññāṇaṃ sukhasampayuttaṃ. Upādārūpānaṃyeva ghaṭṭanā dubbalāti cakkhuviññāṇādīni upekkhāsahagatāni. Tenāha “sesaṃ upekkhāyutta”nti. Sesaṃ chabbidhampi.

Herein, the division into six should be understood in the same way as stated previously. Because of the powerful nature of the striking and friction of the material phenomena that are the support for the body and of the tangible objects that are not extremely desirable, body-consciousness is associated with pleasure. Since the impact of the derived matter only is weak, eye-consciousness and so on are accompanied by equanimity. Therefore, he said: 'The rest is associated with equanimity.' The remainder is also sixfold.

Alobhādosāmohā ceva alobhādosā ca alobhādayo, tehi alobhādīhi vipākahetūhi sampayuttaṃ alobhādivipākahetusampayuttaṃ. Kāmāvacarakusalaṃ viya somanassādibhedatoti yathā kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ somanassupekkhāñāṇasaṅkhārabhedato aṭṭhavidhaṃ, evamidampīti aṭṭhavidhatāya sadisataṃ dasseti. Kāmāvacarabhāvato hīnādito, yonīsu uppattito ca sadisameva, sampayuttadhammato pana ārammaṇato, pavattiākārato ca visadisaṃ. Tathā [M 2.0127] hi kusalaṃ kammadvāravasena pavattati, na idaṃ, vipākānaṃ aviññattijanakattā. Uppattidvāravasena pana imassāpi attheva pavattibhedo pañcadvāramanodvāresu mahāvipākānaṃ tadārammaṇavasena pavattisambhavato. Yathā pana kusalaṃ gativasena pañcavidhaṃ, viññāṇaṭṭhitivasena sattavidhañca, na evamidaṃ tadekadese eva uppajjanato. Tattha ārammaṇato, ekaccapavattiākārato ca visadisataṃ dassetuṃ “yathā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Chasu ārammaṇesūti parittādiatītādiajjhattādippabhedesu chasu ārammaṇesu.

Non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, as well as non-greed and non-hatred, are called 'non-greed and so forth'. Consciousness associated with those roots beginning with non-greed, which are resultant roots, is called 'associated with resultant roots beginning with non-greed'. Just as sense-sphere wholesome consciousness is eightfold through the distinctions of joy, equanimity, knowledge, and prompting, so too is this resultant consciousness shown to be similar in being eightfold. It is indeed similar in being of the sense-sphere, in being inferior and so forth, and in arising in the four modes of birth; however, it is dissimilar with respect to associated states, the object, and the mode of occurrence. For wholesome consciousness occurs by way of the doors of kamma, but this resultant consciousness does not, because resultants are not producers of intimation. However, by way of the doors of arising, there is indeed a distinction in the occurrence of this resultant consciousness as well, because of the possibility of the great resultants occurring by way of registration in the five sense-doors and the mind-door. Furthermore, just as wholesome consciousness is fivefold by way of destinations and sevenfold by way of stations of consciousness, this resultant consciousness is not so, because it arises only in a single part of them. Therein, to show the dissimilarity with respect to the object and a certain mode of occurrence, the phrase beginning with 'yathā pana...' was stated. ‘In the six objects’ means: in the six objects distinguished as limited, etc.; past, etc.; and internal, etc.

Āgamanādivasenāti āgamanapaccayavasena. Tattha ekaccānaṃ ācariyānaṃ matena mukhe calite ādāsatale mukhanimittaṃ calanaṃ viya asaṅkhārassa kusalassa vipāko asaṅkhāro, sasaṅkhārassa kusalassa vipāko sasaṅkhāroti evaṃ āgamanavasena. Ekaccānaṃ pana ācariyānaṃ matena balavantehi vibhūtehi paccayehi kammādīhi uppanno asaṅkhāro, dubbalehi sasaṅkhāroti evaṃ paccayavasena. Sampayuttadhammānanti pāḷiyaṃ sarūpato āgatasampayuttadhammānaṃ. Tesaṃ hi vasena kusalato vipākassa visesābhāvo. Nirussāhanti ettha ussāho nāma anupacchinnāvijjātaṇhāmānasantāne [V 2.0119] vipākuppādanasamatthatāsaṅkhāto byāpāro, so vipākesu natthīti taṃ nirussāhaṃ. Kusalesu pana abhiññāvasapavattesupi atthevāti taṃ saussāhaṃ.

The phrase 'āgamanādivasenāti' means 'by way of its source and conditions.' Herein, according to some teachers, just as when the face moves, the movement of the face's reflection on a mirror's surface occurs, so too the result of an unprompted wholesome act is unprompted, and the result of a prompted wholesome act is prompted—thus, by way of its source. However, according to other teachers, what arises through powerful and manifest conditions such as kamma is unprompted, while what arises through weak conditions is prompted—thus, by way of conditions. The phrase 'sampayuttadhammānaṃ' refers to the associated states that have come forth in their own nature in the Pāli text. For by their means, there is no distinction of the result from the wholesome. Herein, in 'nirussāhaṃ' (without exertion), 'exertion' (ussāha) is the activity designated as the capacity to produce results in a continuity where ignorance, craving, and conceit are not cut off. Since this is absent in results, they are without exertion. However, in wholesome states, even in those proceeding by the power of higher knowledge, it is indeed present—thus, they are with exertion.

Lobhādīnaṃ ekantasāvajjatāya ayonisomanasikārahetukānaṃ natthi vipākabhāvo, alobhādīnampi ekantaanavajjasabhāvānaṃ kāraṇassa tabbidhuratāya nattheva akusalavipākabhāvoti āha “akusalavipākaṃ ahetukamevā”ti. Yathā atiiṭṭhe, iṭṭhamajjhatte ca ārammaṇe vedanābhedasabbhāvato kusalavipākamanoviññāṇadhātu duvidhā hoti somanassasahagatā, upekkhāsahagatāti, na evaṃ atianiṭṭhe, aniṭṭhamajjhatte ca ārammaṇe vedanābhedo atthīti akusalavipākamanoviññāṇadhātu ekamevāti “sattavidha”nti vuttaṃ. Sati hi tattha vedanābhede atianiṭṭhe domanassena bhavitabbaṃ, na ca paṭighena vinā domanassaṃ uppajjatīti.

Due to the entirely blameworthy nature of greed and other defilements, which are rooted in unwise attention, there is no resultant state for them. Similarly, for non-greed and other wholesome states, which are entirely blameless in nature, because the cause is incompatible with them, there is no unwholesome resultant state. Therefore, it is said, 'An unwholesome result is only rootless.' Just as, in the case of a very desirable or moderately desirable object, the wholesome resultant mind-consciousness element is twofold—accompanied by joy or accompanied by equanimity—due to the presence of a difference in feeling, it is not so for a very undesirable or moderately undesirable object. There is no such difference of feeling there. Thus, the unwholesome resultant mind-consciousness element is only one. Therefore, it is said to be 'sevenfold.' For if there were a difference in feeling in that case, when the object is very undesirable, it would have to be accompanied by displeasure. But displeasure does not arise without aversion.

Kāyaviññāṇassa dukkhasahagatatā kusalavipāke vuttavipariyāyena veditabbā. Upekkhā hīnāti ekantanihīnassa akusalassa vipākabhāvato upekkhāpi samānā hīnā eva dukkhasabhāvattā. Tenāha “dukkhaṃ viya [M 2.0128] nātitikhiṇā”ti. Yathā dukkhaṃ ativiya tikhiṇaṃ kaṭukaṃ, na evamayaṃ, tathāpi dukkhasabhāveneva pavattati. Na hi akusalassa vipāko adukkho hoti. Upekkhābhāvo cassa balavatā bādhiyamānassa paṭippaharituṃ asakkontassa dubbalassa purisassa tena kariyamānabādhāya upekkhanā viyāti daṭṭhabbo. Itaresūti kusalavipākesu.

The state of body-consciousness being accompanied by pain should be understood in contrast to what was stated for wholesome results. The phrase 'equanimity is inferior' means that because it is the result of entirely inferior unwholesome kamma, equanimity, even while being equanimity, is still inferior due to its painful nature. Therefore, it is said, 'like pain, though not extremely sharp.' Just as pain is extremely sharp and acute, this equanimity is not so, yet it still operates with a painful nature. For the result of unwholesome kamma is never without suffering. And its state of equanimity should be seen as like the indifference of a weak man who, being oppressed by a strong person and unable to retaliate, is indifferent to the oppression inflicted upon him. 'In others' refers to wholesome results.

Rūpāvacaranti rūpāvacaravipākaviññāṇaṃ. Vipākakathā hesāti. Kusalaṃ viyāti rūpāvacarakusalaṃ viya. Na hi rūpāvacaravipāko tadaññakusalasadiso. Apica sambandhisaddā ete, yadidaṃ “kusalaṃ, vipāko”ti ca. Tasmā yathā “mātaraṃ payirupāsatī”ti vutte attano mātaranti avuttampi siddhamevetaṃ, evaṃ idhāpīti attano kusalaṃ viyāti attho. Kusalasadisatā cettha dhammato, ārammaṇato ca veditabbā. Tathā hi ye phassādayo kusale labbhanti, te vipākepi labbhanti. Yasmiṃ ca ārammaṇe kusalaṃ pavattati, tattheva ayaṃ vipākopi pavattati. Yaṃ panettha pañcamajjhānacittaṃ abhiññāppattaṃ, tassa vipāko eva natthi. Kasmā natthi? Asambhavato, ānisaṃsabhūtattā ca. Tañhi vipākaṃ dentaṃ rūpāvacarameva dadeyya. Na hi aññabhūmikaṃ kammaṃ aññabhūmikaṃ vipākaṃ deti. Kammanimittārammaṇatā ca rūpāvacaravipākassa vuttāti na taṃ aññaṃ ārabbha [V 2.0120] pavattati. Parittārammaṇādiārammaṇañca taṃ na hotīti ayamasambhavo. Jhānassa ānisaṃsabhūtañca dānādīnaṃ tasmiṃ attabhāve paccayalābho viyāti.

'Rūpāvacara' means form-sphere resultant consciousness, for this is a discussion on resultants. 'Like the wholesome' means like the form-sphere wholesome, for the form-sphere resultant is not similar to wholesome states of other kinds. Moreover, these words, 'wholesome' and 'resultant', are related terms. Therefore, just as when it is said, 'he attends upon his mother,' it is understood to mean 'his own mother' even though not explicitly stated, so too here the meaning is 'like one's own wholesome.' Here, the similarity to the wholesome should be understood in terms of its associated states and its object. For the same associated states, such as contact, that are found in the wholesome are also found in the resultant. And in whatever object the wholesome occurs, in that very same object this resultant also occurs. However, the fifth jhāna consciousness that has attained higher knowledge has no result at all. Why is there none? Because of impossibility, and because it is of the nature of a benefit. For if it were to give a result, it would give only a form-sphere result. For kamma belonging to one plane does not give a result belonging to another plane. Furthermore, it has been stated that the form-sphere resultant has the kamma-sign as its object, so it does not arise in relation to another object. And it does not have a limited object, etc., as its object; this is the impossibility. And it is a benefit of the jhāna, like the gain of requisites in that very existence from deeds such as giving.
