Pavattito pana vipākassa, kusalassa ca attheva bhedoti taṃ dassetuṃ “kusalaṃ panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kusalaṃ viya kasiṇugghāṭimākāsādiārammaṇabhedato catubbidhaṃ. Pavattibhedo vuttanayova javanavasena, paṭisandhiādivasena ca pavattanato.

However, there is indeed a distinction between the resultant and the wholesome by way of occurrence; in order to show that distinction, the passage beginning with 'kusalaṃ pana...' was stated. Like the formless-sphere wholesome, it is fourfold due to the distinction of objects such as the space of the removed kasina, etc. The distinction of occurrence is just as was stated, because it occurs by way of impulsion and by way of rebirth-linking, etc.

Catumaggayuttacittaphalattāti catūhi ariyamaggehi sampayuttakusalacittassa phalattā, catubbidhasāmaññaphalasampayuttabhāvatoti attho. Maggavīthiyaṃ dvikkhattuṃ, tikkhattuṃ vā phalasamāpattiyaṃ aparicchinnaparimāṇaṃ pavattamānampi dvīsu ṭhānesu pavattiyā “dvidhā pavattatī”ti vuttaṃ. Sabbampīti tevīsatividhaṃ kāmāvacaravipākaṃ, pañcavidhaṃ rūpāvacaravipākaṃ, catubbidhaṃ arūpāvacaravipākaṃ, catubbidhameva lokuttaravipākanti sabbampi vipākaviññāṇaṃ nātisaṅkhepavitthāranayena chattiṃsavidhaṃ hoti.

‘Catumaggayuttacittaphalattā’ means: because of being the fruit of wholesome consciousness associated with the four noble paths, that is, because of being associated with the four kinds of fruition of recluseship. Although it occurs twice or thrice in the path process, or for an un-delimited measure in the attainment of fruition, it is said to ‘occur in two ways’ because of its occurrence in these two instances. ‘Sabbampi’ (all) means: the twenty-three kinds of sense-sphere resultant, the five kinds of fine-material-sphere resultant, the four kinds of immaterial-sphere resultant, and the four kinds of supramundane resultant. Thus, all resultant consciousness, by a method that is neither too brief nor too extensive, is of thirty-six kinds.

Bhūmibhedato [M 2.0129] tividhaṃ lokuttarassa abhāvato. Lokuttarañhi kiriyacittaṃ natthi ekantena anantaravipākadāyibhāvato. Vuttañhi “samādhimānantarikaññamāhū”ti (khu. pā. 6.5; su. ni. 228). Hotu tāva sekkhānaṃ uppajjamānaṃ anuttaraṃ kusalaṃ puggalantarabhāvūpanayanato saphalaṃ, arahato pana uppajjamānaṃ puggalantarabhāvūpanayanato nipphalaṃ, tassa kiriyabhāvo kasmā na icchitoti? Icchitabbo siyā. Yadi tassa punappunaṃ uppatti siyā, sakiṃyeva pana lokuttarakusalaṃ pavattati. Yadi hi punappunaṃ pavatteyya, maggacittaṃ arahatopi pavattatīti lokuttarakiriyacittaṃ siyā, na cetaṃ atthi payojanābhāvato. Tasmā natthi lokuttarakiriyaviññāṇaṃ. Kiriyaviññāṇanti ca kiriyāmattaṃ viññāṇaṃ, kusalākusalaṃ viya kiñci vipākaṃ anuppādetvā kiriyāmattameva hutvā pavattanakaviññāṇanti attho. Kasmā panetaṃ vipākaṃ na uppādetīti? Vuccate – ettha hi yadetaṃ āvajjanadvayaṃ, taṃ anupacchinnabhavamūlepi santāne pavattaṃ anāsevanatāya dubbalabhāvato abījasāmatthiyaṃ viya pupphaṃ aphalameva hoti. Yaṃ pana ucchinnabhavamūlāyaṃ santatiyaṃ pavattaṃ aṭṭhārasavidhaṃ viññāṇaṃ, taṃ samucchinnamūlāya latāya pupphaṃ viya phaladāyi na hotīti veditabbaṃ. Aññassa asambhavato [V 2.0121] kiriyahetunā nāma alobhādināva bhavitabbanti āha “alobhādikiriyahetuvirahita”nti.

It is threefold due to the division of planes, because of the absence of the supramundane. Indeed, there is no supramundane functional consciousness because it absolutely has the nature of giving an immediate result. For it is said, ‘They call that concentration the one with an immediate result’ (Khu. pā. 6.5; Su. ni. 228). Let it be that for trainees, the supreme wholesome consciousness that arises is fruitful because it leads to the state of another type of individual. But for the Arahant, what arises is fruitless because it does not lead to the state of another type of individual; why, then, is its functional nature not accepted? It should be accepted if it were to arise repeatedly. But the supramundane wholesome consciousness occurs only once. For if it were to occur repeatedly, the path-consciousness would occur even for an Arahant, and thus there would be supramundane functional consciousness. But this does not exist, due to the absence of a purpose. Therefore, there is no supramundane functional consciousness. And ‘functional consciousness’ means consciousness that is merely a function; that is, consciousness that occurs, having become merely a function without producing any result, like wholesome or unwholesome consciousness. But why does it not produce a result? It is said: Herein, the two advertings, though occurring in a continuity with an unsevered root of existence, are weak due to the absence of repetition and are therefore fruitless, like a flower without the capacity for seeds. But the eighteen types of consciousness that arise in a continuity with a severed root of existence, like a flower on a vine with a cut root, do not yield fruit—this should be understood. Because of the impossibility of any other type of cause, a functional cause must be of the nature of non-greed, etc. Therefore, he said, ‘devoid of functional causes such as non-greed, etc.’

Cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ purecarā hutvā rūpādiārammaṇānaṃ vijānanalakkhaṇā cakkhuviññāṇādipurecararūpādivijānanalakkhaṇā. Ayaṃ pana manoviññāṇato uppannāpi visiṭṭhamananakiccābhāvena manomattā dhātūti manodhātu. Tathā hesā manoviññāṇassa paccayo na hoti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana dhātuniddese (visuddhi. 2.517) āgamissati. Āvajjanarasāti ābhogarasā, cittasantānassa vā purimākārato aññathā oṇojanarasā. Bhavaṅgavicchedapadaṭṭhānāti bhavaṅgasantānavicchedapadaṭṭhānā. Apubbārammaṇā sakideva pavattamānā sabbathā visayarasaṃ anubhavituṃ na sakkotīti iṭṭhādīsu sabbattha upekkhāyuttāva hoti.

The mind-element has the characteristic of cognizing visible forms and other objects, having gone before eye-consciousness and so forth; that is, it has the characteristic of cognizing forms and other objects, being the forerunner of eye-consciousness and so forth. However, this mind-element, even though it arises from mind-consciousness, is called merely ‘mind-element’ because it lacks a distinctive cognizing function. Indeed, it is not a condition for mind-consciousness. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation will come in the Exposition of the Elements (Visuddhimagga 2.517). Its function is adverting—that is, the function of turning towards, or the function of inclining the mental continuum otherwise from its previous state. Its proximate cause is the interruption of the life-continuum—that is, the interruption of the continuum of the life-continuum. Because it arises only once toward a new object and cannot fully experience the flavor of the object in all respects, it is invariably associated with equanimity in all cases, whether desirable or otherwise.

Sādhāraṇāti sekkhāsekkhaputhujjanānaṃ sādhāraṇā. Asādhāraṇāti asekkhānaṃyeva āveṇikā. Voṭṭhabbanāvajjanarasāti pañcadvāre santīraṇena gahitārammaṇaṃ vavatthapentī viya pavattanato voṭṭhabbanarasā, manodvāre [M 2.0130] pana vuttanayena āvajjanarasā. Tathābhāvena pañcadvāramanodvāresu yathākkamaṃ voṭṭhabbanāvajjanabhāvena paccupatiṭṭhatīti tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā. Voṭṭhabbanakāle santīraṇakiccānaṃ tissannaṃ ahetukavipākamanoviññāṇadhātūnaṃ āvajjanakāle yassa kassaci bhavaṅgassāti imesaṃ aññatarāpagamo etissā āsannakāraṇanti āha “ahetuka…pe… padaṭṭhānā”ti.

Common means it is common to trainees, non-trainees, and ordinary people. Uncommon means it is unique to the non-trainees alone. Its function is determining and adverting: at the five sense-doors, its function is determining, because it proceeds as if establishing an object grasped by investigation; at the mind-door, however, its function is adverting, as stated previously. Because of its nature of determining and adverting respectively at the five sense-doors and the mind-door, its manifestation is in accordance with this nature. Its proximate cause is the cessation of one of these: either of the three rootless resultant mind-consciousness elements performing the function of investigation at the time of determining, or of any life-continuum at the time of adverting. Hence it is said: “rootless…pe… proximate cause.”

Arahatanti arahataṃyeva asādhāraṇabhāvato. Anuḷāresūti aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikapetarūpādīsu, aññesu vā appaṇītesu vatthūsu. Hasituppādanarasāti hasitasseva uppādanarasā. Tathā hi taṃ cittaṃ “hasituppādana”ntveva vuccati, na aññesaṃ hasituppādakacittānaṃ abhāvato. Aññānipi hi dvādasa somanassasahagatāni parittakusalākusalakiriyacittāni yathārahaṃ puthujjanādīnaṃ hasituppādakāni vijjanti, idaṃ pana cittaṃ vicāraṇapaññāvirahitaṃ parittesu appaṇītesu ārammaṇesu arahantānaṃ somanassamattaṃ uppādentaṃ uppajjati. Bhagavatopi uppajjatīti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ atītaṃsādīsu appaṭihatañāṇaṃ vatvā “imehi tīhi dhammehi samannāgatassa buddhassa bhagavato sabbaṃ kāyakammaṃ ñāṇapubbaṅgamaṃ ñāṇānuparivattī”ti (mahāni. 69; cūḷani. mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 85; paṭi. ma. 3.5) vacanato vicāretabbanti eke[V 2.0122]. Tattha hasituppādacittena pavattiyamānampi bhagavato sitakaraṇaṃ pubbenivāsānāgataṃsasabbaññutaññāṇānaṃ anuvattakattā ñāṇānuparivattiyevāti evaṃ pana ñāṇānuparivattibhāve sati na koci pāḷiaṭṭhakathānaṃ virodho. Evañca katvā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “tesaṃ ñāṇānaṃ ciṇṇapariyante idaṃ cittaṃ uppajjatī”ti vuttaṃ. Avassañca etaṃ evaṃ icchitabbaṃ, aññathā aññassāpi viññattisamuṭṭhāpakassa ahetukacittassa bhagavato uppatti na yujjeyya. Na hi viññattisamuṭṭhāpakassa taṃsamuṭṭhitāya viññattiyā kāyakammādibhāvaṃ āpajjanabhāvo vibandhatīti. Ekantato hadayavatthupadaṭṭhānā pañcavokārabhave eva uppajjanato.

To the Arahants alone, because it is not common to trainees and worldlings. 'In non-excellent objects' (anuḷāresu) means in forms such as that of a skeleton-ghost, or in other ignoble objects. 'Its function is to produce smiling' (hasituppādanarasā) means its function is to produce smiling itself. Indeed, that consciousness is called 'smile-producing' (hasituppādana), not because of the absence of other smile-producing consciousnesses. For there are indeed twelve other sense-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, and functional consciousnesses accompanied by joy that, as is appropriate, produce smiling in worldlings and others. This consciousness, however, being devoid of investigating wisdom, arises while producing mere joy for the Arahants in sense-sphere, ignoble objects. It is said in the commentary, 'It arises also for the Blessed One.' Regarding this, some say it should be investigated based on the passage which, having stated the unobstructed knowledge regarding the past and so on, says: 'Of the Buddha, the Blessed One... all bodily action is preceded by knowledge and follows in accordance with knowledge.' In that regard, even though the Blessed One's act of smiling is brought about by the smile-producing consciousness, because it follows in accordance with the knowledges of past lives, the future, and omniscience, it is indeed one that follows in accordance with knowledge. However, when it is thus a state that follows in accordance with knowledge, there is no contradiction with the Pāḷi and the commentary. And for this reason, it is said in the commentary: 'This consciousness arises at the conclusion of the range of those knowledges.' And this must necessarily be accepted thus; otherwise, the arising for the Blessed One of another rootless consciousness that originates intimation would not be logical. For indeed, the fact that an intimation originated by a consciousness that produces intimation becomes bodily action and so on is not obstructed. Because it arises only in the five-aggregate existence, it exclusively has the heart-base as its proximate cause.

Ayamettha visesoti ayaṃ sekkhaputhujjanānaṃ uppattiyā vipākuppādanasamatthatā, arahataṃ uppattiyā tadabhāvoti ubhayesaṃ santāne uppattisamupalakkhito ettha kusalakiriyaviññāṇesu viseso. Evañca katvā paccayavekallena avipākassāpi kusalākusalassa kiriyabhāvappasaṅgo [M 2.0131] nivattito hoti. Parato kusalato visesoti etthāpi eseva nayo.

Herein lies the distinction: this is the capacity to produce a result by its arising in the mental continuum of trainees and worldlings, and the absence of that capacity by its arising in the mental continuum of Arahants. Thus, this principle, marked by arising in the mental continuum of both types of individuals, is the distinction in these wholesome and functional consciousnesses. And so, the contingency of a wholesome or unwholesome consciousness, even if it is without result due to a deficiency of conditions, becoming functional is averted. Also in the text later on, 'the distinction from the wholesome,' this is the same method.

455. Sabbānipi kusalākusalabyākatāni ekūnanavuti viññāṇāni honti nātisaṅkhepavitthāranayenāti adhippāyo. Paṭisandhiviññāṇādīnaṃ kiccaṃ nāma bhavantarapaṭisandhādinā ākārena pavatti eva. Tabbinimuttañca cittassa aññaṃ kiccaṃ natthīti āha “cuddasahi ākārehi pavattantī”ti.

455. The meaning is that all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states are eighty-nine consciousnesses, by a method that is neither too concise nor too detailed. The function of rebirth-linking consciousness and so on is simply the occurrence in the manner of connecting with another existence and so on. And apart from that occurrence, there is no other function of consciousness. Therefore, it is said, 'They occur in fourteen modes.'

Ānubhāvenāti sāmatthiyena. Katūpacitaṃ hi kammaṃ avasesapaccayasamavāye vipākaṃ dentaṃ attano ānubhāvaṃ vissajjantaṃ viya hoti. Devamanussesūti chasu kāmāvacaradevesu ceva manussesu ca. Kammakammanimittagatinimittānanti ettha kammaṃ nāma katūpacitaṃ kāmāvacarakusalakammaṃ, tañca kho vipākadānāya laddhokāsaṃ. Tenāha “paccupaṭṭhita”nti. Kammanimittaṃ kammāyūhanakkhaṇe cetanāya paccayabhūtaṃ deyyadhammādi. Gatinimittaṃ yaṃ gatiṃ upapajjati, tappariyāpannaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ. Paṇḍakādibhāvanti paṇḍakamūgamammanādibhāvaṃ. Dubbalassa dvihetukakusalassa vipākabhūtā upekkhāsahagatāhetumanoviññāṇadhātu dubbala…pe… manoviññāṇadhātu. Nesanti bhāvitarūpārūpāvacarakusalānaṃ sattānaṃ. Kammanimittamevāti pathavīkasiṇādikaṃ attano kammārammaṇameva.

'By power' means by capability. Indeed, kamma that has been done and accumulated, when giving its result upon the conjunction of the remaining conditions, is as if releasing its own power. 'Among gods and humans' means among the six sense-sphere gods and among humans. Here, in the phrase 'kamma, kamma-sign, and destination-sign,' kamma means accumulated wholesome kamma of the sense-sphere, and it is that which has obtained the opportunity to give its result. Therefore, it is said, 'present.' Kamma-sign is an offering, etc., that has become a condition for volition at the moment of exerting for kamma. Destination-sign is the form-object included in that destination to which one is reborn. 'The state of being a eunuch, etc.,' means the state of being a eunuch, a mute, a stammerer, etc. The rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity, which is the result of weak two-rooted wholesome kamma, is the weak... mind-consciousness-element. 'For them' means for beings who have developed wholesome kamma of the form and formless spheres. 'Only kamma-sign' means just the earth kasiṇa, etc., which is one's own kamma-object.

Evaṃ [V 2.0123] tāvetthāti ettha viññāṇakkhandhaniddese evaṃ saṅkhepato sarūpadassanamatteneva ekūnavīsatiyā vipākaviññāṇānaṃ paṭisandhivasena pavatti veditabbā. Bhavālambanādivibhāgena pana yadettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ paṭiccasamuppādakathāyaṃ āgamissatīti.

Here, in the exposition of the consciousness aggregate, the occurrence of the nineteen resultant consciousnesses by way of rebirth-linking should be known thus in brief, merely by showing their essential nature. However, what should be stated here by way of the classification of the object of becoming and so on, that will come in the discourse on dependent origination.

Taṃ tanti ekūnavīsatiyā paṭisandhiviññāṇesu yaṃ yaṃ uppajjitvā niruddhaṃ, taṃ taṃ anantaraṃ uppattiyā anubandhamānaṃ. Tassa tassevāti yassa yassa kammassa vipākabhūtaṃ paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ, tassa tasseva. Tasmiññevāti kammādike eva. Kammañce paṭisandhiviññāṇassa ārammaṇaṃ, tasmiṃ kamme, atha kammanimittaṃ, gatinimittañca, tasmiṃ kammanimitte gatinimitteti attho. Tādisamevāti yādisaṃ paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ hetuto, sesasampayuttadhammato ca tādisameva. Santānavinivattaketi bhavaṅgasantānassa vinivattanake. Aññasmiṃ āvajjanasaṅkhāte cittuppāde. Kiriyamayacitteneva supinadassanaṃ [M 2.0132] hotīti āha “supinaṃ apassato”ti. Aparimāṇasaṅkhyampi pavattatiyeva, tathā hidaṃ upapattibhavassa aṅgabhāvena pavattanato “bhavaṅga”nti vuccati. Tesaññevāti paṭisandhibhūtānaṃyeva.

As for that: among the nineteen rebirth-linking consciousnesses, whichever has arisen and ceased, that very one follows in sequence by arising immediately after. 'Of that very one' means: of that very kamma of which the rebirth-linking consciousness is the result. 'In that very one' means: in kamma and so on. If kamma is the object of the rebirth-linking consciousness, then in that kamma; or if the kamma-sign and the destination-sign are the object, then in that kamma-sign and in that destination-sign—this is the meaning. 'Just like that' means: just as the rebirth-linking consciousness is in terms of its root-cause and its remaining associated states, so it is. ‘In that which interrupts the continuity’ means: in that which interrupts the bhavaṅga-continuum, that is, in another consciousness-moment called ‘adverting’. Because the seeing of a dream occurs only through a functional consciousness, he said, 'not seeing a dream'. It occurs even an immeasurable number of times. Indeed, because this proceeds as a constituent factor of the rebirth-process existence, it is called 'bhavaṅga' (factor of becoming). 'Of those very ones' means: only of those that have become rebirth-linking.

Indriyānīti cakkhādīni indriyāni. Ārammaṇagahaṇakkhamānīti rūpādiārammaṇaṃ gahetuṃ samatthāni. Mātukucchigatakāle viya hi bahinikkhantakālepi na tāva indriyāni sakiccakāni honti, anukkamena pana visadabhāvaṃ pattakāle eva sakiccakāni honti. Tenevāha “idha paripakkattā āyatanāna”nti. Āpāthagateti yogyadesāvaṭṭhite. Tameva yogyadesāvaṭṭhitaṃ rūpaṃ paṭicca ghaṭṭanā paccayaṃ laddhā. Ghaṭṭanāti paṭighāto, yena byāpārādivisesapaccayantarasahite cakkhussa visaye vikāruppattivisadisuppattivisayassa iṭṭhāniṭṭhabhāvena anuggaho, upaghāto cāti attho. Tatoti ghaṭṭanānantaraṃ. Ghaṭṭanānubhāvenāti ghaṭṭanābalena. Bhavaṅgacalananti bhavaṅgacittassa pakampanaṃ, tathā dvikkhattuṃ pavattiyā visadisassa kāraṇabhāvūpagamananti attho. Tañhi cittasantānassa purimāvatthāya bhinnāvatthāhetutāya calanaṃ viyāti “calana”nti vuttaṃ. Visayavisayībhāvasiddhāya dhammatāya ārammaṇassa abhimukhībhāvena pasādassa tāva ghaṭṭanā hotu, aññasannissitassa pana bhavaṅgassa calanaṃ kathaṃ hotīti? Taṃsambandhabhāvato. Bheritale ṭhapitāsu sakkharāsu ekissā sakkharāya ghaṭitāya tadaññasakkharāyaṃ ṭhitamakkhikā calanaṃ cettha udāharaṇanti. Tadeva rūpanti tadeva bhavaṅgacalanassa paccayabhūtaṃ āpāthagataṃ rūpāyatanaṃ. Bhavaṅgaṃ vicchindamānā viyāti bhavaṅgasantānaṃ vicchindantī [V 2.0124] viya. Tadārammaṇuppattiyā parato bhavaṅgassa uppajjanato visayaggahaṇaṃ pañcadvārāvajjanaṃ vatvā tadanantaraṃ dassanādīsu vattabbesu tāni avatvā manodvārāvajjanassa gahaṇaṃ uddese dvinnaṃ āvajjanānaṃ āvajjanasāmaññena gahitattā.

The faculties are the eye and so forth. 'Capable of grasping objects' means able to grasp objects such as forms. Indeed, just as at the time of being in the mother's womb, and also at the time of having emerged, the faculties are not yet able to perform their own function; only when they gradually reach a state of clarity do they become able to perform their own function. Hence it is said, 'Here, due to the maturation of the sense bases.' 'Come into range' means situated in a suitable location. Depending on that very form situated in a suitable location, having obtained the condition of impact. 'Impact' means collision, by which, in the eye-base which is accompanied by other special conditions such as activity, there is assistance and destruction of the object through its being agreeable or disagreeable; this is the meaning. 'Then' means immediately after impact. 'By the power of impact' means by the force of impact. 'The vibration of the life-continuum' means the agitation of the life-continuum consciousness, and likewise, its becoming a cause for a dissimilar state through occurring twice; this is the meaning. Indeed, because it is the cause of a state different from the previous state of the mind-continuum, it is like a vibration; therefore, it is called 'vibration'. By the natural law established through the relationship of object and subject, let there first be the impact on the sensitivity due to the object's confrontation; but how does the vibration of the life-continuum, which is dependent on something else, occur? It is due to its connection with that. Herein, the vibration of a fly resting on another pebble when one pebble among those placed on a drumhead is struck is an example. 'That very form' means that very form-base which has come into range and has become the condition for the vibration of the life-continuum. 'As if cutting off the life-continuum' means as if interrupting the stream of the life-continuum. The word 'as if' is used because the life-continuum arises again after the arising of the registering consciousness. Having mentioned the five-door adverting, although seeing and so forth should be mentioned immediately after, without mentioning them, the inclusion of mind-door adverting is because in the summary, both advertings were included under the general term 'adverting'.

Āvajjanānantaranti pañcadvārāvajjanānantaraṃ. Ye hadayavatthu viya sampaṭicchanādivīthicittānipi nānujānanti, tesaṃ “sampaṭicchanāya cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā”tiādinā tattha tattha pāḷi āgatā. Na hi sakkā pāḷiṃ paṭisedhetuṃ.

‘Immediately after adverting’ means immediately after five-door adverting. For those teachers who do not permit the process-consciousnesses such as receiving, etc., just as they do not permit the heart-base, for them the Pāli is brought forth by the commentator in various places with phrases such as, 'for the purpose of receiving, the eye-consciousness-element.' Indeed, it is not possible to reject the Pāli.

“Sace [M 2.0133] mahantaṃ hotī”ti idaṃ javanapariyosānāya cittappavattiyā vuccamānattā vuttaṃ. Cuddasacittakkhaṇāyukañhi ārammaṇamidha “mahanta”nti adhippetaṃ, tañca uppajjitvā dviticittakkhaṇātītaṃ hutvā āpāthagamanavasena veditabbaṃ.

The phrase, 'If it is large,' is said because it is spoken of a process of consciousness that ends with impulsion. For here, an object having a lifespan of fourteen mind-moments is intended by 'large,' and it should be understood as having arisen and, after two or three mind-moments have passed, come into range.

Yathāvavatthāpiteti voṭṭhabbanena vuttākārena katavavatthāpane. Āvajjanāya, voṭṭhabbanassa ca vuttattā “avasesakāmāvacarakiriyāna”nti avasesaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Cha satta vāti vā-saddena “pañca vā”ti idampi vuttamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Suttamucchitādikāle hi pañcapi javanāni javantīti.

'As it has been determined' means: when the determination has been made by the determining consciousness in the manner stated. Because adverting and determining have been mentioned, the word 'remaining' is included in the phrase 'remaining sense-sphere functional consciousnesses.' It should be understood that by the word 'or' in 'six or seven,' the phrase 'or five' is also indeed stated. For at times such as being drowsy or faint, even five impulsions run.

Tāniyevāti “aṭṭhannaṃ vā”tiādinā (visuddhi. 2.455) vuttāni ekūnatiṃsa kāmāvacarajavanāniyeva. Ito aññaṃ manodvārāvajjanānantaraṃ uppajjanakacittaṃ nāma natthīti dassanatthaṃ evakāraggahaṇaṃ. “Gotrabhūto”ti idaṃ gotrabhuṭṭhāniyānaṃ parikammavodānānampi gahaṇaṃ, na gotrabhuno eva. Phalacittānīti samāpattivasena pavattanakaphalacittāni. Yaṃ yaṃ laddhapaccayanti yaṃ yaṃ javanaṃ rūpāvacarajavanādivasena gotrabhuanantaraṃ uppattiyā laddhapaccayaṃ.

'These very ones' refers to only the twenty-nine sense-sphere impulsions mentioned with the phrase 'of the eight or...' and so on. The inclusion of the word 'eva' (only) is to show that no other consciousness by name arises immediately after mind-door adverting. 'Gotrabhū' (change-of-lineage) here is an inclusion of preparation and purification, which stand in the place of gotrabhū; it is not an inclusion of gotrabhū only. 'Fruition-consciousnesses' refers to the fruition-consciousnesses that occur by way of attainment. 'Whichever has obtained the condition' means whichever impulsion, such as a form-sphere impulsion, has obtained the condition for arising immediately after gotrabhū.

Atimahantanti soḷasacittakkhaṇāyukaṃ. Tattha hi tadārammaṇacittaṃ uppajjati, na aññattha. Vibhūtanti supākaṭaṃ, tañca kāmāvacarameva. Tattha hi tadārammaṇassa uppatti. Kāmāvacarajavanāvasāneti kāmāvacarajavanasseva avasāne. Na hi taṃ kāmataṇhāhetukakammanibbattaṃ mahaggatānuttarajavanaṃ anubandhati ajanakattā, janakāsadisattā ca. Yathā gehato bahi gantukāmo taruṇadārako janakaṃ, janakasadisaṃ vā anubandhati, na aññaṃ, evamidampi[V 2.0125]. Tatthāpi na sabbasmā javanā sabbaṃ javanena tadārammaṇassa niyametabbato, ārammaṇena ca vedanāya parivattetabbato. Tatthāyaṃ niyamo – parittakusalalobhamohamūlasomanassasahagatakiriyajavanānaṃ aññatarānantaraṃ atimahati visaye pañcannaṃ somanassasahagatānaṃ aññataraṃ tadārammaṇaṃ uppajjati, tathā parittakusalākusalaupekkhāsahagatakiriyajavanānaṃ aññatarānantaraṃ upekkhāsahagatānaṃ channaṃ tadārammaṇānaṃ aññataraṃ pavattati. Iṭṭhārammaṇādīnanti iṭṭhaiṭṭhamajjhattaaniṭṭhārammaṇānaṃ vasenāti sambandho. Tayidaṃ ārammaṇena vedanāparivattidassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. “Purimakammavasenā”ti idaṃ tadārammaṇavisesadassanatthaṃ. Na [M 2.0134] hi paṭisandhijanakameva kammaṃ tadārammaṇaṃ janeti, atha kho aññakammampi. Taṃ pana paṭisandhidāyinā kammena nibbattetabbatadārammaṇato visadisampi nibbattetīti. “Javanacittavasenā”ti idaṃ tadārammaṇaniyamadassanatthaṃ. “Javanena tadārammaṇaṃ niyametabba”nti hi vuttaṃ. Ādi-saddena paṭisandhicittaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tañhi attano ukkaṭṭhatarassa tadārammaṇassa paccayo na hoti. Yo yo paccayo laddho hotīti yathāvuttesu iṭṭhārammaṇādīsu yo yo tadārammaṇassa uppattiyā paccayo samaveto hoti. Kiñci antaranti kiñci khaṇantaraṃ. Udakamivāti paṭisotaṃ gacchantaṃ udakamiva.

"Exceedingly great" refers to an object that has a lifespan of sixteen mind-moments. For in relation to such an object, the registering consciousness arises, not elsewhere. "Clearly evident" means very manifest, and that is only of the sense-sphere. For in relation to that, the arising of the registering consciousness occurs. "At the conclusion of sense-sphere impulsions" means at the conclusion of only the sense-sphere impulsions. For that registering consciousness, which is produced by kamma having sensual craving as its cause, does not follow a sublime or supramundane impulsion, because it is not its own generator and is dissimilar to its generating kamma. Just as a young child wishing to go outside the house follows his father or one like his father, and not another, so too is this. Even so, not every registering consciousness arises from every impulsion, because the registering consciousness is to be determined by the impulsion, and the feeling is to be changed by the object. Herein, this is the rule: immediately after any one of the sense-sphere wholesome, greed-rooted, delusion-rooted, or joy-accompanied functional impulsions, with a very great object, one of the five joy-accompanied registering consciousnesses arises. Similarly, immediately after any one of the sense-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, or equanimity-accompanied functional impulsions, one of the six equanimity-accompanied registering consciousnesses occurs. "Of desirable objects, etc." means the connection is by way of desirable, moderately desirable, and undesirable objects. This is said to show the change of feeling by means of the object. The phrase "by the power of previous kamma" is said to show the distinction of the registering consciousness. For it is not only the kamma that generates rebirth-linking that generates the registering consciousness; rather, other kamma also does. That other kamma, however, produces a registering consciousness that is even dissimilar to the registering consciousness that is to be produced by the kamma that gives rebirth-linking. The phrase "by the power of the impulsion-consciousness" is said to show the determination of the registering consciousness. For it has been said: "The registering consciousness is to be determined by the impulsion." By the word "etc.," it includes the rebirth-linking consciousness. For that rebirth-linking consciousness is not a condition for a registering consciousness more excellent than itself. "Whatever condition is present" means: among the aforementioned desirable objects, etc., whatever condition is present for the arising of the registering consciousness. "Some interval" means some momentary interval. "Like water" means like water going against the current.

Dvikkhattuṃ sakiṃ vāti vacanasiliṭṭhavasena vuttaṃ “aṭṭha vā dasa vā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.11; pārā. 11) viya. Dvikkhattuṃyeva pana vaṇṇenti. Vipākacittattā, āvajjanassa ca vidūrattā, mūlabhavaṅgādibhavaṅgasāmaññasabbhāvato ca bhavaṅgassa ārammaṇe pavattanārahaṃ samānaṃ tassa javanassa ārammaṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ etassāti tadārammaṇanti vuccati ekassa ārammaṇasaddassa lopaṃ katvā “kāmāvacaraṃ, oṭṭhamukha”nti ca yathā. Ettha ca keci “paṭṭhāne ‘kusalākusale niruddhe vipāko tadārammaṇatā uppajjatī’ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.406) vipākadhammadhammānaṃ eva anantaraṃ tadārammaṇaṃ vutta”nti kiriyājavanānantaraṃ na icchanti. Vipphāravantaṃ hi javanaṃ nāvaṃ viya nadīsoto bhavaṅgaṃ anubandhati, na pana chaḷaṅgupekkhāvato santavuttikiriyajavanaṃ paṇṇapuṭaṃ viya nadīsototi. Tayidaṃ labbhamānassāpi kenaci adhippāyena katthaci avacanaṃ dissati, yathā taṃ dhammasaṅgahe akusalaniddese labbhamānopi adhipati na vutto. Yañca paṇṇapuṭaṃ nidassitaṃ, tampi nidassitabbena na samānaṃ. Nāvāpaṇṇapuṭānañhi nadīsotassa āvaṭṭanaṃ, gati ca visadisīti nāvāya nadīsotassa anubandhanaṃ, paṇṇapuṭassa ananubandhanañca yujjati, idha pana kiriyajavanetarajavanānaṃ bhavaṅgasotassa [V 2.0126] āvaṭṭanaṃ, gati ca sadisīti etassa ananubandhanaṃ, itarassa anubandhanañca na yujjati. Tasmā vicāretabbaṃ.

The phrase 'twice or once' is said for the sake of elegant speech, as in passages such as 'eight or ten'. However, they explain it as occurring only twice. Because it is a resultant consciousness, because of the remoteness of the adverting, and because of the existence of the common nature of bhavaṅga, such as the root-bhavaṅga, it is suitable to arise in the object of the bhavaṅga. It is called 'tadārammaṇa' (that whose object is the object of that impulsion) by eliding one word 'ārammaṇa', just as in 'kāmāvacara' and 'oṭṭhamukha'. Here, some do not accept it arising after a functional impulsion, saying, 'In the Paṭṭhāna, it is stated: "When wholesome or unwholesome has ceased, a resultant arises as tadārammaṇa," meaning that tadārammaṇa is stated to occur immediately after only resultant-producing dhammas.' For the bhavaṅga follows a forceful impulsion just as a river current follows a boat; but it does not follow the calm functional impulsion of one possessing six-factored equanimity, just as the current does not follow a leaf-cup. Even though this is obtainable, its non-mention is seen somewhere according to some intention, just as in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, in the exposition of the unwholesome, though the dominance condition (adhipati) is obtainable, it is not mentioned. And the leaf-cup which was given as an example is also not similar to that which is to be exemplified. For, in the case of the boat and the leaf-cup, their turning of the river current and their movement are dissimilar; therefore, it is fitting that the river current follows the boat but not the leaf-cup. Here, however, in the case of the functional impulsion and other impulsions, their turning of the bhavaṅga-stream and their movement are similar; therefore, it is not fitting that it should not follow the one but follow the other. Therefore, this should be carefully considered.

Bhavaṅgamevāti avadhāraṇaṃ bhavapariyosānassa idha na adhippetattā. Aññathā tadārammaṇāvasāne cutipi na hotiyeva. Dassanādīnīti dassanasavanaghāyanasāyanaphusanāni. Iti-saddo ādiattho, tena sampaṭicchanādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Paṭisandhito bhavaṅgameva, bhavaṅgato āvajjanamevāti [M 2.0135] evaṃ pavattacittaniyamavaseneva. Tampīti cuticittampi. Paṭisandhibhavaṅgacittāni viya ekūnavīsatividhameva hoti atthato bhedābhāvato.

The emphasis in 'bhavaṅgameva' is made because the end of existence is not intended here. Otherwise, death would certainly not occur even at the end of the registering consciousness. 'Dassanādīni' refers to seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching. The word 'iti' has the meaning of 'and so on'; by it, the inclusion of receiving and so forth should be understood. After rebirth-linking, it is only the life-continuum; from the life-continuum, it is only adverting—thus it is by the force of this determined sequence of consciousness. 'Tampi' refers to the death-consciousness as well. Like the rebirth-linking and life-continuum consciousnesses, it is also of only nineteen kinds, because in terms of intrinsic nature, there is no difference.

Bhavagatiṭhitinivāsesūti tīsu bhavesu, pañcasu gatīsu, sattasu viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu, navasu sattāvāsesu ca. Yo panettha acittako, so idha na gahetabbo viññāṇakathābhāvato. “Etthā”ti idaṃ “saṃsaramānānaṃ sattāna”nti iminā sambandhitabbaṃ. Ettha etesu vuttanayena saṃsaramānesu sattesu yo pana arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti sammāpaṭipattimanvāyāti adhippāyo. Tassa arahato niruddhameva hoti cittaṃ appaṭisandhikabhāvato.

'In existences, destinations, stations, and abodes' means: in the three existences, in the five destinations, in the seven stations of consciousness, and in the nine abodes of beings. Now, among these, whichever abode is without consciousness should not be included here, as this is a discussion of consciousness. The word 'ettha' should be connected with 'of beings wandering in saṃsāra'. The meaning is: here, among these beings wandering in the manner described, whoever attains Arahantship by following the right practice. For that Arahant, consciousness has indeed ceased, because there is no further rebirth-linking.

Iti viññāṇakkhandhe vitthārakathāmukhavaṇṇanā.

Thus is the explanation of the introduction to the detailed discourse on the aggregate of consciousness.

Vedanākkhandhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Aggregate of Feeling

456. Vedena anubhavanākārena ayitaṃ pavattaṃ vedayitaṃ, vedayitanti lakkhitabbadhammajātaṃ vedayitalakkhaṇaṃ. Taṃ pana atthato vedanā evāti āha “vedayitalakkhaṇaṃ nāma vedanāvā”ti. Atha vā vedayitaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etissāti kappanāsiddhaṃ bhedaṃ nissāya aññapadatthasamāsavasenāpi vedanāva vuccatīti āha “vedayitalakkhaṇaṃ nāma vedanāvā”ti. Vedayati vedayatīti byāpanicchāvasena vacanaṃ vedanāya savisaye abhiṇhappavattidassanatthaṃ. Sabhāvadhammato añño kattā natthīti dassanatthaṃ kattuniddeso. Itīti aniyamato hetuattho. Khoti vacanālaṅkāramattaṃ. Tasmāti tassa niyamanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yasmā yathāpaccayaṃ ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavati, tasmā vedanāti vuccatīti.

456. That which proceeds by way of experiencing is 'what is felt' (vedayitaṃ); the nature of a phenomenon to be marked as 'what is felt' is the characteristic of being felt. But in its own essence, this is just feeling; therefore, he said, 'The characteristic of being felt, indeed, is feeling.' Or alternatively, 'It has the characteristic of being felt'; relying on a distinction established by conceptualization, also by the power of a relative compound (aññapadatthasamāsa), it is feeling itself that is spoken of. Therefore, he said, 'The characteristic of being felt, indeed, is feeling.' The statement 'it feels, it feels' is by way of a desire for pervasion, for the purpose of showing the constant occurrence of feeling in its own domain. The specification of the agent is for the purpose of showing that there is no agent other than the intrinsic nature of the phenomenon. The word 'iti' has the meaning of a cause in an indefinite sense. The word 'kho' is merely an embellishment of speech. The word 'tasmā' is its determination. This is what is said: because it experiences the taste of the object according to conditions, therefore it is called feeling.

“Kusalaviññāṇena [V 2.0127] sampayuttā”ti idaṃ kusalāya vedanāya upalakkhaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yā kāci kusalā vedanā, sabbā sā kusalena viññāṇena sampayuttāti, na pana tassā kusalabhāvasaṃsiddhidassanatthaṃ. Na hi kusalena viññāṇena sampayogato kusalāya vedanāya kusalabhāvo, atha [M 2.0136] kho yonisomanasikārādikato. Tenāha “jātivasenā”ti. Akusalādīsupi eseva nayo. Yathā pana jātivasena kusalādiviññāṇasampayuttatāya tividhā, evaṃ yāva ekūnanavutiviññāṇasampayuttāti ekūnanavutividhā veditabbā. Sabhāvabhedatoti sampayuttabhūmiārammaṇādivasena labbhamānaṃ bhedaṃ aggahetvā kevalaṃ sabhāvakatabhedato evāti attho.

'Associated with wholesome consciousness'—this should be seen as a characteristic mark of wholesome feeling. Whatever wholesome feeling there is, all of it is associated with wholesome consciousness; however, this is not to demonstrate the accomplishment of its wholesome nature. For the wholesome nature of a wholesome feeling does not arise from its association with wholesome consciousness, but rather from wise attention (yonisomanasikāra) and so on. Therefore, he said, 'by way of class.' The same method applies to the unwholesome and other types. Just as, by way of class, feeling is threefold through its association with wholesome and other types of consciousness, so too it should be understood as eighty-ninefold through association with eighty-nine consciousnesses. By 'by difference in intrinsic nature,' the meaning is: taking only the distinction made by its intrinsic nature, without grasping the distinction that is obtained by way of associated bases, objects, and so on.

“Pañcavidhā”ti vatvā taṃ pañcavidhataṃ dassetuṃ “sukha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sukhayatīti sukhaṃ, kāyaṃ, sampayuttadhamme ca laddhassāde karotīti attho. Suṭṭhu vā khādati, khaṇati vā kāyikaṃ ābādhanti sukhaṃ. Sukaraṃ okāsadānaṃ etassāti sukhanti apare. Dukkhayatīti dukkhaṃ, kāyaṃ, sampayuttadhamme ca vibādhatīti attho. Duṭṭhu vā khādati, khaṇati vā kāyikaṃ assādanti dukkhaṃ. Dukkaraṃ okāsadānaṃ etassāti dukkhanti apare. Somanassupekkhānaṃ saddattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Domanassassa somanasse vuttanayānusārena veditabbaṃ. Kiṃ pana kāraṇaṃ mānasetarasātāsātavasena sukhaṃ, dukkhañca vibhajitvā vuttaṃ “sukhaṃ somanassaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassa”nti, upekkhā pana mānasī, itarā ca ekadhāva vuttāti? Bhedābhāvato. Yathā hi anuggahūpaghātakatāya sukhadukkhāni aññathā kāyassa anuggahamupaghātañca karonti, aññathā manaso, na evamupekkhā. Tasmā bhedābhāvato ekadhāva upekkhā vuttāti.

Having stated 'fivefold,' to show that fivefold nature, 'pleasure' (sukha) and so forth were stated. Herein, 'pleasure' (sukha) is so called because it delights (sukhayati); it makes the body and associated states attain satisfaction—this is the meaning. Or, alternatively, it thoroughly eats or digs up and destroys bodily affliction—thus it is called pleasure. Others say it is called 'pleasure' because the giving of opportunity for it is easy. 'Pain' (dukkha) is so called because it causes suffering (dukkhayati); it oppresses the body and associated states—this is the meaning. Or, alternatively, it badly eats or digs up bodily satisfaction—thus it is called pain. Others say it is called 'pain' because the giving of opportunity for it is difficult. The literal meaning of joy (somanassa) and equanimity (upekkhā) has already been stated below. Displeasure (domanassa) should be understood in accordance with the method explained for joy. But what is the reason that pleasure and pain, having been divided by way of mental and non-mental pleasantness and unpleasantness, were stated as 'pleasure, joy, pain, and displeasure,' while equanimity, both mental and otherwise, is stated in only one way? It is due to the absence of division. For just as pleasure and pain, through their supportive and harmful nature, affect the body in one way and the mind in another, so equanimity does not. Therefore, because there is no division, equanimity is stated in one way.

Tattha yena sabhāvabhedena vedanā pañcavidhā, sā pavattiṭṭhāne dassite supākaṭā hotīti pavattiṭṭhānaṃ tāva dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Akusalavipākenāti etthāpi “kāyaviññāṇena sampayutta”nti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Yathā adhikaraṇīmatthake kappāsapicupiṇḍaṃ ṭhapetvā ayokūṭena paharantassa picupiṇḍaṃ atikkamitvā kūṭaṃ adhikaraṇiṃ gaṇhāti, nighaṃso balavā hoti, evaṃ paṭighaṭṭanānighaṃsassa balavabhāvato iṭṭhe, iṭṭhamajjhatte ca ārammaṇe kāyaviññāṇaṃ sukhasahagataṃ hoti. Aniṭṭhe, aniṭṭhamajjhatte ca dukkhasahagatanti āha “kusala…pe… dukkha”nti. Kāmāvacaravipākaviññāṇāni pañca kammārammaṇavasena somanassasahagatāni honti, rūpāvacaravipākāni cattāri kammavasena, sesāni terasa kāmāvacarāni, aṭṭha rūpāvacarāni, dvattiṃsa lokuttarāni, yathārahaṃ [M 2.0137] cetobhisaṅkhārārammaṇapādakādivasena [V 2.0128] somanassasahagatāni hontīti āha “somanassaṃ dvāsaṭṭhiyā viññāṇehi sampayutta”nti. Domanassaṃ dvīhi akusalaviññāṇehi sampayuttaṃ cetobhisaṅkhārārammaṇādivasena.

Therein, by which distinction of intrinsic nature feeling is fivefold, that distinction becomes very clear when the place of its occurrence is shown. Therefore, in order to first show the place of occurrence, the passage beginning with 'Therein' was composed. Also in the phrase 'with unwholesome resultant,' the words 'associated with body-consciousness' should be brought in and connected. Just as when, having placed a ball of cotton-wool on an anvil, one strikes it with an iron hammer, the hammer, having passed over the cotton-wool ball, strikes the anvil, and the impact is strong; similarly, due to the strength of the striking and impact, body-consciousness is accompanied by pleasure in a pleasant or moderately pleasant object. In an unpleasant or moderately unpleasant object, it is accompanied by pain. Therefore, it is said: 'wholesome... pain.' The five sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses are accompanied by joy by way of kamma and object; the four form-sphere resultant consciousnesses are [accompanied by joy] by way of kamma. The remaining thirteen sense-sphere, eight form-sphere, and thirty-two supramundane consciousnesses are, as is appropriate, accompanied by joy by way of mental formation, object, basic jhāna, and so on. Therefore, it is said: 'Joy is associated with sixty-two consciousnesses.' Displeasure, by way of mental formation, object, and so on, is associated with two unwholesome consciousnesses.

Avasesapañcapaññāsāyāti yathāvuttāni chasaṭṭhi viññāṇāni ṭhapetvā avasesāya pañcapaññāsāya. Tattha kusalākusalavipākāni iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu nibbikappakāni sukhadukkhasampayuttāni bhavituṃ yuttānipi dvinnaṃ picupiṇḍānaṃ viya dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ upādārūpānaṃ ghaṭṭanānighaṃsassa mandabhāvato cakkhādisannissitāni aṭṭhapi viññāṇāni sabbattha upekkhāsampayuttāneva honti, tathā balavapaccayatāya sukhadukkhānaṃ tesañca tadabhāvato. Apubbārammaṇanissayappavattīni āvajjanasampaṭicchanaviññāṇāni, asadisānantarappaccayaṃ kiriyārambhassa ādibhūtaṃ voṭṭhabbanaṃ, kāyadukkhapadhānatāya akusalaphalassa tadupanissayabhūtaṃ akusalavipākapaṭisandhiādi, iṭṭhamajjhattārammaṇappavattīni kāmāvacarakusalavipākaviññāṇāni ca upekkhāsahagatāniyeva honti. Kammavasena vā vipākānubhavanassa iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇesu adukkhamasukhabhāvo yutto. Sati ca vipākabhūtāya upekkhāya sukhadukkhamajjhattabhāve kammārammaṇavasena kusalavipākāya iṭṭhabhāvo, akusalavipākāya aniṭṭhabhāvo ca veditabbo. Avasiṭṭhāni pana sattatiṃsa viññāṇāni cetobhisaṅkhārārammaṇapādakādivasena upekkhāsampayuttāni hontīti evaṃ pañcapaññāsāya viññāṇehi upekkhāya sampayuttatā veditabbā.

‘The remaining fifty-five’ means the fifty-five that remain after setting aside the sixty-six consciousnesses mentioned before. Among these, the eight consciousnesses dependent on the eye-faculty and so on are wholesome and unwholesome resultants. Being without deliberation regarding desirable and undesirable objects, and although fit to be associated with pleasure and pain, they are in all cases associated only with equanimity. This is due to the weakness of the striking and rubbing of the pairs of derived matter—like the contact between two balls of cotton—and because pleasure and pain have strong conditions, whereas for these consciousnesses, those strong conditions are absent. The adverting and receiving consciousnesses, because they tend to arise with a new object and a new basis; the determining consciousness, because it has a dissimilar immediately preceding condition and is the beginning of undertaking a functional action; the unwholesome resultant rebirth-linking consciousness, etc., because bodily pain is the predominant factor of an unwholesome result and it is a support condition for that bodily pain; and the sense-sphere wholesome resultant consciousnesses, because they tend to arise with desirable-neutral objects—these too are accompanied only by equanimity. Alternatively, it is fitting that the experiencing of the result in desirable and undesirable objects is a state of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, due to the power of kamma. Furthermore, when there is the state of neutrality between pleasure and pain for the resultant equanimity, it should be understood that, by the power of the kamma and its object, there is a state of being desirable for the wholesome resultant equanimity and a state of being undesirable for the unwholesome resultant equanimity. The remaining thirty-seven consciousnesses, however, are associated with equanimity by the power of mental formation, object, support condition, and so on. Thus, the association of equanimity with these fifty-five consciousnesses should be understood.

Salakkhaṇaṃ nāma dhammānaṃ anaññasādhāraṇo sabhāvo, anubhavanañca sabbavedanānaṃ sādhāraṇalakkhaṇanti taṃ paṭiniyatena ārammaṇena niyametvā dassento āha “iṭṭhaphoṭṭhabbānubhavanalakkhaṇaṃ sukha”nti tassa byabhicārābhāvato. Bhusaṃ brūhanaṃ vaḍḍhanaṃ upabrūhanaṃ. Tayidaṃ kāmañca cetasikasukhepi labbhati, taṃ pana savikappakaṃ cetobhisaṅkhāravasenāpi hoti. Idantu nibbikappakaṃ sabhāvasiddhattā tato sātisayanti āha “sampayuttānaṃ upabrūhanarasa”nti. Assādiyatīti assādo, sukhāvedanā. Tenāha bhagavā “yaṃ, bhikkhave, pañcupādānakkhandhe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, pañcupādānakkhandhesu assādo”ti [M 2.0138] (saṃ. ni. 3.26). Kāyanissitattā kāye bhavo kāyiko, so eva assādo tathā paccupatiṭṭhatīti kāyikaassādapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Kāyindriyapadaṭṭhānaṃ anaññavatthukattā.

What is called the individual characteristic of dhammas is their intrinsic nature, not shared with others; and experiencing is the common characteristic of all feelings. Therefore, defining this by means of a specific object, the author said, 'Pleasure has the characteristic of experiencing a desirable tangible object,' because of its non-deviation. Great enhancement is a great increase or growth. Although this is also obtained in mental pleasure, that, however, has conceptual thought and arises by the power of mental formations. But this is without conceptual thought and, because it is accomplished by its own nature, it is superior to that. Therefore, the author said, 'Its function is the great enhancement of associated states.' 'It is savored,' thus it is savoring (assāda); it is pleasant feeling. For that reason, the Blessed One said: 'Bhikkhus, whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on the five aggregates subject to clinging, this is called the savoring in the five aggregates subject to clinging.' Because it is dependent on the body, what arises in the body is bodily (kāyika). That very savoring manifests as such; thus, its manifestation is as bodily savoring. Its proximate cause is the body faculty because it has no other physical basis.

Dukkhassa lakkhaṇādīni vuttanayānusārena veditabbāni.

The characteristics, etc., of pain should be understood according to the method previously stated.

Sabhāvato[V 2.0129], parikappato vā iṭṭhassa ārammaṇassa anubhavanalakkhaṇaṃ iṭṭhārammaṇānubhavanalakkhaṇaṃ. Tenāha “yathā tathā vā iṭṭhākārasambhogarasa”nti, yathābhūtena vā ayathābhūtena vā iṭṭhākārena ārammaṇassa saṃbhuñjanarasaṃ, paccanubhavanakiccanti attho. “Passaddhipadaṭṭhāna”nti idaṃ “passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedetī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.376; a. ni. 11.12) suttapadaṃ nissāya vuttaṃ, taṃ pana nirāmisasomanassavasena veditabbaṃ.

The characteristic of experiencing a desirable object, whether by its intrinsic nature or by conception, is 'the characteristic of experiencing a desirable object.' For that reason, the author said, 'Its function is the enjoyment of a desirable aspect in whatever way,' the meaning of which is: the function of enjoying an object with a desirable aspect, whether that aspect is real or unreal; the task of directly experiencing it. This phrase, 'having tranquility as its proximate cause,' was said in reliance upon the sutta passage, 'One with a tranquil body experiences pleasure.' This, however, should be understood by way of unworldly joy.

Somanasse vuttavipariyāyena domanassassa lakkhaṇādīni veditabbāni. Domanassassa kāmadhātuyaṃ uppajjanato ekantena hadayavatthupadaṭṭhānatā tato viseso.

The characteristics, etc., of mental pain should be understood in the reverse way to what was stated for mental pleasure. A distinction from mental pleasure is that mental pain arises exclusively in the sense-sphere and thus invariably has the heart-base as its proximate cause.

Majjhattassa, ārammaṇassa majjhattaṃ vā vedayitaṃ anubhavanaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etissāti majjhattavedayitalakkhaṇā. Majjhattānubhavanato eva sampayuttānaṃ nātiupabrūhanamilāpanarasā. “Santabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā”ti idaṃ anavajjāya nirāmisāya upekkhāya vasena veditabbaṃ, na sabbāya.

Its characteristic is the experiencing of a neutral object, or the experiencing of neutrality. Its function, from the very experiencing of neutrality, is neither to greatly enhance nor to cause the associated states to fade. This phrase, 'its manifestation is a peaceful state,' should be understood by way of blameless, unworldly equanimity, not by way of all types.

Iti vedanākkhandhe vitthārakathāmukhavaṇṇanā.

Thus the introductory exposition of the detailed discourse on the aggregate of feeling.

Saññākkhandhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Aggregate of Perception

457. Sañjānanalakkhaṇaṃ nāma saññāvātiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ vedanākkhandhaniddese vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

457. Whatever should be said regarding such passages as 'Perception has the characteristic of perceiving,' should be understood by the very method stated in the exposition on the aggregate of feeling.

Kāmaṃ vedanāyapi vippayuttaṃ viññāṇaṃ natthi, tassā pana sabhāvato bhinnattā kāyaci vedanāya sampayuttampi kāyaci vippayuttaṃ hoti. Saññāya pana īdisaṃ natthīti āha “na hi taṃ viññāṇaṃ…pe… saññāyā”ti.

Indeed, there is no consciousness entirely dissociated from feeling; however, because its (feeling's) nature is distinct, consciousness that is associated with a certain feeling is dissociated from another. But with perception, this is not the case, and so it is said: 'For that consciousness does not exist... without perception.'

Sabbāvāti catubhūmikāpi. Atha vā yathā vedanā bhinnasabhāvattā bhedanalakkhaṇādito vuttā, na evamayaṃ, ayaṃ pana sabbāva sañjānanalakkhaṇā[M 2.0139]. Nīlādibhedassa ārammaṇassa sañjānanaṃ saññaṃ katvā jānanaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etissāti sañjānanalakkhaṇā. Tathā hi sā abhiññāṇena sañjānanato [V 2.0130] paccābhiññāṇarasāti vuccati. Nimittena hi puna sañjānanakiccā paccābhiññāṇarasā. Tassā vaḍḍhakissa dārumhi abhiññāṇaṃ katvā tena abhiññāṇena paccābhijānanakāle pavatti veditabbā. Tenāha “tadeveta”ntiādi. Puna sañjānanassa paccayo punasañjānanapaccayo, tadeva nimittaṃ puna…pe… nimittaṃ, tassa karaṇaṃ, puna…pe… karaṇaṃ, punasañjānanapaccayabhūtaṃ vā nimittakaraṇaṃ puna…pe… karaṇaṃ, tadassā kiccanti punasañjānanapaccayanimittakaraṇarasā. Punasañjānananimittakaraṇaṃ nimittakārikāya, nimittena sañjānanantiyā ca sabbāya saññāya samānaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Abhinivesakaraṇaṃ “idameva sacca”nti (ma. ni. 2.187, 202, 203, 427; ma. ni. 3.27-29) saññābhinivesamatteneva daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathāupaṭṭhitavisayapadaṭṭhānā avikappasabhāvattā. Ñāṇasampayuttā pana saññā ñāṇameva anuvattati, tasmā abhinivesakārikā, viparītaggāhikā ca na hoti. Eteneva samādhisampayuttatāya aciraṭṭhānatā ca na hotīti veditabbā. Evaṃ rāgadiṭṭhimānādisampayuttāya saññāya rāgādianuvattikabhāvoti.

By 'all' is meant that which pertains to the four planes. Alternatively, just as feeling, because of its distinct nature, is said to have the characteristic of differentiating, and so on, this perception is not spoken of in the same way. This perception, however, is entirely characterized by perceiving-by-marking. Perceiving an object with its distinctions, such as blue, by making a mark and knowing it, is its characteristic; hence, it has the characteristic of perceiving-by-marking. Indeed, because it perceives by means of a sign for recognition, it is said to have the function of re-cognition. For, having the task of perceiving again by means of a sign, it has the function of re-cognition. Its process should be understood through the case of a carpenter who, having made a mark on a piece of wood, re-recognizes it at a later time by means of that mark. Therefore, it is said, 'It is just that,' and so forth. The condition for perceiving again is the 'condition-for-perceiving-again'; that very sign... the sign; its making... the making; or the making of the sign that is the condition for perceiving again... the making. That is its function—hence, it has the function of making the sign that is the condition for perceiving again. The making of a sign for perceiving again should be applied equally to all perception, both to that which makes the sign and to that which perceives by means of the sign. The act of insistence—'This alone is true'—should be seen as merely the insistence of perception. Its proximate cause is the object as it has appeared, due to its non-conceptual nature. However, perception associated with knowledge follows knowledge itself; therefore, it is not one that makes an insistence, nor does it grasp perversely. By this same reasoning, it should be understood that because of its association with concentration, it is not of short duration. Thus, the state of following after lust and the like, in the case of perception associated with lust, wrong view, pride, and so on, should be understood.

Iti saññākkhandhe vitthārakathāmukhavaṇṇanā.

Thus, the introductory exposition of the detailed discourse on the aggregate of perception.

Saṅkhārakkhandhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Aggregate of Formations.

458. Rāsikaraṇalakkhaṇanti sampiṇḍanalakkhaṇaṃ, tato saṅkhārā āyūhanarasā vuccanti. Cetanāpadhānatāya hi saṅkhārakkhandhadhammā evaṃ vuttā. Tenevāha “kiṃ pana tanti saṅkhārāyevā”tiādi. Tattha saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharontīti yathā attano phalaṃ saṅkhataṃ sammadeva nipphannaṃ hoti, evaṃ abhisaṅkharontīti attho. Vipphārapaccupaṭṭhānāti ettha vipphāro nāma vipphāravantatā, tasmā sabyāpārapaccupaṭṭhānāti attho.

458. The characteristic of heaping up means the characteristic of accumulating; therefore, formations are said to have the function of accumulating. Indeed, the phenomena of the aggregate of formations are described thus due to the prominence of volition. Therefore, he said, 'But what is that? It is formations indeed,' and so forth. Herein, 'they form the conditioned' means that they form in such a way that their own result, being conditioned, is properly produced. As for 'manifestation as agitation,' herein 'agitation' means the state of being agitated; therefore, the meaning is 'manifestation as activity'.

Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ citte uppanne niyamena uppajjanato niyatā. Sarūpena āgatāti evaṃ piṭṭhivattake akatvā pāḷiyā sarūpeneva āgatā. Kadācideva uppajjanato na niyatāti aniyatā. Yadipi aniyatā ekajjhaṃ [M 2.0140] na uppajjanti, tasmiṃ pana citte uppajjanadhammatāya “chattiṃsā”ti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “uppajjamānāpi ca na ekato uppajjantī”ti.

Because they arise invariably when each consciousness arises, they are called 'determinate'. As for 'they come in their own form,' this means that they come in the Pāḷi in their own form, without being referred back. Because they arise only sometimes, they are not determinate; thus they are 'indeterminate'. Although the indeterminate factors do not arise all at once, they are called 'thirty-six' due to their nature of being able to arise in that consciousness. Therefore, he said: 'And even when arising, they do not arise all at once'.

459. Phusatīti [V 2.0131] kattuniddeso. Yaṃ tattha kāraṇaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Phusanti etenāti vā phasso. Sampayuttadhammā hi ārammaṇe pavattamānā taṃ phusanalakkhaṇena phassena phusantā viya honti. Ārammaṇaphusanamattaṃ vā phassoti sādhanattayampi yujjateva. Sabhāvadhammesu kattukaraṇasādhanavacanaṃ tadākārasamāropanato pariyāyakathā, bhāvasādhanavacanameva nippariyāyakathāti vuttaṃ “phusanalakkhaṇo”ti. Ayañhītiādi yathāvuttalakkhaṇādisamatthanaṃ. Yadi ayaṃ dhammo cetasiko, svāyaṃ arūpadhammo samāno kathaṃ phusanalakkhaṇo, saṅghaṭṭanarasādiko ca hotīti antolīnaṃ codanaṃ hadaye ṭhapetvā tassa sodhanatthaṃ “arūpadhammopi samāno”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “phusanākāreneva pavattatī”ti iminā arūpassāpi tassa dhammassa ayaṃ sabhāvoti dasseti. Sā ca tassa phusanākārappavatti ambilaambapakkādiṃ khādantaṃ passantassa parassa kheḷuppatti, paraṃ vibādhiyamānaṃ disvā dayālukassa sarīrakampanaṃ, rukkhasākhagge duṭṭhitaṃ purisaṃ disvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhitassa bhīrukapurisassa jaṅghacalanaṃ, pisācādibhāyitabbaṃ disvā ūrukhambhoti evamādīsu paribyattā hoti.

459. 'It touches' is an agentive designation. The reason for that has already been stated below. Or, contact is that by which they touch. Indeed, associated states, when occurring in relation to an object, are as if touching it by means of contact, which has the characteristic of touching. Or, contact is merely the touching of the object; thus, all three derivations are indeed applicable. Among intrinsic phenomena, the expression of the agentive and instrumental derivations is a figurative expression due to the superimposition of that form, whereas the expression of the abstract derivation alone is a literal expression, as stated in 'with the characteristic of touching.' The phrase beginning with 'This indeed' is a support for the characteristics, and so forth, as stated. If this phenomenon is a mental concomitant, and being a formless phenomenon, how can it have the characteristic of touching and the function of impact, and so on? Keeping this implicit objection in mind, the phrase beginning with 'though being a formless phenomenon' is stated in order to clarify it. Therein, by the phrase 'it occurs precisely in the manner of touching,' it is shown that this is the intrinsic nature of that phenomenon, even though it is formless. And that occurrence in the manner of touching is clearly evident in such instances as the salivation of another person seeing someone eating sour things, unripe mangoes, and so on; the trembling of a compassionate person seeing another being oppressed; the leg-shaking of a timid man standing on the ground seeing a man precariously perched on a tree branch; or the stiffening of the thighs upon seeing something frightening like a goblin.

Ekadesenāti kaṭṭhadvayādi viya attano ekapassena. Anallīyamānopīti asaṃsiliyamānopi. Rūpasaddehi saha phassassa sāmaññaṃ anallīyamānasaṅghaṭṭanameva, na visayabhāvo. Yathā rūpasaddā cakkhusotāni anallīyamānā eva “phusita”ntiādinā vuttā, evaṃ phassassāpi ārammaṇaphusanasaṅghaṭṭanānīti. Saṅghaṭṭanañca phassassa cittārammaṇānaṃ sannipatanabhāvo eva. Tenāha “cittamārammaṇañca saṅghaṭṭetī”ti. Kiccaṭṭhena rasena saṅghaṭṭanarasatā vuttā, vatthārammaṇasannipātena vā sampajjatīti saṅghaṭṭanasampattiko phasso saṅghaṭṭanaraso vutto. Yathā “dve pāṇī vajjeyyu”ntiādīsu (mi. pa. 2.3.8) pāṇissa pāṇimhi saṅghaṭṭanaṃ tabbisesabhūtā rūpadhammā, evaṃ cittassa ārammaṇe saṅghaṭṭanaṃ tabbisesabhūto eko cetasikadhammo daṭṭhabbo. “Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso”ti (ma. ni. 1.204; 3.421, 425, 426; saṃ. ni. 2.43-44; 4.60) vacanato cakkhurūpaviññāṇādīnaṃ [M 2.0141] saṅgativasena gahetabbattā āha “tikasannipātasaṅkhātassā”tiādi. Tassa phassassa kāraṇabhūto tadanurūpo samannāhāro tajjāsamannāhāro. Indriyassa tadabhimukhabhāvo, āvajjanāya ca ārammaṇakaraṇaṃ visayassa parikkhatatā abhisaṅkhatatā, viññāṇassa visayabhāvakaraṇanti attho. Yathā niccammā gāvī yaṃ yaṃ ṭhānaṃ upagatā, tattha tattha dukkhameva pāpuṇāti, evaṃ phasse sati vedanā uppajjateva. Vedanā ca dukkhasallādisabhāvāti vuttaṃ “vedanādhiṭṭhānabhāvato pana niccammagāvī viya daṭṭhabbo”ti.

‘By a part’ means by one side of itself, like two pieces of wood, etc. ‘Though not adhering’ means though not clinging. The commonality of contact with forms and sounds is merely non-adhering impact, not the state of being an object. Just as forms and sounds are said to ‘touch’ the eye and ear without adhering, so too for contact, there is the touching and impacting of the object. And the impact of contact is simply the state of mind and object coinciding. Therefore, it is said, ‘It impacts the mind and the object.’ Its function as impact is stated in the sense of its function; or, because it is accomplished by the coincidence of the base and the object, contact, which possesses the accomplishment of impact, is said to have impact as its function. Just as in the examples ‘two hands might clap,’ etc., the impact of one hand on another are material phenomena that are a special instance of them, so too the impact of the mind on an object should be seen as a single mental factor that is a special instance of it. From the statement ‘The meeting of three is contact,’ it is said, ‘It is called the meeting of a triad,’ etc., because it is to be understood by way of the meeting of eye, form, and consciousness, etc. The attention that is the cause of that contact and is appropriate to it is attention born therefrom. The meaning is: the faculty's turning towards it, the making of the object by advertence, the object's being prepared and conditioned, and the making of the state of being an object for consciousness. Just as a skinned cow, wherever it goes, only encounters suffering, so too when there is contact, feeling inevitably arises. And since feeling has the nature of a painful dart, etc., it is said, 'On account of its being the basis for feeling, however, it should be seen like a skinned cow.'

460. Abhisandahati [V 2.0132] pabandhati pavatteti. Cetanābhāvo byāpārabhāvo. Āyūhanaṃ cetayanaṃ īriyanaṃ. Saṃvidahanaṃ vicāraṇaṃ. Āyūhanarasāya cetanāya pavattamānāya sabbepi sampayuttadhammā yathāsakaṃ kiccappasutā hontīti sā sakiccaparakiccasādhikā vuttā. Jeṭṭhasisso pare sajjhāyane uyyojento sayampi sajjhāyati. Mahāvaḍḍhakimhi vaḍḍhakikammaṃ kātumāraddhe itarepi karontiyeva. Ussāhanabhāvenāti ādarakaraṇabhāvena. Sā hi sayaṃ ādarabhūtā sampayuttadhamme ādarayatīti. Āyūhanavasena ussāhanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, na vīriyussāhavasena.

460. It binds, connects, and causes to proceed. The state of volition is the state of activity. Striving, urging, setting in motion. Arranging, managing. When volition, which has the function of striving, is occurring, all associated states become diligently engaged in their respective tasks; therefore, it is said to be the accomplisher of its own task and the tasks of others. Just as a senior disciple, while urging other students in recitation, also recites himself; or when a master carpenter has begun to do carpentry work, the other carpenters also indeed do it. 'By the state of exertion' means by the state of acting with respect. For it, being itself respectful, causes the associated states to be respectful. Exertion should be understood by way of striving, not by way of the exertion that is energy.

461. Vīrabhāvoti yena vīro nāma hoti, so dhammoti attho. Vidhinā īretabbaṃ pavattetabbanti vā vīriyaṃ, ussāho, taṃtaṃkiccasamārambho, parakkamo vā. Upatthambhanaṃ sampayuttadhammānaṃ kosajjapakkhe patituṃ adatvā dhāraṇaṃ anubalappadānaṃ, sampaggaṇhanaṃ vā. Saṃsīdanapaṭipakkho dhammo asaṃsīdanaṃ, na saṃsīdanābhāvamattanti asaṃsīdanabhāvena paccupatiṭṭhatīti vuttaṃ “asaṃsīdanabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāna”nti. Saṃvegapadaṭṭhānanti aṭṭhasaṃvegapubbikāya (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.418) kusalakiriyāya vīriyārambhavatthupadaṭṭhānaṃ. “Maggo gantabbo hoti, maggo gato, kammaṃ kātabbaṃ, kammaṃ kataṃ, appamattako ābādho uppanno, gilānā vuṭṭhito hoti, aciravuṭṭhito gelaññā, gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya vicaranto na labhati lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ, labhati…pe… pāripūri”nti evaṃ vuttāni etāni anurūpapaccavekkhaṇāsahitāni aṭṭha vīriyārambhavatthūni, taṃmūlakāni vā paccavekkhaṇāni.

461. The state of a hero means that quality by which one is called a hero; this is the meaning. Or, because it should be aroused and set in motion by a method, it is called energy (vīriya); or it is effort, the undertaking of various tasks, or progressive exertion. Supporting is the sustaining of associated states, not allowing them to fall into the side of laziness; or the giving of subsequent strength, or uplifting. The quality that is the opposite of slackening is non-slackening; it is not merely the absence of slackening. Therefore, it manifests as the state of non-slackening, and thus it is said, 'having non-slackening as its manifestation.' ‘Having a sense of urgency as its proximate cause’ means having the grounds for arousing energy as its proximate cause for wholesome action preceded by the eight kinds of urgency. 'The path is to be traveled, the path has been traveled; the work is to be done, the work has been done; a minor illness has arisen; one has recovered from illness, one has recently recovered from sickness; while wandering for alms in a village or town, one does not obtain as much coarse or fine food as is needed to be satisfied, or one does obtain enough... etc. ...to be satisfied.' These eight grounds for arousing energy, thus stated, together with their appropriate reflections, or the reflections that have those eight as their root.

462. Attanā [M 2.0142] anupāletabbānaṃ sahajātadhammānaṃ anupālanaṃ jīvitassa byāpāro, tañca nesaṃ jīvananti taṃ tassa kāraṇabhāvaṃ purakkhatvā vuttaṃ “jīvanti tenā”ti. Tampi cassa atthato jīvanamevāti āha “jīvanamattameva vā ta”nti.

462. The function of life is the due maintenance of co-nascent states that ought to be maintained by oneself. And since that life is the cause of their living, having placed its state of being a cause foremost, it is said, 'They live by that.' And that life also, in its intrinsic nature, is merely their living; therefore, it is said, 'Or it is merely their living.'

463. Ādhiyatīti ṭhapeti. Avisāro attano eva avisaraṇasabhāvo. Avikkhepo sampayuttānaṃ dhammānaṃ avikkhittatā. Yena sampayuttā avikkhittā honti, so dhammo avikkhepoti. Avūpasamalakkhaṇassa vikkhepassa paṭipakkhatāya cittassa upasamanākārena paccupatiṭṭhatīti upasamapaccupaṭṭhāno. Visesatoti yebhuyyena. Sukhavirahitopi hi atthi samādhīti. Dīpaccinidassanena santānaṭhitibhāvaṃ samādhissa dasseti.

463. Ādhiyati means 'it establishes.' Non-diffusion is the nature of not diffusing of itself. Non-distraction is the state of not being scattered of associated states. That by which associated states are not scattered is non-distraction. Because it is the opposite of distraction, which has the characteristic of non-calmness, it manifests in the manner of the mind's calmness; therefore, it has calm as its manifestation. The word 'especially' (visesato) means 'for the most part,' for indeed, there is also concentration devoid of pleasure. By the example of a lamp's flame, it shows the continuity-based stability of concentration.

464. Saddahanti [V 2.0133] etāyāti saddahanakiriyāya pavattamānānaṃ dhammānaṃ tattha ādhipaccabhāvena saddhāya paccayataṃ dasseti. Tassā hi dhammānaṃ tathāpaccayabhāve sati puggalo saddahatīti vohāro hoti. Saddahanaṃ saddheyyavatthuno pattiyāyanaṃ, taṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etissāti saddahanalakkhaṇā. Okappanalakkhaṇāti anupavisitvā evametanti kappanalakkhaṇā. Kālussiyamalaṃ vidhametvā sampayuttānaṃ, puggalasseva vā pasādanaṃ anāvilabhāvakaraṇaṃ raso etissāti pasādanarasā. Pakkhandanaṃ adhimuccanavasena ārammaṇassa anupavisanaṃ. Akālusabhāvo akālussiyaṃ, anāvilabhāvoti attho. Pasādanīyaṭṭhānesu pasādaviparītaṃ akusalaṃ assaddhiyaṃ, micchādhimutti ca, tappaccanīkova pasādabhūto vatthugato nicchayo adhimutti, na yevāpanakādhimokkho. Ratanattayaṃ, kammaṃ, kammaphalañca saddheyyavatthu. Sappurisasaṃsevanasaddhammasavanayonisomanasikāradhammānudhammappaṭipattiyo sotāpattiyaṅgāni. Kusaladhammānaṃ ādāne hatthaṃ viya, sabbasampattisampadāne vittaṃ viya, amatakasiphalaphalane bījaṃ viya daṭṭhabbā.

464. They believe through it: this shows that faith (saddhā) is a condition by way of dominance for the states occurring in the act of believing. For when it is such a condition for the states, it is conventionally said that a person believes. Believing (saddahana) is trusting in an object to be believed; this is its characteristic. Thus, it has the characteristic of believing. It has the characteristic of placing trust (okappanalakkhaṇā), meaning the characteristic of settling on something as 'it is so' by entering into it. Its function (rasa) is the clarification (pasādana) of associated states by dispelling the stain of mental turbidity (kālussiya), or the clarification of the individual himself, making him undisturbed. Plunging in (pakkhandana) is the entering into the object by way of decisive resolve. Non-turbidity (akālussiya) is the absence of mental disturbance; the meaning is the state of being undisturbed. In places worthy of confidence, the unwholesome opposite of confidence is faithlessness (assaddhiya) and wrong resolve (micchādhimutti). Its very counteragent is conviction (adhimutti), which is a determination that has become confidence, is rooted in the object, and is not the general mental factor of decision (adhimokkha). The Triple Gem, kamma, and the fruit of kamma are the objects of faith. Association with virtuous persons, listening to the good Dhamma, wise attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma are the factors of stream-entry. Faith should be seen as like a hand for taking hold of wholesome states, like wealth for attaining all accomplishments, and like a seed for producing the fruit of the deathless.

465. Saranti tāyāti saraṇakiriyāya pavattamānānaṃ dhammānaṃ tattha ādhipaccabhāvena satiyā paccayataṃ dasseti. Tassā hi dhammānaṃ tathāpaccayabhāve sati taṃsamaṅgipuggalo saratīti vohāro hoti. Udake alābu viya pilavitvā gantuṃ adatvā pāsāṇassa viya niccalassa [M 2.0143] ārammaṇassa ṭhapanaṃ saraṇaṃ asammuṭṭhatākaraṇaṃ apilāpanaṃ. Sammosapaccanīkaṃ kiccaṃ asammoso, na sammosābhāvamattaṃ. “Satārakkhena cetasā”ti (a. ni. 10.20) vacanato ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā. Aññato āgantvā cittavisaye abhimukho bhavati etāyāti visayābhimukhabhāvo, sati. Satiyā vatthubhūtā kāyādayova kāyādisatipaṭṭhānāni, sati eva vā purimā pacchimāya padaṭṭhānaṃ.

465. “They remember by means of this” (Saranti tāyāti): this shows that mindfulness (sati) is a condition, by way of dominance, for the states occurring in the act of remembering. For, when it is such a condition for the states, it is conventionally said that “the person endowed with it remembers.” Remembering (saraṇa) is the placing of the object, making it unmoving like a stone, not allowing it to go floating away like a gourd in water; it is the causing of non-confusion and is non-floating. Its function, the opposite of confusion, is non-forgetfulness (asammosa), not merely the absence of confusion. As stated in the phrase, “With a mind guarded by mindfulness” (AN 10.20), its manifestation is protection. By means of this, the mind, having come from elsewhere, becomes facing towards the object; therefore, the state of facing the object is mindfulness (sati). The body and so forth, which are the basis for mindfulness, are themselves the foundations of mindfulness concerning the body and so forth (kāyādisatipaṭṭhānāni); or, the preceding mindfulness itself is the proximate cause for the subsequent.

466. Kāyaduccaritādīhīti hetumhi karaṇavacanaṃ. Hiriyatīti lajjākārena jigucchati. Tehiyevāti kāyaduccaritādīhiyeva. Ottappatīti ubbijjati. Hirī pāpadhamme gūthaṃ viya passantī jigucchatīti āha “pāpato jigucchanalakkhaṇā hirī”ti. Ottappaṃ te uṇhaṃ viya passantaṃ tato uttasatīti vuttaṃ “uttāsalakkhaṇaṃ ottappa”nti. Vuttappakārenāti lajjākārena, uttāsākārena ca. Attagāravapadaṭṭhānā hirī ajjhattasamuṭṭhānatāya, attādhipatitāya ca. Paragāravapadaṭṭhānaṃ ottappaṃ bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānatāya, lokādhipatitāya ca. Tamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “attānaṃ [V 2.0134] hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ajjhattasamuṭṭhānāditā ca hiriottappānaṃ tattha tattha pākaṭabhāvena vuttā, na panetesaṃ kadāci aññamaññavippayogā. Na hi lajjanaṃ nibbhayaṃ, pāpabhayaṃ vā alajjanaṃ atthīti. Lokapālakāti ettha “dveme, bhikkhave, sukkā dhammā lokaṃ pālentī”ti (a. ni. 2.9; itivu. 42) suttapadaṃ attādhipati, lokādhipatibhāve ca “so attānaṃyeva adhipatiṃ karitvā, so lokaṃyeva adhipatiṃ karitvā”ti (a. ni. 3.40) ca suttapadāni āharitvā vattabbāni.

466. The phrase 'Through bodily misconduct, etc.' (kāyaduccaritādīhi) is in the instrumental case, indicating cause. 'He is ashamed' (hiriyati) means he is disgusted in the manner of shame. 'By those very things' (tehiyeva) means by bodily misconduct, etc., themselves. 'He is apprehensive' (ottappati) means he is alarmed. Shame (hirī), seeing evil qualities as one would see filth, is disgusted by them—thus it was said: 'Shame has the characteristic of disgust for evil.' Apprehension (ottappa), seeing them as one would see a hot iron, is frightened by them—thus it was said: 'Apprehension has the characteristic of being alarmed.' 'In the manner stated' means in the manner of shame and in the manner of being alarmed. Shame (hirī) has self-respect as its proximate cause, due to its internal arising and self-mastery. Apprehension (ottappa) has respect for others as its proximate cause, due to its external arising and the governance of the world. To make this very meaning clearer, the passage beginning 'One is ashamed of oneself...' was stated. The internal arising and so forth of shame and apprehension are stated in various places according to their evident nature, but these two are never disassociated from each other. For there is no shame that is fearless, nor is there a fear of evil that is shameless. Regarding 'Guardians of the world' (lokapālaka), the sutta passage 'Monks, these two bright qualities guard the world' (AN 2.9; Itivuttaka 42) should be cited. And regarding the state of self-mastery and governance of the world, the sutta passages 'Having made oneself the master...' and 'Having made the world the master...' (AN 3.40) should be cited.

467. Yasmā lobhapaṭipakkho alobhoti ye dhammā tena sampayuttā, taṃsamaṅgino vā sattā tena na lubbhanti, sayaṃ kadācipi na lubbhateva, atthato vā alubbhanākāro eva ca hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “na lubbhantī”tiādi. Eseva nayoti “na dussanti tenā”tiādinā kārakattayayojanaṃ atidisati. Agedho agijjhanaṃ anabhikaṅkhanaṃ. Alaggabhāvo anāsattatā. Apariggaho kassaci vatthuno mamattavasena asaṅgaho. Anallīno bhāvo adhippāyo etassāti anallīnabhāvo. Evañhi upamāya sameti.

467. Because non-greed (alobha) is the opposite of greed, the states associated with it, or the beings endowed with it, are not greedy through it; it itself is never greedy; and in essence, it is simply the characteristic of not being greedy. Therefore, it is said, 'they are not greedy,' etc. This is the method: it indicates the application of the three agents to 'they do not hate through it,' etc. Absence of avarice (agedha) is non-covetousness and non-longing. The state of non-clinging (alaggabhāva) is non-attachment. Non-possession (apariggaha) is the non-grasping of any object in terms of 'mine.' The state of non-adherence (anallīnabhāvo) is an unattached state or intention. For thus it accords with the simile.

468. Caṇḍikassa [M 2.0144] bhāvo caṇḍikkaṃ, kopo. Tappaṭipakkho acaṇḍikkaṃ, abyāpādo. Avirodho aviggaho. Anukūlamitto anuvattako. Vinayarasoti vinayanaraso. Sommabhāvo mejjanavasena hilādanīyatā.

468. The state of a harsh person is fierceness (caṇḍikkaṃ), which is anger. Its opposite is non-fierceness (acaṇḍikkaṃ), which is non-ill-will. Non-opposition (avirodha) is non-conflict (aviggaha). A favorable friend (anukūlamitta) is a compliant one (anuvattaka). 'Having the function of dispelling' (vinayarasa) means having the function of dispelling. Gentleness (sommabhāva) is the state of being pleasing by means of affection.

469. Dhammānaṃ yo yo sabhāvo yathāsabhāvo, tassa tassa paṭivijjhanaṃ yathāsabhāvapaṭivedho. Akkhalitaṃ avirajjhitvā paṭivedho akkhalitapaṭivedho. Visayassa obhāsanaṃ tappaṭicchādakasammohandhakāravidhamanaṃ visayobhāsanaṃ. Katthacipi visaye asammuyhanākāreneva paccupatiṭṭhati, sammohapaṭipakkhatāya vā tadabhāvaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetīti asammohapaccupaṭṭhāno. Sabbakusalānaṃ mūlabhūtāti sabbesaṃ catubhūmakakusaladhammānaṃ suppatiṭṭhitabhāvasādhanena patiṭṭhābhūtā, na tesaṃ kusalabhāvasādhanena. Yadi hi tesaṃ kusalabhāvo kusalamūlapaṭibaddho siyā, evaṃ sati taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpesu hetupaccayatā na siyā. Na hi te tesaṃ kusalādibhāvaṃ sādhenti, na ca paccayā na honti. Vuttañhetaṃ “hetū hetusampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ hetupaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.1). Yathā ca kusalabhāvo, evaṃ abyākatabhāvopi abyākatamūlappaṭibaddho siyā. Tathā sati ahetukacittānaṃ [V 2.0135] abyākatabhāvo eva na siyā, akusalesu ca yattha ekaṃyeva mūlaṃ, tassa akusalabhāvo na siyā, ubhayampi hotiyeva. Tasmā na mūlappaṭibaddho kusalādibhāvo, atha kho yonisomanasikārādipaṭibaddho. Tesaṃ pana suppatiṭṭhitabhāvasādhanāni mūlānīti gahetabbaṃ.

469. Whatever is the intrinsic nature of phenomena is 'nature as it is' (yathāsabhāva); the penetration of that very nature is 'penetration of nature as it is' (yathāsabhāvapaṭivedha). Unerring penetration (akkhalitapaṭivedha) is penetration without failure or error. Illuminating the object (visayobhāsana) is the dispelling of the darkness of delusion that conceals it. It manifests as non-delusion in any object, or it establishes the absence of delusion by being the opposite of delusion—thus, it has 'non-delusion as its manifestation' (asammohapaccupaṭṭhāna). Being the root of all wholesome states means they serve as the foundation for all wholesome phenomena of the four planes by accomplishing their well-established state, not by accomplishing their wholesome state. For if their wholesome state were dependent on wholesome roots, then the state of being a root-condition would not apply to the material forms arising from them. Indeed, they do not accomplish the wholesome state, etc., of those forms, yet they are not non-conditions. As it is said: 'Root is a condition by way of root-condition for the phenomena associated with root and for the material forms born of them' (Paṭṭhā. 1.1.1). And just as the wholesome state, so too the indeterminate state would be dependent on indeterminate roots. That being so, the indeterminate state of rootless consciousness would not exist, and in unwholesome states where there is only one root, its unwholesome state would not exist; yet both do exist. Therefore, the state of being wholesome, etc., is not dependent on roots but rather on wise attention and so on. The roots, however, should be understood as those which accomplish the well-established state of those phenomena.

470. Passambhanaṃ darathavūpasamo. Kāyasaddo samūhavācī, so ca kho vedanādikkhandhattayavasenāti āha “kāyoti cettha vedanādayo tayo khandhā”ti.
