Tenevāha “tattha katamā tasmiṃ samaye kāyapassaddhi hoti? Yā tasmiṃ samaye vedanākkhandhassā”tiādi (dha. sa. 40). Daratho sārambho, domanassapaccayānaṃ uddhaccādhikānaṃ kilesānaṃ, tathāpavattānaṃ vā catunnaṃ khandhānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Darathanimmaddanena pariḷāhaparipphandavirahito sītibhāvo aparipphandasītibhāvo. Uddhaccappadhānā kilesā [M 2.0145] uddhaccādikilesā, uddhaccaṃ vā ādiṃ katvā sabbakilese saṅgaṇhāti. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

470. Tranquility is the calming of distress. The term 'body' is a collective expression; specifically, it refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling. Hence it is said: 'Herein, "body" refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling, etc.' Therefore it is also stated: 'What at that time is tranquility of the body? It is the tranquility of the aggregate of feeling,' etc. (Dhs. 40). Distress (daratha) is agitation (sārambho); this is a designation for the defilements which have displeasure as their condition and are predominated by restlessness, or for the four aggregates that have arisen in such a way. The state of coolness, devoid of burning and trembling through the crushing of distress, is undisturbed coolness. Defilements of which restlessness is the principal factor are the defilements beginning with restlessness; or, having taken restlessness as the beginning, it includes all defilements. The same principle applies to the rest as well.

Garubhāvo dandhatā, thinamiddhādhikānaṃ, tathāpavattānaṃ vā catunnaṃ khandhānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Dandhatāya paṭipakkho adandhatā, na dandhatāya abhāvamattaṃ.

The state of heaviness is slowness; this is a designation for the defilements predominated by sloth and torpor, or for the four aggregates that have arisen in such a way. The opposite of slowness is non-slowness, not merely the absence of slowness.

Thaddhabhāvo thambho, diṭṭhimānādhikānaṃ, tappadhānānaṃ vā catunnaṃ khandhānametaṃ nāmaṃ. Thaddhabhāvanimmaddanato eva katthaci ārammaṇe appaṭihatākārena paccupatiṭṭhanti, sampayuttānaṃ vā tattha appaṭighātaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpentīti appaṭighātapaccupaṭṭhānā.

The state of stiffness is rigidity; this is a name for the defilements predominated by wrong view and conceit, or for the four aggregates of which these are the principal factor. Because of the crushing of the state of stiffness, they manifest without opposition in any object, or they establish non-opposition for the associated states therein; thus, they have non-opposition as their manifestation.

Kammani sādhu kammaññaṃ, na kammaññaṃ akammaññaṃ, tassa bhāvo akammaññabhāvo, dānasīlādipuññakiriyāyaṃ ayogyatā. Atthato kāmacchandādisaṃkilesadhammā, tappadhānā vā cattāro akusalakkhandhā. Kammaññabhāveneva sampannākārena ārammaṇassa gahaṇaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇasampatti. Vuttāvasesā kāmacchandādayo, tadekaṭṭhā ca saṃkilesadhammā avasesanīvaraṇādayo. Vinibandhanimmaddanena sukhappavattihetutāya pasādanīyavatthūsu pasādāvahā. Suvaṇṇavisuddhi viyāti yathā suvaṇṇavisuddhi apagatakāḷakā alaṅkāravikativiniyogakkhamā, evamayampi saṃkilesavigamena hitakiriyāviniyogakkhamā.

What is good for action is 'workable'; what is not workable is 'unworkable'. Its state is unworkability, the unsuitability for performing meritorious deeds such as generosity and virtue. In essence, it refers to defilements such as sensual desire, or the four unwholesome aggregates in which they are predominant. By workability itself, the grasping of an object in a complete manner is the accomplishment of making it an object. The remaining [defilements] are sensual desire and so on, and other defiling states that share the same basis, such as the remaining hindrances. By crushing the bonds, and because it is a cause for the pleasant arising [of consciousness], it brings forth confidence towards confidence-inspiring objects. Just as purified gold, devoid of its black tarnish, is fit for application in various ornaments, so too this [workability], through the removal of defilements, is fit for application in beneficial actions.

Kāyacittānaṃ gelaññaṃ, assaddhiyādi, tadekaṭṭhā ca pāpadhammā. Gelaññapaṭipakkho agelaññaṃ[V 2.0136], tabbhāvo lakkhaṇaṃ etāsanti agelaññabhāvalakkhaṇā. Yathāvuttagelaññanimmaddaneneva natthi etāsaṃ ādīnavo doso, na vā etā ādīnaṃ kapaṇaṃ vanti pavattantīti nirādīnavā, tenākārena paccupatiṭṭhanti, taṃ vā sampayuttesu paccupaṭṭhapentīti nirādīnavapaccupaṭṭhānā.

Sickness of body and mind is lack of faith and so on, and other unwholesome states that share the same basis. The opposite of sickness is health. They are 'characterized by the state of health' (agelaññabhāvalakkhaṇā), for that state is their characteristic. Precisely by crushing the aforementioned sickness, there is no danger or fault in them; or, because they do not produce what is miserable and wretched, they are 'free from danger' (nirādīnavā). They manifest in that manner, or they establish that [freedom from danger] in their associated states; thus, they have 'freedom from danger as their manifestation' (nirādīnavapaccupaṭṭhānā).

Kāyasambandhī, cittasambandhī ca ujubhāvoti lakkhitabbatāya kāyacittaajjavalakkhaṇā. Kāyacittānaṃ naṅgalasīsacandakoṭigomuttavaṅkatāsaṅkhātānaṃ kuṭilabhāvānaṃ nimmaddanato kāyacittakuṭilabhāvanimmaddanarasā. Tato eva sabbathāpi ajimhabhāvena paccupatiṭṭhanti, sampayuttānaṃ vā ajimhataṃ paccupaṭṭhapentīti ajimhatāpaccupaṭṭhānā. “Santadosapaṭicchādanalakkhaṇā māyā, asantaguṇasambhāvanalakkhaṇaṃ sāṭheyya”nti evaṃ vuttā tadākārappavattā [M 2.0146] akusalā khandhā, tadekaṭṭhā ca saṃkilesadhammā māyāsāṭheyyādikā. Ettha ca cittapassaddhiādīhi cittameva passaddhaṃ, lahu, mudu, kammaññaṃ, paguṇaṃ, uju ca hoti. Kāyapassaddhiādīhi pana rūpakāyopi. Tenevettha bhagavatā dhammānaṃ duvidhatā vuttā, na sabbattha.

Because they should be characterized as the state of uprightness connected with the body (of mental factors) and connected with the mind, they have the characteristic of straightness of body and mind. Their function is the crushing of the states of crookedness of body and mind, which are reckoned as the crookedness of a plough's tip, a crescent moon, and cow's urine. For that very reason, they manifest in every way as a state of non-crookedness, or they establish non-crookedness in associated states; thus, they have non-crookedness as their manifestation. 'Deceit has the characteristic of concealing existing faults, and fraud has the characteristic of proclaiming non-existent virtues'—unwholesome aggregates that proceed in such a manner, and defiling states that have the same foundation, are called deceit, fraud, and so on. And here, through mental tranquility and so on, the mind itself becomes tranquil, light, malleable, workable, proficient, and upright. But through bodily tranquility and so on, the physical body also becomes so. For that very reason, the Blessed One has spoken of the twofold nature of these states here, not everywhere.

471. Chandanaṃ chando, ārammaṇena atthikatā. “Chando kāmo”tiādīsu (vibha. 564) pana taṇhāpi vuccati, “chandaṃ janeti vāyamatī”tiādīsu (vibha. 432) vīriyampīti tato nivattanatthaṃ “kattukāmatāyetaṃ adhivacana”nti vuttaṃ. Kattukāmatā vuccati karaṇicchā. Cetasikassa ca dhammassa sārammaṇattā karaṇicchā nāma ālambanassa ālambitukāmatāmukheneva hotīti ārammaṇakaraṇicchālakkhaṇo chando kattukāmatālakkhaṇo vutto. Tenevāha “ārammaṇapariyesanaraso, ārammaṇena atthikatāpaccupaṭṭhāno”ti ca. Yadaggena panāyaṃ attano ārammaṇapariyesanaraso, tadaggena sampayuttānampi hotiyeva ekārammaṇatāya tena tesaṃ. Tenevāha “ārammaṇaggahaṇe cāyaṃ cetaso hatthappasāraṇaṃ viya daṭṭhabbo”ti. Svāyaṃ kusalesu uppanno kusalacchandoti vuccati yonisomanasikārasamuṭṭhānattā.

471. Desiring is 'chanda'; it is being concerned with an object. However, in passages such as 'desire is sensual pleasure,' etc. (Vibhaṅga 564), craving is also meant, and in passages such as 'he generates desire, he strives,' etc. (Vibhaṅga 432), energy is also meant. Therefore, to distinguish it from those, it is said, 'This is a designation for the wish to do (kattukāmatā).' The wish to do is called the desire to act (karaṇicchā). And because a mental factor is a state that has an object, the desire to act occurs only by way of the wish to take up an object. Thus, desire, which has the characteristic of wishing to act upon an object, is said to have the characteristic of the wish to do. Therefore, he said, 'It has the function of searching for an object, and its manifestation is being concerned with an object.' Moreover, insofar as it has the function of searching for its own object, to that extent it also occurs for its associated states, because they have a single object with it. Therefore, he said, 'In the grasping of an object, this should be seen like the stretching forth of the mind's hand.' This very desire, when it has arisen in wholesome states, is called wholesome desire because it originates from wise attention (yonisomanasikāra).

472. Adhimuccanaṃ ārammaṇe sanniṭṭhānavasena veditabbaṃ, na pasādanavasena. Yathā tathā vā hi ārammaṇe nicchayanaṃ adhimuccanaṃ anadhimuccantassa pāṇātipātādīsu, dānādīsu vā pavattiyā abhāvā, saddhā pana pasādanīyesu pasādādhimokkhāti ayametesaṃ viseso. Voṭṭhabbanaṃ pana yathā santīrite atthe nicchayanākārena pavattitvā parato ttamānānaṃ tathā pavattiyā paccayo hoti. Yadi evaṃ, vicikicchāsampayuttesu kathanti? Tesampi ekaṃseneva saṃsappanākārassa [V 2.0137] paccayatāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dārakassa viya ito cito ca saṃsappanassa “karissāmi na karissāmī”ti anicchayassa paṭipakkhakiriyā asaṃsappanaṃ, yesu cittuppādesu ayaṃ sanniṭṭhānalakkhaṇo adhimokkho, tesaṃ ārammaṇadhammo eva sanniṭṭheyyadhammo.

472. Determination should be understood as settling decisively upon an object, not as confidence. For, decisiveness regarding an object, in one way or another, is determination, because for one who does not determine, there is an absence of engagement in actions like killing living beings, etc., or giving, etc. Faith, however, is a determination of confidence in inspiring objects. This is the distinction between them. Determining, however, having arisen in the manner of deciding upon a matter that has been investigated, becomes a condition for the subsequent javanas to arise in such a way. If so, how is it in the case of states associated with doubt? In their case too, it should be seen as being a condition exclusively for the state of wavering. Non-wavering is the action that is the opposite of the indecision, 'Shall I do it or not?', which is a wavering to and fro like that of a child. In those states of consciousness where this determination, characterized by decisive settling, arises, the object-dharma itself is the dharma to be decided upon.

473. Kiriyā [M 2.0147] kāroti kārasaddassa bhāvasādhanatamāha. Manamhi kāroti manasi ārammaṇassa karaṇaṃ. Yena hi mano ārammaṇe karīyati ārammaṇenassa saṃyojanato, tato eva tena ārammaṇampi manasi karīyatīti. Purimamanatoti bhavaṅgamanato. Visadisamananti vīthijavanaṃ manaṃ karotīti manasikārasāmaññena vīthijavanapaṭipādake dasseti.

473. By the etymology 'Doing is action' (kiriyā kāro'ti), he states the abstract noun nature of the word 'kāra'. 'Manamhi kāro'ti means the making of the object in the mind. For, by which attention the mind is directed to an object—because of its connecting this mind with the object—for that very reason, by that attention, the object too is directed into the mind. 'Purimamanato' means from the bhavaṅga-mind. 'Visadisamanaṃ'ti means it makes the mind into a cognitive process and javana; thus, by the generality of 'manasikāra', he shows the manasikāras that bring about the cognitive process and javana.

Sampayuttadhamme ārammaṇābhimukhaṃ sārento viya hotīti manasikāro sāraṇalakkhaṇo vutto. Satiyā asammussanavasena visayābhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānatā, manasikārassa pana saṃyojanavasena ārammaṇābhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānatāti ayametesaṃ viseso. Ārammaṇapaṭipādakassa saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannatāvacanaṃ itaramanasikārānaṃ tadaññakkhandhapariyāpannatāmattaṃ jotetīti tathājotitaṃ taṃ viññāṇakkhandhe otāretvā dassetuṃ “vīthipaṭipādako”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Because it is as if directing the associated states towards the object, attention is said to have the characteristic of directing. For mindfulness, the manifestation is the state of facing the object by way of non-forgetfulness; for attention, however, it is the state of facing the object by way of connecting. This is the distinction between them. The statement that the attention which brings about the object is included in the aggregate of formations illuminates that other kinds of attention are merely included in other aggregates. Therefore, to show that which is thus illuminated by including it in the aggregate of consciousness, the words 'that which brings about the cognitive process,' etc., are stated.

474. Tesu dhammesūti yesu dhammesu sayaṃ uppannā, tesu attanā sampayuttesu cittacetasikadhammesu. Anārammaṇattepi hi tesu samappavattesu udāsinabhāvato “tatramajjhattatā”ti vuccati. Samavāhitalakkhaṇāti samaṃ avisamaṃ yathāsakakiccesu pavattanalakkhaṇā. Udāsinabhāvena pavattamānāpi hesā sampayuttadhamme yathāsakakiccesu pavatteti, yathā rājā tuṇhī nisinnopi atthakaraṇe dhammaṭṭhe yathāsakakiccesu appamatte pavatteti. Alīnānuddhatapavattipaccayatā ūnādhikatānivāraṇarasā, kiccavasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yadi evaṃ, sahajātādhipatino kathanti? Tampi tassā kiccameva. Yaṃ sahajātadhammānaṃ adhipatibhāvoti, tassāpi tathāpavattanamevāti nāyaṃ doso. “Idaṃ nihīnakiccaṃ hotu, idaṃ atirekatarakicca”nti evaṃ pakkhapātavasena viya pavatti pakkhapāto, taṃ upacchindantī viya hotīti adhippāyo.

474. Regarding 'in those states': in whichever states it itself has arisen, in those states of consciousness and mental factors associated with itself. Indeed, even though it does not take them as an object, it is called 'neutrality there' (tatramajjhattatā) because of its state of indifference towards those associated states that occur evenly. Its characteristic of being a balanced conductor is the characteristic of causing associated states to proceed evenly, not unevenly, in their respective duties. For although this equanimity proceeds with an attitude of indifference, it causes the associated states to proceed in their respective duties, just as a king, though sitting silently, causes the judges in a court case to proceed heedfully in their respective duties. Because it is the cause for proceeding without contraction or agitation, its function is the prevention of deficiency and excess; and this is stated in terms of its function. If so, what of the co-nascent dominance condition? That too is its function. Since that which is the state of dominance for co-nascent phenomena is also just its way of causing them to proceed thus, there is no fault in this. Proceeding as if by way of partiality, thinking, 'Let this be an inferior function, let this be a superior function,' is called partiality. It is as if cutting that off. This is the meaning.

“Aniyatesu icchantī”ti iminā cetasikantarabhāvena icchantīti dasseti. Adosoyeva mettā. Tathā [V 2.0138] hi soyeva “mettā mettāyanā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1062) niddiṭṭho. Upekkhāti yaṃ upekkhaṃ mettāya saddhiṃ parikappenti, sā tatramajjhattupekkhāyeva.

By the statement, 'They wish among the undetermined,' it is shown that they wish for it to be a different mental factor. Loving-kindness is simply non-aversion. For indeed, that very non-aversion is pointed out by the phrase 'loving-kindness, the state of loving-kindness,' etc. As for equanimity, that equanimity which they conceive in association with loving-kindness, that is just the equanimity that is neutrality (tatramajjhattupekkhā).

475. Kāyaduccaritādivatthūnanti [M 2.0148] parapāṇaparadhanaparaitthiādīnaṃ. Amaddanaṃ maddanapaṭipakkhabhāvo. Kāyaduccaritādivatthuto saṅkocanakiriyāpadesena kāyaduccaritādito eva saṅkocanakiriyā vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi viratiyo duccaritavatthuno akiriyapaccupaṭṭhānā yujjanti, atha kho duccaritassa, viratīnañca soraccavasena saṅkocanaṃ, akiriyānañca hirottappānaṃ jigucchanādivasenāti ayametesaṃ viseso.

475. Regarding 'the bases of bodily misconduct, etc.': they are others' lives, others' wealth, others' wives, and so on. Non-crushing is the state opposite to crushing. It should be understood that by indicating the act of shrinking from the bases of bodily misconduct, etc., the act of shrinking from bodily misconduct, etc., itself is stated. For abstinences are not suitable as having the manifestation of non-action towards the base of misconduct, but rather towards the misconduct itself. Furthermore, for the abstinences, the shrinking and non-doing are by way of gentleness, whereas for shame and fear of wrongdoing, they are by way of disgust, etc. This is the distinction between them.

476. Saṅkhārāti saṅkhārakkhandhadhamme sandhāyāha. Te hi idhādhippetā, aññathā aṭṭhatiṃsāti vattabbaṃ siyā. Yathā cittaṃ, evaṃ taṃsampayuttadhammāpi dutiye sasaṅkhārā evāti āha “sasaṅkhārabhāvamattameva hettha viseso”ti. Avasesā paṭhame vuttadhammā.

476. He said 'saṅkhārā' referring to the phenomena of the aggregate of formations. Indeed, those are intended here; otherwise, it should have been said as 'thirty-eight'. Just as the consciousness, so too the states associated with it are only with prompting in the second; thus, he said, 'Here the only difference is just the state of being with prompting.' The remaining states are those stated in the first.

Avasesā pañcamena sampayogaṃ gacchantīti ettha kathaṃ karuṇāmuditāupekkhāsahagate sambhavantīti? Pubbabhāgabhāvato. Appanāppattā eva hi karuṇāmuditā upekkhāsahagatā na honti, tato aññattha pana upekkhāsahagatāpi hontīti ācariyā.

Regarding the passage, 'The remaining states... become associated,' how do compassion and sympathetic joy arise in a state accompanied by equanimity? Because of being in the preliminary stage. Indeed, it is only when they have reached absorption that compassion and sympathetic joy are not accompanied by equanimity; but elsewhere, they can be accompanied by equanimity, so say the teachers.

Suvisuddhassa kāyakammādikassa cittasamādhānavasena rūpārūpāvacarakusalappavatti, na kāyakammādīnaṃ sodhanavasena, nāpi duccaritadurājīvānaṃ samucchindanapaṭippassambhanavasenāti mahaggatacittuppādesu viratīnaṃ asambhavoyevāti āha “ṭhapetvā viratittaya”nti. Tatoti rūpāvacarapaṭhame vuttacetasikato. Teyevāti rūpāvacarapañcame vuttacetasikā eva. Yadi eva rūpāvacarato ko visesoti āha “arūpāvacarabhāvoyeva hi ettha viseso”ti.

For one with very pure bodily action, etc., the arising of form-sphere and formless-sphere wholesome states is by means of concentrating the mind, not by means of purifying bodily action, etc., nor by means of eradicating and pacifying misconduct and wrong livelihood. Thus, because the non-arising of the abstinences in the arising of sublime consciousness is certain, he said, 'excluding the three abstinences.' `Tato` means: from the mental factors stated in the first form-sphere jhāna. `Teyeva` means: just the mental factors stated in the fifth form-sphere jhāna. If so, what is the difference from the form-sphere? He said, 'Indeed, here the difference is just the state of being formless-sphere.'

Paṭhamajjhāniketi paṭhamajjhānavati. Maggaviññāṇeti catubbidhepi maggaviññāṇe vuttanayeneva veditabbāti sambandho. Dutiyajjhānikādibhede maggaviññāṇeti ettha ādi-saddena tatiyacatutthapañcamajjhānikāni saṅgaṇhāti. “Vuttanayenā”ti vuttaṃ kiṃ avisesenāti codanāyane taṃ dassento “karuṇāmuditāna”ntiādimāha. Tattha maggaviññāṇānaṃ nibbānārammaṇattā, karuṇāmuditānañca sattārammaṇattā na tāsaṃ tattha sambhavo. Maggadhammesu ca pādakādiniyamena [V 2.0139] kadāci sammāsaṅkappaviraho siyā[M 2.0149], na pana virativiraho kāyaduccaritādīnaṃ samucchindanavaseneva ariyamaggassa pavattanatoti niyataviratitā.

`Paṭhamajjhānika` means possessing the first jhāna. `Maggaviññāṇa` should be understood by the method already stated in the fourfold path-consciousness; this is the connection. In the text concerning path-consciousness in the divisions of the second jhānic state and so on, the word `ādi` (etc.) includes the third, fourth, and fifth jhānic states. To the objection, 'Is what was said as "by the method already stated" to be understood without distinction?', showing that it is not so, he said, 'of compassion and sympathetic joy,' etc. Therein, because the path-consciousnesses have Nibbāna as their object, and compassion and sympathetic joy have beings as their object, their arising there is not possible. Furthermore, among the path-factors, by the rule of the foundation jhāna, etc., there might sometimes be an absence of right thought, but not an absence of the abstinences, because the noble path proceeds only by means of eradicating bodily misconduct, etc. Thus, the abstinences are fixed.

478. Na hiriyati na lajjatīti ahiriko, puggalo, cittaṃ, taṃsampayuttadhammasamudāyo vā. “Ahirikka”nti vattabbe ekassa kakārassa lopaṃ katvā “ahirika”nti vuttaṃ. “Na ottappa”nti ottappassa paṭipakkhabhūtaṃ dhammamāha. Ajigucchanaṃ ahīḷanaṃ. Alajjā aviriḷā. Tehevāti kāyaduccaritādīhi eva. Asārajjaṃ nibbhayatā. Anuttāso asambhamo. Vuttapaṭipakkhavasenāti alajjanākārena pāpānaṃ karaṇarasaṃ ahirikaṃ, anuttāsākārena anottappaṃ, vuttappakāreneva pāpato asaṅkocanapaccupaṭṭhānāni attani, paresu ca agāravapadaṭṭhānāni. Gāmasūkarassa viya asucito kilesāsucito ajigucchanaṃ ahirikena hoti, salabhassa viya aggito pāpato anuttāso anottappena hotīti evaṃ vuttappaṭipakkhavasena vitthāro veditabbo.

478. Because one is not ashamed, one is called `ahirika`—be it a person, the mind, or the collection of phenomena associated with it. When it should be said as `ahirikka`, it is said as `ahirika` by eliding one `ka`. By 'not fearing wrongdoing,' it speaks of the state that is the opposite of fear of wrongdoing (`ottappa`). It is non-disgust, non-disdain. It is shamelessness, immodesty. By those very things, that is, by bodily misconduct and so on. Boldness is fearlessness. Lack of dread is lack of agitation. By way of the opposite of what was said: `ahirika` has the characteristic of committing evil in a shameless manner, while `anottappa` has the characteristic of not being terrified. In the manner just stated, they have not shrinking from evil as their manifestation, and disrespect for oneself and for others as their proximate cause. Just as a village pig is not disgusted by filth, so through `ahirika` there is non-disgust for the filth of defilements. Just as a moth has no dread of fire, so through `anottappa` there is no dread of evil. Thus, the detailed explanation should be understood by way of the opposite of what was said.

479. Lubbhanti tenātiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayānusārena veditabbaṃ. Lubbhantīti abhigijjhanti. Muyhantīti na bujjhanti. Ārammaṇaggahaṇaṃ “mama ida”nti taṇhābhinivesavasena abhinivissa ārammaṇassa avissajjanaṃ, na ārammaṇakaraṇamattaṃ. Abhisaṅgo abhimukhabhāvena āsatti. Apariccāgo avijahanaṃ, dummocanīyatā vā. Assādadassanaṃ assādadiṭṭhi. “Assādānupassino ca taṇhā pavaḍḍhatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.52, 54, 57) hi vuttaṃ.

479. In the texts beginning with `lubbhanti tena`, whatever should be said is to be understood in accordance with the method explained previously. `Lubbhanti` means they are intensely greedy. `Muyhanti` means they do not comprehend. Grasping an object is, through the force of adherence which is craving, thinking 'this is mine,' and thus adhering to and not releasing the object; it is not merely the act of taking the object. Clinging (`abhisaṅga`) is adherence by way of facing towards it. Non-relinquishment is non-abandoning, or the state of being difficult to be freed from. Seeing gratification is the view of gratification. For it is said: 'For one who contemplates gratification, craving increases.'

480. Dhammasabhāvassa yāthāvato adassanaṃ cittassa andhabhāvo. Aññāṇaṃ ñāṇapaṭipakkho. Sampaṭivijjhituṃ asamatthatā asampaṭivedho. Yathā ñāṇaṃ ārammaṇasabhāvaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ na labbhati, mohassa tathā pavatti ārammaṇasabhāvacchādanaṃ. Asammāpaṭipattiṃ paccupaṭṭhapeti, sammāpaṭipattiyā paṭipakkhabhāvena gayhatīti vā asammāpaṭipattipaccupaṭṭhāno. Yassa uppajjati, tassa andhakaraṇaṃ andhakāro, tathā paccupatiṭṭhatīti andhakārapaccupaṭṭhāno.

480. Not seeing the true nature of phenomena as it really is, is the state of blindness of the mind. Ignorance is the opposite of knowledge. The inability to penetrate thoroughly is non-penetration. The occurrence of delusion is the concealing of the object's true nature, in such a way that knowledge is unable to penetrate that true nature. It causes wrong practice, or it is taken as being the opposite of right practice, thus it has wrong practice as its manifestation. For whomever it arises, it is the cause of blindness, it is darkness; because it manifests thus, it has darkness as its manifestation.

481. Micchāti dhammasabhāvassa viparītaṃ, niccāditoti attho. Ayoniso abhiniveso anupāyābhiniveso uppathābhiniveso. Dhammasabhāvaṃ [M 2.0150] atikkamitvā parato āmasanaṃ [V 2.0140] parāmāso. Viparītaggāhavasena “idameva saccaṃ, moghamañña”nti (ma. ni. 2.187, 202, 203; 3.27-29) abhinivisanaṃ micchābhiniveso.

481. ‘Wrong’ means contrary to the true nature of things; that is, as permanent, and so on. Unwise adherence is adherence to an improper means, adherence to a wrong path. Having transgressed the true nature of things, grasping it wrongly is misapprehension. Through the power of distorted grasping, the adherence that ‘This alone is true, the other is futile’ is wrong adherence.

482. Yassa dhammassa vasena uddhataṃ hoti cittaṃ, taṃsampayuttadhammā vā, so dhammo uddhaccaṃ. Avūpasamoti asannisinnaappasannabhāvamāha. Anavaṭṭhānarasanti calanakiccaṃ. Bhantattanti paribbhamanākāraṃ. Cetaso avūpasameti nipphādetabbe payojane bhummaṃ, avūpasamapaccayabhūtaṃ ārammaṇaṃ vā “avūpasamo”ti vuttaṃ. Akusaladhammānaṃ ekantanihīnatāya “akusalabhāvena ca lāmakatta”nti vuttaṃ.

482. That state by the power of which the mind becomes agitated, or its associated states, is agitation. ‘Non-subsidence’ refers to the state of being unsettled and not serene. By ‘having the function of instability’ is meant its task of wavering. By ‘the state of bewilderment’ is meant its characteristic of wandering about. The phrase ‘non-subsidence of mind’ is a locative phrase regarding the purpose to be accomplished; or, the object which has become a condition for non-subsidence is called ‘non-subsidence’. Because of the utter baseness of unwholesome states, it is said to be ‘baseness also by its unwholesome nature’.

483. Thinamiddhamettha aniyataṃ, na mānādīti thinamiddhassa aniyatatā ca ettha dutiyacitte paṭhamākusalato viseso.

483. Here, sloth and torpor are indeterminate, unlike conceit and so on. Therefore, the indeterminacy of sloth and torpor is, in this second consciousness, the distinction from the first unwholesome consciousness.

Anussāhanāvasīdanabhāvena saṃhatabhāvo thinaṃ, tena yogato cittaṃ thinaṃ, tassa bhāvoti thinatā. Asamatthatāvighātavasena akammaññatā middhaṃ. Yasmā tato eva tena sampayuttadhammā medhitā vihatasāmatthiyā honti, tasmā “middhanatā middha”nti vuttaṃ. Anussāhalakkhaṇanti ussāhapaṭipakkhalakkhaṇaṃ. Vīriyassa avanodanaṃ khipanaṃ vīriyāvanodanaṃ. Sampayuttadhammānaṃ saṃsīdanākārena paccupatiṭṭhati, tesaṃ vā saṃsīdanaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetīti saṃsīdanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Akammaññatālakkhaṇanti ettha kāmaṃ thinampi akammaññasabhāvameva, taṃ pana cittassa, middhaṃ vedanādikkhandhattayassāti ayamettha viseso. Tathā hi pāḷiyaṃ “tattha katamaṃ thinaṃ? Yā cittassa akallatā akammaññatā. Tattha katamaṃ middhaṃ? Yā kāyassa akallatā akammaññatā”ti (dha. sa. 1162-1163) ca ādinā imesaṃ niddeso pavatto. Onahanaṃ viññāṇadvārānaṃ pidahanaṃ. Līnatā līnākāro ārammaṇaggahaṇe saṅkoco. Yasmā thinena cittasseva saṃhananaṃ hoti, middhena pana vedanādikkhandhattayassa viya rūpakāyassāpi, tasmā taṃ pacalāyikāniddaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetīti pacalāyikāniddāpaccupaṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ. Arati pantasenāsanesu, adhikusaladhammesu ca arocanā. Vijambhikā vijambhanasaṅkhātassa kāyaduṭṭhullassa kāraṇabhūtā saṃkilesappavatti. Arativijambhikādīsūti [M 2.0151] ca ādi-saddena tandiādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Nipphādetabbe payojane cetaṃ bhummavacanaṃ.

The state of contractedness due to non-exertion and sinking is sloth. By connection with that, the mind is slothful; its state is slothfulness. Unwieldiness by way of affliction from incapability is torpor. Because by that very thing, the associated states become dulled and their capability is destroyed, therefore it is called 'torpor.' Its characteristic is non-exertion, that is, it has the characteristic of being the opposite of exertion. Its function is the dispelling and casting away of energy. It manifests in the manner of the sinking of associated states, or it causes their sinking—thus, its manifestation is sinking. Regarding the characteristic of unwieldiness—here, although sloth is also of the nature of unwieldiness, the distinction is that sloth pertains to the mind, while torpor pertains to the three aggregates beginning with feeling. Indeed, in the Pāḷi, by 'Herein, what is sloth? It is the unhealthiness, the unwieldiness of the mind' (Dhs. 1162-1163), and so on, the exposition of these two proceeds. Covering is the shutting of the doors of consciousness. Languor is a languid manner, a shrinking in grasping the object. Because by sloth there is a contraction of the mind only, while by torpor there is a contraction of the material body as well as of the three aggregates beginning with feeling, therefore, it is said to manifest as nodding drowsiness—thus, its manifestation is said to be nodding drowsiness. Discontent is displeasure with remote lodgings and with superior wholesome states. Yawning is the arising of defilement which is the cause of the bodily unwieldiness known as stretching. In the phrase 'discontent, yawning, etc.,' the word 'etc.' includes lassitude and similar states. And this is a locative expression regarding the purpose to be accomplished.

Avasesā [V 2.0141] soḷasa. Māno panettha aniyato hoti, tena saddhiṃ sattaraseva honti. Paṭṭhāne hi “saṃyojanaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca saṃyojano dhammo uppajjati hetupaccayā”ti ettha catukkhattuṃ kāmarāgena, tikkhattuṃ paṭighena ca māno vicikicchā bhavarāgoti tayopete sakadāgāmino saṃyojanānaṃ saṃyojanehi dasavidhā yojanāti dassitāya dasavidhāya yojanāya “kāmarāgasaṃyojanaṃ paṭicca mānasaṃyojanaṃ avijjāsaṃyojana”nti (paṭṭhā. 3.4.1) vatvā “kāmarāgasaṃyojanaṃ paṭicca avijjāsaṃyojana”nti (paṭṭhā. 3.4.1) tathā “mānasaṃyojanaṃ paṭicca bhavarāgasaṃyojanaṃ avijjāsaṃyojana”nti (paṭṭhā 3.4.1) vatvā “bhavarāgasaṃyojanaṃ paṭicca avijjāsaṃyojana”nti (paṭṭhā. 3.4.1) ca evamāgatāhi yojanāhi mānassa aniyatabhāvo pakāsito. Yadi hi māno niyato siyā, kāmarāgassa mānarahitā pavatti na siyā, tathā bhavarāgassa. Evaṃ sati paṭṭhāne catukkhattuṃ kāmarāgena yojanā na siyā, tikkhattuṃyeva siyā. Bhavarāgamūlikā ca na siyā. Evañca saṃyojanānaṃ saṃyojanehi aṭṭhavidhena yojanā siyā, na dasavidhena. Dasavidhāva ca dassitāti. Seyyādivasena uccato namanaṃ unnati. Unnamanavaseneva saṃpaggaharaso. Na vīriyaṃ viya taṃtaṃkiccasādhane abbhussahanavasena. Omānassāpi attānaṃ avaṃ katvā gahaṇampi sampaggahaṇavasenevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ketu vuccati accuggatadhajo, idha pana ketu viyāti ketu, uḷāratamādibhāvo. Taṃ ketubhāvasaṅkhātaṃ ketuṃ kāmetīti ketukamyaṃ, cittaṃ. Yassa dhammassa vasena ketukamyaṃ, sā ketukamyatā. “Aha”nti pavattanato mānassa diṭṭhisadisī pavattīti so diṭṭhiyā saddhiṃ ekacittuppāde na pavattati, attasinehasannissayo cāti āha “diṭṭhivippayuttalobhapadaṭṭhāno”ti.

The remaining are sixteen. Herein, conceit is indeterminate; with it, there are only seventeen. For in the Paṭṭhāna, in the context of “Dependent on a fetter-dharma, a fetter-dharma arises by way of root-condition,” it is shown that in the tenfold combination of fetters with fetters, sensual desire comes four times, aversion comes three times, and conceit, doubt, and craving for existence—these three—each come once. By these combinations that have come thus—having said, “Dependent on the fetter of sensual desire, the fetter of conceit and the fetter of ignorance arise,” and “Dependent on the fetter of sensual desire, the fetter of ignorance arises”; and similarly, having said, “Dependent on the fetter of conceit, the fetter of craving for existence and the fetter of ignorance arise,” and “Dependent on the fetter of craving for existence, the fetter of ignorance arises”—the indeterminate nature of conceit is revealed. For if conceit were determinate, the occurrence of sensual desire without conceit would not be, and similarly for craving for existence. This being so, in the Paṭṭhāna, the combination with sensual desire would not be fourfold; it would be only threefold. And there would be no combination rooted in craving for existence. And thus, the combination of fetters with fetters would be eightfold, not tenfold. But a tenfold combination is indeed shown. Elevation (unnati) is the inclining from on high by way of being superior, etc. Its function is uplifting by way of elevating. It is not like energy, by way of great exertion in accomplishing various tasks. Even in the case of self-deprecation (omāna), the act of considering oneself inferior should be understood as being by way of uplifting. A highly raised banner is called a 'ketu'. Here, however, because it is like a banner, it is called 'ketu', meaning the state of being most excellent, and so on. Because it desires that 'ketu'—designated as the state of a banner—it is 'ketukamyaṃ'; this refers to the mind. That quality, by virtue of which the mind desires prominence, is 'ketukamyatā'. Because it occurs as “I,” the functioning of conceit is similar to that of wrong view. Therefore, it does not arise in the same mind-moment together with wrong view. And it is founded on self-love. Therefore, he said: “It has greed dissociated from wrong view as its proximate cause.”

Etthāpi cāti ca-saddena thinamiddhaṃ ākaḍḍhati.

Here, too, by the word 'ca', sloth and torpor are drawn in.

485. Dussantīti byāpajjanti. Caṇḍikkaṃ kujjhanaṃ. Attano pavattiākāravasena, virūpasaṃsappanakaaniṭṭharūpasamuṭṭhāpanavasena ca visappanaraso. Kāyassa [M 2.0152] vijjhattabhāvāpādanato attano nissayadahanaraso. Dussanaṃ attano, parassa ca upabhogaphalakālesu aniṭṭhattā visasaṃsaṭṭhapūtimuttaṃ viya daṭṭhabboti sabbena sabbaṃ aggahetabbataṃ dasseti.

485. 'Dussanti' means they are corrupted. 'Caṇḍikkaṃ' is anger. By means of its own manner of occurrence, and by producing undesirable forms that are distorted and spreading, its function is to pervade. By causing the body to be scorched, its function is to burn its own support. Corruption is to be seen as like putrid urine mixed with poison, being undesirable for oneself and for others at the times of its application and its result; thus, it demonstrates its complete unacceptability.

486. Yaṃ parasampattīsu issākaraṇaṃ, sā issāti dassento āha “issāyanā issā”ti[V 2.0142]. Usūyanaṃ asahanaṃ. Tatthevāti parasampattīsu eva. Abhiratipaṭipakkhabhūtaṃ issāya kiccaṃ, na abhiratiyā abhāvamattanti āha “anabhiratirasā”ti.

486. Showing that envy is the act of envying others' accomplishments, he said, 'Envy is the act of envying.' 'Usūyanaṃ' is intolerance. 'Right there' means precisely in others' accomplishments. The function of envy is the opposite of delight, not merely the absence of delight; therefore, he said, 'its function is non-delight.'

487. Maccharayogena “maccharī”ti pavattamānaṃ maccharisaddaṃ gahetvā āha “maccharabhāvo macchariya”nti. Niruttinayena pana mā idaṃ acchariyaṃ aññesaṃ hotu, mayhameva hotūti macchariyanti porāṇā. Taṃ macchariyaṃ vuccamānāni lakkhaṇādīni pariyādāya tiṭṭhati. Saṅkocanapaccupaṭṭhānanti attasampattīnaṃ parehi asādhāraṇabhāvakaraṇena saṅkocanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Kaṭukākāragati kaṭukañcukatā. Attasampatti āvāsādi.

487. Taking the word 'maccharī' (one who is stingy), which is used due to its connection with stinginess, he said, 'The state of being stingy is macchariya (stinginess).' However, by way of etymology, the ancients state that macchariya is [the thought]: 'Let this excellent thing not be for others; let it be for me alone.' That stinginess stands by encompassing the characteristics and so forth to be described. Its manifestation is constriction, which arises from making one's own possessions unshared with others. A harsh mode of being is kaṭukañcukatā (defensiveness). One's own possessions are such things as a dwelling.

488. Kukatanti ettha akatampi kukatameva. Evañhi vattāro honti “yaṃ mayā na kataṃ, taṃ kukata”nti. Tathā hi vakkhati “katākatānusocanarasa”nti. Evaṃ katākataṃ duccaritaṃ, sucaritañca kukataṃ, taṃ ārabbha vippaṭisāravasena pavattaṃ pana cittaṃ taṃsahacaritatāya idha “kukata”nti gahetvā “tassa bhāvo kukkucca”nti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pacchā anutāpanaṃ vibādhanaṃ pacchānutāpo. Yathāpavattassa katākatākāravisiṭṭhassa duccaritasucaritassa anusocanavasena virūpaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ vippaṭisāro. Parāyattatāhetutāya dāsabyamiva daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathā hi dāsabye sati dāso parāyatto hoti, evaṃ kukkucce sati taṃsamaṅgī. Na hi so attano dhammatāya kusale pavattituṃ sakkoti. Atha vā katākatākusalakusalānusocane āyattatāya tadubhayavasena kukkuccena taṃsamaṅgī hotīti taṃ dāsabyaṃ viya hotīti.

488. Regarding `kukata`, herein even what is not done is indeed `kukata`. For thus there are those who say, 'What was not done by me, that is `kukata`.' For so it will be said: 'Its characteristic is to regret what has been done and what has not been done.' Thus, bad conduct and good conduct, whether done or not done, is `kukata`. However, the mind that arises by way of remorse concerning that `kukata` is, due to its association with it, taken here as `kukata`, and its state is said to be `kukkucca`; thus it should be understood. Later regret (`pacchānutāpo`) is a later torment, an oppression. Remorse (`vippaṭisāro`) is a distorted recollection, by way of regretting, of bad and good conduct that has occurred, which is characterized by the aspects of what was done and not done. Because it is a cause for dependence on another, it should be seen as being like slavery. For just as, when there is slavery, a slave is dependent on another, so too, when there is remorse, is the one who is endowed with it. Indeed, such a person is not able, by his own nature, to engage in the wholesome. Or alternatively, because of being dependent on regretting unwholesome actions that were done and wholesome actions that were not done, one endowed with remorse becomes dependent by way of both of these; therefore, it is like slavery.

Aniyatesu issādīsu thinamiddhasambhavova cāti ca-saddaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ.

Among the indeterminate factors such as envy, etc., there is also indeed the possibility of the arising of sloth and torpor; thus, the word `ca` should be brought in and connected.

490. Pavattiṭṭhitimattoti [M 2.0153] khaṇaṭṭhitimatto. “Nivāte dīpaccīnaṃ ṭhiti viyā”ti hi evaṃ vuttacittaṭṭhiti viya santānaṭṭhitiyā paccayo bhavituṃ asamattho nicchayābhāvena asaṇṭhahanato cetaso pavattipaccayamattatāya pavattiṭṭhitimatto. Tenāha “dubbalo samādhī”ti. Vigatā cikicchāti cikicchituṃ dukkaratāya vuttaṃ, na sabbathā vicikicchāya cikicchābhāvatoti tadatthamattaṃ dasseti. “Evaṃ nu kho, nanu kho”tiādinā saṃsappanavasena setīti saṃsayo. Kampanarasāti nānārammaṇe cittassa kampanakiccā. Uddhaccañhi attanā gahitākāre [V 2.0143] eva ṭhatvā bhamatīti ekārammaṇasmiṃyeva vipphandanavasena pavattati. Vicikicchā pana yadipi rūpādīsu ekasmiṃyeva ārammaṇe uppajjati, tathāpi “evaṃ nu kho, nanu kho, idaṃ nu kho, aññaṃ nu kho”ti aññaṃ gahetabbākāraṃ apekkhatīti nānārammaṇe kampanaṃ hotīti. Anicchayaṃ dveḷhakaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetīti anicchayapaccupaṭṭhānā. Anekaṃsassa ārammaṇe nānāsabhāvassa gahaṇākārena paccupatiṭṭhatīti anekaṃsagāhapaccupaṭṭhānā.

490. “Having only the stability of occurrence” means having only momentary stability. For, just as it is said, “Like the stability of a lamp's flame in a windless place,” so too, like the aforesaid stability of the mind, being unable to be a condition for the stability of continuity, it is “having only the stability of occurrence” by being merely a condition for the mind's arising, due to the absence of certainty and its lack of firm establishment. Therefore, it is said, “weak concentration.” “The remedy is gone” is said because of the difficulty of treating it; it does not mean there is absolutely no remedy for doubt. Thus, it shows just that much of the meaning. Because it occurs by way of creeping, with thoughts such as, “Is it so? Is it not so?”, it is called “doubt” (saṃsayo). Its characteristic is wavering: it has the function of causing the mind to waver among various objects. Indeed, restlessness (uddhacca), having established itself in the very mode it has grasped, spins about; therefore, it proceeds by way of agitation on a single object. Doubt (vicikicchā), on the other hand, although it arises in regard to a single object such as form, etc., nevertheless anticipates another mode to be grasped, thinking, “Is it so? Is it not so? Is it this? Is it another?” Therefore, there is wavering among various objects. It presents indecision and ambiguity; therefore, its manifestation is indecision. It manifests with the mode of grasping the various natures of an object that is not of one part; therefore, its manifestation is the grasping of multiple aspects.

491. Sattārammaṇattāti sattapaññattiārammaṇattā. Nanu ca paññattiārammaṇāpi vipākā hontīti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “ekantaparittārammaṇā hi kāmāvacaravipākā”ti. Viratiyopi vipākesu na santīti etthāpi nanu kesuci vipākesu viratiyopi santīti codanaṃ manasi katvā āha “pañca sikkhāpadā kusalāyevāti hi vutta”nti, tena lokiyavipākesu viratiyo na santīti dasseti.

491. “Because of having a being as its object” means because of having the concept of a being as its object. Anticipating the objection, “But are there not resultants that also have concepts as their object?”, it is said: “For sense-sphere resultants have exclusively limited objects.” Also, regarding the statement “Abstinences are not present in resultants,” having considered the objection, “But are there not abstinences present in some resultants?”, it is said: “For it is said that the five training rules are exclusively wholesome.” By that, it is shown that abstinences are not present in mundane resultants.

Tesanti rūpāvacarādivipākaviññāṇānaṃ. Janetabbajanakasambandhe hi idaṃ sāmivacanaṃ.

“Tesaṃ” refers to the resultant consciousnesses of the form realm and so on. For indeed, this is a term in the genitive case, in the sense of the relationship between that which is to be generated and that which generates.

492. Teti te ahetukakiriyasaṅkhārā. Tattha kusalavipākamanodhātusampayuttehi samānā ahetukakiriyamanodhātusampayuttā, somanassasahagatasantīraṇasampayuttehi samānā hasituppādasampayuttā, upekkhāsahagatasantīraṇasampayuttehi samānā voṭṭhabbanasampayuttāti imamatthaṃ dassentena “kusala…pe… samānā”ti vatvā tato labbhamānaṃ visesaṃ dassetuṃ “manoviññāṇadhātudvaye panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vīriyasabbhāvato balappatto samādhi hoti “vīriyantaṃ bala”nti katvā.

492. “Te” refers to those rootless functional formations. Among them, the formations associated with the rootless functional mind-element are similar to those associated with the wholesome-resultant mind-element; the formations associated with smile-producing consciousness are similar to those associated with joy-accompanied investigating consciousness; and the formations associated with determining consciousness are similar to those associated with equanimity-accompanied investigating consciousness. Wishing to show this meaning, having said, 'wholesome... etc... similar,' the words beginning with 'But in the two mind-consciousness-elements...' were spoken in order to show the distinction that is obtained therefrom. Having considered that 'the power has effort as its end,' concentration attains the state of a power because of the presence of effort.

Samucchedaviratīhi [M 2.0154] eva arahantānaṃ viramanakiccassa niṭṭhitattā kiriyacittesu viratiyo na santīti āha “ṭhapetvā viratiyo”ti. Kāmāvacarasahetukakiriyasaṅkhārānaṃ kāmāvacarakusalehi viratikato viseso atthi, mahaggatesu pana tādisopi natthīti āha “sabbākārenapī”ti, dhammato, ārammaṇato, pavattiākāratoti sabbapakārenapīti attho.

Because for Arahants the task of abstaining has been completed only by the abstinences of eradication, abstinences do not exist in functional consciousnesses; for this reason, he said, 'except for the abstinences.' There is a distinction, made by the abstinences, of the sense-sphere root-accompanied functional formations from the sense-sphere wholesome formations. But in the sublime formations, even such a distinction does not exist; for this reason, he said, 'in every way.' The meaning is: in all aspects—that is, in terms of associated states, in terms of object, and in terms of mode of occurrence.

Iti saṅkhārakkhandhe vitthārakathāmukhavaṇṇanā.

Thus, the explanation of the introduction to the detailed discourse on the aggregate of formations.

Atītādivibhāgakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Division of the Past, etc.

Abhidhammantogadhampi [V 2.0144] suttantabhājanīyaṃ suttantanayo eva, ekantaabhidhammanayo pana abhidhammabhājanīyanti āha “abhidhamme padabhājanīyanayenā”ti.

Although included in the Abhidhamma, that which is to be analyzed by the Suttanta method is indeed the Suttanta method; but the purely Abhidhamma method is that which is to be analyzed by the Abhidhamma method. For this reason, he said, 'in the Abhidhamma, by the method of the analysis of terms.'

493. Bhagavatā pana evaṃ khandhā vitthāritāti sambandho. Tasmā imāyapi pāḷiyā vasena khandhānaṃ saṃvaṇṇanaṃ karissāmāti adhippāyo. Yaṃ kiñcīti ettha yanti sāmaññena aniyamadassanaṃ. Kiñcīti pakārabhedaṃ āmasitvā aniyamadassanaṃ. Ubhayenāpi atītaṃ vā…pe… santike vā appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā yādisaṃ vā tādisaṃ vā napuṃsakaniddesārahaṃ sabbaṃ byāpetvā gaṇhātīti āha “anavasesapariyādāna”nti. Evaṃ pana aññesupi napuṃsakaniddesārahesu pasaṅgaṃ disvā tattha adhippetatthaṃ aticca pavattanato atippasaṅgassa niyamanatthaṃ rūpanti vuttanti dassento “rūpanti atippasaṅganiyamana”nti āha. Yaṃ kiñcīti ca yaṃ-saddaṃ ekaṃ padaṃ, sanipātaṃ kiṃ-saddañca ekaṃ padanti gahetvā aniyamekatthadīpanato “padadvayenāpī”ti vuttaṃ. Assāti rūpassa. Atītādinā vibhāgaṃ ārabhati atītānāgatapaccuppannantiādinā.

493. However, 'the Blessed One has thus expounded the aggregates in detail'—this is the connection. Therefore, the intention is: 'By means of this Pāli text as well, I shall provide a description of the aggregates.' Herein, in the phrase 'yaṃ kiñci' (whatever), the word 'yaṃ' generally indicates non-specification. The word 'kiñci', having considered the specific variety, indicates non-specification. By both words, it comprehends by pervading all phenomena suitable for designation in the neuter gender—whether past… or near, or little, or much, or of whatever nature, or of such a nature. Thus, he said, 'complete inclusion without remainder.' However, seeing that this would also apply to other things suitable for neuter designation, and because it would proceed by transgressing the intended meaning in that case, the word 'rūpaṃ' was stated in order to restrict that over-application. Showing this, he said, '“rūpaṃ” is for the restriction of over-application.' And in 'yaṃ kiñci', having taken the word 'yaṃ' as one word and the particle-word 'kiṃ' as one word, it was said 'by both words' because it shows a single, non-specific meaning. 'Assa' (its) refers to 'rūpassa' (of form). He begins the division with 'past, etc.,' that is, with 'past, future, present, etc.'

494. Addhāsantatisamayakhaṇavasenāti ettha cutipaṭisandhiparicchinne kāle addhā-saddo vattatīti “ahosiṃ nu kho ahamatītamaddhāna”ntiādisuttavasena (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20) viññāyati. Tathā hi bhaddekarattasuttepi “atītaṃ nānvāgameyyā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 3.272, 275, 276, 277) addhāvaseneva atītādibhāvo vutto. “Tayome, [M 2.0155] bhikkhave, addhā, katame tayo? Atīto addhā anāgato addhā paccuppanno addhā”ti (dī. ni. 3.305; itivu. 63) pana paramatthato paricchijjamāno addhā niruttipathasuttavasena khaṇaparicchinno vutto. Tattha hi “yaṃ, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ jātaṃ…pe… pātubhūtaṃ. Atthīti tassa saṅkhā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.62) vijjamānassa paccuppannatā, tato pubbe, pacchā ca atītānāgatatā vuttā. Tadaññasuttesu pana yebhuyyena cutipaṭisandhiparicchinno atītādiko addhā vuttoti so eva idhāpi “addhāvasenā”ti vutto.

494. Herein, that the word 'addhā' applies to time delineated by death and rebirth-linking is known by way of suttas such as, 'Was I indeed in the past period?' Indeed, in the Bhaddekaratta Sutta also, by the words beginning with, 'One should not pursue the past,' the state of being past, etc., is spoken of by way of the period itself. However, in the sutta, 'Monks, there are these three periods. What three? The past period, the future period, and the present period,' the period, when delineated in the ultimate sense, is spoken of as delineated by moments, by way of the Niruttipatha Sutta. For therein it is said, 'Monks, whatever form is arisen... has manifested. For that, there is the designation: "it is."' The presentness of what is existing, and the pastness and futureness before and after that, are spoken of. However, in other suttas, for the most part, the period which is past, etc., is spoken of as delineated by death and rebirth-linking. Therefore, that very period is here also spoken of as 'by way of the period'.

Sītaṃ sītassa sabhāgo, tathā uṇhaṃ uṇhassa. Yaṃ pana sītaṃ, uṇhaṃ vā sarīre sannipatitaṃ [V 2.0145] santānavasena pavattamānaṃ anūnaṃ anadhikaṃ ekākāraṃ, taṃ eko utūti vuccatīti sabhāgautuno anekattā eka-ggahaṇaṃ kataṃ, evaṃ āhārepi. Ekavīthiekajavanasamuṭṭhānanti pañcachaṭṭhadvāravasena vuttaṃ. Santatisamayakathā vipassakānaṃ upakāratthāya aṭṭhakathāsu kathitā. Janako hetu, upathambhako paccayo, tesaṃ uppādanaṃ, upatthambhanañca kiccaṃ. Yathā bījassa aṅkuruppādanaṃ, pathavīādīnañca tadupatthambhanaṃ, kammassa kaṭattārūpavipākuppādanaṃ, āhārādīnaṃ tadupatthambhanaṃ, evaṃ ekekassa kalāpassa, cittuppādassa ca janakānaṃ kammānantarādipaccayabhūtānaṃ, upatthambhakānañca sahajātapurejātapacchājātānaṃ kiccaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Evaṃ utuādīnaṃ sabhāgavisabhāgatāsambhavato taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ rūpānaṃ santativasena atītādivibhāgo vutto, kammassa pana ekabhavanibbattakassa sabhāgavisabhāgatā natthīti taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ rūpānaṃ santativasena atītādivibhāgaṃ avatvā upatthambhakavaseneva vutto. Yadā pana liṅgaparivattanaṃ hoti, tadā balavatā akusalena purisaliṅgaṃ antaradhāyati, dubbalena kusalena itthiliṅgaṃ pātubhavati. Dubbalena ca akusalena itthiliṅgaṃ antaradhāyati, balavatā kusalena purisaliṅgaṃ pātubhavatīti kammasamuṭṭhānarūpānampi attheva visabhāgatāti tesampi santativasena atītādivibhāgo sambhavati, so pana na sabbakālikoti na gahito.

Cold is of a similar nature to cold; likewise, heat is of a similar nature to heat. Furthermore, when cold or heat that has accumulated in the body occurs by way of continuity, being neither deficient nor excessive and having a uniform characteristic, that is called 'one temperature.' Thus, because there are many kinds of similar temperatures, the term 'one' is used. The same applies to nutriment. The phrase 'arising from a single cognitive process, a single impulsion' is stated with reference to the five doors and the sixth door. The discourse on continuity and time is taught in the commentaries for the benefit of insight meditators. The generator is the cause (hetu); the supporter is the condition (paccayo). Their function is generating and supporting. Just as a seed generates a sprout and earth and so on support it, and as kamma generates materiality produced by kamma and resultants, and nutriment and so on support them, so too, for each material group and arising of consciousness, the function of the generators—which are conditions such as kamma, contiguity, and so on—and of the supporters—which are conascent, prenascent, and postnascent—should be applied as is appropriate. Thus, due to the possibility of similarity and dissimilarity in temperature, etc., the division into past, etc., of material phenomena arising from them is stated in terms of continuity. However, since kamma that generates a single existence has no similarity or dissimilarity, the division into past, etc., of material phenomena arising from it is not stated in terms of continuity but only by way of the supporter. But when a change of gender occurs, by strong unwholesome kamma the male characteristic disappears, and by weak wholesome kamma the female characteristic appears. And by weak unwholesome kamma the female characteristic disappears, and by strong wholesome kamma the male characteristic appears. Thus, for material phenomena originated by kamma, there is indeed dissimilarity, and so for them also, the division into past, etc., by way of continuity is possible. However, since that is not always the case, it is not included.

Taṃtaṃsamayanti ekamuhuttādiko so so samayo etassāti taṃtaṃsamayaṃ, rūpaṃ, taṃtaṃsamayavantanti attho.

Regarding 'taṃtaṃsamayaṃ': For this (materiality), there is that particular time, such as a moment, etc.; therefore, it is called 'taṃtaṃsamayaṃ'. This refers to materiality. The meaning is 'that which possesses that particular time'.

Tato [M 2.0156] pubbeti tato khaṇattayassa pariyāpattito pubbe. Anuppannattā anāgataṃ. Pacchāti tato pacchā. Khaṇattayaṃ atikkantattā atītaṃ. Yassa hetukiccaṃ, paccayakiccañca niṭṭhitattā atikkantaṃ, taṃ atītaṃ uppādakkhaṇe hetukiccaṃ, uppannaphalattā niṭṭhitañcāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tīsupi khaṇesu paccayakiccaṃ. Pathavīādīnaṃ sandhāraṇādikaṃ, phassādīnaṃ phusanādikañca attano kiccaṃ sakiccaṃ, sakiccassa karaṇakkhaṇo sakiccakkhaṇo, saha vā kiccena sakiccaṃ, yasmiṃ khaṇe sakiccaṃ rūpaṃ vā arūpaṃ vā hoti, so sakiccakkhaṇo, tasmiṃ khaṇe paccuppannaṃ. Ettha ca khaṇādikathāyaṃ “tato pubbe anāgataṃ, pacchā atīta”nti vacanaṃ addhādīsu viya bhedābhāvato nippariyāyaṃ. Addhādivasena hi aññeva dhammā atītā aññe anāgatā aññe paccuppannā labbhanti, khaṇādivasena pana natthi dhammato bhedo, kālato eva bhedo. Uppādato pubbe anāgato[V 2.0146], khaṇattaye vattamāno, tato paraṃ atītoti nippariyāyā, addhāpaccuppannādi viya kenaci pariyāyena atītamanāgatanti ca vattabbatābhāvato.

‘Before that’ means before its inclusion in the three moments. Since it has not yet arisen, it is the future. ‘After that’ means after that. Having passed beyond the three moments, it is the past. That of which the causal function and conditional function have passed away because they are completed, is the past. It should be understood that in the moment of arising, the causal function is completed because its result has arisen. The conditional function occurs in all three moments. The supporting, etc., of the earth element and so on, and the contacting, etc., of contact and so on, is its own function (sakicca). The moment of performing its own function is the ‘moment of function’ (sakiccakkhaṇa). Or, it is ‘that which has a function’ (sakicca) because it occurs together with its function. The moment in which a material or immaterial phenomenon that has a function occurs, that is the ‘moment of function’; in that moment, it is the present. And here, in the discussion of moments and so on, the statement, ‘before that is the future, after that is the past,’ is a direct statement, because, unlike in the case of time-periods and so on, there is no difference in the phenomena themselves. For, by way of time-periods and so on, entirely different phenomena are found as past, others as future, and still others as present; but by way of moments and so on, there is no difference in the phenomena themselves, only a difference in time. Before arising, it is future; while occurring in the three moments, it is present; after that, it is past. This is a direct statement because, unlike the time-period present and so on, there is no state of being fit to be called ‘past’ or ‘future’ by some figurative expression.

495. Heṭṭhā vuttaṃ ajjhattikabāhirabhedaṃ sandhāya “vuttanayo evā”ti vatvā tena aparitussamānena yadipi tattha ajjhattameva ajjhattikanti saddattho labbhati, tathāpi attheva ajjhattaajjhattikasaddānaṃ, bahiddhābāhirasaddānañca aññamaññaṃ atthabhedo. Tathā hi ajjhattikasaddo saparasantānikesu cakkhādīsu rūpādīsu bāhirasaddo viya pavattati, ajjhattasaddo pana tassa tassa sattassa sasantānikesveva cakkhurūpādīsu tato aññesu bahiddhāsaddo viya pavattati. Tasmā tamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha idhāti imasmiṃ suttantanaye. Niyakajjhattampi na pubbe vuttaajjhattikameva, parapuggalikampi na pubbe vuttabāhiramevāti adhippāyo.

495. Referring to the distinction between internal (ajjhattika) and external (bāhira) stated below, and having said, 'It is just the method that has been stated,' the commentator was not satisfied with that. Although the word-meaning 'ajjhattika is just ajjhatta' is obtained there, nevertheless, there is indeed a mutual difference in meaning between the words 'ajjhatta' and 'ajjhattika', and between the words 'bahiddhā' and 'bāhira'. For the word 'ajjhattika' applies to the eye, etc., in one's own and others' continuums, just as the word 'bāhira' applies to forms, etc. The word 'ajjhatta', however, applies only to the eye, form, etc., in that particular being's own continuum, just as the word 'bahiddhā' applies to what is other than that. Therefore, to show that meaning, the passage beginning with 'apica' was stated. Therein, 'idha' means 'in this Sutta method'. The meaning is that what is one's own internal phenomenon is not just the 'ajjhattika' previously mentioned, and what belongs to another person is not just the 'bāhira' previously mentioned.

496. Hīnapaṇītabhedo pariyāyato, nippariyāyato ca veditabboti sambandho. Tadeva sudassīnaṃ rūpaṃ. Yatthāti yasmiṃ ārammaṇabhūte. Yaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā akusalavipākaviññāṇaṃ uppajjati, taṃ hīnaṃ aniṭṭhabhāvato. Yaṃ kusalavipākaṃ, taṃ paṇītaṃ iṭṭhabhāvato. Yathā hi akusalavipāko sayaṃ aniṭṭho aniṭṭhe eva uppajjati, na iṭṭhe, evaṃ kusalavipākopi sayaṃ iṭṭho iṭṭhe eva uppajjati, na aniṭṭhe. Tathā hi vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

496. The connection is that the distinction between inferior and superior should be understood both figuratively and literally. That very form of the Sudassī brahmās. 'Wherein' means in whatever has become an object. The object that serves as the basis for the arising of unwholesome resultant consciousness is inferior because it is undesirable. The object that serves as the basis for wholesome resultant consciousness is superior because it is desirable. For just as unwholesome resultant consciousness, being itself undesirable, arises only in relation to an undesirable object and not a desirable one, so too wholesome resultant consciousness, being itself desirable, arises only in relation to a desirable object and not an undesirable one. For so it is said in the commentary—

“Akusalakammajavasena [M 2.0157] aniṭṭhā pañca kāmaguṇā vibhattā, kusalakammajaṃ pana aniṭṭhaṃ nāma natthi, sabbaṃ iṭṭhameva. Kusalakammajavasena iṭṭhā pañca kāmaguṇā vibhattā. Kusalakammajañhi aniṭṭhaṃ nāma natthi, sabbaṃ iṭṭhamevā”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 6) ca.

‘Through the force of what is born of unwholesome kamma, the five strands of sensual pleasure are differentiated as undesirable. However, as for what is born of wholesome kamma, there is nothing called undesirable; all of it is just desirable. Through the force of what is born of wholesome kamma, the five strands of sensual pleasure are differentiated as desirable. Indeed, as for what is born of wholesome kamma, there is nothing called undesirable; all of it is just desirable.’

Tattha manāpānipi kānici hatthirūpādīni akusalakammanibbattāni santi, na pana tāni tesaṃyeva hatthiādīnaṃ sukhassa hetubhāvaṃ gacchanti. Tassa tasseva hi sattassa attanā katena kusalena nibbattaṃ sukhassa paccayo hoti, akusalena nibbattaṃ dukkhassa. Tasmā kammajānaṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhatā kammakārakasattassa vasena yojanārahā siyā. Tattha yaṃ vuttaṃ “kusalakammajaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ nāma natthī”ti, na ca vuttaṃ “akusalakammajaṃ iṭṭhaṃ nāma natthī”ti, tena [V 2.0147] akusalakammajampi sobhanaṃ parasattānaṃ iṭṭhaṃ atthīti anuññātaṃ bhavissati, kusalakammajaṃ pana sabbesaṃ iṭṭhamevāti.

Therein, there are some pleasant things, such as the forms of elephants, produced by unwholesome kamma, but they do not become a cause of happiness for those very elephants, etc. Indeed, for that very being, what is produced by wholesome kamma done by oneself is a condition for happiness; what is produced by unwholesome kamma is a condition for suffering. Therefore, the pleasantness or unpleasantness of things born of kamma should be attributed in accordance with the being who performed the kamma. Therein, it was said, 'There is nothing unpleasant born of wholesome kamma,' but it was not said, 'There is nothing pleasant born of unwholesome kamma.' Thus, it will be acknowledged that even what is born of unwholesome kamma may be beautiful and pleasant for other beings, whereas what is born of wholesome kamma is pleasant for all.

Tiracchānagatānaṃ pana kesañci manussarūpaṃ amanāpaṃ, yato te disvāva palāyanti, manussā ca devatārūpaṃ passitvā bhāyanti, tesampi vipākaviññāṇaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ ārabbha kusalavipākameva uppajjati, tādisassa pana puññassa abhāvā na tesaṃ tattha abhirati hoti. Kusalakammajassa pana aniṭṭhassa abhāvo viya akusalakammajassa ca iṭṭhassa abhāvo vattabbo. Hatthiādīnampi hi akusalakammajaṃ manussānaṃ akusalavipākasseva ārammaṇaṃ, kusalakammajaṃ pana pavatte samuṭṭhitaṃ kusalavipākassa. Iṭṭhārammaṇena pana vomissakattā appakaṃ akusalakammajaṃ bahulaṃ akusalavipākuppattiyā kāraṇaṃ na bhavissatīti sakkā viññātuṃ, vipākaṃ pana na sakkā vañcetunti vipākavasena iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇavavatthānaṃ suṭṭhu yujjati. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “aniṭṭhā pañca kāmaguṇā”ti, taṃ rūpādibhāvasāmaññato kāmaguṇasadisatāya taṃsadisesu tabbohārena vuttaṃ. Iṭṭhāneva hi rūpādīni “kāmaguṇā”ti pāḷiyaṃ (ma. ni. 1.164-165, 177-178, 287; 2.155, 280; 3.57, 190; saṃ. ni. 5.30) vuttāni. Kāmaguṇavisabhāgā vā rūpādayo “kāmaguṇā”ti vuttā asive sivoti vohāro viya, sabbāni vā iṭṭhāniṭṭhāni rūpādīni taṇhāvatthubhāvato kāmaguṇā eva. Vuttañhi “rūpā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpa”ntiādi (dī. ni. 2.400; ma. ni. 1.133). Atisayena pana kamanīyattā suttesu kāmaguṇāti iṭṭharūpādīni vuttāni.

However, for some animals, the human form is unpleasant, since they flee upon seeing it, and humans are frightened upon seeing the form of a deva. Yet, even for them, the resultant consciousness that arises in relation to that form is solely a wholesome result. However, due to the absence of such merit, they do not find delight in it. Furthermore, it should be stated that just as there is no unpleasing form born of wholesome kamma, there is also no pleasing form born of unwholesome kamma. Indeed, even in elephants and so on, that which is born of unwholesome kamma serves only as an object for the unwholesome-resultant consciousness of humans, whereas that which is born of wholesome kamma, arisen in the course of existence, serves as an object for wholesome-resultant consciousness. However, because of being mixed with a pleasing object, it can be understood that a small amount of form born of unwholesome kamma will not be the cause for the frequent arising of unwholesome results. Yet, the result itself cannot be deceived; therefore, the determination of objects as pleasing or unpleasing by way of the result is perfectly justified. As for the statement, 'The five strands of sensual pleasure are unpleasing,' that was said by applying that designation to things similar to them, on account of their general nature as form, etc., and their similarity to sensual pleasures. Indeed, in the Pāḷi, only pleasing forms and the like are called 'strands of sensual pleasure.' Alternatively, forms and other objects that are dissimilar to sensual pleasures are called 'strands of sensual pleasure' by convention, like calling an inauspicious thing auspicious. Or, all forms and the like—whether pleasing or unpleasing—are indeed strands of sensual pleasure because they are a basis for craving. For it is said, 'Forms in the world are of a pleasing nature, of a delightful nature,' and so on. However, in the discourses, pleasing forms and the like are referred to as 'strands of sensual pleasure' because they are exceptionally desirable.

Vuttanayamevāti [M 2.0158] abhidesena lakkhaṇato dūrasantikaṃ dassitanti āha “okāsatopettha upādāyupādāya dūrasantikatā veditabbā”ti. Tattha kittakato paṭṭhāya rūpaṃ okāsavasena santike nāma, kittakato pana paṭṭhāya dūre nāma? Pakatikathāya kathentānaṃ dvādasa hatthā savanūpacāro nāma, tassa orato santike, parato dūre. Tattha sukhumarūpaṃ dūre hontaṃ lakkhaṇatopi okāsatopi dūre hoti, santike hontaṃ pana okāsatova santike hoti, na lakkhaṇato. Oḷārikarūpaṃ santike hontaṃ lakkhaṇatopi okāsatopi santike hoti, dūre hontaṃ okāsatova hoti, na lakkhaṇato. “Upādāyupādāyā”ti pana vuttattā attano rūpaṃ santike nāma, antokucchigatassāpi parassa dūre. Antokucchigatassa santike, bahi ṭhitassa dūreti [V 2.0148] evaṃ antogabbhapamukhapariveṇasaṅghārāmasīmāgāmakhettajanapadarajjasamuddacakkavāḷesu tadantogatabahigatānaṃ vasena dūrasantikatā veditabbā.

Since the distinction of far and near by way of characteristic was shown by the general reference 'It is just the stated method,' he said: 'Herein, the state of being far and near should also be understood by way of location, by taking it into account again and again.' Therein, starting from what extent is materiality called 'near' by way of location? And starting from what extent is it called 'far'? For those speaking with conventional speech, twelve cubits is called the range of hearing. Within that is near; beyond it is far. Therein, subtle materiality, when it is far, is far both by way of characteristic and by way of location. But when it is near, it is near only by way of location, not by way of characteristic. Coarse materiality, when it is near, is near both by way of characteristic and by way of location; when it is far, it is far only by way of location, not by way of characteristic. Furthermore, since it is said 'by taking into account again and again,' one's own materiality is called near; that of another, even if within one's womb, is far. For one within the womb, it is near; for one standing outside, it is far. In this way, the state of being far and near should be understood by way of what is internal and external to an inner chamber, the front of a monastery, a surrounding compound, a monastic residence, a boundary, a village-field, a country, a kingdom, an ocean, and a world-sphere.

497. Tadekajjhanti taṃ ekajjhaṃ ekato. Abhisaṃyūhitvāti saṃharitvā, samūhaṃ vā katvā. Abhisaṅkhipitvāti saṅkhipitvā saṅkhepaṃ katvā. “Sabbampi rūpaṃ…pe… dassitaṃ hotī”ti iminā rūpakhandhasaddānaṃ samānādhikaraṇasamāsabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tenevāha “na hi rūpato añño rūpakkhandho nāma atthī”ti.

497. “Tadekajjhaṃ” (as one whole) means that [materiality] as one whole, together. “Abhisaṃyūhitvā” (having heaped together) means having collected, or having made a group. “Abhisaṅkhipitvā” (having summarized) means having abbreviated, having made a summary. By this [phrase], “All materiality... is shown,” he shows the state of the words “rūpa” and “khandha” being a kammadhāraya compound with a common referent. For that very reason, he said: “For there is indeed no so-called materiality-aggregate other than materiality.”

498. Rāsibhāvūpagamanena vedanākkhandhādayoti dassitā hontīti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ.

498. It should be connected by supplying [the phrase]: “The feeling-aggregate and so on are shown [to be so called] by way of reaching the state of a heap.”

Santativasena, khaṇādivasena cāti ettha addhāsamayavasena atītādivibhāgassa avacanaṃ sukhādivasena bhinnāya atītādibhāvavacanato. Na hi sukhā eva addhāvasena, samayavasena ca atītādikā hoti, tathā dukkhā eva, adukkhamasukhā eva ca kāyikacetasikādibhāvena bhinnā, tena vedanāsamudāyo addhāsamayavasena atītādibhāvena vattabbataṃ arahati samudāyassa tehi paricchinditabbattā, vedanekadesā pana gayhamānā santatikhaṇehi paricchedaṃ arahanti tathā paricchinditvā gahetabbato. Ekasantatiyaṃ pana sukhādīsu anekabhedabhinnesu yo bhedo paricchinditabbabhāvena gahito, tassa ekappakārassa [M 2.0159] pākaṭassa paricchedikā taṃsahitadvārālambanappavattā, avicchedena taduppādakekavidhavisayasamāyogappavattā ca santati bhavituṃ arahatīti tassā bhedantaraṃ anāmasitvā paricchedakabhāvena gahaṇaṃ kataṃ, lahuparivattino vā arūpadhammā parivattaneneva paricchedena paricchindanaṃ arahantīti santatikhaṇavaseneva paricchedo vutto. Ekavidhavisayasamāyogappavattā divasampi buddharūpaṃ passantassa, dhammaṃ suṇantassa pavattasaddhādisahitavedanā paccuppannā. “Pubbantāparantamajjhattagatā”ti etena hetupaccayakiccavasena vuttanayaṃ dasseti.

Here, regarding “by way of continuity and by way of moments, etc.,” the non-mention of the division into past, etc., by way of duration or time is due to the mention of the state of being past, etc., with respect to feeling that is divided by way of pleasant, etc. For indeed, it is not that only pleasant feeling is past, etc., by way of duration or time; similarly, it is not that only painful feeling or only neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, which are divided by way of being bodily, mental, etc., are past, etc. Therefore, the collection of feeling deserves to be spoken of as past, etc., by way of duration and time, because the collection is to be delineated by those. However, when portions of feeling are taken, they deserve delineation by continuity and moments, because they are to be grasped after having been so delineated. Furthermore, in a single continuity, among pleasant feelings, etc., which are divided by numerous distinctions, whatever distinction is taken as that which is to be delineated, the continuity that occurs in connection with the door and object together with that distinction, and occurs without interruption through association with a single kind of object that produces it, is able to be a delineator of that single, manifest type. Thus, without considering its other distinctions, it is taken solely as a delineator. Or, since immaterial phenomena have swift alteration, they deserve to be delineated by the very alteration. Thus, the delineation is spoken of only by way of continuity and moments. For one who sees the Buddha’s form or hears the Dhamma even for a whole day, the feeling, accompanied by faith, etc., that occurs through association with a single kind of object is present. By “gone to the past, future, or present,” this indicates the method already stated by way of the function of cause and condition.

499. Sabyāpārasaussāhasavipākatā kusalādīhi tīhipi sādhāraṇāti asādhāraṇameva dassetuṃ “sāvajjakiriyahetuto”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sāvajjakiriyahetutoti pāṇātipātādigārayhakiriyānimittato. Kilesasantāpabhāvatoti kilesapariḷāhena sadarathabhāvato[V 2.0149]. Vūpasantasabhāvāya kusalāya vedanāya oḷārikā. Sabyāpāratoti saīhato. Tena yathā pavattamānāyassā vipākena bhavitabbaṃ, tathā pavattiṃ vadanto vipākuppādanayogyatamāha. Saussāhatoti sasattito, tena vipākuppādanasamatthataṃ. Savipākatoti vipākasabbhāvato, tena paccayantarasamavāyenassā vipākanibbattanaṃ. Tīhipi padehi vipākadhammataṃyeva dasseti. Kāyakammādibyāpārasabbhāvato vā sabyāpārato, javanussāhavasena saussāhato, vipākuppādanasamatthatāvasena savipākatoti evamettha attho veditabbo. Vipākaṃ anuppādentīpi kiriyā kusalā viya sabyāpārā, saussāhā eva ca hotīti tadubhayaṃ anāmasitvā kiriyābyākatavāre “savipākato” icceva vuttaṃ. Sabyābajjhatoti kilesadukkhena sadukkhato. Vuttavipariyāyatoti anavajjakiriyahetuto, kilesasantāpābhāvato, abyābajjhato ca vūpasantavuttīti evaṃ akusalāya vuttavipallāsato. Yathāyoganti yogānurūpaṃ. Tīsu kāraṇesu yaṃ yaṃ yassā yassā yujjati, tadanurūpanti attho. Kusalākusalavedanāhi vipākabyākatāya tīhipi kāraṇehi oḷārikā. Kiriyābyākatāya savipākato savipākatāvisiṭṭhasabyāpārasaussāhato vāti. Vuttapariyāyenāti vipākabyākatā abyāpārato[M 2.0160], anussāhato, avipākato ca tāhi kusalākusalavedanāhi sukhumā. Kiriyābyākatā avipākato, avipākatāvisiṭṭhasabyāpārasaussāhato vāti evaṃ kusalākusalāya vuttavipallāsena. Kammavegakkhittā hi kammapaṭibimbabhūtā ca kāyakammādibyāpāravirahato nirussāhā vipākā. Saussāhā ca kiriyā avipākadhammā. Savipākadhammā hi sagabbhā viya oḷārikāti.

499. Because the state of having exertion, effort, and result is common to all three beginning with wholesome, in order to show what is uncommon, the passage beginning with “sāvajjakiriyahetuto” was stated. Therein, “sāvajjakiriyahetuto” means because of being the cause of blameworthy actions beginning with the destruction of life. “Kilesasantāpabhāvato” means because of being in a state of distress through the burning of defilements. It is grosser than wholesome feeling, which has a peaceful nature. “Sabyāpārato” means because of being with exertion. By that term, in stating its occurrence in such a way that there must be a result for it as it occurs, he states its suitability for producing a result. “Saussāhato” means because of being with energy; by that, he states its capability to produce a result. “Savipākato” means because of the existence of a result; by that, he states the production of its result through the concurrence of other conditions. By all three terms, he shows precisely the nature of producing a result. Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood thus: `sabyāpārato` is due to the existence of exertion in bodily action and so on; `saussāhato` is by the power of the exertion of impulsion; and `savipākato` is by the power of the capability to produce a result. Although functional feeling does not produce a result, like wholesome feeling, it is indeed with exertion and with effort. Therefore, without touching upon both of these, in the section on functional-indeterminate, only “avipākato” was stated. “Sabyābajjhato” means because of being with affliction, through the suffering of defilements. “Vuttavipariyāyato” means by way of the reverse of what was said for the unwholesome: because it is a cause of blameless action, because of the absence of the affliction of defilements, and because of the absence of affliction, it has a peaceful occurrence. “Yathāyogaṃ” means according to what is suitable. The meaning is: in accordance with whichever of the three causes is suitable for whichever feeling. Indeed, wholesome and unwholesome feelings are grosser than resultant-indeterminate feeling due to all three causes. They are grosser than functional-indeterminate feeling because of having a result, or because of having exertion and effort distinguished by the state of having a result. “Vuttapariyāyena” means by the stated method: resultant-indeterminate feeling, because of being without exertion, without effort, and without result, is more subtle than those wholesome and unwholesome feelings. Functional-indeterminate feeling is more subtle because of being without result, or because of having exertion and effort distinguished by the state of being without result. Thus, it is the reverse of what was said for wholesome and unwholesome. Indeed, results, being flung by the force of kamma and being a reflection of kamma, are without effort due to the absence of exertion in bodily action and so on. And functional feeling, though with effort, does not have the nature of producing a result. Indeed, phenomena that have the nature of producing a result are gross, like a pregnant woman.

500. Nirassādatoti assādābhāvato sukhapaṭikkhepato. Savipphāratoti saparipphandato, anupasantatoti attho. Abhibhavanatoti ajjhottharaṇato. Sukhāya majjhattatā natthi, upekkhāya sātatā. Santatādayo pana sabbattha sukhupekkhāsu labbhantīti “yathāyoga”nti vuttaṃ. Pākaṭatoti sukhito dukkhitoti disvāpi jānitabbattā vibhūtabhāvato. Sā adukkhamasukhā vedanā.

500. “Without enjoyment” (nirassādata) means due to the absence of enjoyment, due to the rejection of pleasure. “Agitated” (savipphāra) means due to its trembling, meaning it is unpacified. “Overwhelming” (abhibhavana) means due to its overpowering. For pleasure, there is no neutrality; for equanimity, there is no pleasantness. However, peacefulness and so forth are found in all pleasant and equanimous feelings, hence it is said “as appropriate” (yathāyoga). “Manifest” (pākaṭa) means due to its being knowable even by seeing “one is happy” or “one is suffering,” thus due to its evident nature. That is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

501. Asamāpannasamāpanna-ggahaṇena cettha bhūmivasenāpi vedanānaṃ oḷārikasukhumatā vuttāti veditabbā. Itarā samāpannassa vedanā.

501. Here, by the inclusion of “one not in attainment” (asamāpanna) and “one in attainment” (samāpanna), the grossness and subtlety of feelings are also stated according to the plane; thus it should be understood. The other is the feeling of one who has attained absorption.

Oghaniyatoti [V 2.0150] oghehi ārammaṇaṃ katvā atikkamitabbato. Tathā yoganiyato, ganthaniyato cāti etthāpi ganthova ganthanaṃ, tassa hitaṃ ārammaṇabhāvena sambandhanatoti ganthaniyaṃ. Evaṃ nīvaraṇiyaṃ, upādāniyañca veditabbaṃ. Saṃkilese niyuttā, saṃkilesaṃ vā arahantīti saṃkilesikā. Sā anāsavā.

“Pertaining to the floods” (oghaniya) means because it is to be overcome, having made the floods an object. Similarly for “pertaining to the yokes” (yoganiya). As for “pertaining to the bonds” (ganthaniya), here too, the bond (gantha) itself is the binding (ganthana); it is called “pertaining to the bonds” (ganthaniya) because it is connected by way of being an object and is beneficial (hita) for that bond. In the same way, “pertaining to the hindrances” (nīvaraṇiya) and “pertaining to clinging” (upādāniya) should be understood. “Connected with defilements” (saṃkilesika) means they are engaged in defilements, or they are worthy of defilements. That is the taint-free feeling.

502. Tatthāti yathāvuttāya oḷārikasukhumatāya. Sambhedoti saṅkaro. “Oḷārikā, sukhumā”ti ca vuttānampi jātiādivasena puna sukhumoḷārikabhāvāpattidoso yathā na hoti, tathā pariharitabbo. Jātivasena sukhumāya vedanāya sabhāvapuggalalokiyavasena oḷārikataṃ pāḷivasena dassetuṃ “vuttañheta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sukhādayopīti ettha akusalā vedanā jātivasena oḷārikā, sabhāvavasena sukhumā. Kusalajjhānasahagatā sukhā vedanā jātivasena oḷārikā, samāpannassa vedanāti katvā puggalavasena sukhumāti evamādinā yojetabbā. “Na parāmasitabbo”ti etena jātiādayo [M 2.0161] cattāro koṭṭhāsā aññamaññaṃ avomissakā eva gahetabbā. Evaṃ sambhedassa parihāro, na aññathāti dasseti. Yathā abyākatamukhena, evaṃ kusalākusalamukhenapi, yathā ca jātimukhena, evaṃ sabhāvādimukhenapi dassetabbanti imamatthaṃ “esa nayo sabbatthā”ti atidisati.

502. `Therein` (tattha) refers to the grossness and subtlety as stated. `Mixture` (sambheda) means mixing (saṅkaro). The fault of again attaining the state of being subtle and gross, by way of birth and so on, for those feelings already stated as ‘gross’ and ‘subtle’, should be avoided so that it does not occur. To show, in accordance with the Pāḷi, the grossness by way of nature, person, and the worldly, of a feeling that is subtle by way of birth, it is said, ‘For this has been stated’ (vuttañhetaṃ), and so on. Herein, regarding ‘Thus, pleasant feelings and so on’ (Evaṃ sukhādayopīti): unwholesome feelings are gross by way of birth, but subtle by way of nature. The pleasant feeling associated with wholesome jhāna is gross by way of birth, but subtle by way of the person, it being considered ‘the feeling of one who has attained’; it should be connected in this way and so on. By ‘It should not be conflated’ (na parāmasitabbo), it is shown that the four divisions—birth and so on—should be taken as mutually unmixed. This shows how mixing is avoided, and not otherwise.
