He applies this meaning by extension with the phrase, ‘This is the method everywhere’ (esa nayo sabbattha): just as it is shown by way of the indeterminate, so too should it be shown by way of the wholesome and unwholesome; and just as it is shown by way of birth, so too should it be shown by way of nature and so on.

Idāni jātiādikoṭṭhāsesupi mitho akusalādīnaṃ upādāyupādāya oḷārikasukhumataṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. “Nissayadahanato”ti iminā dosasahagatāya pākaṭaṃ kurūrappavattiṃ dasseti. Niyatāti micchattaniyāmena niyatā, ānantariyabhāvappattā kappatiṭṭhanakavipākatāya kappaṭṭhitikā devadattādīnaṃ viya. Asaṅkhārikā sabhāvatikhiṇatāya oḷārikā. Diṭṭhisampayuttā mahāsāvajjatāya oḷārikā. Sāpi diṭṭhisampayuttā niyatā oḷārikā, tato kappaṭṭhitikā, tato asaṅkhārikāti tividhāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayattā ekajjhaṃ vuttā visuṃ visuṃyeva yojetabbā. Tenāha “itarā sukhumā”ti. Avisesenāti dosasahagatā, lobhasahagatāti abhedena. Akusalā bahuvipākā dosussannatāya oḷārikā. Tathā kusalā appavipākā. Mandadosattā akusalā appavipākā sukhumā. Tathā kusalā bahuvipākā.

Now, in order to show the state of being gross and subtle among the unwholesome feelings and so forth by comparing them with one another, also within the sections beginning with birth, the passage beginning with 'apica' is commenced. By this text, 'nissayadahanato' (from the burning of the support), it shows the manifest cruel occurrence of the feeling associated with hatred. As for 'niyatā' (fixed): it is a feeling fixed by the fixed course of wrongness. Or, having reached the state of an immediately effective karma, it is 'kappaṭṭhitikā' (aeon-lasting) due to its result lasting for an aeon, like that of Devadatta and others. The unprompted feeling is gross due to its inherent sharpness. The feeling associated with wrong view is gross due to its great blameworthiness. That feeling associated with wrong view, when it is fixed, is also gross. Grosser than that is the aeon-lasting feeling; grosser than that is the unprompted feeling. Thus, although these three types are stated together, due to the method stated previously, they should be applied only individually. Therefore, it is said, ‘the others are subtle’ (itarā sukhumā). As for 'avisesena' (without distinction): it means without differentiating between the feeling associated with hatred and the feeling associated with greed. An unwholesome feeling, when it has much result, is gross due to the predominance of fault. Similarly, a wholesome feeling, when it has little result, [is gross]. Due to having little fault, an unwholesome feeling that has little result is subtle. Similarly, a wholesome feeling, when it has much result, [is subtle].

Oḷārikasukhumanikantivatthubhāvato kāmāvacarādīnaṃ oḷārikasukhumatā, lokuttarā pana ekantasukhumāva. Tatthāpi ca vibhāgaṃ parato vakkhati. Bhāvanāmayāpīti bhāvanāmayāya bhedanena [V 2.0151] dānasīlamayānampi bhedanaṃ nayato dassitanti veditabbaṃ. Bhāvanāya paguṇabalavakālādīsu kadāci ñāṇavippayuttacittenapi manasikāro hotīti vuttaṃ “bhāvanāmayāpi duhetukā”ti. Taṃtaṃbhūmivipākakiriyāvedanāsūti ettha “kāmāvacaravipākā oḷārikā, rūpāvacarā sukhumā”tiādinā yāva arahattaphalā netabbaṃ. “Kāmāvacarakiriyā oḷārikā, rūpāvacarakiriyā sukhumā”tiādinā kāmāvacarā ca “dānākārappavattā oḷārikā, sīlākārappavattā sukhumā”tiādinā yāva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanā netabbaṃ. Yathā ca jātikoṭṭhāse ayaṃ vibhāgo, evaṃ sabhāvakoṭṭhāsādīsupīti dassetuṃ “dukkhādī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

The grossness and subtlety of sense-sphere feelings and so on is due to their being the basis for gross and subtle craving. Supramundane feeling, however, is exclusively subtle. And even therein, a distinction will be stated later. By 'even that consisting of mental development' (bhāvanāmayāpi), it should be understood that by distinguishing that which consists of mental development, a distinction is also shown by implication for that which consists of generosity and morality. During mental development, at times of proficiency, strength, and so on, attention sometimes occurs even with a mind dissociated from knowledge; hence it is said, ‘even that consisting of mental development may be two-rooted’ (bhāvanāmayāpi duhetukā). Here, in the phrase 'in the resultant and functional feelings of the various planes' (taṃtaṃbhūmivipākakiriyāvedanāsu), it should be extended by way of 'the resultant feelings of the sense-sphere are gross, those of the form-sphere are subtle,' and so on, up to the fruition of Arahantship. By way of 'the functional feelings of the sense-sphere are gross, those of the form-sphere are subtle,' and so on, and for sense-sphere feeling, by way of 'feeling that occurs in the mode of generosity is gross, feeling that occurs in the mode of morality is subtle,' and so on, it should be extended up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. And just as this distinction is applied in the section on class, so too in the sections on intrinsic nature and so forth—to show this, ‘suffering, etc.’ (dukkhādi) is stated.

Sabbo [M 2.0162] cāyaṃ vibhāgo lakkhaṇasannissito vuttoti katvā āha “okāsavasena cāpī”tiādi. Sukhāpīti pi-saddena adukkhamasukhaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Sabbatthāti sabbāsu bhūmīsu. Yathānurūpanti yā yā vedanā yattha yattha labbhati, tadanurūpaṃ. Vatthuvasenāti yaṃ vatthuṃ ārabbha vedanā pavattati, tassa vasenāpi. Hīnavatthukāti hīnaṃ vatthuṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā kaṅgubhattaṃ bhuñjantassa vedanā hīnavatthukatāya oḷārikā. Sālimaṃsodanaṃ bhuñjantassa paṇītavatthukatāya sukhumāti.

Having considered that all this distinction is stated as being based on characteristics, he said, ‘and also by way of occasion’ (okāsavasena cāpi), etc. In 'pleasure too' (sukhāpi), the particle ‘pi’ includes the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. ‘In all’ (sabbattha) means in all planes. ‘As is suitable’ (yathānurūpaṃ) means: in accordance with whichever feeling is obtainable in whichever plane. ‘By way of the object’ (vatthuvasena) means: also by the power of the object which feeling takes as its support when it arises. ‘Having an inferior object’ (hīnavatthukā) means: the feeling of one eating millet rice, having taken an inferior thing as its sense-object, is gross due to its having an inferior object. The feeling of one eating fine Sāli rice with meat is subtle due to its having a superior object.

503. Ādinā nayenāti sabbaṃ pāḷigatiṃ āmasati. Jātiādivasena asamānakoṭṭhāsatā visabhāgatā. Dukkhavipākatādivasena asadisakiccatā asaṃsaṭṭhatā, na asampayogo. Yadi siyā, dūravipariyāyena santikaṃ hotīti saṃsaṭṭhatā santikatā āpajjati, na ca vedanāya vedanāsampayogo atthi. Santikapadavaṇṇanāya ca “sabhāgato ca sarikkhato cā”ti vakkhatīti vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Asadisasabhāvatā asarikkhatā. Sabbavāresūti oḷārikasukhumabhede vuttanayānusārena vattabbesu sabbesu vāresu. Jātiādivasena samānakoṭṭhāsatā sabhāgatā, dukkhavipākatādivasena pana sadisasabhāvatā sarikkhatā. Tenāha “akusalā pana…pe… santike”ti.

503. `Ādinā nayena` (by the method beginning with) touches upon the entire course of the Pāḷi. `Visabhāgatā` (dissimilarity) is the state of having dissimilar portions by way of birth and so forth. `Asaṃsaṭṭhatā` (unmixedness) is the state of having a dissimilar function by way of having painful results and so forth; it is not `asampayoga` (non-association). If it were so, then by the reverse of 'distant,' it would be 'proximate'; thus, `saṃsaṭṭhatā` (mixedness) would become `santikatā` (proximity). And there is no association of feeling with feeling. Furthermore, in the explanation of the term `santika` (proximate), it will be said, 'of the same class and alike' (`sabhāgato ca sarikkhato ca`); therefore, the meaning should be understood only by the method already stated. `Asarikkhatā` (unlikeness) is the state of having a dissimilar nature. `Sabbavāresūti` (in all instances) means in all instances that are to be stated in accordance with the method already explained in the distinction of gross and subtle. `Sabhāgatā` (similarity) is the state of having a similar portion by way of birth and so forth; but `sarikkhatā` (alikeness) is the state of having a similar nature by way of having painful results and so forth. Therefore, he said, 'But unwholesome... etc... are near' (`akusalā pana…pe… santike`).

Iti vedanākkhandhassa atītādivibhāge vitthārakathāmukhavaṇṇanā.

Thus is the explanation of the introduction to the detailed discourse on the division of the feeling aggregate into past and so forth.

Kamādivinicchayakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Determination of Order and So Forth

504. Etanti [V 2.0152] evaṃ atītādivibhāge vitthārakathāmukhaṃ. Ñāṇabhedatthanti nānappakāraṃ ñāṇappabhedatthaṃ. Kamatoti desanākkamato, yena kāraṇenāyaṃ desanākkamo kato, tatoti attho. Visesatoti bhedato, khandhupādānakkhandhavibhāgatoti attho. Anūnādhikatoti pañcabhāvato. Upamātoti upamāhi upametabbato. Daṭṭhabbato dvidhāti dvīhi ākārehi ñāṇena passitabbato. Passantassatthasiddhitoti [M 2.0163] yathā passantassa yathādhippetatthanipphattito. Vibhāvināti paññavatā.

504. `Etaṃ` (This) means: thus, the introduction to the detailed discourse on the division into past and so forth. `Ñāṇabhedatthaṃ` (For the sake of the distinction of knowledge) means for the sake of the distinction of various kinds of knowledge. `Kamato` (By order) means: by the sequence of the teaching, or by the reason for which this sequence of the teaching was made; that is the meaning. `Visesato` (By distinction) means: by way of difference, that is, by the division of the aggregates and the aggregates subject to clinging. `Anūnādhikato` (Not deficient or excessive) means: by way of being fivefold. `Upamāto` (By simile) means: by way of being comparable with similes. `Daṭṭhabbato dvidhā` (To be seen in two ways) means: by way of being seen by knowledge in two aspects. `Passantassatthasiddhito` (For the accomplishment of the goal for one who sees) means: by way of the accomplishment of the desired goal for one who sees thus. `Vibhāvinā` (By the discerning) means: by one who is wise.

Uppattikkamoti yathāpaccayaṃ uppajjantānaṃ uppajjanapaṭipāṭi. “Dassanenapahātabbā”tiādinā (dha. sa. tikamātikā 8, 9) paṭhamaṃ pahātabbā paṭhamaṃ vuttā, dutiyaṃ pahātabbā dutiyaṃ vuttāti ayaṃ pahānakkamo. Sīlavisuddhiṃ paṭipajja cittavisuddhi paṭipajjitabbā, tathā tato parāpīti āha “sīlavisuddhi…pe… paṭipattikkamo”ti, anupubbapaṇītā bhūmiyo anupubbena vavatthitāti ayaṃ bhūmikkamo. “Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”tiādiko (vibha. 355) ekakkhaṇepi satipaṭṭhānādisambhavato desanākkamo ca. Dānakathādayo anupubbukkaṃsato kathitā, uppattiādivavatthānābhāvato pana dānādīnaṃ idha desanākkamavacanaṃ. Uppattiādivavatthānahetukatāya hi “paṭhamaṃ kalalaṃ hotī”tiādikā (saṃ. ni. 1.235; kathā. 692) desanāpi samānā uppattiādikamabhāveneva vuttā. Yathāvuttavavatthānābhāvena pana anekesaṃ vacanānaṃ sahapavattiyā asambhavato yena kenaci pubbāpariyena desetabbatāya tena tena adhippāyena desanāmattasseva kamo desanākkamo daṭṭhabbo. Pubbāpariyavavatthānenāti paṭhamaṃ rūpakkhandho, tato vedanākkhandhoti evaṃ pubbāpariyavavatthānena anuppattito. Appahātabbatoti khandhesu ekaccānaṃ pahātabbatāva natthi, kuto pahānakkamo. Sati hi sabbesaṃ pahātabbatāya pahānakkamena nesaṃ desanā siyā. Appaṭipajjanīyatoti sammāpaṭipattivasena na paṭipajjitabbato. “Catubhūmipariyāpannattā”ti iminā vedanādīnaṃ aniyatabhūmikataṃ dasseti. Niyatabhūmikānañhi bhūmikkamo sambhaveyya.

The order of arising (uppattikkama) is the sequence of arising for things that arise according to their conditions. By 'to be abandoned by seeing,' and so forth (Dhs. Tikamātikā 8, 9), what is to be abandoned first is stated first, and what is to be abandoned second is stated second; this is the order of abandonment. Having practiced purification of virtue, one should practice purification of mind, and so on; thus it is said, 'purification of virtue... and so forth... the order of practice.' The successively refined planes are established in sequence; this is the order of planes. And 'the four foundations of mindfulness,' and so forth (Vbh. 355), is an order of teaching, since the foundations of mindfulness and so forth can occur even in a single moment. Discussions on generosity, and so forth, are taught in an ascending order of excellence, but since there is no fixed arrangement of arising and so forth, the term 'order of teaching' is used for generosity and the like here. Indeed, because they are caused by the determination of arising and so forth, even teachings such as 'first there is the kalala,' and so forth (SN 1.235; Kathāvatthu 692), though similar, are spoken of precisely in terms of the order of arising and so forth. However, due to the absence of the aforementioned fixed arrangement, because it is impossible for many statements to occur simultaneously, and because they must be taught in some sequence of before and after, the order of teaching should be understood as merely the sequence of the teaching itself, according to this or that intention. By 'the determination of before and after' is meant: because they do not arise by a determination of before and after, such as 'first the aggregate of form, then the aggregate of feeling.' By 'not to be abandoned' is meant: for some of the aggregates, there is no state of 'to be abandoned' at all; whence could there be an order of abandonment? Indeed, if there were a state of 'to be abandoned' for all of them, there could be a teaching about them with an order of abandonment. By 'not to be practiced' is meant: because they are not to be practiced by way of right practice. By 'because they are included in the four planes,' this indicates the state of not having a fixed plane for feeling and so forth. Indeed, for those that have a fixed plane, an order of planes would be possible.

Abhedenāti rūpādīnaṃ bhedaṃ vibhāgaṃ akatvā ekajjhaṃ piṇḍaggahaṇena. Attagāhapatitanti attagāhasaṅkhāte diṭṭhoghe nipatitaṃ. Samūhaghanavinibbhogadassanenāti rūpato arūpaṃ vivecento rūpārūpasamūhe [V 2.0153] ghanavinibbhujjanadassanena. Cakkhuādīnampi visayabhūtanti ekadesena samudāyabhūtaṃ rūpakkhandhaṃ vadati. Yā ettha iṭṭhaṃ, aniṭṭhañca rūpaṃ saṃvedeti, ayaṃ vedanākkhandhoti iṭṭhāniṭṭharūpasaṃvedanikaṃ vedanaṃ desesīti sambandho. Evaṃ sabbattha. Iṭṭhamajjhattaaniṭṭhamajjhattānampi iṭṭhāniṭṭhasabhāvattā iṭṭhāniṭṭhaggahaṇeneva gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evanti yathāvuttanayena. Saññāya gahitākāre [M 2.0164] visaye abhisaṅkhārappavattīti āha “saññāvasena abhisaṅkhārake”ti. Yathā viññāṇassa sampayuttadhammānaṃ nissayabhāvo pākaṭo, na tathā vedanādīnanti āha “vedanādīnaṃ nissaya”nti. “Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā (dha. pa. 1-2), cittānuparivattino dhammā (dha. sa. dukamātikā 62), chadvārādhipati rājā”ti (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 2.181 erakapatthanāgarājavatthu) vacanato viññāṇaṃ adhipati.

By 'without division' is meant: by taking form, etc., as a single mass, without making a distinction or a separation. By 'fallen into the grasp of self' is meant: fallen into the flood of views called 'grasping at self.' By 'seeing the breaking apart of the compact mass' is meant: by seeing the breaking apart of the compactness in the mass of form and mentality, while distinguishing the formless from form. By the phrase 'being the object of the eye, etc.,' He speaks of the form aggregate, which is a collection, by way of a part. 'Whatever feeling here experiences a form that is pleasant and unpleasant, this is the feeling aggregate'—thus, the connection is that He taught feeling as that which experiences pleasant and unpleasant form. So it is in all cases. Even pleasant-neutral and unpleasant-neutral should be understood as included by the mention of pleasant and unpleasant, since they have the nature of pleasant and unpleasant. 'Thus' means: in the way explained. Because the occurrence of formations is in an object whose aspect has been grasped by perception, it was said, 'formations dependent on perception.' Just as the supporting nature of consciousness for its associated states is evident, it is not so for feeling, etc.; hence, it was said, 'the support for feeling, etc.' Because it is said: 'Mental phenomena are preceded by mind' (Dhp. 1–2), 'mental phenomena follow the mind' (Dhs. Dukamātikā 62), and 'the king, the lord of the six doors' (cf. Dhp-a. III. 226), consciousness is the dominant factor.

505. Rūpakkhandhe “sāsavaṃ upādāniya”nti vacanaṃ anāsavānaṃ dhammānaṃ sabbhāvato rūpakkhandhassa taṃsabhāvatānivattanatthaṃ, na anāsavarūpanivattanatthaṃ.

505. In regard to the form aggregate, the statement 'with taints and subject to clinging' is for the purpose of precluding that [taintless] nature for the form aggregate—due to the existence of taintless phenomena—and not for the purpose of precluding taintless form.

Anāsavāva khandhesu vuttāti ettha aṭṭhānappayutto eva-saddo, anāsavā khandhesveva vuttāti attho. Idha pana visuddhimagge sabbepete khandhāpi upādānakkhandhāpi.

In the phrase 'The taintless alone are spoken of in the aggregates' (Anāsavāva khandhesu vuttā), the particle 'eva' ('alone') is used in the wrong place; the meaning is, 'The taintless are spoken of only in the context of the aggregates' (anāsavā khandhesveva vuttā). Here in the Visuddhimagga, however, all these are both aggregates and also aggregates subject to clinging.

506. Sabbasaṅkhatānaṃ sabhāgena ekajjhaṃ saṅgaho sabbasaṅkhatasabhāgekasaṅgaho. Sabhāgasabhāvena hi saṅgayhamānā sabbasaṅkhatā pañcakkhandhā honti. Tattha ruppanādisāmaññena samānakoṭṭhāsā sabhāgāti veditabbā. Tesu saṅkhatābhisaṅkharaṇakiccaṃ āyūhanarasāya cetanāya balavanti sā “saṅkhārakkhandho”ti vuttā. Aññe ca ruppanādivisesalakkhaṇarahitā phassādayo saṅkhatābhisaṅkharaṇasāmaññenāti daṭṭhabbā, phusanādayo pana sabhāvā visuṃ khandhasaddavacanīyā na hontīti dhammasabhāvaññunā tathāgatena phassakkhandhādayo na vuttāti veditabbā. “Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā sassatavādā sassataṃ attānañca lokañca paññapenti, sabbe te ime eva pañcupādānakkhandhe nissāya paṭicca, etesaṃ vā aññatara”nti evamādisuttānañca vasena attattaniyagāhassa etapparamatā daṭṭhabbā. Etena ca vakkhamānasuttavasena ca khandhe eva nissāya parittārammaṇādivasena na vattabbā ca diṭṭhi uppajjati khandhanibbānavajjassa sabhāvadhammassa abhāvatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Rūpanti ruppanasabhāvaṃ dhammajātamāha. Vedanantiādīsupi eseva nayo. “Sīlakkhandho samādhikkhandho”tiādi (dī. ni. 3.355) vacanato [V 2.0154] aññesañca khandhasaddavacanīyānaṃ [M 2.0165] sīlakkhandhādīnaṃ sabbhāvato na pañcevāti codanaṃ nivattetumāha “aññesaṃ tadavarodhato”ti.

506. The grouping of all conditioned things together by a common part is the 'grouping-of-all-conditioned-things-by-a-common-part.' For, when grouped by the nature of a common part, all conditioned things become the five aggregates. Herein, those with a shared portion by way of the commonality of 'being afflicted,' and so forth, are to be understood as having a common part. Among them, the function of conditioning conditioned things is predominant for volition, which has the function of striving; therefore, that volition is called the 'aggregate of formations.' And it should be understood that other mental states, such as contact, which are devoid of specific characteristics like 'being afflicted,' are included by the commonality of conditioning conditioned things. However, natures such as contact are not separately designated by the word 'aggregate'; therefore, it should be known that the Tathāgata, who knows the nature of phenomena, did not speak of an 'aggregate of contact,' and so forth. Furthermore, by way of suttas such as, 'Bhikkhus, whatever recluses or brahmins who are eternalists proclaim an eternal self and world, all of them do so relying on and dependent on these very five aggregates of clinging, or one of them,' it should be seen that the grasping of 'self' and 'what belongs to self' has these aggregates as its limit. And by this sutta and by way of the sutta to be mentioned later, it is said that a view, which is not classifiable by way of having a sensual-sphere object and so forth, arises relying only on the aggregates, because of the absence of any real phenomenon apart from the aggregates and Nibbāna. 'Form' refers to the class of phenomena that has the nature of being afflicted. The same method applies to 'feeling,' and so forth. To refute the objection that 'there are not only five'—an objection arising because of statements such as 'the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration,' and because of the existence of other things designated by the word 'aggregate,' such as the aggregate of virtue—it was said, 'because of the inclusion of others in that.'

507. Pavattiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ viya hotīti vuttaṃ “nivāsaṭṭhānato”ti. Dukkhadukkhavipariṇāmadukkhasaṅkhāradukkhatāvasena vedanāya ābādhakattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Rāgādisampayuttassa vipariṇāmādidukkhassa itthipurisādiākāragāhikā taṃtaṃsaṅkappamūlabhūtā saññā samuṭṭhānaṃ. Pittādi viya rogassa āsannakāraṇaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ. Utubhojanavisamatāvisamaparihārādi viya mūlakāraṇaṃ nidānaṃ. Cittassa aṅgabhūtā cetasikāti viññāṇaṃ gilānūpamaṃ vuttaṃ. Kuṭṭharogavato siniyhanaṃ tassa bhiyyobhāvāya viya bālassa puññābhisaṅkhārādivasena pavatti vedanādukkhāvahā asappāyasevanasadisī. Vedanattāyāti vedanāsabhāvatthaṃ, vedanattalābhāyāti attho. Kāraṇaṭṭhānatāya, bhojanādhāratāya ca cārakūpamaṃ, bhājanūpamañca rūpaṃ. Subhasaññādivasena vedanākāraṇassa hetubhāvato, vedanābhojanassa chādāpanato ca aparādhūpamā, byañjanūpamā ca saññā. Vedanāhetuto kāraṇakārakūpamo, parivesakūpamo ca saṅkhārakkhandho. Bhattakāro eva yebhuyyena parivisatīti parivesakaggahaṇaṃ. Vedanāya vibādhitabbato, anuggahetabbato ca aparādhikūpamaṃ, bhuñjakūpamañca viññāṇaṃ vuttaṃ.

507. Because it is the place of occurrence, it is like a dwelling place; therefore, it is said 'by reason of being an abode'. The affliction of feeling should be seen by way of suffering as suffering, suffering due to change, and suffering due to formations. Perception, which grasps the aspects of female, male, and so on, and which is the root cause of this or that thought, is the origin of suffering due to change, and so on, associated with lust, and so on. Like bile and so on, the proximate cause of disease is called the origin (samuṭṭhāna). Like the imbalance of climate and food, imbalanced posture, and so on, the root cause is called the source (nidāna). Because mental factors are constituent parts of the mind, consciousness is said to be like a sick person. Just as for one with leprosy, anointing is for its increase, so for the foolish person, existence by way of meritorious formations and so on, bringing the suffering of feeling, is like partaking of what is unsuitable. 'For the state of feeling' (vedanattāya) means for the sake of the nature of feeling, or for obtaining the state of feeling; this is the meaning. Form is said to be like a prison and like a bowl, because it is the place of affliction and because it is the container of food. Perception is said to be like a crime and like a curry, because, by way of the perception of beauty and so on, it is the cause of the affliction that is feeling, and because it makes the food of feeling palatable. The aggregate of formations is said to be like one who inflicts affliction and like a server, because it is a cause of feeling. For the most part, it is the cook who serves; therefore, the term 'server' is used. Consciousness is said to be like a criminal and like an eater, because it is to be afflicted by feeling and because it is to be supported by it.

508. “Pañca vadhakā paccatthikā ukkhittāsikāti kho, bhikkhave, pañcannetaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ adhivacana”nti āsīvisūpame (saṃ. ni. 4.238) vadhakāti vuttā, “bhāroti kho, bhikkhave, pañcannetaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ adhivacana”nti bhārasutte (saṃ. ni. 3.22) bhārāti, “atītampāhaṃ addhānaṃ evameva rūpena khajjiṃ, seyyathāpi etarahi paccuppannena rūpena khajjāmi. Ahañceva kho pana anāgataṃ rūpaṃ abhinandeyyaṃ, anāgatampāhaṃ addhānaṃ evameva rūpena khajjeyyaṃ, seyyathāpi…pe… khajjāmī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 3.79) khajjanīyapariyāye khādakāti, “so aniccaṃ rūpaṃ ‘aniccaṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 3.85) yamakasutte aniccādikāti. Yadipi “idha pana sabbepete ekajjhaṃ katvā khandhāti adhippetā”ti vuttaṃ, bāhullena pana upādānakkhandhānaṃ tadantogadhānaṃ daṭṭhabbatā veditabbā. Vipassanāya bhūmivicāro hesoti.

508. “‘Five murderers, hostile with uplifted swords’—this, monks, is a designation for these five aggregates subject to clinging.” In the Simile of the Viper Sutta, they are called “murderers.” “‘The burden,’ monks, ‘is a designation for these five aggregates subject to clinging.’” In the Burden Sutta, they are called “the burden.” “In the past period, I was consumed by form in this very way, just as I am now consumed by present form. And if I were to delight in future form, in the future period I would be consumed by form in this very way, just as… I am consumed.” By this and so on, in the Discourse on Being Consumed, they are called “the consumers.” “He does not truly understand impermanent form as ‘impermanent form,’” etc. In the Yamaka Sutta, they are called “impermanent,” etc. Although it is said, “Here, however, all these, having been taken together, are intended as the aggregates,” it should be understood that, for the most part, the aggregates subject to clinging included therein are to be seen. For this is an investigation of the ground for insight.

Pheṇapiṇḍo [M 2.0166] viyātiādīsu rūpādīnaṃ evaṃ pheṇapiṇḍādisadisatā daṭṭhabbā, yathā pheṇapiṇḍo [V 2.0155] nissāro paridubbalo agayhupago; gahitopi kiñci atthaṃ na sādheti, chiddāvachiddo anekasandhisaṅghaṭito bahūnaṃ pāṇakānaṃ āvāso anupubbūpacito sabbāvatthanipātī avassaṃbhedī, evaṃ rūpampi niccasārādivirahato nissāraṃ pheggu viya, sukhabhañjanīyato dubbalaṃ, niccanti vā dhuvanti vā ahanti vā mamanti vā na gahetabbaṃ, gahitampi tathā na hoti, bahuchiddaṃ asītisatasandhisaṅghaṭitaṃ anekakimikulāvāsaṃ kalalādivasena anupubbūpacitaṃ kalalakālato paṭṭhāya sabbāsupi avatthāsu vinassati, avassameva ca bhijjati. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.3.95; vibha. aṭṭha. 26 kamādivinicchayakathā) pana parimaddanāsahanameva upamūpameyyasambandho vutto.

In the texts beginning with 'Like a lump of foam,' the similarity of form, etc., to a lump of foam, etc., should be seen in this way: just as a lump of foam is without substance, very weak, and ungraspable; even when grasped, it does not accomplish any purpose; it has holes and gaps, is composed of many joints, is a dwelling place for many creatures, has gradually accumulated, is subject to falling in all conditions, and inevitably breaks apart; so also form, due to being devoid of permanent substance, etc., is without substance like sapwood. Due to being easily broken, it is weak; it should not be grasped as 'permanent,' or 'stable,' or 'I,' or 'mine.' Even when so grasped, it is not so. It has many holes, is composed of one hundred and eighty joints, is a dwelling for many families of worms, and by way of the embryo, etc., it gradually accumulates. Beginning from the time of the embryo, it perishes in all stages, and it inevitably breaks up. However, in the Commentary, only the inability to withstand pressure is stated as the connection between the simile and the object of the simile.

Yathā pubbuḷo nissāro paridubbalo agayhupago, gahitopi na kiñci atthaṃ sādheti, na ciraṭṭhitiko, tathā vedanāpi. Yathā ca pubbuḷo, udakatalaṃ, udakabinduṃ, udakajallikaṃ saṅkaḍḍhitvā puṭaṃ katvā gahaṇavātañcāti cattāri kāraṇāni paṭicca jāyati, evaṃ vedanāpi vatthuṃ, ārammaṇaṃ, kilesajallaṃ, phassasaṅghaṭṭanañcāti cattāri kāraṇāni paṭicca uppajjati. Yathā hi udakatale bindunipātajanito vāto udakajallikasaṅkhātaṃ udakalasikaṃ saṅkaḍḍhitvā puṭaṃ katvā pubbuḷaṃ nāma karoti, evaṃ vatthumhi ārammaṇāpāthagamanajanito phasso anupacchinnaṃ kilesajallaṃ sahakārīpaccayabhāvena saṅkaḍḍhitvā vedanaṃ nāma karoti. Idañca kilesehi mūlakāraṇabhūtehi, ārammaṇassādanabhūtehi ca nibbattaṃ vaṭṭagataṃ vedanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena vā cattāro paccayā vuttā, ūnehipi pana uppajjateva. Idha muhuttaramaṇīyatā upamopameyyasambandho vutto.

Just as a bubble is essenceless, very fragile, ungraspable, serves no purpose even when grasped, and is not long-lasting, so too is feeling. And just as a bubble arises dependent on four causes—the surface of water, a drop of water, water-scum, and the capturing wind—so too does feeling arise dependent on four causes: the physical basis, the object, the defilement-scum, and the impact of contact. For just as wind, generated by a drop falling on the surface of water, gathers the water-viscosity known as water-scum, forms a hollow, and thereby produces what is called a bubble, so too does contact, generated by the object coming into range of the physical basis, gather the uninterrupted defilement-scum by way of being a cooperating condition, and thereby produce what is called feeling. This was said with reference to feeling that belongs to the round of existence, produced by defilements that have become the root cause and the relishing of the object. Or, by way of the supreme classification, four conditions are stated, but it arises even with fewer. Here, the connection between the simile and the object of the simile is stated in terms of momentary delightfulness.

Yathā pana marīcikā asārā agayhupagā. Na hi taṃ gahetvā pātuṃ vā nhāyituṃ vā bhājanaṃ vā pūretuṃ sakkā, evaṃ saññāpi asārā agayhupagā. Yathā ca marīcikā vipphandamānā sañjātūmivegā viya khāyantī mahājanaṃ vippalambeti, evaṃ saññāpi “nīlaṃ pītaṃ dīghaṃ rassa”ntiādinā ārammaṇe pavattamānā sabhāvamatte aṭṭhatvā “subhaṃ sukhaṃ nicca”ntiādimicchāgāhassa kāraṇabhāvena lokaṃ vippalambeti.

Just as a mirage is insubstantial and ungraspable—for it is impossible to take hold of it to drink, bathe, or fill a vessel—so too, perception is insubstantial and ungraspable. And just as a mirage, shimmering and appearing as if with the velocity of a newly-risen wave, deceives the multitude, so too, perception, operating on objects as “blue, yellow, long, short,” etc., not standing in mere own-nature, deceives the world by being the cause of wrong grasping, such as “beautiful, pleasant, permanent,” and so on.

Yathā [M 2.0167] kadalikkhandho asāro agayhupago. Na hi taṃ gahetvā gopānasīādīnaṃ atthāya upanetuṃ sakkā, upanītampi tathā na hoti, bahuvaṭṭisamodhāno ca hoti, evaṃ saṅkhārakkhandhopi [V 2.0156] asāro agayhupago. Na hi taṃ niccādivasena gahetuṃ sakkā, gahitampi tathā na hoti, bahudhammasamodhāno ca. Aññadeva hi phassassa lakkhaṇaṃ, aññaṃ cetanādīnaṃ, te pana sabbe samodhānetvā saṅkhārakkhandhoti vuccati.

Just as a banana trunk is without substance and not to be taken as substance—for indeed, it is not possible to take it and apply it for the purpose of rafters and the like, and even if applied, it does not become so, and it is a collection of many sheaths—so too, the aggregate of formations is without substance and not to be taken as substance. For indeed, it is not possible to take it as permanent and so on, and even if taken, it does not become so, and it is a collection of many phenomena. Indeed, the characteristic of contact is one thing, and that of volition and so on is another; however, having combined all these, it is called the aggregate of formations.

Yathā ca māyā asārā agayhupagā. Na hi taṃ gahetvā kiñci atthaṃ kiccaṃ sādhetuṃ sakkā, ittarā lahupaccupaṭṭhānā amaṇiādimeva maṇiādirūpena dassentī mahājanaṃ vañceti, evaṃ viññāṇampi asāraṃ ittaraṃ lahupaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, teneva cittena āgacchantaṃ viya, gacchantaṃ viya, ṭhitaṃ viya, nisinnaṃ viya ca katvā gāhāpeti, aññadeva cittaṃ āgamane, aññaṃ gamanādīsūti. Evaṃ viññāṇaṃ māyāsadisaṃ.

And just as a magical illusion is without substance and not to be taken as substance—for indeed, it is not possible to take it and accomplish any desired task; it is transient, appears as quickly perishing, and deceives the great multitude by showing what is not a gem and so on in the form of a gem and so on—so too, consciousness is without substance, transient, and appears as quickly perishing. With that very mind, it causes one to grasp it as if coming, as if going, as if standing, and as if sitting, but the mind in coming is one thing, and in going and so on, it is another. Thus, consciousness is like a magical illusion.

Pañcapi upādānakkhandhā asubhādisabhāvā eva saṃkilesāsucivatthubhāvāditoti asubhādito daṭṭhabbā eva, tathāpi katthaci koci viseso sukhaggahaṇīyo hotīti āha “visesato cā”tiādi. Tattha cattāro satipaṭṭhānā catuvipallāsappahānakarāti tesaṃ gocarabhāvena rūpakkhandhādīsu asubhādibhāvena daṭṭhabbatā vuttā.

The five aggregates of clinging, because of being the basis of defilement, impurity, and so on, are indeed of the nature of the unattractive and so on; therefore, they are indeed to be seen as unattractive and so on. Nevertheless, in some cases, a certain distinction is easily grasped as pleasurable, therefore he said, 'and in particular,' and so on. Therein, the four foundations of mindfulness bring about the abandoning of the four perversions; therefore, by way of being their object, the state of being seen as unattractive and so on in the form aggregate and so on is stated.

509. Khandhehi na vihaññati parividitasabhāvattā. Vipassakopi tesaṃ vipattiyaṃ na dukkhamāpajjati, khīṇāsavesu pana vattabbameva natthi. Te hi āyatimpi khandhehi na bādhīyantīti.

509. One is not afflicted by the aggregates because their nature has been thoroughly known. Even the insight meditator does not come to suffering on account of their destruction; but in the case of those whose taints are destroyed, there is nothing at all to be said. For indeed, they are not afflicted by the aggregates even in the future.

Kabaḷīkārāhāraṃ parijānātīti “āhārasamudayā rūpasamudayo”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.56,57) vacanato ajjhattikarūpe chandarāgaṃ pajahanto tassa samudayabhūte kabaḷīkārāhārepi chandarāgaṃ pajahatīti attho. Ayaṃ pahānapariññā. Ajjhattikarūpaṃ pana pariggaṇhanto tassa paccayabhūtaṃ kabaḷīkārāhāraṃ pariggaṇhātīti ñātapariññā. Tassa ca udayabbayānupassī hotīti tīraṇapariññā ca yojetabbā. Evaṃ pariññattaye sijjhante ime vipallāsādayo vidhamīyanti evāti āha “asubhe subhanti vipallāsaṃ pajahatī”tiādi. Tattha kāmarāgabhūtaṃ abhijjhaṃ sandhāyāha “abhijjhākāyagantha”nti. Asubhānupassanāya hi kāmarāgappahānaṃ hoti[M 2.0168], kāmarāgamukhena vā sabbalobhappahānaṃ vadati. Na upādiyati na gaṇhati na uppādeti.

“He fully understands the nutriment of edible food”—this means that, in accordance with the statement, “With the arising of nutriment, form arises,” by abandoning desire and lust for internal form, one also abandons desire and lust for the nutriment of edible food, which is the cause of its arising. This is understanding as abandonment. Furthermore, one who comprehends internal form also comprehends the nutriment of edible food, which is its condition—this is understanding as knowledge. And the understanding as investigation should be applied by observing its rise and fall. When these three kinds of understanding are accomplished, these perversions and so on are certainly destroyed. Therefore, it is said, “He abandons the perversion of perceiving the beautiful in the unattractive,” etc. Herein, “the bodily fetter of covetousness” is said with reference to covetousness that is sensual desire. Indeed, through contemplation of the unattractive, the abandonment of sensual desire occurs; or, with sensual desire as the starting point, he speaks of the abandonment of all greed. He does not cling, grasp, or generate.

“Phassapaccayā [V 2.0157] vedanā”ti (ma. ni. 3.126; saṃ. ni. 2.39; mahāva. 1; udā. 1; netti. 24) vuttattā “vedanāya chandarāgaṃ pajahanto tassā paccayabhūte phassāhārepi chandarāgaṃ pajahatī”tiādinā āhāraparijānane vuttanayena phassaparijānanaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Vedanāya dukkhato dassanena tattha sukhanti vipallāsaṃ pajahati. Sukhatthameva bhavapatthanā hotīti vedanāya taṇhaṃ pajahanto bhavoghaṃ uttarati. Tato eva bhavayogena visaṃyujjati. Bhavāsavena ca anāsavo hoti, sabbavedanaṃ dukkhato passanto attano parena apubbaṃ dukkhaṃ uppāditaṃ, sukhaṃ vā vināsitaṃ na cinteti, tato “anatthaṃ me acarī”tiādi (dha. sa. 1237; vibha. 909) āghātavatthuppahānato byāpādakāyaganthaṃ bhindati. “Sukhabahule sugatibhave suddhī”ti aggahetvā gosīlagovatādīhi suddhiṃ parāmasanto sukhapatthanāvaseneva parāmasatīti vedanāya taṇhaṃ pajahantopi sīlabbatupādānaṃ na upādiyati.

“With contact as condition, there is feeling”—since this is stated, the full understanding of contact should be connected with the method stated in the full understanding of nutriment, thus: “By abandoning desire and lust for feeling, one also abandons desire and lust for the nutriment of contact, which is its condition.” By seeing feeling as suffering, one abandons the perversion of perceiving pleasure in it. Since the aspiration for existence is solely for the sake of pleasure, by abandoning craving for feeling one crosses the flood of existence. From that very reason, one is disjoined from the yoke of existence. And one is without the taint of existence. Seeing all feeling as suffering, one does not think that unprecedented suffering has been produced for oneself by another, or that one’s pleasure has been destroyed. Therefore, by abandoning the grounds for resentment such as, “He has done me harm,” one breaks the bodily knot of ill will. Not grasping, “There is purity in a good-destination existence abounding in pleasure,” one who misapprehends purity through such things as cow-practice and cow-vows does so simply by the power of aspiring for pleasure. Therefore, one who abandons craving for feeling also does not cling to the clinging to rules and vows.

Manosañcetanā saṅkhārakkhandho, saññā pana taṃsampayuttāti saññāsaṅkhāre anattato passanto manosañcetanāya chandarāgaṃ pajahati, tañca pariggaṇhāti, tīreti cāti “saññaṃ saṅkhāre…pe… parijānātī”ti vuttaṃ. Saññāsaṅkhāre anattāti passanto attadiṭṭhimūlakattā sabbadiṭṭhīnaṃ attadiṭṭhiṃ viya sabbadiṭṭhiyopi vidhamatīti dassento “diṭṭhoghaṃ uttarati…pe… attavādupādānaṃ na upādiyatī”ti āha.

Mental volition is the aggregate of formations, and perception is associated with it. Therefore, seeing perception and formations as not-self, one abandons desire and lust for mental volition, comprehends it, and investigates it. Hence, it is said, “One fully understands perception and formations…” Seeing perception and formations as not-self, showing that one dispels all views since they have self-view as their root, just as one dispels self-view, so too does one dispel all views, thus it is said, “One crosses the flood of views… and does not cling to the attachment to the doctrine of self.”

Viññāṇaṃ aniccato passanto aniccānupassanāmukhena tissopi anupassanā ussukkanto tīhipi pariññāhi viññāṇāhāraṃ parijānāti. Visesato panettha anicce niccanti vipallāsaṃ pajahati. Tattha niccaggāhabāhullato avijjāya viññāṇe ghanagahaṇaṃ hotīti ghanavinibbhogaṃ katvā taṃ aniccato passanto avijjoghaṃ uttarati. Tato eva avijjāyogena visaṃyutto avijjāsavena anāsavo ca hoti. Mohabaleneva sīlabbataparāmasanaṃ hotīti taṃ pajahanto “sīlabbataparāmāsakāyaganthaṃ bhindati.

One who sees consciousness as impermanent, by making the contemplation of impermanence the foundation, while striving at the three contemplations, fully understands consciousness-nutriment by means of the three full understandings. Specifically, however, herein one abandons the perversion of perceiving the permanent in the impermanent. Therein, because of the prevalence of grasping it as permanent, through ignorance, the grasping of consciousness as a solid mass occurs. Therefore, having made a breaking up of the solid mass, one who sees that consciousness as impermanent crosses the flood of ignorance. From that very reason, one is both disjoined from the yoke of ignorance and becomes free from the taint of ignorance. It is only by the power of delusion that the misapprehension of precepts and practices occurs. Therefore, one who abandons that delusion breaks the bodily knot of the misapprehension of precepts and practices.

“Yañca [M 2.0169] kho idaṃ, bhikkhave, vuccati cittaṃ itipi, mano itipi, viññāṇaṃ itipi, tatrāssutavā puthujjano nālaṃ nibbindituṃ, nālaṃ virajjituṃ, nālaṃ vimuccituṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Dīgharattaṃ hetaṃ, bhikkhave, assutavato puthujjanassa ajjhositaṃ mamāyitaṃ [V 2.0158] parāmaṭṭhaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.62) –

“And what, bhikkhus, is called mind, or mentality, or consciousness—the uninstructed ordinary person is not capable of becoming disenchanted with it, dispassionate towards it, or liberated from it. What is the reason for that? Because for a long time, bhikkhus, that has been adhered to, taken as ‘mine,’ and grasped by the uninstructed ordinary person as ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’”

Vacanato yathā viññāṇaṃ niccato passanto diṭṭhupādānaṃ upādiyati, evaṃ taṃ aniccato passanto diṭṭhupādānaṃ na upādiyatīti.

According to this statement, just as one who sees consciousness as permanent grasps the clinging to views, so one who sees it as impermanent does not grasp the clinging to views.

Evaṃ mahānisaṃsanti vuttappakārena vipallāsādisakalasaṃkilesavidhamanupāyabhāvato evaṃ vipuludayaṃ. Vadhakādivasenāti ukkhittāsikavadhakādivasena. Passeyyāti ñāṇadassanena paccakkhato passeyya.

Thus, it is of great benefit: because it is a means for dispelling all defilements such as the perversions in the manner stated, it thus has a vast benefit. 'As in the case of a murderer, etc.' means: by way of a murderer with a raised sword, etc. 'One should see' means: one should see directly with the vision of knowledge.

Khandhaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the aggregates is concluded.

Iti cuddasamaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus, the commentary on the fourteenth chapter.

15. Āyatanadhātuniddesavaṇṇanā

15. Commentary on the Exposition of the Sense Bases and Elements

Āyatanavitthārakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Detailed Exposition of the Sense Bases

510. “Khandhāyatanā”tiādinā [M 2.0170][V 2.0159] heṭṭhā uddiṭṭhāni paduddhāravasena “āyatanānī”ti vatvā gaṇanaparicchedenāha “dvādasāyatanānī”ti. Tattha vattabbaṃ parato sayameva vakkhati. Cakkhāyatanantiādi nesaṃ sarūpadassanaṃ.

510. By the words beginning with 'aggregates, sense bases,' having extracted the terms pointed out in brief below and stated them as 'the sense bases,' he then delimited the number by saying 'the twelve sense bases.' What should be said thereon, the commentator himself will state later on. The words beginning with 'the eye-base' are for showing their individual nature.

Attho nāma saddattho, bhāvattho pana lakkhaṇameva. So pana saddattho duvidho – asādhāraṇo sādhāraṇoti. Tattha asādhāraṇo cakkhādisaddattho, sādhāraṇo āyatanasaddattho dvādasannampi samānattā.

The so-called meaning is the meaning of the word; but the intrinsic meaning is just the characteristic. Furthermore, that meaning of the word is of two kinds: uncommon and common. Among them, the uncommon is the meaning of words such as 'eye'; the common is the meaning of the word 'base', because of its being common to all twelve.

Tesu asādhāraṇaṃ tāva dassento “visesato tāvā”tiādimāha. Tattha visesatoti visesatthato, cakkhādisaddatthatoti attho. Assādetīti cakkhati-saddo “madhuṃ cakkhati, byañjanaṃ cakkhatī”ti rasasāyanattho atthīti tassa vasena atthaṃ vadati. “Cakkhuṃ kho pana, māgaṇḍiya, rūpārāmaṃ rūparataṃ rūpasammudita”nti (ma. ni. 2.209) vacanato cakkhu rūpaṃ assādeti. Satipi sotādīnaṃ saddārāmatādibhāve yo “yaṃ cakkhu catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya pasādo”tiādinā (dha. sa. 597) pāḷiyaṃ, “rūpābhighātārahabhūtappasādalakkhaṇa”ntiādinā (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 600; visuddhi. 2.433) aṭṭhakathāyañca vutto atthaviseso, tattheva niruḷhattā cakkhumhi eva cakkhusaddo pavattati gavādīsu gosaddādi viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

First, to show the uncommon among them, he stated the passage beginning with, 'Specifically, first...'. Herein, 'specifically' means by way of a specific meaning, that is, by way of the meaning of words such as 'eye'. The word 'cakkhati' has the meaning of savoring a taste, as in 'he savors honey' or 'he savors curry'; because it has this meaning, he explains the meaning by means of it. Because it is said, 'The eye, indeed, Māgaṇḍiya, delights in forms, is pleased with forms, rejoices in forms,' the eye savors form. Even though there exists for the ear and other faculties the state of delighting in sounds and so on, it is because of being established only in that specific meaning—which is stated in the Pāli as, 'that eye, which is the sensitivity derived from the four great elements,' and in the Commentary as, 'its characteristic is the sensitivity capable of being impinged upon by forms'—that the word 'eye' applies only to the eye-sensitivity, just as the word 'go' (cow) and so on applies to cattle and so on. Thus it should be understood.

Vibhāveti cāti saddalakkhaṇasiddhassa cakkhati-saddassa vasena atthaṃ vadati. Cakkhatīti hi ācikkhati, abhibyattaṃ vadatīti attho. Nettassa ca vadantassa viya samavisamavibhāvanameva [V 2.0160] ācikkhananti katvā āha “vibhāveti cāti attho”ti, anekatthattā vā dhātūnaṃ vibhāvanatthatā ca cakkhati-saddassa daṭṭhabbā. Rattaduṭṭhādikālesu kakaṇṭakarūpaṃ viya, uddarūpaṃ viya ca vaṇṇavikāraṃ āpajjamānaṃ rūpaṃ hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ rūpayati rūpamiva pakāsaṃ karoti, saviggahamiva katvā dassetīti attho. Vitthāraṇaṃ vā [M 2.0171] rūpasaddassa attho, vitthāraṇañca pakāsanamevāti āha “pakāsetīti attho”ti. Anekatthattā vā dhātūnaṃ pakāsanattho eva rūpasaddo daṭṭhabbo. Vaṇṇavācakassa rūpasaddassa rūpayatīti nibbacanaṃ, rūpakkhandhavācakassa ruppatīti ayaṃ viseso. Udāharīyatīti vuccatīti atthe vacanasaddo eva gahito siyā, na ca vacanasaddo evettha saddo, atha kho sabbopi sotaviññeyyoti. Sappatīti sakehi paccayehi sappīyati, sotaviññeyyabhāvaṃ gamīyatīti attho.

By the commentary text which says, 'And it makes clear,' he states the meaning by means of the word 'cakkhati,' which is established in the science of words. Indeed, 'cakkhati' means 'it declares'; 'it speaks manifestly'—this is the meaning. And considering that the very making clear of the even and the uneven by the eye is 'declaring,' just as it is for one who speaks, he said, '“and it makes clear” is the meaning'. Or, because roots have many meanings, it should be understood that the word 'cakkhati' also has the meaning of 'making clear'. At times of lust, anger, and so on, form, undergoing a change of color like the form of a chameleon or like the form of an otter, indicates the state that has gone to the heart. This means: it makes it manifest as if it were a physical form; it shows it, having made it as if it had a body. Or, the meaning of the word 'rūpa' is 'elaboration', and 'elaboration' is indeed 'making manifest'. Therefore, he said, '“it makes manifest” is the meaning'. Or, because roots have many meanings, the word 'rūpa' should be understood as having the meaning of 'making manifest'. For the word 'rūpa' that denotes color, 'rūpayati' is the derivation. For the word 'rūpa' that denotes the aggregate of form, 'ruppati' is the derivation. This is the distinction. If, for 'udāharīyati' (it is uttered), the meaning 'vuccati' (it is spoken) were taken, then only 'the sound of speech' would be understood. But here, 'sound' is not just the sound of speech; rather, it is everything cognizable by the ear. 'Sappati' (it sounds) means: by its own conditions it is made to sound; it is made to arrive at the state of being cognizable by the ear—this is the meaning.

Sūcayatīti attano vatthuṃ apākaṭaṃ gandhavasena “idaṃ sugandhaṃ, duggandha”nti pakāseti, paṭicchannaṃ vā pupphādivatthuṃ “ettha pupphamatthi, campakādiphalamatthi, ambādī”ti pesuññaṃ karontaṃ viya hotīti attho. Rasaggahaṇamūlakattā ajjhoharaṇassa jīvitahetumhi āhārarase ninnatāya jīvitaṃ avhayatīti jivhā niruttilakkhaṇena. Kucchitānaṃ sāsavadhammānaṃ āyoti visesena kāyo vutto anuttariyahetubhāvaṃ anāgacchantesu kāmarāganidānakammajanitesu, kāmarāgassa ca visesapaccayesu ghānajivhākāyesu kāyassa visesatarasāsavapaccayattā. Tena hi phoṭṭhabbasukhaṃ assādentā sattā methunampi sevanti. Uppattidesoti uppattiṭṭhānanti attho, kāyindriyavatthukā vā cattāro khandhā balavakāmāsavādihetubhāvato visesena sāsavāti vuttāti tesaṃ uppattiṭṭhānanti attho.

'It indicates' means it makes its own object, which was not evident, manifest by means of scent, saying, "This is fragrant," or "This is foul." Or, it is as if it were slandering a concealed object like a flower, saying, "Here there is a flower such as a campaka; there is a fruit such as a mango," etc.; this is the meaning. Because ingestion has the grasping of taste as its root, and due to its inclination towards the taste of food which is the cause of life, it is called the tongue (jivhā) by the characteristic of its etymology, as it 'invokes' (avhayati) life. The body (kāya) is specifically mentioned as the 'source' (āya) of contemptible, cankered states because among the nose, tongue, and body—which do not attain the state of being a cause for the supreme, are produced by kamma originating from sensual lust, and are special conditions for sensual lust—the body is a particularly strong condition for the cankered states. For indeed, beings, while savoring tactile pleasure, also engage in sexual intercourse. 'Place of origin' means the place of arising; this is the meaning. Or, the four aggregates that have the body faculty as their physical basis are said to be 'cankered' in a special sense because they are a cause for strong cankers of sensuality and so on; therefore, it is their place of arising. This is the meaning.

Munātīti nāḷiyā minamāno viya, mahātulāya dhārayamāno viya ca ārammaṇaṃ vijānātīti attho. Manate iti vā mano, taṃ taṃ ārammaṇaṃ paricchedavasena jānātīti vuttaṃ hoti. Attano lakkhaṇaṃ dhārentīti ye visesalakkhaṇena āyatanasaddaparā vattabbā, te cakkhādayo tathā vuttāti tato aññe manogocarabhūtā dhammā sāmaññalakkhaṇeneva ekāyatanabhāvaṃ upanetvā vuttā. Yathā hi oḷārikavatthārammaṇamananasaṅkhātehi visayavisayībhāvehi purimāni pākaṭāni, tathā apākaṭā ca aññe manogocarā na attano sabhāvaṃ na dhārentīti imassa atthassa dīpanattho dhammasaddo. Dhārīyanti sāmaññarūpena avadhārīyantīti vā dhammā. Yathā hi rūpādayo cakkhuviññāṇādīhi asādhāraṇato eva yathāsakaṃ [V 2.0161] sabhāvato viññāyanti[M 2.0172], na evamete, ete pana anekadhammabhāvato, sādhāraṇato, sabhāvasāmaññatopi manasā viññāyantīti.

'It measures' (munāti) means it knows the object, like one measuring with a nāḷi basket, or like one weighing with a great balance; this is the meaning. Alternatively, because it knows (manate), it is called mind (mano); it is said that it knows each and every object by way of delimiting it. Those which are said to bear their own characteristic—that is, the eye-base and others, which are to be spoken of following the word 'base' with their specific characteristics—are spoken of thus. Therefore, other phenomena, which are the domain of the mind, are brought under a single base and spoken of only by their general characteristic. For just as the former bases are manifest through the object-subject relationship designated as the gross physical base-object and cognition, so too, the word 'phenomena' (dhamma) serves to clarify this meaning: it is not that other, unmanifest mind-objects do not bear their own nature. Alternatively, they are called phenomena (dhammā) because they are borne (dhārīyanti) or determined (avadhārīyanti) in a general form. For just as forms, etc., are known by eye-consciousness, etc., in a non-common way, each according to its own nature, these are not known in that way. Rather, these are known by the mind due to being multiple phenomena, due to being common, and also due to the generality of their nature.

511. Sena senāti sakena sakena. Uṭṭhahantīti uṭṭhānaṃ karonti. Vāyamantīti ussahanti, attano kiccaṃ karonticceva attho. Imasmiṃ ca atthe āyatanti etthāti āyatanānīti adhikaraṇattho āyatanasaddo, dutiyatatiyesu kattuattho. Te cāti cittacetasike dhamme. Te hi taṃtaṃdvārārammaṇesu ayanti gacchanti pavattantīti āyā. Vitthārentīti pubbe anuppannattā līnāni apākaṭāni pubbantato uddhaṃ pattharenti pākaṭāni karonti, uppādentīti attho. Idañca saṃsāradukkhaṃ. Na nivattatīti anuppādanirodhavasena na nirujjhati. Āyatanaṃ āyatananti āmeḍitavacanaṃ assā samaññāya cakkhādīsu niruḷhabhāvadassanatthaṃ.

511. 'Sena sena' means 'by its own, by its own'. 'They rise up' (uṭṭhahanti) means they make an effort. 'They strive' (vāyamanti) means they endeavor; that is, they perform their own function. And in this meaning, the word 'āyatana' has a locative sense, as in 'they exert themselves (āyatanti) in this (ettha), therefore they are sense bases (āyatanāni)'; in the second and third meanings, it has an agentive sense. And 'these' (te) refers to the phenomena of mind and mental factors. For they go, proceed, or occur in their respective doors and objects, hence they are called 'āyā' (comings). 'They extend' (vitthārenti) means that because they were previously unarisen, they spread forth upwards from a previous state what was latent and unmanifest, make it manifest, and produce it; this is the meaning. And this is the suffering of saṃsāra. 'It does not turn back' (na nivattati) means it does not cease by way of the cessation that is non-arising. The repeated expression 'sense base, sense base' (āyatanaṃ āyatanaṃ) is for the purpose of showing that this designation is established for the eye-base and others.

512. Evaṃ avayavabhedavasena āyatanasaddassa atthaṃ vatvā idāni tattha pariyāyatopi dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Sādhuphalabharitatāya, aparissayatāya ca manoramme.

512. Having thus explained the meaning of the word 'āyatana' by way of analyzing its components, now, to show its meaning through alternative expressions as well, the section beginning with 'furthermore' is commenced. It is pleasing to the mind because it is laden with sweet fruits and is free from danger.

Tattha nivasantīti nivasantā viya honti. Tenāha “tadāyattavuttitāyā”ti. Yattha suvaṇṇaratanādīni nivutthāni viya ākiṇṇāni tiṭṭhanti, so padeso tesaṃ ākaro, evaṃ cittacetasikā cakkhādīsūti te tesaṃ ākaroti dassento āha “cakkhādīsu ca…pe… ākaro”ti. Tannissitattāti ettha mano manoviññāṇādīnaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ nissayapaccayo na hotīti tassa tesaṃ dvārabhāvo nissayabhāvoti daṭṭhabbo. Ahutvā eva paccayasāmaggivasena uppajjantāpi cittacetasikā aneke ekajjhaṃ tattha labbhamānā samosaṭā viya hontīti vuttaṃ “vatthudvārārammaṇavasena samosaraṇato”ti. Na hi dhammānaṃ anāgataddhe vijjamānatālesopi atthi. Tenāha “puñjo natthi anāgate”ti (mahāni. 10). Tattheva uppattitoti tesu cakkhādīsu eva uppattito. Uppattiyā paccayabhūte cakkhādike uppattiṭṭhānaṃ viya katvā upacāravasena vuttaṃ. Na hi arūpadhammānaṃ nippariyāyato uppattideso nāma atthi. Yadaggena vā te [M 2.0173] tesaṃ nissayārammaṇabhūtā, tadaggena sañjātideso. Na hi paccayabhāvamantarena rūpadhammānampi ādhārādheyyabhāvo atthi. Tenāha “nissayārammaṇabhāvenā”ti. Byatirekapadhānatāya kāraṇalakkhaṇassa “tesaṃ abhāve abhāvato” iccevāha, na “bhāve bhāvato”ti.

Herein, 'they reside' means they are as if residing. Hence it is said: 'because their occurrence is dependent on that.' Just as a region where gold, gems, and so on, stand thickly strewn about as if settled there is a mine for them, so the eye, etc., are a mine for consciousness and mental factors. To show this, it is said: 'And in the eye, etc. … a mine.' Regarding 'because they are dependent on it': here it should be understood that since the mind is not a support-condition for mind-consciousness and other mental factors, its being a door for them is its state of being a support. Although consciousness and mental factors arise by the force of a collection of conditions without having existed before, since many of them are found together there, they are as if assembled. Hence it is said: 'because of their converging by way of base, door, and object.' For there is not even a trace of existence for dhammas in the future. Hence it is said: 'There is no heap in the future.' 'Because of arising right there' means because of arising right in the eye, etc. This is said figuratively, by treating the eye, etc., which are a condition for arising, as if they were the place of arising. For there is no literal place of arising for immaterial dhammas. Or, to the extent that these are their support and object, to that extent is the place of their origination designated. For even for material dhammas, there is no relationship of container and contained apart from the state of being a condition. Hence it is said: 'by way of being a support and object.' Because of the predominance of the negative concomitance of the characteristic of a cause, it is said only, 'because of their absence, there is absence,' not, 'because of their presence, there is presence.'

Yathāvuttenatthenāti [V 2.0162] “cakkhatī”tiādinā, “āyatanato āyānaṃ tananato”tiādinā, “nivāsaṭṭhāna”ntiādinā ca vuttappakārena atthena. Dhammāyatanapariyāpannānaṃ dhammānaṃ bahubhāvato yebhuyyena ca te bahū eva hutvā kiccakarāti “dhammā ca te āyatanañcā”ti bahuvacananiddeso.

"By the meaning as stated" means by the meaning in the manner stated with "it sees" (cakkhati), etc.; with "an āyatana because of coming (āyānaṃ) and extending (tananato)," etc.; and with "a dwelling place," etc. Because the dhammas included in the dhamma-base are numerous, and because for the most part they, being many, perform their function, the explanation is in the plural: "they are dhammas and it is a base."

513. Tathā tathā lakkhitabbato lakkhīyati etenāti vā lakkhaṇaṃ, sabhāvo.

513. A characteristic (lakkhaṇa) is so called because it is to be characterized in such and such a way, or because one characterizes by means of it; it is an intrinsic nature (sabhāva).

Tāvabhāvatoti tattakato, tena anūnādhikabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tattha dvādasāyatanavinimuttassa kassaci dhammassa abhāvā adhikabhāvato codanā natthi, salakkhaṇadhāraṇaṃ pana sabbesaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇanti ūnacodanā sambhavatīti taṃ dassento āha “cakkhādayopi hī”tiādi. Bhavaṅgamanasaṅkhātoti dvikkhattuṃ calitvā pavattabhavaṅgamanasaṅkhāto. Calanavasena bhavaṅgappavattiyā sati eva āvajjanuppatti, na aññatthāti āvajjanassāpi kāraṇabhūtanti katvā vuttaṃ “bhavaṅgamanasaṅkhāto…pe… uppattidvāra”nti. Asādhāraṇanti cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ asādhāraṇaṃ. Satipi asādhāraṇabhāve cakkhādīnaṃ dvārabhāvena gahitattā dhammāyatanena aggahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dvārārammaṇabhāvehi vā asādhāraṇataṃ sandhāya “asādhāraṇa”nti vuttaṃ.

"Because of being just that much" (tāvabhāvato) means to that extent; by this it shows the state of being neither deficient nor in excess. Herein, since there is no dhamma whatsoever that is excluded from the twelve bases, there is no objection on the ground of excess. But since the bearing of one's own characteristic is a general characteristic of all, an objection on the ground of deficiency is possible. To show this, it is said: "For the eye, etc., also…." "That which is reckoned as the bhavaṅga-mind" means that which is reckoned as the bhavaṅga-mind that has occurred having vibrated twice. Since the arising of adverting occurs only when there is an occurrence of bhavaṅga by way of vibration, and not otherwise, it is said, "that which is reckoned as the bhavaṅga-mind … a door for arising," because it is also a cause of adverting. "Uncommon" means uncommon to eye-consciousness, etc. Although there is the state of being uncommon for the eye, etc., since they are taken by way of being doors, it should be understood that they are not included by the dhamma-base. Or "uncommon" is said with reference to their uncommonness by way of being doors and objects.

514. Yebhuyyasahuppattiādīhi uppattikkamādīsu ayutti yojetabbā. Yebhuyyena hi cakkhāyatanādīni kassaci kadāci ekato uppajjanti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “kāmadhātuyā upapattikkhaṇe kassaci ekādasāyatanāni pātubhavantī”tiādi (yama. aṭṭha. āyatanayamaka 18-21). Tasmā āyatanānaṃ uppattikkamo tāva na yujjati, na pahānakkamo kusalābyākatānaṃ appahātabbato, na paṭipattikkamo akusalānaṃ ekaccaabyākatānañca appaṭipajjanīyato[M 2.0174], na bhūmikkamo aḍḍhekādasannaṃ āyatanānaṃ ekantakāmāvacarattā, itaresañca catubhūmipariyāpannattā, ekaccassa lokuttarabhāvato cāti. “Ajjhattikesu hī”ti etena ajjhattikabhāvena, visayībhāvena ca ajjhattikānaṃ paṭhamaṃ desetabbataṃ dasseti, tesupi paṭhamaṃ desetabbesu pākaṭattā paṭhamataraṃ cakkhāyatanaṃ desitanti.

514. The unsuitability of a sequence of arising, etc., should be connected with such things as co-arising for the most part. For, for the most part, the eye-base, etc., arise together for someone at some time. For so it is said: "At the moment of rebirth in the sense-sphere realm, for someone eleven bases appear," etc. Therefore, firstly, a sequence of arising is not tenable for the bases; nor a sequence of abandoning, since the wholesome and indeterminate ones are not to be abandoned; nor a sequence of practice, since the unwholesome and some indeterminate ones are not to be practiced; nor a sequence of planes, since ten and a half bases are exclusively of the sense sphere, while the others are included in the four planes, and one is supramundane. By "For among the internal," it shows that the internal bases should be taught first because they are internal and because they are subjects. And among those that should be taught first, the eye-base is taught as the very first because it is the most evident.

Tato ghānāyatanādīnīti ettha bahupakārattābhāvena cakkhusotehi purimataraṃ adesetabbāni, saha vattuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā ekena kamena desetabbānīti ghānādikkamena desitānīti adhippāyo[V 2.0163]. Aññathāpi hi desitesu na na sakkā codetuṃ, na ca sakkā bodhetabbāni na desetunti. Paccuppannārammaṇattā vā cakkhādīni paṭhamaṃ vuttāni ārammaṇato supākaṭānīti, manāyatanaṃ pana kiñci paccunnārammaṇaṃ…pe… kiñci yāva navattabbārammaṇanti pacchā vuttaṃ. Paccuppannārammaṇesupi upādārūpārammaṇāni cattāri paṭhamaṃ vuttāni, tato bhūtarūpārammaṇaṃ. Upādārūpārammaṇesupi dūratare dūre, sīghataraṃ sīghañca ārammaṇasampaṭicchanadīpanatthaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ desanākkamo. Cakkhusotadvayañhi dūragocaranti paṭhamaṃ vuttaṃ, tatrāpi cakkhu dūrataragocaranti sabbapaṭhamaṃ vuttaṃ. Passantopi hi dūratare nadīsotaṃ, na tassa sotapaṭighātasaddaṃ suṇāti. Ghānajivhāsupi ghānaṃ sīghataravuttīti paṭhamaṃ vuttaṃ purato ṭhapitamattassapi bhojanassa gandho gayhatīti. Yathāṭhānaṃ vā tesaṃ desanākkamo. Imasmiñhi sarīre sabbupari cakkhussa adhiṭṭhānaṃ, tassa adho sotassa, tassa adho ghānassa, tassa adho jivhāya, tathā kāyassa yebhuyyato, mano pana arūpibhāvato sabbapacchā vutto. Taṃtaṃgocarattā tassa tassa anantaraṃ bāhirāyatanāni vuttānīti vuttovāyamatthoti evampi imesaṃ kamo veditabbo. Gocaro visayo etassāti gocaravisayo, mano. Kassa pana gocaro etassa visayo? Cakkhādīnaṃ pañcannampi. Viññāṇuppattikāraṇavavatthānatoti cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ uppattikāraṇassa vavatthitabhāvato savibhattibhāvato. Etena cakkhādianantaraṃ rūpādivacanassa ca kāraṇamāha.

Then the nose-base, etc.: here the intention is that because they are not of great service, they should not be taught before the eye and ear; and because they cannot be spoken of together, they should be taught in a single sequence, so they are taught in the sequence beginning with the nose. For even if they were taught otherwise, it is not that one cannot object, nor that what should be understood cannot be taught. Or, the eye, etc., are stated first because they have a present object and are very evident as to their object. The mind-base, however, is stated last because it has some present objects … some objects that cannot be designated as past, present, or future. Even among those with present objects, the four with objects of derived matter are stated first, then the one with an object of primary matter. Even among those with objects of derived matter, the teaching sequence of the eye, etc., is for the purpose of showing the reception of an object at a greater distance and at a distance, and more quickly and quickly. For the pair, the eye and ear, have a distant range, so they are stated first. And among them, the eye has a more distant range, so it is stated first of all. For one sees a river current at a greater distance but does not hear the sound of that current's impact. Among the nose and tongue too, the nose is stated first because its occurrence is quicker, for the smell of food is grasped even when it is merely placed in front. Or the sequence of their teaching is according to their location. For in this body the physical basis of the eye is highest of all, below it that of the ear, below it that of the nose, below it that of the tongue, and likewise for the most part that of the body. But the mind, being immaterial, is stated last of all. This meaning has been stated: 'The external bases are stated immediately after each of these because they are their respective objects.' Thus this sequence of theirs should be understood in this way too. `Gocaravisayo` means: its resort (`gocara`) is its object (`visaya`); this refers to the mind. But whose resort is its object? Of all five, the eye, etc. 'Because of the establishment of the cause for the arising of consciousness' means because the cause for the arising of eye-consciousness, etc., is established and distinguished. By this it also states the reason for the mention of form, etc., immediately after the eye, etc.

515. Saṅgahitattāti gaṇanasaṅgahavasena saṅgahitattā. Jātivasenāti cakkhubhāvasamānatāvasena. Paccayabhedo kammādibhedo. Dānādipāṇātipātādibhedabhinnassa [M 2.0175] hi kusalākusalakammassa, tassa ca sahakārīkāraṇabhūtānaṃ abbhantarānaṃ, bāhirānañca paccayānaṃ bhedena cakkhāyatanaṃ bhinnaṃ visadisaṃ hotīti. Nirayādiko, apadādigatinānākaraṇañca gatibhedo gatīnaṃ, gatīsu vā bhedoti katvā. Hatthiassādiko, khattiyādiko ca nikāyabhedo. Taṃtaṃsattasantānabhedo puggalabhedo. Yā cakkhādīnaṃ vatthūnaṃ anantappabhedatā vuttā, so eva hadayavatthussa bhedo tādisabhedānātivattanato. Tato manāyatanassa anantappabhedatā yojetabbā. Yasmā jhānavirahitaṃ nāma lokuttaraṃ natthi, tasmā pañcannaṃ jhānānaṃ vasena aṭṭha lokuttaracittāni cattālīsaṃ hontīti tāni ekāsītiyā lokiyacittesu pakkhipitvā āha “ekavīsuttarasatappabhedañcā”ti. Vatthūti cakkhādivatthu. Tappabhedena viññāṇaṃ anantappabhedaṃ. Paṭipadā dukkhāpaṭipadādi. Ādi-saddena jhānādhipatibhūmiārammaṇādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Nīlaṃ nīlassa sabhāgaṃ, aññaṃ visabhāgaṃ. Paccayo kammādi. Tatthāpi kusalasamuṭṭhānāditā, sītautusamuṭṭhānāditā [V 2.0164] ca bhedo veditabbo. Ādisaddena gatinikāyabhedo. Sabhāvanānattabhedatoti sukhā dukkhā adukkhamasukhāti evamādiko sabhāvabhedo. Cakkhusamphassajā sotasamphassajāti evamādikaṃ nānattaṃ.

515. `Saṅgahitattā`: because of being included by way of inclusion by enumeration. `Jātivasena`: by way of similarity in kind, that is, by way of the sameness of the eye-state. `Paccayabhedo`: the distinction of condition is the distinction of kamma, etc. For, due to the distinction of wholesome and unwholesome kamma—differentiated by giving, etc., and by the destruction of life, etc.—and due to the distinction of the internal and external conditions that are its auxiliary causes, the eye-base becomes divided and dissimilar. `Gatibhedo`: the distinction of destination, which is the cause of various destinies such as hell, the footless, etc.; it is a distinction of, or among, destinations. `Nikāyabhedo`: the distinction of group, such as elephants and horses, etc., and khattiyas, etc. `Puggalabhedo`: the distinction of individual is the distinction in the continuums of different beings. The infinite diversity that has been stated for the physical bases such as the eye is also the diversity of the heart-base, as it does not surpass such diversity. Hence the infinite diversity of the mind-base should be inferred. Since there is no supramundane consciousness apart from jhāna, the eight supramundane consciousnesses become forty by way of the five jhānas. Including these with the eighty-one mundane consciousnesses, it is said: 'and of one hundred and twenty-one kinds.' `Vatthu`: the physical bases such as the eye. Due to their distinction, consciousness is of infinite distinction. `Paṭipadā`: the painful mode of practice, etc. By the word `ādi`, the inclusion of jhāna, dominant factor, plane, object, etc., should be understood. Blue is similar to blue; another is dissimilar. `Paccayo`: condition, is kamma, etc. Here too, a distinction should be understood, such as origination from wholesome kamma, etc., and origination from the cold season, etc. By the word `ādi`, the distinction of destination and group is included. Regarding `Sabhāvanānattabhedato`: the distinction of nature (`sabhāvabhedo`) is such as pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant. The diversity (`nānattaṃ`) is such as 'born of eye-contact,' 'born of ear-contact,' and so on.

516. “Anāgamanato aniggamanato”ti saṅkhepena vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “na hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pubbantāparantesu avijjamānasarūpattā udayato pubbe kutoci nāgacchanti, vayato ca uddhaṃ na katthaci gacchanti, vijjamānakkhaṇepi ittarakālatāya aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā. Tenāha “atha kho”tiādi. Saparipphandakiriyāvasena īhanaṃ īhā, cintanavasena byāpāranaṃ byāpāro, tattha byāpāraṃ dassento āha “na hi cakkhurūpādīnaṃ evaṃ hotī”ti. Īhaṃ dassento “na ca tānī”tiādi. Ubhayampi pana īhā ca hoti byāpāro cāti uppaṭipāṭivacanaṃ. Dhammatāvāti sabhāvo eva, kāraṇasamatthatā vā īhābyāpārarahitānaṃ dvārādibhāvo dhammatā. Imasmiñca atthe “ya”nti etassa yasmāti attho. Purimasmiṃ sambhavanavisesanaṃ yaṃ-saddo. “Suñño gāmoti kho, bhikkhave, channetaṃ ajjhattikānaṃ āyatanānaṃ adhivacana”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.238) vacanato suññagāmo viya [M 2.0176] daṭṭhabbāni. Annapānasahitanti gahite suññagāme yaṃ yadeva bhājanaṃ parāmasīyati, taṃ taṃ rittakaṃyeva parāmasīyati, evaṃ dhuvādibhāvena gahitāni yoniso upaparikkhiyamānāni rittakāneva etāni dissantīti. Tenāha “dhuvasubhasukhattabhāvavirahitattā”ti. Cakkhādidvāresu abhijjhādomanassuppādakabhāvena rūpādīni cakkhādīnaṃ abhighātakānīti vuttāni. Ahisusumārapakkhīkukkurasiṅgālamakkaṭā cha pāṇakā. Visamabilākāsagāmasusānavanāni tesaṃ gocarā. Tattha visamādiajjhāsayehi cakkhādīhi visamabhāvabilākāsagāmasusānasannissitasadisūpādinnadhammavanabhāvehi abhiramitattā rūpādīnaṃ visamādisadisatā yojetabbā.

516. To explain in detail the meaning stated concisely as 'from not coming, from not going,' the passage beginning 'for not…' was stated. Because they have no real existence in the prior and posterior extremes, they do not come from anywhere before arising nor do they go anywhere after ceasing. Even in the moment of existence, because of their brief duration, they are impermanent, suffering, and have the nature of changing. Hence it is said, 'but rather…' and so on. Striving (`īhā`) is effort by way of the activity of vibration; functioning (`byāpāro`) is activity by way of thinking. Therein, to show the functioning, it is said: 'For it is not so for the eye, forms, and so on.' To show the striving, it is said: 'Nor do they…' and so on. But this statement that there is both striving and functioning is in reverse order. `Dhammatā` (nature) is just intrinsic nature; or it is causal efficacy; or, for those devoid of striving and functioning, their state of being doors and so on is dhammatā. And in this sense, the word `yaṃ` has the meaning of `yasmā` (because). In the former sense, the word `yaṃ` is a qualifier of what can be. They should be seen as like an empty village, in accordance with the statement: 'Bhikkhus, “empty village” is a designation for these six internal bases.' Just as when an empty village is taken to be furnished with food and drink, whatever vessel one touches is touched as empty, so too, when these things taken as permanent and so on are wisely and thoroughly investigated, they are seen to be just empty. Hence it is said: 'because they are devoid of the state of being permanent, beautiful, pleasant, and self.' Because they produce covetousness and displeasure at the sense doors such as the eye, forms and so on are said to be 'strikers' of the eye and so on. A snake, a crocodile, a bird, a dog, a jackal, and a monkey are six creatures. Uneven ground, a hole, the open sky, a village, a charnel ground, and a forest are their respective domains. Therein, because the eye and other senses, which have an inclination for unevenness and so on, delight in clung-to phenomena that are similar to things based on uneven ground, holes, the open sky, villages, and charnel grounds, and in the state of a forest, the similarity of forms and so on to uneven ground and the like should be connected.

Iti āyatanānaṃ vitthārakathāmukhavaṇṇanā.

Thus the explanation of the introduction to the detailed discourse on the bases.

Dhātuvitthārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Detailed Discourse on the Elements.

517. Cakkhussa viññāṇanti cakkhussa kāraṇabhūtassa viññāṇaṃ. Kāmaṃ rūpālokamanasikārādayopi [V 2.0165] tassa viññāṇassa kāraṇā, te pana sādhāraṇakāraṇaṃ, cakkhu asādhāraṇanti asādhāraṇakāraṇenāyaṃ niddeso yathā bherisaddo, yavaṅkuroti. Tathā hi cakkhu puggalantarāsādhāraṇaṃ, nīlādisabbarūpasādhāraṇañcāti sāmibhāvena niddiṭṭhaṃ.

517. 'Consciousness of the eye' means the consciousness of the eye which is the cause. Indeed, although form, light, attention, and so on are also causes of that consciousness, they are a common cause, whereas the eye is the uncommon cause. Therefore, this designation is made by way of the uncommon cause, just as in 'the sound of a drum' or 'a barley sprout.' For indeed, the eye is uncommon to other individuals and common to all forms such as blue; thus, it is designated in the sense of ownership.

Vidahatīti evaṃ evañca tayā pavattitabbanti viniyuñjamānaṃ viya uppādetīti attho. Vidahatīti ca dhātvattho eva visiṭṭho upasaggena dīpīyatīti vināpi upasaggena dhātūti esa saddo tamatthaṃ vadatīti daṭṭhabbo. Kattukammabhāvakaraṇādhikaraṇesu ca dhātusaddasiddhi hotīti pañcāpi te atthā vuttā. Lokuttarā dhātuyo saṃsāradukkhaṃ na vidahanti, aññadatthu vidhaṃsentīti katvā “lokiyā”ti visesitaṃ. Vavatthitāti avatthitā, aññamaññaṃ vā asaṃkiṇṇā. Suvaṇṇarajatādidhātuyo suvaṇṇādīnaṃ bījabhūtā selādayo. Yathāsambhavanti ettha keci “lokiyalokuttarāsu dhātūsu yo yo attho sambhavati, tadanurūpa”nti atthaṃ vadanti, tadayuttaṃ “lokiyā hi dhātuyo”ti visesetvā vuttattā. Atthavasena cetaṃ yathāsambhavaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ, na dhātuvasena[M 2.0177]. Kāmaṃ pañcapi atthā cakkhādīnaṃ sabbesaṃ icchitabbā, tathāpi cakkhādīsu yassa yassa dhammassa yadā kattuvacanicchā, na tadā kammabhāvo. Yadā pana kammavacanicchā, na tadā kattubhāvo. Evaṃ sesesupīti yathāsambhavaggahaṇaṃ. Tenāha “iti cakkhādīsū”tiādi.

`Vidahati` means it produces, as if assigning, 'You should proceed in such and such a way.' And by `vidahati`, the distinguished meaning of the root itself is illuminated by the prefix; thus, it should be understood that even without the prefix, this word `dhātu` expresses that meaning. The word `dhātu` is formed in the senses of agent, object, state, instrument, and location, and thus all five of these meanings have been stated. The supramundane elements do not arrange the suffering of saṃsāra; on the contrary, they demolish it. For this reason, it is specified as 'mundane.' `Vavatthitā` means established, or unmixed with one another. The elements such as gold and silver are the rocks and so on that are the seeds of gold and so on. Regarding 'according to possibility' here, some state the meaning is 'in conformity with whatever meaning is possible among the mundane and supramundane elements.' That is incorrect, because it has been stated with the specification 'for the mundane elements.' And this taking of 'according to possibility' is done by way of meaning, not by way of the elements. Indeed, all five meanings are applicable to all of them, the eye, etc., yet when there is a wish to speak of the agent in regard to some phenomenon among the eye, etc., then there is no state of being the object. But when there is a wish to speak of the object, then there is no state of being the agent. So it is for the remaining cases. This is the taking of 'according to possibility.' Hence it is said: 'Thus, in the eye and so forth…' and so on.

518. Attano sabhāvaṃ dhārentīti dhātuyoti etthāpi dhātīti dhātūti padasiddhi veditabbā dhāraṇattho dhā-saddoti katvā. Kattuatthopi cāyaṃ purimena asadiso vidhānadhāraṇatthānaṃ bhinnasabhāvattā. Nissattasabhāvamattadhāraṇañca dhātusaddassa padhāno atthoti visuṃ vutto. Dhātuyo viya dhātuyoti ettha sīhasaddo viya kesarimhi niruḷhā purise selāvayavesu niruḷho dhātusaddo cakkhādīsu upacaritoti daṭṭhabbo. Ñāṇañca ñeyyañca ñāṇañeyyāni, tesaṃ avayavā tappabhedabhūtā dhātuyo ñāṇañeyyāvayavā. Tattha ñāṇappabhedo dhammadhātuekadeso, ñeyyappabhedo aṭṭhārasāpīti ñāṇañeyyāvayavamattā dhātuyo hontīti. Atha vā ñāṇena ñātabbo sabhāvo aviparīto dhātusaddena vuccamāno ñāṇañeyyo, na diṭṭhiādīhi viparītaggāhakehi ñeyyoti attho, tassa ñāṇañeyyassa avayavā cakkhādayo, visabhāgalakkhaṇāvayavesu rasādīsu niruḷho dhātusaddo tādisesu aññāvayavesu cakkhādīsu upacaritoti daṭṭhabbo. Rasādīsu viya vā cakkhādīsupi niruḷho eva. “Nijjīvamattassetaṃ adhivacana”nti etena nijjīvamattapadatthe dhātusaddassa niruḷhataṃ dasseti. Cha dhātuyo etassāti chadhāturo. Yo loke purisoti dhammasamudāyo [V 2.0166] vuccati, so chadhāturo channaṃ pathavīādīnaṃ nijjīvamattānaṃ sabhāvānaṃ samudāyamatto, na ettha jīvo vā puriso vā atthīti attho.

518. Here too, in the etymology 'they are `dhātus` because they bear their own intrinsic nature,' the derivation of the word `dhātu` from `dhāti` should be known, on the grounds that the root `dhā` has the meaning of bearing. And this, although having the meaning of agent, is dissimilar to the previous one because the meanings of arranging and bearing have different natures. Furthermore, the mere bearing of a non-sentient nature is stated separately as the principal meaning of the word `dhātu`. In the etymology 'elements are like `dhātus`,' it should be understood that just as the word 'lion' (`sīha`), established in reference to a maned beast, is used figuratively for a man, so the word `dhātu`, established in reference to the components of a mountain, is used figuratively for the eye, etc. Knowledge and the knowable are `ñāṇañeyyāni`; the elements, being their parts and divisions, are the parts of knowledge and the knowable. Therein, the division of knowledge is a portion of the dhamma-element, and the division of the knowable comprises all eighteen elements; thus the elements are merely parts of knowledge and the knowable. Or, the undistorted nature to be known by knowledge, when called by the word `dhātu`, is 'knowable by knowledge'; the meaning is that it is not to be known by those who grasp in a distorted way, such as by views, etc. The parts of this 'knowable by knowledge' are the eye, etc. It should be understood that the word `dhātu`, established in reference to parts with dissimilar characteristics such as tastes, etc., is used figuratively for other such parts, the eye, etc. Or, just as it is established in reference to tastes, etc., so it is established in reference to the eye, etc. By the text, 'This is a designation for what is merely lifeless,' he shows that the word `dhātu` is established in the meaning of the term 'merely lifeless.' 'For this one there are six elements,' thus `chadhāturo` (one of six elements). That collection of phenomena in the world which is called a 'person' is one of six elements, a mere collection of six natures that are merely lifeless, such as earth, etc. The meaning is that there is no soul or person here.

519. Cakkhādīnaṃ kamo pubbe vuttoti idhekekasmiṃ tike tiṇṇaṃ dhātūnaṃ kamaṃ dassento āha “hetuphalānupubbavavatthānavasenā”ti. Hetuphalānaṃ anupubbavavatthānaṃ hetuphalabhāvo eva, manodhammadhātūnañca manoviññāṇassa hetubhāvo yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbo.
