Kiriyamanodhātu manoviññāṇassa upanissayakoṭiyā, vipākamanodhātu vipākamanoviññāṇassa anantarādināpi, itarassa sabbāpi upanissayakoṭiyā [M 2.0178] ca, dhammadhātu pana vedanādikā sahajātā sahajātādinā, asahajātā anantarādinā, upanissayena, ārammaṇādinā ca manoviññāṇassa paccayo hotīti dvārabhūtamanovasena vā. Dvārabhūtamanopi hi suttesu manodhātūti vuccatīti tassā vā manodhātuyā manoviññāṇassa hetubhāvo yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbo. Tattha hetūti paccayo adhippeto, phalanti paccayuppannanti āha “cakkhudhātū”tiādi.

519. The sequence of the eye, etc., has been stated before. Here, showing the sequence of the three elements in each triad, he says: 'by way of the arrangement in the sequence of cause and effect.' The arrangement in sequence of cause and effect is just the state of being cause and effect. And the causal status of the mind-element and the dhamma-element for mind-consciousness should be connected as is possible. The functional mind-element is a condition for mind-consciousness by way of a portion of decisive support; the resultant mind-element is a condition for resultant mind-consciousness also by way of contiguity, etc.; and for the other mind-consciousness, all three mind-elements are conditions only by way of a portion of decisive support. The dhamma-element, however—feeling, etc.—when co-nascent, is a condition for mind-consciousness by way of co-nascence, etc.; when not co-nascent, by way of contiguity, etc., by decisive support, and by object, etc.; or by way of the mind that has become the door. For in the suttas, even the mind that has become the door is called the mind-element, so the causal status of that mind-element for mind-consciousness should be connected as is possible. Therein, by 'cause' a condition is intended; by 'effect,' the conditionally arisen is intended. Thus he says: 'the eye-element,' etc.

520. Sabbāsaṃ vasenāti yathāvuttānaṃ ābhādhātuādīnaṃ pañcatiṃsāya dhātūnaṃ vasena. Aparamatthasabhāvassa paramatthasabhāvesu na kadāci antogadhatā atthīti āha “sabhāvato vijjamānāna”nti.

520. ‘By way of all’ means by way of the thirty-five elements, such as the light-element and so on, as stated. Because there is never any inclusion of a reality that is not ultimate in nature within realities that are ultimate in nature, he says, ‘of those existing by their own nature.’

Candābhāsūriyābhādikā vaṇṇanibhā evāti āha “rūpadhātuyeva hi ābhādhātū”ti. Rūpādipaṭibaddhāti rāgavatthubhāvena gahetabbākāro subhanimittanti katvā “rūpādayo evā”ti avatvā paṭibaddhavacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Asatipi rāgavatthubhāve kusalavipākārammaṇaṃ subhadhātūti dutiyo vikappo vutto. Sesāti manoviññāṇadhātusampayuttā. Dhātudvayanirodhamattanti manoviññāṇadhātūnaṃ nirodhamattaṃ catutthāruppacittuppādanirodhabhāvato. Tadaññaviññāṇanirodho viya hi viññāṇadhātumanodhātūnaṃ nirodho samāpattibalasiddhoti katvā dhātudvayaggahaṇaṃ.

Light such as that of the moon and sun is just the radiance of color; thus, he says: ‘for the light-element is indeed the form-element.’ Regarding ‘connected to form and so on’: because the mode to be grasped as a basis for lust is the sign of the beautiful, having considered this, the word ‘connected’ is used instead of saying ‘form and so on itself.’ Even when there is no basis for lust, the object of wholesome resultant consciousness is the beautiful element; thus, the second alternative is stated. ‘The rest’ means the mental factors associated with the mind-consciousness-element. ‘The mere cessation of the two elements’ means the mere cessation of the mind-consciousness-element and the dhamma-element, because it is the cessation of the arising of the fourth immaterial-sphere consciousness. For, like the cessation of mind-consciousness other than that, the cessation of the five sense-consciousness-elements and the mind-element is accomplished by the power of the attainment; having considered this, the two elements are mentioned.

“Dhammadhātumatta”nti idaṃ kāmadhātuyā dhammadhātupariyāpannattā vuttaṃ. Kāmapaṭisaṃyuttoti kāmarāgasampayutto, ārammaṇakaraṇena vā kāmaguṇopasaṃhito. Yaṃ etasmiṃ antareti ye etasmiṃ avīciparanimmitavasavattiparicchinne okāse. Ogāḷhā hutvā adhobhāge ca okāse carantīti etthāvacarā. Aññattha carantāpi yathāvutte eva ṭhāne pariyāpannāti ettha pariyāpannā.

“Merely the element of phenomena”: this is said because the sense-sphere element is included in the element of phenomena. “Connected with the sense-sphere” means associated with sensual desire, or connected to the strands of sensual pleasure by way of making them an object. “That which is within this” means those who are in this space defined by Avīci and Paranimmitavasavatti. “Those who roam here” means that having plunged in, they roam in the lower space. “Included here” means that even while roaming elsewhere, they are included in the very place as stated.

Nekkhammadhātu [V 2.0167] dhammadhātu eva vitakkapakkhe. Sabbepi kusalā dhammāti dānamayapuññakiriyato, sīlamayapuññakiriyato, pabbajjato ca paṭṭhāya yāva aggamaggādhigamā pavattā sabbepi anavajjadhammā. Vihiṃsādhātu cetanā, paraviheṭhanacchando vā. Avihiṃsā karuṇā.

The element of renunciation is indeed the element of phenomena, on the side of thought. “All wholesome states” means all blameless states that occur starting from the meritorious act of giving, the meritorious act of moral conduct, and the going forth, up to the attainment of the highest path. The element of cruelty is volition, or the desire to harm others. The element of non-cruelty is compassion.

Hīnāti [M 2.0179] hīḷitā. Paṇītāti sambhāvitā. “Nātihīḷitā nātisambhāvitā majjhimā”ti khandhaniddese āgatā hīnadukato eva nīharitvā majjhimā dhātu vuttāti veditabbā. Ubhopīti dhammadhātumanoviññāṇadhātuyo.

“Inferior” means despised. “Superior” means esteemed. It should be understood that the middle element is stated by extracting it from the couplet on the inferior, which comes in the Khandha Niddesa thus: “Neither too despised nor too esteemed is the middle.” “Both” means the element of phenomena and the mind-consciousness element.

Viññāṇadhātu yadipi chaviññāṇadhātuvasena vibhattā, tathāpi viññāṇadhātuggahaṇena tassa purecārikapacchācārikattā manodhātu gahitāva hotīti āha “viññāṇadhātu cakkhuviññāṇādisattaviññāṇadhātu saṅkhepoyevā”ti. Anekesaṃ cakkhudhātuādīnaṃ, tāsu ca ekekissā nānappakāratāya nānādhātūnaṃ vasena anekadhātu nānādhātu loko vuttoti āha “aṭṭhārasadhātuppabhedamattamevā”ti.

Although the consciousness element is divided by way of the six consciousness elements, still, by the taking of the consciousness elements, the mind-element is also included because it is their precursor and successor. Thus he says: “The consciousness element is just a summary of the seven consciousness elements such as eye-consciousness.” Because there are many elements such as the eye-element, and because of the diversity of each one of them, the world is said to have “many elements, diverse elements” by way of the various elements. Thus he says: “It is merely the division into the eighteen elements.”

521. Cakkhusotaghānajivhākāyamanodhātumanoviññāṇadhātubhedenāti bahūsu potthakesu likhitaṃ, kesuci “cakkhusotaghānajivhākāyamanomanoviññāṇadhātubhedenā”ti. Tattha na cakkhādīnaṃ kevalena dhātusaddena sambandho adhippeto vijānanasabhāvassa pabhedavacanato. Viññāṇadhātusaddena ca sambandhe kariyamāne dve manogahaṇāni na kātabbāni. Na hi dve manoviññāṇadhātuyo santi. Antarā vā manodhātugahaṇaṃ akatvā “cakkhu…pe… kāyamanoviññāṇadhātumanodhātū”ti vattabbaṃ atulyayoge dvandasamāsābhāvato. Ayaṃ panettha pāṭho siyā “cakkhu…pe… kāyaviññāṇamanomanoviññāṇadhātubhedenā”ti. Tassa viññāṇassa yebhuyyena attavādino tassa ekamekassa attassa advayataṃ, niccattañca pavedentīti anekatāniccatāpakāsanaṃ tesaṃ jīvasaññāsamūhananāya hoti. Khandhāyatanadesanā saṅkhepadesanā, indriyadesanā vitthāradesanā, tadubhayaṃ apekkhitvā ayaṃ anatisaṅkhepavitthārā dhātudesanā. Abhidhamme vā suttantabhājanīye (vibha. 172 ādayo) vuttā dhātudesanā atisaṅkhepadesanā, ābhādhātuādīnaṃ anekadhātunānādhātuantānaṃ vasena desetabbā ativitthāradesanā, tadubhayaṃ apekkhitvā ayaṃ anatisaṅkhepavitthārā.

521. In many books it is written: “by the division into the eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, mind-element, and mind-consciousness-element.” In some it is written: “by the division into the eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, mind-, and mind-consciousness-element.” Here, a connection of “eye,” etc., with the mere word “element” is not intended, because this is a statement about the division of what has the nature of cognizing. And when making the connection with the word “consciousness-element,” two mentions of “mind” should not be made, for there are not two mind-consciousness-elements. Or, without mentioning the mind-element in between, it should be stated as “eye…pe… body-mind-consciousness-element-mind-element,” because there is no dvandva compound in a case of unequal connection. The reading here should be: “by the division into eye…pe… body-consciousness, mind-, and mind-consciousness-element.” Since proponents of a self mostly declare the non-duality and permanence of each individual self of that consciousness, the exposition of its multiplicity and impermanence serves to abolish their perception of a living being. The exposition of the aggregates and bases is a brief exposition; the exposition of the faculties is a detailed exposition. In comparison to both, this exposition of the elements is neither too brief nor too detailed. Or, in the Abhidhamma, in the Suttanta-style analysis, the exposition of the elements that is taught is an extremely brief exposition; the one that should be taught by way of the light element, etc., ending with the many elements and diverse elements, is an extremely detailed exposition. In comparison to both, this one is neither too brief nor too detailed.

Assa [V 2.0168] bhagavato. Saddhammatejasā vihataṃ saddhammatejavihataṃ.

Of this Blessed One. Dispelled by the majesty of the good Dhamma is “dispelled-by-the-majesty-of-the-good-Dhamma.”

522. Saṅkhatoti [M 2.0180] gaṇanato. Jātitoti cakkhubhāvasāmaññato. Atha vā jātitoti cakkhusabhāvato. Tenāha “cakkhupasādo”ti. Vīsati dhammāti saṅkhaṃ gacchati vedanādīnaṃ abhinditvā gahaṇato. Sesakusalākusalābyākataviññāṇavasenāti ettha abyākatāpekkhāya sesaggahaṇaṃ, kusalākusalaṃ pana sabbaso aggahitamevāti.

522. “Conditioned” is from reckoning. “By birth” is from the commonality of the state of being an eye. Or alternatively, “by birth” is from the intrinsic nature of the eye. Therefore he says, “eye-sensitivity.” It reaches the count “twenty phenomena” because feeling and so on are taken without being broken up. In the phrase “by way of the remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate consciousness,” the word “remaining” is with reference to the indeterminate; the wholesome and unwholesome, however, are not taken at all.

523. Tā ca cakkhuviññāṇadhātuādayo pañcapi.

523. And those five also, the eye-consciousness element and so on.

Purimehevāti anantarādīhi eva. Javanamanoviññāṇadhātu pana javanamanoviññāṇadhātuyā āsevanapaccayenāpi paccayo hotīti vuttovāyamattho. Dhammadhātūti pana sahajāto vedanādikkhandho adhippeto. Tenāha “sahajāta…pe… paccayo hotī”ti. Avigatādīhīti ettha ādi-saddena manoviññāṇadhātuyā yathārahaṃ hetuadhipatikammavipākāhārindriyajhānamaggapaccayabhāvo saṅgayhati. Tenāha “bahudhā paccayo hotī”ti. Ekaccā ca dhammadhātu sukhumarūpanibbānappakārā, yā ca sampayogānantarabhāvādīnaṃ abhāvena ārammaṇakaraṇe yogyā. Pañcadvārikavipākavajjanatthaṃ “ekaccāya manoviññāṇadhātuyā”ti vuttaṃ, manodvārikā pana vipākāpi tadārammaṇabhūtā ekaccaṃ dhammadhātuṃ ārabbha pavattatīti. Atha vā “ekaccāya manoviññāṇadhātuyā”ti idaṃ sabbaṃ kāmāvacarakusalaṃ kāmāvacarakiriyaṃ abhiññādvayaṃ āruppadvayanti evarūpaṃ manoviññāṇadhātuṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, lokuttaramanoviññāṇadhātuyā pana ekaccā dhammadhātu ārammaṇapaccayoti pākaṭoyamattho. Cakkhuviññāṇadhātuādīnaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ yathāvuttapaccayadhammato atirekepi paccayadhamme dassetuṃ “na kevala”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha ālokādayoti āloko nāma sūriyālokādi. Tassa suttantanayena upanissayabhāvo veditabbo, evaṃ sesānipi.

“By the preceding ones” means only by the conditions of contiguity and so on. It has already been stated that the impulsion mind-consciousness element is a condition for the impulsion mind-consciousness element also by way of repetition condition. Furthermore, by “element of phenomena,” the conascent aggregates of feeling, etc., are intended. Therefore he says: “by conascence… it is a condition.” In “by non-disappearance, etc.,” the word “etc.” includes the mind-consciousness element’s being a condition, as appropriate, by way of root, dominance, kamma, result, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, and path conditions. Therefore he says: “it is a condition in many ways.” And a certain element of phenomena is of the kind of subtle matter and Nibbāna, which is fit to be made an object due to the absence of association, contiguity, and so on. The words “for a certain mind-consciousness element” are stated to exclude the five-door-process resultants; for the mind-door resultants, which are the registering consciousness for that object, also arise in dependence on a certain element of phenomena. Alternatively, the words “for a certain mind-consciousness element” are stated in reference to the mind-consciousness element of this kind: all sense-sphere wholesome consciousness, sense-sphere functional consciousness, the two direct knowledges, and the two formless-sphere consciousnesses (the second and fourth). But it is plain that a certain element of phenomena is an object condition for the supramundane mind-consciousness element. To show that the eye-consciousness element, etc., have conditioning phenomena in addition to the conditioning phenomena stated for the eye, etc., the passage beginning “not only” was started. Therein, “light, etc.”: light means sunlight and so on. Its being a decisive support condition should be understood in the Suttanta way; likewise for the rest.

Vivaraṃ nāma visesato sotabilaṃ. Vāyu gandhūpasaṃharaṇakavāto. Āpo mukhe pakkhittaāhārassa temanakaudakaṃ. Pathavī kāyappasādassa nissayabhūtā pathavīdhātu. Bhavaṅgamanaṃ dvikkhattuṃ calitaṃ bhavaṅgacittaṃ. Sabbattha manasikāro āvajjanamanasikāro.

“Opening” means specifically the ear-hole. “Air” is the wind that conveys the odor. “Water” is the fluid that moistens the food placed in the mouth. “Earth” is the earth element that has become the support for the body-sensitivity. “Mind of the life-continuum” is the life-continuum consciousness that has vibrated twice. In all cases, “attention” is adverting attention.

524. Avisesato [M 2.0181][V 2.0169] daṭṭhabbākārassa vuccamānattā āha “sabbā evā”ti. Visesato vipassanāya bhūmivicāro esoti “saṅkhatā”ti visesitaṃ. Pubbantāparantavivittatoti ettha “pubbantonāma atīto addhā, aparanto nāma anāgato. Ubhayattha ca saṅkhatā dhātuyo sabhāvavivittā anupalabbhamānasabhāvattā. Pubbanto vā sabhāvadhammassa udayo tato pubbe avijjamānattā. Aparanto vayo tato paraṃ abhāvato. Tasmā pubbantāparantavivittatoti pākābhāvato viddhaṃsābhāvatoti vuttaṃ hoti.

524. Because the mode to be seen is stated without specifics, he says, “all are thus.” Because this exposition of the bases and elements is the investigation of the ground for insight in particular, it is specified as “conditioned.” Herein, regarding “devoid of a former end and a latter end”: the former end is the past time, the latter end is the future. And in both, the conditioned elements are devoid of intrinsic nature because their intrinsic nature is not found. Or the former end is the arising of a real phenomenon, because it did not exist before that. The latter end is its passing away, because it does not exist after that. Therefore, it is said that “devoid of a former end and a latter end” is so because of absence due to prior non-existence and absence due to destruction.

Bheritalaṃ viya cakkhudātu saddassa viya viññāṇassa nissayabhāvato. Ādāsatalādīsupi eseva nayo. Yantaṃ nāma ucchuyantaṃ. Cakkayaṭṭhīti tilamanthaṃ āha. So hi acakkabandhopi taṃsadisatāya cakkayaṭṭhītveva vuccati, cakkabandhameva vā sandhāya tathā vuttaṃ. Imāhi ca upamāhi nijjīvāna. Bheritaladaṇḍādīnaṃ samāyoge, nijjīvānaṃ saddādīnaṃ viya nijjīvānaṃ cakkhurūpādīnaṃ samāyoge nijjīvānaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ pavattīti kāraṇaphalānaṃ dhātumattataṃ, kārakavedakavirahañca dasseti.

The eye-element is like a drum-skin, because it is a support for consciousness just as the drum-skin is for sound. This same method applies to a mirror surface and so on. “A machine” means a sugarcane press. By “wheel-staff” he means a sesame-press pestle. For although it is not bound with a wheel, it is called a “wheel-staff” because of its similarity to one; or it was said so in reference to one that is actually bound with a wheel. And by these similes he shows that just as from the conjunction of lifeless things like a drum-skin and a drumstick there is the occurrence of lifeless things like sound, so from the conjunction of lifeless things like the eye-element and form-element there is the occurrence of lifeless things like eye-consciousness. Thus he demonstrates the mere elemental nature of causes and effects, and the absence of a maker and an experiencer.

Purecarānucarā viyāti nijjīvassa kassaci keci nijjīvā purecarānucarā viyāti attho. Manodhātuyeva vā attano khaṇaṃ anativattantī attano khaṇa anativattantānaṃyeva cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ avijjamānāyapi purecarānucarābhisandhiyaṃ anantarapubbakālāparakālatāya purecarānucarā viya daṭṭhabbā.

“Like precursors and successors”: the meaning is that of some lifeless thing, certain lifeless things are like its precursors and successors. Or, the mind-element itself, not overstepping its own moment, should be seen as if it were the precursor and successor of the eye-consciousness and so on—which also do not overstep their own moment—on account of its being in the immediately preceding time and their being in the subsequent time, even though there is no intention for them to be precursors and successors.

Channañhi viññāṇadhātūnaṃ ekajjhaṃ anekānantarapaccayābhāvato ekajjhaṃ uppattiabhāvo viya aññamaññānantarapaccayatābhāvato anantaruppattipi natthi. Yadi siyā, chaḷārammaṇasannidhāne manasikāramantarenāpi chaḷārammaṇūpaladdhi siyā, na ca hoti, tasmā dassanādianantaraṃ savanādīnaṃ abhāvo viya manoviññāṇadhātānantaraṃ na dassanādīni, na ca dassanādianantaraṃ manoviññāṇadhātu hoti. Tattha bhavaṅgassa, dassanādīnañca bhinnārammaṇatāya manoviññāṇadhātānantaraṃ dassanādīni, dassanādīnaṃ anantarañca savanādīni na uppajjantīti yuttametaṃ. Dassanādīnaṃ, pana santīramaṇassa ca abhinnavisayatāya dassanādianantaraṃ na manāviññāṇadātu hotīti ayuttanti[M 2.0182]? Nayidamevaṃ niyatāniyatavisayānaṃ bhinnavisayabhāvupapattito. Yadi ca dassanādianantaraṃ kāci viññāṇadhātu uppajjeyya, sāpi dassanādidvāratāya [V 2.0170] dassanādiviññāṇadhātu eva siyā, na manoviññāṇadhātu, tato ca dassanādikiccavidhuraṃ cintanaṃ manananti manodvārappavattānaṃ mananakiccāpariccāgo viya dassanaviññāṇadhātuyā dassanakiccāpariccāgo āpajjati. Tathā tadanantarassāti sabbāyapi dassanaviññāṇabhāvato ca viññāṇakāyā na bhaveyyuṃ.

Indeed, for the six consciousness-elements, just as there is no simultaneous arising due to the absence of many immediate conditions at once, so too, there is no immediately successive arising because they are not immediate conditions for one another. If it were so, the apprehension of six objects would occur when the six objects are present, even without attention; but this does not happen. Therefore, just as there is no auditory consciousness, etc., immediately after visual consciousness, etc., so too there is no visual consciousness, etc., immediately after the mind-consciousness-element, nor does the mind-consciousness-element occur immediately after visual consciousness, etc. Herein, it is proper that visual consciousness, etc., do not arise immediately after the mind-consciousness-element (i.e., bhavaṅga), and that auditory consciousness, etc., do not arise immediately after visual consciousness, etc., because they have different objects. But is it improper to say that the mind-consciousness-element does not arise immediately after visual consciousness, etc., given that investigating consciousness and visual consciousness, etc., have an identical object? No, it is not so, because it is established that those with determinate and indeterminate objects have different objective fields. And if some consciousness-element were to arise immediately after visual consciousness, etc., it too, by way of the door of seeing, etc., would be a visual consciousness-element, etc., itself, not the mind-consciousness-element. Consequently, just as what proceeds through the mind-door does not abandon its function of cognizing—which is thinking distinct from the function of seeing, etc.—so it would follow that the visual consciousness-element would not abandon its function of seeing. Similarly for the one subsequent to that; and because every consciousness-element would become a visual consciousness, the six consciousness-bodies would not exist.

Yathā pana manoviññāṇadhātānantaraṃ manodhātu, tato cakkhuviññāṇādīni, evaṃ dassanaviññāṇadhātānantaraṃ manodhātu, tato sotaviññāṇādīni hontīti ce? Na, manodhātuyā dassanadhātubhāvappasaṅgato. Yathā hi manaso nibbisesāvatthā mananamattatāya manodhātu, evaṃ dassanassa nibbisesāvatthā dassanamattatāya dassanadhātu siyā. Tañca cakkhūviññāṇaṃ rūpavisayanti saddādivisayābhogābhāvato savanaviññāṇādīnaṃ asambhavo. Tato ca rūpārammaṇapasutameva viññāṇaṃ siyā manoviññāṇānaṃ viya dassanaviññāṇādīnaṃ samānavatthubhāvappasaṅgato, aññavatthusannissitañca viññāṇaṃ na siyā, na cetaṃ yuttaṃ. Tasmā sukhadukkhānaṃ viya upekkhā cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ, manoviññāṇassa ca byavadhāyikā manodhātu daṭṭhabbā, na cassā upekkhāya viya adukkhamasukhatā adassanādiamananatā, ata kho mananakiccāvisesato manoviññāṇasabhāgatā. Mano hi hadayavatthumhi vattamāno aññavatthusannissitānaṃ viññāṇānaṃ visayaṃ dassetvā nivattamāno aggi viya usumamatte mananamatte ṭhatvā nivattati, aññavatthusannissitaviññāṇanirodhe ca uṭṭhahanto aggi viya usumamatte uṭṭhahati. Paccayānurūpapavattikāni ca mananamattāni manoviññāṇadhātuyā antāni honti. Paṭighasaññāsahagatānañhi pañcannaṃ viññāṇānaṃ indriyārammanapaṭighātajatāya abhinipātamattakiccaṃ, mananalakkhaṇindriyasamuppannassa ca manoviññāṇassa visayavicintanāsambhūtatāya tadanurūpācintanā. Tasmā abhinipātappaccayapaṭighaṭṭanānighaṃsabalena bhavaṅgalakkhaṇaṃ cittaṃ calanāvatthaṃ hutvā nivattamānaṃ cintanāvisesavirahato abhinipātānuguṇaṃ cintanāvasānaṃ mananamattaṃ uppādeti.

If it is said: Just as the mind-element arises immediately after the mind-consciousness-element, and from that, eye-consciousness and so on arise, so too, does the mind-element arise immediately after the seeing-consciousness-element, and from that, do ear-consciousness and so on arise? No, because of the consequence that the mind-element would become a seeing-element. For just as the mind-element is the undifferentiated state of the mind, by being mere cognizing, so a seeing-element would be the undifferentiated state of seeing, by being mere seeing. And that seeing-element would be eye-consciousness, having a form as its object; thus, due to the absence of adverting to objects such as sound, the arising of ear-consciousness and the others would be impossible. And from that, consciousness would be occupied only with a form-object, because of the consequence that seeing-consciousness and the others would have the same physical basis, like mind-consciousnesses. And there would be no consciousness dependent on another physical basis; and this is not proper. Therefore, the mind-element should be seen as intervening between eye-consciousness, etc., and mind-consciousness, just as equanimity intervenes for pleasant and painful feelings. And it is not, like equanimity, a state of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, nor is it non-seeing, non-cognizing, etc.; rather, it partakes of the nature of mind-consciousness because its function of cognizing is undifferentiated. For the mind, existing in the heart-base, having shown the object to consciousnesses dependent on other physical bases, withdraws; like a fire that remains as mere heat, it remains as mere cognizing and withdraws. And when the consciousnesses dependent on other physical bases cease, as it arises, it does so from a state of mere cognizing, just as a fire arises from a state of mere heat. And mere cognitions, which occur in conformity with their conditions, are the boundaries of the mind-consciousness-element. For the five consciousnesses accompanied by perception of resistance have the function of mere impact, since they are produced by the collision of faculty and object. But for mind-consciousness, which arises from the faculty characterized by cognizing, since it is produced from pondering an object, its function is a pondering suitable for that. Therefore, by the force of the collision that is the condition for impact, the citta with the characteristic of the life-continuum, having become a state of vibration and then ceasing, because of the absence of specific pondering, produces a mere cognizing that is in conformity with the impact and is the culmination of pondering.

Dassanādipi [M 2.0183] abhinipātamattaṃ dutiyaṃ khaṇaṃ anativattamānaṃ attānuguṇaṃ cintanāmananasamaññāvirahato dassanādiabhinipātavisesavicittaṃ cittabhāvādinā samānaṃ cintanādimananamattaṃ aññavatthusmiṃ nibbatteti, tasmā vatthukiccehi taṃ manoviññāṇakāyasaṅgahitāpi manodhātu manodvāranikkhamapavesabhūtā ārammaṇantare dvārantaramanasikāratabbisayasampaṭicchanabhāvena [V 2.0171] pañcannaṃ viññāṇadhātūnaṃ yathākkamaṃ purecarā, anucarāti ca vuttā. Sā panāyaṃ satipi viññāṇabhāve manaso sambhūya visiṭṭhamananakiccābhāvato dhātubhāvasāmaññena manomattā dhātu manodhātūti vuccati.

Seeing, etc., being a mere impact not transgressing the second moment, produces on another basis a mere cognizing, such as thinking, that is in conformity with itself, similar in being a citta, etc., variegated by the distinction of impact such as seeing, and is devoid of the designation 'thinking' and 'cognizing'. Therefore, that mind-element—although included in the mind-consciousness-group on account of its basis and functions, its having a similar nature, its being the place of cessation and arising, and its being the end and the beginning of that mind-consciousness—being the exit and entry point of the mind-door, is called the forerunner and follower, respectively, of the five consciousness-elements by way of being, in another object, the attention to another door and the reception of that door's object. But this, although it is a state of consciousness, is called the mind-element (manodhātu)—a mere mind, an element—by the general characteristic of being an element, and because, having arisen from the mind, it lacks a distinct function of cognizing.

Yathāvutteneva ca hetunā matta-saddalopaṃ katvā viññāṇaṭṭhayogato manomattaṃ viññāṇanti manoviññāṇakāyasaṅgahopi cassā yujjati eva. Aññaviññāṇehi pana dvārārammaṇehi ca visesanatthaṃ “manodhātū”ti vuttāti. Manoviññāṇadhātūti pana viññāṇadhātuvisesanaṃ manogahaṇaṃ. Dhātuvisesanatthe ca manoviññāṇaggahaṇe viññāṇavisesanaṃ dvārabhūtamanodassanamevāti dvārasamaññārahattā na manodhātūti vuccati. Tañhi manodvārantogadhaṃ, na ca dassanādipurecarānucaranti manaso viññāṇadhātu, manaso viññāṇanti ca manodvārasamaññārahaṃ, savisesañca tassa mananakiccaṃ, viññāṇakiccañcāti mattasaddassa lopamantarena “manoviññāṇa”nti, nijjīvabhāvavibhāvanatthaṃ “manoviññāṇadhātū”ti ca vuccatīti.

And for the very reason just stated, by eliding the word 'matta' and because of its connection with the meaning of 'consciousness' (viññāṇa), its inclusion in the mind-consciousness-group, by the etymology 'a mere mind is consciousness', is indeed justified. However, to distinguish it from other consciousnesses and from the door and its objects, it is called 'mind-element'. But in the term 'mind-consciousness-element', the inclusion of 'mano' is a qualifier of 'viññāṇadhātu'. And when 'manoviññāṇa' is taken to qualify 'dhātu', the qualification of 'viññāṇa' is simply the indication of the mind that has become a door. Thus, because it is worthy of the designation 'door', it is not called 'mind-element'. For that mind-consciousness is included within the mind-door, and it is not the forerunner and follower of seeing, etc. The consciousness-element of the mind, or consciousness of the mind, is worthy of the designation 'mind-door', and its function of cognizing and its function of special knowing are distinct. Therefore, without eliding the word 'matta', it is called 'mind-consciousness', and to show its nature as being without a living soul, it is called 'mind-consciousness-element'.

Sallamiva sūlamiva tividhadukkhatāsamāyogato daṭṭhabbo. Vedanāsallasūlayogāti vedanāsaṅkhātasallasūlayogato. Āturā viyāti tena āturibhūtā puggalā viya. Āsāyeva dukkhaṃ āsādukkhaṃ, āsāvighātaṃ dukkhaṃ vā. Saññā hi asubhādikampi subhādito sajjānantī āsaṃ, tassā ca vighātaṃ āsīsitasubhādiasiddhiyā janetīti. Vanamigo tiṇapurisaṃ purisoti gaṇhanto ayathābhūccanimittaggāhako, tathā saññāpīti āha “vanamigo viyā”ti. Kammapadhānā saṅkhārāti “paṭisandhiyaṃ pakkhipanato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Jātidukkhānubandhatoti attanā nibbattiyamānena jātidukkhena anubandhatā. Bhavapaccayā jāti hi jātidukkhanti. Padumaṃ viya dissamānaṃ khuracakkaṃ viya rūpampi [M 2.0184] itthiādibhāvena dissamānaṃ nānāvidhupaddavaṃ janeti. Sabbe anatthā rāgādayo, jātiādayo ca visayabhūtā, anupasantā, sappaṭibhayā cāti. Tappaṭipakkhabhūtattā asaṅkhatā dhātu amatādito daṭṭhabbā.

It should be seen as like a dart and like a stake because of its connection with the threefold suffering. 'Connection to the dart and stake of feeling' means connection to the dart and stake designated as feeling. 'Like the afflicted' means like persons who have become afflicted by it. Craving itself is suffering, thus 'suffering of craving'; or the frustration of craving is suffering. For perception, by perceiving even the unattractive, etc., as attractive, etc., generates craving, and it generates the frustration of that craving through the non-attainment of the wished-for attractive, etc. A forest deer, taking a scarecrow for a man, is a grasper of a false sign; so too is perception. Thus he said, 'like a forest deer.' 'Formations have kamma as their chief' is said because 'it casts one into rebirth,' etc. 'Bound by the suffering of birth' means being bound by the suffering of birth that is produced by them. For birth conditioned by becoming is the suffering of birth. Just as a razor-wheel appearing like a lotus generates various calamities, so too a visible form appearing as a woman, etc., generates various calamities. All calamities—lust, etc., and birth, etc.—are like poison, unpeaceful, and fraught with peril. Because it is their opposite, the unconditioned element should be seen as the deathless, etc.

Vavatthānābhāvo “idameva imassa ārammaṇa”nti niyamābhāvo, tena yathā araññamakkaṭo kenaci anivārito gahitaṃ ekaṃ rukkhasākhaṃ muñcitvā aññaṃ gaṇhāti, tampi muñcitvā aññanti katthaci anavaṭṭhito paribbhamati, evaṃ gahitaṃ ekaṃ ārammaṇaṃ muñcitvā aññaṃ, tampi muñcitvā aññanti anavaṭṭhitatā, ārammaṇaṃ aggahetvā pavattituṃ asamatthatā ca makkaṭasamānatāti [V 2.0172] dasseti. Aṭṭhivedhaviddhopi uppathaṃ anugacchanto duṭṭhasso assakhaḷuṅko. Yatthakāmanipātitoti yattha katthaci icchitārammaṇe nipātibhāvato. Nānāvesadhārī raṅganaṭo.

'Absence of stability' is the absence of a fixed rule, 'This alone is its object.' Thereby he shows its similarity to a monkey: just as a forest monkey, unrestrained by anyone, releases a branch it has grasped and grabs another, and releasing that too grabs another, wandering about without settling anywhere, so too its unsettledness consists in releasing one object it has grasped and grabbing another, and releasing that too and grabbing another; and its inability to proceed without grasping an object. A vicious horse, an unruly colt, that follows a wrong path even when pierced by a bone-piercing goad. 'Falling wherever it wishes' means because of its nature of falling upon any desired object whatsoever. An actor on a stage wearing various guises.

Āyatanadātuniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the bases and elements is finished.

Iti pannarasamaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus the commentary on the fifteenth chapter.

16. Indriyasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā

16. Commentary on the Exposition of the Faculties and Truths

Indriyavitthārakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Detailed Discourse on the Faculties

525. Bāvīsatīti [M 2.0185][V 2.0173] gaṇanaparicchedo. Indriyānīti paricchinnadhammanidassanaṃ. Cakkhundriyantiādi tesaṃ sarūpadassanaṃ. Tattha cakkhudvāre indaṭṭhaṃ kāreti cakkhudvārabhāve taṃdvārikehi attano indabhāvaṃ paramissarabhāvaṃ kārayatīti cakkhundriyaṃ. Tañhi te rūpaggahaṇe attānaṃ anuvatteti, te ca taṃ anuvattanti. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Tasmā sotaghānajivhākāyadvāre indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti. Kāyindriyaṃ. Vijānanalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti manindriyaṃ. Itthibhāvalakkhaṇe, parisabhāvalakkhaṇe, anupālanalakkhaṇe, sukhalakkhaṇe, dukkhalakkhaṇe, somanassalakkhaṇe, domanassalakkhaṇe, upekkhālakkhaṇe, adhimokkhalakkhaṇe, paggahalakkhaṇe, upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇe, avikkhepalakkhaṇe, dassanalakkhaṇe, anaññātaṃ ñassāmīti pavatte jānanalakkhaṇe, ñātānaṃ eva dhammānaṃ puna ājānane aññātāvibhāve indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti aññātāvindriyaṃ.

525. “Twenty-two” is the enumeration. “Faculties” is the indication of the delimited phenomena. “The eye faculty” and so forth is the demonstration of their individual natures. Therein, at the eye-door, it causes dominance; in its state as the eye-door, it brings about its own dominance, its supreme lordship, over what is dependent on that door—thus, it is the eye faculty. For in the grasping of forms, it makes them conform to it, and they conform to it. This same method applies to the rest. Therefore, at the ear, nose, tongue, and body doors, it causes dominance—thus, the body faculty. In the characteristic of cognizing, it causes dominance—thus, the mind faculty. In the characteristic of femaleness, the characteristic of maleness, the characteristic of sustaining life, the characteristic of pleasure, the characteristic of pain, the characteristic of joy, the characteristic of sorrow, the characteristic of equanimity, the characteristic of resolution, the characteristic of exertion, the characteristic of mindfulness, the characteristic of non-distraction, the characteristic of seeing, in the characteristic of knowing that occurs as “I shall know the unknown,” in the re-knowing of those very phenomena that have been known, and in the state of one who has final knowledge, it causes dominance—thus, the faculty of one who has final knowledge.

Vijāniyāti vijāneyya. Bhūmito cāti ca-saddo avuttasampipaṇḍanattho, tena tāvatvaṃ saṅgaṇhāti, taṃ pana tāvatvaṃ parato vaṇṇayissāma. Asammasanupagānampi atthibhāvato daṭṭhabbatā idha na gahitā.

“One should know” means one should know. In “And from the ground,” the word “and” has the meaning of gathering together what has not been said; by it, it includes “that much-ness.” But we will explain that “that much-ness” later. The state of being what should be seen is not taken up here simply because of the existence of those [faculties] that have not been reached by comprehension.

Pubbabhāgeti ariyamaggato pubbabhāge. Anaññātanti na aññātaṃ na adhigataṃ. Niccatāya natthi etassa mataṃ bhaṅgo, na vā etasmiṃ adhigate maraṇanti amataṃ, pajjitabbato padañcāti amatapadaṃ nibbānaṃ. “Evaṃ paṭipannassa uppajjanato”ti etena pubbabhāgavasenetaṃ indriyaṃ evaṃ voharīyatīti dasseti. Ājānanatoti paṭhamamaggena diṭṭhamariyādaṃ anatikkamitvāva jānanato. Yena taṃsamaṅgipuggalo, taṃsampayuttadhammā vā aññātāvino honti[V 2.0174], so aññātāvibhāvo pariniṭṭhitakiccajānanakhīṇāsavassa bhāvabhūto hutvā uppattito “khīṇāsavassa uppajjanato”ti vuttaṃ.

“In the preliminary stage” means in the stage prior to the noble path. “The unknown” means not known, not realized. Because of its permanence, for this there is no death or destruction; or, since on attaining it there is no death, it is the deathless; and since it is a state to be attained, it is the deathless state, Nibbāna. By “From the arising for one who practices thus,” it shows that this faculty is so designated on account of the preliminary stage. “From knowing” means from knowing without transgressing the boundary seen with the first path. Because by this the person endowed with it, or the states associated with it, become those who have known, that state of one who has known, having become the very nature of an Arahant whose task of knowing is finished and whose taints are destroyed, is so called from its arising. Thus, it is said, “from the arising for one whose taints are destroyed.”

Liṅgeti gameti ñāpetīti liṅgaṃ, liṅgīyati vā etenāti liṅgaṃ. Kiṃ liṅgeti, kiṃ vā liṅgīyatīti? Indaṃ, indo vā. Indassa liṅga indaliṅgaṃ, indaliṅgassa attho taṃsabhāvo indaliṅgaṭṭho, indaliṅgameva vā indriyasaddassa [M 2.0186] atthoti indaliṅgaṭṭho. Sajjitaṃ uppāditanti siṭṭhaṃ, indena siṭṭhaṃ indasiṭṭhaṃ. Juṭṭhaṃ sevitaṃ. Kammasaṅkhātassa indassa liṅgāni, tena ca siṭṭhānīti kammajāneva yojetabbāni, na aññāni, te ca dve atthā kamme eva yojetabbā, itare ca bhagavati evāti āha “yathāyoga”nti. Tenāti bhagavato, kammassa ca indattā. Etthāti etesu indriyesu. Ulliṅgenti ñāpenti pakāsenti phalasampattivipattīhi kāraṇasampattivipattiavabodhato. “So taṃ nimittaṃ āsevatī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 9.35) gocarakaraṇampi āsevanā vuttāti āha “kānici gocarāsevanāyā”ti. Tattha sabbesaṃ gocarikātabbattepi “kānicī”ti vacanaṃ avipassitabbānaṃ bahulaṃ manasikaraṇena anāsevanīyattā. Paccavekkhanāmattameva hi tesu hotīti. “Tassa taṃ maggaṃ āsevato”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.170) bhāvanā āsevanāti vuttāti bhāvetabbāni saddhādīni sandhāyāha “kānici bhāvanāsevanāyā”ti.

It makes known, thus it is a 'sign.' Or, by this it is indicated, thus it is a 'sign.' What does it make known, or what is indicated by it? Inda, or inda. The sign of inda is indaliṅga. The meaning of indaliṅga is its own nature; or indaliṅga itself is the meaning of the word 'faculty'; thus, the meaning is 'the sign of inda.' 'Prepared' or 'produced' means 'created'; created by inda is indasiṭṭha. 'Frequented' means 'cultivated.' The signs of inda designated as kamma, and those created by it, are to be connected only with what is kamma-born, not with others. And those two meanings should be connected to kamma alone, while the others are to be connected to the Blessed One alone, thus he said: 'according to what is applicable.' 'By that' means because of the lordship of the Blessed One and of kamma. 'Herein' means in these faculties. They indicate, make known, or reveal through the success and failure of the fruit, from understanding the success and failure of the cause. In passages such as 'he cultivates that sign' (AN 9.35), making something an object is also called 'cultivation,' hence it is said: 'some by way of cultivating an object.' Therein, although all could be made objects, the word 'some' is used because things that should not be contemplated by insight should not be cultivated by frequent attention. For in their case there is only mere reviewing. In passages such as 'as he cultivates that path' (AN 4.170), development is called 'cultivation,' hence, referring to faith and so on which are to be developed, it is said: 'some by way of cultivating through development.'

Ādhipaccaṃ indriyapaccayabhāvo. Asatipi ca indriyapaccayabhāve itthipurisindriyānaṃ, attano attano paccayavasena pavattamāne taṃsahitasantāne aññākārena appavattamānehi liṅgādīhi anuvattanīyabhāve ādhipaccaṃ. Imasmiṃ ca atthe indanti parimissariyaṃ karonticceva indriyāni. Cakkhādīsu dassitena nayena aññesañca jīvitādīnaṃ tadanuvattīsu ādhipaccaṃ yathārahaṃ yojetabbaṃ.

Lordship is the state of being a faculty-condition. Even when there is no faculty-condition in the case of the feminine and masculine faculties, lordship consists in this: in the associated continuum, which proceeds by way of its own respective conditions, the characteristics, signs, and so on, which do not proceed in another way, must be conformed to. And in this sense, because they exercise supreme lordship, they are indeed faculties. In the way shown for the eye faculty and so on, the lordship of the others, such as the life faculty and so on, should be applied appropriately in regard to the phenomena that conform to them.

Amohoyeva na visuṃ cattāro dhammā, tasmā tassa saṅkhārakkhandhakathāyaṃ vibhāvitāni lakkhaṇādīni tesañca veditabbānīti adhippāyo. Sesāni tattha khandhaniddese lakkhaṇādīhi arūpeneva āgatāni.

It is only non-delusion; the four states are not separate. Therefore, the meaning is that the characteristics and so forth explained for it in the discourse on the aggregate of formations are to be understood for those four faculties as well. The remaining faculties, in the exposition of the aggregates there, are presented by their own nature only, along with their characteristics and so forth.

526. Sattānaṃ ariyabhūmipaṭilābho bhagavato desanāya sādhāraṇaṃ, padānañca payojananti [V 2.0175] āha “ajjhattadhamme pariññāyā”tiādi. Aññesampi indriyānaṃ attabhāvapariyāpannatāya satipi attabhāvapaññāpanāya mūlabhāvato cakkhādīnaṃ sātisayā attabhāvapariyāpannāti vuttaṃ “attabhāvapariyāpannāni cakkhundiyādīnī”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 219). Abhidhammaṭṭhakathāyaṃ itthipurisindriyānantaraṃ jīvitindriyadesanākkamo vuttoti [M 2.0187] idhāpi “tato jīvitindriya”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ indriyayamakadesanāya (yama. 3.indriyayamaka.1 ādayo) sameti. Indriyavibhaṅge (vibha. 219 ādayo) pana manindriyānantaraṃ jīvitindriyaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ purimapacchimānaṃ ajjhāttikabāhirānaṃ anupālakabhāvadīpanatthaṃ tesa majjhe vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Yañca kiñci vedayitaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ. Yāva ca duvidhattabhāvānupālakassa jīvitindriyassa pavatti, tāva dukkhabhūtānaṃ etesaṃ vedayitānaṃ anivattīti ñāpanatthaṃ, tena ca cakkhādīnaṃ dukkhānubandhatāya pariññeyyataṃ ñāpeti. Paṭipattidassanatthanti pubbabhāgapaṭipattidassanatthaṃ. Tassevāti anaññātaññassāmītindriyasseva. Tato anantaraṃ bhāvetabbattāti bhāvanāmaggasampayuttaṃ aññindriyaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Dassanāntarā hi bhāvanāti.

526. The attainment of the noble plane by beings is a common and primary purpose of the Blessed One’s teaching; therefore, he said, “for the full understanding of internal phenomena,” and so on. Although other faculties are also included in the individual existence, because they are the root for the designation of individual existence, the inclusion of the eye faculty and others in the individual existence is pre-eminent; thus it is said: “The eye faculty and others are included in the individual existence.” In the Abhidhamma Commentary, the order of exposition places the life faculty immediately after the feminine and masculine faculties, hence here too it is said, “Then the life faculty.” This agrees with the exposition in the Indriya Yamaka. In the Indriya Vibhaṅga, however, the life faculty is stated after the mind faculty. This should be understood as being placed in the middle of them to show its role as sustainer of the preceding internal and following external faculties. And whatever feeling is felt, all that is suffering. This is to make known that for as long as the life faculty—which sustains the twofold existence—continues, for so long there is no cessation of these feelings which have become suffering. And by that, it makes known that the eye faculty, etc., are to be fully understood because they are bound up with suffering. “For the purpose of showing the practice” means for the purpose of showing the preliminary-stage practice. “Of that very one” means of the faculty “I shall know the unknown” itself. “Because it is to be developed immediately after that” is said with reference to the faculty of knowledge associated with the path of development. For development is immediately after seeing.

Bhedoti idha sabhāvato bhedo adhippeto, na bhūmipuggalādivasenāti āha “sesānaṃ abhedo”ti. Nanu ca jīvitindriyassa anupālanalakkhaṇaṃ sabhāvo, tenassa duvidhassāpi abhedoti? Saccametaṃ, tassa pana rūpārūpasabhāvakato bhedo gahito, na evaṃ sesānaṃ koci bhedo atthīti tesaṃ abhedoti bhedābhāvo vutto. Nanu cettha vedanā, paññā ca bhinditvā vuttāti? Na, yathā desitesu bāvīsatiyā indriyesu bhedābhedassa adhippetattā.

“Division” here is intended as division by nature, not by way of plane, person, etc.; therefore, it is said, “the rest are without division.” But is not the characteristic of the life faculty sustaining, which is its nature? By that, is there not non-division for it, even though it is of two kinds? This is true. However, its division is taken as that made by its material and immaterial nature. Since no such division exists for the rest, their “non-division” is stated, meaning the absence of division. But are not feeling and wisdom spoken of here as divided? No, because division and non-division are intended with respect to the twenty-two faculties as they have been taught.

527. Cakkhundriyādīnaṃ satipi purejātādipaccayabhāve indriyapaccayabhāvena sādhetabbameva kiccaṃ kiccanti vuttaṃ tassa anaññasādhāraṇattā, indriyakathāya ca adhikatattā. Attano tikkhamandādiākāro attākāro, tassa anuvattāpanaṃ attākārānuvattāpanaṃ. Tenāha “tikkhamandādisaṅkhātaattākārānuvattāpana”nti. Atha vā tikkhamandādisaṅkhātassa ca attākārassa ca anuvattāpanaṃ tikkha…pe… vattāpanaṃ. Visuṃ attākāraggahaṇena cettha rūpāvabhāsanādikassa saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Cakkhundriyassa hi rūpābhihananayogyatāsaṅkhāte rūpāvabhāsanasāmatthiye asati na kadācipi cakkhuviññāṇassa dassanakiccaṃ sambhavati. Esa nayo sotindriyādīsupi. Pubbaṅgamabhāvena manindriyassa vasāvattāpanaṃ hoti, na aññesaṃ. Taṃsampayuttānipi hi indriyāni tabbaseneva hutvā attano attano indriyakiccaṃ sādhenti cetasikabhāvato[V 2.0176], na tesaṃ vasena manindriyaṃ[M 2.0188]. Ayañhissa pubbaṅgamatā. Sabbattha ca indriyapaccayabhāvena sādhetabbanti adhikāro anuvattatīti daṭṭhabbo. Satipi anuppādane, anupatthambhane ca tappaccayānaṃ tappavattane nimittabhāvo anuvidhānaṃ.

527. Regarding the eye faculty and so on, although they can be conditions such as prenascent condition, it is said that their function is what must be accomplished by the faculty-condition, because this is not shared with others and because it is the principal topic in the discourse on faculties. One's own mode is the mode of sharpness, dullness, etc.; causing conformity to that is “causing conformity to one's own mode.” Hence it is said: “causing conformity to one's own mode, designated as sharpness, dullness, etc.” Alternatively, it is the causing of conformity to the mode designated as sharpness, dullness, etc., and to one's own mode. Here, by the separate mention of “one's own mode,” the inclusion of such things as the illumination of form should be understood. For if the eye faculty lacks the capacity to illuminate form—designated as the suitability for being impacted by form—the seeing function of eye-consciousness can never occur. This same method applies to the ear faculty and so on. By being the forerunner, the mind faculty brings associated states under its control, not the others. For even the faculties associated with it, being under its sway, accomplish their own respective faculty-functions because they are mental factors; the mind faculty is not under their sway. This is its forerunnership. And it should be understood that the governing rule “is to be accomplished by the faculty-condition” applies everywhere. Even when there is no production and no support, compliance is being a sign for the occurrence of those things that are conditioned by it.

Chādetvā pharitvā uppajjamānā sukhadukkhavedanā sahajātadhamme abhibhavitvā ajjottharitvā sayameva pākaṭā hoti, sahajātadhammā ca tassā vasena sukhadukkhabāvappatā viya hontīti āha “yathāsakaṃ oḷārikākārānupāpana”nti. Asantassa, apaṇītassapi akusalatabbipākādisampayuttassa yathārahaṃ majjhattākārānupāpanaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Samānajātiyehi vā sukhadukkhehi santapaṇītākārānupāpanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Paṭipakkhābhibhavananti assaddhiyādipaṭipakkhābhibhavanaṃ. Pasannākārādāti pasannapaggahitaupaṭṭhitasamāhitadassanākārānupāpanaṃ yathākkamaṃ saddhādīnaṃ. Byāpādādīti ādi-saddena uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni gahitāni. Maggasampayuttasseva ca aññindriyassa kiccaṃ dassitaṃ. Teneva ca phalasampayuttassa taṃtaṃsaṃyojanappaṭippassaddhipahānakiccatā dassitā hotīti. Katasabbakiccassa aññātāvindriyaṃ aññassa kātabbassa abhāvā amatābhimukhameva tabbhāvapaccayo ca hoti, na itarāni viya kiccantarapasutaṃ. Tenāha “amatābhimukhabhāvapaccayatā cā”ti.

Having covered and pervaded, the arising pleasant and painful feeling, by overcoming and overwhelming its co-arisen states, becomes manifest by itself, and the co-arisen states, through its influence, seem to attain the state of pleasure and pain. Thus it is said: 'the causing to assume a gross aspect according to their respective natures.' For that which is not calm, not refined, and associated with the unwholesome and its resultants, etc., the causing to assume a neutral aspect should be applied as is appropriate. Or, in comparison with pleasure and pain of a similar kind, the causing to assume a calm and refined aspect should be understood. 'Overcoming the opposition' means overcoming opposition such as lack of faith, etc. 'Through the aspect of confidence, etc.' means the causing to assume the aspects of confidence, exertion, establishment, concentration, and seeing, respectively, for faith and the other faculties. 'By ill will, etc.': by the word 'etc.' the higher fetters are included. And the function of the faculty of knowledge is shown only when it is associated with the path. And thereby, for that which is associated with the fruit, the function of abandoning each particular fetter by way of calming it is shown. For one for whom all tasks have been completed, the faculty of one who has final knowledge, because there is no other task to be done, is indeed facing the deathless and is a condition for that state; it is not, like the others, engaged in some other task. Therefore, it is said, 'and its being a condition for the state of facing the deathless.'

528. Bhūmito vinicchayo uttānattho eva. Etthāha – kasmā pana ettakeneva indriyāni vuttāni, etāni eva ca vuttānīti? Ādhipaccaṭṭhavasena, ādhipaccaṃ nāma issariyanti vuttamevetaṃ. Tayidaṃ ādhipaccaṃ attano attano kicce, phale cāti aññesampi sabhāvadhammānaṃ kasmā na labbhati? Paccayādhīnavuttikā hi paccayuppannāti siyā phalahetudhammesu anuvattanānuvattanīyatāti? Saccametaṃ, tathāpi atthi tesaṃ viseso. Svāyaṃ “cakkhuviññāṇādippavattiyañhi cakkhādīnaṃ siddhamādhipacca”ntiādinā (vibha. aṭṭha. 219) aṭṭhakathāyaṃ dassitoyeva. Apica khandhapañcake yāyaṃ sattapaññatti, tassā visesanissayo “cha ajjhattikāni āyatanānī”ti tāni tāva ādhipaccattaṃ upādāya “cakkhundriyaṃ…pe…manindriya”ntiādito (vibha. 219) vuttāni. Svāyaṃ attabhāvo imesaṃ vasena “itthī puriso”ti samaññaṃ labhatīti dassanatthaṃ [M 2.0189] bhāvadvayaṃ. Tayime upādinnadhammā yena dhammena pavattanti, ayaṃ so dhammo tesaṃ ṭhitihetūti dassanatthaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ. Svāyaṃ sattasaññito dhammapuñjo pabandhavasena pavattamāno imāhi vedanāhi saṃkilissatīti [V 2.0177] dassanatthaṃ vedanāpañcakaṃ. Tato visuddhikāmānaṃ vodānasambhāradassanatthaṃ saddhādipañcakaṃ. Sambhavavodānasambhārā imehi visujjanti, visuddhippattā niṭṭhitakiccāva hontīti dassanatthaṃ anaññātaññassāmītindriyādīni tīṇi vuttāni. Sabbattha “ādhipaccattaṃ upādāyā”ti padaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Ettāvatā adhippetatthasiddhīti aññesaṃ aggahaṇaṃ.

528. The analysis by way of planes is plain in meaning. Here it is asked: But why are just these faculties mentioned, and why are only these mentioned? Because of their meaning of dominance. Dominance means sovereignty; this has already been said. Why is this dominance in their respective functions and results not obtained by other phenomena with an intrinsic nature? Is it because conditionally arisen phenomena have a dependent occurrence, so that in the case of phenomena that are causes and effects there is a relationship of conforming and being conformed to? This is true, yet there is a distinction among them. This is shown in the commentary by the passage beginning: 'For in the occurrence of eye-consciousness, etc., the dominance of the eye, etc., is established.' Moreover, in the five aggregates, the designation 'a being' has as its particular basis the 'six internal bases.' These are mentioned first, taking dominance as the basis, as 'the eye faculty... to... the mind faculty.' To show that this individual existence acquires the designations 'woman' or 'man' by means of these, the two sex faculties are mentioned. To show that these clung-to phenomena proceed by means of a certain state, and that this state is the cause of their stability, the life faculty is mentioned. To show that this mass of phenomena designated as 'a being,' proceeding by way of continuity, is defiled by these feelings, the five feeling faculties are mentioned. Then, for those desiring purification, to show the requisites for purification, the five faculties beginning with faith are mentioned. To show that persons who have accumulated the requisites for purification are purified by means of these, and that having attained purification, they have completed their task, the three faculties beginning with the faculty 'I shall come to know the unknown' are mentioned. In all cases, the phrase 'taking dominance as the basis' should be applied. Since the intended meaning is accomplished by this much, others are not included.

Atha vā pavattinivattīnaṃ nissarādidassanattampi etāniyeva vuttāni. Pavattiyā hi visesato mūlanissayabhūtāni cha ajjhattikāyatanāni. Yathāha “chasu loko samuppanno”tiādi (su. ni. 171). Tassa uppatti itthipurisindriyehi visabhāgavatthusarāganimittehi yebhuyyena sattakāyassa abhinibbatti. Vuttañhetaṃ “tiṇṇaṃ kho, mahārāja, sannipātā gabbhassa avakkanti hoti mātā ca utunī hoti, gandhabbo ca paccupaṭṭhito hoti, mātāpitaro ca sannipatitā hontī”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.408; mi. pa. 4.1.6). Avaṭṭhānaṃ jīvitindriyena tena anupāletabbato. Tenāha “āyu ṭhiti yapanā yāpanā”tiādi (dha. sa. 19). Upabhogo vedanāhi. Vedanāvasena hi iṭṭhādisabbavisayūpabhogo. Yathāha “vedayati vedayatīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā vedanāti vuccatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.450). Evaṃ pavattiyā nissayasamuppādaṭṭhitisambhogadassanattaṃ cakkhundriyaṃ yāva upekkhindriyanti cuddasindriyāni desitāni. Yathā cetāni pavattiyā, evaṃ itarāni nivattiyā. Vivaṭṭasannissitena hi nibbattitāni saddhādīni pañcindriyāni nivattiyā nissayo. Uppādo anaññātaññassāmītindriyena tassa nivattivasena paṭhamaṃ uppajjanato. Avaṭṭhānaṃ aññindriyena, upabhogo aññātāvindriyena aggaphalasamupabhogato. Khīṇāsavāhi visavitāya nibbutisukhaṃ paribhujjanti. Evampi etāni eva indriyāni desitāni. Ettāvatā yathādhippetatthasiddhito aññesaṃ aggahaṇaṃ. Imināva nesaṃ desanākkamopi saṃvaṇṇitoti veditabboti.

Or, these very faculties are stated also for the purpose of showing the dependence, etc., of continuance and discontinuance. Indeed, for continuance, the six internal sense bases are especially the root-support. As it is said: 'In the six, the world has arisen,' etc. Its origination is through the female and male faculties; indeed, the production of the aggregate of beings is for the most part caused by intense lust for a dissimilar object. And this was stated: 'Great king, from the conjunction of three things the descent of an embryo occurs: the mother is in season, the gandhabba is present, and the parents are in union,' etc. Its stability is through the life faculty, because it must be maintained by that. Therefore, He said: 'Life-span, stability, subsistence, continuance,' etc. Its enjoyment is through feelings. Indeed, it is by way of feeling that there is enjoyment of all objects, desirable and so on. As it is said: 'It feels, it feels, O bhikkhus, therefore it is called feeling.' Thus, to show the support, origination, stability, and enjoyment of continuance, the fourteen faculties from the eye faculty up to the equanimity faculty are taught. And just as these pertain to continuance, so the others pertain to discontinuance. Indeed, the five faculties beginning with faith, produced by one who is dependent on the rolling back of saṃsāra, are the support for discontinuance. The arising is through the faculty 'I shall come to know the unknown,' because it arises first by way of discontinuance. The stability is through the faculty of final knowledge, and the enjoyment is through the faculty of one who has final knowledge, because of the full enjoyment of the highest fruit. Indeed, those whose taints are destroyed enjoy the bliss of quenching through their mastery. In this way too, these very faculties are taught. Since the intended meaning is accomplished by this much, others are not included. And by this, the order of their exposition is also explained. Thus it should be understood.

Indriyaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Exposition of the Faculties is finished.

Saccavitthārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse Expanding on the Truths

529. Ariyasaddena [M 2.0190][V 2.0178] visesanaṃ akatvā kevalaṃ saccasaddena uddhiṭṭhānipi ariyasaccāni evāti dassento “saccānīti cattāri ariyasaccānī”ti āda. Samāññajotanā hi visese avatiṭṭhati, visesatthinā ca viseso anupayujjitabboti. Ariyasaccesu vā vicāritesu itarānipi atthato vicāritāneva hontīti vipassanāya ca bhūmibhūtāni, ariyasaccānevāti ca katvā “saccānī”ti uddharitvāpi “cattāri ariyasaccānī”ti vuttaṃ.

529. To show that even when they are designated simply by the word 'truth', without the qualification 'noble', they are still the noble truths, it is said: 'The truths are the four noble truths.' For a general designation rests on the specific, and by one who intends the specific, the specific is to be applied. Alternatively, when the noble truths are investigated, the other truths are also investigated in principle. And because they are the ground for insight and are indeed the noble truths, having designated them generally as 'truths,' it is then said, 'the four noble truths.'

Sāsanakkamoti ariyasaccāni vuccanti, ariyasaccadesanā vā. Sakalañhi sāsanaṃ bhagavato vacanaṃ saccavinimuttaṃ natthi pavattinivattitadubhayahetusandassanavasena pavattanato. Tasmā saccesu kamati, sīlasamādhipaññāsaṅkhātaṃ vā sāsanaṃ etesu kamati, pariññādikiccasādhanavasena pavattati, tasmā kamati etthāti kamo, kiṃ kamati? Sāsanaṃ. Sāsanassa kamo “sāsanakkamo”ti saccāni sāsanappavattiṭṭhānāni vuccanti, taṃdesanā ca tabbohārenāti.

By 'the course of the Teaching' are meant the noble truths, or the exposition of the noble truths. For the entire Teaching, the word of the Blessed One, is not apart from the truths, as it proceeds by way of showing the causes for both continuance and discontinuance. Therefore, it pertains to the truths. Or, the Teaching—designated as virtue, concentration, and wisdom—pertains to these, proceeding by way of accomplishing the tasks of full understanding and so on. Therefore, because it proceeds herein, it is the 'course.' What proceeds? The Teaching. The course of the Teaching is 'the course of the Teaching.' Thus the truths are called the established ground for the proceeding of the Teaching, and their exposition is also called by that designation.

Tathāti taṃsabhāvā dukkhādisabhāvā. Avitathāti amusāsabhāvā bādhanādibhāvena bhūtasabhāvā. Anaññathāti aññākārarahitā abādhanādiākāravivittā. Dukkhadukkhatātannimittatāhi adhiṭṭhitattā pīḷanaṭṭho. Samecca sambhūya paccayehi katabhāvo saṅkhataṭṭho. Dukkhadukkhatātannimittatāhi paridahanaṃ, kilesadāhasamāyogo vā santāpaṭṭho. Jarāya, maraṇena cāti dvedā vipariṇāmetabbatā vipariṇāmaṭṭho. Ettha ca pīḷanaṭṭho dukkhassa saraseneva āvibhavanākāro, itare yathākkamaṃ samudayamagganirodhadassanehi āvibhavanākārāti ayaṃ catunnampi viseso. Tatratrābhinandanavasena byāpitvā ūhanaṃ rāsikaraṇaṃ dukkhassa nibbattanaṃ āyūhanaṃ ākārassa byāpanatthattā. Āgacchati samudayatoti vā āyaṃ, dukkhaṃ, tassa ūhanaṃ pavattanaṃ āyūhanaṃ, ayaṃ saraseneva āvibhavanākāro. Nidadāti dukkhanti nidānaṃ, “idaṃ taṃ dukkha”nti sampaṭicchāpentaṃ viya samuṭṭhāpetīti attho. Ayaṃ nidānaṭṭho dukkhadassanena āvibhavanākāro. Saṃsāradukkhena saṃyojanaṃ saṃyogaṭṭho[M 2.0191]. Maggādhigamananivāraṇaṃ palibodhaṭṭho. Ime ca saṃyogapalibodhaṭṭhā nirodhamaggadassanehi āvibhavanākārā. Nissaranti sattā ettha, sayameva vā nissaṭaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ sabbasaṅkhatehi sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggabhāvatoti nissaranaṃ. Ayamassa [V 2.0179] sabhāvena āvibhavanākāro, itare vivekāsaṅkhātāmataṭṭā, samudayakkharaapaccayaavināsitā vā samudayamaggadukkhadassanena āvibhavanākārā.

'Such' means having that nature, the nature of suffering and so on. 'Unerring' means not having a false nature, having a real nature by way of being an affliction and so on. 'Unalterable' means devoid of another mode, free from a mode of non-affliction and so on. Because it is established by the state of suffering as suffering and the state of being its cause, its meaning is oppression. Because it is made by conditions that have come together and combined, its meaning is conditioned. The burning all around by the state of suffering as suffering and the state of being its cause—or the connection with the heat of the defilements—is the meaning of torment. The liability to be changed in two ways, by aging and death, is the meaning of change. Herein, the meaning of oppression is the mode of manifestation of suffering through its own essence alone, while the others are modes of manifestation in sequence through seeing the origin, the path, and cessation. This is the distinction among the four. Accumulation (āyūhana) is the generation of suffering, the heaping up by spreading out through delighting in this and that; this is because the prefix 'ā' has the meaning of 'pervading'. Or, because 'it comes' (āgacchati) 'from the origin' (samudayato), it is an 'income' (āya), which is suffering. The accumulation (ūhana) and bringing forth (pavattana) of that 'income' is 'accumulation' (āyūhana). This is a mode of manifestation through its own essence alone. 'It lays down suffering,' thus it is a 'source'; the meaning is that it makes it arise as if causing one to accept, 'This is that suffering.' This meaning of source is a mode of manifestation through seeing suffering. The 'bondage' is the yoking with the suffering of saṃsāra. The 'obstruction' is the prevention of the attainment of the path. These meanings of bondage and obstruction are modes of manifestation through seeing cessation and the path. 'Beings escape from this,' thus it is an 'escape'; or it is itself escaped, disconnected from all conditioned things, because it is the state of relinquishing all acquisitions. This is its mode of manifestation through its own nature. The others—the meanings of seclusion, the unconditioned, and the deathless, or the destruction of the origin, being without a cause, and indestructibility—are modes of manifestation through seeing the origin, the path, and suffering.

Saṃsārato niggamanaṃ niyyānaṃ. Ayamassa sarasena āvibhavanākāro. Paribodhūpacchedanena nibbānādhigamova nibbānanimittattā maggassa hetuṭṭho. Paññāpadhānattā cassa nibbānadassanaṃ, catusaccadassanaṃ vā dassanaṭṭho. Catusaccadassane, kilesadukkhasantāpavūpasamane ca ādhipaccaṃ karonti maggadhammā sampayuttadhammesūti so maggassa ādhipateyyaṭṭho. Visesato vā ālambanādhipatibhūtā maggadhammā honti “maggādhipatino”ti (dha. sa. tikamātikā 16) vacanatoti so tesaṃ ākāro ādhipateyyaṭṭho. Ete hetudassanādhipateyyaṭṭhā samudayanirodhadukkhadassanehi āvibhavanākārā. Evamādi āhāti sambandho. Abhisamayaṭṭhoti abhisametabbaṭṭho. Abhisamayassa vā visayabhūto attho abhisamayaṭṭho. Atha vā abhisamayassa pavattiākāro abhisamayaṭṭho. So cettha abhisametabbena pīḷanādinā dassitoti daṭṭhabbo.

The going out from saṃsāra is the 'leading out.' This is its mode of manifestation through its own essence. The attainment of Nibbāna by cutting off the obstructions is the 'cause' meaning of the path, because it is the condition for Nibbāna. Furthermore, because wisdom is predominant, the seeing of Nibbāna, or the seeing of the four truths, is its 'seeing' meaning. In the seeing of the four truths and in the pacifying of the torment of defilements and suffering, the path factors exercise sovereignty over the associated states; thus that is the 'sovereignty' meaning of the path. Or specifically, the path factors become a dominant object, because of the statement 'those having the path as sovereign' (Dhs. Tikamātikā 16); thus that mode of theirs is the 'sovereignty' meaning. These meanings—cause, seeing, and sovereignty—are modes of manifestation through seeing the origin, cessation, and suffering. 'Thus he said, and so on'—this is the connection. The 'meaning of comprehension' is 'that which is to be comprehended.' Or, the meaning that is the objective field of comprehension is the 'meaning of comprehension.' Or again, the mode of occurrence of comprehension is the 'meaning of comprehension.' And this should be seen here as shown by that which is to be comprehended, such as oppression and so on.

530. Kucchitaṃ khaṃ dukkhaṃ, gārayhaṃ hutvā asāranti attho.

530. The despicable (kucchitaṃ) and the empty (khaṃ) is suffering (dukkhaṃ); the meaning is that, being reprehensible, it is essenceless.

“Samāgamo sameta”ntiādīsu kevalassa āgamasaddassa, eta-saddassa ca payoge saṃyogatthassa anupalabbhanato, saṃ-saddassa ca saṃyoge upalabbhanato “saṃyogaṃ dīpetī”ti āha anvayato, byatirekato ca tadatthajotakatāsiddhito. Uppannaṃ uditanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Aya-saddo gatiatthe siddho hetusaddoviya kāraṇaṃ dīpeti. Attano phalanipphādanena ayati pavattati, eti vā etasmā phalanti ayoti, saṃyoge uppattikāraṇaṃ samudayoti. Ettha visuṃ payujjamānāpi upasaggasaddā sadhātukaṃ saṃyogatthaṃ, uppādatthañca dīpenti, kiriyāvisesakattāti veditabbā.

In such phrases as 'samāgamo sameta,' because the meaning of combination is not found in the use of the word 'āgama' or the word 'eta' alone, but is found in conjunction with the word 'saṃ-,' it is said that this 'indicates combination.' This is established by its illuminating that meaning both positively and negatively. The same method applies to 'uppannaṃ' and 'uditaṃ.' The word 'aya,' established in the sense of going, indicates a cause, like the word 'hetu.' By producing its own fruit, it proceeds; or, 'from this the fruit comes,' thus it is 'aya.' Therefore, in combination, the cause of arising is 'samudaya.' Here it should be understood that the prefix-words, even when used separately, indicate the meaning of combination and the meaning of arising along with the root, because they are qualifiers of the action.

“Abhāvo [M 2.0192] ettha rodhassāti nirodho”ti etena nibbānassa dukkhavivittabhāvaṃ dasseti. Samadhigate tasmiṃ tadadhigamato puggalassa rodhābhāvo pavattisaṅkhātassa rodhassa paṭipakkhabhūtāya nivattiyā adhigatattāti. Etasmiñca atthe abhāvo etasmiṃ rodhassāti nirodho icceva padasamāso. Dukkhābhāvo panettha puggalassa, na nibbānasseva. Anuppādo eva nirodho anuppādanirodho. Āyatiṃ bhavādīsu appavatti, na pana bhaṅgoti bhaṅgavācakaṃ nirodhasaddaṃ nivattetvā [V 2.0180] anuppādavācakaṃ gaṇhāti. Etasmiṃ atthe kāraṇe phalūpacāraṃ katvā nirodhapaccayo nirodhoti vutto.

By the etymological explanation, 'Absence herein of the prison, thus it is cessation,' he shows the state of Nibbāna as being secluded from suffering. When that is well attained, for the person who has attained it, there is an absence of the prison because the turning back, which is the opposite of the prison designated as continuance, has been attained. And in this meaning, the compounding of words is just this: 'Absence of the prison in this, thus it is cessation.' Herein, the absence of suffering is for the person, not for Nibbāna itself. Non-arising itself is cessation, that is, non-arising-cessation. It is non-occurrence in the future in states of being and so on, but not destruction. Thus, having rejected the word 'nirodha' which denotes destruction, he takes the one that denotes non-arising. In this meaning, having made a metaphorical application of the effect to the cause, Nibbāna, the condition for cessation, is called 'cessation'.

Paṭipadā ca hoti puggalassa dukkhanirodappattiyā. Nanu ca sā eva dukkhanirodappattīti tassā eva sā paṭipadāti na yujjatīti? Na puggalādhigamassa pattibhāvena, yehi so adhigacchati, tesaṃ kāraṇabhūtānaṃ paṭipadābhāvena ca vuttattā. Sacchi kiriyāsacchikaraṇadhammānañhi aññatthābhāvepi puggalasacchikiriyādhammabhāvehi nānattaṃ katvā niddeso katoti. Atha vā yaṃ dukkhanirodhappattiyā niṭṭhānaṃ phalaṃ, sayañca dukkhanirodhappattibhūtaṃ, tassa abhisamayabhūtāya dukkhanirodhappattiyā paṭipadatā daṭṭhabbā.

And there is a path for the person for the attainment of the cessation of suffering. Is it not the case that since that path is itself the attainment of the cessation of suffering, it is unsuitable to say that it is the path for that very attainment? No, because it is spoken of as 'attainment' in the sense of the person's attainment, and as 'path' in the sense of those things, which are the causes, by which one attains. For indeed, although there is no otherness between the act of realization and the dhammas that are the instruments of realization, the exposition is made by making a distinction by way of the person's act of realization and the dhammas as instruments of realization. Alternatively, regarding that fruit which is the culmination of the attainment of the cessation of suffering and is itself the state of having attained the cessation of suffering, its nature as a path for the attainment of the cessation of suffering which is comprehension should be understood.

531. Buddhādayo ariyā paṭivijjhantīti ettha paṭividdhakāle pavattaṃ buddhādivohāraṃ “agamā rājagahaṃ buddho”tiādīsu (su. ni. 410) viya bhāvini bhūte viya upacāroti purimakālepi āropetvā “buddhādayo”ti vuttaṃ. Te hi buddhādayo catūhi maggehi paṭivijjhantīti. Tasmā ariyasaccānīti vuccantīti ettha ariyapaṭivijjhitabbāni saccāni ariyasaccānīti purimapade uttarapadalopo ariyasaccānīti vuccantīti attho. Tathāgatena hi sayaṃ adhigatattā, paveditattā, tato eva ca aññehi adhigamanīrattā tāni tassa hontīti. Ariyabhāvasiddhitopīti ettha ariyasādhakāni saccāni ariyasaccānīti pubbe viya uttarapadalopo daṭṭhabbo. Ariyāni saccānītipīti ettha avitathabhāvena araṇīyattā adhigantabbattā ariyāni, ariyasamaññā vā avisaṃvādake avitathe niruḷhā daṭṭhabbā.

531. Regarding the statement 'The noble ones, the Buddha and others, penetrate them': here, the designation 'Buddha and others,' which applies at the time of penetration, is a figurative expression for a future event as if it were past—like in 'The Buddha went to Rājagaha'—and is thus said, having been applied even to a previous time. Indeed, those noble ones, the Buddha and others, penetrate them with the four paths. Therefore they are called 'Noble Truths.' Here, the meaning is that 'the truths to be penetrated by the noble ones are the Noble Truths,' with the elision of the middle term of the compound to be understood. Or, because the Tathāgata is a noble one, they are his truths, and therefore they are called 'Noble Truths.' Indeed, they are his truths because they were realized by the Tathāgata himself, declared by him, and are to be realized by others only from that. Also, because they bring about the state of nobility: here, 'the truths that make one noble are the Noble Truths,' where the middle term is elided as before. Or, they are 'noble truths': they are 'noble' because they are unerring and because they are to be approached and realized. Or, the designation 'noble' should be seen as established in the sense of what is not deceptive and is unerring.

532. Bādhanalakkhaṇanti [M 2.0193] ettha dukkhadukkhatannimittabhāvo, udayavayapaṭipīḷitabhāvo vā bādhanaṃ. Bhavādīsu jātiādivasena, cakkhurogādivasena ca anekadā dukkhassa pavattanameva puggalassa santāpanaṃ, tadassa kiccaṃ rasoti santāpanarasaṃ. Pavattinivattīsu saṃsāravimokkhesu pavatti hutvā gayhatīti pavattipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Pabhavati etasmā dukkhaṃ nibbattati, purimabhavena pacchimabhavo ghaṭito saṃyutto hutvā pavattatīti pabhāvo. “Evampi taṇhānusaye anūhate, nibbattati dukkhamidaṃ punappuna”nti (dha. pa. 338; netti. 30) evaṃ punappunaṃ uppādanaṃ anupacchedakaraṇaṃ. Bhavanissaraṇanivāraṇaṃ palibodho. Taṇhakkhayādibhāvena sabbadukkhasantatā santi. Accutirasanti accutisampattikaṃ acavanakiccaṃ vā. Kiccanti ca cavanābhāvaṃ [V 2.0181] kiccamiva katvā pariyāyena vuttaṃ, acavanañcassa sabhāvāpariccajanaṃ avikāritā daṭṭhabbā. Pañcakkhandhanimittasuññatāya aviggahaṃ hutvā gayhatīti animittapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Anusayasamucchindanena saṃsāracārakato niggamanūpāyabhāvo niyyānaṃ. Sabbakilesānaṃ anuppādanirodhanaṃ kilesappahānakaraṇaṃ. Nimittato, pavattato ca cittassa vuṭṭhānaṃ hutvā gayhatīti vuṭṭhānapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

532. Herein, affliction is the state of being suffering-as-suffering and the cause thereof, or it is the state of being oppressed by arising and passing away. In states of existence, etc., by way of birth, etc., and by way of afflictions like eye-disease, etc., in many ways the very occurrence of suffering is the tormenting of the individual; this is its function, its taste, thus it has the taste of tormenting. In the round of existence and liberation, it is apprehended as occurrence, thus its manifestation is occurrence. Suffering arises from it, is produced; the subsequent existence, being connected and conjoined with the previous existence, occurs—this is its source. As it is said: 'So long as the underlying tendency to craving is not uprooted, this suffering is produced again and again.' Thus its repeated production is the cause of its non-cessation. It is an obstruction that prevents escape from existence. Through the state of the destruction of craving and so on, the stilling of all suffering is peace. Its taste is the deathless means it is the accomplishment of the deathless, or it has the function of non-passing-away. And the word 'function' is used figuratively, treating the absence of passing away as if it were a function; and its non-passing-away should be seen as the non-abandonment of its intrinsic nature, its immutability. It is apprehended as being without substance because it is empty of the sign of the five aggregates, thus its manifestation is the signless. The state of being a means of escape from the prison of saṃsāra by cutting off the underlying tendencies is deliverance. The non-arising and cessation of all defilements is the effecting of the abandoning of defilements. It is apprehended as the mind's emergence from the sign and from occurrence, thus its manifestation is emergence.

533. Asuvaṇṇādi suvaṇṇādi viya dissamānaṃ māyāti vatthusabbhāvā tassā viparītatā vuttā. Udakaṃ viya dissamānā pana marīci upagatānaṃ tucchā. Vatthumattampi tassā na dissatīti visaṃvādikā vuttā. Marīcimāyāattavidhuro bhāvo tacchāviparītabhūtabhāvo. Ariyañāṇassāti ariyassa avitathaggāhakassa ñāṇassa, tena paṭivedhañāṇaṃ viya paccavekkhaṇañāṇampi gahitaṃ hoti. Tesaṃ gocarabhāvo paṭivijjitabbatā, ārammaṇabhāvo ca daṭṭhabbo. Aggilakkhaṇaṃ uṇhattaṃ. Tañhi katthaci kaṭṭhādiupādānabhede visaṃvādakaṃ, viparītaṃ, abhūtaṃ vākadācipi na hoti. “Jātidhammā jarādhammā, atho maraṇadhammino”ti (a. ni. 3.39; 5.57) evaṃ vuttā jātiādikā lokapakati. Ekaccānaṃ tiracchānānaṃ tiriyaṃ dīghatā, manussādīnaṃ uddhaṃ dīghatā, vuddhiniṭṭhaṃ pattānaṃ puna avaḍḍhananti evamādikā ca lokapakatīti vadanti. Tacchāviparītabhūtabhāvesu pacchimo tathatā. Paṭhamo avitathatā, majjhimo anaññatatāti ayametesaṃ viseso,

533. That which is not gold, etc., appearing like gold, etc., is called māyā (illusion); thus, because of the actual existence of the substance, its contrariety is stated. A mirage (marīci), however, appearing like water, is empty to those who approach it. Not even a mere substance of it is seen; thus, it is called deceptive. A state devoid of the nature of a mirage and illusion is the state of being true, not contrary, and real. 'Of noble knowledge' means of the knowledge of a noble one, who grasps without distortion; by that, reviewing knowledge as well as penetration knowledge is also included. Their state of being a domain should be understood as their state of being that which is to be penetrated and their state of being an object. The characteristic of fire is heat. For it is never at any time deceptive, contrary, or unreal in any difference of fuel, such as wood, etc. As it is said: 'Subject to birth, subject to aging, and also subject to death'—birth and so on, spoken of in this way, are the nature of the world. Some say that for some animals, length is horizontal, while for humans and others, it is vertical; and that for those who have reached the limit of growth, there is no further growth—this and the like is also the nature of the world. Among the states of being true, not contrary, and real, the last is suchness (tathatā), the first is non-distortedness (avitathatā), and the middle is non-otherness (anaññatatā)—this is the distinction among them.

Dukkhā [M 2.0194] aññaṃ na bādhaka nti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu taṇhāpi jāti viya dukkhanimittatāya bādhikāti? Na, bādhakappabhavabhāvena visuṃ gahitattā. Evamhi pavatti, pavattihetu ca asaṅkarato bodhitā honti. Atha vā jātiādīnaṃ viya dukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvo, dukkhadukkhatā ca bādhakatā, na dukkhappabhavatāti natthi taṇhāya pabhavabhāvena visuṃ gahitāya bādhakabhāvapasaṅgo. Tenāha “dukkhā aññaṃ na bādhaka”nti. Bādhakattaniyāmenāti dukkhaṃ bādhakameva, dukkhameva bādhakanti evaṃ dvidhāpi bādhakattāvadhāranenāti attho. Bādhakattaniyāmenāti hi bādhakassa, bādhakatte ca niyāmena. Yatā bādhakattassa dukkhe niyatatā, evaṃ dukkhassa ca bādhakatte niyatatāti.

Why is it said, 'Other than suffering, nothing afflicts'? Does not craving also, like birth, afflict by being a cause of suffering? No, because it is taken separately as being the origin-source of that which afflicts. For in this way, the process of existence and its cause are made known without confusion. Alternatively, like birth and so on, the state of being a basis for suffering and suffering-as-suffering is what is meant by 'affliction,' not the state of being the origin-source of suffering. Therefore, for craving, which is taken separately as being the origin, there is no implication of it having the nature of an afflictor. Therefore, he said, 'Other than suffering, nothing afflicts.' 'By the rule of being an afflictor' means by the twofold determination of the nature of an afflictor, thus: suffering alone is the afflictor, and only suffering is the afflictor. For 'by the rule of being an afflictor' implies a rule of the state of being an afflictor and a rule in the state of being an afflictor. Just as the state of being an afflictor is fixed in suffering, so too is suffering fixed in the state of being an afflictor.

Taṃ vinā nāññatoti satipi avasesakilesaavasesākusalasāsavakusalamūlāvasesasāsavakusaladhammānaṃ [V 2.0182] dukkhahetubhāve na taṇhāya vinā tesaṃ dukkhahetubhāvo atthi, tehi pana vināpi taṇhāya dukkhahetubhāvo atthi kusalehi vinā akusalehi rūpāvacarādikusalehi vinā kāmāvacarādīhi ca taṇhāya dukkhanibbattakattā. Santabhāvassa, santabhāve vā niyāmo santabhāvaniyāmo, tena santabhāvaniyāmena. Tacchaniyyānabhāvattāti dvidhāpi niyāmena taccho niyyānabhāvo etassa, na micchāmaggassa viya viparītatāya, na lokiyamaggassa viya vā anekantikatāya atacchoti tacchaniyyānabhāvo, maggo, tassa bhāvo tacchaniyyānabhāvattaṃ, tasmā tacchaniyyānabhāvattā. Sabbattha dvidhāpi niyāmena tacchāviparītabhūtabhāvo vuttoti āha “iti tacchāvipallāsā”tiādi.

'Without it, there is no other': Although the remaining defilements, remaining unwholesome states, wholesome roots with taints, and remaining wholesome states with taints are causes of suffering, they cannot be causes of suffering without craving.
