Craving, however, can be a cause of suffering even without them, for craving has the nature of producing suffering without wholesome states and with unwholesome states. The rule of the peaceful state is a rule of the peaceful state or a rule in the peaceful state. By that rule of the peaceful state. 'Because it has the nature of a true means of deliverance': This path is a true means of deliverance by a twofold rule; it is not untrue by being perverted like the wrong path, nor is it untrue by being inconclusive like the mundane path. Thus it is a 'true means of deliverance,' the path. The state of that is the nature of a true means of deliverance; therefore, 'because it has the nature of a true means of deliverance.' Because everywhere the state of being true, unperverted, and real has been stated by a twofold rule, he said, 'Thus, true and unperverted,' and so on.

534. Saccasaddassa sambhavantānaṃ atthānaṃ uddharaṇaṃ, sambhavante vā atthe vatvā adhippetassa atthassa uddharaṇaṃ niddhāraṇaṃ atthudvāro. Viratisacceti musāvādaviratiyaṃ. Na hi aññaviratīsu saccasaddo niruḷho. Ye pana “viratisaccaṃ samādānaviratī”ti vadanti, tesampi na samādānamattaṃ viratisaccaṃ, atha kho samādānāvisaṃvādanaṃ. Taṃ pana paṭiññāsaccaṃ musāvādaviratiyeva hoti. “Idameva saccaṃ, moghamañña”nti (ma. ni. 2.187, 202-203, 427; 3.27-29) pavattā diṭṭhi “sacca”nti abhinivisanavuttiyā diṭṭhisaccaṃ. Amosadhammattā nibbānaṃ paramatthasaccaṃ. “Amosadhammaṃ nibbānaṃ, tadariyā saccato vidū”ti (su. ni. 763) hi vuttaṃ, tassa pana taṃsampāpakassa [M 2.0195] ca maggassa pajānanā paṭivedho avivādakāraṇanti dvayampi “ekaṃ hi saccaṃ na dutiyamatthi, yasmiṃ pajā no vivade pajāna”nti imissā (su. ni. 890; mahāni. 119) gāthāya “sacca”nti vuttaṃ.

534. The 'doorway to meaning' (atthudvāra) is the extraction of the meanings that arise from the word 'truth,' or, having stated the meanings that arise, the extraction and determination of the intended meaning. 'Truth as abstinence' refers to abstinence from false speech, for the word 'truth' is not established in usage for other kinds of abstinence. As for those who say, 'Truth as abstinence is abstinence by undertaking,' for them too truth as abstinence is not the mere undertaking, but rather not being deceptive about what has been undertaken. That, however, is the truth of one's promise, which is just abstinence from false speech. The view that occurs as, 'This alone is true, other things are futile,' is 'truth of view' because of its function of adhering to a belief as 'truth.' Because of its undeceptive nature, Nibbāna is the ultimate truth. For it is said: 'Nibbāna has an undeceptive nature; the noble ones know it as truth.' Furthermore, the penetration consisting in the distinct understanding of that Nibbāna and of the path that leads to it is a cause for non-dispute. Therefore both are called 'truth' in this verse: 'For truth is one, there is no second, about which a person who knows would not dispute with another who knows.'

535. “Netaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccanti āgaccheyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti etena jātiādīnaṃ dukkhaariyasaccabhāve aviparītataṃ dasseti ekanteneva bādhakabhāvato. “Aññaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccanti āgaccheyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti iminā dukkhaariyasaccabhāvassa jātiādīsu niyatataṃ dasseti anaññatthabhāvato. Sacepi kathañci koci evaṃcitto āgaccheyya, paññāpane pana sahadhammena ñāpane attano vādassa patiṭṭhāpane samattho natthīti dassetuṃ “ahametaṃ…pe… paññapessāmīti āgaccheyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti vuttaṃ. Jātiādīnaṃ anaññathatā aññassa ca tatābhūtassa abhāvoyevettha ṭhānābhāvo. Sacepi koci āgaccheyya āgacchatu, ṭhānaṃ pana natthīti ayamettha suttattho. Esa nayo dutiyasuttepi. Tattha pana [V 2.0183] attabhāvapaṭilābheneva sattānaṃ jātiādīnaṃ patti, sammukhībhāvo ca hotīti sampattattā, paccakkhatā ca paṭhamatā, yato taṃ bhagavatā paṭhamaṃ desitaṃ, tannimittatā dutiyatā, tadupasamatā tatiyatā, taṃsampāpakatā catutthatāti daṭṭhabbā.

535. 'Should one conclude, "This is not the noble truth of suffering," that is not possible.' By this, he shows the unperverted nature of birth and so on with respect to being the noble truth of suffering, because of their exclusively oppressive nature. 'Should one conclude, "Something else is the noble truth of suffering," that is not possible.' By this, he shows that the state of being the noble truth of suffering is fixed in birth and so on, because it does not occur in anything else. Even if someone were somehow to come with such a thought, to show that there is no one capable of establishing his own thesis by explaining it with reason, it is said: 'Should one come thinking, "I will... proclaim this"... that is not possible.' The absence of a basis here is precisely the fact that birth and so on are not otherwise, and the absence of anything else of such a nature. Even if someone should come, let him come, but there is no basis for it—this is the meaning of the sutta here. This is the method in the second sutta as well. There, however, it is by the very acquisition of an individual existence that beings arrive at and confront birth and so on; therefore, its being first is due to its being attained and directly experienced. Since that suffering was taught first by the Blessed One, its being the cause is second, its being the pacification is third, and its being the means to attain that pacification is fourth—this should be understood.

“Etaparamato”ti etena catūhi ariyasaccehi pavattiādīnaṃ anavasesapariyādānamāha. Nibbutikāmena parijānanādīhi aññaṃ kiñci kiccaṃ kātabbaṃ natti, dhammañāṇakiccaṃ vā ito aññaṃ natthi, pariññeyyādīni ca etaparamānevāti cattāriyeva vuttāni. Taṇhāya ādīnavadassāvīnaṃ vasena taṇhāvatthuādīnaṃ etaparamatāyāti vuttaṃ. Tathā ālaye pañcakāmaguṇasaṅkhāte, sakalavatthukāmasaṅkhāte, bhavattayasaṅkhāte vā dukkhe dosadassāvīnaṃ vasena ālayādīnaṃ eteparamatāyāti vuttaṃ.

'This is the highest': by this he states the complete comprehension of occurrence and so on by means of the four noble truths. For one who desires quenching, there is no other task to be done apart from full understanding and so on; or, there is no task for knowledge of the Dhamma beyond this; and since the things to be fully understood and so on have this as their highest, only these four have been stated. It is said that for those who see the danger in craving, the objects of craving and so on have this as their highest. Similarly, for those who see the fault in suffering—described as attachment, as the five cords of sensual pleasure, as all objects of sensual pleasure, or as the three realms of existence—it is said that attachments and so on have this as their highest.

536. “Oḷārikattā”ti idaṃ jātiādīnaṃ dukkhabhāvassa pacurajanapākaṭatāmattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na ariyena ñāṇena paṭivijjhitabbākāraṃ. Tanti dukkhaṃ. Akatanti anibbattitaṃ, anipphāditakāraṇanti adhippāyo. Kāraṇe hi siddhe phalaṃ siddhameva hoti. “Neva akataṃ āgacchatī”ti ca iminā ahetuvādaṃ [M 2.0196] paṭikkhipati. “Na issaranimmānādito”ti etena pajāpatipurisapakatikālādivāde paṭikkhipati. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ parato āvi bhavissati. “Sahetukena dukkhenā”ti etena dukkhadassanena janitassa saṃvegassa saṃvaḍḍhanamāha. Dukkhassa hi sahetukabhāvasavasena balavasaṃvego jāyati yāvāyaṃ hetu, tāva idaṃ dukkhaṃ avicchedena pavattatīti. Assāsajananatthaṃ nirodhanti saṃvegajātassa assāsaṃ janetuṃ nirodhasaccamāha. Nibbinnasaṃsāradukkhassa hi nirodhakathā vuccamānā ativiya ativiya assāsaṃ sañjaneti.

536. ‘Because of its grossness’—this refers merely to the fact that the suffering nature of birth, etc., is manifest to many people, not to a mode to be penetrated by noble knowledge. That suffering is uncreated, meaning not brought into being; the intention is that its cause has not been produced. For when the cause is established, the result is indeed established. ‘Nor does it come uncreated’—with this he rejects the doctrine of no-cause. ‘Nor from the creation of a Lord, etc.’—with this he rejects doctrines such as those of a Prajāpati, a Puruṣa, Prakṛti, and time. What should be said here will become clear later. ‘With suffering that has a cause’—with this he speaks of the increase of the spiritual urgency born from seeing suffering. For by hearing that suffering has a cause, a strong spiritual urgency arises, with the thought: ‘So long as this cause exists, this suffering will continue without interruption.’ As for ‘Cessation for the purpose of generating solace,’ he speaks of the truth of cessation in order to generate solace for one in whom spiritual urgency has arisen. For to one who is disenchanted with the suffering of saṃsāra, the talk of cessation, when spoken, generates very great solace.

537. Ye te jātiādayo dhammā bhagavatā vuttāti sambandho. Kasmā panettha byādhi na gahitoti? Anekantabhāvato. Tathā hi so kadāci, kesañci ca natthi. Yathāha “tayo rogā pure āsuṃ, icchā anasanaṃ jarā”ti (su. ni. 313). Bākulatterādīnaṃ so nāhosiyeva, dukkhaggahaṇena vā byādhi ettha hitovāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Paramatthato hi dhātukkhobhapaccayaṃ kāyikaṃ dukkhaṃ byādhīti. Upādānakkhandhapañcakaṃ ekaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ katvā “dvādasa dhammā”ti vuttaṃ. Kāmataṇhābhāvasāmaññena ekajjhaṃ katvā “dukkhasamudayo ariyasacca”nti [V 2.0184] aññe antogadhabhede anāmasitvā ekarūpena gahitāpi taṇhā sassatadiṭṭhisahagatā, ucchedadiṭṭhisahagatā, diṭṭhivirahitā kevalaṃ kāmassādabhūtā cāti tidhāva bhinditvā vuttā. “Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo”ti maggasaccabhāvena ekajjhaṃ katvā vuttāpi sabhāvato bhinnā eva te dhammāti āha “aṭṭha dhammā”ti.

537. The connection is: ‘those phenomena, such as birth, etc., that were spoken of by the Blessed One.’ Why is illness not included here? Because it is not invariable. For sometimes, for some beings, it does not exist. As it is said: ‘In the past there were three diseases: desire, hunger, and old age.’ For the Elder Bākula and others, it did not exist at all. Alternatively, it should be understood that illness is indeed included here by the inclusion of suffering. For in the ultimate sense, bodily suffering conditioned by a disturbance of the elements is called illness. The five aggregates subject to clinging are treated as one part, and thus it is said, ‘twelve phenomena.’ Though craving is taken as a single thing and, having been grouped together because of its general nature as craving, is called ‘the noble truth of the origin of suffering’ without touching upon other internal divisions, it is also spoken of as divided in three ways: craving accompanied by the view of eternalism, craving accompanied by the view of annihilationism, and craving devoid of views, which is simply sensual gratification. Though the components of the Noble Eightfold Path are spoken of as grouped together as ‘the noble truth of the path,’ those phenomena are distinct by their intrinsic nature. Hence it is said, ‘eight phenomena.’

Saccaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Exposition of the Truths is finished.

Dukkhaniddesakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Exposition of Suffering

Jātiniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of Birth

Bhaveti ādānanikkhepaparicchinno dhammappabandho bhavo, tasmiṃ bhave. So hi jāyati ettha yonigatiādivibhāgoti jātīti vuccati, jāyanti ettha sattā samānanvayāti jāti, nikāyo. Saṅkhatalakkhaṇeti yattha katthaci uppāde. So hi jananaṭṭhena jāti. Paṭisandhiyanti paṭisandhicittakkhaṇe[M 2.0197]. Sampātijātoti ettha jātisaddena labbhamānaṃ mātukucchito nikkhamanasaṅkhātaṃ jāyanatthaṃ sandhāyāha “pasūtiya”nti, abhijātiyanti attho. Jāyati etāya khattiyādisamaññāti jāti, kulaṃ.

In ‘in existence’ (bhave): existence (bhavo) is the continuous flow of phenomena defined by taking up and laying down; in that existence. Indeed, since the division into wombs, destinies, etc., is born (jāyati) in it, it is called birth (jāti). Beings are born (jāyanti) in it with a common lineage; this is birth (jāti), a class (nikāyo). In ‘having the characteristic of the conditioned’: in any arising whatsoever. For that is birth in the sense of generation. In ‘rebirth-linking’ (paṭisandhi): at the moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness. In ‘actual birth’ (sampātijāti): with reference to the meaning of being born, designated as emergence from the mother's womb, which is obtained here by the word ‘birth,’ he says ‘by parturition’ (pasūtiyā); the meaning is ‘childbirth’ (abhijāti). One is born with a designation such as ‘khattiya’ by means of it; this is birth (jāti), a family (kulaṃ).

538. Sayanti etthāti seyyā, mātukucchisaṅkhāto gabbho seyyā etesanti gabbhaseyyakā, aṇḍajā, jalābujā ca. Itaresanti saṃsedajānaṃ, opapātikānañca. Ayampi cāti “paṭisandhikhandhesvevā”ti anantaraṃ vuttakathāpi, pageva “paṭisandhito paṭṭhāyā”ti vuttakathāyaṃ. Tenāha “tesaṃ tesaṃ paṭhamapātubhāvo jātī”ti.

538. “They lie in it, thus it is a bed (seyyā)”; the womb, designated as the mother's belly, is a bed. “They have a bed,” thus they are “womb-lying” (gabbhaseyyakā), that is, the egg-born and the womb-born. “The others” refers to the moisture-born and the spontaneously arisen. “And this too”: the statement just made, “in the rebirth-linking aggregates themselves,” is already implied in the earlier statement, “from rebirth-linking onwards.” Therefore he said: “The first appearance of these respective beings is birth.”

Ummujjanavasena gayhatīti ummujjanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Vakkhamānavibhāgaṃ dukkhavicittataṃ paccupaṭṭhapetīti dukkhavicittatāpaccupaṭṭhānā.

It is grasped by way of emergence, thus its manifestation is emergence. It presents the diversity of suffering, which has an analysis to be stated, thus its manifestation is the diversity of suffering.

539. “Kasmā panā”ti vadato codakassāyamadhippāyo – ekantadukkhe niraye tāva jātidukkhā hotu, aññāsupi vā duggatīsu pāpakammasamuṭṭhānato sukhasaṃvattaniyakammasamuṭṭhānāsu [V 2.0185] pana sugatīsu kathanti. Itaro “nāyaṃ jāti sabhāvadukkhavasena dukkhāti vuttā, na hi kāci paṭisandhi dukkhavedanāsampayuttā atthi, atha kho dukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato”ti dassento “anekesaṃ dukkhānaṃ vatthubhāvato”tiādimāha. Adukkhasabhāvampi pariyāyato dukkhanti vuccatīti dukkhasabhāvaṃ dukkhasaddena visesetvā vuttaṃ “dukkhadukkha”nti yathā rūparūpanti.

539. This is the intention of the objector who asks, “But why?”: Let birth be suffering in hell, which is exclusively suffering, or in other bad destinations that arise from unwholesome kamma. But how can it be so in the good destinations that arise from kamma conducive to happiness? The other, showing that “This birth is not called suffering by way of being intrinsically suffering—for there is no rebirth-linking associated with painful feeling—but rather because it is the ground for suffering,” says, “because it is the basis for many kinds of suffering,” and so on. Since even what is not intrinsically suffering is called suffering figuratively, in order to specify intrinsic suffering with the word “suffering,” it is said “suffering-as-suffering,” just as one says “form-as-form.”

Dukkhuppattihetutoti “ahu vata me, taṃ vata nāhosī”ti cetasikadukkhuppattihetuto.

“Because it is a cause for the arising of suffering”: because it is a cause for the arising of mental suffering from such thoughts as, “Alas, I had it!” and “Alas, I did not have it!”

“Yadaniccaṃ, taṃ dukkha”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.15, 45, 76, 77, 85; 2.4.1, 4) vacanato tebhūmakā saṅkhārā saṅkhāradukkhaṃ, tattha kāraṇamāha “udayabbayappaṭipāḷitattā”ti. Yañhi abhiṇhaṃ paṭipīḷitaṃ, taṃ dukkhamanatāya dukkhanti, vipassanācārassa adhippetattā tebhūmakaggahaṇaṃ.

In accordance with the saying, “What is impermanent, that is suffering,” the formations of the three planes are the suffering due to formations. He states the reason for this as: “because of being oppressed by arising and passing away.” For what is constantly oppressed is suffering because of its painful nature. The inclusion of the three planes is intended for the practitioner of insight meditation.

Dukkhadukkhanti dukkhadomassupāyāse vadati. “Jātipi dukkhā”tiādinā (vibha. 190) dukkhasaccavibhaṅge āgataṃ.

“Suffering-as-suffering” refers to pain, dejection, and despair. This is found in the Analysis of the Truth of Suffering in the passage beginning “Birth, too, is suffering.”

Bhagavatāpīti [M 2.0198] anāvaraṇañāṇavatā accariyāparimeyyadesanākosallavatā bhagavatāpi. Upamāvasenati aṅgārakāsūpamādiupamāvasena.

‘Even by the Blessed One’: that is, by the Blessed One, possessor of unobstructed knowledge and skill in wonderful and incomparable teaching. ‘By way of similes’: by way of similes such as the simile of the charcoal pit.

540. Puṇḍarīkādīsūti ādi-saddena na maṇikanakarajatapavāḷādiratanasanniccaye, nāpi aṇḍajameṇḍajavāyajātike subhamanuññasayanatale, nāpi ratanamayakuṭṭimamanohare pāsādatale, nāpi sittasammaṭṭhakusumopahāravati pāsādūpacāre, nāpi muttājālasadisavālikāvikiṇṇe viviṭaṅgaṇe, nāpi haritakambalasadisamudusaddalasamotale bhūmibhāgeti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Paramasambādheti ativiya sambādhe. Tibbandhakāreti bahalandhakāre. Pittasemhapubbaruhiragūthodariyādi nānākuṇapasambādhe. Mātā yadi vīsativassā, atha tiṃsa, cattālīsādivassā, tattakaṃ kālaṃ adhotavaccakūpasadisatāya adhimattajegucche. Pūtimacchā di sabbaṃ na sadisūpammaṃ tassa vātādivasena ekaccaduggandhāpagamasabbhāvato. Dasa māseti accantasaṃyoge upayogavacanaṃ, yebhuyyavasena vuttaṃ tato bhiyyopi ekaccānaṃ tatthāvaṭṭhānasambhavato[V 2.0186]. Attano adhomukhaṃ ṭhapitasaṅkucitahatthadvayassa ukkuṭikasseva nisīdato samijjanappasāraṇādirahito.

540. In the text ‘like a white lotus, etc.’ (puṇḍarikādīsu), by the word ‘etc.’ (ādi), the inclusion of the following should be understood: that one is not reborn in a collection of jewels such as gems, gold, silver, or coral; nor on a beautiful and pleasant sleeping surface such as a long-legged couch called an āsandī, a bedstead with figures of lions, etc., or a large rug with long fleece; nor on a charming palace floor made of jewels and inlaid with patterns; nor in the vicinity of a palace that has been sprinkled, swept, and where flowers have been scattered and offered; nor in an open courtyard strewn with white sand like a net of pearls; nor on a plot of ground with a level surface of soft, green grass like a green woolen blanket. ‘Extremely confined’ means exceedingly cramped. ‘Dense darkness’ means very thick darkness. Confined by various impurities such as bile, phlegm, pus, blood, feces, undigested food, etc. If the mother is twenty years old, or thirty, or forty, etc., for that long a time, it is exceedingly repulsive due to being like an unwashed latrine pit. A rotten fish and so on—none of these is an exact simile, because in its case, the removal of some of the foul smell is possible by means of wind, etc. The phrase ‘ten months’ is a term in the accusative case expressing continuous connection; it is stated with respect to the majority, since it is possible for some to remain there even longer than that. Devoid of bending, stretching, etc., like one sitting in a squatting position with one's two contracted hands placed below one's own face.

Abhimukhaṃ kaḍḍhanaṃ ākaḍḍhanaṃ. Parito samantato kaḍḍhanaṃ parikaḍḍhanaṃ. Heṭṭhā dhunanaṃ odhūnanaṃ. Nidhāya nidhāya dhūnanaṃ niddhūnanaṃ. Ākaḍḍhanādisadisañcettha “ākaḍḍhanādī”ti vuttaṃ. Taruṇavaṇasadisaṃ ativiya sukhumālaṃ gabbhagataṃ sarīraṃ sītādiappakampi na sahatīti sītanarakūpapannatādi nidassitaṃ. Tañhi tassa ativiya sītaṃ, ativiya uṇhañca hutvā upatiṭṭhati. Sarīraṃ vāsiyādīhi tacchetvā khārāvasecanakaraṇaṃ khārāpaṭicchakaṃ. Dukkhuppattiṭṭhāneti gabbhāsayasaññitaṃ tatiyaṃ āvaṭṭaṃ sandhāyāha.

Pulling towards is ākaḍḍhana. Pulling all around is parikaḍḍhana. Shaking downwards is odhūnana. Shaking after laying down again and again is niddhūnana. And here, what is similar to pulling, etc., is said to be ‘pulling, etc.’ Because the body in the womb, like a fresh wound and extremely delicate, cannot endure even a little cold or heat, its being in a cold hell, etc., is shown as an example. For that presents itself to it as extremely cold and extremely hot. Planing the body with an adze, etc., and drenching it with an alkaline solution is the ‘alkali treatment.’ With the phrase ‘in the place where suffering arises,’ he speaks referring to the third vortex, called the womb.

Parivattetvāti uddhaṃpādaadhosīsabhāvena parivattetvā. Idaṃ vijāyanamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, yena maraṇadukkhena ca aṭṭitā vedanāppattā sattā katipayamāsamattātikkantampi pavattiṃ vissaranti, mahandhakāraṃ mahāviduggaṃ pakkhandhā viya honti.

‘Having turned over’ means having turned upside down, with feet up and head down. This is suffering rooted in childbirth, by which—and by the suffering of death—beings, afflicted and experiencing painful feeling, forget their course of existence even after only a few months have passed, and are like those plunging into great darkness, into a great impassable place.

Vadhentassāti [M 2.0199] socanaparidevanasīsapaṭihananādinā bādhentassa. Khuppipāsā hi ātapāvaṭṭhānādinā ca ātāpanaṃ. Pañcaggitāpanādinā paritāpanaṃ.

‘Of one slaying’: this means of one who is afflicted by sorrow, lamentation, striking the head, and so on. Scorching is affliction by hunger and thirst, and by standing in the sun, etc. Intense burning is affliction by means of the five-fire austerity, etc.

Imassāti yathāvuttassa sattavidhassa. Sabbassāpīti gabbhakālādīsu tāpanamaddanādinirayaggidāhādisañjanitassa sakalassāpi. Vatthumeva hoti tadabhāve abhāvato. Tenevāha “jāyetha no ce”tiādi.

‘Of this’: of the sevenfold suffering as stated. ‘Of all’: of the whole of it, of all that is generated by scorching, crushing, the burning of the fires of hell, etc., from the time in the womb onwards. Birth is only the basis, because in its absence, this suffering is absent. Therefore he said, ‘If one were not born,’ etc.

541. Vicittanti vividhaṃ, acchariyaṃ vā.

541. ‘Diverse’ (vicittaṃ): various, or wonderful.

Iti jātiniddesavaṇṇanā.

Thus the commentary on the Exposition of Birth.

Jarāniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of Aging

542. Saṅkhātalakkhaṇanti [V 2.0187] “ṭhitassa aññathatta”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.38; a. ni. 3.47; kathā. 214) vuttaṃ khaṇikajaraṃ sandhāyāha. Khaṇḍiccādisammatoti khaṇḍiccapāliccavalittacatādinā samaññato. Sāti khandhapurāṇabhāvasaññitā pākaṭajarā. Khandhaparipāko ekabhavapariyāpannānaṃ khandhānaṃ purāṇabhāvo.

542. The words ‘(aging) has a conditioned characteristic’ are said with reference to momentary aging, which is described as ‘the alteration of what is stable.’ The words ‘designated by such things as broken teeth’ mean designated by such things as broken teeth, grey hair, and wrinkled skin. That is manifest aging, which is designated as the old state of the aggregates. The maturing of the aggregates is the old state of the aggregates included in one existence.

Iti jarāniddesavaṇṇanā.

Thus the commentary on the Exposition of Aging.

Maraṇaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of Death

543. Saṅkhatalakkhaṇanti saṅkhārānaṃ vayasaññitaṃ khaṇikamaraṇamāha. Yaṃ sandhāyāti yaṃ khaṇikamaraṇaṃ sandhāya, “jarāmaraṇaṃ dvīhi khandhehi saṅgahita”nti (dhātu. 71) ettha “maraṇa”nti vuttanti attho. Tanti jīvitindriyupaccedasaññitaṃ pākaṭamaraṇaṃ. “Cavana”nti lakkhitabbatāya cutilakkhaṇaṃ. Viyogarasanti yathādhigatehi sattasaṅkhārehi viyojanarasaṃ. Yathūpapannāya gatiyā vippavāsavasena gayhatīti gativippavāsapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

543. By ‘having the characteristic of the conditioned,’ it refers to momentary death, which is designated as the passing away of formations. As for ‘with reference to which’: it is with reference to this momentary death that in the text, ‘aging and death are included in two aggregates,’ it is said ‘death’; this is the meaning. That is manifest death, designated as the cutting off of the life faculty. Its characteristic is dissolution, because it is to be defined as ‘ceasing.’ As for its function of separation: its function is separation from the formations of a being that have been acquired. Because it is grasped by way of departure from the destiny one has reached, its manifestation is departure from destiny.

Pāpassāti pāpayogena pāpassa, upacitapāpakammassāti attho. Pāpakammādinimittanti pāpakammakammanimittagatinimittasaṅkhātaṃ maraṇakāle upaṭṭhitaṃ [M 2.0200] akusalavipākārammaṇaṃ. Tamhi passantasseva kassaci anubhavantassa viya mahādukkhaṃ hoti. Bhaddassāti bhaddakammassa, katakusalassāti attho. Tassa pana kāmaṃ iṭṭhameva ārammaṇaṃ upaṭṭhāti, piyavippayogavatthukaṃ pana mahantaṃ dukkhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ upaṭṭhāti, piyavippayogavatthukaṃ pana mahantaṃ dukkhaṃ uppajjatīti āha “asahantassa viyogaṃ piyavatthuka”nti. Avisesatoti pāpassa, bhaddassa ca sāmaññato. “Avisesato”ti vatvāpi “sabbesa”nti vacanaṃ taṃ idaṃ dukkhaṃ parimadditasaṅkhārānaṃ ekaccānaṃ khīṇāsavānampi hotiyevāti dassanatthaṃ. Vitujjamānamammānanti sandhibandhanāvacchedakavāyunā vijjhiyamānamammaṭṭhānānaṃ.

As for ‘of an evil person’: of one connected with evil, that is, one who has accumulated unwholesome kamma; this is the meaning. As for ‘the sign of evil kamma, etc.’: the object that is the result of unwholesome kamma which appears at the time of death, designated as the kamma, the kamma-sign, or the destiny-sign. Indeed, for someone, just upon seeing that, great suffering arises as if one were experiencing it. As for ‘of a good person’: of one of good kamma, that is, one who has done wholesome deeds; this is the meaning. For such a person, although a desirable object does indeed appear, great suffering based on separation from what is dear arises; hence it is said: ‘of one unable to bear separation from what is dear.’ As for ‘indiscriminately’: in common for both the evil person and the good person. Although ‘indiscriminately’ is said, the word ‘for all’ is stated to show that this suffering occurs even for some whose formations have been crushed, that is, for some of those whose cankers are destroyed. As for ‘of those whose vital spots are being pierced’: of those whose vital spots are being pierced by the wind that severs the joint-connections.

Iti maraṇaniddesavaṇṇanā.

Thus is the commentary on the Exposition of Death.

Sokaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of Sorrow

544. Soti [V 2.0188] soko. Atthato domanassameva hoti cetasikantarābhāvato. Domanassaviseso pana hoti visayavisese pavattiākāravisesasabbhāvatoti taṃ visesaṃ lakkhaṇādito dassetuṃ “evaṃ santepī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Anto nijjhānaṃ cittasantāpo. Parijjhāpanaṃ rāgadosapariḷāhavisiṭṭhaṃ dahanaṃ. Katākatakusalākusalavisayaṃ vippaṭisārākārena pavattaṃ anusocanaṃ kukkuccaṃ, ñātibyasanādivisayaṃ kevalaṃ cittasanthāpabhūtaṃ anusocanaṃ sokoti anusocanapaccupaṭṭhānattepi ayametesaṃ viseso.

544. ‘So’ is ‘soko’ (sorrow). In terms of its intrinsic nature, it is only displeasure, because of the absence of another mental factor. However, it is a special kind of displeasure because of the existence of a special mode of occurrence in a special object. Therefore, to show that special quality by way of its characteristic, etc., the passage beginning ‘Even so...’ was stated. ‘Internal burning’ is mental torment. ‘Consuming’ is a burning distinguished from the fever of lust and the fever of hatred. Grieving that occurs in the form of remorse, having as its object wholesome and unwholesome deeds done and not done, is worry (kukkucca); grieving that is simply mental torment, having as its object the misfortune of relatives, etc., is sorrow (soko). Thus, although they are the same in having grieving as their manifestation, this is the difference between them.

Visapītaṃ sallaṃ visasallaṃ. Sokavasena atisārādi byādhipi hoti, sokabahulassa sarīraṃ na cirasseva jīrati, balavasokābhibhūto maraṇampi pāpuṇātīti āha “samāvahati ca byādhijarāmaraṇabhedana”nti.

A poisoned dart (visasallaṃ) is a dart smeared with poison. Through the power of sorrow, diseases such as dysentery also occur. For one with much sorrow, the body ages quickly. One overwhelmed by strong sorrow may even reach death. Therefore, it is said, ‘and it brings disease, aging, death, and destruction.’

Iti sokaniddesavaṇṇanā.

Thus the commentary on the Exposition of Sorrow.

Paridevaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of Lamentation

545. Vacīpalāpoti vācāvippalāpo, so atthato saddo eva. Bhiyyoti sokadukkhato upari. Sokasamuṭṭhāno hi paridevo.

545. ‘Wailing’ (vacīpalāpo) is verbal raving (vācāvippalāpo); in terms of its intrinsic nature, it is only sound. ‘Excessively’ (bhiyyo) means on top of sorrow and pain. Indeed, lamentation has sorrow as its origin.

Iti paridevaniddesavaṇṇanā.

Thus the commentary on the Exposition of Lamentation.

Dukkhaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of Suffering

546. Jātiādīnampi [M 2.0201] yathārahaṃ dukkhavatthudukkhadukkhatāhi satipi dukkhabhāve kāyassa pīḷanavasena idaṃ savisesaṃ dukkhamanti āha “dukkhanti visesato vutta”nti.

546. Although for birth and so on there is also a state of suffering, as appropriate, through being a basis for suffering and through being intrinsic suffering, this is a special suffering by way of afflicting the body; therefore, it is said, ‘it is called “suffering” specifically.’

Iti dukkhaniddesavaṇṇanā.

Thus the commentary on the Exposition of Suffering.

Domanassaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of Displeasure

547. Manovighātarasanti [V 2.0189] byāpādasampayogavasena manaso vihaññanakiccaṃ. Cetodukkhasamappitāti cetasikadukkhasamaṅgino. Āvaṭṭantīti āmukhaṃ vaṭṭanti, yaṃdisābhimukhaṃ patitā, taṃdisābhimukhā eva vaṭṭanti. Vivaṭṭantīti viparivattanavasena vaṭṭanti. Uddhaṃpādaṃ papatantīti uddhaṃmukhapādā hutvā patanti. Satthaṃ āharantīti attano sarīrassa vijjhanabhedanavasena satthaṃ upanenti.

547. ‘Having the function of afflicting the mind’ means it has the task of tormenting the mind by way of its connection with ill will. ‘Endowed with mental suffering’ means those endowed with mental suffering. ‘They roll towards’ means they roll towards the front; in whatever direction they have fallen facing, in that very direction they roll. ‘They roll away’ means they roll by way of turning around. ‘They fall with feet upwards’ means they fall with their feet facing upwards. ‘They bring a weapon’ means they bring a weapon to their own body for the purpose of piercing and cutting.

Iti domanassaniddesavaṇṇanā.

Thus the commentary on the Exposition of Displeasure.

Upāyāsaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of Despair

548. Dosoyevāti kāyacittānaṃ āyāsanavasena dosasseva pavattiākāroti attho, yato bhuso āyāsoti upāyāsoti vuccati yathā bhusamādānaṃ upādānanti. Eko dhammoti cuddasahi akusalacetasikehi añño eko cetasikadhammo, yaṃ “visādo”ti ca vadanti. Nitthunanavasena sampajjanato nitthunanaraso, kāye vā nitthunanakaraṇakicco. “Saṅkhāradukkhabhāvato”ti vatvā so panettha sātisayoti dassento “cittaparidahanato, kāyavisādanato cā”ti āha.

548. ‘It is hatred itself’: this means it is the mode of occurrence of hatred itself by way of the vexation of body and mind; because it is intense vexation (bhuso āyāso), it is called despair (upāyāsa), just as intense taking up (bhusaṃ ādānaṃ) is called clinging (upādāna). ‘One state’: this means one mental factor other than the fourteen unwholesome mental factors, which they also call ‘dejection’ (visāda). Its characteristic is groaning, because it is endowed with the nature of groaning; or its function is causing the body to groan. Having said, ‘because of the nature of the suffering of formations,’ to show that this is especially intense here, it is said, ‘because of the burning of the mind and the dejection of the body.’

Ete ca sokaparidevupāyāsā viññattiyā vinā, saha ca yathāpaccayaṃ domanassacittuppādassa pavattiākāravisesoti dassetuṃ “ettha cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha pāko viyāti rajanādino pacitabbavatthuno pāko viya.

To show that these—sorrow, lamentation, and despair—are specific modes of occurrence of the arising of a mind-moment of displeasure, in accordance with conditions, both without and with expression, the passage beginning ‘And here...’ was stated. Therein, ‘like ripening’ means like the ripening of a thing to be ripened, such as dye and so on.

Iti upāyāsaniddesavaṇṇanā.

Thus the commentary on the Exposition of Despair.

Appiyasampayoganiddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of Association with the Disagreeable

549. Samodhānaṃ [M 2.0202][V 2.0190] samāgamo. Kāyikadukkhacittavighātādianatthānaṃ atthibhāvassa paccupaṭṭhāno anatthabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno.

549. ‘Meeting’ (samodhānaṃ) is coming together (samāgamo). Its manifestation is as what is unbeneficial, as it is the proximate cause for the existence of unbeneficial things such as bodily pain and mental distress.

Tesaṃ appiyānaṃ kāyikavācasikapayogasaṅkhāto upakkamo tadupakkamo, tato sambhūto tadupakkamasambhūto.

The assault from those disagreeable ones, reckoned as their bodily and verbal application, is 'their assault'; what has arisen from that is 'arisen from their assault'.

Iti appiyasampayoganiddesavaṇṇanā.

Thus ends the commentary on the exposition of association with the disagreeable.

Piyavippayoganiddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of Separation from the Beloved

550. Upaddavabhāvena paccupatiṭṭhatīti byasanapaccupaṭṭhāno.

550. It is present as a calamity; thus, its manifestation is as disaster.

Iti piyavippayoganiddesavaṇṇanā.

Thus ends the commentary on the exposition of separation from the beloved.

Icchitālābhaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of Not Getting What is Wished For

551. Icchitālābho nāma yassa kassaci attanā icchitassa vatthuno alābho. “Yampicchaṃ na labhatī”ti hi vuttaṃ. Matthakappattaṃ pana icchitālābhaṃ dassetuṃ pāḷiyaṃ “jātidhammānaṃ sattāna”ntiādinā niddiṭṭhanti tameva dassetuṃ “aho vatā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Icchāvāti ettha icchāsahito alābhovāti ca vadanti. Tappariyesanarasāti tesaṃ alabbhaneyyavatthūnaṃ pariyesanarasā. Appatti alābho.

551. ‘Not getting what is wished for’ means the non-acquisition of any thing whatsoever desired by oneself. For it is said: ‘And what one wishes for, one does not get.’ But to show the supreme instance of not getting what is wished for, it is pointed out in the Pāli text by the passage beginning ‘for beings subject to birth,’ and to show just that, the passage beginning ‘Oh, if only!…’ is stated. And here some say that ‘with desire’ means ‘non-acquisition accompanied by desire.’ Its characteristic is searching for those unobtainable things. ‘Non-attainment’ is non-acquisition.

Iti icchitālābhaniddesavaṇṇanā.

Thus ends the commentary on the exposition of not getting what is wished for.

Pañcupādānakkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Five Aggregates Subject to Clinging

552. Yaṃ [V 2.0191] vuttamidhāti idha saccaniddese yaṃ sarūpato vuttaṃ. Avuttanti aññattha dukkhakkhandhabālapaṇḍitasuttādīsu vuttampi idha sarūpato avuttaṃ. Tañca sabbaṃ ime upādānakkhandhe vinā na labbhatīti tattha khandhasannissayameva dukkhaṃ khandhe vibādhatīti dassetuṃ “indanamiva pāvako”ti vuttaṃ. Yathā [M 2.0203] vā lakkhaṃ paharaṇapahārassa vatthu, evaṃ khandhā saṃsāradukkhassa. Yathā ca gorūpaṃ ḍaṃsamakasādivibādhāya, yathā ca khettaṃ nipphannasassalāyanassa, gāmo ca gāmaghātakavibādhāya, evaṃ khandhā jātiādidukkhassa vatthūti dassetuṃ “lakkhamivā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yebhuyyena loke vibādhakā vibādhetabbādhīnā na honti, ime pana vibādhetabbādhīnā evāti dassetuṃ “tiṇalatādīnī”ti vuttaṃ. Kāmaṃ anādimati saṃsāre ādi nāma kassaci natthi, ekabhavaparicchinnassa pana khandhasantānassa vasena vuttaṃ “ādidukkhaṃ jātī”ti. Tenevāha “pariyosānadukkhaṃ maraṇa”nti. Na hettha samucchedamaraṇameva adhippetaṃ. Maraṇassa antike āsanne jātaṃ dukkhaṃ māraṇantikadukkhaṃ. Paridayhanaṃ cittasantāpo. Lālappanaṃ ativiya vippalāpo. Anutthunanaṃ anto nijjhāyanaṃ. Ekamekanti jātiādīnaṃ antarabhedabhinnānaṃ, jātiādīnameva vā upādānakkhandhapañcakānaṃ vā ekamekaṃ. Saṅkhipitvāti samāsetvā, sāmaññaniddesena vā saṅkhepaṃ katvā.

552. ‘What is said here’ refers to what has been stated here in the exposition of the truth by its own nature. ‘Not said’ means that even though it has been mentioned elsewhere, such as in the Dukkhakkhandha Sutta and the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta, it has not been stated here by its own nature. And since all that cannot be found apart from these aggregates subject to clinging, to show that suffering, being dependent on the aggregates, torments the aggregates, it is said, ‘like fire for fuel.’ Or, just as a target is the basis for the strike of a weapon, so the aggregates are for the suffering of saṃsāra. And just as a cow is for the torment by gadflies and mosquitoes, and as a field is for the reaping of the ripened crop, and a village for the affliction by village-raiders, so the aggregates are the basis for the suffering of birth and so on. To illustrate this, it is said, ‘like a target,’ etc. Generally in the world, tormentors are not dependent on the tormented, but these are indeed dependent on the tormented. To show this, it is said, ‘grass, creepers, etc.’ Granted, in beginningless saṃsāra there is no beginning for anything. But with reference to the continuum of aggregates confined to a single existence, it is said, ‘birth is the initial suffering.’ For that very reason, he says, ‘death is the final suffering.’ Here, it is not only annihilation-death that is meant. The suffering that arises near death is the suffering at the time of death. ‘Burning’ is mental agitation. ‘Wailing’ is excessive incoherent talk. ‘Groaning’ is internal brooding. ‘One by one’ refers to each one of birth and so on, differentiated by their internal divisions, or of each one of the five aggregates of clinging themselves, which are birth and so on. ‘Having summarized’ means having condensed, or having made a summary through a general exposition.

Iti dukkhaniddesakathāvaṇṇanā.

Thus is the commentary on the discourse on the exposition of suffering.

Samudayaniddesakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Exposition of the Origin

553. Punabbhavakaraṇaṃ punabbhavo uttarapadalopena, yathā vā apūpabhakkhanasīlo āpūpiko, evaṃ punabbhavakaraṇasīlā, punabbhavaṃ vā phalaṃ arahati, so vā etissā payojananti ponobhavikā. Nandanato, rañjanato ca nandīrāgabhāvaṃ sabbāsu avatthāsu apaccakkhāya vuttiyā nandīrāgasahagatā. Tāya ca sattā tattha tattha bhavādike kimikīṭapaṭaṅgādiattabhāvepi nandanti, rūpābhinandanādibhūtāya rañjanti cāti tatratatrābhinandinī. Tenāha “nandīrāgena sahagatā”tiādi. Tabbhāvattho hi esa sahagatasaddo. Kāmabhavavibhavabhedavasena [V 2.0192] pavattiyā kāmataṇhā, bhavataṇhā, vibhavataṇhā ca veditabbā. Kāmataṇhādibhedaṃ anāmasitvā kevalaṃ taṇhābhāveneva ekabhāvaggahaṇena ekattaṃ upanetvā kassacipi sattassa kenaci sadisatābhāvato taṃtaṃvicittabhāvajanakakammanipphādanena [M 2.0204] ativicittasabhāvā sakalassa dukkhassa hetubhāvato dukkhasamudayo ariyasaccaṃ.

553. ‘Productive of rebirth’: The making of a new existence (`punabbhavakaraṇaṃ`) is called `punabbhavo` by elision of the final word. Or, just as one who is habitually a cake-eater is an `āpūpiko`, so this craving is `ponobhavikā` because it is habitually productive of rebirth; or it deserves rebirth as its fruit; or that new existence is its purpose. ‘Accompanied by delight and lust’: Because of delighting and being attached, it is ‘accompanied by delight and lust,’ its nature being a state of delight and lust that occurs in all situations without being abandoned. And through that craving, beings delight even in such states of being as worms, insects, and moths, and they are attached by that which has become the delighting in forms, etc.; thus it is ‘delighting in this and that.’ Hence he said, ‘accompanied by delight and lust,’ etc. For this word `sahagata` has the meaning of ‘that state.’ By way of its occurrence according to the division into sensual pleasure, existence, and non-existence, it should be understood as craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. Without considering the distinctions such as craving for sensual pleasures, but having brought it to a unity by grasping it as a single state simply in its nature as craving, since it is of an extremely variegated nature—through its accomplishment of kamma that generates those various states of being, as no being whatsoever is similar to any other—and since it is the cause of all suffering, it is the noble truth of the origin of suffering.

Kasmā panettha taṇhāva samudayasaccaṃ vuttāti? Visesahetubhāvato. Avijjā hi bhavesu ādīnavaṃ paṭicchādentī, diṭṭhiādiupādānañca tattha tattha abhinivisamānaṃ taṇhaṃ abhivaḍḍhentī dosādayopi kammassa kāraṇaṃ honti, taṇhā pana taṃtaṃbhavayonigativiññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsasattanikāyakulabhogissariyādivicittataṃ abhipatthentī, kammavicittatāya upanissayataṃ kammassa ca sahāyabhāvaṃ upagacchantī bhavādivicittataṃ niyameti, tasmā dukkhassa visesahetubhāvato aññesupi avijjāupādānakammādīsu sutte (dī. ni. 2.400; ma. ni. 1.133; 3.374) abhidhamme (vibha. 203) ca avasesakilesākusalamūlādīsu vuttesu dukkhahetūsu vijjamānesu taṇhāva samudayasaccanti vuttāti veditabbaṃ.

Why is it that here craving alone is declared as the truth of the origin? Because it is the specific cause. For ignorance, by concealing the danger in states of existence, and clinging to views, etc., by adhering to this and that, intensify craving. Hatred and other defilements also are causes of kamma. Craving, however, by aspiring for the variety of states of existence—such as different realms, wombs, destinies, stations of consciousness, abodes of beings, classes of beings, families, wealth, and sovereignty—and by becoming a decisive support for the variety of kamma and an assistant to kamma, determines the diversity of existence, etc. Therefore, because craving is the specific cause of suffering, it should be understood that although other causes of suffering are mentioned in the suttas and the Abhidhamma—such as ignorance, clinging, kamma, and the remaining defilements, unwholesome roots, etc.—it is craving alone that is declared as the truth of the origin.

Iti samudayaniddesakathāvaṇṇanā.

Thus is the commentary on the discourse on the exposition of the origin.

Nirodhaniddesakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Exposition of Cessation

554. Tassāyevāti yadaggena taṇhā samudayasaccanti vuttā, tadaggena tassāyevāti avadhāraṇaṃ. Sati hi padhānahetunirodhe tadaññahetū niruddhāyeva hontīti byādhinimittavūpasamanena byādhivūpasamo viya hetunirodhena phalanirodhoti āha “samudayanirodhena dukkhanirodho”ti. Na aññathāti yathāvuttassa atthassa ekantikataṃ dasseti.

554. ‘Of that very craving’: By whichever aspect craving is said to be the truth of the origin, by that same aspect the emphasis ‘of that very craving’ is made. For when the principal cause has ceased, other causes are certainly ceased. Just as a disease subsides with the subsiding of its cause, so the fruit ceases with the cessation of its cause. Therefore, it is said, “With the cessation of the origin, there is the cessation of suffering.” The words ‘not otherwise’ show the certainty of the meaning as stated.

Anupaddaveti pāṇakavijjhanasatthappahārādiupaddavarahite. Tato eva daḷhe thire. Sākhādichedanena chinnopi. Taṇhānusayeti kāmarāgabhavarāgānusaye. Anūhateti asamupaghāṭite.

Anupaddaveti means free from dangers such as being pierced by insects, struck by a sword, and so on. Tato eva daḷhe thire means because of this, it is firm and steadfast. Sākhādichedanena chinnopi means even if cut by the severing of its branches and so forth. Taṇhānusayeti means with the underlying tendencies of sensual desire and craving for existence. Anūhateti means not utterly destroyed.

Yathā sīho yenattani saro khitto, tattheva attano balaṃ dasseti, na sare, tathā buddhānaṃ kāraṇe [V 2.0193] paṭipatti, na phale. Yathā pana sārameyyā kenaci leḍḍuppahāre dinne bhussantā leḍḍuṃ khādanti, na [M 2.0205] pahāradāyake uṭṭhahanti, evaṃ aññatitthiyā dukkhaṃ nirodhetukāmā kāyacchedamanuyuñjanti, na kilesanirodhananti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “sīhasamānavuttino”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Just as a lion, when a dart is thrown at it by someone, displays its strength at that very person, not at the dart, so the practice of the Buddhas is on the cause, not on the fruit. And just as dogs, when someone strikes them with a clod of earth, bark and chew the clod, and do not rise up against the one who threw it, so other sectarians, desiring to make suffering cease, engage in mortifying the body, not in the cessation of the defilements. To show this meaning, it is said, 'those whose conduct is like a lion's,' and so on.

555. Virajjati palujjati chijjati samudayo etenāti virāgo vuccati maggo. Virajjanaṃ palujjanaṃ samucchindanaṃ virāgoti pahānaṃ vuccati. Tasmāti yasmā pahānapariyāyo virāgasaddo, nirodhasaddo ca, tasmā. Anusayasamugghātato aseso virāgo aseso nirodhoti sambandhanīyaṃ. Cāgādipadānipi gahetvā vadati sabbāneva etānīti. Yasmā nibbānaṃ vuccati, na dukkhassa nirujjhanamattaṃ, tasmā taṇhāya asesavirāganirodhādipadānipi nibbānavevacanānīti. Vuttamevatthaṃ samattheti “yasmā panā”tiādi. Yathā virāgādipadāni nibbāne yujjanti, taṃdassanaṃ. Tattha taṃ āgammāti taṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇavasena patvā. Taṇhā virajjatīti ariyamaggena accantavirāgavasena taṇhā virajjīyati. Nirujjhatīti nirodhīyati, tena virāganirodhasaddānaṃ adhikaraṇasādhanatamāha. Tadevāti nibbānameva. Cāgādayo hontīti cāgādihetuṃ phalavohārena vadati. “Kāmaguṇālayesū”ti potthakesu likhanti, “kāmaguṇālayādīsū”ti pana pāṭho.

555. The path is called dispassion (virāga) because by it the origin (samudayo), which is craving, fades away, dissolves, and is cut off. Abandonment (pahāna) is called virāga, which is the fading away, dissolving, and eradication. Therefore, since the words 'dispassion' and 'cessation' are synonyms for abandonment, it should be understood that from the uprooting of the underlying tendencies comes complete dispassion and complete cessation. Taking also terms such as 'relinquishment' (cāga), he says that all these are expressions for Nibbāna. Because Nibbāna is spoken of, not merely the cessation of suffering, terms such as 'the complete fading away and cessation of craving' are also expressions for Nibbāna. He supports this very meaning with the passage beginning, 'But since…' This demonstrates how terms like 'dispassion' are applied to Nibbāna. Therein, 'having come to that' means having attained that Nibbāna by making it an object. 'Craving fades away' means that by the noble path, through the power of utter dispassion, craving is made to fade away. 'It ceases' means it is brought to cessation. By this he shows that the words 'dispassion' and 'cessation' are terms indicating the locus of the action. 'That very thing' means Nibbāna itself. When it is said 'relinquishment, etc., occur,' he is speaking of the cause—relinquishment and so on—by using the language of the result. In the manuscripts they write 'kāmaguṇālayesu' ('in the abodes of the strands of sensual pleasure'), but the correct reading is 'kāmaguṇālayādīsu' ('in the abodes of the strands of sensual pleasure, etc.').

556. Tayidantiādi na porāṇapāṭho, saccatthadīpane pana vuttaniyāmena tato ānetvā pacchā ṭhapitaṃ. Tathā hi pubbe vuttānipi lakkhaṇādīni punapi vuttāni. Saṃsāradukkhato nibbinnamānasassa assāsaṃ karonto viya hotīti assāsakaraṇarasaṃ. Rāgādisabbapapañcavūpasamanimittatāya nippapañcataṃ paccupaṭṭhapetīti nippapañcapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

556. The passage beginning 'tayidaṃ' is not an ancient reading; it was brought from the Saccatthadīpanī and inserted here later according to the stated method. For the characteristics and so on that were mentioned before are stated again. Its function is providing solace (assāsakaraṇarasaṃ) because it is as if it gives relief to one whose mind is disenchanted with the suffering of saṃsāra. Its manifestation is non-proliferation (nippapañcapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ) because, by being the cause for the subsiding of all proliferations such as lust, it makes non-proliferation manifest.

557. Nattheva nibbānanti yadi sāmaññato paṭiññā, attanā adhippetanibbānassapi abhāvo āpajjati, tathā sati paṭiññāvirodho. Atha parābhimataṃ nibbānaṃ pati, evaṃ sati dhammiasiddhi, tato ca nissayāsiddho hetu. Anupalabbhanīyatoti kiṃ paccakkhato, udāhu anumānato? Purimasmiṃ pakkhe cakkhādīhi anekantikatā, dutiyasmiṃ paraṃ pati asiddho hetu. Tenāha “na, upāyena upalabbhanīyato”tiādi. Tattha yathā cetopariyañāṇalābhino eva ariyā paresaṃ lokuttaracittaṃ jānanti, tatthāpi ca arahā eva sabbesaṃ, na sabbe, evaṃ nibbānampi [M 2.0206][V 2.0194] sīlasamādhipaññāsaṅkhātasammāpaṭipattibhūtena upāyena upalabbhatīti atthavacanaṃ cetaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, na payogavacanaṃ. Taṃ parato āvi bhavissati.

557. If the assertion, 'Nibbāna does not exist at all,' is a general one, then the non-existence of the Nibbāna intended by oneself also comes about, resulting in a self-contradiction. Alternatively, if the assertion is made with reference to the Nibbāna accepted by others, in that case the subject (dhammin) is unestablished, and from that, the reason is unestablished in its basis. Because it is 'unobtainable': is this by direct perception or by inference? In the first case, the reason is inconclusive on account of the sense faculties such as the eye. In the second case, the reason is unestablished with respect to the other party. Therefore, it is said: 'No, because it is obtainable by a means.' Herein, just as only noble ones who have obtained the knowledge of others' minds know the supramundane consciousness of others—and even among them, only an Arahant knows the supramundane consciousness of all, not all noble ones—so too, Nibbāna is obtained by the means that is the right practice, designated as virtue, concentration, and wisdom. This should be understood as a statement of meaning, not a statement of application. That will become clear later.

558. Natthīti na vattabbaṃ, ariyehi upalabbhanīyatoti adhippāyo. Saṃsārato saṃviggamānasā sammāpaṭipattiyā nibbānaṃ adhigacchantīti sabbasamayasiddhoyaṃ nayo. Tattha sāsanikameva nissāya vadati “paṭipattiyā vañcubhāvāpajjanato”ti. Tenāha “asati hī”tiādi. Sammādiṭṭhipurejavāyāti sammādiṭṭhipubbaṅgamāya. Pubbaṅgamatā cassā padhānabhāvato. Tathā hi sā paṭhamaṃ desanāruḷhā, na sabbapaṭhamaṃ uppajjanato. Na cāyaṃ sammāpaṭipatti vañjhā, nibbānapāpanato nibbānassa sampāpakato. Tava matena pana nibbānasseva abhāvato vañjhabhāvo āpajjatīti yojanā. Abhāvapāpakattāti sammāpaṭipattiyā kilesasamucchindanamukhena khandhānaṃ abhāvasampāpakabhāvato, na vañjhabhāvāpattīti ce vadeyyāsīti attho. Na iti paṭikkhepe. Yaṃ tayā “abhāvapāpakattā”ti vadantena khandhābhāvo nibbānanti paṭiññātaṃ, taṃ na. Kasmā? Atītānāgatābhāvepi nibbānappattiyā abhāvato. Atītānāgatā hi khandhā na santīti tasmiṃ abhāve nibbānaṃ adhigataṃ nāma siyā, so pana natthīti. Na kevalaṃ atītānāgatānameva, atha kho vattamānānampīti tiyaddhagatānaṃ sabbesaṃ khandhānaṃ abhāvo nibbānaṃ. Na hi taṃ ekadesābhāvo bhavituṃ yuttanti vattamānā ce, na na santi, na santi ce, na vattamānāti “vattamānā, na santi cā”ti vippaṭisiddhametanti āha “na, tesaṃ…pe… pajjanato”ti.

558. 'It should not be said, "It does not exist,"' the intention being that it is obtainable by the noble ones. That those whose minds are stirred with urgency by saṃsāra attain Nibbāna through right practice is a principle established in all systems. Here, relying only on the teaching, he says, 'because practice would become barren.' Hence he says, 'For if it were absent,' etc. 'With right view as its precursor' means having right view as its forerunner. Its status as forerunner is due to its being primary. For it is what is first taken up in the teaching, not that it is the very first to arise. And this right practice is not barren, since it leads to Nibbāna, since it is a means for attaining Nibbāna. The connection is: 'But according to your view, since Nibbāna itself does not exist, practice would become barren.' If you should say: '"Because it leads to non-existence" means that right practice, by way of eradicating the defilements, brings about the non-existence of the aggregates, and thus does not become barren'—this is the meaning. 'No' is a rejection. The claim you made in saying 'because it leads to non-existence'—that the non-existence of the aggregates is Nibbāna—is not correct. Why? Because even with the non-existence of past and future aggregates, there is no attainment of Nibbāna. For past and future aggregates do not exist, so in their non-existence Nibbāna would be nominally attained, but this is not the case. Not only of past and future aggregates, but of present ones too—thus Nibbāna is the non-existence of all aggregates belonging to the three times. For it is not right for it to be a partial non-existence. If they are present, they are not non-existent; if they are non-existent, they are not present. Thus 'they are present and they are non-existent' is a contradiction. Hence he says: 'No, because for them… arising…'

Kiñca bhiyyo – yadi vattamānābhāvo nibbānaṃ, yadā ariyamaggo vattati, tadā tassa nissayabhūtā khandhā vattamānāti katvā tadā nibbānassa abhāvo siyā. Tathā ca sati maggakkhaṇepi nibbānasacchikiriyāya abhāvo āpajjatīti dassento “vattamāna…pe… dosato”ti āha. Na mayaṃ sabbesaṃyeva avattamānatāya nibbānaṃ vadāma. Kiñcarahīti, tadā maggakkhaṇe kilesānaṃ avattamānattā, tasmā na doso yathāvuttadosābhāvoti? Yadi kilesānaṃ avattamānatāsaṅkhāto abhāvo nibbānaṃ, evaṃ sati ariyamaggassa niratthakatā āpajjati [M 2.0207] maggakkhaṇato pubbepi tadabhāvasiddhito. Tenāha “ariyamaggassā”tiādi. Tasmā akāraṇametanti yasmā na nibbānassa anupalabbhanīyatā, abhāvamattatā, paṭipattiyā vañjhabhāvo, atītānāgatābhāve nibbānādhigamo ca āpajjati, vattamānānaṃ abhāvopi na sambhavati[V 2.0195], pageva kilesānaṃ avattamānatā, ariyamaggassa ca niratthakabhāvāpatti, tasmā nibbānassa abhāvasādhanatthaṃ yadidaṃ “anupalabbhanīyato, abhāvapāpakattā, tadā kilesānaṃ avattamānattā”ti ca kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ, akāraṇametaṃ, ayuttiresāti attho.

Furthermore, if Nibbāna were the non-presence of the present aggregates, then when the noble path is occurring, since the aggregates that are its support are present, Nibbāna would be non-existent at that time. And that being so, even at the path moment there would be no realization of Nibbāna. To show this, he said: 'The present... because of this fault.'

[The opponent objects:] 'We do not say that Nibbāna is the non-presence of all aggregates whatsoever. What then do we maintain? At that time, at the path moment, it is because of the non-presence of the defilements; therefore there is no fault, because the fault as stated is absent.'

[The author replies:] If Nibbāna were the absence designated as the non-presence of the defilements, this being so, the noble path would be rendered meaningless, since their absence would be established even before the path moment. Hence he says: 'For the noble path...'

Therefore, this is not a valid reason. For it does not follow that Nibbāna is unobtainable, or that it is mere non-existence, or that the practice is barren, or that Nibbāna is attained in the non-existence of past and future aggregates; nor is the non-existence of present aggregates possible. And the noble path would be rendered meaningless because of the non-presence of the defilements even before the path moment. Therefore, the reasons given to establish the non-existence of Nibbāna—namely, 'because it is unobtainable,' 'because it leads to non-existence,' and 'because at that time the defilements are not present'—are not valid reasons. The argument is illogical. This is the meaning.

559. Ādivacanatoti ādi-saddena avasiṭṭhaṃ jambukhādakasuttapadesaṃ (saṃ. ni. 4.314 ādayo), aññampi asaṅkhatāya dhātuyā niddesapāḷiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tathā hi “nibbānaṃ nibbānanti, āvuso sāriputta, vuccati, katamaṃ nu kho, āvuso, nibbānanti? Yo kho, āvuso, rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo, idaṃ vuccati nibbāna”nti jambukhādakasutte (saṃ. ni. 4.314 ādayo), “tattha katamā asaṅkhatā dhātu? Rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo”ti (vibha. 184) āyatanavibhaṅge vuttaṃ. Tatrāyamattho – nibbānaṃ asaṅkhatā dhātu asaṅkhatasabhāvo dhammo. Yasmā taṃ āgamma rāgādayo khīyanti, tasmā rāgakkhayo, dosakkhayo, mohakkhayoti ca vuccatīti. Āgammāti ca sabbasaṅkhārehi nibbinnassa visaṅkhāraninnassa gotrabhunā vivaṭṭitamānasassa maggena sacchikaraṇenāti attho. Sacchikiriyamānañhi taṃ adhigantvā ārammaṇapaccayabhūtañca paṭicca adhipatipaccayabhūte ca tasmiṃ paramassāsabhāvena vinimuttasaṅkhārassa paramagatibhāvena ca patiṭṭhānabhūte patiṭṭhāya khayasaṅkhāto maggo rāgādayo khepetīti taṃsacchikaraṇābhāve rāgādīnaṃ anuppattinirodhagamanābhāvā taṃ āgamma rāgādayo khīyantīti vuccanti. Ekaṃsena cetaṃ evaṃ sampaṭicchitabbaṃ, itarathā yathārutavasena pāḷiyā atthe gayhamāne bahū dosā āpajjantīti te dassetuṃ “arahattassāpī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Arahattañhi aggaphalapamukhā cattāro khandhāti na tassa rāgādikhayamattatā yuttā. Tampi hi…pe… niddiṭṭhaṃ. Tattha yathā rāgādīnaṃ khīṇante uppannattā arahattaṃ “rāgakkhayo”tiādinā niddiṭṭhanti suttassa neyyatthattā. Evaṃ nibbānaṃ āgamma rāgādayo khīyantīti nibbānaṃ “rāgakkhayo”tiādinā niddiṭṭhanti [M 2.0208] imassāpi suttassa neyyatthatā veditabbā. Nibbānassa rāgādikkhayamattatāya bahūdosā āpajjantīti dassetuṃ “kiñca bhiyyo”tiādi āraddhaṃ.

559. By the term 'initial statement,' the word 'etcetera' includes the remaining portion of the Jambukhādaka Sutta passage, and also other Pāḷi texts that give an exposition of the unconditioned element. For instance, in the Jambukhādaka Sutta, it is said: 'Friend Sāriputta, it is said, "Nibbāna, Nibbāna." What, friend, is Nibbāna? The destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion—this, friend, is called Nibbāna.' And in the Analysis of the Bases, it is stated: 'Therein, what is the unconditioned element? The destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion.' The meaning here is this: Nibbāna is the unconditioned element, a phenomenon with an unconditioned nature. Because lust and so on are destroyed by having recourse to it, it is called 'the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion.' 'By having recourse to it' means by realization through the path on the part of one who is disenchanted with all formations, inclined toward the unformed, and whose mind has been turned away by the change-of-lineage consciousness. For when Nibbāna is being realized, having been attained and serving as an object-condition, and depending on it which has become a dominance-condition and a ground of support, and by being established in it—which has the nature of supreme relief and is the supreme goal for one liberated from formations—the path, designated as 'destruction,' eradicates lust and so on. Thus, because in the absence of its realization there would be no arrival at the cessation which is non-re-arising of lust and so on, it is said that lust and so on are destroyed by having recourse to Nibbāna. This must be accepted unequivocally in this way; otherwise, if the meaning of the Pāḷi text is taken literally, many faults arise. To illustrate these faults, the passage beginning 'Even of arahantship...' was stated. For arahantship consists of the four aggregates headed by the supreme fruit, so it is not right for it to be merely the destruction of lust and so on. That too has been pointed out... etc. Therein, just as arahantship is described as 'the destruction of lust' and so on because it arises at the end of the destruction of lust and so on—this is due to the interpretable nature of the sutta—so too, because lust and so on are destroyed by having recourse to Nibbāna, Nibbāna is described as 'the destruction of lust' and so on. It should be understood that this sutta, too, has an interpretable nature. To show that many faults arise if Nibbāna is merely the destruction of lust and so on, the passage beginning with 'Furthermore...' is introduced.

Tattha ittarakālādippattidosatoti rāgādīnaṃ khayamattatāya parittakālatā, saṅkhatalakkhaṇatā, payogena vinā saraseneva adhigandhabbatā, rāgādīhi aparimuttatā, ādittatā, dukkhatā, anupasantatā, bahubhāvo, oḷārikatā, gotrabhumaggānaṃ anārammaṇatāti evamādidosāpajjanato[V 2.0196]. Rāgasseva khayo rāgakkhayo, na dosādīnaṃ. Tathā dosakkhayādayopīti añño rāgakkhayo, añño dosakkhayo, añño mohakkhayoti tiṇṇaṃ akusalamūlānaṃ khayabhūtāni tīṇi nibbānāni, catunnaṃ upādānānaṃ khaye cattāri, pañcannaṃ nīvaraṇānaṃ khaye pañca, channaṃ taṇhākāyānaṃ khaye cha, sattannaṃ anusayānaṃ khaye satta, aṭṭhannaṃ micchattānaṃ khaye aṭṭha, navannaṃ taṇhāmūlakānaṃ khaye nava, dasannaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ khaye dasa, diyaḍḍhakilesasahassassa khaye pāṭiyekkaṃ nibbānanti bahūni nibbānāni honti. Rāgādikkhayo nāma andhabālānampi pākaṭo, antamaso dīpimigamakkaṭādīnampi suviññeyyoti oḷārikaṃ nibbānaṃ hoti. Gotrabhukkhaṇe kilesakkhayassa abhāvato, maggakkhaṇe ca akhīṇattā, ārammaṇakaraṇassa ca asambhavo eva. Tassa nibbānabhāvatoti sabbapariyosānassa rāgādikkhayassa nibbānabhāvato. Yato khayato paṭṭhāya rāgādīnaṃ pavatti na hoti, so “ayaṃ nāmā”ti niyametabbo maggaphalañāṇānaṃ ārammaṇabhūto natthīti āha “na tādisassa khayassa abhāvato”ti.

Therein, because the mere destruction of lust and so on leads to the fault of incurring such defects as these: being of short duration; having the characteristic of the conditioned; being attainable without effort by its own nature; not being free from lust and so on; being inflamed; being suffering; being unpeaceful; being multiple; being coarse; and not being an object for the change-of-lineage and the path. The destruction of lust is just the destruction of lust, not of hatred and so on. Similarly for the destruction of hatred and the others. Thus, the destruction of lust would be one thing, the destruction of hatred another, and the destruction of delusion another. So there would be three Nibbānas that are the destruction of the three unwholesome roots; four for the destruction of the four kinds of clinging; five for the destruction of the five hindrances; six for the destruction of the six bodies of craving; seven for the destruction of the seven underlying tendencies; eight for the destruction of the eight wrongnesses; nine for the destruction of the nine things rooted in craving; ten for the destruction of the ten fetters; and for the destruction of the one and a half thousand defilements there would be a separate Nibbāna for each. Thus there would be many Nibbānas. The destruction of lust and so on is evident even to the blind and foolish, and at least very easily knowable even by tigers, deer, and monkeys; thus Nibbāna would be coarse. At the moment of change-of-lineage, there is no destruction of defilements, and at the moment of the path they are not yet destroyed; thus it is impossible for such a destruction to be made an object. The phrase 'because of its being Nibbāna' refers to the destruction of lust and so on, which is the final end of all, being Nibbāna. He said, 'not because of the absence of such a destruction,' because that destruction—from which onward the arising of lust and so on does not occur, which should be defined as 'this is its name,' and which is the object for the path and fruition knowledges—does not exist.

Kiñca bhiyyo – yo pacchimabhavato tatiyattabhāveyeva rāgādīsu ādīnavaṃ disvā jhānabhāvanāya te vikkhambhetvā aparihīnajjhāno kālaṃ katvā brahmalokaṃ upapanno, tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā idhāgatopi kāmesu vītarāgova hutvā pabbajitvā arahattaṃ patto, yo ca paṭhamavaye eva rāgādito nibbinno te ca jhānena vikkhambhetvā pacchimavaye arahattaṃ patto, tesaṃ rāgādīnaṃ vikkhambhanato paṭṭhāya anuppajjanato nirodhasadisatāya anuppattiyeva nirodho. Te nibbānappattā nāma siyuṃ, na ca honti, tasmā na tādisassa khayassa nibbānabhāvo. Tassāpi ittarakālatādidosasamāyogo evāti āha “bhāvepi cā”tiādi[M 2.0209].

Furthermore, there is more to be said. A person who, even in the third existence from the final one, having seen the danger in lust and so on, suppresses them through the development of jhāna, and with undiminished jhāna, passes away and is reborn in the Brahma world; having stayed there for the full lifespan, even upon returning here, becomes free from lust for sensual pleasures, goes forth, and attains Arahantship. And also a person who, even in the first stage of life, becomes disenchanted with lust and so on, suppresses them by means of jhāna, and in the last stage of life attains Arahantship. For these persons, from the suppression of lust and so on onwards, their non-arising, due to its similarity to cessation, is cessation itself. They might be called 'attainers of Nibbāna,' but they are not. Therefore, such a destruction does not have the nature of Nibbāna. For that too is connected with faults such as being of short duration. Thus, he said, 'bhāvepi ca' ('And even in the case of existence'), and so on.

Yadi “khayo”ti vacanato yato khayato paṭṭhāya rāgādīnaṃ appavatti, taṃ khayamattaṃ nibbānaṃ maññasi, evaṃ sati “khaye ñāṇa”ntiādīsu (dha. sa. dukamātikā 142; 1382) “khayo”ti vuttattā taduppattito paṭṭhāya ca rāgādīnaṃ anuppattīti maggassāpi nibbānabhāvāpattīti dassento “ariyamaggassa cā”tiādimāha.

If, based on the teaching 'destruction,' you consider Nibbāna to be merely that destruction from which the non-occurrence of lust and so on begins, then, this being the case, since the path is called 'destruction' in such passages as 'knowledge in destruction' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Duka-mātikā 142; 1382), and since from its arising onwards lust and so on do not arise, the noble path itself would attain the state of being Nibbāna. To show this, he said, 'ariyamaggassa ca' ('and of the noble path'), and so on.

Yathā niruddhā na santi, evaṃ anuppannāpīti abhāvasāmaññato nirodhasadisatāya anuppatti eva nirodho anuppattinirodho. Ayañhi maggena khepetabbākāro, yadidaṃ uppajjanārahassa anuppattidhammatāpādananti “khayo”ti ca vuccatīti. Taṃ itarakhayato visesento “anuppattinirodhasaṅkhātassa pana khayassā”ti āha. Anipphannatā pana tassa khayassa [V 2.0197] pariyāyena upanissayattāti vuttaṃ. Anuppattinirodhakkhayakarassa hi maggassa ārammaṇabhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ atthato tassa upanissayo viyāti vattabbataṃ labhati. Tadupacārenāti atthato phalabhūtakhayavohārena. Phalūpacārena hi kāraṇaṃ voharīyati yathā “āyu ghataṃ, semho guḷo”ti ca.

Just as what has ceased does not exist, so too what is unarisen. Thus, by the commonality of non-existence and due to its similarity to cessation, non-arising itself is cessation, hence it is the cessation of non-arising. For this is the mode to be exhausted by the path—namely, bringing about the state of non-arising for what is liable to arise—and for this reason it is also called 'destruction.' Distinguishing it from other kinds of destruction, he said, 'but of the destruction designated as the cessation of non-arising.' However, the unproduced nature of that destruction is said to be a support figuratively. For Nibbāna, which is the object for the path that brings about the destruction that is the cessation of non-arising, can, in a real sense, be said to be like its decisive support. This is by that metaphorical usage—that is, by the designation based on the destruction which is the fruit. For a cause is designated by a metaphor based on its effect, as when it is said, 'ghee is long life' and 'molasses is phlegm.'

Assāti nibbānassa. “Idampi kho ṭhānaṃ sududdasa”ntiādinā (dī. ni. 2.64, 66-67; ma. ni. 2.337; saṃ. ni. 1.172; mahāva. 7-8) paccavekkhato bhagavato appossukkabhāvāvahanato. “Tañhi te, māgaṇḍiya, ariyaṃ cakkhuṃ natthi, yena tvaṃ ariyena cakkhunā ārogyaṃ jāneyyāsi, nibbānaṃ passeyyāsī”ti (ma. ni. 2.218) vacanato ariyena cakkhunā passitabbaṃ.

'Of this' means of Nibbāna, because it brought about a state of little enthusiasm in the Blessed One as he reflected, 'This state, too, is very hard to see,' and so on. According to the saying, 'For you, Māgaṇḍiya, do not have that noble eye with which you could know health, with which you could see Nibbāna,' it is to be seen with the noble eye.

560. Yadi nibbānaṃ nāma sabhāvadhammo atthi sattasantānapariyāpanno ca, atha kasmā catumahāpathe sabhā viya sabbasādhāraṇā na labbhatīti āha “maggasamaṅginā pattabbato asādhāraṇa”nti. “Asukassa sammāsambuddhassa kāle uppanna”nti evaṃ purimāya koṭiyā abhāvato appabhavaṃ. Maggabhāveti ariyamaggassa atthibhāve. Bhāvato vijjamānato laddhabbato.

560. If there is a phenomenon called Nibbāna with its own nature, and it is included in the continuity of a being, then why is it not obtained by all in common, like a public hall at a great crossroads? He says, 'It is not common because it is to be attained by one endowed with the path.' It is without origin because it has no prior limit such that one could say, 'It arose at the time of such-and-such a Perfectly Enlightened One.' 'In the existence of the path' means in the existence of the noble path. Because it exists, because it is present, it is attainable.

Aṇuādīnanti aṇupakatikālapurisādīnaṃ. Niccabhāvāpattīti sassatabhāvasiddhi. Kūṭaṭṭhaniccatā hi idhādhippetā. Hetuno abhāvāti upapattiyā sādhanahetuno abhāvā. Niccā te aṇuādayo. Nibbānassa [M 2.0210] niccattāti apekkhadhammattāti hetulakkhaṇānupapatti. “Aṇuādīnaṃ asiddhattā”ti etena “niccā aṇuādayo”ti paṭiññāya dhammiasiddhi, tato ca nissayāsiddho hetūti dasseti.

'Of atoms, etc.' means of atoms, nature, time, persons, etc. 'The attainment of a permanent state' means the establishment of an eternal state. For here, permanence like a mountain peak is intended. 'Because of the absence of a cause' means because of the absence of a proving cause for its existence. Those atoms, etc., are permanent. As for the reason 'because of the permanence of Nibbāna,' since this has the nature of being relative, it does not meet the characteristic of a valid reason. By 'because atoms, etc., are unproven,' he shows that in the proposition 'atoms, etc., are permanent,' the subject of the proposition is unproven, and because of that, the reason is unproven as to its basis.

561. Yathāvuttayuttisabbhāvatoti “appabhavattā”ti attanā vuttaṃ hetuṃ sandhāyāha. Appabhavatā cassa apaccayatāya daṭṭhabbā, tāya tassa purimāya koṭiyā abhāvo. “Rūpasabhāvātikkamato”ti etena yathā rūpadhammānaṃ ruppanasabhāvo, paṭighātavantatāya kalāpaso vuttiyā padesasambandho ca sabhāvo, evaṃ nibbānassa katthaci paṭighāto, sappadesatā ca natthīti dasseti. Na hi nibbānaṃ “asukadisāya, asukadese”ti vā niddisīyati, yato taṃ appatiṭṭhamevāti.

561. 'Because of the existence of the aforesaid reason'—he says this referring to the reason stated by himself, 'because it is without an origin.' And its being without an origin should be seen as its being unconditioned; because of that, it has no prior limit. By 'because it transcends the nature of form,' he shows that just as material phenomena have a nature of being afflicted, and, due to possessing resistance, a nature of occurring in groups and being connected with a location, so for Nibbāna there is no resistance anywhere and no state of having a location. For Nibbāna is not pointed out as 'in such-and-such a direction' or 'in such-and-such a place,' since it is indeed without a foundation.

“Asithila [V 2.0198] …pe… gamanīyato”ti etena nibbānassa ariyānaṃ paccakkhasiddhataṃ dasseti. “Sabbaññuvacanato”ti etena tadaññesaṃ anumānasiddhataṃ, tadubhayena “anupalabbhanīyato”ti panassa hetuno asiddhataṃ dasseti. Paramatthena nāvijjamānaṃ vijjamānamevāti yathāraddhamatthaṃ nigametvā tadatthasādhanaṃ āgamaṃ dassento “vuttañheta”nti-. ādimāha.

By 'Not lax … to be gone to,' he shows that Nibbāna is established for the noble ones by direct experience. By 'Because of the word of the Omniscient One,' he shows that for others it is established by inference. By both of these, however, he shows the unestablished nature of the opponent's reason, 'because it is unapprehendable.' Having concluded the meaning as undertaken—that it is not non-existent in the ultimate sense, but is indeed existent—and showing the scriptural authority that establishes that meaning, he says the passage beginning, 'For this was said…'

Tattha ajātaṃ abhūtaṃ akataṃ asaṅkhatanti (udā. 73; netti. 41) cattāripi padāni aññamaññavevacanāni. Atha vā vedanādayo viya hetupaccayasamavāyasaṅkhātāya kāraṇasāmaggiyā na jātaṃ na nibbattanti ajātaṃ. Kāraṇena vinā, sayameva ca na bhūtaṃ na pātubhūtaṃ na uppannanti abhūtaṃ. Evaṃ ajātattā, abhūtattā ca yena kenaci kāraṇena na katanti akataṃ. Jātabhūtakatabhāvo ca nāma rūpādīnaṃ saṅkhatadhammānaṃ hoti, na asaṅkhatabhāvassa nibbānassāti dassanatthaṃ “asaṅkhata”nti vuttaṃ. Paṭilomato vā samecca sambhūya paccayehi katanti saṅkhataṃ, tathā na saṅkhataṃ saṅkhatalakkhaṇarahitanti ca asaṅkhatanti evaṃ anekehi kāraṇehi nibbattitabhāve paṭisiddhe “pakativādīnaṃ pakati viya siyā nu kho ekeneva kāraṇena etaṃ kata”nti āsaṅkāyaṃ kenaci na katanti dassanatthaṃ “akata”nti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ apaccayampi samānaṃ “sayameva nu kho idaṃ bhūtaṃ pātubhūta”nti [M 2.0211] āsaṅkāyaṃ taṃ nivattanatthaṃ “abhūta”nti vuttaṃ. Ayañcetassa asaṅkhatākatābhūtabhāvo sabbena sabbaṃ ajātidhammattāti dassetuṃ “ajāta”nti vuttaṃ.

Herein, the four terms—'unborn' (ajātaṃ), 'unbecome' (abhūtaṃ), 'unmade' (akataṃ), and 'unconditioned' (asaṅkhataṃ)—are synonyms for one another. Alternatively, like feelings and so on, it is not born, not produced by the assemblage of causes known as the conjunction of causes and conditions; therefore, it is 'unborn'. And without a cause, it is not become by itself, not manifest, not arisen; therefore, it is 'unbecome'. Thus, because it is unborn and unbecome, it is not made by any cause whatsoever; therefore, it is 'unmade'. Furthermore, the state of being born, become, and made belongs to conditioned phenomena such as form, but not to the unconditioned nature of Nibbāna; to show this, it is called 'unconditioned'. Or, conversely, that which is made by causes coming together and assembling is 'conditioned'; as it is not conditioned in that way, and is devoid of the characteristics of the conditioned, it is 'unconditioned'. In this way, when its being produced by many causes has been refuted, to counter the doubt, 'Could it be made by a single cause, like the primordial nature (pakati) of the proponents of primordial nature?', and to show that it is not made by anything, it is called 'unmade'. In this way, although it is without a cause, to dispel the doubt, 'Could this have become manifest by itself?', it is called 'unbecome'. And to show that this state of being unconditioned, unmade, and unbecome is in every respect due to its nature of non-arising, it is called 'unborn'.

Evamettha satthā paramatthato nibbānassa atthibhāvaṃ pavedesi. Pavedento ca “ahaṃ dhammissaro dhammassāmī”ti na attano āṇāmattena pavedesi, apica kho pana padaparame anukampamāno yuttitopi pavedesi. Yathāha –

Thus, herein, the Teacher proclaimed the existence of Nibbāna in the ultimate sense. And in proclaiming it, he did not proclaim it merely by his own authority, saying, 'I am the lord of the Dhamma, the master of the Dhamma,' but rather, out of compassion for those for whom the text is supreme, he proclaimed it also with reason. As was said:

“No cetaṃ, bhikkhave, abhavissa ajātaṃ abhūtaṃ akataṃ asaṅkhataṃ, nayidha jātassa bhūtassa katassa saṅkhatassa nissaraṇaṃ paññāyetha. Yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave, atthi ajātaṃ abhūtaṃ akataṃ asaṅkhataṃ, tasmā jātassa bhūtassa katassa saṅkhatassa nissaraṇaṃ paññāyatī”ti (udā. 73; netti. 41).

“Bhikkhus, if this unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned did not exist, no escape would be discerned here from what is born, become, made, and conditioned. But because, Bhikkhus, there is an unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned, therefore an escape is discerned from what is born, become, made, and conditioned.”

Tassattho [V 2.0199] – bhikkhave, yadi ajātādisabhāvā asaṅkhatā dhātu na abhavissa na siyā, idha loke jātādisabhāvassa rūpādikkhandhapañcakasaṅkhātassa saṅkhatassa nissaraṇaṃ anavasesavūpasamo na paññāyeyya na upalabbheyya na sambhaveyya. Nibbānañhi ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattamānā sammādiṭṭhiādayo ariyamaggadhammā anavasesaṃ saṃkilese samucchindanti, tenettha sabbassāpi vaṭṭadukkhassa apagamo nissaraṇaṃ paññāyati. Evaṃ byatirekavasena nibbānassa atthibhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni anugamanavasenapi taṃ dassetvā nigametuṃ “yasmā ca kho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Its meaning is: O bhikkhus, if the unconditioned element, which has the nature of the unborn and so on, did not exist, were not, then in this world, the escape and appeasement without remainder of the conditioned—designated as the collection of the five aggregates beginning with form, which has the nature of the born and so on—would not be discerned, would not be found, and would not be possible. For the factors of the Noble Path, such as right view and so on, proceeding with Nibbāna as their object, utterly eradicate the defilements without remainder. Therefore, in this world, the removal and escape from all the suffering of the round is discerned. Having thus shown the existence of Nibbāna by way of negative concomitance, now, to show it also by way of positive concomitance and to conclude, 'But since...' and so on was said. The meaning of this should be understood in the way already explained.

Ettha ca yasmā “appaccayā dhammā asaṅkhatā dhammā (dha. sa. dukamātikā 7-8). Atthi, bhikkhave, tadāyatanaṃ, yattha neva pathavī (udā. 71). Idampi kho ṭhānaṃ sududdasaṃ, yadidaṃ sabbasaṅkhārasamatho sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo (dī. ni. 2.64, 67; ma. ni. 2.337; saṃ. ni. 2.172; mahāva. 7-8). Asaṅkhatañca vo, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desessāmi asaṅkhatagāminiñca paṭipada”ntiādīhi (saṃ. ni. 4.366) anekehi suttapadehi “atthi, bhikkhave, ajāta”nti (udā. 73; netti. 41) iminā ca suttapadena nibbānadhātuyā paramatthato sabbhāvo sabbalokaṃ anukampamānena sammāsambuddhena pakāsito, tasmā [M 2.0212] yadipi kattha apaccakkhakārīnampi sāsane abhippasannānaṃ viññūnaṃ saṃsayo natthiyeva. Ye pana paraneyyabuddhino puggalā, tesaṃ vimativinodanatthaṃ ayamettha adhippāyaniddhāraṇamukhena yuttivicāraṇā.

Herein, because through many sutta passages—such as 'Phenomena not conditioned by causes are unconditioned phenomena'; 'There is, O bhikkhus, that base where there is no earth…'; 'This state, too, is very hard to see, namely the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all attachments'; and 'And I will teach you, O bhikkhus, the unconditioned and the path leading to the unconditioned'—and through this sutta passage, 'There is, O bhikkhus, the unborn…,' the real existence of the Nibbāna-element in the ultimate sense has been declared by the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha out of compassion for the whole world of beings. Therefore, although for the wise who have deep confidence in the teaching but have not directly realized it, there is certainly no doubt. However, for those individuals whose understanding depends on others, this is an examination of reasoning here, chiefly by way of determining the intended meaning, for the purpose of dispelling their doubt.

Yathā pariññeyyatāya sauttarānaṃ kāmānaṃ, rūpānañca paṭipakkhabhūtaṃ tabbidhurasabhāvaṃ nissaraṇaṃ paññāyati, evaṃ sabhāvānaṃ sabbesampi saṅkhatadhammānaṃ paṭipakkhabhūtena tabbidhurasabhāvena nissaraṇena bhavitabbaṃ. Yañca taṃ nissaraṇaṃ, sā asaṅkhatā dhātu. Kiñca bhiyyo – saṅkhatadhammārammaṇavipassanāñāṇaṃ, apica anulomañāṇaṃ kilese tadaṅgavasena pajahati, na samucchedavasena pajahituṃ sakkoti. Tathā sammutisaccārammaṇaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīsu ñāṇaṃ vikkhambhanavaseneva kilese pajahati, na samucchedavasena. Iti saṅkhatadhammārammaṇassa, sammutisaccārammaṇassa ca ñāṇassa kilesānaṃ samucchedappahāne asamatthabhāvato tesaṃ samucchedappahānakarassa ariyamaggañāṇassa tadubhayaviparītasabhāvena ārammaṇena bhavitabbaṃ, sā asaṅkhatā dhātu.

Just as, because sensual pleasures and forms, which have a superior, are to be fully understood, an escape is discerned which is their opposite and has a nature dissimilar to them, so too, for all conditioned phenomena whatsoever that possess a nature, there must be an escape which is their opposite and has a nature dissimilar to them. And that escape is the unconditioned element.
