Furthermore, insight knowledge that takes conditioned phenomena as its object, and also conformity knowledge, abandons defilements only by way of temporary abandonment, not by way of eradication. Similarly, knowledge in the first jhāna and so on, which takes conventional reality as its object, abandons defilements only by way of suppression, not by way of eradication. Thus, because the knowledge that takes conditioned phenomena as its object and the knowledge that takes conventional reality as its object are incapable of the eradication of defilements, the noble path knowledge—which performs the eradication of those defilements—must have an object with a nature contrary to both. That object is the unconditioned element.

Tathā [V 2.0200] “atthi, bhikkhave, ajātaṃ abhūtaṃ akataṃ asaṅkhata”nti (udā. 73; netti. 41) evamādi nibbānassa paramatthato atthibhāvajotakavacanaṃ aviparītatthaṃ bhagavatā bhāsitattā. Yañhi bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ, taṃ aviparītatthaṃ yathā taṃ “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā, sabbe saṅkhārā dukkhā, sabbe dhammā anattā”ti (ma. ni. 1.353, 356; dha. pa. 277-279; theragā. 676-678; netti. 5), tathā nibbānasaddo katthaci visaye yathābhūtaparamatthavisayo upacāravuttisabbhāvato. Seyyathāpi sīhasaddoti evamādīhi nayehi yuttitopi asaṅkhatāya dhātuyā paramatthato atthibhāvo veditabbo.

Furthermore, such statements as, 'Bhikkhus, there is the unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned,' which illuminate the existence of Nibbāna in the ultimate sense, have a non-inverted meaning because they were spoken by the Blessed One. For whatever was spoken by the Blessed One has a non-inverted meaning, just as with: 'All formations are impermanent; all formations are suffering; all phenomena are non-self.' Also, the word 'Nibbāna' has as its object the ultimate reality as it actually is, although metaphorical usages of the word exist, just as with the word 'lion.' By such lines of reasoning, and also from reason, the existence of the unconditioned element in the ultimate sense is to be understood.

Aparo nayo – yadi pana nibbānaṃ abhāvamattameva siyā, tassa “gambhīro duddaso duranubodho santo paṇīto atakkāvacaro nipuṇo paṇḍitavedanīyo”ti (dī. ni. 2.64, 67; ma. ni. 2.337; saṃ. ni. 1.172; mahāva. 7-8) gambhīrāditā, “asaṅkhatañca vo, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desessāmī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 4.366) asaṅkhatāditā, “abyākatā dhammā apaccayādhammā”tiādinā abyākatadhammāditā ca na vattabbā siyā. Na hi abhāvassa [M 2.0213] koci sabhāvo atthi, yena so gambhīrāsaṅkhatādiākārato viññāyeyya. Abhāvo hi abhāvo eva, kuto tassa gambhīrāsaṅkhātādibhāvasambandho. Kiñcāyamabhāvo sabbesaṃ kilesānaṃ sabbasattasantānagatānaṃ eko vā bhaveyya aneko vā. Yadi eko, ekeneva maggena sabbakilesābhāvo kato, sacchikato cāti aññassa, aññesañca maggānaṃ niratthakatāti na siyā maggabahutā, ekajjhañca sabbasattānaṃ nibbānādhigamo āpajjati. Siyā panevaṃ eko eva so nibbānasaññito kilesābhāvo, so pana na maggehi kātabbo, atha kho sacchikātabboti. Evaṃ sati visesato maggassa niratthakatā āpajjati, kilesānaṃ appahānatoti ekopi maggo na siyā. Asati ca kilesappahāne dukkhassa anupacchedanato kilesābhāvasacchikiriyā kimatthiyā siyā, atha pana maggānaṃ santānagatasaṃyojanattayappahānādipaṭiniyatakiccatāya catūsu maggesu pāṭiyekkaṃ kilesābhāvo. Evaṃ sati sabhāvapabhedena vinā na bahubhāvoti so kilesakkhayapariyāyena vutto sabhāvadhammo eva siyā.

Another approach: If Nibbāna were merely non-existence, then its being described as 'profound, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of reasoning, subtle, to be experienced by the wise,' its designation as 'the unconditioned,' and its classification among 'undeclared phenomena, phenomena without conditions' could not be stated. For non-existence has no intrinsic nature by which it could be recognized as profound, unconditioned, and so on. Non-existence is simply non-existence—how could it have any connection to qualities like profundity or being unconditioned? Furthermore, would this non-existence of all defilements present in the continua of all beings be one or many? If it were one, then since the non-existence of all defilements would be made and realized by a single path, another path and other paths would be useless. Consequently, there would be no multiplicity of paths, and all beings would attain Nibbāna simultaneously. It might be so that this single non-existence of defilements, called Nibbāna, is not to be made by the paths, but rather to be realized. In that case, the path would be especially useless, because of the non-abandonment of the defilements; thus not even a single path would exist. And when there is no abandonment of defilements, because suffering is not cut off, what would be the purpose of realizing the non-existence of defilements? Or else, because the paths have the specific function of abandoning the three fetters present in the continuum and so on, for each of the four paths there is a respective non-existence of defilements. This being so, without a distinction in intrinsic nature, there is no multiplicity. Therefore, that which is spoken of by the synonym 'destruction of defilements' must be an actual phenomenon with an intrinsic nature.

Yesaṃ abhāvo, tappabhedena abhāve bhedopacāroti ce? Yesaṃ abhāvo, tesaṃ sasabhāvatāya tassa sabhāvopacāropi siyā. Tathā ca te saṃkilesasaṅkhatatādito kilesasaṅkhatatādiupacārāpi [V 2.0201] siyuṃ. No ce te icchitā, tappabhedena bhedopacāropi na icchitabbo. Na ca pahoti upacarito bahubhāvo atthato bahubhāvāya. Na hi jalaṃ analanti upacaritaṃ dahati, pacati vā. Ekattapañhampi cāyamabhāvo asabhāvatāya na sahatīti na sakkā vattuṃ natthibhāvasāmaññato abhedavohāro yuttarūpoti. Ekatte ca pubbe vuttā eva dosā, bahubhāve pana sati vuttanayeneva siddhā sabhāvadhammatā. Sabhāvadhammattepi ca bahubhāvo viya bhāvaṃ bhāvopi bahubhāvaṃ na byabhicareyyāti nibbānassa bahubhāvapasaṅgo siyāti ce? Na bahubhāvasseva abhāvappasaṅgato. Yadi hi yathā kakkhaḷatā bhāvaṃ, evaṃ bhāvopi kakkhaḷataṃ na byabhicareyya. Evaṃ sati sabbesaṃ bhāvānaṃ pathavībhāvāpattito kuto bhāvassa bahubhāvo, tasmā lokavohārānaṃ vicittatāya yadipi bahutā bhāvāpekkhā, bhāvatā pana na bahutāpekkhāti na bhāvassa sato nibbānassa bahubhāvo “ekā niṭṭhā [M 2.0214] na puthu niṭṭhā”ti vacanato. Ekasmiṃyeva ca dassanabhāvanādvayaṃ sambhavati.

If it is said: 'For those defilements of which there is an absence, is there a figurative designation of division in that absence corresponding to their division?' For those defilements of which there is an absence, because they have their own nature, there could also be a figurative designation of own-nature for that absence. And so, because they are defilements, conditioned, and so on, there could also be figurative designations such as 'defilement', 'conditioned', and so on. If these are not wished for, then the figurative designation of division corresponding to their division should also not be wished for. And a figurative multiplicity is not able to become multiplicity in reality. For water figuratively called 'fire' does not burn or cook. Furthermore, since this absence, having no intrinsic nature, cannot sustain even the question of unity, it cannot be said that 'a non-differentiated designation is appropriate due to the commonality of non-existence'. In the case of unity, the faults are just as stated before. But when there is multiplicity, the state of having an own-nature is established in the way already stated. If it is said: 'Even when there is the state of having an own-nature, just as multiplicity does not deviate from existence, so too existence would not deviate from multiplicity; thus there would be the unwanted consequence of multiplicity for Nibbāna?' No, because that would lead to the unwanted consequence of the absence of multiplicity itself. For if, just as hardness does not deviate from existence, so too existence did not deviate from hardness, then since all existing things would acquire the state of earth, whence could there be a multiplicity of existence? Therefore, because of the diversity of worldly conventions, although multiplicity is relative to existence, existence is not relative to multiplicity. Thus for Nibbāna, which is an existent, there is no multiplicity, in accordance with the statement: 'The consummation is one, not many.' And in that one alone, the pair of seeing and development is possible.

Parinibbutānaṃ paccekaṃ nibbānabhāve sattasantānaniyataṃ nāma nibbānaṃ siyā. Tathā ca sati saṅkhatatādidosānativattiyeva, kilesappahānaṃ vā maggakiccaṃ kilesānaṃ abhāvo. Tassa ca ekatte na maggabahutā kiccantarassa kattabbassa abhāvato. Maggabahubhāvo ca maggehi sacchikātabbe ekasmiṃ dhamme indriyānaṃ apāṭavapāṭavapāṭavatarapāṭavatamabhāvena sacchikiriyāvisesena kilesānaṃ pahānabhedena hotīti nibbānassa sabhāvadhammatte eva siyā. Abhāvopi ca kilesānaṃ maggena sakiccakatāya kātabbo eva siyā, na sacchikātabbo. Ko hi sabhāvo abhāvassa? Yo sacchikātabbo siyā, so ce nibbānaṃ ekeneva maggena sabbakilesānaṃ abhāvo eko abhinno kātabbo āpanno. Aññathā maggavasena catubbidhabhāve nibbānassa catubbidhabhāvappasaṅgo, nibbānavisesappasaṅgo ca āpajjeyyāti maggakiccassa ekattena maggabahutā siyā. Bahubhāve pana tesaṃ so vuttanayena ekasmiṃ dhamme sacchikiriyāvisesatoti siddhā nibbānassa sabhāvadhammatā. Khayādhigantabbatāya panetaṃ “khayo”ti vuttaṃ. “Khaye ñāṇa”nti (dha. sa. dukamātikā 142; 1382) hi vacanato ariyamaggo khayo nāma. Tena cetaṃ adhigantabbaṃ sacchikātabbaṃ, tasmā “khayo”ti vuttanti.

If Nibbāna were an individual state for those who have attained Parinibbāna, it would be what is called 'fixed in the continuum of beings.' And if it were so, it would not transcend the faults such as being conditioned. Or, the function of the path, the abandoning of the defilements, is the absence of the defilements. And if that absence is one, there would not be a multiplicity of paths, because there is no other function to be performed. The multiplicity of paths occurs due to the difference in abandoning the defilements through the distinction in realization of the one Dhamma to be realized by the paths, this distinction being due to the faculties being dull, sharp, sharper, and sharpest. Therefore, this multiplicity of paths would only be possible if Nibbāna has an own-nature. Moreover, the absence of the defilements, since its function is performed by the path, would have to be produced, not realized. For what own-nature does absence have that it should be realized? If that absence were Nibbāna, then the one, undifferentiated absence of all defilements would have to be produced by a single path. Otherwise, if that absence were fourfold in accordance with the paths, the unwanted consequence of Nibbāna being fourfold and the unwanted consequence of distinctions in Nibbāna would arise. Thus, if the function of the path is one, there would not be a multiplicity of paths. But when there is a multiplicity of them, that multiplicity is established through the distinction in realization in regard to the one Dhamma in the way stated. Thus, it is established that Nibbāna has an own-nature. But because it is to be attained by the path called 'destruction,' it is called 'destruction.' For, according to the passage 'knowledge in destruction' (Dhs. Dukamātikā 142; §1382), the noble path is called 'destruction.' And by that path, this is to be attained, to be realized; therefore it is called 'destruction.'

Iti nirodhaniddesakathāvaṇṇanā.

Thus ends the Commentary on the Exposition of Cessation.

Magganiddesakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Path

562. Aṭṭha [V 2.0202] dhammāti “katamaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasacca”nti ārabhitvā “sammādiṭṭhī”tiādinā pāḷiyaṃ (vibha. 205) dukkhanirodhagāminipaṭipadāniddese āgatā, tameva ca pāḷiṃ ānetvā uddesavasena idha ca vuttā sammādiṭṭhiādayo aṭṭha dhammā atthato pakāsitā, na maggasaccaniddesavasenāti adhippāyo. Yadi atthato pakāsitā, kimatthiyaṃ pana idha kathananti āha “idha panā”tiādi. Tattha “ekakkhaṇe pavattamānāna”nti idaṃ lokiyakusalacittuppādesu viratiyo nānākkhaṇikā eva [M 2.0215] hontīti katvā vuttaṃ. Sesamaggadhammā pana tatthāpi ekajjhaṃ uppajjantiyeva. Visesāvabodhanatthanti paṭipakkhasamugghātādipavattiākāravisesassa avabodhanatthaṃ. Vitthārato maggakathā parato āvi bhavissatīti āha “saṅkhepato”ti. Catusaccapaṭivedhāya paṭipannassāti yathā catusaccābhisamayo hoti, evaṃ sabbaso pubbabhāgapaṭipattiyā paripūraṇavasena paṭipannassa. Ariyamaggasaṅkhātassa yogassa sabbhāvato yogino. Kāmaṃ avijjānusayasamugghāte tadekaṭṭhakilesānaṃ lesopi nāvasissati, vijjāya pana avijjā ujuvipaccanīkadhammoti dassanatthaṃ “avijjānusayasamugghātaka”nti vuttaṃ. Parato micchāsaṅkappādiggahaṇepi eseva nayo. Dhātuppakāsanarasāti paramatthapakāsanarasā, catusaccavibhāvanakiccāti attho. Maggadhammānaṃ paṭipakkhavidhamanākāro sātisayaṃ pākaṭo hutvā upaṭṭhātīti avijjānusayasamugghātakataṃ sammādiṭṭhiyā vatvāpi avijjandhakāraviddhaṃsanapaccupaṭṭhānatā vuttā.

562. Regarding 'eight factors': The meaning is that the eight factors beginning with right view—which are found in the Pāḷi's exposition of the path leading to the cessation of suffering, beginning with 'What is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering?' and 'Right view,' etc., and which are also stated here by way of a summary, quoting that very Pāḷi text—are explained according to their meaning, not by way of an exposition of the truth of the path. If they are explained according to their meaning, for what purpose are they stated here? He says: 'But here,' etc. Therein, the words 'arising in a single moment' are stated because in worldly wholesome mind-moments the abstinences occur at different moments. But the remaining path factors arise together even there. For the purpose of understanding the special features: for the purpose of understanding the special mode of occurrence, such as the eradication of the opposites. He says 'in brief' because a detailed discussion of the path will become clear later. Of one who has undertaken the practice for the penetration of the four truths: of one who has undertaken the practice by way of fulfilling the preliminary practice in all respects so that there is the realization of the four truths. Of a yogī, because of the existence of the practice called the noble path. Granted, when the underlying tendency to ignorance is eradicated, not even a trace of the defilements that have a common basis with it remains; but to show that knowledge is the direct opponent of ignorance, it is called 'the uprooter of the underlying tendency to ignorance.' The same method applies below in the case of wrong thought, etc. Its function is to reveal the ultimate reality: its function is to reveal the ultimate reality; the meaning is that its task is to make the four truths clear. Because the way the path factors demolish their opposites becomes exceedingly clear and present, even after stating that right view is the uprooter of the underlying tendency to ignorance, its manifestation as the dispeller of the darkness of ignorance is stated.

Tathā sampannadiṭṭhinoti yathā avijjānusayasamugghāto hoti, tathā maggasammādiṭṭhiyā sampannadiṭṭhino. Evañhi catusaccapaṭivedhāya paṭipannassa yoginoti imamatthaṃ tathā-saddo upasaṃharati. Nibbānārammaṇatā pana taṃsampayuttavacaneneva bodhitā. Micchāsaṅkappanighātakanti kāmasaṅkappādimicchāsaṅkappasamucchedakaṃ. Appanārasoti nibbānārammaṇe maggacittassa samuppādavasena pavattanato appanākicco.

'Of one endowed with such a view': of one endowed with the right view of the path in such a way that there is the uprooting of the underlying tendency to ignorance. For the word 'tathā' (such) summarizes this meaning: 'of a yogī who has undertaken the practice for the penetration of the four truths.' But its having Nibbāna as object is understood from the words associated with it. 'The crusher of wrong thought': the uprooter of wrong thoughts such as sensual thought. 'Its function is absorption': because it proceeds by way of the arising of path-consciousness with Nibbāna as its object, its task is absorption.

Tathā passato vitakkayato cāti vuttappakārāya sammādiṭṭhiyā passato, nibbānārammaṇe ca sammāsaṅkappena cittaṃ abhiniropayato. Vacīduccaritasamugghātikāti catubbidhassapi vacīduccaritassa samucchedikā. Musāvādādīnaṃ visaṃvādanādikiccatāya lūkhānaṃ apariggāhakānaṃ [V 2.0203] paṭipakkhabhāvato siniddhabhāvena sampayuttadhammānaṃ pariggāhakasabhāvā sammāvācāti āha “sā pariggahalakkhaṇā”ti. Kāyikakiriyā kiñci kattabbaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, sayañca samuṭṭhahanaṃ ghaṭanaṃ hotīti sammākammantasaṅkhātā viratipi samuṭṭhānasabhāvā vuttā. Sampayuttadhammānaṃ vā ukkhipanaṃ samuṭṭhāpanaṃ kāyikakiriyāya bhārukkhipanaṃ viya.

'Of one seeing thus and thinking thus': of one seeing with right view of the kind described, and applying the mind with right thought to Nibbāna as object. 'The uprooter of verbal misconduct': the uprooter of all four kinds of verbal misconduct. Because it is the opponent of things that are rough and unembracing—since lying, etc., has the function of deceiving, etc.—right speech has the nature of embracing the associated states with a quality of smoothness. Thus he says: 'It has the characteristic of embracing.' Bodily action originates something to be done, and originating itself is an exertion; therefore the abstinence called right action is also said to have the nature of originating. Or, the lifting up, the originating, of the associated states is like the lifting of a burden by bodily action.

Assāti yogino. Tasmiṃ sati visujjhanato visuddhibhūtā. Jīvamānassa sattassa, sampayuttadhammānaṃ vā suddhi vodānaṃ, ājīvasseva vā jīvitindriyavuttiyā[M 2.0216]. Ñāyājīvassa abuddhapaṭikuṭṭhāya sammājīvikāya pavattihetutāya ñāyājīvapavattiraso. Imassa hi pavattito paṭṭhāya micchājīvo na pavattatīti.

'Of this one': of the yogī. When that is present, it is of the nature of purity because it purifies. It is the purity, the cleansing, of a living being, or of the associated states, or of livelihood itself by the functioning of the life faculty. Its function is the occurrence of a right livelihood because it is the cause for the occurrence of a right livelihood that is methodical and not despised by the wise. For from the time this occurs, wrong livelihood does not occur.

Sabbākusalaviddhaṃsakopi sammāvāyāmo ujupaṭipakkhadassanavasena kosajjasamucchedako vutto. Saṃkilesapakkhatopi tassa paggaṇhanaṃ paggaho. Kāyādīsu subhādiākārupadhāraṇavasena pavattā subhasaññādipubbaṅgamā akusalakkhandhā micchāsati, tassā viddhaṃsano micchāsativiniddhunano. Asammosoti sammosaviddhaṃsanato tappaṭipakkho. Ārammaṇassa yathāsabhāvasallakkhaṇaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ. “Ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā”ti, “satārakkhena cetasā”ti (dī. ni. 3.348) ca vacanato visesato sati kusalacittassa ārakkhāti āha “satiyā saṃrakkhiyamānacittassā”ti.

Although it destroys all unwholesome states, right effort is called the uprooter of laziness by way of showing its direct opposite. From the side of the defilements too, its exertion is exertion. The unwholesome aggregates—preceded by the perception of beauty, etc., and occurring by way of attending to the aspect of beauty, etc., in the body, etc.—are wrong mindfulness; the destroyer of that is the shaker-off of wrong mindfulness. As for non-confusion, because it destroys confusion, it is the opposite of that. Establishment is the correct marking of an object's intrinsic nature. In accordance with the statements, 'its manifestation is protection,' and, 'with a mind guarded by mindfulness' (DN 33), mindfulness is specifically the protection of a wholesome mind; thus, he says, 'of a mind being protected by mindfulness.'

563. Saccañāṇassāti saccāni ārabbha pavattanakañāṇassa, na paṭivedhañāṇaṃ viya sakideva bujjhati, atha kho punappunaṃ uppajjanato anu anu bodho anubodho, anussavākāraparivitakkadiṭṭhinijjhānakkhantianugato vā bodho anubodho, tadeva ñāṇanti anubodhañāṇaṃ. Na hi taṃ paccakkhato bujjhati, anussavādivasena pana kappanamukhena bujjhati. Kiccatoti parijānanādito. Taṃkiccakaraṇeneva hi pariññeyyādīni viya tānipi tassa pākaṭāni honti. Vivaṭṭānupassanāya hi saṅkhārehi patilīyamānamānasassa uppajjamānaṃ maggañāṇaṃ visaṅkhāraṃ dukkhanissaraṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā dukkhaṃ paricchindati, dukkhagatañca taṇhaṃ pajahati, nirodhañca sacchikaroti phusati. Ādicco viya pabhāya sammāsaṅkappādīhi saha samuppannaṃ taṃ maggaṃ bhāveti, na ca saṅkhāre amuñcitvā pavattamānena ñāṇena etaṃ sabbaṃ kātuṃ sakkā nimittapavattehi avuṭṭhitattā. Tasmā etāni kiccāni karontaṃ taṃ ñāṇaṃ dukkhādīni vibhāveti [V 2.0204] tattha sammohanivattanenāti “cattāripi saccāni paṭivijjhatī”ti vuttaṃ, ekapaṭivedhenāti adhippāyo.

563. As for ‘knowledge of the truth,’ it is the knowledge that arises taking the truths as its object. It is not like the knowledge of penetration, which understands only once; but rather, because it arises again and again, the repeated knowing is a subsequent knowing (anubodha). Or, a knowing that follows upon oral tradition, reflection on reasons, pondering on views, and approval through patient endurance is a subsequent knowing; that very thing is knowledge, thus it is subsequent knowledge (anubodhañāṇa). For it does not understand through direct experience, but rather it understands by means of conceptualization through the power of oral tradition and so on. As for ‘by its function,’ it is from full understanding and so on. For by the very performance of that function, those truths become manifest to it, just as the things to be fully understood, etc., become manifest. For through the contemplation of turning away, for one whose mind is withdrawing from formations, the path knowledge that arises, having made the unconditioned—the escape from suffering—its object, fully understands suffering, abandons the craving that pertains to suffering, and realizes and touches cessation. Like the sun with its light, it develops that path, which has arisen together with right intention and so on. And it is not possible for a knowledge that operates without having abandoned formations to do all this, because it has not emerged from that which proceeds by way of signs. Therefore, that knowledge, while performing these functions, clarifies suffering and so on by dispelling delusion regarding them. Thus it is said, ‘it penetrates all four truths,’ the intention being ‘by a single penetration.’

Dukkhasamudayampi so passatīti kālantaradassanaṃ sandhāya vuttanti ce? Na, “yo nu kho, āvuso, dukkhaṃ passati, dukkhasamudayampi so passatī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 5.1100) ekadassino aññattayadassitāvicāraṇāyaṃ taṃsādhanatthaṃ āyasmatā [M 2.0217] gavampatittherena imassa suttassa ānītattā, paccekañca saccesu dissamānesu aññattayadassanassa yojitattā. Aññathā anupubbābhisamaye purimadiṭṭhassa pacchā adassanato samudayādidassino dukkhādidassitā na yojetabbā siyā. Yojitā ca sā “yo dukkhasamudayaṃ passati, dukkhampi so passatī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 5.1100). Lokiyaṃ saccañāṇaṃ. Tattha lokiyañāṇe. Pariyuṭṭhānasaṅkhāto abhibhavo pariyuṭṭhānābhibhavo, tassa vasena. Suddhasaṅkhārapuñjamattadassanato sakkāyadiṭṭhipariyuṭṭhānaṃ nivatteti. “Lokasamudayaṃ kho, kaccāna, yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passato yā loke natthitā, sā na hotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.15) vacanato samudayadassanaṃ hetuphalapabandhāvicchedadassanato pariyuṭṭhānābhibhavavasena pavattamānaṃ ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ nivatteti. “Lokanirodhaṃ kho…pe… passato yā loke atthitā, sā na hotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.15) vacanato nirodhadassanaṃ hetunirodhā phalanirodhadassanato sassatadiṭṭhiṃ nivatteti. Attakārassa paccakkhadassanato maggadassanaṃ “natthi attakāre, natthi parakāre, natthi purisakāre”tiādikaṃ (dī. ni. 1.168) akiriyadiṭṭhiṃ pajahati. “Natthi hetu, natthi paccayo sattānaṃ saṃkilesāya, ahetū appaccayā sattā saṃkilissanti, natthi hetu…pe… visuddhiyā, ahetū appaccayā sattā visujjhantī”tiādikā (dī. ni. 1.168; ma. ni. 2.101, 227; saṃ. ni. 3.212) ahetukadiṭṭhi ca idha akiriyādiṭṭhiggahaṇeneva gahitāti daṭṭhabbā. Sāpi hi visuddhimaggadassanena pahīyatīti. Dukkhe ñāṇaṃ samudayaphalassa dukkhassa addhuvādibhāvaṃ passatīti phale vippaṭipattiṃ nivatteti.

If it is said that the statement, 'He also sees the origin of suffering,' was spoken with reference to seeing at a different time, [the reply is:] No. This is because this sutta was brought by the Venerable Gavampati Thera to establish that meaning in the investigation of how one who sees one truth also sees the other three, with the words beginning, 'Friend, one who sees suffering, he also sees the origin of suffering,' and because the seeing of the other three is applied when each of the truths is seen individually. Otherwise, in the case of gradual penetration, because what was seen first is not seen later, the seeing of suffering, etc., should not be applied to one who sees the origin, etc. And that is indeed applied by the words beginning, 'One who sees the origin of suffering, he also sees suffering.' This is mundane knowledge of the truth. Therein, in mundane knowledge, by means of overcoming obsession, it dispels the obsession of personality view by seeing merely a heap of bare formations. Because it is said, 'Kaccāna, for one who, with right wisdom, sees the origin of the world as it really is, that non-existence which is in the world does not occur,' the seeing of the origin—by seeing the unbroken continuity of the cause-and-effect series—which proceeds by way of overcoming obsession, dispels the annihilationist view. And because it is said, 'Kaccāna, for one who… sees the cessation of the world… that existence which is in the world does not occur,' the seeing of cessation—by seeing the cessation of the effect from the cessation of the cause—dispels the eternalist view. The seeing of the path, by directly perceiving one's own action, abandons the inactionist view that 'there is no self-action, there is no other-action, there is no personal effort.' And the view of causelessness—'There is no cause, no condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled without cause, without condition. There is no cause… for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause, without condition'—should be understood here as included by the taking of the inactionist view itself, for that too is abandoned by seeing the path to purification. Knowledge concerning suffering, by seeing the state of impermanence, etc., of suffering, which is the fruit of the origin, dispels wrong practice regarding the fruit.

Issaro lokaṃ pavatteti sajjeti nivatteti saṃharatīti issarakāraṇino vadanti. Padhānato loko āvi bhavati, tattheva ca patilīyatīti padhānakāraṇino.

A Lord brings the world into being and creates it, causes it to cease and withdraws it—so say the proponents of a Lord as cause. From primordial matter the world becomes manifest, and into that very same matter it dissolves—so say the proponents of primordial matter as cause.

“Kālo [V 2.0205] karoti bhūtāni, kālo saṃharatī pajā;

Kālo sutte jāgarati, kālo hi duratikkamo”ti. –

“Time creates beings, time consumes creatures; Time is awake among the sleeping, for time is truly hard to overcome.”

Kālavādino. Kaṇṭakassa tikhiṇabhāvo viya, kapiṭṭhaphalādīnaṃ parimaṇḍalatā viya, migapakkhisarīsapādīnaṃ vicittatā viya ca sabhāveneva loko sambhoti, vibhoti cāti sabhāvavādino. Ādi-saddena aṇūhi [M 2.0218] loko pavattati, sabbaṃ pubbekatahetu, loko niyato acchejjasuttāvutābhejjamaṇisadiso, na ettha kassaci purisakāroti niyativādino.

[So say] the proponents of time. Just as the sharpness of a thorn, the roundness of fruits like the wood-apple, and the variegated nature of beasts, birds, and reptiles come to be, so the world arises and ceases by its own intrinsic nature—so say the proponents of intrinsic nature. By the word ‘etc.’ are included the views that the world proceeds from atoms; that everything is caused by past action; and the view of the determinists, who hold that the world is fixed, like an unbreakable gem strung on an uncuttable thread, and that there is no personal effort here for anyone.

“Yadicchāya pavattanti, yadicchāya nivattare;

Yadicchāya sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ, tasmā yādicchakī pajā”ti. –

“By chance they proceed, by chance they turn back; By chance come happiness and suffering, therefore beings are governed by chance.”

Yadicchāvādino, ye adhiccasamuppattivādinoti ca vuccanti. Evamādiakāraṇavādasaṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Rāmudakaāḷārādīnaṃ viya, arūpaloke nigaṇṭhānaṃ viya ca lokathūpikāyaṃ apavaggo mokkhoti gahaṇaṃ apavaggagāho. Ādi-saddena padhānassa appavatti, guṇaviyuttassa attano sakattani avaṭṭhānaṃ, brahmunā salokatā, samīpatā, saṃyogo, diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādāti evamādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ettha ca padhānassa appavatti mahatādibhāvena apariṇāmo, anabhibyatti vā. “Ahamañño, pakati aññā”ti evaṃ pavattapakatipurisantarajānanena attasukhadukkhamohesu avibhāgaggahaṇe kira nivattite vuttanayena padhānaṃ nappavattati, so vimokkhoti kāpilā. Guṇaviyuttassāti buddhisukhadukkhaicchādosappayattadhammādhammasaṅkhārehi navahi attaguṇehi viyuttassāti kaṇādamatānusārino. Salokatā brahmunā samānalokatā. Samīpatā tassa samīpappavattitā. Saṃyogo tena ekībhāvūpagamanaṃ. “Indriyatappanaputtamukhadassanādīhi vinā apavaggo natthī”ti gahetvā tathā pavattanaṃ kāmasukhallikānuyogo. Anasanakesaluñcanāditapacariyāya naggasīlagosīlakukkurasīlādīhi ca attaparitāpanena mokkho hotīti attakilamatho.

The proponents of chance, who are also called proponents of spontaneous origination. Thus, the inclusion of the doctrine of causelessness, etc., should be understood. The grasping that release is liberation—like that of Rāma, Udaka, Āḷāra, and others in the formless realm, and like that of the Nigaṇṭhas in the lokathūpikā (the realm of non-percipient beings, like the pinnacle of the corporeal world)—is the ‘grasping at release.’ By the word ‘etc.’ should be understood the inclusion of such views as: the non-activity of primordial matter; the subsistence of the self, devoid of qualities, in its own selfhood; co-existence with Brahmā, proximity to him, and union with him; and the doctrines of Nibbāna in this very life. Herein, the non-activity of primordial matter means its non-transformation into the great principle, etc., or its non-manifestation. When, it is said, the grasping of non-distinction with regard to the self, pleasure, pain, and delusion has been dispelled by the knowledge of the difference between primordial nature and the person, which proceeds as ‘I am one, nature is another,’ then primordial matter no longer evolves in the aforesaid manner; this, according to the followers of Kapila, is liberation. ‘Devoid of qualities’ means devoid of the nine qualities of the self—intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, righteousness, unrighteousness, and formations—according to the followers of Kaṇāda's view. ‘Co-existence’ means sharing the same world as Brahmā. ‘Proximity’ means dwelling near him. ‘Union’ means becoming one with him. The indulgence in sensual pleasures is to hold the view that ‘there is no release without the gratification of the senses, seeing the faces of one's children, etc.’ and to act accordingly. Self-mortification is the view that liberation comes through tormenting oneself with ascetic practices such as fasting, pulling out the hair, and with observances such as the naked practice, the cow practice, and the dog practice.

Svāyaṃ sabbo micchāgāho saccañāṇe sati patiṭṭhaṃ na labhatīti vuttamevatthaṃ saṅgaṇhanto “loke lokappabhave”ti gāthamāhāti.

All this wrong grasping does not find a footing when there is knowledge of the truth. Summing up this very meaning that has been stated, he spoke the verse beginning, “In the world, in the origin of the world.”

Ñāṇakiccato vinicchayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the determination with respect to the function of knowledge.

564. Sesā [M 2.0219][V 2.0206] sabbadhammāti sesā ekāsīti lokiyadhammā. Ajjhattikabāhiresu dvādasasu āyatanesu kāmabhavavibhavataṇhāvasena dvādasatikā chattiṃsa taṇhāvicaritāni, khuddakavatthuvibhaṅge vā āgatanayena kālavibhāgaṃ anāmasitvā vuttāni. Tadāmasane hi aṭṭhasataṃ honti. Asammissanti ekakattā kenaci asammissaṃ, kuto tadantogadhappabhedoti adhippāyo. Vīmaṃsiddhipādādīnaṃ bodhipakkhiyānaṃ satipi kiccanānatte atthato ekattā sammādiṭṭhiyā saṅgahoti sammādiṭṭhimukhena tadantogadhatā vuttā.

564. ‘All remaining phenomena’ means the remaining eighty-one mundane phenomena. With respect to the twelve internal and external bases, there are thirty-six courses of craving—twelve triads by way of craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence—stated without touching upon the division by time, in the way it comes in the Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga. For when that is touched upon, there are one hundred and eight. ‘Unmixed’ means unmixed with anything because of its singularity; the intention is: How then could there be subdivisions included within it? Although the aids to enlightenment, such as the basis for spiritual power consisting of investigation, have a variety of functions, because they are one in meaning, they are included in right view. Thus their inclusion within it is stated by way of right view.

Tayo nekkhammavitakkādayoti lokiyakkhaṇe alobhamettākaruṇāsampayogavasena bhinnā, maggakkhaṇe lobhabyāpādavihiṃsāsamucchedanavasena tayoti ekopi vutto. Esa nayo sammāvācādīsu. Appicchatāsantuṭṭhitānaṃ pana bhāve sammāājīvasambhavato tena tesaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Bhavantarepi jīvitahetupi ariyehi avītikkamanīyattā ariyakantānaṃ sammāvācādisīlānaṃ gahaṇena yena saddhāhatthena tāni gahetabbāni, so saddhāhattho gahito eva hotīti tato anaññāni saddhindriyasaddhābalāni tattha antogadhāni vuttāni. Chando pana saddhānuguṇoti katvā chandiddhipādassāpi tadantogadhatā vuttā. Tesaṃ atthitāyāti saddhindriyasaddhābalachandiddhipādānaṃ atthitāya sīlassa atthibhāvato tividhenāpi sīlena te tayopi gahitāti tattha antogadhā. Cittasamādhīti cittiddhipādaṃ vadati. “Cittaṃ paññañca bhāvaya”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.23, 192; peṭako. 22; mi. pa. 2.1.9) hi cittamukhena samādhi vuttoti samādhimukhena cittampi vattabbataṃ arahati. Cittiddhipādabhāvanāya pana samādhipi adhimatto hotīti vīmaṃsiddhipādādivacanaṃ viya cittiddhipādoti avatvā idha “cittasamādhī”ti vuttaṃ. “Pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedeti, sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.466; 3.359; saṃ. ni. 5.376; a. ni. 3.96; 11.12) vacanato samādhiupakārā pītipassaddhiyo, tasmā samādhiggahaṇena gahitā. Upekkhā pana samādhiupakārakato, taṃsadisakiccato ca. Tasmā samādhisīsena etesaṃ antogadhatā daṭṭhabbā.

The three, namely thoughts of renunciation and so forth, are distinct at the mundane moment by way of their association with non-greed, loving-kindness, and compassion. At the path moment, the three are also spoken of as one by way of cutting off greed, ill will, and cruelty. This same method applies to right speech and so on. Since right livelihood arises for one with few wishes and contentment, their inclusion should be understood by that. Also in future existences, since the virtues of right speech and so on, which are dear to the noble ones, are not to be transgressed by them even for the sake of life, when these are to be grasped with the hand of faith, that hand of faith is indeed taken. Therefore the faith faculty and the faith power, being not other than that, are said to be included therein. And since desire is in conformity with faith, the inclusion of the basis for spiritual power of desire is also spoken of. Because of their existence—that is, because virtue exists due to the existence of the faith faculty, the faith power, and the basis for spiritual power of desire—those three are grasped by the threefold virtue and are thus included therein. 'Concentration of mind' refers to the basis for spiritual power of mind. For it is said, 'Develop the mind and wisdom'; thus, as concentration is spoken of by way of the mind, so the mind is fit to be spoken of by way of concentration. However, since concentration also becomes pre-eminent through the development of the basis for spiritual power of mind, instead of saying 'basis for spiritual power of mind'—like the expression 'basis for spiritual power of investigation,' etc.—here it is called 'concentration of mind.' Based on the statement, 'For one with a joyful mind, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one feels pleasure; the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated,' rapture and tranquility are assistants to concentration; therefore, they are included by the grasping of concentration. Equanimity, too, is included because it assists concentration and because its function is similar. Therefore, their inclusion should be understood under the heading of concentration.

Antogadhānaṃ pabhedavinicchayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the analysis and determination of the included factors is concluded.

565. Bhāro [M 2.0220] viya dukkhasaccaṃ vighātakattā, saṃharaṇīyavasena vihantabhāvatoti attho. Bhārādānamiva tattha tattha bhave uppajjanakavighātassa hetubhāvato. Bhāranikkhepanamiva pavattidukkhavūpasamabhāvato[V 2.0207]. Rogo viya, dubbhikkhamiva ca bādhakattā. Roganidānaṃ viya, dubbuṭṭhi viya ca pabhavalakkhaṇattā. Dubbuṭṭhīti ca avassanaṃ vā ativassanaṃ vā. Rogavūpasamo viya, subhikkhamiva ca santilakkhaṇattā, sukhabhāvato. “Nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukha”nti (dha. pa. 203-204) hi vuttaṃ. Bhesajjamiva, suvuṭṭhi viya ca dukkhassa hetupacchedato, tassa ca apagamūpāyabhāvato. Niyyānalakkhaṇañhi maggasaccaṃ. Aniṭṭhabhāvato, sāsaṅkasappaṭibhayato ca dukkhaṃ verivisarukkhabhayaorimatīrūpamaṃ. Veraṃ byāpādo, paccatthikabhāvo vā. Verasamugghāto veravūpasamo mettā. Verasamugghātupāyo saṅgahavatthūni.

565. The truth of suffering is like a burden because it is oppressive; the meaning is that it has the nature of being oppressive by way of being something to be carried along. The truth of the origin is like taking up the burden because it is the cause of the affliction of arising in various existences. The truth of cessation is like laying down the burden because it is the subsiding of the suffering of ongoing existence. Suffering is like a disease and like a famine because it oppresses. The origin is like the cause of disease and like a bad rain because it has the characteristic of being a source. 'Bad rain' is either no rain or too much rain. Cessation is like the subsiding of disease and like a time of abundance because it has the characteristic of peace and is a state of happiness. For it is said: 'Nibbāna is the supreme happiness.' The path is like medicine and like good rain because it cuts off the cause of suffering and is the means for its removal. For the truth of the path has the characteristic of an outlet. Because it is undesirable and because it is perilous and fearful, suffering has the form of an enemy, a poisoned tree, fear, and the near shore. Enmity is ill will or the state of being an adversary. The uprooting of enmity is loving-kindness, which is the appeasement of enmity. The means for uprooting enmity are the bases of sympathy.

Upamāto vinicchayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the determination by way of similes is concluded.

566. Esa nayo samudayādīsūti atthi cettha samudayo, na ariyasaccaṃ, atthi ariyasaccaṃ, na samudayo, atthi samudayo ceva ariyasaccañca, atthi neva samudayo na ariyasaccanti. Sesasaccadvayepi eseva nayo. Na ariyasaccaṃ pariññeyyapahātabbāsaṅkhataniyyānabhāvābhāvato. Itaraṃ pana ariyasaccadvayanti samudayamaggasaccadvayamāha. Siyā dukkhaṃ saṅkhāradukkhatāya. Tenāha “aniccato”ti. Tathattenāti tathasabhāvena, pariññeyyabhāvenāti attho. Etena taṃ ariyasaccadvayaṃ “siyā dukkhaṃ, na ariyasaccaṃ, siyā ariyasaccaṃ, na dukkha”nti imamatthaṃ dasseti. Ariyasaccasaddaparā hi dukkhādisaddā pariññeyyādibhāvaṃ vadanti. Teneva ariyasaccasaddānapekkhaṃ dukkhasaddaṃ sandhāya maggasampayuttasāmaññaphaladhammānaṃ ādipadasaṅgaho vutto, ariyasaccasaddāpekkhaṃ pana sandhāya catutthapadasaṅgaho.

566. This is the method regarding the origin, etc.: Here, there is an origin but not a noble truth; there is a noble truth but not an origin; there is both an origin and a noble truth; and there is neither an origin nor a noble truth. This same method applies to the remaining two truths. It is not a noble truth because of the absence of the state of being something to be fully understood, to be abandoned, unconditioned, or leading out. Furthermore, the other two noble truths—which he states are the two truths of origin and path—might be suffering due to the suffering of formations. Therefore, he said, 'as impermanent.' 'By its being-so' means by its true nature; the meaning is, by its nature of being something to be fully understood. By this, he shows this meaning concerning those two noble truths: 'It might be suffering but not a noble truth; it might be a noble truth but not suffering.' For the words 'suffering,' etc., when following the word 'noble truth,' denote the state of being something to be fully understood, etc. For that very reason, with reference to the word 'suffering' irrespective of the word 'noble truth,' the inclusion of the states associated with the path and the fruits of recluseship under the first phrase is stated; but with reference to it as dependent on the word 'noble truth,' the inclusion under the fourth phrase is stated.

Sabbākārenāti sabbappakārena. Yathā maggasampayuttadhammādayo ekaṅgavikalā, evaṃ ahutvā sabbaṅgayogena dukkhatāya ceva ariyasaccatāya cāti attho. “Upādānakkhandhapañcaka”nti vutte taṇhāyapi saṅgaho siyāti taṃnivattanatthaṃ “aññatra taṇhāyā”ti vuttaṃ tassā visuṃ ariyasaccabhāvato. Samudayādīsu avasesakilesādayo pabhavaṭṭhena samudayo, na ariyasaccaṃ suttantasaṃvaṇṇanā ayanti katvā[M 2.0221]. Nirodho ariyasaccaṃ, na samudayo. Itaraṃ pana ariyasaccadvayaṃ siyā samudayo attano phalassa paccayaṭṭhena, na pana yassa pahānāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati tathattena, sabbākārena pana taṇhāsamudayo ceva ariyasaccañca. Maggasampayuttadhammā, sāmaññaphalāni ca yassa pahānāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati tathattena neva samudayo, na ariyasaccaṃ. Saṅkhāranirodho, nirodhasamāpatti ca nirodho, na ariyasaccaṃ. Samudayo [V 2.0208] ariyasaccaṃ, na nirodho. Itaraṃ pana ariyasaccadvayaṃ siyā nirodho khaṇanirodhasabbhāvato, na pana yassa sacchikiriyāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati tathattena. Sabbākārena pana asaṅkhatā dhātu nirodho ceva ariyasaccañca. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Ariyamaggato aññāni maggāni maggo, na ariyasaccaṃ. Nirodho ariyasaccaṃ, na maggo. Itaraṃ pana saccadvayaṃ siyā maggo bhavagāminipaṭipadābhāvato, na pana yassa bhāvanāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati tathattena, sabbākārena pana nirodhagāminipaṭipadā maggo ceva ariyasaccañca. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

‘In all aspects’ means in every way. The meaning is that it is not like the path-associated states and so on, which are deficient in one factor, but by being endowed with all factors, it is both suffering and a noble truth. When ‘the five aggregates of clinging’ is said, craving might also be included; to exclude it, ‘apart from craving’ is said, because it is separately a noble truth. Among the origins, etc., the remaining defilements and so on are an origin in the sense of being a source, but not a noble truth, this being a Suttanta commentary. Cessation is a noble truth, not an origin. But the other two noble truths might be an origin in the sense of being a condition for their own fruit, but not in the sense of that for the abandoning of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. In all aspects, however, craving is both an origin and a noble truth. The states associated with the path and the fruits of recluseship are, in the sense of that for the abandoning of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One, neither an origin nor a noble truth. The cessation of formations and the attainment of cessation are cessation, but not a noble truth. The origin is a noble truth, not cessation. But the other two noble truths might be cessation because of the existence of momentary cessation, but not in the sense of that for the realization of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. In all aspects, however, the unconditioned element is both cessation and a noble truth. The rest is in the way already stated. Paths other than the noble path are a path, but not a noble truth. Cessation is a noble truth, not the path. But the other two truths might be a path because they are a practice leading to existence, but not in the sense of that for the development of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. In all aspects, however, the practice leading to cessation is both the path and a noble truth. The rest is in the way already stated.

Catukkato vinicchayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the analysis by way of the tetrad.

567. Suññānīti vedakādīhi bāhirakaparikappitehīti adhippāyo. Dukkhañhi vedanīyampi santaṃ vedakarahitaṃ, kevalaṃ pana tasmiṃ attano paccayehi pavattamāne dukkhaṃ vedetīti vohāramattaṃ hoti. Esa nayo itaresupi.

567. 'Empty'—the intention is: empty of a feeler and so on, which are imagined by outsiders. For suffering, though it is something to be felt, is devoid of a feeler. Indeed, it is merely a conventional expression that 'one feels suffering' when that suffering is occurring because of its own conditions. This same method applies to the other truths as well.

“Dukkhamevā”ti avadhāraṇena nivattitamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “na koci dukkhito”ti vuttaṃ. Kiriyāva vijjatīti samudayasaccaṃ sandhāya vadati. Purimasaccadvayassa vipākavaṭṭakammavaṭṭasaṅgahato kārakassa vā dukkhasaccasabhāvamāha. Kātabbāpi hi kiriyā kārakarahitā kevalaṃ attano paccayehi tāya pavattamānāya dukkhasaññite dhammappabandhe kiriyaṃ karotīti vohāramattaṃ hoti. Nibbutagamakesupi eseva nayo. “Maggo atthī”ti vattabbe “maggamatthī”ti okārassa abhāvo katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Gamakoti nibbutiṃ gantā.

To show the meaning excluded by the emphasis in 'Suffering only exists,' it is said, 'There is no one who suffers.' The statement 'Action alone exists' is said in reference to the truth of the origin. Or, because the first two truths are included in the round of results and the round of kamma, he speaks of the state of the doer as being the truth of suffering. For although an action is to be done, it is devoid of a doer; it is merely a conventional expression that 'one performs an action' in the continuum of phenomena designated as suffering, when that action occurs simply by its own conditions. This very same method applies also in the case of those who go to Nibbāna. It should be understood that when 'the path exists' (maggo atthi) should be said, the absence of the 'o' sound is made, resulting in 'maggamatthi'. 'One who goes' means one who goes to Nibbāna.

Kilesāsucipaggharaṇaṭṭhena sāsavatā asubhatāti katvā anāsavattā nirodhamaggā subhā eva. Dukkhādīnaṃ pariyāyena samudayādibhāvo ca atthi[M 2.0222], na pana nirodhabhāvo, nirodhassa vā na dukkhādibhāvoti nirodhāvasesattayānaṃ na aññamaññasamaṅgitāti āha “nirodhasuññāni vā”tiādi.

Because of the meaning of causing the impurity of defilements to flow out, the state of being with taints is impurity. And because they are without taints, cessation and the path are indeed pure. Furthermore, suffering and so on may, by way of figure of speech, have the state of being the origin and so on, but not the state of being cessation; and cessation, in turn, does not have the state of being suffering and so on. Therefore, because there is no mutual applicability among cessation and the remaining three truths, he said, 'or empty of cessation,' and so on.

Samudaye dukkhassābhāvatoti ponobhavikāya taṇhāya punabbhavassa abhāvato. Yathā vā pakativādīnaṃ vikārā avikāribhāvato, pubbe patipalīnā ca pakatibhāveneva tiṭṭhanti, na evaṃ samudayasampayuttampi dukkhaṃ samudayabhāvena tiṭṭhatīti āha “samudaye dukkhassābhāvato”ti[V 2.0209]. Magge ca nirodhassa abhāvatoti sambandho. Yathā avibhattehi vikārehi mahāhaṅkāratammattavisesindriyabhūtavisesehi pakatibhāveneva ṭhitehi pakati sagabbhā icchitā pakativādīhi, evaṃ na phalena sagabbho hetūti attho. “Dukkhasamudayānaṃ nirodhamaggānañca asamavāyā”ti etaṃ vivaranto āha “na hetusamavetaṃ hetuphala”ntiādi. Tattha “idha tantūsu paṭo, kapālesu ghaṭo, bīraṇesu kaṭo dvīsu aṇūsu dviaṇuka”ntiādinā idha vuddhivohārajanako avisuṃ siddhānaṃ sambandho samavāyo, tena samavāyena kāraṇesu dvīsu aṇūsu dviaṇukaṃ phalaṃ samavetaṃ ekībhūtamiva sambaddhaṃ, tīsu aṇūsu tiaṇukanti evaṃ mahāpathavīmahāudakamahāaggimahāvātakkhandhapariyantaṃ phalaṃ attano kāraṇesu samavetanti samavāyavādino vadanti. Evaṃ pana vadantehi aparimāṇesu kāraṇesu mahāparimāṇaṃ ekaṃ phalaṃ samavetaṃ attano antogadhehi kāraṇehi sagabbhaṃ asuññanti vuttaṃ hoti. Evamidha samavāyābhāvā phale hetu natthīti hetusuññaṃ phalanti attho.

‘Because of the absence of suffering in the origin’: this is because of the absence of renewed existence in the craving that leads to renewed existence. Or, just as for the proponents of pakati (nature), their modifications, having previously reverted, remain only in their natural state, so too suffering, even when associated with the origin, does not remain in the state of the origin. Therefore, he said, ‘because of the absence of suffering in the origin.’ And ‘because of the absence of cessation in the path’: this is the connection. Just as the proponents of pakati hold that nature is pregnant with its unmanifested modifications—the great principle (mahat), the ego-principle, the subtle elements, the specific sense faculties, and the specific gross elements—which remain in their natural state, so the cause is not pregnant with the effect. This is the meaning. Explaining ‘because of the non-inherence of suffering and origin, and of cessation and path,’ he said, ‘the effect of a cause does not inhere in the cause,’ etc. Therein, as in the examples ‘a cloth in the threads, a pot in the potsherds, a mat in the reeds, a dyad in two atoms,’ etc., the relation of inseparably established things, which generates the cognition and conventional usage of ‘here [it is],’ is inherence (samavāya). By this inherence, the proponents of inherence (samavāya-vādins) say that the effect—a dyad—inheres in its causes, the two atoms, connected as if unified; a triad inheres in three atoms; and so on up to the great mass of the earth, water, fire, and air aggregates, the effect inheres in its own causes. When they speak thus, it is said that a single effect of great magnitude, inhering in innumerable causes, is pregnant with its internal causes and is not empty. So here, because of the absence of inherence, the cause is not in the effect; thus the meaning is that the effect is empty of the cause.

Suññato vinicchayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the analysis with respect to emptiness is finished.

Iti magganiddesakathāvaṇṇanā.

Thus the explanation of the exposition of the path.

Ekavidhādivinicchayakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Analysis Beginning with the Onefold

568. Pavattibhāvatoti saṃsārassa pavattibhāvato. Catuāhārabhedatoti catuāhārappaccayavisesato. Etena cattāro kabaḷīkārādiāhāravisese, ajjhoharaṇīyavatthu, saḷāyatana, avijjā, abhisaṅkhārasaṅkhāte tappaccayabhūtadhammavisese ca saṅgaṇhāti[M 2.0223], ojaṭṭhamakarūpa, vedanā, paṭisandhiviññāṇa, nāmarūpasaṅkhāte tannibbattadhammavisese ca.

568. ‘Because of the state of occurring’: because of the state of saṃsāra’s occurring. ‘Because of the division of the four nutriments’: because of the specific conditions of the four nutriments. By this, it includes the four specific nutriments beginning with edible food; and the specific phenomena that are their conditions, namely, the object to be ingested, the six sense bases, ignorance, and volitional formations; and also the specific phenomena produced by them, namely, matter with nutritive essence as its eighth factor, feeling, rebirth-linking consciousness, and name-and-form.

Pavattakabhāvato pavattidukkhassa. Rūpābhinandanādibhedo rūpakkhandhādiabhinandanabhedo, rūpārammaṇādivasenāpīti vadanti. Rūpataṇhādīnaṃ paccekaṃ anekabhedattā cha taṇhākāyā, tesaṃ bhedato.

‘Because of its nature as a producer’: of the suffering of what occurs. ‘The division of delight in form, etc.’: is the division of delight in the form aggregate, etc.; they say it is also by way of form-objects, etc. Because craving for form, etc., each has many divisions, there are six bodies of craving; because of their division.

Upādānehi upādīyatīti upādi, upādānakkhandhapañcakaṃ. Tannissaraṇabhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ, tassa vūpasamo taṃsantīti katvā tassa yāva pacchimaṃ cittaṃ, tāva sesataṃ, tato paraṃ anavasesatañca [V 2.0210] upādāya saupādisesanibbānadhātu, nirupādisesanibbānadhātūti dvidhā voharīyati. Yathā cāyaṃ bhedo vohārato, evamitarepīti te katipaye dassetuṃ “tividho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aññathā ekassa sato nibbānassa kuto bhedoti.

What is clung to by the clingings is the ‘clung-to’ (upādi), that is, the five aggregates subject to clinging. Nibbāna is the escape from that. Taking it as the calming of that, the stilling of that, then based on the fact that for as long as the final consciousness exists there is a remainder, and after that there is no remainder, it is designated in two ways as the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining and the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining. And just as this distinction is by way of conventional designation, so too are the others. To show a few of them, it is said ‘threefold,’ etc. Otherwise, how could there be distinctions for the one Nibbāna that exists?

Samathavipassanābhedatoti ettha sammādiṭṭhisammāsaṅkappā vipassanā, itare samathāti vadanti. Sīlampi hi samathassa upakārakattā samathaggahaṇena gayhatīti tesaṃ adhippāyo. Atha vā yānadvayassa vasena laddho maggo samatho vipassanāti āgamanavasena vuttoti daṭṭhabbo. Ayanti ariyamaggo. Sappadesattāti sīlakkhandhādīnaṃ ekadesattāti attho. Ekadeso hi padissati avayavabhāvena apadisīyatīti padeso, attano samudāyaṃ pati saha padesenāti sappadesoti vuccati yathā “sanidassanā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. dukamātikā 9), sīlakkhandhādayo ca sabbalokiyalokuttarasīlādisaṅgāhakā, ariyamaggo lokuttaro evāti tadekadeso hoti.

‘Because of the division into serenity and insight’: here, they say, right view and right intention are insight; the others are serenity. Their intention is that virtue, too, is included by the term ‘serenity’ because it is helpful to concentration. Or, it should be seen that ‘the path attained by means of the two vehicles is serenity and insight’ is said according to the textual tradition. This is the noble path. ‘Because it has parts’: the meaning is, because it is a part of the aggregates of virtue, etc. A part (ekadeso) is pointed out (padissati); it is designated as a component (avayavabhāvena), hence it is a padeso. Because it exists with a part in relation to its own collection, it is called ‘having a part’ (sappadeso), as in ‘phenomena that are with a visible counterpart.’ And the aggregates of virtue, etc., comprise all worldly and supramundane virtue, etc., but the noble path is only supramundane; thus it is a part of them.

Sajātitoti samānajātito, vacīduccaritaviratiādibhedesu samānāya sīlajātiyāti attho.

‘Because it is of the same kind’: because it is of a similar kind; the meaning is, of the same kind of virtue in the divisions such as abstinence from misconduct in speech.

Onatasahāyo viya vāyāmo paggahakiccasāmaññato. Aṃsakūṭaṃ datvā ṭhitasahāyo viya sati apilāpanavasena niccalabhāvakaraṇasāmaññato. Sajātitoti savitakkasavicārādibhedesu samānāya samādhijātiyāti attho. Kiriyatoti samādhianurūpakiriyato. Tato eva hi “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā samādhinimittā, cattāro sammappadhānā [M 2.0224] samādhiparikkhārā”ti (ma. ni. 1.46) sativāyāmānaṃ samādhissa nimittaparikkhārabhāvo vutto.

Effort is like a companion who stoops to help, because of the similarity of its function of exertion. Mindfulness is like a companion standing with braced shoulder, because of the similarity of its function of making things steady by way of non-wavering. ‘Because it is of the same kind’: the meaning is, of the same kind of concentration in the divisions such as that with applied and sustained thought. ‘Because of its action’: because of action that is suitable for concentration. For it is for this reason that the role of mindfulness and effort as the sign and requisite for concentration is stated: ‘The four establishments of mindfulness are the sign of concentration; the four right strivings are the requisites of concentration.’

Ākoṭentena viyāti “aniccaṃ anicca”ntiādinā paññākiccasadisena kiccena samantato koṭentena viya, “aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhena, dukkhaṃ bhayaṭṭhenā”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 1.48) parivattentena viya ca ādāya ūhitvā dinnameva paññā paṭivijjhati. Dvinnaṃ samānakālattepi paccayabhāvena sammāsaṅkappassa purimakālassa viya niddeso kato. Sajātitoti “dukkhe ñāṇa”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.8) samānāya paññājātiyā. Kiriyatoti ettha paññāsadisaṃ kiccaṃ “kiriyā”ti vuttaṃ, pubbe pana samādhiupakārakaṃ tadanurūpakiccanti ayamettha viseso.

‘Like one striking’: wisdom penetrates only what has been given to it, after taking it up and considering it, just as if one were striking all around with an action similar to the function of wisdom, saying ‘impermanent, impermanent,’ etc., and as if one were turning it over, saying ‘impermanent in the sense of destruction, suffering in the sense of fear,’ etc. Although the two are simultaneous, right intention is described as if it were prior because it is a condition. ‘Because it is of the same kind’: by the same kind of wisdom as in ‘knowledge in suffering,’ etc. ‘Because of its action’: here an action similar to the function of wisdom is called ‘action,’ whereas previously, in the section on the aggregate of concentration, an action that assists concentration and is suitable for it was called ‘action.’ This is the difference here.

“Sabbaṃ[V 2.0211], bhikkhave, abhiññeyya”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.46) vacanato cattāripi abhimukhaṃ paccakkhato ñātabbāni, abhivisiṭṭhena vā ñāṇena ñātabbānīti abhiññeyyāni.

Because of the statement, ‘All, bhikkhus, is to be directly known,’ all four truths are to be known directly, face to face, or to be known by distinguished knowledge; thus they are ‘to be directly known’ (abhiññeyyāni).

569. Aññamaññaṃ sabhāgānīti aññamaññasamānabhāgāni, sadisarūpānīti attho.

569. ‘Mutually of a similar nature’ means having similar portions in relation to each other, having a similar nature; this is the meaning.

Durabhisambhavataranti abhisambhavituṃ sādhetuṃ asakkuṇeyyataraṃ, sattivighātena duradhigamanti attho. Asananti kaṇḍaṃ. Atipāteyyāti khipeyya. Koṭiyāti kaṇḍassa koṭiyā vālaggena. Koṭinti vālasseva koṭiṃ. Paṭivijjheyyāti paṭimukhabhāvena vijjheyya.

‘More difficult to accomplish’ means more impossible to bring about or achieve; the meaning is ‘difficult to attain’ because of the exhaustion of one's ability. ‘Asana’ means an arrow. ‘Atipāteyya’ means one would shoot. ‘Koṭiyā’ means with the tip of the arrow, with the tip of a hair. ‘Koṭiṃ’ means the very tip of the hair. ‘Paṭivijjheyya’ means one would pierce face to face.

Bādhakapabhavasantiniyyānalakkhaṇehi vavatthānaṃ salakkhaṇavavatthānaṃ. Duravagāhatthena gambhīrattāti oḷārikā dukkhasamudayā. Tiracchānagatānampi hi dukkhaṃ, āhārādīsu ca abhilāso pākaṭo. Pīḷanādiāyūhanādivasena pana “idaṃ dukkhaṃ, idamassa kāraṇa”nti yāthāvato ogāhituṃ asakkuṇeyyattā gambhīrā. Saṇhasukhumadhammattā nirodhamaggā sabhāvato eva gambhīraṭṭhena duravagāhā. Teneva uppanne magge natthi nirodhamaggānaṃ anavagāhoti. Nibbānampi maggena adhigantabbattā tassa phalanti apadisīyatīti āha “phalāpadesato”ti. Vuttañhetaṃ “dukkhanirodhe ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 719). Maggopi nirodhassa sampāpakabhāvato “hetū”ti [M 2.0225] apadisīyatīti āha “hetuapadesato”ti. Vuttampi cetaṃ “dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 719).

The determination by means of the characteristics of oppressing, originating, pacifying, and escaping is the determination of individual characteristics. As for the statement ‘profound in the sense of being difficult to fathom,’ suffering and its origin are gross. For even for animals suffering is evident, and longing for food and so on is manifest. But because of the inability to fathom them as they really are—‘this is suffering, this is its cause’—by way of their aspects of affliction, accumulation, and so on, they are profound. Because they are subtle and refined phenomena, cessation and the path are by their very nature difficult to fathom in the sense of being profound. For that very reason, when the path has arisen, there is no non-fathoming of cessation and the path. Since Nibbāna is to be attained by the path, it is designated as its fruit; thus he said, ‘by designation as the fruit.’ For it was said: ‘Knowledge of the cessation of suffering is the analytical knowledge of meaning.’ Since the path is the means for accomplishing cessation, it is designated as ‘cause’; thus he said, ‘by designation as the cause.’ For this too was said: ‘Knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of suffering is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma.’

Iti evaṃ pakārehīti iti vijaññāti sambandho. Tattha itisaddena vijānanakkamaṃ dasseti. Evaṃ pakārehīti evaṃ-saddena vijānanakāraṇabhūtena eva.

The connection is: ‘Thus, in these ways… thus one should understand.’ Therein, the word ‘iti’ (thus) shows the sequence of understanding. In the phrase ‘in these ways’ (evaṃ pakārehi), by the word ‘evaṃ’ (thus), it indicates only the methods that are the cause for understanding.

Sabhāgavisabhāgatovinicchayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the analysis concerning the similar and dissimilar is finished.

Indriyasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the exposition of the faculties and the truths is finished.

Iti soḷasamaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus is the explanation of the sixteenth chapter.

17. Paññābhūminiddesavaṇṇanā

17. The Commentary on the Exposition of the Ground of Wisdom

Paṭiccasamuppādakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on Dependent Origination

570. Imissā [M 2.0226][V 2.0212] paññāyāti imissā yathādhigatāya vipassanāya. Bhūmibhūtesūti pavattiṭṭhānabhūtesu. Kāmañcāyaṃ paṭiccasamuppādapaṭiccasamuppannasamaññā pitāputtasamaññā viya apekkhāsiddhā, hetuphaladhammesu pana yathākkamaṃ vavatthitāvāti “paṭiccasamuppādo cevā”tiādinā vibhajja vuttaṃ. Ādisaddenāti “paṭiccasamuppādādibhedā”ti ettha vuttaādisaddena. Avasesā honti, saṃvaṇṇanāvasenāti adhippāyo. Tenāha “tesaṃ vaṇṇanākkamo anuppatto”ti.

570. ‘By this wisdom’ (imissā paññāya) means by this insight that has been attained. ‘In what has become the ground’ (bhūmibhūtesu) means in what serves as the basis of occurrence. And although this designation of ‘dependent origination’ and ‘dependently arisen phenomena’ is, like the designation of ‘father’ and ‘son,’ established by mutual relation, yet in regard to causal and resultant phenomena they are established sequentially. Thus it is stated in detail with the words ‘dependent origination and…,’ etc. ‘By the word “etc.”’ (ādisaddena) means by the word ‘etc.’ stated here in ‘the distinctions beginning with dependent origination.’ The meaning is that the remaining things are included by way of commentary. Therefore he says: ‘The turn for their commentary has come.’

Avijjādayo dhammā paṭiccasamuppādo, na samuppattimattaṃ. Svāyamattho iminā suttapadena veditabboti dassento “vuttañheta”ntiādiṃ vatvā paṭiccasamuppanne pana dassetuṃ “jarāmaraṇādayo panā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Kasmā panettha anulomato paṭiccasamuppādadhammā dassitā, paṭilomato paṭiccasamuppannā dhammāti? Yato te paccayato uppannā, tassa samanantaradassanatthaṃ.

The causal phenomena beginning with ignorance are ‘dependent origination,’ not merely co-arising. To show that this is the meaning to be understood by this sutta passage, he said, ‘For this has been said,’ etc. Then, to show the dependently arisen phenomena, he began with, ‘But aging-and-death, etc.’ Why, in this case, are the phenomena of dependent origination shown in forward order, and the dependently arisen phenomena in reverse order? Because they have arisen from a particular cause, it is for the purpose of showing them immediately after that cause.

Na niccaṃ na sassatanti aniccaṃ. Samecca sambhūya paccayehi katanti saṅkhataṃ. Paṭicca paccayārahaṃ paccayaṃ nissāya sahitameva uppannanti paṭiccasamuppannaṃ. Khayanasabhāvaṃ khayadhammaṃ. Vayanasabhāvaṃ vayadhammaṃ. Virajjanasabhāvaṃ palujjanasabhāvaṃ virāgadhammaṃ. Nirujjhanasabhāvaṃ nirodhadhammaṃ. Sesaṃ yadettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ parato āvi bhavissati.

‘Not permanent, not eternal’ means impermanent. ‘Made by conditions coming together’ means conditioned. ‘Arisen together in dependence on a suitable condition’ means dependently arisen. ‘Having the nature of wasting away’ means subject to wasting away. ‘Having the nature of vanishing’ means subject to vanishing. ‘Having the nature of fading away, having the nature of crumbling’ means subject to fading away. ‘Having the nature of ceasing’ means subject to cessation. Whatever else should be said here will become clear later.

571. Etthāti etesu yathāvuttesu suttapadesu. Saṅkhepoti atthasaṅkhepo.

571. ‘Herein’ means in these aforesaid sutta passages. ‘In brief’ means a summary of the meaning.

Jātipaccayāti jātisaṅkhātā paccayā. Hetumhi nissakkavacanaṃ. Ṭhitāva sā dhātūti yāyaṃ jarāmaraṇassa idappaccayatā “jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa”nti, esā dhātu esa sabhāvo. Sā [V 2.0213] tathāgatānaṃ uppādato pubbe, uddhañca aviññāyamāno, majjhe ca viññāyamāno, na tathāgatehi uppādito, atha kho sambhavantassa jarāmaraṇassa sabbakālaṃ jātipaccayato sambhavoti ṭhitā eva. Kevalaṃ pana sayambhūñāṇena [M 2.0227] abhisambujjhanato, “ayaṃ dhammo tathāgatena adhigato”ti pavedanato ca tathāgato “dhammassāmī”ti vuccati na apubbassa uppādanato. Tena vuttaṃ “ṭhitāva sā dhātū”ti. Sā eva jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇanti ettha vipallāsābhāvato evaṃ avabujjhamānassa etassa sabhāvassa, hetuno vā tatheva bhāvato ṭhitatāti dhammaṭṭhitatā. Jāti vā jarāmaraṇassa uppādaṭṭhiti pavattaāyūhanasaṃyogapalibodhasamudayahetupaccayaṭṭhitīti taduppādādibhāvenassā ṭhitatā “dhammaṭṭhitatā”ti phalaṃ patisāmatthiyato hetumeva vadati.

‘With birth as condition’ means because of the condition designated as birth. This is a term in the ablative case in the sense of cause. ‘That very element remains’: this specific conditionality of aging-and-death, namely, ‘with birth as condition, aging-and-death [arises],’ this is the element, this is the nature. It is not cognized before or after the arising of Tathāgatas but is cognized in between; it is not created by the Tathāgatas. Rather, for aging-and-death that is arising, its arising is always from birth as its condition; thus it just remains. But it is simply because he fully awakens to it with self-originating knowledge and because he proclaims, ‘This Dhamma has been attained by the Tathāgata,’ that the Tathāgata is called ‘the Lord of the Dhamma,’ not because he originates something that did not exist before. Therefore it is said: ‘That very element remains.’ Because there is no distortion here concerning this nature, which is thus understood as ‘with birth as condition, aging-and-death,’ or concerning the cause, its being just so is the stability of the Dhamma. Or, birth is for aging-and-death the condition for arising, the condition for continuance, the condition for accumulation, the condition for connection, the condition for obstruction, the condition for origination, the condition as a root-cause, and the condition as a supporting cause; thus its stability, by way of being its origination and so on, is called ‘the stability of the Dhamma.’ By its capacity in relation to the effect, it speaks only of the cause.

Atha vā dhārīyati paccayehīti dhammo, tiṭṭhati tattha tadāyattavuttitāya phalanti ṭhiti, dhammassa ṭhiti dhammaṭṭhiti. Dhammoti vā kāraṇaṃ, paccayoti attho. Dhammassa ṭhitisabhāvo, dhammato ca añño sabhāvo natthīti dhammaṭṭhiti, paccayo. Tenāha “paccayapariggahe paññā dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.45). Dhammaṭṭhiti eva dhammaṭṭhitatā. Sā eva dhātu “jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa”nti imassa sabhāvassa, hetuno vā aññathattābhāvato “na jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa”nti viññāyamānassa tabbhāvābhāvato niyāmatā vavatthitabhāvoti dhammaniyāmatā. Phalassa vā jarāmaraṇassa jātiyā sati sambhavo dhamme hetumhi ṭhitatāti dhammaṭṭhitatā. Asati asambhavo dhamme niyatatāti dhammaniyāmatāti evaṃ phalena hetuṃ vibhāveti. Taṃ “ṭhitāva sā dhātū”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.20) vuttaṃ idappaccayataṃ abhisambujjhati paccakkhakaraṇena abhimukhaṃ bujjhati yāthāvato paṭivijjhati. Abhisametīti tassa vevacanaṃ. Ādito kathento ācikkhati, uddisatīti attho. Tameva uddesaṃ pariyosāpento deseti. Yathāuddiṭṭhamatthaṃ niddisanavasena pakārehi ñāpentā paññapeti. Pakārehiyeva patiṭṭhapento paṭṭhapeti. Yathāniddiṭṭhamatthaṃ paṭiniddisanavasena vivarati vibhajati, vivaṭañhi vibhattañca atthaṃ hetudhāraṇadassanehi pākaṭaṃ karonto uttānīkaroti. Uttānīkaronto tathāpaccakkhabhūtaṃ katvā nigamanavasena passathāti cāha.

Or, it is a 'dhamma' because it is borne by conditions; the effect 'stands' there, its occurrence being dependent on that, so this is 'stability'; the causal basis for the standing of the effect is dhammaṭṭhiti. Or, 'dhamma' is the cause; the meaning is 'condition'. The nature of the standing of the cause, and because there is no other nature apart from the cause, it is called dhammaṭṭhiti, the condition. Hence it is said: 'Wisdom in the grasping of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena' (Paṭis I 45). Dhammaṭṭhiti itself is dhammaṭṭhitatā. That very element is the fixedness, the established state, which is the determinacy of phenomena, because there is no otherness of this nature—or of its cause—'with birth as condition, aging-and-death,' and because of the absence of that state when it is cognized as 'not with birth as condition, aging-and-death.' Or, when birth exists, the occurrence of the effect, aging-and-death, is dhammaṭṭhitatā, the state of being established in the dhamma as cause. When birth is absent, the non-occurrence is dhammaniyāmatā, the state of being fixed in the dhamma. Thus he clarifies the cause by means of the effect. He fully awakens to that specific conditionality stated in the words 'That very element remains,' etc. He knows it directly by making it directly present; he penetrates it as it really is. 'He comprehends' is a synonym for this. In the beginning, speaking, he tells; the meaning is, he states the theme. Bringing that very statement to a conclusion, he teaches. He makes known the meaning as stated by way of detailed explanation in various ways. Establishing it by means of those very ways, he establishes it. He opens it up and analyzes the meaning as explained by way of further detailed explanation. Indeed, making the opened up and analyzed meaning plain by showing causes and examples, he makes it manifest. Making it manifest, and having made it a matter of direct experience, he also says by way of conclusion, 'See!'

572. Paccayalakkhaṇoti paccayabhāvalakkhaṇo, paccayoti vā lakkhitabbo. Pavattidukkhassa [V 2.0214] anubandhāpanakiccatāya dukkhānubandhanaraso. Nibbānagāmimaggassa uppathabhāvato kummaggapaccupaṭṭhāno.

572. It has the characteristic of the state of being a condition, or it is to be characterized as a condition. Its function is the continuation of suffering, because its task is to cause the suffering of ongoing existence to follow in succession. It is manifested as a wrong path, because it is a contrary path to the path leading to Nibbāna.

So [M 2.0228] panāyaṃ paṭiccasamuppādo. Yāvattakehi paccayehi yaṃ phalaṃ uppajjanārahaṃ, avikaleheva tehi tassa uppatti, tadaññena ca tassa payojanaṃ natthīti āha “anūnādhikehevā”ti. Yathā taṃ cakkhurūpālokamanasikārehi cakkhuviññāṇassa, etena taṃtaṃphalanipphādanena tassā paccayasāmaggiyā tapparatā tathatāti dasseti. Sāmagginti samodhānaṃ, samavāyanti attho. Asambhavābhāvatoti anuppajjanassa abhāvato. Paccayasāmaggiyañhi sati anuppajjane tassā vitathatā siyā. Aññadhammappaccayehīti aññassa phaladhammassa paccayehi. Aññadhammānuppattitoti tato aññassa phaladhammassa anuppajjanato. Na hi kadāci cakkhurūpālokamanasikārehi sotaviññāṇassa sambhavo atthi, yadi siyā, tassā sāmaggiyā aññathatā nāma siyā, na cetaṃ atthīti “anaññathatā”ti vuttaṃ. Paccayatoti paccayabhāvato. Paccayasamūhatoti etthāpi eseva nayo.

Now, this is dependent origination. A certain effect is fit to arise from a certain number of conditions; its arising occurs from just those without deficiency, and there is no contribution from another; thus he says, 'from conditions that are neither deficient nor excessive.' For example, the arising of eye-consciousness from eye, form, light, and attention. By this, he shows that the devotion of that assemblage of conditions to producing that particular effect is its thusness (tathatā). 'Assemblage' means coming together; the meaning is conjunction. 'Because of the absence of non-occurrence' means because of the absence of non-arising. For if, when the assemblage of conditions is present, there were non-arising, that assemblage would be futile. 'From conditions for another phenomenon' means from the conditions for a different resultant phenomenon. 'Because of the non-arising of another phenomenon' means because a different resultant phenomenon does not arise from them. For ear-consciousness never arises from eye, form, light, and attention. If it did, that assemblage would be called 'otherness,' but since this is not so, it is called 'non-otherness.' 'From the condition' means from the state of being a condition. 'From the collection of conditions': here too the same method applies.

573. Idappaccayā eva idappaccayatāti tā-saddena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ, na kiñci atthantaraṃ yathā devo eva devatāti. Idappaccayānaṃ vā samūho idappaccayatāti samūhatthaṃ tā-saddamāha yathā “janānaṃ samūho janatā”ti. Nanu ca “atthi idappaccayā jarāmaraṇanti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. Kiṃ paccayā jarāmaraṇanti iti ce vadeyya, jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇanti iccassa vacanīya”nti (dī. ni. 2.96) jātisaddapaccayasaddasamānādhikaraṇena kiṃ-saddena idaṃsaddassa samānādhikaraṇatādassanato idappaccayasaddassa kammadhārayasamāso dissati, na hettha “imassa paccayā idappaccayā”ti jarāmaraṇassa, aññassa vā paccayato jarāmaraṇasambhavapucchā sambhavati viditabhāvato, asambhavato ca, jarāmaraṇassa pana paccayapucchā sambhavati. Paccaya-saddena ca samānādhikaraṇatāya idaṃ-saddassa imasmā paccayāti paccayapucchā yujjati. Sā ca samānādhikaraṇatā bāhiratthasamāsepi labbhati. Tato ca aññapadatthavacanicchābhāve kammadhārayasamāso labbhati.

573. 'Idappaccayatā' is simply 'idappaccayā'; the word is augmented by the suffix '-tā' with no difference in meaning, just as 'deva' becomes 'devatā.' Or, 'idappaccayatā' means a collection of specific conditions, as the suffix '-tā' indicates a collective sense, just as 'janatā' means 'a collection of people.' But is it not so? In the passage: 'Ānanda, if one is asked, “Is there aging-and-death from a specific condition?” one should say, “There is.” If one should say, “With what as condition is there aging-and-death?” one should say, “With birth as condition is there aging-and-death”' (DN 15), because it is seen that the word `idaṃ` is in apposition with the word `paccaya` (just as the words `kiṃ` and `jāti` are), the word `idappaccaya` is seen to be a kammadhāraya compound. For here, analyzing `idappaccayā` as 'the condition of this' (`imassa paccayā`), a question about the arising of aging-and-death from the condition of aging-and-death itself, or of something else, is not possible, both because it is already known and because it is impossible. A question, however, about the condition for aging-and-death is possible. And because the word `idaṃ` is in apposition with the word `paccaya`, a question about the condition, analyzed as 'from this condition' (`imasmā paccayā`), is fitting. And that apposition is also found in an exocentric compound. And from that, when there is no wish to state the meaning of another term, a kammadhāraya compound is obtained.

Sāmivacanasamāse pana samānādhikaraṇatā natthīti na kathañci kammadhārayasamāsasambhavoti? Nayidamevaṃ vacanicchantarabhāvato. Paṭiccasamuppādavacanicchā hesā “idappaccayatā [V 2.0215] paṭiccasamuppādo”ti ettha. “Atthi idappaccayā [M 2.0229] jarāmaraṇa”nti ettha pana jarāmaraṇassa paccayamattaparipucchā, tasmā yathā idaṃ-saddassa paṭiccasamuppādavisesanatā, pucchitabbapaccayavisesanatā ca hoti, tathā samāsavikappo ettha, tattha ca kātabboti na samāsantaradassanaṃ sāmivacanasamāsabādhakaṃ. Kasmā panetthāpi kammadhārayasamāso na icchitoti? Hetuppabhavānaṃ hetu paṭiccasamuppādoti imassatthassa kammadhārayasamāse asambhavato, “imassa attano paccayānurūpassa anurūpo paccayo idappaccayo”ti imassa ca atthassa icchitattā. Yo panettha idaṃ-saddena gahito attho, so “atthi idappaccayā jarāmaraṇa”nti ettha jarāmaraṇaggahaṇeneva gahitoti idaṃ-saddo paṭiccasamuppannato abhassitvā aññāsambhavato paccaye avatiṭṭhati, tasmā tattha kammadhārayasamāso. Ettha pana idaṃ-saddassa tato pariccajanakāraṇaṃ natthīti sāmivacanasamāso eva. Evampi na idappaccayo eva idappaccayabhāvo bhavituṃ yuttoti idappaccayatāya paṭiccasamuppādatānupapattīti? Nāyaṃ doso atthantarābhāvatoti vuttovāyamattho.

But in a genitive determinative compound, since there is no common referent, is it not so that an appositional compound is by no means impossible? That is not so, because of a difference in the intended expression. For here, in ‘this-conditionality is dependent origination,’ the intention is to express dependent origination. But in ‘is there aging-and-death from this condition?,’ the question is merely about the condition for aging-and-death. Therefore, just as the word ‘this’ can be a specifier of dependent origination and a specifier of the condition being asked about, so a choice of compound should be made in this case and that. Thus, pointing to another compound does not invalidate the genitive determinative compound. But why is an appositional compound not intended here as well? Because the meaning ‘dependent origination is the cause of things that arise from a cause’ is impossible with an appositional compound, and because this meaning is intended: ‘A specific condition is a condition suitable for this, its own effect which corresponds to its cause.’ Here, the meaning taken by the word ‘this’ is already taken by the mention of ‘aging-and-death’ in the phrase ‘is there aging-and-death from this condition?’ Thus the word ‘this,’ having been dislodged from what is dependently arisen and because no other meaning is possible, stands for the condition. Therefore, an appositional compound is intended there. Here, however, there is no reason for dislodging the word ‘this’ from that, so it is indeed a genitive determinative compound that is intended. Even so, is it not the case that it is not proper for a specific condition itself to be the state of being a specific condition, and thus that the identification of this-conditionality with dependent origination is untenable? This is not a fault, for there is no other meaning. This point has already been stated.

Atha vā pana hotu idappaccayabhāvo idappaccayatāti. Bhāvoti cettha avinābhāviphalaṃ pati hetuno satvaṃ. Tathā hi idappaccaya-saddo jātiādīsu niruḷho. Tañca idappaccayasatvaṃ idappaccayato aññaṃ natthi. Yadi aññaṃ siyā, taṃ avijjamānaṃ siyā. Na hi satā aññaṃ vijjamānaṃ hoti. Atha satvaṃ saṃ nāma, yassa sato bhāvo, taṃ asaṃ nāma siyā. Na hi taṃ satvaṃ sabhāvaṃ satvato aññattā, tasmā sato bhāvo satvanti niddeso na yujjati. Na ca saṃ-sambandhena asaṃ saṃ nāma hoti, pageva saṃ-sambandhena. Asati ca saditiggahaṇaṃ viparītaggāhoti na gahaṇato saṃsiddhi. Sadisakappanāyañca māṇavakassa sīhabhāvo viya na asato saṃ-sabhāvatā. Yasmā pana idappaccayabhāvo yathāvuttaṃ satvaṃ, na asatvaṃ. Nāpi yassa taṃ satvaṃ, tadasaṃ, tasmā idappaccayabhāvo idappaccayasarūpaṃ sabhāvantarehi vinivattabhāvadassanatthaṃ imassāyanti visesetvā idappaccayatāti vuttanti na idappaccayatāya paṭiccasamuppādabhāvāsambhavo.
