Or else, let the state of being a specific condition be this-conditionality. Herein, ‘state’ is the existence of a cause with respect to its inseparable fruit. For the term ‘specific condition’ is established in regard to birth and so on. And that existence as a specific condition is not other than the specific condition. If it were other, it would be non-existent. For indeed, what is other than an existent thing is not existent. Alternatively, if existence is called ‘being,’ then that existent thing of which it is the state would be called ‘non-being.’ For that existent thing is not its own nature, which is existence, due to its otherness from that existence; therefore the designation ‘the state of what is is existence’ is not tenable. And a non-being does not become a being by connection with a being, how much less so by connection with a non-being. And when something is non-existent, grasping it as 'it is existent' is a perverse grasp; therefore, its being is not established by grasping. And by supposing a likeness, a non-existent thing does not acquire the nature of a being, just as a young man does not acquire the state of being a lion. However, since the state of being a specific condition is, as stated, existence, not non-existence, and that of which it is the existence is not non-existent, therefore, in order to show that the state of being a specific condition is the intrinsic nature of the specific condition—a state turned away from other natures—it is specified as 'this is the state of this' and thus spoken of as 'this-conditionality.' Thus, there is no impossibility of this-conditionality being the state of dependent origination.

Paṭicca samuppajjati etasmāti paṭiccasamuppādoti tassāpi hetuatthabhāvato jātiādipadānaṃ evameva hetubhāvavācakatāya hetupadhānatā yojetabbā hetuppabhavānaṃ hetu paṭiccasamuppādoti katvā[M 2.0230]. Tathā hi “dasabalasamannāgato, bhikkhave, tathāgato catūhi vesārajjehi [V 2.0216] samannāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti, imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti yāva ‘evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī’”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.21-22) anena sīhanādasuttena pakāsito evamattho. “Kiṃ vādī panāyasmato satthā kimakkhāyī”ti puṭṭhena āyasmatā assajittherena –

‘It arises dependently from this’; thus it is ‘dependent origination.’ Since this too has the meaning of a cause, in just the same way, for the terms 'birth', etc., their pre-eminence as a cause should be understood because they express the state of being a cause, on the grounds that ‘dependent origination is the cause of things that arise from a cause.’ For this meaning is clarified by this Lion’s Roar Sutta thus: ‘Bhikkhus, endowed with the ten powers, the Tathāgata, endowed with the four kinds of intrepidity, claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the supreme wheel, teaching: “When this exists, that comes to be … down to … Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.”’ And by the venerable elder Assaji, who was asked: ‘What does the venerable one's teacher state, what does he proclaim?’—

“Ye dhammā hetuppabhavā, tesaṃ hetuṃ tathāgato āha;

Tesañca yo nirodho, evaṃvādī mahāsamaṇo”ti. (mahāva. 60; apa. thera 1.1.286) –

‘Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has stated their cause, and also their cessation. Such is the teaching of the Great Ascetic.’

Vutto. Tena viññāyati hetuppabhavānaṃ hetu paṭiccasamuppādoti. Sesamettha vattabbaṃ parato āvi bhavissati.

This was spoken. By this it is understood that dependent origination is the cause of things that arise from a cause. The rest to be said on this will become clear hereafter.

574. Paṭiccāti taṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ nissāya. Sammāti aviparītaṃ aniccato aniccassa uppādoti katvā. Niccato hi kāraṇato phalassa uppādo viparīto. Tenāha “titthiya…pe… nirapekkho”ti. “Uppādo paññāyatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.38; a. ni. 3.47; kathā. 214) evaṃ vuttasaṅkhatalakkhaṇato añño “paccayato khaṇato”ti ettha vuttapaccayalakkhaṇo eko ākāro uppādoti tesaṃ adhippāyo. Yaṃ sandhāya te “jātiādīnaṃ hetavo jātiādayo”ti vadanti, taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ, nibbattilakkhaṇavinimuttassa tādisassa kassaci abhāvato. Tenāha “taṃ na yujjatī”tiādi. Gambhīranayāsambhavatoti gambhīrānaṃ nayānañca asambhavato. Saddabhedatoti saddavināsato saddāyogato. Suttaṃ natthi “paṭiccasamuppādaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmī”tiādisuttapadehi (saṃ. ni. 2.1, 20) uppādamattassa appakāsitattā. Ayameva hi attho heṭṭhā dassito idānipi dassīyati. Taṃ uppādamattaṃ. Viharāmi tasmiṃ paṭhamābhisambuddhakāleti adhippāyo. Viharāmīti vā kālavipallāsena vuttaṃ, vihāsinti attho. Tatrāti tasmiṃ padesavihāre. Paccayākāradassanenāti yenākārena paccayadhammo paccayuppannassa paccayo hoti, so paccayākāro paccayabhāvo, tassa dassanena. Idha pana vedanānaṃ paccayabhāvo adhippeto. Tenāha [M 2.0231] “micchādiṭṭhipaccayāpi vedayita”ntiādi. Vedanānaṃyeva hi paccayaṃ passantena vuttavihāro paṭiccasamuppādassa ekadesameva passato vihāroti [V 2.0217] katvā padesavihāro jāto, anantanayasamantapaṭṭhānamanasikāro paṭhamābhisambuddhavihāro. Tañhi nippadesato paccayākāradassananti eke. Padesavihārasuttavirodho āpajjati tassa vedanānaṃ paccayadhammamanasikāravibhāvanato.

574. ‘Dependently’: relying on this or that cause. ‘Rightly’: not pervertedly, on the grounds that it is the arising of the impermanent from the impermanent. For the arising of an effect from a permanent cause is perverted. Therefore he said: ‘The sectarians …pe… are unconcerned.’ Their intention is that apart from the characteristic of the conditioned stated thus, ‘arising is discerned,’ there is another mode, ‘arising,’ which has the characteristic of a condition stated here as ‘from a condition, from a moment.’ With reference to which they say, ‘The causes of birth, etc., are birth, etc.’—that is merely their opinion, since there is no such thing devoid of the characteristic of production. Therefore he said: ‘That is not tenable,’ etc. ‘Because of the impossibility of the profound methods’: because of the impossibility of the profound and of the methods. ‘Because of the difference in term’: because of the corruption of the term or the misapplication of the term. There is no sutta: because mere arising is not declared in sutta passages such as ‘Bhikkhus, I will teach you dependent origination.’ This very meaning was shown above and is being shown now. That is mere arising. The intention is: ‘I am dwelling in that at the time of my first full awakening.’ Or ‘I am dwelling’ is stated with a temporal displacement; the meaning is ‘I dwelt.’ ‘There’: in that partial dwelling. ‘By seeing the mode of conditions’: the mode by which a condition-phenomenon is a condition for a conditionally arisen phenomenon is the mode of condition, the state of being a condition; by seeing that. Here, however, the state of being a condition for feelings is intended. Therefore he said: ‘Feeling conditioned by wrong view,’ etc. For the dwelling of one seeing only the condition for feelings becomes a partial dwelling, since it is a dwelling of one who sees only a part of dependent origination; whereas the dwelling of the first full awakening is the attention to the endless methods of the Universal Correlation. Some say that this is seeing the mode of conditions non-partially. But this would contradict the Sutta on Partial Dwelling, because it explains the attention to the phenomena that are conditions for feelings.

Loko samudeti etasmāti lokasamudayo, avijjādiko paccayagaṇo, na lokasamudayamattaṃ. Tenāha “anulomapaṭiccasamuppādo”ti. Natthitāti sabbaso abhāvo, naranvayavināso ucchedoti attho. Natthitāsahacaraṇato pana ucchedadiṭṭhi natthitāti adhippetā. Paccayānuparamo paccayānaṃ avicchedo. Yathā hi atītahetupañcakasannissayena etarahiphalapañcakaṃ viya hetupañcakampi hoti, evaṃ etarahihetupañcakasannissayena āyatiṃphalapañcakampi bhavissati. Tenāha “paccayānuparame phalānuparamato”ti.

‘The world originates from this,’ thus it is the ‘origin of the world,’ which is the collection of conditions beginning with ignorance, not the mere origination of the world. Therefore he said: ‘the forward order of dependent origination.’ ‘Non-existence’ means complete absence, destruction without a successor; annihilation is the meaning. But because of its association with ‘non-existence,’ the view of annihilation is intended by ‘non-existence.’ ‘Non-cessation of conditions’ is the non-interruption of conditions. For just as, in dependence on the past fivefold cause-group, the present fivefold cause-group also comes to be, like the present fivefold fruit-group, so too, in dependence on the present fivefold cause-group, the future fivefold fruit-group will also come to be. Therefore he said: ‘because of the non-cessation of the fruit when the conditions do not cease.’

Taṃ gambhīrattaṃ uppādamatte natthi asabhāvadhammattā. Ekattanayādayo nayā sabhāvadhammesu labbhamānato uppādamatte kathañcipi na labbheyyunti āha “nayacatukkaṃ uppādamatte natthī”ti.

That profundity does not exist in mere arising, because it is not a real phenomenon. Since methods such as the method of oneness are found in real phenomena, they cannot in any way be found in mere arising. Therefore he said: ‘The fourfold method does not exist in mere arising.’

575. Samāne kattarīti ekasmiṃyeva kattari uppajjanakiriyāya yo kattā, tasmiṃyeva paccayanakiriyāya ca kattubhūteti attho. Yathā “nhatvā bhuñjati, bhutvā sayatī”ti. “Pubbakāle”ti idañca tvāsaddantānaṃ padānaṃ yebhuyyena purimakālakiriyāya dīpanato vuttaṃ, na idha paṭiccasaddassa purimakālatthattā. Evañhi “cakkhuṃ paṭiccā”ti nidassanavacanaṃ nidassitabbena saṃsandeyya. Atha vā kāmañcettha ubhinnaṃ kiriyānaṃ samakālatā uppajjanakiriyāya pubbe paccayanakiriyāya asambhavato, tathāpi phalakiriyāya hetukiriyā purimakālo viya voharituṃ yuttā. Evamettha hetuphalavavatthānaṃ supākaṭaṃ hotīti upacārasiddhaṃ purimakālaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ “pubbakāle”ti. Atthasiddhikaroti vākyatthapaṭiviññattikaro. Paṭiccasamuppādoti hi ettha vākyatthāvabodho idha atthasiddhīti adhippeto. Payujjamāno paṭiccasaddo uppādasaddena vuccamānassa [M 2.0232] samānassa “kattu abhāvato”ti padaṃ ānetvā yojetabbaṃ. Ayañhettha attho “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇa”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.204, 400; 3.421, 425-426; saṃ. ni. 2.43-44; 2.4.60; kathā. 465) paccayanakiriyāya, uppajjanakiriyāya ca viññāṇameva kattāti samānakattukatā labbhati.

575. “In the case of the same agent” means that for one and the same agent, that which is the agent of the action of arising is also the agent of the action of depending. For example: “Having bathed, he eats; having eaten, he sleeps.” And this phrase “in prior time” is stated because words ending in “tvā” generally indicate an action of a prior time, not because the word “paṭicca” has the meaning of prior time here. For in this way, the illustrative statement “dependent on the eye” accords with what is being illustrated. Alternatively, although here the two actions are simultaneous—since the action of depending cannot occur before the action of arising—it is still proper to speak of the causal action as if it were prior to the resultant action. In this way, the distinction between cause and effect becomes very clear. Therefore, having taken a 'prior time' that is established by metaphorical usage, it is stated “in prior time.” “It establishes the meaning” means it makes the meaning of the sentence intelligible. For here, in the context of 'paṭiccasamuppāda', the understanding of the meaning of the sentence is what is intended by “establishment of the meaning,” on account of the absence of a common agent for the word 'paṭicca' as used and for that which is expressed by the word 'uppāda'. For this is the meaning here: In such passages as “Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises,” consciousness alone is the agent of both the action of depending and the action of arising; thus, the state of having the same agent is obtained.

“Paṭiccasamuppādo”ti [V 2.0218] ettha pana uppādasaddassa bhāvasādhanatāya kiriyāva vuttāti samānakattulakkhaṇo saddappayogo na sambhavatīti. Tenāha “saddabhedaṃ gacchatī”ti, apasaddappayogo hotīti attho. Na cettha parāvarayogo (pāṇinī 3.4.20) “appatvā nadiṃ pabbato, atikkamma pabbataṃ nadī”tiādīsu viya, nāpi lakkhaṇahetuādipayogo “sīhaṃ disvā bhayaṃ hoti, ghataṃ pivitvā balaṃ jāyate, ‘dha’nti katvā daṇḍo patito”tiādīsu viya. Nevettha saddabhedo. Na hi hatthatale āmalakaṃ viya sabbaññeyyaṃ paccakkhaṃ katvā ṭhitānaṃ mahesīnaṃ vacane akkharacintakānaṃ vippalāpo avasaraṃ labhati. Labhatu, vākyatthena saddasiddhito “nhatvā gamanaṃ, bhutvā sayana”ntiādīsu viyāti. Evampi na ca kiñci atthaṃ sādheti. Yadipi paccekaṃ padattho labbhati, vākyattho pana na yujjati, tasmā dasadāḷimādivākyāni viya asambandhatthatāya niratthakaṃ hotīti adhippāyo.

In the phrase “dependent origination” (paṭiccasamuppādo), however, since the word “uppāda” (arising) is a verbal noun (bhāvasādhana) denoting action, a verbal construction characterized by the same agent is not possible. Hence, it is said, “it involves a violation of the word,” meaning an incorrect verbal construction occurs. Here, neither the construction of proximity and remoteness—as in examples like “the mountain not reaching the river, the river passing beyond the mountain”—nor the construction based on characteristics or cause—as in examples like “seeing a lion, fear arises; drinking ghee, strength arises; after uttering ‘dha,’ the stick fell”—applies. In this case, however, there is no violation of the word. For in the speech of the great seers who stand having directly realized all that is knowable as if it were an āmalaka fruit on the palm of their hand, the idle chatter of those who are mere grammarians finds no opportunity. Or let it be granted that the word is established by the meaning of the sentence, as in such cases as “bathing, going” and “eating, sleeping.” Even so, this does not establish any meaning. Although the meaning of each word is obtained, the meaning of the sentence is not coherent. Therefore, the intention is that, like such sentences as “ten pomegranates,” it is meaningless because of the unconnectedness of the meaning.

Nāmapade vutte appayuttānipi “atthi, hoti, vijjatī”ti evarūpāni kiriyāpadāni ānetvā sambandhitabbānīti ñāyaṃ sandhāyāha “hotisaddena saddhiṃ yojayissāmā”ti. Imesūti yathāvuttesu desanāpaṭiññāpucchānigamanavasena vuttesu paṭiccasamuppādapadesu. Nidassanamattañcetaṃ, aññesupi “paṭiccasamuppādameva sādhukaṃ yoniso manasi kāroti. Yadidaṃ idappaccayatā paṭiccasamuppādo (dī. ni. 2.67; ma. ni. 2.337; sa. ni. 1.172; mahāva. 7). Gambhīro cāyaṃ, ānanda, paṭiccasamuppādo”ti (dī. ni. 2.95; saṃ. ni. 2.60) evamādīsupi ekenapi saddhiṃ hoti-saddo sambandhaṃ na gacchati. Yogaṃ na gacchati tathā sambandhavasena avuttattā. “Na ca uppādo hotī”ti idaṃ asabhāvadhammattā uppādassa nibbattilakkhaṇāyogaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yathā hi vināsassa vināso natthi, evaṃ uppādassa vināso viya uppādopi natthi. Yadi siyā, yena uppādena uppādo uppādavā, sopi uppādavāti [M 2.0233] anavaṭṭhānameva āpajjeyyāti vuttovāyamattho. Tenāha “sace heyyā”tiādi. Yadi evaṃ, kathaṃ samudayo hotīti? Nāyaṃ doso nibbattiyā anadhippetattā. Evaṃ dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo pātubhāvo sambhavatīti ayañhettha attho, idha pana paṭiccasamuppādo hotīti tassa atthibhāvacodanāti katvā hoti, jāyatīti nibbatticodanā katā siyāti adhippāyena vuttaṃ “na uppādo hotī”ti.

Referring to the rule that when a noun is stated, even if they are not explicitly used, such verbs as “exists,” “is,” and “occurs” should be supplied and connected, he says, “We will connect it with the word ‘is.’” “In these” means in these passages on dependent origination that have been mentioned according to the divisions of exposition, proposition, question, and conclusion. This is merely an example. In other instances as well—such as, “One should carefully and wisely attend to dependent origination itself, that is, this specific conditionality, dependent origination,” or “This dependent origination is deep, Ānanda”—the word “is” does not connect with any of them. It does not form a connection because it is not stated in such a way as to be connected. The statement “And arising is not” is stated with reference to the unsuitability of the characteristic of production for arising, because it is not a substantial phenomenon. For just as there is no destruction of destruction, so too, like the destruction of arising, there is no arising of arising. If there were, then the arising by which an arising is endowed with arising would itself be endowed with arising, and thus one would fall into an infinite regress. This meaning has indeed been stated. Hence he says, “if it were so,” etc. If so, how is there origination? This is not a fault, because production is not intended. The meaning here is this: In this way, the origin, the appearance, of this mass of suffering is possible. But here, when it is said “dependent origination is,” this is an assertion of its existence; thus, if it were said “it is” or “it is born,” that would be an assertion of its production. It is with this intention that it is said, “arising is not.”

576. Imesaṃ saṅkhārādīnaṃ paccayā idappaccayā, avijjādayo, tesaṃ bhāvo idappaccayatā[V 2.0219]. Ko pana so bhāvoti āha “bhāvo ca nāmā”tiādi. Tassattho – yenākārena avijjādayo saṅkhārādipātubhāvahetū honti, tasmiṃ avijjādīnaṃ pavattiākāravisese vikāre paṭiccasamuppādoti ayaṃ samaññāti. Tesaṃ vādīnaṃ taṃ maññanaṃ. Hetuvacanatoti hetubhāvavacanato.

576. The conditions for these—formations and so on—are specific conditions, namely, ignorance and so on. Their state of being so is specific conditionality. But what is that state? It is said: “And the state is…” and so on. The meaning is this: The designation “dependent origination” refers to that particular mode of occurrence, that specific modification, by which ignorance and so on become the causes for the manifestation of formations and so on. That is the opinion of those theorists. “Because it expresses the cause” means because it expresses the state of being a cause.

577. Etthāti paṭiccasamuppādapade. Samuppādapadhānavacanaviññeyyo sasattiko hetu paṭiccasamuppādoti aviparītaṃ atthaṃ ajānantānaṃ aññattha samuppādasaddassa bhāvasādhanassa dassanato tathā idhāpi byañjanacchāyāya uppādoyevāyaṃ vutto, na hetūti yā saññā uppajjati, sā imassa paṭiccasamuppādapadassa evaṃ idāni vuccamānākārena atthaṃ gahetvā vūpasametabbā vinodetabbā.

576. “Here” means in the term “dependent origination.” For those who do not know the unerring meaning that “dependent origination” is a potent cause to be understood from the word which has “origination” as its principal part, the following perception arises. Because they have seen elsewhere that the word “origination” is a verbal noun, here too, due to the semblance of the expression, they think that this is just origination that is spoken of, not a cause. That perception should be allayed and dispelled by grasping the meaning of this term “dependent origination” in the way now being explained.

Dvedhāti gāthāya ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – yasmā attano paccayavasena pavatto paccayuppannadhammasamūho paccetabbato paṭicco ca so saha uppajjanato samuppādo ca, paṭicca vā kāraṇasāmaggiṃ apaccakkhāya saha uppajjanato evāti ca evaṃ dvedhā “paṭiccasamuppādo”ti idaṃ vacanaṃ icchitabbaṃ, tasmā tassa paccayadhammopi phalūpacārena paṭiccasamuppādo icceva vuttoti.

577. Of the verse beginning 'Dvedhā', this is the summary meaning: Since the collection of conditionally arisen phenomena, which proceeds by way of its own conditions, is 'dependent' (paṭicca) because it is to be cognized, and 'origination' (samuppāda) because it arises together; or, because it arises together dependently, without rejecting the causal assemblage—thus, in two ways, this expression 'dependent origination' is to be accepted. Therefore, its conditioning phenomenon is also called 'dependent origination' by a metaphor based on the fruit.

Paccayatāyāti paccayasamūhato. Pavattoti nibbatto. Dhammasamūhoti paccayuppannadhammapuñjo. Patīyamānoti ñāṇagatiyā abhimukhaṃ upeyamāno, abhisamiyamānoti attho. Hitāya sukhāya cāti lokuttarahitāya, lokuttarasukhāya ca. Saha uppajjati ekekassa kadācipi [M 2.0234] uppattiyā abhāvato. Sammā uppajjati ahetuto, visamahetuto ca anuppajjanato. Saha uppajjatīti ekajjhaṃ uppajjati antamaso aṭṭhannaṃ dhammānaṃ uppajjanato. Na paccakkhāyāti apaṭikkhipitvā, attano paccayabhūtadhammasamudāyena kenaci na vināti attho. Tassāti yvāyaṃ “paṭiccasamuppādo”ti vutto paccayuppannadhammasamūho, tassa ayaṃ avijjādiko hetusamūho. “Tappaccayattā”ti etena paṭiccasamuppādapaccaye paṭicca samuppādasamaññāti dasseti. Tenāha “yathā loke”tiādi. Yathā hi loke “pittaṃ mathitaṃ, sūrā dadhi, tipusaṃ jaro, semho guḷo, āyu ghata”nti ca paccayo phalavohārena vuccati, evaṃ phalūpacārena paṭiccasamuppādo vuttoti veditabbo.

“By conditionality” means from the assemblage of conditions. “Proceeds” means produced. “Collection of phenomena” means the heap of conditionally arisen phenomena. “Being approached” means being approached face-to-face by the path of knowledge, that is, being fully realized. “For welfare and for happiness” means for supramundane welfare and for supramundane happiness. “It arises together” because there is never an arising of each one individually. “It arises rightly” because it does not arise from no cause or from a discordant cause. “It arises together” means it arises all at once, since at the minimum eight phenomena arise. “Not rejecting” means not repudiating; that is, not without any of its own assemblage of conditioning phenomena. “Of that” means of that collection of conditionally arisen phenomena called “dependent origination,” this is the assemblage of causes beginning with ignorance. By the phrase “because it is conditioned by that,” he shows that the designation “dependent origination” is applied to the condition for dependent origination. Hence he says, “As in the world,” etc. For just as in the world the cause is called by the name of the effect in such expressions as “churned milk is bile,” “curds are liquor,” “cucumber is fever,” “jaggery is phlegm,” and “ghee is longevity,” so too “dependent origination” should be understood as spoken of by a metaphor based on the fruit.

578. Paṭicca-sadde [V 2.0220] paṭi-saddo abhimukhattho, icca-saddo gammatthoti dassento āha “paṭimukhamito”ti. Kassa pana paṭimukhaṃ, kena vā ito, ko vā itoti codanattaye pacchimaṃ vissajjento “hetusamūho”ti āha. Tasmiñhi vissaṭṭhe hetusamūho nāma paccayasāmaggīti tattha aññamaññassa paṭimukhaṃ, aññamaññeneva ca itoti vissaṭṭhovāyamattho hotīti. Sahiteti samudite avinibbhutte. Soti hetusamūho. Samuppādo iti vuttoti yojanā.

578. Showing that in the word “paṭicca,” the prefix “paṭi” has the meaning of “facing” and the word “icca” has the meaning of “gone,” he says, “gone towards.” To the three questions—“But facing what?,” “By what is it gone?,” and “What is it that has gone?”—answering the last, he says, “The assemblage of causes.” For when that has been answered, since “assemblage of causes” means the causal nexus, this meaning is thereby also answered: that they are facing one another and have gone by means of one another. “Together” means assembled, inseparable. The connection is: “That assemblage of causes is called ‘origination.’”

Pātubhāvāyāti uppādāya. Kāmaṃ pāḷiyaṃ “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.1; udā. 1; mahāva. 1; netti. 24; vibha. 225) avijjāva paccayabhāvena vuttā, tathāpi na avijjā ekāva paccayo hoti, atha kho sahajātadhammavatthuārammaṇādayo, yonisomanasikārādayo, taṇhupādānādayo ca dhammā yathārahaṃ saṅkhāruppādane avijjāya sahakārīkāraṇaṃ hontiyeva. Evaṃ saṅkhārādayopi viññāṇādīnanti āha “avijjādiekekahetusīsena niddiṭṭho hetusamūho”ti. Sādhāraṇaphalanipphādakaṭṭhenāti taṃsamūhapariyāpannānaṃ hetudhammānaṃ sādhāraṇassa phalassa nibbattakabhāvena. Avekallaṭṭhenāti anūnabhāvena. Tasmiñhi hetusamūhe ekaccāsādhāraṇañcetaṃ phalaṃ, ekacceheva ca nibbattetabbaṃ siyā, sabbesaṃ tesaṃ paccayadhammānaṃ aññamaññāpekkhā natthīti paṭimukhagamanābhāvato paṭiccattho na paripūreyyāti. Sāmaggiaṅgānanti paccayasāmaggiyā aṅgabhūtānaṃ, samūhīnanti attho[M 2.0235]. Niddhāraṇe cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Phaladhammānaṃ sahitatā nāma visuṃ abhāvo, na hetudhammānaṃ viya aññamaññāpekkhāti āha “aññamaññaṃ avinibbhogavuttidhamme”ti avinibbhogaggahaṇañcettha rūpadhammānampi saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ. Aññathā sampayuttadhammeti vucceyya.

‘For arising’ means for production. Although in the Pāḷi it is said, ‘With ignorance as condition, formations [arise]’ (saṃ. ni. 2.1; udā. 1; mahāva. 1; netti. 24; vibha. 225), and ignorance alone is stated as the condition, nevertheless, ignorance is not the sole condition. Rather, dhammas such as co-nascent states, physical bases, and objects, as well as wise attention and the like, and craving, clinging, and the like, are, as appropriate, indeed cooperative causes with ignorance in the production of formations. Similarly, formations, etc., are to be understood as conditions for consciousness, etc. Thus it is said: ‘a collection of causes indicated under the heading of each single cause such as ignorance.’ ‘By the characteristic of producing a common result’ means by the fact of producing a result that is common to the causal dhammas included in that collection. ‘By the characteristic of completeness’ means by being without deficiency. For in that collection of causes, if this result were not common to some, and if it were to be produced by only some, then because there would be no mutual dependence among all those conditional dhammas, the meaning of ‘paṭicca’ would not be fulfilled due to the absence of a convergent approach. ‘Of the members of the assemblage’ means of those that are members of the assemblage of conditions; that is, of the collected items. And this is a genitive of specification. The togetherness of resultant dhammas is their non-existence separately; it is not a mutual dependence like that of causal dhammas. Hence it is said: ‘dhammas with an inseparable mode of occurrence.’ And the inclusion of ‘inseparable’ here is for the purpose of including material dhammas as well. Otherwise, it would have been said ‘associated dhammas.’

579. Paccayatāti ayaṃ avijjādiko paccayasamūho. Aññoññanti aññamaññaṃ. Paṭiccāti nissāya sahakārīkāraṇaṃ laddhā. Samanti avisamaṃ avekallena. Sahāti ekajjhaṃ. Dhammeti attano paccayuppannadhamme. Yasmā uppādeti, tatopi tasmāpi. Evaṃ paṭiccasamuppādoti muninā bhagavatā bhāsitāti yojanā. Na apaṭicca paṭiccevāti avadhāraṇatthaṃ dassento gāthāyaṃ eva-kāro luttaniddiṭṭhoti dasseti.

579. ‘Conditionality’ refers to this collection of conditions beginning with ignorance. ‘Mutually’ means reciprocally. ‘Having depended’ means having relied upon, having obtained a cooperative cause. ‘Evenly’ means without disparity, with completeness. ‘Together’ means at once. ‘Dhammas’ means the dhammas arisen from their respective conditions. ‘Because it originates them, for that reason also.’ The construction is: ‘Thus, “dependent origination” was spoken by the Sage, the Blessed One.’ To show the emphatic sense, ‘not undependently but dependently indeed,’ he points out that the particle ‘eva’ is indicated as elided in the verse.

Ekekadesanti phalasamudāyassa ekadesekadesaṃ, bhāgasoti attho. Pubbāparabhāvenāti paṭipāṭiyā[V 2.0221]. Sabbametaṃ rūpārūpakalāpuppādanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Atthānusāravohārakusalenāti paramatthadhammānugatavohāranipuṇena.

‘Each single part’ means each single part of the aggregate of results; the meaning is ‘as a portion.’ ‘In sequence’ means in their due order. All this is said with reference to the production of material and immaterial groups. ‘By one skilled in expression that accords with the meaning’ means by one adept in expression that follows the ultimate dhammas.

580. Purimena padenāti yojanā. Sassatādīnanti sassatabhāvādīnaṃ, sassatavādādīnaṃ vā. Sassatasahacaritā hi vādāpi sassatādayoti vuccanti yathā “dukkhadesanā dukkha”nti. Ucchedādīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Vighāto vināso, pahānanti attho. Ñāyoti antadvayavirahitā majjhimā paṭipatti.

580. The connection is ‘with the preceding word.’ ‘Of eternalism, etc.’ means of the state of being eternal, etc., or of the doctrines of eternalism, etc. For doctrines associated with eternalism, etc., are also called ‘eternalism, etc.,’ just as ‘the teaching on suffering is suffering.’ ‘Annihilationism, etc.’: here too the same method applies. ‘Vighāta’ means destruction; the meaning is ‘abandoning.’ ‘The method’ is the Middle Path, which is devoid of the two extremes.

Pavattidhammānanti pavattibhūtānaṃ dhammānaṃ, kilesavaṭṭādīnanti attho. “Sassato attā ca loko cā”tiādinayappavatto (dī. ni. 1.31) sassatavādo. “Natthi hetu, natthi paccayo sattānaṃ saṃkilesāyā”tiādinayappavatto (dī. ni. 1.168; ma. ni. 2.101, 227; saṃ. ni. 3.212) ahetuvādo. Pakati aṇukālādivasena loko pavattatīti evaṃ pavatto visamahetuvādo. Issarapurisapajāpativādā vasavattivādā. Ahetuvādaggahaṇeneva cettha sabhāvaniyati yadicchāvādānampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Keci pana “cakkhu eva cakkhussa kāraṇa”nti evamādiko visamahetuvādo. Issarādivādo ahetuvādantogadho. Sabhāveneva dhammā pavattantīti vādo “vasavattivādo”ti vadanti. Kiṃ [M 2.0236] hi paccayasāmaggiyā payojananti adhippāyo. Samuppādapadena paridīpito hotīti yojanā. Paridīpanassa pana aviparītakāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “paccayasāmaggiyaṃ dhammānaṃ uppattito”ti vuttaṃ. Vihatāti abbhāhatā. “Purimapurimapaccayavasenā”ti iminā avicchedavasena pavattamānaṃ ucchedadiṭṭhinivattakaṃ hetuphalapabandhaṃ dasseti. Tenāha “kuto ucchedo”ti. Ucchedābhāvakathaneneva cettha ucchedavādassāpi abhāvaṃ dassetīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Of ongoing dhammas' means of the dhammas that have become ongoing, that is, the round of defilements, etc. The doctrine of eternalism is that which proceeds in the manner of 'the self and the world are eternal,' etc. The doctrine of non-causality is that which proceeds in the manner of 'there is no cause, no condition for the defilement of beings,' etc. The doctrine of uneven causality is that which proceeds thus: 'the world proceeds by way of nature, atoms, time, etc.' The doctrines of a Lord (Issara), a Primal Person (Puruṣa), or a Creator (Pajāpati) are doctrines of a controller. And here, by the inclusion of the doctrine of non-causality, the inclusion of the doctrines of determinism by nature, fatalism, and accidentalism should also be understood. Some, however, say the doctrine of uneven causality is such as 'the eye itself is the cause of the eye.' The doctrine of a Lord, etc., is included within the doctrine of non-causality. The view that 'dhammas proceed purely by their own nature' they call 'the doctrine of a controller.' The intention is: 'For what is the use of an assemblage of conditions?' The construction is: 'is illuminated by the term 'origination' (samuppāda).' But to show the non-erroneous reason for the illumination, it is said: 'because of the arising of dhammas in an assemblage of conditions.' 'Refuted' means struck down. By 'by way of preceding and preceding conditions,' he shows the chain of cause and effect that proceeds without interruption, which counters the view of annihilationism. Therefore he says: 'Whence is annihilation?' And here, it should be understood that by stating the absence of annihilation, he also shows the absence of the doctrine of annihilationism.

Tassā tassā paccayasāmaggiyāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ hetupaccayasamavāye. Santatiṃ avicchinditvāti hetuphalapabandhasaṅkhātassa santānassa avicchindanena. Tesaṃ tesaṃ paccayuppannadhammānaṃ sambhavato uppajjanato sassatucchedasaṅkhātaṃ antadvayaṃ anupaggamma yathāsakaṃ paccayehi anurūpaphaluppatti idha majjhimapaṭipadāti adhippetā. Kammavaṭṭassa, vipākavaṭṭassa ca bhinnasabhāvattā, bhinnakālattā ca so karoti so paṭisaṃvedetīti vādappahānaṃ. Kusalākusalakkhandhappavattiyañhi kārakavohāro, vipākakkhandhapavattiyaṃ vedakavohāroti. Yasmiṃ santāne [V 2.0222] kammaṃ nibbattaṃ, tattheva tassa phalassa nibbattanato añño karoti añño paṭisaṃvedetīti vādappahānaṃ. Na hi katassa vināso, akatassa vā abbhāgamo atthi. “Itthī, purisā”ti vohārena janapadanirutti. Tattha yasmā paṇḍitāpi loke “pañcakkhandhe ānetu, nāmarūpaṃ āgacchatū”ti avatvā itthī, purisotveva voharanti, tasmā “itthī evāyaṃ, puriso evāyanti apariññātavatthukānaṃ hoti abhiniveso. Viddasuno pana paṭiccasamuppādaṃ jānantassa tathā tathā pavattamāne dhamme upādāya paññattimattato tattha paramatthato na abhinivesoti āha “janapadaniruttiyā anabhiniveso”ti. Samaññāyāti lokasamaññāya. Anatidhāvananti anatikkamanaṃ. “Satto”ti hi vutte “ko ettha satto, kiṃ rūpaṃ, udāhu vedanādayo”ti vibhāgaṃ akatvā lokasamaññāvaseneva lokiyehi viya lokiyo attho samaññaṃ avilaṅghantena voharitabbo.

'In each particular assemblage of conditions' means in each particular combination of causes and conditions. 'Without interrupting the continuity' means by not severing the continuum reckoned as the chain of cause and effect. Because those dhammas arisen from their respective conditions arise, without approaching the two extremes of eternalism and annihilationism, the arising of a corresponding result from its own proper conditions is here intended as the Middle Path. Because the round of kamma and the round of its result have different natures and different times, the view 'the one who acts is the one who experiences' is abandoned. For in the occurrence of the wholesome and unwholesome aggregates there is the convention of an 'agent'; in the occurrence of the resultant aggregates, there is the convention of an 'experiencer.' Because the result is produced in the very same continuum in which the kamma was produced, the view 'one acts and another experiences' is abandoned. For there is no perishing of what has been done, nor an arising of what has not been done. The terms 'woman' and 'man' are provincial expressions. Herein, since even the wise in the world do not say, 'Bring the five aggregates,' or 'Let name-and-form come,' but speak only in terms of 'woman' and 'man,' therefore, for those for whom the underlying reality is not fully understood, there is an adherence: 'This is indeed a woman, this is indeed a man.' But for a wise person who knows dependent origination, since it is merely a designation based on phenomena that are proceeding in such and such a way, there is no adherence to it in an ultimate sense. Thus it is said: 'non-adherence to provincial expressions.' 'By convention' means by worldly convention. 'Not overrunning' means not transgressing. For when 'a being' is mentioned, without making a division such as 'Who here is the being? Is it form, or is it feeling, etc.?' the worldly meaning should be used in accordance with worldly convention, just as by worldly people, without violating the convention.

Aparo nayo – paccetumarahatīti paṭicco. Yo hi naṃ pacceti abhisameti, tassa accantameva dukkhavūpasamāya saṃvattati. Sammā, saha ca uppādetīti samuppādo. Paccayadhammo hi attano phalaṃ uppādento sampuṇṇameva [M 2.0237] uppādeti, na vikalaṃ. Ye ca dhamme uppādeti, te sabbe saheva uppādeti, na ekekaṃ. Iti paṭicco ca so samuppādo cāti paṭiccasamuppādo. Atha vā paṭicca paṭimukhaṃ itvā kāraṇasāmaggiṃ appaṭikkhipitvā sahite uppādetīti paṭiccasamuppādo. Paṭimukhagamanañca paccayassa kāraṇasāmaggiyā aṅgabhāvena phalassa uppādanameva. Appaṭikkhipitvāti ca na vinā tāya kāraṇasāmaggiyā, aṅgabhāvaṃ agantvā sayameva na uppādetīti attho. Etena kāraṇabahutā dassitā, “sahite”ti iminā paccayuppannadhammabahutā. Ubhayenāpi “ekaṃ na ekato”tiādinā (visuddhi. 2.617) parato vuccamāno sāsananayo dīpito hoti.

Another method: It is 'paṭicca' because it is fit to be directly perceived. For indeed, to one who directly perceives it and fully comprehends it, it conduces utterly to the stilling of suffering. It is 'samuppāda' because it causes to arise (uppādeti) completely (sammā) and together (saha). For indeed, a conditional phenomenon, when causing its own fruit to arise, causes it to arise only completely, not deficiently. And whatever phenomena it causes to arise, it causes them all to arise only together, not one by one. Thus, because it is that which is directly perceived (paṭicco) and that which causes to arise completely and together (samuppādo), it is called 'paṭiccasamuppādo.' Alternatively, 'paṭiccasamuppādo' is so called because, having approached face-to-face and without rejecting the assemblage of causes, it causes co-arisen phenomena to arise. And the 'approaching face-to-face' is simply the causing to arise of the fruit by the condition through its being a constituent part of the assemblage of causes. And 'without rejecting' means that it does not cause to arise by itself alone, without that assemblage of causes, without having become a constituent part. By this, the multiplicity of causes is shown; by this word 'sahite' (co-arisen), the multiplicity of dependently arisen phenomena is shown. By both, the method of the teaching to be stated later, beginning with 'not one from one,' is illuminated.

Atha vā paṭicca paccetabbaṃ paccayaṃ paṭigantvā na vinā tena sambandhassa uppādo paṭiccasamuppādo (udā. aṭṭha. 1). Paṭiccasamuppādoti cettha samuppādappadhānavacanaviññeyyo sasattiko hetūti veditabbo. Tattha “paṭiccā”ti vutte kiṃ paṭiccāti vattabbanti āha “paccetabba”nti. So ca paccayadhammoti katvā vuttaṃ “paccaya”nti. Idāni paṭiccasaddassa atthamāha “paṭigantvā”ti. Kāraṇassa sabhāvena tappaṭilābhagatiyā patvā. Kathaṃ na vinā tena? Sati eva tasmiṃ, tassa ca phalassa uppādato eva, na aññathā. Asati, nirodhato cāti [V 2.0223] ayaṃ paccayaṭṭhiti paṭiccasaddassa attho. Tenāyaṃ paṭiccasaddo yathā “imasmiṃ sati imassuppādo”ti ete saddā bhummanissakkavacanajotanīyena idaṃ-saddavacanīyassa hetumato hetuāyattabhāvena bhāvuppāduttarakiriyāpekkhena yāyassa tadāyattatā, tāya samatthatāya hetuṃ vadanti, evaṃ gantvā-saddantaravacanīyena taṃviññeyyasseva paccayanakiriyākattuhetumato hetupaccayanena hetuāyattabhāvena samuppāduttarakiriyāpekkhena yāyassa tadāyattatā, tāya samatthatāya hetumāha. Evañca katvā “avijjā paṭicca, saṅkhārā paṭiccasamuppannā”tiādi (paṭi. ma. 1.46) saṅkhārapiṭake vuttaṃ. Samatthatā cettha nidānādibhāvo. So ca tadavinābhāviphalaṃ pati satvameva. Sambandhassāti ca saṃyojanānurūpatāvasena jātiādinā sambandhassa jarāmaraṇādipaccayuppannassa. Uppādoti uppajjanaṃ. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ paṭiccasaddappayogo, nanu samānakattukānaṃ pubbakāle īdiso saddappayogoti? “Bhutvā gacchati, kasitvā vapatī”tiādīsu saccametaṃ, taṃ pana yebhuyyavasena daṭṭhabbaṃ [M 2.0238] samānāparakāle, asamānakattuke ca dassanato. Samānakāle tāva –

Alternatively, having approached a condition that is to be approached, the arising of a connected effect, not being without that condition, is Dependent Origination. And herein, 'Dependent Origination' should be understood as the cause together with its power, which is to be known through the expression in which 'origination' is primary. Therein, when 'having depended on' is said, it should be asked, 'Having depended on what?' Therefore, it is said: 'that which is to be approached.' And that, being a conditioning thing, is called a 'condition.' Now, the meaning of the word 'paṭicca' is stated as 'having approached,' that is, having reached it by the fact of the cause's existence, by way of attaining it. How so? Not without that cause. Only when that cause exists is there the arising of its effect, not otherwise; when it does not exist, there is its cessation. This state of being a condition is the meaning of the word 'paṭicca'. Therefore, this word 'paṭicca' indicates the cause. Just as the words 'When this exists, this arises' indicate the cause by that capacity—namely, the dependence on the cause of the effect (which is expressed by the word 'this', anticipates the subsequent actions of 'being' and 'arising', and is indicated by the locative and ablative cases)—so too 'paṭicca' indicates the cause by that capacity—namely, the dependence on the cause of the effect (which is the agent of the action of conditioning expressed by the other word 'gantvā' and anticipates the subsequent action of 'arising'). And for this reason, it was said in the Saṅkhārapiṭaka: 'Ignorance is a condition (paṭicca); formations are dependently arisen (paṭiccasamuppannā),' and so on. And herein, 'capacity' is the state of being a source, etc. And that exists only in relation to a fruit that is inseparable from it. And 'of the connection' refers to that of the dependently arisen phenomena, such as aging and death, which is connected with birth, etc., by way of its suitability for conjunction. 'Arising' means coming into being. If so, how is the word 'paṭicca' used? Is it not that such a word is used for a prior action of the same agent? In cases like 'having eaten, he goes' and 'having plowed, he sows,' this is true. But this should be seen as the general rule, for its usage is also found in cases of simultaneous and subsequent time, and when the agents are different. First, regarding simultaneous time:

“Andhakāraṃ nihantvāna, uditāyaṃ divākaro;

Vaṇṇapaññāvabhāsehi, obhāsetvā samuggato”ti. –

“Having dispelled the darkness, this sun has risen; having illuminated with the radiances of physical form and wisdom, He has fully arisen.”

Udāharaṇaṃ. Keci pana “mukhaṃ byādāya sayati, akkhīni parivattetvā passatī”ti udāharanti. Apare “nisajja adhīte, ṭhatvā kathetī”ti.

This is an example. Some, however, cite: “Having opened his mouth, he sleeps; having rolled his eyes, he looks.” Others cite: “Having sat down, he studies; having stood up, he speaks.”

Tattha byādānaparivattanuttarakālabhāvisayanadassanakiriyāpekkhā pubbuttarakālatā atthi, sā ca bhedānupalakkhaṇā kehici na lakkhīyati. “Nisajja adhīte, ṭhatvā kathetī”ti ca samānakālatāyapi ajjhenakathanehi pubbepi nisajjaṭṭhānāni hontīti sakkā pubbuttarakālatā sambhāvetuṃ, tasmā purimāniyeva udāharaṇāni yuttāni. Udayasamakālameva hi tannivattaniyanivattananti. Aparakāle “dvāramāvaritvā pavisati, āvaritvā nikkhamatī”ti. Keci pana “ḍakkacca patito daṇḍo”ti udāharanti. Abhighātabhūtasahajātāya pana abhighātajasaddassa samānakālatā ettha labbhati, tasmā idhāpi purimāniyeva udāharaṇāni yuttāni. Purimatāvacanicchāvaseneva pana lakkhaṇahetukiriyānaṃ lakkhaṇahetubhāvavacanicchāti lakkhaṇabhāvato purimakālo icceva “nihantvānā”ti saddasiddhi icchitā, evañca paccayanakiriyā [V 2.0224] samuppajjanakiriyāya purimikāvāti paṭicca-saddasiddhi. Tattha yuttaṃ paccakkhato kattudassanato. Idha pana tadabhāvato na yuttanti ce? Nāyaṃ doso. Idhāpi anumānato siddho. Jarāmaraṇādiko kattā attheva “ñatvā kiriyato vaya”nti evamādipayogadassanato avassaṃ anumiyamānena kattunā īdiso saddapayogo icchitabbo. Asamāne pana kattari “pisācaṃ disvā bhayaṃ hoti, paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā hontī”ti (ma. ni. 1.271; 2.182; pu. pa. 204) evamādi veditabbaṃ. Yathā ca tattha pisācadassanādipurisabyāpāro, evamidhāpi paccayanaṃ paccayabyāpāro attano phaluppādanaṃ, tañca satvaṃ samuppādovāti “paccaye sati, paccayassa uppādā”ti paccayanassa samuppādahetutāya gamako samānassa kattu abhāvepi paṭicca-saddo siddhoti veditabbo. Yadi paṭiccasambandhassa uppādo paṭiccasamuppādo, kathaṃ paccayo [M 2.0239] paṭiccasamuppādoti? Heṭṭhā vicāritovāyamattho. Apica yoyaṃ samuppāda-saddavibhāvitānaṃ paccayuppannānaṃ paṭiccasaddavibhāvito sasattiko hetu adhippeto, tassa samuppādābhimukhatāya padhānavacanaviññeyyasabhāvattā tathā vuttoti.

In those examples, with respect to the actions of sleeping and seeing which occur at a time subsequent to the actions of opening and turning, there is a state of being prior and subsequent in time; but since its distinction is imperceptible, it is not perceived by some. And in 'having sat down, he studies; having stood up, he speaks,' although there is simultaneity, it is possible to conceive of a prior-subsequent sequence, since the acts of sitting and standing also occur before the studying and speaking. Therefore, only the former examples are suitable. For the cessation of that which is to be made to cease by it occurs at the very same time as its arising. As an example of a subsequent time: 'having closed the door, he enters; having closed it, he exits.' Some, however, cite as an example: 'the stick fell with a 'ḍakka' sound.' But here, simultaneity is obtained between the sound born of the impact and the action of falling which is co-nascent with the impact. Therefore, here too, only the former examples are suitable. However, it is only by the power of the wish to speak of priority that there is a wish to speak of the state of characteristic-actions and cause-actions as being characteristics and causes. Thus, because it is a characteristic, it is intended that it is only a prior time; for this reason, the establishment of the word 'nihantvāna' is intended. And similarly, the action of conditioning is only prior to the action of arising; therefore, the word 'paṭicca' is established. There, it is suitable because the agent is directly perceived. But if it is said that here it is not suitable because of the absence of that agent, this is not a fault. Here too, an agent is established by inference. An agent such as aging-and-death certainly exists. Because of seeing such usages as 'having known decay from action,' such a verbal usage must necessarily be intended for an inferred agent. But when the agent is different, it should be understood through such examples as: 'Having seen a goblin, fear arises,' and 'Having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.' And just as there, seeing a goblin, etc., is the activity of a person, so here too, conditioning is the activity of a condition—its own production of a fruit. And that, being, is just arising. Thus, as in 'when there is a condition, because of the arising from the condition,' it should be understood that the word 'paṭicca' is established, even in the absence of a single agent, as it indicates that the action of conditioning is a cause for the arising. If 'paṭiccasamuppādo' is the arising of a connected effect which has been conditioned, how then is the condition 'paṭiccasamuppādo'? This matter has already been investigated below. Moreover, this cause with its potency, distinguished by the word 'paṭicca'—which is the intended cause of the dependently arisen phenomena distinguished by the word 'samuppāda'—is so called because of its orientation towards arising and because its nature is to be known through the primary expression.

Kiṃ pana kāraṇaṃ samuppādapadhānena vacanena samuppādassa hetu veditabbo, na pana sahetuko samuppādo evāti? Vuccate – diṭṭhassa dukkhassa yo paccayo paccayaniddesena tassa vibhāvitattā. Kathaṃ? Yathāha –

What, then, is the reason that by this expression in which 'origination' is primary, the cause of the origination should be understood, and not simply the origination as being with its cause? It is said: because the condition for the suffering that is seen has been made clear by the exposition of the condition. How? As He said:

“Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu parivīmaṃsamāno parivīmaṃsati ‘yaṃ kho idaṃ anekavidhaṃ nānappakārakaṃ dukkhaṃ loke uppajjati jarāmaraṇaṃ, idaṃ nu kho dukkhaṃ kiṃ nidānaṃ kiṃ samudayaṃ kiṃ jātikaṃ kiṃ pabhavaṃ, kismiṃ sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hoti, kismiṃ asati jarāmaraṇaṃ na hotī’ti. So parivīmaṃsamāno evaṃ pajānāti ‘yaṃ kho idaṃ…pe… idaṃ kho dukkhaṃ jātinidāna’”miccādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.51) –

Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, investigating, investigates thus: ‘This suffering of many kinds and various sorts that has arisen in the world, that is, aging-and-death: what is the source of this suffering, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its provenance? When what exists does aging-and-death come to be? When what does not exist does aging-and-death not come to be?’ Investigating thus, he understands: ‘This suffering… this suffering has birth as its source,’ and so on.

Diṭṭhassa dukkhassa nidānaṃ parivīmaṃsasutte vuttaṃ. Taṃ pajānanañca nidānampi viññātabbanti. Yathā cāha –

In the Sutta on Investigation, the source of the suffering that is seen is stated. And that knowing is to be understood in terms of the source. As it is also said:

“Pubbe me, bhikkhave, sambodhā anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva sato etadahosi ‘kicchaṃ [V 2.0225] vatāyaṃ loko āpanno jāyati ca jīyati ca mīyati ca cavati ca upapajjati ca, atha ca panimassa dukkhassa nissaraṇaṃ nappajānāti jarāmaraṇassa. Kudāssu nāma imassa dukkhassa nissaraṇaṃ paññāyissati jarāmaraṇassā’ti…pe… tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, yoniso manasikārā ahu paññāya abhisamayo ‘jātiyā kho sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hoti, jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa’”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.10) –

“Bhikkhus, before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, this thought occurred to me: ‘Alas, this world has fallen into trouble, in that it is born, ages, and dies, it passes away and is reborn, and yet it does not know the escape from this suffering, that is, from aging-and-death. When, indeed, will an escape from this suffering, from aging-and-death, be discerned?’… Then, bhikkhus, for me, through wise attention, there occurred a breakthrough with wisdom: ‘Indeed, when there is birth, aging-and-death comes to be; with birth as a condition, aging-and-death comes to be.’”

Ādinā diṭṭhassa dukkhassa paccayavīmaṃsābhisamayā vuttā. Paccayo hi ñātabbo. Tadabhisamayāyattañca dukkhanissaraṇapajānananti yo ca ñātabbo, so pavedetabboti paṭiccasamuppādasaddo yaṃ yadidaṃ samuppādasaddavibhāvitaṃ diṭṭhaṃ dukkhaṃ, taṃ paccayaṃ paṭicceva, na aññathāti evaṃ paccayavibhāvanatthaṃ vuccati. Bhavati hi ñātuṃ, pavedetuñca icchitabhāvena padhānassāpi kenaci visesena ñātabbatāya appadhānabhāvena niddeso yathā [M 2.0240] “ko sotāpanno, yassa tīṇi saṃyojanāni pahīnāni. Ko devadatto, yassa uccatarāni gehānī”ti, evamidhāpi paccayapaccayanapavedanaṭṭhena niddese sattivisesena attano phalena paccanīyatāya ñātabbabhāvena “paṭiccā”ti pariyāyena paccayo vutto.

By the preceding, the investigation of and breakthrough to the cause of the suffering that is seen are stated. For the cause must be known. And since the understanding of the escape from suffering is dependent on the breakthrough to that, what is to be known must also be declared. Thus the term ‘dependent origination’ is spoken for the purpose of clarifying the cause, thus: ‘Whatever suffering is seen, clarified by the word “origination,” that arises only in dependence on a cause, not otherwise.’ For it happens that even what is primary, being desired to be known and to be declared, is designated in a secondary way because it is to be known by some special quality, as in: ‘Who is a stream-enterer? One for whom the three fetters are abandoned. Who is Devadatta? One whose houses are taller.’ So here too, in this exposition which has the purpose of making the cause known, the cause is spoken of by the alternative term ‘paṭicca’ because it is to be known by its special power and by its being depended upon by its own fruit.

Yo cāyaṃ “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādiko niddeso, so ca sakalassa dukkhakkhandhassa mūlato paṭṭhāya paccayānaṃ pavedanāya niddiṭṭhoti pariyosānepi “evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hotī”ti evaṃ-saddena samugghātaṃ dukkhaṃ dassetvā tassa yathāvutte paccaye taṃsamudayābhimukhe katvā nigamitā paccayā. Paṭipadāsuttepi (saṃ. ni. 2.3) “avijjāpaccayā…pe… samudayo hotī”ti vatvā “ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, micchāpaṭipadā”ti vuttaṃ. Na ca paṭiccasamuppannabhāvena gahitaṃ dukkhaṃ micchāpaṭipadaṃ, atha kho dukkhasamudayabhūtā paccayāti. Yathā ca “pañcaṅgiko sammāsamādhi (dī. ni. 3.335), pañcañāṇiko sammāsamādhī”ti (dī. ni. 3.355) aṅgañāṇapaṭivedanatthattā desanāya sammāsamādhipadhānehi saddehi aṅgañāṇapaṭivedanaṃ kataṃ, evamidhāpi samuppādapadhānena saddena paccayapaṭivedanaṃ katanti veditabbaṃ.

And this exposition beginning, ‘With ignorance as condition, formations,’ is stated starting from the root of the entire mass of suffering in order to make the causes known. Thus, at the conclusion, by saying, ‘Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering,’ the aggregate of suffering is shown by means of the word ‘thus,’ and the causes are brought to a conclusion by being directed toward that origin. In the Discourse on the Path, too, after stating, ‘With ignorance as condition… the origin occurs,’ it is said, ‘This, bhikkhus, is called the wrong path.’ But suffering, grasped as a dependently arisen phenomenon, is not the wrong path; rather, the causes that are the origin of suffering are the wrong path. And just as in the statements, ‘Right concentration has five factors’ and ‘Right concentration has five kinds of knowledge,’ the making known of the factors and the kinds of knowledge is effected by means of terms that make right concentration primary, as the teaching is for the purpose of making them known; so too here, it should be understood that the making known of the causes is effected by means of a term that makes ‘origination’ primary.

581. Yā panāyaṃ tantīti sambandho. Nikkhittāti ṭhapitā, desitāti attho. Yathādhippetassa atthassa tananato tanti, gantho. “Kiṃ vādī, bhante, sammāsambuddho”ti pucchitena [V 2.0226] “vibhajjavādī, mahārājā”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.tatiyasaṅgītikathā; kathā. aṭṭha. nidānakathā) moggaliputtatissattherena vuttattā sammāsambuddhasāvakā vibhajjavādino. Te hi satthārā venayikādibhāvaṃ vibhajja vuttaṃ anuvadanti, somanassādīnaṃ, cīvarādīnañca sevitabbāsevitabbabhāvaṃ. Sassatucchedavāde vā vibhajja vadanti. “Sassato attā ca loko cā”tiādīnaṃ (dī. ni. 1.31) ṭhapanīyānaṃ ṭhapanato, rāgādikkhayassa sassatassa, rāgādikāyaduccaritādiucchedassa ca vacanato, na pana ekaṃsabyākaraṇīyādike tayo pañhe apanetvā vibhajjabyākaraṇīyameva vadanti. Vibhajjavādīnaṃ maṇḍalaṃ samūho vibhajjavādimaṇḍalaṃ. Vibhajjavādino vā bhagavato parisā vibhajjavādimaṇḍalantipi vadanti, vibhajja vā sassatucchede ubho ante anupagamma majjhimapaṭipadābhūtassa paṭiccasamuppādassa desanato bhagavā, tadanuvādato tassa sāvakā ca vibhajjavādinoti. Sesaṃ purimasadisaṃ.

581. As to this canon (tanti): this is the connection. ‘Laid down’ (nikkhittā) means placed, that is, taught. Because it expounds (tananato) the intended meaning, it is a canon (tanti), a text. When asked, ‘Venerable sir, what is the doctrine of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One?’ the Elder Moggaliputtatissa replied, ‘He is an analyst, great king.’ Thus the disciples of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One are analysts. For they repeat what the Teacher has taught analytically: the state of being one to be trained, and the suitability and unsuitability of cultivating things such as gladness and using things such as robes. Alternatively, they speak analytically with regard to the doctrines of eternalism and annihilation: by setting aside what should be set aside, such as the view ‘The self and the world are eternal’; by declaring that the destruction of lust, etc., is eternal; and by declaring the annihilation of bodily misconduct, etc., rooted in lust. But they do not, having dismissed the three types of questions such as those requiring a categorical answer, speak only of what requires an analytical answer. The circle (maṇḍalaṃ) of analysts, their assembly (samūho), is the vibhajjavādimaṇḍalaṃ. Alternatively, they also say that the assembly of the Blessed One, the Analyst, is the vibhajjavādimaṇḍalaṃ. Alternatively, because the Blessed One, having analyzed and not approached the two extremes of eternalism and annihilation, taught dependent origination, which is the middle path, he is an analyst; and because his disciples repeat his teaching, they too are analysts. The rest is as before.

Otaritvāti [M 2.0241] ogāhetvā, vibhajjavādī hutvāti attho. Na hi sayaṃ avibhajjavādī samāno vibhajjavādīnaṃ antare ṭhānamattena vibhajjavādimaṇḍalaṃ otiṇṇo nāma hoti. Ācariyehi avuttaviparītatthadīpanena te naabbhacikkhantena. Avijjā puññāneñjābhisaṅkhārānampi hetu paccayo hotīti vadanto, kathāvatthumhi paṭikkhitte puggalavādādike ca vadanto sakasamayaṃ vokkamati nāma, tathā avokkamantena. Parasamayaṃ dosāropanabyāpāravirahena anāyūhantena. “Idampi suttaṃ gahetabba”nti parasamayaṃ asampiṇḍentenāti keci vadanti. “Tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi, yathā tadevidaṃ viññāṇaṃ sandhāvati saṃsarati anañña”ntiādīni (ma. ni. 1.396) vadanto suttaṃ paṭibāhati nāma, tathā apaṭibāhantena. “Tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi, yathā yeme antarāyikā dhammā vuttā bhagavatā, te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāya (ma. ni. 1.234; pāci. 417, 418), supinante kato vītikkamo āpattikaro hotī”ti ca evamādiṃ vadanto vinayaṃ paṭilometi nāma, tabbipariyāyena taṃ anulomentena. Paṭilomento hi kammantaraṃ bhindanto, dhammatañca vilomento kuto kilesavinayaṃ anulometi. Sutte (dī. ni. 2.187 ādayo; a. ni. 4.180) vutte cattāro mahāpadese, aṭṭhakathāyañca vutte suttasuttānulomaācariyavādaattanomatimahāpadese olokentena. Tadolokanena hi sutte, vinaye ca santiṭṭhati nātidhāvati.

Having descended into (otaritvā) means having plunged into it; that is, having become an analyst. For one who is not himself an analyst does not become one who has descended into the circle of analysts merely by standing among them. By not falsely accusing the teachers by expounding a meaning contrary to what they have said. One who says that ignorance is the cause and condition for meritorious and imperturbable formations, or who speaks of the personalist doctrine and so on that are refuted in the Kathāvatthu, is said to deviate from his own system; thus, by not deviating. By not attacking another's system, being free from the business of imputing faults to it. Some say this means: by not conflating it with another's system, saying, 'This sutta too should be accepted.' One who says, 'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that runs on and transmigrates, not another,' is said to obstruct the Sutta; thus, by not obstructing it. One who says, 'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things said by the Blessed One to be obstructions are not able to be an obstruction for one who indulges in them,' and, 'A transgression committed in a dream entails an offense,' is said to go against the Vinaya; thus, by conforming to it, which is the opposite. For how can one who goes against it—who breaks a formal act and violates the nature of things—conform to the discipline for the removal of defilements? By examining the four great authorities mentioned in the Suttas, and the great authorities mentioned in the commentary, namely, the Sutta, what conforms to the Sutta, the teachers' tradition, and one's own opinion. For by examining these, one stands firm in the Sutta and the Vinaya and does not transgress.

Dhammanti [V 2.0227] paṭiccasamuppādapāḷiṃ. Atthanti tadatthaṃ. Hetu, hetuphalāni vā ayamettha hetu dhammo, idamettha hetuphalaṃ atthoti. Dhammanti vā dhammataṃ. Yathā eke “uppādā vā tathāgatānaṃ anuppādā vā tathāgatānaṃ ṭhitāva sā dhātū”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.20) suttapadassa atthaṃ micchā gāhentā “nicco paṭiccasamuppādo”ti paccayākāradhammaṃ micchā dīpenti, evaṃ adīpetvā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva attano phalaṃ pati kāraṇassa vavatthitasabhāvaṃ dīpentena. Yathā ca eke “anirodhaṃ anuppāda”ntiādinā paṭiccasamuppādassa atthaṃ micchā gāhenti, evaṃ gāhe akatvā vuttanayeneva aviparītaṃ atthaṃ saṅgāhentena. “Dukkhādīsu aññāṇaṃ avijjā”ti vuttamatthaṃ parivattetvā puna “pubbante aññāṇa”ntiādīhi (dha. sa. 1067) aparehipi pariyāyehi niddisantena[M 2.0242]. “Saṅkhārā iminā pariyāyena bhavoti vuccanti, taṇhā iminā pariyāyena upādāna”ntiādinā niddisantenāti ca vadanti. Pakatiyāti yathāvuttavidhānaṃ anāmasitvā kevalameva.

Dhamma means the Pāli of dependent origination. Attha means its meaning. Or, the cause and the fruits of the cause; herein, this cause is the Dhamma, and this fruit of the cause is the meaning. Or, Dhamma means specific conditionality. Just as some, wrongly grasping the meaning of the Sutta passage, 'Whether Tathāgatas arise or not, that element stands,' declare that 'dependent origination is permanent,' thus wrongly expounding the principle of conditionality; so, by not expounding it thus, but by expounding, in the way stated below, the fixed nature of a cause in relation to its own fruit. And just as some wrongly grasp the meaning of dependent origination with such phrases as 'non-cessation, non-arising'; so, by not grasping it thus, but by correctly grasping the unerring meaning in the way stated. By pointing out in other ways the meaning stated as 'Ignorance is unknowing regarding suffering, etc.,' varying it with such phrases as 'unknowing regarding the past,' etc. And some say: by pointing out, 'Formations in this sense are called becoming,' and 'Craving in this sense is called clinging,' etc. Pakatiyā means: simply, without touching upon the method stated.

Saccanti catusaccaṃ. Sattoti sattasuññatāti vadanti, sattasuññesu pana saṅkhāresu sattavohāro, sattatthakiccasiddhi ca. Paccayākārameva cāti paccayākāro eva ca, ma-kāro padasandhikaro. Paccayadhammānaṃ attanoyeva phalassa paccayabhāvo paṭiccasamuppādoti attho.

Sacca means the four truths. Satta: some say this means the emptiness of a being. But in formations that are empty of a being, there is the conventional expression 'a being' and the accomplishment of the function of a being. And Paccayākārameva ca is paccayākāro eva ca; the letter 'm' is for euphonic junction. The meaning is that dependent origination is the state of conditioning phenomena being a condition for their own fruit.

Tasmāti vuttanayena atthavaṇṇanāya kātabbattā, dukkarattā ca patiṭṭhaṃ nādhigacchāmīti yattha ṭhitassa vaṇṇanā sukarā hoti, tassā patiṭṭhābhūtaṃ taṃ nayaṃ attanoyeva ñāṇabalena nādhigacchāmīti attho. Nissayaṃ pana ācikkhanto “sāsanaṃ panida”ntiādimāha. Idha sāsananti pāḷidhammamāha, paṭiccasamuppādameva vā. So hi anulomapaṭilomādinānādesanānayapaṭimaṇḍito abbocchinno ajjāpi pavattatīti nissayo hoti. Tadaṭṭhakathāsaṅkhāto ca pubbācariyamaggo. “Taṃ suṇātha samāhitā”ti ādarajanane, ussāhane ca kiṃ payojananti ce, taṃ dassento āha “vuttañheta”ntiādi. Aṭṭhi katvāti atthaṃ katvā. Yathā vā na nassati, evaṃ aṭṭhigataṃ viya karonto aṭṭhiṃ katvā. Pubbakālato aparakāle bhavaṃ pubbāpariyaṃ. Visesanti paṭhamārambhato pabhuti khaṇe khaṇe ñāṇavisesaṃ, kilesakkhayavisesañca labhatīti attho.

Therefore: because the explanation of the meaning has to be made in the way stated, and because it is difficult. I do not find a footing: the meaning is, I do not by the power of my own knowledge find that method which constitutes the footing, standing upon which the explanation becomes easy. But indicating his resort, he said, 'But this Dispensation,' etc. Here, by 'Dispensation' he refers to the Pāli Dhamma, or to dependent origination itself. For this, adorned with the various methods of teaching such as the forward and reverse orders, continues uninterrupted even today; thus it is a resort. And so is the path of the ancient teachers, which is reckoned as its commentary. If it is asked what is the purpose of the words, 'Listen to it attentively,' which are for generating respect and rousing energy, he said, 'For it is said,' etc., to show that. Having made it a core concern (aṭṭhi katvā) means having made it one's goal. Or, making it as if it were established in the bone so that it is not lost. Before and after (pubbāpariyaṃ): what occurs in a later time from an earlier time. Distinction: the meaning is that from the very beginning, moment by moment, one obtains a distinction in knowledge and the distinction of the destruction of the defilements.

582. Desanābhedatoti desanāvisesato. Atthato, lakkhaṇādito, ekavidhādito ca atthalakkhaṇekavidhādito[V 2.0228]. Aṅgānañca vavatthānāti avijjādīnaṃ dvādasannaṃ aṅgānaṃ vavatthānadassanato.

582. By the divisions in the teaching means by the distinctions in the teaching. By way of meaning, characteristic, etc., and by way of being onefold, etc., means by way of meaning, characteristic, being onefold, etc. And by the determination of the factors means by determining the twelve factors beginning with ignorance.

Kammavipākakilesavaṭṭānaṃ mūlakāraṇattā, ādito vuttattā ca avijjā paṭiccasamuppādassa mūlaṃ. Tattha valliyā mūle diṭṭhe tato pabhuti valliharaṇaṃ viya paṭiccasamuppādassa mūle diṭṭhe tato pabhuti paṭiccasamuppādadesanāti upamāsaṃsandanā na kātabbā. Na hi bhagavato idameva diṭṭhaṃ, idaṃ adiṭṭhanti vibhajanīyaṃ atthi sabbassa diṭṭhattā. Mūlato pabhuti pana valliharaṇaṃ viya mūlato pabhuti paṭiccasamuppādadesanā katāti idamettha sāmaññaṃ [M 2.0243] adhippetaṃ, bodhaneyyajjhāsayavasena vā bodhetabbabhāvena mūlādidassanasāmaññaṃ yojetabbaṃ.

Because it is the root cause of the round of kamma, results, and defilements, and because it is stated at the beginning, ignorance is the root of dependent origination. Here, the simile should not be applied thus: 'Just as when the root of a creeper is seen, one takes the creeper starting from there, so when the root of dependent origination is seen, the teaching of dependent origination proceeds from there.' For there is no distinction for the Blessed One that 'this was seen, this was not seen,' since everything has been seen by him. Rather, this is the general point intended here: just as one takes a creeper starting from its root, so the teaching of dependent origination was given starting from its root. Or else the general point of seeing the root, etc., should be connected with the fact that it has to be taught according to the disposition of the person to be taught.

Tassāti –

Of that:

“Sa kho so, bhikkhave, kumāro vuddhimanvāya indriyānaṃ paripākamanvāya pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito…pe… rajanīyehi. So cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā piyarūpe rūpe sārajjati, appiyarūpe rūpe byāpajjati, anupaṭṭhitakāyasati ca viharati parittacetaso, tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti, yatthassa te pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti. So evaṃ anurodhavirodhaṃ samāpanno yaṃ kiñci vedanaṃ vedeti sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā, so taṃ vedanaṃ abhinandati abhivadati, ajjhosāya tiṭṭhatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.408) –

“Bhikkhus, as that boy grows up and his faculties mature, he is provided and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure … that are enticing. Having seen a form with the eye, he becomes attached to agreeable forms and is repelled by disagreeable forms. He dwells with mindfulness of the body unestablished and with a limited mind, and he does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder. Thus, having fallen into favouring and opposing, whatever feeling he feels—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he delights in that feeling, welcomes it, and remains holding to it.”

Evaṃ vuttassa. Evaṃ sotadvārādīsupi. Tassa abhinandatoti sappītikataṇhāya abhimukhabhāvena nandato. Abhivadatoti “aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha”nti vacībhedakaraṇapavattāya balavataṇhāya “ahaṃ, mamā”ti abhivadato. Tato balavatiyā mocetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya ajjhosāya tiṭṭhato. Tatopi balavatī pana upādānabhūtā taṇhā nandī. Ettha ca abhinandanādinā taṇhā vuttā, nandivacanena tappaccayaṃ upādānaṃ catubbidhampi nanditātadavippayogatāhi, taṇhādiṭṭhābhinandanabhāvehi cāti veditabbaṃ.

The same applies to the ear-door and so on. ‘He delights in it’ means: he rejoices with a craving accompanied by joy, by way of turning towards it. ‘He welcomes it’ means: with a strong craving that gives rise to verbal expressions such as, ‘Oh, bliss! Oh, bliss!’, he asserts ‘I’ and ‘mine.’ ‘He remains holding to it’ means: with a stronger craving, being unable to get free, he remains engrossed. But stronger even than this is delight (nandī), which is craving that has become clinging. Here, by ‘delighting,’ etc., craving is expressed. By the word ‘delight,’ the fourfold clinging dependent on it should be understood, both through its nature as delight and its inseparability, and through its nature as delighting in craving and views.

Jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇantiādikañca tattheva mahātaṇhāsaṅkhayasutte vuttaṃ.

“With birth as condition, aging and death,” and so on, is stated in that same Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta.

Vipākavaṭṭabhūte [V 2.0229] paṭisandhipavattiphassādike kammasamuṭṭhānañca ojaṃ sandhāya “cattāro āhārā taṇhānidānā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vaṭṭūpathambhakā pana itarepi āhārā taṇhāpabhave tasmiṃ avijjamāne na vijjantīti “taṇhānidānā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭanti.

With reference to contact and so on, which belong to the round of results during rebirth-linking and ongoing life, and to the nutritive essence that arises from kamma, it is said: “The four nutriments have craving as their source,” etc. But since the other nutriments, which support the round, also do not exist when that which is produced by craving is non-existent, it is proper to say that they “have craving as their source.”

583. Tato [M 2.0244] tatoti catubbidhāsu desanāsu tato tato desanato. Ñāyappaṭivedhāya saṃvattatīti ñāyoti maggo, so eva vā paṭiccasamuppādo “ariyo cassa ñāyo paññāya sudiṭṭho hotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.41; 5.1024) vacanato. Sayameva hi so samantabhaddakattā tathā tathā paṭivijjhitabbattā tāya tāya desanāya attano paṭivedhāya saṃvattati. Catubbidhagambhīrabhāvappattiyāti dhammatthadesanāpaṭivedhagambhīresu patiṭṭhādhigamanena patiṭṭhitattāti attho.

583. The phrase ‘From this and that’ means: from this and that teaching in the fourfold expositions. ‘It leads to the penetration of the method’: Here, ‘method’ (ñāya) is the Noble Path, or it is dependent origination itself, because of the statement: “And this noble method has been well seen by him with wisdom.” For, being altogether auspicious and needing to be penetrated in such and such a way, it itself, by means of this and that teaching, conduces to the penetration of itself. ‘Through the attainment of the fourfold profundity’ means: because of being established by gaining a footing in the profundities of the Dhamma, the meaning, the exposition, and the penetration.

Samantabhaddakatā, desanāvilāsappatti ca catunnampi desanānaṃ samānaṃ kāraṇanti visesakāraṇaṃ vattukāmo āha “visesato”ti. Assāti assa bhagavato desanā, assa vā paṭiccasamuppādassa desanāti yojetabbaṃ. Pavattikāraṇavibhāgo avibhattasabhāvā avijjādayova, kāraṇanti vā gahitānaṃ pakatiādīnaṃ, avijjādīnañca akāraṇatā, kāraṇatā ca. Tattha sammūḷhā keci akāraṇaṃ kāraṇanti gaṇhanti, keci na kiñci kāraṇaṃ bujjhantīti tesaṃ yathāsakehi anurūpehi kāraṇehi saṅkhārādipavattisandassanatthaṃ, saṃsārappavattisandassanatthanti attho. Pavattiādīnavapaṭicchādikā avijjā ādi, tato saṅkhārā uppajjanti, tato viññāṇanti evaṃ pavattiyā uppattikkamasandassanatthaṃ, gabbhaseyyakādivasena vā tattha tattha bhave attabhāvassa uppajjanānupubbisandassanatthañca anulomadesanā pavattāti. Itarāsaṃ tadatthatāsambhavepi na tāsaṃ tadatthameva pavatti atthantarasabbhāvato. Ayaṃ pana tadatthā evāti etissā tadatthatā vuttā.

Since being altogether auspicious and the attainment of grace in exposition are common reasons for all four expositions, wishing to state the specific reason, the author said ‘especially.’ ‘Of this’ should be construed as ‘of this Blessed One’s exposition’ or ‘of this exposition of dependent origination.’ The analysis of the cause of occurrence is simply ignorance and so on, whose nature is unanalyzed; or, it is the non-causality of primordial nature and so on, which are taken as the cause, and the causality of ignorance and so on. In this regard, some who are deluded take a non-cause as the cause, while others do not understand any cause at all; therefore, it is for showing them the occurrence of formations, etc., from their own suitable causes, that is, for showing the occurrence of saṃsāra. Ignorance, which conceals the danger of occurrence, is the beginning; from that, formations arise; from that, consciousness arises. Thus, the forward-order exposition is given to show the sequence of the arising of the process, or to show the succession of the arising of individual existence in various states of being, such as lying in the womb. Although the other expositions could have this purpose, their occurrence is not for this purpose alone, as they have other meanings. This one, however, has only this purpose; thus its having this purpose is stated.

Anuvilokayato yo sambodhito pubbabhāge taṃtaṃpaccayuppannāvabodhasaṅkhāto pubbabhāgapaṭivedho pavatto, tadanusārena tadanugamena jarāmaraṇādikassa jātiādikāraṇaṃ yaṃ adhigataṃ, tassa sandassanatthaṃ ayaṃ paṭilomadesanā pavattā. Anuvilokayato paṭilomadesanā pavattāti vā sambandho. Desentopi hi bhagavā kicchāpannaṃ lokaṃ anuviloketvā pubbabhāga…pe… sandassanatthaṃ desesīti. Āhārataṇhādayo paccuppannaddhā, saṅkhārāvijjā atītaddhāti iminā adhippāyenāha [V 2.0230] “yāva atītaṃ addhānaṃ atiharitvā”ti. Āhārā vā taṇhāya pabhāvetabbā anāgato addhā, taṇhādayo paccuppanno[M 2.0245], saṅkhārāvijjā atītoti. Paccakkhaṃ pana phalaṃ dassetvā tannidānadassanavasena phalakāraṇaparamparadassanaṃ yujjatīti āhārā purimataṇhāya uppāditā paccuppanno addhā, taṇhādayo atīto, saṅkhārāvijjā tatopi atītataro saṃsārassa anādibhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttoti. Yāva atītaddhānanti yāva atītataraṃ addhānanti attho yuttoti. Āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbattiāhārakā vā cattāro āhārā “āhāretītāhaṃ na vadāmi…pe… evaṃ pana maṃ avadantaṃ yo evaṃ puccheyya ‘kissa nu kho, bhante, viññāṇāhāro’ti, esa kallo pañho, tatra kallaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ, viññāṇāhāro āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbattiyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.12) vacanato, taṃsampayuttattā phassacetanānaṃ, tappavattihetuttā ca kabaḷīkārāhārassa. Tena hi upatthambhitarūpakāyassa, tañca icchantassa kāmaviññāṇāyūhanaṃ hoti. Bhojanañhi saddhādīnaṃ, rāgādīnañca upanissayoti vuttaṃ. Tasmā te kammavaṭṭasaṅgahitā āhārā paccuppanno addhāti imasmiṃ pariyāye purimoyeva attho yutto.

For one who reviews, that penetration of the preliminary stage occurred, which is called the understanding of what has arisen from this or that condition in the preliminary stage of enlightenment. This reverse-order exposition is given to show the cause that was understood in accordance with that, namely, that birth and so on is the cause of aging and death and so on. Or the connection is: the reverse-order exposition is given for one who reviews. Indeed, when teaching, the Blessed One, having reviewed the world that has fallen into suffering, taught in accordance with the penetration of the preliminary stage for the purpose of clearly showing the cause—understood by Himself—of this and that suffering, such as aging and death. With the intention that nutriment, craving, etc., are the present time, and formations and ignorance are the past time, it is said, ‘as far as traversing the past time.’ Alternatively, nutriments to be generated by craving are the future time; craving, etc., are the present; and formations and ignorance are the past. But since it is logical to show the manifest result and then, by showing its source, to show the series of result and cause, it is said that nutriments produced by a former craving are the present time; craving, etc., are the past; and formations and ignorance are a still more remote past, in order to show the beginningless nature of saṃsāra. Thus the meaning ‘as far as the past time’ is suitably ‘as far as the more remote past time.’ Alternatively, the four nutriments are for renewed existence in the future, according to the text: ‘I do not say… but if someone were to ask me, who does not speak thus, “Venerable sir, for what is consciousness-nutriment a nutriment?” that would be a proper question. Therein, the proper answer is: “Consciousness-nutriment is for the arising of a new existence in the future”’ (SN 12.12). This is also because of the association of contact and volition with it, and because physical nutriment is the cause for its occurrence. For, in one whose physical body is sustained by that physical nutriment, and who desires it, an accumulation of kamma-consciousness occurs. For it is said that food is a decisive support condition for faith, etc., and for lust, etc. Therefore, in this exposition, since those nutriments are included in the round of kamma and are the present time, the former meaning is the suitable one.

Atītaddhato pabhuti “iti kho, bhikkhave, avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.2) atīte, tato parañca hetuphalapaṭipāṭiṃ paccakkhabhūtānaṃ āhārānaṃ nidānadassanavasena ārohitvā nivattanena vinā abujjhantānaṃ taṃsandassanatthaṃ sā ayaṃ desanā pavattāti attho. Anāgataddhahetusamuṭṭhānato pabhutīti anāgatassa bhavassa hetubhūtānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppattito paṭṭhāya. Anāgataddhasandassanatthanti anāgataddhuno appaṭivijjhantānaṃ apassantānaṃ paccakkhaṃ paccuppannaṃ hetuṃ dassetvā hetuphalaparamparāya tassa sandassanatthanti attho. Ettha ca ādito paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānā, pariyosānato ca paṭṭhāya yāva ādi pavattā desanā dvādasaṅgā, tato eva tisandhi catusaṅkhepā. Majjhato paṭṭhāya yāva ādi pavattā desanā aṭṭhaṅgā dvisandhi tisaṅkhepā. Majjhato pana paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānā pavattā desanā chaḷaṅgā dvisandhi tisaṅkhepā. “Saṃyojaniyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu assādānupassino viharato taṇhā pavaḍḍhati, taṇhāpaccayā upādāna”ntiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.53, 57) majjhato paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānā pavattā desanā ekasandhi dvisaṅkhepā. Evaṃ ayaṃ anekaṅgā eva [M 2.0246] paṭiccasamuppādadesanā āgatā. Ekaṅgavasenāpi ca paṭiccasamuppādadesanā labbhateva. Yathāha –

The meaning is this: this exposition is given for the purpose of clearly showing the sequence of cause and effect to those who cannot understand it, having traced it from the past time onwards—beginning with, ‘Thus, bhikkhus, with ignorance as condition, formations arise,’ and so on, in the past and thereafter—by way of showing the cause of manifest nutriments, without reversal. Beginning from the arising of causes for the future time means starting from the arising of phenomena that are causes for future existence. For the purpose of showing the future time means that for those who do not penetrate or see the future time, it is for the purpose of showing it to them by showing the manifest present cause and the series of cause and effect. Herein, the exposition that proceeds from the beginning to the end, and from the end back to the beginning, has twelve factors, and for that very reason, three connections and four sections. The exposition that proceeds from the middle back to the beginning has eight factors, two connections, and three sections. Furthermore, the exposition that proceeds from the middle to the end has six factors, two connections, and three sections. With the text beginning, ‘Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that are objects of the fetters, craving increases; with craving as condition, clinging arises,’ and so on, the exposition that proceeds from the middle to the end has one connection and two sections. Thus this exposition of dependent origination has come down with many factors indeed. And an exposition of dependent origination is certainly obtained also by way of a single factor. As it is said:

“Tatra, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako paṭiccasamuppādaṃyeva sādhukaṃ yoniso manasi [V 2.0231] karoti ‘iti imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti, imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjati. Imasmiṃ asati idaṃ na hoti, imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhatī’ti. Sukhavedaniyaṃ, bhikkhave, phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhavedanā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.62) –

“Here, bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple attends carefully and wisely to dependent origination itself thus: ‘When this is, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this is not, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.’ Bhikkhus, dependent on a contact to be felt as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises.”

Ādi. Ettha hi “phassapaccayā”ti ettako eva paṭiccasamuppādo vutto. Tenetaṃ viññāyati “ekaṅgapaṭiccasamuppādo”ti.

And so on. For in this sutta only this much of dependent origination is stated: ‘with contact as condition.’ Therefore this is known as ‘single-factored dependent origination.’”

Tattha imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hotīti imasmiṃ avijjādike paccaye sati idaṃ saṅkhārādikaṃ phalaṃ hoti. Imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjatīti imassa avijjādikassa paccayassa uppādā idaṃ saṅkhārādikaṃ phalaṃ uppajjatīti attho.
