Imasmiṃ asati idaṃ na hoti, imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhatīti avijjādīnaṃ abhāve saṅkhārādīnaṃ abhāvassa, avijjādīnaṃ nirodhā saṅkhārādīnaṃ nirodhassa ca vacanena purimasmiṃ paccayalakkhaṇe niyamo dassito hoti “imasmiṃ sati eva, na asati, imassa uppādā eva, na nirodhā”ti. Tenetaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ antogadhaniyamaṃ idha paṭiccasamuppādassa vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Herein, 'When this exists, that comes to be' means: when this condition, such as ignorance, exists, this result, such as formations, comes to be. 'With the arising of this, that arises' means: with the arising of this condition, such as ignorance, this result, such as formations, arises. This is the meaning. By the statement, 'When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases,' which speaks of the absence of formations, etc., in the absence of ignorance, etc., and of the cessation of formations, etc., with the cessation of ignorance, etc., a rule is shown concerning the former characteristic of a condition, namely: 'only when this exists, not when it does not exist; only with the arising of this, not with its cessation.' Therefore it should be understood that this characteristic, which includes a rule, is stated here for dependent origination.

Nirodhoti ca avijjādīnaṃ virāgādhigamena āyatiṃ anuppādo appavatti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “avijjāyatveva asesavirāganirodhā”tiādi (mahāva. 1; udā. 3). Nirodhavirodhī ca uppādo, yena so uppādavirodhibhāvena vutto “imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhatī”ti, tenetaṃ dasseti “anirodho uppādo nāma, so cettha atthibhāvotipi vuccatī”ti. “Imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hotī”ti idameva hi lakkhaṇaṃ pariyāyantarena “imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjatī”ti vadantena parena purimaṃ visesitaṃ hoti, tasmā na dharamānataṃyeva sandhāya “imasmiṃ satī”ti vuttaṃ, atha kho maggena aniruddhabhāvañcāti viññāyati. Yasmā ca “imasmiṃ asati idaṃ na hoti, imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhatī”ti (udā. 2) dvidhāpi uddiṭṭhalakkhaṇassa nirodhassa niddesaṃ vadantena “avijjāyatveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho”tiādinā (mahāva. 1; udā. 3) nirodho [M 2.0247] eva vutto, tasmā natthibhāvopi nirodho evāti natthibhāvaviruddho atthibhāvo anirodhoti dassitaṃ hoti. Tena anirodhasaṅkhātena atthibhāvena uppādaṃ viseseti. Tato na idha attalābhamattaṃ uppādoti adhippeto, atha kho anirodhasaṅkhāto atthibhāvo cāti ayamattho vibhāvitoti [V 2.0232] evametaṃ lakkhaṇadvayavacanaṃ aññamaññaṃ visesanavisesitabbabhāvena sātthakanti veditabbaṃ.

And cessation is the future non-arising and non-occurrence of ignorance, etc., through the attainment of dispassion. For it is said: 'With the utter fading away and cessation of that very ignorance…' and so on. And arising is the opposite of cessation, by which reason that cessation is spoken of as being the opposite of arising in the statement 'with the cessation of this, that ceases.' By this it is shown that 'non-cessation is called arising, and here it is also called existence.' For this very characteristic, 'When this exists, that comes to be,' is specified by the latter statement, 'With the arising of this, that arises,' which says the same thing in another way. Therefore, it is understood that 'when this exists' is not said merely with reference to the state of being present, but also to the state of not having been eradicated by the path. And since, when explaining the characteristic of cessation stated in two ways as 'When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases,' it is only cessation that is spoken of with the words 'with the utter fading away and cessation of that very ignorance, formations cease,' etc., therefore non-existence is also just cessation. Thus it is shown that existence, the opposite of non-existence, is non-cessation. He thereby specifies arising by means of existence, which is designated as non-cessation. Hence, what is intended here by 'arising' is not the mere acquisition of an individual existence, but also existence designated as non-cessation. This meaning is thus clarified. In this way, it should be understood that these two statements of the characteristics are meaningful in that they mutually specify and are specified by each other.

Ko panāyaṃ anirodho nāma, yo atthibhāvo, uppādoti ca vuccatīti? Appahīnabhāvo, anibbattitaphalatāppahīnārahatāhi phaluppādanārahatā ca. Ye tehi pahātabbā akusalā dhammā, tesaṃ ariyamaggena asamugghātitabhāvo, ye pana na pahātabbā kusalābyākatā dhammā, yāni tesu saṃyojanāni akhīṇāsavānaṃ, tesaṃ aparikkhīṇatā ca. Asamugghātitānusayatāya hi sasaṃyojanākhandhappavatti paṭiccasamuppādo. Tathā hi vuttaṃ –

But what is this 'non-cessation,' which is called 'existence' and 'arising'? It is the state of non-abandonment, and the fitness to produce a result owing to the fact that its fruit has not been produced and its fitness has not been abandoned. It is the state of the unwholesome states that are to be abandoned not having been uprooted by the noble path; and, in the case of wholesome and indeterminate states that are not to be abandoned, it is the non-exhaustion of the fetters in them for one whose taints are not destroyed. For dependent origination is the occurrence of the aggregates together with the fetters because the underlying tendencies have not been uprooted. For thus it has been said:

“Yāya ca, bhikkhave, avijjāya nivutassa bālassa, yāya ca taṇhāya sampayuttassa ayaṃ kāyo samudāgato, sā ceva avijjā bālassa appahīnā, sā ca taṇhā aparikkhīṇā. Taṃ kissa hetu? Na, bhikkhave, bālo acari brahmacariyaṃ sammā dukkhakkhayāya, tasmā bālo kāyassa bhedā kāyūpago hoti, so kāyūpago samāno na parimuccati jātiyā jarāmaraṇenā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.19) –

'Bhikkhus, this body has come to be for the fool who is enveloped by that ignorance and yoked to that craving. That very ignorance has not been abandoned by the fool, and that craving has not been exhausted. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, the fool has not lived the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, with the breakup of the body, the fool is bound for a body. Being bound for a body, he is not freed from birth, aging, and death.'

Ādi. Khīṇasaṃyojanānaṃ pana avijjāya abhāvato saṅkhārānaṃ, taṇhupādānānaṃ abhāvato upādānabhavānaṃ na sambhavoti vaṭṭassa upacchedo paññāyati. Tenevāha –

And so on. But for those whose fetters are destroyed, since there is no ignorance, there is no arising of formations; and since there is no craving and clinging, there is no arising of clinging and becoming. Thus the cutting off of the round is discerned. Therefore he said:

“Channantveva, phagguna, phassāyatanānaṃ asesavirāganirodhā phassanirodho, phassanirodhā vedanānirodho”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.12) –

'Phagguna, with the utter fading away and cessation of the six bases for contact themselves, there is the cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling.'

Ādi. Na hi aggamaggādhigamato uddhaṃ yāva parinibbānā saḷāyatanādīnaṃ appavatti, atha kho natthitā, nirodhasaddavacanīyatā, khīṇasaṃyojanatāti nirodho vutto. Apica cirakatampi kammaṃ anibbattitaphalatāya, appahīnārahatāya ca phalārahaṃ santaṃ eva nāma hoti, na nibbattitaphalaṃ, nāpi [M 2.0248] pahīnārahanti phaluppattipaccayānaṃ avijjāsaṅkhārādīnaṃ vuttanayena phalārahabhāvo anirodhoti veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ aniruddhabhāveneva hi yena vinā phalaṃ na sambhavati, taṃ kāraṇaṃ atītādipi “imasmiṃ satī”ti iminā vacanena vuttaṃ. Tato eva ca avusitabrahmacariyassa appavattidhammataṃ anāpanno paccayuppādo kālabhedaṃ anāmasitvā anivattitāya [V 2.0233] eva “imassuppādā”ti vutto. Atha vā avasesapaccayasamavāye avijjamānassāpi vijjamānassa viya pageva vijjamānassa yā phaluppattiabhimukhatā, sā “imassuppādā”ti vuttā. Tadā hi tato phalaṃ uppajjatīti tadavatthaṃ kāraṇaṃ phalassa uppādanabhāvena upaṭṭhitaṃ uppatitaṃ nāma hoti, na vijjamānampi atadavatthanti tadavatthatā uppādoti veditabbā.

And so on. For from the attainment of the highest path up to parinibbāna, it is not that the six sense bases, etc., do not occur; rather, 'cessation' is spoken of as non-existence, as being describable by the word 'cessation,' and as the destruction of the fetters. Moreover, a kamma, even one done long ago, being fit to fruit because its fruit has not been produced and its fitness has not been abandoned, is indeed called 'existing'; a kamma whose fruit has been produced is not, nor is one whose fitness has been abandoned. Thus, in the way stated for ignorance, formations, etc., which are conditions for the production of fruit, their state of being fit to fruit should be understood as 'non-cessation'. Indeed, it is precisely by reason of this state of non-cessation that a cause, without which a fruit cannot arise, even if it is past, etc., is spoken of by the phrase 'when this exists.' For that very reason, in the case of one who has not lived the holy life, the arising of a condition, not having reached a state of non-occurrence, is spoken of as 'with the arising of this,' without regard to the distinction of time, precisely because it has not turned back. Alternatively, when the remaining conditions have come together, that readiness for the production of fruit—which belongs even to a non-existent cause as if it were existent, and how much more so to an existent one—is called 'with the arising of this.' For then the fruit arises from it; therefore, a cause that is in that state, being present as the producer of the fruit, is called 'arisen.' Even if it exists, if it is not in that state, it is not so considered. Therefore, that very state should be understood as 'arising'.

Tattha “satī”ti iminā vijjamānatāmattena paccayabhāvaṃ vadanto abyāpārataṃ paṭiccasamuppādassa dasseti. Uppādāti uppattidhammataṃ, asabbakālabhāvitaṃ, phaluppattiabhimukhatañca dīpento aniccataṃ paṭiccasamuppādassa dasseti. “Sati, na asati, uppādā, na nirodhā”ti pana hetuatthehi bhummanissakkavacanehi samatthitaṃ nidānasamudayajātipabhavabhāvaṃ paṭiccasamuppādassa dasseti. Hetuatthatā cettha bhummavacane yassa bhāvena tadavinābhāviphalassa bhāvo lakkhīyati, tattha pavattiyā veditabbā, yathā adhanānaṃ dhane ananuppadīyamāne dāliddiyaṃ vepullamagamāsi (dī. ni. 3.91), nipphanne sasse subhikkhaṃ jāyatīti ca. Nissakkavacanassāpi hetuatthatā phalassa pabhave pakatiyañca pavattiyā, yathā “kalalā hoti abbudaṃ, abbudā jāyate pesī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.235; kathā. 692), “himavatā gaṅgā pabhavati, siṅgato saro jāyatī”ti ca. Avijjādibhāvena ca tadavinābhāvisaṅkhārādibhāvo lakkhīyati, avijjādīhi ca saṅkhārādayo pabhavanti, pakarīyanti cāti tesaṃ pabhavo, pakati ca, tasmā tadatthadīpanatthaṃ “imasmiṃ sati imassuppādā”ti hetuatthā bhummanissakkaniddesā katā.

Herein, by the word 'exists,' stating conditionality by way of mere presence, he shows the non-active nature of dependent origination. By the word 'arises,' by indicating the nature of arising, its not existing at all times, and its orientation towards the production of a fruit, he shows the impermanence of dependent origination. But by 'exists, not does not exist; from the arising, not from the cessation,' which is established by the locative and ablative cases in the sense of cause, he shows the nature of dependent origination as source, origin, birth, and production. Herein, the sense of cause in the locative case should be understood as applying where the existence of a fruit that is an invariable consequent of something is observed through the existence of that thing, as in: 'When wealth is not given to the poor, poverty increases,' and 'When the crop is harvested, there is abundance.' The sense of cause in the ablative case also applies to the production and nature of the fruit, as in: 'From the embryo comes the 'abbuda'; from the 'abbuda' is born the fleshy piece,' and 'The Ganges originates from the Himalayas; a sound is born from a horn.' And by the existence of ignorance, etc., the existence of formations, etc., which are its invariable consequents, is observed. And from ignorance, etc., formations, etc., originate and are produced; thus that is their production and nature. Therefore, to clarify that meaning, the locative and ablative indications in the sense of cause have been made as 'When this exists; from the arising of this...'

Yasmā cettha “imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti, imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjatī”ti saṅkhepena uddiṭṭhassa paṭiccasamuppādassa “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādiko niddeso, tasmā yathāvutto atthibhāvo, uppādo ca tesaṃ [M 2.0249] tesaṃ paccayuppannadhammānaṃ paccayabhāvoti viññāyati. Na hi aniruddhatāsaṅkhātaṃ atthibhāvaṃ, uppādañca anivattasabhāvatāsaṅkhātaṃ, udayāvatthatāsaṅkhātaṃ vā “satiyeva, na asati, uppādā eva, na nirodhā”ti antogadhaniyamehi vacanehi pakāsitaṃ muñcitvā añño paccayabhāvo nāma atthi, tasmā yathāvutto atthibhāvo, uppādo ca paccayabhāvoti veditabbo. Yepi hi paṭṭhāne āgatā hetuādayo catuvīsati paccayā, tepi etasseva paccayabhāvassa visesāti veditabbā. Tathā yvāyaṃ mūlahetunidānasambhavapabhavādipariyāyehi[V 2.0234], uppādaṭṭhiti pavattaṭṭhiti nimittaṭṭhiti āyūhanaṭṭhiti saṃyogaṭṭhiti palibodhaṭṭhitītiādipariyāyehi ca pakāsito kāraṇattho, sopi ettheva antogadhoti daṭṭhabbo.

And since here the exposition of dependent origination, which was stated in brief as 'When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises,' begins 'With ignorance as condition, formations come to be,' etc., therefore it is understood that the aforesaid existence and arising constitute the conditionality of the respective conditionally arisen phenomena. For there is no other conditionality apart from that revealed by the words containing an invariable rule, 'only when it exists, not when it does not exist; only from the arising, not from the cessation'—namely, existence designated as non-cessation, and arising designated as the state of not having turned back or as the state of being in the moment of arising. Therefore it should be understood that the aforesaid existence and arising are conditionality. For even the twenty-four conditions—root-condition, etc.—that come in the Paṭṭhāna should be understood as specific instances of this same conditionality. Likewise, the meaning of 'cause' explained by such synonyms as root, cause, origin, source, production, etc., and by such synonyms as the state of arising, the state of continuance, the state of being a sign, the state of accumulation, the state of connection, the state of obstruction, etc.—this too should be seen as included herein.

584. Mūlakāraṇasaddaṃ apekkhitvā na akāraṇanti napuṃsakaniddeso, akāraṇāti attho. Akāraṇaṃ yadi siyā, suttaṃ paṭibāhitaṃ siyāti dassento “āsavasamudayā”ti suttaṃ āharati. Pariyāyo kāraṇaṃ. Vaṭṭakathāya sīsabhāvo vaṭṭahetuno kammassāpi hetubhāvo. Tattha bhavataṇhāyapi hetubhūtā avijjā, tāya paṭicchāditādīnave bhave taṇhāya uppajjanato avijjā visesena sīsabhūtāti “mūlakāraṇa”nti vuttā.

584. With reference to the word 'root cause,' the neuter designation is used to show that it is not a non-cause; the meaning is that it is not without a cause. To show that if it were without a cause, the sutta would be contradicted, he adduces the sutta passage 'from the arising of the taints.' A synonym for cause is condition. In the discourse on the round, its being the head is the state of being a cause even for kamma, which is the cause of the round. Therein, ignorance is the cause even for craving for existence, for because craving arises for an existence whose dangers are concealed by that ignorance, ignorance is specifically what has become the head; thus it is called the 'root cause'.

Purimāya koṭiyā apaññāyamānāya uppādavirahato niccataṃ gaṇheyyāti āha “evaṃ cetaṃ, bhikkhave, vuccatī”tiādi. Tena ito pubbe uppannapubbatā natthīti apaññāyanato purimakoṭiapaññāyanaṃ vuttanti imamatthaṃ dasseti.

He said, 'And so, bhikkhus, it is said,' etc., because when the first point is not discerned, one might, from the absence of an origin, grasp the idea of permanence. By this he shows the following meaning: the non-discernment of a first point is stated because a previous state of having arisen before this is not discerned.

585. Avijjātaṇhāhetukkamena phalesu vattabbesu “sugatiduggatigāmino”ti vacanaṃ saddalakkhaṇāvirodhanatthaṃ. Pūjitassa hi dvande pubbanipāto. Savarā kira maṃsassa aṭṭhinā alagganatthaṃ punappunaṃ tāpetvā koṭṭetvā uṇhodakaṃ pāyetvā virittaṃ sūnaṃ aṭṭhito muttamaṃsaṃ gāviṃ mārenti. Tenāha “aggisantāpā”tiādi. Tattha yathā vajjhagāvī ca avijjābhibhūtatāya yathāvuttaṃ uṇhodakapānaṃ ārabhati, evaṃ puthujjano yathāvuttaṃ duggatigāmikammaṃ. Yathā pana sā uṇhodakapāne ādīnavaṃ disvā taṇhāvasena sītudakapānaṃ ārabhati, evaṃ puthujjano avijjāya nātibalavabhāvato duggatigāmikamme ādīnavaṃ disvā taṇhāvasena [M 2.0250] sugatigāmikammaṃ ārabhati. Dukkhe hi avijjaṃ taṇhā anuvattati, sukhe taṇhaṃ avijjāti.

585. When the fruits should be stated according to the sequence of their causes—ignorance and craving—the statement 'leading to good and bad destinations' is for the purpose of not contradicting a grammatical rule. For in a dvandva compound, the honored term is placed first. It is said that the Savaras, in order to prevent the flesh from sticking to the bone, repeatedly heat and pound it, make the cow drink hot water, and then kill the purged and swollen cow, its flesh freed from the bone. Therefore, he said, 'scorched by fire,' etc. In this context, just as the cow to be slaughtered, being overwhelmed by ignorance, undertakes the drinking of hot water as described, so the worldling undertakes action leading to a bad destination as described. But just as that cow, seeing the danger in drinking hot water, undertakes the drinking of cold water through the power of craving, so the worldling, because ignorance is not too strong, sees the danger in action leading to a bad destination and undertakes action leading to a good destination through the power of craving. For in the case of suffering, craving follows ignorance; in the case of happiness, ignorance follows craving.

586. Katthaci sutte. Ekadhammamūlikaṃ desananti avijjātaṇhāsu ekoyeva dhammo mūlaṃ etissāti ekadhammamūlikā, taṃ, tattha ekaṃ eva dhammaṃ mūlaṃ katvā paṭiccasamuppādadesanaṃ desetīti attho. Upanisīdati phalaṃ etthāti upanisā, kāraṇaṃ, avijjā upanisā etesanti avijjūpanisā. Assādānupassinoti upādāniyesu tebhūmakadhammesu visayabhūtesu assādetabbato assādasaññitaṃ [V 2.0235] sukhasomanassaṃ anupassanasīlassa. Appahīnāvijjatāya bālalakkhaṇayogena bālassa. Evanti avijjānivutattā, taṇhāsaṃyuttattā ca. Ayaṃ kāyoti ayaṃ mamañceva tumhākañca paccakkhabhūto saviññāṇakakāyo khandhapañcakaṃ. “Saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso”ti (mahāva. 1; udā. 1) vacanato phassakāraṇañcetaṃ vuccatīti āyatanacchakkaṃ vā. Samudāgatoti uppanno. Bahiddhā ca nāmarūpanti bahiddhā saviññāṇakakāyo khandhapañcakaṃ, saḷāyatanāni vā. Itthetanti itthaṃ etaṃ. Attano ca paresañca pañcakkhandhā dvādasāyatanāni dvārālambanabhāvena vavatthitāni dvayaṃ nāmāti attho. Dvayaṃ paṭicca phassoti aññattha cakkhurūpādīni dvayāni paṭicca cakkhusamphassādayo vuttā, idha pana ajjhattikabāhirāni āyatanāni, mahādvayaṃ nāma kiretanti vuttaṃ. Ayamettha adhippāyo – aññattha “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.204, 400; 3.421, 425, 426; saṃ. ni. 2.44; 4.60; kathā. 465) cakkhu ceva rūpā ca…pe… mano ceva dhammā cāti vuttāni dvayāni paṭicca cakkhusamphassādayo vuttā. Idha pana “ayañceva kāyo”ti cakkhādinissaye sesadhamme cakkhādinissite eva katvā vuttaṃ cakkhādikāyaṃ ekattena “ajjhattikāyatana”nti gahetvā, “bahiddhā ca nāmarūpa”nti vuttaṃ rūpādiārammaṇaṃ ekatteneva “bāhirāyatana”nti tāni ajjhattikabāhirāni āyatanāni paṭicca phasso vutto, tasmā mahādvayametanti.

586. In a certain sutta. A teaching rooted in one thing: for this teaching, among ignorance and craving, only one dhamma is the root; for this reason, it is called `ekadhammamūlikā`. The meaning is: having made just one dhamma among those two the root, the teaching of dependent origination is taught. Support (`upanisā`): in this, the fruit 'sits near' (`upanisīdati`), thus it is `upanisā`; it means 'cause'. Having ignorance as support (`avijjūpanisā`): for these formations, ignorance is the cause (`upanisā`), thus they are `avijjūpanisā`. Of one who contemplates gratification: of one who has the nature of repeatedly contemplating the pleasure and gladness—designated as 'gratification' because it is to be enjoyed—in the phenomena of the three planes which are subject to clinging and have become objects of gratification. Of the fool: of the worldling called a fool, because of having unabandoned ignorance and because of being endowed with the characteristic of a fool. Thus: because of being obstructed by ignorance and because of being conjoined with craving. This body: this body with consciousness, which is directly manifest to me and to you, is the five aggregates. Or, because of the statement, 'Conditioned by the sixfold sense base, contact arises,' this, being the cause of contact, is also spoken of; therefore, the sixfold sense base is called `kāyo` (body). Has come to be: has arisen. And external name-and-form: externally, the body with consciousness, which is the five aggregates; or, the six sense bases. `Itthetaṃ` is to be parsed as `itthaṃ etaṃ`. The meaning of a dyad is that one's own and others' five aggregates and twelve sense bases, established by way of being doors and objects, are called a dyad. Contact dependent on a dyad: elsewhere, contacts such as eye-contact are said to arise in dependence on dyads such as the eye and forms. Here, however, contact is said to arise in dependence on the internal and external sense bases, and this, it is said, is called the 'great dyad'. This is the intention here: elsewhere, by such statements as 'Dependent on the eye and on forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact,' contacts such as eye-contact are said to arise in dependence on the stated dyads, namely, eye and forms... mind and mental objects. Here, however, by the phrase 'this very body,' having treated the remaining phenomena that are the support for the eye, etc., as being included in what is dependent on the eye, etc., and having taken the 'body of the eye, etc.' thus spoken of collectively as the 'internal sense base'; and by the phrase 'and external name-and-form,' having taken the object, such as form, spoken of collectively as the 'external sense base'; contact is said to arise in dependence on those internal and external sense bases. Therefore, this is the 'great dyad'.

Evañca katvā attano ca parassa ca pañcahi khandhehi, chahi āyatanehi cāti ayamattho dīpetabbovāti vuttaṃ. “Ayaṃ kāyo”ti hi vuttāni sanissayāni cakkhādīni attano pañcakkhandhā, “bahiddhā nāmarūpa”nti vuttāni rūpādīni [M 2.0251] paresaṃ. Tathā ayaṃ kāyo attano cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni, bahiddhā nāmarūpaṃ paresaṃ bāhirānīti. Aññathā ajjhattikāyatanamatte eva “ayaṃ kāyo”ti vuttena ajjhattikāyatanāneva attano pañcakkhandhā hontīti attano ca paresañca pañcahi khandhehi dīpanā na sambhaveyyāti. Saḷevāyatanānīti saḷeva phassakāraṇāni, yehi kāraṇabhūtehi āyatanehi uppannena phassena phuṭṭho bālo sukhadukkhaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti. Ādi-saddena “etesaṃ vā aññatarena. Avijjānīvaraṇassa, bhikkhave, paṇḍitassa taṇhāya sampayuttassā”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.19) yojetabbaṃ. Imasmiñhi sutte saṅkhāre avijjātaṇhānissite eva katvā kāyaggahaṇena viññāṇanāmarūpasaḷāyatanāni gahetvā tasmiṃ kāye saḷāyatanānaṃ phassaṃ taṃnissitameva [V 2.0236] katvā vedanāya visesapaccayabhāvaṃ dassentena bhagavatā bālapaṇḍitānaṃ atītaddhāvijjātaṇhāmūlako vedanānto paṭiccasamuppādo dassito. Puna ca bālapaṇḍitānaṃ visesaṃ dassentena –

And having done so, it is said that this meaning should be explained in terms of one's own and others' five aggregates and six sense bases. For 'this body' refers to the eye and other sense bases with their supports, which are one's own five aggregates, while 'external name-and-form' refers to forms and so on, which are the five aggregates of others. Similarly, 'this body' refers to one's own six internal sense bases, while 'external name-and-form' refers to the external sense bases of others. Otherwise, if 'this body' were said to mean only the internal sense bases, then one's own five aggregates would be just the internal sense bases, and the explanation in terms of the five aggregates of both oneself and others would not be possible. The six sense bases: just the six are the causes of contact, for it is when touched by contact arisen from these sense bases as cause that the fool experiences pleasure and pain. By the word 'etc.' one should connect 'or by any one of these. For the wise person, bhikkhus, obstructed by ignorance and yoked to craving...' etc. For in this sutta, the Blessed One has shown the dependent origination for fools and the wise that is rooted in past ignorance and craving and ends with feeling. He did so by treating formations as dependent on ignorance and craving, by taking 'body' to include consciousness, name-and-form, and the sixfold sense base, and by treating contact, the result of the six sense bases in that body, as dependent only on them, thus showing that they are a specific condition for feeling. And further, showing the difference between the fool and the wise person—

“Yāya ca, bhikkhave, avijjāya nivutassa bālassa, yāya ca taṇhāya sampayuttassa ayaṃ kāyo samudāgato, sā ceva avijjā bālassa appahīnā, sā ca taṇhā aparikkhīṇā. Taṃ kissa hetu? Na, bhikkhave, bālo acari brahmacariyaṃ sammā dukkhakkhayāya. Tasmā bālo kāyassa bhedā kāyūpago hoti, so kāyūpago samāno na parimuccati jātiyā…pe… dukkhasmāti vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.19) –

‘Bhikkhus, for the fool who is enveloped by that ignorance and conjoined with that craving, this body has arisen. That same ignorance has not been abandoned by the fool, and that same craving has not been exhausted. For what reason? The fool, bhikkhus, has not lived the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, with the breakup of the body, the fool is one who goes to a body. Being one who goes to a body, he is not freed from birth… from suffering, I say.’

Vedanāpabhavaṃ sāvijjaṃ taṇhaṃ dassetvā, upādānabhave ca tannissite katvā “kāyūpago hotī”tiādinā jātiādike dassentena paccuppannahetusamuṭṭhānato pabhuti ubhayamūlavasena paṭiccasamuppādo vutto, tabbipariyāyena ca paṇḍitassa paccuppannahetuparikkhayato pabhuti ubhayamūlako paṭilomapaṭiccasamuppādoti.

Having shown craving—which originates from feeling and is accompanied by ignorance—and having treated clinging and becoming as dependent on it, by showing birth and so on with the words 'he is one who goes to a body,' etc., the dependent origination has been stated on the basis of both roots, beginning from the arising of present causes. And conversely, for the wise person, the dependent origination in reverse, based on both roots, has been stated, beginning from the exhaustion of present causes.

587. Pūretunti vaḍḍhetuṃ, upacinitunti attho. Duggatigāmikammassa visesapaccayattā avijjā “avindiyaṃ vindatī”ti vuttā, tathā visesapaccayo vindiyassa na hotīti “vindiyaṃ na vindatī”ti ca. Attanissitāni katvā [M 2.0252] cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ pavattanaṃ uppādanaṃ āyatanaṃ. Sammohabhāveneva anabhisamayabhūtattā aviditaṃ aññātaṃ karoti. Antavirahite javāpetīti vaṇṇāgamavipariyāyavikāravināsadhātuatthavisesayogehi pañcavidhassa niruttilakkhaṇassa vasena a-kāra vi-kāra ja-kāre gahetvā aññesaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ lopaṃ, ja-kārassa ca dutiyassāgamaṃ katvā “avijjā”ti vuttaṃ. Byañjanatthaṃ vatvā sabhāvatthaṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ vatthārammaṇāni “idaṃ vatthu, idaṃ ārammaṇa”nti avijjāya ñātuṃ na sakkāti avijjā tappaṭicchādikā vuttā. Vatthārammaṇasabhāvachādanato eva avijjādīnaṃ paṭiccasamuppādabhāvassa, jarāmaraṇādīnaṃ paṭiccasamuppannabhāvassa ca chādanato paṭiccasamuppādapaṭiccasamuppannacchādanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

587. `Pūretuṃ` means to increase; the meaning is to accumulate (`upacinituṃ`). Because ignorance is a specific condition for kamma leading to a bad destination, it is said that it 'finds what should not be found'; similarly, because it is not a specific condition for what should be found, it is said that it 'does not find what should be found.' `Āyatana` (source) is the production, the occurrence of eye-consciousness, etc., making them dependent on itself. Precisely because of its nature of delusion and because it is contrary to penetration, it makes the unknown unknown. It is called `avijjā` because 'it makes beings run on (`javāpeti`) in what is without end (`antavirahite`),' this derivation being made according to the fivefold characteristic of etymology—by way of letter interpolation, reversal, alteration, elision, and combination with a specialized root meaning—by taking the letters `a`, `vi`, and `ja`, eliding the other letters, and interpolating a second `ja`. Having stated the literal meaning, in order to show the meaning according to its intrinsic nature, 'Moreover,' etc., is said. Because it is not possible through ignorance to know the bases and objects of eye-consciousness, etc., as 'This is the base, this is the object,' ignorance is said to be what conceals them. Precisely because it conceals the intrinsic nature of the bases and objects, and because it conceals the fact that ignorance, etc., are dependently originated and that aging-and-death, etc., are dependently arisen, it should be understood as concealing dependent origination and the dependently arisen phenomena.

Apaccakkhitvāti [V 2.0237] paccakkhānaṃ akatvā apaṭikkhipitvā. Upakārakaṭṭho paccayaṭṭho yathā piṇḍapātādi sarīrassa.

Not having rejected means not having made a refusal, not having repudiated. The meaning of 'support' is the meaning of 'condition,' just as almsfood and so on are for the body.

Saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharontīti yathā saṅkhataṃ hoti, evaṃ abhisaṅkharonti. Saṅkhārasaddaggahaṇena āgatā saṅkhārā saṅkhārasaddena āgatasaṅkhārā. Yadipi avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāpi saṅkhārasaddena āgatā, te pana imissā desanāya padhānāti visuṃ vuttā, tasmā “duvidhā”ti ettha saṅkhārasaddena āgatasaṅkhāresu abhisaṅkharaṇakasaṅkhāraṃ vajjetvā tadaññe saṅkhārasaddena āgatasaṅkhārā yojetabbā. Saṅkhārasaddena āgatasaṅkhārāti vā samudāyo vutto. Tadekadesā ca idha vaṇṇetabbabhāvena gahitā avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā, tasmā vaṇṇetabbasabbasaṅgāhakavasena duvidhatā vuttāti veditabbā. “Paṭhamaṃ nirujjhati vacīsaṅkhāro”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.464) vitakkavicāraassāsapassāsasaññāvedanāvacīsaṅkhārādayo vuttā, na avijjāpaccayā saṅkhāresu vuttā kāyasañcetanādayo.

They form the formed means: they form it in the way that it is formed. Formations included under the term 'formations' are formations included under the term 'formations.' Although formations conditioned by ignorance are also included under the term 'formations,' they are the principal topic in this discourse and are therefore stated separately. Therefore, here in the term 'twofold,' among the formations included by the term 'formations,' the formative formation should be excluded and the other formations included by the term 'formations' should be connected. Alternatively, 'formations included under the term "formations"' refers to the aggregate. And a portion of that, namely, the formations conditioned by ignorance, are taken here as the subject to be explained. Therefore, it should be understood that the twofoldness is stated by way of encompassing all that is to be explained. By the passage beginning, 'First, the verbal formation ceases,' verbal formations and so on—applied thought and sustained thought, in-breathing and out-breathing, perception, and feeling—are mentioned, not the bodily volitions, etc., stated among the formations conditioned by ignorance.

Saṅkhatasaṅkhārā nāma yathāsakaṃ paccayehi saṅkhatattā. Satipi paccayanibbattānaṃ sabbesampi saṅkhatabhāve “mametaṃ phala”nti tatthābhimukhena viya kammunā nibbattitattā tebhūmakavipākakaṭattārūpesu sātisayo saṅkhatabhāvoti adhippāyena aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (visuddhi. 2.587) kammanibbattānaṃ abhisaṅkhatasaṅkhāratā vuttā. Pāḷiyaṃ pana tathā āgataṭṭhānassa abhāvato “tepi [M 2.0253] …pe… ettheva saṅgahaṃ gacchantī”ti vuttaṃ. Aniccā vata saṅkhārāti vuttā ubhuādisamuṭṭhānāpi sabbadhammā. Abhisaṅkharaṇakasaṅkhāroti vuccati attano phalassa abhisaṅkharaṇato. Kāyapayogasamuṭṭhāpanavīriyaṃ kāyikavīriyaṃ. Abhisaṅkhārassāti payogavegassa.

Formed formations are so called because they are formed by their respective conditions. Although all things produced by conditions have a formed nature, because they are produced by kamma as if facing it with the thought 'this is my fruit,' there is a pre-eminent formed nature in the resultant and kamma-produced matter of the three planes. With this intention, in the commentary, the state of being a 'volitionally formed formation' is ascribed to kamma-produced phenomena. However, since there is no passage in the Pāḷi Canon stating this, it is said: 'These too... are included right here.' When it is said, 'Impermanent, alas, are formations,' this refers to all phenomena, even those originating from temperature, etc. It is called the 'formative formation' because it forms its own fruit. Energy that originates from bodily application is bodily energy. 'Of the formation' means of the force of application.

Vācaṃ saṅkharotīti vacīsaṅkhāro. Kāyena saṅkharīyatīti kāyasaṅkhāro. Cittena saṅkharīyati, cittaṃ vā saṅkharotīti cittasaṅkhāro. Saṅkhepato pana sabbepi yathārahaṃ saṅkharonti, saṅkharīyantīti ca saṅkhārāti veditabbā. Vuttanti saṅkhāraṭṭhapaccayaṭṭhādimāha.

It forms speech, therefore it is a verbal formation. It is formed by the body, therefore it is a bodily formation. It is formed by the mind, or it forms the mind, therefore it is a mental formation. In brief, however, all formations, as is fitting, both form and are formed, and thus should be understood as 'formations'. By the word `vuttaṃ`, he states the meaning of 'formation', the meaning of 'condition', and so on.

Namatīti ekantasārammaṇatāya ārammaṇābhimukhaṃ namati. Paritassatīti pipāsati, taṇhāparitāpatāya vā vicalati. Upādiyatīti daḷhaṃ ādiyati. Bhavatīti upapattibhavaṃ sandhāyāha. Bhāvayatīti kammabhavaṃ. Cuti khandhānaṃ maraṇanti “maranti etenā”ti vuttaṃ. Dukkhā vedanā [V 2.0238] uppādadukkhā, ṭhitidukkhāti ca katvā “dvedhā khaṇatī”ti vuttaṃ. Āyāso parissamo visādo.

'It bends' means: because of being exclusively with an object, it inclines towards the object. 'It trembles' means: it thirsts, or it is agitated by the torment of craving. 'It clings' means: it grasps firmly. Regarding 'it becomes,' he speaks with reference to rebirth-existence. Regarding 'it brings into being,' he speaks with reference to kamma-existence. The passing away of the aggregates is death; therefore it is said, 'they die by this.' Because painful feeling is suffering at arising and suffering in duration, it is said, 'it afflicts in two ways.' Distress is fatigue, despair.

Niddiṭṭhanayadassananti yathāniddiṭṭhavidhisandassanaṃ. Kevala-saddo asammissavācako ca hoti “kevalā sālayo”tiādīsu, niravasesavācako ca “kevalā aṅgamagadhā”tiādīsu, tasmā dvidhāpi atthaṃ vadati. Tattha asammissassāti sukharahitassa. Na hi ettha kiñci uppādavayarahitaṃ atthi. Sakalassāti sabbabhavādigatassa, sabbakālikassa ca.

'Exposition of the indicated method' means showing the procedure as it has been indicated. The word `kevala` expresses 'unmixed,' as in 'purely sāl trees,' and it expresses 'without remainder,' as in 'the whole of Aṅga and Magadha.' Therefore, it conveys the meaning in two ways. Therein, 'of the unmixed' means of that which is devoid of pleasure. For herein, in this collection of phenomena, there is nothing devoid of arising and passing away. 'Of the entire' means of that which pertains to all existences, etc., and of that which is of all time.

588. “Lakkhaṇekavidhādito”ti ettha ādi-saddo paccekaṃ parisamāpetabboti dassento āha “lakkhaṇādito”ti. Sampayutte, taṃsamaṅgipuggale vā sammohayatīti sammohanarasā. Ārammaṇasabhāvassa chādanaṃ hutvā gayhatīti chādanapaccupaṭṭhānā. “Āsavasamudayā avijjāsamudayo”ti (ma. ni. 1.103) vacanato āsavapadaṭṭhānā. Paṭisandhijananatthaṃ āyūhanti byāpāraṃ karontīti āyūhanarasā. Rāsikaraṇaṃ vā āyūhanaṃ. Cetanāsabhāvattā cetanā hutvā gayhatīti cetanāpaccupaṭṭhānā. Nāmarūpassa purecārikabhāvena pavattatīti pubbaṅgamarasaṃ. Purimabhavena saddhiṃ ghaṭanaṃ hutvā gayhatīti paṭisandhipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Viññāṇena saha, aññamaññañca sampayujjatīti sampayogarasaṃ. Samaṃ pakārehi yogo [M 2.0254] sampayogo. Visuṃ abhāvo avinibbhogo. Rūpaṃ sampayogābhāvato vikiratīti vikiraṇarasaṃ. Tato eva hi pisiyamānā taṇḍulādayo vikiranti, cuṇṇībhūtā viddhaṃsanti, nāmassa kadāci kusalādibhāvopi atthīti tato visesanatthaṃ “abyākatapaccupaṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ. “Acetano abyākato”ti (visuddhi. 1.311; vibha. aṭṭha. 173) ettha viya anārammaṇatā vā abyākatatā daṭṭhabbā. Āyatanalakkhaṇanti ghaṭṭanalakkhaṇaṃ, āyānaṃ tananalakkhaṇaṃ vā. Dassanassa yathāsakaṃ visayaggahaṇassa karaṇato dassanarasaṃ. “Dassanādirasa”nti pana sammohavinodaniyaṃ vuttaṃ. Vatthudvārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ yathārahaṃ viññāṇamanoviññāṇadhātūnanti adhippāyo. Vatthuggahaṇañcettha cakkhādipañcakāpekkhaṃ. Akusalavipākupekkhāya aniṭṭhabhāvato dukkhena, itarāya iṭṭhabhāvato sukhena saṅgahitattā “sukhadukkhapaccupaṭṭhānā”ti vuttaṃ. Dukkhasamudayattā hetulakkhaṇā taṇhā. “Tatratatrābhinandinī”ti (ma. ni. 1.91, 460; saṃ. ni. 5.1081; vibha. 203; mahāva. 14) vacanato abhinandanarasā. Cittassa, puggalassa vā rūpādīsu atittabhāvo hutvā gayhatīti atittabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā. Amuñcanarasaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhābhinivesavasena. Taṇhādaḷhattaṃ [V 2.0239] hutvā kāmupādānaṃ, sesāni diṭṭhi hutvā upaṭṭhahantīti taṇhādaḷhattadiṭṭhipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Kammupapattibhavavasena bhavassa lakkhaṇādayo yojetabbā.

588. In 'from the characteristic, onefold, etc.,' the word 'etc.' is to be applied to complete each point, as shown by 'from the characteristic, etc.' It deludes those associated with it or the person endowed with it—this is its function of delusion. It manifests as concealing the intrinsic nature of the object. It has the taints as its proximate cause, in accordance with the text: 'With the arising of the taints, there is the arising of ignorance' (MN 9). It strives to generate rebirth-linking—this is its function of accumulation. Or, accumulation is the making of a collection. It manifests as volition, due to its nature as volition. It occurs as the precursor to name-and-form—this is its function as a forerunner. It is grasped as connecting with the previous existence—this is its manifestation as rebirth-linking. It is associated with consciousness and with one another—this is its function of association. Association is connection in like ways. Inseparability is the absence of being separate. Form scatters due to the absence of association—this is its function of dispersing. Indeed, for this very reason, grains of rice and so on, when being milled, scatter, and when pulverized are destroyed. Since name sometimes also has the state of being wholesome, etc., to distinguish it from that, it is said to have an 'indeterminate manifestation.' Or, as in the passage 'non-mental and indeterminate,' indeterminacy should be seen as being without an object. The characteristic of a base is the characteristic of impinging, or the characteristic of extending the sources. It facilitates the grasping of its respective object—this is its function of seeing. But 'the function of seeing, etc.' is stated in the Sammohavinodanī. The manifestation as basis and door is intended with respect to the consciousness-element and the mind-consciousness-element, as is appropriate. And here, the term 'basis' refers to the pentad of sense faculties beginning with the eye. Because unwholesome resultant equanimity is undesirable, it is included under suffering, while the other is desirable and included under pleasure; thus it is said to have 'pleasure and suffering as its manifestation.' Craving has the characteristic of a cause because it is the origin of suffering. It has the function of delighting, in accordance with the text: 'delighting in this and that.' It is grasped as the insatiability of the mind or the person toward forms, etc.—this is its manifestation as insatiability. Its function is not letting go, by way of adherence to craving and views. Clinging to sensual pleasures manifests as the strengthening of craving, while the others manifest as views—thus it has the strengthening of craving and views as its manifestation. The characteristics, etc., of existence should be applied in terms of kamma-existence and rebirth-existence.

589. Mohādibhāvatoti ettha ādi-saddena ananubodhādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Dukkhādīsu aññāṇavasena appaṭipatti, asubhādīsu subhādivipallāsavasena micchāpaṭipatti. Diṭṭhivippayuttavasena vā appaṭipatti, diṭṭhisampayuttavasena micchāpaṭipatti. Dvārārammaṇatoti dvārato, ārammaṇato ca chasu dvāresu, chasu ārammaṇesu ca pavattanato. Ayaṃ pana vibhāgo na avijjāya eva, aññesupi paṭiccasamuppādaṅgesu arūpadhammānaṃ labbhatīti āha “sabbesupī”ti.

589. Herein, in the phrase 'by way of being delusion, etc.,' by the word 'etc.' is included non-comprehension and so on. In regard to suffering, etc., there is non-penetration by way of ignorance; in regard to the foul, etc., there is wrong penetration by way of the perversion of seeing it as beautiful, etc. Alternatively, there is non-penetration by way of being dissociated from views, and wrong penetration by way of being associated with views. As for 'by way of door and object,' it is because of occurring by way of door and by way of object in the six doors and in the six objects. However, this division is obtained not only in the case of ignorance but also for the formless states among other factors of dependent origination; thus, he said 'in all.'

Vipākadhammadhammādibhāvatoti ettha ādi-saddena nevasekkhānāsekkhasaṃyojaniyādibhāve saṅgaṇhāti. Catuyonisaṃvattanatoti catuyonipariyāpannattabhāvanibbattanato.

Herein, in the phrase 'by way of being a resultant state, etc.,' by the word 'etc.' he includes the states of being neither-a-trainee-nor-a-non-trainee, being subject to the fetters, and so on. As for 'by way of revolving through the four kinds of generation,' it is because it produces an individual existence included in the four kinds of generation.

Lokiyavibhāgādibhāvatoti [M 2.0255] ettha ādi-saddena abyākatasappaccayasaṅkhatādibhāve saṅgaṇhāti. Sahetukāhetukāditoti ādi-saddena sasaṅkhārāsaṅkhārādibhede saṅgaṇhāti.

Herein, in the phrase 'by way of the mundane division, etc.,' by the word 'etc.' he includes the states of being indeterminate, having a condition, being formed, and so on. In the phrase 'with cause, without cause, etc.,' by the word 'etc.' he includes the distinctions of with prompting, without prompting, and so on.

Kāmaṃ nāmarūpaṃ paccuppannaddhavasena vuccati, tathāpi yathā paccuppannaṃ, evaṃ atītānāgatampīti addhadvayapariyāpannassāpi nayato gahetabbattā vuttaṃ “atītādito tividha”nti.

Granted, name-and-form is spoken of by way of the present time-period; nevertheless, because it should be grasped by a method as also being included in the two time-periods—for just as it is present, so too it is past and future—it is said to be 'threefold, beginning with the past.'

Sañjātisamosaraṇaṭṭhānatoti viññāṇataṃsampayuttadhammānaṃ uppattipavattidesabhāvato. “Bhūtappasādaviññāṇato”ti pāṭho yutto. “Viññāṇādito”ti pana paṭhanti. Ekasesanayena bāhirāyatanassāpi saṅgahe sati ādi-saddena tassa saṅgahitatā daṭṭhabbā. Nobhayagocaranti manāyatanamāha. Na hi arūpadhammānaṃ desavasena āsannatā, dūratā vā atthi aviggahattā, tasmā manāyatanassa gocaro manāyatanaṃ sampatto, asampatto vāti na vuccati. Phassādīnampīti ettha phasso tāva phusanasabhāvato, lokiyasāsavādibhāvato ca ekavidho. Paṭighasamphassaadhivacanasamphassabhedato, sahetukādibhāvato ca duvidho. Bhavattayapariyāpannato, vedanāttayasampayogato[V 2.0240], ahetukaduhetukatihetukato ca tividho. Yonigativasena catubbidho, pañcavidho ca.

“By way of being a place of birth and assembly” means by being the location for the arising and proceeding of consciousness and its associated states. The reading “from consciousness based on the primary elements and sensitive matter” is suitable. But some read “from consciousness, etc.” When the external bases are also included by the method of one-remainder, it should be seen that they are included by the word “etc.” “Not the domain of both” refers to the mind base. For indeed, for formless phenomena, because they are without physical shape, there is no nearness or distance by way of location; therefore, it is not said that the object of the mind base has reached the mind base or not reached it. Regarding “contact, etc.”: here, contact, in the first place, is onefold by way of its nature of touching, and by way of being mundane and subject to taints. It is twofold by the distinction between sensory-impression contact and designation contact, and by way of being with a cause, etc. It is threefold by way of being included in the three realms of existence, by its association with the three kinds of feeling, and by being rootless, two-rooted, or three-rooted. It is fourfold and fivefold by way of generation and destiny.

Vedanā anubhavanalakkhaṇato, lokiyasāsavādibhāvato ca ekavidhā. Pañcadvārikamanodvārikabhedato duvidhā. Sukhādibhedato tividhā. Yonigativasena catubbidhā, pañcavidhā ca. Chaḷārammaṇabhedato chabbidhā.

Feeling is onefold by its characteristic of experiencing and by being worldly and with taints. It is twofold by the distinction of the five doors and the mind door. It is threefold by the distinction of pleasant, etc. It is fourfold by way of generation, and fivefold by way of destiny. It is sixfold by the distinction of the six objects.

Taṇhā lokassa samudayabhāvato ekavidhā. Duvidhā diṭṭhisampayuttavippayuttabhāvato. Tividhā kāmabhavavibhavataṇhābhedato. Catubbidhā catumaggapaheyyato. Pañcavidhā rūpābhinandanādibhāvato. Chabbidhā chataṇhākāyabhedato.

Craving is onefold by being the origin of the world. It is twofold by being associated with or dissociated from view. It is threefold by the distinction of craving for sensual pleasure, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. It is fourfold by being abandonable by the four paths. It is fivefold by being a delighting in forms, etc. It is sixfold by the distinction of the six classes of craving.

Upādānaṃ ekavidhaṃ daḷhaggāhabhāvato. Duvidhaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhibhedato. Tividhaṃ bhavattayūpanissayabhāvato. Catubbidhaṃ kāmupādānādibhedato. Pañcavidhaṃ pañcagatisaṃvattanato.

Clinging is onefold by its nature of firm grasping. It is twofold by the distinction of craving and view. It is threefold by being a decisive support condition for the three kinds of existence. It is fourfold by the distinction of clinging to sensual pleasures, etc. It is fivefold by conducing to the five destinations.

Bhavo [M 2.0256] ekavidho lokiyasāsavādibhāvato. Duvidho kammupapattibhedato. Tividho kāmabhavādibhedato. Catubbidho caturupādānapaccayato. Pañcavidho pañcagatisaṃvattanato. Chabbidho kāmakammabhavādibhedato. Sattavidho sattaviññāṇaṭṭhitisaṅgahato. Aṭṭhavidho caturupādānapaccayakammabhavādibhedato. Navavidho kāmabhavādibhedato.

Existence is onefold by being worldly, with taints, and so on. It is twofold by the distinction of kamma-existence and rebirth-existence. It is threefold by the distinction of sense-sphere existence, and so on. It is fourfold by being conditioned by the four kinds of clinging. It is fivefold by conducing to the five destinations. It is sixfold by the distinction of sense-sphere kamma-existence, and so on. It is sevenfold by its inclusion in the seven stations of consciousness. It is eightfold by the distinction of the four kamma-existences conditioned by the four kinds of clinging and the four rebirth-existences. It is ninefold by the distinction of kamma-existence, and so on.

Jāti ekavidhā tattha tattha bhave paṭhamābhinibbattibhāvato. Duvidhā rūpakkhandhasaṅkhārakkhandhasaṅgahato. Tividhā bhavattayapariyāpannato. Yonigativasena catubbidhā, pañcavidhā ca. Iminā nayena jarāmaraṇādīnampi ekavidhādibhāvo veditabbo.

Birth is onefold by being the initial arising in this or that existence. It is twofold by the inclusion of the aggregate of form and the aggregate of formations. It is threefold by being included in the three kinds of existence. It is fourfold by way of modes of generation and fivefold by way of destinations. By this method, the onefold nature and other classifications of aging-and-death, and so on, should also be understood.

590. Sokādīnampi gahitattā aṅgabahuttappasaṅge “dvādasevā”ti aṅgavavatthānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Na hi sokādayo aṅgabhāvena vuttā, phalena pana kāraṇaṃ avijjaṃ mūlaṅgaṃ dassetuṃ te vuttā. Jarāmaraṇabbhāhatassa hi bālassa te sambhavantīti sokādīnaṃ jarāmaraṇakāraṇatā vuttā, na pana “kāyikāya dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho”ti ca sutte jarāmaraṇanimittañca dukkhaṃ saṅgahitanti taṃ tannimittānaṃ jarāmaraṇabbhāhatassa sambhave sādhakabhāvena vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana jarāmaraṇeneva [V 2.0241] sokādīnaṃ ekasaṅkhepo kato, tasmā tesaṃ jātipaccayatā yujjati. Jarāmaraṇapaccayabhāve hi avijjāya ekasaṅkhepo kātabbo siyā. Jātipaccayā pana jarāmaraṇaṃ[M 2.0257], sokādayo ca sambhavantīti tattha jarāmaraṇaṃ ekantikaṃ aṅgabhāvena gahitaṃ. Sokādayo pana rūpabhavādīsu abhāvato anekantikā kevalaṃ pākaṭena phalena avijjānidassanatthaṃ gahitā. Tena anāgate jātiyā sati tato parāya paṭisandhiyā hetuhetubhūtā avijjā dassitāti bhavacakkassa avicchedo dassito hotīti. Suttañca sokādīnaṃ avijjā kāraṇanti etasseva atthassa sādhakaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, na sokādīnaṃ bālassa jarāmaraṇanimittatāmattassa. “Assutavā puthujjano”ti hi vacanena avijjā sokādīnaṃ kāraṇanti dassitā, na ca jarāmaraṇanimittameva dukkhaṃ dukkhanti.

590. Lest there be the problem of too many links because sorrow and so on are also included, the determination of the links as 'just twelve' should be understood. For sorrow and so on are not stated as links in themselves; rather, they are stated in order to show ignorance as the root link by way of its result. Because they arise for a fool afflicted by aging-and-death, it is said that aging-and-death is their cause. And it is not that that sutta is cited as proof for the arising of those signs in one afflicted by aging-and-death, on the grounds that in the sutta passage 'touched by painful bodily feeling,' suffering, which is also a sign of aging-and-death, is included. Since, however, a single summary of sorrow and so on is made with aging-and-death itself, their being conditioned by birth is justified. For if they were conditioned by aging-and-death, a single summary would have to be made with ignorance. But since aging-and-death and sorrow and so on arise conditioned by birth, aging-and-death is included there as an invariable link. Sorrow and so on, however, are not invariable since they are absent in the form existence, etc.; they are included merely to illustrate ignorance by way of a manifest result. Thus it is shown that when there is birth in the future, ignorance is the cause of the cause for the subsequent rebirth-linking; in this way the uninterruptedness of the wheel of existence is shown. And the sutta should be seen as proving this very meaning—that ignorance is the cause of sorrow and so on—not merely that sorrow and so on are a sign of aging-and-death for a fool. For by the words 'the uninstructed worldling,' it is shown that ignorance is the cause of sorrow and so on, and not that suffering is only the suffering that is a sign of aging-and-death.

Aparo nayo jarāmaraṇampi paccayo, aññathā dvādasaṅgāni na paripūrenti. Kassa pana so paccayo? Sokādīnaṃ. Yadi evaṃ kasmā “jarāmaraṇapaccayā sokādayo sambhavantī”ti avatvā “jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ, sokādayo ca sambhavantī”ti vuttanti? Yasmā tadaññenapi dukkhadhammena phuṭṭhassa te sambhavanti, tasmā appahīnasaṃyojanassāpi tesaṃ tappaccayatā na ekaṃsikāti jātipaccayatāva vuttā. Atha vā jarāmaraṇaggahaṇena upapattibhavo saṅgahito. Upādinnakkhandhaparipāko hi āyuno saṃhāni, indriyānaṃ paripāko ca jarā, tesañca bhedo maraṇanti. Sati ca upapattibhave tattha katupacitaṃ, porāṇaṃ vā kammaṃ kammabhavo, kammādiupaṭṭhāne cutianantaraṃ paṭisandhiṃ janetīti upapattibhavo jātiyā paccayo, tasmā jarāmaraṇampi jātiyā paccayatāya paṭiccasamuppādo. Yasmā pana “bhavapaccayā jātī”ti ettheva upapattibhavassa jātiyā paccayatā saṅgahitā, tasmā vuttapariyāyasaṅgahato ca “jarāmaraṇapaccayā jātī”ti na vuttaṃ. Evaṃ jarāmaraṇassāpi paccayabhāvasiddhito paṭiccasamuppādatāti dvādasaṅgatā vavatthitāti veditabbā. Tenāha “dvādasevā”tiādi. Ayaṃ tāvāti “desanābhedato”tiādinā vuttaṃ atthasaṃvaṇṇanaṃ sandhāyāha.

Another method: Aging-and-death is also a condition; otherwise the twelve links would not be complete. For what is it a condition? For sorrow and so on. If so, why is it not said, 'From aging-and-death as condition, sorrow and so on arise,' but instead, 'From birth as condition, aging-and-death, and sorrow and so on arise'? Because they also arise for one afflicted by other phenomena of suffering, their being conditioned thus is not invariable even for one who has not abandoned the fetters; therefore it is stated that they are conditioned by birth. Alternatively, by the term 'aging-and-death,' rebirth-existence is included. For aging is the maturation of the clung-to aggregates, the decline of the life-faculty, and the maturation of the sense faculties; death is their breakup. And when there is rebirth-existence, kamma-existence—that is, kamma accumulated therein or past kamma—generates rebirth-linking immediately after decease when kamma, etc., presents itself. Thus rebirth-existence is a condition for future birth. Therefore aging-and-death is also part of dependent origination through its being a condition for future birth. However, since the conditionality of rebirth-existence for birth is already included right there in 'from existence as condition, birth,' and because of the inclusion by the stated method, it is not said 'from aging-and-death as condition, birth.' Thus, since the status of aging-and-death as a condition is also established, it is part of dependent origination, and so the state of having twelve links is established; this should be understood. Hence it is said, 'Just twelve,' etc. This, for now, is said with reference to the explanation of the meaning stated by 'by the distinction in the teaching,' etc.

Avijjāpaccayāsaṅkhārapadakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Exposition of the Phrase 'Conditioned by Ignorance, Volitional Formations'

591. Ayaṃ panāti idāni vakkhamānaṃ. “Katamā ca, bhikkhave, avijjā dukkhe aññāṇa”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 1.103) suttantesu catuṭṭhānikā avijjā vuttāti “suttantapariyāyenā”ti [V 2.0242] vuttaṃ. Nikkhepakaṇḍe (dha. sa. 1106) pana suttantesu catūsu ṭhānesu kathitāya eva avijjāya aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu kiccajātito kathitattā tadatthavaṇṇanāvasena vibhāvanaṃ kātuṃ “abhidhammapariyāyenā”ti ārabhitvā “vuttañheta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Ahāpetvā vibhajitabbaṃ. Vibhajanañhi abhidhammapariyāyo. “Aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu aññāṇa”nti ānetvā taṃ sambandhitabbaṃ. Sesaṭṭhānesūti dukkhasamudayesu, pubbantādīsu ca. Ārammaṇavasenāti ārammaṇakaraṇavasenāpi. Idhāti imasmiṃ “dukkhe aññāṇa”ntiādike pāṭhe. Sāti avijjā. Uppannāti asamūhatuppannā, pageva paccuppannā. “Paṭicchādetvā”ti ettha vuttaṃ paṭicchādanākāraṃ dassetuṃ “yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ na detī”ti vuttaṃ. Rasitabbo paṭivijjhitabbo sabhāvo raso, attano raso saraso, yāthāvo yathābhūto saraso yāthāvasaraso, yo “pīḷanaṭṭho”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 2.8) vutto [M 2.0258] dukkhasaccappabhedā eva ca pubbantādayo, so eva lakkhitabbattā yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇaṃ. Taṃ paṭivijjhituṃ paccakkhato jānituṃ na deti.

591. Now, this refers to what is about to be said. In the discourses, it is said: “And what, bhikkhus, is ignorance? Not knowing suffering,” etc., where ignorance is described in four instances; hence, it is said, “according to the Sutta method.” However, in the Nikkhepakaṇḍa, ignorance, which is spoken of in four places in the suttas, is discussed in eight instances based on its function and nature. To explain its meaning, the exposition “according to the Abhidhamma method” is begun with the words, “For it has been said,” etc. It should be analyzed without omission, for analysis is the Abhidhamma method. The phrase “not knowing in eight instances” should be brought in and connected to that. The remaining instances are in suffering and its origin, and in the past, etc. “By way of object” means also by way of making something an object. Here, in this passage “not knowing suffering,” etc., ‘that’ refers to ignorance. “Arisen” means it has arisen uneradicated; how much more so is it presently arisen. Here, regarding “concealing,” to show the manner of concealment it is said: “it does not allow the characteristic of the true own-nature to be penetrated.” The nature to be savored and penetrated is the essence (rasa); its own essence is sarasa; the true, real own-essence is yāthāvasarasa. That yāthāvasarasa is what is described as “the meaning of oppression,” etc., and the past and so on are themselves divisions of the truth of suffering. That very true own-nature, because it is to be characterized, is the “characteristic of the true own-nature.” It does not allow that to be penetrated, to be known directly.

Tadubhayanti pubbantañceva aparantañca atītaṃ, anāgatañca khandhapañcakaṃ. Pubbantāparantabhāgavantatāya vā paccuppannaddhabhūto majjhanto pubbantāparanto. Ayaṃ avijjā ime saṅkhārāti idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppannadhammesu paccakkhato jānanākāradassanaṃ. Etthāti etesu dukkhādīsu. Yadipi avijjā dukkhādīsu ārammaṇakaraṇavasenapi pavattati, yathā pana nirodhamagge ārammaṇaṃ kātuṃ asakkontī te jānitukāmassa tappaṭicchādanavasena, anirodhamaggesu nirodhamaggaggahaṇakāraṇabhāvena ca pavattamānā te yāthāvato paṭivijjhituṃ na deti, evaṃ dukkhādīsupīti veditabbaṃ. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “paṭicchādanavaseneva idhādhippetā”ti. Dukkhādivisayo andhatamakaro, lobhādīnañca andhatamakarānaṃ paccayabhūto adassanākāro aññāṇaṃ.

‘That which is both’ means the former end and the latter end, which are the five aggregates of the past and the future. Or, because it possesses parts of the former and latter ends, the middle part, which is the present time, is called ‘the former and latter ends.’ The statement, ‘This is ignorance, these are formations,’ is the showing of the mode of knowing directly in regard to dependently arisen phenomena with their specific conditionality. ‘Here’ means in these things, such as suffering. Although ignorance also proceeds by way of making suffering, etc., its object, it should be understood thus: just as, being unable to make cessation and the path its object, it does not allow one who wishes to know them to penetrate them as they really are—by way of concealing them and by proceeding in regard to what is not cessation and the path as a cause for grasping them as cessation and the path—so too is it in regard to suffering, etc. For so it was said: “Here it is intended precisely by way of concealment.” Ignorance is that which makes for blindness and darkness in the domain of suffering, etc., and it is the aspect of not-seeing which is a condition for greed, etc.—which also make for blindness and darkness.

592. Puññādayoti puññābhisaṅkhārādayo. Tattha punāti attano santānaṃ apuññaphalato, dukkhasaṃkilesato ca sodhetīti puññaṃ. Hitasukhajjhāsayena puññaṃ karotīti tannipphādanena kārakassa ajjhāsayaṃ pūreti, pujjabhavaṃ nibbattetīti vā puññaṃ. Iti pūrako, pujjanibbattako ca niruttinayena puññanti veditabbo. Puññañca so attano phalassa abhisaṅkharaṇaṭṭhena abhisaṅkhāro cāti puññābhisaṅkhāro. Puññapaṭipakkhato apuññanti vuttavipariyāyena apuññābhisaṅkhāro veditabbo. Samādhipaccanīkānaṃ atidūratāya na iñjati, aniñjañca [V 2.0243] bhavaṃ abhisaṅkharotīti āneñjābhisaṅkhāro. Kāyena pavattito, kāyato vā pavatto, kāyassa vā saṅkhāroti kāyasaṅkhāro. Vacīcittasaṅkhāresupi eseva nayo. Tattha paṭhamattiko parivīmaṃsanasuttādivasena gahito. Tattha hi “puññaṃ ce saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti, puññūpagaṃ hoti viññāṇa”ntiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.51) āgataṃ. Dutiyattiko vibhaṅgasuttavasena. Tattha hi “tayome, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā. Katame tayo? Kāyasaṅkhāro vacīsaṅkhāro cittasaṅkhāro”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.28) vuttaṃ.

592. “Meritorious, etc.” means meritorious volitional formations and so on. Therein, “merit” (puñña) is so called because it cleanses (punāti) or purifies one's own continuum from the fruit of demerit and from the defilement of suffering. Because one performs merit with an intention for welfare and happiness, by accomplishing that, it fulfills (pūreti) the doer’s intention; or, it is called “merit” because it generates a venerable existence. Thus, by way of etymology, “merit” should be understood as that which fulfills and that which generates a venerable existence. And that merit, in the sense of constructing its own fruit, is also a formation (abhisaṅkhāra); thus, it is a meritorious volitional formation. Demerit (apuñña) is so called because it is the opposite of merit; thus, the demeritorious volitional formation should be understood in the opposite way to what has been said. The imperturbable volitional formation is so called because, being very far from things hostile to concentration, it does not stir (iñjati), and it constructs an imperturbable existence. A bodily formation is that which is set in motion by the body, or proceeds from the body, or is a formation of the body. This same method applies to verbal and mental formations as well. Therein, the first triad is taken by way of the Parivīmaṃsana Sutta and others, for there it is stated: “If one constructs a meritorious formation, consciousness becomes one that partakes of merit,” and so on. The second triad is taken by way of the Vibhaṅga Sutta, for there it is said: “Bhikkhus, there are these three formations. What three? Bodily formation, verbal formation, and mental formation.”

Vitthārato panātiādi puññābhisaṅkhārādīnaṃ sarūpato, pabhedato ca vibhāvanaṃ. Bhāvanāvaseneva pavattā, na dānasīlavasenāti tattha labbhamānaṃ puññakiriyavatthuṃ dasseti. Evañca katvā arūpāvacaracetanāpi “bhāvanāvaseneva [M 2.0259] pavattā”ti vuttā. Ye pana “bhāvanāvasenevā”ti avadhāraṇena abhiññācetanaṃ nivattetīti vadanti, tadayuttaṃ tāsampi avijjāpaccayatāya viya puññābhisaṅkhārabhāvassa ca icchitattā. Aññathā abhiññācittuppādassa puññakiriyavatthūsu asaṅgaho eva siyā, na ca yuttaṃ “kusalañca puññakiriyavatthuñca na hotī”ti. Pāṇātipātādīti ādi-saddena na tadavasiṭṭhaakusalakammapathānaṃyeva gahaṇaṃ, atha kho anavasesaakusalakammassāpi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The passage beginning “Now, in detail” is an explanation of meritorious volitional formations and so on in terms of their nature and their divisions. The words “arisen solely by way of mental development, not by way of giving and virtue” show the ground of meritorious action obtainable therein. And having said this, even formless-sphere volitions are said to be “arisen solely by way of mental development.” But those who say that the restrictive particle in “solely by way of mental development” excludes the volition of direct knowledge are incorrect, for its state as a meritorious volitional formation is also intended, just like its being conditioned by ignorance. Otherwise, the arising of the mind of direct knowledge would simply not be included among the grounds of meritorious action, and it is not right to say that “it is wholesome, but it is not a ground of meritorious action.” Regarding “killing living beings, etc.,” by the word “etc.” one should understand the inclusion not only of the remaining paths of unwholesome kamma, but of all unwholesome kamma without remainder.

Itaresu panāti kāyasaṅkhārādīsu. Puññābhisaṅkhārādayo pavattamānā imehi dvārehi pavattantīti dvārato pavattidassanatthaṃ. “Samavīsati cetanā”ti kasmā vuttaṃ, yadi kāyavacīviññattiyo samuṭṭhāpentiyo kusalākusalacetanā kāyasaṅkhāro, vacīsaṅkhāroti ca vuccanti, evaṃ sante abhiññācetanāyapi kusalāya tathā pavattāya vacīsaṅkhārabhāvo vattabboti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “abhiññācetanā”tiādi. Etthāti kāyavacīsaṅkhāraggahaṇe, kāyavacīsañcetanāggahaṇe vā. Na gahitāti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ na gahitā “abhiññācetanā viññāṇassa paccayo na hotī”ti. Kasmā pana na hoti, nanu sāpi kusalā, vipākadhammā cāti? Saccametaṃ, anupacchinnataṇhāvijjamāne pana santāne sabyāpārappavattiyā tassā kusalatā, vipākadhammatā ca vuttā, na vipākuppādanena. Sā pana vipākaṃ uppādentī rūpāvacarameva uppādeyya. Na hi aññabhūmikaṃ kammaṃ aññabhūmikaṃ vipākaṃ uppādetīti. Attanā sadisārammaṇaṃ tiṭṭhānikameva ca uppādeyya cittuppādakaṇḍe rūpāvacaravipākassa kammasadisārammaṇasseva vuttattā. Na ca rūpāvacaravipāko parittādiārammaṇo atthi, abhiññācetanā [V 2.0244] ca parittādiārammaṇāva hoti. Tasmā vipākaṃ na uppādetīti viññāyati. Kasiṇesu ca uppāditassa catutthajjhānasamādhissa ānisaṃsabhūtā abhiññā. Yathāha “so evaṃ samāhite citte”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.244-245; ma. ni. 1.384-386, 431-433; pārā. 12). Tasmā samādhiphalasadisā sā, na ca phalaṃ deti. Dānasīlānisaṃsabhūto tasmiṃ bhave paccayalābho viyāti sāpi vipākaṃ na uppādetīti.

“But in the others” refers to bodily formations and so on. This is for the purpose of showing their occurrence by way of doors, that is, that meritorious formations and the like, when occurring, occur through these doors. Why is it said, “twenty volitions”? In reference to the objection—“If the wholesome and unwholesome volitions that originate bodily and verbal intimations are called ‘bodily formation’ and ‘verbal formation,’ then, this being so, it should be said that the wholesome volition of direct knowledge, occurring in the same way, is also a bodily and verbal formation”—the text says “the volition of direct knowledge,” etc. “Here” means in the inclusion of bodily and verbal formations, or in the inclusion of bodily and verbal volitions. “Is not included” means it is not included in the commentary, thus: “The volition of direct knowledge is not a condition for consciousness.” But why is it not? Is it not also wholesome and subject to ripening? This is true. However, in a continuum where craving and ignorance are not cut off, its wholesomeness and its nature of being subject to ripening are spoken of because of its active occurrence, not because of producing a result. But if it were to produce a result, it would produce only a form-sphere result, for kamma of one plane does not produce a result in another plane. And it would produce only a three-functional result with an object similar to its own, because in the chapter on the arising of consciousness it is said that form-sphere results have an object similar to their kamma. And there is no form-sphere result that has a sense-sphere object, etc., whereas the volition of direct knowledge has only a sense-sphere object, etc. Therefore, it is understood that it does not produce a result. And direct knowledge is a benefit of the concentration of the fourth jhāna produced in regard to the kasiṇas. As it is said: “When his mind is thus concentrated…” Therefore, it is similar to the fruit of concentration, and a fruit does not yield a fruit. Just like the acquisition of requisites in that existence, which is a benefit of giving and virtue, so too it does not produce a result.

“Yathā ca abhiññācetanā, evaṃ uddhaccacetanāpi na hotī”ti idaṃ uddhaccasahagatadhamme visuṃ uddharitvā “tesaṃ vipāke ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 725) vuttattā [M 2.0260] vicāretabbaṃ. Sā pana vicāraṇā heṭṭhā khandhaniddesavaṇṇanāyaṃ akusalakathāyaṃ vicāritā evāti tattha vicāritanayeneva veditabbā. Apicettha yadeke vibhajja vadanti, dassanabhāvanānaṃ abhāvepi yesaṃ puthujjanānaṃ, sekkhānañca dassanabhāvanāhi bhavitabbaṃ, tesaṃ taduppattikāle tehi pahātuṃ sakkuṇeyyā akusalā dassanena pahātabbā, bhāvanāya pahātabbāti ca vuccanti. Puthujjanānaṃ pana bhāvanāya abhāvā bhāvanāya pahātabbacintā natthi. Tena tesaṃ pavattamānā dassanena pahātuṃ asakkuṇeyyāpi bhāvanāya pahātabbāti na vuccanti. Yadi vucceyyuṃ, dassanenapahātabbā bhāvanāyapahātabbānaṃ kesañci kenaci kadāci ārammaṇaārammaṇādhipatiupanissayapaccayehi paccayo bhaveyyuṃ? Na ca paṭṭhāne dassanenapahātabbā bhāvanāyapahātabbānaṃ kenaci paccayena paccayoti vuttā. Sekkhānaṃ pana vijjamānā bhāvanāya pahātuṃ sakkuṇeyyāti bhāvanāya pahātabbā. Teneva sekkhānaṃ dassanena pahātabbā, cattattā vantattā muttattā pahīnattā paṭinissaṭṭhattā ukkheṭitattā samukkheṭitattā assāditabbā, abhinanditabbā ca na honti. Pahīnatāya eva somanassahetubhūtā, avikkhepahetubhūtā ca na domanassaṃ, uddhaccañca uppādentīti na te tesaṃ ārammaṇaārammaṇādhipatibhāvaṃ, pakatūpanissayabhāvañca gacchanti. Na hi pahīne upanissāya ariyo rāgādikilese uppādeti.

The statement, “Just as the volition of direct knowledge is not, so too the volition of restlessness is not,” should be investigated by setting apart the states accompanied by restlessness, since it is said: “Knowledge in their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning” (Vibh 725). But that investigation has already been conducted below in the commentary on the Exposition of the Aggregates, in the Discourse on the Unwholesome, so it should be understood in the way it was investigated there. Moreover, here some, making a distinction, say that for those worldlings and trainees for whom vision and development are yet to be accomplished, even in their absence, at the time of the arising of those paths, the unwholesome states that could be abandoned by them are called ‘to be abandoned by vision’ and ‘to be abandoned by development.’ But for worldlings, since there is no development, there is no consideration of what is to be abandoned by development. Therefore, for them, occurring states that cannot be abandoned by vision are not called ‘to be abandoned by development.’ If they were so called, would states to be abandoned by vision be a condition for some states to be abandoned by development at some time by way of object, object-dominance, or decisive support conditions? And in the Paṭṭhāna it is not said that states to be abandoned by vision are a condition for states to be abandoned by development by any condition. For trainees, however, since the existing unwholesome states can be abandoned by development, they are called ‘to be abandoned by development.’ For that very reason, for trainees, states to be abandoned by vision are not to be savored or delighted in, because they have been given up, vomited out, released, abandoned, relinquished, eradicated, and utterly eradicated. Precisely because they have been abandoned, being a cause for gladness and a cause for non-distraction, they do not produce displeasure and restlessness. Therefore, they do not attain the state of being an object, object-dominance, or natural decisive support condition for those other states. For a noble one does not generate defilements such as lust by depending on what has been abandoned.

Vuttañhetaṃ “sotāpattimaggena ye kilesā pahīnā, te kilese na puneti na pacceti na paccāgacchati…pe… arahattamaggena…pe… paccāgacchatī”ti (mahāni. 80; cūḷani. mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddesa 27). Na ca puthujjanānaṃ dassanena pahātuṃ sakkuṇeyyā, itaresaṃ na kenaci paccayena paccayo hontīti na sakkā vattuṃ “diṭṭhiṃ assādeti abhinandati, taṃ ārabbha rāgo uppajjati, diṭṭhi, vicikicchā, uddhaccaṃ uppajjati. Vicikicchaṃ ārabbha vicikicchā[V 2.0245], diṭṭhi, uddhaccaṃ uppajjatī”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.407) diṭṭhivicikicchānaṃ uddhaccārammaṇapaccayabhāvassa vuttattā. Ettha hi uddhaccanti uddhaccasahagatacittuppādaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Evañca katvā adhipatipaccayaniddese “diṭṭhiṃ garuṃ katvā assādeti abhinandati, taṃ garuṃ katvā rāgo uppajjati, diṭṭhi uppajjatī”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.415) ettakameva [M 2.0261] vuttaṃ, na vuttaṃ “uddhaccaṃ uppajjatī”ti. Tasmā dassanabhāvanāhi pahātabbānaṃ atītādibhāvena na vattabbattepi yādisānaṃ tāhi anuppattidhammatā āpādetabbā, tesu puthujjanesu vattamānā dassanaṃ apekkhitvā tena pahātuṃ sakkuṇeyyā dassanena pahātabbā, sekkhesu vattamānā bhāvanaṃ apekkhitvā tāya pahātuṃ sakkuṇeyyā bhāvanāya pahātabbā.

For this has been said: “He does not return to, does not revert to, does not come back to those defilements that have been abandoned by the path of stream-entry... (and so on up to) ... by the path of arahantship... does not come back” (MNi 80; CNi 27). And it cannot be said that for worldlings, states that could be abandoned by vision are not a condition for other states by any condition whatsoever, because it is said: “He savors and delights in a view; taking that as object, lust arises; a view, doubt, and restlessness arise. Taking doubt as object, doubt, a view, and restlessness arise” (Paṭṭh 1.1.407), for it has been stated that views and doubt have the status of object-condition for restlessness. Here, ‘restlessness’ is said with reference to a consciousness-moment accompanied by restlessness. This being so, in the exposition of the dominance condition, only this much is said: “Having made a view weighty, he savors and delights in it; having made that weighty, lust arises, a view arises” (Paṭṭh 1.1.415); it is not said, “restlessness arises.” Therefore, although states to be abandoned by vision and development cannot be spoken of in terms of being past, etc., for those for whom the state of non-arising is to be brought about by these, among them, the present states in worldlings that can be abandoned by vision are called ‘to be abandoned by vision’ in anticipation of that future vision; and the present states in trainees that can be abandoned by development are called ‘to be abandoned by development’ in anticipation of that future development.

Tesu bhāvanāya pahātabbā sahāyavirahā vipākaṃ na janayantīti bhāvanāya pahātabbacetanāya nānākkhaṇikakammapaccayabhāvo na vutto, apekkhitabbadassanabhāvanārahitānaṃ pana puthujjanesu uppajjamānānaṃ sakabhaṇḍe chandarāgādīnaṃ, uddhaccasahagatacittuppādassa ca saṃyojanattayatadekaṭṭhakilesānaṃ anupacchinnatāya aparikkhīṇasahāyānaṃ vipākuppādanaṃ na sakkā paṭisedhitunti uddhaccasahagatadhammānaṃ vipāko vibhaṅge vutto. Yadi evaṃ, apekkhitabbadassanabhāvanārahitānaṃ akusalānaṃ nevadassanena-nabhāvanāyapahātabbatāya navattabbatā āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati, appahātabbānaṃ “nevadassanena-nabhāvanāya pahātabbā”ti (dha. sa. tikamātikā 9) vuttattā, appahātabbaviruddhasabhāvattā ca akusalānaṃ.

Among them, states to be abandoned by development, being devoid of allies, do not generate a result; thus the state of being a differently-momented kamma condition for a volition to be abandoned by development is not stated. However, for worldlings devoid of the vision and development that are to be regarded, since the three fetters and the defilements that have the same basis have not been cut off, their allies are not exhausted, and thus the production of a result by desire and lust, etc., for one's own belongings and by the arising of consciousness accompanied by restlessness cannot be denied. Thus the result of states accompanied by restlessness is stated in the Vibhaṅga. If so, does it follow that for the unwholesome states of those devoid of the vision and development that are to be regarded, they are to be stated as 'to be abandoned neither by vision nor by development'? It does not follow, because it is said of states that are not to be abandoned, 'to be abandoned neither by vision nor by development,' and because the nature of unwholesome states is contrary to that which is not to be abandoned.

Evampi te imasmiṃ tike “navattabbā”ti vattabbā āpajjantīti? Nāpajjanti, cittuppādakaṇḍe dassitānaṃ dvādasaakusalacittuppādānaṃ dvīhi padehi saṅgahitattā. Yathā hi dhammavasena sabbe saṅkhatadhammā saṅgahitāti uppannattike kālavasena asaṅgahitāpi atītā “navattabbā”ti na vuttā cittuppādarūpabhāvena gahitesu navattabbassa abhāvā, evamidhāpi cittuppādabhāvena gahitesu navattabbassa asaṅgahitassa abhāvā navattabbatā navuttāti veditabbā. Yattha hi cittuppādo koci niyogato navattabbo atthi, tattha tesaṃ catuttho koṭṭhāso atthīti yathāvuttapadesu viya tatthāpi bhinditvā bhajāpetabbacittuppāde bhinditvā bhajāpeti “siyā navattabbā parittārammaṇā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1422). Tadabhāvā uppannattike, idha ca tathā na vuttā.

Even so, does it follow that they should be called 'not to be stated' in this triad? It does not follow, because the twelve unwholesome arisings of consciousness shown in the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness are included under the two terms. For just as in the triad on the arisen, because all conditioned states are included by way of states, past states, though not included by way of time, are not called 'not to be stated' because among things taken as arisings of consciousness and material form, there is nothing that is 'not to be stated.' So too here, it should be understood that the category of 'not to be stated' is not mentioned because among those unwholesome states taken as arisings of consciousness, there is nothing unincluded that is 'not to be stated.' For wherever there is any arising of consciousness that is necessarily 'not to be stated,' there is a fourth division for them, and just as in the passages mentioned, there too one analyzes and distributes the arisings of consciousness that are to be analyzed and distributed, saying: 'It may be "not to be stated" with a limited object,' and so on. Due to its absence, it is not stated thus in the triad on the arisen, nor here.

Atha [V 2.0246] vā yathā sappaṭighehi samānasabhāvattā rūpadhātuyaṃ tayo mahābhūtā sappaṭighāti vuttā. Yathāha “asaññasattānaṃ anidassanasappaṭighaṃ ekaṃ mahābhūtaṃ paṭicca dve mahābhūtā, dve mahābhūte paṭicca ekaṃ mahābhūta”nti[M 2.0262], evaṃ puthujjanānaṃ pavattamānā bhāvanāya pahātabbasamānasabhāvā bhāvanāya pahātabbāti vucceyyunti? Natthi navattabbatāpasaṅgo. Evañca sati puthujjanānaṃ pavattamānāpi bhāvanāya pahātabbā sakabhaṇḍe chandarāgādayo parabhaṇḍe chandarāgādīnaṃ upanissayapaccayo, rāgo ca rāgadiṭṭhīnaṃ adhipatipaccayoti ayamattho laddho hoti. Yathā pana aphoṭṭhabbattā rūpadhātuyaṃ tayo mahābhūtā na paramatthato sappaṭighā, evaṃ apekkhitabbabhāvanārahitā puthujjanesu vattamānā sakabhaṇḍe chandarāgādayo na paramatthato bhāvanāya pahātabbāti bhāvanāya pahātabbānaṃ nānākkhaṇikakammapaccayatā na vuttā. Na ca dassanenapahātabbā bhāvanāyapahātabbānaṃ kenaci paccayena paccayoti vuttā. Ye hi dassanena pahātabbapaccayā kilesā, na te dassanato uddhaṃ pavattanti. Dassanena pahātabbapaccayassapi pana uddhaccasahagatassa sahāyavekallamattameva dassanena kataṃ, na tassa koci bhāvo dassanena anuppattidhammataṃ āpāditoti tassa ekantabhāvanāyapahātabbatā vuttā. Tasmā tassa tādisasseva sati sahāye vipākuppādanavacanaṃ, asati ca vipākānuppādanavacanaṃ na virujjhatīti.

Alternatively, just as the three great elements in the form realm are said to be 'resistant' because they have the same nature as resistant things—as it is said: 'For non-percipient beings, dependent on one invisible resistant great element, two great elements arise; dependent on two great elements, one great element arises'—so too, could it be said that states occurring in worldlings, which have the same nature as states to be abandoned by development, are 'to be abandoned by development'? Then there is no occasion for their being 'not to be stated.' And this being so, the meaning is obtained that states to be abandoned by development, such as desire and lust for one's own belongings, even when occurring in worldlings, are a decisive support condition for desire and lust for others' belongings, and that lust is a dominance condition for lust and views. However, just as the three great elements in the form realm are not ultimately resistant because they are intangible, so too, desire and lust for one's own belongings occurring in worldlings, who are devoid of the development that is to be looked for, are not ultimately 'to be abandoned by development.' Therefore, the status of states to be abandoned by development as a differently-momented kamma condition is not stated. Nor is it said that states to be abandoned by vision are a condition for states to be abandoned by development by any condition whatsoever. For those defilements that are conditioned by states to be abandoned by vision do not proceed beyond the path of stream-entry.
