However, for the restlessness-accompanied state, which is also conditioned by states to be abandoned by vision, only the mere lack of an ally is effected by vision; no state of it is brought to the nature of non-arising by vision. Therefore, it is said to be exclusively 'to be abandoned by development.' Thus, for such a state, when an ally exists, the statement about the production of a result is not contradicted; and when it does not exist, the statement about the non-production of a result is not contradicted.

Tayidaṃ sabbaṃ tesaṃ ācariyānaṃ ahopurisikāmattanti apare. Kasmā? Uddhaccasahagatassa ekantena bhāvanāya pahātabbattā. Evañhi vuttaṃ bhagavatā “katame dhammā bhāvanāya pahātabbā? Uddhaccasahagato cittuppādo”ti (dha. sa. 1406). Yadi hi taṃ icchitaṃ siyā, yathā atītārammaṇattike “niyogā anāgatārammaṇā natthī”ti (dha. sa. 1433) vatvā vibhajja vuttaṃ, evamidhāpi “niyogā bhāvanāya pahātabbā natthī”ti vatvā “uddhaccasahagato siyā bhāvanāya pahātabbo, siyā na vattabbo”ti vadeyya. Yā ca taṃ samatthentena “yadi vucceyyu”ntiādinā yutti vuttā, sāpi ayutti. Kasmā? Yasmā dassanena pahātabbārammaṇānaṃ rāgadiṭṭhivicikicchāuddhaccānaṃ dassanena pahātabbabhāvo eva icchitoti. Yaṃ pana uddhaccaggahaṇena pāḷiyaṃ uddhaccasahagato cittuppādo vuttoti vatvā taṃ sādhetuṃ adhipatipaccayaniddese uddhaccassa anuddharaṇaṃ nibandhanaṃ vuttaṃ, tampi anibandhanaṃ paṭṭhāne sāvasesapāṭhadassanato. Tathā hi “atīto dhammo paccuppannassa dhammassa, anāgato dhammo paccuppannassa dhammassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti [M 2.0263] (paṭṭhā. 2.18.2) etesaṃ vibhaṅge cetopariyañāṇaggahaṇaṃ [V 2.0247] katvā “paccuppanno dhammo paccuppannassa dhammassā”ti etassa vibhaṅge labbhamānampi na uddhaṭaṃ.

All this is merely a display of those teachers' manliness, say others. Why? Because the state accompanied by restlessness is to be abandoned exclusively by development. For thus it was said by the Blessed One: “What states are to be abandoned by development? An arising of consciousness accompanied by restlessness.” If that were intended, just as in the triad on past objects it was said after analysis, “There are no necessary future objects,” so here too one would say, “There are no necessary things to be abandoned by development,” and then state, “An arising of consciousness accompanied by restlessness might be one to be abandoned by development, or it might not be said to be so.” And the reasoning stated by those who attempt to prove it, beginning “If it were said…,” is also invalid. Why? Because it is intended that states such as lust, wrong view, doubt, and restlessness—which have as their objects things to be abandoned by vision—are indeed to be abandoned by vision. Moreover, the argument put forward—saying that by the term 'restlessness' in the Pāḷi, an arising of consciousness accompanied by restlessness is meant, and then, to establish this, citing as a binding reason the non-extraction of restlessness in the exposition of the dominance condition—that too is not a binding reason, because the Pāḷi text in the Paṭṭhāna has omissions. For thus, in the analysis of the passages 'A past state is a condition for a present state by way of object condition; a future state is a condition for a present state by way of object condition,' the knowledge of others’ minds is included; yet in the analysis of 'a present state is a condition for a present state,' it is not extracted, though it could be found there.

Bhāvanāya pahātabbassa vipākadānaṃ pati dassanena pahātabbassa sahāyabhāvūpagamanaṃ vicāretabbaṃ. Kiṃ avijjādi viya dānasīlādīnaṃ uppattiyāyeva vipākadānasāmatthiyā ṭhānavasena dassanenapahātabbaṃ bhāvanāyapahātabbassa sahāyabhāvaṃ upagacchati, udāhu kilesā viya kammassa paṭisandhidānaṃ patīti? Kiñcettha – yadi tāva purimo pakkho pahīnadassanappahātabbattā sekkhasantāne pavattino bhāvanāpahātabbassa kiriyabhāvo āpajjati pahīnāvijjātaṇhāmāne santāne pavattadānādi viya. Atha dutiyo, tassāpi dassanenapahātabbatā āpajjati apāyagamanīyasabhāvānativattanato, tasmā heṭṭhā vicāritanayeneva uddhaccasahagatassa vipākadānaṃ pati pāḷiyā, aṭṭhakathāya ca avirujjhanavasenettha atthavinicchayo veditabbo.

It should be investigated how that which is to be abandoned by seeing becomes an accomplice to that which is to be abandoned by cultivation with respect to the giving of fruit. Does that which is to be abandoned by seeing become an accomplice to that which is to be abandoned by cultivation—like ignorance and so on, by way of establishing the capacity for giving, virtue, and so on to give fruit merely upon their arising? Or is it like the defilements with respect to the giving of rebirth-linking by kamma? Herein, there is a further point: if the first alternative is taken, then because that which is to be abandoned by seeing has been abandoned, that which is to be abandoned by cultivation occurring in the continuum of a trainee would attain the state of being functional, just like giving and so on occurring in the continuum of one who has abandoned ignorance, craving, and conceit. But if the second alternative is taken, it too would become something to be abandoned by seeing, as it does not transcend the nature that leads to the planes of misery. Therefore, by the method investigated previously, the determination of the meaning herein concerning the giving of fruit by that which is accompanied by restlessness should be understood in a way that does not conflict with the Pāḷi and the Commentary.

Sāpīti uddhaccacetanāpi. Viññāṇassa paccayabhāveti sampuṇṇassa vipākaviññāṇassa paccayabhāve. Yadi apanetabbā, kasmā “samavīsati cetanā”ti vuttanti tassa kāraṇaṃ dassento āha “avijjāpaccayā pana sabbāpetā hontī”ti. Abhiññācetanāyapi paccayabhāvaṃ dasseti. Yadi evaṃ abhiññācetanāya saha ekavīsatīti vattabbaṃ, na, tathā avacanassa vuttakāraṇattā. Taṃ pana itarāvacanassāpi kāraṇanti samānarūpāya ekissā avacane yaṃ kāraṇaṃ apekkhitvā ekā na vuttā, tena kāraṇena vuttāyapi avattabbataṃ dasseti. Ayaṃ tikoti kāyasaṅkhārattiko. Purimattikanti puññābhisaṅkhārattikaṃ. Pavisatīti kathaṃ pavisati. Puññābhisaṅkhāro hi aṭṭhakāmāvacaracetanāpabhedo kāyaduccaritato viramantassa siyā kāyasaṅkhāro, vacīduccaritato viramantassa siyā vacīsaṅkhāro, manodvāre pana uppannā terasapi cetanā puññābhisaṅkhāro ca hoti cittasaṅkhāro ca. Apuññābhisaṅkhāropi kāyaduccaritavasena pavattiyaṃ siyā kāyasaṅkhāro, vacīduccaritavasena pavattiyaṃ siyā vacīsaṅkhāro, dve dvārāni muñcitvā manodvāre pavattiyaṃ siyā cittasaṅkhāro, āneñjābhisaṅkhāro cāti evaṃ dutiyattiko purimattikameva [M 2.0264] pavisati. Tena vuttaṃ “atthato puññābhisaṅkhārādīnaṃyeva vasena avijjāya paccayabhāvo veditabbo”ti.

“That also” means the volition of restlessness also. “In the state of being a condition for consciousness” means: in the state of being a condition for the resultant consciousness that is complete by way of rebirth-linking and the course of existence. If this volition is to be excluded, why is it said, “There are twenty volitions”? To explain the reason for this, it is stated: “But with ignorance as condition, all of them are.” This also shows the conditioning role of the volition of direct knowledge. If so, it should be said, “There are twenty-one,” including the volition of direct knowledge. No, because of the stated reason for its omission. That, however, is also the reason for not mentioning the other; for, having regard to the reason why one of a similar nature was not mentioned, it shows by that same reason that even the one that was mentioned should not have been mentioned. “This triad” is the triad of bodily formations. “The previous triad” is the triad of meritorious formations. Regarding “it enters,” how does it enter? The meritorious formation, a division of the eight sense-sphere volitions, may be a bodily formation for one who abstains from bodily misconduct, and a verbal formation for one who abstains from verbal misconduct; but the thirteen volitions that arise at the mind-door are both meritorious formation and mental formation. The demeritorious formation also, when occurring by way of bodily misconduct, may be a bodily formation; when occurring by way of verbal misconduct, it may be a verbal formation; and having left aside the two doors, when occurring at the mind-door, it may be a mental formation. The imperturbable formation is only a mental formation. Thus, the second triad enters right into the first triad itself. Therefore, it is said: “In meaning, the conditioning role of ignorance should be understood by way of the meritorious formations and so on themselves.”

593. Avijjābhāve [V 2.0248] bhāvatoti avijjāya atthibhāve saṅkhārānaṃ bhāvato. Na hi avijjāya asati kadāci saṅkhārā sambhavanti. Idāni taṃ avijjāya bhāvaṃ dassento “aññāṇaṃ appahīnaṃ hotī”ti āha. Tena maggena anirodho idha avijjāya atthibhāvo, na dharamānatā evāti dasseti. Svāyamattho heṭṭhā vibhāvitoyeva. “Avijjāsaṅkhāta”nti ca iminā ñāṇābhāvādiṃ nivatteti. Ayañhi a-kāro “ahetukā dhammā (dha. sa. dukamātikā 2) abhikkhuko āvāso”tiādīsu (cūḷava. 76) taṃyoganivattiyaṃ dissati. Abhāvo hettha dīpito. “Appaccayā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. dukamātikā 7) taṃsambandhitānivattiyaṃ. Paccayuppannañhi paccayasambandhīti appaccayuppannattāti taṃsambandhitā ettha jotīyati. “Anidassanā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. dukamātikā 9) taṃsabhāvanivattiyaṃ. Nidassanañhi daṭṭhabbatā. Atha cakkhuviññāṇaṃ nidassanaṃ na passatīti taggahetabbatānivattiyaṃ. Tathā “anāsavā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. dukamātikā 15). “Appaṭighā dhammā (dha. sa. dukamātikā 10), anārammaṇā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. dukamātikā 55) taṃkiccanivattiyaṃ. “Arūpino dhammā (dha. sa. tikamātikā 11), acetasikā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. dukamātikā 57) tabbhāvanivattiyaṃ. Tadaññathā hi ettha pakāsīyati. “Amanusso”ti (dī. ni. 2.321) tabbhāvamattanivattiyaṃ. Manussattamattaṃ natthi, aññaṃ samānanti sadisatā hettha sūcīyati. “Assamaṇo samaṇapaṭiñño (a. ni. 3.13, 27; pu. pa. 91, 124), aputto”ti tathā sambhāvanīyaguṇanivattiyaṃ. Garahā hi ettha ñāyati. “Kacci bhoto anāmayaṃ (jā. 1.15.146; 2.20.129), anudarā kaññā”ti tadanappabhāvanivattiyaṃ. “Anuppannā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. tikamātikā 17) taṃsadisabhāvanivattiyaṃ. Atītānañhi uppannapubbattā, uppādidhammānañca paccayekadesanibbattiyā āraddhuppādabhāvā, kālavinimuttassa ca vijjamānattā uppannānukūlatā, pageva paccuppannānanti tabbidhurabhāvo ettha viññāyati. “Asekkhā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. tikamātikā 11) tadapariyosānanivattiyaṃ. Tanniṭṭhānañhettha pakāsīyati. Imesaṃ pana atthānaṃ asambhavato pārisesena yathā kusalapaṭipakkhā dhammā akusalā, evaṃ vijjāpaṭipakkhā avijjāti katvā ñāṇapaṭipakkho dhammo aññāṇanti veditabbaṃ.

593. “From the being of ignorance, there is being” means that from the existence of ignorance, there is the being of formations. For when ignorance is absent, formations never arise. Now, showing the existence of that ignorance, he says: “Non-knowledge is not abandoned.” By that, he shows that here the existence of ignorance is its non-cessation by the path, not merely its persistence. This meaning has already been explained above. And by the term “designated as ignorance,” he excludes such meanings as the absence of knowledge. For this prefix “a-” is seen in the sense of negating connection with something, as in “causeless states” and “a residence without bhikkhus.” Here absence is shown. In “states without a condition,” it negates relation to that. For what has arisen from a condition is related to a condition; therefore, because these states have not arisen from a condition, the state of not being related to that condition is illuminated here. In “invisible states,” it negates the nature of that. For `nidassana` is the state of being visible. Or, eye-consciousness is `nidassana` because it sees; in that case, `anidassana` is in the sense of negating the state of being graspable by that eye-consciousness. Similarly in “taintless states.” In “non-impinging states” and “objectless states,” it negates the function of that. In “immaterial states” and “states not associated with the mental,” it negates the state of being that. For here the state of being other than that is clarified. In “non-human,” it negates just the state of being that. Just the state of being human is absent; other aspects are the same. Thus, similarity is indicated here. In “not a recluse, though claiming to be one” and “sonless,” it negates a quality that should be esteemed in that way. For here censure is understood. In “Are you well?” and “a slender-waisted maiden,” it negates an abundance of that. In “unarisen states,” it negates being of a similar state. For past states, because they have arisen previously, and states that are bound to arise, because their arising has been initiated by the completion of a part of their condition, and the timeless Nibbāna, because of its existence, have a conformity with the arisen—how much more so present states. Therefore, the state of being dissimilar to that arisen state is understood here. In “states of one beyond training,” it negates the non-completion of it. For here its completion is clarified. But since these meanings are impossible here, by the method of elimination, just as unwholesome states are the opposite of wholesome states, so having construed that ignorance is the opposite of knowledge, it should be understood that non-knowledge is the state that is the opposite of knowledge.

Sukhasaññāya [M 2.0265] gahetvā dukkhadukkhavipariṇāmadukkhasaṅkhāradukkhatāhi viññūhi dukkhantveva gahetabbaṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ sukhanti saññāya abhinivisitvā, etena tattha taṇhāpavattiṃ dasseti. Ārabhatīti [V 2.0249] nibbatteti. Taṇhāparikkhāreti taṇhāya “sukhaṃ subha”ntiādinā saṅkhate parikkhate, alaṅkateti attho. Taṇhā hi dukkhassa samudayoti ajānanto bālo “aho vatāhaṃ kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā khattiyamahāsālānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjeyya”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 1.442) paritassanto kāyasaṅkhāre parikkharoti. Taṇhāparikkhāreti vā taṇhāya parivārabhūte. Taṇhāvatthuṃ hi cakkhādiṃ, rūpādiñca abhisaṅkharitvā taṃsamaṅgīnaṃ dentā saṅkharā taṇhāya upanentā tassā parivārā viya hontīti. Gativisese brahmalokādike. Anekasatapasubaddhabhiṃsano vājapeyyādiko yañño. Amaraṇatthāti gahitā dukkarakiriyā amaratapo. Amaro vā devo vā bhaveyyaṃ, devaññataro vāti pavattitā vatacariyā amaratapo. Dukkhattā vā maro mārako tapo amaratapo. Diṭṭhe adiṭṭhasaddo viya mare amarasaddo daṭṭhabbo.

By firmly adhering with the perception of pleasure to the suffering of saṃsāra as 'pleasure'—which should be understood by the wise only as suffering, by way of being suffering as pain, suffering as change, and suffering as conditioned formations—by this, it shows the occurrence of craving therein. Ārabhati means it generates. Taṇhāparikkhāre means fashioned, prepared, and adorned by craving with notions like “pleasure,” “beauty,” and so on; this is the meaning. Indeed, the foolish person, not knowing that craving is the origin of suffering, yearning with thoughts such as, “Oh, how wonderful it would be if, after the breakup of the body, after death, I were to be reborn into the companionship of wealthy Khattiya nobles!”, fashions the three kinds of formations by means of that craving. Alternatively, taṇhāparikkhāre means being the retinue of craving. Indeed, having specially fashioned the bases of craving, such as the eye, and its objects, such as forms, the formations, by giving these to persons endowed with that craving and bringing them to craving, are like the retinue of that craving. Thus it should be known. In special destinies, such as the brahma worlds. The Vājapeyya sacrifice and so on, which is terrifying by the binding of many hundreds of animals, is called a sacrifice. Amaraṇatthā means for the sake of deathlessness; the difficult practice undertaken is the “deathless austerity.” The practice of vows undertaken with the thought, “May I be a deathless one or a deva or some other kind of deva,” is the “deathless austerity.” Alternatively, because it is suffering, the austerity is a killer; hence it is called “deathless austerity” by irony. Just as the word 'unseen' is used in the sense of 'seen', so the word 'deathless' should be understood in the sense of 'killer'.

Jātiādipapātadukkhajananato maruppapātasadisatā puññābhisaṅkhārassa vuttā. “Mahāpariḷāhajanika”nti iminā anudahanaṭṭhena tiṇukkāsadisataṃ puññaphalassa dasseti. Appassādatañcāti ca-saddena adhikuṭṭanavinivijjhanaaṅgapaccaṅgapalibhañjanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tappaccayanti tassa vipariṇāmadukkhasabhāvassa sugatiphalassa paccayabhūtaṃ. Ramaṇīyabhāvena ca assādabhāvena ca gayhamānaṃ puññaphalaṃ dīpasikhāmadhulittasatthadhārāsadisaṃ. Tadattho ca puññābhisaṅkhāro taṃnipātalehanasadiso vutto. “Sukho imissā paribbājikāya taruṇāya mudukāya lomasāya bāhāya samphasso”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.469) sukhasaññāya asubhabhāvassa asallakkhaṇeneva ekaccakāmaparibhogoti bālo viya gūthakīḷanaṃ, kilesābhibhūtatāya kodhāratiabhibhūto asavaso maritukāmo viya visakhādanaṃ sampati kiriyākhaṇe, āyatiṃ phalakkhaṇe ca jigucchanīyaṃ, dukkhañca apuññābhisaṅkhāraṃ ārabhati. Lobhasahagatassa vā gūthakīḷanasadisatā, dosasahagatassa visakhādanasadisatā yojetabbā. Sabhayassāpi pisācanagarassa kāmaguṇasamiddhiyā sukhavipallāsahetubhāvo viya āruppavipākānaṃ [M 2.0266] nirantaratāya, anupalakkhiyamānauppādavayānaṃ dīghasantānatāya agayhamānavipariṇāmānaṃ saṅkhāravipariṇāmadukkhabhūtānampi niccādivipallāsahetubhāvoti, tesaṃ pisācanagarasadisatā, tadabhimukhagamanasadisatā ca āneñjābhisaṅkhārassa yojetabbā.

The meritorious formation is said to be like falling from a mountain precipice because it generates the suffering of the fall into birth and so on. By the words 'It generates a great blaze,' it shows, in the sense of burning in succession, that the fruit of merit is like a grass torch. And by the word 'ca' in the phrase 'and little gratification,' it includes chopping on a block, piercing, the breaking of major and minor limbs, and so on. 'Because of that' means being a condition for that fruit of a happy destination, which has the nature of suffering due to change. The fruit of merit, being grasped because of its delightfulness and its gratifying nature, is like the flame of a lamp and the honey-smeared edge of a sword. And the meritorious formation undertaken for its sake is said to be like falling into that flame and licking that sword's edge. By not perceiving the repulsive nature through the perception of pleasure, as in the passage beginning, 'Pleasant is the touch of this young, tender, soft-haired female wanderer’s arm,' one indulges in some sensual pleasure like a fool playing with excrement. Or, overcome by defilements, overwhelmed by anger and discontent, one who is powerless and wishes to die eats poison. Thus one undertakes an unmeritorious formation, which is disgusting and painful both now at the moment of action and in the future at the moment of the result. The similarity to playing with excrement should be applied to what is accompanied by greed, and the similarity to eating poison to what is accompanied by hatred. Just as a city of goblins, although frightening, is a cause for the perversion of happiness due to its abundance of sensual pleasures, so too, the formless results—because of their uninterruptedness, the long continuity of their imperceptible arising and passing away, and their ungraspable change, even though they are suffering inherent in formations and suffering due to change—are a cause for the perversions of permanence, etc. Thus, their similarity to a city of goblins, and the similarity of heading towards it, should be applied to the imperturbable formation.

Avijjābhāvatova saṅkhārabhāvo, na abhāvatoti saṅkhārānaṃ avijjāpaccayabhāve saṅkhepena anvayato, byatirekato ca vuttamatthaṃ suttena samatthetuṃ “vuttampi ceta”ntiādinā suttapadaṃ ābhataṃ[V 2.0250]. Tattha avidvāti aviddasu. Avijjāgatoti avijjāya samannāgato, appahīnāvijjoti adhippāyo.

The existence of formations is only due to the existence of ignorance, not to its non-existence. To support with a sutta the meaning that has been stated concisely—in terms of presence and absence—about formations having ignorance as their condition, the sutta passage beginning, 'And this was said...' is adduced. Therein, 'one who does not know' means an unwise person. 'One who has come to be in ignorance' means one who is endowed with ignorance; the intended meaning is 'one whose ignorance has not been abandoned'.

Paṭṭhānapaccayakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on Conditional Relations

594. Tāvāti vattabbantarāpekkho nipāto, tena “avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo”ti idaṃ tāva siddhaṃ, idaṃ pana aparaṃ vattabbanti dasseti. “Idaṃ pana vattabba”nti yamatthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ paccayadhammā nāma yesaṃ paccayā honti, yathā vā paccayā honti, tadubhayesaṃ bahubhāvato anekadhāva paccayā hontīti avijjāyapi taṃ āsaṅkanto pucchi “katamesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ kathaṃ paccayo hotī”ti, puññābhisaṅkhārādayo bahū saṅkhārā vuttā. Avijjā ca tesaṃ paccayo hoti, na sabbesaṃ ekadhāva hoti, tasmā imesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ evaṃ paccayo hotīti idaṃ vattabbanti attho. Tatrāti tasmiṃ paccayabhāve. Yadipi “katamesaṃ saṅkhārāna”ntiādinā asādhāraṇato pucchā āraddhā, ekadesena pana samudāyopalakkhaṇametanti dvādasannaṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṅgānaṃ yathāsakaṃ paccayuppannānaṃ paccayabhāvo vattabboti taṃ dassetuṃ, avijjāya vā paccayabhāve pucchite tappasaṅgena sabbesampi paccayadhammānaṃ paccayabhāvaṃ visajjetukāmo paccaye tāva pāḷinayeneva dassetuṃ “bhagavatā hī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha ca bhagavatā catuvīsati paccayā vuttāti sambandho. Tesaṃ vasena avijjādīnaṃ paccayabhāvo veditabboti adhippāyo.

594. The particle `tāva` looks forward to another statement. Thus it shows that the statement 'ignorance is a condition for formations' is established for now, but something more is to be said. To show what is meant by 'But this is to be said': Conditioning states are conditions for certain conditioned states, and they are conditions in certain ways. Due to the multiplicity of both of these—the conditioned states and the modes of conditioning—they are conditions in many ways. Suspecting this also in the case of ignorance, one asks: 'For which formations and how is it a condition?' Many formations have been mentioned, such as meritorious formations. And ignorance is a condition for them, but it is not a condition for all of them in the same way. Therefore, the meaning is that this should be stated: 'It is a condition for these formations in this way.' 'Therein' means in that state of being a condition. Although the question beginning 'For which formations…' is posed in a specific way, it is a designation of the whole by way of a part. Thus, to show that the conditional relation for each of the twelve links of dependent origination with their respective conditioned phenomena should be stated, or because, when the conditional nature of ignorance is asked about, he wishes to explain the conditional nature of all conditioning states in that connection, he begins with 'For by the Blessed One…' in order to first set forth the conditions according to the method of the Pāḷi. And therein, the connection is that the Blessed One has spoken of twenty-four conditions. The intended meaning is that the conditional nature of ignorance and the other factors should be understood by way of these.

“Hetu ca so paccayo cā”ti iminā vacanena hetuno, adhipatipaccayādibhūtassa ca gahaṇaṃ siyāti taṃ nivārento āha “hetu hutvā paccayo”ti. Evampi so eva doso āpajjatīti puna āha “hetubhāvena paccayoti vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Tena na idha hetusaddena dhammaggahaṇaṃ [M 2.0267] kataṃ, atha kho dhammassa sattiviseso gahitoti dasseti. Tassa hi paccayasaddassa ca samānādhikaraṇataṃ sandhāya “hetu ca so paccayo ca, hetu hutvā paccayo”ti ca vuttaṃ. Evañca katvā parato pāḷiyaṃ “hetū hetu…pe… hetupaccayena paccayo”tiādinā (paṭṭhā. 1.1.1) tena tena hetubhāvādiupakārena tassa tassa dhammassa upakārakattaṃ vuttaṃ. Abhidhammaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “yo hi dhammo yaṃ dhammaṃ appaccakkhāya tiṭṭhati vā uppajjati vā, so tassa paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. aṭṭha. paccayuddesavaṇṇanā), “mūlaṭṭhena upakārako dhammo hetupaccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. aṭṭha. paccayuddesavaṇṇanā) ca evamādinā dhammapaṭṭhānaniddesena [V 2.0251] dhammato aññā dhammasatti nāma natthīti dhammeheva dhammasattivibhāvanaṃ katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Idhāpi vā “hetu ca so paccayo cā”ti dhammeneva dhammasattiṃ dasseti. Na hi “hetupaccayo”tiādiko uddeso kusalādiuddeso viya dhammappadhāno, atha kho dhammānaṃ upakārakabhāvappadhānoti.

With the statement, 'It is a root and it is a condition,' one might take this to mean the root as well as what has become the predominance condition, etc. To prevent this, he says, 'Being a root, it is a condition.' Since even with this the same fault arises, he says further, 'It is said to be a condition by way of being a root.' He thereby shows that here the word 'root' does not signify a state, but rather a specific power of a state is signified. For it is with reference to the co-referentiality of that word 'root' and the word 'condition' that it is said, 'It is a root and it is a condition' and 'Being a root, it is a condition.' And so, later in the Pāḷi, in the passage beginning, 'Roots as root… by way of root condition,' the supportive nature of a particular state is stated in terms of its particular way of being a supportive root, etc. But in the Abhidhamma Commentary it should be understood that by such an exposition in which the states are primary, as in 'Whatever state, without being absent, persists or arises for another state, is a condition for it' and 'A state that is supportive in the sense of a root is a root condition,' the clarification of the powers of states is made by means of the states themselves, since there is no such thing as a 'power of a state' separate from the state itself. Alternatively, here too, by 'It is a root and it is a condition,' he shows the power of a state by means of the state itself. For the enumeration beginning 'root condition' is not, like the enumeration 'wholesome, etc.,' one where the states are primary; rather, it is one where the supportive nature of the states is primary.

“Eseva nayo”ti iminā tabbhāvena paccayabhāvaṃ ārammaṇādīsu atidisati “ārammaṇañca taṃ paccayo cāti ārammaṇapaccayo, ārammaṇaṃ hutvā paccayo, ārammaṇabhāvena paccayoti attho”ti, na kammadhārayamattaṃ.

By 'This is the same method,' he extends the principle of being a condition in that same way to the object condition and the others, thus: 'It is an object and it is a condition, thus object condition; being an object, it is a condition; the meaning is, a condition by way of being an object.' It is not merely a descriptive determinative compound.

595. Vacanāvayavoti sādhanāvayavaṃ sandhāyāha. Vacanasabhāvañhi sādhanaṃ paresaṃ aviditatthañāpanato loke sādhananti pākaṭaṃ paññātaṃ. Tathā hi naṃ avayavalakkhaṇaṃ, vacanasabhāvañca sādhanaṃ, avayavapakkhādīni vacanāni sādhananti ca ñāyavādino vadanti. Paṭiññā, hetūtiādīsūti paṭiññā, hetu, udāharaṇa, upanaya, nigamanāni. Udāharaṇasādhammiyā sādhyasādhanaṃ hetu. Virūpo hetūti ca evamādīsu kāraṇaṃ yaṃ kiñci kāraṇalakkhaṇaṃ, sampāpakalakkhaṇampi vā. Ādi-saddena tassāpi saṅgahetabbatāya, ñāpakalakkhaṇaṃ pana vacanāvayavaggahaṇena gahitaṃ. Kāmaṃ mūlampi kāraṇalakkhaṇaṃ kāraṇameva, kāraṇanti panettha paccayahetu gahito. Mūlanti hetuhetūti kāraṇavisesavisayattā mūlassa visuṃ gahaṇaṃ. Etīti etassa atthavacanaṃ vattatīti, tañca uppattiṭṭhitīnaṃ sādhāraṇavacanaṃ. Tenevāha “tiṭṭhati vā uppajjati vā”ti. Ekacco hi paccayo ṭhitiyā eva upakārako hoti yathā pacchājātapaccayo, ekacco [M 2.0268] uppattiyā eva yathā anantarādiko, ekacco ubhayassa yathā hetuādayo.

595. 'Component of a statement' refers to a component of a proof. For the nature of speech is a proof, since it makes known to others a meaning they did not know; thus in the world it is widely known as a 'proof' (sādhana). For so the proponents of logic say that a proof has the characteristic of a component and the nature of speech, and that statements which are components—the thesis, etc.—are proofs. In 'proposition, reason, etc.' are included the proposition, reason, example, application, and conclusion. The reason is the proof of the thesis by its similarity with the example. And in such cases as 'the reason is dissimilar,' 'cause' (kāraṇa) means anything with the characteristic of a cause, or also with the characteristic of bringing to attainment, since this latter should also be included by the word 'etc.' (ādi). The characteristic of making known, however, is included by the term 'component of a statement.' Although the root (mūla) too has the characteristic of a cause and is a cause, here by 'cause' (kāraṇa) a conditioning cause (paccayahetu) is meant. The root is mentioned separately because it pertains to a specific kind of cause, the root-cause (hetuhetu). The meaning of 'eti' is 'it proceeds,' and this is a term common to arising and persisting. Therefore he says, 'it persists or it arises.' For one kind of condition is supportive only of persistence, like the postnascence condition; one is supportive only of arising, like the contiguity condition, etc.; and one is supportive of both, like the root condition, etc.

Upakārakalakkhaṇoti ca dhammena dhammasattiṃ upakāraṃ dassetīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Hinoti patiṭṭhāti etthāti hetu, anekatthattā dhātusaddānaṃ hi-saddo mūlasaddo viya patiṭṭhattho veditabbo. Hinoti vā etena kammanidānabhūtena uddhaṃ ojaṃ atiharantena mūlena viya pādapo tappaccayaṃ phalaṃ gacchati pavattati vuddhiṃ viruḷhiṃ āpajjatīti hetu. Attano phalaṃ karotīti kāraṇaṃ. Nidadāti dassentaṃ viya hotīti nidānaṃ. Sambhavati taṃ etasmāti sambhavo. Pabhavati etasmāti pabhavoti paccayahetusaddehi itaresampi samānatthatā veditabbā. Evaṃ santepi kāraṇavisesavisayo [V 2.0252] hetusaddo, kāraṇasāmaññavisayo paccayasaddoti dassento “mūlaṭṭhenā”tiādimāha. Hetuattho, paccayaṭṭho ca heṭṭhā papañcavasena vuttoti taṃ saṅkhippaṃ dassento āha “saṅkhepato…pe… hetupaccayo”ti.

And by 'having the characteristic of being supportive,' it should be understood that it shows the support, which is the power of a state, by means of the state itself. 'Hinoti,' it is established in this, thus 'hetu'; because verbal roots have many meanings, the root 'hi' should be understood in the sense of 'establishment,' like the word 'mūla.' Or, 'hinoti' (it proceeds); by means of this, the fruit dependent on it proceeds—attaining growth and development—just as a tree does by means of a root which is the cause of its actions and carries nutriment upwards; thus 'hetu.' It makes ('karoti') its own fruit, thus 'kāraṇa' (cause). It is as if it lays down ('nidadāti') or shows, thus 'nidāna' (source). From this ('etasmā') it well comes to be ('sambhavati'), thus 'sambhava' (origin). From this it originates ('pabhavati'), thus 'pabhava' (source). The other terms should be understood to have a similar meaning to the words 'paccaya' and 'hetu.' Even so, showing that the word 'hetu' pertains to a specific cause, while the word 'paccaya' pertains to a general cause, he says, 'in the sense of a root,' etc. Because the meaning of 'hetu' and the meaning of 'paccaya' have been stated previously in detail, showing this in brief, he says, 'In brief… root condition'.

Yathā sālivīhibījādīni taṃtaṃosadhīnaṃ sālivīhiādibhāvassa sādhakāni, maṇiādippabhāvatthūni ca nīlādivaṇṇāni nīlādippabhāsādhakāni, evaṃ hetupaccayo yathārahaṃ attanā sampayuttadhammānaṃ kusalādibhāvassa sādhakoti imamatthaṃ dasseti “so sāliādīna”ntiādinā. Ācariyānanti ca revatācariyaṃ sandhāyāha. Evaṃ santeti hetupaccayo yadi kusalādibhāvasādhako, evaṃ sati. Na sampajjati na sijjhati. Yathā kusalākusalahetu taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpassa kusalākusalabhāvāya na pariyatto, evaṃ abyākatopi hetu taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpassa abyākatabhāvāya. Sabhāveneva hi taṃ abyākatanti āha “na hi so tesaṃ kusalādibhāvaṃ sādhetī”ti. Hetupaccayo ca tesaṃ hotiyevāti āha “na ca paccayo na hotī”ti. Idāni tamatthaṃ pāḷiyā samatthetuṃ “vuttañheta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Vinā etenāti etena hetunā abyākatabhāvasādhakena vinā ahetukattā, abyākatabhāvo siddho sabhāvenevāti adhippāyo.

Just as seeds of fine rice, coarse grain, and so on are producers of the state of being fine rice, coarse grain, and so on for their respective annual plants, and just as bases of radiance such as gems, and objects of blue and other colors, are producers of blue and other radiances, so the root condition, as is appropriate, is the producer of the wholesome or other nature of the states associated with it—this meaning is shown by the phrase 'like rice, etc.' and so on. And by 'of the teachers,' he refers to the Elder Revata. 'This being so' means: if the root condition is the producer of the wholesome or other nature, this being the case, 'it does not succeed,' it is not accomplished. Just as a wholesome or unwholesome root is not sufficient to bring about the wholesome or unwholesome nature of the materiality co-arisen with it, so too an indeterminate root is not sufficient to bring about the indeterminate nature of the materiality co-arisen with it. For that is indeterminate by its own nature—thus he says: 'For it does not produce their wholesome or other nature.' And a root condition does exist for them—thus he says: 'And it is not that it is not a condition.' Now, to support that meaning with the Pāḷi, what begins 'For this has been said' is stated. 'Without this' means: without this root that produces the indeterminate nature, because it is rootless, the indeterminate nature is established by its own nature—this is the intention.

“Yoniso, bhikkhave, manasi karoto anuppannā ceva kusalā dhammā uppajjanti, uppannā ca kusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhantī”tiādi (a. ni. 1.67) vacanehi kusalabhāvassa [M 2.0269] yonisomanasikārappaṭibaddhatā siddhāti āha “yonisomanasikārappaṭibaddho kusalabhāvo”ti. Eteneva akusalaabyākatabhāvāpi kusalabhāvo viya na hetupaṭibaddhāti dassitaṃ hoti. Yaṃ paneke maññeyyuṃ “ahetukahetussa akusalabhāvo viya sahetukahetūnampi sabhāvatova kusalādibhāvo, aññesaṃ taṃsampayuttānaṃ hetupaṭibaddho”ti, tassa uttaraṃ vattuṃ “yadi cā”tiādimāha. Alobho kusalo vā siyā abyākato vāti yadi alobho sabhāvato kusalo, so kusalasabhāvattā abyākato na siyā. Atha abyākato taṃsabhāvattā kusalo na siyā alobhasabhāvassa adosattābhāvo viya. Yasmā pana ubhayathāpi hoti, tasmā yathā ubhayathā hontesu saddhādīsu sampayuttesu hetupaṭibaddhaṃ kusalādibhāvaṃ pariyesetha, na sabhāvato, evaṃ hetūsupi kusalāditā aññapaṭibaddhā pariyesitabbā, na sabhāvatoti yaṃ vuttaṃ “sampayuttahetūsu sabhāvatova kusalādibhāvo”ti, taṃ na yujjati. Sā pana pariyesiyamānā yonisomanasikārādipaṭibaddhā [V 2.0253] hotīti hetūsu viya sampayuttesupi yonisomanasikārādipaṭibaddho kusalādibhāvo, na hetupaṭibaddhoti siddhaṃ hotīti adhippāyo.

By such words as, 'O bhikkhus, for one who attends wisely, unarisen wholesome states arise, and arisen wholesome states increase' (AN 1.67), the dependence of the wholesome state on wise attention is established. Thus he says: 'The wholesome state is dependent on wise attention.' By this it is shown that the states of being unwholesome and indeterminate, like the state of being wholesome, are not dependent on the roots. As to what some might think—'Just as the unwholesome state of a rootless root is from its own nature, so too for roots accompanied by other roots, their wholesome or other state is from their own nature, while for other associated factors, it is dependent on the roots'—to answer this, he states what begins 'And if…' 'Non-greed might be wholesome or indeterminate' means: if non-greed is wholesome by its own nature, then because of its wholesome nature it could not be indeterminate. Or if it were indeterminate, because of that nature it could not be wholesome, just as the nature of non-greed is not the state of being non-hatred. But since it can be both, therefore, just as in the case of associated states like faith, which can be both, one should seek their wholesome or other state as dependent on the roots, not as from their own nature, so too in the case of the roots themselves, their wholesome or other state should be sought as dependent on something else, not as from their own nature. Thus, what was said—'For associated roots, the wholesome or other state is from their own nature'—is not tenable. And when that state is sought, it is found to be dependent on wise attention and so on. Therefore, just as in the case of the roots, so too in the case of the associated states, the wholesome or other state is dependent on wise attention and so on, not dependent on the roots. This is the established meaning.

Viruḷhamūlā viyāti etena mūlāni viya mūlānīti dasseti. Tenevāha “suppatiṭṭhitabhāvasādhanenā”ti. Svāyaṃ “kusalo dhammo kusalassa, kusalo dhammo abyākatassa, kusalo dhammo kusalābyākatassa, akusalo dhammo akusalassa, akusalo dhammo abyākatassa, akusalo dhammo akusalābyākatassa, abyākato dhammo abyākatassā”ti evaṃ sattadhā pañhāvāre niddiṭṭho. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ hetukiccaṃ dassentena “hetū hetusampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ, taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ hetupaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.1), tattha paṭhamo hetusaddo paccattaniddiṭṭho paccayadhammaniddeso, tenassa hetubhāvena upakārakatā hetupaccayatāti dasseti. Dutiyo paccayuppannavisesanaṃ, tena na yesaṃ kesañci sampayuttakānaṃ hetū hetupaccayena paccayo, atha kho hetunā sampayuttānamevāti dasseti. Nanu ca sampayuttasaddassa [M 2.0270] sāpekkhattā dutiye hetusadde avijjamānepi aññassa apekkhitabbassa aniddiṭṭhattā hetū attanāva sampayuttakānaṃ hetupaccayena paccayoti ayamattho viññāyatīti? Nāyamekanto. Hetusaddo hi paccattaniddiṭṭho “hetupaccayena paccayo”ti ettheva byāvaṭo yadā gayhati, na tadā sampayuttavisesanaṃ hotīti sampayuttaavisiṭṭhā ye keci gahitā bhaveyyunti. Nanu ca yathā “arūpino āhārā sampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ, arūpino indriyā sampayuttakānaṃ dhammāna”nti ca vutte dutiyena āhāraggahaṇena, indriyaggahaṇena ca vināpi āhārindriyasampayuttakāva gayhanti, evamidhāpi siyāti? Na, āhārindriyāsampayuttassa vajjetabbassa abhāvato. Vajjetabbābhāvato hi tattha dutiye āhārindriyaggahaṇe asatipi taṃsampayuttakāva gayhantīti taṃ na kataṃ, idha pana vajjetabbaṃ atthīti kattabbaṃ dutiyaṃ hetuggahaṇaṃ. Evampi “hetū hetusampayuttakāna”nti ettha hetusampayuttakānaṃ so eva sampayuttakahetūti visesanassa akatattā yo koci hetu yassa kassaci hetusampayuttassa hetupaccayena paccayoti āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati, paccattaniddiṭṭhasseva hetuno puna sampayuttavisesanabhāvena vuttattā. Etadatthameva hi vināpi dutiyena hetusaddena hetusampayuttabhāve siddhepi tassa gahaṇaṃ kataṃ.

By `viruḷhamūlā viya` (like well-grown roots), he shows that they are roots because they are like roots (`mūlāni viya mūlāni`). Therefore it is said: 'by establishing a well-established state.' This root condition is set forth in seven ways in the Question Section: 'A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state... for an indeterminate state... for a wholesome and indeterminate state; an unwholesome state is a condition for an unwholesome state... for an indeterminate state... for an unwholesome and indeterminate state; an indeterminate state is a condition for an indeterminate state.' As to what was said when showing the function of a root, 'Roots are a condition for states associated with the roots, and for the material phenomena co-arisen with them, by way of root condition' (Paṭṭh 1.1.1), in that statement the first word 'roots' is a specific designation, a designation of the conditioning state; by this it shows that its helpfulness by way of being a root is the root condition. The second is a qualifier of the conditioned states; by this it shows that roots are not a condition by way of root condition for just any associated states whatsoever, but only for those associated with the roots. But is it not the case that since the word 'associated' is relational, even if the second word 'roots' were absent, because nothing else to be related to is designated, the meaning 'roots are a condition for states associated with themselves by way of root condition' would be understood? This is not certain. For when the word 'roots,' being a specific designation, is taken as occupied only with 'are a condition by way of root condition,' it is not then a qualifier of 'associated,' and thus any unspecified associated states might be taken. But is it not the case that just as when it is said, 'Immaterial nutriments are a condition for associated states... immaterial faculties are a condition for associated states...,' even without the second mention of 'nutriments' or 'faculties,' only states associated with nutriments or faculties are taken, so it might be here too? No, because there is nothing unassociated with nutriments and faculties to be excluded. Because there is nothing to be excluded there, even without the second mention of 'nutriments' or 'faculties,' only states associated with them are taken, so that mention is not made. But here there is something to be excluded, so the second mention of 'roots' should be made. Even so, in the phrase 'roots for root-associated states,' since no qualification is made that they are associated with that very same root, would it not follow that any root is a condition by way of root condition for any root-associated state? It does not follow, because the very root that is specifically designated is stated again as a qualifier of 'associated'. Indeed, it is for this very purpose that its inclusion is made, even though the state of being associated with a root is established even without the second word 'roots'.

Atha vā asati dutiye hetusadde hetusampayuttakānaṃ hetupaccayena paccayo, na pana hetūnanti evampi gahaṇaṃ siyāti tannivāraṇatthaṃ so vutto. Tena hetusampayuttabhāvaṃ ye labhanti, tesaṃ [V 2.0254] sabbesaṃ hetūnaṃ, aññesampi hetū hetupaccayena paccayoti dassitaṃ hoti. Yasmā pana hetujhānamaggā patiṭṭhāmattādibhāvena aññadhammanirapekkhā, na āhārindriyā viya sāpekkhā eva, tasmā etesveva dutiyaṃ hetādiggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Āhārindriyā pana āharitabbaīsitabbāpekkhā eva, tasmā te vināpi dutiyena āhārindriyaggahaṇena attanā eva āharitabbe, īsitabbe ca āhārindriyabhūte, aññe ca sampayuttake paricchindantīti taṃ tattha na kataṃ. Idha ca dutiyena hetuggahaṇena paccayuppannānaṃ hetunā, paccayabhūteneva ca sampayuttānaṃ hetūnaṃ, aññesañca paricchinnattā puna visesena kiccaṃ natthīti pañhāvāre “kusalā [M 2.0271] hetū sampayuttakānaṃ khandhāna”ntiādīsu dutiyaṃ hetuggahaṇaṃ na katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Alternatively, if the second word 'hetu' were absent, the meaning might be taken thus: 'it is a condition by way of root condition for states associated with a root, but not for the roots themselves.' To prevent this, that word is stated. By this, it is shown that for all those states that attain association with a root—both for the roots themselves and for the other associated states—the roots are a condition by way of root condition. And since roots, jhānas, and paths, by way of being merely a foundation and so on, are independent of other states—not dependent like nutriment and faculties—therefore, the second mention of 'root,' etc., is made only in these cases. Nutriments and faculties, however, are dependent on what is to be nutrified and what is to be dominated. Therefore, even without a second mention of 'nutriment' or 'faculty,' they by themselves delimit the associated states: those to be nutrified and dominated, those that are themselves nutriment and faculty, and others; thus, that second mention is not made there. And here, because the conditioned states—both the roots and the others associated with the very root that is the condition—are delimited by the second mention of 'hetu', there is no further need for a special qualification. Thus, it should be seen that in the Question Section, in such phrases as 'wholesome roots for the associated aggregates,' the second mention of 'hetu' is not made.

596. Ārammaṇabhāvenāti visayabhāvena, ālambitabbabhāvenāti attho. Ārabhitvāpīti pi-saddena imamatthaṃ dasseti – rūpāyatanādimatte yasmiṃ kismiñci ekasmiṃ aṭṭhatvā “yaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ ārabbhā”ti (paṭṭhā 1.1.2) aniyamena sabbarūpāyatanānaṃ…pe… sabbadhammāyatanānañca ārammaṇapaccayabhāvassa vuttattā rūpādibhedena chabbidhesu saṅkhatāsaṅkhatapaññattidhammesu na koci dhammo ārammaṇapaccayo na hotīti. Svāyaṃ ārammaṇapaccayabhāvo heṭṭhā vibhāvito eva. Ālambitvāti gahetvā. Ekantasārammaṇabhāvato anārabbha pavatti eva natthīti āha “ārabbhevā”ti. Svāyaṃ “kusalo dhammo kusalassa, kusalo dhammo akusalassa, kusalo dhammo abyākatassa, akusalo dhammo akusalassa, kusalassa, abyākatassa, abyākato dhammo abyākatassa, kusalassa, akusalassā”ti evaṃ navappakāro veditabbo.

596. 'By way of object' means by way of being a sense-field; the meaning is 'by way of being that which is to be taken as an object.' By the particle 'pi' in 'even having taken as an object,' it shows this meaning: since it has been stated—not being confined to any single thing such as the mere form-base, but without restriction, by the text 'Whatever state one takes as an object...' (Paṭṭh 1.1.2)—that the state of being an object-condition applies to all form-bases...pe...all mind-object-bases, therefore, among the six kinds of states distinguished by way of form and so on—conditioned, unconditioned, and conceptual states—there is no state that is not an object-condition. This nature of the object condition has already been explained. 'Having taken as an object' means having grasped. Because consciousness is exclusively with an object, there is no occurrence whatsoever without taking an object; thus it is said, 'only after having taken as object.' This should be understood as being of nine kinds: 'A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state, for an unwholesome state, for an indeterminate state; an unwholesome state is a condition for an unwholesome state, for a wholesome state, for an indeterminate state; an indeterminate state is a condition for an indeterminate state, for a wholesome state, for an unwholesome state.'

597. Jeṭṭhakaṭṭhenāti pamukhabhāvena. Attādhīnānañhi patibhūto dhammo adhipati. So tesaṃ pamukhabhāvena pavattati. “Chandavato kiṃ nāma na sijjhatī”tiādikaṃ purimābhisaṅkhārūpanissayaṃ labhitvā uppajjamāne cittuppāde chandādayo dhurabhūtā jeṭṭhakabhūtā sampayuttadhamme sādhayamānā vase vattayamānā hutvā pavattanti, sampayuttadhammā ca tesaṃ vasena vattanti hīnādibhāvena tadanuvattanato, tena te adhipatipaccayā honti. Garukātabbampi ārammaṇaṃ tanninnapoṇapabbhārānaṃ assādanapaccavekkhaṇamaggaphalānaṃ attano vase vattayamānaṃ viya paccayo hoti. Tasmā ayaṃ attādhīnānaṃ patibhāvena upakārakattā adhipatipaccayoti daṭṭhabbo. Chandādhipatīti chandasaṅkhāto adhipati, chandaṃ dhuraṃ chandaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā cittuppattikāle uppannassa kattukamyatāchandassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Kasmā pana yathā hetupaccayaniddese [V 2.0255] “hetū hetusampayuttakāna”nti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.1) vuttaṃ, evamidha “adhipatī adhipatisampayuttakāna”nti avatvā “chandādhipati chandasampayuttakāna”ntiādinā (paṭṭhā. 1.1.3) nayena vuttanti? Ekakkhaṇe [M 2.0272] abhāvato. Hetavo hi dve tayopi ekakkhaṇe hetupaccayā honti, mūlaṭṭhena upakārakabhāvassa avijahanato. Adhipati pana jeṭṭhakaṭṭhena upakārako, na ca ekakkhaṇe bahū jeṭṭhakā honti. Tasmā ekato uppannānampi tesaṃ ekakkhaṇe adhipatipaccayabhāvo natthīti “adhipatī adhipatisampayuttakāna”nti avatvā “chandādhipati chandasampayuttakāna”ntiādinā nayena vuttaṃ.

597. By the meaning of 'foremost' is meant by way of being the chief. Indeed, a state that is the master of those states dependent on it is a dominant factor. It proceeds by way of being their chief. In line with such sayings as, 'What indeed is not accomplished for one with desire?', when a state of consciousness arises having obtained a previous volitional formation as its decisive support, desire and other factors, being the leaders and the foremost, proceed while accomplishing the associated states and bringing them under their power. And the associated states proceed under their power, following them by way of being subordinate, etc. Therefore they are a dominance condition. Even an object that is to be revered is a condition for the states of enjoying, reviewing, path, and fruition of those who are inclined, bent, and sloping towards it, as if bringing them under its own power. Therefore, this should be seen as a dominance condition because it is helpful by way of being a master for those dependent on it. 'Desire as dominance' means the dominant factor called desire. This is the name for the desire-to-act that has arisen at the time of the arising of consciousness, having made desire the leader, having made desire the foremost. The same method applies to the remaining cases. But why, just as in the exposition of the root condition it is said, 'Roots are a condition for states associated with roots,' is it not said here, 'A dominant factor is a condition for states associated with a dominant factor,' but is stated by the method beginning, 'Desire as dominance is a condition for states associated with desire'? Because of their non-existence in a single moment. For two or three roots can be a root condition in a single moment, since they do not abandon their nature of being helpful by way of being a root. But a dominant factor is helpful by way of being the foremost, and there cannot be many foremost things in a single moment. Therefore, even though they arise together, they do not have the nature of a dominance condition in a single moment. Thus, it is not said, 'A dominant factor is a condition for states associated with a dominant factor,' but is stated by the method beginning, 'Desire as dominance is a condition for states associated with desire.'

Yaṃ yaṃ dhammanti yaṃ yaṃ ārammaṇadhammaṃ. Garuṃ katvāti garukāracittīkāravasena vā assādanavasena vā garukārikaṃ laddhabbaṃ avijahitabbaṃ anavaññātaṃ katvā. Te te dhammāti te te garukātabbā dhammā. Tesaṃ tesanti taṃtaṃgarukārakadhammānaṃ. Adhipatipaccayenāti ārammaṇādhipatipaccayena. Svāyaṃ “kusalo dhammo kusalassa sahajātārammaṇehi, akusalassa ārammaṇeneva, abyākatassa sahajātārammaṇehi, kusalābyākatassa sahajātenevāti kusalamūlā cattāro, akusalo dhammo akusalassa sahajātārammaṇehi, abyākatassa sahajāteneva, tathā akusalābyākatassāti akusalamūlā tayo, abyākato dhammo abyākatassa sahajātārammaṇehi, kusalassa ārammaṇeneva, tathā akusalassāti abyākatamūlā tayo”ti saṅkhepato dasappakāro adhipatipaccayo. Ettha ca sattadhā sahajātādhipati, sattadhā ārammaṇādhipati veditabbo.

'Whatever state' means whatever object-state. 'Having made it weighty' means having made it something to be respected, to be obtained, not to be abandoned, and not to be slighted, doing so either by way of reverence and esteem or by way of enjoyment. 'Those states' means those states that are to be revered. 'Of those' means of those states that one makes revered. 'By way of dominance condition' means by way of object-dominance condition. In brief, this dominance condition is tenfold: 'A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state by conascence-dominance and object-dominance; for an unwholesome state only by object-dominance; for an indeterminate state by conascence-dominance and object-dominance; for a wholesome-and-indeterminate state only by conascence-dominance'—thus there are four rooted in the wholesome. 'An unwholesome state is a condition for an unwholesome state by conascence-dominance and object-dominance; for an indeterminate state only by conascence-dominance; likewise for an unwholesome-and-indeterminate state'—thus there are three rooted in the unwholesome. 'An indeterminate state is a condition for an indeterminate state by conascence-dominance and object-dominance; for a wholesome state only by object-dominance; likewise for an unwholesome state'—thus there are three rooted in the indeterminate. And here, conascence-dominance should be understood as sevenfold, and object-dominance as sevenfold.

598. Antarāyatīti antaraṃ, byavadhāyakanti attho. Nāssa antaraṃ vijjatīti anantaro, anantaro ca so paccayo cāti anantarapaccayo. “Atthānantaratā anantarapaccayo, kālānantaratā samanantarapaccayo”tiādinā bahudhā papañcayanti, asāraṃ ganthavitthāraṃ karonti. Yathā pavattiokāsadānavisesabhāvena natthivigatapaccayā vuttā, na evaṃ anantarasamanantarapaccayā, ete pana cittaniyamahetubhāvena vuttāti taṃ cittaniyamahetubhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “yo hi esā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha manoviññāṇadhātūtiādi cittaniyamoti ettha ādi-saddena santīraṇānantarā voṭṭhabbanaṃ, cutianantarā paṭisandhīti yassa yassa cittassa anantarā yaṃ yaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati, tassa tassa tadanantaruppādaniyamo taṃtaṃsahakāripaccayavisiṭṭhassa purimapurimacittasseva vasena ijjhatīti dasseti.

598. 'It makes an interval' (antarāyati), thus 'interval' (antaraṃ); the meaning is 'that which separates.' 'There is no interval for it,' thus 'without interval' (anantaro). And that is a condition without interval, thus 'proximity condition' (anantarapaccayo). They proliferate in many ways with such statements as, ‘Immediacy in substance is the proximity condition, immediacy in time is the contiguity condition,’ making an essenceless expansion of the text. The proximity and contiguity conditions are not stated in the way the absence and disappearance conditions are, namely, as having the special nature of giving an opportunity for occurrence. Rather, these are stated as being the cause for the fixed order of consciousness. To show this nature of being the cause for the fixed order of consciousness, the passage beginning ‘yo hi esā’ etc. was introduced. Therein, in the phrase ‘the mind-consciousness element, etc., is the fixed order of consciousness,’ the word ‘etc.’ indicates that determination arises immediately after investigating consciousness, and rebirth-linking arises immediately after death. It shows that for whichever consciousness arises immediately after whichever other consciousness, the fixed order of its arising immediately after that is accomplished by the power of the immediately preceding consciousness itself, which is distinguished by its specific cooperative conditions.

Atthānantaratāyāti [M 2.0273] atthena kenaci dhammena anantaratāya. Kālānantaratāyāti kālabhedena anantaratāya[V 2.0256]. Ācariyānanti idhāpi revatācariyameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tasmiṃ kālānantaratāya samanantarapaccayabhāve, tasmiṃ vā yathāvuttavirodhe. Bhāvanābalena pana vāritattāti ettha yathā rukkhassa vedhe dinne pupphituṃ samatthasseva pupphanaṃ na hoti, vedhe pana apanīte tāya eva samatthatāya pupphanaṃ hoti, evamidhāpi bhāvanābalena vāritattā samuṭṭhāpanasamatthasseva asamuṭṭhāpanaṃ, tasmiñca apagate tāya eva samatthatāya samuṭṭhāpanaṃ hotīti adhippāyo. Tampi vacanaṃ kālānantaratā natthi sattāhādinā kālena antaritabhāvato. Etadeva “kālantaritatā atthi” icceva vadāma. Nanu ca kālo nāma koci paramatthato natthīti vadeyyāti āsaṅkanto āha “kālānantara…pe… laddhī”ti.

‘By proximity of meaning’ means by proximity through some phenomenon as meaning. ‘By proximity of time’ means by proximity through a difference in time. ‘Of the teachers’: here too it is said with reference to the teacher Revata. ‘Therein’ means in that state of being a contiguity condition due to proximity of time, or in that aforesaid opposition. ‘But because it is restrained by the power of cultivation’: here, just as when a wedge is driven into a tree that is capable of flowering, it does not flower, but when the wedge is removed, it flowers by that very same capability; so too here, because it is restrained by the power of cultivation, there is the non-arising of that which is indeed capable of arising, and when that restraint is removed, it arises by that very same capability. This is the intended meaning. Regarding that statement too, there is no proximity of time because of being separated by a period of time such as seven days. This is precisely what we say: ‘There is separation by time.’ Anticipating that someone might say, ‘But surely, time as such does not exist in an ultimate sense,’ he said: ‘Proximity of time… is the view.’

Byañjanamattatovettha nānākaraṇaṃ paccetabbaṃ, na atthatoti upacayasantatiadhivacananiruttipadānaṃ viya saddatthamattato nānākaraṇaṃ, na vacanīyatthatoti adhippāyo. Teneva saddatthavisesaṃ dassetuṃ “katha”ntiādimāha. Tattha purimapacchimānaṃ nirodhuppādantarābhāvato nirantaruppādanasamatthatā anantarapaccayabhāvo. Rūpakalāpānaṃ viya saṇṭhānābhāvato, paccayapaccayuppannānaṃ sahāvaṭṭhānābhāvato ca “idamito heṭṭhā, uddhaṃ, tiriya”nti vibhāgābhāvā attanā ekattamiva upanetvā suṭṭhu anantarabhāvena uppādanasamatthatā samanantarapaccayatā. Uppādanasamatthatāti ca abyāpārattā dhammānaṃ yasmiṃ yadākāre niruddhe, vattamāne vā sati taṃtaṃvisesavanto dhammā honti, tassa sova ākāro vuccatīti daṭṭhabbo. Dhammānaṃ pavattimattameva ca upādāya kālavohāroti nirodhā vuṭṭhahantassa nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaphalasamāpattīnaṃ [M 2.0274] asaññabhavā cavantassa, purimacutipacchimapaṭisandhīnañca nirodhuppādanirantaratāya kālantaratā natthi. Na hi tesaṃ antarā arūpadhammappavatti atthi, yaṃ upādāya kālantaratā vucceyya, na ca rūpadhammappavatti arūpadhammappavattiyā antaraṃ karoti aññasantānattā. Rūpārūpasantatiyo hi dve aññamaññaṃ visadisasabhāvattā aññamaññūpakārabhāvena pavattamānāpi visuṃyeva honti. Ekasantatiyañca purimapacchimānaṃ majjhe pavattamānaṃ taṃsantatipariyāpannatāya antarakārakaṃ hoti. Tādisañca kiñci nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaphalasamāpattīnaṃ majjhe natthi, na ca abhāvo antarakārako hoti abhāvattā eva. Tasmā javanānantarassa javanassa viya, bhavaṅgānantarassa bhavaṅgassa viya ca nirantaratā suṭṭhu anantaratā hotīti tathā uppādanasamatthatā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanacutīnampi daṭṭhabbā. Uppattiyā paccayabhāvo cettha anantarapaccayādīnaṃ pākaṭoti uppādanasamatthatāva vuttā[V 2.0257]. Paccuppannānaṃ pana dhammānaṃ pubbantāparantaparicchedena gahitānaṃ uppajjatīti vacanaṃ alabhantānaṃ “atīto dhammo paccuppannassa dhammassa anantarapaccayena paccayo”tiādinā (paṭṭhā. 2.18.4) anantarādipaccayabhāvo vuttoti na so uppattiyā evāti viññāyati. Na hi kusalādiggahaṇaṃ viya paccuppannaggahaṇaṃ aparicchedaṃ. Yato uppattimattasamaṅgino eva gahaṇaṃ siyā. Teneva ca atītattike paṭiccavārādayo na santīti. Tassa “kusalo dhammo kusalassa, kusalo dhammo abyākatassa, akusalo dhammo akusalassa, akusalo dhammo abyākatassa, abyākato dhammo abyākatassa, abyākato dhammo kusalassa, abyākato dhammo akusalassā”ti sattadhā bhedo veditabbo.

Herein, the distinction should be understood as one of phrasing only, not of meaning. The intention is that, like the terms ‘accumulation’ and ‘continuity’, or ‘designation’ and ‘etymology’, the distinction is one of word-meaning only, not of the meaning to be expressed. For that reason, to show the specific word-meaning, he said, ‘How?’ etc. Therein, because there is no interval between the cessation of the preceding and the arising of the subsequent, the capability to cause an uninterrupted arising is the proximity condition. Because there is no shape, as in the case of material groups, and because there is no co-existence of condition and conditioned phenomenon, there is no division such as ‘this is below, above, or across from that’; thus, having brought it to a state of unity with itself, as it were, the capability to cause an arising in a perfectly immediate manner is the contiguity condition. And ‘capability to cause arising’ should be understood thus: because dhammas are without agency, when a certain condition in a certain mode has ceased or is present, dhammas possessing those specific qualities come to be; that very mode of the former is spoken of. Moreover, the convention of time is used with reference to the mere occurrence of dhammas. Thus, because of the uninterruptedness of cessation and arising, there is no temporal interval for one emerging from the attainment of cessation, for one passing away from non-percipient existence, and between the preceding death and subsequent rebirth-linking. For there is no occurrence of immaterial dhammas between them with reference to which a temporal interval might be spoken of; nor does the occurrence of material dhammas create an interval for the occurrence of immaterial dhammas, because they belong to a different continuity. For the two continuities of materiality and immateriality, though proceeding by way of mutual assistance, are quite distinct because their intrinsic natures are dissimilar. And in a single continuity, what occurs between the preceding and the subsequent creates an interval by reason of its inclusion in that continuity. But there is nothing of that sort in the middle of the attainment of the fruition of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and an absence does not create an interval precisely because it is an absence. Therefore, just as for an impulsion immediately after an impulsion, or for a life-continuum moment immediately after a life-continuum moment, the uninterruptedness is a perfect immediacy, so the capability to cause an arising should be understood also for the death-consciousnesses of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and of non-percipient existence. Since the nature as a condition for arising is manifest here for the proximity condition, etc., the ‘capability to cause arising’ has been stated. But for present dhammas, which are taken as delimited by a past and future boundary, since they do not obtain the term ‘is arising,’ the nature of the proximity condition, etc., is stated in such passages as, ‘A past dhamma is a condition for a present dhamma by way of proximity condition.’ From this it is understood that it is not a condition for arising only. For the taking up of ‘present’ is not without delimitation, like the taking up of ‘wholesome,’ etc., in which case there would be the taking up only of that which is endowed with the mere moment of arising. And for that very reason, in the past triad, there are no sections on dependent origination, etc. Its sevenfold division should be understood as: a wholesome dhamma for a wholesome dhamma; a wholesome dhamma for an indeterminate dhamma; an unwholesome dhamma for an unwholesome dhamma; an unwholesome dhamma for an indeterminate dhamma; an indeterminate dhamma for an indeterminate dhamma; an indeterminate dhamma for a wholesome dhamma; and an indeterminate dhamma for an unwholesome dhamma.

599. Uppajjamānova saha uppādanabhāvenāti etthāpi uppattiyā paccayabhāvena pākaṭena ṭhitiyāpi paccayabhāvaṃ nidassetīti daṭṭhabbaṃ, aññathā padīpanidassanaṃ na yujjeyya. Padīpo hi pabhāsassa ṭhitiyāpi paccayo, na uppattiyā eva. Paccayuppannānaṃ sahajātabhāvena upakārakatā sahajātapaccayatā. Okkantikkhaṇeti paṭisandhikkhaṇe. Tasmiṃ hi khaṇe nāmarūpaṃ okkantaṃ viya paralokato āgantvā idha mātukucchiādiṃ pavisantaṃ viya uppajjati, tasmā so khaṇo okkantikkhaṇoti vuccati. Ettha ca rūpanti hadayavatthuyeva adhippetaṃ. Tañhi nāmassa, nāmañca tassa sahajātapaccayo hoti. Cittacetasikāti pavattiyaṃ cattāro khandhā paṭisandhikkhaṇe cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ abhāvato. Rūpino dhammāti hadayavatthuṃ sandhāyāha. Tattha yadipi pubbe “okkantikkhaṇe nāmarūpa”nti vuttaṃ, tathāpi tena khaṇantare sahajātapaccayabhāvo rūpadhammānaṃ na nivāritoti tannivāraṇatthamidaṃ vuttanti gahetabbaṃ. Kiñci kāleti keci kismiñci kāleti attho, tena rūpino dhammā keci vatthubhūtā kismiñci paṭisandhikāleti aññesaṃ rūpadhammānaṃ, vatthuno ca pavattiyaṃ arūpadhammānaṃ [M 2.0275] sahajātapaccayabhāvaṃ pubbe anivāritaṃ nivāreti. Evañca katvā “kiñci kāla”nti vā “kismiñci kāle”ti vā vattabbe tathā avatvā vibhattivipallāsaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Tena kiñcīti upayogekavacanaṃ. “Rūpino dhammā”ti etena sambandhe paccattabahuvacanaṃ jāyati. “Kāle”ti etena sambandhe bhummekavacananti dīpitanti veditabbaṃ. Purimena ca “eko khandho, vatthu ca tiṇṇannaṃ khandhāna”nti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.419) ādivacanena nāmasahitaṃ eva vatthu nāmassa paccayoti vattabbe āpanne itarena kevalassa ca tathāvattabbataṃ dasseti. Svāyaṃ sahajātapaccayo “kusalo dhammo kusalassa, abyākatassa, kusalābyākatassa, akusalo dhammo akusalassa[V 2.0258], abyākatassa, akusalābyākatassa, abyākato dhammo abyākatassa, kusalābyākato dhammo abyākatassa, akusalābyākato dhammo abyākatassā”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.419) navavidho veditabbo.

599. In the phrase, 'When it is arising, by its nature of arising,' here too, it should be understood that by its manifest conditionality for arising, it also indicates its conditionality for presence; otherwise, the illustration of the lamp would not be appropriate. For a lamp is a condition for the presence of light, not only for its arising. The co-nascence condition is the state of being helpful to conditioned phenomena by way of co-existence. 'At the moment of descent' means at the moment of rebirth-linking. For at that moment, name-and-form arises as if it has descended, having come from another world and entered here into a mother’s womb, and so on. Therefore, that moment is called the 'moment of descent.' And here, by 'form,' only the heart-base is intended. For that is a co-nascence condition for name, and name is a co-nascence condition for it. By 'mind and mental factors' are meant the four aggregates during the course of existence, due to the absence of mind-originated phenomena at the moment of rebirth-linking. 'Material phenomena' is said with reference to the heart-base. In this regard, although it was said earlier, 'at the moment of descent, name-and-form,' that did not preclude the co-nascence conditionality of material phenomena at other moments; therefore, it should be understood that this latter statement was said in order to preclude that. 'Kiñci kāle' means 'some at some time.' Thereby, by the statement that 'some material phenomena that are bases are conditions at a certain time, that is, at the time of rebirth-linking,' it precludes what was not precluded before: the co-nascence conditionality for other material phenomena, and of the base for immaterial phenomena during the course of existence. And so, when it should have been said 'kiñci kālaṃ' or 'kismiñci kāle,' it was said with a transposition of case endings. Thus, it should be understood as shown that 'kiñci' is an accusative singular; in connection with 'rūpino dhammā,' it becomes a nominative plural, and in connection with 'kāle,' it becomes a locative singular. And by the previous statement beginning 'one aggregate and the base for the three aggregates…,' when it would follow that the base together with name is a condition for name, the other statement shows that this can also be stated for the base alone. This co-nascence condition should be understood as ninefold: a wholesome phenomenon is a condition for a wholesome phenomenon, for an indeterminate phenomenon, and for a wholesome-and-indeterminate phenomenon; an unwholesome phenomenon is a condition for an unwholesome phenomenon, for an indeterminate phenomenon, and for an unwholesome-and-indeterminate phenomenon; an indeterminate phenomenon is a condition for an indeterminate phenomenon; a wholesome-and-indeterminate phenomenon is a condition for an indeterminate phenomenon; and an unwholesome-and-indeterminate phenomenon is a condition for an indeterminate phenomenon.

600. Attano upakārakassa upakārakatā aññamaññapaccayatā. Tathā hissa tidaṇḍaṃ nidassitaṃ. Upakārakatā ca aññamaññatāvaseneva daṭṭhabbā, na sahajātatādivasena. Sahajātādipaccayo hontoyeva hi koci aññamaññapaccayo na hoti, na ca sahajātādipaccayadhammehi vinā imassa pavatti atthi. Tathā hi sahajātādipaccayo ca hontoyeva hi koci aññamaññapaccayo hoti. Yadi ca attano upakārakassa upakārakatāmattaṃ aññamaññapaccayo siyā, purejātapacchājātabhāvena upakārassa upakārakā vatthukhandhā aññamaññapaccayā siyuṃ, na ca taṃ icchitaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “upakārakatā ca aññamaññavaseneva daṭṭhabbā”ti. Ayañca uppattiyā, ṭhitiyā ca upakārakoti veditabbo. Ayaṃ pana “kusalo dhammo kusalassa, akusalo dhammo akusalassa, abyākato dhammo abyākatassā”ti tividho veditabbo.

600. The mutuality condition is the state of being helpful in return to that which is helpful to oneself. Thus indeed, the tripod is shown as its illustration. And helpfulness should be understood only by way of mutuality, not by way of co-nascence and so on. For indeed, some phenomenon, while being a co-nascence condition, etc., is not a mutuality condition; and the latter cannot occur without phenomena that are co-nascence conditions, etc. Thus indeed, some phenomenon is a mutuality condition only while it is also a co-nascence condition, etc. And if the mutuality condition were merely the state of being helpful to that which is helpful to it, then the physical basis and the mental aggregates, which are helpful to that which helps them by way of pre-nascence and post-nascence, would be mutuality conditions; but that is not intended. Therefore it was said: “And helpfulness should be understood only by way of mutuality.” And this condition should be understood as being helpful for arising and for presence. This condition, furthermore, should be understood as threefold: a wholesome phenomenon is a condition for a wholesome one, an unwholesome phenomenon for an unwholesome one, and an indeterminate phenomenon for an indeterminate one.

601. Taruādīnaṃ pathavī viya adhiṭṭhānākārena pathavīdhātu sesadhātūnaṃ, cakkhādayo cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ upakārakā cittakammassa paṭādayo viya nissayākārena khandhādayo taṃtaṃnissayānaṃ khandhādīnaṃ. Pathavīdhātuyaṃ patiṭṭhāya eva hi sesadhātuyo upādārūpāni viya yathāsakaṃ kiccaṃ karonti.

601. The earth element is helpful to the remaining elements, and the eye, etc., to eye-consciousness, etc., in the manner of a foundation, just as the earth is for trees and so on; the aggregates, etc., are helpful to their respective dependent aggregates, etc., in the manner of a support, just as a cloth, etc., is for a painting. For indeed, it is only by being established on the earth element that the remaining elements, like derived materiality, perform their respective functions.

Adhiṭṭhānākārenāti [M 2.0276] ādhārākārena. Ādhārākāro cettha tesaṃ sātisayaṃ tadadhīnavuttitāya veditabbo. Yato bhūtāni aniddisitabbaṭṭhānāni vuccanti, evañca katvā cakkhādīnampi adhiṭṭhānākārena upakārakatā suṭṭhu yujjati. Na hi yathāvuttaṃ tadadhīnavuttitāvisesaṃ muñcitvā añño cakkhādīsu adesakānaṃ arūpadhammānaṃ adhiṭṭhānākāro sambhavati. Yadipi yaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca ye ye dhammā uppajjanti, tesaṃ sabbesaṃ tadadhīnavuttibhāvo. Yena pana paccayabhāvavisesena cakkhādīnaṃ paṭumandabhāvesu cakkhuviññāṇādayo tadanuvidhānākāreneva pavattanti, svāyamidha tesaṃ tadadhīnavuttitāsiddho visesoti. Evañhi paccayabhāvasāmaññe satipi ārammaṇapaccayato nissayapaccayassa viseso vibhāvito hoti. Svāyaṃ nayo heṭṭhā pakāsitova. Chaṭṭho panāti ettha “rūpino [V 2.0259] dhammā arūpīnaṃ dhammānaṃ kismiñci kāle”ti idaṃ na labbhati. Yaṃ panettha labbhati “rūpino dhammā kecī”ti, tattha te eva dhamme dassetuṃ “cakkhāyatana”ntiādi niddiṭṭhaṃ. Yaṃ rūpanti hadayavatthuṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ pana nissayapaccayo terasavidho. Kathaṃ? Sahajātato kusalamūlā tayo, tathā akusalamūlā, abyākatamūlesu pana purejātaṃ labbhati. Abyākatañhi abyākatassa sahajātampi paccayo hoti, purejātampi kusalassa purejātameva, tathā akusalassa, kusalābyākataṃ sahajātapurejātato kusalassa, sahajātato eva abyākatassa, tathā akusalābyākata”nti evaṃ terasa.

“In the manner of a foundation” means in the manner of a basis. Here, the manner of a basis should be understood as the pre-eminent dependence of those phenomena upon it. Since the great elements are said to have an unspecifiable location, it is quite appropriate that the eye and other sense faculties are helpful in the manner of a foundation. For apart from this specific state of dependence as described, no other manner of foundation is possible for immaterial phenomena, which have no location, in the eye and other faculties. Although for all phenomena that arise in dependence on whatever other phenomena, there is a state of being dependent on them, that specific kind of conditionality by which, when there are states of sharpness and dullness of the eye and other faculties, eye-consciousness and so on proceed only in a manner conforming to that—this here is that specific feature established by their state of being dependent on them. For thus, even when there is a generality of conditionality, the distinction of the support condition from the object condition is made clear. This method has already been explained below. But as to the sixth permutation, the statement “a material phenomenon for an immaterial phenomenon at some time” is not found here. What is found here is “some material phenomena,” and to show those very phenomena, “the eye-base,” etc., is specified. The phrase “that material form” is stated with reference to the heart-base. This support condition, however, is of thirteen kinds. How? By way of co-nascence, there are three rooted in the wholesome, and likewise three rooted in the unwholesome. But among those rooted in the indeterminate, pre-nascence is found. For an indeterminate phenomenon is a condition for an indeterminate one by co-nascence and also by pre-nascence. It is a condition for a wholesome phenomenon only by pre-nascence; likewise for an unwholesome one. A wholesome-and-indeterminate phenomenon is a condition for a wholesome one by co-nascence and pre-nascence, but for an indeterminate one only by co-nascence; likewise for an unwholesome-and-indeterminate one. Thus there are thirteen.

602. Tadadhīnavuttitāya attano phalena nissitoti yaṃ kiñci kāraṇaṃ nissayoti vatvā tattha yo bhuso nissayo, taṃ upanissayoti niddhāreti. Balavakāraṇabhāvena upakārakoti ārammaṇabhāvavasena anantaraṃ anurūpacittuppādanasamatthatāvasena, kevalañca balavantaṃ kāraṇaṃ hutvā upakārako. Tenāha “so”tiādi.

602. Having stated, 'Because its occurrence is dependent on that, it is supported by its own fruit; thus, any cause whatsoever is a support,' the text then defines that among them, a powerful support is a decisive support. It is helpful by being a strong cause: by way of being an object, by way of being capable of producing a suitable succeeding consciousness, and simply by being a powerful cause that is helpful. Therefore it is said: “That…” etc.

Tattha dānaṃ datvāti deyyadhammaṃ cajitvā. Yāya vā cetanāya so diyyati, sā cetanā dānaṃ. Datvāti taṃ cetanaṃ pariyodapetvā visuddhaṃ katvā. Sīlaṃ samādiyitvāti pañcaṅgadasaṅgādivasena niccasīlaṃ gaṇhitvā. Iminā samādānaviratiyeva dassitā, sampattaviratisamucchedaviratiyo pana loke “sīla”nti apākaṭattā na vuttā. Kiñcāpi na vuttā, ārammaṇapaccayo [M 2.0277] pana hontiyeva. Tattha samucchedavirati sekkhānaṃyeva kusalassa ārammaṇaṃ hoti, na itaresaṃ. Uposathakammanti “pāṇaṃ na hane, na cādinnamādiye”ti (su. ni. 402) evaṃ vuttaṃ uposathasīlaṃ. Taṃ garuṃ katvā paccavekkhatīti taṃ yathāvuttaṃ kusalaṃ sekkhopi puthujjanopi paccavekkhati, arahāpi taṃ paccavekkhateva. Arahatopi hi pubbe kataṃ kusalaṃ kusalameva. Yena pana cittena paccavekkhati, taṃ kiriyacittaṃ nāma hoti. Tasmā “kusalo kusalassā”ti imasmiṃ adhikāre na labbhati. Pubbe suciṇṇānīti “datvā katvā”ti hi āsannakatāni vuttāni, iminā na āsannakatānīti veditabbāni, dānādīhi vā sesāni kāmāvacarakusalāni dassetuṃ idaṃ vuttaṃ. Jhānā vuṭṭhahitvāti jhānaṃ samāpanno jhānato vuṭṭhahitvā. “Jhānaṃ vuṭṭhahitvā”tipi pāḷi. Sekkhā gotrabhunti sotāpannaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. So hi gotrabhuṃ paccavekkhati. “Vodāna”nti idaṃ pana sakadāgāmianāgāmino sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tesañhi taṃ cittaṃ vodānaṃ nāma hoti. Sekkhāti sotāpannasakadāgāmianāgāmino[V 2.0260]. Maggā vuṭṭhahitvāti maggaphalabhavaṅgātikkamavasena attanā paṭiladdhamaggā vuṭṭhahitvā, suddhamaggatoyeva pana vuṭṭhāya paccavekkhaṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ādi-saddena “kusalaṃ aniccato dukkhato anattato vipassantī”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.404) evamādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Yadipi nānattaṃ akatvāva vibhatto, tathāpi idampi ārammaṇādhipatiārammaṇūpanissayānaṃ visesoti dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Herein, ‘having given a gift’ means having relinquished an object to be given. Or the volition by which it is given—that volition is the gift. ‘Having given’ means having purified and cleansed that volition. ‘Having undertaken virtue’ means having taken up the fivefold, tenfold, and other precepts as constant virtue. By this, only abstinence as undertaking is shown; but abstinence as coincidence and abstinence as eradication are not mentioned because they are not evident in the world as ‘virtue.’ Although they are not mentioned, they still serve as object conditions. Among them, abstinence as eradication is an object for the wholesome only for trainees, not for others. ‘The Uposatha observance’ refers to the Uposatha virtue as stated: “One should not kill living beings, nor take what is not given” (Snp 402), and so on. ‘Reflecting on it with respect’: both a trainee and a worldling reflect on that wholesome deed as described, and even an arahant reflects on it. For an arahant’s past wholesome deed is indeed wholesome. However, the consciousness with which one reflects is called functional consciousness. Therefore, in this context, ‘the wholesome for the wholesome’ does not apply. ‘Previously well-practiced’: whereas ‘having given, having done’ refers to recently performed deeds, by this it should be understood as deeds not recently performed; or this is said to show the remaining sense-sphere wholesome deeds apart from giving and so on. ‘Having emerged from jhāna’ means one who has attained jhāna having emerged from jhāna. The Pāli also has ‘jhānaṃ vuṭṭhahitvā’. ‘A trainee at the change-of-lineage’ is said with reference to a stream-enterer, for he reflects on the change-of-lineage consciousness. ‘Purification’ is said with reference to a once-returner or a non-returner, for their consciousness is called purification. ‘Trainees’ refers to stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners. ‘Having emerged from the path’ means having emerged from the path one has personally attained by transcending path, fruition, and bhavaṅga. However, there is no such thing as reflection by emerging from the bare path alone. By the word ‘etc.’, it includes such things as “they contemplate the wholesome as impermanent, as suffering, as non-self” (Paṭṭh 1.1.404). Although it is analyzed without making a distinction, nevertheless, to show that this too is a specific case of object-dominance and object-decisive support conditions, the words ‘herein,’ etc., are stated.

Nesaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ anantarapaccayaanantarūpanissayānaṃ nikkhepaviseso atthi. Yasmā purimo abyākatadhammavasena pavatto, itaro kusalādivasenapīti sopi nikkhepaviseso atthato ekībhāvameva gacchati sabbesupi cittuppādesu tadubhayassa icchitabbattā. Evaṃ santepītiādi anantaraanantarūpanissayānaṃ visesadassanaṃ. Yathā hītiādi anantarūpanissayassa sambhavadassanaṃ.

There is a specific analysis for these states of consciousness and mental factors that are contiguity condition and contiguity-decisive support condition. Since the former occurs by way of indeterminate states and the latter by way of wholesome states, etc., that specific analysis also in meaning becomes one, because both are desirable in all arisings of consciousness. The phrase ‘Even so, etc.’ shows the distinction between contiguity and contiguity-decisive support conditions. The phrase ‘Just as, etc.’ shows the occurrence of the contiguity-decisive support condition.

Pakatoti ettha pa-kāro upasaggo, so attano phalassa uppādanasamatthabhāvena suṭṭhukatataṃ dīpeti. Tathā ca kataṃ attano santāne kataṃ hotīti āha “attano santāne”tiādi. Karaṇañca duvidhaṃ nipphādanaṃ, upasevanañcāti taṃ dassetuṃ “nipphādito vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha nipphādanaṃ [M 2.0278] hetupaccayasamodhānena phalassa nibbattanaṃ. Upasevanaṃ pana kāye allīyāpanavasena upayogūpasevanaṃ, vijānanasañjānanādīnaṃ vasena ārammaṇūpasevanañca. Teneva anāgatānampi utusampadādīnaṃ ārammaṇūpasevanena upasevitānaṃ pakatūpanissayatā vuttā hoti, pageva atītapaccuppannānaṃ. Paccuppannassāpi hi “paccuppannaṃ utubhojanaṃ senāsanaṃ upanissāya jhānaṃ uppādetī”tiādivacanato (paṭṭhā. 2.18.8) pakatūpanissayabhāvo labbhatīti. Pakatiyā evāti paccayantarasaṅkararahitena attano sabhāveneva. Upanissayoti balavakāraṇaṃ katvā. Anekappakārato pabhedo veditabbo pañhāvāre āgatanayena. Paccayavāre pana –
