Herein, in the word ‘pakata,’ the prefix ‘pa-’ indicates something well done (suṭṭhukata) because of its capacity to produce its own result. And since what is done is done in one’s own continuity, it says ‘in one’s own continuity,’ etc. And doing is twofold: producing and resorting. To show this, it is said ‘produced or...,’ etc. Herein, producing is the generation of a result through the convergence of cause and conditions. Resorting, however, is resorting by way of use through application to the body, and resorting by way of object through cognizing, perceiving, etc. By that very resorting to an object, the state of natural decisive support is spoken of even for future things that are resorted to, such as a favorable climate, etc.—how much more so for past and present ones. For even of the present, the state of natural decisive support is obtained from such statements as: ‘Relying on present climate, food, and lodging, one generates jhāna’ (Paṭṭh 2.18.8). ‘By its own nature’ means by its own intrinsic nature, free from admixture with other conditions. ‘Decisive support’ means a strong reason. The distinction into numerous kinds should be understood according to the method that comes in the Question Section. In the Condition Section, however—

“Purimā purimā kusalā dhammā pacchimānaṃ pacchimānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upanissayapaccayena paccayo, purimā purimā kusalā dhammā pacchimānaṃ pacchimānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ kesañci, kusalā abyākatānaṃ, akusalā akusalānaṃ, kusalānaṃ kesañci, akusalā abyākatānaṃ, abyākatā abyākatānaṃ, abyākatā kusalānaṃ, abyākatā akusalānaṃ[V 2.0261], puggalopi, senāsanampi upanissayapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.9).

“Preceding, preceding wholesome states are a condition for succeeding, succeeding wholesome states by way of decisive support condition; preceding, preceding wholesome states for succeeding, succeeding unwholesome states in some cases; wholesome states for indeterminate states; unwholesome states for unwholesome states, and for wholesome states in some cases; unwholesome states for indeterminate states; indeterminate states for indeterminate states; indeterminate states for wholesome states; indeterminate states for unwholesome states. A person, and also lodging, are a condition by way of decisive support condition” (Paṭṭh 1.1.9).

Tattha ye purimā yesaṃ pacchimānaṃ anantarūpanissayo honti, te tesaṃ sabbesampi ekanteneva honti, na kesañci kadāci. Tasmā yesu padesu anantarūpanissayo labbhati, tesu “kesañcī”ti na sakkā vattunti na vuttaṃ. Ye pana purimā yesaṃ pacchimānaṃ ārammaṇūpanissayo vā pakatūpanissayo vā honti, te tesaṃ, na sabbesaṃ ekantena honti. Yesaṃ uppattivibandhakā paccayā balavanto honti, tesaṃ na bhavanti, itaresaṃ bhavanti. Tasmā yesu padesu anantarapaccayo na labbhati, tesu “kesañcī”ti vuttaṃ. Siddhānaṃ paccayadhammānaṃ yehi paccayuppannehi bhavitabbaṃ, tesaṃ “kesañcī”ti ayamettha attho.

Herein, those preceding states that are the contiguity-decisive support for succeeding ones are so for all of them absolutely, not for some, sometimes. Therefore, in those sections where contiguity-decisive support is found, it is not possible to say ‘for some,’ so it is not said. But those preceding states that are the object-decisive support or natural decisive support for succeeding ones are not so for all of them absolutely. For those for which obstructive conditions to their arising are strong, they are not a condition; for others, they are. Therefore, in those sections where the contiguity condition is not found, it is said ‘for some.’ This is the meaning here: of the established conditioning states, it is for some of those conditioned phenomena that should arise.

Kasiṇapaññattiyā ārammaṇūpanissayatābhāvato ekaccāya paññattiyā saddhiṃ sabbo dhammo ārammaṇūpanissayo, anantarātīto cittacetasikarāsi anantarūpanissayo, kusalākusalavipākakiriyārūpavasena pañcavidho [M 2.0279] pakatūpanissayoti ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana paṭṭhānaṭṭhakathāyaṃ veditabbo.

Since a kasiṇa concept does not have the state of being an object-decisive support, all phenomena together with certain concepts are an object-decisive support. The immediately past aggregate of consciousness and mental factors is a contiguity-decisive support. Natural decisive support is fivefold by way of wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional, and matter. This is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, should be understood from the Paṭṭhāna Commentary.

603. Paṭhamataranti paccayuppannato puretaraṃ. Ayañhi purejātapaccayo rūpadhammavaseneva labbhati. Paccayuppanno ca arūpadhammāyeva. Tenāha “vattamānabhāvena upakārako”ti. Nissayārammaṇākārādīhi visiṭṭhā purejātabhāvena vinā upakārakabhāvaṃ agacchantānaṃ vatthārammaṇānaṃ purejātākārena upakārakatā purejātapaccayatā. Evaṃ vatthārammaṇavasena duvidhe purejātapaccaye “cakkhāyatana”ntiādi vatthuvasena vuttaṃ, “rūpārammaṇa”ntiādi ārammaṇavasena.

603. Earlier means earlier than the conditioned phenomenon. For this pre-nascence condition is obtained only by way of material phenomena, while the conditioned phenomenon consists only of immaterial phenomena. Hence it is said, ‘helpful by way of presence.’ Pre-nascence conditionality is the helpfulness in the mode of pre-nascence of those bases and objects which, although distinguished by modes such as support, object, etc., do not become helpful without the state of pre-nascence. Thus, in the twofold pre-nascence condition by way of base and object, ‘eye-base,’ etc., is stated by way of base, and ‘visible form as object,’ etc., is stated by way of object.

Yaṃ rūpanti hadayavatthuṃ sandhāyāha. Tattha “kiñci kāle”ti pavattikālavasena vuttaṃ. “Kiñci kālena” iti paṭisandhikālavasena. Yāni ārammaṇapurejātena vinā na vattanti, tesaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ ārammaṇapurejātadassanena manodvārepi yaṃ yaṃ ārammaṇapurejātena vattati, tassa tassa ārammaṇapaccayabhūtaṃ sabbaṃ rūparūpaṃ ārammaṇapurejātanti dassitameva hoti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ pañhāvāre “ārammaṇapurejātaṃ sekkhā vā puthujjanā vā cakkhuṃ aniccato [V 2.0262] dukkhato anattato vipassantī”tiādi (paṭṭhā. 1.1.424). “Abyākato dhammo abyākatassa dhammassa purejātapaccayena paccayo, abyākato dhammo kusalassa dhammassa purejātapaccayena paccayo, abyākato dhammo akusalassa dhammassa purejātapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.424) abyākatamūlakā tayova vārā. Te ca paccekaṃ vatthupurejātaṃ, ārammaṇapurejātanti dvidhā vibhattā.

‘What material form’ refers to the heart-base. Therein, ‘at some time’ is said with reference to the time of occurrence; the words ‘not at some time’ are said with reference to the time of rebirth-linking. By showing the object pre-nascence for eye-consciousness and so on—which do not occur without object pre-nascence—it is also shown that for whatever occurs at the mind-door with object pre-nascence, all produced material form that serves as its object condition is object pre-nascence. For so it is said in the Question Section: ‘As object pre-nascence, trainees or worldlings contemplate the eye as impermanent, as suffering, as non-self,’ etc. ‘An indeterminate phenomenon is a condition for an indeterminate phenomenon by way of pre-nascence condition; an indeterminate phenomenon is a condition for a wholesome phenomenon by way of pre-nascence condition; an indeterminate phenomenon is a condition for an unwholesome phenomenon by way of pre-nascence condition’—these are the three sections rooted in the indeterminate. And they are each divided in two as base pre-nascence and object pre-nascence.

604. Paccayuppannadhammassa puretaraṃ siddhabhāve sati paccayadhammassa pacchājātatāti vuttaṃ “purejātāna”nti. Ayañca nayo rūpadhammesu eva labbhati, na arūpadhammesūti vuttaṃ “rūpadhammāna”nti. Yadi paccayuppannadhammā puretarameva jātā, kathaṃ paccayabhāvoti āha “upathambhakattenā”ti. Pacchājātena hi vinā santānāvicchedahetubhāvaṃ agacchantānaṃ dhammānaṃ ye pacchājātākārena upakārakā, tesaṃ sā vippayuttākārādīhi visiṭṭhā upakārakatā [M 2.0280] pacchājātapaccayatā. Evaṃ sabbapaccayānaṃ paccayantarākāravisiṭṭhā upakārakatā yojetabbā. “Gijjhapotakasarīrānaṃ āhārāsācetanā viyā”ti etena manosañcetanāhāravasena pavattamānehi arūpadhammehi rūpakāyassa upatthambhitabhāvaṃ dasseti. Teneva “āhārāsā viyā”ti avatvā cetanāggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Kāyassāti catusamuṭṭhānikabhūtupādāyarūpasaṅkhātassa rūpakāyassa. Saṅkhepato ṭhapetvā rūpadhamme avisiṭṭho arūpakkhandho pacchājātapaccayo. So jātivasena kusalo, akusalo, vipāko, kiriyāti catubbidhoti veditabbaṃ.

604. “Of prior-nascent things” is said because when the conditionally arisen phenomenon is established as having arisen earlier, the conditioning phenomenon is later-born. This principle is found only in material phenomena, not in immaterial phenomena; hence it is said, “of material phenomena.” If the conditionally arisen phenomena have arisen earlier, how can there be the state of being a condition? It is said: “by way of supporting.” Indeed, whatever immaterial phenomena are helpful in the mode of being later-born to those material phenomena that, without a later-born phenomenon, do not attain the state of being a cause for the non-interruption of the continuity—the helpfulness of those phenomena, which is distinct from the modes of dissociation and so on, is the post-nascence condition. Thus the helpfulness of all conditions, distinguished by the modes of other conditions, should be applied. By “like the volition associated with craving for food for the bodies of vulture chicks,” he shows how the material body is supported by immaterial phenomena that occur by way of mental volition as nutriment. For that reason, without saying “like the craving for food,” the word “volition” is used. “Of the body” refers to the material body comprised of primary and derived matter with a fourfold origin. In brief, setting aside material phenomena, the undifferentiated immaterial aggregate is the post-nascence condition. It should be understood as fourfold by way of its class: wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional.

605. Kusalādibhāvena attanā sadisassa payogena karaṇīyassa punappunaṃ karaṇaṃ pavattanaṃ āsevanaṭṭho, attasadisasabhāvatāpādanaṃ vāsanaṃ vā. Purimapurimābhiyogo viyāti uggahaṇasavanadhāraṇādipurimāpurimāsevanā viya. Tīsu pana etesu purimā purimāti samanantarātītā daṭṭhabbā. Kasmā panettha anantarapaccaye viya “purimā purimā kusalā dhammā pacchimānaṃ pacchimānaṃ abyākatāna”ntiādinā bhinnajātiyehi saddhiṃ niddeso na katoti? Attano gatiṃ gāhetuṃ asamatthattā. Bhinnajātikā hi bhinnajātikānaṃ āsevanaguṇena paguṇabalavabhāvaṃ sampādentā attanova kusalādibhāvasaṅkhātaṃ gatiṃ gāhetuṃ na sakkuṇanti. Tasmā tehi saddhiṃ niddesaṃ akatvā ye yesaṃ vāsanāsaṅkhātena āsevanaguṇena paguṇabalavabhāvavisiṭṭhaṃ attano kusalādibhāvasaṅkhātaṃ gatiṃ gāhetuṃ samatthā, tesaṃ tehi samānajātikeheva saddhiṃ niddeso katoti daṭṭhabbo.

605. The meaning of repetition is the repeated performance or continuation of what is to be done by an effort similar to oneself in being wholesome, etc.; or it is the imprinting that produces a nature similar to oneself. 'Like the earlier and earlier application' means like the earlier and earlier repetition of learning, listening, memorizing, and so on. Why here, unlike in the contiguity condition, is an exposition not made together with those of a different class, such as 'earlier and earlier wholesome states are a condition for later and later indeterminate states'? Because of their inability to make the other grasp their own course. For those of a different class, even when they produce a proficient and strong state for those of a different class by the quality of repetition, are unable to make them grasp their own course, designated as wholesome, etc. Therefore, it should be understood that, without making an exposition in connection with them, the exposition is made only in connection with those of the same class, which are capable of making others grasp their own course—distinguished by a proficient and strong state through the quality of repetition known as imprinting—which is designated as wholesome, and so on.

Atha [V 2.0263] vipākābyākataṃ kasmā na gahitaṃ? Āsevanābhāvato. Vipākābyākatañhi kammavasena vipākabhāvappattaṃ kammapariṇāmitaṃ hutvā pavattamānaṃ nirussāhaṃ dubbalaṃ santaṃ āsevanaguṇena attano sabhāvaṃ gāhetvā paribhāvetvā neva aññaṃ vipākaṃ pavatteti, na ca purimavipākānubhāvaṃ gahetvā uppajjati, atha kho kammavegakkhittaṃ patitaṃ viya hutvā uppajjati. Tasmā sabbathāpi vipāke āsevanā natthīti na gahitaṃ. Kusalākusalakiriyānantaraṃ uppajjamānampi sakammapaṭibaddhavuttitāya āsevanaguṇaṃ na gaṇhātīti kusalādayopi tassa āsevanapaccayo na honti. Nānājātikattāpi cete tassa āsevanādhānaṃ na [M 2.0281] karonteva. Bhūmito, pana ārammaṇato vā nānājātikatā nāma natthīti parittakusalakiriyā mahaggatakusalakiriyānaṃ, saṅkhārārammaṇañca kusalaṃ nibbānārammaṇassa āsevanapaccayo hotiyeva. Svāyaṃ “kusalo dhammo kusalassa, akusalo dhammo akusalassa, abyākato dhammo abyākatassa āsevanapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.426) tidhāva vutto. Abyākataggahaṇena āvajjanavajjitā kiriyadhammā gahitā.

Why, then, is the resultant indeterminate not included? Because of the absence of repetition. For the resultant indeterminate—having reached the state of a result by the force of kamma, being transformed by kamma, occurring without effort, weak, and tranquil—neither grasps and imbues its own nature by the quality of repetition, nor does it cause another result to occur, nor does it arise by taking up the power of a previous result. Therefore, since there is absolutely no repetition in a result, it is not included. Even when arising immediately after wholesome, unwholesome, or functional states, it does not acquire the quality of repetition because its occurrence is bound to its own kamma; thus wholesome states, etc., are not a condition for it by way of repetition condition. Moreover, because they are of a different class, they do not provide a basis for its repetition. However, there is no such thing as being of a different class from the standpoint of plane or object. Thus, a wholesome or functional action of the sense sphere can be a repetition condition for sublime wholesome or functional actions, and a wholesome state with formations as its object for one with Nibbāna as its object. Thus this is stated in three ways: 'A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state, an unwholesome state for an unwholesome state, and an indeterminate state for an indeterminate state by way of repetition condition.' By the term 'indeterminate,' functional phenomena, apart from the two advertences, are included.

606. Cittapayogo cittakiriyā, āyūhananti attho. Yathā hi kāyavacīpayogo viññatti, evaṃ cittapayogo cetanā. Tena hi sā uppannakiriyatāvisiṭṭhe santāne sesapaccayasamāgame pavattamānānaṃ vipākakaṭattārūpānampi teneva santānavisesena kiriyābhāvena upakārikā hoti. Tassa hi kiriyābhāvassa pavattattā tesaṃ pavatti, na aññathā. Sahajātānaṃ pana āyūhanakiriyābhāvena pavattamānā upakārikāti kiṃ vattabbaṃ. Kammanti ca cetanākammameva adhippetaṃ. Na hi cetanāsampayuttaṃ kammaṃ abhijjhādi kammapaccayo hoti. Satipi vipākadhammabhāve cetanāvajjānaṃ ataṃsabhāvattā vipākāpi cetanā sahajātakammapaccayo hotiyeva, svāyaṃ kammapaccayo jātivasena catubbidhoti sabbaṃ vattabbaṃ.

606. Mental application is mental action; the meaning is striving. For just as bodily and verbal application is intimation, so mental application is volition. Therefore, in a continuity distinguished by arisen action, when the remaining conditions are present, it is helpful even to resultant and kamma-born material phenomena that are occurring, by that very state of being an action which is a distinction of the continuity. For their occurrence is due to the occurrence of that nature as action, not otherwise. But for co-nascent states, what need be said that it is helpful, occurring with the nature of an action of striving? And by 'kamma,' only volition as kamma is intended. For kamma associated with volition, such as covetousness, is not the kamma condition. Even though there are resultant states, since resultant states other than volition do not have that nature, resultant volition is indeed a conascence-kamma condition. This kamma condition, it should be said, is fourfold by way of class.

607. “Nirussāhasantabhāvenā”ti etena saussāhehi vipākadhammadhammehi kusalākusalehi sārammaṇādibhāvena sadisānampi asadisaṃ vipākabhāvaṃ dasseti. So hi vipākānaṃ payogena asādhetabbatāya payogena, aññathā vā sesapaccayesu siddhesu kammassa kaṭattā eva sijjhanato nirussāho santabhāvo hoti, na kilesavūpasantabhāvo. Tathāsantabhāvato eva hi bhavaṅgādayo duviññeyyā. Pañcadvārepi hi javanappavattiyā rūpādīnaṃ gahitatā viññāyati, abhinipātasampaṭicchanasantīraṇamattā pana vipākā duviññeyyā eva. Nirussāhasantabhāvāyāti [V 2.0264] nirussāhasantabhāvatthāya. Etena tappaccayavantānaṃ avipākānampi rūpadhammānaṃ vipākānukūlaṃ pavattiṃ dasseti. Pavattetiādi pañhāvāranayaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ. Paṭiccavāre pana “vipākā cattāro [M 2.0282] khandhā arūpino aññamaññaṃ vipākapaccayena paccayo”tiādinā (paṭṭhā. 1.1.14) āgatā. Ettha ca yesaṃ ekantena vipāko vipākapaccayo hoti, tesaṃ vasena nayadassanaṃ katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi āruppe kāmarūpabhūmīsu viya vipāko rūpassa paccayo hoti.

607. By 'by being without exertion and tranquil,' he shows the dissimilar nature of the resultant, even though it is similar to the wholesome and unwholesome states—which involve exertion and are the basis for resultants—in having an object, etc. For since a resultant is not to be accomplished by effort, but is accomplished simply because the kamma has been done when the other conditions are established, it is a state that is without exertion and tranquil; it is not the pacification of defilements. It is precisely because of such a tranquil nature that the life-continuum and other states are difficult to discern. For even in the five-door process, the grasping of forms, etc., is discerned during the impulsion phase, but the resultants—which are merely impinging, receiving, and investigating—are indeed difficult to discern. 'For the sake of being without exertion and tranquil' means for the purpose of being without exertion and tranquil. By this he shows the occurrence, in a way conformable to a resultant, even of non-resultant material phenomena that are dependent on that condition. The words 'it causes to occur,' etc., are stated adopting the method of the question section. In the section on conditionality, however, it is stated: 'The four immaterial resultant aggregates are a condition for one another by way of resultant condition,' and so on. And here it should be understood that the exposition of the method is made with reference to those for which a resultant is exclusively a resultant condition. For in the formless realm, unlike in the sense-sphere and form-sphere realms, a resultant is not a condition for material phenomena.

608. Satipi janakabhāve upatthambhakattaṃ āhārānaṃ padhānakiccanti āha “rūpārūpānaṃ upatthambhakattenā”ti. Upatthambhakattañhi satipi janakatte arūpīnaṃ āhārānaṃ, āhārajarūpasamuṭṭhāpakarūpāhārassa ca hoti. Asatipi catusamuṭṭhānikarūpūpatthambhakarūpāhārassa, asati pana upatthambhakatte āhārānaṃ janakattaṃ natthīti upatthambhakattaṃ padhānaṃ. Atha vā janayamānopi āhāro avicchedavasena upatthambhento janetīti upatthambhanabhāvo eva āhārabhāvoti “upatthambhakattenā”ti vuttaṃ. Keci pana “rūpāhāro attanā janitassa āhārapaccayo na hoti, aññena janitassa hoti, tasmā ‘upatthambhakattenā’ti vutta”nti vadanti. Taṃ “āhāro rūpassa paccayo honto āhārapaccayo na hotīti viruddhameta”nti apare nānujānanti. Rūpāhāro cettha rūpadhammānaṃ eva āhārapaccayo hoti. Arūpāhārā pana rūpadhammānampi āhārapaccayo honti. Tañca kho na kevalaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ rūpānameva, atha kho kadāci kaṭattārūpānampīti dassetuṃ “pañhāvāre panā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

608. He says, 'by supporting material and immaterial phenomena,' because, even when there is a generative state, the primary function of nutriments is supporting. For the state of supporting exists for immaterial nutriments even when they generate, and for material nutriment that originates nutriment-born matter; and also for material nutriment that supports matter with fourfold origination even when it does not generate. But when there is no supporting, there is no generation by nutriments; thus supporting is the primary function. Alternatively, since even when generating, nutriment generates by supporting in the sense of non-interruption, the very nature of supporting is the nature of nutriment; thus it is said, 'by supporting.' Some, however, say: 'Material nutriment is not a nutriment condition for what it itself generates, but for what is generated by another; hence it is said, "by supporting."' Others do not approve of this, saying: 'This is a contradiction: that nutriment, while being a condition for matter, is not a nutriment condition.' Here, material nutriment is a nutriment condition only for material phenomena, whereas immaterial nutriments are nutriment conditions for material phenomena as well. And to show that this is so not only for mind-originated matter but sometimes also for kamma-born matter, it is said: 'But in the question section,' etc.

609. Adhipatiyaṭṭhenāti ettha na adhipatipaccayadhammānaṃ viya pavattinivārake abhibhavitvā pavattanena garubhāvo adhipatiyaṭṭho, atha kho dassanādikiccesu cakkhuviññāṇādīhi, jīvane kammajarūpehi arūpadhammehi ca jīvantehi, manane sampayuttadhammehi, sukhitādibhāve sukhitādīhi, adhimokkhapaggahūpaṭṭhānāvikkhepapajānanesu, “anaññātaṃ ñassāmī”ti pavattiyaṃ ājānane, aññātāvibhāve ca saddhādisahajātehīti evaṃ taṃtaṃkiccesu cakkhādipaccayehi dhammehi cakkhādīnaṃ anuvattanīyatā. Tesu hi kiccesu cakkhādīnaṃ issariyaṃ, tappaccayānañca tadanuvattanena tattha pavatti. Kasmā panettha itthipurisindriyadvayaṃ na gahitaṃ, nanu cetampi liṅgādīhi anuvattīyatīti? Saccaṃ anuvattīyati, na pana paccayabhāvato. Yathā hi jīvitāhārā [M 2.0283] yesaṃ paccayā honti, tesaṃ anupālakaupatthambhakā[V 2.0265], atthiavigatapaccayabhūtā ca honti, na evaṃ itthipurisabhāvā liṅgādīnaṃ kenaci pakārena upakārakā honti. Yato paccayā siyuṃ, kevalaṃ pana yathāsakehi eva paccayehi pavattamānānaṃ liṅgādīnaṃ yathā itthiādiggahaṇassa paccayabhāvo hoti, tato aññenākārena taṃsahitasantāne appavattito liṅgādīhi anuvattanīyatā, indriyatā ca tesaṃ vuccati. Tasmā na tesaṃ indriyapaccayabhāvo vutto. Cakkhādayo arūpadhammānaṃyevāti ettha sukhindriyadukkhindriyānipi cakkhādiggahaṇena gahitānīti daṭṭhabbāni.

609. Herein, by 'in the sense of dominance,' the meaning of dominance is not, as in the case of the dominance condition, a state of weightiness occurring by overpowering other dominance-condition states that obstruct its arising. But rather, it is the state of being followed: in the functions of seeing and so on, the eye and so on are followed by eye-consciousness and so on; in the function of living, the life faculty is followed by living kamma-born matter and immaterial states; in the function of cognizing, the mind faculty is followed by associated states; in the state of being happy and so on, the feeling faculty is followed by states associated with pleasure and so on; in the functions of decision, exertion, establishment, non-distraction, and discernment, and in the arising with the thought, 'I will know the unknown,' in precise knowing, and in the state of one who has known, the respective faculties are followed by faith and other co-nascent states. Thus, in these respective functions, it is the state of the eye and so on being followed by those phenomena for which they are a condition. For in these functions, the eye and so on have mastery, and the phenomena conditioned by them occur there by following them. But why are the two faculties of femininity and masculinity not included here? Are they not also followed by gender characteristics and so on? It is true, they are followed, but not from the state of being a condition. For just as life and nutriment are sustainers and supporters for those things of which they are conditions, and are conditions by way of presence and non-disappearance, so the states of femininity and masculinity do not assist the gender characteristics and so on in any way that they could be conditions. Rather, since the gender characteristics and so on arise merely from their own respective conditions, and since they do not occur in the continuity associated with them in any other way than that whereby there is a conditionality for the apprehension of 'female,' etc., their state of being followed by gender characteristics and so on, and their faculty-nature, are spoken of. Therefore, their state as a faculty condition is not stated. In the statement, 'The eye, etc., are only for immaterial phenomena,' it should be understood that the faculties of pleasure and pain are also included by the term 'the eye, etc.'

610. Lakkhaṇārammaṇūpanijjhānabhūtānaṃ vitakkādīnaṃ vitakkanādivasena ārammaṇaṃ upagantvā nijjhānaṃ pekkhanaṃ, cintanaṃ vā vitakkādīnaṃyeva āveṇiko byāpāro upanijjhāyanaṭṭho. “Ṭhapetvā dvipañcaviññāṇe sukhadukkhavedanādvaya”nti vatvāpi “satta jhānaṅgānī”ti vacanena ajhānaṅgānaṃ upekkhācittekaggatānaṃ nivattanaṃ katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yadi evaṃ “satta jhānaṅgānī”ti eteneva siddhe “ṭhapetvā sukhadukkhavedanādvaya”nti kasmā vuttaṃ? Vedanābhedesu pañcasu sukhadukkhadvayassa ekantena ajhānaṅgabhāvadassanatthaṃ jhānaṅgaṭṭhāne niddiṭṭhattā, satipi vā jhānaṅgavohāre vedanābhedadvayassa ekantena jhānapaccayattābhāvadassanatthaṃ. Upekkhācittekaggatānaṃ pana yadipi jhānapaccayattābhāvo atthi, najhānapaccayabhāvo pana natthīti sabbānipi satta jhānaṅgānīti ettha gahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Tattha “sabbānipī”ti vacanaṃ sabbakusalādibhedasaṅgaṇhanatthaṃ, na pana sabbacittuppādagatasaṅgaṇhanatthanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yesaṃ pana “ṭhapetvā dvipañcaviññāṇe vedanāttaya”nti pāṭho, tesaṃ yathāvutto vicāro cittekaggatāvaseneva veditabbo.

610. The meaning of 'close contemplation' (upanijjhāyana) is the unique function of initial application (vitakka) and so on—which are the close contemplation of characteristics and the close contemplation of the object—that consists of the seeing which is contemplation, or the thinking, after having approached an object by way of initial application and so on. Although it is said, 'Excluding the pair of feelings, pleasure and pain, in the two sets of five consciousnesses,' it should be understood that by the statement 'seven jhāna factors,' the exclusion of equanimity and one-pointedness of mind (which are not jhāna factors in those consciousnesses) has been made. If so, why was it said, 'Excluding the pair of feelings, pleasure and pain,' when this is established by 'seven jhāna factors' alone? It was said to show that among the five kinds of feeling, the pair of pleasure and pain are entirely not jhāna factors, because they are specified in the section on jhāna factors; or, alternatively, to show that even though there is the designation 'jhāna factor,' this pair of feeling-divisions is entirely not a jhāna-condition. As for equanimity and one-pointedness of mind, although there are instances where they are not a jhāna-condition, it is not the case that they are never a jhāna-condition. Thus, they are included here in 'all seven are jhāna factors.' Therein, the word 'all' should be understood as for including all divisions such as wholesome, etc., and not for including them as present in every consciousness-moment. For those who have the reading, 'Excluding the triad of feeling in the two sets of five consciousnesses,' the aforesaid investigation should be understood by way of one-pointedness of mind only.

611. Yato tato vāti sammā vā micchā vāti attho. Pañhāvāre panātiādi yadipi paccayaniddese taṃsamuṭṭhānaggahaṇena so attho ñāpito eva, pañhāvāre pana sarūpeneva gahitoti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Ete pana dvepi…pe… na labbhanti “yathāsaṅkhya”nti vacanaseso veditabbo. Paṭṭhānaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “dvepi jhānamaggapaccayā ahetukacittesu na labbhantī”ti vuttaṃ. Tenassa kathamavirodhoti? Adhippāyavasena[M 2.0284]. Ayañhi tattha adhippāyo – ahetukacittesu eva jhānamaggapaccayā na labbhanti, na sahetukacittesūti sahetukacittesu alābhābhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na ahetukacittesu lābhābhāvadassanatthanti. Evañhi atthe gayhamāne ahetukacittesu katthaci kassaci lābho na nivāritoti viññāyati. Tena savitakkāhetukacittesu jhānapaccayassa sambhavo anuññāto hoti. Tattha hi yena alābhena dhammasaṅgaṇiyaṃ [V 2.0266] manodhātuādīnaṃ saṅgahasuññatavāresu jhānaṃ na uddhaṭaṃ, taṃ alābhaṃ sandhāya jhānapaccayassapi ahetukacittesu alābho vutto. Yathā hi sahetukacittuppādesu vitakkādīnaṃ sahajāte saṅkaḍḍhitvā ekattagatabhāvakaraṇaṃ upanijjhāyanabyāpāro balavā, na tathā ahetukacittuppādesūti. Idha pana dubbalampi upanijjhāyanaṃ yadi kiñcimattampi atthi, na tena upakārakatā na hotīti savitakkāhetukacittesupi jhānapaccayaṃ anujānantena “ete pana dvepi jhānamaggapaccayā dvipañcaviññāṇāhetukacittesu na labbhantī”ti (paṭṭhā. aṭṭha. paccayuddesavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ. Paccayakathā nāma samantapaṭṭhānanissitā, na dhammasaṅgaṇīnissitāti.

611. 'From this or that' means 'whether right or wrong.' 'In the question section, etc.': although in the exposition of conditions that meaning is indicated by taking the co-arisen, this is said to show that in the question section it is taken by its own nature. 'But these two... are not obtained': the remainder of the statement, 'respectively,' should be understood. In the Paṭṭhāna commentary, however, it is said: 'The two, the jhāna and path conditions, are not obtained in rootless consciousnesses.' How is this not a contradiction? By way of intention. For this is the intention there: The jhāna and path conditions are not obtained only in rootless consciousnesses; they are not unobtainable in rooted consciousnesses. Thus, the statement was made to show that there is no non-obtainment (i.e., there is obtainment) in rooted consciousnesses, not to show the non-obtainment in rootless consciousnesses. For when the meaning is taken in this way, it is understood that the obtainment of some jhāna factor in some rootless consciousness is not precluded. Therefore, the possibility of the jhāna-condition is permitted in rootless consciousnesses accompanied by initial application. For there, with reference to that non-obtainment by which jhāna was not extracted in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī in the sections on the emptiness of inclusion regarding the mind-element, etc., the non-obtainment of the jhāna-condition in rootless consciousnesses is also stated. For just as in the arising of rooted consciousnesses the function of close contemplation—which draws in the co-nascent factors like initial application and brings them to a state of unity—is strong, it is not so in the arising of rootless consciousnesses. Here, however, on the principle that even a weak close contemplation, if there is any at all, is not unhelpful, the jhāna-condition is allowed even in rootless consciousnesses accompanied by initial application, and so it is said: 'But these two, the jhāna and path conditions, are not obtained in the rootless consciousnesses of the two pentads of sense consciousness' (Paṭṭhāna-aṭṭhakathā, Exposition of the enumeration of conditions). The discourse on conditions is based on the Samantapaṭṭhāna, not on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī.

612. Samaṃ avisamaṃ, sammā, saha vā pakārehi yuttatāya ekībhāvūpagamena viya upakārakatā sampayuttapaccayatā. Kā pana sā pakārehi yuttatāti āha “ekavatthukaekārammaṇaekuppādekanirodhasaṅkhātenā”ti. Tattha ye ekavatthukā, te sampayuttāti ettake vuccamāne avinibbhogarūpesu ekaṃ mahābhūtaṃ sesamahābhūtupādārūpānaṃ nissayapaccayo hoti, tena tāni ekavatthukāni, cakkhādinissayabhūtāni vā bhūtāni ekaṃ vatthu etesu nissitanti ekavatthukānīti kappentassa tesaṃ sampayuttatāpatti siyāti tannivāraṇatthaṃ ekārammaṇaggahaṇaṃ. Ye ekavatthukā, ekārammaṇā ca, te sampayuttāti evampi cutiāsannānaṃ sampaṭicchanasantīraṇādīnaṃ sampayuttatā āpajjeyyāti ekuppādaggahaṇaṃ. Ye ekavatthukekārammaṇekuppādā, te sampayuttāti kiṃ pana nānānirodhāpi evaṃtividhalakkhaṇā honti, udāhu ekanirodhā evāti vicāraṇāyaṃ ekanirodhā eva evaṃlakkhaṇā hontīti dassanatthaṃ “ekanirodhā”ti vuttaṃ.

612. Helpfulness, like an approach to unity, by reason of being endowed with modes—equally, without discrepancy, or rightly, or together—is the association condition. But what is that 'being endowed with modes'? It is said: 'By that which is designated as having a single base, a single object, a single arising, and a single cessation.' Therein, if it were stated simply that 'those which have a single base are associated,' then among inseparable material forms, one great element is a support condition for the remaining great elements and derived material forms, and thus they have a single base; or, for one who imagines that the elements that are the support for the eye, etc., have a single base because one thing is dependent on them, the undesirable consequence of their being associated might arise. To prevent this, the inclusion of 'single object' is made. If it is stated that 'those which have a single base and a single object are associated,' the association of receiving, investigating, etc., close to death might occur. Thus, the inclusion of 'single arising' is made. 'Those which have a single base, a single object, and a single arising are associated.' But upon consideration of whether those with different cessations also have this threefold characteristic, or only those with a single cessation, the term 'single cessation' is stated to show that only those with a single cessation have these characteristics.

Paṭilomato vā ekanirodhā sampayuttāti vuccamāne ekasmiṃ khaṇe nirujjhamānānaṃ rūpārūpadhammānaṃ sampayuttatā āpajjeyyāti “ekuppādā”ti [M 2.0285] vuttaṃ. Evampi avinibbhogarūpānaṃ atthi ekuppādekanirodhatāti tesampi sampayuttatā āpajjeyyāti tannivāraṇatthaṃ ekārammaṇaggahaṇaṃ. Ye ekārammaṇā hutvā ekuppādekanirodhā, te sampayuttāti ayañca nayo ekavatthukesu eva labbhati, na nānāvatthukesūti dassanatthaṃ ekavatthukaggahaṇaṃ. Ye ekavatthukekārammaṇekuppādekanirodhā, te sampayuttāti pañcavokārabhavāpekkhāya cetaṃ ekavatthukaggahaṇaṃ. Āruppe pana vatthuyeva natthīti kuto ekavatthukaggahaṇassa avasaro.

Or, arguing in reverse, if it were said, 'Those with a single cessation are associated,' the association of material and immaterial phenomena ceasing in a single moment would result; hence, 'single arising' is stated. Even so, inseparable material forms have a state of single arising and single cessation; thus their association would also result. To prevent that, the inclusion of 'single object' is made. 'Those that, having a single object, have a single arising and a single cessation, are associated.' This principle, however, is found only in cases with a single base, not in cases with different bases; to show this, the inclusion of 'single base' is made. 'Those that have a single base, a single object, a single arising, and a single ceasing are associated.' This inclusion of 'single base' is with reference to existence in the five-constituent planes. But in the formless realm, there is no base at all, so where is there an opportunity for the inclusion of 'single base'?

613. Aññamaññaṃ [V 2.0267] sambandhatāya yuttānampi samānānaṃ vippayuttabhāvena visaṃsaṭṭhatāya nānattūpagamena upakārakatā vippayuttapaccayatā. Ayañca vippayuttatā na sampayuttapaccayatāya viya aññamaññaṃ paccayapaccayuppannadhammavasena gahetabbā, atha kho visuṃyeva. Tattha hi arūpadhammānaṃ samānajātiyatāya samadhuraṃ, idha rūpārūpadhammānaṃ vijātiyatāya vidhuraṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “yuttānampi…pe… vippayuttapaccayatā”ti. Na hi vatthusahajātapacchājātavasena ayuttānaṃ rūpādīnaṃ ārammaṇādibhāvena upakārakānaṃ vippayuttānampi vippayuttapaccayatā atthi. Yathā hi “vatthu khandhānaṃ vippayuttapaccayena paccayo, sahajātā kusalā khandhā cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ rūpānaṃ, pacchājātā kusalā khandhā purejātassa imassa kāyassa vippayuttapaccayena paccayo”tiādivacanato (paṭṭhā. 1.1.434) vatthunā, sahajātapacchājātavasena ca yuttānaṃ atthi vippayuttapaccayabhāvo, na evaṃ ayuttānaṃ atthīti. Yadi evaṃ rūpānaṃ rūpehi kasmā vippayuttapaccayo na vuttoti? Rūpānaṃ rūpehi satipi avinibbhoge sampayogo viya vippayogo (dhātu. 3) natthīti na tesaṃ vippayuttapaccayatā. Vuttañhi “catūhi sampayogo, catūhi vippayogo”ti. Sampayujjamānānañhi arūpānaṃ rūpehi, rūpānañca tehi siyā sampayogāsaṅkāti tesaṃ aññamaññaṃ vippayuttapaccayatā vuttā. Rūpānaṃ pana rūpehi sampayogo natthīti na tesaṃ vippayuttapaccayatā vuttā.

613. The helpfulness of phenomena that, though associated by being mutually connected, are helpful by way of being in a state of dissociation, unmixedness, and otherness, is the dissociated condition. And this dissociation is not to be understood, like that in the associated condition, in terms of mutually conditioning and conditioned phenomena, but as entirely separate. For in that case, there is an equal yoke due to the similar nature of the immaterial phenomena, while here there is an unequal yoke due to the different natures of material and immaterial phenomena. Therefore it is said: “Though associated… this is the dissociated condition.” For there is no dissociated conditionality for material phenomena, etc., that are unassociated by way of basis, co-nascence, or post-nascence, even if they are dissociated and are helpful by way of being an object, etc. Just as, according to the statement, “The physical basis is a condition for the mental aggregates by way of the dissociated condition; co-nascent wholesome aggregates are a condition for mind-originated matter…; post-nascent wholesome aggregates are a condition for this pre-nascent body by way of the dissociated condition,” there is a dissociated condition for things associated by way of basis, co-nascence, and post-nascence, so there is no such condition for things that are unassociated. If so, why is a dissociated condition not spoken of for material phenomena with other material phenomena? Because for material phenomena with other material phenomena, though there is inseparability, just as there is no association, there is also no dissociation; therefore their dissociated conditionality is not stated. For it is said: “Association is with the four, dissociation is with the four.” For, in the case of immaterial phenomena that are associating with each other, a doubt might arise about association with material phenomena, and of material phenomena with them; therefore, their mutual dissociated conditionality is stated. But since there is no association of material phenomena with other material phenomena, their dissociated conditionality is not stated.

Rūpino dhammā arūpīnaṃ dhammānaṃ, arūpinopi rūpīnanti ettha arūpaggahaṇaṃ catunnaṃ khandhānaṃ vasena veditabbaṃ. Arūpadhammesu hi cattāro eva khandhā sahajātapurejātānaṃ rūpadhammānaṃ vippayuttapaccayā honti. Nibbānaṃ pana yathā [M 2.0286] arūpadhammānaṃ sampayuttapaccayo na hoti, evaṃ rūpadhammānaṃ vippayuttapaccayo na hoti. “Catūhi sampayogo, catūhi vippayogo”ti (dhātu. 3) hi vuttaṃ. Tasmā arūpadhammesu catunnaṃ khandhānameva vippayuttapaccayatā. Vuttañca pañhāvāre “sahajātā kusalā khandhā cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ rūpānaṃ vippayuttapaccayena paccayo”tiādi (paṭṭhā. 1.1.434). Rūpino dhammāti cetaṃ hadayavatthuno ceva cakkhādīnañca vasena veditabbaṃ. Rūpadhammesu hi cha vatthūniyeva arūpakkhandhānaṃ vippayuttapaccayo. Rūpāyatanādayo pana ārammaṇadhammā kiñcāpi vippayuttadhammā, vippayuttapaccayo pana na honti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Sampayogāsaṅkābhāvato. Arūpakkhandhā hi cakkhādīnaṃ vatthūnaṃ abbhantarato nikkhamantā viya uppajjantīti siyā tattha āsaṅkā “kiṃ nu kho ime imehi sampayuttā, udāhu vippayuttā”ti? Ārammaṇadhammā pana vatthusannissayena uppajjamānānaṃ ārammaṇamattaṃ hontīti natthi tesu sampayogāsaṅkāti [V 2.0268] na te vippayuttā. Sampayogāsaṅkāsabbhāvato vatthūniyeva vippayuttapaccayā honti. Vuttampi cetaṃ pañhāvāre “vatthu kusalānaṃ khandhānaṃ vippayuttapaccayena paccayo, vatthu akusalānaṃ khandhānaṃ, cakkhāyatanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā”tiādi. Svāyaṃ vippayuttapaccayo “sahajātapacchājātato kusalena abyākataṃ, tathā akusalena abyākataṃ, sahajātapurejātapacchājātato abyākatena abyākataṃ, vatthupurejātato abyākatena kusalaṃ, tathā akusalanti kusalamūlamekaṃ, akusalamūlamekaṃ, abyākatamūlāni tīṇī”ti pañcavidho veditabbo.

In the text 'Material phenomena for immaterial phenomena, and immaterial phenomena for material phenomena,' the term 'immaterial' should be understood by way of the four aggregates. For among immaterial phenomena, only the four aggregates are a condition by dissociation for material phenomena that are co-nascent and pre-nascent. Nibbāna, however, just as it is not a condition by association for immaterial phenomena, so too it is not a condition by dissociation for material phenomena. For it is said, 'Association is with four, dissociation is with four.' Therefore, among immaterial phenomena, the state of being a condition by dissociation pertains only to the four aggregates. And it is said in the Pañhāvāra: 'Co-nascent wholesome aggregates are a condition, by way of dissociation condition, for material phenomena originated by consciousness,' and so on. And this phrase 'material phenomena' should be understood by way of the heart-base and the eye, etc. For among material phenomena, only the six bases are a condition by dissociation for the immaterial aggregates. But objective phenomena such as the visible-form-sphere, although they are dissociated phenomena, are not a condition by dissociation. For what reason? Because of the absence of doubt about association. For the immaterial aggregates arise as if emerging from within the bases such as the eye, so there might be a doubt there: 'Are these associated with those, or are they dissociated?' But objective phenomena are merely an object for immaterial phenomena that arise depending on a base; therefore, there is no doubt about association regarding them, and thus they are not conditions by dissociation. Because of the existence of doubt about association, only the bases are conditions by dissociation. And this is also stated in the Pañhāvāra: 'The base is a condition by dissociation for the wholesome aggregates; the base for the unwholesome aggregates; the eye-base for the eye-consciousness element,' and so on. This condition by dissociation should be understood as fivefold: from co-nascence and post-nascence, the wholesome for the indeterminate; similarly, the unwholesome for the indeterminate; from co-nascence, pre-nascence, and post-nascence, the indeterminate for the indeterminate; from pre-nascent base, the indeterminate for the wholesome, and similarly for the unwholesome—thus, one wholesome root, one unwholesome root, and three indeterminate roots.

614. Paccuppannalakkhaṇenāti paccuppannasabhāvena. Tena “atthi me pāpakammaṃ kataṃ, atthi puggalo attahitāya paṭipanno”ti (pu. pa. catukkauddesa 24) ca evamādīsu vuttaṃ nibbattitūpalabbhamānatālakkhaṇaṃ atthibhāvaṃ nivāreti. Satipi janakatte upatthambhakattappadhānā atthibhāvena upakārakatāti āha “upatthambhakattenā”ti. Idañca upatthambhakattaṃ vatthārammaṇasahajātādīnaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ atthibhāvena upakārakattanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Sattadhā mātikā nikkhittā”ti vuttamatthaṃ pāḷiyā eva dassetuṃ “yathāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “cattāro khandhā arūpino”tiādinā sahajātavasena atthipaccayodassito[M 2.0287], “cakkhāyatana”ntiādinā purejātavasena, “yaṃ rūpaṃ nissāyā”tiādinā sahajātapurejātavasena. Evamayaṃ pāṭho sahajātapurejātaatthipaccayavaseneva āgato.

614. 'By the characteristic of the present' means by the nature of being present. By that, in such passages as, 'There is evil kamma done by me,' and 'There is a person practicing for their own welfare,' it precludes the state of existence which has the characteristic of being that which has arisen and is obtainable. Even when there is a generative state, because the assistance by means of the state of existence is primarily that of being a support, it is said, 'by being a support.' And this state of being a support should be understood as the state of assisting by means of the state of existence, which is common to the base, object, co-nascent states, and so on. In order to show the meaning that was stated as, 'The mātikā is laid out in seven ways,' by the Pāḷi itself, 'as it is said,' etc., is stated. Therein, by 'the four immaterial aggregates,' etc., the presence condition is shown by way of co-nascence; by 'the eye-base,' etc., by way of pre-nascence; and by 'depending on which form,' etc., by way of co-nascence and pre-nascence. Thus, this passage has come only by the power of the co-nascent presence and pre-nascent presence conditions.

Aññattha pana tato aññathāpi āgatoti dassetuṃ “pañhāvāre panā”tiādimāha. Taṃ tena pacchājātāhārindriyavasenāpi atthipaccayattaṃ vibhāveti. Purimapāṭhe pana sāvasesā desanā katāti veditabbaṃ. Sati ca yesaṃ paccayā honti, tehi ekato, puretaraṃ, pacchā ca uppannabhāve sahajātādipaccayattābhāvato āhāro, indriyañca sahajātādibhedaṃ na labhanti, tadabhāvo ca tesaṃ dhammasabhāvavasena daṭṭhabbo. Svāyaṃ atthipaccayo “sahajātato kusalena kusalaṃ, sahajātapacchājātato kusalena abyākataṃ, sahajātato eva kusalena kusalābyākatanti kusalamūlā tayo, tathā akusalamūlā. Sahajātapurejātapacchājātāhārindriyato pana abyākatena abyākataṃ, vatthārammaṇapurejātato abyākatena kusalaṃ, tathā akusalaṃ. Sahajātapurejātato kusalañca abyākatañca kusalassa, sahajātapurejātapacchājātāhārindriyato kusalañca abyākatañca abyākatassa, sahajātapurejātato akusalañca abyākatañca akusalassa, sahajātapurejātapacchājātāhārindriyato [V 2.0269] akusalañca abyākatañca abyākatassā”ti evaṃ terasavidho. Saṅkhepena kusalākusalavipākakiriyarūpavasena pañcavidho atthipaccayo, na nibbānaṃ. Yo hi atthibhāvābhāvena anupakārako atthibhāvaṃ labhitvā upakārako hoti, so atthipaccayo hoti. Nibbānañca nibbānārammaṇānaṃ na attano atthibhāvābhāvena anupakārakaṃ hutvā atthibhāvalābhena upakārakaṃ hotīti, uppādādiyuttānaṃ vā natthibhāvopakārakatāviruddho upakārakabhāvo atthipaccayatāti, na nibbānaṃ atthipaccayo hoti.

However, elsewhere, to show that it also comes in another way than that [text], he said, 'But in the Question Section...' and so on. By that [text], he also clarifies that state of being a presence condition by way of post-nascence, nutriment, and faculty conditions. In the earlier text, however, it should be understood that the teaching was given with a remainder. And although [nutriment and faculty] are in a state of having arisen simultaneously with, earlier than, and after those [dhammas] for which they are conditions, because of the absence of the state of being a conascence, etc., condition, nutriment and faculty do not obtain the distinction of conascence, etc. And the absence of that [state of being a conascence, etc., condition] for them should be understood by way of the intrinsic nature of dhammas. This presence condition is thus thirteenfold: 'By conascence, the wholesome for the wholesome; by conascence and post-nascence, the wholesome for the indeterminate; by conascence alone, the wholesome for the wholesome-and-indeterminate'—thus there are three rooted in the wholesome; similarly, [three] rooted in the unwholesome. 'However, by conascence, pre-nascence, post-nascence, nutriment, and faculty, the indeterminate for the indeterminate; by base-object pre-nascence, the indeterminate for the wholesome, and similarly for the unwholesome. By conascence and pre-nascence, the wholesome and indeterminate for the wholesome; by conascence, pre-nascence, post-nascence, nutriment, and faculty, the wholesome and indeterminate for the indeterminate. By conascence and pre-nascence, the unwholesome and indeterminate for the unwholesome; by conascence, pre-nascence, post-nascence, nutriment, and faculty, the unwholesome and indeterminate for the indeterminate.' In brief, the presence condition is fivefold by way of wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional, and material [conditions]; but not Nibbāna. For, whatever dhamma, being unsupportive due to the absence of its state of presence, becomes supportive upon attaining a state of presence, that is a presence condition. And Nibbāna, for those [dhammas] that have Nibbāna as their object, does not become supportive by the attainment of a state of presence after having been unsupportive due to the absence of its own state of presence. Or, for dhammas connected with arising, etc., the state of being supportive which is the opposite of being supportive through a state of absence is the state of being a presence condition. Therefore, Nibbāna is not a presence condition.

615. Ārammaṇe phusanādivasena pavattamānānaṃ phassādīnaṃ anekesaṃ sahabhāvo natthīti ekasmiṃ phassādisamudāye sati dutiyo na hoti, asati pana hotīti tena natthibhāvena upakārakatā natthipaccayatā. Satipi purimataracittānaṃ natthibhāve na tena tāni natthibhāvena upakārakāni, anantarameva pana attano atthibhāvena pavattiokāsaṃ [M 2.0288] alabhamānaṃ natthibhāvena okāsaṃ dadamānaṃ viya upakārakaṃ hotīti “pavattiokāsadānena upakārakā”ti āha. Paṭuppannānanti paccuppannānaṃ.

615. Of the many instances of contact, etc., that occur in an object by way of touching and so on, there is no co-existence. Thus, when one assemblage of contact, etc., is present, a second does not arise; but when it is not present, another arises. Therefore, the state of being helpful by means of that non-existence is the absence condition. Even with the non-existence of much earlier consciousnesses, they are not helpful by means of that non-existence. Rather, it is only the immediately preceding consciousness that, by its non-existence, becomes helpful—as if giving an opportunity to those subsequent states that were not obtaining an opportunity to arise on account of its own existence. Thus, he said, 'They are helpful by giving the opportunity for arising.' 'Present' means presently occurring.

“Te evā”ti etena natthivigatapaccayānaṃ dhammato visesābhāvamāha. Evaṃ santepi abhāvamattena upakārakatā okāsadānaṃ natthipaccayatā, sabhāvāvigamena appavattamānānaṃ sabhāvavigamena upakārakatā vigatapaccayatā. Natthitā ca nirodhānantarā suññatā, vigatatā nirodhappattatāti ayametesaṃ viseso.

By the phrase 'They are just that,' he states the lack of distinction, in terms of their nature, between the absence and disappearance conditions. Even so, the state of being helpful by mere non-existence, which is the giving of an opportunity, is the absence condition. For those mental states that cannot arise due to the non-departure of a preceding state's own nature, the state of being helpful by the departure of its own nature is the disappearance condition. Alternatively, non-existence is the voidness immediately after cessation; disappearance is the state of having reached cessation. This is the distinction between them.

Atthipaccayadhammā eva cāti ca-saddo sampiṇḍanattho. Tena na kevalaṃ natthivigatapaccayā eva dhammato avisiṭṭhā, atha kho atthiavigatapaccayāpīti imamatthaṃ dīpeti. Yadipime paccayā dhammato avisiṭṭhā, tathāpi atthitāya sasabhāvatāya upakārakatā atthipaccayatā, sabhāvāvigamena nirodhassa appattiyā upakārakatā avigatapaccayatāti paccayabhāvaviseso dhammāvisesepi veditabbo. Dhammānañhi samatthatāvisesaṃ sabbaṃ yāthāvato abhisambujjhitvā bhagavatā catuvīsatipaccayavisesā vuttāti dhammassāmimhi saddhāya “evaṃ visesā ete dhammā”ti sutamayañāṇaṃ uppādetvā cintābhāvanāmayehi tadabhisamayāya yogo karaṇīyo.

In the phrase 'And only the phenomena of the presence condition,' the word 'ca' has an aggregative meaning. By this, it indicates that it is not only the absence and disappearance conditions that are non-distinct in nature, but also the presence and non-disappearance conditions. Although these conditions are non-distinct in nature, nevertheless, the state of being helpful by presence, by being with its own nature, is the presence condition; the state of being helpful by the non-departure of its own nature, by not having yet reached cessation, is the non-disappearance condition. Thus, even when there is no distinction in their nature, the distinction in their conditional function should be understood. For indeed, the Blessed One, having thoroughly understood all the distinct capacities of phenomena exactly as they are, taught the twenty-four distinct conditions. Therefore, with faith in the Lord of the Dhamma, having generated knowledge based on hearing that 'these phenomena have such distinctions,' effort should be made to comprehend that through knowledge born of thinking and meditation.

Ettha [V 2.0270] ca ārammaṇaanantarasamanantaraupanissayapurejātaāsevanasampayuttanatthivigatapaccayā arūpadhammānaṃyeva, pacchājātapaccayo rūpadhammānaṃyeva, itare cuddasa rūpārūpadhammānaṃ.

And here, the object, contiguity, proximity, decisive support, pre-nascence, repetition, association, absence, and disappearance conditions are for immaterial phenomena only. The post-nascence condition is for material phenomena only. The remaining fourteen conditions are for both material and immaterial phenomena.

Hetuanantarasamanantarāsevanapacchājātakammavipākajhānamaggasampayuttanatthivigatapaccayā arūpadhammā eva, purejātapaccayo rūpameva, ubhayaṃ ārammaṇūpanissaye ṭhapetvā sesā, te dve paññattisabhāvāpi honti.

The root, contiguity, proximity, repetition, post-nascence, kamma, result, jhāna, path, association, absence, and disappearance conditions are immaterial phenomena only. The pre-nascence condition is a material phenomenon only. Setting aside the object and decisive support conditions, the remaining are both. Those two also have a conceptual nature.

Anantarasamanantarāsevananatthivigatapaccayā atītā eva. Ārammaṇārammaṇādhipatiārammaṇūpanissayā tikālikā, kālavinimuttā ca. Kammapaccayo atītapaccuppannavasena dvikāliko. Sesā pañcadasa paccuppannāva.

The contiguity, proximity, repetition, absence, and disappearance conditions are past only. The object, object-dominance, and object-decisive-support conditions are of the three times and also free from time. The kamma condition is of two times, by way of past and present. The remaining fifteen are present only.

Tathā anantarasamanantaraanantarūpanissayapakatūpanissayāsevanapaccayā, nānākkhaṇikakammapaccayo, natthivigatapaccayā cāti ime paccayā janakā eva, na upatthambhakā. Pacchājātapaccayo upatthambhako eva, na janako[M 2.0289]. Sesā janakā ca upatthambhakā cāti ayampi viseso veditabbo.

Similarly, the contiguity, proximity, contiguity-decisive-support, natural-decisive-support, repetition, kamma-at-different-moments, absence, and disappearance conditions—these conditions are generative only, not supportive. The post-nascence condition is supportive only, not generative. The remaining are both generative and supportive. This distinction should also be understood.

Avijjāpaccayāsaṅkhārapadavitthārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Detailed Exposition of the Phrase 'Conditioned by Ignorance are Formations'

616. Paccayesūti niddhāraṇe bhummaṃ. Duvidhā dvippakārena. Anekadhāti sattarasadhā ārammaṇapaccayādivasena.

616. 'In conditions' (paccayesu) is the locative case in the sense of determination. 'Twofold' (duvidhā) means of two kinds. 'Manifold' (anekadhā) means seventeenfold, by way of the object condition and so on.

Abhiññācittenāti cetopariyapubbenivāsaanāgataṃsañāṇasaṅkhātāhi abhiññāhi sahagatacittena. Samohacittajānanakāleti paresaṃ, attano ca samohassa cittassa jānanakāle. Avijjāpubbaṅgamā akusalappavattiyo yā kāci vipattiyo, sabbā tā mohamūlikāti ca avijjāya ādīnavadassanena avijjāsamatikkamatthāya vivaṭṭābhipatthanāyāti attho. Dvinnampi tesaṃ puññābhisaṅkhārānaṃ. Avijjāsammūḷhattāti bhavādīnavappaṭicchādikāya avijjāya sammūḷhattā. Tāneva puññānīti tāneva yathāvuttāni kāmāvacararūpāvacarapuññāni. Upanissayapaccayena paccayo hotīti sambandho.

'With the abhiññā mind' (abhiññācittena) means with the mind accompanied by the higher knowledges (abhiññā), namely, the knowledge of others' minds, the recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of the future. 'At the time of knowing a deluded mind' (samohacittajānanakāle) means at the time of knowing the mind of others and of oneself that is accompanied by delusion. And regarding the statements, 'Unwholesome occurrences are preceded by ignorance,' and 'Whatever misfortunes there are, all are rooted in delusion,' the meaning is: with the aspiration for the Unbinding for the purpose of transcending ignorance by seeing the danger in ignorance. 'For both of those meritorious formations' (dvinnampi tesaṃ puññābhisaṅkhārānaṃ). 'Due to being utterly deluded by ignorance' (avijjāsammūḷhattā) means due to being utterly deluded by ignorance which conceals the danger of existence. 'Those very merits' (tāneva puññāni) means those very sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere merits as have been stated. The connection is that it 'is a condition by way of decisive support condition' (upanissayapaccayena paccayo hoti).

Rāgādīnanti [V 2.0271] rāgadiṭṭhivicikicchuddhaccadomanassānaṃ. Avijjāsampayuttattā rāgādīnaṃ rāgādiassādanakālesu avijjaṃ ārabbha uppatti veditabbā. Garuṃ katvā assādanaṃ rāgadiṭṭhisampayuttāya eva avijjāya yojetabbaṃ. Assādanañca rāgo, tadaviyuttā ca diṭṭhīti assādanavacaneneva yathāvuttaṃ avijjaṃ garuṃ karontī diṭṭhi ca vuttāti veditabbā. Rāgādīhi ca pāḷiyaṃ sarūpato vuttehi taṃsampayuttasaṅkhārassa avijjārammaṇāditaṃ dasseti. Anādīnavadassāvinoti pāṇātipātādīsu na ādīnavadassino. Avijjāya anārammaṇassa, paṭhamajavanassa ca ārammaṇādhipatianantarādipaccayavacanesu avuttassa, vuttassa ca sabbassa saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ “yaṃ kiñcī”ti āha.

'Of lust, etc.' (rāgādīnaṃ) means of lust, views, doubt, restlessness, and displeasure. Because lust, etc., are associated with ignorance, their arising should be understood as taking ignorance as a support during times of savoring them. Savoring, when made weighty, should be connected only with ignorance that is associated with lust and views. And savoring is lust, and view is not dissociated from it; thus, it should be understood that by the very word 'savoring,' view, which makes the aforesaid ignorance weighty, is also stated. And by lust, etc., which are stated in the Pāḷi in their own form, it is shown that the formations associated with them have ignorance as their object, etc. 'Of one who does not see the danger' (anādīnavadassāvino) means of one who does not see the danger in the destruction of life, etc. For the sake of including all that is stated and all that is not stated in the statements about object, dominance, contiguity, and other conditions—namely, that which does not have ignorance as its object and the first impulsion—he said 'whatever' (yaṃ kiñci).

Vuttanayenāti samatikkamabhavapatthanāvasena puññābhisaṅkhāre vuttanayena.

'By the method stated' (vuttanayena) means by the method stated in regard to meritorious formations, by way of transcending ignorance and aspiring for formless existence.

617. Kiṃ panāyantiādinā codakassa ayamadhippāyo – “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā sambhavantī”ti ettha sambhavanti evāti avadhāraṇaṃ na yujjati[M 2.0290], avasesapaccayasamavāyābhāve saṅkhārānaṃ sambhavābhāvato. Tathā saṅkhārā evāti avadhāraṇampi na yujjati. Kasmā? Aññesañca paccayuppannadhammānaṃ sambhavassa tato icchitabbattā. Vākyassa avadhāraṇaphalattā avijjāpaccayā eva saṅkhārā sambhavantīti avadhāraṇe gayhamānepi ayaṃ doso. Kasmā? Yasmā lobhādikammanidānaupādānavatthārammaṇamanasikārādayo aññepi paccayā labbhantiyevāti. Tattha ekāti asahāyā, kāraṇantaranirapekkhāti attho. Aññepi paccayā sahakārikāraṇabhūtā. Dosamettha vattukāmo codako pucchatīti ñatvā ācariyo āha “kiṃ panetthā”ti. Ettha avijjāya paccayantarena rahitabhāve ca sahitabhāve ca kiṃ pana vattabbaṃ, asamattā te codanā, avasiṭṭhañca tāva kathehīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ekakāraṇavādo āpajjatīti dosappasaṅgo vutto. Aniṭṭho hi ekakāraṇavādo sabbattha sabbakālaṃ sambhavāpattito, ekasadisāsabhāvāpattito ca.

617. By the words beginning with 'Kiṃ panāyanti...', this is the objector's intention: In the text 'With ignorance as a condition, formations come to be,' the emphasis 'they certainly come to be' is not fitting, because of the non-arising of formations in the absence of a conjunction of the remaining conditions. Similarly, the emphasis 'formations only' is also not fitting. Why? Because the arising of other dependently arisen phenomena from that is also to be desired. Because the sentence has the effect of emphasis, even when the emphasis is taken to mean that 'formations arise only from ignorance as a condition,' this fault arises. Why? Because other conditions, such as greed, etc., kamma as source, clinging, physical basis, object, attention, and so on, are indeed obtained. Therein, 'eka' (one/sole) means without a companion, not depending on another cause. Other conditions are also co-operating causes. Knowing that the objector, wishing to state the fault here, asks, the teacher said, 'What then here?' This means: 'In this matter, regarding the state of ignorance being without another condition and its state of being together with one, what is there to be said? Your objection is incomplete; first state the remainder.' The entailment of the fault, 'the doctrine of a single cause would result,' is stated. Indeed, the doctrine of a single cause is undesirable, because it would lead to arising everywhere at all times, and because it would lead to the state of being of one similar nature.

Yasmā ekaṃ na ekatotiādīsu tīsu pakāresu avijjamānesu pārisesena anekato anekamevāti etasmiṃ catutthe eva pakāre vijjamāne ekahetuphaladīpane attho atthi, tasmā na nupapajjati upapajjatiyeva. Ekaṃ phalaṃ ekato natthi, anekampi ekato natthi. Anekatopi ekaṃ phalaṃ no atthīti sambandho.

Because, since the three modes, beginning with 'one is not from one,' are non-existent, and by elimination, it is only in this fourth mode, 'from many, many only,' that there is existence, there is a purpose in the exposition of a single cause and a single effect. Therefore, it is not unsuitable; it is indeed suitable. One effect is not from one cause; many effects are also not from one cause; from many causes also, one effect is not—this is the connection.

Ekekahetuphaladīpananti [V 2.0272] “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti ekahetudīpanaṃ, “saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇa”nti ekaphaladīpananti evaṃ tattha tattha ekekahetuphaladīpanaṃ kataṃ.

The exposition of each single cause and effect means: 'Conditioned by ignorance are formations' is the exposition of a single cause; 'Conditioned by formations is consciousness' is the exposition of a single effect. In this way, in each respective case, the exposition of each single cause and effect is made.

Veneyyānaṃ anurūpatoti veneyyānaṃ ajjhāsayassa anurūpato. Ekasseva hetuno, phalassa ca dīpanā satthu desanāvilāsato vā veneyyapuggalānaṃ ajjhāsayato vā. Tadubhayassa panettha kāraṇaṃ tattha tattha desetabbassa atthassa padhānatā, pākaṭatā, asādhāraṇatā ca. Desanāvilāsappattā ca buddhā bhagavanto te desetabbe atthe bahūsupi pariyāyesu labbhamānesu yathārucitaṃ gahetvā dhammaṃ desenti, sā desanāvilāsānurūpatā. Tattha pana yena pariyāyena ye veneyyā bujjhanti, teneva tesaṃ bodhanaṃ, sā veneyyajjhāsayānurūpatā.

Suitability for those to be taught means suitability according to the inclination of those to be taught. The exposition of a single cause and its result is due either to the Teacher’s delight in exposition or to the inclination of the individuals to be taught. Here, the reason for both is the prominence, manifestness, and uncommonness of the meaning to be taught in each respective case. The Blessed Ones, the Buddhas, having attained the delight of exposition, teach the Dhamma by taking up whichever method they please from among the many available methods concerning the meaning to be taught; this is suitability to the delight of exposition. Moreover, among those methods, by whichever method certain individuals to be taught understand, their awakening is by that very method; this is suitability to the inclination of those to be taught.

Yathāphassaṃ [M 2.0291] vedanāvavatthānatoti “sukhavedanīyaṃ, bhikkhave, phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhā vedanā”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 4.129), “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.204, 400; 3.421, 425, 426; saṃ. ni. 2.43-44; 2.4.60; kathā. 465, 467) ca sukhavedanīyaphassādicakkhusamphassādianurūpena sukhavedanādicakkhusamphassajāvedanādīnaṃ vavatthānato. Samānesupi hi cakkhurūpādīsu phassavasena sukhādivipariyāyābhāvato, samānesu rūpamanasikārādīsu cakkhādisaṅghaṭṭanavasena cakkhusamphassajādivipariyāyābhāvato, aññapaccayasāmaññepi cakkhusamphassavasena sukhādicakkhusamphassajādīnaṃ oḷārikasukhumādisaṅkarābhāvato cāti attho. Yathāvuttaphassassa sukhādīnaṃ aviparīto paccayabhāvo eva yathāvedanaṃ phassavavatthānaṃ. Kāraṇaphalavisesena vā phalakāraṇavisesanicchayo hotīti ubhayatthāpi nicchayo pavatthānanti vutto.

‘Determination of feeling according to contact’ is because of the determination of pleasant feeling, etc., and feeling born of eye-contact, etc., in accordance with pleasant-feeling-producing contact, etc., and eye-contact, etc., as stated in passages such as: ‘Monks, dependent on a contact that is to be felt as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises,’ and ‘Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, there is feeling.’ For this is the meaning: even when the eye and forms, etc., are the same, there is no reversal of pleasant feeling, etc., due to contact; even when forms and attention, etc., are the same, there is no reversal of feeling born of eye-contact, etc., by the power of the impingement of the eye, etc.; and even when other conditions are common, there is no confusion of gross, subtle, etc., regarding pleasant feeling, etc., and feeling born of eye-contact, etc., due to eye-contact. The unreversed state of the aforementioned contact as a condition for pleasant feelings, etc., is itself the determination of contact according to feeling. Alternatively, by means of the distinction between cause and effect, there is the determination of the distinction between effect and cause; therefore, in both cases, determination is called ‘establishment’.

Kammādayoti kammaāhārautuādayo apākaṭā semhapaṭikārena rogavūpasamanato. Semhassa mandabhāvādinā ca semhaṃyeva pākaṭaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Ayamidha avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ hetubhāvena dīpitāti sambandho. Assādānupassino taṇhā pavaḍḍhatīti vacanatoti “saṃyojaniyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu assādānupassino taṇhā pavaḍḍhati, taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ, upādānapaccayā bhavo”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.53) iminā suttena taṇhāya saṅkhārakāraṇabhāvassa vuttattāti attho. Puna tassāpi avijjāya kāraṇanti dassanatthaṃ “avijjāsamudayā āsavasamudayoti ca vacanato”ti āha[V 2.0273]. Taṇhā vā caturupādānabhūtā kāmāsavadiṭṭhāsavā ca saṅkhārassa kāraṇanti pākaṭā avijjāhetukāti suttadvayenāpi avijjāya pākaṭaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ kāraṇabhāvameva dasseti. “Assādānupassino”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.53) hi vacanena bhavādīnavappaṭicchādanakiccā avijjā taṇhāya kāraṇanti dassitā hoti. Yasmā avidvā, tasmā puññābhisaṅkhārādike abhisaṅkharotīti avijjāya saṅkhārakāraṇabhāvassa pākaṭattā aviddasubhāvova saṅkhārakāraṇabhāvena vutto. Khīṇāsavassa saṅkhārābhāvato, asādhāraṇattā ca puññābhisaṅkhārādīnaṃ sādhāraṇakāraṇāni vatthārammaṇādīnīti [M 2.0292] puññabhavādīnavappaṭicchādikā avijjā puññābhisaṅkhārādīnaṃ asādhāraṇaṃ kāraṇanti vā attho daṭṭhabbo. Eteneva “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā, saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇa”nti (ma. ni. 3.126; saṃ. ni. 2.1; udā. 1; mahāva. 1; netti. 24) ettha pana padhānattā, pākaṭattā, asādhāraṇattāti ekekahetuphaladīpanaparihāravacanena sabbattha “phassapaccayā vedanā, vedanāpaccayā taṇhā”tiādīsu bodhaneyyajjhāsayavasena dhammassa bodhanasaṅkhātaṃ payojanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Karma and so on (kammādayo) refers to karma, nutriment, season, etc., which are unmanifest causes because disease is pacified by counteracting phlegm. And due to the weakness of phlegm, etc., phlegm itself is the manifest cause. Here, the connection is that ignorance is shown as the cause of formations. The statement 'For one who sees gratification, craving grows' (assādānupassino taṇhā pavaḍḍhati) means that by the sutta 'Monks, for one who sees gratification in things that can fetter, craving grows; from craving as condition, clinging arises; from clinging as condition, becoming arises,' craving is stated to be the cause of formations. Furthermore, to indicate that ignorance is also the cause of that craving, it says, 'With the arising of ignorance, the taints arise.' Alternatively, craving, and the taints of sensual pleasure and views, which become the four clingings, are manifest as causes of formations; they have ignorance as their cause. Thus, by both suttas, only the manifest nature of ignorance as the cause of formations is shown. Indeed, by the phrase 'for one who sees gratification,' ignorance, whose function is to conceal the dangers of existence, is shown to be the cause of craving. Because one is ignorant, one fabricates wholesome formations, etc.; thus, because the nature of ignorance as the cause of formations is manifest, the very state of being ignorant is stated as the cause of formations. This is because there is an absence of formations for one whose taints are destroyed, and because of its (ignorance's) uncommonness. Or, the meaning should be understood as follows: while base, object, and so on are common causes for meritorious formations and the like, ignorance, which conceals the danger of existence resulting from meritorious formations, is the uncommon cause for meritorious formations and the like. By this very explanation—'due to prominence, manifestness, and uncommonness'—which resolves the exposition of each single cause and effect, the purpose, known as the instruction of the Dhamma, should be understood. This applies here in the passage 'With ignorance as condition, formations arise; with formations as condition, consciousness arises,' and everywhere in passages such as 'With contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises,' in accordance with the disposition of those to be taught.

618. “Ekantāniṭṭhaphalāyā”ti etena viruddhabhāvaṃ, “sāvajjāyā”ti etena vijātiyabhāvaṃ avijjāya joteti. Puññāneñjābhisaṅkhārā hi iṭṭhavipākatāya, anavajjasabhāvatāya ca tassā viruddhā, vijātiyā cāti. Kathaṃ na yujjissatītiādi samādhānaṃ, tena yvāyaṃ ekantāniṭṭhaphalatādihetupadeso, tassa anekantikataṃ dasseti. Ayaṃ hettha adhippāyo – yāyaṃ tayā codanā “evaṃ santepī”tiādinā katā, sā yuttā vipākaṃ pati. Na hi aniṭṭhavepakkaṃ kāraṇaṃ iṭṭhaṃ phalati, iṭṭhavepakkaṃ vā aniṭṭhaṃ. Yasmā panettha paccayuppannadhammānaṃ paccayabhāvalakkhaṇadhammānaṃ dhammatā adhippetā, tatra cāyaṃ niyamo natthi vicittarūpattā tassāti. Tenāha “viruddho cā”tiādi.

618. By 'leading exclusively to unpleasant results' (ekantāniṭṭhaphalāya), it illuminates the contradictory nature (viruddhabhāvaṃ) of ignorance; by 'being blameworthy' (sāvajjāya), it illuminates its dissimilar nature (vijātiyabhāvaṃ). For meritorious and imperturbable volitional formations (puññāneñjābhisaṅkhārā) are indeed contradictory to it (ignorance) and of a different kind (vijātiyā) because they have agreeable results (iṭṭhavipākatāya) and a blameless nature (anavajjasabhāvatāya). The reconciliation, 'How could this not be fitting?' and so forth, thereby shows the non-absoluteness (anekantikataṃ) of this indication of a reason (hetupadeso) that it leads exclusively to unpleasant results and so forth. Here is the intended meaning: The objection you raised, saying, 'Even so...' and so forth, is valid with regard to results. For a cause that has an unpleasant result (aniṭṭhavepakkaṃ) does not bear a pleasant fruit, nor does one that has a pleasant result (iṭṭhavepakkaṃ) bear an unpleasant one. However, since here the natural law (dhammatā) of conditioning phenomena (paccayabhāvalakkhaṇadhammānaṃ) in relation to conditionally arisen phenomena (paccayuppannadhammānaṃ) is intended, and in that regard this fixed rule (niyamo) does not exist due to its diverse nature (vicittarūpattā). Therefore, it is said, 'It is contradictory...' and so forth.

Tattha dhammānanti sabhāvadhammānaṃ. Ṭhānanti avaṭṭhānaṃ. Tasmā ṭhānaviruddhoti atthitāviruddho. Keci pana “paṭisandhiādīniṭhānānī”ti vadanti. Evaṃ sati “purimacittaṃ pacchimacittassa ṭhānaviruddho paccayo”ti nayidaṃ ekantikaṃ siyā. Bhavaṅgampi hi bhavaṅgassa anantarapaccayo, javanaṃ javanassa, na ca sippādīnaṃ paṭisandhiādiṭṭhānaṃ atthi, tasmā na taṃ idha adhippetaṃ. Kammaṃ rūpassa namanaruppanavirodhā, sārammaṇānārammaṇādivirodhā ca sabhāvaviruddho paccayo[V 2.0274]. Khīrādīni dadhiādīnaṃ madhurambilarasādisabhāvavirodhā. Avijānanakicco āloko vijānanakiccassa viññāṇassa. Amadanakiccā ca guḷādayo madanakiccassa āsavassa.

Here, 'dhammas' (dhammānaṃ) means phenomena in their own nature (sabhāvadhammānaṃ). 'Position' (ṭhānaṃ) means existence (avaṭṭhānaṃ). Therefore, 'opposed in position' (ṭhānaviruddho) means opposed in existence (atthitāviruddho). Some, however, say 'positions such as rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and so forth.' If this were so, the statement 'the preceding consciousness is a condition for the subsequent consciousness by being opposed in position' would not be absolute. For life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is indeed the immediately preceding condition for life-continuum, and impulsion (javana) for impulsion; and there is no position such as rebirth-linking and so forth for things like skills (sippādīnaṃ). Hence, that is not intended here. Kamma is a condition for materiality (rūpassa) by being opposed in nature (sabhāvaviruddho) due to the opposition of bending (namana) and being afflicted (ruppana), and the opposition of having an object (sārammaṇa) and not having an object (anārammaṇa), and so forth. Milk and so forth are a condition for curd and so forth, being opposed in nature due to the opposition of sweet and sour tastes, and so forth. Light, which has the function of not-knowing, is a condition for consciousness, which has the function of knowing. And molasses and so forth, which have the function of non-intoxication, are a condition for fermented drinks (āsava), which have the function of intoxication.

Golomāvilomādītiādīsu golomāvilomāni dubbāya, avīti ca rattā eḷakā veditabbā. Visāṇaṃ sarassa. Dadhitilapiṭṭhaguḷāni bhūtiṇakassa. Sevālaṃ taṇḍuleyyakassa, kharavaḷavā assatarassāti evamādi ādi-saddena saṅgahito. Yasmā vipākā eva na, tasmā dukkhavipākāyapi [M 2.0293] avijjāya adukkhavipākānaṃ puññāneñjābhisaṅkhārānaṃ paccayattaṃ na na yujjatīti attho.

In such phrases as 'cow-hair and sheep-wool,' cow-hair and sheep-wool are for dubbā grass. And by 'avi,' red sheep should be understood. A horn is for arrow grass. Curd, sesame flour, and molasses are for fragrant grass. Moss is for taṇḍuleyyaka spinach. A male donkey and a mare are for a mule. Thus, and so forth, is included by the word 'ādi.' Because they are not only results, therefore, it is not unfitting that ignorance, which has a painful result, is a condition for meritorious and imperturbable formations, which have non-painful results. This is the meaning.

Tadavipākattepi sāvajjatāya tadaviruddhānaṃ, taṃsadisānañca apuññābhisaṅkhārānameva paccayo, na itaresanti etassa pasaṅgassa nivāraṇatthaṃ “viruddho cāviruddho ca, sadisāsadiso tathā. Dhammānaṃ paccayo siddho”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmā tamatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ karonto “iti ayaṃ avijjā”tiādimāha.

Even though it is not its result, due to its faultiness, it is a condition only for demeritorious formations that are not opposed to it and are similar to it, and not for the others. In order to prevent this implication, it was said: 'Opposed and unopposed, similar and dissimilar likewise; the condition of phenomena is established.' Therefore, making that meaning clear, he said, 'Thus, this ignorance...' and so forth.

619. Sabbattha khandhānaṃ bhedo maraṇanti cutiṃ aggaṇhantoti idha cuti nāma tattha tattha bhavādīsu rūpādīnaṃ khandhānaṃ maraṇasaññito carimo bhedoti yāthāvato ajānanto. Sattassa sato vijjamānasseva. Dehantarasaṅkamanaṃ aññena kāyena samāgamo.

619. As for the view of not grasping that cessation is 'the breakup of the aggregates everywhere, which is death': this means not knowing as it really is that here, what is called 'cessation' is the final breakup, designated as death, of the aggregates of form and so forth in various existences here and there. This view holds that death is the transmigration to another body, the meeting with another body, of a being that is truly existing.

Sabbattha khandhānaṃ pātubhāvoti tattha tattha bhavādīsu khandhānaṃ paṭhamābhinibbatti. Navasarīrapātubhāvoti idha jiṇṇassa sarīrassa nikkhepe paralokapariyāpannassa navakāyassa uppādo. Yatheke vadanti –

'The manifestation of the aggregates everywhere' means the first arising of the aggregates in various existences here and there. 'The appearance of a new body' means, here, upon the casting off of the old body, the arising of a new body that is included in another world. As some say:

“Vatthāni jiṇṇāni yathā pahāya,

Navāni gaṇhāti naro parāni;

Nikkhippa dehaṃ idha jiṇṇamevaṃ,

Gaṇhāti attābhinavaṃ sukhesī”ti.

"Just as a person, having abandoned worn-out clothes, takes up other, new ones; so too, here, the self, having laid down the old, worn-out body, seeking happiness, takes up a new one."

Ayaṃ sattoti ayamattā, yo sāmī, nivāsī, kārako, vedako cāti adhippeto. Satto [V 2.0275] marati, satto upapajjatīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tīsupi ṭhānesu ādi-saddena issarakuttabrahmakuttādivikappanaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

'This being' means this self, which is intended as the owner, the dweller, the agent, and the experiencer. In 'a being dies, a being is reborn,' this is the same method. In all three instances, the word 'and so forth' includes speculations such as creation by a Lord, creation by Brahmā, and so forth.

Sabhāvalakkhaṇanti’ruppanānubhavanādiṃ, kakkhaḷaphusanādisabhāvameva vā. Sāmaññalakkhaṇanti aniccatādiṃ. Saṅkhāre attato attaniyatoti rūpādīsu ekaccaṃ attato, tadaññaṃ attaniyato.

'Individual characteristic' refers to affliction, experience, and so forth, or the intrinsic nature of things such as hardness, contact, and so forth. 'General characteristic' refers to impermanence and so forth. 'Regarding formations as self or as belonging to self' means regarding one among form and so forth as self, and another as belonging to self.

Attā jānāti vāti vikappeti kāpilādayo viya. Na jānāti vāti kāṇādājīvikādayo viya. Kāṇādopi hi attā sabhāvena na jānāti. Yadā buddhiguṇena saṃyujjati, tadā jānātīti icchati. So eva karoti ca kāreti cāti yo parattha sukhadukkhaṃ anubhavati, so eva puññāpuññaṃ sayaṃ karoti, aññañca kāreti, na aññoti adhippāyo[M 2.0294]. Saṇṭhapentāti dviaṇukādiuppādanavasena, icchāvasena ca sampādentā. Soti attasaññito satto. Indriyasampannoti cakkhādīhi indriyehi samannāgato, tena saḷāyatanappavattiṃ dasseti. Sabbañhetaṃ yathāpaccayaṃ pavattamānānaṃ avijjādīnaṃ kiccaṃ attano byāpāraṃ katvā diṭṭhigatiko vimuyhatīti dassanavasena vuttaṃ. Acchejjasuttāvutābhejjamaṇīnaṃ viya pubbāpariyavavatthānaṃ niyati, niyatiyā, niyati eva vā saṅgati samāgamo niyatisaṅgati, tāya bhāvesu pariṇatā manussadevavihaṅgādibhāvaṃ pattā niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇatā. Niyatiyā, saṅgatiyā, bhāvasaṅkhātena sabhāvena ca pariṇatā nānappakārataṃ pattā niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇatāti ca atthaṃ vadanti.

'The self knows' is speculated thus by the followers of Kāpila and so forth. 'It does not know' is speculated thus by the followers of Kaṇāda, the Ājīvikas, and so forth. For even Kaṇāda holds that the self by its own nature does not know; he holds that when it is conjoined with the quality of intellect, then it knows. As for 'He himself does and causes to be done,' the meaning is that whoever experiences happiness and suffering in a future existence, that very person himself performs meritorious and demeritorious actions and causes another to perform them, not another. 'They establish' means they bring to completion by means of the arising of dyads and so forth, and by means of desire. 'He' is the being conceived as a self.
