By the statement 'Craving is conditioned by feeling,' when the consequence of craving arising for every person who has feeling occurs due to the existence of the condition, in order to prevent that consequence, he says, 'And also conditioned by feeling,' etc.

Nanu “anusayasahāyā vedanā taṇhāya paccayo”ti vacanassa abhāvā atippasaṅganivattiṃ na sakkā kātunti? Na, vaṭṭakathāya pavattattā. Vaṭṭassa ca anusayavirahe abhāvato anusayasahitāva paccayoti atthato vuttamevetaṃ hotīti. Atha vā “avijjāpaccayā”ti anuvattamānattā anusayasahitāva paccayoti viññāyati. Vedanāpaccayā taṇhāti cettha vedanāpaccayā eva taṇhā, na vedanāya vināti ayaṃ niyamo icchito, na vedanāpaccayā taṇhā hotiyevāti, tasmā atippasaṅgo ettha natthi evāti.

Is it not that because there is no statement saying, 'feeling accompanied by latent tendencies is a condition for craving,' it is not possible to prevent over-application? No, it is possible, because this is spoken in the context of the round of existence. And because the round of existence is absent when latent tendencies are absent, it is indeed said in meaning that only feeling accompanied by latent tendencies is a condition. Alternatively, because 'conditioned by ignorance' is carried forward, it is understood that only feeling accompanied by latent tendencies is a condition. And here, the intended rule is this: craving is conditioned by feeling only (in that it does not arise without feeling); it is not intended that craving necessarily arises when conditioned by feeling. Therefore, there is no over-application here at all.

Vusīmatoti vusitavato, vusitabrahmacariyavāsassāti attho. Vussatīti vā vusīti maggo vuccati, so etassa vuttho atthīti vusīmā, ukkaṭṭhaniddesena arahā. Aggaphalaṃ vā pariniṭṭhitavāsattā “vusī”ti vuccati, taṃ etassa atthīti vusīmā.

'Vusīmā' means one who has dwelt, that is, one who has dwelt the holy life. Or, because it is practiced, the path is called 'vusī'; that practiced path exists for him, hence he is 'vusīmā', which by highest designation means an Arahant. Alternatively, the highest fruit, because of the completion of dwelling, is called 'vusī'; he possesses that, hence he is 'vusīmā'.

Taṇhāpaccayāupādānapadavitthārakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Detailed Account of the Section on Clinging Conditioned by Craving

645. Atthavibhāgo atthassa vibhajanā. Vatthusaṅkhātaṃ kāmanti kāmaguṇasaññitaṃ rūpādiārammaṇamāha. Upādiyatīti kāmavasena gaṇhāti, daḷhaṃ assādetīti attho. Kāmaṃ upādiyatīti ettha kammasādhano kāmasaddo[M 2.0327], kāmo ca soti ettha kattusādhano kilesakāmassa adhippetattā. Upādānasaddo pana ubhayatthāpi kattusādhanova. Daḷhattho bhusattho. Yathā bhuso āyāso [V 2.0307] upāyāso, bhusaṃ kuṭṭhaṃ upakuṭṭhaṃ, evaṃ idhāpīti āha “upāyāsaupakuṭṭhādīsu viyā”ti. Purimadiṭṭhiṃ uttaradiṭṭhi upādiyatīti purimadiṭṭhiṃ sassatabhāvena gaṇhantī upādiyati, purimadiṭṭhiākārena vā uttaradiṭṭhi uppajjamānā teneva purimadiṭṭhiṃ daḷhaṃ karontī taṃ upādiyatīti vuttā. Atha vā purimadiṭṭhiṃ uttaradiṭṭhi upādiyatīti “sassato attā”ti (dī. ni. 1.31) idaṃ purimadiṭṭhiṃ upādiyamānaṃ uttaradiṭṭhiṃ nidassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Yathā hi esā daḷhīkaraṇavasena purimaṃ uttarā upādiyati, evaṃ “natthi dinna”ntiādikāpīti (ma. ni. 1.445; 2.94; 3.91, 116, 136; dha. sa. 1221; vibha. 938). Attaggahaṇaṃ pana attavādupādānanti na idaṃ diṭṭhupādānadassananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Loko cāti vā attaggahaṇavinimuttaṃ gahaṇaṃ diṭṭhupādānabhūtaṃ idha purimadiṭṭhiuttaradiṭṭhivacanehi vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

645. The analysis of meaning is the division of meaning. By 'sensual pleasure reckoned as a basis', he refers to the objects such as form, etc., designated as sensual qualities. 'Clings' (upādiyati) means: he grasps by way of sensual desire and enjoys firmly; this is the meaning. Here, in 'clings to sensual pleasure' (kāmaṃ upādiyati), the word 'sensual pleasure' (kāma) is derived in the object sense; here, in 'and that is sensual desire' (kāmo ca so), it is derived in the agent sense, because defilement-desire is intended. The word 'clinging' (upādāna), however, is in both cases derived only in the agent sense. The meaning of 'firm' is 'abundant'. Just as intense effort becomes 'great effort' (upāyāso), and a severely censured act becomes 'greatly censured' (upakuṭṭhaṃ), so it is here too; thus he said, 'as in the case of upāyāsa, upakuṭṭha, etc.' As for 'the later view clings to the former view', it clings by grasping the former view as being eternal; or, the later view, arising in the manner of the former view, thereby makes the former view firm, and so it is said that it clings to it. Alternatively, the phrase 'the later view clings to the former view' is said to illustrate the later view that clings to this former view: 'the self is eternal.' For just as this later view clings to the former by way of strengthening it, so too do views like 'there is no result of what is given,' etc. However, it should be understood that the grasping of a self is clinging to a doctrine of self, and thus this is not an illustration of clinging to views. Or, it should be known that here, a grasping that is free from the grasping of a self and has become clinging to views—such as '[the self and] the world [are eternal]'—is spoken of by the words 'former view' and 'later view'.

Sīlabbataṃ upādiyatīti ettha asuddhimaggagosīlādisamādānavasena sīlaṃ, avītikkamanavasena vataṃ. Ubhayathāpi vā sīlaṃ, tapokammabhāvena gahitatāya vataṃ, gavādipakatibhāvanā. Attano vā gavādibhāvādhiṭṭhānaṃ sīlaṃ, “gacchanto bhakkheti, tiṭṭhanto muttetī”tiādinā gavādikiriyākaraṇaṃ vataṃ. Taṃtaṃakiccasammatato vā nivatti sīlaṃ, taṃsamādānavatovesa bhojanakiccakaraṇādivisesapaṭipatti vataṃ, taṃ sīlabbataṃ asuddhimaggaṃ “suddhimaggo”ti parāmasanto tathā abhinivisanto upādiyati, taṃ gāhaṃ daḷhaṃ gaṇhātīti attho. Sīlabbatasahacaritaṃ parāmāsaṃ sīlabbatanti gahetvā āha “sīlabbatañca taṃ upādānañcā”ti. Gosīlagovatādīnīti ca tathābhūtaṃ diṭṭhiṃ vadati. Tenevāha “sayameva upādānānī”ti. Abhinivesatoti abhinivesabhāvato, abhinivisanato vā. Attavādupādānanti “attā”ti vādassa paññāpanassa, gahaṇassa ca kāraṇabhūtā diṭṭhīti attho. Attavādamattamevāti attassa abhāvā “attā”ti idaṃ vacanamattameva. Upādiyantīti daḷhaṃ gaṇhanti. Kathaṃ? “Attā”ti. “Attā”ti hi abhinivisantā vacanamattameva daḷhaṃ katvā gaṇhantīti atthoti. Evaṃ “attavādamattameva upādiyantī”ti vuttaṃ[M 2.0328]. Attavādamattanti vā vācāvatthumattamevāha. Vācāvatthumattameva hi “attā”ti upādiyanti attassa abhāvāti.

In the phrase 'One clings to rules and observances' (sīlabbataṃ upādiyati): Here, by way of undertaking practices such as cow-conduct, which are not a cause of purity, it is 'sīla' (rules); by way of not transgressing, it is 'vata' (observances). Or, in both ways it is 'sīla'; because it is undertaken as an austere practice, it is 'vata'; the cultivation of the nature of a cow and so forth. Or, the determination of oneself to have the nature of a cow and so forth is 'sīla'; the performance of cow-like actions, such as 'while walking, it eats; while standing, it urinates,' is 'vata'. Or, refraining from what is designated as this or that improper action is 'sīla'; for one who has undertaken that, the special practice concerning appearance, eating, performing difficult tasks, and so on, is 'vata'. Misapprehending that practice of rules and observances, which is not the path to purity, as 'the path to purity,' and adhering to it as such, one clings to it. The meaning is: one firmly grasps that view. Taking the misapprehension that accompanies rules and observances as 'rules and observances,' it is said: 'and those rules and observances which are that clinging.' And by 'cow-conduct, cow-observances, etc.,' he speaks of such a view. Therefore, he said: 'they themselves are clingings.' As for 'from adherence' (abhinivesato): it is because of the state of adherence, or because of adhering. 'Clinging to the doctrine of self' (attavādupādāna) means: the view that is the cause for the saying, the proclaiming, and the grasping of 'self.' This is the meaning. As for 'merely the doctrine of self': because of the non-existence of a self, this 'self' is merely a word. 'They cling' (upādiyanti) means they grasp firmly. How? As 'self.' For those adhering to 'self' make firm merely the word and grasp it. This is the meaning. Thus it is said: 'they cling merely to the doctrine of self.' Or, by 'merely the doctrine of self,' he speaks of merely the basis for the word. For they cling merely to the basis for the word as 'self,' because of the non-existence of a self.

“Dhammasaṅkhepavitthāre pana kāmupādānaṃ saṅkhepato taṇhādaḷhattaṃ, sesupādānattayaṃ diṭṭhimattameva, vitthārato panā”ti evaṃ dhammasaṅkhepavitthārasamudāyato tadavayavabhūtaṃ saṅkhepaṃ, vitthārañca niddhāretīti. Dhammasaṅkhepavitthāreti niddhāraṇe bhummaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kāmesūti pañcasu kāmaguṇesu[V 2.0308]. Kāmacchandoti kāmasaṅkhāto chando, na kattukamyatāchando, na ca dhammacchando. Kāmanavasena, rañjanavasena ca kāmoyeva rāgo kāmarāgo, evaṃ sabbattha kāmatthaṃ viditvā kāmo eva nandanaṭṭhena kāmanandī, taṇhāyanaṭṭhena kāmoyeva kāmataṇhā, sinehanaṭṭhena kāmo eva kāmasneho, paridayhanaṭṭhena kāmapariḷāho, mucchanaṭṭhena kāmamucchā, gilitvā pariniṭṭhāpanaṭṭhena kāmajjhosānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Appattavisayapatthanā taṇhā ārammaṇe paritassanabhāvato, sampattavisayaggahaṇaṃ upādānaṃ ārammaṇe daḷhaggāhabhāvato. Appicchatāpaṭipakkhā taṇhā visayābhimukhabhāvato, santuṭṭhipaṭipakkhā upādānaṃ taṇhādaḷhattaṃ hutvā atricchatābhāvato. Pariyesanadukkhamūlā taṇhā appattavisayapatthanābhāvato, ārakkhadukkhamūlaṃ upādānaṃ sampattavisayaggahaṇabhāvato.

"In the summary and detailed explanation of the Dhamma, clinging to sensual pleasures is, in brief, the intensity of craving, while the remaining three types of clinging are merely views. But in detail..." Thus, from the comprehensive collection of the summary and detailed explanation of the Dhamma, the brief and the detailed are distinguished. Regarding 'Dhammasaṅkhepavitthāre,' the locative case should be understood as indicating determination. 'In sensual pleasures' refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Desire for sensual pleasures' means desire designated as sensual, not the desire to act, nor the desire for the Dhamma. By way of desire and attachment, sensuality itself is lust—sensual lust. Similarly, in all instances, understanding the meaning of 'sensual', sensuality itself is delight in the sense of enjoyment, craving in the sense of thirsting, affection in the sense of fondness, torment in the sense of burning, infatuation in the sense of delusion; and it should be understood as sensual obsession in the sense of swallowing and bringing to completion. Craving is the longing for unattained objects because of thirsting for the object, while clinging is the grasping of attained objects because of firmly grasping the object. Craving is opposed to wanting little due to its tendency toward objects, while clinging is opposed to contentment by becoming the intensity of craving, leading to insatiability. Craving is the root of suffering in seeking due to the longing for unattained objects, while clinging is the root of suffering in guarding due to the grasping of attained objects.

Natthi dinnantiādīsu dinnanti dānamāha, taṃ aphalattā rūpaṃ viya dānaṃ nāma na hotīti paṭikkhipati. Yiṭṭhaṃ vuccati mahāvijitayaññasadiso mahāyāgo. Hutanti āhunapāhunamaṅgalakiriyā. Tattha āmantetvā havanaṃ dānaṃ āhunaṃ, pāhunānaṃ atithīnaṃ atithikiriyā pāhunaṃ, āvāhādīsu maṅgalatthaṃ dānaṃ maṅgalakiriyā, dasa kusalakammapathā sukatakammāni nāma, dasa akusalakammapathā dukkaṭakammāni nāma, phalaṃ vipākoti nissandādiphalañceva nippariyāyavipāko ca natthīti yojanā. Yathā cettha, evaṃ “natthi dinna”ntiādīsupi phalavipākapaṭikkhepova daṭṭhabbo. Natthi ayaṃ lokoti paraloke ṭhito imaṃ lokaṃ “natthī”ti gaṇhāti. Imaṃ hi lokaṃ avekkhitvā paraloko, parañca lokaṃ avekkhitvā ayaṃ loko hoti gantabbato, āgantabbato cāti paralokato idhāgamanassa abhāvā tattheva ucchijjanato cittena paraloke ṭhito imaṃ lokaṃ “natthī”ti gaṇhātīti attho. Na hi ayaṃ diṭṭhi paraloke ṭhitasseva hotīti. Natthi paralokoti idhaloke [M 2.0329] ṭhito paralokaṃ “natthī”ti gaṇhāti. Idhāpi vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Ayaṃ vā ettha attho – saṃsaraṇappadeso idhaloko, paraloko ca nāma koci natthi saṃsaraṇassa abhāvā tattha tattheva ucchijjanatoti.

In 'There is no gift,' etc., by 'gift' (dinna) it refers to giving, and this is rejected because, being fruitless like material form, it is not what is called a 'gift'. 'Sacrifice' (yiṭṭha) is said to be a great offering like the Mahāvijita sacrifice. 'Offered' (huta) refers to the rites of offering to the invited (āhuna), hospitality to guests (pāhuna), and auspicious ceremonies (maṅgala). Therein, inviting and giving an offering is the offering called āhuna; hospitality for guests is called pāhuna; giving for auspicious purposes such as weddings is called maṅgala rites. The ten unwholesome courses of action are called bad deeds. 'Fruit and result' (phalaṃ vipāko) means that both the consequential fruit and the direct kamma-result do not exist; this is the construing. Just as here, so too in 'there is no gift,' etc., a denial of fruit and result should be understood. 'There is no this world' means one who stands in the other world regards this world as 'non-existent.' For, by considering this world, the other world exists; and by considering the other world, this world exists, as a place to be gone to and a place to be come from. Since there is no coming here from the other world, and since one is annihilated right there, the meaning is that one, mentally standing in the other world, regards this world as 'non-existent.' Indeed, this view does not belong only to one who stands in the other world. 'There is no other world' means one who stands in this world regards the other world as 'non-existent.' Here too, the meaning should be understood in the same way as stated before. Or the meaning here is this: there is no place of wandering whatsoever called 'this world' or 'the other world', because there is no wandering—one is annihilated in that very place.

Purimabhavato pacchimabhave upapatanaṃ upapāto, so yesaṃ sīlaṃ, te opapātikā. Te pana cavanakaupapajjanakasattā natthīti dassento āha “natthi sattā opapātikā”ti. Natthi loke samaṇa…pe… pavedentīti anulomapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannattā sammaggatā sammāpaṭipannā dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇā [V 2.0309] lokasmiṃ natthi, ye imañca lokaṃ, parañca lokaṃ attanā eva abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇena paccakkhato ñatvā pavedanasamatthā sabbaññubuddhā nāma natthīti dasseti. Rūpaṃ attato samanupassatītiādīsu vattabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

Arising from a previous existence into a subsequent existence is called 'arising' (upapāta). Those for whom this is their nature are 'spontaneously arisen' (opapātikā). But showing that there are no beings who are subject to passing away and arising, he said: 'There are no spontaneously arisen beings.' As for 'There are no ascetics... proclaiming in the world,' this shows that there are no righteous ascetics and brahmins in the world who, because of having practiced the concordant path, are rightly gone and rightly practicing, and who, by their own superior knowledge, having directly known both this world and the next, are capable of proclaiming it—that is, those called omniscient Buddhas do not exist. What should be said regarding 'one regards form as self,' etc., has already been stated previously.

Pakatiaṇuādīnaṃ sassataggāhapubbaṅgamo, sarīrassa ucchedaggāhapubbaṅgamo ca tesaṃ gāhānaṃ sāmibhūto koci sassato, ucchijjamāno vā attā atthīti attaggāho kadāci hotīti “yebhuyyenā”ti vuttaṃ. Svāyaṃ attaggāho atthato khandhārammaṇo eva daṭṭhabbo. Yebhuyyena paṭhamaṃ attavādupādānantiādināva sambandho. Yadipi bhavarāgajavanavīthi paṭhamaṃ pavattati gahitapaṭisandhikassa bhavanikantiyā pavattitabbattā, so pana bhavarāgo taṇhādaḷhattaṃ na hotīti maññamāno na kāmupādānassa paṭhamuppattimāha.

The grasping of a self (attaggāha)—which is preceded by the grasping of permanence concerning fundamental particles, etc., and by the grasping of annihilation concerning the body—is the view that there is some self which is the master of these graspings and is either permanent or being annihilated. Since this sometimes occurs, it is said 'for the most part' (yebhuyyena). This grasping of a self should, in essence, be seen as having only the aggregates as its object. Alternatively, 'for the most part' is connected with 'clinging to the doctrine of self', etc., which comes first. Although the javana-process of lust for existence arises first—because for one who has taken up rebirth-linking, delight in existence is bound to occur—still, considering that this lust for existence is not a state of firm craving, he does not state the first arising to be clinging to sensual pleasures.

Taṇhā kāmupādānanti pana vibhāgassa akaraṇe sabbāpi taṇhā kāmupādānaṃ, karaṇepi vā kāmarāgato aññāpi taṇhā daḷhabhāvaṃ pattā kāmupādānanti tassa arahattamaggavajjhatā vuttā.

Furthermore, when no distinction is made between craving and clinging to sensual pleasures, all craving is clinging to sensual pleasures. Or, even when a distinction is made, any craving other than sensual lust, having reached a state of firmness, is clinging to sensual pleasures. Therefore, its nature of being abandoned by the path of Arahantship is stated.

Uppattiṭṭhānabhūtā cittuppādā visayo. Pañcupādānakkhandhā ālayo. Tattha ramatīti ālayarāmā, pajā. Teneva sā ālayarāmatā sasantāne, parasantāne ca pākaṭā hoti. Kāmānanti vatthukāmānaṃ. “Sukhadukkhaṃ kammunā hotī”ti aggahetvā kotūhalamaṅgalādibahulo hoti. Sā kotūhalamaṅgalādibahulatā. Assa kāmupādānavato. Tanti diṭṭhupādānaṃ, anattani dhammamatte “attā”ti micchābhinivesassa sukhumataradhammupādānatāya sukhumatā vuttā. Upanissayavacanena ārammaṇānantarapakatūpanissayā [M 2.0330] vuttāti anantarapaccayādīnampi saṅgaho kato hoti.

The arisings of consciousness, which are the place of origination, are the object. The five aggregates of clinging are the abode. Delighting therein, beings are called 'those who delight in the abode.' Therefore, that delight in the abode becomes apparent in one's own continuum and in the continuum of others. 'Sensual pleasures' refers to objective sensual pleasures. Not grasping that 'happiness and suffering arise from kamma,' one becomes engrossed in curiosity, auspicious ceremonies, and the like. That engrossment in curiosity, auspicious ceremonies, and the like belongs to one who has clinging to sensual pleasures. The subtlety of clinging to views is stated because of the very subtle clinging to phenomena, which is the wrong adherence to 'self' in what is merely a phenomenon and not self. By the term 'dependence-condition,' the object, contiguity, and natural dependence conditions are stated; thus, the inclusion of the contiguity condition and others is also made.

Upādānapaccayābhavapadavitthārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Detailed Exposition of the Section on Becoming Conditioned by Clinging

646. Atthatoti vacanatthato. Dhammatoti sabhāvadhammato. Sātthatoti sātthakato, pubbe vuttassapi puna vacanassa sappayojanato. Bhedasaṅgahāti bhedato saṅgahato, vibhāgato ceva vibhattassa saṅkhipanato cāti attho. Yaṃ yassa paccayoti yaṃ yaṃ upādānaṃ yassa yassa bhavassa paccayo hoti, tato cāti attho.

646. 'In terms of meaning' means by way of the word's meaning. 'In terms of nature' means by way of its intrinsic nature. 'With purpose' means being purposeful, because the repetition of what was stated before has a purpose. 'By analysis and synthesis' means by way of analysis and by way of synthesis, that is, the meaning is both by way of classification and by way of condensing what has been classified. 'Whatever is a condition for whatever' means whatever clinging is a condition for whatever becoming, and from that; this is the meaning.

Bhavatīti [V 2.0310] bhavoti phalavohārena kammabhavo vutto. Upapattibhavanibbacanameva hi dvayassapi sādhāraṇaṃ katvā vuttaṃ, bhavati etasmā upapattibhavoti vā. Dutiyo pana kammabhavo sattassa punabbhavabhāvena savisesaṃ bhavatīti bhavo. Tato eva na sabbassa bhavantarassa, taṃhetuno vā bhavabhāvappasaṅgo. Duvidhenāti dvīhi ākārehi pavattitoti attho. Duvidhenāti vā paccattatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, duvidhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Atthīti saṃvijjati.

'It becomes, therefore it is becoming'—by this definition, kamma-becoming is stated by the designation of its fruit. Indeed, the very definition of rebirth-becoming is stated as being common to both. Or: 'Rebirth-becoming becomes from this.' However, the second, which is rebirth-becoming, becomes in a special way from that kamma-becoming as the renewed existence of a being; therefore, it is called 'becoming.' Precisely for that reason, the designation 'becoming' does not apply to everything that arises, nor to its cause. 'In two ways' means it proceeds in two modes; this is the meaning. Alternatively, 'in two ways' (duvidhena) is an instrumental case used in the sense of the nominative case; thus, it is said to be 'twofold' (duvidho). 'There is' means it exists.

647. Attano paccayehi karīyatīti kammaṃ, attano phalaṃ karotīti kammanti keci, “kamma”nti evaṃ vattabbā kammasaṅkhātā. Parittabhūmakoti kāmabhūmako. Mahābhūmakoti mahaggatabhūmako. Sabbanti anavasesaṃ. Bhavaṃ gacchati, gameti cāti bhavagāmi. Gacchatīti ca nipphādanasamatthatāvasena, attano pavattikāle bhavābhimukhaṃ hutvā pavattatīti attho, nibbattanameva vā gamanaṃ adhippetaṃ. “Bhavagāmī”ti ca etena kammakkhayakaraṃ kammaṃ nivatteti. Ayañhi vaṭṭakathā, tañca vivaṭṭanissitanti. Apuññābhisaṅkhāroti dvādasa cetanāti uddhaccasahagatacetanāyapi gahaṇaṃ “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti ettha viya veditabbaṃ. “Bhavapaccayā jātī”ti ettha pana “saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇa”nti (ma. ni. 3.126; mahāva. 1; saṃ. ni. 2.1; udā. 1; netti. 24) ettha viya sāpi apanetabbā. Mandabahuvipākatāti appamahāvipākatā.

647. It is called 'kamma' because it is done by its own conditions; 'it is called kamma because it produces its own result,' so say some; that which is designated as kamma is what is to be called 'kamma.' 'Of a limited sphere' (parittabhūmaka) refers to the sense-sphere (kāmabhūmaka). 'Of a great sphere' (mahābhūmaka) refers to the exalted sphere (mahaggatabhūmaka). 'All' (sabba) means without remainder. 'Leading to becoming' (bhavagāmi) means it goes to becoming or causes one to go to becoming. The term 'goes' (gacchati) implies the ability to produce, meaning that at the time of its occurrence, it proceeds toward becoming—this is the meaning. Alternatively, 'going' here refers simply to the act of arising. By the term 'leading to becoming,' the kamma that brings about the destruction of kamma is excluded. For this teaching is a discourse on the round of existence, and that kamma is dependent on the Unrounding, Nibbāna. In 'unwholesome volitional formations' (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), which are the twelve volitions, the inclusion of volition accompanied by restlessness (uddhaccasahagata-cetanā) should be understood here, just as in the phrase 'volitional formations are conditioned by ignorance' (avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā). But in the phrase 'birth is conditioned by becoming' (bhavapaccayā jāti), here, as in 'consciousness is conditioned by volitional formations' (saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇa), that too should be excluded. 'Producing weak and abundant results' (mandabahuvipākatā) means producing small and great results (appamahāvipākatā).

“Sabbampi bhavagāmikammanti iminā cetanāsampayuttā abhijjhādayo vuttā”ti etena ācayagāmitāya tesaṃ kammasaṅkhātatā vuttāti kammabhavapariyāpannataṃ [M 2.0331] pariyāyena vadati, nippariyāyena pana cetanāva kammabhavo. Vuttañhi “kammabhavo tīhi khandhehi ekenāyatanena ekāya dhātuyā sampayutto, ekena khandhena ekenāyatanena ekāya dhātuyā kehici sampayutto”ti (dhātu. 244). Upapattibhavo tīhipi tikehi vutto upādinnakkhandhova. Yathāha “upapattibhavo… kāmabhavo… saññābhavo… pañcavokārabhavo pañcahi khandhehi ekādasahāyatanehi sattarasahi dhātūhi saṅgahito”tiādi (dhātu. 67). Yadi hi anupādinnakānampi gahaṇaṃ siyā, “dvādasahi āyatanehi aṭṭhārasahi dhātūhī”ti vattabbaṃ siyāti. Kāmataṇhāya kāmetabbato kāmanissayatāya bhogā viya, kāmasahacaritatāya “kuntā pacarantī”ti viya, kāmārammaṇatāya “sukhaṃ rūpa”nti viya, kāmapaccayaṭṭhānatāya “sukho saggo”ti viya kāmāti avīciparanimmitavasavattiparicchinnā upādinnakkhandhā vuccanti[V 2.0311]. Rūpāvirāgato yaṃ nissitā, tadupacārena “mañcā ghosantī”ti viya, “phandanadevatā”ti viya ca “rūpa”nti vuccanti brahmakāyikākaniṭṭhaparicchinnā upādinnakkhandhā.

By this statement, 'By “All kamma leading to existence,” covetousness and so on associated with volition are mentioned,' because of their nature of leading to accumulation, their designation as 'kamma' is stated. Thus, it speaks indirectly of their inclusion in kamma-existence; but directly, volition itself is kamma-existence. For it has been said: 'Kamma-existence is associated with three aggregates, one sense base, and one element; and in some cases, with one aggregate, one sense base, and one element.' Rebirth-existence, spoken of by the three triads, is simply the clung-to aggregates. As it is said: 'Rebirth-existence… sensual existence… five-constituent existence is comprised of five aggregates, eleven sense bases, and seventeen elements,' and so on. For if there were an inclusion of the unclung-to as well, it would have to be said, 'with twelve sense bases and eighteen elements.' Because they are desirable through sensual craving, because they are a basis for sensual desire like enjoyments, because they are associated with sensual desire like 'the spears are advancing,' because they are an object of sensual desire like 'form is pleasant,' and because they are a location for the conditions of sensual pleasure like 'heaven is happiness'—for these reasons, the clung-to aggregates bounded by the Avīci and Paranimmittavasavatti realms are called 'sensualities.' Because of non-dispassion towards form, on which they depend, by a figure of speech—like 'the couches are shouting' or 'the deity of the Phandana tree'—the clung-to aggregates bounded by the Brahmakāyika and Akaniṭṭha realms are called 'form.'

Rūpameva bhavo rūpabhavo, tathā arūpanti ākāsānañcāyatanabhavaggaparicchinnā cattāro upādinnakkhandhā vuccanti. Arūpameva bhavo arūpabhavo. Kāmo eva bhavoti kāmabhavo, so pana yasmā yathāvuttenatthena “kāmo”ti vattabbo hoti, tasmā “kāmasaṅkhāto bhavo”ti vuttaṃ. Kāmāvacarasaññito vā bhavo “kāmasaṅkhāto bhavo”ti vutto. Tathā rūpārūpabhavoti āha “esa nayo rūpārūpabhavesū”ti. Saññāvataṃ bhavoti ettha vantu-saddassa lopo daṭṭhabbo. Tassa vā atthe akāraṃ katvā “saññabhavo”tipi pāṭho. Tenāha “saññāvā”tiādi. Vokiṇṇoti etena vokārasaddassa kammasādhanatamāha. Vokirīyati pasārīyati vitthārīyatīti vokāro, vokiraṇaṃ vā vokāro, so ekasseva khandhassa vasena pavattattā “eko vokāro”ti vutto, pasaṭuppattīti attho.

Form itself is becoming, namely, form-becoming. Similarly, the four grasped aggregates delimited by the sphere of infinite space and the highest existence are called 'formless'. The formless itself is becoming, namely, formless-becoming. Sensual desire itself is becoming, namely, sensual-desire-becoming. However, since in the sense explained it is known as 'sensual desire,' it is therefore said to be 'becoming designated as sensual desire.' Or, becoming designated as belonging to the sensual sphere is called 'becoming designated as sensual desire.' Similarly for form- and formless-becoming, it is said: 'This is the method in the case of form- and formless-becomings.' In the phrase saññāvataṃ bhavo (becoming of those with perception), the elision of the suffix '-vantu' should be seen here. Or, by forming the suffix '-a' in its sense, there is also the reading saññabhavo (perception-becoming). Therefore, it is said, 'one with perception,' and so on. By the word vokiṇṇo (scattered), it states the formation of the word vokāra in the passive sense. Because it is scattered, spread out, and expanded, it is vokāra; or, the act of scattering is vokāra. Since that occurs by way of only one aggregate, it is called 'one vokāra,' the meaning of which is 'widespread arising'.

648. Kiñcāpi bhavaniddese “sabbampi bhavagāmikammaṃ kammabhavo”ti (vibha. 234) iminā cetanāsampayuttadhammāpi vuttā. Puññābhisaṅkhārādayovāti pana avadhāraṇaṃ [M 2.0332] paccayadhammavisesepi atthappabhedena saṅkhārabhavaggahaṇesu attheva visesoti dassanatthaṃ kataṃ. Tenāha “evaṃ santepī”tiādi. Saṅkhārabhavānaṃ dhammabhedato na saṅkhārā eva puna vuttāti “sātthakamevidaṃ punavacana”nti etaṃ ayuttanti ce? Na, bhavekadesabhāvena saṅkhārānaṃ bhavoti puna vuttattā. Parena vā dhammavisesaṃ aggahetvā punavacanaṃ coditanti codakābhilāsavasena “sātthakamevidaṃ punavacana”nti vuttaṃ.

648. Although in the exposition of becoming it is stated, 'All kamma leading to becoming is kamma-becoming' (Vibh. 234), by which states associated with volition are also stated, however, the specification 'meritorious formations and so on' is made to show that there is indeed a distinction in the taking of the terms 'formations' and 'becoming', through a difference in meaning and even in the specific conditional state. Therefore, it is said, 'Even so,' and so on. If it is said: 'This statement, "This repetition is indeed meaningful," is inappropriate, because due to the difference in nature between formations and becoming, it is not that formations alone are stated again.' No, for formations are stated again as 'becoming' due to their being a part of becoming. Or, since the repetition was questioned by another who did not grasp the specific nature of the states, it was said, 'This repetition is indeed meaningful,' in accordance with the questioner's inclination.

649. Kāmabhavādinibbattakassa kammassa kāmabhavādibhāvo phalavohārena aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutto. Sahajātaviññāṇassapi paccayabhūtaṃ avijjāhetukaṃ saṅkhāraggahaṇena yaṃ kiñci kammaṃ pubbe vuttaṃ, idha pana “sabbampi bhavagāmikamma”nti (vibha. 234) vacanato bhavassa nibbattakaṃ upādānahetukaṃ vipaccanāya katokāsameva bhavoti adhippeto. Yaṃ kāmupādānapaccayā rūpabhavanibbattakaṃ, arūpabhavanibbattakañca kammaṃ karīyati, so kammabhavo, tadabhinibbattā khandhā upapattibhavoti imamatthaṃ “esa nayo rūpārūpabhavesū”ti atidisati. Dve kāmabhavāti [V 2.0312] kāmakammabhavo, kāmūpapattibhavoti dve kāmabhavā. Evaṃ “dve rūpabhavā, dve arūpabhavā”ti etthāpi. Antogadhe hi visuṃ aggahetvā abbhantaragate eva katvā kāmabhavādike kammūpapattibhavavasena duguṇe katvā āha “cha bhavā”ti.

649. The state of being sensual-desire becoming and so forth, of the kamma that produces it, is stated in the commentary by way of the designation of its result. Whatever kamma, being a condition even for co-nascent consciousness and having ignorance as its cause, was previously stated by the term 'formations'—here, however, on account of the saying 'all kamma leading to becoming' (Vibh. 234), it is intended that 'becoming' is the very kamma that produces becoming, has clinging as its cause, and has been given the opportunity to ripen. The kamma that is performed, conditioned by sensual clinging, which produces form-becoming and also formless-becoming—that is kamma-becoming; the aggregates produced by that are rebirth-becoming. This meaning is indicated by extension with 'this is the method for form and formless becomings.' 'Two sensual-desire becomings' means sensual-sphere kamma-becoming and sensual-sphere rebirth-becoming; thus, there are two sensual-desire becomings. Likewise, this also applies to 'two form becomings, two formless becomings.' For, not taking those that are included within as separate, but treating them as simply internal, and having made the sensual-desire becomings and so forth twofold by way of kamma-becoming and rebirth-becoming, he says, 'six becomings.'

Avisesenāti upādānavasena bhedaṃ akatvā. Upādānabhedākaraṇeneva ca dvādasappabhedassa saṅgahavasena saṅgahato “cha bhavā”ti vuttaṃ. Anupagammāti anissāya, anāmasitvāti attho.

'Without distinction' means not making a distinction by way of clinging. And precisely because of not making a distinction by way of clinging, 'six becomings' is stated as a summary, by way of summarizing the twelvefold division. 'Without approaching' means not depending upon, not touching upon; this is the meaning.

650. Gosīlena, kukkurasīlena ca samattena samādinnena gunnaṃ, kukkurānañca sahabyatā vuttāti “sīlabbatupādānavato jhānabhāvanā na ijjhatī”ti maññamānā tena rūpārūpabhavā na hontīti keci vadanti. Vakkhamānena pana pakārena paccayabhāvato “taṃ na gahetabba”nti āha. Asuddhimagge ca suddhimaggaparāmasanaṃ sīlabbatupādānanti suddhimaggaparāmasanena rūpārūpāvacarajjhānānaṃ nibbattanaṃ na na yujjatīti.

650. Because it is stated that through the cow-practice and dog-practice, undertaken perfectly and well, companionship with cows and dogs is attained, some, thinking, 'For one with clinging to rites and rituals, the development of jhāna does not succeed,' say that because of that clinging, form and formless becomings do not arise. However, he says, 'That should not be accepted,' because it is a condition in the manner that will be explained. Furthermore, since clinging to rites and rituals is the misapprehension of the path to purity within an impure path, the arising of form-sphere and formless-sphere jhānas through such misapprehension of the path to purity is not unsuitable.

Anussavavasenāti “setavadhayajjaṃ ālabhate bhūtikāmo”ti ādinnaanussavavasena, yathā ime manussaloke kāmā samiddhā, evaṃ devaloke [M 2.0333] ito samiddhatarāti diṭṭhānusārena vā. Purāṇabhāratasītāharaṇapasubandhavidhiādisavanaṃ assaddhammassavanaṃ. Ādi-saddena asappurisūpanissayaṃ pubbe ca akatapuññataṃ, attamicchāpaṇidhiñca saṅgaṇhāti. Kāyaduccaritādīnipīti attano adhippetānaṃ kāmānaṃ anupāyabhūtānipi kāyaduccaritādīni karoti, cirasaggādiatthaṃ yuddhādivasenāti adhippāyo. Sandiṭṭhike vā pana rajjasenāpatiṭṭhānādisaṅgahe kāme. Tadantogadhā evāti tasmiṃ duccaritanibbatte, sucaritanibbatte ca kāmabhave antogadhā evāti attho. Antogadhāti ca saññābhavapañcavokārabhavānaṃ ekadesena antogadhattā vuttaṃ. Na hi te niravasesā kāmabhave antogadhāti.

‘By hearsay’ means by way of hearsay, such as, ‘One who desires prosperity should perform the sacrifice of a white goat,’ and so on; or by following what is seen, as in the belief that just as these sensual pleasures are abundant in the human world, so too are they even more abundant in the heavenly realm. Listening to the Purāṇas, the Bhārata, the abduction of Sītā, the methods of animal sacrifice, and so on—this is listening to the non-Dhamma. By the word ‘and so on’ (ādi), it includes associating with ignoble people, having no merit made in the past, and wrong aspiration for oneself. As for ‘Even unwholesome bodily actions, etc.’: although they are not the means for the sensual pleasures one desires, one performs unwholesome bodily actions, etc., by way of fighting and so on, for the sake of long-lasting heavenly bliss, etc. This is the intended meaning. Or, it refers to sensual pleasures in the visible realm, which are comprised of kingship, the position of a general, and so on. ‘They are included in that’ means they are included in that sensual-sphere existence which is produced by both misconduct and good conduct. And ‘included’ is said because they are partially included in perception-becoming and five-aggregate-becoming. For those becomings are not included in the sensual realm without remainder.

Sappabhedassāti sugatiduggatimanussādippabhedavato.

'Of varied kinds' means having distinctions such as good and bad destinies, humans, and so on.

Kāmāvacarasampattibhave paṭhamadutiyaucchedavādavasena, rūpabhave tatiyaucchedavādavasena, arūpabhave sesaucchedavādavasena ayamattā suucchinno hotīti tadupagaṃ kammaṃ karotīti āha “ayaṃ [V 2.0313] attā nāmā”tiādi. Tattha suucchinnoti sakalavaṭṭadukkhasamucchedena suṭṭhu ucchinno, apunabbhavuppattiko hotīti attho.

In the sensual-sphere attainment-becoming, by way of the first and second annihilationist views; in form-becoming, by way of the third annihilationist view; and in formless-becoming, by way of the remaining annihilationist views, one performs kamma leading to that, thinking, 'This self is utterly annihilated.' Therefore, it says, 'This self,' and so on. Here, 'utterly annihilated' means well cut off by the complete cessation of the entire round of suffering, becoming one who has no further rebirth—this is the meaning.

“Kāmāvacarasampattibhave”ti idaṃ paṭhamadiṭṭhadhammanibbānavādavasena vuttaṃ, sesaṃ itaradiṭṭhadhammanibbānavādavasena. Tattha kiñcāpi pāḷiyaṃ (dī. ni. 1.93 ādayo) rūpāvacarajjhānavaseneva upari cattāro diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā āgatā, diṭṭhigatiko pana yaṃ kiñci gahetvā yathā tathā abhinivisatīti arūpabhavaggahaṇaṃ, arūpajjhānānampi vā catutthajhānasaṅgahato arūpabhavaggahaṇaṃ, santasukhatāya vā taṃsamaṅgino sukhitabhāvasāmaññato. Vigatapariḷāhoti yathābhilāsitavisayūpahārena, pahānena ca vūpasantakāmarāgapariḷāho, diṭṭheva dhamme nibbānappattoti attho.

“In sensual-sphere attainment-becoming”—this is stated by way of the first view of Nibbāna in this very life; the rest is stated by way of the other views of Nibbāna in this very life. Here, although in the Pāḷi the four higher views of Nibbāna in this very life are described only by way of the form-sphere jhānas, one holding wrong views, however, grasps anything and clings to it in whatever way; therefore, there is the inclusion of formless-becoming. Or, there is the inclusion of formless-becoming because the formless jhānas are also included in the fourth jhāna. Or, because of having peaceful happiness, due to the similarity in the blissful state of one endowed with them. “Free from torment” means that through the provision of desired sense-objects and through abandonment, the torment of sensual desire is pacified, and thus one has attained Nibbāna in this very life; this is the meaning.

Suddhimaggaparāmasanavasena pavattitaṃ yaṃ kiñci lokiyaṃ sīlaṃ, jhānañca sīlabbatamicceva idhādhippetanti āha “idaṃ sīlabbataṃ nāmā”tiādi. Kamena avatvā sīlabbatupādānassa ante bhavapaccayatāvacanaṃ attavādupādānaṃ viya abhiṇhaṃ asamudācārato, attavādupādānanimittattā ca.

Whatever mundane virtue and jhāna are practiced by way of adherence to the path of purity is here intended as merely “rules and vows”; therefore, he said, “This is called rules and vows,” and so on. The statement of the conditionality of becoming by clinging to rules and vows at the end, without stating it in sequence, is like the clinging to the doctrine of self, because it does not occur frequently and because it has the clinging to the doctrine of self as its cause.

Kammabhaveti [M 2.0334] niddhāraṇe bhummaṃ. Hetupaccayappabhedehīti ettha maggapaccayo ca vattabbo. Diṭṭhupādānādīni hi sahajātakammabhavassa maggapaccayā hontīti, tasmā tāni sahajātādīsu hetupaccayaṃ apanīya maggapaccayaṃ pakkhipitvā sattadhā paccayā hontīti veditabbāni. Sabbāni pana anantarasamanantaraanantarūpanissayanatthivigatāsevanapaccayehi paccayā honti. Nānantarassa upanissayapaccayena paccayā honti. Kadāci ārammaṇapaccayādināpi, taṃ pana upanissayapaccayeneva saṅgahetvā vuttaṃ “vippayuttassa pana upanissayapaccayenevā”ti.

In “kamma-becoming,” the locative case is used for specification. And in the phrase “in the divisions of root-condition,” the path-condition should also be stated. Indeed, clinging to views, etc., are path-conditions for co-nascent kamma-becoming. Therefore, it should be understood that they are conditions in seven ways, having removed the root-condition from among the co-nascent conditions, etc., and having inserted the path-condition. Furthermore, all four clingings are conditions for the immediately succeeding unwholesome kamma-becoming by way of contiguity, immediate contiguity, contiguity decisive support, absence, disappearance, and habitual recurrence conditions. For that which is not immediately succeeding, they are conditions by way of decisive-support condition. Sometimes they are also conditions by way of object-condition, etc., but that, however, is included under the decisive-support condition and stated as: “but for the dissociated, only by way of decisive-support condition.”

Bhavapaccayājātiādipadavitthārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Detailed Exposition of Terms Such as “Birth Conditioned by Becoming”

651. Jātītiādīsūti ādi-saddena “jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā sambhavantī”ti (ma. ni. 3.126; saṃ. ni. 2.1; mahāva. 1; udā. 1; netti. 24) sabbaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tenāha “jātiādīna”ntiādi. Upapattibhavuppattiyeva [V 2.0314] jātīti āha “na upapattibhavo”ti. Jāyamānassa pana jāti jātīti upapattibhavopi asati abhāvā jātiyā paccayoti sakkā vattuṃ. Jāyamānarūpapadaṭṭhānatāpi hi rūpajātiyā vuttā “upacitarūpapadaṭṭhāno upacayo, anuppabandharūpapadaṭṭhānā santatī”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 641).

651. In the phrase “birth, etc.,” the word “etc.” includes all that is stated as: “From birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be.” Therefore, he said, “of birth, etc.” The very arising of rebirth-becoming is birth; therefore, he said, “it is not rebirth-becoming.” However, since the arising of an arising aggregate is birth, it can be said that even rebirth-becoming is a condition for birth, because in its absence, there is no birth. Indeed, the state of having arising form as its proximate cause is also stated with reference to the birth of form, as it is said: “Accumulation has accumulated form as its proximate cause; continuity has uninterruptedly arising form as its proximate cause.”

Jātānaṃ khandhānaṃ uññātatā, abhimatatā ca hīnapaṇītatā. Aniṭṭhañhi hīnaṃ, iṭṭhaṃ paṇītaṃ. Ādi-saddena suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇahīnuttamādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Yamakānampi satanti yamakabhāvena nibbattānampi samānānaṃ. So ca sattānaṃ viseso. Bhinnasantānikassa visesakāraṇassa sabbena sabbaṃ abhāvato “ajjhattasantāne”ti vuttaṃ. Aññassa kāraṇassa abhāvatoti attasantānagatato aññassa visesakāraṇassa anupalabbhamānattā, sati ca tasmiṃ sabbadā sabbesaṃ abhāvatoti pasaṅgassa dunnivāraṇato kāraṇe avisiṭṭhe phalavisesassa ayujjamānakattā. Tenāha “kammabhavahetukovā”ti.

The inferiority and superiority of arisen aggregates are their being despised and esteemed, respectively. Indeed, what is undesirable is inferior, and what is desirable is superior. By the word “etc.,” it includes having a beautiful complexion or an ugly complexion, a short lifespan or a long lifespan, and so on. And that distinction among beings is seen even among those who are similar, having been born as a pair (twins). Because there is absolutely no distinguishing cause in a different continuum, it was said, “in the internal continuum.” “Because there is no other cause” means: because no other distinguishing cause is found apart from that which is in one's own continuum; and because, if such a cause existed, it would be difficult to prevent the undesirable consequence that it would be absent for all beings at all times; and because a distinction in the result is unsuitable when the cause is not distinct. Therefore, he said, “It is caused by kamma-becoming.”

Tena tenāti ñātibyasanādinā jarāmaraṇato aññena dukkhadhammena. Jarāmaraṇanimittañhi uppannā sokādayo jarāmaraṇābhisambandhā, tadaññe anabhisambandhā. Upanissayakoṭiyāti upanissayaṃsena, upanissayalesenāti [M 2.0335] attho. Yo hi paṭṭhāne anāgato sati bhāvā, asati ca abhāvā suttantapariyāyena upanissayo, so “upanissayakoṭī”ti vuccati. Paccayamahāpadeso kireso, yadidaṃ upanissayoti.

By “this and that” is meant by a phenomenon that is a cause of suffering other than aging and death, such as the loss of relatives, etc. Indeed, sorrows and so on that have arisen due to the cause that is aging and death are connected with aging and death; others are not connected. By “the category of decisive support” is meant by way of a portion of decisive support, or by way of a hint of decisive support. Indeed, whatever decisive support condition, though not found in the Paṭṭhāna, is a decisive support according to the Suttanta method—because of the existence of the effect when the cause is present, and its non-existence when the cause is absent—is called “the category of decisive support.” It is said that this is the great domain of conditions, that is to say, decisive support.

Bhavacakkakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Wheel of Becoming

652. Na kevalaṃ sokādīnaṃyeva jāti paccayo hoti, sokādīnaṃ pana paccayattā avijjāyapi paccayo evāti dassetuṃ “yasmā panā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Etthāti paṭiccasamuppādadesanāyaṃ. Aviditādi midanti ma-kāro padasandhikaro. Satatanti sabbakālaṃ yāva aggamaggādhigamā. Samitanti saṅgataṃ, abbocchinnanti attho.

652. Not only is birth a condition for sorrow, etc., but to show that because it is a condition for sorrow, etc., it is also a condition for ignorance, the passage beginning with “But since...” is introduced. Here, that is, in the teaching of dependent origination. In “aviditādi midaṃ,” the letter “ma” is a euphonic connector. “Satataṃ” means at all times, until the attainment of the highest path. “Samitaṃ” means connected, uninterrupted—this is the meaning.

Tesūti sokādīsu. Siddhesūti labbhamānesu. Siddhā hoti avijjā avinābhāvato.

In “them,” that is, in sorrow, etc. In “accomplished,” that is, in what is obtained. Ignorance is established because of its inseparability.

Kāmayānassāti [V 2.0315] kāmayamānassa, kāmo vā yānaṃ etassāti kāmayāno, tassa kāmavasena yāyamānassāti attho. Chandajātassāti jātataṇhāchandassa. Parihāyantīti vigacchanti. Ruppatīti sokādinā kuppati.

By “kāmayānassa” is meant “of one who desires,” or “kāmayāno” is one whose vehicle is desire, meaning “of one who proceeds by way of desire”—this is the meaning. By “chandajātassa” is meant “of one in whom the desire that is craving has arisen.” “Parihāyanti” means they depart. “Ruppati” means one is ruined by sorrow, etc.

Pariyuṭṭhānatāya tiṭṭhanasīlo pariyuṭṭhānaṭṭhāyī. “Pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyino”ti vā pāṭho. Tattha pariyuṭṭhātīti pariyuṭṭhaṃ, diṭṭhipariyuṭṭhānaṃ, tena tiṭṭhatīti pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyīti attho daṭṭhabbo.

One whose nature is to stand by way of obsession is “pariyuṭṭhānaṭṭhāyī.” Alternatively, the reading is “pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyino.” Therein, “it obsesses,” thus it is “pariyuṭṭhaṃ,” the obsession of wrong view; “he stands by that,” thus he is “pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyī”—this meaning should be understood.

Pañca pubbanimittānīti “mālā milāyanti, vatthāni kilissanti, kacchehi sedā muccanti, kāye vevaṇṇiyaṃ okkamati, devo devāsane nābhiramatī”ti (itivu. 83) vuttāni pañca maraṇapubbanimittānīti attho. Tāni hi disvā kammanibbattakkhandhasaṅkhāte upapattibhave bhavacchandabalena devānaṃ balavasoko uppajjatīti.

By “five preceding omens” is meant the five omens preceding death spoken of thus: “Garlands fade, clothes become soiled, sweat is released from the armpits, discoloration appears on the body, and the deity no longer delights in the divine seat”—this is the meaning. For, having seen those omens, great sorrow arises in the deities by the power of their desire for existence in the rebirth-becoming which is designated as the aggregates produced by kamma.

Bāloti avidvā. Tena avijjāya kāraṇabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tividhaṃ dukkhanti tassāruppakathāsavana, kammakāraṇādassana, maraṇakālakammopaṭṭhānanidānaṃ sokādidukkhaṃ.

‘Bālo’ means one who is ignorant. By that, it shows the state of ignorance as a cause. By ‘threefold suffering’ is meant the suffering of sorrow, etc., which has as its causes: hearing talk that is unsuitable for him, seeing the causes of kamma, and the presentation of kamma at the time of death.

Āsave sādhentīti āsave gamenti bodhentīti attho.

Regarding ‘āsave sādhenti,’ the meaning is that they cause the cankers to be known, they awaken them.

Evaṃ [M 2.0336] satīti evaṃ bhavacakkassa aviditāditāya anādibhāve sati. Ādimattakathananti avijjāvasena ādisabbhāvakathanaṃ. Ādi etassa atthīti hi ādimaṃ, bhavacakkaṃ. Tassa bhāvo ādimattaṃ, tassa kathanaṃ ādimattakathanaṃ. Visesanivattiattho vā mattasaddo, sati anādibhāve avijjā ādimhi, majjhe, pariyosāne ca sabbattha siyāti ādimattāya avijjāya kathanaṃ virujjhatīti attho. “Avijjā padhānā”ti vatvā tassā padhānabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “avijjāggahaṇenā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha avijjāggahaṇenāti avijjāya uppādanena, appahānena vā, attano santāne sannihitabhāvakaraṇenāti attho. Kammādīnīti kammavipākavaṭṭāni. Palibodhentīti nānādukkhaparibyūḷhe saṃsāracārake nirodhenti. Tehīti kilesakammavipākavaṭṭehi. Vaṭṭassa kāraṇabhāvena padhānattā “padhānadhammo”ti avijjā kathitā.

By ‘thus it is so’ is meant: when the wheel of existence is without a beginning due to its unknown origin. By ‘the statement of a mere beginning’ is meant the statement of the existence of a beginning by means of ignorance. Indeed, because it has a beginning, it is called ‘having a beginning’ (ādimaṃ), that is, the wheel of existence. Its state is ‘a mere beginning’ (ādimattaṃ), and the statement of that is ‘the statement of a mere beginning’ (ādimattakathanaṃ). Or, the word ‘matta’ has the meaning of excluding a specification; when there is beginninglessness, because ignorance might be at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end, everywhere, the statement of ignorance as a mere beginning is contradicted; this is the meaning. Having said, ‘Ignorance is primary,’ to show its primary nature, the passage beginning with ‘by the grasping of ignorance’ is commenced. Therein, ‘by the grasping of ignorance’ means by producing ignorance, or by not abandoning it, thereby causing it to be established in one's own continuum; this is the meaning. ‘Kamma and so on’ means the rounds of kamma and result. ‘They obstruct’ means they confine beings in the prison of saṃsāra, which is filled with various kinds of suffering. ‘By them’ means by the rounds of defilements, kamma, and result. Because it is primary in being the cause of the round, ignorance is called ‘the primary factor’.

Tato avijjādito. Brahmādināti ādi-saddena pajāpatissarapurisādike saṅgaṇhāti. Vadatīti [V 2.0316] vado, taṃ taṃ hitāhitaṃ pavattāti attho. Vedeti, vediyatīti vā vedeyyo, sukhādiṃ anubhavati, sabbavisaye vā jānāti, “sukhito dukkhito”tiādinā attanā, parehi ca jānāti, ñāyati cāti attho. Brahmādinā vā attanā vāti vā-saddo ca-saddattho. Tenāha “kārakavedakarahita”nti ca-saddatthasamāsaṃ.

From that, from ignorance, etc. By ‘Brahmā, etc.’ is meant: with the word ‘etc.’ (ādi), it includes Pajāpati, Issara, Purisa, and so on. Because one speaks (vadati), one is a speaker (vado); the meaning is, one declares what is beneficial or harmful. Because one feels (vedeti), or is felt (vediyati), one is an experiencer (vedeyyo); one experiences pleasure, etc., or knows all objects; by way of ‘I am happy,’ ‘I am suffering,’ etc., one knows by oneself and is known by others; this is the meaning. In ‘by Brahmā, etc., or by oneself,’ the word ‘vā’ (or) has the meaning of ‘ca’ (and). Therefore, he said ‘devoid of an agent and an experiencer,’ which is a compound with the meaning of ‘and’.

Dvādasavidhasuññatāsuññanti avijjādīnaṃ dvādasannaṃ suññasabhāvānaṃ suññatāya suññaṃ dvādasavidhasuññatāsuññaṃ, dhuvabhāvādisuññatāya vā catubbidhampi suññataṃ ekaṃ katvā dvādasaṅgagatattā dvādasavidhāti tāya dvādasasuññatāya suññanti attho.

By ‘empty with the twelvefold emptiness’ is meant: it is empty with the emptiness of the twelve things, beginning with ignorance, which are empty in nature; this is ‘empty with the twelvefold emptiness.’ Or, having made the fourfold emptiness one by way of the emptiness of a permanent nature, etc., because it pertains to the twelve factors, it is ‘twelvefold.’ Thus, it is empty with that twelvefold emptiness; this is the meaning.

653. Pubbantāharaṇatoti pubbantato atītakoṭṭhāsato paccuppannavipākassa āharaṇato. Vedanāvasānaṃ paricchinnaṃ ekaṃ bhavacakkaṃ hoti. Bhavacakkekadesopi hi bhavacakkanti vuccati. Vedanā vā taṇhāsahāyāya avijjāya paccayo hotīti vedanāto avijjā, avijjāto saṅkhārāti sambajjhanato vedanāvasānaṃ bhavacakkaṃ paripuṇṇamevāti [M 2.0337] daṭṭhabbaṃ. Avijjāggahaṇena vā taṇhupādānāni tadavinābhāvato. Saṅkhāraggahaṇena bhavo, viññāṇādiggahaṇena jātijarāmaraṇāni, sokādayo ca gahitāti evampi vedanāvasānaṃ bhavacakkanti yuttamevetaṃ. Evaṃ taṇhāmūlake ca yojetabbaṃ. Dvinnampi hi aññamaññānuppaveso hotīti. Avijjā dhammasabhāvaṃ paṭicchādetvā viparītābhinivesaṃ kārentī diṭṭhicarite saṃsāre nayati, tesaṃ vā saṃsāraṃ saṅkhārādipavattiṃ nayati pavattetīti saṃsāranāyikā vuttā. Taṇhāya taṇhācaritānaṃ saṃsāranāyikābhāve vattabbameva natthi.

653. By ‘drawing from the past’ is meant drawing the present resultant from the past portion. One wheel of existence is defined as ending with feeling. Indeed, even a part of the wheel of existence is called ‘the wheel of existence.’ Alternatively, feeling is a condition for ignorance, which is accompanied by craving; thus, by linking from feeling to ignorance, and from ignorance to formations, the wheel of existence ending with feeling should be understood as complete. Alternatively, by the grasping of ignorance, craving and clinging are included due to their inseparability from it. By the grasping of formations, becoming is included; by the grasping of consciousness and so on, birth, aging, death, and sorrow, etc., are also included. Thus, in this way also, it is indeed appropriate that the wheel of existence ends with feeling. Similarly, this should be applied to the wheel of existence rooted in craving as well. For there is a mutual interpenetration of both. Ignorance, by concealing the true nature of phenomena and causing wrong adherence, leads those characterized by wrong views in saṃsāra. Alternatively, it leads their cycle of existence—the occurrence of formations, etc.—and causes it to proceed; thus, it is called the leader in saṃsāra. As for craving, there is no need to say that it is the leader in saṃsāra for those characterized by craving.

Paṭhamaṃ bhavacakkaṃ. Phaluppattiyāti kattuatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, karaṇatthe eva vā. Viññāṇādipaccuppannaphaluppatti hi idha diṭṭhā, adiṭṭhānaṃ purimabhave attano hetūnaṃ avijjāsaṅkhārānaṃ phalaṃ anuppādetvā anupacchijjanaṃ pakāseti, pakāsanassa vā karaṇaṃ hotīti. Atha vā purimabhavacakkaṃ dutiyena sambandhaṃ vuttanti vedanāsaṅkhātassa phalassa uppattiyā taṇhādīnaṃ hetūnaṃ anupacchedaṃ pakāseti, tasmā phaluppattiyā kāraṇabhūtāya paṭhamassa bhavacakkassa hetūnaṃ anupacchedappakāsanatoti attho. Saṅkhārādīnameva vā phalānaṃ uppattiyā avijjādīnaṃ hetūnaṃ phalaṃ ajanetvā anupacchedameva, viññāṇādihetūnaṃ vā saṅkhārādīnaṃ anuppabandhameva pakāseti paṭhamaṃ bhavacakkaṃ, na dutiyaṃ viya pariyosānampīti “phaluppattiyā hetūnaṃ [V 2.0317] anupacchedappakāsanato”ti vuttaṃ. Anupubbapavattidīpanatoti “saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 3.126; saṃ. ni. 2.1; udā. 1) dhammānaṃ anupubbato pavattiyā dīpanato. “Viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti hi ettha aparipuṇṇāyatanaṃ kalalarūpaṃ vatvā tato uddhaṃ “nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatana”nti saḷāyatanappavatti vuttā. Sahuppattidīpanatoti “upādānapaccayā bhavo, bhavapaccayā jātī”ti vā upapattikkhandhānaṃ ekajjhaṃ uppattiyā dīpanato. Na hi ettha paṭhame viya bhavacakke āyatanānaṃ kamena uppatti vuttā.

The first wheel of existence. The phrase ‘by the arising of the result’ (phaluppattiyā) is the instrumental case in the sense of the agent, or simply in the instrumental sense. For, the arising of the present result, beginning with consciousness, is seen in this present life; it reveals the non-cessation of one's own unseen causes in the previous existence—ignorance and volitional formations—without producing their result. Or, it is the means of revealing. Alternatively, since it is said that the first wheel of existence is connected to the second, it reveals the non-cessation of the causes, such as craving, by the arising of the result known as feeling. Therefore, the meaning is: ‘because it reveals the non-cessation of the causes of the first wheel of existence by means of the arising of the result which has become a cause.’ Or, by the arising of the results, namely volitional formations and so on, without generating a result for the causes, namely ignorance and so on, it reveals only the non-cessation. Or, the first wheel of existence reveals only the uninterrupted continuity of volitional formations and so on, which are the causes for consciousness and so on; it does not reveal the conclusion as the second wheel does. Thus it is said, ‘because it reveals the non-cessation of the causes by the arising of the result.’ ‘Because it illustrates the sequential occurrence’ means: because it illustrates the sequential occurrence of phenomena through such statements as, ‘With volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form.’ For here, in the phrase ‘With consciousness as condition, name-and-form,’ having stated the embryonic form with its undeveloped sense bases, thereafter the arising of the six sense bases is stated with ‘With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases.’ ‘Because it illustrates simultaneous arising’ means: because it illustrates the simultaneous arising of the rebirth-aggregates through such statements as ‘With clinging as condition, existence’ or ‘With existence as condition, birth.’ For here, unlike in the first wheel of existence, the sequential arising of the sense bases is not described.

654. Hetuādipubbakā tayo sandhī etassāti hetuphalahetupubbakatisandhi, bhavacakkaṃ. Hetuphalahetuphalavasena catuppabhedo aṅgānaṃ saṅgaho etassāti catubhedasaṅgahaṃ. Sarūpato avuttāpi tasmiṃ [M 2.0338] tasmiṃ saṅgahe ākirīyanti avijjāsaṅkhārādiggahaṇehi pakāsīyantīti ākārā. Atītahetuādīnaṃ vā pakārā ākārā. Kilesakammavipākā vipākakilesakammehi sambandhā hutvā punappunaṃ parivattantīti tesu vaṭṭanāmaṃ āropetvā “tivaṭṭa”nti vuttaṃ, vaṭṭekadesattā vā “vaṭṭānī”ti vuttāni.

654. For this wheel of existence, there are three links preceded by cause, etc.; thus, it is called 'that which has three links preceded by cause, result, and cause'. For this wheel of existence, there is a fourfold classification of the factors by way of past cause and present result, and present cause and future result; thus, it is called 'the fourfold classification'. Although not stated in their own form, in each of those classifications they are indicated by the inclusion of such terms as ignorance and formations; thus, they are called 'aspects'. Or, the aspects are the modes of past causes and so on. Defilements, kamma, and results, having become connected in sequence with results, defilements, and kamma, revolve again and again; thus, having ascribed the name 'round' to them, they are called the 'three rounds'. Or, because they are a part of the round, they are called 'rounds'.

Sandhīnaṃ ādipariyosānavavatthitāti sandhīnaṃ pubbāparavavatthitāti attho.

The links are established in their beginning and end, meaning the links are established in their preceding and succeeding parts.

Paritassatīti taṃ taṃ vatthuṃ pariggahakaraṇavasena tassati, taṇhāyatīti attho. Upādiyatīti daḷhagāhaṃ gaṇhāti. Purimakammabhavasminti purimakammabhave sati.

One thirsts (`paritassati`), meaning one thirsts for (`tassati`) and craves (`taṇhāyati`) this and that object by way of taking possession of it. One clings (`upādiyati`), meaning one takes a firm hold. `In a previous kamma-existence` (`purimakammabhavasmim`) means when there is a previous kamma-existence.

Tassa ca sabbhāvo kariyamānatā evāti āha “kammabhave kariyamāneti attho”ti. Dukkhādīsu mohoti dukkhādīnaṃ ādīnavapaṭicchādako appahīno moho. Āyūhanāti sampiṇḍanakā dānādikiriyāya pavattanakā. Ekaṃ āvajjanaṃ etesanti ekāvajjanā, tesu ekāvajjanesu. Sattame cetanā bhavo. “Yā kāci vā pana cetanā bhavo, sampayuttā āyūhanā saṅkhārā”ti idaṃ yathādassitāya dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇabhājanīye vuttāya paṭisambhidāpāḷiyā (paṭi. ma. 1.45) vasena vuttaṃ. Tattha hi “cetanā bhavo”ti āgatā. Bhavaniddese pana “sātthato”ti ettha “cetanāva saṅkhārā, bhavo pana cetanāsampayuttāpī”ti vibhaṅgapāḷivasena dassitaṃ. “Tattha katamo puññābhisaṅkhāro? Kusalā cetanā kāmāvacarā”tiādinā hi saṅkhārānaṃ [V 2.0318] cetanābhāvo vibhaṅgapāḷiyaṃ (vibha. 226) vutto. Tattha paṭisambhidāpāḷiyaṃ “cetanāsampayuttā vipākadhammattā savipākena āyūhanasaṅkhātena saṅkhatābhisaṅkharaṇakiccena saṅkhārā”ti vuttā. Vibhaṅgapāḷiyaṃ “sabbampi bhavagāmikammaṃ kammabhavo”ti (vibha. 234) bhavassa paccayabhāvena bhavagāmibhāvato, kammasaṃsaṭṭhasahāyatāya kammabhāvato ca upapattibhavaṃ bhāventīti “bhavo”ti vuttā. Upapattibhavabhāvanākiccaṃ pana cetanāya sātisayanti paṭisambhidāpāḷiyā cetanā “bhavo”ti vuttā. Bhavābhisaṅkharaṇakiccaṃ cetanāya sātisayanti vibhaṅgapāḷiyaṃ “kusalā cetanā”tiādinā (vibha. 226) cetanā “saṅkhārā”ti vuttā. Tasmā tena tena pariyāyena [M 2.0339] ubhayaṃ ubhayattha vattuṃ yuttanti natthettha virodho. Tassa phale upapattibhave nikāmanāti “tassa sutaṃ hoti ‘cātumahārājikā devā dīghāyukā vaṇṇavanto sukhabahulā’ti”ādisutānusārena bhāvini upapattibhave abhikaṅkhanā. Gahaṇanti kāmupādānaṃ kiccenāha. Parāmasananti itarāni. Āyūhanāvasāneti tīsupi atthavikappesu vuttassa āyūhanassa avasāne.

And its existence is simply the state of being made; thus, it is said: 'The meaning is "being made in kamma-bhava."' Delusion regarding suffering, etc., is the unabandoned delusion that conceals the danger of suffering, etc. Accumulations are those which amass and which cause the arising of actions such as giving. They have one adverting, thus they are 'of single adverting'; in those of single adverting. In the seventh [javana], volition is becoming. 'Whatever volition there is, that is becoming; the associated accumulations are formations.' This is stated by way of the Paṭisambhidāmagga-pāḷi spoken in the exposition on the knowledge of the stability of phenomena, as has been shown. For there it comes as: 'Volition is becoming.' In the exposition of becoming, however, in the section 'with its meaning,' it is shown by way of the Vibhaṅga-pāḷi: 'Volition itself is formations, but becoming can also be that which is associated with volition.' For by the text beginning, 'Therein, what is the meritorious formation? Wholesome volition pertaining to the sense-sphere,' and so on, the state of formations as volition is stated in the Vibhaṅga-pāḷi. Therein, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga-pāḷi, it is said that [phenomena] associated with volition are called 'formations' because they are result-giving phenomena, and by their function of forming the conditioned, which is termed accumulation that has a result. In the Vibhaṅga-pāḷi, with the text 'All kamma leading to becoming is kamma-bhava,' they are called 'becoming' because they produce rebirth-becoming: by being a condition for becoming and by leading to becoming; and by being a companion associated with kamma and by being kamma. The function of producing rebirth-becoming, however, is pre-eminent for volition; thus, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga-pāḷi, volition is called 'becoming.' The function of forming becoming is pre-eminent for volition; thus, in the Vibhaṅga-pāḷi, by the text beginning 'Wholesome volition,' volition is called 'formations.' Therefore, by this and that method, it is suitable to state both in both places, so there is no contradiction here. The phrase 'desire for its result, rebirth-becoming' means the longing for a future rebirth-becoming, in accordance with what has been heard, such as, 'He has heard that "the devas of the Four Great Kings are long-lived, beautiful, and have much happiness."' By 'grasping,' he speaks of sensual clinging by way of its function. By 'adhering,' he speaks of the others. 'At the end of accumulation' means at the end of the accumulation spoken of in all three alternative meanings.

Idhāti imasmiṃ paccuppannabhave. Bhavantarassa atītabhavassa iminā paccuppannabhavena paṭisandhānaṃ bhavantarapaṭisandhānaṃ, bhavantarabhāvena vā paṭisandhānaṃ bhavantarapaṭisandhānaṃ, tassa vasena. Yaṃ paṭisandhīti vuccati, taṃ viññāṇanti sambandho. Tathā hi viññāṇaṃ “paṭisandhānapaccupaṭṭhāna”nti vuccati. Gabbheti mātukucchiyaṃ, gabbhāvatthāyaṃ vā.

'Here' means in this present existence. The linking of another existence, a past existence, with this present existence is called 'bhavantarapaṭisandhāna' (relinking to another existence); or, the linking in the manner of another existence is 'bhavantarapaṭisandhāna'. By virtue of that, that which is called 'relinking' is consciousness; thus is the connection. For indeed, consciousness is said to have 'the manifestation of relinking'. 'In the womb' means in the mother's belly, or in the embryonic stage.

Dvīsu atthavikappesu vutte āyūhanasaṅkhāre “tassa pubbabhāgā”ti āha, tatiye atthavikappe vutte “taṃsampayuttā”ti. Taṃsampayuttā avijjā gahitāva hotīti sambandho. Daharassa cittappavatti bhavaṅgabahulā yebhuyyena bhavantarajanakakammāyūhanasamatthā na hotīti “idha paṭipakkattā āyatanāna”nti vuttaṃ. “Kammakaraṇakāle sammoho dassito”ti etena kammassa paccayabhūtaṃ sammohaṃ dasseti, na kammasampayuttameva.

Regarding the formations of exertion stated in the two interpretations of meaning, he said, 'They are the preliminary part of that (sensual existence).' In the third interpretation of meaning, it is stated that ignorance associated with that (craving and clinging) is indeed included; thus is the connection. The process of consciousness of a young person is abundant in `bhavaṅga` and, for the most part, is not capable of exerting kamma that can generate another existence; therefore, it is said, 'here, due to the maturity of the sense bases.' By the phrase, 'delusion is shown at the time of performing the action,' it shows the delusion that is a condition for the kamma, not merely the delusion that is associated with the kamma.

“Tattha purimabhavasmiṃ pañca kammasambhārā, etarahi pañca vipākadhammā, etarahi pañca kammasambhārā, anāgate pañca vipākadhammāti dasa dhammā kammaṃ, dasa dhammā vipāko, iti dvīsu ṭhānesu kammaṃ, kammavaṭṭaṃ, dvīsu ṭhānesu vipāko, vipākavaṭṭanti kammasaṅkhepo ca vipākasaṅkhepo [V 2.0319] ca, kammabhavo ca vipākabhavo ca kammavaṭṭañca vipākavaṭṭañca, kammapavattañca vipākapavattañca, kammasantati ca vipākasantati ca, kiriyā ceva kiriyāphalañcāti –

Therein, in that round of existence: in the previous existence, there are five constituents of kamma; in the present, five resultant states. In the present, there are five constituents of kamma; in the future, five resultant states. Thus, ten states are kamma, and ten states are result. Thus, in two instances, kamma is the round of kamma; in two instances, result is the round of result. Therefore, there is the summary of kamma and the summary of result; kamma-existence and resultant-existence; the round of kamma and the round of result; the process of kamma and the process of result; the continuity of kamma and the continuity of result; and both action and the fruit of action—thus it should be known.

“Evaṃ samuppannamidaṃ sahetukaṃ,

Dukkhaṃ aniccaṃ calamittaraddhuvaṃ;

Dhammehi dhammā pabhavanti hetuso,

Na hettha attāva parova vijjati.

Thus arisen, this (round of existence) is with cause; it is suffering, impermanent, unstable, fleeting, and not lasting. States arise from states by way of cause; indeed, herein no being called 'self' or 'other' is found.

“Dhammā dhamme sañjanenti, hetusambhārapaccayā;

Hetūnañca nirodhāya, dhammo buddhena desito.

States, having causes, constituents, and conditions, produce other states. And for the cessation of causes, the Dhamma was taught by the Buddha.

“Hetūsu [M 2.0340] uparuddhesu, chinnaṃ vaṭṭaṃ na vaṭṭati;

Evaṃ dukkhantakiriyāya, brahmacariyidha vijjati;

Satte ca nupalabbhante, nevucchedo na sassata”nti. (vibha. aṭṭha. 242);

When the causes are obstructed, the round, being cut off, does not revolve. Thus, for the purpose of making an end of suffering, the holy life exists here. And when a being is not found, there is neither annihilation nor eternalism.

Tattha kammāneva vipākaṃ sambharanti vaḍḍhentīti kammasambhārā, kammaṃ vā saṅkhārabhavā, tadupakārakāni avijjātaṇhupādānāni kammasambhārā. Paṭisandhidāyako vā bhavo kammaṃ, tadūpakārakā yathāvuttā āyūhanasaṅkhārā, avijjādayo ca kammasambhārāti kammañca kammasambhārā ca kammasambhārāti ekasesavasena kammasambhāraggahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Dasa dhammā kammanti avijjādayopi kammasahāyatāya kammasarikkhakā, tadūpakārā cāti “kamma”nti vuttā. Saṅkhippanti ettha avijjādayo, viññāṇādayo cāti saṅkhepo, kammaṃ, vipāko ca. “Kammaṃ vipāko”ti evaṃ saṅkhipīyatīti vā saṅkhepo, avijjādayo, viññāṇādayo ca. Saṅkhepabhāvasāmaññena pana ekavacanaṃ katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, saṅkhepasaddo vā bhāgādhivacananti kammabhāgo kammasaṅkhepo.

Therein, kammas alone produce and increase the result—thus, they are called constituents of kamma. Or, the formational existences are kamma, and its supporters—ignorance, craving, and clinging—are the constituents of kamma. Alternatively, the existence that provides rebirth-linking is kamma, and its supporters—the accumulating formations as mentioned, and ignorance, etc.—are the constituents of kamma. Thus, kamma and the constituents of kamma are collectively called 'constituents of kamma'; the taking of this term should be understood by way of the ekasesa method. Regarding the statement 'ten things are kamma,' ignorance and so on are also called 'kamma' because they are companions to kamma, are similar to kamma, and are its supporters. It is a summary (saṅkhepa) because herein ignorance, etc., and consciousness, etc., are summarized, that is, kamma and its result. Or, it is a summary because it is summarized thus: 'kamma and result,' and herein ignorance, etc., and consciousness, etc., are comprised. But it should be understood that the singular is used due to the commonality of being a summary. Or, the word 'summary' (saṅkhepa) is a designation for a part; thus, the kamma-part is the kamma-summary.

Evaṃ samuppannanti kammatopi vipāko. Tatthāpi “avijjāto saṅkhārā”ti evaṃ samuppannaṃ, tisandhiādivasena vā samuppannaṃ idaṃ bhavacakkanti attho. Ittaranti gamanadhammaṃ, vinassadhammanti [V 2.0320] attho. Tena uppādavayavantatādīpakena aniccasaddena, vikārāpattidīpakena calasaddena ca adīpitaṃ kālantaraṭṭhāyitābhāvaṃ vibhāveti. Addhuvanti etena thirabhāvābhāvanissārataṃ. Hetu eva sambhārā hetusambhārā. “Ṭhānaso hetuso”ti (kathā. 355; paṭi. ma. 1.44) ettha evaṃ vuttaṃ vā ṭhānaṃ, aññampi tassa tassa sādhāraṇaṃ kāraṇaṃ sambhāro, asādhāraṇaṃ hetu. Evanti evaṃ hetuto dhammamattasambhave, hetunirodhā ca vaṭṭacchede dhamme ca taṃnirodhāya desite satīti attho. Brahmacariyaṃ idha brahmacariyidha satte cāti ettha ca-saddo “evaṃ brahmacariyañca vijjati, sassatucchedā ca na hontī”ti samuccayattho. Evañhi hetuāyatte dhammamattasambhave satto nupalabbhati, tasmiñca upalabbhante sassato, ucchedo vā siyāti nupalabbhante tasmiṃ neva ucchedo na sassatanti vuttaṃ hoti.

Thus, the result is also arisen from kamma. Therein also, 'from ignorance, formations arise'—thus arisen, or arisen by way of the threefold connection, etc., this is the meaning of 'the wheel of existence.' 'Transient' means it is of a nature to pass away, or of a nature to perish; this is the meaning. By that (word 'ittaraṃ'), it reveals the absence of enduring for another period of time, which is not indicated by the word 'impermanent,' which indicates the state of having arising and passing away, nor by the word 'unstable' (cala), which indicates the state of undergoing alteration. By this (word 'addhuvaṃ'), it reveals the unsubstantiality which is the absence of a stable state. 'Causal constituents' means the causes themselves are the constituents. In the passage 'by way of ground, by way of cause,' either `ṭhāna` (ground) is what is thus mentioned, or another common cause for each respective thing is `sambhāro` (constituent), while the specific cause is `hetu` (cause). 'Thus' means: in this way, when a mere phenomenon arises from a cause, and with the cessation of the cause there is the cutting off of the round, and the Dhamma has been taught for its cessation. In the phrase 'the holy life here, and beings here,' the word 'and' has a conjunctive sense: 'thus the holy life also exists, and eternalism and annihilationism do not occur.' For thus, when there is the arising of a mere phenomenon dependent on a cause, a being is not found. And if that being were found, it would be eternalism or annihilationism. Therefore, since that being is not found, there is neither annihilationism nor eternalism—this is what is said.

655. Saccappabhavatoti saccato, saccānaṃ vā pabhavato ca.

655. 'Because of arising from truth' means: because of arising from the cause which is truth, or because of the arising of the truths.

Kusalākusalaṃ [M 2.0341] kammanti vaṭṭakathāya vattamānattā sāsavanti viññāyati. Avisesenāti “cetanā cetanāsampayuttakā”ti visesaṃ akatvā, sabbampi taṃ kusalākusalaṃ kammaṃ samudayasaccanti vuttanti attho. “Taṇhā ca…pe… avasesā ca sāsavā kusalā dhammā”ti (vibha. 208-210) hi cetanācetanāsampayuttavisesaṃ akatvā vuttanti, ariyasaccavisesaṃ vā akatvā samudayasaccanti vuttanti attho. Saccavibhaṅge hi sabbepi kilesā sabbampi bhavagāmikammaṃ “samudayasacca”nti vuttaṃ. Dutiyasaccaṃ pabhavo etassāti dutiyasaccapabhavaṃ. Upādānapaccayā bhavoti upapattibhavassa, kammabhavassa ca adhippetattā vuttaṃ “paṭhamadutiyasaccadvaya”nti.

Regarding 'wholesome and unwholesome kamma': since this is a discussion on the round of existence, it is understood as tainted. 'Without distinction' means that without making a distinction such as 'volition and its associated states,' all that wholesome and unwholesome kamma is said to be the truth of the origin—this is the meaning. For it is said in the passage, 'craving and… the remaining tainted wholesome states,' without making a distinction between volition and its associated states; or, the meaning is that it is said to be the truth of the origin without making a distinction of the noble truths. Indeed, in the Analysis of the Truths, all defilements and all kamma leading to existence are called 'the truth of the origin.' 'Having its origin in the second truth' means 'the second truth is the origin of this.' Because in the phrase 'with clinging as condition, existence,' 'existence' (bhava) is intended to mean both existence-as-rebirth and kamma-existence, it is called 'the pair of the first and second truths'.

656. Vatthūsūti ārammaṇesu, dukkhādīsu vā paṭicchādetabbesu vatthūsu. Sammohetīti dhammasabhāvaṃ jānituṃ paṭivijjhituṃ adentī tassa paṭicchādanavasena sammoheti. Vatthunti idha ārammaṇaṃ adhippetaṃ. Aññamaññañca upatthambheti aññamaññasannissayena vinā ṭhātuṃ asakkontā dve naḷakalāpā viya. Savisayeti yathāsakaṃ visaye rūpāyatanādike. Jāyamānānaṃ khandhānaṃ vikārabhāvena labbhamānā jāti te janentī viya hotīti vuttaṃ “khandhe ca janetī”ti. Tenāha “tesaṃ abhinibbattibhāvena pavattattā”ti. Pākabhedabhāvañca adhitiṭṭhatīti etthāpi “khandhe janetī”ti ettha vuttanayeneva attho gahetabbo. Pākabhedavasena vattaticceva attho[V 2.0321]. Paccatīti pāko, bhijjatīti bhedo, pāko ca bhedo ca pākabhedaṃ, tassa bhāvaṃ paccanaṃ, bhijjanañcāti attho. Sokādīnaṃ adhiṭṭhānattāti tesaṃ kāraṇattā, tehi siddhāya avijjāya sahitehi saṅkhārehi paccayo ca hoti bhavantarapātubhāvāyāti adhippāyo. Cuticittaṃ vā paṭisandhiviññāṇassa anantarapaccayo hotīti “paccayo ca hoti bhavantarapātubhāvāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ pana cuticittaṃ avijjāsaṅkhārarahitaṃ bhavantarassa paccayo na hotīti sasahāyattadassanatthamāha “sokādīnaṃ adhiṭṭhānattā”ti. Dvedhāti attano attano sarasena, dhammantarapaccayabhāvena cāti dvedhā dvedhā. Byāpanicchālopena hi niddeso.

656. ‘On the bases’ (vatthūsu) means on the objects, or on the bases that are to be concealed, such as suffering, etc. ‘It deludes’ (sammoheti) means that by concealing the true nature of phenomena, it prevents one from knowing and penetrating it. Here, ‘base’ (vatthu) is intended to mean the object. ‘And they support one another’: like two sheaves of reeds that cannot stand without leaning on each other. ‘In their respective spheres’: in their own domains, such as the form base, etc. ‘And it generates the aggregates’: birth, which is the alteration-state of the arising aggregates, is as if it generates them; thus it is said. Therefore he says: ‘because they proceed by way of bringing them about.’ ‘And it presides over the state of ripening and breaking’: here too, the meaning should be taken in the way stated in the context of ‘and it generates the aggregates.’ The meaning is simply that it proceeds by way of ripening and breaking. ‘Ripens’ (paccati), thus ‘ripening’ (pāko); ‘breaks’ (bhijjati), thus ‘breaking’ (bhedo). Ripening and breaking is pākabheda; its state is the process of ripening and breaking. ‘Because it is the foundation of sorrow, etc.’: because it is their cause. The meaning is that by the formations accompanied by ignorance—which is established by them (sorrow, etc.)—it becomes a condition for the manifestation of another existence. Or, the death consciousness is the immediate condition for the rebirth-linking consciousness; thus it is said, ‘it becomes a condition for the manifestation of another existence.’ But that death consciousness, when devoid of ignorance and formations, is not a condition for another existence. To show its state of having companions, he says, ‘because it is the foundation of sorrow, etc.’ ‘In two ways’: in two ways for each, that is, by its own essence and by being a condition for other phenomena. For this is an instruction by elision.

657. “Avijjāpaccayā [M 2.0342] saṅkhārā”ti etena saṅkhārānaṃ paccayuppannatādassanena “ko nu kho abhisaṅkharotīti esa no kallo pañho”ti dasseti, tenetaṃ kārakadassananivāraṇaṃ. Attā bhavato bhavantaraṃ saṅkamatīti dassanaṃ attasaṅkantidassanaṃ, taṃ saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇuppattivacanena nivāritaṃ hoti. Pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ abhedato eko attāti gahaṇaṃ ghanasaññā, taṃ yamakatālakandaṃ bhindantena viya “viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpamattameta”nti vacanena nivāritaṃ hoti. “Evamādidassananivāraṇa”nti etena “socati paridevati dukkhito”tiādidassananivāraṇamāha. Sokādayopi hi paccayāyattā avasavattinoti “jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ soka…pe… sambhavantī”ti (ma. ni. 3.126; saṃ. ni. 2.1; udā. 1) etena vuttamevāti. Micchādassananivāraṇatopīti kārakadassanādinānāvidhamicchābhinivesanivāraṇatopi.

657. “With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise”—by showing the conditionally arisen nature of volitional formations, it is shown that the question, “Who now performs the formations?” is not appropriate. Thus, this refutes the view of a doer. The view that a self transmigrates from one existence to another is the view of self-transmigration, which is refuted by the statement that consciousness arises with volitional formations as condition. The grasping of the five aggregates as an undivided single self is the perception of compactness. This is refuted by the statement, like one splitting a double palm-tuber, that “with consciousness as condition, there is only name-and-form.” By “Thus, the refutation of such views,” it speaks of the refutation of such views as “one grieves, laments, suffers,” and so on. For sorrow and the like are indeed dependent on conditions and not under one's control, as is stated: “With birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow… come to be.” “Also from the refutation of wrong views” means also from the refutation of various kinds of wrong adherence, such as the view of a doer.

658. “Salakkhaṇasāmaññalakkhaṇavasenā”ti etena sabbappakārena dhammānaṃ yāthāvato adassanamāha tadubhayavinimuttassa dhammesu paramatthato passitabbabhāvassa abhāvato. Upakkhalanaṃ viya dukkhuppattihetuto. Patanaṃ viya bhavantarapapātato. Gaṇḍapātubhāvo viya dukkhatāsūlayogato, kilesāsucipaggharaṇato ca. Gaṇḍabhedapīḷakā viyāti bhedanatthaṃ paccamāne gaṇḍe tassa upari jāyamānā khuddakapīḷakā viya, gaṇḍassa vā anekadhābhede pīḷakā viya. Ghaṭṭanaṃ viya saṅghaṭṭanarasatāya phasso. Ghaṭṭanadukkhaṃ viyāti ghaṭṭanato jātaṃ dukkhaṃ viya tividhadukkhatāvasena tissannampi vedanānaṃ dukkhabhāvato. Paṭikārābhilāso viyāti samudāyassa ekadesanidassanabhāvenāha.
