Asappāyaggahaṇaṃ viya bahuvidhānatthuppattinimittato. Asappāyalepanaṃ viya dukkhahetuno sasantāne sannidhāpanato. Gaṇḍavikārapātubhāvo viya attabhāvagaṇḍassa nibbattivikārabhāvato[V 2.0322], tannimittañcassa sūnabhāvādisambhavato. Sūnatāsarāgapubbaggahaṇādayo hi gaṇḍavikārā. Sarasato gaṇḍassa bhijjanaṃ pākena vinā na hotīti bhedaggahaṇenevassa pākopi gahitoti katvā āha “gaṇḍabhedo viya jarāmaraṇa”nti. Gaṇḍassa vā visadisāpatti, bhijjanañca gaṇḍabhedo, tattha visadisāpatti pākoti veditabbaṃ.

658. “By way of specific and general characteristics”: by this is meant the not seeing of phenomena as they really are in every way, because in phenomena liberated from both of these, there is ultimately nothing to be seen. Like stumbling, because it is a cause for the arising of suffering. Like falling, because it is a plunge into another existence. Like the appearance of a tumor, because of its connection with the stake of the threefold painfulness and the oozing of the impurity of defilements. Like the pustules on a bursting tumor: like the small pustules that arise on a tumor when it is ripening to burst, or the pustules when a tumor bursts in many ways. Like collision, because contact has the nature of impact. Like the pain from a collision: like the pain that arises from a collision, because all three kinds of feeling are of a painful nature by way of the threefold painfulness. Like the desire for a remedy: this is said by way of showing one part of the whole. Like grasping what is unsuitable, because it is a sign for the arising of various kinds of disadvantage. Like applying an unsuitable ointment, because of placing the cause of suffering in one's own continuity. Like the appearance of a tumor's affliction, because it is the state of the affliction of the arising of the tumor of individual existence, and its sign is the occurrence of swelling and so on. For swelling, discoloration, pus formation, and the like are the afflictions of a tumor. Because the bursting of a tumor by its own nature does not occur without ripening, its ripening is included by the mention of its bursting. Thus it is said: “Like the bursting of a tumor is aging and death.” Or, the bursting of a tumor is its deterioration and its breaking apart; therein, the deterioration should be understood as the ripening.

Upamāhi [M 2.0343] bhavacakkaṃ viññāpentena ekādhiṭṭhānehi upamāvisesehi taṃ viññāpetvā idāni nānādhiṭṭhānehi viññāpetuṃ “yasmā vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha paṭalābhibhūtacakkhuko rūpāni na passati, kiñci passantopi viparītaṃ passati, evaṃ avijjābhibhūto dukkhādīni na paṭipajjati na passati, micchā vā paṭipajjatīti paṭalaṃ viya avijjā. Kosakārakimi viya attanāva katattā, vaṭṭassa attano eva paribbhamanakāraṇattā ca kosappadesā viya saṅkhārā. Saṅkhārapariggahaṃ vinā patiṭṭhaṃ alabhamānaṃ viññāṇaṃ pariṇāyakapariggahaṃ vinā patiṭṭhaṃ alabhamāno rājakumāro viyāti pariggahena vinā patiṭṭhālābho ettha upamopameyyasāmaññaṃ. Upapattinimittanti kammādiārammaṇamāha. Parikappanatoti ārammaṇakaraṇato, sampayuttena vā vitakkena vitakkanato. Devamanussamigavihaṅgādivividhappakāratāya māyā viya nāmarūpaṃ. Patiṭṭhāvisesena vuddhivisesāpattito vanappagumbo viya saḷāyatanaṃ. Āyatanānaṃ visayivisayabhūtānaṃ aññamaññābhimukhabhāvo āyatanaghaṭṭanaṃ. Tato āyatanaghaṭṭanato dvayasaṅghaṭṭanuppattito, vedanādukkhahetuto ca aggi viya phasso. Sapariḷāhato dāho viya vedanā. Uparūpari taṇhāpavaḍḍhanato loṇūdakapānaṃ viya visayānubhavanaṃ. Ārammaṇe pātukamyatābhāvato pipāsā viya taṇhā. Tadassupādānanti taṃ abhilāsakaraṇaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhābhinandanaṃ assa taṃsamaṅgino puggalassa, tadassa vā bhaveyya upādānaṃ. Byasanāvahatāya ajānanato bhavupādānaṃ macchassa baḷisupādānaṃ viya. Ettha ca saṅkhārādīnaṃ kosappadesapariṇāyakādīhi dvīhi dvīhi sadisatāya dve dve upamā vuttāti veditabbā.

The commentator, having explained the wheel of becoming with special similes having a single foundation, now stated the passage beginning “Because…” in order to explain it with similes having various foundations. Therein, just as a person whose eyes are overcome by a cataract does not see forms, or even if seeing something, sees it distortedly, so too one who is overcome by ignorance does not comprehend or see suffering and so forth, or comprehends it wrongly—thus ignorance is like a cataract. Formations are like a silkworm because they are made by oneself, and like the parts of a cocoon because they are the cause of one's own revolving in the round of existence. Consciousness, which does not obtain a footing without the support of formations, is like a prince who does not obtain a footing without the support of a guardian—thus, herein, the non-obtaining of a footing without support is the commonality between the simile and the thing illustrated. By “the sign of rebirth,” it refers to the object, such as kamma. As for “from conceptualizing,” it means from making it an object, or from thinking with associated thought. Name-and-form is like an illusion due to its diverse manifestations, such as gods, humans, beasts, and birds. The sixfold sense base is like a thicket in the woods because it attains special growth through a special basis. The state of the sense bases, which are the sense faculty and its object, facing one another is the “striking of the sense bases.” From that striking of the sense bases, from arising from the impact of the pair, and because it is a cause of the suffering of feeling, contact is like a fire. Feeling is like a burning due to its torment. The experiencing of sense objects is like drinking salt water because it increases craving more and more. Craving is like thirst due to the state of desiring to partake of objects. As for “that grasping of his,” it is the making of a wish for it, the delighting through craving and views, on the part of that person endowed with it; or, it would be the grasping of that person. The grasping of existence is like a fish's grasping of a hook, due to not knowing that it brings ruin. And herein, it should be understood that for formations and so on, two similes each are stated because of their similarity with two things each, such as the parts of a cocoon and a guardian.

659. Koci agambhīro eva gambhīro viya khāyati purāṇatiṇapaṇṇādibharito pabbatasaṅkhepe jalāsayo viya, na evamayaṃ. Ayaṃ pana gambhīrova hutvā obhāsati pakāsati dissatīti gambhīrāvabhāso. Yathārahanti atthādivasena yathānurūpaṃ.

659. Just as some reservoir in a mountain cleft, filled with old grass, leaves, and so on, though it is in fact not deep, appears as if it were deep; this is not so. Rather, this, being truly deep, shines forth and is manifest; thus, it is of deep appearance. “As is fitting” means: suitably, by way of meaning and so on.

Jātito jarāmaraṇaṃ na na hoti, hoti evāti avadhāraṇe siddhe “siyā nu kho jarāmaraṇaṃ [V 2.0323] jātito, aññatopī”ti āsaṅkāyaṃ tadāsaṅkānivattanatthaṃ “na ca jātiṃ vinā aññato hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha aññaggahaṇaṃ jātiyā paṭiyogīvisayaṃ, na aññamattavisayaṃ [M 2.0344] “jātiṃ vinā”ti vacanato. Tenassa nāññaṃ jātiyā sahakārīkāraṇabhūtaṃ nivattitaṃ hoti. Esa nayo ito paresupi. Itthanti idaṃ pakāraṃ, iminā pakārenāti attho. Jātipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭhoti jātipaccayasambhūtaṃ hutvā sahitassa attano paccayānurūpassa uddhaṃ uddhaṃ āgatabhāvo, anuppavattaṭṭhoti attho. Atha vā sambhūtaṭṭho ca samudāgataṭṭho ca sambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho. “Na jātito jarāmaraṇaṃ na hoti, na ca jātiṃ vinā aññato hotī”ti hi jātipaccayasambhūtaṭṭho vutto. Itthañca jātito samudāgacchatīti jātipaccayasamudāgataṭṭho, yā yā jāti yathā yathā paccayo hoti, tadanurūpapātubhāvoti attho.

From birth, aging-and-death does not not occur; it certainly occurs. When this determination is established, should the doubt arise, 'Could aging-and-death come from birth, and also from something else?', to dispel that doubt, it is stated: 'Nor does it occur from something else without birth.' Here, the term 'something else' refers to a counterpart to birth, not merely to anything different—as indicated by the phrase 'without birth.' By this, another factor that is a cooperative cause along with birth is not negated. This principle applies to the subsequent links as well. 'Thus' (`ittham`) means 'in this manner.' The meaning of 'arisen and come forth conditioned by birth' is this: having been produced by birth as condition, it is the state of its own corresponding effect having come about progressively higher and higher; the meaning is 'proceeding in conformity.' Alternatively, the meaning of 'arisen and come forth' is composed of the meaning 'arisen' and the meaning 'come forth.' For by the statement, 'Aging-and-death does not not occur from birth, nor does it occur from another cause without birth,' the meaning 'arisen conditioned by birth' is stated. And by 'And thus it comes forth from birth,' the meaning 'come forth conditioned by birth' is stated; that is, in whatever way any birth is a condition, its manifestation occurs in conformity with that.

Tattha “na jātito jarāmaraṇaṃ na hotī”ti iminā jarāmaraṇassa jātipaccayatāya avitathataṃ dasseti, “na jātiṃ vinā aññato jarāmaraṇaṃ hotī”ti iminā anaññathattaṃ, “itthañca jātito samudāgacchatī”ti iminā tathataṃ. Tena ca yathā paccayadhammā attano paccayuppannānaṃ paccayabhāve, tathā avitathā anaññathā, evaṃ paccayuppannadhammāpi tabbhāveti dasseti. Esa nayo sesesupi. “Hetuphale ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”ti etena vacanena atthassa hetuphalabhāvo kathaṃ ñātabboti? “Atthapaṭisambhidā”ti etassa samāsapadassa avayavapadatthaṃ dassentena “hetuphale ñāṇa”nti vuttattā. “Atthe paṭisambhidā atthapaṭisambhidā”ti ettha hi “atthe”ti etassa atthaṃ dassentena “hetuphale”ti vuttaṃ, “paṭisambhidā”ti etassa atthaṃ dassentena “ñāṇa”nti, tasmā hetuphalaatthasaddā ekatthā, ñāṇapaṭisambhidā cāti imamatthaṃ vadantena sādhito atthassa hetuphalabhāvo.

Herein, by the statement, 'It is not the case that aging and death do not occur from birth,' the unfailing nature of birth as a condition for aging and death is shown. By, 'Aging and death do not occur from anything else apart from birth,' its not-otherness is shown. By, 'And in this way it comes forth from birth,' its thusness is shown. And by this it is shown that just as conditioning phenomena, in their role as conditions for the phenomena that arise from them, are thus, unfailing, and not otherwise, so too are the conditionally arisen phenomena in that very state. This same principle applies to the subsequent sections. How is the nature of meaning as cause and effect to be known from the statement, 'Knowledge of cause and effect is the analytical knowledge of meaning'? Because it is said, 'knowledge in cause and effect,' when showing the meaning of the component words of the compound 'atthapaṭisambhidā.' For in 'Analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā) of meaning (atthe) is atthapaṭisambhidā,' the meaning of 'atthe' is shown by 'in cause and effect,' and the meaning of 'paṭisambhidā' is shown by 'knowledge.' Therefore, the words 'cause-and-effect' and 'meaning' are synonymous, as are 'knowledge' and 'analytical knowledge.' By stating this, the nature of meaning as cause and effect is established.

Yenākārenāti yena pavattiākārena. Sabhāvadhammā hi paccayavisesasiddhena pavattiākārena visiṭṭhākārā honti. Tenāha “sabbe dhammā sabbākārena buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇamukhe āpāthamāgacchantī”ti (mahāni. 156; cūḷani. mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 85). Yadavatthāti yāya avatthāya avatthitā. Avatthāvisesavanto hi dhammā tena tena avatthāvisesena taṃ taṃ atthakiccaṃ sādhetuṃ samatthā honti. Svāyaṃ pavattiākāro, avatthāviseso ca avijjāyapi anupacitakusalasambhārehi duravabodhato eva ñāṇena alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭho [M 2.0345][V 2.0324] cāti āha “tassa…pe… gambhīro”ti. Tassa ākārassa, avatthāya ca. Hetumhi ñāṇanti ettha hetuno dhammapariyāyatā vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

'By whatever mode' means by whatever mode of occurrence. For phenomena by their nature possess a distinguished mode through a mode of occurrence established by specific conditions. Hence it is said: 'All phenomena in all their modes come within the range of the Blessed One the Buddha's knowledge.' 'In whatever state' means the state in which they are established. For phenomena endowed with particular states are capable of accomplishing their respective functions by means of those particular states. And this mode of occurrence and this particular state, even in the case of ignorance, being difficult to comprehend for those who have not accumulated a store of wholesome merits, is for that very reason a foundation unattainable by knowledge. Therefore it is said: 'That... is deep'—that is, of that mode and of that state. In 'knowledge in the cause,' the status of 'cause' as a synonym for 'dhamma' should be understood in the way already explained.

Assāti paṭiccasamuppādassa. Tena tena kāraṇenāti tena tena veneyyānaṃ bujjhanānuguṇatāsaṅkhātena kāraṇena. Tatthāti tasmiṃ desanappakāre. Anulomapaṭilomatoti nayidha paccayuppādā paccayuppannuppādasaṅkhātaṃ anulomaṃ, paccayanirodhā paccayuppannanirodhasaṅkhātañca paṭilomamāha. Ādito pana antagamanamanulomaṃ, antato ca ādigamanaṃ paṭilomamāha. Ādito paṭṭhāya anulomadesanāya, antato paṭṭhāya paṭilomadesanāya ca tisandhicatusaṅkhepaṃ. “Ime cattāro āhārā kiṃnidānā”tiādikāya (saṃ. ni. 2.11) vemajjhato paṭṭhāya paṭilomadesanāya, “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā”tiādikāya (ma. ni. 1.204, 400; ma. ni. 3.421, 425-426; saṃ. ni. 2.43-45; 2.4.60; kathā. 465, 467) anulomadesanāya ca dvisandhitisaṅkhepaṃ. “Saṃyojanīyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu assādānupassino viharato taṇhā pavaḍḍhati, taṇhāpaccayā upādāna”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.53, 57) ekasandhidvisaṅkhepaṃ. Katthaci ekaṅgopi ca paṭiccasamuppādo desito, so “tatra, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.62) dassito eva.

“Of this” means of dependent origination. “For this and that reason” means for the reason designated as suitability for the awakening of various persons to be trained. “Therein” means in that mode of teaching. By “in forward and reverse order”: here this does not refer to the forward order as the arising of the conditioned from the arising of the condition, and the reverse order as the cessation of the conditioned from the cessation of the condition. Rather, it refers to the forward order as going from the beginning to the end, and the reverse order as going from the end to the beginning. By the forward teaching from the beginning, and by the reverse teaching from the end, there are three connections and four sections. By the reverse teaching starting from the middle with “These four kinds of nutriment, what is their source?” (SN 12.11), and by the forward teaching with “Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, feeling,” etc. (MN 1.204, 400; MN 3.421, 425-426; SN 12.43-45; SN 12.60; Kathā. 465, 467), there are two connections and three sections. In such passages as, “For one, monks, who dwells contemplating gratification in things that fetter, craving increases; with craving as condition, clinging...” (SN 12.53, 57), there is one connection and two sections. And in some places dependent origination is taught with even a single factor, as is shown by the passage beginning, “Here, monks, a learned noble disciple...” (SN 12.62).

Avijjādīnaṃ sabhāvo paṭivijjhīyatīti paṭivedho. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “tesaṃ tesaṃ vā tattha tattha vuttadhammānaṃ paṭivijjhitabbo salakkhaṇasaṅkhāto aviparītasabhāvo paṭivedho”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā). Jānanalakkhaṇassa ñāṇassa paṭipakkhabhūto avijjāya aññāṇaṭṭho. Ārammaṇassa paccakkhakaraṇena dassanabhūtassa paṭipakkhabhūto adassanaṭṭho. Yena panesā dukkhādīnaṃ yāthāvasarasaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ na deti, chādetvā pariyonandhitvā tiṭṭhati, so tassā saccāsampaṭivedhaṭṭho. Apuññābhisaṅkhārekadeso sarāgo, añño virāgo. Rāgassa vā apaṭipakkhabhāvato rāgapavaḍḍhako apuññābhisaṅkhāro sabbopi sarāgo, itaro [M 2.0346] tappaṭipakkhabhāvato virāgo. “Dīgharattaṃ hetaṃ, bhikkhave, assutavato puthujjanassa ajjhositaṃ mamāyitaṃ parāmaṭṭhaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.62) attaparāmāsassa viññāṇaṃ visesato vatthu vuttanti viññāṇassa suññataṭṭho gambhīro. Attā vijānāti saṃsaratīti sabyāpāratāsaṅkanti abhinivesabalavatāya abyāpāraṭṭhaasaṅkantipaṭisandhipātubhāvaṭṭhā [V 2.0325] ca gambhīrā. Nāmarūpassa paṭisandhikkhaṇe ekuppādo, pavattiyaṃ visuṃ visuṃ yathārahaṃ ekuppādo, nāmassa rūpena, rūpassa ca nāmena asampayogato vinibbhogo, nāmassa nāmena, rūpassa ca rūpena, ekaccassa ekaccena avinibbhogo yojetabbo. Ekuppādekanirodhe hi avinibbhoge adhippete so rūpassa ca ekakalāpavuttino labbhati. Atha vā ekacatuvokārabhavesu nāmarūpānaṃ asahavattanato aññamaññavinibbhogo, pañcavokārabhave sahavattanato avinibbhogo ca veditabbo.

It is called 'penetration' (paṭivedha) because the inherent nature of ignorance and so on is penetrated. For this was said in the commentary: 'Alternatively, penetration is the undistorted inherent nature, designated as its own characteristic, of those various phenomena taught in their respective contexts, which is to be penetrated' (Dhs-a. Nidānakathā). The meaning of not-knowing, which is the opponent of knowledge that has the characteristic of knowing, is the meaning of ignorance. The meaning of not-seeing is that which is the opponent of the seeing that directly experiences the object. Moreover, that by which this ignorance does not allow the penetration of the true inherent nature of suffering and so on, but stands covering and enveloping it, that is its meaning of non-penetration of the truths. One part of demeritorious formations is with lust; the other is without lust. Or, because it is not the opponent of lust and promotes lust, all demeritorious formation is with lust; the other, because it is its opponent, is without lust. 'For a long time, O bhikkhus, this has been clung to, cherished, and wrongly grasped by the uninstructed worldling thus: “This is mine, this I am, this is my self”' (SN 22.81). Because consciousness is stated as the special basis for the wrong grasping of self, the meaning of the voidness of consciousness is profound. Because of the strength of the adherence to the view of activity and transition—as in 'A self knows, it transmigrates'—the meaning of non-activity and the meaning of the appearance of rebirth-linking without transition are also profound. For name-and-form, the following should be applied: simultaneous arising at the moment of rebirth-linking; in the course of existence, separate simultaneous arising as appropriate; the dissociation of name from form and of form from name due to non-conjunction; and the non-dissociation of a certain name with a certain name, and of a certain form with a certain form. For when non-dissociation is intended as simultaneous arising and cessation, this is also obtained for form that occurs in a single group. Alternatively, in the one- and four-constituent planes of existence, because name-and-form do not occur together, their mutual dissociation should be understood; in the five-constituent plane of existence, because they occur together, their non-dissociation should be understood.

Adhipatiyaṭṭho nāma idha indriyapaccayabhāvo. “Lokopeso dvārāpesā khettampeta”nti (dha. sa. 598-599) vuttā lokādiatthā cakkhādīsu pañcasu yojetabbā. Manāyatanassāpi lujjanato, manosamphassādīnaṃ dvārakhettabhāvato ca ete atthā sambhavanti eva. Āpāthagatānaṃ rūpādīnaṃ pakāsanayogyatālakkhaṇaṃ obhāsanaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ visayibhāvo, manāyatanassa vijānanaṃ. Saṅghaṭṭanaṭṭho visesato cakkhusamphassādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ, itare channampi yojetabbā. Phusanañca phassassa sabhāvo, saṅghaṭṭanaṃ raso, itare upaṭṭhānākārā. Ārammaṇarasānubhavanaṭṭho rasavasena vutto, vedayitaṭṭho lakkhaṇavasena. Sukhadukkhamajjhattabhāvā yathākkamaṃ tissannaṃ vedanānaṃ sabhāvavasena vuttā. Attā vedayatīti abhinivesassa balavatāya nijjīvaṭṭho vedanāya gambhīro. Nijjīvāya vā vedanāya vedayitaṃ nijjīvavedayitaṃ, nijjīvavedayitameva attho nijjīvavedayitaṭṭho. Sappītikataṇhāya abhinanditaṭṭho, balavatarataṇhāya gilitvā pariniṭṭhāpanaṃ ajjhosānaṭṭho. Itaro sādhāraṇavasena veditabbo. Ādānaggahaṇābhinivesaṭṭhā catunnampi upādānānaṃ samānā, parāmāsaṭṭho vutto diṭṭhupādānādīnameva, tathā duratikkamaṭṭho. “Diṭṭhikantāro”ti (dha. sa. 392) hi vacanato diṭṭhīnaṃ duratikkamatā, daḷhaggahaṇattā [M 2.0347] vā catunnampi duratikkamaṭṭho yojetabbo. Duratikkamatāyapi hi taṇhāya samuddaṭṭho vutto. Yonigatiṭhitinivāsesukhipananti samāse bhummavacanassa alopo daṭṭhabbo. Evañhi tena āyūhanābhisaṅkharaṇapadānaṃ samāso hoti. Jarāmaraṇaṅgaṃ maraṇappadhānanti maraṇaṭṭhā eva khayādayo gambhīrāti dassitā. Navanavānañhi khayena khaṇḍiccādiparipakkappavatti jarāti, khayaṭṭho vā jarāya vuttoti daṭṭhabbo. Navabhāvāpagamo hi khayoti vattuṃ yuttoti. Vipariṇāmaṭṭho dvinnampi. Santativasena vā jarāya khayavayabhāvo, sammutikhaṇikavasena maraṇassa bhedavipariṇāmatā yojetabbā.

Here the meaning of dominance is the state of being a faculty condition. The meanings of world, etc., stated as 'this is the world, this is the door, this is the field' (Dhs. §§598-599), should be applied to the five beginning with the eye. These meanings are possible for the mind base too, because it perishes and because it is the door and field for mind-contact, etc. Illumination, characterized by the suitability for manifesting visible forms, etc., that have come into range, is the subjectivity of the eye, etc.; for the mind base, it is cognizing. The meaning of impinging is especially for the five kinds of contact beginning with eye-contact; the other meanings should be applied to all six. Touching is the nature of contact, impinging is its function, the others are its manifestations. The meaning of experiencing the flavor of the object is stated in terms of function; the meaning of being felt is stated in terms of characteristic. The states of pleasure, pain, and neutrality are stated, in order, in terms of the intrinsic nature of the three feelings. Because of the strength of the adherence 'a self feels,' the meaning of lifelessness is profound for feeling. Or, what is felt by a lifeless feeling is a lifeless feeling-experience; the meaning of lifeless feeling-experience is just that. The meaning of delighting is for craving accompanied by zest; the meaning of devouring is the swallowing and consuming by a stronger craving. The other should be understood as general. The meanings of taking up, grasping, and adhering are common to all four kinds of clinging. The meaning of misapprehending is stated only for clinging to views, etc., likewise the meaning of being hard to overcome. For it is said, 'the wilderness of views' (Dhs. §392), thus indicating the difficulty of overcoming views. Or because of their firm grip, the meaning of being hard to overcome should be applied to all four. Indeed, because it is hard to overcome, the meaning of 'ocean' is stated for craving. In the compound 'yonigatiṭhitinivāsesukhipana,' the non-elision of the locative plural ending should be seen. For thus there is a compound of the words 'accumulating' and 'forming' with it. The link of aging-and-death has death as its principal part; thus it is shown that the meanings of decay, etc., which are indeed meanings of death, are profound. For aging is the occurrence of maturation, such as brokenness of teeth, etc., through the destruction of what is new and newer. Or it should be seen that the meaning of decay is stated for aging. For it is right to say that decay is the departure of newness. The meaning of alteration applies to both. Alternatively, aging's state of decay and decline should be applied in terms of continuity, while death's state of breaking up and alteration should be applied in terms of conventional and momentary destruction.

660. Atthanayāti atthānaṃ nayā, avijjādiatthehi ekattādī sakena bhāvena nayanti gamentīti [V 2.0326] ekattādayo, tesaṃ nayāti vuttā. Nīyantīti hi nayāti. Atthā eva vā ekattādibhāvena nīyamānā ñāyamānā atthanayāti vuttā. Nīyanti etehīti vā nayā, ekattādīhi ca atthā “eka”ntiādinā nīyanti, tasmā ekattādayo atthānaṃ nayāti atthanayā.

660. ‘Methods of meaning’ (atthanayā) means the methods (nayā) of the meanings (atthānaṃ). Unity and so on are said to be their methods because, by their own nature, they make known the things such as ignorance by way of unity and so on. For a method (naya) is so called because by it things are known (nīyanti). Alternatively, the meanings themselves, being known by way of unity and so on, are called 'methods of meaning.' Or, methods (nayā) are so called because by them things are known. And by unity and so on, the meanings are known as 'one,' etc. Therefore, unity and so on are the methods of the meanings, hence 'methods of meaning'.

Aṅkurādibhāvenāti aṅkurapattanāḷakhandhasākhāpallavapalāsādibhāvena pavattamāne avayave ekajjhaṃ gahetvā santānānupacchedena bījaṃ rukkhabhāvaṃ pattaṃ rukkhabhāvena pavattaṃ tañca ekattena vuccatīti santānānupacchedo yathā ekattaṃ, evaṃ idhāpi avijjāsaṅkhārādihetuhetusamuppannānaṃ santānānupacchedo ekasantatipatitatā ekattanayoti dasseti. “Hetuphalasambandhenā”ti etena santānānupacchedaṃ vibhāveti. Satipi hi hetuphalānaṃ paramatthato bhede hetubhāvena, phalabhāvena ca tesaṃ sambandhabhāvoyevettha santānānupacchedo, yato yasmiṃ santāne kammaṃ nibbattaṃ, tattheva phaluppattīti katassa vināso, akatassa abbhāgamo ca natthīti. Ekattaggahaṇatoti hetuphalānaṃ bhedaṃ anupadhāretvā hetuṃ, phalañca abhinnaṃ katvā ubhinnaṃ ekabhāvassa abhedassa gahaṇena. “Tadeva viññāṇaṃ sandhāvati saṃsaratī”tiādinā sassatadiṭṭhiṃ upādiyati.

By the state of sprout, etc.: Just as when one takes together the developing parts—such as the sprout, leaf, stalk, stem, branch, shoot, and foliage—the seed that has reached the state of a tree and is developing as a tree is, due to the unbroken continuity, spoken of as a unity; so too here, it is shown that the method of unity is the unbroken continuity, the falling into a single continuum, of the causes, such as ignorance and formations, and the effects arisen from those causes. By the phrase 'by the connection of cause and result,' he clarifies the unbroken continuity. For even though cause and result are different in an ultimate sense, their state of connection as cause and as result is itself the unbroken continuity here. Because of this, since the result of a kamma arises in the very same continuum in which the kamma was performed, there is no destruction of a deed that was done, nor the arrival of a result for a deed that was not done. By grasping unity: by not investigating the difference between cause and result, by making the cause and the result non-different, and by grasping the non-difference, the single state, of the two. By thinking, 'That same consciousness runs on and transmigrates,' etc., one adopts the eternalist view.

Lakkhaṇavavatthānanti sabhāvavavatthānaṃ hetuno, phalassa ca bhinnasabhāvatāvabodho. Bhinnasantānassevāti sambandharahitassa nānattassa gahaṇato [M 2.0348] añño mato, añño jāto, tasmā “sattantaro ucchinno, sattantaro uppanno”ti gaṇhanto ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ upādiyati.

Ascertainment of characteristics: This is the ascertainment of intrinsic nature, the understanding that cause and result have different intrinsic natures. Of a broken continuum itself: Because of grasping the diversity of what is disconnected, devoid of connection, one holds: 'One dies, another is born.' Thus, by holding that 'one being is annihilated, another being has arisen,' one adopts the annihilationist view.

Amhehi uppādetabbanti ānetvā sambandho. Byāpārābhāvo anabhisandhitāya abyāvaṭatā. Sammā passantoti “nirīhā nijjīvā dhammamattā”ti passanto. Sabhāvo eva niyamo sabhāvaniyamo “sasambhāraggino uddhamukhatā, sasambhāravāyuno tiriyagamana”nti evamādi viya. Tena siddho yathāsakaṃ paccayuppannassa hetubhāvo. “Kassaci kattuno abhāvā na kāci kiriyā phalapabandhinī”ti akiriyadiṭṭhiṃ upādiyati.

The connection is made by supplying the words, 'is to be produced by us.' Absence of activity is non-involvement due to absence of intention. Seeing rightly is seeing that 'they are without striving, lifeless, mere phenomena.' Intrinsic nature itself is the law, a natural law, like 'the upward tendency of fire with its fuel, the horizontal movement of wind with its fuel,' and so on. Thereby, the state of being a cause for that which has arisen from its own respective conditions is established. By holding that 'because there is no doer, no action is connected with a result,' one adopts the view of non-action.

“Khīrato dadhi, na udakato, tilato telaṃ, na vālikato”ti sabbato sabbasambhavābhāvadassanena ahetukadiṭṭhiṃ hetuanurūpameva phalaṃ passanto akiriyadiṭṭhiṃ pajahati. Yato kutocīti yadi aññasmā aññassa uppatti siyā, vālikato telassa, ucchuto khīrassa [V 2.0327] kasmā uppatti na siyā, tasmā na koci kassaci hetu atthīti ahetukadiṭṭhiṃ, avijjamānepi hetumhi niyatatāya tilagāvīsukkasoṇitādīhi telakhīrasarīrādīni pavattantīti niyativādañca upādiyatīti viññātabbaṃ yathārahaṃ.

By seeing that 'curd comes from milk, not from water; oil from sesame, not from sand,' and thus seeing the absence of an arising of everything from everything, one abandons the view of non-causality; and seeing that the result conforms to the cause, one abandons the view of non-action. If the arising of one thing from another could happen from anything whatsoever, why would the arising of oil from sand, or of milk from sugarcane, not happen? Therefore, holding that 'nothing is a cause of anything,' one adopts the view of non-causality; or, holding that 'even though a cause is non-existent, things such as oil, milk, and bodies proceed from things such as sesame, cows, semen and blood due to a fixed nature,' one adopts the doctrine of fatalism. This should be understood as appropriate.

661. Kasmā? Yasmā idañhi bhavacakkaṃ apadāletvā saṃsārabhayamatīto na koci supinantarepi atthīti sambandho. Agādhaṃ appatiṭṭhaṃ duratiyānaṃ duratikkamaṃ. Asanivicakkamivāti asanimaṇḍalamiva. Tañhi nimmathanameva, nānimmathanaṃ pavattati, evaṃ bhavacakkampi ekantadukkhuppādanatova “niccanimmathana”nti vuttaṃ.

661. Why? The connection is this: because without shattering this wheel of existence, there is no one, even in a dream, who has overcome the fear of saṃsāra. It is profound, without footing, hard to cross, hard to overcome. 'Like a thunderbolt-wheel' means like the disk of a thunderbolt. For that is only crushing; it does not proceed without crushing. So too, the wheel of existence is called 'constantly crushing' precisely because it produces nothing but suffering.

Ñāṇāsinā apadāletvā saṃsārabhayamatīto natthīti etassa sādhakasuttaṃ dassento “vuttampi ceta”ntiādimāha. Tantūnaṃ ākulakaṃ tantākulakaṃ, tantākulakamiva jātā tantākulakajātā, kilesakammavipākehi ativiya jaṭitāti attho. Kuliyā sakuṇiyā nīḍaṃ kulikaṃ, taṃ viya jātā kulikuṇḍikajātā. Muñcā viya, pabbajā viya ca bhūtā jātā muñjapabbajabhūtā. Tadubhayaṃ [M 2.0349] kira tiṇaṃ ākulaṃ jaṭitaṃ hutvā vaḍḍhati. Vaḍḍhiyā abhāvato apāyaṃ, dukkhagatibhāvato duggatiṃ, sukhasamussayato vinipatitattā vinipātañca, catubbidhaṃ apāyaṃ “khandhānañca paṭipāṭī”tiādinā (visuddhi. 2.619; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.95 āpasādanāvaṇṇanā; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.60; a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.4.199; vibha. aṭṭha. 226 saṅkhārapadaniddesa; dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā; su. ni. aṭṭha. 2.523; udā. aṭṭha. 39; itivu. aṭṭha. 14, 58; theragā. aṭṭha. 1.67, 99; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.1.117; cūḷani. aṭṭha. 6; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 2.58) vuttaṃ saṃsārañca nātivattati. Saṃsāro eva vā sabbo idha vaḍḍhiapagamādiatthehi apāyādināmako vutto kevalaṃ dukkhakkhandhabhāvato.

To show the supporting text for the statement, 'There is no one who has transcended the fear of saṃsāra without having shattered it with the sword of wisdom,' he says: 'This has also been stated,' and so on. A tangle of threads is a `tantākulaka`; born like a tangle of threads is `tantākulakajātā`. The meaning is: exceedingly entangled by defilements, kamma, and results. The nest of a `kuli` bird is a `kulika`; born like that is `kulikuṇḍikajātā`. Having become like muñja grass and babbaja grass is `muñjapabbajabhūtā`. It is said that both these kinds of grass grow tangled and matted. Because it is devoid of progress, it is a 'state of loss' (`apāya`); because it is a state of suffering, it is a 'woeful destination' (`duggati`); and because it is a falling away from the accumulation of happiness, it is a 'downfall' (`vinipāta`). One does not transcend the fourfold plane of misery—and saṃsāra, which is described as 'and the sequence of the aggregates,' etc. Or, all of saṃsāra itself is here called by such names as `apāya` in the senses of being devoid of progress, etc., solely because it is a mass of suffering.

Paññābhūminiddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Ground of Wisdom is concluded.

Iti sattarasamaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus the commentary on the seventeenth chapter.

18. Diṭṭhivisuddhiniddesavaṇṇanā

18. The Commentary on the Exposition of the Purification of View

Nāmarūpapariggahakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on Comprehending Name-and-Form

662. Yā [M 2.0350][V 2.0328] visuddhiyo sampādetabbāti sambandho. Imesu yathāvicāritesu khandhādīsu vipassanāya bhūmibhūtesu dhammesu. Ganthassa uggaṇhanaṃ vācuggatakaraṇaṃ uggaho, parito sabbathāpi atthassa ñātumicchā paripucchā, savanupaparikkhādivasena tadatthassa manasikāravidhi, tadubhayavasena yasmā tatthapi ñāṇaṃ svāsevitaṃ hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “uggahaparipucchāvasena ñāṇaparicayaṃ katvā”ti, khandhādīsu sutamayaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppādetvāti attho. Vitthāritameva, tasmā tattha vitthāritanayānusārena sīlavisuddhi sampādetabbāti adhippāyo. Upacārasamādhipi appanāsamādhi viya vipassanāya adhiṭṭhānabhāvato cittavisuddhiyevāti āha “saupacārā”ti. Veditabbāti attano santāne nibbattanavaseneva veditabbā. Evañhi tā paccakkhato viditā nāma honti, tasmā veditabbā sampādetabbāti vuttaṃ hoti. Veditabbāti vā samāpattisukhādhigamavasena anubhavitabbāti attho. Na hi kevalena jānanamattena cittavisuddhiyaṃ patiṭṭhito nāma hoti, na ca tattha apatiṭṭhāya uparivisuddhiṃ sampādetuṃ sakkāti.

662. 'The purifications that are to be accomplished'—this is the connection. In these things that have become the ground for insight, the aggregates, etc., which have been investigated as they are. Grasping (uggaho) is the learning of the text, making it familiar by recitation; thorough inquiry (paripucchā) is the wish to know the meaning from all sides, in every way. The method of attending to that meaning is by way of listening, examining, etc. Since by means of both of these, knowledge becomes well practiced in that regard, it is therefore said: 'having become familiar with knowledge by way of grasping and thorough inquiry.' The meaning is: having generated the knowledge consisting of learning concerning the aggregates, etc. It has been explained in detail; therefore, the intention is that the purification of virtue should be accomplished there in accordance with the detailed method. Access concentration, too, like absorption concentration, is indeed purification of mind because it is a foundation for insight; thus he says 'along with access concentration.' 'They should be known' means they should be known by way of causing them to arise in one's own continuity. For in this way they are known directly. Therefore it is said, 'they should be known, they should be accomplished.' Or, 'they should be known' means they should be experienced by way of attaining the bliss of meditative attainment. For one is not established in the purification of mind merely by knowing alone, nor can one accomplish the higher purifications without being established in it.

Nāmarūpānaṃ yāthāvadassananti nāmassa, rūpassa ca vibhajja yathābhūtasabhāvadassanaṃ. Nāmaggahaṇena cettha vedanādīnaṃ catunnaṃ tebhūmakānaṃ khandhānaṃ gahaṇaṃ, na “viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti ettha viya viññāṇaṃ vinā, nāpi “nāmañca rūpañcā”ti (dī. ni. 3.304, 352; dha. sa. dukamātikā 109) ettha viya sanibbānehi lokuttarakkhandhehi saddhinti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Seeing name-and-form as it really is' means seeing the real nature of name and of form by analyzing them. Here, by the taking up of 'name' is meant the taking up of the four aggregates belonging to the three planes, beginning with feeling; not without consciousness, as in the passage 'with consciousness as condition, name-and-form comes to be,' nor should it be understood as being together with the supramundane aggregates along with Nibbāna, as in the passage 'name and form'.

663. Yāti pajjati etenāti yānaṃ, samathova yānaṃ samathayānaṃ, taṃ etassa atthīti samathayāniko. Jhāne, jhānūpacāre vā patiṭṭhāya vipassanaṃ anuyuñjantassetaṃ nāmaṃ, tena samathayānikena[V 2.0329]. “Ṭhapetvā nevasaññānāsaññāyatana”nti idaṃ bhavaggadhammānaṃ ādikammikassa duppariggahatāya vuttaṃ. Lakkhaṇarasādivasena pariggahetabbā ñāṇena paricchijja gahetabbā, pariggahavidhi pana khandhaniddese (visuddhi. 2.421 ādayo) vuttā evāti adhippāyo. Ārammaṇābhimukhanamanaṃ ārammaṇena vinā appavatti, tena namanaṭṭhena, nāmakaraṇaṭṭhena [M 2.0351] vā. Vedanādayo hi arūpadhammā sabbadāpi ca phassādināmakattā pathavīādayo viya kesakumbhādināmantarānāpajjanato attanāva katanāmatāya nāmakaraṇaṭṭhena “nāma”nti vuccanti. Atha vā adhivacanasamphasso viya adhivacanaṃ nāmaṃ antarena anupacitasambhārānaṃ gahaṇaṃ na gacchantīti nāmāyattaggahaṇatāya vedanādayo “nāma”nti vuccanti, rūpaṃ pana vināpi nāmasavanaṃ attano ruppanasabhāveneva gahaṇaṃ gacchati. Vavatthāpetabbanti asaṅkarato ṭhapetabbaṃ, aññamaññaṃ, rūpena ca amissitaṃ katvā citte ṭhapetabbanti attho.

663. That by which one goes (yāti) or proceeds (pajjati) is a vehicle (yāna); serenity itself is the vehicle, thus samathayāna (serenity vehicle). One who possesses this is a samathayānika (a serenity-vehicle practitioner). This is the designation for one who practices insight established in jhāna or its access concentration. 'Excluding the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception'—this is said because the states of the peak of existence are difficult for a beginner to comprehend. They should be comprehended by way of characteristic, function, etc.; they should be grasped by being defined by knowledge. The intention is that the method of comprehension has been stated in the Exposition of the Aggregates. It bends towards an object; it does not occur without an object. Due to this sense of bending (namana), or due to the function of naming (nāmakaraṇa), it is called 'name' (nāma). For feelings and other immaterial phenomena are called 'name' (nāma) due to the function of naming, because they always have names such as 'contact,' etc., and because—unlike things such as earth—they do not come to have other names like 'hair' or 'pot,' and because they have a name made by themselves. Alternatively, since for those who have not accumulated the proper conditions, apprehension does not proceed without a designation or name—as in the case of 'contact of designation'—feelings and so on are called 'name' because their apprehension is dependent on a name. Form, however, can be apprehended by its own nature of being afflicted even without hearing its name. 'They should be defined' means they should be established without confusion, unmixed with each other and with form, and established in the mind—this is the meaning.

Nāmarūpapariggaho ca nāma yāvadeva tassa paṭinissajjanatthanti tadanurūpameva nidassanaṃ dassento “yathā nāmā”tiādimāha. Ruppanatoti ettha ruppanaṭṭho “sītādivirodhipaccayasannipāte visadisuppattī”tiādinā (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 2.432) khandhaniddesavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttoyeva. Evaṃ visuṃ nāmapariggahaṃ, rūpapariggahañca dassetvā idāni ekajjhaṃ nāmarūpapariggahaṃ dassetuṃ “tato namanalakkhaṇa”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

The comprehension of name-and-form is for the purpose of relinquishing it. Showing an illustration suitable for this, he says: 'Just as...' and so on. Here, regarding 'is afflicted,' the meaning of affliction as 'the arising of a dissimilar state upon the conjunction of contrary conditions such as cold, etc.' has already been stated in the commentary on the Exposition of the Aggregates. Having thus shown the comprehension of name and the comprehension of form separately, now to show the comprehension of name-and-form together, it is said: 'Then, the characteristic of bending...' and so on.

664. Iti arūpamukhena vipassanābhinivesaṃ dassetvā idāni rūpamukhena taṃ dassento “suddhavipassanāyāniko panā”tiādimāha. Tattha samathayānikassa samathamukhena vipassanābhiniveso, vipassanāyānikassa pana samathaṃ anissāyāti āha “suddhavipassanāyāniko”ti, samathabhāvanāya amissitavipassanāyānavāti attho. Ayameva vā samathayānikoti yathāvutto samathayāniko eva vā. Tena samathayānikassāpi rūpamukhena vipassanābhiniveso labbhati, na arūpamukhenevāti dasseti. Tesaṃ tesaṃ dhātupariggahamukhānanti “yaṃ thaddhalakkhaṇaṃ, ayaṃ pathavīdhātū”tiādinā (visuddhi. 1.308) saṅkhepamanasikārādivasena vuttesu terasasu dhātupariggahamukhesu. Kammasamuṭṭhāno nāma keso cammabbhantaragato. Tatthevāti tasmiṃyeva kammasamuṭṭhāne kese. Kāyappasādassa viya bhāvassāpi sakalasarīrabyāpitāya “bhāvassa atthitāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Puna tatthevāti tasmiṃyeva kesasaññite rūpasamudāye. Aparānipīti pubbe vuttāni kammasamuṭṭhānāni vīsati, imāni āhārasamuṭṭhānādīni catuvīsati [V 2.0330] rūpānīti sabbānipi catucattālīsa, tañca [M 2.0352] kho tattha labbhamānasantatisīsasāmaññena veditabbaṃ. “Catucattālīsā”ti ca idaṃ saddassa aniyatattā vuttaṃ. Na hi sabbakālaṃ utucittato rūpaṃ uppajjantaṃ sasaddameva uppajjatīti. Evanti yathā kese, evaṃ lomādīsu catusamuṭṭhānikesu. Catuvīsatikoṭṭhāsesūti dvattiṃsāya koṭṭhāsesu vakkhamāne aṭṭha koṭṭhāse apanetvā catuvīsatikoṭṭhāsesu. Sedādīnaṃ ātapūpatāpādinā, cittavikārena ca uppajjanato te utucittasamuṭṭhānā vuttā.

664. Having thus shown the entry into insight by way of the formless, now, wishing to show it by way of form, he says: 'But a bare-insight practitioner...' and so on. Therein, for a serenity-vehicle practitioner, the entry into insight is by way of serenity; but for an insight-vehicle practitioner, it is without relying on serenity. Thus he says 'a bare-insight practitioner,' the meaning of which is one whose vehicle is insight unmixed with the development of serenity. Or this very one is a serenity-vehicle practitioner, that is, the aforementioned serenity-vehicle practitioner. He thus shows that for a serenity-vehicle practitioner, too, the entry into insight can be obtained by way of form, not only by way of the formless. 'Through the various doors of comprehending the elements' refers to the thirteen doors of comprehending the elements stated by way of brief attention, etc., beginning with 'Whatever has the characteristic of hardness, that is the earth element.' Kamma-originated hair is that which is within the skin. 'Therein' means in that very kamma-originated hair. Because the sex faculty, like the body sensitivity, pervades the entire body, it is said 'because of the existence of the faculty.' 'Again, therein' means in that very collection of matter designated as 'hair.' 'And others too': the twenty previously mentioned kamma-originated types of matter, and these twenty-four nutriment-originated, etc., types of matter, making forty-four in all. And this should be understood by the commonality of the principal continuity obtainable there. And 'forty-four' is said because sound is not fixed, for matter arising from temperature and mind does not always arise together with sound. 'Thus' means: as in the case of the hair of the head, so too in the case of the body hairs, etc., which have four origins. 'In the twenty-four parts' means in the twenty-four parts after removing the eight parts to be mentioned from the thirty-two parts. Since sweat, etc., arise from the sun's heat, burning, etc., and from a change of mind, they are said to be temperature-originated and mind-originated.

Dvattiṃsakoṭṭhāsagatesu rūpesu pākaṭesu jātesu tadaññānipi pākaṭāni hontīti tānipi dassetuṃ “apare”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha apare dasa ākārāti tejovāyokoṭṭhāsavasena apare dasa ākārā. Kammajeti bhūtakathanaṃ, na visesanaṃ asitādiparipācakassa tejassa akammajassa abhāvato. Tathā cittajeti ca ekantacittasamuṭṭhānattā assāsapassāsānanti keci, taṃ na, acittajasantāne pavattānaṃ utujabhāvato. Abbhantaraṭṭhā eva hi te cittajā, na bahiddhā, tasmā tattha “cittaje”ti idaṃ visesanameva, ayañca attho heṭṭhā ānāpānakathāyaṃ vuttoyeva. Sesesūti santappanādivasena ceva uddhaṅgamādivasena ca pavattesu tejovāyokoṭṭhāsesu.

When the material phenomena situated in the thirty-two parts have become manifest, other material parts also become manifest. Therefore, to show these also, it is said: 'other...' and so on. Therein, 'ten other aspects' means ten other aspects by way of the parts of the fire element and air element. 'Kamma-born' is a statement of fact, not a qualification, because of the absence of a fire element that digests what is eaten, etc., that is not kamma-born. Similarly, some say that 'mind-born' is also a statement of fact and not a qualification, because the in-breaths and out-breaths arise exclusively from mind. But that is not so, because those that occur in a non-mind-born continuity are born of temperature. For they are mind-born only when internal, not when external. Therefore, in that case, 'mind-born' is only a qualification. And this meaning has already been stated above in the discourse on mindfulness of breathing. 'In the remaining ones' means in the parts of the fire and air elements that occur by way of heating, etc., and by way of moving upwards, etc.

Cakkhudasakādīsu padhānarūpaṃ cakkhādayoti tesu labbhamānaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ avayavakiccaṃ samudāye āropetvā vuttaṃ “vatthudvāravasena pañca cakkhudasakādayo”ti. Vatthuvasena hadayavatthudasakañcāti yojetabbaṃ, ekayoganiddiṭṭhānampi ekadeso anuvattatīti. Sabbānipīti yathāvuttagaṇanāyaṃ catunnavuticatusatādhikāni sahassarūparūpāni. Koṭṭhāsāvayavānaṃ pana tadavayavakalāpānañca bhede gayhamāne ativiya tato bahutaro rūpabhedo hoti, so pana bhedo idha ādikammikassa duppariggahoti na gahetabbo.

In the eye-decad, etc., the principal form is the eye, etc. The function of the part—the state of being a physical base and a door, which is found in them—is attributed to the aggregate, hence it is said: 'Five, beginning with the eye-decad, by way of physical base and door.' It should be connected thus: 'and the heart-base decad by way of physical base.' For even of what is indicated by a single connection, a part is carried over. 'All' means that according to the aforementioned enumeration, there are 1,494 material phenomena. However, when the distinction between the parts of the bodily portions and their constituent kalāpas is apprehended, the divisions of material phenomena become far more numerous. But that distinction, being difficult for a beginner to apprehend here, should not be grasped.

Kāmaṃ vatthuvasenāpi arūpadhammā pākaṭā honti, dvāravasena pana pariggaho anākuloti katvā vuttaṃ “dvāravasena arūpadhammā pākaṭā hontī”ti[M 2.0353]. Sabbasaṅgāhikavasena “ekāsīti lokiyacittānī”ti vuttaṃ, lābhino eva pana mahaggatacittāni supākaṭāni honti. Avisesenāti sādhāraṇato. Phassādayo hi satta cetasikā cakkhuviññāṇādīhipi uppajjanato sabbacittuppādasādhāraṇā. Sabbepi teti ekāsīti lokiyacittāni, taṃsampayuttaphassādayoti [V 2.0331] sabbepi te arūpadhamme. Ārammaṇādivibhāgena pana cittuppādabhede gayhamāne tato bahutaro eva hoti, so pana idha nādhippeto.

Granted, immaterial states also become manifest by way of a physical base, but because their apprehension by way of a door is unconfused, it is said: 'Immaterial states become manifest by way of a door.' In an all-inclusive sense, it is said, 'eighty-one mundane consciousnesses'; but only for one who has attained jhāna are the sublime consciousnesses very manifest. 'Without distinction' means generally. For the seven mental factors beginning with contact, arising even with eye-consciousness and so on, are common to the arising of all consciousness. 'All those' means the eighty-one mundane consciousnesses and the associated factors of contact, etc.—all these are the immaterial states. But when the divisions in the arising of consciousness are apprehended by way of the distinction of object, etc., they become far more numerous; however, that is not intended here.

665. Assa cakkhupasādassa nissayabhūtā pana catasso dhātuyoti sambandho. Sahajātarūpāni tassa cakkhupasādassa icceva sambandho. Tatthevāti tasmiṃyeva sasambhāracakkhupadese. Anupādinnarūpānīti pubbe vuttarūpānaṃ upādinnarūpattā vuttaṃ, akammajarūpānīti attho. Sesānīti paṭhamaṃ cakkhuno vuttattā tato sesāni, tena pana saddhiṃ catupaññāsa rūpāni honti. Cakkhudasakādīsu ekassapi aggahetabbato “avasesāni tecattālīsa rūpānī”ti vuttaṃ. Saddassa aniyatattā taṃ aggahetvā “tecattālīsa rūpānī”ti vatvā puna utucittasamuṭṭhāne dve sadde gahetvā “pañcacattālīsā”ti kecivādo dassito.

665. The connection is: 'the four great elements are the support for this eye-sensitivity.' The connection is just so: 'the co-nascent material phenomena of that eye-sensitivity.' 'In that very place' means in that very region of the eye with its components. The term 'non-appropriated material phenomena' is used because the previously mentioned material phenomena are appropriated; the meaning is 'non-kamma-generated material phenomena.' 'The rest' means those remaining after the eye, since the eye was mentioned first; together with it, there are fifty-four material phenomena. Because not even one of the eye-decad, etc., is to be grasped, it is said: 'the remaining forty-three material phenomena.' Because sound is non-fixed, having not grasped it, it is said 'forty-three material phenomena'; then, having grasped the two sounds that are temperature-originated and mind-originated, the view of some that there are 'forty-five' is shown.

Avasesarūpānīti “dasa dhātuyo”ti vutte dvādasa rūpadhamme ṭhapetvā avasesāni cha nipphannarūpāni. Rūparūpāneva hi idha pariggayhanti, na rūpaparicchedavikāralakkhaṇāni. Cakkhusannissayarūpārammaṇabhāvasāmaññena, cittabhāvasāmaññena ca kusalākusalavipākatāya duvidhampi cakkhuviññāṇaṃ cittantveva vuttaṃ. Evanti iminā “cakkhuṃ nissāyā”tiādinā vuttaṃ, avuttañca “sotaṃ nissāyā”tiādikaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Manoviññāṇadhātūti etthapi “ekā”ti padaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ “ekā manoviññāṇadhātū”ti. Aḍḍhena ekādasa aḍḍhekādasa, aḍḍhaṃ vā ekādasamaṃ etāsanti aḍḍhekādasa. Aḍḍhaṭṭhamāti etthāpi eseva nayo.

By 'remaining material phenomena' is meant the six remaining produced material phenomena, after setting aside the twelve material phenomena when 'ten elements' is said. For here only concrete material phenomena are apprehended, not the phenomena of delimitation, alteration, and characteristics. By the commonality of having the eye-sensitivity as support and form as object, and by the commonality of being a state of consciousness, the twofold eye-consciousness—wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant—is spoken of simply as 'consciousness.' By this 'Thus,' what is stated, beginning with 'dependent on the eye,' and what is unstated, such as that beginning with 'dependent on the ear,' is included. In the phrase 'mind-consciousness element' too, the word 'one' should be supplied and connected, as 'one mind-consciousness element.' Eleven with a half are 'ten and a half' (aḍḍhekādasa); or, for these, the half is the eleventh, hence 'ten and a half.' In 'seven and a half' (aḍḍhaṭṭhama) too, this is the same method.

666. Cakkhudhātuyaṃ vuttanayenevāti “yaṃ loko setakaṇhamaṇḍalavicitta”ntiādinā (visuddhi. 2.665) vuttanayena.

666. 'In the same way as was said for the eye-element' means in the way stated beginning with the words: 'that which in the world is variegated with white and black circles...'

667. Idha bhikkhu imasmiṃ sarīreti ajjhattaṃ vipassanābhinivesadassanavasena vuttaṃ. Teneva hi ekasseva bhāvassa gahitattā “sattarasa [M 2.0354] rūpāni sammasanupagānī”ti āha. Sammasituṃ sakkuṇeyyāni sammasanaṃ upagacchantīti sammasanupagāni, sammasanīyānīti attho. Ākāra-ggahaṇena viññattidvayaṃ vuttaṃ, vikāra-ggahaṇena lahutādittayaṃ, itarena ākāsadhātūti vadanti. Ākāra-ggahaṇena pana viññattidvayena saddhiṃ lakkhaṇarūpamāha. Tampi hi rūpānaṃ uppajjanādiākāramattanti. Antaraparicchedoti taṃtaṃkalāpānaṃ asaṅkarakāraṇatāya antarabhūto paricchedo[V 2.0332]. Yadi na sammasanupagāni, ākārādimattāni ca, kathaṃ rūpānīti āha “apica kho”tiādi.

667. 'Here a bhikkhu, in this body' is said by way of showing the initial internal application of insight. For it is because only one gender phenomenon has been grasped that he said: 'Seventeen material phenomena are accessible to comprehension.' 'Accessible to comprehension' (sammasanupagāni) means they are phenomena that can be comprehended, or they attain comprehension; the meaning is that they are fit for comprehension. By the term 'mode' (ākāra), the pair of intimations is meant; by the term 'alteration' (vikāra), the triad beginning with lightness is meant; by the other term, they say, is meant the space element. But by the term 'mode', he states the characteristic phenomena along with the two intimations. For that too is the intervening delimitation, being the cause for the non-confusion of the various kalāpas. If they are not accessible to comprehension and are mere modes, etc., how can they be material phenomena? To this he says, 'But furthermore...'

668. Evaṃ dvācattālīsāya koṭṭhāsānaṃ vasena vitthārato rūpapariggahaṃ tadanusārena vitthārato eva nāmapariggahaṃ vibhāvetvā tato saṃkhittasaṃkhittatarasaṃkhittatamavasena, aṭṭhārasadhātuvasena, dvādasāyatanavasena, pañcakkhandhavasena ca rūpārūpapariggahaṃ dassetvā atisaṃkhittanayenāpi dassetuṃ “yaṃ kiñci rūpa”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

668. Thus, having first clarified in detail the apprehension of material form by way of the forty-two bodily parts, and in accordance with that the apprehension of name in detail, and then having shown the apprehension of name-and-form in a condensed, more condensed, and most condensed manner—that is, by way of the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates—in order to show it also by the most condensed method, the passage beginning 'Whatever material form...' was stated.

Yathā ca dhātuādivasena, evaṃ indriyasaccapaṭiccasamuppādavasenapi rūpārūpapariggaho veditabbo. Kathaṃ? Indriyavasena tāva cakkhādīni pañca, itthipurisindriyāni cāti satta indriyāni rūpaṃ, manindriyaṃ, pañca vedanindriyāni, saddhādīni pañca cāti ekādasa nāmaṃ, jīvitindriyaṃ nāmañca rūpañca, pacchimāni tīṇi idha anadhippetāni lokuttarattā. Dukkhasaccaṃ nāmañca rūpañca, samudayasaccaṃ nāmaṃ, itarāni idha nādhippetāni lokuttarattā. Paccayākāre ādito tīṇi aṅgāni nāmaṃ, catutthapañcamāni nāmañca rūpañca, chaṭṭhasattamaaṭṭhamanavamāni nāmaṃ, dasamaṃ nāmañceva nāmarūpañca, pacchimāni dve paccekaṃ nāmañca rūpañcāti evaṃ tattha tattha vuttanayānusārena indriyasaccapaccayākāravasenapi nāmarūpapariggaho kātabbo. Evaṃ pana nāmarūpapariggahassa vibhāgena kathane payojanaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

And just as by way of the elements, etc., so too the apprehension of name-and-form should be understood by way of the faculties, the truths, and dependent origination. How? First, by way of the faculties: the five beginning with the eye, and the femininity and masculinity faculties—these seven faculties are material form. The mind faculty, the five feeling faculties, and the five beginning with faith—these eleven are name. The life faculty is both name and material form. The last three faculties are not intended here as they are supramundane. The truth of suffering is both name and material form; the truth of the origin is name; the other truths are not intended here as they are supramundane. In the causal chain, the first three factors are name; the fourth and fifth are name-and-form; the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth are name; the tenth is both name and name-and-form; the last two are each name-and-form. Thus, in accordance with the method stated in each of those cases, the apprehension of name-and-form should also be undertaken by way of the faculties, the truths, and the causal chain. The purpose of explaining the apprehension of name-and-form by way of classification in this way has already been stated previously.

669. Kāmaṃ vedanādīsu arūpadhammesu na uttaruttarā viya purimapurimā sukhumā, tathāpi saṅghaṭṭanena vikāraāpajjanake rūpadhamme upādāya sabbepi te sukhumā evāti āha “sukhumattā arūpaṃ na upaṭṭhātī”ti. Sammasitabbanti sammadeva lakkhaṇādito vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. Manasikātabbanti tathā citte ṭhapetabbaṃ. Pariggahetabbanti paricchedakārikāya paññāya paricchijja gahetabbaṃ. Vavatthapetabbanti aññamaññaṃ asaṅkarato vinicchitabbaṃ. Assāti yogino[M 2.0355]. Suvikkhālitanti suvisodhitaṃ. Ādikammikassa hi kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariggaṇhantassa yāva dhammā suparibyattaṃ na upatiṭṭhanti, tāva te tappaṭicchādakasammohabalena abhibhūtā avisuddhā nāma honti, asaṅkarato upaṭṭhānābhāvato aññamaññañca jaṭitā. Yadā pana sammasanādividhinā taṃ vibhūtaṃ hoti, tadā te suvikkhālitā, nijjaṭā ca nāma honti. Tenāha “yathā yathā hī”tiādi. Ādikammikassa arūpadhammā yebhuyyena rūpadhamme ārabbha pavattanākārena [V 2.0333] gahaṇaṃ gacchantīti katvā vuttaṃ “tadārammaṇā arūpadhammā”ti. Teneva hi heṭṭhā “tassevaṃ pariggahitarūpassa dvāravasena arūpadhammā pākaṭā hontī”ti vuttaṃ, na vatthuvasenāti.

669. Granted, among the immaterial states such as feeling, etc., the earlier ones are not as subtle as the later ones; nevertheless, in comparison with material phenomena, which are liable to alteration through collision, all of them are indeed subtle. Hence it is said: 'Because of its subtlety, the immaterial does not become manifest.' 'To be comprehended' means to be investigated properly as to characteristics, etc. 'To be attended to' means to be placed in the mind accordingly. 'To be apprehended' means to be apprehended by delimiting them with the wisdom that effects delimitation. 'To be defined' means to be determined without confusing them with one another. 'Of him' means of the meditator. 'Thoroughly clarified' means well cleansed. For a beginner apprehending a meditation subject, so long as the states do not appear very clearly, they are called 'impure,' being overwhelmed by the power of the delusion that conceals them, and are entangled with one another due to their failure to appear unconfusedly. But when this becomes manifest by the method of comprehension, etc., then they are called 'thoroughly clarified' and 'disentangled.' Hence he says: 'For in whatever way...' For a beginner, the immaterial states are for the most part apprehended in the mode of occurring with material phenomena as their object; therefore it is said: 'The immaterial states have that as their object.' For this very reason it was stated previously: 'For one who has thus apprehended material form, the immaterial states become manifest by way of the door,' not 'by way of the physical base.'

Idāni rūpapariggaho arūpapariggahassa upāyo, upatthambho cāti yathāvuttamatthaṃ upamāhi pakāsetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Mukhanimittanti mukhassa paṭibimbaṃ. Tatridaṃ upamāsaṃsandanaṃ – cakkhumā puriso viya yogāvacaro, tassa cakkhu viya yogino kammaṭṭhānapariggāhakañāṇaṃ, ādāsaṃ viya rūpapariggaho, mukhanimittaṃ viya arūpapariggaho, ādāsassa aparisuddhakālo viya rūpapariggahassa avikkhālitakālo, tadā mukhanimittassa apaññāyanaṃ viya rūpapariggahassa avisuddhatāya arūpadhammānaṃ anupaṭṭhānaṃ, ādāsassa punappunaṃ parimajjanaṃ viya rūpapariggahassa punappunaṃ visodhanaṃ, suparimajjite ādāse subyattaṃ mukhanimittassa paññāyanaṃ viya suvikkhālite nijjaṭe rūpapariggahe arūpadhammānaṃ suṭṭhu upaṭṭhānanti. Iminā nayena telatthikopamādīsupi yathārahaṃ upamāsaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tilapiṭṭhanti tilacuṇṇaṃ. Katakaṭṭhinti katakabījaṃ. Kalalakaddamanti tanukaddamaṃ.

Now, in order to clarify with similes the meaning already stated—that the grasping of form is the means and support for the grasping of the immaterial—the passage beginning 'Just as...' was stated. 'The sign of the face' (mukhanimitta) means the reflection of the face. Therein, this is the application of the simile: the meditator is like a person with sight; the yogi's knowledge that grasps the meditation subject is like that person's eye; the grasping of form is like a mirror; the grasping of the immaterial is like the image of the face; the time when the grasping of form is uncleaned is like the time when the mirror is unclean; the non-manifestation of the immaterial states due to the impurity of the grasping of form is like the non-appearance of the image of the face at that time; the repeated cleansing of the grasping of form is like the repeated wiping of the mirror; and the clear manifestation of the immaterial states when the grasping of form is well-cleaned and disentangled is like the clear appearance of the image of the face in a well-wiped mirror. In this way, the application of the simile should be understood as is fitting in the similes of the oil-seeker and others as well. 'Sesame paste' (tilapiṭṭha) means sesame powder. 'Clearing-nut' (katakaṭṭha) means the kataka seed. 'Liquid mud' (kalalakaddama) means thin mud.

Tappaccanīkakilesāti tassa arūpadhammapariggāhakañāṇassa vibandhabhāvena paṭipakkhabhūtā sammohādikilesā. Ucchuādiupamāsu idaṃ mukhamattassa dassanaṃ – yathā ucchurasaṃ gahetukāmo ucchūni ucchuyante pakkhipitvā ekavāraṃ dvivāraṃ yantakkamanamattena ucchurase anikkhamante na ucchūni chaḍḍetvā gacchati, yathā vā core gahetvā tehi katakammaṃ jānitukāmo dvattippahāramattena tesu tamatthaṃ akathentesu na te muñcati, yathā vā pana godammako goṇaṃ dametukāmo dhure taṃ yojetvā ekavāraṃ dvivāraṃ tasmiṃ pathena agacchante na vissajjeti, yathā [M 2.0356] ca dadhiṃ manthetvā navanītaṃ gahetukāmo dadhikalasiyaṃ manthaṃ pakkhipitvā sakiṃ, dvikkhattuṃ vā manthassa bhamanamattena navanīte anuppajjante na dadhiṃ chaḍḍeti, yathā vā pana macche pacitvā khāditukāmo ekavāraṃ dvivāraṃ aggidānamattena macchesu apaccantesu na te chaḍḍeti. “Atha kho naṃ punappunaṃ parimajjatī”ti ettha vuttanayānusārena “atha kho naṃ ucchuyante punappunaṃ uppīḷetī”tiādinā sabbattha upamattho yojetabbo.

The opposing defilements: these are the defilements such as strong delusion that are hostile, being an obstruction to that knowledge which comprehends immaterial phenomena. In the similes of sugarcane and so on, this is a mere indication of the method: Just as one who wishes to extract sugarcane juice, after putting the canes in the sugarcane press, does not discard the canes and go away if the juice does not come out by the mere working of the press once or twice; or as one who, having caught thieves and wishing to know the deed done by them, does not release them if they do not speak about that matter after a mere two or three blows; or as a bull-tamer, wishing to tame a bull, yokes it to the yoke and does not release it if it does not go along the path once or twice; and as one who, wishing to get butter by churning curd, having put the churning stick in the pot of curds, does not discard the curd if butter is not produced by the mere turning of the churning stick once or twice; or as one who, wishing to cook and eat fish, does not discard them if the fish are not cooked by the mere application of fire once or twice. Here, in the passage, “Then indeed he rubs it again and again,” in accordance with the method stated therein, the meaning of the similes should be connected everywhere thus: “Then indeed he crushes them again and again in the sugarcane press,” and so on.

Arūpadhammānaṃ upaṭṭhānākārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentarial Explanation on the Mode of Manifestation of Immaterial Phenomena

670. Ākirīyanti [V 2.0334] abhimukhā honti etehīti ākārā, arūpadhammānaṃ upaṭṭhānassa mukhabhūtā phusanānubhavanavijānanappakārāti āha “arūpadhammā tīhi ākārehi upaṭṭhahantī”tiādi. Ārammaṇe pavattamānesu cittacetasikesu asatipi pubbāpariye phusanalakkhaṇo phasso, tattha sabbapaṭhamaṃ abhinipatanto viya hotīti vuttaṃ “paṭhamābhinipāto phasso”ti. Tenassa phusanākārena supākaṭabhāvena upaṭṭhānaṃ dasseti. Phasse pana upaṭṭhite yasmiṃ ārammaṇe so phasso, tassa anubhavanalakkhaṇā vedanā, sañjānanalakkhaṇā saññā, āyūhanalakkhaṇā cetanā, paṭivijānanalakkhaṇaṃ viññāṇanti imepi pākaṭā hontīti āha “taṃsampayuttā vedanā”tiādi. Evaṃ salakkhaṇasaṅkhepato catudhātuvavatthānavasena phassamukhena arūpapariggahaṃ dassetvā idāni vitthārato catudhātuvavatthānavasena taṃ dassetuṃ “tathā kese”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kese pathavīdhātūti kesasaṅkhāte pathavīkoṭṭhāse pathavīdhātu. Lakkhaṇavibhattito hi dhātuvavatthānadassanametaṃ.

670. Modes (ākārā) are so called because by means of them things are presented and face one; they are the principal types—touching, experiencing, and cognizing—which are the grounds for the manifestation of immaterial phenomena. Hence it is said: “Immaterial phenomena are established in three modes,” and so on. Although among the mind and mental factors occurring in relation to an object there is no before and after, contact, which has the characteristic of touching, is as if it were the very first to fall upon it; thus it is said, “contact is the first impact.” By this is shown its manifestation as being very clear through the mode of touching. When contact has arisen, then feeling, which has the characteristic of experiencing that object where contact occurs; perception, which has the characteristic of perceiving; volition, which has the characteristic of accumulating; and consciousness, which has the characteristic of cognizing—these too become manifest. Thus it is said: “the feeling associated with it,” and so on. Having thus shown the comprehension of the immaterial with contact as primary, by way of the determination of the four elements in brief according to their specific characteristics, now, to show it in detail by way of the determination of the four elements, it is said: “So too in the hair,” and so on. Herein, “the earth element in the hair” means the earth element in the bodily part designated as hair. For this is the showing of the determination of the elements by way of their classified characteristics.

Punapi dvinnaṃ dhātuvavatthānānaṃ vasena vedanāmukhena arūpapariggahaṃ dassetuṃ “ekassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tassa rasānubhavanakavedanāti thaddhabhāvasaṅkhātassa phoṭṭhabbasabhāvassa anubhavanavasena pavattavedanā.

Again, to show the comprehension of the immaterial with feeling as primary, by way of the determination of two elements, it is said, “of one,” and so on. Herein, “that feeling which experiences its essence” is the feeling that occurs by way of experiencing the nature of the tangible, which is designated as the state of hardness.

Aparassāti etthāpi vuttanayeneva sambandho veditabbo. Tattha ārammaṇapaṭivijānananti thaddhatāsaṅkhātaphoṭṭhabbārammaṇapaṭivijānanaṃ. Kāyadvārābhinihataṃ, kevalaṃ vā manodvārikajavanaviññāṇamāha. Tañhi “pathavīdhātu [M 2.0357] kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā”ti paṭivijānāti, itaraṃ pana kakkhaḷalakkhaṇapaṭivijānanamattamevāti.

‘Of another’: here too the connection should be understood in the way already stated. Therein, ‘cognizing the object’ is the cognizing of the tangible object designated as hardness. He speaks of the consciousness arisen from impact at the body-door, or purely of the mind-door impulsion-consciousness. For the latter cognizes, “The earth element has the characteristic of hardness,” whereas the former is the mere cognizing of the characteristic of hardness.

Eteneva upāyenāti yvāyaṃ salakkhaṇasaṅkhepato, salakkhaṇavibhattito ca dhātuvavatthānavasena rūpapariggahaṃ dassetvā tattha ṭhitassa phassādimukhena arūpapariggaṇhanupāyo dassito, eteneva upāyena. Kammasamuṭṭhānakeseti catusamuṭṭhānakesato niddhārite kammasamuṭṭhānakese. Kakkhaḷalakkhaṇātiādinā nayenāti ādi-saddena na kevalaṃ “paggharaṇalakkhaṇā āpodhātū”tiādinā lakkhaṇavisesena saddhiṃ dhātvantarāniyeva, atha kho ekasamuṭṭhānādibhedāni koṭṭhāsantarānipīti [V 2.0335] daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenevāha “dvācattālīsāya dhātukoṭṭhāsesū”ti. Sabbaṃ nayabhedaṃ anugantvāti yvāyaṃ dvācattālīsāya dhātukoṭṭhāsesu pathavīdhātuādīnaṃ lakkhaṇādito vavatthāpanavasena nānāvidho rūpapariggahanayo vutto, taṃ sabbaṃ nayabhedaṃ nayavisesaṃ anugantvā, cakkhudhātuādīsu rūpapariggahamukhesu arūpapariggahadassanavasena yojanā kātabbāti adhippāyo. Tatridaṃ yojanāmukhamattadassanaṃ – ekassa tāva “cakkhudhātu rūpābhighātārahabhūtappasādalakkhaṇā, daṭṭhukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtappasādalakkhaṇā vā”tiādinā (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 600) nayena dhātuyo pariggaṇhantassa “paṭhamābhinipāto phasso, taṃsampayuttā vedanā”ti sabbaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Tathā “yathāvuttalakkhaṇāya cakkhudhātuyā rasānubhavanakavedanā vedanākkhandho”tiādi yojetabbaṃ. Tathā “yathāvuttalakkhaṇā cakkhudhātū”ti, “ārammaṇapaṭivijānanaṃ viññāṇaṃ viññāṇakkhandho”tiādinā sabbaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Āyatanādivasena rūpapariggahamukhesupi eseva nayo.

By this very method: that is, the method of comprehending the formless by means of contact and so on, which was shown for one established in the comprehension of form—which itself was shown by way of defining the elements in summary according to their specific characteristics and by way of analysis of their specific characteristics—by this very method. In the hair originated from kamma: in the hair originated from kamma when this has been determined out of the hair from the four origins. By the method beginning with “the characteristic of hardness,” etc.: by the word “etc.” it should be understood not only the other elements with their specific characteristics, such as “the water element has the characteristic of trickling,” and so on, but also the other parts with their distinctions of single origination and so on. Therefore he says: “in the forty-two elemental parts.” Having followed all the distinctions of method: the meaning is that having followed every distinction of method, that is, the various methods of comprehending form that have been stated by way of defining the characteristics, etc., of the earth element and so on in the forty-two elemental parts, the application should be made by showing the comprehension of the formless in the approaches to the comprehension of form, such as the eye element, etc. This is the intention. Here is a mere indication of the method of application: For one who comprehends the elements by the method beginning, “The eye element has the characteristic of a sensitivity suitable for the impact of forms, or it has the characteristic of a sensitivity originated from kamma which is the cause of the desire to see,” etc., everything should be connected thus: “The first impact is contact; the feeling associated with it,” etc. Similarly, it should be connected thus: “The feeling that experiences the flavor of the eye element with its aforementioned characteristic is the feeling aggregate,” etc. Similarly, everything should be connected thus: “The eye element with its aforementioned characteristic…,” and “The consciousness that cognizes the object is the consciousness aggregate,” etc. This same method applies also in the approaches to the comprehension of form by way of the bases, etc.

671. Yathā nāma heṭṭhimajhānaṃ subhāvitaṃ vasībhāvaṃ pāpitameva uparijhānassa pādakaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, na paṭiladdhamattaṃ, evaṃ rūpapariggaho suvisuddho nijjaṭo niggumbo eva arūpapariggahassa pādakaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, na avisuddho, tasmā rūpārūpassa ekadesepi anupaṭṭhite so avisuddho eva nāma hoti, pageva bahūsu anupaṭṭhitesūti dassento āha “sace hī”tiādi. Pabbateyyā gāvī viya bālā abyattā akhettaññū.

671. Just as only a lower jhāna that has been well-developed and brought to a state of mastery serves as the basis and proximate cause for a higher jhāna, and not one that has been merely attained; in the same way, only a comprehension of form that is thoroughly purified, without tangles, and without thickets, serves as the basis and proximate cause for the comprehension of the formless, and not an impure one. Therefore, wishing to show that if even one part of derived form has not appeared, that comprehension of form is indeed called impure—how much more so when many have not appeared—he said the words beginning with, “If, indeed…,” and so on. Like a mountain cow: foolish, unskilled, not knowing the pasture.

Khaggenāti [M 2.0358] khaggaggena. Samugganti mañjūsāsadisaṃ mahāsamuggaṃ. Apariggahitakammaṭṭhānassa avibhattaṃ viya upaṭṭhahantampi nāmarūpaṃ vibhattasabhāvameva, tassa ca vibhāgo kammaṭṭhānapariggahesu pākaṭo hotīti ca dassanatthaṃ samuggavivaraṇaṃ, yamakatālakandaphālanañca nidassanabhāvena vuttaṃ. Yamakatālakandañhi bhinnasantānampi abhinnaṃ viya upaṭṭhāti, evaṃ rūpārūpadhammāti. Sabbepi tebhūmake dhamme nāmañca rūpañcāti dvedhā vavatthapetīti ettha kiñcāpi sabba-saddo anavasesapariyādāyako, nāmarūpabhāvo pana aññamaññavidhuroti na tadubhayaṃ samudāyavasena parisamāpayetabbaṃ, tasmā “yadettha namanalakkhaṇaṃ, taṃ nāmaṃ. Yaṃ ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ, taṃ rūpa”nti evaṃ dvedhā vavatthapetīti attho. Evaṃ vavatthapentoyeva ca tadubhayavinimuttassa tebhūmakadhammesu kassaci dhammassa abhāvato “sabbepi tebhūmakadhamme nāmañca rūpañcāti dvedhā vavatthapetī”ti vuccati. “Nāmañca rūpañcā”ti eteneva [V 2.0336] tassa duvidhabhāve siddhe “dvedhā vavatthapetī”ti idaṃ nāmarūpavinimuttassa aññassa abhāvadassanatthaṃ. Tenevāha “nāmarūpamattato uddha”ntiādi. “Sabbepi tebhūmake dhamme”ti pana sabbaggahaṇañcettha sammasamanupagassa dhammassa anavasesetabbatāya vuttaṃ. Tañhi anavasesato pariññeyyaṃ ekaṃsato virajjitabbaṃ, tato ca cittaṃ virājayaṃ pamocetabbaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā –

With a sword: with the tip of a sword. A casket: a large casket similar to a chest. The opening of the casket and the splitting of the twin palm-shoot are mentioned as illustrations to show that although name-and-form presents itself as if undivided to one who has not comprehended the meditation subject, its nature is in fact divided, and its division becomes manifest in the comprehension of the meditation subjects. For a twin palm-shoot, though its continuity is split, appears as if unsplit; so too with form and formless phenomena. In the phrase ‘He defines all phenomena of the three planes in two ways as name and form,’ here, although the word “all” is inclusive without remainder, since the state of name and the state of form are mutually distinct, the two should not be summed up by way of a collection. Therefore, the meaning is that he defines them in two ways thus: “Whatever herein has the characteristic of bending is name; whatever has the characteristic of being afflicted is form.” And it is just because he defines them in this way, and because among the phenomena of the three planes there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is devoid of both, that it is said: “He defines all phenomena of the three planes in two ways as name and form.” Since its twofold nature is established just by the words “name and form,” the phrase “defines in two ways” is for the purpose of showing the absence of anything else devoid of name and form. Therefore he said: “Beyond mere name-and-form,” and so on. Further, the inclusion of “all” in “all phenomena of the three planes” is stated because the phenomenon that is subject to comprehension must be taken without remainder. For it must be fully understood without remainder, one must become completely dispassionate towards it, and by causing dispassion towards it, one must liberate the mind from it. Therefore the Blessed One said:

“Sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, anabhijānaṃ aparijānaṃ tattha cittaṃ avirājayaṃ appajahaṃ abhabbo dukkhakkhayāya. Sabbañca kho, bhikkhave, abhijānaṃ parijānaṃ tattha cittaṃ virājayaṃ pajahaṃ bhabbo dukkhakkhayāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.26-27).

“Bhikkhus, without directly knowing and fully understanding the All, without causing dispassion towards it and abandoning it, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering. But, bhikkhus, by directly knowing and fully understanding the All, by causing dispassion towards it and abandoning it, one is capable of the destruction of suffering.”

Yadi tebhūmakaṃ dhammajātaṃ anavasesato gahitaṃ “nāmarūpa”nti, yaṃ ito bāhirakehi padatthabhāvena parikappitaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – pakatiādi drabyādi jīvādi kāyādi. Tattha kathaṃ paṭipajjitabbanti? Ummattakavipallāsasadise asammāsambuddhapavedite kā tattha aññā paṭipatti aññatra ajjhupekkhanato. Atha vā tepi nāmarūpantogadhabhāvābhāvavasena nicchitā evāti veditabbā. Kathaṃ? Pakati, mahā, ahaṃkāro, tammattāni, indriyāni, bhūtāni, purisoti ete pakatiādayo. Tattha samabhāvena pavattamānānaṃ sattarajatamasaṅkhātānaṃ sukhadukkhamohānaṃ samudāyo pakati, padhānanti ca vuccati. Sattamattasampavedanīyo mahā, buddhīti keci. Sattarajādīsu [M 2.0359] abhimāno ahaṃkāro, asmimattāti keci. Saddaphassarūparasagandhā tammattāni aññamaññavisiṭṭhānaṃ pathavīādīnaṃ ekuttaratādassanato ekuttarāni tammattānīti vijjhavāsiekalakkhaṇehi tammattehi ekalakkhaṇā visesā sajiyanti, sukhumabhāvena pana nesaṃ sampavesanato ekuttaratāti keci. Sotādīni pañca savanādivuttikāni buddhindriyāni, vacanādānavicaraṇussaggānandakiccāni vācādīni pañca kammindriyāni. Mano antokaraṇaṃ, itaraṃ bāhirakaraṇaṃ. Gandhādīhi āraddhāni pathavīudakaaggivāyuākāsāni bhūtāni, cetanāsabhāvo purisoti evaṃ pakatiādīni sarūpato veditabbāni.

If the collection of phenomena in the three planes is grasped without remainder as 'name-and-form', what of that which is conceived by those outside this teaching as a fundamental reality, namely: nature (pakati), substance (dabba), soul (jīva), body (kāya), and so on? If it is asked, 'How should one act in regard to them?' In regard to what is proclaimed by those who are not Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, which resembles the deranged speech of a madman, what other practice is there apart from disregarding it? Or else, it should be understood that even these are determined by way of their inclusion or non-inclusion in name-and-form. How so? Nature (pakati), the great (mahā), ego (ahaṃkāra), the subtle elements (tanmātra), the faculties (indriya), the gross elements (bhūta), and the person (purisa)—these are the principles beginning with 'nature'. Among them, the aggregate of pleasure, pain, and delusion—called sattva, rajas, and tamas—which proceed in equilibrium is 'nature' (pakati); it is also called 'the primary' (padhāna). The principle which is known as mere existence is 'the great' (mahā); some call it 'intellect' (buddhi). Conceit regarding sattva, rajas, and so on, is 'ego' (ahaṃkāra); some call it 'the mere sense of “I am.”' Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the 'subtle elements' (tanmātra). Because a state of one being pre-eminent is seen among the gross elements—earth and so on—which are distinct from one another, the subtle elements are also pre-eminent one by one. From the subtle elements, which have a single undifferentiated characteristic, the distinct gross elements are produced. However, some say that this pre-eminence is due to their subtle pervasion. The five beginning with the ear, which have the function of hearing and so on, are the faculties of cognition. The five beginning with speech, which have the functions of speaking, taking, moving about, excreting, and enjoying, are the faculties of action. The mind is the internal instrument; the others are the external instruments. The gross elements—earth, water, fire, air, and space—are produced from the subtle elements beginning with smell. The 'person' (purisa) has the nature of consciousness. Thus, the principles beginning with 'nature' should be understood according to their own nature.

Tattha hi pakati tāva sukhadukkhamohamattatāya nāmaṃ, samavisamabhāvāpattito aniccā, dukkhā, saṅkhatā ca āpannā. Mahāpi “tasmā aliṅgato liṅgavisesāmatto mahā uppajjatī”ti vacanato, buddhibhāvānujānanato ca nāmaṃ, aniccaṃ, saṅkhatameva ca āpannaṃ. “Tasmā [V 2.0337] mahato cha visesā sajiyantī”ti sakkate vacanato “asmī”ti gahaṇanimittabhāvānujānanena ahaṃkāro abhimānoti katvā nāmaṃ, tato eva aniccasaṅkhatabhāvāpatti cassa siddhā. Itaraṃ tammattapañcakaṃ gandharasarūpaphassasaddabhāvānujānanato rūpaṃ, arūpanti pana kāpilānaṃ micchābhinivesamattaṃ.
