Te hi soḷasa visesā pañca bhūtāni, ekādasindriyāni bhūtehi bhūtavisesānīti gandhāditammattehi tannissayāni pathavīāpotejovāyoākāsasaṅkhātāni bhūtāni icchitāni. “Tabbisesā ca nānājātikā ahaṃkārato ca indriyānī”ti vacanato sotakāyacakkhujivhāghānavācāpāṇipādapāyūpatthāni ceva mano cāti ekādasindriyāni.

Here, 'nature' (pakati), in the first place, is name because it is merely the state of pleasure, pain, and delusion. Because it attains states of equilibrium and disequilibrium, it has become impermanent, suffering, and conditioned. The 'great' (mahā) too, according to the statement, 'Therefore, from the unmanifested, the mere specific manifestation arises as the great,' and because it is acknowledged as having the nature of intellect, is name, and has come to be impermanent and conditioned. According to the statement in the Sanskrit text, 'Therefore, from the great, six specific modifications are produced,' and because it is acknowledged as the cause for grasping 'I am,' egoism, being considered conceit, is name; precisely from that, its attainment of the state of being impermanent and conditioned is also established. The other pentad of subtle elements—acknowledged as having the nature of smell, taste, form, touch, and sound—is form. But the view of the followers of Kapila that they are formless is merely a wrong adherence. For them, the sixteen modifications are the five subtle elements and the eleven faculties. The gross elements are modifications of the subtle elements; thus, from the subtle elements of smell and so on, the gross elements dependent on them—called earth, water, fire, air, and space—are posited. And according to the statement, 'Their modifications are of various kinds, and from egoism the faculties arise,' the eleven faculties are posited: the ear, body, eye, tongue, nose, speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals, and the mind.

Tattha mano nāmaṃ, itarāni sabbāni rūpaṃ. Vācāti cettha atthāvajotakassa akkharasamudāyassa gahaṇaṃ. Imesaṃ pana dhammino dhammassa anaññatthassa icchitattā siddhāva aniccatā pariṇāmapakkhe, abhibyattipakkhepi yadi tabbisayañāṇuppādena abhibyañjanaṃ siddhāva aniccatā, atha tato pubbepi ñāṇaṃ attheva. Akkhabyattivādo pana siyāti idamettha disāmattaṃ. Drabyaguṇakammasāmaññavisesasamavāyā drabyādikā. Tattha pathavī āpo [M 2.0360] tejo vāyu ākāso kālo disā attā manoti nava drabyāni. Sadda rūpa rasa gandha phassa saṅkhā parimāṇāni puthūtva saṃyoga viyoga paratvā paratva buddhi sukha dukkha icchā dosa payatta gurutva dravatva sneha vegā saṅkhārā diṭṭhā ceti evamete tevīsati guṇā. Ukkhepanaṃ avakkhepanamākucanaṃ pasāraṇaṃ gamanamiti pañca kammāni. Aññamaññavisiṭṭhesu avisiṭṭhamabhidhānaṃ paccayo hoti. Saṃ-iti yato drabyaguṇakammesu sā atthi evāti etaṃ mahāsāmaññaṃ. Pathavīādīsu anuvattibyāvuttibuddhinimittaṃ drabyatvādi, taṃ yathā drabyatva guṇatva kammatva ghaṭatvādi, eso sāmaññaviseso. Iha tantesu paṭo, kapālesu ghaṭoti iheti yato hetuhetuphalānaṃ sambandho samavāyoti vutto, samavāyoti evamete drabyādikā.

Among these, mind is name; all the others are form. Here, by 'speech' is meant the grasping of a collection of syllables that illuminates the meaning. For these thinkers, since it is held that a property is not other than its possessor, impermanence is indeed established on the theory of transformation. Even on the theory of manifestation, if manifestation occurs through the arising of knowledge that has that as its object, impermanence is indeed established. But if knowledge exists even before that, the theory of manifestation itself would not be possible. This here is merely a pointer. Substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence are what are called 'substance, etc.' Among them, earth, water, fire, air, space, time, direction, self, and mind—these are the nine substances. Sound, form, taste, smell, touch, number, measure, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, heaviness, fluidity, viscosity, momentum, dispositions, and the unseen—thus these are the twenty-four qualities. Lifting up, putting down, contracting, extending, and going—these are the five actions. That which is the cause of an undifferentiated designation for things that are distinct from each other is generality. The designation 'existence'—since it exists in substances, qualities, and actions, it is called 'great generality'. The cause for cognitions of inclusion and exclusion with regard to earth, etc., is substance-ness, etc.—for example, substance-ness, quality-ness, action-ness, pot-ness, etc. This is 'particular generality'. Regarding 'cloth here in the threads' and 'pot here in the potsherds'—since the connection of cause and effect is expressed as 'here', it is called 'inherence'. Thus are these, substance and so on, to be understood.

Tattha pathavī āpa teja vāyū bhūtarūpaṃ, ākāsaṃ tesaṃ abhāvamattaṃ, paricchedo vā, candasūriyādiparivattanaṃ, dhammappavattiñca upādāya paññattimattaṃ kālo. Tathā disā, attā ca. Mano nāmaṃ. Saddarūparasagandhā rūpameva. Tathā phasso bhūtattayasabhāvato. Saṅkhā ekādikā taṃ taṃ upādāya paññattimattaṃ. Tathā avayavasamudāye guṇavisesavasena, saṇṭhānavisesavasena vā mahantaṃ dīghaṃ, tabbipariyāyato aṇu rassanti bhinnalakkhaṇadesesu puthutvanti. Bhinnadesajānaṃ sahabhāve saṃyogoti. Tadapāye viyogoti. Samānadisādesagatānaṃ rūpānaṃ mahadabbantarānaṃ vasena paramaparanti [V 2.0338] paññattimattaṃ. Buddhisukhadukkhaicchādosapayattā nāmameva. Gurutva dravatva snehavegā rūpadhammānaṃ pavattivisesato gahetabbākārā. Itaro saṅkhāro ñāṇassa pavattiviseso. Adiṭṭhopi dhammādhammabhāvato nāmameva. Ukkhepanaṃ avakkhepanaṃ ākucanaṃ pasāraṇaṃ gamananti rūpadhammānaṃ pavattimattaṃ. Sadisāsadisatāyaṃ sāmaññavisesasaññā, ayuttasambandhe samavāyasamaññāti drabyādīnampi nāmarūpantogadhatā daṭṭhabbā.

Herein, earth, water, fire, and air are primary matter. Space is either merely their absence or a limitation. Time is merely a concept made in dependence on the revolution of the moon, sun, and so on, and on the occurrence of phenomena. Likewise are direction and self. Mind is name. Sound, form, taste, and smell are just form. Likewise, contact, due to its nature as a composite of the three primary elements, is just form. Number, beginning with one, is merely a concept made in dependence on this or that. Likewise, in an aggregate of parts, 'large' and 'long' are by way of a specific quality or a specific configuration, and conversely 'small' and 'short'; 'separateness' is in things with distinct characteristics and locations. When things born of different locations are together, it is 'conjunction'; in their separation, it is 'disjunction.' 'Far' and 'near' are merely concepts by way of large or small intervals between material phenomena situated in the same direction and location. Cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort are just name. Heaviness, fluidity, viscosity, and momentum are modes to be grasped from the specific occurrence of material phenomena. The other formation is a specific occurrence of knowledge. The unseen, too, due to its being dhamma and adhamma, is just name. Lifting up, putting down, contracting, extending, and going are merely the occurrence of material phenomena. The designations 'generality' and 'particularity' pertain to similarity and dissimilarity; the designation 'inherence' pertains to an inseparable connection. Thus the inclusion of 'substance' and so on within name-and-form should be understood.

Jīvājīvabandha puñña pāpāsava saṃvaranijjaravimokkhā jīvādikā. Tattha jīvoti attā. Puggaladhammādhammākāsakālesu ajīvasaññā. Tesu saddaphassarūparasagandhasaṇṭhānabandhabhedasukhumaparaaparāghātappabhācchāyojjākatamāni puggalalakkhaṇanti puggalo rūpaṃ rūpadhammānaṃ pavattiākāramattato. Dhammādhammā jīvapuggalānaṃ gatiṭṭhitimattatāya tadavisiṭṭhā[M 2.0361]. Ākāsakālā paññattimattaṃ. Bandho “kammapuggalantarasaṃyogo”ti vacanato tehi anañño. Puññapāpāni nāmanti pākaṭameva. “Kammapuggalānamāsavo”ti vacanato puññāpuññasambhave āsavasamaññāti tato avisiṭṭho āsavo. “Āsavanirodho saṃvaro”ti vacanato paṭipakkhena puññāpuññanirodho saṃvaro. “Kammaphalappavattiyā pakatiyā appavatti nijjaro”ti vacanato vipākanirodhanimittaṃ nijjaro. Mokkhopi “sabbakammavimokkho”ti vacanato kammapuggalajīvaviyogo. Tattha kammapuggalānaṃ saddādilakkhaṇatāya rūpamattatā puññāpuññamattatāya arūpatā. Jīvo ca arūpamattamevāti ayaṃ drabyamokkho. Bhāvamokkho pana jīvassa rāgādibhāvāpariṇāmo rāgādayo nāmamevāti jīvādayopi nāmarūpantogadhā eva.

Soul, non-soul, bondage, merit, demerit, influx, restraint, wearing away, and liberation are the categories of 'soul,' and so on. Here, 'soul' (jīva) means the self. The designation 'non-soul' (ajīva) applies to matter (pudgala), dharma, adharma, space, and time. Among these, the characteristics of matter are sound, touch, form, taste, smell, shape, combination, division, subtlety, impact, light, shade, radiance, and darkness. Matter is form, being merely a mode of occurrence of material phenomena. Dharma and adharma are not distinct from soul and matter, being merely the principles of their motion and rest. Space and time are mere concepts. Bondage, according to the statement 'the union of karma and matter,' is not different from them. That merit and demerit are name is evident. According to the statement 'the influx of karmic matter,' the designation 'influx' applies to the arising of merit and demerit; hence influx is not distinct from them. According to the statement 'restraint is the cessation of influx,' restraint is the cessation of merit and demerit through their opposite. According to the statement 'the natural non-occurrence of the ripening of karmic fruit is wearing away,' wearing away is the cause for the cessation of ripening. Liberation too, according to the statement 'the release from all karma,' is the separation of the soul from karmic matter. Here, karmic matter, having the characteristics of sound and so on, is merely form; and merit and demerit, being merely such, are formless. And soul is merely formless. This is liberation of substance. Liberation of state, however, is the non-transformation of the soul's states of lust, etc.; and lust and so on are just name. Thus 'soul' and so on are also included within name-and-form.

Kāyappavattigatijātibandhāpavaggā kāyādikā. Tattha pathavīāpatejavāyuattasukhadukkhesu kāyasamaññā. Tadavisiṭṭhā pavattigatijātibandhāpavaggā, “bhāvoti attho, kāyoti anatthantara”nti vacanato kāyato aññaṃ kiñci natthi. “Pavattisaññā kiriyāsaṃyogavibhāgesū”ti vacanato gatiādippakārena pavattā pathavīādayo eva pavatti upacāro. “Tasmiṃ anatthantara”nti vacanato kāyato anaññā suramanujapetatiracchānanarakūpapattiyo gatiyo. Tāsu purimāpurimāvisiṭṭho gatīsu jātassa nicchayopi pavattimattanti tato anaññā kaṇhanīlarattapītasukkaatisukkasaṅkhātā jātiyo. Tā uttaruttaravisiṭṭhā aññāṇamoharāgadosatatvāsandassanappāyā sukkajāti, antā accantavimuttā avagāhitatvā cāti sukkajāti[V 2.0339]. “Dosesu bandhasamaññā”ti vacanato aññāṇādilakkhaṇassa bandhassa jīvato anaññatā. Aññāṇādidosābhāvato apavaggasiddhīti kāyādayopi nāmarūpamattameva.

Body, occurrence, destiny, birth, bondage, and release are the categories of 'body,' and so on. Here, the designation 'body' applies to earth, water, fire, air, the self, pleasure, and pain. Occurrence, destiny, birth, bondage, and release are not distinct from it. According to the statement, 'The meaning is existence; "body" is not something different,' there is nothing other than the body. According to the statement, 'The designation "occurrence" applies to actions, conjunctions, and disjunctions,' earth and so on, occurring in the mode of destiny, etc., are 'occurrence' only by metaphor. According to the statement, 'Since it is not different in meaning,' the destinies—rebirth as gods, humans, ghosts, animals, and hell-beings—are not different from the body. Among them, the determination of one born into destinies that are successively more distinguished is merely an occurrence, and thus not different from it are the births called black, blue, red, yellow, white, and exceedingly white. These are successively more distinguished. The white birth is mostly characterized by not seeing the reality of ignorance, delusion, lust, and hatred. The final one is the exceedingly white birth, as it is completely liberated and has penetrated the truth. According to the statement, 'The designation "bondage" applies to defilements,' bondage, which is characterized by ignorance and so on, is not different from the living being. Release is accomplished through the absence of defilements such as ignorance. Thus 'body' and so on are merely name-and-form.

Yopi tattha tattha “puriso attā jīvo”tiādipariyāyehi vutto attapadattho, sopi yathārahaṃ nāmarūpamattaṃ upādāya paññatto, nāmarūpamattameva vā. Tena vuttaṃ “tepi nāmarūpantogadhabhāvābhāvavasena nicchitā evā”ti.

Even the meaning of the term 'self,' expressed in such phrases as 'the person is the self, the living principle,' is, as is appropriate, a designation made in dependence on mere name-and-form, or it is just mere name-and-form. Therefore it is said: 'They too are definitively determined by way of the presence or absence of inclusion within name-and-form.'

Sambahulasuttantasaṃsandanākathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition Correlating with Numerous Suttas

672. Soti [M 2.0362] so vipassanākammiko yogāvacaro. Evanti vuttappakāraparāmasanaṃ. Yāthāvasarasatoti yathābhūtasabhāvato. Nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapetvā etamatthaṃ saṃsandetvā vavatthapetīti sambandho. Lokasamaññāyapi pahānatthāya, pageva “satto jīvo”ti pavattanakamicchābhinivesassāti adhippāyo. Nāmarūpamattatāya avinicchatattā, santānādighanabhedassa ca akatattā abhinivesena vinā samūhekattaggahaṇavasena “satto”ti pavatto sammoho sattasammoho. Tassa vikkhambhanā asammohabhūmi. Sambahulasuttantavasenāti “yathāpī”tiādinā idha vuttānaṃ, avuttānañca “rūpañca hidaṃ, mahāli, attā abhavissa, nayidaṃ rūpaṃ ābādhāya saṃvatteyyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.59; mahāva. 20) evamādinā sambahulānaṃ suttantānaṃ vasena. “Nāmarūpamattamevā”tiādinā vuttamevatthaṃ sandhāyāha “etamattha”nti.

672. So: that yogin engaged in insight meditation. Evaṃ: the reviewing of the manner already described. Yāthāvasarasato: according to its actual nature. The connection is: 'Having determined name-and-form, he correlates and determines this meaning.' The intention is for the purpose of abandoning even worldly convention, let alone the wrong adherence that perpetuates the notions 'a being,' 'a living soul.' Because it has not been determined to be mere name-and-form, and because the breaking up of the mass of continuity and so on has not been done, the delusion that proceeds as 'a being' by way of grasping a collection as a unity, without wrong adherence, is the delusion concerning a being (sattasammoho). The suppression of this is the plane of non-delusion. By way of numerous suttas: by way of the numerous suttas mentioned here beginning with 'Just as...,' and those not mentioned, such as: 'For if, Mahāli, this form were the self, this form would not lead to affliction' (SN 22.59). Referring to this very meaning stated in the passage beginning 'mere name-and-form,' he says 'this meaning.'

Aṅgasambhārāti aṅgasambhārahetu. Tannimittaṃ taṃ amuñcitvā sati eva tasmiṃ “satto”ti vohāro.

Aṅgasambhārā: because of the cause which is the assemblage of parts. Because of that cause, not abandoning that assemblage, only when it is present is there the designation 'a being.'

Agārantvevāti yathā kaṭṭhādīni paṭicca upādāya tesaṃ nāmaṃ vissajjetvā agāramicceva saṅkhaṃ samaññaṃ gacchati, evaṃ aṭṭhiādīni paṭicca upādāya tesaṃ nāmaṃ vissajjetvā rūpaṃ sarīramicceva saṅkhaṃ gacchatīti yojanā.

As for 'a house indeed': Just as, in dependence on wood and so on, having discarded their names, it comes to be counted and designated simply as 'a house,' so too, in dependence on bones and so on, having discarded their names, it comes to be counted simply as 'form' or 'a body.' This is the application.

Dukkhameva sambhotīti dukkhadukkhatādibhedaṃ tividhaṃ dukkhameva sambhavati, yathāpaccayaṃ uppajjati, tadeva dukkhaṃ khaṇaṭṭhitipabandhaṭṭhitivasena tiṭṭhati ceva khaṇanirodhaāyukkhayanirodhādivasena [V 2.0340] nirujjhati cāti attho. Idāni dukkhamevāti evakārena nivattitamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “nāññatrā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho – yathāvuttaṃ dukkhaṃ ṭhapetvā tato aññaṃ kiñci dhammajātaṃ na sambhavati, yo “satto”ti vā “jīvo”ti vā vucceyya, sabbena sabbaṃ abhāvā kuto tassa nirodhoti.

'Only suffering arises': This means that the threefold suffering, with its divisions such as suffering-as-suffering, is what arises, what originates in accordance with conditions. The meaning is that this very suffering both persists—by way of momentary duration and the duration of the continuum—and ceases—by way of momentary cessation, the cessation at the exhaustion of the life-span, and so on. Now, to show the meaning excluded by the particle 'only' in 'only suffering,' the passage beginning 'apart from...' is stated. Its meaning is: Setting aside the suffering as described, no other kind of phenomenon arises apart from it that could be called 'a being' or 'a living principle.' Since this is entirely non-existent, whence could its cessation be?

Upamāhināmarūpavibhāvanākathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition Clarifying Name-and-Form by Way of Similes

673. Ekenākārena saṇṭhitesūti yena pakārena akkhādīsu sanniviṭṭhesu rathasamaññā, tena ekena ākārena samavaṭṭhitesu ekajjhaṃ rāsikatesu[M 2.0363]. Evamevanti sannivesavisiṭṭhe avayavasamudāye santānavasena pavattamāne yathā “ratho gehaṃ muṭṭhi vīṇā senā nagaraṃ rukkho”ti vohāramattaṃ, paramatthato pana rathādi nāma kiñci natthi, evamevaṃ. Upādānakkhandhesūti upādānakkhandhasaññitesu rūpārūpadhammesu samuditesu santānavasena pavattamānesu “satto jīvo”ti vohāramattaṃ, paramatthato pana satto vā jīvo vā natthīti yāthāvato jānanaṃ. Idaṃ yathābhūtadassanaṃ “diṭṭhivisuddhī”ti vuccati.

673. 'When they are established in one way': This means: in that one way in which the designation 'chariot' arises when parts such as the axle are arranged, when they are established together, heaped together. 'Just so': Just as, when a collection of parts with a specific arrangement proceeds as a continuum, there is the mere verbal usage 'chariot,' 'house,' 'fist,' 'lute,' 'army,' 'city,' or 'tree,' but in an ultimate sense there is nothing at all called a chariot, etc.—just so... 'In the aggregates subject to clinging': When the material and immaterial phenomena designated as the aggregates subject to clinging have arisen together and proceed as a continuum, there is the mere verbal usage 'a being' or 'a living principle'; the knowing, as it really is, that in an ultimate sense there is no being or living principle—this seeing things as they really are is called 'purification of view'.

674. Tassāti sattoti gahitassa attano. Vināsanti niruddhassa vināsaṃ. Avināsanti avinassanaṃ, niccatanti attho. Dvayavaseneva hi attavādino ṭhitā, sassato attā, ucchijjatīti vā, ekaccasassatavādopi ettheva samavaruddhoti. Avināsaṃ anujānantoti buddhiādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ vināsaṃ icchantopi “dhammī nicco kūṭaṭṭho”ti attano vināsābhāvaṃ anujānanto. Sassateti sassatagāhe. Patati katavināsaakatabbhāgamādidosappasaṅgatoti adhippāyo. Khīranvayassāti khīrassa anvayabhūtassa, phalabhūtassāti attho. Tadanvayassāti tassa attano anvayabhūtassa aññassa kassaci abhāvato. Olīyati nāmāti “sassato attā”ti abhinivesena bhavābhirato hutvā bhavanirodhato saṅkocanaṃ āpajjanto bhaveyeva nilīyati nāma. Atidhāvati nāmāti tattha tattheva hi bhave attā ucchijjatīti ucchedavādī “ucchijjati attā”ti gaṇhanto paraṃ maraṇā santaṃ bhavaṃ “natthī”ti atikkamanto atidhāvati nāmāti vadanti. Kilesanirodhe pana kammassa avipaccanato bhavanirodhe icchitabbe tathā aggahetvā “taṃ taṃ bhavavisesaṃ āgamma attā ucchijjatīti evaṃ bhavanirodho hotī”ti gaṇhanto taṃ atidhāvati nāma.

674. 'Of that' (tassa): of the self that is grasped as 'a being.' 'Destruction' (vināsaṃ): the destruction of what has ceased. 'Non-destruction' (avināsaṃ): not perishing; the meaning is permanence. For the proponents of a self are established on a duality: either 'the self is eternal' or 'it is annihilated.' The doctrine of partial eternalism is also included right here. 'One who affirms non-destruction' (avināsaṃ anujānanto): one who, while wishing for the destruction of phenomena such as consciousness, affirms the non-destruction of the self, thinking, 'The possessor of the phenomena is permanent, immutable.' 'In the eternal' (sassate): in the grasp of eternalism. The intention is that this is because of the fault of entailing the destruction of what has been done and the partaking of what has not been done. 'Of the successor of milk' (khīrannayassa): of what has succeeded from milk, that is, of what is its result. 'Of its successor' (tadanvayassa): because there is no other successor of that self. 'He clings' (olīyati nāma): adhering to the view 'the self is eternal,' he delights in existence, and shrinking from the cessation of existence, he indeed hides away in existence. 'He overruns' (atidhāvati nāma): they say that the annihilationist, who holds 'the self is annihilated here and there in existence,' overruns by transgressing, thinking 'after death, existing being is not.' But when, on the cessation of defilements, kamma does not ripen and the cessation of existence is to be wished for, not grasping it thus, one who holds, 'The self is annihilated by reaching this or that particular existence; thus there is a cessation of existence,' is said to 'overrun' it.

Pariyuṭṭhitāti [V 2.0341] abhibhūtā. Cakkhumantoti yathābhūtadassanasaṅkhātena ñāṇacakkhunā cakkhumanto.

'Beset' (pariyuṭṭhitā) means overwhelmed. 'Those with eyes' (cakkhumanto) means those possessing the eye of knowledge, termed the vision of things as they really are.

Kāmabhavādibhedo bhavo āramitabbaṭṭhena ārāmo etesanti bhavārāmā. Tasmiṃ bhave ratā abhiratāti bhavaratā. Bhave sammodaṃ āpannāti bhavasammuditā. Tīhipi padehi bhavassādagadhitatāva vuttā. Cittaṃ na pakkhandatīti bhavassādagadhitattā eva bhavanirodhāvahe dhamme cittaṃ na [M 2.0364] anuppavisati. Nappasīdatīti na okappati. Na santiṭṭhatīti na patiṭṭhahati. Nādhimuccatīti na adhimuccati.

Existence, which has distinctions such as sensual existence, is a 'delight' (ārāma) for them in the sense that it is to be delighted in; therefore, they are 'delighters in existence' (bhavārāmā). Those who are fond of and delighted in that existence are 'fond of existence' (bhavaratā). Those who have found gladness in existence are 'gladdened by existence' (bhavasammuditā). By all three terms, only the state of being infatuated with the gratification in existence is expressed. 'The mind does not leap toward it': precisely because of being infatuated with the gratification in existence, the mind does not enter the Dhamma that brings about the cessation of existence. 'It does not become confident' (nappasīdati): it does not trust in it. 'It does not stand firm' (na santiṭṭhati): it does not become established. 'It is not resolved upon it' (nādhimuccati): it is not decided upon it.

Aṭṭīyamānāti dukkhāpiyamānā. Harāyamānāti lajjamānā. Jigucchamānāti hīḷentā. Vibhavanti ucchedaṃ. Abhinandantīti vuttaabhinandanākāradassanaṃ “yato kira bho”tiādi.

'Being distressed' (aṭṭīyamānā) means being afflicted by suffering. 'Being ashamed' (harāyamānā) means feeling shame. 'Feeling revulsion' (jigucchamānā) means despising. 'Non-existence' (vibhavaṃ) means annihilation. 'They welcome it' (abhinandanti): this shows the manner of welcoming that was stated, as in the passage beginning, 'For, sirs...'

Bhūtanti khandhapañcakaṃ. Tañhi yathāsakaṃ paccayehi jātattā, paramatthato vijjamānattā ca bhūtanti vuccati. Bhūtatoti yathābhūtasabhāvato, salakkhaṇato, sāmaññalakkhaṇato ca.

'What has come to be' (bhūtaṃ) means the five aggregates. For it is called 'what has come to be' because it has been born from its own respective causes and because it exists in an ultimate sense. 'From what has come to be' (bhūtato) means according to its actual nature, and according to its specific characteristic and its general characteristics.

675. Evaṃ sattagāhato avalīyanātidhāvanadose, yathābhūtadassanato nibbidādiguṇe ca suttavaseneva dassetvā idāni nāmarūpamattepi gamanādiattakiccasiddhiṃ dassetuṃ “tasmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tasmāti yasmā “asmī”ti vā “aha”nti vā gāhassa vatthubhūto satto nāma natthi, paramatthato nāmarūpamattameva, tasmā. Sace koci attā nāma natthi, kathamidha nāmarūpamatte gamanādiattakiccasiddhīti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “dāruyanta”ntiādi. “Khāyatī”ti etena yathā nijjīve dārumayayante abbhantare vattamānassa jīvassa vasena saīhassa sabyāpārassa viya upaṭṭhānamattaṃ paccayavisesato, evaṃ nijjīve nāmarūpamatte paccayavisesato gamanādiattakiccasiddhīti saīhassa sabyāpārassa viya upaṭṭhānanti dasseti.

675. Having thus shown by way of the sutta the faults of shrinking back and overrunning that arise from grasping at a being, and the virtues such as disenchantment that arise from the vision of things as they really are, now, in order to show the accomplishment of the functions of a self, such as going, even in mere name-and-form, the passage beginning 'Therefore...' is stated. Therein, 'therefore' means: since there is no being that is the basis for the grasp 'I am' or 'I,' but in an ultimate sense there is only mere name-and-form, therefore... Referring to the objection, 'If there is no self, how is the function of a self, such as going, accomplished here in mere name-and-form?' he says the passage beginning 'a wooden puppet...' By this word 'it appears,' he shows that just as in a lifeless wooden machine there is, due to specific conditions, the mere appearance as if it had volition and activity by means of a life-principle existing inside, so too in lifeless mere name-and-form, there is, due to specific conditions, the accomplishment of the functions of a self, such as going, which is an appearance as if it had volition and activity.

Saccatoti bhūtato, paramatthatoti attho. Suññaṃ jīvena yantamiva abhisaṅkhataṃ paccayavasena pavattīti adhippāyo. Dukkhassa puñjo niccāturatāya tiṇakaṭṭhasadiso attasuññatāyāti attho. Etaṃ nāmarūpaṃ.

'Truly' (saccato) means 'actually' (bhūtato); 'in an ultimate sense' (paramatthato) is the meaning. The intention is that, like a machine, it is fabricated, empty of a living principle, and proceeds by way of conditions. The meaning is that, as a heap of suffering, it is like grass and sticks due to its constant affliction and its emptiness of self. This is name-and-form.

Yamakanti [V 2.0342] yugaḷakaṃ. So ca kho yamakabhāvo aññamaññasannissitabhāvenāti āha “ubho aññoññanissitā”ti. Tato eva ca ekasmiṃ bhijjamānasmiṃ ubho bhijjanti. Na hi kadāci pañcavokārabhave rūpe nirujjhante arūpaṃ anirujjhantaṃ, arūpe vā nirujjhante rūpaṃ anirujjhantaṃ atthi. Svāyaṃ bhaṅgo paccayā paccayanirodheneva, nāmarūpanirodhoti attho. Paccayāti vā paccayabhūtā, aññamaññassa paccayā hontāpi ubho bhijjantiyevāti attho.

'A pair' (yamakaṃ) means a couple. And this state of being a pair is due to their state of mutual dependence, thus it is said: 'Both are dependent on each other.' For that very reason, when one breaks, both break. For in the five-constituent existence, it is never the case that when materiality is ceasing, the immaterial does not cease, or that when the immaterial is ceasing, materiality does not cease. This breaking is from a condition, that is, by the cessation of the condition itself; the meaning is 'by the cessation of name-and-form.' Or, 'from the condition' (paccayā) means being a condition; the meaning is that although they are conditions for each other, both indeed break.

676. Daṇḍābhihatanti [M 2.0365] visesanena daṇḍaṃ, daṇḍābhighātassa paccayaṃ purisavāyāmañca dasseti, bheriyā pana visesitabbatā saddassa asādhāraṇakāraṇatāya. Teneva hi “aññā bherī”ti bherīyeva gahitā, na daṇḍādayo. Adissamānarūpatāya saddaṃ nāmaṭṭhāniyaṃ katvā “evameva”ntiādinā upamāsaṃsandanaṃ karoti.

676. By the specification 'struck by a stick,' he indicates the stick and the person's effort, which is the cause of the strike with the stick. But the drum is to be specified because it is the uncommon cause of the sound. For that very reason, by 'another drum,' only the drum is taken, not the stick and so on. Because sound has an invisible form, having placed it in the position of 'name' (in the name-and-form pair), he makes the connection with the simile by the words 'just so...'

Na cakkhuto jāyareti na cakkhāyatanato niggacchanavasena jāyanti. Na hi cakkhāyatanassa paccayabhāvūpagamanato pubbe phassapañcamakā labbhanti, na ca padesavanto, yena te tato niggaccheyyuṃ. Tenevāha “puñjo natthi anāgate”ti (mahāni. 10). Na rūpatoti etthāpi eseva nayo. “No ca ubhinnamantarā”ti idaṃ pana tesaṃ arūpadhammattā appadesatāya vuttaṃ. Kevalaṃ pana yasmiṃ khaṇe paccayasamavāyo, tadā uppajjanamattamevāti āha “hetuṃ paṭicca pabhavanti saṅkhatā”ti, cakkhurūpālokamanasikārādibhedaṃ dhammajātaṃ nissāya paccayabhūtaṃ kāraṇaṃ labhitvā tehi samecca sambhūya katattā saṅkhatā phassādayo dhammā uppajjantīti attho. Tassā pana dhammānaṃ uppattiyā pākaṭaṃ rūpadhammapavattiṃ dassento “yathāpi saddo pahaṭāya bheriyā”ti āha. Phassapañcamaggahaṇañcettha pākaṭaarūpadhammānaṃ dassanaṃ. Sesagāthāsupi eseva nayo.

'They do not arise from the eye' means they do not arise in the sense of emerging from the eye-base. For before the eye-base has come to be a condition, the pentad headed by contact is not found, nor are they localized, so that they could emerge from it. Hence it is said: 'There is no heap in the future' (Mahāni. 10). The same method applies also to 'nor from form.' But 'nor from between the two' is said because, being immaterial states, they are non-localized. However, at the moment there is a convergence of conditions, there is merely an arising—this is what is meant by 'Dependent on a cause, conditioned things arise.' The meaning is: having obtained a cause that is a condition by relying on the collection of phenomena such as eye, form, light, and attention, the conditioned states headed by contact arise, having been formed by their combination and co-arising. To show the manifest occurrence of a material phenomenon in the arising of those states, he said: 'just as sound from a struck drum.' And here, the taking up of the pentad headed by contact is a demonstration of manifest immaterial states. The same method applies to the remaining verses as well.

Vatthurūpāti hadayavatthuto. Tannissayānaṃ arūpadhammānaṃ bahubhedattā sāmaññavohārena te dassetuṃ “saṅkhatā”ti vuttaṃ.

'Material basis' means the heart-base. Because the immaterial states dependent on it are of many kinds, to indicate them with a general designation, it is said 'conditioned'.

677. Nittejanti tejahīnaṃ ānubhāvarahitaṃ. Yathā pana taṃ nittejaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “na khādatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Na hi aññathā saddahanussahanādīsu nāmaṃ “nitteja”nti sakkā vattuṃ, nāpi rūpaṃ sandhāraṇābandhanādīsu. Teneva hi “rūpaṃ nitteja”nti vatvā “na hi tassa khāditukāmatā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Atha kho”tiādinā byatirekavasenāpi nāmarūpānaṃ nittejataṃyeva [V 2.0343] vibhāveti. Aññamaññasannissayena hi nāmarūpassa attakiccasiddhipi paccekaṃ asamatthatāvibhāvanameva. Tathā hi nāmarūpassa attasuññatā, nirīhatā, byāpāravirahatā ca suṭṭhutaraṃ pākaṭā honti.

677. 'Powerless' means devoid of power, without influence. To show how it is powerless, it is said, 'It does not eat,' etc. For name cannot otherwise be called 'powerless' in regard to believing, striving, etc., nor can form in regard to supporting, binding, etc. For that very reason, having said 'form is powerless,' it is said, 'For it has no desire to eat,' etc. By means of 'But rather,' etc., he clarifies the very powerlessness of name-and-form by way of contrast. For the accomplishment of their respective functions by name-and-form through mutual dependence is itself a demonstration of their individual incapacity. Thus the emptiness of self, the inertia, and the inactivity of name-and-form become exceedingly clear.

Kathaṃ pana paccekaṃ asamatthānaṃ samuditabhāve samatthatā hoti? Asāmaggiyaṃ ahetūnaṃ sāmaggiyampi ahetubhāvāpattito. Na hi paccekaṃ [M 2.0366] daṭṭhuṃ asakkontānaṃ andhānaṃ satampi sahassampi samuditaṃ daṭṭhuṃ sakkotīti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “imassa panatthassā”tiādi. Imaṃ upamaṃ udāharanti aṭṭhakathācariyā upamāyapi asiddhassa atthassa sādhetabbato. Tenevāha “upamaṃ te karissāmi, upamāyapidhekacce viññū purisā bhāsitassa atthaṃ jānantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.67). Tuṭṭhahaṭṭhoti yadipāhaṃ cakkhukaraṇīyaṃ kātuṃ na sakkomi, pādakaraṇīyaṃ pana kātuṃ sakkomi, tvañca cakkhukaraṇīyaṃ, tasmā amhākaṃ ubhinnaṃ sahitānañca vasena icchitadesasampatti sijjhatīti tuṭṭhahaṭṭho jaccandho. Tattha jaccandhotiādi upamopameyyasaṃsandanaṃ. Dhammānaṃ attalābho parapaṭibaddhoti vattabbameva natthi tato pubbe avijjamānattā, paṭiladdhattalābhassāpi parapaṭibaddhameva atthakiccanti dassetuṃ “na sakena tejena uppajjati, na tāsu tāsu kiriyāsu pavattatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tesaṃ nāmarūpānaṃ aññamaññaṃ nissāya uppatti vā pavatti vā na ca na hotīti jaccandhapīṭhasappiupamāya sādhitamatthaṃ nigamento “asāmaggiyaṃ ahetūnaṃ sāmaggiyampi ahetukabhāvāpattito”ti yathāvuttassa hetuno anekantikabhāvaṃ vibhāveti.

But how can there be capability in combination for things that are individually incapable? Since what are non-causes when disunited would also be non-causes when united. Referring to the objection, 'For a hundred or even a thousand blind men who are individually unable to see cannot see when they are combined,' he says, 'But regarding this meaning…' etc. The commentators cite this simile because a point that is not established has to be proven even by a simile. Hence he said: 'I will make a simile for you, for by a simile some wise people here understand the meaning of what has been said' (Saṃ. Ni. 2.67). 'Delighted and joyful': The man born blind is delighted and joyful, thinking: 'Although I cannot do the work of the eyes, I can do the work of the feet, and you can do the work of the eyes; therefore, by means of us both together, the attainment of the desired place is accomplished.' Here, 'the man born blind,' etc., is the correlation of the simile and the thing illustrated. It is not even possible to say that the acquisition of an existence by states is dependent on another, because they do not exist prior to that. But to show that even for one that has acquired an existence, its function is dependent on another, it is said: 'It does not arise by its own power, nor does it proceed in those various functions.' Concluding the meaning established by the simile of the man born blind and the cripple—that the arising or occurrence of this name-and-form through mutual dependence does indeed happen—he clarifies the inconclusiveness of the aforesaid reason, 'since what are non-causes when disunited would also be non-causes when united'.

Paradhammavasānuvattinoti paresaṃ attato aññesaṃ hetupaccayasaṅkhātānaṃ dhammānaṃ vasena anuvattanasīlā. Attadubbalāti attanā dubbalā asamatthā. Parapaccayatoti paresaṃ dhammānaṃ paccayabhāvato. Etena janakapaccayaṃ vadati. Tenevāha “jāyare”ti. Paraārammaṇatoti paresaṃ dhammānaṃ ārammaṇabhāvato. Etena upatthambhakapaccayaṃ vadati. Paccayaggahaṇaṃ vā rūpāpekkhaṃ, ārammaṇaggahaṇaṃ nāmāpekkhaṃ. “Paradhammehī”ti idaṃ ārammaṇapaccayānaṃ visesanaṃ. Purimatthena hi vuttamevatthaṃ pacchimatthena pākaṭaṃ karoti. Pabhāvitāti uppāditā.

'Following the power of other things' means they are wont to conform to the power of other things, designated as causes and conditions, which are other than themselves. 'Weak in themselves' means weak and incapable by themselves. 'From another as condition' means because of other things being a condition. By this he speaks of the generative condition. Hence he says, 'they are born.' 'From another as object' means because of other things being an object. By this he speaks of the supporting condition. Alternatively, the taking up of 'condition' is with reference to form, the taking up of 'object' is with reference to name. 'By other things' is a qualification of 'object' and 'condition'. For with the latter half of the verse, he makes clear the very meaning that was stated with the first half. 'Produced' means generated.

Nāvāyantikūpamāyapi nāmarūpānaṃ avasavattitaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “yathāpī”tiādinā tisso gāthā vuttā. Nissāyāti patiṭṭhāya. Yantīti gacchanti. Manusse nissāyāti netubhūte niyāmakakammakārakādimanusse apassāya. Na hi tesaṃ araṇaggahaṇalaṅkārasaṇṭhāpanaudakussiñcanādikiriyāya [V 2.0344] vinā nāvā icchitadesaṃ pāpuṇāti. Ubhoti aññamaññaṃ nāvaṃ nissāya manussā, manusse nissāya nāvāti attho.

Also by the simile of the boat and the boatmen, three verses beginning with 'Just as…' have been stated to clarify the non-subservience of name-and-form. 'Depending on' means relying on. 'They go' means they proceed. 'Depending on people' means by relying on the people who are the guides, the helmsmen, the crew, etc. For without their actions such as taking the helm, adjusting the sail, and bailing out water, the boat does not reach the desired destination. 'Both' means mutually: the people depending on the boat, and the boat depending on the people—this is the meaning.

Evanti [M 2.0367] vuttappakārena. Nānānayehīti paṭhamādīnaṃ sattannaṃ jhānānaṃ, tesaṃ upacārānañca vasena cuddasa arūpapariggahamukhāni, catudhātuvavatthāne vuttānaṃ terasannaṃ dhātupariggahamukhānaṃ dhātāyatanakhandhamahābhūtavasena, idha vuttānaṃ avuttānañca indriyasaccapaṭiccasamuppannānaṃ vasena samavīsati rūpapariggahamukhāni, tāni paccekaṃ “phasso vedanā citta”nti imesaṃ sammukhabhāvena upaṭṭhitānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ arūpadhammānaṃ vasena tiguṇitāni samasaṭṭhi, cuddasa arūpapariggahamukhāni, tāni cāti catusattatiyā nāmarūpapariggahanayehi ceva sambahulasuttantarathagehamuṭṭhivīṇāsenārukkhadāruyantanaḷakalāpibherijaccandhapaṅguḷanāvāmanussūpamāhi ca nāmarūpapamattatāvavatthāpananayehi ca. Sattasaññaṃ abhibhavitvāti anādikālabhāvitaṃ khandhapañcake attagāhaṃ vikkhambhetvā. Nāmarūpānaṃ yāthāvadassananti “idaṃ nāmaṃ, ettakaṃ nāmaṃ, na ito bhiyyo. Idaṃ rūpaṃ, ettakaṃ rūpaṃ, na ito bhiyyo”ti ca tesaṃ lakkhaṇasallakkhaṇamukhena dhammamattabhāvadassanaṃ. Attadiṭṭhimalavisodhanato diṭṭhivisuddhīti veditabbaṃ. Etassevāti nāmarūpassa yāthāvadassanasseva.

'Thus' means in the manner explained. 'By various methods' refers to the seventy-four methods of apprehending name-and-form and the methods of establishing the mere-phenomenon-ness of name-and-form through numerous similes from the suttas: the chariot, house, fist, lute, army, tree, wooden machine, sheaf of reeds, drum, the man born blind and the cripple, the boat and the men. The seventy-four methods are as follows: there are fourteen approaches to apprehending the immaterial, by way of the seven jhānas beginning with the first and their access concentrations. There are twenty approaches to apprehending the material, comprising the thirteen approaches to apprehending elements stated in the Definition of the Four Elements, the approaches stated herein by way of elements, sense bases, aggregates, and great elements, and those by way of the faculties, truths, and dependent origination which are not stated herein. These twenty, when tripled by way of the three immaterial states of contact, feeling, and consciousness that have arisen as prominent, become sixty. These sixty, together with the fourteen approaches to apprehending the immaterial, total seventy-four. 'Having overcome the perception of a being' means having suppressed the grasping at a self in the five aggregates, which has been cultivated since beginningless time. 'The seeing of name-and-form as it really is' is the seeing of them as mere phenomena by way of defining their characteristics, thus: 'This is name, so much is name, no more than this. This is form, so much is form, no more than this.' It should be understood as 'purification of view' because it cleanses the stain of self-view. 'Of this very' means of this very seeing of name-and-form as it really is.

Diṭṭhivisuddhiniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Exposition of the Purification of View is concluded.

Iti aṭṭhārasamaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus the commentary on the Eighteenth Chapter.

19. Kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiniddesavaṇṇanā

19. Commentary on the Exposition of the Purification by Overcoming Doubt

Paccayapariggahakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Comprehension of Conditions

678. Anantaraniddiṭṭhāya [M 2.0368][V 2.0345] diṭṭhivisuddhiyā visayabhāvena dassitattā “etassevā”ti vuttaṃ, na tadaññato visesanatthaṃ tadaññasseva abhāvato. Ajjhattaṃ vā hi vipassanābhiniveso hotu bahiddhā vā, ajjhattasiddhiyaṃ pana lakkhaṇato sabbampi nāmarūpaṃ anavasesato pariggahitameva hotīti. Paccayapariggahenāti hetumhi karaṇavacanaṃ. Paccayapariggahahetu hissa addhattayakaṅkhāvitaraṇaṃ hotīti, karaṇe vā etaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ paccayapariggahassa sādhakatamabhāvato kaṅkhāvitaraṇakiriyāya. Yadā hissa suparisuddho nijjaṭo niggumbo paccayapariggaho sijjhati, tadānena kaṅkhā vitarīyatīti. Vitaritvāti atikkamitvā, vikkhambhetvāti attho. Taṃ pana ñāṇaṃ tathādhigataṃ vasībhāvappattaṃ jhānaṃ viya yogino santāne pabandhavasena pavattatīti katvā vuttaṃ “ṭhitaṃ ñāṇa”nti.

678. Because it was shown as the object for the purification of view, which was set forth immediately before, it is said “of this very,” not to distinguish it from something else, since there is nothing else apart from it. For whether one’s application to insight is internal or external, with the accomplishment of the internal, all name-and-form is fully comprehended without remainder by way of its characteristics. “By the comprehension of conditions”—this is the instrumental case in the sense of cause. For because of the comprehension of conditions, one’s overcoming of doubt concerning the three periods of time occurs. Alternatively, this is the instrumental case in the sense of instrument, since the comprehension of conditions is the most effective means for the act of overcoming doubt. For when one’s comprehension of conditions becomes thoroughly purified, freed from tangles and thickets, then by this yogī doubt is overcome. ‘Having overcome’ means having surmounted, having suppressed; this is the meaning. Furthermore, that knowledge, having been thus attained and having reached a state of mastery, proceeds in the yogī’s continuum by way of an unbroken stream, like a jhāna. Therefore, it is called “established knowledge.”

Tanti kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiṃ. Taṃ sampādetukāmo āpajjatīti sambandho. Yāthāvato diṭṭhaṃ nāmarūpaṃ tividhadukkhatāyogato rogo viya. Paccayā cassa rogasamuṭṭhānaṃ viya upaṭṭhahantīti imamatthaṃ dassento “yathā nāma…pe… pariyesatī”ti āha. Saṃsāradukkhanimuggassa santānassa tato vimocetukāmatāvasena anukampitabbatā labbhatīti tamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “yathā vā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Evameva ṭhite yadeke vadanti “anukampetabbakumārakadassanena tassa mātāpituāvajjanaṃ idha anudāharaṇaṃ nirodhetabbatāya nāmarūpassa anukampitabbatābhāvato”ti, tadapāhataṃ hoti. Avassañcetaṃ evaṃ icchitabbaṃ, aññathā veneyyapuggalasantāne satthu mahākaruṇāpavatti eva vicāretabbā siyā. Mandabuddhitāya mandaṃ. Vuḍḍhataropi koci mandabuddhi hotīti tato visesanatthaṃ “kumāra”nti vuttaṃ. Yo koci paṭhamavaye vattamāno “kumāro”ti vuccatīti tato visesanatthaṃ “dahara”nti vuttaṃ. Evampi yo ādhāvitvā paridhāvitvā vicāraṇako taruṇadārako, sopi [M 2.0369] “daharo”ti [V 2.0346] vuccatīti tato nivattanatthaṃ “uttānaseyyaka”nti vuttaṃ. Catūhipi padehi karuṇāyitabbataṃyeva dasseti. Āpajjatīti karoti.

That purification by overcoming doubt. He who desires to accomplish that undertakes it—this is the connection. Name-and-form, seen as it truly is, appears like a disease because of its connection with the threefold suffering. And its conditions appear like the cause of the disease—to show this meaning, he said, “Just as … he seeks.” To show that compassion should be exercised out of a desire to liberate the continuum immersed in the suffering of saṃsāra, it is said: “Or just as…,” and so on. This being so, the statement by some—“The seeing of a boy who is to be pitied and the parents’ attention to him is not an example here, because name-and-form is not to be pitied since it is to be brought to cessation”—is refuted. And this must certainly be accepted in this way; otherwise, the very arising of the Teacher’s great compassion in the continuum of persons to be trained would have to be questioned. A slow one (manda) because of his dull intelligence. Since even an older person can be of dull intelligence, to distinguish from him, “boy” (kumāra) is said. Since anyone in the first stage of life is called a “boy,” to distinguish from him, “young” (dahara) is said. And since even a young child who can run about and investigate is called “young,” to exclude him, “an infant lying on his back” (uttānaseyyaka) is said. With these four terms he shows only that the child is to be pitied. “He undertakes” means he does.

Yathā panassa hetupaccayapariyesanāpatti hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “so”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha byatirekamukhena attho sādhito sammadeva sādhito hotīti ahetukabhāvaṃ tāva paṭikkhipanto “na tāvidaṃ nāmarūpaṃ ahetuka”nti vatvā tattha kāraṇamāha “sabbatthā”tiādinā. Hetumantarena sati sambhave sabbadhammānaṃ hetuabhāvo samānoti sabbasamānatā siyā, tathā ca sati sotapadesādīsu, bahiddhā ca cakkhuviññāṇādihetuabhāvoti sabbattha, cakkhādīnaṃ uppattito pubbe, paribhedato uddhañca hetuabhāvoti sabbadā ca andhādīnaṃ arūpīnaṃ, asaññīnañca hetuabhāvoti sabbesañca cakkhuviññāṇādīhi bhavitabbaṃ, hetuabhāvā visesato tañca natthīti āha “sabbattha sabbadā sabbesañca ekasadisabhāvāpattito”ti. Nidassanamattañcetaṃ yadidaṃ “cakkhuviññāṇādīsu hī”ti. Yattakā loke visesā, tehi sabbesaṃ, sabbakālañca bhavitabbanti adhippāyo. Ādi-saddena vā tesampi gahaṇaṃ katamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tasmā ahetukabhāve visiṭṭhatāya asambhavo evāti sabbattha ekasadisabhāvāpattito, sabbadā ekasadisabhāvāpattito, sabbesaṃ ekasadisabhāvāpattitoti paccekaṃ sambandho veditabbo. Evaṃ ahetubhāve paṭisiddhe visamahetuvādī vadeyya “na idaṃ ahetukaṃ kiñcarahi sahetukaṃ, kena pana hetunā sahetukanti? Issarādinā”ti.

Now, to show how the undertaking of the search for cause and condition comes to be for that yogī, the passage beginning 'So...' was stated. Therein, because the meaning is well established by the method of exclusion, first, refuting the state of causelessness, having said, 'This name-and-form is not without a cause,' he stated the reason with the words beginning 'everywhere...' For if there were an arising without a cause, since the absence of a cause is the same for all things, there would be universal sameness. And that being so, because the absence of a cause for eye-consciousness and so forth is the same in places like the ear and externally, it would have to arise everywhere; and because the absence of a cause is the same before the arising of the eye and so forth and after its dissolution, it would have to arise always; and because the absence of a cause is the same for the blind, for formless beings, and for non-percipient beings, eye-consciousness and so forth would have to arise for all, because of the non-difference with respect to the absence of a cause. And that is not the case. Therefore, he said: 'because it would entail a state of absolute uniformity everywhere, always, and for all.' And this, namely 'eye-consciousness and so forth,' is merely an illustration. The intention is that whatever distinctions exist in the world, they would have to exist for all and at all times. Or, it should be understood that by the word 'etc.' their inclusion is also made. Therefore, since in a state of causelessness there is certainly an impossibility of distinction, the connection should be known with each term individually: 'because of entailing a state of absolute uniformity everywhere,' 'because of entailing a state of absolute uniformity always,' and 'because of entailing a state of absolute uniformity for all.' When the state of causelessness is thus refuted, a proponent of a dissimilar cause might say: 'This is not without a cause. What then? It has a cause. But by what cause does it have a cause? By a Lord (Īśvara), etc.'

Ādi-saddena pakatipurisapajāpatikālādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ, taṃ paṭikkhipanto āha “na issarādihetuka”ntiādi. Na nāmarūpaṃ issarādihetukaṃ nāmarūpato aññassa anupalabbhamānattā issarapakatiādinameva abhāvato. Yadi pana asato issarādito nāmarūpassa uppatti, evaṃ sati sā eva sabbattha sabbadā sabbesaṃ ekasadisatā āpajjati. Atha nāmarūpamattameva issarādihetukaṃ, nāmarūpañca ahutvā sambhavantaṃ, hutvā ca vinassantaṃ dissatīti issarādīhipi tādisehi bhavitabbaṃ. Tathā ca tadapi sappaccayaṃ saṅkhatamevāti tassāpi paccayapariggaho kātabbo. Atha [M 2.0370] taṃ nuppajjati, ahetukatā tassa āpannā. Tenāha “ahetukabhāvāpattito”ti.

By the word 'ādi' (etc.), the inclusion of primordial nature (pakati), spirit (purisa), Prajāpati, time, and so on should be understood. Rejecting this, he said, “It is not caused by a Lord, etc.” and so on. Name-and-form is not caused by a Lord or the like, because nothing other than name-and-form is found, and due to the very non-existence of a Lord, primordial nature, and so forth. If, however, name-and-form were to arise from a non-existent Lord or the like, then that very state of uniformity would result for all, everywhere, and always. If, on the other hand, only name-and-form has a Lord or the like as its cause, and name-and-form is seen to arise without having been and to perish after having been, then the Lord and the like must also be of such a nature. And so, that too would be with a cause and merely conditioned, and its cause would also have to be comprehended. But if that (Lord) does not arise, causelessness is entailed for it. For that reason, he said, “because it would entail the state of being causeless.”

Apica na issarādihetukaṃ nāmarūpaṃ. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Kamena uppattito. Yadi hi evaṃ niccaṃ [V 2.0347] issarādisaññitaṃ kammakilesindriyārammaṇādinirapekkhakāraṇampi siyā, sabbesaṃyeva ekajjhaṃ uppatti siyā, yattakehi tato uppajjitabbaṃ. Kasmā? Kāraṇassa sannihitabhāvato. Yadi pana tassa icchāvasena tassa uppattiṃ parikappeyyuṃ, tāsañca icchānaṃ ekajjhaṃ uppattiyaṃ ko vibandho. Atha aññampi kiñci kammakilesindriyārammaṇādiapekkhitabbaṃ atthīti ce? Tadeva hetu kāraṇaṃ, kimaññena adiṭṭhasāmatthiyena parikappitena payojanaṃ? Diṭṭhañhi kammādīnaṃ sāmatthiyaṃ tadaññapaccayasannidhānepi tadabhāve abhāvato. Yathā hi rūpālokamanasikārasannidhānepi cakkhuno abhāve cakkhuviññāṇassa abhāvaṃ, bhāve ca bhāvaṃ disvā cakkhuno cakkhuviññāṇuppādanasamatthatā atthīti viññāyati. Yathā ca yvāyaṃ yamakānampi samānānaṃ janakajananīsukkasoṇitādibāhirapaccayasamabhāvepi sattānaṃ hīnapaṇītatādiviseso dissati, so ca sasantāne tādisassa aññassa hetuno abhāvā kammakilesahetukoti tassa tattha samatthatā atthīti viññāyati, na evamissarādikassa. Kāraṇassa hi bhāvābhāve phalassa bhāvābhāvehi kāraṇassa samatthatā viññāyeyya. Na ca sannihite tadakāraṇassa nāmarūpassa issarādivekallena katthaci anuppatti diṭṭhā, tasmā akāraṇamissaro.

Furthermore, name-and-form is not caused by a Lord or the like. What is the reason? Because it arises sequentially. For if there were a single, permanent cause designated as a Lord, etc., which is independent of kamma, defilements, faculties, objects, and so on, then all that should arise from it would arise simultaneously. Why? Because of the presence of the cause. If, however, one were to suppose that its arising is by the power of that one's will, what hindrance would there be to the simultaneous arising of those volitions? Or if it is supposed that there is something else to be depended upon, such as kamma, defilements, faculties, objects, and so on, then that very thing is the true cause. What is the use of another postulated cause with unseen power? For the efficacy of kamma and so forth is seen, because in their absence there is an absence of the effect, even when other supporting conditions are present. For example, just as it is known that the eye faculty has the capacity to produce eye-consciousness—having seen the absence of eye-consciousness in the absence of the eye faculty and its presence in its presence, even when form, light, and attention are present. And just as, even in the case of similar twins, when the external conditions such as the semen and blood of the father and mother are the same, a distinction among beings, such as inferiority and superiority, is seen; and because of the absence of another such cause in their own continuum, it is known that this distinction is caused by kamma and defilements and that they have the efficacy for that. It is not so in the case of a Lord or the like. For the efficacy of a cause should be known by the presence and absence of the effect corresponding to the presence and absence of the cause. And the non-arising of name-and-form anywhere due to the lack of a Lord, etc., when that supposed cause is present, has not been seen. Therefore, a Lord is not the cause.

Athāpi saggo evaṃ issarādihetuko vucceyya, sopi saggappakāro sabbakālaṃ tato nibbatteyya. Na hi sannihitakāraṇassa phalassa anuppatti yuttā. Nicce ca sati aññanirapekkhakāraṇe saggassa ādiyeva na yutto, yāva issarādikaṃ kāraṇaṃ, tāva sabbassa atthibhāvappasaṅgato. Athāpi vadeyya “aññepi yathārahaṃ paccayā hontiyeva, issarādikampi tesaṃ sahakārīkāraṇaṃ hotī”ti. Yadettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Yadi paro vadeyya “idha buddhipubbo bhāvānaṃ racanāviseso diṭṭho, yathā taṃ ghaṭagehādīnaṃ. Atthi ca ajjhattikabāhirānaṃ sarīrapadumādīnaṃ racanāviseso, tasmā tenāpi buddhipubbena bhavitabbaṃ. Yassa ca so buddhipubbo, so issarādiko, tasmā tena nāmarūpasaññitassa lokassa kāraṇena bhavitabba”nti. Tayidaṃ asiddhaṃ, racitā sarīrapadumādayoti [M 2.0371] tattheva uppannattā. Uppannassa hi sannivesavasena tathā tathā paṭṭhapanaṃ “racanā”ti vuccati. Anekantiko cāyaṃ abuddhipubbassāpi diṭṭhattā. Diṭṭho hi nhāruādīnaṃ aggisaṃyogena racanāviseso, tathā visussantānaṃ pubbacammādīnaṃ. Yadi panāyamissarādiko gavassajagadrabhādīnaṃ karīsāvatte paṭimahutaṃ raceyya, ummatto viya vikkhitto siyā. Kiñcāyaṃ lokaṃ sajjento attatthaṃ vā sajjeyya lokatthaṃ vā.

Or alternatively, if it were said that creation has a cause such as Issara, then that kind of creation would be produced from that cause at all times. Indeed, the non-arising of a result from a well-established cause is not suitable. And when there is a permanent cause that is independent of anything else, the very beginning of creation is not suitable; because for as long as the cause, such as Issara, exists, it would follow that creation exists. Or alternatively, if one were to say: 'Other conditions also exist according to what is appropriate, and Issara and so on is a cooperative cause for them.' What should be said here has already been stated below. If another were to say: 'Here, a distinctive arrangement of things preceded by intelligence is seen, as in the case of pots, houses, and so on. And there is a distinctive arrangement of internal and external things, such as bodies, lotuses, and so on; therefore, that too must be preceded by intelligence. And he whose intelligence precedes it is Issara and so on; therefore, he must be the cause of the world designated as name-and-form.' This is unproven—that bodies, lotuses, and so on are arranged—because they arise just as they are. For the establishment of what has arisen in such and such a way by means of its composition is called 'arrangement'. And this is inconclusive, because it is also seen without being preceded by intelligence. For a distinctive arrangement of sinews and so on is seen through contact with fire, and likewise of drying flowers, leather, and so on. But if this Issara and so on were to create a cow, horse, goat, donkey, and so on in a coil of dung every moment, he would be like a madman, distracted. Furthermore, in creating the world, would he create it for his own benefit or for the world’s benefit?

Tattha [V 2.0348] ca yadi purimo makkho katakicco na siyā lokena sādhetabbassa atthibhāvato. Atha dutiyo, kasmā lokassa ahitadukkhāvahaṃ pāpaṃ nirayādiṃ, jarāmaraṇādiñca sajati? Atha tadubhayaṃ anāmasitvā kīḷatthaṃ sajati. Kīḷā ca nāma ratiatthā hoti. Vinā kīḷāya ratiṃ ajānantānaṃ ratiatthañca kīḷamārabhanto ratiyaṃ issaro anissaro siyā. Atha payojananirapekkho, sabbakālaṃ sajeyya, tassa cāyaṃ sajanasamatthatā ahetukā vā siyā sahetukā vā. Ahetukā ce, sabbesaṃ siyā sahetukā vā. Ahetukā ce, sabbesampi siyā. Atha sahetukā, so cassa hetu parato vā sambhūto siyā attato vā. Tattha parato ce sambhūto, yadassa so laddho, tassāyaṃ veyyāvaccakarasadiso siyā. Atha attato taduppattito pubbe ayaṃ kīdiso loko cāti sabbamidaṃ ālunavisiṇaṃ ākulabyākulaṃ goyūthena gatamaggasadisapheṇapiṇḍasamaṃ avimaddakkhamaṃ asāraṃ. Tiṭṭhatu pasaṅgo, yathādhikatameva vaṇṇayissāma. Tasmāti yasmā idaṃ nāmarūpaṃ na ahetukaṃ, nāpi issarādivisamahetukaṃ, tasmā. Teti hetupaccayā.

Among those two alternatives, if it were the first, he would not be one who has completed his task, because there exists something to be accomplished by means of the world. Now, if it were the second, why does he create evil that brings non-benefit and suffering to the world, such as hell, and aging and death? Then, not considering either of the two, he creates for the sake of sport. But sport is for the sake of pleasure. For one who does not know pleasure without sport and who undertakes sport for the sake of pleasure, the Lord would not be a master in regard to pleasure. Then, being indifferent to any purpose, he would create always, and this creative ability of his would be either without a cause or with a cause. If it were without a cause, it would belong to everyone. Now, if it were with a cause, that cause of his would have arisen either from another or from himself. Among these two, if it arose from another, from whom he obtained that cause, this Lord would be like a servant to that one. Now, if from himself, then before its arising, what was this Lord like, and what was the world like? All this is cut up and scattered, confused and confounded, like a path trodden by a herd of cattle, like a lump of foam, unable to withstand pressure, insubstantial. Let this digression stand; we shall comment only upon what has been transmitted. Therefore: because this name-and-form is not without a cause, nor does it have an un-uniform cause such as a Lord, therefore... 'Those' means the causes and conditions.

679. Oḷārikattā, supākaṭattā ca rūpassa paccayapariggaho sukaroti “imassa tāva rūpakāyassā”tiādinā paṭhamaṃ tassa paccayapariggahavidhiṃ ārabhati. Tattha yathā nāmarūpassa paccayapariggaho ahetuvisamahetuvādanivattiyā hoti, evaṃ nibbidāvirāgāvahabhāvena tattha abhiratinivattiyāpi icchitabboti taṃ gabbhaseyyakavasena dassento nibbattaṭṭhānassa sucibhāvapaṭisedhanamukhena asucibhāvaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “ayaṃ kāyo”tiādimāha. Tattha uppalādīni asuciṭṭhāne nibbattānipi [M 2.0372] sayaṃ sucisammatānevāti taṃdassanatthaṃ abbhantaraggahaṇaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā –

679. Because of the grossness and manifestness of material form, the grasping of its conditions is easy; thus, with the words, “first, of this material body…,” he first begins the method of grasping its conditions. Here, just as the grasping of conditions for name-and-form is for the purpose of dispelling the theories of causelessness and un-uniform cause, so too it should be desired for the purpose of dispelling delight in it, by way of its leading to disenchantment and dispassion. In order to show this by way of the lying in the womb, and to clarify its impurity by means of denying the purity of its place of origin, he says, “this body….” Here, lotuses and the like, though arisen in an impure place, are themselves considered pure; for the purpose of showing this distinction, the word “internal” is included. Therefore the Blessed One said:

“Yathā saṅkāradhānasmiṃ, ujjhitasmiṃ mahāpathe;

Padumaṃ tattha jāyetha, sucigandhaṃ manorama”nti. (dha. pa. 58);

“Just as upon a rubbish heap, cast away on the highway, a lotus might grow there, of pure fragrance and delightful to the mind.”

“Nibbattatī”ti idaṃ mātukucchiyaṃ paṭisandhipavattīsu rūpakāyassa nibbattanasāmaññato gahetvā vuttaṃ, na paṭhamābhinibbattimattaṃ. Evañca katvā āhārassa upatthambhakapaccayatāvacanaṃ, udarapaṭalassa pacchato karaṇādivacanaṃ, duggandhajegucchapaṭikkūlatāvacanañca samatthitaṃ hoti. Evamavaṭṭhite yadekaccehi piṭṭhito, purato ca karaṇaṃ kiṃ siyā paṭisandhikāletiādi vuttaṃ, taṃ [V 2.0349] apāhataṃ hoti. “Nibbattakattā”ti iminā bījaṃ viya aṅkurassa avijjādayo rūpakāyassa asādhāraṇakāraṇatāya hetūti dasseti. “Upatthambhakattā”ti iminā pana aṅkurassa pathavīsalilapārisiādayo viya āhāro sādhāraṇakāraṇatāya paccayoti dasseti.

The term ‘is produced’ is stated by taking it in a general sense with regard to the production of the material body during relinking and the course of existence in the mother’s womb, not merely its initial production. And by doing so, the statement about food as a supporting condition, the statement about the abdominal membrane being behind, etc., and the statement of its foul smell, loathsomeness, and repulsiveness are all established. When this is thus established, what has been said by some—such as, 'How could there be a making of a back and front at the time of relinking?'—is refuted. By the term ‘by being a producer,’ it shows that ignorance and so forth are generating causes (hetu) in the sense of being the uncommon causes of the material body, like a seed for a sprout. But by the term ‘by being a supporter,’ it shows that food is a supporting condition (paccaya) in the sense of being a common cause, like earth, water, the sun's rays, etc., for a sprout.

Pañca dhammā hetupaccayāti avijjādayo pañca dhammā yathārahaṃ hetu ca paccayo cāti attho. Bhavesu vijjamānadosapaṭicchādanapatthanā daḷhaggāhabhāvena saṅkhārabhavānaṃ hetubhūtā janakasahāyatāya bhavanikanti taṃsahajātaāsannakāraṇattā abhisaṅkhārikā, apassayabhūtā cāti “mātā viya dārakassa upanissayā”ti vuttā. Yathā pitu janitasukke puttassa uppattīti pitā janako, evaṃ kammaṃ sattassa uppādakattā janakaṃ vuttaṃ. Yathā dhāti jātassa dārakassa posanavasena sandhārikā, evaṃ āhāro uppannassa kāyassāti sandhārako vutto.

‘Five things are causes and conditions’ means that the five things beginning with ignorance are, as is fit, both a generating cause and a supporting condition. Ignorance, craving, and clinging—by their nature of concealing the faults existing in states of existence, desiring, and strong grasping, respectively—become the cause for formations and existence. By assisting the generator [kamma], and because craving delights in existence while ignorance and clinging are its co-nascent and proximate causes, they are formative and a support. Thus, they are said to be 'a decisive support like a mother for a child.' Just as a father is the generator because of the production of a son in the sperm he has generated, so kamma is called the generator because it produces a being. Just as a wet-nurse is the sustainer of a born child by way of nourishing it, so food is called the sustainer of the arisen body.

Kāmañcettha avijjādayo nāmakāyassāpi paccayo, pakārantarena pana tassa pākaṭaṃ paccayapariggahavidhiṃ dassetuṃ “cakkhuñca paṭiccā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha cakkhuñcāti ca-saddo samuccayattho. Tena cakkhuviññāṇassa āvajjanādiajjhattaṃ sabbaṃ paccayajātaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Rūpe cāti pana ca-saddena yathā bahulaṃ bāhirarūpaṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa ārammaṇapaccayo, evaṃ aññampi bāhiraṃ paccayajātaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Paṭiccāti paccayabhūtaṃ [M 2.0373] laddhāti attho. Tena cakkhussa nissayapurejātaindriyavippayuttaatthiavigatavasena, rūpassa ārammaṇapurejātaatthiavigatavasena, itaresañca saṅgahitānaṃ anantarādisahajātādivasena paccayabhāvaṃ dasseti. Vacanabhede pana kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Ādi-saddena ca phassādīnaṃ viya sahapaccayehi sotaviññāṇādīnaṃ saṅgaho veditabbo “tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso”tiādipāṭhassa (ma. ni. 1.204; 3.421, 425-426; saṃ. ni. 2.43-45; kathā. 465, 467) viya “sotañca paṭiccā”tiādipāṭhassa saṅgahitattā. Evaṃ sammasanupagaṃ sabbaṃ nāmaṃ sahapaccayena saṅgahitaṃ hoti. Tenāha “nāmakāyassa paccayapariggahaṃ karotī”ti.

Although here ignorance and so on are also conditions for the mental body, nevertheless, in order to show the method of grasping its conditions in another, manifest way, the passage beginning ‘dependent on the eye and…’ was stated. Here, in ‘the eye and,’ the word ‘and’ has the sense of collection. By this, it includes the entire set of internal conditions for eye-consciousness, such as adverting. And in ‘and forms,’ by the word ‘and,’ just as an external form is for the most part the object condition for eye-consciousness, so too it includes the other external sets of conditions. ‘Dependent on’ means ‘having obtained the state of being a condition.’ By this it shows the conditionality of the eye by way of dependence, pre-nascence, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance; of form by way of object, pre-nascence, presence, and non-disappearance; and of the other included factors by way of contiguity, co-nascence, and so on. The reason for the difference in wording has been stated above. And by the word ‘etc.’, the inclusion of ear-consciousness and so on with their accompanying conditions should be understood, just like the inclusion of contact and so on, because the passage beginning ‘dependent on the ear and…’ is included, just as the passage beginning ‘the meeting of the three is contact’ is. In this way, all mentality that is subject to comprehension is included along with its conditions. Therefore it is said: ‘he makes a grasping of the conditions for the mental body.’

Pavattiṃ disvāti etarahi pavattiṃ disvā. Evanti iminā na kevalaṃ sappaccayatāmattameva paccāmaṭṭhaṃ, atha kho yādisehi paccayehi etarahi pavattati, tādisehi avijjādipaccayeheva atītepi pavattitthāti paccayasadisatāpi paccāmaṭṭhāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

‘Having seen the occurrence’ means having seen the occurrence at the present time. ‘Thus’: by this, it should be understood that not only is the mere fact of conditionality reviewed, but the similarity of conditions is also reviewed, namely, that just as it occurs now with certain conditions, so too in the past it occurred with those same kinds of conditions, such as ignorance and so on.

680. Pubbantanti [V 2.0350] atītaṃ khandhappabandhakoṭṭhāsaṃ. Ārabbhāti uddissa. Ahosiṃ nu kho, na nu kho ahosinti sassatākāraṃ, adhiccasamuppattiākārañca nissāya atīte attano vijjamānataṃ, avijjamānatañca kaṅkhati. Kiṃ nu kho ahosinti jātiliṅgūpapattiyo nissāya “khattiyo nu kho ahosiṃ, brāhmaṇādīsu gahaṭṭhādīsu devādīsu aññataro nu kho”ti kaṅkhati. Kathaṃ nu khoti saṇṭhānākāraṃ nissāya “dīgho nu kho ahosiṃ, rassaodātakāḷapamāṇikaappamāṇikādīnampi aññataro”ti kaṅkhati. Issaranimmānādiṃ nissāya “kena nu kho pakārena ahosi”nti nibbattākārato kaṅkhatīti ca vadanti. Kiṃ hutvā kiṃ ahosinti jātiādiṃ nissāya “khattiyo hutvā nu kho brāhmaṇo ahosiṃ…pe… devo hutvā nu kho manusso ahosi”nti attano aparāparuppattiṃ kaṅkhati. Sabbattheva ca addhānanti kālādhivacanaṃ. Bhavissāmi nu khoti sassatākāraṃ, ucchedākārañca nissāya anāgate attano vijjamānataṃ, avijjamānatañca kaṅkhati. Sesamettha vuttanayameva. Etarahi vā pana paccuppannaṃ addhānanti idāni vā paṭisandhimādiṃ katvā cutipariyantaṃ sabbampi vattamānakālaṃ. Ajjhattaṃ kathaṃkathī hotīti attano khandhesu vicikicchā hoti. Ahaṃ nu khosmīti attano atthibhāvaṃ kaṅkhati. Ayuttaṃ [M 2.0374] panetanti. Yuttaṃ ayuttanti kā ettha cintā. Ummattako viya hi bālaputhujjano. No nu khosmīti attano natthibhāvaṃ kaṅkhati. Kiṃ nu khosmīti khattiyova samāno attano khattiyabhāvaṃ kaṅkhati. Esa nayo sesesu. Kathaṃ nu khosminti vuttanayameva. Kevalañhettha “abbhantare jīvo nāma atthī”ti gahetvā tassa dīghādibhāvaṃ kaṅkhanto “kathaṃ nu khosmi”nti kaṅkhatīti veditabbo. Paccuppannaṃ pana attano sarīrasaṇṭhānaṃ ajānanto nāma natthi. Kuto āgato, so kuhiṃ gāmī bhavissatīti attabhāvassa āgatigatiṭṭhānaṃ kaṅkhati. Sā sabbāpi pahīyatīti sā yathāvuttā soḷasavidhāpi vicikicchā vikkhambhanavasena pahīyati.

680. ‘The past’ means the past portion of the continuum of aggregates. ‘Concerning’ means having aimed at. ‘Did I exist? Did I not exist?’—he doubts his own existence and non-existence in the past, based on the mode of eternalism and the mode of fortuitous origination. ‘What was I?’—he doubts based on birth, characteristics, and rebirth, wondering: ‘Was I a khattiya, or some other among brahmins, etc.?’ ‘How was I?’—he doubts based on the mode of physical form, wondering: ‘Was I tall, or some other among the short, fair, dark, of medium size, or of immeasurable size, etc.?’ And some say that based on creation by a Lord, etc., he doubts the mode of his coming into being, wondering, ‘In what way did I exist?’ ‘Having been what, what did I become?’—he doubts his successive rebirths based on birth, etc., wondering: ‘Having been a khattiya, did I become a brahmin?… Having been a deva, did I become a human?’ And in all cases, ‘the time’ is a designation for a temporal period. ‘Will I exist? Will I not exist?’—he doubts his own existence and non-existence in the future, based on the mode of eternalism and the mode of annihilationism. The rest here is just as has been stated. ‘Or now, the present time’ means the entire present time, from rebirth-linking up to the end at death. ‘He is doubtful internally’ means he has doubt about his own aggregates. ‘Am I?’—he doubts his own existence. But this is inappropriate. What thought is there here of ‘appropriate’ or ‘inappropriate’? For the foolish worldling is like a madman. ‘Am I not?’—he doubts his own non-existence. ‘What am I?’—though he is a khattiya, he doubts his own state of being a khattiya. This is the method for the rest. ‘How am I?’ is just as has been stated. It should be understood that here, however, having grasped that ‘there is an inner being called a self,’ he doubts its being long, etc., and thus doubts, ‘How am I?’ But there is no one who does not know the shape of his own present body. ‘From where has this being come? Where will it go?’—he doubts the place of arrival and departure of his individual existence. ‘All that is abandoned’ means that all sixteen kinds of doubt as described are abandoned by way of suppression.

681. Kusalādibhedato sabbappakārassāpi nāmassa sādhāraṇo paccayoti, tato pavattito manasikārādiko kusalādibhedato sabbappakārassāpi nāmassa asādhāraṇo paccayoti ca yojetabbaṃ. Kusalādibhedatoti kusalākusalavipākakiriyabhedato. Tassāpi somanassasahagatādiaññatarabhedavasena sabbappakārassāpi. Yaṃ ekantato chadvārikaṃ, tampi chadvāraggahaṇeneva gahitaṃ yathā chaṭṭhārammaṇaṃ chaḷārammaṇaggahaṇenātipi vuttaṃ “sabbappakārassāpī”ti. Tatoti cakkhurūpādito. Manasikārādikoti yonisomanasikāraayonisomanasikārādiko[V 2.0351], kammabhavaṅgādiko ca. Kāmañcettha dvāracchakkayonisomanasikārādivasena nāmasseva sādhāraṇo, asādhāraṇo ca paccayo vutto, taṃ pana avisesavasena vuttaṃ. Visesato pana kammaṃ vipākanāmassa, kammasamuṭṭhānarūpānañca cittaṃ cetasikanāmassa, cittasamuṭṭhānarūpānañca sādhāraṇo paccayo, yathāvuttasseva ca nāmassa, rūpassa ca tadaññanāmarūpāpekkhāya asādhāraṇo paccayo. Tathā sabhāgo, utusabhāgo ca āhāro taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpānaṃ sādhāraṇo paccayo, tadaññāpekkhāya asādhāraṇoti rūpassāpi sādhāraṇo, asādhāraṇo ca paccayo yathārahaṃ niddhāretabbo. Paccayapariggaho nāma anadhigatārahattena kātabboti tadapekkhāya “yonisomanasikārasaddhammassavanādiko kusalassevā”ti vuttaṃ. Ādi-saddena sappurisūpanissayassa, catunnampi vā sampatticakkānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Viparīto akusalassāti vacanato yathā yonisomanasikārādiviparīto akusalasseva [M 2.0375] paccayo, tathā yonisomanasikārādi kusalasseva paccayo hotīti attho. Yassa vā kusalaṃ sambhavati, akusalaṃ sambhavati, kusalākusalāni vā, tassāti atthasiddhametaṃ. Kammādikoti ādi-saddena avijjādayo viya gatikālādayopi saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbā. Bhavaṅgādikoti bhavaṅgasantīraṇaparittakiriyārahattādiko. Tattha bhavaṅgaṃ pañcadvāramanodvārāvajjanakiriyānaṃ, santīraṇaṃ voṭṭhabbanassa, parittakiriyā yathārahaṃ parittamahaggatakiriyānaṃ, arahattaṃ āvajjanavajjānaṃ sabbakiriyānaṃ paccayoti veditabbaṃ.

681. It should be connected thus: '...is a common condition for every kind of mentality, distinguished as wholesome, etc.,' and 'attention, etc., which arises from that, is an uncommon condition for every kind of mentality, distinguished as wholesome, etc.' 'Distinguished as wholesome, etc.' means distinguished as wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional. And of that also, by way of the distinction of being one or another among those accompanied by joy, etc., it is of every kind. That which is exclusively six-doored is also included by the taking of the six doors, just as the sixth object is included by the taking of the six objects; thus it is said 'for every kind.' 'From that' means from eye and form, etc. 'Attention, etc.' means wise attention, unwise attention, etc., and kamma, life-continuum, etc. Although here, by way of the six doors, wise attention, etc., a common and an uncommon condition for mentality alone are stated, this is said in a general way. Specifically, however, kamma is a common condition for resultant mentality and for materiality originating from kamma; and consciousness is a common condition for mental factors and for materiality originating from consciousness. And for that same mentality and materiality as stated, it is an uncommon condition with respect to other mentality-and-materiality. Similarly, temperature of the same nature and nutriment of the same nature are a common condition for materiality originating from them, and an uncommon condition with respect to other materiality. Thus, for materiality too, the common and uncommon conditions should be determined as is appropriate. The comprehension of conditions is to be undertaken by one who has not attained arahantship; with reference to this it is said: 'Wise attention, hearing the good Dhamma, etc., are for the wholesome only.' By the word 'etc.,' association with superior persons or the four wheels of accomplishment should be understood as included. From the statement 'The opposite is for the unwholesome,' the meaning is that just as what is the opposite of wise attention, etc., is a condition for the unwholesome only, so wise attention, etc., is a condition for the wholesome only. Or, for that worldling or trainee in whom the wholesome can arise, the unwholesome can arise, or both wholesome and unwholesome can arise—this meaning is established by the sense. 'Kamma, etc.': by the word 'etc.,' it should be understood that just as ignorance, etc., so too destination, time, etc., are included. 'Life-continuum, etc.' means life-continuum, investigating, limited functional, arahantship, etc. Herein, it should be known that life-continuum is a condition for the five-door and mind-door adverting functional consciousnesses; investigating is for determining; limited functional consciousness is, as appropriate, for limited and sublime functional consciousnesses; and arahantship is for all functional consciousnesses except adverting.

Kammanti cetanāva adhippetā, sā ca kho kusalākusalā. Vuttañhetaṃ “kusalākusalacetanā vipākānaṃ khandhānaṃ, kaṭattā ca rūpānaṃ kammapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.427). Na cittaṃ viya sasampayuttā. Cittañhettha sasampayuttaṃ adhippetaṃ “hetū hetusampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ, taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ hetupaccayena paccayo”tiādivacanato (paṭṭhā. 1.1.1). Tatthāti tesu kammādīsu rūpajanakapaccayesu. Atītato eva kammato phalaṃ uppajjati, na vattamānatoti vuttaṃ “kammaṃ atītameva kammasamuṭṭhānassa rūpassa paccayo”ti. Yadi hi paccuppannato kammato phalaṃ uppajjeyya, āyūhanakkhaṇe eva phalena uppajjitabbaṃ bhaveyya, na ca taṃ diṭṭhamicchitaṃ vā. Na hi loke kudācanaṃ kariyamānameva kammaṃ phalaṃ dentaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, tathārūpo vā āgamo atthīti. Nanu ca idamapi na diṭṭhaṃ, yaṃ vinaṭṭhato hetuto phalaṃ uppajjamānaṃ, mato vā kukkuṭo vassantoti? Saccamadiṭṭhaṃ rūpadhammānaṃ pabandhavicchede, idaṃ pana arūpaṃ pabandhopi atthīti upamā na saṃsandati. Kammato hi atītato [V 2.0352] eva kammassa katattā, upacitattā ca phalaṃ uppajjati. Vuttañhetaṃ “kāmāvacarassa kusalassa kammassa katattā upacitattā vipākaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ uppannaṃ hotī”tiādi (dha. sa. 431). Yasmā anantarādipaccayalābhato uppādakkhaṇe eva cittassa balavatā, tasmā taṃ uppajjamānameva rūpaṃ janetīti āha “cittaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānassa uppajjamāna”nti. Rūpassa paccayo hotīti sambandho. Yasmā pana rūpassa ṭhitikkhaṇe balavatā pacchājātādipaccayalābhato, tasmā vuttaṃ “utuāhārā…pe… hontī”ti, bāhiraṃ utuṃ, āhārañca paccayaṃ labhitvā attano ṭhitikkhaṇe utuāhārā rūpaṃ janentīti attho.

By 'kamma,' volition is intended, and that is wholesome and unwholesome. For it is said: 'Wholesome and unwholesome volition is a condition by way of kamma-condition for the resultant aggregates and for materiality produced by that kamma' (Paṭṭh. 1.1.427). Unlike consciousness, it is not intended along with its associated states. For here, consciousness is intended as associated with its conascent states, because of such statements as: 'Roots are a condition by way of root-condition for root-associated states and for materiality originated by them' (Paṭṭh. 1.1.1). 'Therein' means among those conditions that generate materiality, such as kamma. The result arises from past kamma only, not from present kamma; thus it is said: 'Only past kamma is a condition for kamma-originated materiality.' For if the result were to arise from present kamma, the result would have to arise at the very moment of exertion, which is neither seen nor desired. For it is never seen in the world that a kamma being performed gives its result, nor is there any such scriptural text. But is it not also unseen that a result arises from a cause that has perished, or that a dead rooster crows? True, this is unseen when the continuity of material phenomena is interrupted, but since for this immaterial phenomenon there is continuity, the simile does not fit. For the result arises from past kamma only because the kamma has been done and has been accumulated. For it is said: 'Because a wholesome kamma of the sense-sphere has been done and accumulated, resultant eye-consciousness has arisen,' etc. (Dhs. 431). Because consciousness is powerful at the very moment of arising due to obtaining conditions such as proximity, therefore, just as it is arising it generates materiality. Thus he said: 'consciousness, while arising, for consciousness-originated [materiality].' The connection is: 'is a condition for materiality.' But because materiality is powerful at its static moment due to obtaining postnascence condition, etc., it is said: 'Temperature and nutriment... are.' The meaning is that temperature and nutriment, having obtained an external temperature and nutriment as condition, generate materiality at their own static moment.

Evanti [M 2.0376] “sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇavasenā”tiādinā vuttappakārena.

'Thus' means in the way stated beginning with 'by way of common and uncommon.'

682. Saṅkhārānanti saṅkhatasaṅkhārānaṃ. Bhaṅganti maraṇaṃ. Jarāmaraṇaṃ nāma jātiyā satītiādi phaladassanānupubbiyā hetudassanakkamena nāmarūpassa paccayapariggaho sukaroti katvā dassito. Tattha bhave satīti kammabhave sati.

682. 'Of formations' means of conditioned formations. 'Breaking up' means death. It is shown in the manner beginning with 'When there is birth, there is aging-and-death,' having considered that the comprehension of the conditions for mentality-materiality becomes easy by the sequence of seeing the fruit and by the order of seeing the cause. Therein, 'when there is existence' means when there is kamma-existence.

683.
