Pubbe vitthāretvā dassitaanulomapaṭiccasamuppādavasenāti pariyosānato paṭṭhāya paṭilomanayena ādipāpanavasena vitthāretvā dassitaanulomapaṭiccasamuppādavasena. “Asati jātiyā natthi jarāmaraṇa”ntiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.4) hi paṭilomavasena dassite paccayākāre “yassa abhāvā yassa abhāvo, so tassa paccayo”ti byatirekato, anvayato ca nāmarūpassa paccayapariggaho sukaroti.

683. “By way of the dependent origination in forward order explained in detail before” means by way of the dependent origination in forward order explained in detail by the reverse method, starting from the end and leading back to the beginning. For when the conditional structure is shown in reverse order with the words, “When birth is absent, there is no aging-and-death,” etc., the comprehension of the conditions for mentality-materiality becomes easy both negatively—“that because of the absence of which this is absent, is its condition”—and positively.

684. Purimakammabhavasmiṃ mohotiādi vuttatthameva. Kammasahāyattā kilesavaṭṭaṃ kammavaṭṭe pakkhitvā vuttaṃ “kammavaṭṭavipākavaṭṭavasenā”ti.

684. “Delusion, etc., in the previous kamma-existence” has the meaning already stated. Because it is an associate of kamma, the round of defilements is included in the round of kamma, and thus it is said, “by way of the round of kamma and the round of results.”

685. Diṭṭhadhammo vuccati paccakkhabhūto paccuppanno attabhāvo, tattha veditabbaphalaṃ kammaṃ diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ. Paccuppannabhavato anantaraṃ veditabbaphalaṃ kammaṃ upapajjavedanīyaṃ. Aparāpariyāyeti diṭṭhadhammānantarānāgatato aññasmiṃ attabhāvapariyāye attabhāvaparivatte. Ahosikammanti ahosi eva kammaṃ, na tassa vipāko ahosi, “atthi, bhavissati vā”ti evaṃ vattabbakammaṃ. Paṭipakkhehi anabhibhūtatāya, paccayavisesena paṭiladdhavisesatāya ca balavabhāvaṃ pattā tādisassa [V 2.0353] pubbābhisaṅkhārassa vasena sātisayā hutvā pavattā paṭhamajavanacetanā tasmiṃyeva attabhāve phaladāyinī diṭṭhadhammavedanīyā nāma. Sā hi vuttākārena balavati javanasantāne guṇavisesayuttesu upakārāpakāravasappavattiyā, āsevanālābhena appavipākatāya ca paṭhamajavanacetanā itaradvayaṃ viya pavattasantānuparamāpekkhaṃ, okāsalābhāpekkhañca kammaṃ na hotīti idheva pupphamattaṃ viya pavattivipākamattaṃ phalaṃ deti. Tathā asakkontanti kammassa vipākadānaṃ nāma upadhipayogādipaccayantarasamavāyeneva hotīti tadabhāvato [M 2.0377] tasmiṃyeva attabhāve vipākaṃ dātuṃ asakkontaṃ. Atthasādhikāti dānādipāṇātipātādiatthassa nipphādikā. Kā pana sāti āha “sattamajavanacetanā”ti. Sā hi sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā vuttanayena paṭiladdhavisesā, purimajavanacetanāhi laddhāsevanā ca samānā anantarattabhāve vipākadāyinī upapajjavedanīyakammaṃ nāma. “Sati saṃsārappavattiyā”ti iminā asati saṃsārappavattiyaṃ ahosikammapakkhe tiṭṭhati vipaccanokāsassa abhāvatoti dīpeti.

685. The “presently visible state” (diṭṭhadhamma) is said to be the directly perceived, present individual existence. Kamma whose fruit is to be experienced therein is kamma-to-be-experienced-in-the-here-and-now (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya). Kamma whose fruit is to be experienced immediately after the present existence is kamma-to-be-experienced-in-the-next-life (upapajjavedanīya). “In a subsequent life” (aparāpariyāye) means in another turn of existence, other than the present existence and the one immediately following it. “Defunct kamma” (ahosikamma) is kamma that has indeed occurred, but its result has not occurred, is not occurring, nor will it occur; it is kamma spoken of in this way. Having become powerful because it is not overcome by opposing factors and has attained a special quality through a particular condition, the first javana-volition, by way of such a prior volitional formation, becomes exceedingly potent and, being productive of fruit in that very same existence, is called kamma-to-be-experienced-in-the-here-and-now. For that first javana-volition—being powerful in the aforesaid manner in the javana-process, occurring by way of benefiting or harming those endowed with special qualities, and due to not obtaining the condition of repetition and having a weak result—is not, like the other two, kamma that awaits the cessation of the ongoing process or the gaining of an opportunity. Thus it gives its fruit right here, a mere result in the course of life like a mere flower. Similarly, “being unable” means that since the giving of a kamma’s fruit occurs only through the conjunction of other conditions such as the substrates of existence and effort, in their absence it is unable to give its fruit in that very existence. “Accomplishing the purpose” means accomplishing the purpose of acts such as giving or destroying life. What is that? It is said to be the “seventh javana-volition.” For that concluding volition, having attained a special quality in the way stated and having obtained the condition of repetition from the preceding javana-volitions, gives its fruit in the immediately following existence and is called kamma-to-be-experienced-in-the-next-life. By the words “as long as the round of rebirths continues,” it is shown that when the round of rebirths does not continue, it falls into the category of defunct kamma because there is no opportunity for it to ripen.

686. Yaṃ garukanti yaṃ akusalaṃ mahāsāvajjaṃ, kusalaṃ mahānubhāvaṃ kammaṃ. Yaṃ bahulanti yaṃ bahulaṃ abhiṇhaso kataṃ samāsevitaṃ. Maraṇakāle anussaritanti paribyattabhāvena maraṇassa āsannakāle anussaritaṃ. Āsannakāle kate vattabbameva natthīti hi vuttaṃ. “Punappunaṃ laddhāsevana”nti iminā “yaṃ bahula”nti vuttakammato viseseti. Tathā diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ nivatteti paṭisandhiākaḍḍhanānujānanato. Paṭisandhijanakavasena hi garukādikammacatukkaṃ vuttaṃ.

686. “What is weighty” refers to that kamma which, if unwholesome, is greatly reprehensible, and if wholesome, is of great power. “What is habitual” refers to that which is done many times, constantly, and well-practiced. “Remembered at the time of death” refers to that which is remembered with clarity at the time near death. For indeed, it is said that there is nothing to be said of kamma done at the time near death. By this phrase, “repeatedly practiced,” it specifies from the kamma called “what is habitual.” Thus, because it allows the drawing towards rebirth-linking, it prevents kamma that is to be experienced in the here-and-now from taking effect. For the fourfold kamma beginning with the weighty is stated in terms of generating rebirth-linking.

Tattha garukaṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ vipaccati. Tathā hi taṃ garukanti vuttaṃ. Garuke asati bahulīkataṃ, tasmiṃ asati āsannaṃ, tasmimpi asati “kaṭattā vā panā”ti vuttaṃ purimajātīsu katakammaṃ vipaccati. Bahulāsannapubbakatesu ca balābalaṃ vā jānitabbaṃ, pāpato pāpantaraṃ, kalyāṇañca, kalyāṇato ca kalyāṇantaraṃ, pāpañca, bahulīkatato ca mahato ca pubbakatādi, appañca. Bahulānussaraṇena vippaṭisārādijananato paṭipakkhassa aparipuṇṇatāya āraddhavipākassa kammassa, kammasesassa vā aparāpariyāye vedanīyassa aparikkhīṇatāya santatiyā pariṇāmavisesatoti tehi tehi kāraṇehi āhitabalaṃ paṭhamaṃ vipaccati. Mahānāradakassapajātake videharañño senāpati alāto, bījako dāso, rājakaññā rucā ca ettha nidassanaṃ. Tathā hi vuttaṃ bhagavatā –

Among these, the weighty kamma ripens first of all. For that is why it is called “weighty.” In the absence of weighty kamma, the habitual ripens. In its absence, the death-proximate ripens. In its absence, as it is said, “or because it has been done,” kamma done in previous lives ripens. And among the habitual, death-proximate, and previously done kammas, their relative strength and weakness should be known. From an evil kamma, another evil kamma or a good kamma may ripen; from a good kamma, another good kamma or an evil kamma; from a habitual, great, or previously done kamma, a small kamma. That kamma which has been empowered for these various reasons ripens first: because of generating remorse and the like through frequent recollection; because of the incompleteness of an opposing kamma; because of the non-exhaustion of a kamma whose result has begun to manifest, or of the remainder of a kamma to be experienced in a subsequent life; and because of a special transformation of the continuity. The general Alāta of King Videha, the slave Bījaka, and the princess Rucā in the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka are examples here. For so it was said by the Blessed One:

“Tatrānanda[V 2.0354], yvāyaṃ puggalo idha pāṇātipātī…pe… micchādiṭṭhi kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati. Pubbe vāssa taṃ kataṃ hoti pāpakammaṃ dukkhavedanīyaṃ, pacchā vāssa taṃ kataṃ hoti pāpakammaṃ dukkhavedanīyaṃ[M 2.0378], maraṇakāle vāssa hoti micchādiṭṭhi samattā samādinnā, tena so kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati. Yañca kho so idha pāṇātipātī hoti…pe… micchādiṭṭhi hoti, tassa diṭṭhe vā dhamme vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti upapajja vā apare vā pariyāye.

“Ānanda, in this world, a certain person is one who destroys life... holds wrong view. On the dissolution of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, a place of downfall, in hell. Either that evil kamma which is to be experienced as painful was done by him previously, or that evil kamma which is to be experienced as painful was done by him subsequently, or at the time of death wrong view was taken up and undertaken by him. Because of that, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, a place of downfall, in hell. And as for the fact that this person here is one who destroys life... holds wrong view, he experiences the result of that either in this very life, or in the next life, or in a subsequent life.”

“Tatrānanda, yvāyaṃ puggalo idha pāṇātipātī…pe… micchādiṭṭhi kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. Pubbe vāssa taṃ kataṃ hoti kalyāṇakammaṃ sukhavedanīyaṃ, pacchā vāssa taṃ kataṃ hoti kalyāṇakammaṃ sukhavedanīyaṃ, maraṇakāle vāssa hoti sammādiṭṭhi samattā samādinnā, tena so kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. Yañca kho so idha pāṇātipātī hoti…pe… micchādiṭṭhi hoti, tassa diṭṭhe vā dhamme vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti upapajja vā apare vā pariyāye.

Ānanda, here a certain person is one who destroys life... holds wrong view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Either he has previously done a good kamma that is to be experienced as pleasant, or he has subsequently done a good kamma that is to be experienced as pleasant, or at the time of death right view has been adopted and undertaken by him. Because of that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. And as for the fact that this person here is one who destroys life... holds wrong view, he experiences the result of that either in this very life, or in the next existence, or on a subsequent occasion.

“Tatrānanda, yvāyaṃ puggalo idha pāṇātipātā paṭivirato…pe… sammādiṭṭhi kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. Pubbe vāssa taṃ kataṃ hoti kalyāṇakammaṃ sukhavedanīyaṃ, pacchā vāssa taṃ kataṃ hoti kalyāṇakammaṃ sukhavedanīyaṃ, maraṇakāle vāssa hoti sammādiṭṭhi samattā samādinnā, tena so kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. Yañca kho so idha pāṇātipātā paṭivirato…pe… sammādiṭṭhi hoti, tassa diṭṭhe vā dhamme vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti upapajja vā apare vā pariyāye.

Ānanda, here a certain person is one who abstains from destroying life... holds right view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Either he has previously done a good kamma that is to be experienced as pleasant, or he has subsequently done a good kamma that is to be experienced as pleasant, or at the time of death right view has been adopted and undertaken by him. Because of that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. And as for the fact that this person here abstains from destroying life... holds right view, he experiences the result of that either in this very life, or in the next existence, or on a subsequent occasion.

“Tatrānanda, yvāyaṃ puggalo idha pāṇātipātā paṭivirato…pe… sammādiṭṭhi kāyassa bhedā paraṃ…pe… nirayaṃ upapajjati. Pubbe vāssa taṃ kataṃ hoti pāpakammaṃ dukkhavedanīyaṃ, pacchā vāssa taṃ kataṃ hoti pāpakammaṃ dukkhavedanīyaṃ, maraṇakāle vāssa hoti micchādiṭṭhi samattā samādinnā, tena so kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ [V 2.0355] …pe… nirayaṃ upapajjati. Yañca kho so idha pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hoti…pe… sammādiṭṭhi [M 2.0379] hoti, tassa diṭṭhe vā dhamme vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti upapajja vā apare vā pariyāye”ti (ma. ni. 3.303).

Ānanda, here a certain person is one who abstains from destroying life... holds right view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn... in hell. Either he has previously done an evil kamma that is to be experienced as painful, or he has subsequently done an evil kamma that is to be experienced as painful, or at the time of death wrong view has been adopted and undertaken by him. Because of that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a plane of misery... in hell. And as for the fact that this person here abstains from destroying life... holds right view, he experiences the result of that either in this very life, or in the next existence, or on a subsequent occasion.

Kiṃ bahunā yaṃ taṃ tathāgatassa mahākammavibhaṅgañāṇaṃ, tassevāyaṃ visayo, yadidaṃ tassa tassa kammassa tena tena kāraṇena pubbāparavipākatā sāmatthiyaṃ.

What more is there to say? This is the domain of the Tathāgata's knowledge of the great analysis of kamma, namely, the capacity for the earlier and later ripening of this or that kamma for this or that reason.

687. Paṭisandhidānādivasena vipākasantānassa nibbattakaṃ janakaṃ. Tenāha “taṃ paṭisandhiyampi pavattepi rūpārūpavipākakkhandhe janetī”ti. Sukhadukkhasantānassa, nāmarūpappabandhassa vā ciratarappavattihetubhūtaṃ upatthambhakaṃ. Tenāha “sukhadukkhaṃ upatthambheti, addhānaṃ pavattetī”ti. Upapīḷakaṃ sukhadukkhappabandhe pavattamāne saṇikaṃ saṇikaṃ taṃ hāpeti. Tenāha “sukhadukkhaṃ pīḷeti bādhati, addhānaṃ pavattituṃ na detī”ti. Ghātetvāti upacchinditvā. Kammassa upacchindanaṃ nāma tassa vipākapaṭibāhanamevāti āha “tassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā”ti. Tañca attano vipākuppattiyā okāsakaraṇanti vuttaṃ “attano vipākassa okāsaṃ karotī”ti. Vipaccanāya katokāsaṃ kammaṃ vipakkameva nāma hotīti āha “evaṃ pana kammena kate okāse taṃ vipākaṃ uppannaṃ nāma vuccatī”ti. Upapīḷakaṃ aññassa vipākaṃ upacchindati, na sayaṃ attano vipākaṃ deti. Upaghātakaṃ pana dubbalaṃ kammaṃ upacchinditvā attano vipākaṃ uppādetīti ayametesaṃ viseso. Bavhābādhatādipaccayūpanipātena vipākassa vibādhakaṃ upapīḷakaṃ, tathā vipākasseva upacchedakaṃ upaghātakaṃ. Kammaṃ upaghātetvā attano vipākassa okāsakaraṇena vipaccane sati janakameva siyā, janakādibhāvo nāma vipākaṃ pati icchitabbo, na kammaṃ patīti vipākasseva upaghātakatā yuttā viya dissati, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ.

687. Kamma that produces the continuity of result by way of giving rebirth-linking and so on is generative kamma. Therefore, it is said: 'It generates the resultant aggregates of form and formlessness both at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence.' Kamma that has become the cause for a more prolonged continuation of the continuity of pleasure and pain, or of the sequence of mentality-materiality, is supportive kamma. Therefore, it is said: 'It supports pleasure and pain and makes the duration continue.' As the sequence of pleasure and pain is proceeding, obstructive kamma gradually causes it to diminish. Therefore, it is said: 'It afflicts and obstructs pleasure and pain, not allowing the duration to continue.' 'Having destroyed' means having cut off. The cutting off of a kamma is just the warding off of its result; therefore, it is said: 'having warded off its result.' And that is said to be the making of an opportunity for its own result to arise: 'it makes an opportunity for its own result.' A kamma for which an opportunity has been made for ripening is indeed called 'ripened'; therefore, it is said: 'But when an opportunity has been made by kamma in this way, that result is said to have arisen.' Obstructive kamma cuts off the result of another kamma; it does not itself give its own result. Destructive kamma, however, having cut off a weak kamma, produces its own result—this is the distinction between them. That which obstructs the result through the impact of conditions such as much illness is obstructive kamma; similarly, that which cuts off the result itself is destructive kamma. If, having destroyed a kamma, there is ripening by making an opportunity for its own result, it would be only generative kamma. The state of being generative, etc., should be understood in relation to the result, not in relation to the kamma. Therefore, the quality of being destructive appears as if it were proper to the result itself. This should be investigated.

Kammantaranti kammaviseso kammānaṃ balābalabhedo. Vipākantaranti vipākaviseso, tassa hīnapaṇītatādibhedo. Aparo nayo – yasmiṃ kamme kate paṭisandhiyaṃ, pavatte ca vipākakaṭattārūpānaṃ uppatti hoti, taṃ janakaṃ. Yasmiṃ pana kate aññena janitassa iṭṭhassa vā aniṭṭhassa vā phalassa vibādhakavicchedakapaccayānuppattiyā, upabrūhanapaccayuppattiyā ca janakānubhāvānurūpaṃ pariposaciratarappabandhā honti, taṃ upatthambhakaṃ. Janakena [M 2.0380] nibbattitaṃ kusalaphalaṃ vā akusalaphalaṃ vā yena paccanīkabhūtena rogadhātusamatādinimittatāya bādhīyati, taṃ upapīḷakaṃ[V 2.0356]. Yena pana kammunā janakasāmatthiyavasena ciratarappabandhārahampi samānaṃ phalaṃ vicchedakapaccayuppattiyā upahaññati vicchijjati, taṃ upaghātakaṃ. Tattha keci dutiyassa kusalabhāvaṃ itthannāmagatassa appābādhadīghāyukatāsaṃvattanavasena, pacchimānaṃ dvinnaṃ akusalabhāvaṃ bavhābādhaappāyukatāsaṃvattanavasena vaṇṇenti. Devadattādīnaṃ, pana nāgādīnaṃ, ito anupadinnena yāpanakapetānañca narakādīsu akusalavipākupatthambhanupapīḷanupaghātakāni na na santīti catunnampi akusalākusalabhāvo na virujjhati. Buddhāveṇikatāya asādhāraṇasseva ñāṇassa gocarabhāvato kammantarādi “asādhāraṇaṃ sāvakehī”ti vuttaṃ. Ekadesato jānitabbaṃ anavasesato jānituṃ na sakkā avisayattā. Sabbena sabbaṃ ajānane paccayapariggaho na paripūratīti.

'The diversity of kamma' means the variety of kamma, its division into strong and weak. 'The diversity of result' means the variety of result, its division into inferior, superior, and so forth. Another method: When a kamma has been performed, and there is the arising of resultant kamma-born materiality at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence, this is generative kamma. However, when a kamma is performed, whereby for a desirable or undesirable fruit generated by another, a nourished and longer-lasting sequence occurs in accordance with the power of the generative kamma—through the arising of an afflicting and intercepting condition, as well as an enhancing condition—that is supportive kamma. That by which a wholesome or unwholesome fruit produced by a generative kamma is afflicted, it being an opponent in the form of a cause of illness, elemental balance, and so forth, is obstructive kamma. But that kamma by which a fruit, though fit for a long-lasting sequence by the power of the generative kamma, is destroyed and cut off by the arising of an intercepting condition, is destructive kamma. Therein, some describe the second type as wholesome for one who has attained such a state, on account of its conducing to little illness and long life, and the last two types as unwholesome on account of their conducing to much illness and short life. However, for Devadatta and others, for nāgas and others, and for the ghosts who sustain themselves on what is not given from here, supportive, obstructive, and destructive kammas for unwholesome results in the hells, etc., are certainly not absent. Thus, that all four types can be wholesome or unwholesome is not contradicted. Because the diversity of kamma and so on is the domain of a knowledge that is unique to the Buddhas and not shared with the disciples, it is said to be 'not shared by disciples.' It is to be known in part; it cannot be known completely because it is beyond their range. If one does not know it in every way, the full comprehension of conditionality is not perfected.

688. Yathāvuttaṃ kammaṃ vattamānavipākappabandhanimittameva adhippetanti kammekadesatāya “dvādasavidhaṃ kammaṃ kammavaṭṭe pakkhipitvā”ti vuttaṃ. Kilesavaṭṭampi kammasahāyatāya kammavaṭṭapakkhikameva katvā āha “kammavaṭṭavipākavaṭṭavasenā”ti. Yādisato paccayato paccuppanne addhāne nāmarūpassa pavatti, tādisato eva itarasmimpi addhadvayeti yathā atītānāgate nayaṃ neti, taṃ dassento “ida”ntiādimāha. Tattha anāgatepi kammavaṭṭavipākavaṭṭavasenevāti ettha vuttaṃ eva-saddaṃ “etarahi atītepī”ti etthāpi ānetvā vattabbaṃ addhattayepi kiriyākiriyaphalamattatādassanaparattā codanāya. Iti kammañcevātiādi vuttassevatthassa nigamanavasena vuttaṃ. Aparāparaṃ vaṭṭanaṭṭhena vaṭṭaṃ. Tathā pavattanaṃ pavattaṃ. Hetuphalabhāvena sambandhatīti santati, pabandho. Karaṇaṭṭhena, paccayehi karīyatīti vā kiriyā.

688. Since the aforesaid kamma is intended simply as the cause for the sequence of present result, it is said, 'having included the twelvefold kamma in the kamma-round,' due to its being a partial aspect of kamma. Having also treated the defilements-round as belonging only to the side of the kamma-round due to its being an assistant to kamma, he says: 'by way of the kamma-round and the result-round.' To show how one applies the method to the past and future—'just as from such a condition there is the occurrence of mentality-materiality in the present period, so too from such a condition in the other two periods'—he says, 'this,' etc. Here, the word 'eva' in the phrase 'even in the future, by way of the kamma-round and the result-round' should also be brought to bear on 'now and also in the past,' because the objection is primarily concerned with showing that in all three periods of time there is only action and the fruit of action. Thus, 'kamma indeed,' etc., is stated by way of a conclusion to the meaning already explained. It is a 'round' (vaṭṭa) in the sense of revolving again and again. Similarly, 'occurrence' (pavatta) is so called in the sense of proceeding. Because it connects by way of cause and fruit, it is 'continuity' (santati), a 'sequence' (pabandho). 'Action' (kiriyā) is so called in the sense of doing, or because it is done by conditions.

Kammāti kammato. Sambhavati etasmāti sambhavo, kammaṃ sambhavo etassāti kammasambhavo, vipāko.

'From kamma' (kammā) means from action (kammato). 'It arises from this,' thus 'origin' (sambhavo). 'Kamma is its origin,' thus 'kamma-originated' (kammasambhavo), which means the result.

Kāraṇasāmaggiyaṃ dānādīhi sādhitakiriyāya vattamānāya kāraṇamatte kattuvohāroti āha “neva kāraṇato uddhaṃ kārakaṃ passatī”ti. Karotīti hi kārakaṃ. Vipākapaṭisaṃvedakaṃ na passatīti sambandho[M 2.0381]. Kāmaṃ bālāpi “kārako paṭisaṃvedako”ti vadantā atthato paññattimattameva vadanti, te pana viparītābhinivesavasenāpi vadantīti taṃ appamāṇanti āha “samaññāmattena paṇḍitā voharantī”ti.

When, in the assemblage of causes, an action accomplished by giving, etc., is occurring, the designation 'doer' applies to the mere cause. Thus he said: 'One does not see a doer apart from the cause.' For a 'doer' (kāraka) is one who does (karoti). The connection is: 'one does not see an experiencer of the result.' Although fools, saying 'the doer is the experiencer,' in reality speak only of a mere concept, since they also speak under the influence of perverse adherence, that is not authoritative. Thus he said: 'The wise use speech only as a convention.'

689. Evetanti [V 2.0357] evaṃvidhaṃ etaṃ dassanaṃ, sammadassanaṃ, aviparītadassananti attho. Bījarukkhādikānaṃvāti yathā bījato rukkho, rukkhato puna bījanti anādikālikattā bījarukkhasantānassa pubbakoṭi natthi, evaṃ kammapaccayā vipāko, vipākapaccayā kammanti anādikālikattā kammavipākasantānassa pubbakoṭi na paññāyati. Ādi-saddena “kukkuṭiyā aṇḍaṃ, aṇḍato kukkuṭī, punapi kukkuṭiyā aṇḍa”nti evamādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Anāgatepi saṃsāreti yathā atīte, evaṃ anāgatepi addhāne “khandhānañca paṭipāṭī”tiādinā (visuddhi. 2.619; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.95 apasādanāvaṇṇanā; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.60; a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.4.199; dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā; vibha. aṭṭha. 226 saṅkhārapadaniddesa; su. ni. aṭṭha. 2.523; udā. aṭṭha. 39; itivu. aṭṭha. 14, 58; theragā. aṭṭha. 1.67, 99; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.1.117; cūḷani. aṭṭha. 6; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 2.58) vutte saṃsāre sati kammavipākānaṃ appavattaṃ na dissati, kammavipākānaṃ appavatti na dissati, pavattati evāti attho.

689. ‘Thus this’ means: this view is of such a nature, it is right view, an unperverted view. This is the meaning. ‘Like seeds, trees, etc.’ means: just as from a seed comes a tree, and from a tree again a seed, so because the continuity of seed and tree is beginningless, a prior limit does not exist. Similarly, from kamma as condition comes its result, from the result as condition comes kamma; thus, because the continuity of kamma and its result is beginningless, a prior limit is not discerned. By the word ‘etc.’ it includes such instances as ‘from the hen, the egg; from the egg, the hen; and again from the hen, the egg.’ Just as in the past, so also in the future period, when there is the saṃsāra spoken of as ‘the sequence of the aggregates,’ etc., the non-occurrence of kamma and its results is not seen; the non-occurrence of kamma and its results is not seen; it just continues to occur. This is the meaning.

Etamatthanti “kammassa kārako natthī”tiādinā (visuddhi. 2.689) vuttamatthaṃ. Asayaṃvasīti na sayaṃvasino, micchābhinivesaparavasāti attho. Aññamaññavirodhitāti itarītaravirodhitā, diṭṭhiyo, diṭṭhiyā vā aññamaññena virodhitā viruddhā.

‘This meaning’ refers to the meaning stated in the passage beginning ‘There is no doer of the kamma,’ etc. ‘Not self-mastered’ means not being their own masters; the meaning is that they are subservient to perverse adherence. ‘Mutually contradictory’ means contradictory to one another; the views, or a view, are mutually contradictory, opposed.

Gambhīrañāṇagocaratāya gambhīraṃ. Tathā nipuṇaṃ. Sattasuññatāya, aññamaññasabhāvasuññatāya ca suññaṃ. Paccayanti nāmarūpassa paccayaṃ, tappaccayapaṭivedheneva ca sabbaṃ paṭividdhaṃ hotīti. Kammaṃ natthi vipākamhītiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

It is ‘profound’ because it is the domain of profound knowledge. Likewise, ‘subtle.’ It is ‘empty’ because of its emptiness of a being and its emptiness of mutual substance. ‘Condition’ means the condition for mentality-materiality, for by penetrating that very condition, everything is penetrated. Regarding ‘kamma does not exist in the result,’ etc., what should be said has already been stated below.

Paccayasuññaṃ phalanti yathāvuttamatthaṃ upamāya vibhāvetuṃ “yathā na sūriye”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tesanti sūriyādīnaṃ. Soti aggi. Sambhārehīti ātapādīhi kāraṇehi.

To clarify by a simile the aforesaid meaning that 'the fruit is empty of a cause,' the passage beginning 'Just as not in the sun' is stated. 'Of them' (tesaṃ) means of the sun, etc. 'It' (so) means fire. 'With the components' (sambhārehi) means with causes such as heat, etc.

Yadi [M 2.0382] ca hetu ca phalañca aññamaññarahitaṃ, kathaṃ hetuto phalaṃ nibbattatīti āha “kammañca kho upādāyā”ti. Na kevalaṃ kammaphalameva suññaṃ katturahitaṃ, sabbampi dhammajātaṃ kārakarahitanti dassetuṃ “na hettha devo”ti gāthā vuttā. Hetusambhārapaccayāti hetusamūhanimittaṃ, hetupaccayanimittaṃ vā.

If cause and fruit are devoid of each other, how is the fruit produced from the cause? To this he says: 'But depending on kamma...' To show that not only are kamma and fruit empty, devoid of a doer, but that the whole mass of phenomena is devoid of an agent, the verse 'Here there is no deva...' was stated. 'By the cause which is an assemblage of conditions' (hetusambhārapaccayā) means on account of the collection of causes, or on account of the cause as condition.

690. Cutipaṭisandhivasena [V 2.0358] viditā hontīti kammavaṭṭavipākavaṭṭavasena paccayapariggahassa katattā cutipaṭisandhivasena viditā hontīti vadanti. Vuttanayena pana sappaccayanāmarūpassa dassanena tīsu addhāsu pahīnavicikicchassa addhattayapariyāpannā dhammā atītapaccuppannānāgatabhavesu ca cutipaṭisandhivasena viditā honti, na anupadadhammavasena tathāpariggahassa akatattā. Sāssa hoti ñātapariññāti yāya nāmarūpapariggahaṃ, tassa ca paccayapariggahaṃ karoti, sā assa yogino “idaṃ nāmaṃ, ettakaṃ nāma”ntiādinā, “tassa ayaṃ paccayo, ettako paccayo”tiādinā ca paricchedavasena ñātavatī paññāti katvā ñātapariññā.

690. They are known by way of death and rebirth-linking—this is because the grasping of conditions has been undertaken in terms of the round of kamma and the round of kamma-result; thus they are known by way of death and rebirth-linking, so the teachers say. However, by the stated method, for one who has abandoned doubt in the three periods of time by seeing name-and-form together with its conditions, the phenomena included in the three periods of time are known by way of death and rebirth-linking in past, present, and future existences—but not in terms of momentary phenomena, because they have not been grasped in that way. That wisdom of the yogī by which he accomplishes the grasping of name-and-form and the grasping of its conditions, which knows by way of delimitation such as, 'This is name, so much is name,' and, 'This is its condition, so much is the condition,' is, by etymology, his 'full understanding as the known' (ñātapariññā).

Idāni yena kāraṇena addhattayapariyāpannā dhammā cutipaṭisandhivasena viditā honti, taṃ dassetuṃ “so evaṃ pajānātī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tena dhammānaṃ bhavantarasaṅkamo nāma na kadācipi atthi, tattha tattheva nirujjhanatoti dasseti. Sajjhāya mantodakapāna mukhamaṇḍana padīpasīkhūpamāhi tameva dhammānaṃ saṅkamābhāvaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “apica kho”tiādimāha.

Now, to show the reason why the phenomena included in the three periods of time are known by way of death and rebirth-linking, the passage beginning 'He understands thus' was stated. By this it is shown that there is never any so-called transition of phenomena from one existence to another, for they cease right there where they arise. Furthermore, to clarify this very absence of transition of phenomena by means of the similes of recitation, drinking incanted water, face adornment, and a lamp flame, he states the passage beginning 'Moreover.'

Manodhātuanantaranti kiriyamanodhātuyā anantaraṃ labbhamānaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Na ceva āgatanti kiriyamanodhātuto na ceva āgataṃ kiriyamanodhātuyaṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa abhāvato. Nāpi na nibbattaṃ anantaranti kiriyamanodhātuto anāgacchantampi paccayasāmaggilābhena tato anantaraṃ nāpi na nibbattaṃ, nibbattameva hoti. Yathāyaṃ pavattiyaṃ cittappavatti, tatheva paṭisandhimhi vattate cittasantati, cuticittato anāgacchantampi paṭisandhicittaṃ tato anantaraṃ nāpi na nibbattati, paccayasāmaggivasena nibbattatevāti attho. Santatigahaṇena cettha kutoci āgamābhāvameva vibhāveti. Hetuphalabhāvena hi sambandhatāti dhammappavatti santatīti. Tenāha “purimaṃ bhijjate citta”ntiādi. Purimanti cuticittaṃ. Bhijjateti [M 2.0383] nirujjhati. Pacchimanti paṭisandhicittaṃ. Tatoti cuticittato anantarameva jāyati. Yattha hi cuticittato dūrepi kālantarepi uppajjamānaṃ paṭisandhicittaṃ anantarameva jāyatīti vuccati. Tasmā tesaṃ antarikā natthi tesaṃ cutipaṭisandhicittānaṃ byavadhāyakaṃ kiñci natthi. Vīci tesaṃ na vijjatīti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Itoti cuticittato anantaraṃ na ca gacchati kiñci cittaṃ. Tañhi sasampayuttadhammaṃ tatheva nirujjhati. Paṭisandhi cāti paṭisandhiviññāṇañca aññameva yathāpaccayaṃ jāyati nibbattatīti punapi saṅkamābhāvameva vibhāvento sappaccayanāmarūpadassanaṃ nigameti.

"Immediately after the mind-element" means the eye-consciousness that is obtained immediately after the functional mind-element. "And it has not come" means it has not come from the functional mind-element, because eye-consciousness is absent in the functional mind-element. "Nor is it not produced immediately" means that although it does not come from the functional mind-element, it is not the case that it is not produced immediately after it; on obtaining the assembly of conditions, it is indeed produced. Just as this process of consciousness occurs in the course of life, so the continuity of consciousness proceeds at rebirth-linking. Although the rebirth-linking consciousness does not come from the death-consciousness, it is not that it is not produced immediately after it; the meaning is that it is produced by way of the assembly of conditions. Here, by the term "continuity," he clarifies the very absence of coming from anywhere. For the process of phenomena is a continuity because it is connected by way of cause and effect. Therefore, he said: "The prior consciousness breaks up," etc. "Prior" is the death-consciousness. "Breaks up" means ceases. "Subsequent" is the rebirth-linking consciousness. "After that" means it arises immediately after the death-consciousness. For where a rebirth-linking consciousness arises even after a long time from the death-consciousness, it is said to arise "immediately." Therefore, there is no interval between them; there is nothing that intervenes between those death and rebirth-linking consciousnesses. "No gap exists between them" is a synonym for that. "From this" means that immediately after the death-consciousness, no consciousness goes forth. For that consciousness, together with its associated states, ceases right there. "And rebirth-linking" means that the rebirth-linking consciousness, being quite another, arises, is produced, according to its conditions. Again clarifying the absence of transmigration, he concludes with the seeing of name-and-form with its conditions.

691. Nāmarūpaggahaṇena[V 2.0359], tassa ca paccayadhammaggahaṇena aggahitassa tebhūmakadhammassa abhāvato “viditasabbadhammassā”ti vuttaṃ. Na cettha lokuttaradhammā adhigatā. Thāmagataṃ hoti anekākāravokārapaccayapariggahavidhino anuṭṭhitattā. Suṭṭhutaraṃ pahīyati tiyaddhagatadhammappavattiyā vigatasammohattā. Sā evāti soḷasavidhā kaṅkhā eva. Yasmā ettha “buddho, dhammo, saṅgho, sikkhā”ti ca kaṅkhāya gocarabhūtā lokiyā dhammā adhippetā. Na hi lokuttaradhamme ārabbha kilesā pavattituṃ sakkonti. Pubbantoti atītā khandhāyatanadhātuyo. Aparantoti anāgatā. Pubbantāparantoti tadubhayaṃ, addhāpaccuppannaṃ vā tadubhayabhāgayuttattā. Evaṃ buddhādiggahaṇena, paṭiccasamuppannadhammaggahaṇena ca gahito aṭṭhamo kaṅkhāvisayo nāmarūpamattaṃ, idappaccayatāggahaṇena pana tassa paccayo gahito, tasmā soḷasavatthukāya kaṅkhāya pahīnāya aṭṭhavatthukā kaṅkhā appatiṭṭhāva hotīti āha “na kevalañca…pe… pahīyatiyevā”ti.

691. Because, by grasping name-and-form and by grasping its conditioning phenomena, there is an absence of any ungrasped phenomena of the three planes, it is said, 'one who has understood all phenomena.' And here, supramundane phenomena are not attained. It becomes strong because the method of grasping conditions in their many aspects and details has been undertaken. Doubt is more thoroughly abandoned due to the absence of delusion about the continuity of phenomena across the three times. That itself is the sixteen kinds of doubt. For here, what is intended are the worldly phenomena that are the domain of doubt—such as [doubt about] the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Sangha, and the training. Indeed, defilements are not able to arise in relation to the supramundane phenomena. 'The past end' refers to the past aggregates, sense bases, and elements. 'The future end' refers to the future ones. 'The past and future ends' refer to both, or to the temporal present, since it is connected with both parts. Thus, the eighth subject of doubt, which is grasped by grasping the Buddha, etc., and by grasping dependently arisen phenomena, is mere name-and-form; moreover, by grasping specific conditionality, its condition is grasped. Therefore, when the doubt with sixteen bases is abandoned, the doubt with eight bases has no footing. Hence it is said: 'Not only…pe… it is indeed abandoned.'

Diṭṭhekaṭṭhattā vicikicchāya yathā diṭṭhi samucchijjamānā vicikicchāya saddhiṃyeva samucchijjati, evaṃ vicikicchā vikkhambhiyamānā diṭṭhiyā saddhiṃyeva vikkhambhīyatīti āha “dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhigatāni vikkhambhantī”ti. Attābhinivesūpanissayā hi “ahosiṃ nu kho aha”ntiādi (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20) nayappavattā soḷasavatthukā kaṅkhā, sā eva ca pubbantādivatthukabhāvena vuttā. Attābhinivesavatthukāni ca dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhigatāni, buddhādivatthukā ca kaṅkhā tadekaṭṭhāti. Dharīyanti [M 2.0384] attano paccayehīti dhammā, tiṭṭhati ettha tadāyattavuttitāya phalanti ṭhiti, dhammānaṃ ṭhiti dhammaṭṭhiti, paccayadhammo. Atha vā dhammoti kāraṇaṃ “dhammapaṭisambhidā”tiādīsu (vibha. 718 ādayo) viya, dhammassa ṭhiti sabhāvo, dhammato ca añño sabhāvo natthīti paccayadhammānaṃ paccayabhāvo dhammaṭṭhiti, dhammaṭṭhitiyaṃ ñāṇaṃ dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ. Saṅkhārānaṃ yaṃ yaṃ bhūtaṃ aniccatādi yathābhūtaṃ, tattha ñāṇanti yathābhūtañāṇaṃ. Sammā passatīti sammādassanaṃ.

Because doubt and view have the same foundation, just as view, when being eradicated, is eradicated together with doubt, so too doubt, when being suppressed, is suppressed together with view. Therefore, it is said: 'The sixty-two views are suppressed.' Indeed, the sixteen-point doubt, which proceeds in the manner of 'Was I in the past?' etc., has the adherence to self as its decisive support; and that very doubt is also spoken of as having the past end, etc., as its grounds. The sixty-two views are founded on the adherence to self, and doubt concerning the Buddha, etc., has the same foundation. 'They are borne by their own conditions,' thus they are 'dhammas.' 'Standing' (ṭhiti) is so called because herein the fruit 'stands' (tiṭṭhati), its occurrence being dependent on that cause. The standing-ground of dhammas is 'dhammaṭṭhiti,' which is the conditioning phenomenon. Alternatively, 'dhamma' means cause, as in 'analytical knowledge of cause' (dhammapaṭisambhidā), etc.; the stability of a cause is its nature, and since there is no nature other than the cause, the causal nature of conditioning phenomena is 'dhammaṭṭhiti.' Knowledge of the stability of dhammas is 'dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa.' Whatever is the true nature of formations, such as impermanence, is 'as it really is' (yathābhūta); knowledge therein is 'knowledge of things as they really are' (yathābhūtañāṇa). 'One sees rightly,' thus it is 'right view' (sammādassana).

Avijjā paccayoti avijjā hetuādivasena saṅkhārānaṃ yathārahaṃ paccayo. Tato eva saṅkhārā paccayasamuppannā. Ubhopeteti yasmā avijjāpi āsavādivasena paccayasambhūtāva, tasmā avijjā saṅkhārāti ubhayepi ete dhammā paccayasamuppannā. Itīti evaṃ. Paccayapariggahe paññāti paccayānaṃ paricchijja gahaṇavasena pavattā paññā. Vuttanayena dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ.

'Ignorance is a condition' means that ignorance, by way of being a root cause, etc., is a condition for formations in a suitable way. For that very reason, formations are dependently arisen. 'Both of these' means that since ignorance itself has also arisen from conditions by way of the taints, etc., therefore both these phenomena—ignorance and formations—are dependently arisen. 'Thus' means 'in this way.' 'Wisdom in the comprehension of conditions' is the wisdom that proceeds by way of grasping conditions after having delimited them. By the method stated, this is the knowledge of the stability of dhammas.

Nimittanti [V 2.0360] saṅkhāranimittaṃ, atthato pañcakkhandhā. Te hi ghanasaññāpavattiyā vatthubhāvato nimittaṃ, saviggahabhāvena upaṭṭhānato vā. Yasmā aniccatā nāma saṅkhārānaṃ aviparītākāro. Tattha niccatāya lesassāpi abhāvato aniccato passanto yathābhūtaṃ jānāti. Tañca ñāṇaṃ aviparītaggahaṇatāya sammādassanaṃ. Taṃsamaṅginā ca paccuppannesu viya atītānāgatesupi nayaṃ nentena te suparividitā honti.

The 'sign' is the sign of formations; in substance, the five aggregates. For they are a 'sign' because they are a basis for the occurrence of the perception of compactness, or because they appear with their individual essence. Because impermanence is the true aspect of formations, one who sees them as impermanent—there being not even a trace of permanence in them—knows them as they really are. And that knowledge, because it is a non-distorted grasping, is right view. By one endowed with that knowledge, who applies the method to the past and future just as to the present, they are thoroughly understood.

Aniccatā ca nāma uppattimato, uppādo ca paccayavasenāti aniccatā sijjhamānā saṅkhārānaṃ sappaccayataṃ sādhentī yathāvuttakaṅkhappahānāya saṃvattatīti imamatthaṃ dassento “aniccato…pe… pahīyatī”ti āha. Tattha tadanvayenāti paccakkhato diṭṭhassa anugamanena. Etthāti yathādiṭṭhesu dhammesu. Dukkhato manasi karontotiādīsupi eseva nayo. Pavattanti upādinnakkhandhappavattaṃ. Tañhi kilesābhisaṅkhārehi pavattitattā sātisayaṃ dukkhabhāvena upaṭṭhāti. Pavattanti ṭhānanisajjādivasena dukkhadukkhatādivasena ca saṅkhārappavattanti apare. “Nimittaṃ, pavatta”nti ca vutte ajjhattabahiddhāsantānasaññite sabbasmiṃ sappaccaye nāmarūpe yāthāvato pavattā ekāva paññā pariyāyavasena “yathābhūtañāṇa”ntipi “sammādassana”ntipi tattha kaṅkhāvikkhambhanena “kaṅkhāvitaraṇā”tipi vuccati. Yathā “rukkho pādapo tarū”ti imamatthaṃ dassento āha “yañca yathābhūtañāṇa”ntiādi.

To show this meaning—that since impermanence belongs to what has an origin, and origin is dependent on conditions, the establishing of impermanence proves that formations are conditioned and thus leads to the abandonment of the aforesaid doubt—he said: 'By seeing as impermanent... it is abandoned.' Therein, 'by inference from that' means by following what has been directly seen. 'Herein' means in the phenomena as seen. The same method applies to 'attending to as suffering,' etc. 'Occurrence' refers to the occurrence of the aggregates subject to clinging. For since it occurs through defilements and volitional formations, it appears as suffering in the highest degree. Others say 'occurrence' is the process of formations by way of postures like standing and sitting, and by way of the suffering due to suffering, etc. When 'sign' and 'occurrence' are mentioned, the single wisdom that proceeds correctly regarding all conditioned name-and-form—internal and external, designated as a continuity—is called by various names: 'knowledge of things as they are' (yathābhūtañāṇa), 'right view' (sammādassana), and, because it suppresses doubt therein, 'overcoming of doubt' (kaṅkhāvitaraṇa). To show this meaning, just as a tree is called 'rukkha,' 'pādapa,' and 'taru,' he said: 'And that which is knowledge of things as they are…' etc.

Paramatthato [M 2.0385] sāsane assāso nāma ariyaphalaṃ, patiṭṭhā nāma ariyamaggo, ayaṃ pana anadhigatamaggaphalopi tadadhigamupāyapaṭipattiyaṃ ṭhitattā laddhassāso viya, laddhapatiṭṭho viya ca hotīti vuttaṃ “laddhassāso laddhapatiṭṭho”ti. Aparihīnakaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiko vipassako lokiyāhi sīlasamādhipaññāsampadāhi samannāgatattā uttari appaṭivijjhanto sugatiparāyaṇo ca hotīti vuttaṃ “niyatagatiko”ti. Tato eva cūḷasotāpanno nāma hoti. Sotāpanno hi khīṇāpāyaduggativinipātoti.

In the ultimate sense, in the Dispensation, 'solace' is the noble fruit, and 'footing' is the noble path. But this person, although not having attained the path and fruit, because of being established in the practice that is the means for their attainment, is as if he has gained solace and as if he has gained a footing; thus it is said, 'one who has gained solace, one who has gained a footing.' The insight meditator who is undiminished in the Purification by Overcoming Doubt, because of being endowed with the worldly accomplishments of virtue, concentration, and wisdom, although not penetrating further, has a good destination as his resort; thus it is said, 'one of fixed destiny.' For that very reason, he is called a 'lesser stream-enterer.' Indeed, a stream-enterer is one for whom the fall into a plane of misery, a bad destination, is destroyed.

Atha vā laddhassāso diṭṭhivisuddhisamadhigamena. Nāmarūpaparicchedena hi khandhādike sabhāvasarasato sallakkhetvā sāsane dhammupasaṃhitapāmojjappaṭilābhena laddhassāso hoti. Laddhapatiṭṭho kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhisamadhigamena. Sappaccayanāmarūpadassanena hi parimadditadiṭṭhikaṇṭako viniddhataahetuvisamahetuvādo yathāsakaṃ paccayeheva dhammamattaṃ jānitvā sāsane [V 2.0361] patiṭṭhitasaddho laddhapatiṭṭho nāma hoti. Nāmarūpavavatthānena dukkhasaccaṃ, dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇena samudayasaccaṃ, tasseva aparabhāgena aniccato manasikārādividhinā maggasaccañca abhiññāya pavattiyā dukkhabhāvaṃ disvā appavatte nirodhe ekaṃseneva ninnajjhāsayatāya lokiyeneva ñāṇena catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ adhigatattā apāyesu abhabbuppattiko, sotāpannabhūmiyaṃ bhabbuppattiko ca hotīti vuttaṃ “niyatagatiko”ti. Tenāha “cūḷasotāpanno nāma hotī”ti.

Alternatively, one has gained solace through the attainment of the Purification of View. Indeed, by clearly noting things such as the aggregates according to their own intrinsic nature through the discernment of name-and-form, and by gaining joy connected with the Dhamma in the Dispensation, one has gained solace. One has gained a footing through the attainment of the Purification by Overcoming Doubt. For, by seeing name-and-form with its conditions, one has crushed the thorn of wrong view and dispelled the doctrines of causelessness and dissimilar cause; and by knowing mere phenomena as arising only from their own respective causes, one whose faith is established in the Dispensation is called 'one who has gained a footing.' By defining name-and-form, one knows with higher knowledge the truth of suffering; by the knowledge of the stability of phenomena, the truth of origin; and in the subsequent part of that very knowledge, by the method of attending to impermanence and so forth, the truth of the path. Having seen the suffering nature of the continuity of existence, and because of having an inclination that tends solely and certainly towards cessation, which is non-occurrence, and because of having attained the four noble truths with only worldly knowledge, one becomes incapable of arising in the planes of misery and capable of arising in the stage of a stream-enterer. Thus it is said, 'one of fixed destiny.' Therefore, he said, 'he is called a lesser stream-enterer.'

Tasmāti yasmā evaṃ mahānisaṃsametaṃ yathābhūtañāṇaṃ, tasmā. Sadāti sabbakālaṃ rattiñceva divā ca. Sabbasoti nibbattakahetuādipariggaṇhanavasena sabbappakārena.

The word tasmā (therefore) is used because this knowledge of things as they really are is of such great benefit. The word sadā (always) means at all times, both in the night and in the day. The word sabbaso (in every way) means in all ways, by way of comprehending the generative causes and so on.

Kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the Purification by Overcoming Doubt is finished.

Iti ekūnavīsatimaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus ends the commentary on the nineteenth chapter.

20. Maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhiniddesavaṇṇanā

20. Commentary on the Exposition of the Purification of Knowledge and Vision of the Path and Not-Path

Sammasanañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Knowledge of Comprehension

692. Evaṃ [M 2.0386][V 2.0362] maggañca amaggañca ñatvā ṭhitaṃ ñāṇanti ayaṃ upakkilesavinimuttā vīthipaṭipannā vipassanāpaññā ariyamaggassa pubbabhāgamaggo, ayaṃ obhāsādibhedo dasavidho upakkileso na maggoti evaṃ maggañca amaggañca yāthāvato vavatthapetvā ṭhitaṃ ñāṇaṃ.

692. Knowledge that stands having known the path and the not-path means: This insight-wisdom, freed from the corruptions, entered upon the right course, is the path that is the preliminary part of the noble path; this tenfold corruption distinguished as illumination and so on is not the path—thus it is knowledge that stands having defined the path and the not-path as they really are.

Atītādivasena anekabhedabhinne dhamme kalāpato saṅkhipitvā sammasanaṃ kalāpasammasanaṃ, ayaṃ kira jambudīpavāsīnaṃ abhilāpo. “Yaṃ kiñci rūpa”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 1.361; 2.113; 3.86; a. ni. 4.181) nayena hi dhammānaṃ vipassanā nayavipassanā, ayaṃ kira tambapaṇṇidīpavāsīnaṃ abhilāpo. Tenevāha “kalāpasammasanasaṅkhātāya nayavipassanāyā”ti. Tāva-saddo kamattho, tena sammasanappakārānaṃ bahubhedataṃ dīpeti. Bahubhāvato hi tesaṃ paṭhamaṃ nayavipassanāya yogārambhaṃ anusāsati “nayavipassanāya tāva yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Kasmāti codakavacanaṃ. Tassāyaṃ adhippāyo – yadi maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi sampādetabbā, atha kasmā “nayavipassanāya ādito yogo kātabbo”ti vuttanti. Itaro tassāyaṃ adhigamūpāyoti dassento “āraddhavipassakassā”tiādimāha. Tenetaṃ dasseti “vipassanāya sati udayabbayañāṇuppādo, udayabbayañāṇe sati obhāsādiupakkilesasambhavo, tato maggāmaggavavatthānaṃ, tasmā tassa āditova ārambhassa sambhavo natthīti vipassanā paṭhamaṃ āraddhabbā”ti. Evampi paṭhamaṃ nayavipassanāva kasmā āraddhabbāti āha “vipassanāya ca kalāpasammasanaṃ ādī”ti. Tañhi atītādibhedabhinnānaṃ dhammānaṃ saṅkhipitvā vavatthānavasena pavattanato ādikammikassa sukaraṃ sammasananti ādibhūtaṃ.

The comprehension of phenomena divided by many distinctions, such as past, etc., by summarizing them into groups, is 'comprehension by groups' (kalāpasammasana). This, it is said, is the term of the elders who dwell in Jambudīpa. Indeed, insight into phenomena by the method beginning 'Whatever kind of form...' is 'insight by method' (nayavipassanā). This, it is said, is the term of the elders who dwell on the island of Tambapaṇṇi. Therefore, he said, 'by insight by method, which is designated as comprehension by groups.' The word 'tāva' is in the sense of sequence; by it, it indicates that there are many kinds of comprehension. Indeed, because of their multiplicity, he first instructs the undertaking of the practice of insight by method, saying, 'First, the practice of insight by method should be done.' 'Why?' This is the questioner's statement. This is its meaning: If the purification of knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path is to be accomplished, then why is it said, 'From the beginning, the practice of insight by method should be undertaken'? The other, showing that this is the means for its attainment, says what begins with 'for one who has begun insight...' By this he shows: 'When there is insight, the arising of the knowledge of rise and fall occurs; when the knowledge of rise and fall is present, the occurrence of corruptions such as illumination, etc., happens; then comes the defining of the path and the not-path. Therefore, there is no possibility of undertaking that from the very beginning. Hence, insight should be undertaken first.' Even so, to the question, 'Why should insight by method itself be undertaken first?' he says, 'And for insight, comprehension by groups is the beginning.' For since it proceeds by way of defining after summarizing phenomena divided by distinctions such as past, etc., it is easy for a beginner to comprehend, and so it is the initial step.

Tasmāti [V 2.0363] ādibhūtattā. Atha vā tasmāti yasmā āraddhavipassakassa…pe… kalāpasammasanaṃ ādi, tasmā. Etanti kalāpasammasanaṃ. Apicātiādi kalāpasammasanasseva vipassanāya ādibhāve upacayahetudassanaṃ. Udayabbayañāṇapariyosānā tīraṇapariññā, asampatte [M 2.0387] eva ca udayabbayañāṇe maggāmaggavavatthānaṃ hotīti āha “tīraṇapariññāya vattamānāyā”ti. Kalāpasammasane tāva yogo kātabboti etthāpi tasseva paṭhamārambhe kāraṇaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Yasmā kalāpasammasanaṃ nāma ekavisuddhiyampi na antogadhaṃ, ekacce ca taṃ anāmasitvāva vipassanācāraṃ vaṇṇenti. Evaṃ santepi taṃ suttantesu ekadesena, anavasesato ca dassitaṃ. Paṭisambhidāyaṃ ādikammikānaṃ manasikārasukaratāya vipassanāya ādibhāvena ṭhapitaṃ. Vipassantassa ca obhāsādīsu uppannesu maggāmaggañāṇasambhavo, tasmā “taṃ sampādetukāmenā”tiādinā ayaṃ vicāro katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Therefore: because it is the beginning. Or, therefore: because for one who has begun insight... comprehension by groups is the beginning, therefore. This refers to comprehension by groups. The words 'Moreover,' etc., show the accumulation of causes for comprehension by groups being the beginning of insight. Full understanding by discerning ends with the knowledge of rise and fall, and the defining of the path and not-path occurs even before the knowledge of rise and fall is reached; thus he said, 'while full understanding by discerning is occurring.' In the phrase 'First, the practice of comprehension by groups should be done,' the reason for its being undertaken first should be understood in the way already stated. Because comprehension by groups is not included even in a single purification, and some describe the practice of insight without even touching upon it. Even so, it is shown in the Suttas partially and also completely. In the Paṭisambhidā, it is established as the beginning of insight because it is easy for beginners to attend to. And for one practicing insight, when illumination and so on have arisen, the arising of the knowledge of the path and not-path occurs. Therefore, it should be seen that this investigation beginning 'by one who wishes to accomplish that...' was undertaken.

693. Tatrāti tasmiṃ tīraṇapariññāya ñātapariññānantarabhāve, tāsu vā pariññāsu. Vinicchayoti sarūpato, kiccato, bhūmito ca sanniṭṭhānaṃ. Lokuttarāpi purimasmiṃ saccadvaye maggasampayuttā tividhāpi pariññā kiccavasena labbhatīti “lokiyapariññā”ti visesetvā vuttaṃ. Sabhāvadhammānaṃ lakkhaṇasallakkhaṇato ñeyyaabhimukhā paññā abhiññāpaññā. Ñātaṭṭheti ñātabhāvanimittaṃ. Abhiññeyyassa jānanahetu “ñāṇa”nti vuccati. Pariññāpaññāti aniccādilakkhaṇāni paricchijja jānanapaññā. Tīraṇaṭṭheti sammasanabhāvahetu. Pahānapaññāti pahātabbassa pajahanapaññā. Vedayitādilakkhaṇavidhuratāya ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ paccattalakkhaṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Tesaṃyeva paccattalakkhaṇasallakkhaṇavasena gahitadhammānaṃyeva. Yathā pathavīphassādīnaṃ kakkhaḷaphusanādilakkhaṇāni tīsupi khaṇesu sallakkhitabbāni paṭiniyatarūpatāya sabhāvasiddhāneva hutvā gayhanti, na evamaniccatādilakkhaṇāni. Tāni pana bhaṅgudayabbayapīḷāvasavattanākāramukhena gahetabbato samāropitarūpāni viya gayhantīti vuttaṃ “sāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā”ti. Lokiyapariññānaṃyeva adhippetattā lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanāva “pahānapariññā”ti vuttā.

693. Therein: in that state immediately following full understanding of the known, or among those full understandings. Decision: a conclusion as to its own nature, function, and plane. Since even the supramundane threefold full understanding associated with the path in the first two truths is obtained by way of function, it is specified as 'mundane full understanding.' Wisdom that faces the knowable by clearly marking the characteristics of phenomena with their own nature is wisdom as direct knowledge. In the sense of the known: because of the state of being known. Because it is the cause of knowing what is to be directly known, it is called 'knowledge.' Wisdom as full understanding is the wisdom that knows by delimiting the characteristics of impermanence, etc. In the sense of discerning: because of the state of comprehension. Wisdom as abandoning is the wisdom that abandons what is to be abandoned. Just as the characteristics of hardness, contact, etc., of the earth element, contact, etc., are to be marked in all three moments and are grasped as established by their own nature in a definite way, so it is not with the characteristics of impermanence, etc. But since these have to be grasped by way of the mode of dissolution, rise and fall, oppression, and non-control, they are grasped as if they were superimposed; hence it is said, 'having superimposed the general characteristic.' Because only mundane full understandings are intended, insight that has characteristics as its object is called 'full understanding as abandoning.'

Saṅkhārapaṭicchedatoti nāmarūpavavatthānato, yā “diṭṭhivisuddhī”ti vuttā. Keci pana “khandhādīnaṃ vipassanāya bhūmibhāvato sabbopi khandhādivicāro saṅkhāraparicchedo”ti vadanti. “Paccattalakkhaṇapaṭivedhasseva ādhipacca”nti iminā nāmarūpapaccayapariggahapaññānaṃ tīraṇapahānāsamatthataṃ [V 2.0364] dasseti[M 2.0388]. Tāsampi pana “namanalakkhaṇaṃ nāmaṃ, ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ rūpa”nti arūparūpānaṃ sādhāraṇākārasallakkhaṇavasena pavattiyā ekenākārena tīraṇapariyāyo, diṭṭhikaṅkhāvikkhambhanena pahānapariyāyo labbhatīti siyā tīraṇapahānesupi ādhipaccanti vadanti. Ukkaṭṭhaniddesena pana yathā diṭṭhivisuddhiyāva saṅkhāraparicchedatā, evaṃ lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanāya eva tīraṇapahānakiccatā veditabbā. Evaṃ hi tissopi pariññā vavatthitā honti, aññathā saṅkāro siyā. Tīraṇapariññāya bhūmi tattha paññāya aniccatādilakkhaṇasantīraṇato. Tenāha “etasmiṃ…pe… ādhipacca”nti. Kāmaṃ udayabbayañāṇampi kañci micchābhinivesaṃ pajahati, tassa pana athāmagatattā na sātisayaṃ pahānanti vuttaṃ “bhaṅgānupassanaṃ ādiṃ katvā upari pahānapariññāya bhūmī”ti. Aniccato anupassantoti aniccākārato saṅkhāre anupassanto sammasanto. Niccasaññanti “te niccā sassatā”ti pavattaṃ micchāsaññaṃ. Saññāsīsena diṭṭhicittānampi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Eseva nayo ito paresupi. Nibbindantoti aniccānupassanādisambhūtāya nibbidānupassanāya saṅkhāre nibbijjanavasena passanto. Nandinti sappītikataṇhaṃ. Virajjantoti virāgānupassanāya virajjanavasena yathā saṅkhāresu rāgo nuppajjati, evaṃ anupassanto. Tathābhūto hi rāgaṃ pajahatīti vuccati. Nirodhentoti nirodhānupassanāya yathā saṅkhārā nirujjhantiyeva, na āyatiṃ punabbhavavasena uppajjanti, evaṃ anupassanto. Tathābhūto hi saṅkhārānaṃ samudayaṃ pajahati nāma anuppattidhammatāpādanato. Paṭinissajjantoti paṭinissaggānupassanāya yathā saṅkhārā na puna ādiyanti, evaṃ vossajjanto. Tenāha “ādānaṃ pajahatī”ti, niccādivasena vā gahaṇaṃ vissajjetīti attho. Sādhitattāti sampāditattā. Itarāti tīraṇapahānapariññā. Evaṃ pariññā niddisitvā pariññākkamavasenapi kaṅkhāvitaraṇānantaraṃ “kalāpasammasane yogo kātabbo”ti yvāyamattho vutto, taṃ nigamavasena paccāharanto “tena vutta”ntiādimāha, taṃ vuttatthameva.

By 'the discernment of formations' is meant the determination of name-and-form, which is called 'the purification of view.' Some, however, say that all examination of the aggregates and so forth is 'the discernment of formations' because it is the ground for insight. By 'predominance lies only in the penetration of individual characteristics,' it is shown that the wisdoms that comprehend name-and-form and their conditions are incapable of investigation and abandonment. However, some say that even for those wisdoms, since they proceed by way of discerning the common mode of immaterial and material phenomena—that 'name has the characteristic of bending, and form has the characteristic of being afflicted'—a phase of investigation is obtained in one way, and by the suppression of wrong view and doubt, a phase of abandonment is obtained. Therefore, they say, there can be predominance even in investigation and abandonment. But by the pre-eminent explanation, just as the discernment of formations is solely the purification of view, so the function of investigation and abandonment should be understood as belonging only to insight that has the characteristics as its object. In this way, the three kinds of full understanding are established; otherwise, there would be confusion. The ground for the full understanding by investigating is there, because of the wisdom's investigation of the characteristics of impermanence, etc. Hence it is said: 'In this… the predominance lies.' Granted, the knowledge of rise and fall also abandons some wrong adherence, but since it has not reached its full strength, it is not an outstanding abandonment. Thus it is said: 'Beginning with the contemplation of dissolution, the higher stages are the ground for the full understanding by abandonment.' 'Contemplating as impermanent' means contemplating and examining formations from the standpoint of impermanence. 'The perception of permanence' is the wrong perception that occurs as 'they are permanent, everlasting.' Under the heading of perception, the inclusion of views and thoughts should also be understood. The same method applies to the subsequent terms. 'Growing disenchanted' means seeing formations by way of disenchantment with the contemplation of disenchantment born from the contemplation of impermanence, etc. 'Delighting' is craving accompanied by zest. 'Becoming dispassionate' means contemplating by way of dispassion with the contemplation of dispassion, so that lust does not arise in regard to formations. For one who is so is said to abandon lust. 'Causing to cease' means contemplating with the contemplation of cessation, so that formations just cease and do not arise again in a future existence. For one who is so is said to abandon the arising of formations by bringing them to a state of non-recurrence. 'Relinquishing' means letting go with the contemplation of relinquishment, so that formations are not taken up again. Hence it is said, 'he abandons grasping,' or the meaning is that he gives up the grasping in terms of permanence, etc. 'Because it is accomplished' means because it is fulfilled. 'The others' are the full understanding by investigating and the full understanding by abandonment. Having thus explained full understanding, and also by way of the sequence of full understanding, after overcoming doubt, the meaning that has been stated—'one should apply oneself to the comprehension of groups'—is brought to a conclusion when he says, 'Therefore it was said,' etc., which has the meaning already stated.

694. Tatrāti tasmiṃ kalāpasammasane vibhāvetabbe, tassa vā kalāpasammasanassa ādibhāve. Ayaṃ pāḷīti dassiyamānaṃ paṭisambhidāmaggapāḷimāha. Tattha saṅkhipitvā vavatthāne paññāti atītādibhedabhinne dhamme [M 2.0389] ekato saṅgahetvā aniccādivasena vinicchaye sādhetabbe taṃsādhanīyā paññā. Sammasane aniccatādivasena tīraṇe ñāṇanti pavuccati, sā kathaṃ hotīti attho. Vavatthāne sammasaneti ca nipphādetabbe bhummavacanaṃ. Yaṃ kiñci rūpantiādīni padāni [V 2.0365] heṭṭhā vuttatthāneva. Sabbaṃ rūpaṃ aniccato vavatthapetītiādīni pana yasmā parato vaṇṇiyissanti, tasmā tattheva nesaṃ atthaṃ vibhāvayissāma.

694. ‘Therein’ means in that comprehension of groups that is to be clarified, or at the beginning of that comprehension of groups. By the words ‘This is the Pāḷi,’ he stated the Pāḷi text from the Paṭisambhidāmagga that is to be shown. Therein, ‘wisdom in determination by summarizing’ is the wisdom that is the means for accomplishing the determination by way of impermanence, etc., having gathered together as one the phenomena divided by the distinctions of past, etc. The investigation by way of impermanence, etc., in comprehension is called ‘knowledge.’ The meaning is: How does that wisdom come to be? And the words ‘in determination’ and ‘in comprehension’ are in the locative case in the sense of that which is to be accomplished. The phrases beginning ‘whatever form…’ have the same meaning as stated previously. However, since the phrases beginning ‘one should determine all form as impermanent…’ will be explained later, we will clarify their meaning only there.

Pāḷivavatthānaṃ pana evaṃ veditabbaṃ – ettha hi ādikammikānaṃ vipassanāmanasikārasukhatthaṃ “yaṃ kiñci rūpa”ntiādinā paṭhamaṃ tāva pañcakkhandhā atītādivibhāgamukhena gahitā, te pana khandhā yasmā dvārārammaṇehi saddhiṃ dvārappavattadhammavasena vibhāgaṃ labbhanti, tasmā tadanantaraṃ dvārachakkādivasena dasa chakkā gahitā. Yasmā pana lakkhaṇesu anattalakkhaṇaṃ dukkhavibhāgaṃ, tasmā tassa vibhāvanāya cha dhātuyo gahitā. Tato yesu kasiṇesu ito bāhirakānaṃ attābhiniveso, tāni imesaṃ jhānānaṃ ārammaṇabhāvena upaṭṭhānākāramattānīti dassanatthaṃ dasa kasiṇāni gahitāni. Tato dukkhānupassanāya parivārabhāvena paṭikkūlākāravasena dvattiṃsa koṭṭhāsā gahitā. Pubbe khandhavasena saṅkhepato gahitā dhammā nātisaṅkhepavitthāranayena, vitthāranayena ca manasi kātabbāti dassanatthaṃ dvādasāyatanāni, aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo ca gahitā. Tesu ime dhammā satipi suññanirīhaabyāpārabhāve dhammasabhāvato ādhipaccavasena pavattantīti anattalakkhaṇavibhāvanatthaṃ indriyāni gahitāni. Evaṃ anekabhedabhinnāpime dhammā bhūmittayapariyāpannatāya tividhāva hontīti dassanatthaṃ tisso dhātuyo gahitā.

The arrangement of the Pāḷi should be understood as follows: Here, for the sake of ease of attention in insight for beginners, first the five aggregates are taken up by way of the division into past, etc., with the text beginning 'whatever form...' Since these aggregates, however, are divided by way of phenomena occurring at the sense doors together with their objects, immediately after, the ten sixes are taken up by way of the six doors, etc. Since among the characteristics, the characteristic of not-self is difficult to analyze, the six elements are taken up for its clarification. Then, to show that the kasiṇas in which those outside this Dispensation have an adherence to self are merely the mode of their appearance as objects for these jhānas, the ten kasiṇas are taken up. Next, as a support for the contemplation of suffering, the thirty-two parts of the body are taken up by way of their repulsive aspect. To show that the phenomena previously taken up briefly by way of the aggregates should be attended to by a method that is neither too brief nor too detailed, and by a detailed method, the twelve sense bases and the eighteen elements are taken up. To clarify the characteristic of not-self—that these phenomena, though void of self, desireless, and without activity, proceed by way of dominance from their own intrinsic nature—the faculties are taken up. To show that although these phenomena are divided in many ways, they are just threefold by being included in the three planes of existence, the three elements are taken up.

Ettāvatā nimittaṃ dassetvā pavattaṃ dassetuṃ kāmabhavādayo nava bhavā gahitā. Ettake abhiññeyyavisese pavattamanasikārakosallena saṇhasukhumesu nibbattitamahaggatadhammesu manasikāro pavattetabboti dassanatthaṃ jhānappamaññāruppāni gahitāni. Tattha jhānāni nāma vuttāvasesārammaṇāni rūpāvacarajjhānāni. Paccayapaccayuppannavibhāgato ime dhammā bhinditvā manasi kātabbāti dassanatthaṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṅgāni gahitāni. Paccayākāramanasikāro hi lakkhaṇattayaṃ sukhena, suṭṭhutarañca vibhāveti, tasmā pacchato gahito. Evamete sammasanīyabhāvena gahitā [M 2.0390] khandhādivasena koṭṭhāsato pañcavīsatividhā. Pabhedato pana atītādibhedaṃ anāmasitvāva gayhamānā dvīhi ūnāni dvesatāni honti.

Having thus far shown the sign of formations, in order to show the internal process, the nine existences, beginning with sensual existence, are taken up. To show that with skill in attention directed to so many special things to be directly known, one should direct attention to the sublime states that have been produced in what is fine and subtle, for this purpose the jhānas, the boundless states, and the formless attainments are taken up. Herein, the jhānas are the fine-material sphere jhānas, which have the remaining things mentioned as their objects. To show that these phenomena should be attended to by analyzing them according to the division into conditions and conditionally arisen phenomena, the factors of dependent origination are taken up. For attention to the conditional structure clarifies the triad of characteristics easily and very well; therefore it is taken up afterwards. Thus these phenomena, taken up as things to be comprehended, are of twenty-five kinds by way of categories, by way of the aggregates, etc. But by way of classification, when taken without considering the division into past, etc., they amount to one hundred and ninety-eight.

Tattha aniccato vavatthapetītiādiko paṭhamo lakkhaṇavavatthāpanavāro. Aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhenātiādiko dutiyo hetuvāro lakkhaṇānaṃ hetukittanato. Aniccaṃ saṅkhatantiādiko pana hetupatiṭṭhāpanavāro [V 2.0366] pākaṭabhāvasallakkhaṇato. Khayaṭṭhenāti hi khayasabhāvato yasmā rūpaṃ khayasabhāvaṃ uppajjitvā khayaṃ vayaṃ bhedaṃ gacchati, tasmā aniccanti attho. Bhayaṭṭhenāti bhāyitabbabhāvato yasmā rūpaṃ pabhaṅguratāya bhayānakaṃ, tasmā dukkhanti. Tenāha bhagavā “yadaniccaṃ, taṃ dukkha”nti (saṃ. ni. 30.15, 45, 46, 76, 85; 2.4.14; paṭi. ma. 2.10). Asārakaṭṭhenāti asārakabhāvato, attasāravirahatoti attho. Tatiyavāre pana “rūpaṃ anicca”nti vatvā tassa hetuṃ patiṭṭhāpetuṃ “saṅkhata”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Yasmā samecca sambhūya paccayehi kataṃ, anurūpe ca paccaye paṭicca, na vinā tehi samaṃ, sammā ca uppannaṃ, tasmā khayavayavirāganirodhadhammanti. Na hi paccayanibbattaṃ anirujjhanakaṃ nāma atthi. Tenāha bhagavā “yaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ jātaṃ bhūtaṃ saṅkhataṃ palokadhammaṃ, taṃ vata mā palujjīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.379). Etena aniccā pathavīdhātu paccayanibbattattā tadaññaṃ paccayanibbattaṃ viyāti dasseti. Esa nayo sesadhammesupi.

Therein, the first section, beginning with 'one should determine as impermanent,' is the section on the determination of characteristics. The second, beginning with 'impermanent in the sense of destruction,' is the section on the reason, because it states the reason for the characteristics. But the one beginning with 'impermanent because it is conditioned' is the section on establishing the reason, because of the good discernment of its manifest nature. For 'in the sense of destruction' means: because of its nature of destruction. Since form, having arisen, goes to destruction, vanishing, and breakup, therefore it is impermanent. 'In the sense of the fearsome' means: because of its nature of being something to be feared. Since form is terrifying on account of its fragility, therefore it is suffering. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'What is impermanent, that is suffering.' 'In the sense of being without a core' means: because of its coreless nature, that is, its lack of a core of self. In the third section, however, after stating 'form is impermanent,' 'conditioned,' etc., was said in order to establish the reason for that. Because it is made by conditions that have come together and assembled, and it has arisen together and rightly in dependence on suitable conditions, not without them, therefore it has the nature of destruction, vanishing, fading away, and cessation. For there is nothing whatsoever produced by conditions that is not subject to cessation. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'That form which is born, come to be, conditioned, and subject to breakup—that it should not break up, indeed, this possibility does not exist.' By this, it is shown that the earth element is impermanent because it is produced by conditions, just like anything else produced by conditions. This is the method for the remaining phenomena as well.

Idāni anvayato, byatirekato ca saṅkhatadhammānaṃ aniccataṃ patiṭṭhāpetuṃ “jātipaccayā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aniccalakkhaṇasseva cettha patiṭṭhāpanaṃ tasmiṃ patiṭṭhāpite sesalakkhaṇadvayassapi patiṭṭhāpanasiddhito.

Now, to establish the impermanence of conditioned phenomena both positively and negatively, it is said, 'because of birth as condition,' etc. Here, the establishment is of the characteristic of impermanence alone, for when that is established, the establishment of the other two characteristics is also accomplished.

Iminā peyyālena ime dhammarāsayo saṃkhittāti sambandho. “Dvārārammaṇehi saddhiṃ dvārappavattā dhammā, pañcakkhandhā”ti idaṃ abhiññeyyaniddese “cakkhuṃ, bhikkhave, abhiññeyya”ntiādinā (paṭi. ma. 1.3; saṃ. ni. 4.46) dvārārammaṇehi saddhiṃ dvārappavatte dhamme dassetvā tesaṃ pañcahi khandhehi saṅgahitataṃ dassetuṃ “rūpaṃ abhiññeyyaṃ…pe… viññāṇaṃ abhiññeyya”nti āgatattā vuttaṃ. Paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.48) pana “yaṃ kiñci rūpa”ntiādinā paṭhamaṃ pañcakkhandhe dassetvā “cakkhu”ntiādinā dvārārammaṇehi saddhiṃ dvārappavattā dhammā dassitā. Tathādassane kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

The connection is that by this abbreviation these collections of dhammas are summarized. The statement, 'The dhammas that have arisen at the doors along with the door-objects are the five aggregates,' is made because in the Exposition of the Directly Knowable, after showing the dhammas that have arisen at the doors along with the door-objects with the words, 'Bhikkhus, the eye is to be directly known,' etc., the passage 'Form is to be directly known… consciousness is to be directly known' is given in order to show their inclusion by the five aggregates. In the Paṭisambhidāmagga, however, first the five aggregates are shown with 'whatever form,' etc., and then the dhammas that have arisen at the doors along with the door-objects are shown with 'the eye,' etc. The reason for showing it thus has already been stated previously.

Kasmā [M 2.0391] panettha ime dhammarāsayo saṃkhittāti pāḷiyaṃ vitthārato āgatattāti dassento “vuttaṃ heta”ntiādimāha. Tenevāha “taṃ tattha…pe… saṃkhitta”nti. Tattha tanti abhiññeyyaṃ. Etthāti abhiññeyyaniddese. “Viññāṇaṃ mano dhammā”tiādinā tattha tattha koṭṭhāse ye lokuttaradhammā āgatā. Keci pana “etthāti paṭisambhidāya”nti vadanti, taṃ na [V 2.0367] sundaraṃ. Sammasanupagā eva hi dhammā paṭisambhidāyaṃ gahitā sammasanavārassa adhippetattā, na abhiññeyyaniddese (paṭi. ma. 1.3; saṃ. ni. 4.46) viya sabbeva abhiññeyyā dhammā. Ye rūpārūpadhammā. Yassāti yogino. Tesu tena sammasanaṃ ārabhitabbaṃ yathāpākaṭaṃ vipassanābhinivesoti katvā. Pacchā pana anupaṭṭhahantepi upāyena upaṭṭhahāpetvā anavasesatova sammasitabbā.

To show why these collections of dhammas are summarized here—namely, because they are set forth in detail in the Pāḷi—he says, 'For this has been said,' etc. For that reason he says, 'That therein… is summarized.' Therein, 'that' is what is to be directly known. 'Here' means in the Exposition of the Directly Knowable. By 'consciousness, mind, mental objects,' etc., are meant the supramundane dhammas that occur in the various sections. Some, however, say, '“Here” means in the Paṭisambhidāmagga,' but that is not good. For only dhammas suitable for comprehension are included in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, since the section on comprehension is intended, not all directly knowable dhammas as in the Exposition of the Directly Knowable. These are the material and immaterial dhammas. 'Of whom' refers to the yogi. Comprehension of them should be undertaken by him, since the initial application to insight proceeds according to what is manifest. Afterwards, however, even those that are not manifest should be made to manifest by skillful means and comprehended without remainder.

695. “Atītaṃ rūpaṃ anicca”ntiādinā aniccato sammasanassa atītādivibhāgā pavattiṭṭhānabhūtāti āha “ekādasahi okāsehī”ti. Vavatthāpanaṃ nāma sanniṭṭhānaṃ. Aniccato sanniṭṭhānañcettha “anicca”nti vipassanāvāti āha “aniccanti sammasatī”ti.

695. By 'Past form is impermanent,' etc., the divisions, such as past, etc., are the basis for the proceeding of the comprehension as impermanent; thus he says, 'in eleven instances.' Defining, indeed, is ascertainment. And here, the ascertainment as impermanent is insight itself as 'impermanent'; thus he says, 'one comprehends as “impermanent.”'

Kathanti sammasanākāro pucchitoti taṃ parato idheva pāḷiyaṃ dutiyavāre vuttanayenevāti saṅkhepeneva vissajjeti. Idāni tamatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “vuttañheta”ntiādimāha. Tattha hī-ti hetuatthe nipāto. Yasmā “rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhenā”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā iminā vuttanayena aniccanti sammasatīti yojanā.

The question 'How?' asks about the mode of comprehension. He answers this briefly, stating that it is by the very method taught later in the second section here in this very Pāḷi. Now, to make that meaning clearer, he says, 'For this has been said,' etc. Therein, 'hi' is a particle in the sense of reason. The connection is: because it is said, 'Past, future, and present form is impermanent in the sense of destruction,' therefore 'by this stated method, one comprehends it as impermanent.'

Evampi saṅkhepoyevāti vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “esā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Atīteti atīte bhave. Ādikammikassa hi idaṃ sammasanavidhānaṃ, tasmā bhavavasena addhābhedo adhippeto. Tenāha “nayimaṃ bhavaṃ sampattantī”ti. Ettha iti-saddo hetuattho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yaṃ atītabhave pariyāpannaṃ rūpaṃ, taṃ atīteyeva bhave khīṇaṃ, tato na imaṃ bhavaṃ sampattaṃ, tasmā aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhena khayasabhāvattāti sammasatīti. Esa nayo yaṃ anāgatantiādīsupi.

To show by analyzing that even this is just a summary, the words beginning with 'This...' were spoken. 'In the past' means in a past existence. For this is the method of comprehension for a beginner; therefore, a division of time by way of existence is intended. For that reason, he says, 'it does not reach this existence.' Here the word 'iti' has the sense of reason. This is what is said: Whatever form was comprised in a past existence perished in that very past existence; from there it did not reach this existence. Therefore, one comprehends: 'It is impermanent in the sense of perishing because it has the nature of perishing.' This is the method also in regard to 'what is future,' etc.

Yaṃ [M 2.0392] bahiddhā, tampi bahiddhā eva khīyati, na ajjhattabhāvaṃ gacchatīti aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhenāti, yaṃ oḷārikaṃ, tampi tattheva khīyatīti aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhenātiādinā yojetabbaṃ.

It should be connected thus: 'Whatever form is external also perishes externally and does not become internal; thus it is impermanent in the sense of perishing.' And: 'Whatever form is gross also perishes right there; thus it is impermanent in the sense of perishing,' and so on.

Idaṃ sabbampīti idaṃ atītādibhedassa rūpassa sammasanato sabbaṃ ekādasavidhampi sammasanaṃ ekaṃ sammasanaṃ aniccato sammasananti katvā.

'All this' means that because it is the comprehension of form which has divisions such as past, etc., all this elevenfold comprehension is a single comprehension, being taken as the comprehension of impermanence.

Tanti taṃ ekādasavidhampi rūpaṃ. Sappaṭibhayatāyāti bhayānakatāya. Bhayāvahaṃ hotīti appahīnavipallāsassa [V 2.0368] “ahaṃ vinassāmi, mama santakaṃ vinassatī”ti cintentassa bhayajanakaṃ hoti. Sīhopamasutte devānaṃ viyāti sīhopamasutte desiyamāne devānaṃ viya. Tattha hi –

'That' means that elevenfold form. 'Because of its fearfulness' means because of its terrifying nature. 'It brings fear' means it is fear-generating for one whose perversions have not been abandoned, who thinks, 'I will perish, my possessions will perish.' 'Like for the devas in the Sīhopama Sutta' means like for the devas when the Sīhopama Sutta was being taught. For there—

“Yadā tathāgato loke uppajjati arahaṃ sammāsambuddho…pe… so dhammaṃ deseti ‘iti rūpaṃ, iti rūpassa samudayo, iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo. Iti vedanā… iti saññā… iti saṅkhārā… iti viññāṇaṃ, iti viññāṇassa samudayo, iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo’ti. Yepi te, bhikkhave, devā dīghāyukā vaṇṇavanto sukhabahulā uccesu vimānesu ciraṭṭhitikā, tepi tathāgatassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā yebhuyyena bhayaṃ saṃvegaṃ santāsaṃ āpajjanti ‘aniccāva kira bho mayaṃ samānā niccamhāti amaññimha, addhuvāva…pe… asassatāva kira bho mayaṃ samānā sassatamhāti amaññimha, mayampi kira bho aniccā addhuvā asassatā sakkāyapariyāpannā’”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.78; a. ni. 4.33) –

'When the Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One... he teaches the Dhamma thus: “This is form, this is the origin of form, this is the cessation of form. This is feeling... this is perception... these are formations... this is consciousness, this is the origin of consciousness, this is the cessation of consciousness.” Then, bhikkhus, even those devas who are long-lived, beautiful, abounding in happiness, dwelling for a long time in lofty mansions, on hearing the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, for the most part experience fear, agitation, and terror, thinking: “It seems, sirs, that though we are impermanent, we regarded ourselves as permanent; though we are unstable... though we are non-eternal, we regarded ourselves as eternal. It seems, sirs, that we too are impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, included within the existing body.”' (Saṃ. Ni. 3.78; A. Ni. 4.33)

Evaṃ devānaṃ bhayuppatti āgatā.

Thus the arising of fear for the devas has come.
