Khandhapañcakaṃ, tadekadeso vā attavādīhi “attā”ti parikappīyati, tañca ekantato aniccaṃ, dukkhañcāti āha “yañhi aniccaṃ, taṃ dukkha”ntiādi. Tīsu dukkhatāsu saṅkhāradukkhatāva byāpinī, “yadaniccaṃ, taṃ dukkha”nti ca adhippetāti vuttaṃ “aniccataṃ vā udayabbayapaṭipīḷanaṃ vā”ti. Attā abhavissāti “kārako vedako sayaṃvasī”ti evaṃbhūto attā abhavissāti adhippāyo. Evañhi sati rūpassa ābādhāya saṃvattanaṃ ayujjamānakaṃ siyā. Yathā rūpakkhandhe abhedato tividhaṃ sammasanaṃ, bhedato tettiṃsavidhaṃ, evaṃ vedanākkhandhādīsupīti imamatthaṃ “esa nayo”ti [M 2.0393] atidisati. Tena khandhavasena tāva bhedato pañcasaṭṭhiadhikā sataṃ sammasanavārā dassitā honti. Iminā nayena dvārachakkādīsupi yathārahaṃ sammasanabhedo veditabbo.

The pentad of aggregates, or a part of it, is conjectured to be 'self' by the proponents of a self-doctrine, but it is entirely impermanent and suffering. Hence he says, 'For what is impermanent is suffering,' etc. Among the three kinds of suffering, the suffering due to formations is pervasive, and 'what is impermanent is suffering' is intended, as is said: 'impermanence or oppression by rise and fall.' The meaning of 'if there were a self' is that there would be a self that is 'a doer, an experiencer, one who has mastery.' For if this were so, it would be illogical for form to be subject to affliction. Just as in the case of the form aggregate there is comprehension in three ways without division and in thirty-three ways with division, so it is for the aggregates of feeling and the rest. He extends this meaning by saying, 'This is the method.' Thus, with respect to the aggregates, when divided, one hundred and sixty-five occasions for comprehension are shown. By this method, the divisions of comprehension should be understood as is suitable in regard to the six sense bases, etc.

696. Niyamato saṅkhatādibhedaṃ hotīti ekaṃsena saṅkhatatādivisesavantaṃ hoti asaṅkhatādisabhāve aniccatāya asambhavato. Assāti aniccassa. Pariyāyadassanatthanti vevacanadassanatthaṃ, taṃ pana “khayadhamma”ntiādīnaṃ vasena veditabbaṃ, na purimānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ. Na hi [V 2.0369] tadeva tassa pariyāyo hoti, nāpi saṅkhatapaṭiccasamuppannapadāni hutvā abhāvadīpanato pākabhāvadīpanato. Pākabhāvadīpanena pana aniccatāya sādhanapakkhe tiṭṭhanti. Teneva hi sabbesaṃ padānaṃ pariyāyatābhāvato “nānākārehi vā”ti vikappantaraṃ gahitaṃ. Manasikārappavattīdassanatthanti aniccatāya upabrūhanamanasikārapavattidassanatthaṃ.

696. 'It necessarily has the distinction of being conditioned, etc.' means that it is definitively possessed of the distinctions of being conditioned, etc., because impermanence is impossible in a state that is unconditioned, etc. 'Of it' means of the impermanent. 'For the purpose of showing synonyms' means for the purpose of showing alternative expressions. This, however, should be understood in relation to such terms as 'subject to perishing,' etc., not the first three. For that very term is not a synonym for itself, nor are the terms 'conditioned' and 'dependently arisen,' as they indicate prior non-existence. However, by indicating prior non-existence, they stand on the side of proving impermanence. It is precisely because not all the terms are synonyms that the alternative 'or in various ways' is taken. 'For the purpose of showing the occurrence of attention' means for the purpose of showing the occurrence of attention that reinforces the comprehension of impermanence.

Cattārīsākāraanupassanākathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Discourse on Contemplation in Forty Aspects

697. Soti yogāvacaro. Tassāti yathāvuttabhedassa aniccatādisammasanassa. Thirabhāvatthāyāti daḷhabhāvatthāya aniccādiākārassa punappunaṃ manasikāro viya bahulīkārabhāvato. Yaṃ taṃ bhagavatā etassa vibhaṅge aniccādisammasanaṃ vuttanti sambandho. Anulomikanti ariyamaggādhigamassa anukūlaṃ. Khantinti ñāṇakhantiṃ. Ñāṇañhi visayasabhāvaṃ ogāhetvā vavatthāne khamati sahatīti khantīti vuccati. Sammattaniyāmanti ariyamaggaṃ. So hi sammādiṭṭhiādisammattañceva anivattidhammatāya niyāmo cāti vuccati. “Ādinā nayenā”ti iminā “pañcakkhandhe dukkhato passanto anulomikaṃ khantiṃ paṭilabhati, khandhānaṃ nirodho sukhaṃ nibbānanti passanto sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.38) evamādiko pāṭhaseso rogādipaṭipakkhayojanāvasena vitthāretabbo. “Khandhānaṃ nirodho niccaṃ nibbāna”nti vacanena saṅkhārānaṃ dukkharogatādipaṭipakkho nibbānassa sukhārogyādibhāvo “ādinā nayenā”ti ettha nayaggahaṇena dīpitoti. Avaseso sabbo pāṭho pakāsito eva hotīti.

697. 'He' is the yogi. 'Of that' refers to the contemplation of impermanence, etc., with its divisions as stated. 'For the sake of firmness' means for the sake of stability—due to frequent cultivation, which is like repeated attention to the aspects of impermanence, etc. The connection is thus: that contemplation of impermanence, etc., which was spoken by the Blessed One in the analysis of this. 'Conducive' means favorable for the attainment of the noble path. 'Patience' refers to the patience of knowledge. For knowledge, having penetrated the intrinsic nature of its object, is able to endure it in making a determination; thus it is called 'patience.' 'The right determination' refers to the noble path. For it is called 'rightness' because it consists of right view and so on, and 'determination' because it is of an irreversible nature. By 'by the method beginning with' is meant that the remaining passage, such as: 'One who sees the five aggregates as suffering gains the conducive patience; one who sees that the cessation of the aggregates is happiness, Nibbāna, enters the right determination,' should be elaborated by way of applying the opposites of disease, etc. By the statement, 'The cessation of the aggregates is permanent, Nibbāna,' it is indicated through the inclusion of the term 'method' here in 'by the method beginning with' that Nibbāna's nature of happiness, health, etc., is the opposite of the suffering, disease, etc., of formations. Thus, the entire remaining passage is indeed clarified.

Kāmañcetaṃ [M 2.0394] cattārīsāya ākārehi sammasanaṃ anulomañāṇe bhāvetabbavidhānaṃ. Tenāha “anulomañāṇaṃ vibhajantena…pe… vutta”nti, ito paṭṭhāya pana kataparicayasseva kiccāvahaṃ hotīti idhāpi vuttantīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tassāpīti na kevalaṃ kalāpasammasanasseva, atha kho yathādassitassa cattālīsappabhedassa aniccādisammasanassapi. Tañhi anulomikakhantipaṭilābhāya, sammattaniyāmokkamanāya ca saṃvattanato ekaṃsato icchitabbaṃ. Vuttañhi –

Indeed, this contemplation in forty aspects is the method by which it should be developed in the stage of conformity knowledge. Therefore it was said: '...was stated by the one analyzing conformity knowledge....' However, it should be understood that from this point onwards it is effective only for one who has already practiced it, and thus it is stated here as well. 'Of that too' means not only of the contemplation of groups, but also of the forty-fold contemplation of impermanence, etc., as shown. For that is certainly to be desired, since it leads to the attainment of conducive patience and to entry into the right determination. For it is said:

“So vata, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kañci saṅkhāraṃ niccato samanupassanto anulomikāya khantiyā samannāgato bhavissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati, anulomikāya khantiyā [V 2.0370] asamannāgato sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati, sammattaniyāmaṃ anokkamamāno sotāpattiphalaṃ vā…pe… arahattaṃ vā sacchikarissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. So vata, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sabbasaṅkhāre aniccato samanupassanto”ti (a. ni. 6.98; paṭi. ma. 3.36) –

“Indeed, O bhikkhus, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who regards any formation as permanent will be endowed with conducive patience. It is impossible that one not endowed with conducive patience will enter the right determination. It is impossible that one not entering the right determination will realize the fruit of stream-entry... or arahantship. Indeed, O bhikkhus, a bhikkhu regarding all formations as impermanent...”

Ādi sukkapakkho vitthāretabbo. Tathā “so vata, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kañci saṅkhāraṃ sukhato, dukkhato, kañci dhammaṃ attato, anattato”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.36) vitthāretabbo.

The bright side beginning thus should be elaborated in full. Similarly, the passage should be elaborated in full for regarding any formation 'as pleasant' or 'as suffering,' and any phenomenon 'as self' or 'as not-self'.

698. Ekekaṃ khandhaṃ aniccādisammasanassa vasena sammasatīti sambandho. Tassa pana sammasanassa pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ sādhāraṇatāya “ekekaṃ khandha”nti vuttaṃ. Anaccantikatāyāti accantikatābhāvato, asassatatāyāti attho. Sassatañhi accantikaṃ parāya koṭiyā abhāvato. Ādiantavantatāyāti pubbāparakoṭivantatāya, udayabbayadhammatoti attho. Aniccato sammasatīti sambandho. Esa nayo sabbattha.

698. The connection is that one contemplates each aggregate by way of the contemplation of impermanence, etc. But since this contemplation is common to the five aggregates, the words 'each aggregate' are used. 'Because of non-ultimacy' means because of the absence of ultimacy; the meaning is 'because of non-eternality.' For the eternal is ultimate because it is without a final limit. 'Because of having a beginning and an end' means because of having a former and a latter limit; that is, because it has the nature of arising and passing away. The connection is: 'one contemplates it as impermanent.' This is the method in all cases.

Aniccatoti ca addhuvato. Etañhi na niccaṃ, khaṇikatāya asadābhāvitāya vā na iccaṃ na upagantabbanti aniccaṃ. Uppādavayapaṭipīḷanatāyāti uppādena, vayena ca pati pati khaṇe khaṇe taṃsamaṅgino vibādhanasabhāvattā, tehi vā sayameva vibādhetabbattā. Udayabbayavanto hi dhammā abhiṇhaṃ tehi paṭipīḷitā eva honti, yā pīḷanā “saṅkhāradukkhatā”ti vuccati. Dukkhavatthutāyāti [M 2.0395] tividhassāpi dukkhassa, saṃsāradukkhassa ca adhiṭṭhānabhāvato. Paccayayāpanīyatāyāti yathārahaṃ paccayehi yāpetabbatāya. Rogamūlatāyāti mūlabyādhi viya anubandhabyādhīnaṃ mūlabhāvato, padadvayenāpi yāpyarogasadisatoti dasseti. Yāpyabyādhi hi rogo itaro ābādhoti. Dukkhatāsūlayogitāyāti tividhadukkhatāsaṅkhātena rujjanena yujjatāya. Kilesāsucipaggharaṇatāyāti yathārahamārammaṇavasena, samannāgamavasena ca rāgādikilesāsucivissandanato. Ahutvā sambhavato uppattiyā uddhumātatā.

'As impermanent' means because it is unstable. For this is not permanent because of its momentariness; or, because of its not existing always, it is not desirable or to be approached, thus it is 'impermanent.' 'Because of being oppressed by arising and passing away' means because of having the nature of afflicting the person endowed with them by arising and passing away at every single moment, or because they themselves must be afflicted by them. For phenomena that have arising and passing away are constantly oppressed by them, and this oppression is called 'the suffering of formations.' 'Because it is a basis for suffering' means because it serves as the foundation for the threefold suffering and for the suffering of saṃsāra. 'Because it is sustained by conditions' means because it must be maintained by appropriate conditions. 'Because it is the root of disease' means because, like a root-disease, it is the root of subsequent illnesses; by both terms it shows that it is like a chronic disease. For a chronic illness is a 'disease' (roga), while the other is an 'ailment' (ābādha). 'Because of its connection with the dart of suffering' means because it is connected with the pain designated as the threefold suffering-nature. 'Because it is a discharge of the impurity of defilements' means because it oozes the impurity of defilements such as lust, according to the object and one's possession of them. Because it arises after not having been, it is bloated by origination.

Antotudanatāyāti abbhantare tudanato. Dukkhavedanādayo viya hi ime saṅkhārā attabhāvassa abbhantaragatā eva udayabbayavasena tudanti. Ariyamaggasaṇḍāsena vinā nīharituṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya dunnīharaṇīyatā taṇhādiṭṭhābhinivesadaḷhabhāvato. Aghanti pāpaṃ viya ariyajanehi [V 2.0371] vigarahitabbaṃ. Sattānaṃ anatthajananato avaḍḍhiāvahaṃ, pāpassa ca vatthubhūtaṃ khandhapañcakanti āha “vigaraha…pe… aghato”ti. Aseribhāvajanakatāyāti paravasatājananato. Yathā gilāno aññehi saṃvesanavuṭṭhāpanādinā parapaṭibaddhasarīravuttiko aserī, evametepi aseribhāvajanakā. Avasatāyāti avasavattanato. Yathā parosatanto puriso parassa vasaṃ na gacchati, evaṃ subhasukhādibhāvena vase vattetuṃ asakkuṇeyyato. Avidheyyatāyāti “mā jīratha, mā mīyathā”tiādinā vidhātuṃ asakkuṇeyyato. Palujjanatāyāti byādhiādīhi pakārehi chijjanato vinassanato. Tehi eva vā ābyasanato. Byasanattho hi lokasaddo, pasaddo bhusattho daṭṭhabbo. Byādhiādīhi ca khandhānaṃ byasananti. Byasanāvahabhāvena etīti īti, āgantukānaṃ akusalapakkhiyānaṃ byasanahetūnaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Khandhā ca edisāti āha “anekabyasanāvahatāya ītito”ti.

'Because of being a goad within' means because it goads from within. For these formations, like painful feelings, being internal to one's own being, goad by way of arising and passing away. Because they are hard to extract, being unable to be removed without the pincers of the noble path, due to the firmness of the adherence to craving and views. 'As a calamity' means like an evil, something to be censured by the noble ones. It brings harm to beings, leads to decline, and is the basis for evil—this five-aggregate mass. Thus it is said: '...because it is to be censured... as a calamity.' 'Because it generates a state of non-mastery' means because it generates dependence on others. Just as a sick person, whose bodily life depends on others for lying down, getting up, and so on, is not his own master, so too do these aggregates generate a state of non-mastery. 'Because of being uncontrollable' means because it does not submit to one's will. Just as a man who is his own master does not submit to the will of another, so too these aggregates cannot be brought under one's own will to be beautiful, pleasant, and so on. 'Because of being unbiddable' means because one cannot command them, saying, 'Do not grow old, do not die.' 'Because of crumbling' means because of being broken up and destroyed in various ways by disease, etc. Or because of being greatly afflicted by them. The word `loka` here has the sense of calamity (`byasana`); the prefix `pa-` should be understood as an intensifier. And the calamity for the aggregates is through disease and so on. 'It comes' (`eti`) 'bringing calamity' (`byasanāvaha`), thus it is a 'disaster' (`īti`). This is a term for the adventitious, unwholesome causes of calamity. The aggregates are of such a nature. Thus it is said: 'because they bring many calamities, they are a disaster.'

Upaddavatīti upaddavo, anatthaṃ janento abhibhavati ajjhottharatīti attho, rājadaṇḍādīnaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Khandhā ca edisāti vuttaṃ “aviditānaṃ…pe… upaddavato”ti. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikabhayāvahato, abhayapaṭipakkhato ca khandhā bhayanti āha “sabbabhayānaṃ…pe… bhayato”ti. Bahiddhā ñātibyasanādīhi, ajjhattaṃ rāgādīhi anatthehi upasajjanaṭṭhena, upasaggasadisatāya [M 2.0396] ca upasaggo. Upasaggoti ca devatūpasaṃhāravasena pavatto byādhiādianattho. So atthakāmena muhuttampi na ajjhupekkhitabbo hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “anekehi…pe… upasaggato”ti. Dosūpasaṭṭhatāyāti ārammaṇato, sampayogato ca rāgādidosehi upetatāya. Lokadhammā lābhādihetukā anunayapaṭighā, tehi, byādhiādīhi ca anavaṭṭhitatā pacalitatā.

'It oppresses' (`upaddavati`), thus it is an 'oppression' (`upaddavo`); the meaning is that it overpowers and overwhelms while generating harm. This is a term for things like royal punishment. And that the aggregates are of such a nature is stated: '...because they are an oppression... for the uninformed....' Because they bring fear in this present life and in future lives, and because they are the opposite of safety, the aggregates are a 'fear.' Thus it is said: '...because they are a fear... of all fears....' Because of being attached to by harms—externally, such as the loss of relatives, and internally, such as lust—and because of their similarity to an affliction, they are an 'affliction' (`upasagga`). 'Affliction' also refers to a harm such as a disease that occurs due to the influence of a deity. That should not be neglected even for a moment by one who desires his own welfare. Therefore it was said: '...because it is an affliction... by many....' 'Because of being beset by faults' means because of being endowed with faults such as lust, both in relation to the object and by way of association. Worldly conditions are attraction and aversion caused by gain and so on; due to them, and due to disease and so on, there is instability and vacillation.

Upakkamenāti attano, parassa vā payogena. Sarasenāti sabhāvena. Pabhaṅgupagamanasīlatā bhiduratā. Sabbāvatthanipātitāyāti rukkhaphalaṃ viya atitaruṇakālato paṭṭhāya sabbāsu avatthāsu nipatanasīlatāya. Anipatassapi sabbena sabbaṃ asāratāya thirabhāvassa abhāvatāya. Thirañhi dhuvaṃ nāma hoti. Tāyituṃ rakkhituṃ asamatthatāya na tāyanoti atāyano, tabbhāvo atāyanatā. Tāṇāsīsāya upagatassa alabbhaneyyakhematā. Dukkhabhītiyā upalīyanādhippāyena allīyituṃ. Dukkhanivattanaṃ leṇakiccaṃ. Jātiādibhayānaṃ hiṃsanaṃ vidhamanaṃ bhayasārakattaṃ. Yathāparikappitehīti paramatthato avijjamānehi bālehi parikappitappakārehi. Rittatāyāti vivittatāya, virahitatāyāti [V 2.0372] attho. Antosārābhāvo rittatā. Sā eva ca tucchatāti āha “rittatāyeva tucchato”ti. Appakattāti parittattā, lāmakattā vā. Dhuvasārābhāvādīhi saddhiṃ attasārābhāvaṃ rittapadena vatvā nibbattitamattasārābhāvameva suññapadena dassetuṃ “sāmi…pe… suññato”ti vuttaṃ. Yathā kenaci sāmiādilakkhaṇena attanā suññā ete, evaṃ sayampi ataṃsabhāvoti āha “sayañca…pe… anattato”ti. Na attāti hi anattāti.

“By effort” means by one’s own or another’s exertion. “By its own nature” means by its intrinsic nature. The nature of tending towards breaking up is fragility. “Because of its liability to fall in all states” means because of its nature of falling in all states, starting from a very tender age, like the fruit of a tree. Even for that which has not fallen, this is because of its complete essencelessness, due to the absence of a stable state. For what is stable is called permanent. Because of the inability to protect or guard, it is “no protection”; its state is “the state of no protection.” For one who has approached seeking a refuge, it is the unobtainability of security. To cling with the intention of taking shelter out of fear of suffering. The function of a shelter is the warding off of suffering. The destroying and dispelling of the fears of birth, etc., is the state of being a dispeller of fear. “As imagined” means in the ways imagined by fools, which do not exist in an ultimate sense. “As empty” means as secluded; the meaning is “as devoid.” The absence of an inner core is emptiness. And that very thing is hollowness, thus he says, “from emptiness itself as hollowness.” “As insignificant” means because of being trifling, or because of being base. Having stated the absence of a self-essence along with the absence of a permanent essence and so on with the word “empty,” in order to show with the word “void” just the absence of an essence in what has merely come to be, it is said: “…as void of a master… etc.” Just as these are void of a self characterized as a master and so on, so too is one oneself devoid of that nature. Thus he says: “…and oneself… as not-self.” For 'not a self' is indeed 'not-self'.

Pavattidukkhatāyāti bhavapavattidukkhabhāvato. Bhavapavatti ca pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ aniccādiākārena pavattanameva, so ca ādīnavo. Yathāha “yaṃ, bhikkhave, pañcupādānakkhandhā aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu ādīnavo”ti. Tenāha “dukkhassa ca ādīnavatāyā”ti. Ādīnanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso yathā “ekamanta”nti (dī. ni. 1.165), ativiya kapaṇanti attho. Bhusattho hi ayaṃ ā-kāro. Yathā [M 2.0397] “dvidhā chiddakaṃ vicchiddaka”nti ettha dvi-saddassa atthe vi-saddo, evamidhāpīti āha “dvedhā pariṇāmapakatitāya vipariṇāmadhammato”ti. Vipariṇāmo ca viparītasabhāvāpatti. Dubbalatāyāti sarasabhiduratāya balābhāvato. Dubbalampi kiñci mudukammaññābhāvena duppadhaṃsiyā. Ime pana supadhaṃsiyā evāti āha “pheggu viya sukhabhañjanīyatāya cā”ti. Aghassa pāpassa hetutā aghahetutā. Khandhapaṭibaddhameva hi sabbaṃ kibbisanti. Ime rūpādayo sukhahetu, na dukkhahetūti janitavissāsānaṃ hananasīlatāya, khandhesu hi “etaṃ mamā”ti gāhavasena sattā byasanaṃ pāpuṇanti, vissāsaṃ vā hanantīti vissāsaghātino, tabbhāvato.

“As the suffering in the round” means because of being the suffering in the round of existence. And the round of existence is just the proceeding of the five aggregates in the modes of impermanence, etc., and that is a danger. As it is said: “Bhikkhus, these five aggregates subject to clinging are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. This, bhikkhus, is the danger in the five aggregates subject to clinging.” Therefore he says, “and because of being the danger of suffering.” `Ādīna` is a verbal noun in the neuter gender, as in `ekamantaṃ`; the meaning is “very wretched.” For this `ā` has an intensive meaning. Just as in the phrase `dvidhā chiddakaṃ vicchiddakaṃ` the word `vi` has the meaning of the word `dvi`, so too here, he says, “because of its twofold nature of change, as being subject to change.” And change is the attainment of a contrary state. “As frailty” means because of the absence of strength, due to its fragile nature. Something weak might be hard to crush because of its softness and malleability. But these are easy to crush, thus he says, “and because of being easily broken like sapwood.” Being a cause of `agha`, that is, of evil, is “being a cause of `agha`.” For all wrongdoing is connected with the aggregates. Because of their nature of slaying those who have generated trust that “these things, form, etc., are a cause of pleasure, not a cause of suffering”; for by the power of grasping the aggregates with the thought “this is mine,” beings meet with disaster, or they slay trust, thus they are “trust-slayers”; because of being that.

Vigatabhavatāyāti apagatavaḍḍhitāya. Vibhavataṇhā, vibhavadiṭṭhi ca vibhavo uttarapadalopena, tato vibhavato, pitusadisassa vā sabhāvahetuno vibhavato vināsato sambhūtatāya. Āsavānaṃ ārammaṇādinā paccayabhāvo āsavapadaṭṭhānatā. Bījādiko asādhāraṇo hetu, bhūtasalilādiko sādhāraṇo paccayo. Esa nayo ajjhattepi. Tehi samecca sambhūya kato saṅkhato. Maccumārassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvena, kilesamārassa paccayabhāvena saṃvaḍḍhanato āmisabhūtatā, khandhāpi khandhānaṃ āmisabhūtā paccayabhāvena saṃvaḍḍhanato, tadantogadhā abhisaṅkhārā. Devaputtamārassa pana “mameta”nti adhimānavasena āmisabhāvoti khandhādimārānampi imesaṃ yathārahaṃ āmisabhūtatā vattabbā. Dhammasaddo “jātidhammāna”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.373; paṭi. ma. 1.33) viya pakatiattho[V 2.0373], “dhammapaṭisambhidā”tiādīsu (vibha. 718 ādayo) viya hetuattho cāti āha “jātijarābyādhimaraṇapakatitāya, sokaparidevaupāyāsahetutāyā”ti. Saṃkilesattayaggahaṇena tadekaṭṭhānaṃ dasannaṃ kilesavatthūnampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tadārammaṇāpi hi dhammā tadanativattanato saṃkilesikā eva. Tathā khuddā, taṇhā, jaṭādīsu sarīrassa, saṃkilesassa ca saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

“Due to the state of being devoid of existence” means due to being devoid of growth. Craving for non-existence and the view of non-existence are called `vibhava` by elision of the final word. From that `vibhava`, or because of being produced from destruction, that is, from the perishing of an intrinsic cause similar to a father. Being a condition for the taints by way of object, etc., is the state of being a proximate cause for the taints. A specific, uncommon cause is like a seed, etc.; a common condition is like earth and water, etc. This is the method internally as well. That which is made by them coming together and combining is 'conditioned.' Because it promotes Māra as death by being his basis, and Māra as defilements by being their condition, it is the state of being bait. The aggregates too are bait for the aggregates by being their condition for promotion, and the formations are included within them. But for Māra as a devaputta, the state of being bait is due to the conceit “this is mine.” Thus, the state of being bait for these, the Māras of the aggregates, etc., should be stated as is appropriate. The word `dhamma`, as in “subject to birth,” etc., has the meaning of nature, and as in “discrimination of `dhamma`,” etc., it has the meaning of cause. Thus he says: “because of having the nature of birth, aging, sickness, and death, and because of being a cause for sorrow, lamentation, and despair.” By the taking up of the three kinds of defilement, the inclusion of the ten bases of the defilements, which have the same standing, should be understood. For phenomena that have them as object are also defiling because they do not transcend them. Similarly, in the case of hunger, thirst, aging, etc., the inclusion of the body and of defilement should be understood.

Cattārīsāpi sammasanāni tīsu anupassanāsu antogadhānevāti tadantogadhabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “ettha hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aniccānupassanāni sarūpato[M 2.0398], pariyāyato ca aniccabhāvavibhāvanato. Esa nayo itaresupi. “Asārakato”ti idaṃ niccasārābhāvavibhāvanaṃ.

The forty kinds of comprehension are also included in the three kinds of insight-contemplation; thus, to show their inclusion, it is said, “For here…,” etc. They are insight-contemplations of impermanence because they make manifest the state of impermanence both in its own nature and discursively. This is the method for the others too. The phrase “as essenceless” is the making manifest of the absence of a permanent essence.

Ettāvatā kalāpato dhamme saṅgahetvā nayato sammasanamattaṃ dassitaṃ, na tāva anupadadhammavipassanā vihitāti “sammasanārambhavidhāna”nti. Vuttaṃ.

Thus far, having grouped phenomena into aggregates and by way of method, only the mere comprehension has been shown, not yet the insight that analyzes phenomena one by one. Thus this is called “The Instruction on the Beginning of Comprehension.”

Indriyatikkhakāraṇanavakakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on the Nine Causes for Making the Faculties Keen

699. Ekaccassa tikkhindriyassa mahāpaññassa nayavipassanāvaseneva udayabbayañāṇaṃ uppajjati, itarassa nuppajjati. Taṃ sandhāya “yassa pana…pe… na sampajjatī”ti vuttaṃ. Udayabbayañāṇuppatti hi idha nayavipassanāya sampajjananti adhippetaṃ. Tena “navahākārehi indriyāni tikkhāni bhavanti…pe… antarā ca abbosānenā”ti evaṃ vuttānaṃ navannaṃ ākārānaṃ vasena indriyāni tikkhāni katvā sappāyāni sevamānena sammasitabbanti sambandho.

699. For a certain one with keen faculties and great wisdom, the knowledge of arising and passing away arises just by the power of methodical insight, but for another it does not arise. With reference to that one, it is said: “But for one for whom…pe… it is not accomplished.” Indeed, the arising of the knowledge of arising and passing away is intended here as the accomplishment of methodical insight. Therefore, the connection is that one should contemplate, having made the faculties keen by means of the nine modes stated thus, “By nine ways… and without giving up,” while resorting to what is suitable.

Tenāti yoginā. Navahākārehīti vakkhamānehi navahi ākārehi. Indriyānīti saddhādīni indriyāni. Tikkhānīti tikhiṇāni visadāni sūrāni. Uppannuppannānanti khaṇe khaṇe uppannānaṃ uppannānaṃ. Saṅkhārānanti vipassiyamānānaṃ rūpārūpadhammānaṃ. Khayamevāti paṭhamaṃ uppādaṃ disvā taṃ muñcitvā khayameva bhaṅgameva passati. Tassa tathākhayadassanapasutassa vipassanāpaññā tikkhā sūrā vahati, itarāni ca indriyāni. Tatthāti khayadassane. Sakkaccakiriyāyāti ādarakāritāya, yathā khayadassanaparameneva vipassanāñāṇaṃ pavattati, evaṃ taṃ ādarajāto sampādeti. Sātaccakiriyāyāti avicchedakiriyāya, yathā vipassanāñāṇaṃ khayadassanavasena nirantarameva pavattati, evaṃ yuttappayutto naṃ sampādeti. Sappāyakiriyāyāti anurūpakiriyāya āvāsādisattavidhasappāyāsevanakiriyāya[V 2.0374]. Nimittaggāhenāti yathā manasikarontassa vipassanāsamādhi uppanno, tassa ākārassa sallakkhaṇavasena samathanimittaggahaṇena sampādetīti sambandho. Anupavattanatāyāti anurūpato pavattanena bhāvanācittassa līnabhāve pītivīriyadhammavicayasambojjhaṅgānaṃ uddhatabhāve passaddhisamādhiupekkhāsambojjhaṅgānaṃ brūhanenāti attho. Kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhatanti attano kāye asucibhāvena bāhirakaaviññāṇakakuṇape [M 2.0399] viya jīvite ahitāvahapaccatthike viya nirapekkhacittaṃ upaṭṭhapeti. Tattha ca abhibhuyya nekkhammenāti tasmiṃ kāyacitte anapekkhabhāvena indriyānaṃ tikkhabhāvāpādanena uppannaṃ uppannaṃ dukkhaṃ vīriyena abhibhavitvā bhāvanaṃ sampādeti. Antarāti yathādhippetāya bhāvanāsiddhiyā antarāva. Abbosānenāti asaṅkocanena.

By that: that is, by the yogi. By the nine ways: that is, by the nine modes about to be explained. Faculties: that is, the faculties beginning with faith. Keen: that is, sharp, clear, and valiant. Of what has arisen and arisen: that is, of formations that have arisen moment by moment. Of formations: that is, of the material and immaterial phenomena being contemplated with insight. Only destruction: that is, having first seen arising, having abandoned that, one sees only destruction, only dissolution. For one thus intent on seeing destruction, the insight-wisdom flows keen and valiant, and so do the other faculties. Therein: that is, in the seeing of destruction. By careful action: that is, by acting with respect; just as the insight-knowledge proceeds with the seeing of destruction as its supreme object, so one, having generated respect, accomplishes it. By continuous action: that is, by uninterrupted action; just as the insight-knowledge proceeds continuously by way of seeing destruction, so one who is yoked and devoted accomplishes it. By suitable action: that is, by appropriate action, by the action of resorting to the seven kinds of suitable conditions beginning with lodging. By grasping the sign: the connection is that one accomplishes this by grasping the sign of serenity, by way of discerning the features of that mode in which insight-concentration arose for one who was attending. By making it proceed conformably: the meaning is, by making it proceed appropriately, by developing the enlightenment factors of rapture, energy, and discrimination of states when the meditation mind is sluggish, and by developing the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity when it is agitated. By non-concern for body and life: that is, one establishes a mind of non-concern for one's own body, regarding it as impure like an external, non-sentient corpse, and for life, regarding it as an enemy bringing harm. And therein by the renunciation that overcomes: that is, in regard to that body and mind, by means of non-concern, in bringing the faculties to a state of keenness, one accomplishes the development by overcoming with energy suffering as it repeatedly arises. In between: that is, in the interim, before the intended accomplishment of the development. Without cessation: that is, without shrinking back.

Evaṃ vuttānanti evaṃ “navahākārehi indriyāni tikkhāni bhavantī”tiādinā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttānaṃ. Ettha ca yathā nāma sukhumānaṃ muttāpavāḷādīnaṃ vijjhane sukhumatarena vedhanena bhavitabbaṃ, evameva saṇhasukhumānaṃ rūpārūpadhammānaṃ, paccayassa ca pariggaṇhane tikkhena ñāṇena bhavitabbaṃ. Tesaṃ pana khayavayadassane tikkhatarena bhavitabbaṃ. Tikkhataratā cassa nisānasilāyaṃ saṇhamaṭṭhatāya karaṇena viya pharasudhārāya nisitabhāvāpādanena indriyānaṃ tikkhabhāvāpādanena sādhetabbā. Tañca yehi navahi ākārehi hoti, tesu khaṇikānaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇe khaṇe bhijjanākāradassanaṃ paṭhamaṃ vuttaṃ “uppannuppannānaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ khayameva passatī”ti. Asati ñāṇassa tikkhatarabhāve tadabhāvato sesindriyatikkhatā tassa sambhārabhāvato vuttā, avinābhāvato vā. Sakkaccakiriyādiggahaṇaṃ pana tassa upāyadassanaṃ. Asappāyāni bhojanādīni anupayujjanādivasena vajjetvā sappāyāni mattaso sevamānena. Rūpārūpadhammānaṃ accantavidhuratāya ekajjhaṃ asammasitabbattā, tathā sammasanassa ca idha anadhippetattā “kālena rūpaṃ sammasitabbaṃ, kālena arūpa”nti vuttaṃ. Tatthāpi ca rūpassa oḷārikatāya suviññeyyattā paṭhamaṃ sammasitabbatā vuttā. Nibbatti passitabbāti paṭhamaṃ tāva āgamānusārato anumānavasena daṭṭhabbā. Tato paraṃ anukkamena balappatte bhāvanāñāṇe paccakkhatopi dissatīti.

Of what was thus stated: this refers to what was stated in the commentary beginning, “By nine modes the faculties become keen,” etc. Here, just as in piercing subtle pearls, corals, and so on, it must be done with a subtler piercing instrument, so too, in comprehending delicate and subtle material and immaterial phenomena and their conditions, it must be done with keen wisdom. But in seeing their destruction and passing away, it must be with even keener wisdom. This greater keenness should be accomplished by making the faculties keen, just as sharpness is produced in an axe-blade by making it fine and smooth on a whetstone. As to the nine modes by which this comes about, among them the seeing of the mode of the momentary breaking up of formations from moment to moment is stated first: “He sees only the destruction of formations that have arisen again and again.” When there is no greater keenness of wisdom, it is because of the absence of keenness in the other faculties; the keenness of the remaining faculties is mentioned because it is a requisite for that keen wisdom, or because of its inseparability from it. The mention of careful action and so on is to show the means for that. This is done by one who avoids unsuitable things such as food by not using them, and who resorts in moderation to what is suitable. Because material and immaterial phenomena are extremely disparate, they should not be contemplated together, and because contemplating them in that way is not intended here, it is said: “At one time material form should be contemplated, at another time the immaterial.” There too, it is said that material form should be contemplated first because of its grossness and easy cognizability. “Occurrence should be seen”: first, it should be seen by way of inference in accordance with the scriptures. Thereafter, when the meditation-knowledge has successively gained strength, it is also seen directly.

Rūpanibbattipassanākārakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on the Mode of Observing the Arising of Materiality

700. Sabbesanti [V 2.0375] kāmāvacarādiaṇḍajādibhedabhinnānaṃ sabbesaṃ sattānaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ kammato nibbattati taṃmūlakattā utujādirūpānaṃ. Parato pavattanakakāyadasakādivasena labbhamānaṃ pabandhattayaṃ, santatisīsaṃ vā sandhāya “tisantativasenā”ti vuttaṃ.

700. Of all beings: of all beings distinguished by divisions such as those of the sense-sphere, etc., and those who are egg-born, etc. First, it arises from kamma, because materiality produced by temperature, etc., has that kamma-born materiality as its root. Subsequently, referring to the threefold continuity obtained by way of the body-decade, etc., occurring later, or to the head of the continuity, it is said, 'by way of three continuities'.

Dandhaṃ [M 2.0400] mandaṃ cirena nirodho etassāti dandhanirodhaṃ sattarasacittakkhaṇāyukattā. Tenāha “garuparivattī”ti. Tenāti tasmā, yasmā “tato sīghataraṃ kho, bhikkhave, āyusaṅkhārā khīyantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.228) vacanato rūpadhammāpi ittarakālā eva, arūpadhammā pana tehi sātisayaṃ ittarakālā, tasmā āha bhagavāti attho. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vicāritameva. Tehi sadisāti cittassa uppādabhaṅgakkhaṇehi sadisā. Sabbesampi hi saṅkhārānaṃ uppādabhaṅgakkhaṇesu visadisatā natthi, samānakālāva te. Ṭhānappattanti ṭhitikkhaṇappattaṃ. Tenāti dutiyabhavaṅgacittena. Vatthurūpaṃ ekassa cittassa nissayo hutvā aññassa na hoti ṭhapetvā maraṇāsannaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “tena saddhi”ntiādi.

“Slow cessation” means that its cessation is slow, sluggish, and long-lasting, because its lifespan is seventeen mind-moments. Hence it is said to be “slow to change.” “By that” means therefore. Because it is said, “More quickly than that, bhikkhus, the life-formations are exhausted” (SN 2.228), material phenomena are of short duration, but immaterial phenomena are exceedingly more short-lived than them; therefore the Blessed One spoke thus—this is the meaning. Whatever should be said on this point has already been examined below. “Similar to them” means similar to the moments of arising and perishing of consciousness. For in regard to all formations, there is no dissimilarity in their moments of arising and perishing; they are of the same duration. “Having reached its station” means having reached the moment of presence. “By that” means by the second life-continuum consciousness. The base-materiality, having been a support for one consciousness, is not a support for another, except near death. Therefore it is said, “together with that,” and so on.

Evaṃ paṭisandhito paṭṭhāya yāva cuticittassa uppatti, taṃ dassetvā idāni nirodhaṃ dassetuṃ “paṭisandhicittassā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha ṭhānakkhaṇeti paṭisandhicittassa ṭhitikkhaṇe. Yāva pavatti nāma atthīti yāva saṃsārappavatti nāma atthi, yāva vā cittassa pavatti nāma atthi. Asaññūpapattiyañhi natthi cittappavattīti. Rūpūpapattiyaṃ saṃsedajā opapātikasadisāti opapātikānaṃyeva gahaṇaṃ. Opapātikānampīti pi-saddena vā saṃsedaje sampiṇḍeti. Sattasantativasenāti cakkhudasakādīnaṃ sattannaṃ santatisīsānaṃ vasena.

Having thus shown the process from rebirth-linking up to the arising of the death-consciousness, now, to show the cessation, the text begins with “of the rebirth-linking consciousness….” Therein, “at the moment of presence” means at the moment of presence of the rebirth-linking consciousness. “As long as there is an occurrence” means as long as the process of saṃsāra occurs, or as long as the process of consciousness occurs. For in the realm of non-percipient beings there is no occurrence of consciousness. In the fine-material realm, moisture-born beings are similar to spontaneously born beings; hence only the spontaneously born are mentioned. “And of the spontaneously born”: the particle “pi” (and) includes the moisture-born. “By way of the seven continuities” means by way of the seven heads of continuity, beginning with the eye-decade and so on.

701. Tatthāti kammato rūpapavattiyaṃ. Nānākkhaṇikakammapaccayabhūtaṃyeva idha kammanti adhippetanti āha “kammaṃ nāma kusalākusalacetanā”ti. Jīvitanavakaṃ cakkhudasakādiantogadhameva katvā “samasattatirūpa”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ vā cakkhudasakādi viya sukhapariggahaṃ na hotīti. Tadevāti yathāvuttaṃ vipākakkhandhakaṭattārūpamāha. Kammañhi kammajassa janakaṃ, paripācakampi hoti jīvitindriyassa, kammajaggino ca vasena anurakkhaṇasabbhāvato, āhārādipaṭilābhahetutāya upatthambhakanimittato ca. Tenāha “upatthambhakapaccayopi hotī”ti. Upatthambhakapaccayatā [V 2.0376] cassa upanissayapaccayavaseneva veditabbā. Kammaṃ paccayo etassāti kammapaccayaṃ, tadeva cittaṃ, taṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ etassāti kammapaccayacittasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Vipākacetasikānampi kammapaccayacittasamuṭṭhānatā vattabbā, na vā vattabbā kammasamuṭṭhānakammapaccayaggahaṇena gahitattā. Ṭhānappattā ojā aññaṃ ojaṭṭhamakaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti āhārānugate sarīreti gahetabbaṃ.

701. “Therein”: that is, in the continuous occurrence of materiality from kamma. To show that here kamma is intended as only that which has become a kamma-condition at different moments, he says: “Kamma, namely, is wholesome and unwholesome volition.” Having included the life-ennead within the eye-decade and so on, it is called “the seventy-seven material phenomena.” Or, it is not easily apprehended like the eye-decade and so on. “That very same”: this refers to the aforesaid resultant aggregates and kamma-born materiality. For kamma is the generator of what is kamma-born; it is also the preserver, because of the existence of preservation by way of the life faculty and the kamma-born fire element, and because it is the cause for obtaining nutriment, etc., and a supporting factor. Therefore he says: “it is also a supporting condition.” And its nature as a supporting condition should be understood only by way of decisive support condition. “Kamma is its condition,” thus kamma-conditioned; “that same consciousness is its origin,” thus originated from kamma-conditioned consciousness. It should be stated that resultant mental factors also originate from kamma-conditioned consciousness; or rather, it need not be stated, since they are included by the taking up of “kamma-originated” and “kamma-conditioned.” Nutritive essence that has reached its station produces another nutritive octad: this should be understood as occurring in a body sustained by nutriment.

Tatrāpīti [M 2.0401] kammasamuṭṭhānāhārasamuṭṭhānepi ojaṭṭhamake. Catasso vā pañca vā pavattiyo ghaṭetīti sadisasantativasena catasso vā pañca vā rūpakalāpappavattiyo santāneti. Bāhirapaccayavisesena pana visadisā bahūpi pavattiyo ghaṭetīti vadanti. Yathā kammapaccayāhārasamuṭṭhāne paveṇighaṭanā, evaṃ kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānepīti taṃ dassetuṃ “kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ nāmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ettha ca yathā tattha tattha koṭṭhāse paramparappavattiṃ dassentena akammajā dutiyādipavattiyo asambhedena dassitā, evaṃ kammajāhārasamuṭṭhānautuvasena, kammajautusamuṭṭhānāhāravasena, kammapaccayacittajāhārautusamuṭṭhānautuāhāravasena ca sambhedavasenāpi rūpappavatti dassetabbāti vadanti. Tattha kammajato pavattaāhārā visesapaccayalābhe sati yathāvuttaparimāṇāhi pavattīhi uddhampi pavattiyo na ghaṭentīti na sakkā vattuṃ. Tathā hi “dasa dvādasa vāre pavattiṃ ghaṭetī”ti (visuddhi. 2.703), “evaṃ dīghampi addhānaṃ anupādinnapakkhe ṭhatvāpi utusamuṭṭhānaṃ pavattati evā”ti (visuddhi. 2.704) ca vakkhati.

“Even there”: that is, in the nutritive octad which is originated from nutriment that is originated from kamma. “It connects four or five occurrences” means that by way of a similar continuity, it extends four or five occurrences of material groups. But some say that due to special external conditions, many dissimilar occurrences may also be connected. Just as there is a serial connection in what is kamma-conditioned and nutriment-originated, so too in what is kamma-conditioned and temperature-originated; to show this, the passage beginning “what is called kamma-conditioned and temperature-originated…” is stated. And here, they say that just as in the various sections, the commentator, in showing the successive continuity, has shown the non-kamma-born occurrences from the second onwards unmixed, so too the occurrence of materiality should be shown by way of combination: by way of temperature originated from kamma-born nutriment; by way of nutriment originated from kamma-born temperature; and by way of temperature and nutriment originated from the nutriment and temperature that are born of kamma-conditioned consciousness. Herein, it cannot be said that when nutriment that has arisen from what is kamma-born obtains special conditions, it does not connect occurrences even beyond the occurrences of the aforesaid limit. For it will be said: “it connects an occurrence ten or twelve times” (Vism XX, 117), and “thus for a long time, even having stood on the side of the unappropriated, what is temperature-originated continues to occur indeed” (Vism XX, 118).

702. Janakājanakā matāti purimakā tikoṭṭhāsasaṅgahitā janakā, pacchimakoṭṭhāsikā “soḷasā”ti vuttā ajanakāti matā ñātā. Kusalakiriyatoti kusalato ca kiriyato ca. Iriyāya kāyikakiriyāya pavattiṭṭhānatāya pathabhāvato iriyāpatho, gamanādi, atthato tadavatthā rūpappavatti. Kāmañcettha rūpavinimutto iriyāpatho, viññatti ca natthi, tathāpi na sabbaṃ rūpasamuṭṭhāpakacittaṃ iriyāpathūpatthambhakaṃ, viññattivikāruppādakañca hoti. Yaṃ pana cittaṃ viññattijanakaṃ, taṃ ekaṃsato itarassa janakaṃ avinābhāvato, tathā iriyāpathūpatthambhakaṃ rūpassa. Etassa visesassa dassanatthaṃ “rūpaṃ, iriyāpathaṃ, viññattiñcā”ti samuccayo kato. Vipākavajjānīti ettha vipākābhiññādvayavajjānīti vattabbaṃ tadaññesaṃyeva sesaggahaṇena gahetabbattā. Na vā vattabbaṃ sesaggahaṇeneva abhiññācittānampi nivattetabbato. Na viññattiṃ janayanti [V 2.0377] mahaggatakusalādīnaṃ santabhāvena avipphārikabhāvato. Vipphārikameva hi kāmāvacarakusalādiviññattiṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, iriyāpathūpatthambhakāni pana honti satipi santabhāve jhānavegena saussāhattā, yato tesaṃ javanakiccatā. Pañca bhavaṅgacittānīti [M 2.0402] sambandho. Rūpameva janayanti, na iriyāpathaṃ nirussāhasantabhāvena paridubbalabhāvato. Kiriyāmayacittehi avimissabhavaṅgappavattikāle khandhādisarīrāvayavānaṃ niccalabhāvenāvaṭṭhānaṃ. Tathā hi abbokiṇṇe bhavaṅge pavattamāne aṅgāni osīdanti paviṭṭhāni viya honti. “Dvattiṃsā”ti pana ādinā vuttesu jāgaraṇacittesu vattamānesu aṅgāni upatthaddhāni yathāpavattairiyāpathabhāveneva pavattantīti. Dvepañcaviññāṇāni sabbadubbalatāya rūpaṃ na janenti. Paṭisandhicittaṃ vatthudubbalatāya. Khīṇāsavānaṃ cuticittanti ettha –

702. “Generators and non-generators are intended”: the former, included in the three sections, are the generators; the latter, the sixteen mentioned, are intended and known as non-generators. “From wholesome and functional” means from what is wholesome and from what is functional. Posture (iriyāpatha) is so called because it is the basis for the occurrence of bodily action, being the path for it, such as walking; in meaning, it is the occurrence of materiality in that state. Granted, here posture is devoid of materiality and there is no intimation (viññatti), yet not every consciousness that originates materiality supports posture or produces a modification of intimation. But a consciousness that generates intimation is, because of inseparability, definitely a generator of the other two. Similarly, a consciousness that supports posture is a generator of materiality. To show this distinction, the collection “materiality, posture, and intimation” is made. “Excluding resultant”: here it should be said “excluding the pair, resultant and direct knowledge,” because only those other than them are to be taken by the word “the rest.” Or, it need not be said, because the direct-knowledge consciousnesses are also to be excluded by the very word “the rest.” The sublime wholesome states and so on do not generate intimation because of their tranquil and non-forceful nature. For only what is forceful, such as sense-sphere wholesome consciousness, originates intimation. But they do support posture, even though they are tranquil, because they are energetic due to the impetus of jhāna, since their function is impulsion. The connection is with “the five life-continuum consciousnesses.” They generate only materiality, not posture, because they are very weak due to their lack of energy and tranquil nature. At a time when the life-continuum is occurring unmixed with functional consciousnesses, the bodily parts such as the shoulders remain motionless. For when the life-continuum occurs unmixed, the limbs sink down as if they have entered into something. But when the waking consciousnesses mentioned beginning with “thirty-two” are occurring, the limbs are firm and continue in the same posture as they were. The two sets of fivefold sense consciousness do not generate materiality because they are the weakest of all. The rebirth-linking consciousness does not generate it because its base is weak. Here, regarding “the death-consciousness of the arahants”—

“Kāmāvacarānaṃ pacchimacittassa uppādakkhaṇe yassa cittassa anantarā kāmāvacarānaṃ pacchimacittaṃ uppajjissati, rūpāvacare arūpāvacare pacchimabhavikānaṃ, ye ca rūpāvacaraṃ arūpāvacaraṃ upapajjitvā parinibbāyissanti, tesaṃ cavantānaṃ tesaṃ vacīsaṅkhāro nirujjhissati, no ca tesaṃ kāyasaṅkhāro nirujjhissatī”ti (yama. 2.saṅkhārayamaka.88) –

“For beings of the sense-sphere at the arising-moment of the final consciousness; for those immediately after whose consciousness the final consciousness of sense-sphere beings will arise; for those in their final existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms; and for those who, having been reborn into the fine-material or immaterial realm, will attain Parinibbāna—for all of them, as they are passing away, their verbal formation will cease, but their bodily formation will not cease.” (yama. 2.saṅkhārayamaka.88) –

Pana vacanato aññesampi cuticittaṃ rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpetīti viññāyati. Na hi rūpasamuṭṭhāpakacittassa gabbhagatatādivibandhābhāve kāyasaṅkhārāsamuṭṭhāpane kāraṇaṃ atthi, na ca yuttaṃ cuto ca cittasamuṭṭhānarūpañcassa pavattati, nāpi “cuticittaṃ rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpetī”ti pāḷi atthi, “khīṇāsavāna”nti, pana visesanaṃ appaṭisandhikanirodhena nirujjhantassa tesaṃ cuticittassa rūpasamuṭṭhāpanaṃ pākaṭanti katvā katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Soḷasa cittānīti paricchijja gahaṇaṃ tesaṃ rūpajanane ekaṃsato niyametabbattā, aññāni pana bahūni arūpe uppannāni anokāsagatattā rūpaṃ na janentiyeva. Na ṭhitikkhaṇe, bhaṅgakkhaṇe vā rūpaṃ janentīti sambandho. Uppādakkhaṇe pana balavaṃ anantarādipaccayalābhato.

However, from this statement it is understood that the death-consciousness of others too does not originate materiality. For when there is no impediment such as being in the womb, there is no reason for a consciousness that originates materiality not to originate bodily formations. Nor is it right that for one who has passed away, materiality originated by his consciousness should continue to occur. Nor is there a canonical text that says, “The death-consciousness originates materiality.” However, the qualification “of those with taints destroyed” should be seen as having been made with the consideration that the non-origination of materiality by their death-consciousness, which ceases with a cessation that has no relinking, is evident. The specific inclusion of “sixteen consciousnesses” is because their non-generation of materiality must be definitely determined. But many other consciousnesses, having arisen in the immaterial sphere, do not generate materiality at all since they have not come to a location for it. The connection is: “They do not generate materiality at the moment of presence or at the moment of dissolution.” But at the moment of arising, it is powerful because it obtains the proximity condition and others.

Yathā pathavīādayo rūpadhammā cittahetukā cittasamuṭṭhānā, evaṃ vedanādayopīti vuttaṃ “cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma tayo arūpino khandhā, saddanavaka”ntiādi. Tenevāha – “katame dhammā cittasamuṭṭhānā? Vedanākkhandho saññākkhandho saṅkhārakkhandho kāyaviññatti vacīviññattī”ti (dha. sa. 1201, 1535). Tattha [V 2.0378] kāyaviññattiādīnaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānatā pariyāyato vuttāti veditabbā tesaṃ anipphannattā. “Evaṃ vuttaṃ catusamuṭṭhānarūpa”nti iminā ataṃsamuṭṭhānasseva cittajarūpassa cittapaccayatā dassitā. Yathā pana kammapaccayaṃ dassitaṃ[M 2.0403], evaṃ cittapaccaye gayhamāne taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpassa, sahajātavedanādīnañca cittapaccayatā siyā. Cittasamuṭṭhānacittapaccaye pana asaṅkarato dassetuṃ pacchājātapaccayavaseneva cittapaccayaṃ uddhaṭanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Cittasamuṭṭhānautuāhārehi kammasamuṭṭhānautuāhārā balavanto hontīti tesaṃ vasena catupañcapavattighaṭanaṃ vuttaṃ, cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ pana vasena dvattippavattighaṭanaṃ taṃpākatikacittavasena, mahaggatānuttaracittavasena pana bahutarāpi pavattiyo icchitabbā. Taṃnibbattānaṃ cittajarūpānaṃ uḷārapaṇītabhāvato.

Just as material phenomena such as the earth element have mind as their cause and are originated from mind, so too, regarding feeling and so on, it is said: 'What is called 'originated from mind'? The three immaterial aggregates, the sound nonad,' etc. Therefore, He said: 'Which phenomena are originated from mind? The feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, the formations aggregate, bodily intimation, and verbal intimation' (Dhs. 1201, 1535). Therein, it should be understood that the state of being mind-originated for bodily intimation and so on is stated figuratively, because of their being non-produced matter. By this text, 'Thus it is said: matter with four origins,' the state of having mind as a condition is shown only for mind-born matter that is not originated from that same mind. However, just as the kamma-condition is shown, so too, when the mind-condition is taken, there would be a state of having mind as a condition for matter originated from that mind and for co-nascent feeling, etc. However, it should be seen that in order to show the mind-originated phenomena and the mind-condition without confusion, the mind-condition is presented only by way of the post-nascence condition. Kamma-originated temperature and nutriment are stronger than mind-originated temperature and nutriment; therefore, by their power, the connecting of a series of four or five occurrences is stated. But by the power of the mind-originated, the connecting of a series of two or three occurrences is stated; that is by the power of ordinary consciousness. By the power of sublime and supramundane consciousness, however, even many more occurrences should be expected, due to the magnificent and refined nature of the mind-born matter produced by them.

703. “Upādinnaṃ kammajarūpaṃ paccayaṃ labhitvā”ti etena bahiddhā anupādinnaojā rūpāharaṇakiccaṃ na karotīti dasseti. Paccayalābho cassa kammajabhūtasannissayatāvasenāti āha “tattha patiṭṭhāyā”ti. Tattha kammapaccayacittasamuṭṭhānādirūpassapi kammamūlakattā siyā kammajapariyāyoti taṃnivattanatthaṃ “upādinna”nti visesetvā vuttaṃ. Āhārapaccayassa āhāro na kevalaṃ upatthambhakova, atha kho janakopīti dassetuṃ “catusamuṭṭhānarūpa”nti vuttaṃ. “Dasa dvādasa vāre”ti vatvā kathaṃ imasseva dasa dvādasa vāre pavattighaṭanāti anuyogaṃ sandhāyāha “ekadivasaṃ paribhuttāhāro”tiādi. Dārakassa sarīraṃ pharitvāti nābhimūlānugatāhi rasaharaṇīhi pharitvā, aññathā jalābuantarike kāye makkhanāvasena na sammāviniyogo āhārassa sambhavatīti.

703. By 'Having obtained appropriated kamma-born matter as a condition,' it is shown that external, unappropriated nutritive essence does not perform the function of producing matter. And because its acquisition of a condition is by way of dependence on kamma-born primary elements, it is said, 'therein established.' Here, even for matter originated by mind with kamma as its condition, etc., since it has kamma as its root-cause, the term 'kamma-born' might apply. To preclude that, the specific term 'appropriated' is used. To show that for matter conditioned by nutriment, nutriment is not merely supportive but also generative, the phrase 'matter with four origins' is used. Having stated 'ten or twelve times,' in anticipation of the question, 'How does the connection of the process for this very matter happen ten or twelve times?' it is said, 'the nutriment consumed in a single day,' etc. 'Having pervaded the child's body' means having pervaded it through the nutrient-carrying channels that follow from the root of the navel; otherwise, a proper distribution of the nutriment would not be possible by way of smearing it on the body inside the womb.

Upādinnako anupādinnakoti duvidhe āhāre pubbe anupādinnako āhārapaccayaāhāro dassitoti itaraṃ dassetuṃ “kammajāhāro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ kammapaccayāhārasamuṭṭhāne vuttanayameva. Tenāha “catasso vā pañca vā pavattiyo ghaṭetī”ti. Āhārapaccayautunopi utupaccayāhārassa viya dasa dvādasa vāre pavattighaṭanā veditabbā. Vuttanayattā na uddhatanti vadanti. Sesānanti kammacittautusamuṭṭhānānaṃ tisantatirūpānaṃ. Kabaḷīkārāhāro hi aññāhārasamuṭṭhitassa, tisantatirūpānañca upatthambhakavasena attanā uppāditassa janako hutvā paccayo hoti. Evaṃ āhārapaccayo hontoyeva atthiavigatavasenāpi paccayo hoti, nissayabhāvo pana paṭṭhānanayena natthi. Āhārapaccayā pavattamānāni rūpāni āhāranissayāni [M 2.0404][V 2.0379] nāma hontīti suttantanayena vuttoti daṭṭhabbo. Parato utuno nissayajotanāyapi eseva nayo.

In regard to the two kinds of nutriment, appropriated and unappropriated, since the unappropriated, which is nutriment as a condition for nutriment, was previously shown, in order to show the other, 'kamma-born nutriment,' etc., was said. That is the very same method as stated in the section on nutriment originating from kamma as a condition. Therefore, it is said, 'it connects four or five occurrences.' For temperature conditioned by nutriment, the connecting of the process ten or twelve times should be understood, just as for nutriment conditioned by temperature. Because the method has been stated, it is not cited, so they say. 'Of the remaining' means of the material phenomena of the three continuities that originate from kamma, mind, and temperature. For edible food is a condition by being a generator for what is produced by itself, and by way of being a supporter for material phenomena arisen from other nutriment and for the material phenomena of the three continuities. Thus, while being a nutriment-condition, it is also a condition by way of presence and non-disappearance; but the state of being a dependence-condition does not exist according to the Paṭṭhāna method. It should be understood that it is stated according to the Suttanta method that 'material phenomena occurring due to the nutriment-condition are called nutriment-dependent.' Subsequently, in the explanation of the dependence on temperature, this is the very same method.

704. Kammasamuṭṭhānādivasena catubbidhāyapi tejodhātuyā rūpuppādane samatthabhāvato “utu nāma catusamuṭṭhānā tejodhātū”ti vuttaṃ. Esa duvidho hotīti esa utu tejodhātubhāvāvisesepi tikkhamandatāvisesena uṇho, sītoti duvidho hoti. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vicāritameva. Yadipi utu upādinnakena vināpi rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, indriyabaddhe pana tena vinā tassa rūpuppādanaṃ natthīti āha “upādinnakaṃ paccayaṃ labhitvā”ti. Tenāha “catusamuṭṭhāno utū”ti. Utusamuṭṭhānoyeva hi utu upādinnakena vinā rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Utupaccayaṃ nāma catusamuṭṭhānikaṃ rūpaṃ. Yañhi utusamuṭṭhānaṃ pannarasavidhaṃ rūpaṃ, yañca tadaññatisantatirūpaṃ, tassa sabbassapi sabhāgo utuupatthambhakapaccayo hotīti. Yasmā visabhāgo utu himādi viya padumādīnaṃ visadisarūpuppattihetubhūtaṃ purimarūpaṃ vināsentaṃ viya hoti, tasmā sabhāgaṃ, visabhāgañca ekajjhaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ “utu catusamuṭṭhānikarūpānaṃ pavattiyā ca vināsassa ca paccayo hotī”ti.

704. Because the fire element, in its fourfold aspect as originating from kamma, etc., is capable of producing material form, it is said: 'Temperature is the fire element with four origins.' This is of two kinds: although there is no difference in its nature as the fire element, this temperature is of two kinds, hot and cold, due to the difference in intensity and dullness. Whatever is to be said on this has already been discussed below. Although temperature can produce matter even without appropriated matter, in the case of what is bound up with the faculties, the production of matter does not occur without it; hence it is said: 'having obtained appropriated matter as a condition.' Therefore it is stated: 'Temperature has four origins.' For only temperature originated from temperature produces matter without appropriated matter. Matter conditioned by temperature is matter with four origins. For the fifteen kinds of material form originated by temperature, and for the other matter of the three continuities, similar temperature is a supporting condition for all of it. Because dissimilar temperature, like frost for lotuses, is like a destroyer of the previous matter, being a cause for the arising of dissimilar matter, therefore, having taken both similar and dissimilar together, it is said: 'Temperature is a condition for the occurrence and for the destruction of material form with four origins.'

Dīghampi addhānanti “dasa dvādasa vāre”ti aññassa vuttaparicchedato dīghampi kālaṃ. Utu hi sabhāgasantativasena laddhapaccayaṃ ciratarampi kālaṃ sadisākāraṃ rūpappavattiṃ santāneti upādinnakasannissayena vinā, pageva itarathā. Tenāha “anupādinnapakkhe ṭhatvāpī”ti, maṃsavinimuttakesalomanakhacammakhilatilakādivasena jīvamānasarīre aññattha matakaḷevarādivasenāti adhippāyo. Rūpassa nibbattiyā diṭṭhāya tassa bhaṅgopi diṭṭhoyeva hoti ittarakālattā dhammappavattiyāti āha “nibbattiṃ passanto kālena rūpaṃ sammasati nāmā”ti. Na hi nibbattimattadassanaṃ sammasanaṃ nāma hoti, udayabbayadassanañca adhikatanti. Esa nayo ito paresupi nibbattiggahaṇesu.

'For a long time' means for a long time beyond the limit of 'ten or twelve times' stated for another. For temperature, having obtained a condition by way of the continuity of the similar, extends a process of matter of a similar kind for a very long time without dependence on appropriated matter, how much more so with it. Therefore it is said, 'even when it stands on the side of the unappropriated,' the meaning is: in a living body, in the sense of hair, body hair, nails, calluses, moles, etc., that are detached from flesh; and elsewhere, in the sense of a dead corpse, etc. When the origination of matter is seen, its dissolution is also seen indeed, because the occurrence of phenomena is for a short time; thus it is said, 'seeing origination, one in time indeed comprehends matter.' For the mere seeing of origination is not called comprehension; and the seeing of rise and fall is what is intended. This is the method in the subsequent graspings of origination as well.

Arūpanibbattipassanākārakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Mode of Insight into Formless Arising

705. Lokiyacittuppādavasenevāti avadhāraṇaṃ itarassa avisayattā.

705. The phrase 'only by way of the arising of worldly consciousness' is a specification, because the other is not its domain.

Nibbattati [M 2.0405][V 2.0380] taṃtaṃbhavavasena. Tadeva ekūnavīsatippabhedaṃ cittaṃ bhavaṅgavasena nibbattatīti sambandho. Tathā cutivasena tadārammaṇavasenāti etthāpi. Tatthāti tesu ekūnavīsaticittuppādesu. Anantaracittato paṭṭhāyātiādināpi pavattiyeva vuttā.

It arises according to the respective becoming. That same consciousness, of nineteen kinds, arises by way of the life-continuum—this is the connection. So too here with 'by way of death' and 'by way of that object.' 'Tattha' means: among those nineteen arisings of consciousness. Also by the phrase beginning with 'from the immediately preceding consciousness,' only the process is described.

So pana paṭisandhicittānaṃyeva pavattiyaṃ pavattanākāroti suddhappavatticittānaṃ uppattiṃ dassento “pavatte panā”tiādimāha. Asambhinnattāti avinaṭṭhattā. “Asambhinnattā cakkhussā”tiādinā saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “cakkhupasādassa hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Ṭhitippattamevā”ti iminā yathā nirujjhamānaṃ rūpaṃ kassaci paccayo na hoti, evaṃ uppajjamānampīti dasseti. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ uppajjatīti sambandho. Evaṃ sesesupi. Kāmāvacarakusalākusalakiriyacittesu ekaṃ vā pañca, satta vā javanāni hutvā uppajjatīti sambandho. Upekkhāsahagatāhetukaṃ cittaṃ vāti vā-saddaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Voṭṭhabbanañhi sandhāya evaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ pana dutiyamoghavāravasena veditabbaṃ. Pañca javanāni suttamucchitādikāle, satta pākatikakāle veditabbāni. Javanārammaṇānurūpanti “tihetukaṃ ce javanaṃ, tihetukaṃ, dvihetukaṃ vā”tiādinā, “iṭṭhaṃ ce ārammaṇaṃ, somanassasahagata”ntiādinā ca javanassa, ārammaṇassa ca anurūpaṃ. Sesadvāresūti sotadvārādisesadvāresu.

But that mode of occurrence in the course of life pertains only to rebirth-linking consciousnesses. To show the arising of purely process-consciousness, he says, 'But in the course of life…' `Asambhinnattā` means: because it is not destroyed. To explain the meaning stated concisely by the phrase 'because of the unbrokenness of the eye,' the passage beginning 'for of the eye-sensitivity…' was stated. By this phrase 'only when it has reached the stage of presence,' he shows that just as ceasing materiality is not a condition for anything, so too arising materiality is not. The connection is: 'eye-consciousness arises.' So too in the other cases. The connection is: 'among the sense-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, and functional consciousnesses, it arises as one consciousness, or as five or seven impulsions.' The word 'or' should be supplied and connected thus: 'or the rootless consciousness accompanied by equanimity.' For this was said with reference to the determining consciousness, but that should be understood by way of the second ineffective process. Five impulsions should be understood at a time of drowsiness, fainting, and the like; seven at a normal time. `Javanārammaṇānurūpaṃ` means: in conformity with the impulsion and its object, as by 'if the impulsion is triple-rooted, then the tadārammaṇa is triple-rooted or double-rooted,' etc., and by 'if the object is desirable, then the tadārammaṇa is accompanied by gladness,' etc. `Sesadvāresu` means: in the remaining doors, that is, the ear-door and the other remaining doors.

Anukkamenāti udayabbayañāṇādhigamānukkamena paññābhāvanaṃ sampādeti arahattaṃ adhigacchati.

`Anukkamena` means: by means of the sequence of attaining the knowledge of arising and passing away and so forth, he accomplishes the development of wisdom and attains Arahantship.

Rūpasattakasammasanakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Sevenfold Comprehension of Materiality

706. Rūpesu manasikārasattakaṃ rūpasattakaṃ, rūpadhammesu sattahākārehi manasi kārotīti attho. Evaṃ arūpasattakampi veditabbaṃ. Imehi ākārehīti imehi ādānanikkhepanamanasikārādippakārehi, imehi vā yathāvuttakoṭṭhāsehi. Āropetvāti tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā.

706. The sevenfold method concerning materiality (`rūpasattakaṃ`) is a set of seven kinds of attention to materiality; the meaning is: attention to material phenomena in seven ways. The sevenfold method concerning the formless should also be understood in the same way. `Imehi ākārehi` means: by these modes, that is, by the types of attention such as taking up and laying down; or by these sections as stated. `Āropetvā` means: having applied the three characteristics.

Ādānanikkhepanatoti bhavassa gahaṇavissajjanato, jātito, maraṇato cāti attho. Vayovuḍḍhatthagāmitoti vayasā vuḍḍhassa atthagāmibhāvato, atthaṅgamato icceva attho. Āhāratoti āhārahetu[M 2.0406][V 2.0381], rūpassa paccayabhūtaāhāratoti attho. Ayalohādibhūmipāsāṇādibhedaṃ vividhavaṇṇasaṇṭhānaṃ kammānapekkhaṃ sabhāvasiddhaṃ rūpaṃ dhammatārūpaṃ. Sattāti sattadhā sattahākārehi. Vipassatīti taṃ taṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā vipassati sammasati.

`Ādānanikkhepanato` means: from the taking up and laying down of existence, that is, from birth and from death. `Vayovuḍḍhatthagāmito` means: from the state of passing away of that which is advanced in age; the meaning is simply 'from passing away.' `Āhārato` means: from nutriment as a cause; the meaning is from nutriment that is a condition for materiality. Materiality that is established by its own nature, independent of kamma, of various colors and shapes, differentiated as iron, bronze, etc., and earth, stones, etc., is materiality as a natural phenomenon. `Sattā` means: sevenfold, in seven ways. `Vipassati` means: he sees with insight, he comprehends, by superimposing the three characteristics on each respective section.

“Bhārādānaṃ dukhaṃ loke”ti vacanato khandhabhārassa ādito gahaṇanti katvā “ādānanti paṭisandhī”ti āha. “Sabbeva nikkhipissanti, bhūtā loke samussaya”nti (dī. ni. 2.220; saṃ. ni. 1.186) pana vacanato khandhabhāranikkhepoti katvā “nikkhepananti cutī”ti vuttaṃ. “Yo ciraṃ jīvati, so vassasata”nti (dī. ni. 2.7; saṃ. ni. 1.145-146; a. ni. 7.74) vacanato tato ūnādhikabhāvo appamāṇanti vuttaṃ “ekaṃ vassasataṃ paricchinditvā”ti. Etthantare sabbe saṅkhārāti etasmiṃ ādānanikkhepantare pavattā sabbe bhūtupādāyarūpappabhedā saṅkhārā. Rūpadhammesu hi idaṃ sammasanavidhānanti. “Aniccā”ti gahitamattaṃ yuttito hadaye patiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ “kasmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha uppādavayavattitoti uppajjanavasena, nirujjhanavasena ca pavattanato, ahutvā sambhavato hutvā vayūpagamanatoti attho. Vipariṇāmatoti santānassa purimuttaravisadisabhāvatoti vadanti. Taṃ vassasataparicchinne rūpe idaṃ sammasananti adhippāyeneva vuttaṃ siyā, jarāmaraṇena vipariṇāmetabbatoti attho. Asatipi dhammabhede avatthābhedo icchitabbo. Na hi uppādāvatthā eva bhaṅgāvatthāti yuttā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “jarāya ceva maraṇena cāti dvedhā pariṇāmapakatitāyā”ti. Sabhāvavigamo eva vā ettha vipariṇāmo. Khaṇikatā tāvakālikatā. Niccasabhāvābhāvo eva niccapaṭikkhepo. Aniccadhammā hi teneva attano sabhāvena jānantānaṃ niccataṃ paṭikkhipanti nāma. Yato na niccanti aniccaṃ, uppādakkhaṇe yadavatthā saṅkhārā, na tadavatthā ṭhitikkhaṇeti avatthantarappattiyā ñāyati tesaṃ kilamanākāroti āha “ṭhitiyaṃ jarāya kilamantī”ti, svāyamattho pākaṭajarāya veditabbo. Ye pana saṅkhārānaṃ ṭhitiṃ na sampaṭicchanti, tattha vattabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Dhammānaṃ sabhāvo nāma duratikkamo jarānantaraṃ bhaṅgoti āha “jaraṃ patvā avassaṃ bhijjantī”ti. Tasmāti yasmā uppādajarābhaṅgavasena [M 2.0407] saṅkhārānaṃ nirantarabādhatā, tato ca nesaṃ dussahatāya dukkhamatā, tissannaṃ dukkhatānaṃ, saṃsāradukkhassa ca adhiṭṭhānatāya dukkhavatthutā, tasmā. Abhiṇha…pe… dukkhāti yojanā.

Based on the statement, 'Taking up the burden is suffering in the world,' and considering this to mean the taking up of the burden of the aggregates from the beginning, he said: '“Taking up” is rebirth-linking.' And based on the statement, 'All beings in the world will lay down their composite forms,' and considering this to mean the laying down of the burden of the aggregates, it was said: '“Laying down” is death.' Based on the statement, 'One who lives long lives for a hundred years,' and because being more or less than that is not the standard measure, it was said, 'having defined it as one hundred years.' `Etthantare sabbe saṅkhārā` means: all formations—differentiated as primary and derived materiality—that occur in this interval between taking up and laying down. For this is the method of comprehension concerning material phenomena. To establish in the heart by reasoning what has been grasped as 'impermanent,' the passage beginning 'Why?' was stated. Therein, `uppādavayavattito` means: because of occurring by way of arising and passing away; that is, from having not been it comes to be, and having been it goes to destruction. `Vipariṇāmato` means: because of the dissimilar nature of the earlier and later continuity, so they say. This may have been said with the very intention that this is a comprehension of materiality that is limited to a hundred years; the meaning is that it is alterable by aging and death. Even when there is no difference in the phenomena, a difference in state should be accepted. For it is not right that the state of arising is the same as the state of dissolution. For so it is said: 'because of the twofold nature of alteration, namely, by aging and death.' Or here alteration is simply the disappearance of its nature. Momentariness is temporariness. The absence of a permanent nature is itself the rejection of permanence. For impermanent phenomena, by their very own nature, indeed reject permanence for those who know them. Because they are not permanent (`na nicca`), they are impermanent (`anicca`). The state of formations at the moment of arising is not their state at the moment of presence; because they reach another state, their mode of affliction is known. Thus he says: 'they are afflicted by aging in the stage of presence.' This meaning should be understood by way of manifest aging. But as for those who do not accept a stage of presence for formations, what should be said on that has already been said below. The nature of phenomena is indeed difficult to transgress; after aging comes dissolution. Thus he says: 'having reached aging, they inevitably break up.' The connection (`yojanā`) of `tasmā` is as follows: since formations are continuously oppressed by way of arising, aging, and dissolution, and from that, due to their unbearableness, they are in a state of suffering, and because they are the ground for the three kinds of suffering and for the suffering of saṃsāra, they are a basis for suffering, therefore they are 'constantly... suffering.'

“Sukhapaṭikkhepato”ti [V 2.0382] idaṃ vuttanayameva. Ṭhitiṃ mā pāpuṇantu, uppajjamānākāreneva pavattantūti adhippāyo. “Uppannā”ti iminā uppādakkhaṇasamaṅgitā vuttā. Ṭhānappattā mā jīrantūti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu atthato ṭhiti eva jarāti? Saccametaṃ, jarāvasena pana yo kilamatho, so idha jarāggahaṇena gahitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Mā bhijjantūti niccataṃ āsīsati. Kassaci dhammissarassāpi bhagavato vasavattibhāvo natthi. Na hi lakkhaṇaññathattaṃ kenaci kātuṃ sakkā. Bhāvaññathattameva hi iddhivisayo. Suññā saṅkhārā tena tīsu ṭhānesu vasavattanākārena. Tasmāti vuttakāraṇaparāmasanaṃ. Suññatoti nivāsīkārakavedakaadhiṭṭhāyakavirahena tato suññato, na nissabhāvatoti ekaccaparikappitasabhāvasuññato. Assāmikatoti sāmibhūtassa kassaci abhāvato. Etena anattaniyataṃ dasseti. Avasavattitoti yathāvuttavasavattibhāvābhāvato. Attapaṭikkhepatoti paraparikappitassa attano paṭikkhipanato. “Suññato”tiādinā hi dhammānaṃ bāhirakaparikappitaattaviraho vutto, iminā pana ataṃsabhāvato attā na hotīti.

‘From the rejection of happiness’: this is in the same way as stated. The intention is: ‘May they not reach the stage of presence; may they proceed only in the mode of arising.’ By ‘arisen,’ their being endowed with the arising-moment is stated. Why was it said, ‘Having reached their stage of presence, may they not age’? Is not aging in reality the same as the stage of presence? That is true, but it should be seen that the affliction that comes by way of aging is included here by the term ‘aging.’ ‘May they not break up’—this expresses a wish for permanence. Even for the Blessed One, a master of phenomena, there is no exercising of control. For it is not possible for anyone to make the characteristics otherwise. The domain of psychic power is only making the state otherwise. Formations are empty of that mode of exercising control in the three instances. Therefore (`tasmā`) is a reference to the reason already stated. Because of emptiness (`suññato`) means: empty because of the absence of an indweller, a maker, a feeler, or a controller; not empty in the sense of being without a nature, that is, empty of a nature imagined by some. Because of being without a master (`assāmikato`) means: because of the absence of any master. By this he shows that it is not one's own. Because of not being subject to control (`avasavattito`) means: because of the absence of the aforesaid exercising of control. From the rejection of a self (`attapaṭikkhepato`) means: from the rejection of a self imagined by others. For by the words beginning with ‘because of emptiness,’ the absence in phenomena of a self imagined by outsiders is stated; but by this latter phrase it is said that there is no self because it does not have that nature.

707. Ettha ca “uppādavayavattito”tiādinā catūhi kāraṇehi aniccā, “abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanato”tiādinā catūhi kāraṇehi dukkhā, “suññato”tiādinā catūhi kāraṇehi anattāti rūpadhamme niruḷhaṃ lakkhaṇattayaṃ pubbe attanā asallakkhitaṃ sallakkhetvā sammasanto taṃ tattha āropetīti vuccati. Tathā panānena ādānanikkhepanavasena sammasitattā āha “rūpe tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā”ti.

707. And here, they are impermanent for the four reasons beginning with ‘because of proceeding by way of arising and passing away’; they are suffering for the four reasons beginning with ‘because of constant oppression’; they are not-self for the four reasons beginning with ‘because of emptiness.’ When one comprehends by discerning the three characteristics established in material phenomena, which were previously not discerned by oneself, it is said that one ‘superimposes’ them thereon. However, because he has comprehended by way of taking up and laying down, he says, ‘having superimposed the three characteristics on materiality.’

Tattha ca yasmā aniccalakkhaṇaggahaṇapubbakaṃ dukkhalakkhaṇaggahaṇaṃ, dukkhalakkhaṇaggahaṇapubbakaṃ vā anattalakkhaṇaggahaṇaṃ. Aniccalakkhaṇañcettha rūpabhedena dassiyamānaṃ yathoḷārikato dīpetabbanti taṃ vassasataparicchedena paṭhamaṃ dassentena vassasataṃ ṭhitassa “dasa vā vīsati vā”tiādinā [M 2.0408] vibhajitvā anukkamena yāvauddharaṇādikoṭṭhāsavasena rūpassa bhaṅgaṃ disvā tato “aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā”ti tilakkhaṇāropanaṃ vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgamato sammasananti dassetuṃ “tameva vassasata”ntiādinā vayavasena rūpassa sammasanavidhi āraddho. Tattha yasmā oḷārikavasenevāyaṃ ādito rūpabhedo gayhati, tasmā na vassasataṃ samakoṭṭhāsavasena vibhattaṃ, majjhimāvatthāya vā tathārūpattā majjhimavaye ekaṃ vassaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ.

And among these characteristics, because the grasping of the characteristic of suffering is preceded by the grasping of the characteristic of impermanence, or the grasping of the characteristic of not-self is preceded by the grasping of the characteristic of suffering; and because the characteristic of impermanence, being shown here through the breaking up of material form, should be explained in accordance with its grossness, therefore, the method of contemplating material form by way of age is begun with 'that very hundred years,' etc. This is in order to show that contemplation by way of the decline of old age is the application of the three characteristics as 'impermanent, suffering, not-self,' after one has first shown that characteristic of impermanence with the limit of a hundred years, having divided that which has stood for a hundred years by 'ten or twenty,' etc., and having successively seen the breaking up of material form up to the portion of final dissolution. Therein, because this breaking up of material form is at first grasped only in a gross way, the hundred years is not divided into equal portions; or, because the middle state is of such a nature, one year is added in the middle age.

708. Mandatābāhullena [V 2.0383] pavattaṃ vassānaṃ dasakaṃ mandadasakaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi.

708. A decade of years that proceeds with an abundance of dullness is the 'decade of dullness.' This same method applies to the rest.

Tadāti paṭhame vassadasake. Soti puggalo. Capaloti anavaṭṭhitakiriyatāya taralo. Tena momūhabhāvato viseseti. Na hesa navamadasake viya momūhabhāvena mando, atha kho capalatāyāti. Tenāha “kumārako”ti. Tatiye dasake maṃsapāripūriyā yathārahaṃ chavivaṇṇo vippasīdatīti āha “vaṇṇāyatanaṃ vepullaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti. Catutthe dasake aṭṭhīnaṃ, nhārūnañca thirabhāvappattiyā balañca thāmo ca vepullaṃ pāpuṇāti. Pañcame dasake yobbanamadassa dūrībhāvena yebhuyyena kilesatanutāya paññā yathārahaṃ suvisadā hoti. Khiḍḍāya rati khiḍḍārati. Kapallikādinissayavisesena padīpassa suddhatādi viya nissayavisesena pañcamachaṭṭhadasakesu paññāya buddhihāniyo veditabbā. Purato pabbhāro hoti kaṭisandhigīvāsandhīnaṃ vasena rassassāpi, pageva dīghassa. Pabbhāroti ca garubhāvena palambako. Momūho hoti satipaññāvippavāsato. Sayanabahulova hoti ṭhānādivasena sarīrabhāraṃ vahituṃ asakkonto.

‘At that time’ means in the first decade of years. ‘He’ means the person. ‘Fickle’ means unsteady because of unstable activity. By this, it is distinguished from the state of delusion. For this person is not dull through delusion as in the ninth decade, but rather through fickleness. Therefore, he said, ‘a little boy.’ In the third decade, with the fullness of flesh, the skin's complexion brightens appropriately; thus it is said, ‘the sphere of appearance attains fullness.’ In the fourth decade, with the attainment of firmness of bones and sinews, strength and stamina reach their fullness. In the fifth decade, with the passing away of the intoxication of youth and generally through the attenuation of the defilements, wisdom becomes very clear as is suitable. Delight in play is ‘delight-in-play.’ Just as the purity, etc., of a lamp depends on the specific support such as the bowl, so too the increase and decline of wisdom in the fifth and sixth decades should be understood as depending on a specific support. He is bent forward on account of the hip and neck joints, even a short person, how much more so a tall one. And ‘bent forward’ means stooping due to heaviness. He becomes deluded due to the absence of mindfulness and wisdom. He is much given to lying down, being unable to bear the burden of the body while standing and so on.

709. Tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vassānanti yebhuyyatāya vuttaṃ. Catuvassikopi hi eko koṭṭhāso hotīti. Dvisataṃ koṭṭhāse katvā ekekaayanavasenātipi veditabbaṃ.
