709. ‘Of three and three years’ is said as a general rule. For there is also a four-year portion. It should also be understood thus: having made two hundred portions, by way of each half-year.

Vassāne pavattarūpanti sambandho.

The connection is: 'material form that has occurred in the rainy season.'

Taṃ [M 2.0409] pana vassānaṃ dvidhā samattaṃ, na pubbe viya catumāsanti āha “dvemāsa”nti. Accantasaṃyoge cetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. So pana vassāno utu sāvaṇapoṭṭhapādamāsā, assayujakattikamāsā sarado, migasiraphussamāsā hemanto, māghaphaggunamāsā sisiro, cittavesākhamāsā vasanto, jeṭṭhāsaḷhamāsā gimho utūti veditabbo. Cha koṭṭhāse katvāti dasadasanāṭikāvasena cha koṭṭhāse katvā.

But that rainy season is two months long, not four months as before; hence it is said, ‘two months.’ And this is a term in the accusative case in the sense of continuous duration. Furthermore, that rainy season (vassāna) is the season of the months Sāvaṇa and Poṭṭhapāda; autumn (sarada) is Assayuja and Kattika; the cool season (hemanta) is Migasira and Phussa; the cold season (sisira) is Māgha and Phagguna; spring (vasanta) is Citta and Vesākha; summer (gimha) is Jeṭṭha and Āsāḷha—thus the seasons should be understood. ‘Having made six portions’ means having made six portions by way of periods of ten nāṭikās each.

710. Abhimukhaṃ purato kamanaṃ abhikkamo. Paṭinivattanavasena kamanaṃ paṭikkamo. Āmukhaṃ lokanaṃ ālokanaṃ. Vividhaṃ ito cito ca lokanaṃ vilokanaṃ. Hatthapādānaṃ saṅkucanaṃ samiñjanaṃ. Āyamanaṃ pasāraṇaṃ.

710. Going forward, facing forward, is advancing (abhikkama). Going by way of returning is retreating (paṭikkama). Looking towards the front is looking at (ālokana). Looking variously here and there is looking around (vilokana). The contracting of the hands and feet is bending in (samiñjana). Stretching forth is stretching out (pasāraṇa).

Pāduddharaṇakāleti [V 2.0384] dutiyapāduddharaṇakāle. Pādassāti uddhaṭapādassa. Omattāti sattito hīnappamāṇā. Tenāha “mandā”ti. Itarāti tejovāyodhātuyo. Yathā pādassa uddharaṇaṃ sijjhati, tathā pavattacittasamuṭṭhānarūpesu ekaṃsato tejovāyodhātūnaṃ adhimattatā icchitabbā sallahukasabhāvatāya tāsaṃ. Tato eva ca itarāsaṃ omattatā garusabhāvattā. Taṃsambandhattā pana sesaṃ tisamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ taggatikameva hoti. Kāyavacīviññattipavattiyaṃ vāyopathavīadhimattatā imassa atthassa nidassananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Purato haraṇe, pacchato haraṇe ca uddharaṇe viya sallahukasabhāvarūpappavattīti tāsaṃyeva dvinnaṃ dhātūnaṃ adhimattatā icchitabbāti āha “tathā atiharaṇavītiharaṇesū”ti. Yathā uddharaṇādīsu sallahukasabhāvattā pacchimānaṃ dvinnaṃ dhātūnaṃ kiccaṃ adhikaṃ hoti, itarāsaṃ hīnaṃ, evaṃ vossajjanādīsu tīsu garusabhāvattā purimānaṃ dvinnaṃ kiccaṃ adhikaṃ hoti, itarāsaṃ hīnanti dassento āha “vossajjane”tiādi.

'At the time of lifting the foot' means at the time of lifting the second foot. 'Of the foot' means of the first foot that has been lifted. 'Deficient' means of a measure less than its own power. Therefore, he said, 'sluggish.' 'The others' means the fire and air elements. Just as the lifting of the foot is accomplished, so in the material phenomena arisen from consciousness that are occurring, a preponderance of the fire and air elements is certainly to be desired, because of their light nature. And for that very reason, there is a deficiency of the other two elements, because of their heavy nature. And because of this connection, the remaining material form from the three other origins follows the very same course. The preponderance of the air and earth elements in the occurrence of bodily and verbal intimation should be seen as an illustration of this meaning. In carrying forward and in carrying sideways, just as in lifting, there is an occurrence of light-natured material form; therefore, a preponderance of just those two elements is to be desired. Thus he said, 'similarly in carrying forward and carrying sideways.' Just as in lifting and so forth, due to their light nature, the function of the latter two elements is greater and that of the others is lesser, so too in the three actions of setting down and so forth, due to their heavy nature, the function of the former two is greater and that of the others is lesser. To show this, he says, 'in setting down,' etc.

Tadupādāyarūpānīti tā dhātuyo nissāya pavattaupādārūpāni. Etthevāti uddharaṇeyeva. Tenāha “atiharaṇaṃ appatvā”ti. Itīti evaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ uddharaṇādikoṭṭhāse. Pabbaṃ pabbantiādi [M 2.0410] tesaṃ dhammānaṃ koṭṭhāsantarasaṅkarābhāvadassanaṃ. Taṭataṭāyantāti taṭataṭāyanti viya, tena nesaṃ pavattikkhaṇassa ittarataṃ dasseti.

'Derived material forms' means the derived material forms that occur in dependence on those elements. 'Just here' means only in the lifting. Therefore he said, 'without reaching the carrying forward.' 'Thus' means in this way. 'In this and that' means in this and that portion of lifting, etc. 'Joint by joint,' etc., shows the absence of confusion between the portions of those phenomena. 'Crackling' means as if crackling; by this it shows the briefness of their moment of occurrence.

711. Assāti sammasanassa. Dārutiṇukkādīsūti dāruukkātiṇukkādīsu. “Kiṃ andhabāla ekaghanaṃ satataṃ sabbadābhāviṃ ekanti maññasī”ti adhippāyenāha “kimettha manāpa”nti. Idampīti yadidaṃ telavaṭṭikkhayena padīpassa apaññāyanaṃ vuttaṃ, idampi. Aṅgulaṅgulantareti aṅguliyā mitaṃ aṅgulanti aṅgulappamāṇe padeseti attho. Tantuno avayavalesabhūtaṃ paramasukhumabhāvappattaṃ aṃsuṃ sandhāyāha “aṃsuṃ pana muñcitvā”ti.

711. 'Of this' means of the contemplation. 'In wood-torches, grass-torches, etc.' means in wood-torches, grass-torches, and so on. With the intention, 'Why, you blind fool, do you think this is a single solid mass, constant, ever-existing, a single flame?' he says, 'What here is agreeable?' 'This too' means this which was said: the non-appearance of the lamp due to the exhaustion of the oil and wick, this too. 'Between finger-breadths' means a finger-breadth is what is measured by a finger; the meaning is 'in a space the measure of a finger-breadth.' Referring to a fiber that is a tiny particle of a thread and has reached a state of extreme subtlety, he says, 'but having released the fiber.'

Tatthātiādi upamāsaṃsandanaṃ. Tattha kāmaṃ upameyye viya upamāyaṃ pākaṭo kālabhedo natthi, ekakoṭṭhāsagataṃ pana koṭṭhāsantaraṃ na pāpuṇātīti ettāvatā upamābhāvo veditabbo. Upamāyampi vā tāva yāvāti kālassa bhedamattā labbhatevāti tassā gahaṇe kālabhedavasenāpi upamā yojetabbā.

'There,' etc., is the connection with the simile. Therein, it is true, there is no manifest difference of time in the simile as there is in the thing to be compared; but the nature of the simile should be understood to this extent: that what belongs to one portion does not reach another portion. Or, since in the simile too a mere measure of the difference of time is obtained as 'for as long as... for so long...,' in taking it up the simile should also be applied by way of the difference of time.

712. Pubbe ādānanikkhepādivasena catusantatirūpaṃ saṅgharitvā dassitaṃ, idāni āhārasamuṭṭhānādivasena [V 2.0385] bhinditvā dassento “tadeva rūpaṃ visaṅkharitvā”tiādimāha. Tattha visaṅkharitvā vibhajitvā. “Visaṅgharitvā”ti vā pāṭho, ayamevattho. Āhāramayanti āhārena nibbattaṃ. Jhattanti milātaṃ. Kilantanti khinnaṃ. Dhātanti tittaṃ. Pīṇitanti maṃsūpacayasampattiyā pīṇitaṃ. Tato eva mudu. Siniddhanti siniddhacchavitāya saṇhaṃ. Tato eva phassavantaṃ.

712. Previously, material form in its four continuities was shown collected together by way of taking up, putting down, etc. Now, showing it broken down by way of what is originated by nutriment, etc., he says, 'Having dismantled that very material form,' etc. Here, 'having dismantled' means having divided. Or the reading is 'having disassembled,' and the meaning is the same. 'Nutriment-made' means produced by nutriment. 'Withered' means faded. 'Worn out' means exhausted. 'Satisfied' means satiated. 'Nourished' means nourished by the acquisition of an increase of flesh. Hence, it is soft. 'Oily' means smooth on account of an oily complexion. Hence, it is pleasant to touch.

713. Uṇhakāle samuṭṭhitaṃ rūpanti uṇhasantāpena santattaṃ rūpaṃ sandhāyāha. Sītautunāti sappāyena sītautunā.

713. 'Material form arisen in the hot season' refers to material form scorched by the burning of the heat. 'By the cold season' means by a suitable cold season.

714. Āyatanadvāravasenāti āyatanasaṅkhātadvāravasena. Kammadvāranivattanatthaṃ āyatanaggahaṇaṃ. Kāyadvāreti pasādakāyadvāre. Manodvāraṃ nāma sāvajjanaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ. Tassa nissayabhāvato hadayavatthuṃ sandhāya nissitavohārena “manodvāre”ti vuttaṃ, yattha manodvāruppatti.

714. 'By way of the base-doors' means by way of the doors designated as bases. The taking up of 'bases' is for the purpose of excluding the kamma-doors. 'At the body-door' means at the sensitive body-door. The mind-door, by name, is the life-continuum together with adverting. Because the heart-base is its support, 'at the mind-door' is said with reference to the heart-base by way of a designation based on what is dependent, where the arising of the mind-door occurs.

715. Somanassitadomanassitavasenāti [M 2.0411] somanassitadomanassitapuggalavasena, somanassitadomanassitakālavasena vā.

715. 'By way of being joyful or displeased' means either by way of a person who is joyful or displeased, or by way of a time of joy or displeasure.

Ayamatthoti ayaṃ idāni vuccamāno saṅkhārānaṃ atiittarakhaṇatāsaṅkhāto attho.

'This is the meaning': this meaning which is now being stated, designated as the extremely brief momentariness of formations.

Jīvitanti jīvitindriyaṃ. Sukhadukkhāti sukhadukkhavedanā. Upekkhāpi hi sukhadukkhāsu eva antogadhā iṭṭhāniṭṭhabhāvato. Attabhāvoti jīvitavedanāviññāṇāni ṭhapetvā avasiṭṭhadhammā vuttā. Saññāti keci. Kevalāti attanā niccabhāvena vā avomissā. Ekacittasamāyuttāti ekekena cittena sahitā. Lahuso vattate khaṇoti vuttanayena ekacittakkhaṇikatāya lahuko atiittaro jīvitādīnaṃ khaṇo vattati.

'Life' means the life faculty. 'Pleasure and pain' means pleasant and painful feelings. Indeed, equanimity also is included right within pleasant and painful feelings because of its nature of being desirable and undesirable. By the term 'individual existence', the remaining phenomena are meant, having excluded life, feeling, and consciousness. Some say 'perception'. 'Mere' means unmixed, either by self or by a permanent nature. 'Conjoined with a single consciousness' means together with each single consciousness. Because of the momentariness of a single mind-moment, the moment of life and so on proceeds, being quick and extremely brief.

Cullāsītisahassāni kappanti caturāsītisahassaparimāṇaṃ kappaṃ, accantasaṃyoge etaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Kappanti ca sāmaññavasena ekavacanaṃ. Marūti devā. Dvīhi cittehi samohitāti evaṃ cirajīvinopi te dvīhi cittehi sahitā hutvā na tiṭṭhanti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti [V 2.0386] – tesampi santāne jīvitādīni dvīhi cittehi saha na tiṭṭhanti, ekena cittena saha uppannāni teneva saha nirujjhanato yāva dutiyā na tiṭṭhantīti.

'Eighty-four thousand eons' means for the duration of an eon measuring eighty-four thousand; this is a term in the accusative case in the sense of continuous connection. And 'eon' is a singular term by way of a general class. 'Marū' means gods. 'Combined with two consciousnesses' means that even though they are so long-lived, they do not remain, having become endowed with two consciousnesses. This is what is said: even in their continuum, life and other such phenomena do not remain together with two consciousnesses; because, having arisen together with one consciousness, they cease together with that very one, they do not last until a second.

Ye niruddhā marantassāti cavantassa sattassa cuticittena saddhiṃ niruddhāti vattabbā ye khandhā. Tiṭṭhamānassa vā idhāti ye vā idha pavattiyaṃ tiṭṭhantassa dharantassa bhaṅgappattiyā niruddhakkhandhā. Sabbepi sadisā te sabbepi ekasadisā atthaṅgatā appaṭisandhikā puna āgantvā paṭisandhānābhāvena vigatā. Yathā hi cutikkhandhā na nibbattanti, evaṃ tato pubbepi khandhā. Tasmā ekacittakkhaṇikaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitanti adhippāyo.

“Those that ceased while one was dying” means those aggregates which are said to have ceased together with the death-consciousness of a being who is passing away. “Or of one who remains here” means those aggregates which have ceased on reaching dissolution for one who remains, who subsists, here in the course of existence. They are all identical, just the same: having reached cessation, they are without relinking, departed due to the absence of relinking by coming again. For, just as the aggregates at death do not arise, so too the aggregates that have ceased prior to that do not arise. Therefore, the intended meaning is that the life of beings is of a single mind-moment.

Anantarā ca ye bhaggāti ye saṅkhārā anantarameva bhaggā niruddhā. Ye ca bhaggā anāgateti ye ca saṅkhārā anāgate bhaggā bhañjanasīlā bhijjissanti. Tadantarā niruddhānanti tesaṃ atītānāgatānaṃ antarā vemajjhe paccuppannataṃ patvā niruddhānaṃ bhaggānaṃ. Vesamaṃ natthi lakkhaṇeti tesaṃ tividhānampi bhaṅgalakkhaṇanimittaṃ visamatā visadisatā natthi.

“And those that broke immediately” means: the formations that broke and ceased immediately before. “And those that will break in the future” means: and the formations that, in the future, being of a nature to break, will break. “Of those that ceased in between” means: of those formations that broke, that ceased, having reached the state of being present in the very middle between those past and future ones. “There is no disparity in their characteristic” means: there is no unevenness or dissimilarity on account of the characteristic mark of breaking among these three kinds of formations.

Anibbattena [M 2.0412] na jātoti anuppannena cittena jāto na hoti, ajāto nāma hoti. Paccuppannena vattamānena cittena jīvati jīvamāno nāma hoti. Cittabhaṅgā mato lokoti cuticittassa viya sabbassapi tassa tassa cittassa bhaṅgappattiyā ayaṃ loko paramatthato mato nāma hoti niruddhassa appaṭisandhikattā. Evaṃ santepi paññatti paramatthiyā yāyaṃ taṃ taṃ santaṃ sanissayaṃ cittaṃ upādāya “tisso jīvati, phusso jīvatī”ti evaṃ vacanappavattiyā visayabhūtā santānapaññatti, sā ettha paramatthiyā paramatthabhūtā. Tathā hi vadanti “nāmagottaṃ na jīratī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.76).

“Not born by the unproduced” means: one is not born by a mind that has not arisen; one is called ‘unborn.’ One lives by the present, existing mind; one is called ‘living.’ “At the mind’s breaking, the world is dead” means: just as with the death-consciousness, so too, through the attainment of breaking of each and every mind, this world is in an ultimate sense called ‘dead,’ because what has ceased is without relinking. Even so, there is a concept that is ultimately real: this concept of continuity, which is the object of the occurrence of such speech as “Tissa lives, Phussa lives,” arisen by depending on this or that existing mind with its basis, is here ultimately real, being of ultimate reality. For thus it is said: “Name and clan do not decay.”

Anidhānagatā bhaggāti ye bhaggā, na te katthaci nidhānaṃ gatā, atha kho abhāvameva gatā. Puñjo natthi anāgate yato āgaccheyyuṃ vattamānabhāvaṃ. Nibbattā yepīti ye paṭiladdhattabhāvā paccuppannā, tepi āragge sāsapūpamā tiṭṭhanti. Yathā nāma sūciyaṃ ṭhitāyaṃ sāsapo khitto tassā sikhaṃ phuṭṭhamatto vigacchati na tiṭṭhati, evaṃ saṅkhārā uppajjitvā bhijjanti, na tesaṃ avaṭṭhānaṃ atthīti.

“Those that broke have gone to no store” means: those formations that broke have not gone to any store in any place, but rather have gone only to non-existence. There is no heap in the future from which they might come to the present state. “Even those that have arisen” means: those present formations that have gained existence, they too stand on the point of an awl like a mustard seed. Just as a mustard seed tossed onto the tip of a standing needle, merely upon touching its very tip, rolls away and does not stay, so too formations, having arisen, break up; they have no stability.

Bhaṅgo [V 2.0387] nesaṃ purakkhatoti tesaṃ nibbattadhammānaṃ bhaṅgo nāma purato eva kato, ekaṃsabhāvī na apasakkatīti attho. Purāṇehīti purimakehi atītehi.

“Their breaking is placed in front” means: the breaking of those arisen phenomena is indeed placed before them; the meaning is that it is certain and does not retreat. “By the old ones” means: by the former, past ones.

Adassanatoti apassitabbato. Āyantīti āgacchanti. “Uppajjantī”ti imināpi kutoci rāsito āgamanābhāvamevāha. Bhaggā gacchantudassananti bhaggāpi katthaci upagamanābhāvato sabbena sabbaṃ adassanaṃ abhāvameva gacchanti. Tattha nidassanamāha “vijjuppādo…pe… vayanti cā”ti.

“From not seeing” means because they are not to be seen. “They come” means they arrive. By this word “arising,” too, he states the absence of coming from any heap. “The broken go to invisibility” means: since the broken do not go anywhere, they go completely and entirely to invisibility, to non-existence. Therein, he gives an illustration: “The arising of lightning… and they vanish.”

716. “Vivaṭṭakappato paṭṭhāya uppajjanakarūpa”nti iminā sayameva uppajjanakadhammatāya “dhammatārūpa”nti anvatthanāmataṃ dasseti. Ayalohādīsu ayo nāma kāḷalohaṃ. Lohaṃ nāma jātilohaṃ vijātilohaṃ kittimalohaṃ pisācalohanti catubbidhaṃ. Tattha ayo rajataṃ suvaṇṇaṃ tipu sīsaṃ tambalohaṃ vekantakalohanti imāni satta jātilohāni. Nāganāsikalohaṃ vijātilohaṃ. Kaṃsalohaṃ vaṭṭalohaṃ [M 2.0413] hārakūṭanti tīṇi kittimalohāni. Morakkhakādi pisācalohaṃ. Tattha tambalohaṃ vekantakanti imehi dvīhi jātilohehi saddhiṃ sesaṃ sabbampi idha “loha”nti gahitanti. Tipūti setatipu. Sīsanti kāḷatipu. Suvaṇṇaṃ ākaruppannarasaviddhādibhedaṃ. Muttā sāmuddikamuttādi. Maṇīti veḷuriyalohitaṅgamasāragallāni ṭhapetvā avaseso sabbo maṇiviseso. Veḷuriyo vaṃsavaṇṇamaṇi. Saṅkho sāmuddikasaṅkho. Silāti kāḷasilāpaṇḍusilādibhedā sabbāpi ratanasammatasilā. Pavāḷaṃ nāma vaṭṭumaṃ viddhamaṃ. Lohitaṅgaṃ rattamaṇi. Masāragallaṃ kabaramaṇi. Bhūmiādayo pākaṭāva. Tadassāti taṃ dhammatārūpaṃ assa yogino.

716. By this phrase “matter that has been arising since the aeon of evolution,” he shows that because of its nature of arising by itself, it has the etymological name “natural matter.” Among metals, “ayo” is black metal. “Loha” (metal) is of four kinds: natural metal, non-genuine metal, manufactured metal, and demonic metal. Among these, the seven natural metals are: iron, silver, gold, tin, lead, copper, and vekantaka metal. Non-genuine metal is nāganāsika metal. The three manufactured metals are: bronze, brass, and hārakūṭa. Demonic metal is morakkhaka, etc. Here, “metal” is to be understood as all the rest together with these two natural metals, copper and vekantaka. “Tipu” is white tin. “Sīsa” is black tin. Gold is of different kinds such as that produced from a mine, that produced by alchemy, etc. Pearls are ocean pearls, etc. “Maṇi” (gem) means every kind of gem remaining after excluding beryl, ruby, and masāragalla. “Veḷuriya” is a gem the color of bamboo. “Saṅkha” is an ocean conch. “Silā” (stone) means all kinds of stone considered precious, such as black stone, pale stone, etc. “Pavāḷaṃ” (coral) is round or pierced. “Lohitaṅgaṃ” is a red gem. “Masāragalla” is a variegated gem. Earth and so on are evident. “Tadassā” means that natural matter belongs to the yogi.

Taruṇapallavavaṇṇanti ambādīnaṃ taruṇapallavena samānavaṇṇaṃ. Sabhāgarūpasantatinti vaṇṇādinā samānabhāgaṃ rūpasantānaṃ. Anuppabandhāpayamānanti hetuphalaparamparāya sambandhanavasena pavattanti.

“The color of a tender shoot” means having a color similar to the tender shoot of a mango tree or the like. “A continuity of similar matter” means a continuity of matter that is similar in regard to color and so on. “Continuing in sequence” means they proceed by way of connection in a series of cause and effect.

Soti yogī. Tanti asokarukkhapaṇṇaṃ. Pariggahetvāti ñāṇena paricchijja gahetvā. Iminā nayenāti iminā asokapaṇṇe vuttena nayena. Sabbampi ayalohādibhedaṃ dhammatārūpaṃ. Tampi hi sītakāle sītalaṃ, uṇhakāle sūriyasantāpena uṇhataraṃ hoti. Tattha sītabhāvena pavattaṃ [V 2.0388] rūpaṃ uṇhaṃ uṇhabhāvena pavattaṃ rūpaṃ sītaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Tattha tattheva taṭataṭāyantaṃ bhijjatītiādinā yojetabbaṃ.

“He” means the yogi. “That” means a leaf of an asoka tree. “Having comprehended” means having defined and grasped it with knowledge. “By this method” means by this method spoken of in connection with the asoka leaf. All natural matter, differentiated as iron, bronze, etc. For that too becomes cool in the cold season, and hotter in the hot season through the sun’s heat. There, the matter that has occurred with a cool nature does not reach a hot state, and the matter that has occurred with a hot nature does not reach a cool state. It should be connected with “it breaks up right there with a crackling sound,” and so on.

Arūpasattakasammasanakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on the Comprehension of the Formless Heptad

717. Kalāpatoti arūpadhammakalāpato.

717. By “from a group” is meant from a group of formless phenomena.

Yasmā tattha phassapañcamakā dhammā sabbacittuppādasādhāraṇā supākaṭā, suviññeyyā ca, tasmā tesaṃ vasena dassento “kalāpatoti phassapañcamakā dhammā”ti āha. Ye ime sammasane uppannā phassapañcamakā dhammā, sabbe te vinaṭṭhāti sambandho.

Because the phenomena with contact as the fifth are common to all arisings of consciousness, very clear, and easily cognizable, he therefore showed them by this means, saying: “A group is the phenomena with contact as the fifth.” The connection is: “All these phenomena with contact as the fifth that arose during comprehension have perished.”

Pavattaṃ cittanti sattasu ṭhānesu sammasanavasena pavattaṃ cittaṃ. Sammasantoti ekajjhaṃ gahetvā sammasanto. Taṃ yuttataranti taṃ ariyavaṃsakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ yuttataraṃ āsannabhāvena vibhūtataraṃ rūpasattake sammasanaṃ saha gahetvā sammasanassa vuttattā. Apica rūpasattake sammasanassa [M 2.0414] rūpadhammesu sātisayaṃ ghanavinibbhogaṃ katvā pavattattā tabbisayaṃ arūpasammasanaṃ sātisayaṃ aniccādilakkhaṇappaṭivedhāya sampavattatīti taṃ yuttataraṃ, na pana apubbakesādisammasanaṃ katvā tabbisayaṃ pavattitaṃ. Tathā sati kammaṭṭhānaṃ navaṃ navaṃ eva siyā, pubbe gahitaṃ sammasanavisayaṃ chaḍḍetvā aññassa sammasanavisayassa gaṇhanato. Sesānipīti yamakato sammasanādīnipi. Tenevāti ariyavaṃsakathānayeneva.

By 'the mind that has occurred' is meant the mind that has occurred by way of comprehending in the seven instances. By 'comprehending' is meant comprehending by taking them together. By 'that is more appropriate' is meant that what is said in the Discourse on the Noble Lineages is more appropriate, being more manifest on account of its nearness, because the comprehension of the material heptad is spoken of as a comprehension by taking things together. Moreover, because the comprehension of the material heptad proceeds by making an exceedingly intense analysis of the dense mass of material phenomena, the comprehension of immaterial phenomena, having that as its object, proceeds exceedingly for the penetration of the characteristics of impermanence and so on. Thus that is more appropriate, and not that which proceeds having as its object a comprehension made of newly arisen things like hair, etc. If that were so, the meditation subject would be ever new, since one would be abandoning the previously taken object of comprehension and taking up another. By 'the remaining ones as well' is meant the comprehensions by pairs and so on. By 'by that very means' is meant by the very method of the Discourse on the Noble Lineages.

718. Tampi cittanti ādānanikkhepato sammasanavasena pavattacittuppādampi. Cittasīsena hi niddeso. Esa nayo sabbattha. Yamakato sammasati nāma nāmarūpadhamme ārabbha yugaḷavasena sammasanassa pavattanato. Ayañhi pubbe rūpasattakavasena sammasitvā ṭhitopi idāni ādānanikkhepādivasena sammasitvāva taṃ sammasati. Khaṇikato sammasanādīsupi eseva nayo.

718. By 'that mind too' is meant also the mind-moment that has arisen by way of comprehension through taking up and putting down. For the exposition is headed by 'mind.' This is the method everywhere. It is called 'comprehends by way of pairs' because comprehension proceeds by way of a couple, taking mentality-materiality phenomena as its object. For although this yogi has previously stood having comprehended by way of the material heptad, now, after comprehending by way of taking up and putting down and so on, he comprehends that mind. This very same method applies also to comprehension by way of the momentary and so on.

719. Etampīti etaṃ catutthasammasanacittampi. Paṭhamacittanti ādānanikkhepādivasena rūpaṃ [V 2.0389] sammasitacittaṃ, yaṃ rūpapariggāhakacittanti adhippetaṃ. Sammasitasammasitacittasammasanena tesaṃ khaṇikabhāvassa vibhāvanato idaṃ sammasanaṃ “khaṇikato sammasana”nti vuttaṃ.

719. By 'this too' is meant this fourth comprehension-mind as well. By 'the first mind' is meant the mind that has comprehended materiality by way of taking up and putting down, etc., which is intended as the mind that grasps materiality. Because their momentary nature is made clear by comprehending the mind that has comprehended the already comprehended, this comprehension is called 'comprehension by way of the momentary.'

720. Idameva ca sammasanaṃ diguṇitaṃ anekasammasanapaṭipāṭisambhavato “paṭipāṭito sammasana”nti vuttaṃ. Vaṭṭeyyāti sambhaveyya. Tathā sati paṭipāṭisammasanapasutā eva bhāvanā siyā, na mūlakammaṭṭhānupakārī, na cāyaṃ samāpatticāro. Yasmā ca tattakena rūpadhammesu, arūpadhammesu ca aniccādilakkhaṇāni suṭṭhu vibhūtāni honti, tasmā vuttaṃ “yāva dasamacittasammasanā…pe… ṭhapetabba”nti. Ṭhapetabbanti ca na ekādasamaṃ dvādasamena sammasitabbanti paṭipāṭito sammasanassa paricchedadassanaparaṃ, na tato sammasanato oramanadassanaparaṃ, tasmā punapi rūpaṃ pariggahetvā yāva dasamacittasammasanā bhāvanamanuyuñjateva. Vuttanti ariyavaṃsakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ.

720. This very comprehension, being doubled, is called 'comprehension by sequence' because of the arising of a sequence of many comprehensions. 'It would be proper' means 'it could occur.' If that were so, the development would be one devoted only to sequential comprehension, not helpful to the basic meditation subject, nor is this the practice for attainment. And because by that much the characteristics of impermanence, etc., in material and immaterial phenomena become very manifest, it is said: '…up to the comprehension of the tenth mind… it should be set aside.' And by 'it should be set aside' is not meant that the eleventh should be comprehended with the twelfth, but this is for the purpose of showing the limit of sequential comprehension, not for showing a cessation from that comprehension. Therefore, having again grasped materiality, one should indeed apply oneself to the development up to the comprehension of the tenth mind. By 'it is said' is meant what was said in the Discourse on the Noble Lineages.

721. Visuṃ sammasananayo nāma natthīti aniccādimanasikāravinimutto añño vipassanāmanasikāro natthi. Vipassanāya ca diṭṭhiādivikkhambhanā idha diṭṭhiugghāṭanādayoti adhippetā. Vipassanāya eva hi pavattivisesena [M 2.0415] diṭṭhiugghāṭanādayo ijjhantīti dassento “yaṃ paneta”ntiādimāha. Tattha sattasaññāti sattā atthīti uppajjanakasaññā. Dubbalāya attadiṭṭhiyā sahagatasaññātipi vadanti. Sattasaññaṃ ugghāṭitacittenāti sattasaññāya vikkhambhanavasena pavattacittena diṭṭhi nuppajjati, saññāvipallāsahetuuppajjanakā cittadiṭṭhivipallāsā tadabhāvena hontīti. Māno nāma yo diṭṭhūpanissayo apāyagamanīyo, so diṭṭhiyā vikkhambhitāya vikkhambhito eva hoti, diṭṭhiyā samucchinnāya samucchijjanatoti āha “diṭṭhiugghāṭita…pe… māno nuppajjatī”ti. Māno vikkhambhiyamāno taṇhāya pavattiṃ nivāreti, abhimatavisayesu eva taṇhāya pavattanatoti vuttaṃ “mānasamugghāṭita…pe… taṇhā nuppajjatī”ti. Taṇhāti idha sukhumā nikanti adhippetāti āha “taṇhāya…pe… pariyādinnā nāma hotī”ti.

721. That there is no separate method of comprehension means that there is no other insight-attention apart from the attention to impermanence, etc. By 'the suppression of views, etc., by insight,' here 'the uprooting of views, etc.' is intended. Showing that it is by a special progression of insight itself that the uprooting of views, etc., is accomplished, he said: 'But this…' and so on. Herein, 'perception of a being' is the perception that arises with the notion 'beings exist.' Some also say it is the perception associated with a weak self-view. By 'with a mind that has uprooted the perception of a being' is meant that with a mind that proceeds by way of suppressing the perception of a being, view does not arise; for in the absence of the distortion of perception, the distortions of mind and view, which have it as their cause, do not occur. Conceit, which has view as its support and leads to the plane of misery, is suppressed when view is suppressed; because it is cut off when view is cut off, he said: 'when view is uprooted… conceit does not arise.' Conceit, being suppressed, prevents the occurrence of craving, because craving occurs only in relation to agreeable objects; thus it is said: 'when conceit is uprooted… craving does not arise.' By 'craving' here a subtle liking is intended, thus he said: 'by craving… is fully brought to an end.'

Ayaṃ nayoti idāni vuccamāno sammasanavidhi.

By 'this method' is meant the procedure of comprehension now being explained.

Mama vipassanāti imassāpi attaniyasaññitāya vipassanāya sāmibhūto attā parāmasīyatīti [V 2.0390] diṭṭhigāhatāti tathā “gaṇhato hi diṭṭhisamugghāṭanaṃ nāma na hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Kāmañcāyaṃ diṭṭhivisuddhikaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhisamadhigamena visuddhadiṭṭhiko, maggena pana asamugghāṭitattā anoḷārikāya ca diṭṭhiyā vasenevaṃ vuttaṃ.

By 'my insight': because even with this insight, when it is perceived as 'mine,' a self as owner is being grasped, it is a grasping of view. Thus it is said: 'For one who so grasps, there is indeed no uprooting of view.' And although this person has purified view through the attainment of the purification of view and the purification by overcoming doubt, it is stated thus because it has not been uprooted by the path and on account of the non-gross view.

Suṭṭhūti sammā. Manāpanti ca kiriyāvisesanaṃ, manavaḍḍhanākārenāti attho. Ubhayenāpi vipassanāvisayaṃ adhimānamāha. Tena vuttaṃ “mānasamugghāṭo nāma na hotī”ti.

By `suṭṭhu` is meant 'rightly.' And `manāpaṃ` is an adverb, meaning 'in a way that increases the mind.' By both, he indicates conceit regarding the object of insight. Therefore it is said: 'There is no uprooting of conceit.'

Vipassituṃ sakkomīti tattha samatthatāpadesena guṇavisesayogato vipassanāya assādetabbatā dassīyati, cittaṃ vipassituṃ sakkomi. Tasmā vipassanto eva kālaṃ vītināmessāmīti vipassanaṃ assādentassāti yojanā.

By the thought 'I am able to practice insight,' the savoriness of insight is shown here by indicating capability, due to its connection with a special quality. The connection for one who savors insight is as follows: 'I am able to practice insight into the mind. Therefore, I will spend my time only practicing insight.'

Yasmā diṭṭhisamugghāṭanaṃ nāmettha visesato anattānupassanāya hoti, tasmā taṃ dassentena “sace saṅkhārā”tiādinā anattānupassanāvidhiṃ vatvā yasmā pana anattato anupassantena saṅkhārā aniccatopi [M 2.0416] dukkhatopi anupassitabbā eva tadupabrūhanato, tasmā “hutvā abhāvaṭṭhenā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Because the uprooting of view is here accomplished especially through the contemplation of not-self, therefore, the author, wishing to show this, stated the method of contemplating not-self with 'if formations,' etc. And because formations must indeed be contemplated as impermanent and as suffering by one who contemplates them as not-self—as this strengthens that contemplation—it is for this reason stated: 'by the meaning of non-existence after having been,' etc.

Yasmā mānasamugghāṭanaṃ nāma aniccānupassanāya hoti. Khaṇe khaṇe bhijjanake saṅkhāre passantassa kuto mānassa avasaro. Aniccasaññā bhāvetabbā asmimānasamugghāṭāyāti hi vuttaṃ.

Because the uprooting of conceit occurs through the contemplation of impermanence. For one who sees formations as breaking up from moment to moment, where is the opportunity for conceit? For it is said: 'The perception of impermanence should be developed for the uprooting of the conceit "I am".'

Yasmā nikantipariyādānaṃ nāma dukkhānupassanāya hoti. Na hi sabhāvato, dukkhavatthuto ca dukkhabhūte saṅkhāre passantassa tattha īsakampi abhirato hoti. Assādānupassino hi tattha taṇhā uppajjeyya. Sesaṃ anattalakkhaṇe vuttanayameva. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – vuttanayena paṭipāṭito sammasanaṃ pasutassa yogino yadā anattānupassanā tikkhā sūrā visadā pavattati, itarā dvepi tadanugatikā, tadānena diṭṭhiugghāṭanaṃ kataṃ hoti. Attadiṭṭhimūlikā hi sabbā diṭṭhiyo. Anattānupassanā ca attadiṭṭhiyā ujupaṭipakkhā.

Because the exhaustion of liking occurs through the contemplation of suffering. For one who sees formations that are suffering—by their intrinsic nature and as a basis for suffering—there is not even the slightest delight in them. Indeed, for one who contemplates gratification, craving would arise there. The rest is just as by the method stated under the characteristic of not-self. Here this is the concise meaning: for a yogi devoted to sequential comprehension according to the stated method, when the contemplation of not-self proceeds keenly, boldly, and clearly—the other two also following it—then the uprooting of view has been accomplished by him. For all views are rooted in self-view, and the contemplation of not-self is the direct opposite of self-view.

Yadā pana aniccānupassanā tikkhā sūrā visadā pavattati, itarā dvepi tadanugatikā[V 2.0391], tadānena mānasamugghāṭanaṃ kataṃ hoti. Sati hi niccagāhe mānajappanā “idaṃ niccaṃ, idaṃ dhuva”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 1.501) bakabrahmuno viya. Aniccānupassanā ca niccagāhassa ujupaṭipakkhā.

When, however, the contemplation of impermanence proceeds keenly, boldly, and clearly—the other two also following it—then the uprooting of conceit has been accomplished by him. For when there is the grasping of permanence, there is the vaunting of conceit, like that of Baka Brahmā, with such thoughts as 'This is permanent, this is stable,' etc. And the contemplation of impermanence is the direct opposite of the grasping of permanence.

Yadā pana dukkhānupassanā tikkhā sūrā visadā pavattati, itarā dvepi tadanugatikā, tadānena nikantipariyādānaṃ kataṃ hoti. Sati hi sukhasaññāya taṇhāgāhova, dukkhānupassanā ca nikantiyā ujupaṭipakkhā. Evaṃ tissannaṃ anupassanānaṃ kiccavisesavasena diṭṭhiugghāṭanādīni honti. Tena vuttaṃ “iti ayaṃ vipassanā attano attano ṭhāneyeva tiṭṭhatī”ti. Anupassanānaṃ yathārahaṃ sakakiccakaraṇañhi sakaṭṭhāneyeva ṭhānaṃ, tasmā visuṃ sammasananayo natthīti na vattabbanti adhippāyo.

When, however, the contemplation of suffering proceeds keenly, boldly, and clearly—the other two also following it—then the exhaustion of liking has been accomplished by this one. For when there is the perception of pleasure, there is the grasping of craving, and the contemplation of suffering is the direct opposite of liking. Thus, the uprooting of view and so on occurs by way of the special functions of the three contemplations. Therefore it is said: 'Thus this insight stands in its own respective place.' For the contemplations' performing of their own function as is fit is indeed their standing in their own place. Therefore, the intended meaning is that it should not be said, 'There is no separate method of comprehension.'

722. Sabbākāratoti idha viya ekadesena avatvā sabbākārato sarūpato, kiccato ca anavasesato vattabbā. Idhevāti tīraṇapariññāyameva. Ekaccānaṃyevettha anupassanānaṃ paṭilābhoti āha “ekadesaṃ paṭivijjhanto”ti, tā pana sayameva sarūpato dassessati[M 2.0417]. Tappaṭipakkhe dhammeti yā anupassanā idha sambhavanti, tāsaṃ paṭipakkhe dhamme niccasaññādike pajahati vikkhambheti.

722. By 'in all aspects': unlike here where it is spoken of in part, it should be spoken of in all aspects—in terms of nature and function, and without remainder. By 'just here' is meant in the full understanding by investigation alone. Because there is the attainment here of only some of the contemplations, he said 'penetrating one part'; but the commentator himself will show them in terms of their nature. By 'states that are their opposites' is meant: he abandons and suppresses the states that are the opposites of those contemplations that arise here, such as the perception of permanence and so on.

Khayānupassananti saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇabhaṅgānupassanaṃ. Bhāventoti vaḍḍhento. Ghanasaññanti santatisamūhakiccārammaṇānaṃ vasena ekattaggahaṇaṃ. Khayānupassananti hutvā abhāvānupassananti vadanti. Yāya paññāya ghanavinibbhogaṃ katvā “aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhenā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.48) passati, sā khayānupassanā. Bhaṅgānupassanato paṭṭhāya tassā pāripūrīti ghanasaññāya pahānaṃ hoti, tato pubbe aparipuṇṇatāya taṃ na hoti. Evamaññatthāpīti paripuṇṇāparipuṇṇatā pahānatīraṇapariññāsu vipassanāpaññāya daṭṭhabbā. Paccakkhato, anvayato ca saṅkhārānaṃ bhaṅgaṃ disvā tattheva bhaṅgasaṅkhāte nirodhe adhimuttatā vayānupassanā, tāya āyūhanaṃ pajahati. Yadatthaṃ, yāya ca āyūhati, tasmiṃ pavatte taṇhāya cassa cittaṃ na namatīti. Tena vuttaṃ “vayānupassanaṃ bhāvento āyūhanaṃ pajahatī”ti. Jātassa jarāmaraṇehi dvidhā pariṇāmadassanaṃ, rūpasattakādivasena vā pariggahitassa taṃtaṃparicchedato paraṃ aññabhāvadassanaṃ vipariṇāmānupassanā, tāya dhuvasaññaṃ thirabhāvagahaṇaṃ pajahati.

"Contemplation of destruction" is the contemplation of the momentary dissolution of formations. "Developing" means increasing. "Perception of solidity" is the grasping of oneness by way of continuity, group, function, and object. Some say "contemplation of destruction" is the contemplation of non-existence after having been. The wisdom by which one penetrates solidity and sees "impermanent in the sense of destruction" is the contemplation of destruction. Beginning from the contemplation of dissolution, its fulfillment brings about the abandoning of the perception of solidity; before that, due to its non-fulfillment, this does not occur. Similarly in other cases, the fulfillment and non-fulfillment of the wisdom of insight should be seen in the full understanding as abandoning and the full understanding as investigating. Having seen the dissolution of formations both directly and by inference, the resolve upon that very cessation designated as dissolution is the contemplation of vanishing. Through it, one abandons striving. For what purpose and with what craving one strives, his mind inclines neither toward that continuity of existence nor toward that craving. Therefore it is said: "Developing the contemplation of vanishing, one abandons striving." Seeing the twofold alteration of what is born through aging and death, or seeing its alteration into another state beyond the specific demarcation of what has been grasped by way of the material septad, etc., is the contemplation of alteration. Through it, one abandons the perception of permanence, that is, the grasping of a stable nature.

Animittānupassanādayo [V 2.0392] aniccānupassanādayo eva. Nimittanti santatiyaṃ, samūhe ca ekattasaññāya gayhamānaṃ kālantarāvaṭṭhāyibhāvena, niccabhāvena ca saṅkhārānaṃ sakiccaparicchedatāya saviggahaṃ viya upaṭṭhānamattaṃ. Paṇidhinti sukhapatthanaṃ, rāgādipaṇidhiṃ vā, atthato taṇhāvasena saṅkhāresu ninnataṃ. Abhinivesanti attābhinivesaṃ. Etesañhi nimittādīnaṃ paṭipakkhabhāvena aniccānupassanādayo animittādināmehi vuttāti aniccānupassanādīhi pahātabbā niccasaññādayo viya nimittaggāhādayova paṭipakkhāti daṭṭhabbā. Rūpādiārammaṇaṃ ñatvā tadārammaṇassa cittassa bhaṅgaṃ disvā saṅkhārā eva bhijjanti, saṅkhārānaṃ maraṇaṃ, na añño koci atthīti bhaṅgavasena suññataṃ gahetvā pavattā vipassanā adhipaññā ca sā dhammesu ca vipassanāti adhipaññādhammavipassanā, tāya niccasārādiādānavasena pavattaṃ abhinivesaṃ sataṇhaṃ diṭṭhiṃ pajahati. Yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ nāma sappaccayanāmarūpadassanaṃ. Tena “ahosiṃ nu kho ahamatītamaddhāna”nti [M 2.0418] (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20) evamādikaṃ, “issarato loko sambhavatī”ti evamādikañca sammohābhinivesaṃ pajahati. Bhayatupaṭṭhānavasena uppannaṃ sabbabhavādīsu ādīnavadassanañāṇaṃ ādīnavānupassanā, tāya kassacipi ālayanissayaadassanato ālayābhinivesaṃ tathāpavattaṃ taṇhaṃ pajahati. Saṅkhārānaṃ muñcanassa upāyabhūtaṃ paṭisaṅkhāñāṇaṃ paṭisaṅkhānupassanā, tāya aniccādīsu appaṭisaṅkhātattā paṭisaṅkhānassa paṭipakkhabhūtaṃ avijjaṃ pajahati. Saṅkhārupekkhā, anulomañāṇañca vivaṭṭānupassanā. Tassā hi vasena tassa padumapalāse udakabindu viya sabbasaṅkhārehi cittaṃ patilīyati patikuṭati, tasmā tāya saṃyogābhinivesaṃ kāmasaṃyogādikilesappavattiṃ pajahati. Aniccānupassanādayo satta anupassanā heṭṭhā atthato vibhattāti, parato ca saṃvaṇṇīyantīti idha na vuttā.

The contemplations of the signless and so on are the very contemplations of impermanence and so on. The sign is what is grasped as a unity in continuity and in a collection, appearing as something stable over time and as permanent due to the demarcation of formations by their own function, like a mere appearance with a body. Longing is the aspiration for happiness or the longing for lust and so on; in essence, it is an inclination toward formations by way of craving. Adherence is adherence to a self. Because the contemplations of impermanence and so on are the opposites of these things beginning with the sign, they are called by the names signless and so on. Therefore, just as the perceptions of permanence and so on are to be abandoned by the contemplations of impermanence and so on, so too the grasping of signs and so on should be seen as their opposites. Having known an object such as form and having seen the dissolution of the mind that takes it as object, one understands that formations simply disintegrate—that it is the death of formations, and nothing else exists. Insight proceeds by grasping emptiness through the mode of dissolution. And that is higher wisdom and insight into phenomena—thus, it is called 'higher-wisdom-insight-into-phenomena.' By means of this, one abandons adherence, which is view accompanied by craving that arises from grasping at formations as permanent, a core, and so on. Knowledge and vision of things as they really are is the seeing of name-and-form with its conditions. Through this, one abandons the adherence of delusion, such as, "Did I exist in the past?" (MN 2; SN 12:20) and so on, or "The world arises from a creator," and so on. The knowledge that arises by way of the appearance of fear, seeing the danger in all states of existence and so on, is the contemplation of danger. By this, since one sees no resort or support in anything, one abandons the adherence to a resort, which is craving that proceeds in such a way. The knowledge of reflection, which is the means for release from formations, is the contemplation of reflection. By this, one abandons ignorance, which is the opponent of reflection, because one has not reflected on impermanence and so on. Equanimity toward formations and conformity knowledge are the contemplation of turning away. For by means of this, the mind recoils and shrinks back from all formations like a water drop on a lotus leaf. Therefore, by this, one abandons the adherence to the fetters—the proceeding of the defilements such as the fetter of sensual desire. The seven contemplations beginning with the contemplation of impermanence have been analyzed above in terms of meaning and will be explained later, so they are not discussed here.

Tāsūti aṭṭhārasasu mahāvipassanāsu. Imināti yoginā. Tasmāti aniccādilakkhaṇattayavasena saṅkhārānaṃ diṭṭhattā. Taṃdassanañhi aniccādianupassanāti. Paṭividdhāti paṭiladdhā. Yadaggena hi ñāṇena savisayo paṭividdho, tadaggena taṃ paṭiladdhaṃ nāma hoti. Byañjanameva nānaṃ yathā “rukkho pādapo tarū”ti. Tāpi animittāpaṇihitasuññatānupassanā.

Tāsu means: among the eighteen great insights. Iminā means: by the yogī. Tasmā means: because formations have been seen by way of the three characteristics beginning with impermanence. For that seeing is the contemplation of impermanence, etc. Paṭividdhā means: attained. For by whatever portion of knowledge its object has been penetrated, by that portion it is said to have been attained. The expression alone is different, as in 'rukkho, pādapo, taru.' These too are the contemplations of the signless, the desireless, and emptiness.

Sabbāpi vipassanā, tasmā ekadesena paṭividdhā hontīti adhippāyo. Kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiyā [V 2.0393] eva saṅgahitaṃ, tasmā taṃ pageva siddhanti attho. Tenāha “idampi dvayaṃ paṭividdhameva hotī”ti. Sesesu nibbidānupassanādīsu dasasu. “Kiñci paṭividdhaṃ kiñci appaṭividdha”nti iminā tesaṃ ekadesapaṭivedhamāha. Aniccānupassanāya hi siddhāya nirodhānupassanā, khayānupassanā, vayānupassanā, vipariṇāmānupassanā ca ekadesena siddhā nāma honti, dukkhānupassanāya siddhāya nibbidānupassanā, ādīnavānupassanā ca, anattānupassanāya siddhāya itarāti.

The meaning is: it is all insight; therefore, they are penetrated in part. It is included only in the purification by overcoming doubt; therefore the meaning is that it is accomplished beforehand. Hence he said: “This pair, too, is indeed penetrated.” Regarding the remaining ten, beginning with the contemplation of disenchantment, by this phrase, “Some is penetrated, some is not penetrated,” he indicates their partial penetration. For when the contemplation of impermanence is accomplished, the contemplations of cessation, destruction, vanishing, and alteration are said to be accomplished in part. When the contemplation of suffering is accomplished, so too are the contemplations of disenchantment and danger. When the contemplation of not-self is accomplished, so too are the others.

Udayabbayañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

An Exposition of the Discourse on the Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away

723. Parato [M 2.0419] paṭipadāñāṇadassanakathāyaṃ abbhādivigamena ākāsassa viya, paṅkamalavigamena udakassa viya, kāḷakāpagamena suvaṇṇassa viya saṃkilesavigamena ñāṇassa parisuddhīti āha “niccasaññādīnaṃ pahānena visuddhañāṇo”ti. Anekākāravokārasaṅkhāresu lakkhaṇattayasallakkhaṇasammasanassa katattā vuttaṃ “sammasanañāṇassa pāraṃ gantvā”ti. Tattha sammasanañāṇassāti nayavipassanāsaṅkhātassa kalāpasammasanañāṇassa. Tasseva hi thirabhāvāya itare sammasanavisesāti vadanti. Sammasanañāṇassāti vā kalāpasammasanādisammasanañāṇassa. Anupadadhammavipassanāya sadisā hi sā. Tāya hi diṭṭhiugghāṭanādi sambhavatīti. Vitthārato bhāvanāvidhānaṃ parato vattukāmo “saṅkhepato tāva ārabhatī”ti āha. Saṅkhepato hi ārambho ādikammikassa sukaro. Tatrāti saṅkhepena ārambhe.

723. In the following discussion on the knowledge and vision of the path, just as the sky is purified by the departure of clouds, water by the removal of mud and defilements, and gold by the removal of dross, so too is knowledge purified by the removal of defilements. Thus it is said: “Through the abandoning of perceptions of permanence and so on, one’s knowledge is purified.” Because one has thoroughly comprehended the three characteristics in formations of various and diverse kinds, it is said: “Having gone beyond the knowledge of comprehension.” Therein, “the knowledge of comprehension” refers to the knowledge of comprehension by groups, which is known as insight by way of method. For they say that the other special kinds of comprehension are for the sake of its stability. Or, “the knowledge of comprehension” refers to the knowledge of comprehension by groups and so on. For this is indeed similar to insight into each successive phenomenon; through it, the uprooting of views and so on becomes possible. Wishing to explain the method of development in detail later on, the author says: “For now, he begins in brief.” For a beginner, a brief beginning is easy. Therein, this means in the brief beginning.

Kathanti kathetukamyatāpucchā. Yaṃ “paccuppannānaṃ…pe… udayabbayānupassane ñāṇa”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ kathaṃ ñātabbanti ceti attho. Santatipaccuppanne, khaṇapaccuppanne vā dhamme udayabbayadassanābhiniveso kātabbo, na atītānāgateti vuttaṃ “paccuppannānaṃ dhammāna”nti. Udayadassanañcettha yāvadeva vayadassanatthanti vayadassanassa padhānataṃ dassetuṃ “vipariṇāmānupassane paññā”ti vatvā taṃ pana vayadassanaṃ udayadassanapubbakanti āha “udayabbayānupassane ñāṇa”nti.

“How?” This is a question prompted by the desire to explain. The meaning is: that which was said, “…knowledge in observing the arising and passing away of present phenomena…”—how is that to be known? One should be intent on seeing the arising and passing away of phenomena in the continuous present or the momentary present, not in the past or future. Hence it is said, “of present phenomena.” Herein, the seeing of arising is only for the sake of seeing passing away. To show the pre-eminence of seeing passing away, it is said, “wisdom in observing alteration.” But since that seeing of passing away is preceded by the seeing of arising, it is said, “knowledge in observing arising and passing away.”

Jātanti nibbattaṃ paṭiladdhattabhāvaṃ. Ayaṃ hi jātasaddo khaṇattayasamaṅgitaṃ sandhāya vutto “ye dhammā jātā bhūtā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 1046) viya, na atītaṃ

“Born” means produced, having acquired an individual existence. For this word “born” is used in reference to what is endowed with the three moments, as in such passages as “those phenomena that are born, have come to be” (Dhs §1046), and does not mean the past.

“Ye [V 2.0394] te jātā na te santi, ye na jātā tattheva te;

Laddhattabhāvā no bhaggā, teva santi sabhāvato”ti. –

“Those that have been born exist no more; those that have not been born, they likewise do not exist. Those that have acquired existence and have not yet perished, only they exist by their intrinsic nature.”

Ādīsu viya, nāpi jātatāmattaṃ “yaṃ taṃ jātaṃ bhūtaṃ saṅkhata”ntiādīsu viya. Tenāha “jātaṃ rūpaṃ paccuppanna”nti (dī. ni. 2.207; saṃ. ni. 5.379), paccuppannarūpaṃ nāma jātaṃ khaṇattayapariyāpannanti attho. Taṃ pana ādito duppariggahanti santatipaccuppannavasena vipassanābhiniveso kātabbo. Tassāti rūpassa. Paccayalakkhaṇapapañcaṃ [M 2.0420] anāmasitvā nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ udayoti nibbattanasaññitaṃ saṅkhatalakkhaṇaṃ udayo uppādo. Vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ vayoti vipariṇāmasaññitaṃ saṅkhatalakkhaṇaṃ vayo vināso. Anupassanāñāṇanti yā udayassa, vayassa ca anupekkhanā, taṃ ñāṇaṃ. Kiñcāpi kalāpasammasanādīsu jātijarāmaraṇasīsena jātijarāmaraṇavanto dhammā vuttā, idha pana udayabbayañāṇaniddese “jāti paccuppannā, tassā nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ udayo, vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ vayo”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 1.49) vuccamāne jātijarāmaraṇānaṃ jātijarāmaraṇavantatā, nipphannatā ca anuññātā viya hotīti taṃ pariharituṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṅgesu bhavapariyosānāva desanā katā.

Nor does it mean mere born-ness, as in such passages as “whatever is born, become, conditioned.” Therefore it is said: “Born form is present form,” the meaning being that what is called present form is born and comprised within the three moments. But since this is difficult to grasp at first, one should apply oneself to insight by way of the continuous present. 'Of that' means of form. Without considering the proliferation of the characteristic of condition, the characteristic of production is arising; that is, the conditioned characteristic designated as production is arising, origination. The characteristic of alteration is passing away; that is, the conditioned characteristic designated as alteration is passing away, dissolution. 'Knowledge of observation' is the knowledge that is the contemplation of arising and of passing away. Although in the comprehension of groups, etc., phenomena possessing birth, aging, and death are spoken of under the heading of birth, aging, and death, here, however, in the exposition of the knowledge of arising and passing away, when it is said, “Birth is present; its characteristic of production is arising, its characteristic of alteration is passing away,” it is as if the fact that birth, aging, and death themselves possess birth, aging, and death, and their accomplished nature, were being admitted. To avoid this, the teaching on the links of dependent origination was made to conclude with becoming.

Soti yogī. Iminā pāḷinayenāti imāya “jātaṃ rūpaṃ paccuppanna”ntiādinā dassitāya pāḷigatiyā. Jātinti na pasūtiṃ, na ca paṭhamābhinibbattimattaṃ, atha kho uppādaṃ nibbattivikāraṃ. Svāyaṃ vikāro yasmā saṅkhārānaṃ abhinavāvaṭṭhānajarā viya navabhāvāpagamoti āha “abhinavākāra”nti. Samanupassatīti sambandho. Anuppannassa rāsi vā nicayo vā natthi yato āgaccheyya uppajjamānaṃ aladdhattabhāvassa sabbena sabbaṃ avijjamānattā. Tenāha “uppajjamāna…pe… natthī”ti. Yathā anāgate addhani ime dhammā sabbena sabbaṃ natthi, evaṃ atītepi addhanīti dassento “nirujjhamānassāpī”tiādiṃ vatvā avijjamānānaṃyeva rūpārūpadhammānaṃ hetupaccayasamavāye uppādo, uppajjitvā ca sabbaso abhāvūpagamoti imamatthaṃ samudāyagataṃ tadekadesabhūtāya upamāya vibhāvetuṃ “yathā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha rāsitoti rāsibhāvena samussito puñjo rāsi. Yathā tathā piṇḍibhūto nicayo. Bhūmiyaṃ nidahitvā ṭhapitaṃ nidhānaṃ. Upavīṇeti etenāti upavīṇaṃ, vīṇāvādanaṃ.

He means the yogi. 'By this textual method' means by this course of the text shown by such passages as “born form is present form.” 'Born' means not parturition, nor merely the first production, but rather origination, the change that is production. Because this change is the fresh state of formations, and not the departure from a new state like aging, he says 'fresh appearance.' 'He closely observes' is the connection. For what has not arisen, there is no heap or store from which it might come when arising, because what has not yet acquired existence is in every way non-existent. Therefore it is said: “What is arising... does not exist.” In the future period, for these material and immaterial phenomena which are in every way entirely non-existent, upon the conjunction of causes and conditions, there is arising, and having arisen, there is a coming to complete non-existence. To clarify this meaning, which pertains to the aggregate, by means of a simile that is a part of it, it is said, “Just as...” and so on. Therein, 'heap' means a pile raised up as a heap. A mass formed in any way whatsoever is a 'store.' A 'deposit' is what is laid down and placed in the ground. `Upavīṇaṃ` is so called because 'one plays the lute with this' (`upavīṇeti etena`); it means the plectrum for playing the lute.

724. Evaṃ [V 2.0395] saṅkhepato udayabbayamanasikāravidhiṃ dassetvā idāni vitthārato dassetuṃ “puna yānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha avijjāsamudayāti avijjāya uppādā, atthibhāvāti attho. Nirodhavirodhīhi uppādo atthibhāvavācakopi hotīti vuttovāyamattho. Tasmā purimabhavasiddhāya avijjāya sati imasmiṃ bhave rūpassa uppādo hotīti [M 2.0421] attho. Paccayasamudayaṭṭhenāti paccayassa uppannabhāvena, atthibhāvatoti attho. Avijjādīhi ca tīhi atītakālikāni tesaṃ sahakārīkāraṇabhūtāni upādānādīnipi gahitānevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

724. Having thus shown in brief the method of attending to arising and passing away, now to show it in detail, it is said, “Again, which...” and so on. Therein, 'with the arising of ignorance' means: from the origination of ignorance, or from its existence. It has been said that origination, being the opposite of cessation, can also be expressive of existence. Therefore, the meaning is that when there is ignorance established in a previous existence, the origination of form occurs in this existence. 'In the sense of the arising of the condition' means: because the condition has arisen, or because of its existence. And it should be understood that by the three past conditions—ignorance and so on—their auxiliary causes, such as clinging and so on, are also included.

Pavattipaccayesu kabaḷīkārāhārassa balavatāya so eva gahito “āhārasamudayā”ti. Tasmiṃ pana gahite pavattipaccayatāsāmaññena utucittānipi gahitāneva hontīti catusamuṭṭhānikarūpassa paccayato udayadassanaṃ vibhāvitamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Avijjātaṇhupanissayasahiteneva kammunā rūpakāyassa nibbatti. Asati ca avijjupanissayāya bhavanikantiyā jātiyā asambhavo evāti. Yathā ca rūpassa avijjātaṇhupanissayatā, evaṃ vedanādīnampi daṭṭhabbā. Āhāro pana uppannassa rūpassa posako, kabaḷīkārāhārassa adhippetattā, kāmadhātādhiṭṭhānattā ca desanāya. Ukkaṃsaniddesena vā āhāraggahaṇaṃ. “Nibbattilakkhaṇa”ntiādinā kālavasena udayadassanamāha. Tattha addhānavasena pageva udayaṃ passitvā ṭhito idha santativasena disvā anukkamena khaṇavasena passati. Pañca lakkhaṇānīti [V 2.0396] avijjā taṇhā kammaṃ āhāroti imesaṃ paccayānaṃ atthitāsaṅkhātalakkhaṇāni ceva rūpassa nibbattilakkhaṇañcāti imāni pañca lakkhaṇāni. Tesaṃ atthitā hi rūpassa udayo lakkhīyati etehīti lakkhaṇānīti vuccanti. Nibbatti pana saṅkhatalakkhaṇamevāti.

Among the conditions for continuance, because of the strength of physical nutriment, that alone is taken up with the words 'from the arising of nutriment.' But when that is taken up, by the commonality of being conditions for continuance, temperature and mind are also included. Thus it should be understood that the seeing of the arising of form from conditions—form which has four origins—is thereby explained. The production of the material body is through kamma accompanied by the support of ignorance and craving. And when there is no delight in becoming which has ignorance as its support, the impossibility of birth is certain. Just as form has ignorance and craving as its support, so too should it be understood of feeling and so on. Nutriment, however, is a supporter of form that has already arisen, since physical nutriment is intended and the teaching is based on the sense-sphere. Or the inclusion of nutriment is by way of a pre-eminent exposition. By 'the characteristic of production,' etc., he speaks of seeing arising by way of time. Therein, one who has already seen arising by way of duration and is established in that, here sees it by way of continuity and then successively by way of moments. The five characteristics are these: the characteristics consisting in the existence of these conditions—ignorance, craving, kamma, and nutriment—and the characteristic of the production of form. They are called 'characteristics' because the arising of form is marked by their existence. Production, however, is just the conditioned characteristic.

Avijjānirodhā rūpanirodhoti aggamaggañāṇena avijjāya anuppādanirodhato anāgatassa rūpassa anuppādanirodho hoti paccayābhāve abhāvato. Paccayanirodhaṭṭhenāti avijjāsaṅkhātassa anāgate uppajjanakarūpapaccayassa niruddhabhāvena. Taṇhānirodhā kammanirodhāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Āhāranirodhāti pavattipaccayassa kabaḷīkārāhārassa abhāve. Rūpanirodhoti taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpassa abhāvo hoti. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayānusārena veditabbaṃ. Vipariṇāmalakkhaṇanti bhaṅgakālavasena tesaṃ vayadassanaṃ. Tasmā taṃ addhāvasena pageva passitvā ṭhito idha santativasena disvā anukkamena khaṇavasena passati. Pañca lakkhaṇānīti idha avijjādīnaṃ catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ anuppādanirodho, rūpassa khaṇanirodho cāti imāni pañca lakkhaṇāni. Tesañhi anuppādanirodho, rūpassa accantanirodho lakkhīyati etehīti lakkhaṇānīti vuccanti.

“With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of form”: through the knowledge of the highest path, from the non-arising-cessation of ignorance, there is the non-arising-cessation of future form, because of the non-existence of the effect in the absence of the cause. “In the sense of the cessation of the condition” means because of the state of having ceased of the condition for form that would arise in the future, designated as ignorance. “With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of kamma”: here too the same method applies. “With the cessation of nutriment” means in the absence of physical food, the condition for continuance. “Cessation of form” means there is the absence of form originating from that. The rest should be understood according to the method stated previously. “The characteristic of alteration” is the seeing of their passing away by way of the time of dissolution. Therefore, one who has already seen it by way of duration and is established therein, here sees it by way of continuity and then successively by way of moments. Herein, these are the five characteristics: the non-arising-cessation of the four conditions beginning with ignorance, and the momentary cessation of form. For by these, their non-arising-cessation and the final cessation of form are marked; thus they are called ‘characteristics’.

Vipariṇāmo [M 2.0422] saṅkhatalakkhaṇameva. Esa nayo vedanākkhandhādīsu. Ayaṃ pana viseso – “phuṭṭho vedeti, phuṭṭho sañjānāti, phuṭṭho cetetī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.93), “phassapaccayā vedanā, cakkhusamphassajā vedanā, saññā, cetanā”ti, ca vacanato phasso vedanā (vibha. 231) saññā saṅkhārakkhandhānaṃ pavattipaccayo, taṃnirodhā ca tesaṃ nirodho, mahāpadāna (dī. ni. 2.60) mahānidānasuttesu, abhidhamme ca aññamaññapaccayavāre “nāmarūpapaccayā viññāṇa”nti (kathā. 719) vacanato nāmarūpaṃ viññāṇassa pavattipaccayo, taṃnirodhā tassa nirodhoti vuttaṃ “phassasamudayā vedanāsamudayo”tiādi.

Change is indeed a characteristic of the conditioned. This method applies to the aggregates of feeling and so on. Here, however, is the distinction: “Being touched, one feels; being touched, one perceives; being touched, one intends”; and because of such statements as “With contact as condition, feeling [arises]; feeling, perception, and volition [arise] born of eye-contact,” contact is a condition for the occurrence of the aggregates of feeling, perception, and volitional formations, and with its cessation their cessation occurs. As stated in the Mahāpadāna and Mahānidāna Suttas, and in the Abhidhamma in the section on mutual conditionality, “With name-and-form as condition, consciousness [arises],” name-and-form is a condition for the occurrence of consciousness, and with its cessation, its cessation occurs. Thus it is said: “With the arising of contact, there is the arising of feeling,” and so on.

Ettha ca keci tāva āhu “arūpakkhandhānaṃ udayabbayadassanaṃ addhāsantativaseneva, na khaṇavasenā”ti. Tesaṃ matena khaṇato udayabbayadassanameva na siyā. Apare panāhu “paccayato udayabbayadassane atītādivibhāgaṃ anāmasitvā sabbasādhāraṇato avijjādipaccayā vedanāsambhavaṃ labbhamānataṃ passati, na uppādaṃ. Avijjādiabhāve ca tassā asambhavaṃ alabbhamānataṃ passati, na bhaṅgaṃ. Khaṇato udayabbayadassane paccuppannānaṃ uppādaṃ, bhaṅgañca passatī”ti, taṃ yuttaṃ. Santativasena hi rūpārūpadhamme udayato, vayato ca manasi karontassa anukkamena bhāvanāya balappattakāle ñāṇassa tikkhavisadabhāvappattiyā khaṇato udayabbayā upaṭṭhahantīti. Ayañhi paṭhamaṃ paccayato udayabbayaṃ manasi karonto avijjādike paccayadhamme vissajjetvā udayabbayavante khandhe gahetvā tesaṃ paccayato udayabbayadassanamukhena khaṇatopi udayabbayaṃ manasi karoti.

Here, some first say: “The observation of the arising and passing away of the formless aggregates is only by way of duration and continuity, not by way of individual moments.” According to their view, the observation of arising and passing away by moments would not be possible at all. Others, however, say: “In observing arising and passing away by way of conditions, without touching upon the division into past, etc., because it is common to all, one sees that the arising of feeling is possible and obtainable due to conditions such as ignorance, but not the actual arising. And in the absence of ignorance, etc., one sees that its arising is impossible and unobtainable, but not the actual passing away. In observing arising and passing away by way of moments, one sees both the arising and the passing away of present phenomena.” That is correct. For when one attends to the arising and passing away of material and immaterial phenomena by way of a continuum, and the meditation has gradually reached a state of power, because the knowledge has reached a state of sharpness and clarity, the arising and passing away by way of moments become manifest. Indeed, this yogi, first attending to arising and passing away by way of conditions—not setting aside the conditional phenomena such as ignorance, but grasping the aggregates that are subject to arising and passing away—also attends to their arising and passing away by way of moments, with the observation by way of conditions as the primary approach.

Tassa yadā ñāṇaṃ tikkhaṃ visadaṃ hutvā pavattati, tadā rūpārūpadhammā khaṇe khaṇe uppajjantā, bhijjantā ca hutvā upaṭṭhahanti. Tena vuttaṃ “evampi rūpassa udayo”tiādi. Tattha evampi rūpassa udayoti evaṃ vuttanayena avijjāsamudayāpi. Taṇhā…pe… kamma…pe… āhārasamudayāpi rūpassa sambhavo. Evampi rūpassa vayoti evaṃ vuttanayeneva avijjānirodhāpi taṇhā…pe… āhāranirodhāpi rūpassa vayo anuppādoti paccayato vitthārena manasikāraṃ karoti[V 2.0397]. Evampi rūpaṃ udetīti evaṃ vuttanayena nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ passantopi kammasamuṭṭhānarūpampi āhārautucittasamuṭṭhānarūpampi udeti uppajjati nippajjatīti. Evaṃ vuttanayeneva vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ passanto kammasamuṭṭhānarūpampi āhārautucittasamuṭṭhānarūpampi [M 2.0423] veti nirujjhatīti khaṇato vitthārena manasikāraṃ karotīti yojanā.

When his knowledge becomes sharp and clear and proceeds, then material and immaterial phenomena appear as arising and breaking up moment by moment. Therefore, it is said, “Thus too is the arising of form,” and so on. Here, “Thus too is the arising of form” means in the way stated: from the arising of ignorance too, from the arising of craving... from the arising of kamma... from the arising of nutriment too is the production of form. “Thus too is the passing away of form” means in the very way stated: from the cessation of ignorance too, from the cessation of craving... from the cessation of nutriment too is the passing away, the non-arising, of form. Thus he attends extensively by way of conditions. “Thus too form arises” means: in the way stated, while seeing the characteristic of generation, [he attends that] kamma-born form, and form born of nutriment, temperature, and mind, also arises, is produced, is generated. In the very way stated, while seeing the characteristic of change, [he attends that] kamma-born form, and form born of nutriment, temperature, and mind, also passes away, ceases. Thus he attends extensively by way of moments—this is the connection.

725. Evaṃ manasi karoto na yāva udayabbayañāṇaṃ uppajjati, tāva udayabbayā suṭṭhu pākaṭā na hontīti katvā vuttaṃ “iti kirime dhammā…pe… paṭiventī”ti, nayadassanavasena vā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Paṭhamañhi paccuppannadhammānaṃ udayabbayaṃ disvā atha atītānāgate nayaṃ neti. Dukkhādisaccappabhedā, anulomādipaṭiccasamuppādappabhedā, ekattādinayappabhedā, aniccatādilakkhaṇappabhedā ca saccapaṭiccasamuppādanayalakkhaṇappabhedā. Paṭiccasamuppādaggahaṇeneva cettha paṭiccasamuppannadhammānampi gahaṇaṃ, tesampi attano phalaṃ pati paṭicca samuppādabhāvato.

725. For one who attends in this way, as long as the knowledge of arising and passing away has not arisen, arising and passing away are not very evident. It is because of this that it is said: “Thus, it seems, these phenomena… are penetrated.” Or, this is stated by way of seeing the method. For at first one sees the arising and passing away of present phenomena, and then one extends the method to the past and future. The distinctions of the truths such as suffering, the distinctions of dependent origination such as the forward order, the distinctions of methods such as oneness, and the distinctions of characteristics such as impermanence are the distinctions of the truths, of dependent origination, of method, and of characteristics. Here, by the very grasping of dependent origination, dependently arisen phenomena are also grasped, because they too have the nature of causing dependent origination in relation to their own fruit.

726. Yanti karaṇe paccattavacanaṃ, yena ñāṇenāti atthaṃ vadanti. Yanti vā kiriyāparāmasanaṃ. Khandhānaṃ samudayaṃ passati, khandhānaṃ nirodhaṃ passatīti ettha yadetaṃ dassananti attho. Yaṃ panāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Ettha ca yathā avijjādisamudayanirodhato khandhānaṃ samudayanirodhassa aññattā “avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayo”tiādivacanabhedo (paṭi. ma. 1.50) kato, na evaṃ nibbattivipariṇāmalakkhaṇehi khandhānaṃ udayabbayassa bhedo atthi abhinnādhikaraṇattāti “nibbattilakkhaṇavipariṇāmalakkhaṇāni passanto khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ passatī”ti vacanabhedaṃ akatvā vuttaṃ. Uppattikkhaṇeyeva hīti hi-saddo hetuattho. Yasmā uppādakkhaṇeyeva nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ, bhaṅgakkhaṇeyeva ca vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ, tasmā tāni passanto khaṇato khandhānaṃ udayabbaye passati nāmāti “yaṃ panā”tiādinā vuttamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ karoti.

726. The word 'yanti' is a term in the nominative case in the sense of the instrumental; they say the meaning is 'by which knowledge.' Or, 'yanti' is a reference to the action. When it says, 'one sees the arising of the aggregates, one sees the cessation of the aggregates,' the meaning is 'that seeing.' As for 'yaṃ pana,' the same method applies here also. And here, just as a distinction of expression is made—such as 'from the arising of ignorance, the arising of form'—because the arising and cessation of the aggregates is different from that of ignorance and so on, so, in the same way, no such distinction is made for the arising and passing away of the aggregates from the characteristics of generation and change, because they have an identical basis. Thus, it is stated without making a verbal distinction, as 'seeing the characteristics of generation and change, one sees the arising and passing away of the aggregates.' The word 'hi' in 'Uppattikkhaṇeyeva hi' has the sense of cause. Because the characteristic of generation is at the very moment of arising, and the characteristic of change is at the very moment of breaking up, therefore one who sees them is said to see the arising and passing away of the aggregates by way of moments. The passage beginning 'yaṃ pana' makes the very meaning that was stated even clearer.

727. Iccassevanti ettha iti-saddo hetuattho. Yasmā “avijjā samudayā”tiādi paccayato khandhānaṃ udayabbayadassanaṃ, “nibbattilakkhaṇa”ntiādi khaṇato, tasmāti attho. Assāti yogino. Evanti vuttappakāraparāmasanaṃ. Ye pana “iccassa paccayato”ti paṭhanti, tesaṃ itīti vuttappakāraparāmasanaṃ. Janakāvabodhatoti khandhānaṃ janakassa avijjādipaccayassa avabujjhanato[V 2.0398]. Jātidukkhāvabodhatoti jātisaṅkhātassa dukkhassa avabujjhanato. Dukkhasaccaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti ekadesadassanena pabbatasamuddādidassanakānaṃ [M 2.0424] viya. Maraṇadukkhāvabodhatoti etthāpi eseva nayo. “Paccayānuppādenā”ti etena paccayānaṃ anuppādanirodho idha paccayanirodhoti dasseti. Paccayavatanti paccayato uppajjanakānaṃ. Yañcassa udayabbayadassananti yaṃ assa yogino paccayato, khaṇato ca udayabbayānaṃ dassanaṃ. Tattha asammoho, tappadhāno vā vitakkādidhammapuñjo maggo vāyaṃ lokikoti niyyānānulomato lokiko maggo evāyaṃ. Iti tasmā maggasaccaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti sabhāvāvabodhato. Tenāha “tatra sammohavighātato”ti, tadaṅgavasenāti attho. Atha vā yathāvutto sammādiṭṭhisaṅkhāto maggo ariyamaggassa upāyabhūto asammohasabhāvo attānampi pakāseti padīpo viyāti maggasaccaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti. Svāyaṃ pākaṭabhāvo mohandhakāravidhamanenāti āha “tatra sammohavighātato”ti.

727. In the phrase 'iccassevanti,' the particle 'iti' has the sense of cause. The meaning is: because the seeing of the arising and passing away of the aggregates by way of conditions is expressed by 'with the arising of ignorance,' etc., and by way of moments by 'the characteristic of generation,' etc., therefore, this is the meaning. 'Assa' refers to the yogi. 'Evam' is a reference to the manner stated. But for those who read 'iccassa paccayato,' 'iti' is a reference to the manner stated. 'By understanding the generator' means by thoroughly understanding the condition that generates the aggregates, namely, ignorance, etc. 'By understanding the suffering of birth' means by thoroughly understanding the suffering described as birth. The truth of suffering becomes evident through seeing a part, just as it is for those who see mountains, oceans, and so forth. The same method applies to 'by understanding the suffering of death.' By the phrase 'through the non-arising of conditions,' it is shown that here the cessation of conditions means the cessation which is the non-arising of conditions. 'Paccayavataṃ' means 'of things that arise from conditions.' 'And his seeing of arising and passing away' means the yogi’s seeing of arising and passing away by way of conditions and by way of moments. Therein, non-delusion, or the collection of mental states such as applied thought, etc., with that as predominant, is the path. This is the mundane path because it conforms to the path of deliverance. Thus the truth of the path becomes evident through thoroughly understanding its intrinsic nature. Hence he says, 'by the removal of delusion therein,' which means, by way of momentary abandonment. Alternatively, the path described as right view, as stated, being a means to the noble path and having the nature of non-delusion, illuminates itself like a lamp; thus the truth of the path becomes evident. This state of being evident comes about by dispelling the darkness of delusion; hence he says, 'by the removal of delusion therein.'

728. “Avijjāpaccayā”tiādiko anulomo paṭiccasamuppādo pavattiyā anulomanato. “Avijjāsamudayā”tiādinā avijjādīsu santesūti ayamattho vuttoti āha “imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hotīti avabodhato”ti. Pavattiyā vilomanato “avijjāyatveva asesavirāganirodhā”tiādiko paṭilomo paṭiccasamuppādo. Te ca saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā “jarāmaraṇaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppanna”ntiādivacanato (saṃ. ni. 2.20). Paṭiccasamuppannassa ca pākaṭatā paccayākārapākaṭatāya eva “imassetaṃ phala”nti avabodhato.

728. The dependent origination beginning with “Dependent on ignorance” is the forward order, because it conforms to the process of occurrence. By the text beginning with “With the arising of ignorance,” the meaning “when ignorance and the other conditions exist” is stated; thus he says, “by understanding ‘when this exists, that comes to be.’” The dependent origination beginning with “With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same ignorance” is the reverse order, because it is the reverse of the process of occurrence. And those conditioned things are dependently arisen, on the basis of such statements as: “Bhikkhus, aging-and-death is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen.” And the manifestation of what is dependently arisen is precisely through the manifestation of the conditional structure, that is, by understanding, “This is the fruit of that.”

729. Purimapurimānaṃ nirodho uttaruttarānaṃ uppādānubandhoti ayamattho paccayato udayadassanena sijjhamāno ekattanayādhigamāya hoti. Yato “añño karoti, añño paṭisaṃvedayatī”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.17) vohārasiddhiyā ucchedadiṭṭhiyā anokāsatā. Tenāha “hetuphalasambandhenā”tiādi. Saṅkhārā khaṇe khaṇe uppajjantīti ayamattho khaṇato udayadassanena sijjhamāno nānattanayādhigamāya hoti. Yato paccayapaccayuppannānaṃ sabhāvabhedāvabodhato “so karoti, so paṭisaṃvedayatī”tiādinayappavattāya sassatadiṭṭhiyā anokāsatā. Tenāha “khaṇato udayadassanenā”tiādi. Paccayato [M 2.0425] udayabbayadassanena paccaye sati phalassa bhāvo, asati abhāvoti imassa atthassa siddhiyā atthitāmatteneva te dhammā kāraṇanti abyāpāranayo pākaṭo hoti. Yato attadiṭṭhiyā anokāsatā vasavattitāya alabbhaneyyato[V 2.0399]. Tena vuttaṃ “dhammāna”ntiādi. Avasavattibhāvo parāyattatā, sā ca sappaccayatāya veditabbā. Paccayato udayadassanena tehi tehi paccayehi ime dhammā uppajjanti, uppajjamānā ca paccayānurūpameva uppajjantīti hetuphalassa hetuanurūpato siddhiyā akiriyadiṭṭhiyā anokāsatāvāti āha “paccayato panā”tiādi. Sati kāraṇe kuto akiriyavādo. Karotīti hi kāraṇaṃ.

729. The cessation of the preceding is followed by the arising of the subsequent—this meaning, established by seeing the arising from a condition, leads to the comprehension of the principle of unity. Because of this, there is no opportunity for the annihilationist view, which is based on the convention that 'one person acts, another experiences.' Hence it is said, 'through the connection of cause and effect,' and so on. The meaning that formations arise moment by moment, established by seeing the arising from moment to moment, leads to the comprehension of the principle of diversity. Because of this, by understanding the difference in nature between conditions and conditionally arisen phenomena, there is no opportunity for the eternalist view, which holds that 'he who acts is the same as he who experiences.' Hence it is said, 'by seeing the arising from moment to moment,' and so on. By seeing the arising and passing away from a condition, the principle of non-agency becomes manifest through the establishment of this meaning: when a condition exists, its effect occurs, and when it is absent, it does not occur; thus those phenomena are causes merely by their existence. Because of this, there is no opportunity for the view of self, since control is unobtainable. Hence it is said, 'of phenomena,' and so on. The state of being beyond control is dependence on others, and that is to be known through its conditioned nature. By seeing the arising from a condition, one understands that these phenomena arise from these and those conditions, and in arising they do so in conformity with their conditions. Thus, by establishing the conformity of the effect with the cause, there is no opportunity for the view of non-action. Hence it is said, 'but from a condition,' and so on. When a cause exists, how can there be a doctrine of non-action? For a cause is indeed what acts.

730. Paccayato udayaṃ passato paccaye sati sabhāve sati phalassa sambhavoti atthitāmattena upakārakatāti saṅkhatānaṃ nirīhatā, asati ca abhāvoti paccayādhīnavuttitā ca viññāyamānā attasuññataṃ vibhāvetīti āha “paccayato cassa…pe… tāvabodhato”ti. Aniccalakkhaṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti khaṇato udayabbayadassanena saṅkhārānaṃ udayabbayato paricchinnatāya viññāyamānattā. Tenāha “hutvā abhāvāvabodhato”ti. Uppajjitvā nirujjhanañhi hutvā abhāvo. Pubbantāparantaviveko atītānāgatabhāvasuññatā. Na hi saṅkhārā khaṇattayato pubbe, pacchā ca vijjanti, tasmā pubbantāparantavivekāvabodhatoti ādiantavantatāpaṭivedhatoti attho. Dukkhalakkhaṇampi pākaṭaṃ hoti udayabbayadassanenāti sambandho. Uppajjitvā bhijjantā saṅkhārā uppādato uddhaṃ jarābhaṅgāvatthantaruppattiyā nirantaraṃ vibādhīyanteva. Sā ca nesaṃ vibādhiyamānatā sammā udayabbayadassanena vibhūtā hotīti āha “dukkha…pe… bodhato”ti.

730. For one who sees arising from a condition, the conditioned things' lack of striving is discerned as their being helpful by mere existence—since when a condition and its nature exist, the effect occurs—and their dependence on conditions is discerned—since when it is absent, there is no effect. This clarifies the emptiness of self. Hence it is said: 'And for him, by way of conditions... up to the point of understanding.' The characteristic of impermanence becomes manifest by seeing the arising and passing away from moment to moment, because formations are discerned as being limited by their arising and passing away. Therefore, it is said: 'through the understanding of their non-existence after having been.' For non-existence after having been is ceasing after having arisen. Discernment of the former and latter ends is the emptiness of past and future states. For formations do not exist before or after the three moments. Therefore, 'understanding the discernment of the former and latter ends' means penetrating their having a beginning and an end. The characteristic of suffering also becomes manifest by seeing the arising and passing away—this is the connection. Formations, having arisen and breaking up, are constantly oppressed indeed from their arising onwards by the arising of the distinct states of aging and breaking up. And that state of being oppressed of theirs becomes fully evident through the correct seeing of arising and passing away. Hence it is said: 'Suffering... up to... understanding.'
