Sabhāvalakkhaṇampīti udayabbayadassanena na kevalaṃ aniccadukkhalakkhaṇameva, atha kho pathavīphassādīnaṃ kakkhaḷaphusanādisaññitaṃ sabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ lakkhaṇampi pākabhāvaviddhaṃ sabhāvāvacchinnaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti. Tenāha “udayabbayaparicchinnāvabodhato”ti. Sabhāvalakkhaṇeti sabhāvasaññite lakkhaṇe, taṃtaṃdhammānaṃ salakkhaṇe. Saṅkhatalakkhaṇassa tāvakālikattampīti uppādādisaṅkhatalakkhaṇassa uppādakkhaṇādiparittakālikatāpi khaṇantarānavaṭṭhānato [M 2.0426] tassa. Tenāha “udayakkhaṇe”tiādi. Udayavayamattaggahaṇañcettha udayabbayadassanavaseneva imassa ñāṇassa pavattanato, na ṭhitikkhaṇassa abhāvā.

Also the characteristic of specific nature: by seeing arising and passing away, not only are the characteristics of impermanence and suffering alone manifest, but also the characteristic reckoned as specific nature—designated as hardness, contact, etc., of the earth element, contact, etc.—becomes manifest, being delimited by the state of maturity and destruction. Hence it is said, 'through the understanding of what is delimited by arising and passing away.' 'The characteristic of specific nature' means in the characteristic designated as specific nature, in the individual characteristic of each respective phenomenon. Also the temporariness of the conditioned characteristic: the very brief duration of the conditioned characteristic, such as the moment of arising, also becomes manifest. This is because of its not persisting into another moment. Hence it is said, 'at the moment of arising,' and so on. And here, the grasping of mere arising and passing away is because this knowledge proceeds by way of seeing arising and passing away, not because of an absence of the moment of presence.

731. Na kevalañca niccanavā, atha kho parittakālaṭṭhāyino. Kathanti āha “sūriyuggamane”tiādi. Tattha udake daṇḍena katalekhā udake daṇḍarāji. Ussāvabinduādayo pañca kiccāpi uttaruttari atiparittaṭṭhāyibhāvadassanatthaṃ nidassitā, tathāpi te dandhanirodhā eva [V 2.0400] nidassitā, tatopi lahutaranirodhattā saṅkhārānaṃ. Tathā hi gamanassādānaṃ devaputtānaṃ heṭṭhupariyāyena paṭimukhaṃ dhāvantānaṃ sirasi pāde ca bandhakhuradhārā sannipātatopi sīghataro rūpadhammānaṃ nirodho vutto, pageva arūpadhammānaṃ. Na kevalaṃ niccanavā, nāpi parittakālaṭṭhāyinova, atha kho asārā. Kathanti āha “māyā”tiādi. Māyādayo hi maṇiādivasena dissamānā ataṃsabhāvatāya asārā. Tattha mantosadhabhāvitā indajālādikā māyā. Migataṇhikā marīci. Supinameva supinantaṃ. Maṇḍalākārena āvijjhiyamānaṃ alātameva alātacakkaṃ. Gandhabbadevaputtānaṃ kīḷanicchāvasena nagaraṃ viya ākāse upaṭṭhānamattaṃ gandhabbanagaraṃ.

731. Not only are they ever new, but they are also of brief duration. How so? It is said: 'At sunrise,' etc. Therein, a line made in water with a stick is a stick-line in water. The five examples, beginning with a dewdrop, are adduced to show a state of progressively more and more brief duration; yet they are shown as slow to cease, because the cessation of formations is even swifter than that. For the cessation of material phenomena is said to be swifter than the clashing of sharp razor-blades bound to the head and feet of devaputtas who delight in running as they rush towards each other, one from below and one from above—how much more so for immaterial phenomena. Not only are they ever new, nor are they merely of brief duration, but they are also essenceless. How so? It is said: 'Like a magical illusion,' etc. For magical illusions and so on, though appearing as gems and so on, are essenceless because their nature is not that of such things. Therein, māyā is a magical illusion, etc., produced by spells and herbs. A mirage is a mirage. A dream itself is a dream-state. A firebrand itself, being whirled in a circle, is a firebrand-circle. A mere appearance in the sky like a city, owing to the playful wish of the gandhabba devaputtas, is a gandhabbas' city.

Ettāvatāti yvāyaṃ “jātaṃ rūpaṃ paccuppanna”ntiādipāḷinayānusārena (paṭi. ma. 1.49), “yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppanna”ntiādipāḷinayānusārena (ma. ni. 1.347, 361; 2.113; 3.86, 89; paṭi. ma. 1.48) vā yāva udayabbayapaṭivedhā bhāvanāvidhi āraddho, ettāvatā. Kalāpasammasanādikopi hi sabbo bhāvanāvidhi udayabbayañāṇuppādanasseva, na parisaparisarīrakarabandhoti. Vayadhammamevāti bhijjanasabhāvameva. Vayaṃ upeti attano dhammatāya. Yañhi upakkamena vinassatīti vuccati, tampi attano dhammatāya eva vinassati ahetukattā vināsassa. Upakkamahetu pana visadisuppādo hoti. Iminā ākārenāti “yaṃ kiñci samudayadhammaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhamma”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 16; paṭi. ma. 2.30) hi vuttaṃ, tasmā vayaṃ anālambitvāpi “vayadhammameva uppajjatī”ti udayassa, “uppannañca idaṃ vayaṃ upetī”ti vayassa ca iminā yathāvuttena paccakkhakaraṇākārena. Adhunā uppannaṃ, na tāva balappattanti āha “taruṇavipassanāñāṇa”nti. Kalāpasammasanādivasena pavattaṃ [M 2.0427] sammasanaṃ na nippariyāyena vipassanāsamaññaṃ labhati, udayabbayānupassanādivasena pavattameva labhatīti āha “yassādhigamā āraddhavipassakoti saṅkhaṃ gacchatī”ti.

‘Up to this point’ means: by this much, that is, the method of meditation that has been undertaken—in accordance with the scriptural method, ‘Material form that has been born is present,’ etc., or in accordance with the scriptural method, ‘Whatever material form, whether past, future, or present,’ etc.—up to the penetration of arising and passing away. For the entire method of meditation, beginning with the comprehension of groups, is indeed only an accessory for the production of the knowledge of arising and passing away. ‘Only that which is of a nature to pass away’ means only that which has a nature to break up. It goes to passing away by its own nature. For what is said to be destroyed by an external agency also perishes only by its own nature, because destruction is without a cause. The external agency, however, is a cause for a dissimilar arising. ‘In this way’ means: for it is said, ‘Whatever is of a nature to arise, all that is of a nature to cease.’ Therefore, even without taking passing away as an object, by this aforesaid manner of direct experience, one understands regarding arising, ‘only that which is of a nature to pass away arises,’ and regarding passing away, ‘and this, having arisen, goes to passing away.’ He said ‘tender insight-knowledge’ because it has just arisen and has not yet gained strength. Comprehension that proceeds by way of the comprehension of groups, etc., does not obtain the designation ‘insight’ in a definitive sense; only that which proceeds by way of the contemplation of arising and passing away, etc., obtains it. Hence he said, ‘Through the attainment of which one is reckoned as one who has begun insight.’

Vipassanupakkilesakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Corruptions of Insight

732. Imāya udayabbayānupassanāsaṅkhātāya taruṇavipassanāya vasena, na āraddhavipassanānaṃ bhaṅgānupassanādisaṅkhātāya taruṇavipassanāya, nāpi nibbidānupassanādisaṅkhātāya [V 2.0401] balavavipassanāya vasenāti attho. Na hi tadā vipassanupakkilesā uppajjantīti. Āraddhavipassakassāti ca āraddhavipassakassevāti eva-kāro luttaniddiṭṭho. Tenāha “vipassanupakkilesā hī”tiādi. Diṭṭhigāhādivatthubhāvena vipassanaṃ upakkilesantīti vipassanupakkilesā. “Ariyasāvakassā”ti idaṃ ukkaṭṭhaniddesena vuttaṃ balavavipassanāpattassāpi anuppajjanato. Vippaṭipannakassāti sīlavipattiādivasena yathā tathā vippaṭipannakassa. Tassa pana paṭipattiyā garahitabbataṃ dassento “vippaṭipannakassā”ti āha. Ca-saddo uparipadadvayepi yojetabbo. Nikkhittakammaṭṭhānassāti vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā antarā vosānaṃ āpannassa. Kusītapuggalassāti sīlasampannasseva kosajjena bhāvanaṃ ananuyuñjantassa. Atha vā vippaṭipannakassāti vipassanābhāvanāsaṅkhātāya sammāpaṭipattiyā abhāvena vigarahitapaṭipattikassa. Vipassanāpaṭipattiyeva hi sasambhārā pubbabhāge sammāpaṭipatti, tadaññā vippaṭipatti, sā ca tattha nikkhittadhurassa hoti. Nikkhittadhuratā ca kosajjenāti vuttaṃ “nikkhittakammaṭṭhānassa kusītapuggalassā”ti. Yuttappayuttassāti yogena ñāṇena bhāvanamanuyuñjantassa. Sā pana yuttappayuttatā samathavasenāpi hotīti āha “āraddhavipassakassā”ti. Uppajjantiyeva na nuppajjanti aññathā maggāmaggañāṇasseva asambhavato.

732. The meaning is this: The corruptions of insight arise by means of this immature insight designated as the contemplation of arising and passing away; for those who have undertaken insight, they do not arise by means of the immature insight designated as the contemplation of dissolution, etc., nor by means of the powerful insight designated as the contemplation of disenchantment, etc. For at that time, the corruptions of insight do not arise. And "for one who has begun insight" means indeed for one who has begun insight—the particle "eva" has been elided in the citation. Hence it is said, "for the corruptions of insight, indeed…" and so on. They are "corruptions of insight" because they corrupt insight by serving as a basis for adhering to wrong views, etc. "For a noble disciple" is said as a supreme instance, since they do not arise even for one who has attained powerful insight. "For one who has gone astray" means for one who has gone astray in some way, such as through a lapse in virtue. To show that his practice is blameworthy, it is said, "for one who has gone astray." The word "ca" should be connected with the two subsequent phrases as well. "For one who has abandoned the meditation subject" means for one who, having begun insight, has given up in the middle. "For a lazy person" means for one who, though accomplished in virtue, does not apply himself to the development of meditation due to laziness. Alternatively, "for one who has gone astray" means for one whose practice is blameworthy due to the absence of right practice, which is the development of insight. For it is the practice of insight with its requisites in the preliminary stage that is right practice; any other is wrong practice, and this is the case for one who has abandoned the task. And abandoning the task is due to laziness; thus it is said: "for one who has abandoned the meditation subject, for a lazy person." "For one who is properly engaged" means for one who applies himself to the development of meditation with the appropriate knowledge. But since this proper engagement can also be by way of serenity, it is said, "for one who has begun insight." They certainly do arise; it is not that they do not arise, for otherwise the knowledge of path and not-path itself would be impossible.

Obhāsādīsu “ariyadhammo”ti pavattaṃ uddhaccaṃ vikkhepo dhammuddhaccaṃ, tena dhammuddhaccena vipassanāvīthito ukkamanena virūpaṃ gahitaṃ pavattitaṃ mānasaṃ dhammuddhaccaviggahitamānasaṃ. Obhāso dhammoti kāraṇūpacārenāha, īdisaṃ obhāsaṃ vissajjento mama ariyamaggoti attho. Obhāsaṃ āvajjati “nibbāna”nti vā “maggo”ti vā “phala”nti vā. Nibbānanti gaṇhanto [M 2.0428] tattha pavattadhamme maggaphalabhāvena gaṇhāti, ñāṇādike pana maggaphalabhāveneva gaṇhāti. Tato vikkhepo uddhaccanti tato obhāsahetu yo vikkhepo, taṃ uddhaccanti attho. “Uddhaccena viggahitamānaso”ti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “aniccato”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Regarding the light and other corruptions, the restlessness and distraction that arises with the thought 'this is a noble phenomenon' is restlessness concerning the Dhamma. By this restlessness concerning the Dhamma, the mind, deviating from the path of insight, is wrongly grasped and directed; thus it is called 'a mind seized by restlessness concerning the Dhamma.' The statement 'The light is the Dhamma' is a metaphorical expression based on the cause; the meaning is: 'The Dhamma that produces such a light is my noble path.' One attends to the light as 'Nibbāna,' or as 'the path,' or as 'the fruit.' Taking it as Nibbāna, one grasps the phenomena occurring then as the path and fruit; and one grasps knowledge and the other corruptions as the path and fruit. Then, the distraction that arises from it is restlessness—that is, the distraction caused by the light is restlessness. To elaborate on the meaning stated concisely as 'a mind seized by restlessness,' the passage beginning 'as impermanent' was stated.

Tattha anicca…pe… nappajānāti “maggaṃ pattosmī”ti saññāya aniccatādivasena manasikārasseva abhāvato. Ayañca attho –

Herein, he does not properly know things as impermanent… and so on, because of the very absence of attention by way of impermanence, etc., due to the perception, 'I have attained the path.' And this meaning is as follows:

“Yo hi koci, āvuso, bhikkhu vā bhikkhunī vā mama santike arahattappattiṃ [V 2.0402] byākaroti, sabbo so catūhi maggehi, etesaṃ vā aññatarena. Katamehi catūhi? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu samathapubbaṅgamaṃ vipassanaṃ bhāveti, tassa samathapubbaṅgamaṃ vipassanaṃ bhāvayato maggo sañjāyati, so taṃ maggaṃ āsevati bhāveti bahulīkaroti. Tassa taṃ maggaṃ āsevato…pe… karoto saṃyojanāni pahīyanti anusayā byantīhonti.

“Friends, whatever monk or nun declares in my presence the attainment of arahantship, they all do so by means of four paths, or by one of them. What four? Here, friends, a monk develops insight with serenity as its forerunner. As he develops insight with serenity as its forerunner, the path arises for him. He cultivates that path, develops it, and makes it manifold. As he cultivates that path… the fetters are abandoned, the underlying tendencies are brought to an end.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu vipassanāpubbaṅgamaṃ samathaṃ bhāveti…pe… samathavipassanaṃ yuganaddhaṃ bhāveti…pe….

“Furthermore, friends, a monk develops serenity with insight as its forerunner… he develops serenity and insight yoked together….

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno dhammuddhaccaviggahitaṃ mānasaṃ hoti, hoti so, āvuso, samayo yaṃ taṃ cittaṃ ajjhattameva santiṭṭhati sannisīdati ekodi hoti samādhiyati, tassa maggo sañjāyati…pe… anusayā byantīhontī”ti (a. ni. 4.170) –

“Furthermore, friends, a monk's mind is seized by restlessness concerning the Dhamma. There comes a time, friends, when that mind itself inwardly settles down, subsides, becomes unified, and is concentrated. For him the path arises… the underlying tendencies are brought to an end.”

Iminā suttapadeneva veditabbo. Ettha hi catutthamaggavissajjane yathāvuttamaggaphalanibbānadhammā dhammo. Tattha uddhaccaṃ “adhigatamaggādikohamasmī”ti amaggādīsu vikkhepo dhammuddhaccaṃ, tena upaddutaṃ viggahitamānasaṃ hoti. Nikanti obhāsādīsu apekkhā sukhumarūpā taṇhā, sā vipassanābhiratiākārena upaṭṭhahantī adhimānikena “dhammo”ti gayhatīti āha “nikanti ‘dhammo’ti nikantiṃ āvajjatī”ti.

This should be understood by this very sutta passage. Here, in the explanation of the fourth path, the aforementioned dhammas—path, fruition, and Nibbāna—are the Dhamma. Therein, restlessness concerning the Dhamma is the distraction towards what is not the path, etc., with the thought, 'I am one who has attained the path, etc.'; by this, the mind becomes afflicted and seized. Delight is a subtle craving, a longing for the light, etc. That craving, appearing in the guise of delight in insight, is grasped as 'the Dhamma' by one who is conceited. Therefore, it is said, 'one attends to delight as “the Dhamma”.'

733. Vipassanobhāsoti vipassanācittasamuṭṭhitaṃ, sasantatipatitaṃ utusamuṭṭhānañca bhāsuraṃ rūpaṃ. Tattha vipassanācittasamuṭṭhitaṃ yogino [M 2.0429] sarīraṭṭhameva pabhassaraṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati, itaraṃ sarīraṃ muñcitvā ñāṇānubhāvānurūpaṃ samantato pattharati, taṃ tasseva paññāyati, tena phuṭṭhokāse rūpagatampi passati, passanto ca cakkhuviññāṇena passati, udāhu manoviññāṇenāti vīmaṃsitabbanti vadanti. Dibbacakkhulābhino viya taṃ manoviññāṇaviññeyyamevāti vuttaṃ viya dissatīti. Vipassanāvīthi nāma paṭipāṭiyā pavattamānā vipassanāva. Ukkantā nāma hoti yoginā “maggappattomhī”ti adhimānena vissaṭṭhattā, tassa vā [V 2.0403] yogino vipassanā tato eva vīthi ukkantā nāma hoti. Mūlakammaṭṭhānanti vipassanamevāha.

733. The illumination of insight is a radiant material form arisen from the insight-mind, fallen upon one's own continuum, and also arisen from temperature. Therein, that which is arisen from the insight-mind remains, being radiant, only within the yogī’s body. The other, having left the body, spreads all around in accordance with the power of his knowledge. It appears only to him. In the space touched by it, he also sees the collection of material forms. And while seeing, whether he sees with eye-consciousness or with mind-consciousness—this, they say, should be investigated. It appears as if it has been said that, like for one who has obtained the divine eye, it is cognizable only by mind-consciousness. The 'path of insight' is simply insight itself, proceeding in sequence. It is called 'deviated' because it has been abandoned by the yogī through the conceit, 'I have attained the path,' or, for that yogī, the insight is called 'deviated from the path' because of that very conceit. He speaks of insight itself as 'the root meditation subject'.

Vemattatāyāti appavipulatāvasena visadisatāya. Assāti obhāsassa. Dvīhi kuṭṭehi paricchinnaṃ gehaṃ dvikuṭṭagehaṃ. Tassa kira abbhantarepi ekā bhitti hoti bahipi, ubhinnaṃ antare anupariyāyapathaṃ hoti, sāyanhe tattha santharitāni pañcavaṇṇāni kusumāni, visadañāṇassa obhāsena pharitaṭṭhāne rūpagatañca dibbacakkhuno viya paññāyanti. Tena vuttaṃ “bhante mayha”ntiādi.

'By diversity' means by dissimilarity, by way of being small and extensive. 'Of this' means of the light. A 'two-walled house' is a house enclosed by two walls. It is said that there is one wall on the inside and also on the outside, and between the two there is a circumambulatory path. In the evening, flowers of five colors are spread there. For one of clear knowledge, in the place pervaded by the light, the collection of material forms also appears as if to one with the divine eye. Therefore, it was said: 'Venerable sir, for me…' and so on.

Evaṃ obhāsassa vemattatāya vatthuṃ dassetvā cirakālavippalambane vatthuṃ dassetuṃ “ayaṃ panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ayaṃ pana vipassanupakkilesoti vakkhamānappakāraṃ sandhāyāha, na sabbaṃ. Soti so samathavipassanālābhī adhimāniko.

Having thus shown the story concerning the diversity of the light, in order to show the story concerning the long-term deception, the passage beginning 'But this…' was stated. There, 'But this corruption of insight' is said referring to the type about to be described, not to all of them. 'He' means: he who has obtained serenity and insight and is conceited.

Divāsaneti divāṭṭhāne nisīditabbaāsane. Paṭhamaṃ “pañhaṃ pucchissāmī”ti cintitattā vuttaṃ “pañhaṃ, bhante, pucchituṃ āgatomhī”ti.

'On the day-seat' means on a seat for sitting in the daytime dwelling place. First, because he thought, 'I will ask a question,' he said, 'Venerable sir, I have come to ask a question.'

Pacchā upāyena puthujjanabhāvaṃ viññāpetvā kammaṭṭhāne niyojessāmīti cintitattā vuttaṃ “avassayo bhavissāmiccevāhaṃ āgato”ti, tassa ca padhānattā sāvadhāraṇaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ dhammoti ayaṃ ariyamaggānugato paṭisambhidādhammoti therassa ajjhāsayavasena vadati. Samādhinti abhiññāsamādhiṃ. Añcitakaṇṇoti niccalaṭṭhapitakaṇṇapuṭo. Palāyituṃ āraddho bhayena. Tenāha “thero kira dosacarito”ti. Dosacaritassa hi sūrassāpi sahasā bhayaṃ uppajjati. Tenassa khīṇāsavatthero ajjhāsayaṃ ñatvā “iminā upāyena puthujjanabhāvaṃ jānāpessāmī”ti [M 2.0430] hatthinimmāpanādimakāsi. Dosacaritattā hi thero khippaṃ paṭivijjhi. Khippavirāgī hi dosacarito.

Later, because he thought, 'By some means I will make him understand his status as a worldling and then engage him in a meditation subject,' he said, 'I have come to be a refuge,' and because of its importance, he spoke with emphasis. 'This Dhamma'—he speaks according to the elder’s disposition, meaning, 'this Dhamma of the analytical knowledges that follows the noble path.' 'Concentration' means the concentration of direct knowledge. 'With ears pricked up' means with ear-flaps held motionless and fixed. He began to flee out of fear. Hence it is said, 'The elder, it seems, was of an aversive character.' For fear arises suddenly even for a hero who is of an aversive character. Therefore, the elder whose taints were destroyed, knowing his disposition, thought, 'By this means I will make him know his status as a worldling,' and he created a phantom elephant, etc. Because he was of an aversive character, the elder quickly penetrated the truth. For one of an aversive character is quick to become dispassionate.

734. Tassāti udayabbayañāṇaṃ matthakaṃ pāpentassa yogino. “Evampi rūpaṃ udeti, evampi rūpaṃ vetī”tiādinā udayabbayānupassanamevettha tulanaṃ, tīraṇañca veditabbaṃ. Yathā devānamindena khittaṃ vajiraṃ amoghaṃ, appaṭihatañca hoti, evamidampi ñāṇaṃ nipuṇaṃ udayabbayadassaneti [V 2.0404] vuttaṃ “vissaṭṭhaindavajiramivā”tiādi. Tattha tikhiṇanti akuṇṭhaṃ. Sūranti tejavantaṃ. Ativisadanti nisitabhāvena ativiya paṭutaraṃ ñāṇaṃ uppajjati. Tathā hinena yogī “maggappattosmī”ti maññati.

734. 'Of him' refers to the yogi who is bringing the knowledge of arising and passing away to its culmination. Here, 'weighing' and 'judging' should be understood as the very contemplation of arising and passing away, beginning with 'Thus does form arise, thus does form pass away.' Just as the thunderbolt released by the king of the devas is unfailing and unimpeded, so too this knowledge is skilled in seeing arising and passing away; hence the phrase 'like the released thunderbolt of Indra,' and so on was stated. There, 'sharp' means unblunted. 'Powerful' means potent. 'Extremely clear' means that a knowledge arises that is exceedingly acute on account of its sharpness. Thus, by this knowledge, the yogi thinks, 'I have attained the path.'

Vipassanāpītīti vipassanācittasampayuttā pīti. Khuddakādayo pītiyo heṭṭhā vaṇṇitā eva. Yasmā udayabbayānupassanāya vīthipaṭipannāya anukkamena pañca pītiyo uppajjanti, tasmā vuttaṃ “ayaṃ pañca…pe… uppajjatī”ti. Matthakappattena pana udayabbayañāṇena saddhiṃ pharaṇāpītiyeva hoti. Upacārappanākkhaṇato aññadāpi hi pharaṇāpīti hotiyeva. Tenāha “sakalasarīraṃ pūrayamānā uppajjatī”ti.

`Vipassanāpīti` is the joy associated with the consciousness of insight. The minor and other types of joy have already been described below. Because, when one proceeds systematically with the contemplation of arising and passing away, five types of joy arise in sequence, therefore it is said, 'These five... arise.' But with the knowledge of arising and passing away that has reached its culmination, only pervasive joy arises. Indeed, pervasive joy also arises at other times than at the moment of access and absorption. Hence it is said, 'It arises filling the entire body.'

Passaddhiādīni cha yugaḷakāni aññamaññāviyoginīti passaddhiyā uppannāya itarāpi uppannā eva hontīti kiccadassanamukhena tā sabbāpi dassento “kāyacittānaṃ neva daratho, na gārava”ntiādimāha. Tattha kāyaggahaṇena rūpakāyassapi gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ, na vedanādikkhandhattayasseva. Kāyappassaddhiādayo hi rūpakāyassāpi darathādinimmaddikāti. Kāyacittāni passaddhāni…pe… ujukāniyeva honti tesaṃ apassaddhādibhāvassa hetubhūtānaṃ uddhaccādithinamiddhādidiṭṭhimānādisesanīvaraṇādiassaddhiyādimāyāsātheyyādisaṃkilesadhammānaṃ vidhamanavasena tadā vipassanācittuppādassa pavattanato. Tasmiṃ samayeti tasmiṃ udayabbayañāṇuppattisamaye. Manussānaṃ ayanti mānusī, manussayoggā kāmasukharati, tādisehi manussavisesehi anubhavitabbatānativattanato dibbā ratipi saṅgahitā, mānusīsadisatāya kāmasukhabhāvena dibbā ratipi vā, tassā atikkantatāya na mānusīti amānusī.

The six pairs, beginning with tranquility, are inseparable from one another—meaning when tranquility arises, the others also arise. Thus, showing all of them through the perspective of function, it is said, 'There is no distress or heaviness in body and mind,' and so on. Here, by the term 'body,' the physical body should also be understood, not just the three aggregates of feeling and so on. For tranquility of body and the like also eliminate distress and so on of the physical body. Body and mind become tranquil... and straightened because at that time the arising of insight-consciousness occurs by way of destroying the defiling states—such as restlessness, sloth and torpor, wrong view, conceit, the remaining hindrances, lack of faith, deceit, craftiness, and so on—which are the cause of their state of non-tranquility. 'At that time' means at the moment of the attainment of the knowledge of arising and passing away. `Mānusī` (human) means 'of humans,' that is, the delight of sensual pleasure suitable for humans. Because it does not transcend what is to be experienced by those exceptional humans, divine delight is also included. Or, due to its similarity to human delight in being a sensual pleasure, divine delight is also included. Because it transcends that, it is not human, thus it is `amānusī` (non-human).

Suññāgāranti [M 2.0431] yaṃ kiñci vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ, vipassanaṃ eva vā. Sāpi hi niccabhāvādisuññatāya, yogino sukhasannissayatāya ca “suññāgāra”nti vattabbataṃ labhati. Cittassa anupassanakarānaṃ kilesānaṃ vigamena santacittassa. Saṃsāre bhayassa ikkhanena bhikkhuno. Sammā ñāyena rūpārūpadhammānaṃ udayabbayānupassanādivasena vipassato. Sammasato anāraddhavipassanānaṃ manussānaṃ avisayatāya amānusī. Vipassanāpītisukhasaññitā rati hotīti ayamettha gāthāya saṅkhepattho. Dutiyagāthā pana udayabbayañāṇameva sandhāya vuttā. Tattha yato yatoti rūpato vā arūpato vā.

An 'empty dwelling' refers to any secluded lodging, or to insight meditation itself. For it also obtains the designation 'empty dwelling' because it is empty of permanence and so on, and because it is a resort of happiness for the yogi. For a bhikkhu—whose mind is peaceful through the removal of defilements that cause non-pacification of the mind, and who sees the danger in the cycle of existence—who sees with insight and comprehends material and immaterial phenomena by way of the right method through the contemplation of their arising and passing away and so on, there arises a non-human delight, as it is beyond the scope of humans who have not undertaken insight. This delight is known as the joy and happiness of insight. This is the brief meaning of the first verse here. The second verse, however, is spoken with reference to the knowledge of arising and passing away itself. Therein, 'from wherever' means from the material or from the immaterial.

Vipassanāsukhanti [V 2.0405] vipassanācittasampayuttaṃ cetasikasukhaṃ. Yasmā taṃsamuṭṭhitehi atipaṇītarūpehi sabbo kāyo pariphuṭo, paribrūhito ca hoti. Tasmā vuttaṃ “sakalasarīraṃ abhisandayamāna”nti.

The happiness of insight is the mental happiness associated with insight-consciousness. Because the whole body is permeated and suffused by the extremely refined matter arisen from that happiness, it is therefore said, 'pervading the whole body.'

Adhimokkhoti saddhā, na yevāpanakādhimokkhoti adhippāyo. Sā cettha na kammaphalaṃ, ratanattayaṃ vā saddahanavasena pavattā, atha kho kilesakālussiyāpagamena sampayuttānaṃ ativiya pasannabhāvahetubhūtā. Tenāha “vipassanāsampayuttā…pe… saddhā uppajjatī”ti.

'Resolution' is faith; the meaning is that it is not a resolution based on deduction. Herein, it does not proceed by way of believing in the fruit of kamma or the Triple Gem, but rather, through the removal of the stain of the defilements, it becomes the cause for the exceedingly clear state of its associated phenomena. Therefore, he said: 'Faith associated with insight... arises.'

Purimuppannabhāvanābalasaṃsiddhaṃ samappavattaṃ vīriyaṃ sampayuttadhammānaṃ saṃkilesapakkhato kosajjato paggaṇhanato paggaho. Tenāha “paggahoti vīriya”ntiādi.

Energy, accomplished by the power of previously arisen development and proceeding evenly, is called 'exertion' (paggaha) because it uplifts its associated states from the side of defilement, that is, from laziness. Therefore, he said, 'Exertion is energy,' and so on.

Supaṭṭhitāti sabhāvasallakkhaṇena ārammaṇe suṭṭhu upaṭṭhitā. Supatiṭṭhitāti paṭipakkhavigamena tena acalanīyatāya suṭṭhu patiṭṭhitā. Tato eva nikhātā viya acalā. Acalabhāveneva pabbatarājasadisāti tīhipi padehi supatiṭṭhitameva dasseti. Soti yogāvacaro. Yaṃ yaṃ ṭhānanti yaṃ yaṃ attano upatiṭṭhānaṭṭhānaṃ rūpaṃ vā arūpaṃ vā. Okkhanditvāti anupavisitvā. Pakkhinditvāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Dibbacakkhuno paribhaṇḍabhūtassa yathākammūpagañāṇassa upaṭṭhahante paralokasaññite satte sandhāyāha “dibbacakkhuno paraloko viyā”ti na dibbacakkhuno paralokavisayattā. Vaṇṇāyatanavisayañhi tanti. Assa sati upaṭṭhāti khāyati, upatiṭṭhatīti vā attho. Yadaggena hi sati ārammaṇaṃ okkhanditvā [M 2.0432] upatiṭṭhati, tadaggena ārammaṇampissa okkhanditvā upatiṭṭhatīti vuccati.

"Well-present" means: it is well present on the object by clearly marking its own-nature. "Well-founded" means: it is well-founded because of the removal of opposing factors, due to its unshakable nature by them. For that very reason, it is immovable, like a post dug in. Because of its very immovable nature, it is like a king of mountains. Thus, with these three terms, it shows that it is well-founded. "He" is the yogi. "Whatever position" means whatever basis for his mindfulness, whether it is form or a formless state. `Okkhanditvā` means having penetrated (`anupavisitvā`); `Pakkhinditvā` is a synonym for it. With reference to beings known as 'in the next world' who appear to the knowledge of rebirth according to kamma—which is an accessory of the divine eye—he said, "like the next world for the divine eye." This is not because the next world is the object of the divine eye, for indeed, its object is the sense base of forms. It is present, it appears, to his mindfulness; or, it is established. This is the meaning. For, in whatever way mindfulness, having entered the object, is present, in that same way, it is said, the object also, having entered, is present to that mindfulness.

Vicinitavisayattā saṅkhārānaṃ vicinane majjhattabhāvena ṭhitā vipassanupekkhā. Sā pana atthato tathāpavattā tatramajjhattupekkhāva. Manodvārāvajjanacittasampayuttā cetanā āvajjane ajjhupekkhanavasena pavattiyā “āvajjanupekkhā”ti vuttā. Udayabbayānaṃ suṭṭhutaraṃ upaṭṭhānato tadanupassanāyaṃ majjhattabhūtā idha vipassanupekkhā nāma. Te pana udayabbayā sabbasaṅkhārānanti āha “sabbasaṅkhāresu majjhattabhūtā”ti. Āvajjanāya indavajiratattanārācasadisatā, sūratikkhabhāvo ca sabbaññutaññāṇapurecarā viya tadanucarañāṇassa tathābhāvena daṭṭhabbā.

Because its object has been investigated, the equanimity that stands with neutrality in the investigation of formations is insight-equanimity. But that, in essence, having occurred in such a way, is simply equanimity-as-neutrality-in-that-context. The volition associated with the mind-door-adverting consciousness is called "adverting-equanimity" because it proceeds by way of looking on with equanimity in adverting. Because of the very clear appearance of arising and passing away, that which has become neutral in the contemplation of them is here called insight-equanimity. And since that arising and passing away belongs to all formations, he said, "neutral toward all formations." The similarity of the adverting to Indra's thunderbolt and a red-hot arrow, and its brave and sharp nature, should be seen as being like the forerunner of the knowledge of omniscience, because the subsequent knowledge is of such a nature.

Vipassanānikantīti [V 2.0406] vipassanāya nikāmanā apekkhā. Obhāsādayo vipassanāya vijambhanabhūtā tassā alaṅkāro viya hontīti āha “obhāsādipaṭimaṇḍitāyā”ti. Ālayanti apekkhaṃ. Sukhumā, santākārāti sukhumākārā, santākārā ca, sā cassā sukhumasantākāratā bhāvanāya sātisayappavattiyā, yato kilesabhāvopissā duviññeyyo hoti. Tenāha “yā nikanti kilesoti…pe… hotī”ti.

Delight in insight means desire and longing for insight. Illumination and other factors, being the flourishing of insight, are like its ornaments; hence, he said, 'adorned with illumination and so on.' Clinging means longing. Subtle and peaceful in appearance means having a subtle and peaceful nature, and this subtle and peaceful nature of it comes about by the exceeding progress of the meditation practice, whereby even its nature as a defilement becomes difficult to discern. Therefore, he said, 'The delight which is a defilement... and so on... becomes.'

Etesupīti yathādassitesu ñāṇādīsupi. “Aññatarasmiṃ uppanne”ti idaṃ uppanne aññatarasmiṃ “maggappattomhī”tiādiggahaṇadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na aññataraññatarasseva uppajjanato. Na vāpi hi upakkilesā ekakkhaṇepi uppajjanti, paccavekkhaṇā pana visuṃ visuṃ hoti. “Na vata me ito pubbe evarūpā nikanti uppannapubbā”ti idaṃ dhammasabhāvadassanavasena vuttaṃ, na pana tadā yogino tathācittappavattivasena. Na hi so tadā taṃ “nikantī”ti jānāti, tathā sati tabbisayassa “maggappattomhī”tiādiggahaṇassa asambhavo eva. Tasmā evamassa siyā “na vata me evarūpā bhāvanābhirati uppannapubbā, addhā maggappattomhī”ti.

Even in these—that is, in the knowledges and so on as previously described—'when one arises' is said to illustrate the grasping, such as 'I have attained the path,' when any one of them has arisen; it is not said because only one or another arises. For indeed, the nine corruptions (other than delight) can arise even in a single moment or simultaneously, but the reviewing of each occurs separately. 'Indeed, such a delight has never arisen in me before'—this is said from the perspective of seeing the nature of phenomena, not from the yogi's mental state at that time. For at that time, he does not know it as 'delight,' and if that were so, the grasping which takes that as its object, such as 'I have attained the path,' would be impossible. Therefore, it might occur to him thus: 'Indeed, such delight in meditation practice has never arisen in me before; truly, I have attained the path.'

735. Upakkilesavatthutāyāti nippariyāyato diṭṭhimānataṇhā idha upakkilesā tesaṃ vatthutāya uppattiṭṭhānatāya. Na sabhāvatoti āha “na akusalattā”ti. Yathā pana obhāsādayo, evaṃ nikantipi diṭṭhigāhādīnaṃ [M 2.0433] ṭhānaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ “upakkilesavatthu cā”ti. Vatthuvasenevāti gāhe anāmasitvā gāhānaṃ vatthutāvaseneva. Attavādī hi “ahaṃbuddhinibandhano”ti parikappito attā obhāsassa sāmibhūto “mamā”ti sāmivacanassa visayabhāvena gahitoti āha “mama obhāso uppannoti gaṇhato hi diṭṭhigāho”ti. Obhāsassa manāpaggahaṇamukhena tena attānaṃ seyyādito dahatīti vuttaṃ “manāpo vata obhāso uppannoti gaṇhato mānagāho”ti. Assādayatoti sampiyāyato. Tesanti diṭṭhigāhādisaññitānaṃ upakkilesānaṃ vasena. Obhāsādīsūti obhāsādinimittaṃ. Kampanaṃ yathāraddhavipassanāya aṭṭhatvā vikkhepāpatti, sā ca obhāsādīsu taṇhādigāhoti dassento “obhāsādīsu kampati…pe… samanupassatī”ti āha.

735. Because it is the basis for corruptions: directly, view, conceit, and craving are the corruptions here; because of being their basis, the ground for their arising. Not by its own nature: he says, 'not because of unwholesomeness.' Just as light and so on are a basis, so too delight is a ground for clinging to views and so on; thus it is said: 'and a basis for corruptions.' By way of the basis alone: without touching upon the graspings, only by virtue of being the basis for the graspings. For one who holds a doctrine of self, the self conceived as 'bound by the notion “I”' is imagined as the owner of the light and is thus taken as the object of the possessive word 'mine'; hence he says: 'for one who grasps, “my light has arisen,” there is indeed the grasping of views.' Through the principal means of grasping the light as pleasant, by that he places himself as superior, etc.; hence it is said: 'for one who grasps, “Oh, how delightful, the light has arisen,” there is the grasping of conceit.' Finds pleasure: is very fond of. Those: by means of the corruptions called the grasping of views and so on. In light and so on: on account of the sign of light and so on. Agitation is not standing in the insight as it has been undertaken, which is the falling into distraction; and showing that this is the grasping of craving and so on in regard to light and so on, he says: 'one is agitated regarding light and so on… observes.'

Obhāsanimittaṃ cittaṃ vikampatīti sambandho. Obhāse vā visayabhūte upakkilesehi cittaṃ [V 2.0407] vikampatīti yojanā. Tenāha “yehi cittaṃ pavedhatī”ti. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Upaṭṭhāneti satiyaṃ. Upekkhāya cāti vipassanupekkhāya ca.

On account of the sign of light, the mind trembles—this is the connection. Or, with light as the object, the mind trembles because of the corruptions—this is the construction. Therefore, he said, 'by which the mind trembles.' In the remaining phrases also, this is the same method. In attending: in mindfulness. And with equanimity: and with insight-equanimity.

Maggāmaggavavatthānakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Determination of Path and Not-Path

736. Kusalo panātiādīsu kammaṭṭhānakosallayogena kusalo. Paripakkañāṇatāya paṇḍito. Āgamabyattiyā byatto. Upakkilesatabbisodhanesu ādīnavānisaṃsāvabodhayogato buddhisampanno. Ayaṃ kho soti yo so ācariyena kammaṭṭhānadānakāle udayabbayañāṇuppattisamaye uppajjatīti vutto, ayaṃ kho so obhāso uppannoti upakkilesavatthubhāvavavatthānaṃ dassetvā idānissa vipassanāya visayabhāvūpanayanavidhiṃ dassento “so kho panā”tiādimāha. Tattha paṭhamanaye aniccalakkhaṇavibhāvanameva dassitaṃ, tasmiṃ siddhe itarampi lakkhaṇadvayaṃ siddhameva hoti. Dutiyanaye pana obhāsādike nissāya uppajjanakadiṭṭhigāhādīnaṃ ugghāṭanasamugghāṭanapariyādānavasena manasikāravidhiṃ dassetuṃ “sace obhāso attā bhaveyyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Arūpasattake “sace saṅkhārā attā bhaveyyu”ntiādi [M 2.0434] (visuddhi. 2.721) sabbasaṅkhārasaṅgaṇhanavasena sāmaññato vuttaṃ, idha obhāsādivasena saṅkhāre vibhajja vuttaṃ. Seso manasikāravidhi tattha vuttanayovāti āha “sabbaṃ arūpasattake vuttanayena vitthāretabba”nti.

736. In the passage beginning, “But one is skilled,” one is skilled through proficiency in the meditation subject. One is wise due to mature knowledge. One is proficient through expertise in the scriptures. One is endowed with intelligence through being endowed with the understanding of the danger and benefit regarding the corruptions and their purification. The phrase “This indeed is that” refers to what was said by the teacher to arise at the time of giving the meditation subject and at the time of the arising of the knowledge of arising and passing away, namely, “This indeed is that illumination which has arisen.” Having thus shown the determination of its nature as a basis for the corruptions, he now, in order to show the method of introducing it as an object for insight, states, “But this…” and so on. Therein, in the first method, only the elucidation of the characteristic of impermanence is shown. When that is accomplished, the other two characteristics are also accomplished indeed. In the second method, however, to show the method of attention by way of uprooting, completely uprooting, and exhausting the grasping of views and so on that arise in dependence on the illumination and other phenomena, it is said, “If the illumination were self…” and so on. In the section on the formless septad, it is said generally, “If formations were self…” and so on, by way of comprehending all formations. Here, it is stated by analyzing formations by way of illumination and so on. The rest of the method of attention is just as was stated there; thus he said, “Everything should be elaborated in the way stated in the section on the formless septad.”

Obhāsaṃ “netaṃ mamā”ti samanupassanto taṇhāgāhato cittaṃ visodheti, “nesohamasmī”ti samanupassanto mānagāhato, “na meso attā”ti samanupassanto diṭṭhigāhato. Tenāha “obhāsaṃ netaṃ mamā”tiādi. Esa nayo ñāṇādīsupi.

Contemplating the illumination thus, 'This is not mine,' one purifies the mind from the grasp of craving. Contemplating thus, 'This am I not,' one purifies it from the grasp of conceit. Contemplating thus, 'This is not my self,' one purifies it from the grasp of views. Therefore, he said, 'The illumination is not mine,' and so on. This is the method for knowledge and so on as well.

Imāni dasa ṭhānānīti imāni yathāvuttāni obhāsādīni dasa upakkilesakāraṇāni. Paññā yassa pariccitāti yassa yogino paññā obhāsādīsu aniccatādiggahaṇavasena paricitavatī pariggahetvā upaparikkhitvā ṭhitā. Dhammuddhaccassa samaggabhāvajānanena dhammuddhaccakusalo hoti.

“These ten items” means these ten causes of the corruptions as stated, namely illumination and so on. “His wisdom is familiar” means: the wisdom of whichever yogī has become familiar by way of grasping impermanence and so on in regard to illumination and the other corruptions, having comprehended, examined, and established it. By knowing the nature of restlessness about the Dhamma as not being the path, one becomes skilled in regard to restlessness about the Dhamma.

Vīthipaṭipannanti udayabbayānupassanāvasena vipassanāvīthipaṭipannaṃ.

“Entered upon the course” means one who has entered upon the course of insight by way of the contemplation of arising and passing away.

Diṭṭhivisuddhiyanti [V 2.0408] diṭṭhivisuddhiyaṃ adhigatāyaṃ, diṭṭhivisuddhiñāṇena vā diṭṭhiyā visodhane dukkhasaccassa vavatthānaṃ kataṃ hoti dukkhasaccapariyāpannassa nāmarūpassa vavatthānato. Nāmarūpassa paccayā nāmarūpasamudayapakkhiyāti āha “kaṅkhā…pe… samudayasaccassa vavatthānaṃ kata”nti. Abhidhammanayena hi sabbakilesā, kammañca samudayasaccaṃ. Imissanti imāyaṃ. Sammāti aviparītaṃ. Maggassāti ariyamaggassa upāyabhūtamaggassa.

“In the purification of view” means: when the purification of view has been attained, or by the knowledge of the purification of view in purifying the view, the determination of the truth of suffering is accomplished, because of the determination of name-and-form, which is included in the truth of suffering. The conditions of name-and-form belong to the side of the origin of name-and-form; thus he says: “By overcoming doubt… the determination of the truth of origin is accomplished.” For according to the Abhidhamma method, all defilements and kamma are the truth of origin. “In this” means in this (Purification by Knowledge and Vision of Path and Not-Path). “Rightly” means correctly. “Of the path” means of the noble path, of the insight-path that is the means.

Maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhiniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of Path and Not-Path is finished.

Iti vīsatimaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus ends the commentary on the twentieth chapter.

21. Paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddesavaṇṇanā

21. Commentary on the Exposition of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way of Practice

Upakkilesavimuttaudayabbayañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away Freed from Corruptions

737. Vipassanācārassa [M 2.0435][V 2.0409] matthakappattiyā saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ sikhāppattā vipassanā. Sikhāppatti panassa udayabbayañāṇādīnaṃ attaṭṭhamānaṃvasena jātāti āha “aṭṭhannaṃ pana ñāṇānaṃ vasena sikhāppattā vipassanā”ti. Oḷārikoḷārikassa saccapaṭicchādakamohatamassa vigamanena saccappaṭivedhānukūlattā “saccānulomikañāṇa”nti anulomañāṇamāha. Tāni pana ñāṇāni sarūpato dassetuṃ “aṭṭhannanti cā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha udayabbayadassanena saṅkhārānaṃ aniccalakkhaṇaṃ, tadanusārena itaralakkhaṇāni ca vibhāventīyeva udayabbayānupassanā pavattatīti katvā “vīthipaṭipannavipassanāsaṅkhātaṃ udayabbayānupassanāñāṇa”nti vuttanti keci. Tayidaṃ tassa sabbaso tīraṇapariññābhāvameva maññamānehi vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi hi udayabbayañāṇaṃ tīraṇapariññantogadhameva, udayabbayādīnaṃ pana jānanaṭṭhena, paccakkhato dassanaṭṭhena ca ñāṇadassanāni, udayabbayañāṇādīni. Tāniyeva paṭipakkhato visuddhattā ñāṇadassanavisuddhi, sā eva ariyamaggo paṭipajjati etāyāti paṭipadā cāti paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhīti vuttaṃ. Taṃ pana uppannamattaṃ appaguṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Paguṇañhi niccasaññādipahānasiddhiyā pahānapariññāya adhiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ. Yato tadavigamena aṭṭhārasasu mahāvipassanāsu ekaccā adhigatā eva honti. Na hi udayabbayānaṃ paccakkhato paṭivedhena vinā sāmaññākārānaṃ tīraṇamattena sātisayaṃ paṭipakkhapahānaṃ sambhavati. Asati ca paṭipakkhapahāne kuto ñāṇādīnaṃ vajiramiva avihatavegatā, tikhiṇavisadāditā vā. Tasmā paguṇabhāvappattaṃ udayabbayañāṇaṃ pahānapariññāpakkhiyameva daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sabbasaṅkhārānaṃ bhaṅgasseva anupassanā bhaṅgānupassanā, tadeva ñāṇaṃ bhaṅgānupassanāñāṇaṃ. Yathābhūtadassāvī bhāyati etasmāti bhayaṃ, tebhūmakadhammā, tesu bhayato upaṭṭhitesu bhāyitabbākāragāhiñāṇaṃ bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ. Muñcituṃ icchatīti muñcitukamyaṃ, cittaṃ, puggalo vā, tassa bhāvo muñcitukamyatā[V 2.0410], tadeva ñāṇaṃ muñcitukamyatāñāṇaṃ. Puna [M 2.0436] paṭisaṅkhānākārena pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ paṭisaṅkhānupassanāñāṇaṃ. Nirapekkhatāya saṅkhārānaṃ upekkhanavasena pavattañāṇaṃ saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ. Tasmāti yasmā upakkilesavimuttaṃ udayabbayañāṇādinavavidhañāṇaṃ paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi, tasmā.

737. Because of reaching the summit of the practice of insight, the knowledge of equanimity towards formations is called insight that has reached the summit. Furthermore, its reaching of the summit arises by way of the knowledges beginning with the knowledge of arising and passing away, with itself as the eighth. Therefore, he said: 'Furthermore, insight reaches the summit by way of the eight knowledges.' Because of its conformity to the penetration of the truths through the removal of the very gross darkness of delusion that conceals the truths, he calls conformity knowledge 'knowledge that conforms to the truths.' Furthermore, to show those knowledges in their own nature, the passage beginning 'And of the eight...' was begun. Therein, some say that, thinking thus: 'The contemplation of arising and passing away proceeds while making manifest the characteristic of impermanence of formations by seeing their arising and passing away, and, in accordance with that, the other characteristics as well,' it is called 'the knowledge of the contemplation of arising and passing away, designated as insight that has entered upon the course.' This, however, was said by those who consider it to be entirely the state of full understanding by discerning. Although indeed the knowledge of arising and passing away is included in the full understanding by discerning, nevertheless, the knowledges of arising and passing away and so on are 'knowledges and visions' in the sense of knowing and in the sense of seeing directly. Those very same knowledges, because of being purified from their opposites, are the purification of knowledge and vision. And that very purification is also the 'way of practice' (paṭipadā) because the noble path is entered upon by means of it; therefore, it is called the purification by knowledge and vision of the way of practice. But that was said with reference to it when it has just arisen and is not yet proficient. For the proficient knowledge, through the accomplishment of abandoning the perception of permanence, etc., is the foundation for the full understanding of abandoning. Wherefore, by attaining it, some of the eighteen great insights are indeed attained. Indeed, without the direct penetration of arising and passing away, the superior abandoning of the opposites is not possible by the mere discerning of general characteristics. And when there is no abandoning of the opposites, whence could there be for the knowledges and so on an unimpeded force like a diamond, or sharpness, clarity, and so on? Therefore, the knowledge of arising and passing away that has reached a state of proficiency should be understood as belonging to the side of the full understanding of abandoning. The contemplation of only the dissolution of all formations is the contemplation of dissolution; that very contemplation is the knowledge, hence the knowledge of the contemplation of dissolution. 'Fear' (bhaya) is that from which one who sees things as they truly are fears, that is, the phenomena of the three planes. When they appear as fearful, the knowledge that grasps the aspect of what is to be feared is the knowledge of the appearance of the fearful. Because one wishes (icchati) to be liberated (muñcituṃ), one is called 'wishing to be liberated' (muñcitukamyaṃ), which refers to the mind or the person. The state (bhāvo) of that is the 'wish for deliverance' (muñcitukamyatā). That very state is the knowledge; hence, it is the knowledge of the wish for deliverance. Again, knowledge that proceeds in the mode of reflection is the knowledge of the contemplation of reflection. Knowledge that proceeds by way of equanimity towards formations due to non-concern is the knowledge of equanimity towards formations. As for 'therefore': because the ninefold knowledge beginning with the knowledge of arising and passing away, when freed from the corruptions, is the purification by knowledge and vision of the way of practice, therefore...

738. “Upakkilesavimutta”nti visesanena vibhāvitamatthaṃ anavabujjhanto codako “puna udayabbayañāṇe yogo kimatthiyo”ti pucchati. Tattha kimatthiyoti kiṃ payojano niratthako, pageva nibbattitattā pakkassa pacanaṃ viyāti adhippāyo. Atha vā lakkhaṇasallakkhaṇādihetupaṭipāṭiggahaṇavasena tamatthaṃ ñāpetukāmo ācariyova kathetukamyatāvasena “kimatthiyo”ti pucchati. Lakkhaṇasallakkhaṇatthoti aniccādilakkhaṇānaṃ sammadeva upadhāraṇattho. Tattha kāraṇaṃ dassento “udayabbayañāṇaṃ hī”tiādimāha. Nanu ca udayabbayañāṇaṃ nāma saṅkhārānaṃ udayabbayameva passati, na aniccādilakkhaṇattayaṃ, tena kathaṃ aniccatādilakkhaṇattayasallakkhaṇaṃ hotīti? Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ “udayabbayañāṇaṃ lakkhaṇattayavisayaṃ hotī”ti. Udayabbaye pana paṭividdhe aniccalakkhaṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Tato “yadaniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.15; 45, 77; 4.1, 4; paṭi. ma. 2.10) itaralakkhaṇampi. Atha vā udayabbayaggahaṇena hutvā abhāvākāro, abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanākāro, avasavattanākāro ca vibhūtataro hotīti kāraṇabhāvena udayabbayañāṇe yogassa lakkhaṇattayasallakkhaṇatthatā veditabbā, na sammukheneva. Heṭṭhāti maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhito heṭṭhā. Tañhi obhāsādiuppattihetutāya tikkhaṃ visadaṃ hutvā pavattampi diṭṭhiādīhi upakkiliṭṭhattā kuṇṭhaṃ avisadameva jātaṃ. Tenāha “dasahi…pe… nāsakkhī”ti.

738. The questioner, not understanding the meaning clarified by the qualification “freed from corruptions,” asks: “Why is there application again to the knowledge of arising and passing away?” Here, “why?” means: what is the purpose? Is it not useless, like cooking what has already been cooked, since it has already been produced beforehand? This is the intention. Or else, the teacher himself, wishing to make that meaning known by way of taking up the sequence of causes, such as the thorough marking of characteristics, asks “Why?” out of a desire to speak. As for the phrase, “For the purpose of thoroughly marking the characteristics,” this means for the purpose of rightly ascertaining the characteristics of impermanence, and so on. Stating the reason for this, he says: “For the knowledge of arising and passing away….” But surely, does not the knowledge of arising and passing away, so-called, see only the arising and passing away of formations, and not the three characteristics of impermanence, etc.? How then, through that knowledge, is there the thorough marking of the three characteristics of impermanence and so on? This, however, should not be seen thus: “The knowledge of arising and passing away has the three characteristics as its object.” Rather, when arising and passing away are penetrated, the characteristic of impermanence becomes manifest and presents itself. Thereafter, the other characteristics also present themselves thus: “What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self.” Or else, by grasping arising and passing away, the aspect of non-existence after having been, the aspect of constant oppression, and the aspect of being uncontrollable become more manifest. Thus, the purpose of application to the knowledge of arising and passing away should be understood as being for the thorough marking of the three characteristics by way of being a cause, not directly. “Below” means below the purification by knowledge and vision of path and not-path. For that knowledge, although it proceeded sharply and clearly because it was the cause for the arising of illumination, etc., became blunt and unclear because it was corrupted by views, etc. Hence he said: “by the ten… he was not able….”

739. Amanasikārāti hetumhi nissakkavacanaṃ. “Kissa amanasikārā”ti hi idaṃ “kena paṭicchannattā”ti pucchitassa paṭicchādakassa hetupucchā. Santatiyā hissa paṭicchannattā aniccalakkhaṇaṃ na upaṭṭhāti, sā ca santati udayabbayāmanasikārena paṭicchādikā jātā. Iriyāpathehi paṭicchannattā dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ na upaṭṭhāti, te ca iriyāpathā abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanāmanasikārena paṭicchādakā jātā. Ghanena paṭicchannattā anattalakkhaṇaṃ [M 2.0437] na upaṭṭhāti, te ca ghanā nānādhātuvinibbhogāmanasikārena paṭicchādakā jātāti. Udayabbayaṃ passato [V 2.0411] na udayāvatthā vayāvatthaṃ pāpuṇāti, vayāvatthā vā udayāvatthaṃ. Aññova udayakkhaṇo, aññova vayakkhaṇoti ekopi dhammo khaṇavasena bhedato upaṭṭhāti, pageva atītādikoti āha “udayabbayaṃ pana…pe… upaṭṭhātī”ti. Tattha santatiyā vikopitāyāti pubbāpariyena pavattamānānaṃ dhammānaṃ aññoññabhāvasallakkhaṇena santatiyā ugghāṭitāya. Na hi sammadeva udayabbayaṃ sallakkhentassa dhammā sambandhabhāvena upaṭṭhahanti, atha kho ayosalākā viya asambandhabhāvenāti suṭṭhutaraṃ aniccalakkhaṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti.

739. The word 'amanasikārā' is an ablative expression in the sense of a cause. For the question, 'By non-attention to what?' is an inquiry into the cause of the concealer, which was asked about with the words 'By what is it concealed?' Because it is concealed by continuity, the characteristic of impermanence does not become apparent; and that continuity has become a concealer through non-attention to arising and passing away. Because it is concealed by the postures, the characteristic of suffering does not become apparent; and those postures have become concealers through non-attention to the constant oppression. Because it is concealed by compactness, the characteristic of non-self does not become apparent; and those compact masses have become concealers through non-attention to the separate analysis of the various elements. For one who sees arising and passing away, the state of arising does not reach the state of passing away, nor does the state of passing away reach the state of arising. The moment of arising is one thing, the moment of passing away is another. Thus, even a single phenomenon appears as divided by way of moments; how much more so those of the past, etc. Therefore, it was said: 'But arising and passing away... becomes apparent.' Herein, 'when continuity is disrupted' means when the continuity of phenomena occurring in sequence is uncovered by discerning their nature of being other than one another. For to one who rightly discerns arising and passing away, phenomena do not appear as connected, but rather as unconnected, like iron rods. Thus, the characteristic of impermanence becomes exceedingly clear.

Abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanaṃ manasi katvāti yathāpariggahitaudayabbayavasena saṅkhārānaṃ nirantaraṃ paṭipīḷiyamānataṃ vibādhiyamānataṃ manasi karitvā. Iriyāpathe ugghāṭiteti iriyāpathe labbhamānadukkhapaṭicchādakabhāve ugghāṭite. Ekasmiñhi iriyāpathe uppannassa dukkhassa vinodakaṃ iriyāpathantaraṃ tassa paṭicchādakaṃ viya hoti, evaṃ sesāpīti iriyāpathānaṃ taṃtaṃdukkhapaṭicchādakabhāve yāthāvato ñāte tesaṃ dukkhapaṭicchādakabhāvo ugghāṭito nāma hoti saṅkhārānaṃ nirantaraṃ dukkhābhitunnatāya pākaṭabhāvato. Tenāha “dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ yāthāvasarasato upaṭṭhātī”ti. Nānādhātuyoti nānāvidhā pathavīādidhātuyo nānāvidhe sabhāvadhamme. Vinibbhujitvāti “aññā pathavīdhātu, aññā āpodhātū”tiādinā, “añño phasso, aññā vedanā”tiādinā ca visuṃ visuṃ katvā. Ghanavinibbhoge kateti samūhaghane, kiccārammaṇaghane ca pabhedite. Yā hesā aññamaññūpatthaddhesu samuditesu rūpārūpadhammesu ekattābhinivesavasena aparimadditasaṅkhārehi gayhamānā samūhaghanatā, tathā tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ kiccabhedassa satipi paṭiniyatabhāve ekato gayhamānā kiccaghanatā, tathā sārammaṇadhammānaṃ satipi ārammaṇakaraṇabhede ekato gayhamānā ārammaṇaghanatā ca, tā dhātūsu ñāṇena vinibbhujitvā dissamānā hatthena parimajjiyamāno pheṇapiṇḍo viya vilayaṃ gacchanti, “yathāpaccayaṃ pavattamānā suññā ete dhammā dhammamattā”ti anattalakkhaṇaṃ pākaṭataraṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “nānādhātuyo…pe… upaṭṭhātī”ti.

'Having attended to the constant oppression' means: having attended to the state of formations being constantly oppressed and afflicted, in accordance with their arising and passing away as previously comprehended. 'When the postures are uncovered' means: when their nature of concealing the suffering found in the postures is uncovered. For when suffering has arisen in one posture, another posture that dispels it is like a concealer of it; so too for the others. Thus, when the way each posture conceals its particular suffering is known as it really is, their nature of concealing suffering is said to be uncovered, because the state of formations being unceasingly pierced and oppressed by suffering has become manifest. Hence it was said: 'the characteristic of suffering... becomes apparent.' 'The various elements' means the various kinds of elements such as the earth element, etc., and the various kinds of phenomena with their intrinsic natures. 'Having analyzed' means having separated them individually by thinking: 'The earth element is one thing, the water element is another,' etc., and 'Contact is one thing, feeling is another,' etc. 'When the analysis of the compact is made' means when the compact as a group, and the compact as function and object, are broken down. For there is this compactness of a group, which is grasped as a unity by those who have not crushed the formations, through adherence to oneness in regard to the aggregated material and immaterial phenomena that support one another. Similarly, there is the compactness of function, which is grasped as one despite the definite distinction in the functions of those respective phenomena; and the compactness of object, which is grasped as one despite the distinction in the way phenomena with an object take their object. When these are seen as analyzed by knowledge into the elements, they dissolve away like a lump of foam being rubbed by the hand. Then the characteristic of non-self becomes clearer: 'These phenomena, which proceed according to conditions, are empty, mere phenomena.' Therefore it was said: 'the various elements... becomes apparent.'

740. Dhuvabhāvapaṭikkhepato [M 2.0438] na niccanti aniccaṃ, khandhapañcakaṃ. Yathāha “rūpaṃ kho, rādha, aniccaṃ, vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ anicca”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.172). Tattha kāraṇaṃ vadanto “uppādavayaññathattabhāvā”ti āha. Uppādo nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ, vayo vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ, aññathattaṃ jarā, tesaṃ sabbhāvatoti attho. Hutvā abhāvatoti [V 2.0412] uppajjitvā vinassanato. Ettha ca purimena jātijarāmaraṇasabbhāvato aniccanti dasseti, dutiyena pākabhāvaviddhaṃsābhāvato. Yassa bhāvena khandhapañcakaṃ “anicca”nti vuccati, taṃ aniccalakkhaṇanti dassetuṃ “uppādavayaññathatta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tena hi taṃ “anicca”nti lakkhīyati. Ākāravikāroti ākāravikati. Abhāvākāro hi vikatirūpena labbhati, virūpattā na uppādākāro. Ākāravikāroti vā ākāraviseso. Hutvā abhāvo hi pākabhāvato bhinno viddhaṃsābhāvattā tattha ca aniccalakkhaṇaṃ niruḷhaṃ. Aniccākāro hi dukkhānattākārehi viya uppādākārato ca visiṭṭho. Tathā hi saddassa viddhaṃsābhāvo saṅkhatabhāvenapi sādhīyati.

740. Because of the rejection of a permanent nature, the five aggregates are 'not permanent,' that is, impermanent (anicca). As it was said: 'Form, O Rādha, is impermanent; feeling... perception... formations... consciousness is impermanent' (Saṃ. Ni. 3.172). There, stating the reason, it was said: 'Because of the existence of arising, passing away, and otherwiseness.' Arising has the characteristic of production; passing away, the characteristic of alteration; otherwiseness is aging. The meaning is 'because of the actual existence of these.' 'Because of non-existence after having been' means: because of perishing after having arisen. And here, the first shows impermanence because of the existence of birth, aging, and death; the second, because of prior non-existence and non-existence as destruction. To show that the nature by which the five aggregates are called 'impermanent' is the characteristic of impermanence, the words 'arising, passing away, and otherwiseness,' etc., were stated. For by that it is characterized as 'impermanent.' 'Alteration of mode' means a distortion of mode. For the mode of non-existence is obtained in the form of a distortion; because it is a disfigurement, it is not the mode of arising. Or 'alteration of mode' means a specific mode. For 'non-existence after having been' is different from prior non-existence because it is non-existence as destruction, and in that the characteristic of impermanence is established. The mode of impermanence is distinct from the modes of suffering and non-self, and also from the mode of arising. Thus the non-existence as destruction of sound is established also by its conditioned nature.

Saṅkhatabhāvo ca atthato uppādavantatā. Uppādo ca pākabhāvasādhitā dharamānāvatthā. Iminā nayena dukkhānattālakkhaṇāni veditabbāni. Apica yathā niccapaṭikkhepato aniccanti niccākārapaṭikkhepato yathāvutto abhāvākārasaṅkhāto aniccākāro aniccalakkhaṇaṃ, evaṃ sukhapaṭikkhepato dukkhanti sukhākārapaṭikkhepato abhiṇhapaṭipīḷanākārasaṅkhāto dukkhākāro dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ, tathā attapaṭikkhepato anattāti attākārapaṭikkhepato avasavattanākārasaṅkhāto anattākāro anattalakkhaṇanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Te yime tayopi ākārā asabhāvadhammattā khandhapariyāpannā na honti. Khandhehi vinā anupalabbhanīyato khandhavinimuttāpi na honti. Khandhe pana upādāya vohāravasena labbhamānā tadādīnavavibhāvanāya visesakāraṇabhūtā tajjāpaññattivisesāti veditabbā.

And the conditioned nature is, in meaning, the possession of arising. And arising is the state of presence established by prior non-existence. By this method, the characteristics of suffering and non-self are to be understood. Furthermore, it should be seen that just as 'impermanent' is so called from the rejection of the permanent, so the characteristic of impermanence is the mode of impermanence—reckoned as the mode of non-existence as described above—from the rejection of the mode of permanence. So too, just as 'suffering' is so called from the rejection of pleasure, so the characteristic of suffering is the mode of suffering—reckoned as the mode of constant oppression—from the rejection of the mode of pleasure. And so too, just as 'non-self' is so called from the rejection of self, so the characteristic of non-self is the mode of non-self—reckoned as the mode of non-control—from the rejection of the mode of self. These three modes, because they are not real phenomena, are not included in the aggregates. Since they are not apprehended without the aggregates, they are not liberated from the aggregates either. However, being obtained by way of convention in dependence on the aggregates, and being a special cause for the demonstration of their danger, they should be understood as specific concepts derived from them.

Tayidaṃ sabbampīti yathāvuttalakkhaṇattayañceva lakkhitabbañca khandhapañcakaṃ. “Udayabbayānupassanāñāṇena yāthāvasarasato sallakkhetī”ti idaṃ tadatthe tabbohāravasena vuttaṃ. Udayabbayañāṇatthañhi lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanā “udayabbayañāṇa”nti kathitā. Na hi udayabbayañāṇaṃ dukkhalakkhaṇādivisayaṃ[M 2.0439]. Tabbisayatte vā udayabbayañāṇameva na siyā, udayabbayañāṇaṃ pana tikkhaṃ, visadañca kātukāmena lakkhaṇattayatīraṇameva kātabbaṃ. Parikammasadisañhetaṃ tassa. Esa nayo sesañāṇesupīti.

'All this' means both the three aforesaid characteristics and the five aggregates that are to be characterized. The statement 'he discerns it according to opportunity with the knowledge of contemplation of arising and passing away' is said with reference to that by way of its designation. For it is insight that has the characteristics as its object which, being for the sake of the knowledge of arising and passing away, is called 'knowledge of arising and passing away.' The knowledge of arising and passing away does not have the characteristic of suffering, etc., as its object. Or if it did have them as its object, it would not be the knowledge of arising and passing away at all. However, by one who wishes to make the knowledge of arising and passing away sharp and clear, the investigation of the three characteristics must be done. For this is like preliminary work for it. This is the method for the remaining knowledges as well.

Upakkilesavimuttaudayabbayañāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away Free from Corruptions is finished.

Bhaṅgānupassanāñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Knowledge of Contemplation of Dissolution

741. Vahatīti [V 2.0413] pavattati. Ñāṇassa tikkhabhāvo bhāvanāya paguṇabhāvena. Paguṇā ca bhāvanā vikkhepābhāvato ārammaṇe appitā viya pavattatīti ñāṇassa tikkhabhāvena saṅkhārānaṃ lahuupaṭṭhānatā dassitā. Saṅkhāresu pana udayabbayavasena lahuṃ lahuṃ upaṭṭhahantesu udayadassanañca “uppādavato vināso”ti yāvadeva vayadassanatthaṃ tassa nibbidāvahattāti vaye evassa ābhogasamannāhāro manasikāro pavattati, tena uppādādiṃ muñcitvā vayamevārabbha ñāṇaṃ uppajjati. Tena vuttaṃ “uppādaṃ vā”tiādi. Tattha uppādanti nibbattivikāraṃ. Ṭhitinti ṭhitippattaṃ, jaranti attho. Pavattanti upādinnakappavattaṃ. Nimittanti saṅkhāranimittaṃ. Yaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ samudayādighanavasena, sakiccaparicchedatāya ca saviggahānaṃ viya upaṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ saṅkhāranimittaṃ. Keci pana “pavattaṃ nāma saṅkhārānaṃ avicchedena pavattanaṃ uppādova, nimittaṃ nāma uppannānaṃ vijjamānatā ṭhānaparamparā, tasmā uppādameva gaṇhāti ce, pavattaṃ gaṇhāti nāma. Ṭhitiṃyeva gaṇhāti ce, nimittaṃ gaṇhāti nāmā”ti vadanti, taṃ “uppādaṃ vā”tiādivacanena virujjhati. Na hi asati bhede vikappo yutto. Na sampāpuṇāti aggahaṇato. Kiṃ pana sampāpuṇātīti āha “khaya…pe… santiṭṭhatī”ti. Tattha nirodhasaddo anuppādepi dissatīti bhedasaddena visesitaṃ, bhedasaddo visesavācakopi hotīti vayasaddena visesitaṃ, sopi anirodhavācakopi atthīti khayasaddena visesitaṃ, khayavayabhedasaṅkhāte khaṇikanirodheti attho. Sati santiṭṭhatīti satisīsena ñāṇamāha. Etasmiṃ ṭhāneti upakkilesavinimuttassa udayabbayañāṇassa tikkhabhāvāpattiyaṃ vuttanayena udayampi muñcitvā vayasseva manasikārakāle.

741. “It flows,” means it proceeds. The sharpness of knowledge is due to the proficiency of meditation. And because meditation is proficient, it proceeds without distraction, as if absorbed in its object—thus, the swift appearance of formations is shown by the sharpness of knowledge. Now, when formations appear very swiftly in terms of arising and passing away, the observation of arising is for the sole purpose of seeing their passing away, since that brings about disenchantment. Hence, the yogi's attention and mental advertence proceed only on passing away; having let go of arising and the rest, knowledge arises focused solely on passing away. Therefore, it is said, “arising or…” etc. Therein, “arising” means production and alteration. “Persistence” means having reached a state of persistence—that is, aging. “Continuity” refers to the continuity of the appropriated aggregates. “Sign” means the sign of formations—that is, whatever appearance there is of formations as a mass in terms of collection, etc., and by the delineation of their function, as if they had a physical body, that is the sign of formations. Some, however, say: “Continuity is the uninterrupted proceeding of formations—arising itself. The sign is the existence of what has arisen, a succession of states. Thus, if one grasps arising, it is called grasping continuity. If one grasps persistence, it is called grasping the sign.” This is contradicted by the statement, “arising or…” etc. For without a difference, an alternative is not justified. It does not attain them, because it does not grasp them. What, then, does it attain? It is said: “destruction… is established.” Therein, the term “cessation” is also seen in the sense of non-arising, hence it is specified by the term “dissolution.” The term “dissolution” can also be a specific designation, so it is specified by the term “passing away.” That too can be a term for non-cessation, hence it is specified by the term “destruction.” The meaning is momentary cessation, designated as destruction, passing away, and dissolution. Mindfulness “is established”—this refers to knowledge headed by mindfulness. “At this stage” means: at the time when the knowledge of arising and passing away, free from imperfections, has attained sharpness, and when, in the way stated, one has let go of arising and applies the mind only to passing away.

Ārammaṇapaṭisaṅkhāti rūpavedanādiārammaṇaṃ khayavayavaseneva paṭisaṅkhāya. Yakāralopena hi niddeso “sayaṃ abhiññā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.28, 405) viya. Yathāvuttassa [M 2.0440] vā ārammaṇassa khayavayabhedavasena paṭisaṅkhā ārammaṇapaṭisaṅkhā. Bhaṅgānupassaneti yo tadārammaṇassa cittassa bhaṅgo, tassa anupassane. Paññāti pakārato jānanā. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ idāneva saṃvaṇṇīyati.

Ārammaṇapaṭisaṅkhā means: having known the object—such as form, feeling, etc.—only by way of its destruction and passing away. This is the indicated text with the elision of the letter 'y', as in such cases as 'sayaṃ abhiññā' (dī. ni. 1.28, 405) viya. Or, the knowing of the aforesaid object by way of its destruction, passing away, and dissolution is ārammaṇapaṭisaṅkhā. Bhaṅgānupassanā means: in the contemplation of the dissolution of the insight-consciousness that has that as its object. Paññā is knowing in various ways. What should be said in this matter will be explained right now.

742. Yaṃ kiñci ārammaṇanti rūpaṃ yāva jarāmaraṇanti vipassitabbabhāvena gahitaṃ sabbaṃ saṅkhāragatamāha[V 2.0414]. Paṭisaṅkhānaṃ nāma jānanaṃ, tañca bhaṅgānupassanāya adhippetattā bhaṅgato dassanamevāti āha “jānitvā khayato vayato disvāti attho”ti. Tassa ñāṇassāti sambandho.

742. By the phrase 'yaṃ kiñci ārammaṇaṃ', he speaks of all that is included among formations—from form up to aging and death—which is grasped as a phenomenon to be contemplated with insight. What is called paṭisaṅkhāna is knowing. And since that knowing is intended by the contemplation of dissolution, it is simply seeing from the point of view of dissolution. Therefore, he says: 'The meaning is: having known, having seen it as destruction and passing away.' The connection is with 'of that knowledge'.

Rūpārammaṇameva rūpārammaṇatā yathā “devo eva devatā”ti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “rūpārammaṇaṃ citta”nti vuttaṃ. Rūpārammaṇatāti vā bhummatthe paccattavacananti dassento “atha vā rūpārammaṇabhāve”ti āha. Aparena cittena bhaṅgaṃ anupassatīti vipassanāvisayaṃ bhaṅgānupassanamāha. Evañhi bhaṅgānupassanā paguṇā hoti, ārammaṇañcassa vibhūtataraṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Ñātanti ārammaṇamāha anupassanāvasena ñātattā. Ñāṇanti anupassanāñāṇaṃ. Ubhopi vipassatīti tadubhayampi khayato vayato vipassatīti. Ayaṃ hettha saṅkhepattho – rūpassa yāva jarāmaraṇassa khayato vayato dassanaṃ ārammaṇapaṭisaṅkhātaṃ, dassanakañāṇassa khayato vayato dassanaṃ ārammaṇapaṭisaṅkhāya bhaṅgassa anupassananti ubhayattha paññā. Purimaṃ vā tadabhāve abhāvato pacchimāyaṃ pakkhipitvā pacchimā eva paññā vipassane ñāṇanti.

Rūpārammaṇatā is rūpārammaṇa itself, just as devatā is deva itself. To show this meaning, it is said, 'the mind with form as its object.' Or, showing that rūpārammaṇatā is a nominative expression in the locative sense, he says, 'or in the state of having form as object.' By the phrase 'he contemplates dissolution with a subsequent mind,' he speaks of the contemplation of dissolution, which has insight as its domain. For in this way, the contemplation of dissolution becomes proficient, and for that yogi, the object, having become more distinct, appears. By ñātaṃ (the known), he refers to the object, because it is known by way of contemplation. By ñāṇaṃ (knowledge), he refers to the knowledge of contemplation. Ubhopi vipassati (he sees both with insight) means that he sees both of them—the object and the subject—as destruction and passing away. Here is the condensed meaning: The seeing of the destruction and passing away of form up to aging and death is called ārammaṇapaṭisaṅkhā. The seeing of the destruction and passing away of the knowledge that sees is the contemplation of the dissolution of the knowledge that knows the object. Thus, in both cases, it is wisdom. Alternatively, having included the former wisdom in the latter—because in the absence of that former wisdom, the latter is also absent—only the latter wisdom is the knowledge in insight.

Etthāti “tassa cittassa…pe… bhaṅgaṃ anupassatī”ti ettha. Anekehi ākārehīti aniccato anupassanādīhi anekehi ākārehi. Anu-saddo “bhiyyo”ti etasmiṃ attheti āha “punappunaṃ passatī”ti.

“Here” means here in the phrase “he contemplates the dissolution… of that mind.” “In many ways” means in many ways, such as by contemplating as impermanent, etc. The prefix “anu-” is in the sense of “further,” hence it is said, “he sees again and again.”

Idha saṅkhatadhammo nāma jātijarāmaraṇapakatiko, tassa jāti ādikoṭi, jarā majjhimakoṭi, maraṇaṃ osānakoṭi. Tattha kiñcāpi uppādāditividhampi saṅkhatalakkhaṇatāya aniccalakkhaṇaṃ, tathāpi jātijarāsu diṭṭhāsu na tathā aniccalakkhaṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti yathā vayakkhaṇeti āha “bhaṅgo nāma aniccatāya paramā koṭī”ti, uttamā koṭi [M 2.0441] pariyosānakoṭīti attho. Yathā hi jarādhammaṃ, maraṇadhammameva ca jāyatīti jāti aniccatāya ādi koṭi, tathā jātidhammaṃ, maraṇadhammameva ca jīratīti jarā majjhimā koṭi, jātidhammaṃ, jarādhammameva ca bhijjatīti bhaṅgo paramā koṭīti. Aniccato anupassatīti na kalāpato sammasanto viya “aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhenā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.48) anumānavasena, nāpi āraddhavipassako viya udayaggahaṇapubbakavayadassanavasena, atha kho udayabbayañāṇānubhāvena paccakkhato upaṭṭhitesu udayavayesu vuttanayena udayaṃ muñcitvā bhaṅgadassanavaseneva aniccato anupassati, evaṃ anupassato panassa niccagāhassa lesopi natthīti [V 2.0415] āha “no niccato”ti. Tathā hesa niccasaññaṃ pajahatīti vuccati. Ettha ca “aniccato eva anupassatī”ti eva-kāro luttaniddiṭṭhoti tena nivattitamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “no niccato”ti vuttaṃ. Na cettha dukkhato anupassanādinivattanamāsaṅkitabbaṃ paṭiyogīnivattanaparattā, eva-kārassa upari desanāruḷhattā ca tāsaṃ. Dukkhato anupassatītiādīsupi eseva nayo.

Here, a conditioned phenomenon is by nature subject to birth, aging, and death. Of that, birth is the initial stage, aging is the middle stage, and death is the final stage. Among these, although the threefold process beginning with arising is also the characteristic of impermanence due to being a characteristic of the conditioned, nevertheless, when birth and aging are seen, the characteristic of impermanence does not appear as manifestly as it does in the moment of passing away. Hence, it is said: “Dissolution is the ultimate stage of impermanence,” meaning the supreme stage, the concluding stage. For, just as that which is subject to aging and that which is subject to death is born, therefore birth is the initial stage of impermanence; similarly, as that which is subject to birth and that which is subject to death ages, therefore aging is the middle stage; and as that which is subject to birth and that which is subject to aging dissolves, therefore dissolution is the ultimate stage. “One contemplates as impermanent” means: not by way of inference, like one comprehending by way of groups, thinking “impermanent in the sense of destruction,” nor like one who has begun insight practice by way of seeing passing away preceded by the grasping of arising. Rather, through the power of the knowledge of arising and passing away, when arising and passing away are present as directly perceived, having let go of arising in the way stated, one contemplates as impermanent solely by way of seeing dissolution. Now, for one who contemplates in this way, not even a trace of grasping at permanence exists; hence, it is said: “Not as permanent.” For thus, this one is said to abandon the perception of permanence. And here, the particle 'eva' in “contemplates only as impermanent” is indicated as elided; therefore, the phrase “not as permanent” is stated to show the meaning excluded by it. And here, one should not suspect the exclusion of the contemplation as suffering, etc., because the particle 'eva' is chiefly concerned with excluding its counterpart, and because those contemplations are established in the teaching later on. This same method applies also to “contemplates as suffering,” etc.

Aniccato tāva anupassanā bhaṅgānupassakassa yuttā “bhaṅgo nāma aniccatāya paramā koṭī”ti, dukkhādito pana kathanti āha “aniccassa dukkhattā”tiādi. Etena yaṃ aniccaṃ, taṃ ekantato dukkhaṃ anattā, tato ca na abhinandaniyādirūpaṃ. Tasmā upari nibbattetabbato ñāṇaparikammatthañca itarāsampi channaṃ anupassanānaṃ vasena anupassatīti dasseti. Keci panettha “aniccato anupassati, no niccatotiādinā visuṃ dassanakiccaṃ natthi, bhaṅgadassaneneva sabbaṃ diṭṭhaṃ hotī”ti vadanti, taṃ bhaṅgānupassanāya matthakappattiyaṃ yuttaṃ, tato pana pubbabhāge anekākāravokārā anupassanā icchitabbāva. Aññathā “aniccato anupassatī”tiādikā (paṭi. ma. 1.51) pāḷi, “anekehi ākārehi punappunaṃ passatī”ti āgatā tassā aṭṭhakathā ca virodhitā siyā. Tadeva aniccato diṭṭhameva sabbasaṅkhāragataṃ.

First, contemplation as impermanent is suitable for one who contemplates dissolution, since 'dissolution is the ultimate limit of impermanence.' But how is it with regard to suffering and so on? He said, 'Because what is impermanent is suffering,' etc. By this it is shown that whatever is impermanent is entirely suffering and not-self, and therefore not of a nature to be delighted in, or the like. Therefore, it is shown that for the purpose of the preliminary work for the knowledge to be generated hereafter, one also contemplates by way of the other six contemplations. Some, however, say: 'There is no separate task of seeing in “One contemplates as impermanent, not as permanent,” and so on; everything is seen through the vision of dissolution alone.' This is fitting when the contemplation of dissolution has reached its peak. However, prior to that, contemplation in various ways and modes is certainly to be desired. Otherwise, the Pāḷi passage 'One contemplates as impermanent,' etc., and the commentary on it that says, 'One sees again and again in many ways,' would be contradicted. That very thing seen as impermanent is the entirety of conditioned phenomena.

Na taṃ abhinanditabbanti taṃ saṅkhāragataṃ taṇhādiṭṭhābhinandanavasena “etaṃ mama, eso me attā”ti na abhinanditabbaṃ. Na tattha rañjitabbanti tattha saṅkhāragate rañjanavasena na pavattitabbaṃ, kāmarāgo, bhavarāgo vā na pavattetabboti [M 2.0442] attho. Rāgaṃ nirodhetīti rāgaṃ vikkhambhananirodhaṃ pāpeti, vikkhambhetīti attho. Tenāha “lokikeneva tāva ñāṇenā”ti. Sati ca vikkhambhane kathaṃ samudayoti āha “no samudeti, samudayaṃ na karotī”ti.

‘One should not delight in that’ means: one should not delight in conditioned phenomena by way of delighting with craving and views, thinking, ‘This is mine, this is my self.’ ‘One should not be enamored of that’ means: one should not act out of enamorment towards conditioned phenomena; the meaning is that sensual lust or lust for existence should not be aroused. ‘He brings lust to cessation’ means: he brings lust to cessation by suppression; the meaning is, he suppresses it. And when there is suppression, how can arising occur? Thus it is said: ‘it does not arise, one does not cause it to arise.’

Evaṃ virattoti evaṃ bhaṅgānupassanānusārena viratto. Yathā diṭṭhaṃ sampati upaṭṭhitaṃ saṅkhāragataṃ nirodheti nirodhaṃ manasi karoti, adiṭṭhampi atītānāgataṃ anvayañāṇavasena yathā idaṃ etarahi, evaṃ itarepīti anuminanto nirodheti manasikatassāpi nirodhaṃ karoti. No samudetīti etthāpi eseva nayo, no samudayaṃ manasi karotīti attho.

‘Thus dispassionate’ means being dispassionate in accordance with the contemplation of dissolution.
