Just as one brings to cessation—that is, gives attention to the cessation of—the conditioned phenomena that have been seen and are presently arisen, so too, regarding that which has not been seen, the past and future, one brings them to cessation by inferring through consequential knowledge, ‘Just as this ceases now, so too do the others.’ One also brings to cessation that which has been given attention to. ‘It does not arise’: here too the same method applies; the meaning is that one does not give attention to arising.

Evaṃ paṭipannoti evaṃ vuttappakārena aniccānupassanādivasena paṭipanno. Saddhiṃ khandhābhisaṅkhārehi [V 2.0416] kilesānaṃ pariccajanatoti khandhehi, abhisaṅkhārehi ca saha kilesānaṃ pajahanato. Kilese hi pajahanto tannimittakakammaṃ, tato nibbattanake khandhe ca pajahati nāma. Saṅkhatadosadassanenāti saṅkhatadhammesu aniccadukkhatādiādīnavadassanena. Tabbiparīteti niccasukhādisabhāve. Tanninnatāyāti tadadhimuttatāya. Paṭinissaggasaddo pariccāgattho, pakkhandanattho cāti paṭinissaggassa duvidhatā vuttā. Tattha pakkhandanaṃ adhimuccanaṃ. Yathāvuttenāti tadaṅgādippahānappakārena, tanninnappakārena ca. Nibbattanavasenāti uppādanavasena. Nibbattento hi kilese ādiyatīti te anibbattento kilese na ādiyati nāma. Adosadassitāvasenāti dosānaṃ adassāvibhāvena. Saṅkhatārammaṇaṃ ādiyatīti yojanā. Anādīnavadassitāya hi saṅkhāre ādiyatīti ādīnavadassitāya te na ādiyati na gaṇhāti.

Thus practicing: practicing in the manner described, by way of contemplating impermanence, etc. Abandoning the defilements together with the aggregates and formations: because of abandoning the defilements together with the aggregates and formations. For in abandoning defilements, one is said to abandon also the kamma that has them as its cause and the aggregates that will be produced from it. Seeing the fault in the conditioned: by seeing the danger, such as impermanence and suffering, in conditioned phenomena. Opposite to that: in the nature of permanence, happiness, and so on. Inclined towards that: by being resolved on that. The term “relinquishment” has two meanings: abandonment and leaping into. Herein, leaping into is resolution. As stated: in the manner of abandoning by substitution, etc., and in the manner of being inclined towards it. By way of generating: by way of producing. For one who generates defilements takes them up; thus, one who does not generate them is said not to take them up. By way of not seeing fault: by the state of not perceiving faults. Taking up the conditioned as object: this is the connection. For one takes up formations by not seeing their danger; thus, by seeing their danger, one does not take them up or grasp them.

743. Assāti yogino. Tehi ñāṇehīti aniccānupassanādiñāṇehi. Tanti pahānaṃ. Niccasaññanti niccagāhaṃ, saññāsīsena niddeso. Sukhasaññaṃ attasaññanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Sappītikaṃ taṇhanti sauppilāvitaṃ abhipatthanaṃ.

743. Of him: of the yogi. By those knowledges: by the knowledges beginning with the contemplation of impermanence. That: abandonment. The perception of permanence: the grasping of permanence; the designation is made with perception as the principal thing. The perception of pleasure, the perception of self: here too this is the method. Craving with delight: longing together with elation.

744. “Vatthusaṅkamanā”ti ettha vipassanāya pavattiṭṭhānabhāvato rūpādiārammaṇaṃ “vatthū”ti adhippetanti dassento “rūpassā”tiādimāha. Tattha saṅkamanāti vipassanābhāvasāmaññato ekattanayena vuttaṃ[M 2.0443], aññathā aññadeva rūpabhaṅgavisayaṃ ñāṇaṃ, aññadeva tadārammaṇacittabhaṅgavisayanti kuto saṅkamanā. Paññāvivaṭṭanāyapi eseva nayo. Paññāyāti udayabbayadassanavasena pavattamānāya vipassanāpaññāya. Vayasseva gahaṇavasena udayato vinivaṭṭanā. Tenāha “udayaṃ pahāya vaye santiṭṭhanā”ti. “Anantarameva āvajjanasamatthatā”ti iminā bhaṅgānupassanāya paguṇabalavabhāvamāha.

744. “The shifting of the base”—here, to show that “base” is intended to mean the object, such as form, etc., because it is the place where insight occurs, he said, “of form, etc.” Here, “shifting” is stated in terms of unity due to the commonality of the state of insight; otherwise, the knowledge that has the dissolution of form as its object is one thing, and the knowledge that has the dissolution of the mind that takes that as its object is another—how could there be shifting? The same method applies to the turning away of wisdom. “By wisdom” means by the insight-wisdom that proceeds by way of seeing arising and passing away. Turning away from arising is by way of grasping only passing away. Therefore, he said, “abandoning arising and becoming established in passing away.” By “the ability to advert immediately,” he indicates the proficient and powerful nature of the contemplation of dissolution.

745. Ubhoti diṭṭhādiṭṭhabhāvena dvepi ārammaṇāni. Ekavavatthanāti khaṇabhaṅguratāya samānāti vavatthāpanā.

745. “Both” means both objects, in being seen and unseen. “Single determination” means the determination that they are similar due to momentary dissolution.

Saṃvijjamānamhīti paccakkhato upalabbhamāne paccuppanne. Visuddhadassanoti bhaṅgadassanassa paribandhavidhamanena visuddhañāṇo, suvisuddhabhaṅgadassanoti attho. Tadanvayaṃ netīti tassa paccuppannasaṅkhārabhaṅgadassino ñāṇassa anvayaṃ anugatabhūtaṃ ñāṇaṃ pavatteti. Kattha pana pavattetīti [V 2.0417] āha “atītanāgate”ti, atīte, anāgate ca saṅkhāragate. Sabbepītiādi tassa pavattanākāradassanaṃ.

“In what is present” means in what is directly experienced in the present. “One with pure vision” means one whose knowledge is purified by the dispelling of obstacles to the vision of dissolution; the meaning is, one with a very pure vision of dissolution. “Leads in conformity with that” means one sets in motion a knowledge that follows in conformity with that knowledge of one who sees the dissolution of present formations. But where does one set it in motion? He says, “in the past and future,” that is, concerning the collection of formations in the past and in the future. The words beginning with “All” show the manner of its proceeding.

Bhaṅgasaṅkhāte nirodhe, na nibbānasaṅkhāteti adhippāyo. Esāti yā ārammaṇanvayena ubho diṭṭhādiṭṭhe khaṇabhaṅguratāya ekabhāvena vavatthāpanā, esā vayalakkhaṇe vipariṇāmalakkhaṇe vipassanā bhaṅgānupassanāti attho.

The intended meaning is: in cessation designated as dissolution, not in that designated as Nibbāna. “This” refers to the determination, by way of the sequence of the object, of both the seen and the unseen as a single nature because of their momentary dissolution. This insight into the characteristic of vanishing, the characteristic of change, is the contemplation of dissolution. This is the meaning.

746. Ārammaṇañca paṭisaṅkhātiādi bhaṅgānupassanāya duppaṭivijjhattā vuttassevatthassa daḷhīkaraṇaṃ. Tayidaṃ bhaṅgadassanaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ avasavattanāvabodhanena anattalakkhaṇapaṭivedhāyāti taṃ dassento “suññato ca upaṭṭhāna”nti āha. Ārammaṇassa hi bhaṅgārammaṇacittassa ca bhaṅgamanupassato visesato saṅkhārā suññā hutvā upaṭṭhahanti. Tenāha “tasseva”ntiādi.

746. “And reflecting on the object,” etc., is a strengthening of the meaning already stated, because the contemplation of dissolution is difficult to penetrate. This vision of dissolution is for the penetration of the characteristic of not-self through the understanding of the unruliness of formations. Showing this, he said, “and the manifestation as empty.” For to one who contemplates the dissolution of the object and of the mind that has dissolution as its object, formations especially manifest as empty. Hence he said, “of that very,” etc.

Na catthi aññoti ettha imasmiṃ loke añño khandhavinimutto attā nāma koci natthi. Tesaṃ khayaṃ passatīti tesaṃ dhammānaṃ khaṇe khaṇe upaṭṭhahantaṃ bhaṅgaṃ passati. Yathāvuttāya appamādapaṭipattiyā appamatto. Yathā kiṃ? Maṇiṃva vijjhaṃ vajirena yoniso yathā nāma kusalo puriso upāyena maṇiṃ vijjhanto maṇissa chiddameva passati manasi karoti[M 2.0444], na maṇissa vaṇṇādiṃ, evameva saṅkhārānaṃ nirantaraṃ bhaṅgameva yoniso manasi karoti, na saṅkhāreti adhippāyo. Yathā vā vajirena maṇiṃ vijjhantassa viddhaṭṭhānaṃ na puna ruhati, evaṃ vajirasadisena bhaṅgānupassanāñāṇena bhaṅge diṭṭhe na puna niccagāho ruhati, evaṃ bhaṅgameva passatīti attho.

There is no other: in this world, there is no so-called self apart from the aggregates. He sees their destruction: he sees the dissolution of those phenomena presenting itself from moment to moment. He is diligent through the practice of diligence as described. How so? Like wisely piercing a gem with a diamond: just as a skilled person, skillfully piercing a gem, attends only to the hole in the gem, not to its color, etc., so too one wisely attends only to the continuous dissolution of formations, not to the formations themselves—this is the intended meaning. Or, just as the place pierced by a diamond does not grow back, so too, when dissolution is seen with the diamond-like knowledge of the contemplation of dissolution, the grasping at permanence does not grow back. Thus, he sees only dissolution—this is the meaning.

Yā ca ārammaṇapaṭisaṅkhāti “rūpārammaṇatā cittaṃ uppajjitvā bhijjati, taṃ ārammaṇaṃ paṭisaṅkhā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.51) evamāgatā yā ca ārammaṇapaṭisaṅkhā, “tassa cittassa bhaṅgaṃ anupassatī”ti evaṃ vuttā yā ca bhaṅgānupassanā, “saṅkhārāva bhijjanti, tesaṃ bhedo maraṇaṃ, na añño koci atthī”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ yañca suññato upaṭṭhānaṃ, ayaṃ evaṃ tidhā vuttāpi adhipaññāvipassanā nāmāti attho.

And that reflection on the object which is handed down thus: “The mind having a form as its object arises and breaks up; one reflects on that object”; and that contemplation of dissolution which is stated thus: “One contemplates the dissolution of that mind”; and that manifestation as empty which is stated thus: “Only formations break up; their breaking up is death; there is no other”—this, though spoken of in these three ways, is called the insight of higher wisdom. This is the meaning.

747. Aniccānupassanādīsūti aniccadukkhānattānupassanāsu. Nibbidādīsūti nibbidāvirāganirodhapaṭinissaggānupassanāsu[V 2.0418]. Tayo upaṭṭhāneti aniccādivasena tividhe upaṭṭhāne. Khayato vayato upaṭṭhānañhi aniccato upaṭṭhānaṃ, bhayato upaṭṭhānaṃ dukkhato, suññato upaṭṭhānaṃ anattatoti. Diṭṭhīsūti diṭṭhinimittaṃ na vedhati. Tā hi asaṃhīratāya na calati.

747. In the contemplations of impermanence, etc.: in the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, and not-self. In disenchantment, etc.: in the contemplations of disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, and relinquishment. Three manifestations: in the threefold manifestation by way of impermanence, etc. Indeed, the manifestation as destruction and as vanishing is the manifestation as impermanence; the manifestation as fear is as suffering; the manifestation as empty is as not-self. In regard to views: one does not tremble on account of the sign of views. For one does not waver, due to not being carried away by them.

748. Dubbalabhājanassa viyāti tintaāmamattikābhājanassa viya bhedameva passatīti sambandho. Ettha ca dubbalabhājanūpamā sarasabhiduratādassanatthaṃ, vippakiriyamānasukhumarajūpamā aññamaññaṃ asambandhatādassanatthaṃ, bhijjiyamānatilūpamā khaṇe khaṇe bhijjanakabhāvadassanatthanti daṭṭhabbā. Bhedamevāti vināsameva passati uppādādīnaṃ aggahaṇato. Evamevāti yathā udakabubbuḷakāni udakatalādipaccayaṃ paṭicca uppannāni na ciraṭṭhitikāni sīghaṃ sīghaṃ bhijjanti, evameva sabbe rūpārūpadhammā kammādipaccayaṃ paṭicca uppannā khaṇaṭṭhitikā sīghaṃ sīghaṃ bhijjantīti bhedameva passati. Turitaturitañhi nesaṃ bhedadassanatthaṃ “bhijjanti bhijjantī”ti āmeḍitavacanaṃ.

748. Like a fragile vessel: the connection is thus: just as one sees only the breaking of a pot of moist, unbaked clay. And here it should be understood that the simile of the fragile vessel is for the purpose of showing its liability to break by its own nature; the simile of scattered fine dust is for the purpose of showing the lack of connection with one another; and the simile of roasted sesame seeds is for the purpose of showing the nature of breaking up from moment to moment. Only dissolution: one sees only destruction, because of not grasping arising and so forth. Just so: just as water bubbles, having arisen dependent on conditions such as the surface of the water, are not long-lasting and quickly, quickly break up, even so all material and immaterial phenomena, having arisen dependent on conditions such as kamma, are of momentary duration and quickly, quickly break up—thus one sees only dissolution. Indeed, for the purpose of showing their very rapid dissolution, the repeated phrase “they break, they break” is stated.

Marīcipi ittarakālikāva, nissayapabandhavasena pana ciratarupaṭṭhānanti “yathā passe marīcika”nti vuttaṃ, na ayāthāvupaṭṭhānatova. Lokanti khandhalokaṃ. Maccurājā na passati arahattādhigamena punabbhavābhāvato.

A mirage, too, is of short duration, but because it appears to last longer due to the continuity of its supporting conditions, it is said, “as one would see a mirage,” and not only because of its deceptive appearance. The world: the world of the five aggregates. The King of Death does not see him: because, through the attainment of arahantship, there is no further renewed existence.

749. Bhavadiṭṭhippahānanti [M 2.0445] sassatadiṭṭhiyā vikkhambhanaṃ. Na hi nirantaraṃ bhaṅgameva passato sassatadiṭṭhiyā avasaro atthi. Tato eva jīvite nirālayattā jīvitanikantipariccāgo. Sadāti sabbakālaṃ rattindivaṃ. Bhāvanāya yuttappayuttatā. Icchācārānaṃ dūrībhāvato visuddhājīvitā. Ussukkappahānaṃ kiccākiccesu abyāvaṭatā tibbasaṃvegattā. Vigatabhayatā kutocipi nibbhayatā attasinehābhāvato. Khantisoraccapaṭilābho aniccatāya sudiṭṭhattā. Pantasenāsanesu adhikusalesu ca aratiyā, kāmaguṇesu ratiyā ca sahanato abhibhavanato aratiratisahanatā.

749. Abandonment of the view of being is the suppression of the eternalist view. Indeed, for one who sees only continuous dissolution, there is no opportunity for the eternalist view. Therefore, because of being without attachment to life, there is the relinquishment of craving for life. Always means at all times, day and night. Being exceedingly devoted to the development of meditation. Purity of livelihood because of being far from wrongful conduct. Abandonment of eagerness is not being occupied with duties and non-duties, because of intense spiritual urgency. Freedom from fear is fearlessness from any quarter, because of the absence of affection for a self. The attainment of patience and gentleness is because impermanence has been well seen. The state of enduring discontent and delight comes from enduring and overcoming discontent with remote lodgings and with higher wholesome states, and delight in sensual pleasures.

Imāni aṭṭhagguṇamuttamānīti liṅgavipallāsena vuttaṃ. Ma-kāro ca padasandhikaro, bhavadiṭṭhippahānādike ime aṭṭha uttamānisaṃseti attho. Tahinti tattha bhaṅgānupassanāyanti attho.

The phrase Imāni aṭṭhagguṇamuttamāni ('These supreme qualities are eight') is stated with a change of gender. The letter ‘ma’ is for euphonic conjunction; the meaning is: these eight supreme benefits, beginning with the abandonment of the view of being. Tahiṃ means: ‘therein, in the contemplation of dissolution.’

Bhaṅgānupassanāñāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Knowledge of the Contemplation of Dissolution is finished.

Bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Knowledge of Appearance as Terror

750. Sabbasaṅkhārānanti [V 2.0419] tebhūmakānaṃ sabbasaṅkhārānaṃ. Adhikāravasena hi padesasabbavisayo idha sabbasaddo. Āsevantassāti ādaravasena sevantassa pavattentassa. Bhāventassāti vaḍḍhentassa brūhentassa. Bahulīkarontassāti punappunaṃ karontassa yuñjantassa. Pabhedakāti khaṇe khaṇe bhijjanavasena pabhedakā. Ājīvikā byādhiādinimittaṃ maritukāmassa, amaritukāmassāpi sūrassa bhāyitabbampi na bhayato upaṭṭhātīti “sukhena jīvitukāmassa bhīrukapurisassā”ti vuttaṃ. Yathā bhīrukajātikassa sīhādayo santāsanimittaṃ bhayānakabhāvato, tathā yogino bhaṅgato dissamānā saṅkhārāti āha “sīha…pe… upaṭṭhahantī”ti. Paccuppannāti addhāpaccuppannā oḷārikā dīghatarapabandhā, khaṇapaccuppannā sukhumatarā ittarakālā, santatipaccuppannā majjhimā idha ādito pariggahetabbā. Bhayato bhāyitabbato upatiṭṭhanakesu ñāṇaṃ bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ.

750. Regarding 'all formations': this means all formations belonging to the three planes. Here, by virtue of the context, the word 'all' has a specific, partial scope. 'To one who attends to': this means to one who attends to with respect, who makes them occur. 'To one who develops': this means to one who increases, who cultivates. 'To one who makes much of': this means to one who does so again and again, who strives unceasingly. 'They are constantly breaking up': this means they are constantly breaking up by way of perishing moment by moment. For one who wishes to die on account of livelihood, disease, or other such reasons, and even for a brave person who does not wish to die, what should be feared does not appear as a terror; therefore, it is said, “for a timid person who wishes to live happily.” Just as for a person of a timid nature, a lion and so on are a cause of terror due to their frightening quality, so for the yogī are the formations that are seen as dissolving; therefore, he said, “a lion… appear.” 'Present': the temporal present formations are gross and have a particularly long continuity; the momentary present formations are more subtle and have a short duration; the continuous present formations, which are intermediate, should be grasped here from the beginning. The knowledge concerning those things that appear as terror, as fit to be feared, is the knowledge of the appearance as terror.

Yathā [M 2.0446] itthiyā puttānaṃ sīsassa chinnatā chijjamānatā gayhamānā bhayāvahā, evaṃ yogino tiyaddhagatānaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ nirodhā gayhamānāti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “ekissā kira itthiyā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Just as for a woman, when the state of her sons' heads having been cut off or being in the process of being cut off is apprehended, it brings forth fear, so too for the yogī, when the cessations of formations belonging to the three periods of time are apprehended, they bring forth fear. To show this meaning, it is said, “Of a certain woman, it is said…” and so on.

Yathā pūtibhūtaṃ odanādi na sabhāvena tiṭṭhati vinassati, evaṃ yassā itthiyā vijātavijātā puttā na jīvanti maranti eva, sā “pūtipajā”ti vuttā. Pūtipajāggahaṇañcettha visesato gabbhagatamaraṇacintādassanena yogino anāgatasaṅkhāranirodhasanniṭṭhānadassanatthaṃ. Atītapaccuppannasaṅkhāranirodho hissa supākaṭo evāti na so upamāya sādhetabbo. Antimabhavikassa ca yogino sattakkhattuṃ paramādibhāvino atīte dukkhabahutāya, anāgatadukkhaparittatāya ca dassanatthaṃ bahupajāva itthī nidassitā.

Just as putrid rice and so forth does not remain in its natural state but perishes, so a woman whose sons, whenever they are born, do not live but only die, is called 'one with putrid offspring'. And here, the taking up of the term 'one with putrid offspring' is specifically for the purpose of showing the yogī, by demonstrating the contemplation of death occurring in the womb, the firm establishment in the cessation of future formations. Indeed, for this yogī, the cessation of past and present formations is already very plain, so that does not need to be established by a simile. Moreover, for a yogī in his final existence—one who is destined to be a seven-times-returner at most, and so on—a woman with many children is pointed out as an example in order to show the abundance of suffering in the past and the littleness of suffering in the future.

Tattha yathā tassā nava puttā matā, evaṃ ajjhattādippabhedā atītā saṅkhārā, vusitapubbā vā nava sattāvāsā daṭṭhabbā, mīyamānaputto viya paccuppannā saṅkhārā, pavattamāno vā sattāvāso daṭṭhabbo. Ajātaputto viya anāgatā saṅkhārā, bhāvī vā sattāvāso daṭṭhabbo. Evamavaṭṭhite yadeke dasaputtamātaraṃ aggahetvā navaputtamātuggahaṇaṃ sātthakanti vadanti, tadapāhataṃ hoti[V 2.0420]. Dārakānaṃ maraṇassa cirakālikattā maraṇānussaraṇanti vuttaṃ. Gabbhagato appaccakkhatāya bhāvīpakkheyeva tiṭṭhatīti adhippāyena kucchigato anāgatasaṅkhāraṭṭhāniyo vutto. Etasmiṃ khaṇeti bhaṅgadassanamukhena saṅkhārānaṃ bhayānakabhāvena upaṭṭhānakkhaṇe.

Therein, just as her nine sons have died, so too should be seen the past formations, distinguished as internal, etc., or the nine abodes of beings that have been previously inhabited. Like the son who is dying, the present formations should be seen, or the ongoing abode of beings. Like the son yet to be born, the future formations should be seen, or the abode of beings yet to come. This being so, that which some say—'Not taking the mother of ten sons, the taking of the mother of nine sons is meaningful'—is refuted. It is called ‘recollection of death’ because the death of the children is a long-past event. With the intention that ‘the one in the womb, because of not being directly perceived, stands only on the side of the future,’ the one in the womb is said to be in the position of future formations. ‘At this moment’ means at the moment of their appearance as terrifying, due to the fearsome nature of formations, with the seeing of dissolution as the principal method.

751. Na bhāyati ñāṇassa bhāyanākārena appavattanato. Paṭighacittuppādavasena hi bhāyanaṃ, ñāṇaṃ pana bhāyitabbavatthuṃ bhāyitabbanti yāthāvato jānāti. Tenāha “atītā…pe… tīraṇamattamevā”ti, tisso aṅgārakāsuyo atitāpena tikkhamajjhamudubhedāti adhippāyo. Kāmabhavādīnañhi tiṇṇaṃ bhavānaṃ nidassanabhāvena tāsaṃ gahaṇaṃ, tathā khadirādisūlattayassa appaṇītādibhāvato. Tenāha “kevalaṃ hī”tiādi. Assāti ñāṇassa. Byasanāpannāti nānāvidhavipulānatthapatitā. Bhayatoti bhāyitabbato.

751. It does not fear, because knowledge does not proceed in the mode of fearing. For fearing occurs by way of the arising of a mind-state of aversion, but knowledge knows the object fit to be feared as ‘to be feared’ exactly as it is. Hence it is said, ‘past… is mere discernment.’ The meaning is that the three charcoal pits are distinguished as sharp, medium, and mild by their excessive heat. Their being taken is as an illustration of the three kinds of existence—sensual existence, etc.—just as the three stakes of khadira wood, etc., are taken because of their being unalluring, etc. Therefore he said, ‘For merely…’ etc. ‘Of it’ (assa) means of knowledge. ‘Fallen into calamity’ (byasanāpannā) means fallen into various and vast misfortunes. ‘As terror’ (bhayato) means because it is fit to be feared.

Saṅkhāranimittanti [M 2.0447] “saṅkhārānaṃ samūhādighanavasena, sakiccaparicchedatāya ca saviggahānaṃ viya upaṭṭhāna”nti vuttovāyamattho. Saṅkhārānaṃ pana tathā upaṭṭhānaṃ saṅkhāravinimuttaṃ na hotīti āha “atītā…pe… adhivacana”nti. Maraṇamevāti bhaṅgameva. Tenāti bhaṅgadassanena. Khaṇe khaṇe bhaṅgameva passato hi nimittasaññitaṃ saṅkhāragataṃ aniccatāya vuttanayena sappaṭibhayaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Pavattaṃ nāma kāmaṃ sabbā bhavapavatti, matthakappattāya pana bhaṅgānupassanāya sabbabhavesu abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanassa suṭṭhutaraṃ upaṭṭhānato santasukhābhimatāpi bhavā dukkhasabhāvatāya bhayato upaṭṭhahantīti dassanatthaṃ “pavattanti rūpārūpabhavapavattī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ubhayanti nimittaṃ, pavattañca. Dvayampi hi taṃ attasuññameva hutvā upaṭṭhahatīti.

“The sign of formations” means: “the appearance of formations as if they had substance, by way of being a mass, a solid block, etc., and by being delimited by their own function.” This is the meaning already stated. But since such an appearance of formations is not separate from the formations, he said, “past… a designation.” “Death itself” means just dissolution. “By that” means by the seeing of dissolution. For to one who sees only dissolution moment by moment, the collection of formations, designated as a “sign,” appears as fraught with terror in the way described for impermanence. Indeed, “occurrence” (pavatta) is all occurrence of being; but because, when the contemplation of dissolution has reached its climax, the constant oppression in all kinds of existence appears more clearly, even kinds of existence considered peaceful and happy appear as terror due to their nature of suffering. To show this, it was said, “‘Occurrence’ means the occurrence of form and formless existence,” etc. “Both” means the sign and the occurrence. For indeed, both of them appear as being empty of self.

Bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Knowledge of Appearance as Terror is concluded.

Ādīnavānupassanāñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Knowledge of Contemplation of Danger

752. Tāṇanti saṅkhārahetukā anattato rakkhaṇaṃ. Neva paññāyati sabbabhavādīnaṃ sādīnavatāya ekasadisattā. Leṇanti tassa pariharaṇatāṇāya upalīyanaṃ. Gatīti tadatthaṃ gantabbaṭṭhānaṃ. Paṭisaraṇanti tasseva paṭisaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ. Patthanāti āsīsanā na hoti. Etena “netaṃ [V 2.0421] mamā”ti taṇhāgāhābhāvamāha. Parāmāsoti diṭṭhiparāmāso. Tena “eso me attā”ti diṭṭhigāhābhāvamāha. Taṇhāgāhābhāveneva cettha “esohamasmī”ti mānagāhābhāvopi vuttoyeva hoti, vā-saddaggahaṇena vā.

752. Protection (tāṇa) means guarding from the harm that is caused by formations. It is not found, because all existences, etc., are of one and the same nature in being fraught with danger. Shelter (leṇa) means a hiding place for avoiding that harm. Destination (gati) means a place to be gone to for that purpose. Refuge (paṭisaraṇa) means a place for destroying that very harm. Aspiration (patthanā) means there is no wishing for. By this, he shows the absence of the grasp of craving expressed as 'This is mine.' Clinging (parāmāsa) means the clinging to views. By this, he shows the absence of the grasp of views expressed as 'This is my self.' And here, by the very absence of the grasp of craving, the absence of the grasp of conceit expressed as 'This I am' is also stated to be so, or else by the inclusion of the word 'or'.

Idāni patthanādīnamabhāve kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “tayo bhavā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tayo bhavā aṅgārakāsuyo viya jātiādidukkhādhiṭṭhānabhāvena mahābhitāpatāya. Cattāro mahābhūtā kaṭṭhamukhapūtimukhaaggimukhasatthamukhasaṅkhātā ghoravisaāsīvisā viya kāyassa thaddhatāvissandanadāhacchedadukkhavidhānato visesato, avisesato pana āsayato, visavikārato, anatthadānato, durupacārato, durāsadato, akataññuto, avisesakārito, anekādīnavūpaddavato ca. “Cattāro āsīvisā uggatejā ghoravisāti kho, bhikkhave[M 2.0448], catunnetaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ adhivacana”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.238) hi vuttaṃ. Pañcakkhandhā ekakkhandhabhede aññakkhandhānavaṭṭhānato. Aññamaññāghātanato, maraṇadukkhāvahanato ca ukkhittāsikavadhakā viya. Vuttampi cetaṃ “ukkhittāsiko vadhakoti kho, bhikkhave, pañcannetaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ adhivacana”nti. Cha ajjhattikāyatanāni attattaniyabhāvena gahitānipi tato rittabhāvato suññagāmo viya bhojanādigayhupagamettha atthīti paviṭṭhasuññagāmo viya. Tathā hi vuttaṃ –

Now, to show the reason for the absence of aspirations and so on, 'the three kinds of existence,' etc., is said. Herein, the three kinds of existence are like a pit of embers, since they are a basis for suffering such as birth and so on, and are greatly scorching. The four great elements are like fierce, deadly venomous snakes—described as wood-mouthed, putrid-mouthed, fire-mouthed, and sword-mouthed—because they inflict the suffering of stiffness, oozing, burning, and cutting on the body; and also because of their disposition, their venomous effects, their causing of harm, their being hard to manage, their being hard to approach, their ungratefulness, their indiscriminate action, and their many dangers and calamities. For it is said: 'Bhikkhus, "four snakes of fierce energy and terrible venom" is indeed a designation for these four great elements' (SN 35.238). The five aggregates are like an executioner with a raised sword because when one aggregate is destroyed, the others cannot endure, because they mutually destroy one another, and because they bring the suffering of death. And this is said: 'Bhikkhus, "an executioner with a raised sword" is a designation for these five aggregates subject to clinging.' The six internal sense bases, though grasped as self or what belongs to self, are like an empty village because they are devoid of that; like an empty village that one has entered thinking, 'Here there is food and other things to be taken.' For so it is said:

“Suññagāmoti kho, bhikkhave, channetaṃ ajjhattikānaṃ āyatanānaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Cakkhuto cepi naṃ, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto medhāvī upaparikkheyya, rittakaññeva khāyati, tucchakaññeva khāyati, suññakaññeva khāyatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.238) –

'Empty village,' bhikkhus, is indeed a designation for these six internal sense bases. If a wise, competent, intelligent person were to investigate it by way of the eye, it would appear simply empty, simply hollow, simply void' (SN 35.238).

Ādi. Cha bāhirāyatanāni gāmaghātakacorā viya sabbathāpi ghātakabhāvato. Tenevāha “corā gāmaghātakāti kho, bhikkhave, channetaṃ bāhirānaṃ āyatanānaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Cakkhu, bhikkhave, haññati manāpāmanāpesu rūpesū”tiādi. Rāgaggiādīhi ekādasahi aggīhi. Vuttañhetaṃ –

The six external sense bases are like village-plundering thieves because in every way they are of a destructive nature. Therefore he said: '“Village-plundering thieves,” bhikkhus, is indeed a designation for these six external sense bases. The eye, bhikkhus, is assailed by agreeable and disagreeable forms,' and so on. By the eleven fires, such as the fire of lust. For this has been said:

“Cakkhu, bhikkhave, ādittaṃ. Kena ādittaṃ? Rāgagginā dosagginā mohagginā jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.28) –

'Bhikkhus, the eye is burning. With what is it burning? With the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion; with birth, aging, and death; with sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair' (SN 35.28).

Ādi[V 2.0422]. Saṅkhārānaṃ gaṇḍādisadisatā heṭṭhā vuttāyeva. Nirassādāti assādetabbarahitā dukkhasabhāvattā. Nirasāti sampattirahitā vipattipariyosānattā. Sabbattha yathā heṭṭhā nirassādā nirasā mahāādīnavarāsibhūtā hutvā upaṭṭhahantīti sambandho, evaṃ uparipi “savāḷakamiva vanagahana”ntiādīsu taṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ.

And so on. The similarity of formations to a boil and so on has already been stated below. Devoid of gratification (nirassādā) means devoid of anything to be gratified by, because their nature is suffering. Devoid of substance (nirasā) means devoid of success, because they end in ruin. The connection is that everywhere, just as below, they appear as being devoid of gratification, devoid of substance, and a great mass of danger. Similarly, above too, in such phrases as 'like a dense forest full of savage beasts,' this should be brought in and connected.

Sasaddūlāti sabyagghā. Gāhā kumbhilādayo. Rakkhaso dakarakkhaso. “Nirasaṃ nirassāda”nti iminā ādīnavassa abbokiṇṇataṃ dasseti. Tathā hissa yogino sabbesu bhavādīsu sabbepi saṅkhārā nissaggato nirantaraṃ sappaṭibhayāva hutvā upaṭṭhahanti. Yañca sappaṭibhayaṃ, taṃ sādīnavaṃ. Tenāha “tasseva”ntiādi.

'With savage beasts' means with tigers. 'Seizers' means crocodiles and so on. 'A demon' means a water-demon. By the phrase 'without substance, without gratification,' he shows the unadulterated nature of the danger. For to that yogi, in all existences and so on, all formations, by their very nature, continuously appear as fraught with peril. And whatever is fraught with peril is fraught with danger. Therefore he said, 'of that very thing,' etc.

Yanti [M 2.0449] ādīnavañāṇaṃ. Idaṃ vuttanti idaṃ dasavatthukaṃ dvādasavārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ anvayabyatirekavasena tasseva padabhājanaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ vuttaṃ.

That which is the knowledge of danger. This has been said: this analysis of its terms, which has ten bases and is adorned with twelve sections, has been stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga by way of positive and negative correlation.

Uppādo bhayanti saṅkhārānaṃ uppādo akhemaṭṭhena bhayavatthutāya bhayaṃ. Uppādamūlakañhi sabbaṃ taṃ sabbavatthukanti sabyasanaṃ. Pavattaṃ bhayantiādīsupi eseva nayo. Natthi etassa uppādo, na vā etasmiṃ adhigate saṅkhārānaṃ āyatiṃ uppādoti anuppādo, nibbānaṃ. Tañca sabbaso bhayābhāvato paramassāsabhūtattā nibbhayaṭṭhena khemanti. Santipadeti sabbasaṅkhārūpasamabhūte amatapade. Appavattantiādīhipi pavattādipaṭikkhepamukhena nibbānameva vadati. Pavattiyaṃ ādīnavaṃ disvā tadanantarameva nivattiyaṃ ānisaṃsadassanavasena sīghaṃ vipassanaṃ ussukkāpentānaṃ vasena “uppādo bhayaṃ, anuppādo khema”nti tatiyavāro vutto. Eseva nayo chaṭṭhavārādīsupi. Ettha ca uppādo viseso, bhayaṃ visesitabbaṃ sāmaññabhāvatoti satipi dvinnaṃ padānaṃ samānādhikaraṇabhāve liṅgabhedo gahito. Yathā “dukkhasamudayo ariyasacca”nti (dī. ni. 3.354; ma. ni. 3.374). Esa nayo “gati bhaya”ntiādīsupi.

'Arising is fear' means: the arising of formations is fear in the sense of being unsafe, because it is a basis for fear. For indeed, that fear, being rooted in arising and having everything as its basis, is accompanied by destruction. This same method applies also to 'continuance is fear,' etc. 'Non-arising' (anuppādo) means there is no arising of this, or, when this is attained, there is no future arising of formations; this is Nibbāna. And that, because it is utterly without fear and is the ultimate consolation, is 'safety' (khema) in the sense of being fearless. 'In the peaceful state' means in the deathless state which is the calming of all formations. By 'non-continuance,' etc., too, he speaks only of Nibbāna by way of rejecting continuance, etc. The third section, 'Arising is fear, non-arising is safety,' is stated for those who, having seen the danger in continuance, immediately thereafter see the benefit in cessation and thus are urged to strive for insight quickly. This same method applies to the sixth section, etc. And here, although the two words are in apposition, a difference in gender is taken, because 'arising' is the qualifier and 'fear' is the general term to be qualified. As in 'the origin of suffering is a noble truth.' This same method applies to 'destination is fear,' etc.

Uppādo saṅkhārāti ettha pana sabbesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ uppādaṃ sāmaññena gahetvā saṅkhārā bhedato vihitā sabbatthakameva tesaṃ vibhāgato vipassiyamānattāti vacanabhedo kato.

In the phrase 'Arising is formations,' however, a difference in grammatical number is made because, while the arising of all formations is taken in general, the formations are set forth by way of division, since they are contemplated everywhere according to their classification.

Āyūhanaṃ paṭisandhiṃ “dukkha”nti passatīti sambandho. Ñāṇaṃ ādīnave idanti ādīnave visayabhūte [V 2.0423] idaṃ pañcavatthukaṃ ñāṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ñāṇaṃ santipadeti santipade ninnādibhāvena ṭhitaṃ idaṃ ñāṇanti attho.

The connection is: 'He sees accumulation and rebirth-linking as suffering.' 'This is knowledge in danger' means: this five-based knowledge, which has danger as its object, should be understood. 'Knowledge in the peaceful state' means: this is the knowledge that stands inclined towards the peaceful state.

753. Kammapaccayā paccuppannabhave uppajjamānānaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ uppādo pākaṭataro hutvā upaṭṭhātīti āha “purimakammapaccayā idha uppattī”ti. Pavattaṃ nāma idha pavattiyaṃ dhammappavattīti āha “uppannassa pavattī”ti. Sabbampīti tiyaddhagataṃ rūpārūpaṃ ajjhattabahiddhādivibhāgaṃ sabbampi. Kammanti etarahi pavattaṃ kammaṃ. Ettha ca uppādapavattaāyūhanaggahaṇena paccuppannaddhapariyāpannā saṅkhārā gahitā, paṭisandhiggahaṇena anāgataddhapariyāpannā upādittā. Uppādaggahaṇena ca atītaddhapariyāpannā kammasaṅkhārā ulliṅgattā. Nimittaggahaṇena pana sabbepi gahitā. Yāya gatiyā sā paṭisandhi hoti sā [M 2.0450] nirayādibhedā gati sucaritaduccaritavasena gantabbattā, sā panatthato taṃtaṃkammaniyamitā bhavasamaññārahā vipākakkhandhā, kaṭattā ca rūpanti veditabbā. Khandhānaṃ nibbattananti sabbesampi khandhānaṃ nibbattanaṃ. Pākaṭā eva saccavibhaṅge lakkhaṇādivasena niddiṭṭhattā. Vatthuvasenāti ārammaṇasaṅkhātapavattiṭṭhānavasena. Yadi te pañceva vatthubhāvena icchitā, atha kasmā sesā vuttāti āha “sesā tesaṃ vevacanavasenā”ti. Tena vipassakānaṃ ñāṇavipphārassa visayasaṃvaḍḍhanatthaṃ desanā vaḍḍhitāti dasseti.

753. He said, 'Here, arising is conditioned by past kamma,' because the arising of formations that are being produced in the present existence conditioned by kamma appears more clearly. He said, 'the continuance of what has arisen,' because what is called 'continuance' is the continuous occurrence of phenomena during the period of continuance in this present existence. 'All' means all that is comprised in the three time periods, divided into material and immaterial, internal and external, etc. 'Kamma' means the kamma occurring now. And here, by taking 'arising,' 'continuance,' and 'accumulation,' formations included in the present time period are taken. By taking 'rebirth-linking,' formations included in the future time-period are taken, because they are aggregates that are clung to. And by taking 'arising,' kamma-formations included in the past time-period are taken, because they are causes indicated by their effect. But by taking 'sign,' all formations are taken. That destination (gati) by which there is that rebirth-linking—that destination, of kinds such as hell, etc., is called 'destination' because it is to be gone to by way of good and bad conduct. But in meaning, it is the resultant aggregates, determined by this or that kamma and worthy of the designation 'existence,' and also form produced by kamma; thus it should be known. 'The production of aggregates' means the production of all aggregates. They are evident because they are described in the Saccavibhaṅga by way of characteristics, etc. 'By way of basis' means by way of the place of occurrence, which is known as the object. If only those five were intended as the basis, why were the others stated? He said: 'The others are by way of synonyms for them.' By this he shows that the teaching was expanded to broaden the scope of knowledge for insight meditators.

Anvayato dassitassa ādīnavañāṇassa byatirekato dassanatthaṃ paṭipakkhañāṇadassanaṃ “yattha uppādo natthi, tattha sabbena sabbaṃ bhayampi natthī”ti. “Bhayatupaṭṭhānena vā”tiādinā pavattiṃ dassetvā nivattidassanaṃ buddhānaṃ, anubuddhānañca āciṇṇametaṃ yathā purimaṃ saccadvayaṃ dassetvā nirodhasaccadesanāti dasseti. Yathā loke kassaci ādīnavadassanaṃ niratthakampi hoti, na tathā idaṃ, idaṃ pana sātthakamevāti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “yasmā vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tappaṭipakkhaninnaṃ cittaṃ hoti dāhābhibhūtassa sītaninnatā viya suṭṭhu diṭṭhādīnavato ekaṃsena muñcitukamyatābhāvato.

To show by way of contrast the knowledge of danger that was shown by way of affirmation, there is the showing of the opposing knowledge: 'Where there is no arising, there is no fear at all.' He shows that having shown occurrence by means of 'or by the appearance as fearful,' etc., the showing of non-occurrence is the practice of the Buddhas and the Anubuddhas, just as the teaching of the truth of cessation is given after showing the first two truths. To show this meaning—that just as in the world someone's seeing of danger can be fruitless, this is not so, but this is indeed fruitful—'or because,' etc., was said. The mind becomes inclined to its opposite, like the inclination to coolness of one overcome by heat, because, from having well seen the danger, there arises the state of desiring to be completely liberated.

Bhayanti bhāyitabbaṃ. “Niyamato dukkha”nti etenassa dukkhabhāvena bhāyitabbatāti bhāyitabbatā dukkhabhāvaṃ na byabhicaratīti dasseti. Vaṭṭāmisaṃ upādinnakkhandhāti vadanti. Tividhampi vaṭṭaṃ, vaṭṭasannissitañca vaṭṭāmisaṃ. Kilesehi āmasitabbato lokāmisaṃ, pañca kāmaguṇā[V 2.0424]. Kilesā eva kilesāmisaṃ. Saṅkhāramattamevāti ettha eva-saddena visaṅkhāraṃ nivatteti. Na hi tattha sāmisatālesopi atthīti. Matta-saddena pana aparipuṇṇataṃ vibhāveti. Na hi sabbasaṅkhāragataṃ sāmisanti. Tasmāti “bhaya”nti vuttassa dukkhādibhāvena niyatattā. Yadi yaṃ bhayaṃ, taṃ dukkhādisabhāvameva, tathā sati bhayādīsu ekeneva atthasiddhi. Kasmā sabbāni gahitānīti anuyogaṃ manasi katvā āha “evaṃ santepī”tiādi. Yathā tesu eva saṅkhāresu aniccato dukkhato anattato pavattivasena ākāranānattato anupassanānānattaṃ, evaṃ bhayākārādiākāranānattato pavattivasenevettha ñāṇassa nānattaṃ[M 2.0451]. Tattha bhayākārena pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ, itarākāravasena pavattaṃ ādīnavañāṇanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Bhayanti means that which should be feared. By this text, “as a rule, it is suffering,” it is shown that because of its nature as suffering, the state of being something to be feared does not transgress the state of suffering. They say that the bait of the round of existence is the aggregates subject to clinging. The threefold round of existence, as well as that which is dependent on the round, is the bait of the round. The bait of the world, which is to be touched by defilements, is the five cords of sensual pleasure. The defilements themselves are the bait of defilements. Here, in the phrase “merely formations,” by the word `eva`, the unconditioned is excluded, for not even a trace of the state of being bait exists there. The word `matta` (mere), however, indicates an incompleteness, for not all that has become a formation is bait. Therefore, because what is called “fear” is fixed by its nature as suffering, etc., if what is fear is indeed of the nature of suffering, etc., then the meaning would be accomplished by just one of these, such as “fear.” Having kept in mind the objection, “Why are all taken?” he said, “Even so,” etc. Just as in those very formations, there is a diversity of insight contemplation due to the diversity of aspects in the way they proceed—as impermanent, as suffering, and as not-self—so too here, the diversity of knowledge should be understood as arising precisely from the diversity of aspects in the way they proceed, such as the aspect of fear. Therein, knowledge that proceeds with the aspect of fear is the knowledge of the appearance of what is fearful, while knowledge that proceeds by way of other aspects should be understood as the knowledge of drawbacks.

Yasmā ādīnavañāṇassa visayabhāvena vuttā pannarasāpi atthā uppādādīsu pañcasveva antogadhā, tattha ca ñāṇaṃ anvayabyatirekavasena pavattanato dasavidhaṃ hoti. Tasmā āha “dasa ñāṇe pajānātī”ti. Pajānanañca sātisayaṃ visayagatasammohavigamena asammūḷhaṃ, attanipi asammūḷhamevāti attānampi pajānantaṃ viya hotīti katvā vuttaṃ. Tenāha “paṭivijjhati sacchikarotī”ti. Dvinnanti dvīsu kusalasaddayogena hi bhummatthe sāmivacanaṃ yathā “kusalā naccagītassā”ti (jā. 2.22.94). Kusalatāti karaṇe paccattavacananti āha “dvinnaṃ kusalatāyā”ti. Dvinnanti vā dvinnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ vasenāti attho. Pavattiyā yāthāvato diṭṭhatāya tappaṭipakkhato santipadaṃ suvinicchitameva hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Tenassa cittaṃ paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānādimicchāgāhavasena na vicalati. Tattha suparidiṭṭhādīnavattāti āha “nānādiṭṭhīsu na kampatī”tiādi. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

Because the fifteen meanings spoken of as the domain of the knowledge of drawbacks are included in just the five—arising, etc.—and because knowledge proceeds therein by way of positive and negative correlation, it becomes tenfold. Therefore, he said, “He understands ten knowledges.” And this understanding is excellent, unconfused through the removal of confusion concerning its object; and since it is also unconfused in itself, it is said to be as if it understands itself. Hence, he said, “He penetrates, he realizes.” Regarding `dvinnam` (of two): this is a genitive in the sense of the locative, by connection with the word “skilled,” as in “skilled in dance and song.” `Kusalatā` (skill) is a nominative in the sense of the instrumental; hence he said, `dvinnaṃ kusalatāya` (by skill in two). Alternatively, `dvinnam` means by way of two knowledges. Because the continuity of existence is seen as it really is, the state of peace, its opposite, presents itself as very well-discerned. Thereby his mind does not waver through the wrong grasp of such things as a supreme Nibbāna realizable in this very life. Because the state of having drawbacks in that continuity has been thoroughly seen, he said, “He does not waver among diverse views,” and so on. The rest here has a plain meaning.

Ādīnavānupassanāñāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The knowledge of contemplation of drawbacks is completed.

Nibbidānupassanāñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Knowledge of Contemplation of Disenchantment.

754. Saṅkhāragateti sabbasmiṃ tebhūmake saṅkhāre. Nibbindatīti ñāṇanibbidena nibbedaṃ āpajjati. Tathābhūto ca tattha ukkaṇṭhanto, anabhiramanto ca nāma hotīti vuttaṃ “ukkaṇṭhati nābhiramatī”ti.

754. Regarding `saṅkhāragate`: in all formations belonging to the three planes. Regarding `nibbindati`: he attains disenchantment by means of the disenchantment that is knowledge. And one who has become so is one who feels revulsion for that and does not delight in it; thus it is said: “he feels revulsion, he does not delight.”

Tattha [V 2.0425] anabhiramaṇassa upamaṃ dassetuṃ “seyyathāpī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Anotattadahaṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitesu dviyojanasatubbedhesu yathākkamaṃ sānuañjanarajatasuvaṇṇasattaratanamayesugandhamādanakāḷakelāsasudassanacittakūṭabhedesu pañcasu himavato mahāsikharesu pacchimo cittakūṭapabbato nāma. Sīhapapātādīsu sattasu mahāsaresu.

Therein, to show an illustration of not delighting, the phrase “Just as...” and so on, was stated. Among the five great peaks of the Himavanta—namely Gandhamādana, Kāḷa, Kelāsa, Sudassana, and Cittakūṭa—which stand enclosing Lake Anotatta, are two hundred yojanas high, and are made respectively of emerald, añjana stone, silver, gold, and the seven kinds of gems, the last of these is called Cittakūṭa mountain. In the seven great lakes, beginning with Sīhapapāta...

Suvaṇṇapañjareti [M 2.0452] suvaṇṇamaye sīhapañjare. Pakkhittoti niruddho. Tividhe sugatibhaveti kāmasugatiādike tividhe sampattibhave.

Regarding `suvaṇṇapañjare` (in a golden cage): in a golden lion-cage. Regarding `pakkhitto` (placed in): confined. Regarding `tividhe sugatibhave` (in the threefold happy existence): in the threefold existence of attainment, such as the happy sense-sphere destination.

Hatthapādavālavatthikosehi bhūmiphusanehi sattahi patiṭṭhitoti sattapatiṭṭho. Nagaramajjhe nābhiramati dvārapañjaranāḷanādiavabādhanabhayena. Diṭṭheti adhimuttipubbakena anvayadassanena diṭṭhe. Tenāha “tanninnatappoṇatappabbhāramānaso”ti.

Established by seven parts touching the ground—its trunk, four feet, tail, and sheath—it is called “seven-established.” It does not delight in the midst of a city, due to fear of being awakened by things such as the striking of doors, cages, and gongs. Regarding `diṭṭhe` (when seen): when seen by means of sequential inference preceded by resolve. Therefore, it is said: “with a mind sloping, tending, and inclining to that.”

Nibbidānupassanāñāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The knowledge of contemplation of disenchantment is completed.

755. Taṃ panetanti nibbidāñāṇamāha. Ñāṇadvayenāti bhayatupaṭṭhānādīnavānupassanāñāṇadvayena. Yasmā bhayato dissamānā eva saṅkhārā mahādīnavā, nibbinditabbā ca hutvā upaṭṭhahanti, tasmā ekampi taṃ ñāṇaṃ tathābhāvanābalappattiyā avatthāvisesayuttaṃ tividhakiccasāmatthiyavantaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ “atthato eka”nti. Tenāha “sabbasaṅkhāre”tiādi.

755. By the phrase `taṃ panetaṃ`, he speaks of the knowledge of disenchantment. “By two knowledges” means by the pair of knowledges: the knowledge of the appearance of what is fearful and the knowledge of contemplation of drawbacks. Because formations, being seen as fearful, appear as having great drawbacks and as things to be disenchanted with, therefore even that single knowledge, by attaining the power of such development, becomes endowed with a special stage and possessed of the capacity for a threefold function—thus it is said, “one in meaning.” Hence he says, “all formations,” and so on.

Tayidaṃ tāsaṃ anupassanānaṃ matthakappattivasena vuttaṃ, ādimhi pana bhinnasabhāvā eva pavattanti. Uppādesīti pātvākāsi, vibhāvesīti attho.

This is said by way of those contemplations having reached their culmination, but in the beginning they proceed as having distinct natures. `Uppādesi` (he produced) means `pātu akāsi` (he made manifest); the meaning is `vibhāvesi` (he clarified).

Muñcitukamyatāñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Knowledge of the Desire for Deliverance.

756. Na sajjati bahvādīnavatāya diṭṭhattā. Muñcitukāmaṃ nissaritukāmaṃ hoti anādikālikassa khandhassa pariññāyamānattā. Muñcitukāmatā tato attānaṃ nibbedhetukāmatā nissaritukāmatā apagantukāmatā. Pañjarapakkhittoti pañjarena samoruddho. Evamādayoti ādi-saddena ādittaaṅgāraupasaṭṭhadesabyāḷasāpadākulavanagahanādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

756. One does not cling, because the state of having many drawbacks has been seen. One desires to be freed, desires to escape, because the aggregate from beginningless time is being fully comprehended. The desire to be freed (`muñcitukāmatā`) is the desire to release oneself from that; the desire to escape (`nissaritukāmatā`) is the desire to depart. `Pañjarapakkhitto` (placed in a cage) means well confined by a cage. Regarding `evamādayo` (and so on): by the word `ādi` (etc.), the inclusion of things such as a house ablaze, an afflicted region, and a forest thicket confused with vicious snakes and beasts of prey should be understood.

Muñcitukamyatāñāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The knowledge of the desire for deliverance is completed.

Paṭisaṅkhānupassanāñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Knowledge of Contemplation by Reflection.

757. “Sabbabhava [M 2.0453][V 2.0426] …pe… muñcitukāmo”ti vatvā puna sabbasmā saṅkhāragatāti sabbaggahaṇaṃ sātisayamuttidassanatthaṃ adhikavacanaṃ aññamatthaṃ bodhetīti. Yañhi saṅkhārehi ananubandhassa muñcanaṃ, taṃ sātisayaṃ muñcanaṃ. Taṃ pana vuccamānāya paṭisaṅkhānupassanāya hotīti taṃ dassetuṃ “puna te evaṃ saṅkhāre”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā saṅkhārapariggaṇhanaṃ pubbepi katanti punaggahaṇaṃ. Bhavādigatassa saṅkhārassa aparitulitassa abhāvato “te”ti vuttaṃ. Anupassanākārassa apubbassapi atthitāya “eva”nti vuttaṃ. Idāni vuccamānākārenāti hi attho. Saṅkhārānaṃ pariggaṇhanaṃ nāma paripuṇṇalakkhaṇavaseneva hotīti “tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā”ti vuttaṃ.

757. Having said, 'Desirous of release from all existence… etc.,' again, the inclusion of 'all' in 'from all that has become conditioned' is for the purpose of showing the excellent release, for 'an additional statement indicates another meaning.' Indeed, the release of one who is not followed by formations is an excellent release. And that release is by means of the contemplation of reflection that is about to be spoken of; to show that, it was said, 'again, those formations thus…' and so on. The comprehending of formations by superimposing the three characteristics has been done before, hence the re-comprehending. Because of the absence of any unweighed formation belonging to existence, etc., 'those' was said. Because of the existence of a mode of contemplation that is also new, 'thus' was said. Indeed, the meaning of `evaṃ` is 'in the manner about to be spoken of now.' The comprehending of formations occurs only by way of the complete characteristics; therefore, 'by superimposing the three characteristics' was said.

Anaccantikatotiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Paṭhamena ādi-saddena “ādiantavantato niccapaṭikkhepato”ti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho.

In 'as not final,' etc., whatever should be said, that has already been said below. By the first `ādi`-word, the inclusion of such as 'because of having a beginning and an end, because of the rejection of permanence' should be understood.

Dutiyena “udayabbayapaṭipīḷanato sukhapaṭikkhepato”ti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho.

By the second `ādi`-word, the inclusion of such as 'because of the oppression by arising and passing away, because of the rejection of pleasure' should be understood.

Ajaññatoti amanuññato, asobhanato vā. Jegucchatoti “dhī”ti jigucchitabbato. Paṭikkūlatoti abhiruciyā paṭilomanena paṭikkūlabhāvato. Na maṇḍanena hatā amaṇḍanahatā, amaṇḍanena sakkā etesaṃ subhabhāvaṃ hantunti attho. Amaṇḍanena vā tesaṃ asubhatā pākaṭā hotīti amaṇḍanahatā. Maṇḍanena vā na hantabbasabhāvā “asūriyapassā”ti viya amaṇḍanahatā. Tato amaṇḍanahatabhāvatoti rūpasaṅkhāre sandhāya vadati. Virūpatoti asundarato. Paṭighasaṃyojanavatthutāya passante attani bandhatīti bībhacchaṃ ativiya virūpaṃ. Yaṃ diṭṭhamattameva domanassuppattinimittaṃ hoti. Ajaññajigucchanīyatā hi gūthaṃ viya pariccajitabbaṃ vā bībhacchaṃ. Idha ādi-saddena “asucito amanāpato”ti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho.

'As ignoble' (`ajaññato`) means because of being disagreeable, or because of being unattractive. 'As contemptible' (`jegucchato`) means because of being fit to be abhorred, as in 'Fie!'. 'As repulsive' (`paṭikkūlato`) means because of being repulsive by being contrary to delight. `Amaṇḍanahatā` is explained as `na maṇḍanena hatā`. This can be interpreted as 'destroyed by non-adornment'; the meaning is that by not adorning, it is possible to destroy their beautiful nature. Or, they are called `amaṇḍanahatā` because by not adorning, their foulness becomes evident. Or, they are `amaṇḍanahatā` because they have a nature not to be destroyed by adornment, like 'those not seen by the sun' (`asūriyapassā`). Then, 'because of the state of being `amaṇḍanahatā`' is said with reference to material formations. 'As deformed' (`virūpato`) means because of being ugly. 'Horrible' (`bībhacchaṃ`) means that which binds those who see it by being a basis for the fetter of aversion; it is extremely deformed. It is that which, upon the mere sight of it, is a cause for the arising of displeasure. Or, 'horrible' is that which should be abandoned like excrement because of its ignoble and contemptible nature. Here, by the word 'etc.' (`ādi`), the inclusion of such as 'as impure' and 'as disagreeable' should be understood.

Catutthena ādi-saddena “apariṇāyakato attapaṭikkhepato”ti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho.

By the fourth `ādi`-word, the inclusion of such as 'as being without a guide' and 'as a rejection of self' should be understood.

758. Ayanti [M 2.0454][V 2.0427] yogāvacaro. Muñcanassāti puna ananubandhanatthaṃ sumuttamuñcanassa. Upāyasampādanatthanti aniccādivasena suṭṭhu pariggaṇhanaṃ parimaddanā upāyo, tassa sādhanatthaṃ.

758. 'This one' (`ayaṃ`) means the meditator. 'Of release' (`muñcanassa`) means of a well-freed release, for the purpose of not being followed again. 'For accomplishing the means' (`upāyasampādanatthaṃ`) means for the purpose of achieving that means; the means is the crushing, which is the thorough comprehending by way of impermanence and so on.

Macchagahaṇatthaṃ udake tattha tattha khipanti etanti khippaṃ, macchānaṃ gahaṇakūṭapaṃ. Oḍḍāpesīti osāresi, khipīti attho. Sappanti kaṇhasappaṃ. Gahaṇeti yathāgahitaṃ sappaṃ achaḍḍetvā gahaṇe. Hatthaṃ nibbeṭhetvāti sappena attano bhogena veṭhitaṃ hatthapadesaṃ nibbeṭhetvā mocetvā. Āvijjhitvā āveṭhikappahāpanena bhametvā. Nissajjitvāti chaḍḍetvā.

A `khippaṃ` is what one casts here and there in the water to catch fish; a trap for catching fish. `Oḍḍāpesi` means he submerged it, or cast it; that is the meaning. `Sappaṃ` means a black snake. `Gahaṇe` means in the holding, without letting go of the snake as it was caught. `Hatthaṃ nibbeṭhetvā` means having unwound and freed the part of the hand that was encircled by the snake with its own coil. `Āvijjhitvā` means having whirled it around by causing it to abandon its coiling. `Nissajjitvā` means having discarded it.

Tatthātiādi upamāsaṃsandanaṃ. Tattha āditovāti viññutaṃ pattakāle. Ghanavinibbhogaṃ katvāti kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā samūhādighanaggahaṇaṃ bhinditvā. Sumuttanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso “visamaṃ candimasūriyā parivattantī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.70) viya. Saṅkhārānaṃ niccādiākārena upaṭṭhātuṃ asamatthatā aniccasaññādibhedāya vipassanāya sātisayaṃ balavabhāvappattiyā, sā ca saṅkhārānaṃ aniccādiākārassa suṭṭhutaraṃ sallakkhaṇenāti āha “tilakkhaṇāropanena…pe… pāpetvā”ti. Yathā hi nibbuddhakaraṇe balavatarena paṭimallena tattha tattha muṭṭhippahārādinā vimathito itaro tena yujjhituṃ asamatthataṃ pāpito hoti. Na kevalaṃ asamatthataṃ pāpitova hoti, atha kho maraṇamattaṃ dukkhaṃ vā maraṇaṃ vā pāpuṇāti, evametepi saṅkhārā evaṃ dubbalabhāvaṃ pāpitā upariñāṇānubhāvena nibbisevanataṃ, sabbaso bhaṅgañca pāpuṇantīti.

“Tattha,” etc., is the connection with the simile. Therein, “āditova” means: at the time of attaining discernment. “Having made a breakdown of the compact” (`ghanavinibbhogaṃ katvā`) means: having taken up the meditation subject and having broken down the grasping of compactness as a mass, etc. “Sumuttaṃ” is a neuter designation for development, like in the text beginning with, “The moon and sun revolve unevenly,” etc. The inability of formations to present themselves in the manner of permanence, etc., is due to insight—differentiated as the perception of impermanence, etc.—having attained a state of sublime power; and that attainment of a powerful state is through discerning very thoroughly the characteristic of impermanence, etc., of formations. Therefore, he said, “By superimposing the three characteristics… leading to…” For just as in a boxing match, the other boxer, being pummeled by a stronger opponent with blows of the fist, etc., here and there, is brought by him to the inability to fight. Not only is he brought to inability, but he also attains pain amounting to death, or even death itself. So too, these formations, having been brought to such a weakened state, through the power of the higher knowledges, attain a state of non-indulgence and complete dissolution.

759. Ettāvatāti evaṃ “anaccantikato”tiādinā parocattālīsāya ākārehi saṅkhārānaṃ aniccādibhāvasallakkhaṇavasappavattena paṭisaṅkhānena.

759. “Thus far” (`ettāvatā`) means: by the reflection that proceeds by way of discerning the state of impermanence, etc., of formations in the forty-odd modes beginning with “as not final,” and so on.

Aniccato manasikarototiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ bhayatupaṭṭhānakathāyaṃ (visuddhi. 2.750) vuttanayameva.

Regarding “he gives attention as impermanent,” etc., what is to be said follows the method stated in the discourse on the appearance as terror.

Ayaṃ pana viseso – “paṭisaṅkhā”ti padassa “jānitvā”ti atthaṃ vatvā paṭisaṅkhānuppajjanakiriyānaṃ samānakhaṇattā asatipi pubbāparakālatte saddavohāramattena evaṃ vuttanti dassento “kāma”ntiādimāha. Tena “kusalaṃ [M 2.0455] dhammaṃ paṭicca kusalo dhammo uppajjati hetupaccayā [V 2.0428] (paṭṭhā. 1.1.53), nihantvā timiraṃ sabbaṃ, uggatoyaṃ divākaro”ti ca evamādīsu viya samānakālavasenāyaṃ saddapayogoti. Tathā manañca dhamme ca paṭhamaṃ paṭicca pacchā na manoviññāṇassa uppatti, evamidhāpīti dassetuṃ “manañca paṭiccā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ediso saddapayogo yebhuyyena loke pubbakālavaseneva dissatīti pubbakālavaseneva idhāpi taṃ dassetuṃ “ekattanayena vā…pe… veditabba”nti āha. Tassattho – aparāparaṃ uppannesu ñāṇesu purimassa vasena paṭisaṅkhānakiriyā, tadaññassa vasena uppajjanakiriyā ca yojetabbā, na ca tāni bhedato apekkhitabbāni ekasantānapatitatāya ekattanayavasena gahitattāti. Itarasmiṃ padadvayeti “pavattaṃ paṭisaṅkhā, nimittañca pavattañca paṭisaṅkhā”ti imasmiṃ padadvaye.

However, this is the distinction: having stated the meaning of the word 'paṭisaṅkhā' as 'having known,' to show that it is stated thus merely by verbal convention even though there is no state of being a prior and a later time because the act of reflection and the act of arising are of the same moment, he says 'kāmaṃ,' etc. Therefore, just as in such examples as, 'Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises through the root condition,' and, 'Having dispelled all darkness, this sun has risen,' this verbal usage is by way of simultaneity. Likewise, to show that just as the arising of mind-consciousness does not occur later, having first depended on the mind and mental objects, so too is it here, 'dependent on the mind,' etc., is stated. To show that such a verbal usage is for the most part seen in the world by way of a prior time, and here too to show that meaning by way of a prior time, he says, 'or by the single method… it should be known.' Its meaning is: among knowledges that have arisen successively, the act of reflection should be connected by way of the prior knowledge, and the act of arising by way of another, subsequent knowledge; and those knowledges should not be regarded separately, because they are taken by way of the single method due to falling within a single continuum. In the other pair of phrases—that is, in this pair of phrases: 'he reflects on what has occurred' and 'he reflects on the sign and what has occurred.'

Paṭisaṅkhānupassanāñāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Knowledge of Contemplation by Reflection is concluded.

Saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations

760. Saṅkhārānaṃ aniccadukkhākārādipariggaṇhanavasena pavattampi paṭisaṅkhānupassanāñāṇaṃ visesato anattākārapariggaṇhanapadhānanti vuttaṃ “sabbe saṅkhārā suññāti pariggahetvā”tiādi. Tasmiñhi sati saccasampaṭivedho ijjhati, na asati. Tadabhāvato hi aniccadukkhalakkhaṇapaññāpakampi sarabhaṅgasatthārādīnaṃ sāsanaṃ aniyyānikameva jātaṃ. Atha vā tesaṃ niccasārādīhi rittakaṃ sandhāya “sabbe saṅkhārā suññāti pariggahetvā”ti vuttaṃ. Yañhi yato rittakaṃ, taṃ tena suññanti. Saṅkhārānaṃ attasuññatāya duviññeyyabhāvato anekavāraṃ paṭividdhāyapi suññatānupassanāya daḷhībhāvāpādanatthaṃ “puna suññamida”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha yadaggena saṅkhārā anattatā, tadaggena anattaniyā. Sati hi attani attaniyena bhavitabbanti vuttaṃ “suññamidaṃ attena vā attaniyena vā”ti. Dvikoṭikanti dviaṃsikaṃ, attānaṃ neva disvā ñāṇacakkhunā paccakkhato, anumānato ca tassa anupalabbhanīyatoti adhippāyo. Paraṃ aññaṃ sattaṃ, saṅkhāraṃ vā parikkhārabhāve attano sukhadukkhasādhanabhāve ṭhitaṃ na disvāti yojanā. Puna pariggaṇhātīti sambandho. Etthāti etasmiṃ suññatānupassanādhikāre.

760. Although the Knowledge of Contemplation by Reflection occurs by way of comprehending the aspects of impermanence, suffering, and so on of formations, it is said to have the comprehension of the aspect of not-self as its principal feature, as in 'having comprehended that all formations are empty,' and so on. For when this is present, the penetration of the truths is accomplished; when absent, it is not. For due to its absence, the teaching of the teacher Sarabhaṅga and others, although it makes known the characteristics of impermanence and suffering, became one that is not a means of escape. Alternatively, with reference to those formations being devoid of a permanent essence and so on, it is said, 'having comprehended that all formations are empty.' For whatever is devoid of something, that is empty of it. Due to the difficulty in understanding the emptiness of self in formations, although it has been penetrated many times, for the purpose of strengthening the contemplation of emptiness, the passage beginning 'Again, this is empty,' and so on, is commenced. Therein, to the extent that formations are not-self, to that extent they are not what belongs to a self. For if a self exists, there must be what belongs to a self; therefore it is said, 'This is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self.' `Dvikoṭikaṃ` means having two parts; the meaning is that one does not see a self with the eye of wisdom, neither directly nor by inference, because of its unattainability. The connection is: not seeing another being or formation existing in the state of being an accessory, in the state of being a means for one's own happiness and suffering. The connection is with 'again, comprehends.' `Ettha` means: in this section on the contemplation of emptiness.

Kvacīti [M 2.0456][V 2.0429] katthaci ṭhāne, kāle, dhamme vā. Atha vā kvacīti ajjhattaṃ, bahiddhā vā. Attano attānanti sakattānaṃ. “Ayaṃ kho bhavaṃ brahmā mahābrahmā…pe… seṭṭho sajitā vasī pitā bhūtabhabyāna”ntiādinā (dī. ni. 1.42) parehi parikappitaṃ attānañca kassaci kiñcanabhūtaṃ na passatīti dassento “kassacī”tiādimāha. Tattha parassāti “parajāti, paro puriso”ti ca evaṃ gahitassa. Na ca mama kvacanīti ettha mama-saddo aṭṭhāne payuttoti āha “mama-saddaṃ tāva ṭhapetvā”ti. Parassa cāti attato aññassa. “Paro puriso”ti evaṃbhūto attho mamatthāya ṭhito, tassa vasena mayhaṃ sabbaṃ sijjhatīti evaṃ ekaccadiṭṭhigatikaparikappitavasena paraṃ attānaṃ tañca attano kiñcanabhūtaṃ na passatīti dassento “na ca kvacanī”tiādimāha. Ettha ca nāhaṃ kvacanīti sakaattano abhāvaṃ passati. Na kassaci kiñcanatasminti sakaattano eva kassaci anattaniyataṃ passati. Na ca mamāti etaṃ dvayaṃ yathāsaṅkhyaṃ sambandhitabbaṃ. Atthīti paccekaṃ. Na ca kvacani parassa attā atthīti parassa attano abhāvaṃ passati. Tassa parassa attano mama kiñcanatā na catthīti parassa attano anattaniyataṃ passati. Evaṃ ajjhattaṃ, bahiddhā ca khandhānaṃ attattaniyasuññatā suddhasaṅkhārapuñjatā catukoṭikasuññatāpariggaṇhanena diṭṭhā hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “evamaya”ntiādi.

“In some place” (kvaci) means in any location, time, or phenomenon. Alternatively, “in some place” refers to internally or externally. “One’s own self” (attano attānaṃ) means one’s own self. By stating, “This, indeed, is the venerable Brahmā, the Great Brahmā… the foremost, the creator, the sovereign, the father of all that has been and will be,” and so on (Dī. Ni. 1.42), he shows that he does not perceive any self conceived by others as belonging to anyone, hence the phrase “to anyone,” etc. Here, “another’s” (parassa) refers to what is understood as “another being, another person.” “And not mine anywhere” (na ca mama kvacani)—here, the word “mine” (mama) is inappropriately applied, hence it is said, “First, set aside the word ‘mine.’” “And another’s” (parassa ca) means of someone other than oneself. “Another person”—such a concept is imagined as being for the sake of ‘me’ (mamatthāya) thinking, “Through him, everything is accomplished for me.” Thus, showing that one does not perceive another as a self or as belonging to oneself, according to the views of those gone astray, he states, “and not anywhere,” etc. Here, “nor am I anywhere” (nāhaṃ kvacani) means one perceives the absence of one’s own self. “I am not a ‘something’ of anyone’s” (na kassaci kiñcanatasminti) means one perceives that one’s own self does not belong to anyone else. “And not mine” (na ca mama)—this pair should be connected in respective order. “Is” (atthi)—is applied to each part. “Nor is there anywhere a self of another” (na ca kvacani parassa attā atthi)—one perceives the absence of another’s self. “Of that other’s self, there is no state of being mine” (tassa parassa attano mama kiñcanatā na catthi)—one perceives that another’s self does not belong to oneself. Thus, internally and externally, the emptiness of the aggregates with regard to self and what belongs to a self—that is, their nature as a mere heap of conditioned phenomena—is seen by comprehending the four-fold emptiness. Therefore, it is said, “Thus, this,” etc.

761. “Chahākārehī”tiādinā niddesādīsu tattha tattha āgate pakāre suññatānupassanāya paribrūhanaṃ saṅgahetvā dasseti. Tattha chahākārehīti chahi gahaṇākārehi, gahetabbākārehi vā. Niccenāti “nicco”ti parikappitena attanā vā aññena vā kenaci. Niccenāti vā niccabhāvena. Dhuvādayo “nicco”ti gahitasseva gahetabbākārā. Tabbibhāgena hi imassa chakkatā. Tattha niccatā nāma kūṭaṭṭhatā. Dhuvabhāvo thiratā. Sadā bhāvitā sassatatā. Nibbikāratā avipariṇāmadhammatā. Yāva jarāmaraṇāti peyyālaṃ akatvā pariyosānapadameva dasseti.

761. By “in the six ways” (chahākārehi) and so on, he shows the development of the contemplation of emptiness by including the aspects that appear in the explanations and elsewhere. Herein, “in the six ways” means by six modes of grasping, or by modes of what is to be grasped. “Permanent” (niccena) means (grasped as) “permanent” by a self conceived by oneself or by another. Or, “permanent” means by the state of permanence. “Enduring” (dhuvādayo) and so on are modes of what is to be grasped, of that very thing taken as “permanent.” Indeed, by their division, this becomes a sixfold group. Herein, permanence (niccatā) is immutability (kūṭaṭṭhatā). The state of being enduring (dhuvabhāvo) is stability (thiratā). Always existing (sadā bhāvitā) is perpetuity (sassatatā). Unchanging (nibbikāratā) is the state of not being subject to change (avipariṇāmadhammatā). “Until old age and death” (yāva jarāmaraṇā): without elaborating the ellipsis, he shows only the concluding phrase.

762. Na sāranti asāraṃ, natthi etassa sāranti nissāraṃ. Sārato apagataṃ, sāraṃ vā tato apagatanti sārāpagataṃ. Keci panettha [M 2.0457] “niccasārasārena vā sukhasārasārena vā attasārasārena vā”ti pāḷīti adhippāyena “asāraṃ nissāraṃ sārāpagata”nti padattayaṃ eko suññatāpariggahākāro, aññathā satteva ākārā siyuṃ, na aṭṭhāti vadanti. Apare pana “subhasārasārenātipi [V 2.0430] pāḷiyaṃ atthīti ‘asāraṃ nissāraṃ sārāpagata’nti idaṃ padattayaṃ ‘niccasārasārenā’tiādīsu paccekaṃ yojetabba”nti vadanti. Setavacchoti setavaruṇako. “Minarukkho”tipi vadanti. Pāḷibhaddakoti kiṃsuko.

762. ‘It is not essence’ (na sāraṃ), hence it is called worthless (asāraṃ); ‘there is no essence in this’ (natthi etassa sāraṃ), hence it is called without essence (nissāraṃ). ‘Departed from essence’ (sārato apagataṃ), or ‘essence has departed from it’ (sāraṃ vā tato apagataṃ), hence it is called devoid of essence (sārāpagataṃ). Some here say that with the intention of the Pāli text “by the essence of permanence, or by the essence of pleasure, or by the essence of self,” the three terms “worthless,” “without essence,” and “devoid of essence” constitute a single mode of comprehending emptiness; otherwise, there would be only seven aspects, not eight. Others, however, say that since the phrase “by the essence of the beautiful” also exists in the Pāli, these three terms—“worthless,” “without essence,” and “devoid of essence”—should each be applied separately to “by the essence of permanence,” etc. “Setavaccho” refers to the white varuṇaka tree. Some also call it the “Minarukkho.” “Pāḷibhaddako” refers to the kiṃsuka tree.

763. Niccasārādīnaṃ abhāvato rittato passati. Parittato, lāmakattā vā tucchato. Attasārābhāvena suññato. Sayaṃ anattatāya anattato. Issariyassa abhāvato, kenaci issariyaṃ kāretuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya ca anissariyato. Pheṇapiṇḍena bhājanādiṃ kātukāmassa viya rūpassa niccatādiṃ kātukāmassa taṃ na sijjhati, sakaicchāvasena vā kāci kiriyā natthīti akāmakāriyato. “Evaṃ rūpaṃ hotu, mā eva”nti alabbhanīyato. Sayaṃ aññassa vase na vattati, nāpi aññaṃ attano vase vattetīti avasavattakato. Yasmiṃ santāne sayaṃ tassa paro viya avidheyyatāya parato. Kārakādi viya kāraṇehi, phalena ca vivittato. Na hi kāraṇena phalaṃ, phalena vā kāraṇaṃ sagabbhaṃ tiṭṭhati. Esa nayo vedanādīsupi.

763. One sees it as empty because of the absence of an essence of permanence and so on. Because of being insignificant or inferior, one sees it as worthless. As void because of the absence of an essence of self. As not-self because it is itself not-self. As without mastery, both because of the absence of mastery and because of the inability for anyone to effect mastery. Just as for one wishing to make a vessel from a lump of foam that does not succeed, so too for one wishing to effect permanence, etc., in form, that does not succeed; or, because there is no action whatsoever according to one’s own will, it is as not doable according to one's wish. As unobtainable because it is not obtainable through the wish, 'May form be thus; may it not be thus.' It does not itself proceed under the power of another, nor does it make another proceed under its own power; thus, it is as not subject to control. In whatever continuum it itself exists, because of its unmanageability with respect to that continuum, as if it were an outsider, one sees it as other. As separate from causes and from the effect, just as it is from an agent and so on. For indeed, the effect does not exist latent within the cause, nor the cause within the effect. This is the method also in regard to feeling and the rest.

764. Rūpaṃ na sattotiādīsu yo lokavohārena satto, rūpaṃ so na hotīti ayamattho idha nādhippeto tassāvuttasiddhattā. Na hi loko rūpamattaṃ “satto”ti voharati, bāhirakaparikappito pana attā “satto”ti adhippeto. So hi tehi rūpādīsu sattavisattatāya paresaṃ sañjāpanaṭṭhena “satto”ti vuccati, rūpaṃ so na hotīti attho. Suññatāpariggaṇhanañhetanti. Esa nayo na jīvotiādīsupi. Tattha jīvanaṭṭhena jīvo. Naranaṭṭhena netubhāvena naro. “Ahamasmī”ti mānuppattiṭṭhānatāya māno ettha vāti pavattatīti mānavo. Thiyati ettha gabbhoti itthī. Padhānabhāvena puri setīti puriso[M 2.0458]. Āhito ahaṃmāno etthāti attā. Paccattaṃ tassa tassa ahaṃkāravatthutāya “aha”nti ca diṭṭhigatikehi attā vuccati, rūpaṃ pana tādisaṃ na hotīti suññatāpariggaṇhanavidhiṃ dassetuṃ “rūpaṃ na satto”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tasmā aṭṭhahipi padehi rūpassa attasuññatāva dassitā. Itarehi catūhi tassa kiñcanatābhāvo. Tattha na mamāti mayhaṃ attano santakaṃ na hoti, tathā aññassa attano santakaṃ na hoti, kassacipi attano santakaṃ na hoti attanoyeva abhāvato. “Na attaniya”nti padena pakāsito evattho pariyāyantarehi tīhipi padehi pakāsito. Esa nayo vedanādīsupi.

764. In the phrase 'form is not a being,' etc., the meaning intended here is not that form is not the being spoken of by worldly convention, for that meaning is established without being stated. For the world does not refer to mere form as a 'being.' Rather, what is intended as a 'being' is the self conceived by outsiders. For that self is called a 'being' by them because of its nature of clinging and being attached to form and the like, and because of its meaning of causing others to become attached. The meaning is that form is not such a self. This is the comprehension of emptiness. This same method applies to 'not a living soul,' and so on. Therein, a 'living soul' (jīvo) is so called in the sense of living. A 'person' (naro) is so called in the sense of leading, by being one who leads. A 'human being' (mānavo) is so called because conceit (māno) arises or proceeds herein, it being the ground for the arising of the conceit 'I am.' A 'woman' (itthī) is so called because a fetus is established herein. A 'man' (puriso) is so called because he lies (seti) in front (puri) in a prominent way. A 'self' (attā) is so called because the conceit 'I' (ahaṃmāno) is placed herein. Because for each and every one it is the basis for the 'I-making' view, it is called 'I' and it is called 'self' by those with wrong views. But form is not of such a nature. Thus, to show the method for comprehending emptiness, 'form is not a being,' etc., was said. Therefore, by these eight terms, the emptiness of self in regard to form is shown. With the other four terms, its state of having no belongings is shown. Therein, 'not mine' means it is not the possession of my self; likewise, it is not the possession of another's self; it is not the possession of anyone's self, because of the very absence of a self. The very meaning explained by the term 'not of a self' is also explained by these three terms, which are alternative expressions. This same method applies to feeling and so on.

765. Heṭṭhā [V 2.0431] kalāpasammasanassa daḷhabhāvāya vuttasammasananayāpi suññatānupassanāya daḷhabhāvāya saṃvattantīti dassento “tīraṇapariññāvasenā”tiādimāha. Tattha bhayassa ahiṃsanena asaraṇato. “Saraṇa”nti gahetuṃ ayuttatāya asaraṇībhūtato. “Anassādato”ti idaṃ pāḷiyaṃ natthi. Sati ca tecattālīsa ākārā siyuṃ. Rūpappavattiyaṃ sabbādīnavūpaladdhiyā ādīnavato. “Samudayato atthaṅgamato”ti idaṃ dvayaṃ yathā aniccato dassanaṃ panāḷikāya, niccasāravirahadīpanena vā suññatāvibhāvanaṃ hoti, evaṃ suññatāvibhāvananti katvā vuttaṃ. Tathā “yaṃ kho rūpaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, ayaṃ rūpassa assādo”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.26) dassanaṃ paccayapaccayuppannatāvibhāvanena suññatāvibhāvanaṃ. “Yaṃ rūpaṃ aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, ayaṃ rūpassa ādīnavo”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.26) ca dassanaṃ niccatādisuññatābhāvanato. Tathā “yo rūpe chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ, idaṃ rūpassa nissaraṇa”nti evaṃ samudayādidassanānaṃ, itaresañca yathārahaṃ suññatānupassanānubrūhanatā daṭṭhabbā. Yaṃ pana ādīnavato dassanaṃ, pubbe vatvāpi puna vacanaṃ assādapaṭikkhepato dassanaṃ sandhāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Vedanādīsupi dvācattālīsa ākārā netabbāti āha “vedanaṃ…pe… viññāṇaṃ aniccato…pe… nissaraṇato passatī”ti.

765. To show that the aforesaid methods of comprehension, intended to strengthen the comprehension of groups below, also conduce to the strengthening of the contemplation of emptiness, he said: 'by way of the full understanding of investigation,' and so on. Herein, because it offers no protection from fear, it is without refuge. Because it is improper to take it as 'a refuge,' it has become without refuge. The phrase 'from being without gratification' is not found in the Pāli text; if it were, there would be forty-three aspects. In the occurrence of form, by perceiving all drawbacks, it is seen as a drawback. The pair 'from arising' and 'from passing away' is said to be a manifestation of emptiness, just as the seeing as impermanent, by showing the absence of a permanent essence, is a manifestation of emptiness. Likewise, the seeing of 'Whatever pleasure and joy arise dependent on form, this is the gratification in form' (SN 22.26) is a manifestation of emptiness by manifesting the arising of effects from conditions. And the seeing of 'Whatever form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, this is the drawback in form' (SN 22.26) is so by manifesting the emptiness of permanence and so on. Similarly, with 'The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for form, this is the escape from form,' the seeings of arising and so on, and of the others as is appropriate, should be understood as augmenting the contemplation of emptiness. As for the seeing as a drawback, though mentioned before, its repetition should be understood as stated in reference to the seeing which rejects gratification. The rest is by the same method as stated below. He says that forty-two aspects should be applied to feeling and the other aggregates as well: 'He sees feeling... pe... consciousness as impermanent... pe... as an escape.'

Vuttampi ca niddese etaṃ suññatāpariggaṇhanakathāsandassanaṃ “asukāya pāḷiyā ayaṃ niddeso”ti dassanatthaṃ, tassa phalasandassanatthañca.

And this presentation of the discourse on comprehending emptiness has also been stated in the Niddesa in order to show, 'This is the exposition of such and such a Pāli passage,' and in order to show its fruit.

766. Evaṃ [M 2.0459] tīraṇapariññāvasena paccekaṃ khandhesu dvācattālīsāya ākārehi suññataṃ pariggahetvāpi tividhānupassanāvaseneva bhāvanaṃ anuyuñjantassa saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇuppattīti dassento “evaṃ suññato”tiādimāha. Tattha pariggaṇhantoti sammasanto. Bhayañca nandiñca vippahāyāti ajjhupekkhakatāya saṅkhārānaṃ vipattiṃ nissāya uppajjanakabhayañceva tesaṃ sampattiṃ nissāya uppajjanakapītiñca pajahitvā. Atha vā bhayatupaṭṭhānavasena uppajjanakañāṇabhayañca sammasanavasena uppajjanakapītisaṅkhātaṃ nandiñca pahāya. Na hi sabbaso suññatāya diṭṭhāya bhayanandīnaṃ avasaro atthi, atha kho upekkhāva saṇṭhāti. Tenāha “saṅkhāresu udāsīno hotī”ti. Tattha yena micchāgāhena anudāsīnatā siyā, tadabhāvaṃ dassento “ahanti vā mamanti vā na gaṇhātī”ti āha. Idānissa udāsīnatāya upamaṃ dassento “vissaṭṭhabhariyo viya puriso”tiādimāha.

766. To show that for one who, having comprehended emptiness in each aggregate in forty-two aspects by way of the full understanding of investigation, still applies himself to the development by way of the threefold contemplation, the knowledge of equanimity towards formations arises, he said: 'Thus, as empty,' and so on. Herein, 'comprehending' means contemplating. 'Having abandoned fear and delight' means, through equanimity, having abandoned the fear that arises based on the failure of formations and the delight that arises based on their success.
