For even food and so on would become factors of enlightenment. By this, it is shown that being encompassed within the arising of the path-consciousness is not a reason for being a factor of enlightenment.

Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “maggamaggaparivāradhammā ca bodhipakkhiyā”ti, tattha parivāraṭṭho kiṃ sahapavattiattho, udāhu parikkhāraṭṭhoti? Yadi purimo pakkho, so pageva nillocito. Atha dutiyo, idaṃ vicāretabbaṃ. Kathaṃ pavattamānaṃ jhānaṃ maggassa parikkhāro? Yadi sahajātādipaccayabhāvena, evaṃ sati phassādīnampi maggaparikkhāratā āpajjati. Atha paṭipakkhavidhaṃsanena, na sabbe jhānadhammā paṭipakkhavidhaṃsanasamatthā. Na hi vicāro, vedanā ca kassaci saṃkilesadhammassa ujupaṭipakkhabhāvena pavattanti. Yaṃ pana peṭake “sukhaṃ uddhaccakukkuccassa, vicāro vicikicchāya paṭipakkho”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ pariyāyena vuttaṃ. Na hi sukhaṃ sayaṃ uddhaccakukkuccassa paṭipakkho, paṭipakkhassa pana samādhissa paccayatāya paṭipakkho. Na ca vicāro paññā viya, adhimokkho viya vā vicikicchāya paṭipakkho, paṭipakkhassa paṭirūpatāya pana paṭipakkho [M 2.0494] vutto. Tathā pītipi na byāpādassa adoso viya ujupaṭipakkho, adosasampayogato pana paṭipakkho vutto. Tena vuttaṃ “taṃ pariyāyena vutta”nti. Vitakkasamādhayo eva pana jhānadhammesu ujukaṃ paṭipakkhavidhaṃsanasamatthāti paṭipakkhaviddhaṃsanasamatthassa paripuṇṇassa jhānakoṭṭhāsassa abhāvato na cassa bodhipakkhiyesu saṅgaho kato. Yasmā pana sammāsaṅkappo, sammāsamādhi ca maggapariyāpannā jhānadhammā, tasmā te sandhāya taṃsampayuttatāya vā itarepi gahetvā pariyāyena vuttaṃ pāḷiyaṃ “yasmiṃ samaye lokuttaraṃ jhānaṃ bhāveti niyyānika”ntiādi (dha. sa. 277).

As for what was said, “The dhammas that are the retinue of the path are also factors of enlightenment,” here, does the meaning of ‘retinue’ imply ‘co-arising,’ or does it imply ‘requisite’? If the former, that has already been examined. If the latter, this should be investigated: In what way does an occurring jhāna serve as a requisite for the path? If it is by way of being a co-nascence condition and so on, then in that case, contact and other factors would also have to be considered requisites of the path. If it is by way of destroying the opponent, not all jhāna factors are capable of destroying an opponent. For sustained thought and feeling do not arise as direct opponents to any defiling factor. As for what is stated in the Peṭakopadesa, “Happiness is the opponent of restlessness and remorse; sustained thought is the opponent of doubt,” this is stated figuratively. For happiness itself is not the opponent of restlessness and remorse; rather, it is called an opponent because it is a condition for concentration, which is the opponent. And sustained thought is not an opponent to doubt in the way that wisdom or resolve are; rather, it is called an opponent because of its resemblance to the opponent. Likewise, rapture is not a direct opponent to ill will in the way that non-aversion is; rather, it is called an opponent because it is associated with non-aversion. Therefore it was said, “This is stated figuratively.” Among the jhāna factors, only initial thought and concentration are capable of directly destroying an opponent. Thus, due to the absence of a complete set of jhāna factors capable of destroying an opponent, this jhāna-component is not included among the factors of enlightenment. However, since right thought and right concentration are jhāna factors included in the path, it is with reference to them—or by their association, thereby including the other factors as well—that it is stated figuratively in the Pāḷi: “At the time when one develops the supramundane jhāna that leads to release,” etc.

Vuṭṭhānabalasamāyogakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Discourse on the Combination of the Powers of Emergence

827. Vuṭṭhānaṃ nimittato, pavattato ca vuṭṭhānaṃ. Balasamāyogo samathavipassanābalehi sampayuttatā. Pariññābhisamayādivasena dukkhādīsu visesadassanaṭṭhena maggapaññāpi vipassanāti vuccatīti “lokiyavipassanā”ti visesetvā vuttaṃ. Tenevāha “vuṭṭhānaṭṭhena samathavipassanaṃ yuganaddhaṃ bhāvetī”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.5). Nimittārammaṇattā nevanimittā vuṭṭhāti, pavatti…pe… chindanato na pavattā vuṭṭhātīti yojanā. Tattha nimittato vuṭṭhānaṃ saṅkhāranimittaṃ nissajjitvā nibbānārammaṇakaraṇaṃ. Pavattato vuṭṭhānaṃ hetunirodhena āyatiṃ vipākappavattassa [V 2.0465] anuppavattidhammatāpādanaṃ. Tenāha “samudayassa asamucchindanato pavattā na vuṭṭhātī”ti.

827. Emergence is from the sign, and emergence is from the continuum. The combination of powers is the state of being associated with the powers of serenity and insight. Because path-wisdom, in the sense of seeing distinctly in regard to suffering and so forth by way of full understanding, penetration, and so on, is also called 'insight,' it is specifically stated as 'mundane insight.' Therefore, He said: 'In the sense of emergence, one develops serenity and insight yoked together.' The connection is as follows: because it has the sign as its object, it does not emerge from the sign; because of not cutting off the origin, it does not emerge from the continuum. Here, emergence from the sign is the abandoning of the sign of formations and making Nibbāna the object. Emergence from the continuum is the bringing about of the nature of non-arising for the future continuum of resultants through the cessation of their cause. Therefore, He said: 'Because of not cutting off the origin, one does not emerge from the continuum.'

Dubhatoti ubhato, da-kārāgamaṃ katvā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Dubhāti vā padantaramevetaṃ ubhayasaddena samānatthaṃ. Dassanaṭṭhenāti pariññābhisamayādilakkhaṇena catusaccadassanaṭṭhena. Micchādiṭṭhiyāti dvāsaṭṭhippabhedāyapi micchādiṭṭhiyā. Tadanuvattakakilesehīti apāyagamanīyatāya tassā micchādiṭṭhiyā anuvattakehi vicikicchādikilesehi. Khandhehīti etthāpi tadanuvattakasaddo ānetvā sambandhitabbo. Te ca micchādiṭṭhiādipaccayā uppajjanārahā veditabbā. Micchāsaṅkappātiādīsupi tadanuvattakakilesehi ca khandhehi ca vuṭṭhāti. Bahiddhā ca sabbanimittehi vuṭṭhātīti pāḷi saṃkhittā. Yathā micchādiṭṭhimicchāsaṅkappā, evaṃ micchāvācādayopi apāyagamanīyā eva veditabbā. Micchāvācākammantājīvā cetanāsabhāvā. Micchāsati tathāpavattā cattāro khandhā. Uparimaggattaye sammādiṭṭhi taṃtaṃmaggavajjhā [M 2.0495] mānato vuṭṭhāti. So hi “ahamasmī”ti pavattiyā diṭṭhiṭṭhāniyo, micchāmaggato panettha vuṭṭhānaṃ anuddharitvā taṃtaṃmaggavajjhasaṃyojanānusayeheva vuṭṭhānaṃ uddhaṭaṃ.

‘Dubhato’ means ‘from both sides’; it is said thus by adding the augment ‘da-’. Or ‘dubha’ is simply another word with the same meaning as the word ‘ubhaya’ (both). ‘In the sense of seeing’ means in the sense of seeing the four truths, characterized by full understanding, penetration, and so on. ‘From wrong view’ means from wrong view, even that which has sixty-two divisions. ‘From the defilements that follow it’ means from the defilements such as doubt that follow that wrong view, due to its nature of leading to the lower realms. ‘From the aggregates’—here too, the word ‘that which follows it’ should be brought in and connected. And those aggregates should be understood as liable to arise due to conditions such as wrong view. In the cases of wrong intention and so forth as well, the Pali text stating that one ‘emerges from the defilements and aggregates that follow them, and externally from all signs’ is condensed. Just as wrong view and wrong intention are states that lead to the lower realms, so too should wrong speech and the others be understood as states that lead to the lower realms. Wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood are of the nature of volition. Wrong mindfulness is the four aggregates occurring in that way. In the higher three paths, right view emerges from pride, which is to be abandoned by the respective path. For that pride, due to its occurrence as ‘I am’, stands in the place of a view. Here, however, without extracting the emergence from the wrong path, the emergence from the very fetters and latent tendencies to be abandoned by the respective path is extracted.

Aṇusahagatāti aṇubhāvaṃ gatā pattā, tanubhūtāti attho.

‘Aṇusahagatā’ means having attained a subtle state, reached it, become subtle—this is the meaning.

828. Evaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ dassetvā idāni balasamāyogaṃ dassetuṃ “lokiyānañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Samathabalaṃ adhikaṃ hoti samādhibhāvanābhāvato. Vipassanābalaṃ adhikaṃ hoti ñāṇuttarattā vipassanābhāvanāya. Samānabhāvena yuge naddhā baddhā viya hontīti yuganaddhā. Tenāha “aññamaññaṃ anativattanaṭṭhenā”ti, kiccato anūnādhikabhāvenāti attho. Tato eva samāyogoti samaparicchedayogoti attho.

828. Having thus shown emergence, now, to show the combination of powers, the passage beginning ‘and of the mundane’ was stated. The power of serenity is greater due to the development of concentration. The power of insight is greater due to the superiority of knowledge in the development of insight. Because they are, as it were, tied and bound to a yoke in an equal manner, they are called ‘yuganaddhā’ (yoked together). Therefore, it is said: ‘in the sense of not surpassing each other,’ which means, with respect to function, being neither deficient nor excessive. For that very reason, there is combination, which means the union of equal measure.

Samādhipaṭipakkhadassanatthaṃ “uddhaccasahagatakilesehī”ti vuttaṃ, uddhaccapadhānehi kilesehīti adhippāyo. Avikkhepo samādhīti samucchindanena vikkhepassa ujupaṭipakkhabhūto samādhi. Nirodhagocaroti nibbānārammaṇo. Vuṭṭhānaṭṭhenāti vuṭṭhānakabhāvena nimittato, pavattato ca vuṭṭhahamānavasena. Ekarasāti samānakiccā.

For the purpose of showing the opposing factor to concentration, it is said, 'from defilements accompanied by restlessness'; the meaning is, from defilements predominated by restlessness. As for 'non-distraction is concentration': concentration is the direct opposite of distraction by way of utterly cutting it off. As for 'having cessation as its object': it has Nibbāna as its object. As for 'in the sense of emergence': by way of being the emergence, by the power of emerging from the sign and from the internal occurrence. As for 'of one essence': they have the same function.

Pahātabbadhammapahānakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Discourse on the Abandoning of Phenomena to Be Abandoned

829. Ye [V 2.0466] dhammāti ye saṃkilesadhammā. Saṃyojanādīsu saṃyojanaṭṭhena bandhanaṭṭhena saṃyojanāni, vibādhanaṭṭhena, upatāpanaṭṭhena vā kilesā, micchāsabhāvāti micchattā, loke dhammā lokapariyāpannā dhammāti lokadhammā, maccherassa bhāvo, kammaṃ vāti macchariyaṃ, viparītaṭṭhena vipallāsā, ganthanaṭṭhena ganthā, ayuttā gatīti agati, āsavantīti āsavā, ohanantīti oghā, yojanaṭṭhena yogā, nīvarantīti nīvaraṇāni, dhammasabhāvaṃ atikkamma parato āmasantīti parāmāsā, bhusaṃ ādiyantīti upādānāni, appahīnabhāvena santāne anu anu sentīti anusayā, malīnabhāvakaraṇaṭṭhena malā, akusalakammāni ca tāni sugatiduggatīnaṃ, tattha nibbattanakasukhadukkhānañca pathā cāti akusalakammapathā, cittaṃ uppajjati etthāti cittuppādo, cittacetasikarāsi[M 2.0496], akusalo ca so cittuppādo cāti akusalacittuppādoti akusalasaddaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ.

829. As for 'which phenomena' (ye dhammā), it means which defiling phenomena. In terms of fetters and the like: fetters (saṃyojanāni) are so called because of the meaning of fettering or the meaning of binding; defilements (kilesā) are so called because of the meaning of oppressing or tormenting; because they have a wrong nature, they are called wrongnesses (micchattā); because they are phenomena in the world, phenomena included in the world, they are called worldly phenomena (lokadhammā); stinginess (macchariyaṃ) is the state or act of a miser; perversions (vipallāsā) are so called because of the inverted meaning; bonds (ganthā) are so called because of the meaning of tying in knots; a wrong course (agati) is an improper course; influxes (āsavā) are so called because they flow out; floods (oghā) are so called because they submerge; yokes (yogā) are so called because of the meaning of yoking; hindrances (nīvaraṇāni) are so called because they hinder; misapprehensions (parāmāsā) are so called because they transgress the true nature of phenomena and grasp wrongly; graspings (upādānāni) are so called because they grasp intensely; latent tendencies (anusayā) are so called because they lie dormant again and again in the mental continuum due to the state of not yet being abandoned; stains (malā) are so called because of the meaning of causing a state of stain. And they are unwholesome actions, and those are also the paths to good and bad destinations and to the pleasure and pain to be produced therein; therefore, they are called unwholesome courses of action (akusalakammapathā). An arising of mind (cittuppādo) is so called because the mind arises therein; it is a mass of mind and mental factors. And that arising of mind is unwholesome; thus, the word 'unwholesome' should be brought in and connected, as 'unwholesome arising of mind' (akusalacittuppādo).

Khandhehi khandhānanti idhalokakkhandhehi paralokakkhandhānaṃ. Yāvañhi teti te rūparāgādayo yāva pavattanti na samucchijjanti, tāva etesaṃ khandhaphaladukkhānaṃ anuparamo avicchedoti. Etena tesaṃ saṃyojanatthaṃ vibhāveti. Uddhanti rūpārūpabhavesu, tatiyamagguppattiyā vā uddhaṃ. Uddhaṃ bhajantīti uddhaṃbhāgā, rūpārūpabhavā, tesaṃ avicchedahetutāya hitāni uddhaṃbhāgiyāni.

‘From aggregates, aggregates’ means the aggregates of the next world from the aggregates of this present world. For as long as those, such as lust for form, etc., continue to arise and are not utterly cut off, so long is there no cessation, no cutting off, of this suffering which is the result of the aggregates. By this, their meaning as a fetter is made clear. ‘Uddhaṃ’ (upward) means in the form and formless existences, or upward from the arising of the third path. ‘They resort to what is upward’, thus they are called ‘uddhaṃbhāgā’ (pertaining to the upper part), which are the form and formless existences. Because they are conducive to the non-cessation of those upper existences, they are called ‘uddhaṃbhāgiyāni’ (pertaining to the upper part).

Kilissanti, kilesenti cāti duvidhampi atthaṃ dassento “sayaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhattā”tiādimāha.

Showing both meanings, namely, ‘they are defiled’ and ‘they defile’, he said the passage beginning, ‘because of being defiled oneself’.

Micchāvimutti “lokathūpikādīsu mokkho”ti pavattamicchāvimokkho. Abhinivisanādivasena micchā viparītaṃ na sammā pavattanato micchāñāṇaṃ mohova.

‘Wrong liberation’ is the wrong liberation that occurs as the view ‘this is liberation’ in regard to worldly peaks, etc. Because it occurs wrongly, pervertedly, and not rightly, by the power of firm adherence, etc., ‘wrong knowledge’ is simply delusion.

Lokappavattiyāti khandhappavattiyaṃ sati. Anuparamadhammakattāti puññapāpavasena aparāparaṃ avicchijjanato. “Lābhahetuko lābho”tiādinā kāraṇopacārena.

‘In the occurrence of the world’ means when there is the occurrence of the aggregates. ‘Because of being a state of non-cessation’ means because of its successive, unbroken occurrence by the power of merit and demerit. By such phrases as ‘gain which has gain as its cause’, it is by way of causal metaphor.

Āvāse macchariyaṃ, āvāsahetukaṃ vā macchariyaṃ āvāsamacchariyaṃ.

Stinginess regarding a dwelling (āvāsamacchariyaṃ) is stinginess in regard to a dwelling, or stinginess that has a dwelling as its cause.

Tayoti [V 2.0467] vatthuṃ abhinditvā vuttaṃ, bhinditvā pana vuccamāne dvādasa honti.

‘Three’ is said without dividing the subject matter. But when it is spoken of having divided it, there are twelve.

Ganthakaraṇaṃ kāraṇabhāvena paṭibaddhatākaraṇaṃ ganthananti taṃ rūpakāyepi labbhatīti āha “nāmakāyassa ceva rūpakāyassa cā”ti. Tattha byāpādassāpi abhisajjanupanayhavasena pavattanato ganthanaṭṭho veditabbo, yato tassa paṭighasaṃyojanabhāvo vutto.

The making of a bond, by way of being a cause, is the making of a state of being bound; this is called ‘binding’ (ganthanaṃ). Since that is also found in the physical body, he said, ‘of the mental body and of the physical body’. Therein, the meaning of ‘binding’ should also be understood for ill will, because it occurs by the power of clinging and grudge-bearing, for its state as the fetter of aversion has been stated.

Chandadosamohabhayehīti chandadosamohabhayahetu. Tañhīti akattabbakaraṇaṃ, kattabbākaraṇañca.

‘By desire, aversion, delusion, and fear’ means because of the cause that is desire, aversion, delusion, and fear. ‘That indeed’ means the doing of what should not be done and the not doing of what should be done.

Savanāti pavattanato. Savanatoti kilesāsucibhāvena vissandanato. Puna savanatoti pasavanato.

‘Flowing’ (savanā) is because it occurs (pavattanato). ‘From flowing’ (savanato) is because it oozes (vissandanato) with the impurity of defilements. ‘Again, from flowing’ (puna savanato) is because it generates (pasavanato).

Ākaḍḍhanaṭṭhena[M 2.0497], duruttaraṇaṭṭhena cāti etena oghā viya oghāti dasseti. Ārammaṇena, dukkhena ca viyogassa appadānasaṅkhātena yojanaṭṭhena yogāti dasseti, saṃkilesakaraṇaṭṭhenāti attho. Tesaññevāti kāmarāgādīnaṃyeva. Te hi sotavasena vattamānā soto viya sotapatite satte apāyasamuddaṃ pāpenti, saṃsārasamuddato ca sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ na denti, yathāgahitañca ārammaṇaṃ vissajjituṃ na denti, yādisañca pāpaṃ katvā dukkhappatte punapi tādisena yojenti.

By the meaning of dragging down and by the meaning of being hard to cross, it is shown that because they are like floods, they are called 'floods'. By the meaning of yoking, which is described as the non-giving of separation from the object and from suffering, it is shown that they are called 'yokes'; the meaning is by the act of causing clinging. 'Of those very things' means of sensual desire and the rest only. For they, occurring by way of a current, like a stream, cause beings who have fallen into the stream to reach the ocean of the lower realms; they do not allow them to lift their heads from the ocean of saṃsāra, nor do they allow them to release the object as it was grasped; and having done whatever evil and reached suffering, they yoke them again with a similar kind.

Cittassāti kusalacittassa, visesato jhānacittassa. Ādito varaṇaṃ āvaraṇaṃ. Kilesavāsanaṃ netvā varaṇaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ. Kuṭṭakavāṭādīhi viya pidahanaṃ paṭicchādanaṃ, taṃ pana kusalādīni saṅgaṇhituṃ, pariññātuṃ, ñātuñca appadānavasena daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Of the mind' means of the wholesome mind, specifically the jhānic mind. In the beginning, obstructing (varaṇa) is an obstruction (āvaraṇa). Leading away the latent tendencies of defilements, obstructing (varaṇa) is a hindrance (nīvaraṇa). Like a closing by means of a wall, a door-leaf, and so on, it is a covering. But that should be seen by way of not allowing the grasping, fully understanding, and knowing of wholesome states and so on.

Tassa tassa dhammassa sabhāvanti kāyādikassa tassa tassa dhammassa asubhādisabhāvaṃ. Abhūtaṃ sabhāvanti subhādisabhāvaṃ.

'The true nature of each and every phenomenon' means the true nature of foulness and so on of each and every phenomenon such as the body. 'The unreal nature' means the unreal, mistaken nature of beauty and so on.

Thāmagataṭṭhenāti thāmagatabhāvena. Thāmagatanti ca anaññasādhāraṇo kāmarāgādīnaṃ sabhāvo daṭṭhabbo. Yena te eva bhagavatā “anusayā”ti vuttā. Anusayanañca maggena appahīnabhāvena paccayasamavāye uppajjanārahatā. Tenāha “punappunaṃ kāmarāgādīnaṃ uppattihetubhāvena anusentiyevā”ti.

'By the meaning of having reached strength' means by the state of having reached strength. And 'having reached strength' should be understood as the intrinsic nature of sensual lust and so on, which is not shared with other defilements. For which reason, they alone were called 'latent tendencies' by the Blessed One. And 'lying dormant' is the state of being fit to arise when there is a conjunction of conditions, due to not yet being abandoned by the path. Therefore, he said: 'Because they are the cause for the repeated arising of sensual lust and so on, they indeed lie dormant.'

Dummocanīyabhāvena [V 2.0468] pavattiṃ sandhāyāha “telañjanakalalaṃ viyā”ti.

With reference to the occurrence being difficult to be freed from, he said: 'like a mire of oil and soot.'

830. Sesāti anapāyagamanīyā. Sukhumā kāmarāgapaṭighāti sambandho. Catutthañāṇavajjhā evāti avadhāraṇena paṭhamañāṇādivajjhatā nivattīyati. Tayidaṃ niyamadassanaṃ aññatthāpi netabbanti dassento “parato”tiādimāha. Tattha “niyamaṃ na karissāmā”ti etena niyame akate heṭṭhimamaggavajjhatāpi anuññātā eva hotīti.

'The rest' means those that are not 'leading to the lower realms'. The connection is: 'subtle sensual lust and aversion'. By the emphasis in 'to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge only', the state of being abandoned by the first knowledge and so on is precluded. Showing that this showing of a definite rule should be applied elsewhere also, he said 'from another,' and so on. Therein, by this statement, 'We will not make a definite rule,' when a definite rule is not made, the state of being abandoned by the lower paths also is indeed permitted.

Lobha…pe… catutthañāṇavajjhānītiādīsu paṭhamañāṇādīhi hatāpāyagamanīyādibhāvānīti adhippāyo veditabbo. Ādisaddena oḷārikasukhumatā gahitā.

830. In such phrases as 'Greed... and so on... are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge,' the meaning should be understood thus: the states of being liable to lead to the plane of misery, etc., have been destroyed by the first knowledge, etc. By the word 'etc.' (ādi), coarseness and subtlety are included.

Yaseti parivāre.

'Glory' (yasa) is in the context of the retinue.

Agatīsu [M 2.0498] chandādayo kiñcāpi uparimaggavajjhā, tathāpi taṃmūlakassa akattabbakaraṇassa, kattabbākaraṇassa ca apāyagamanīyatāya paṭhamamaggavajjhā.

Although desire and so forth, in the context of the wrong courses, are to be abandoned by the higher paths, nevertheless, because the doing of what should not be done and the not-doing of what should be done are rooted in them, they are to be abandoned by the first path due to their nature of leading to the plane of misery.

Katākatākusalākusalavisayaṃ yaṃ vippaṭisārabhūtaṃ kukkuccaṃ, taṃ idha tatiyañāṇavajjhaṃ vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana “kukkuccapakatatāya āpattimāpajjatī”ti (pāci. aṭṭha. 438; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. nidānavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ kukkuccaṃ, taṃ sandhāya “kukkuccavicikicchā sotāpattimaggena pahīyantī”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1176) aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tasmā dvinnaṃ vacanānaṃ adhippāyo veditabbo. Aññesupi edisesu ṭhānesu adhippāyo maggitabbo, na virodhato paccetabbo. Oḷārikānavasesappahānaṃ vā sandhāya kukkuccassa paṭhamatatiyañāṇavajjhatā vuttāti veditabbaṃ. “Bhagavatā paṭikkhittaṃ anuvasitvā anuvasitvā āvasathapiṇḍaṃ bhuñjitu”nti, “kukkuccāyanto na paṭiggahesī”ti (pāci. 204) pana āgataṃ kukkuccaṃ, na nīvaraṇaṃ arahato uppajjanato, nīvaraṇapaṭirūpakaṃ pana “kappati na kappatī”ti vīmaṃsanabhūtaṃ vinayakukkuccaṃ nāma, taṃ tathāpavattacittuppādova.

That remorse which is the nature of regret concerning unwholesome deeds that have been done and wholesome deeds that have not been done, is said here to be abandoned by the third knowledge. But as for the remorse that is mentioned thus, 'One commits an offense due to being overcome by remorse,' it is with reference to that remorse that it is said in the Aṭṭhasālinī, 'Remorse and doubt are abandoned by the path of stream-entry.' Therefore, the intention of the two statements should be understood. In other such instances, the intention should be sought and not assumed to be contradictory. Or, it should be known that the state of remorse being abandoned by the first and third knowledges is stated with reference to the abandonment of the gross form and the abandonment without remainder. As for the remorse that is found in the passage, 'Thinking, "It has been forbidden by the Blessed One to eat almsfood from a guest-house day after day," he, being scrupulous, did not accept it,' this is not a hindrance, because it arises in an Arahant. It is, however, a counterfeit of a hindrance, called 'disciplinary scruples' (vinayakukkucca), which is a state of investigation, thinking, 'Is this allowable or not allowable?' It is merely a mind-moment that arises in such a way.

Kāmarāgapaṭighānusayā aṇusahagatā tatiyañāṇavajjhā. Oḷārikānaṃ pana dutiyañāṇavajjhatā heṭṭhā vuttanayāva.

The underlying tendencies of sensual lust and aversion, being subtle, are to be abandoned by the third knowledge. As for the gross forms, their state of being abandoned by the second knowledge is just according to the method stated previously.

Cittuppādaggahaṇena [V 2.0469] cettha makkhapaḷāsamāyāsāṭheyyapamādathambhasārambhādīnaṃ saṅgaho katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

And it should be understood that here, by the inclusion of 'thought-arising' (cittuppāda), the inclusion of denigration, contentiousness, deceit, hypocrisy, heedlessness, stubbornness, presumption, and so on, is made.

831. Aphalo vāyāmoti ettha atītānaṃ tāva pajahane aphalo hotu vāyāmo niruddhattā, anāgatānaṃ pana kathanti tesampi vakkhamānaṃ aviparītamatthaṃ ajānanto natthitāmattaṃ gahetvā codeti, tathāpi “aphalo”ti pubbe pahātabbānaṃ natthitāya codanā katā, idāni pahānassa. Yadi hi pahānaṃ atthi, kathaṃ pahātabbā santi? Atha pahātabbā santi, kathaṃ pahānaṃ hoti? Pahātabbā ca santi, pahānañca hotīti vippaṭisiddhametaṃ. Kasmā? Pahātabbesu santesu pahānassa asambhavato tadupago vāyāmo aphalo ālokatamānaṃ sahāvaṭṭhāne sati ālokassa aphalatā viya. Athāpi kathañci pahānaṃ siyā? Saṃkilesikā ca maggabhāvanā āpajjati pahātabbapahāyakānaṃ sahāvaṭṭhānato[M 2.0499]. Vippayuttatā vā kilesānaṃ cittavippayuttasaṅkhāravādīnaṃ vippayuttasaṅkhārānaṃ viyāti adhippāyo. Taṃ pana nesaṃ vādīnaṃ yathā matimattaṃ, evamidhāpīti dassento āha “na ca paccuppannakileso cittavippayutto nāma atthī”ti. Arūpadhammā hi ekavatthukādibhāvena vattamānā khaṇattayapariyāpannā paccuppannā, te kathaṃ cittena vippayuttā nāma siyuṃ, tasmā nattheva vippayuttatā kilesānaṃ. Āveṇikāti asādhāraṇā, sayameva uppāditā pāḷi anāruḷhāti adhippāyo. Pāḷiyaṃyeva hi paṭikkhittanti sambandho. Svāyaṃ puggalo. Hañcīti yadi.

In this text, 'The effort is fruitless': Firstly, in the abandoning of past defilements, let the effort be fruitless, because they have ceased. But regarding the abandoning of future ones, how is it? Thus, not knowing the correct meaning that will be stated concerning them as well, and grasping merely their non-existence, one raises an objection. Nevertheless, the objection 'fruitless' was made previously based on the non-existence of what is to be abandoned; now, it is regarding the abandoning itself. For if abandoning exists, how can there be things to be abandoned? And if there are things to be abandoned, how does abandoning occur? That there are things to be abandoned and that abandoning happens—this is contradictory. Why? Because as long as the things to be abandoned exist, abandoning cannot occur; the effort directed toward it is fruitless, just like the fruitlessness of light when light and darkness coexist. Furthermore, if by some means abandoning were to occur, the development of the path would become associated with defilement, due to the co-existence of the things to be abandoned and that which abandons. Or, the intention is that there might be a disassociation of the defilements, like the disassociated formations of those who advocate for mind-disassociated formations. But just as that is merely the opinion of those theorists, so it is here too—showing this, he said: 'There is no so-called present-moment defilement that is disassociated from the mind.' For immaterial dhammas, occurring by way of having a single basis, etc., and being included in the three moments, are 'present'. How could they be called 'disassociated from the mind'? Therefore, there is indeed no disassociation of the defilements. 'Āveṇikā' means: not shared, produced by oneself (the commentator), not found in the Pāḷi canon; this is the meaning. For it is rejected in the Pāḷi itself—this is the connection. 'This individual' (svāyaṃ puggalo). 'Hañci'—If.

Vinibaddhoti mānena patthaddhacitto. Parāmaṭṭhoti micchābhiniviṭṭho. Thāmagatoti thāmagatakileso thirabhāvagatānusayo. Tena hi natthi maggabhāvanāti yasmā tīsupi kālesu kilesānaṃ pahānaṃ na yujjati, tikālikā ca kilesā, tasmā natthi maggabhāvanā, tāya sādhetabbaṃ kiccaṃ natthīti attho. “Na hi natthi maggabhāvanā”tiādinā catukkhattuṃ vuttassa paṭikkhepassa paṭikkhepo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ “pāḷiyaṃyeva hī”tiādiṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ.

Bound: his mind is rigid with pride. Clinging: he is entrenched in wrong views. Obstinate: his defilements have become tenacious and his underlying tendencies have become fixed. Therefore, there is no development of the path—because the abandoning of defilements is not suitable in the three time periods, and the defilements are of the three time periods; therefore, there is no development of the path, and there is no task to be accomplished by it—this is the meaning. The phrase ‘Indeed, it is not that there is no development of the path,’ and so on, is the refutation of the rejection that was stated four times. This should be connected by bringing in what was stated in the Pāḷi itself.

Evamevāti yathā ajātaphale taruṇarukkhe mūle chinne asati chedane āyatiṃ uppajjanārahāni chedanapaccayā anuppajjamānāni vinaṭṭhāni nāma honti, evameva maggabhāvanāya asati uppajjanārahā kilesā maggabhāvanāya anuppajjamānā “pahīnā”ti vuccantīti upamāsaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Uppādoti uppādasīsena uppādavanto khandhā vuttā. Anuppādeti [V 2.0470] nibbāne. Ajātāyeva na jāyanti, tasmā pahīnā nāma hontīti “natthi kilesappahāna”nti paravādinā kato paṭikkhepo “na hī”ti paṭikkhitto. Te pana neva uppajjitvā vigatā, nāpi bhavissanti, na ca uppannāti “atīte kilese pajahatī”tiādi na vattabbanti dasseti. Hetunirodhāti dukkhahetūnaṃ kilesānaṃ nirodhā. Dukkhanirodhoti āyatiṃ uppajjanakadukkhassa nirodho. Uppādapavattanimittāyūhanā paccuppannabhavavasena gahitā.

So it is: just as with a young tree that has not yet borne fruit, when its root is cut, the fruits that would have been fit to arise in the future (had there been no cutting) do not arise because of the cutting, and are thus called 'destroyed'; so too, the defilements that were fit to arise (if there were no development of the path) do not arise because of the development of the path, and are thus said to be 'abandoned.' This application of the simile should be understood thus. 'Arising': by this are meant the aggregates that possess arising, with arising as their chief characteristic. 'In non-arising': this means in Nibbāna. Because they are unborn, they do not arise; therefore they are called 'abandoned.' Thus the rejection made by the opponent—'there is no abandoning of defilements'—is refuted by 'indeed not.' Furthermore, those defilements have neither ceased after having arisen, nor will they come to be, nor are they arising. This shows that it should not be said, 'one abandons past defilements,' and so on. 'From the cessation of the cause' means from the cessation of the defilements that are the cause of suffering. 'Cessation of suffering' means the cessation of suffering that would arise in the future. The accumulation of signs of arising and continuation is grasped in relation to present existence.

832. Etenāti “ajātāyeva na jāyantī”tiādivacanena. Vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtaṃ upādānakkhandhapañcakasaṅkhātaṃ bhūmipavattiṭṭhānaṃ laddhavanto bhūmiladdhā yathā “aggiāhito”ti, laddhabhūmikāti attho[M 2.0500]. Vattamānādiuppannavidhuratāya bhūmiladdhuppannā eva nāma teti vuttaṃ.

832. By this is meant: by the statement beginning, 'Being unborn, they do not arise.' Having obtained the ground—the place of occurrence—which is the object of insight and is designated as the five aggregates of clinging, they are 'ground-attained,' just as in the example 'one who has placed the fire'; the meaning is 'having an obtained ground.' It is said that they are indeed called 'arisen having obtained the ground' because of being distinct from what has arisen, such as the present.

833. Anubhavitvā, bhavitvā ca apagataṃ bhūtāpagataṃ. Anubhūtabhūtā hi bhūtatāsāmaññena bhūtasaddena vuttā. Sāmaññameva hi upasaggena visesīyatīti. Anubhūtasaddo ca kammavacanicchāya abhāvato anubhāvakavācako daṭṭhabbo. Vikappagāhavasena rāgādīhi, tabbipakkhehi ca akusalaṃ, kusalañca ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavati, na vipāko kammavegakkhittattā, nāpi kiriyā ahetukānaṃ atidubbalatāya, sahetukānañca khīṇakilesassa chaḷaṅgupekkhāvato uppajjamānānaṃ atisantavuttittā. Ettha ca purimanaye kusalākusalameva vattuṃ adhippāyavasena “bhūtāpagata”nti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ “uppannānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.651-662; vibha. 390-391) ettha “uppanna”nti gahetvā taṃsadisānaṃ pahānaṃ, vuddhi ca vuttā. Pacchimanaye ca-saddena kusalākusalañca ākaḍḍhitvā sabbaṃ saṅkhataṃ vuttaṃ bhutvāpagatabhāvābhidhānādhippāyena. Vipaccituṃ okāsakaraṇavasena uppattitaṃ atītaṃ kammañca tato uppajjituṃ āraddho vipāko ca anāgato okāsakatuppannoti vutto okāso kato etena, okāso kato etassāti ca atthadvayavasena, yaṃ uppannasaddena vināpi viññāyamānaṃ uppannaṃ sandhāya “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sañcetanikānaṃ kammāna”ntiādi (a. ni. 10.217, 219) vuttaṃ.

833. Having experienced and having been, that which is gone is 'past and gone.' Indeed, 'experienced' and 'been' are spoken of by the word 'been' due to the commonality of their nature as 'what has been.' For it is just the general meaning that is specified by the prefix. And the word 'experienced' should be understood as denoting the experiencer, due to the absence of the intention to express the passive voice. By way of grasping through conceptualization, the unwholesome (such as lust, etc.) and the wholesome (their opposites) experience the flavor of the object; the resultant does not, because it is thrown by the force of kamma; nor does the functional, in the case of the rootless, due to their extreme weakness, and in the case of the root-accompanied, which arise for one with defilements destroyed and who possesses six-factored equanimity, due to their extremely tranquil occurrence. And here, in the first method, it is said as 'past and gone' with the intention of speaking only of the wholesome and unwholesome. Regarding that, in the passage 'for the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states, for the maintenance of arisen wholesome states,' having taken it as 'arisen,' the abandoning and growth of similar states are spoken of. In the latter method, by the word 'and,' having drawn in the wholesome and unwholesome as well, all that is conditioned is spoken of with the intention of denoting the state of having been and gone. Past kamma that has become present by way of making an opportunity to ripen, and the future resultant that has begun to arise from that, are called 'arisen by opportunity made.' This is said in a twofold sense: 'an opportunity was made by this' and 'an opportunity was made for this.' Referring to that which is understood as 'arisen' even without the word 'arisen,' it is said: 'Monks, I do not say of intentional actions...' and so on.

Tāsu tāsu bhūmīsūti manussadevādiattabhāvasaṅkhātesu upādānakkhandhesu. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ santāne [V 2.0471] anuppattidhammataṃ anāpāditatāya asamūhataṃ. Asamūhatattāyeva hissa natthīti navattabbatāya uppannavohāro.

'In those various planes' means: in the aggregates of clinging designated as the individual existences of humans, devas, and so on. In each respective continuity, it is uneradicated because the state of having the nature of non-arising has not yet been brought about. Indeed, precisely because it is uneradicated, it should not be said, 'it does not exist'; hence, there is the conventional expression 'arisen'.

834. “Kā bhūmi, ko vā bhūmiladdho”ti āsaṅkaṃ nivattetuṃ “ettha cā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. “Vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtā”ti etena khandhānaṃ apariññātataṃ dasseti, na ārammaṇabhāvamattaṃ tebhūmakaggahaṇeneva tassa siddhattā. Apariññātā hi khandhā kilesānaṃ bhūmīti adhippetā. Khandhesu vatthubhūtesu. Ārammaṇavasenāti ārammaṇakaraṇavasena. Atītānāgate, pageva paccuppanneti adhippāyo. Tanti taṃ aññasantānagataṃ [M 2.0501] kilesajātaṃ. Tato aññasmiṃ santāne ārammaṇakaraṇamattena bhūmiladdhaṃ nāma yadi siyāti sambandho. Tassāti kilesajātassa. Appaheyyato parasantatipatitattā na koci bhavamūlaṃ pajaheyya. Bhūmiladdhañhi anusayitaṃ nāma hotīti adhippāyo. Vatthuvasenāti uppattiṭṭhānavasena. Yattha yattha bhave, santāne vā. Pariññātānaṃ abhūmibhāvato “apariññātā”ti vuttaṃ. Uppādato pabhutīti tesaṃ khandhānaṃ uppajjanato paṭṭhāya. Kilesānaṃ appahīnabhāvaṃ ṭhapetvā aññassa kāraṇassa abhāvato tesu khandhesu kilesajātaṃ anuseti, tasmā taṃ anusayitaṃ kilesajātaṃ, teneva anusayanasaṅkhātena appahīnaṭṭhena bhūmiladdhanti veditabbaṃ.

834. To dispel the doubt, 'What is the ground, or what is ground-acquired?,' 'Here too,' etc., is begun. By 'being an object for insight,' this shows the uncomprehended state of the aggregates, not merely their being objects, since that is established by the very inclusion of the three planes. For the uncomprehended aggregates are intended as the ground of defilements. In the aggregates, which are the basis. 'By way of object' means by way of making an object. Past and future, not to mention the present—this is the meaning. 'That' refers to that group of defilements existing in another's continuum. If, in a different continuum, it were to be called 'ground-acquired' merely by being an object—this is the connection. 'Of that' refers to that group of defilements. Because it is not to be abandoned, as it falls into another's continuum, no one would abandon the root of existence. For what is ground-acquired is called latent—this is the meaning. 'By way of basis' means by way of the place of origination. In whatever existence or continuum. Because the comprehended are not a ground, it is said 'uncomprehended.' 'From arising onwards' means from the arising of those aggregates onwards. Since there is no other cause besides their state of non-abandonment, the group of defilements lies latent in those aggregates; therefore, that latent group of defilements should be understood as 'ground-acquired' by that very un-abandoned state designated as latency.

835. Tattha ca bhūmibhūtesu khandhesu na sabbe sabbesaṃ vatthū honti, atha kho viseso atthīti taṃ dassento āha “yassa yesū”tiādi. Tattha yassāti yassa puggalassa. Yesūti satipi ajjhattabhāvasāmaññe yesu atītādikāmāvacarādibhedabhinnesu khandhesu. Te eva yathānusayitā khandhā. Kiṃ panete kilesā ārammaṇaṃ karontā viya paricchijja paricchijja anusentīti? Yato te eva khandhā tesaṃ kilesānaṃ vatthūti vuttā, na heva kho anusayānaṃ vatthuṃ paricchijja pavatti atthi. Atītādikāmāvacarādivasena pana yathāparicchinne vatthusmiṃ yo kilesānaṃ appahīnaṭṭho, so paricchijja pavatto viya hotīti “atītakkhandhesū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tena vatthuvasena bhūmiladdhaṃ hotīti vatthubhedena siyā tassa bhedoti dasseti. Tathāvavatthitabhāvato eva hi “aññataro lolajātiko taṃ rasapathaviṃ aṅguliyā sāyī”tiādivacanaṃ (dī. ni. 3.120) kāmāvacarakkhandhesu anusayitānaṃ rasataṇhādīnaṃ rūpārūpāvacarakkhandhe atikkamitvā puna kāmāvacarakkhandhavatthukataṃ vibhāveti. Tenāha “tathā kāmāvacarakkhandhesū”tiādi[V 2.0472]. Yathā cettha rūpārūpāvacarakkhandhe atikkamitvā pavatti, evaṃ kāmāvacarakkhandhe atikkamitvā pavatti hotīti āha “esa nayo rūpārūpāvacaresū”ti.

835. And therein, regarding the aggregates that have become the ground, not all of them are the basis for all defilements; rather, there is a distinction. To show this, it is said: “For whom, in which…” etc. Therein, “for whom” means for which person. “In which” refers to the aggregates—differentiated by the distinctions of past, etc., and sense-sphere, etc.—even though there is the commonality of being internal. Those very aggregates are the ones in which they have lain latent. But do these defilements lie latent by dividing and subdividing, as if taking an object? Since those very aggregates are said to be the basis for those defilements, there is certainly no occurrence for the latent tendencies by way of dividing up the basis. However, by way of the past, etc., and the sense-sphere, etc., in a basis that is divided accordingly, the unabandoned nature of the defilements occurs as if it were divided; thus, it is said: “In past aggregates…” etc. By that, it becomes ‘ground-acquired’ by way of the basis; thus, he shows that there might be a distinction for it due to the distinction of the basis. Indeed, precisely because of its nature of being thus established, the statement, “a certain person of a greedy nature tasted that savory earth with his finger…” (DN 3.120), clarifies that cravings for tastes, etc., which lie latent in the sense-sphere aggregates, having transcended the form-sphere and formless-sphere aggregates, again take the sense-sphere aggregates as their basis. Therefore, he said: “similarly, in the sense-sphere aggregates…” etc. And just as here there is an occurrence that transcends the form-sphere and formless-sphere aggregates, so too there is an occurrence that transcends the sense-sphere aggregates; thus, he said: “this is the method in the form-sphere and formless-sphere.”

Pariyuṭṭhānābhibhavanavasena ca kilesānaṃ anusayanaṭṭho anumīyati tadabhāve abhāvato. Yassa ye anusayā pahīnā, tesaṃ vatthu tena [M 2.0502] samatikkantaṃ pariññātattāti kuto nesaṃ bhūmisamaññāti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “sotāpannādīsu panā”tiādi. Idha vaṭṭamūlakilesāti anusayā adhippetā, na avijjā, bhavataṇhā ca. Yaṃ kiñci cetanācetasikabhedaṃ, kāyikādibhedaṃ vā. Itīti evaṃ, appahīnānusayattāti adhippāyo. Assāti puthujjanassa. Te panete anusayā atītādikāmāvacarādivasena yathāparicchinne tattha tattha vatthusmiṃ anusayantāpi te te pañcupādānakkhandhe avibhāgeneva vatthuṃ katvā anusentīti dassento “tassetaṃ vaṭṭamūla”ntiādimāha.

And, the state of latency of the defilements is inferred by way of the overpowering nature of their manifestation, because of the absence of the manifestation when that latency is absent. To show that for one whose latent tendencies are abandoned, their object has been transcended because of being fully understood, and therefore, whence could there be the designation 'ground' for them, it is said: 'But in the case of stream-enterers and so on...' Here, by 'root defilements of the round,' the latent tendencies are intended, not ignorance and craving for existence. This refers to whatever action, whether distinguished as volitional and mental, or distinguished as bodily, etc. 'Thus' means: because of having unabandoned latent tendencies; this is the meaning. 'For him' means for the ordinary person. But these latent tendencies, although they lie latent in this or that object delimited by way of the past, etc., and the sense-sphere, etc., lie latent having made those five aggregates of clinging their undivided object. Showing this, he said: 'For him, this is the root of the round...' and so on.

836. Idāni tamatthaṃ anvayabyatirekavasena upamāya vibhāvetuṃ “pathavīrasādi viyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Rukkhagacchalatādīnaṃ paccayabhūto sasambhārapathaviyā raso pathavīraso. Āporasepi eseva nayo. Sākhā nāma khuddakasākhā. Pasākho viṭapo. Rukkhapaveṇinti rukkhaparāparaṃ. Santānayamāneti aparāparaṃ anuppabandhante.

836. Now, to clarify that meaning by way of positive and negative concomitance and by a simile, it is said: 'Like the essence of the earth, etc.' The essence of the earth (pathavīrasa) is the sap of the earth with its constituents, which is a condition for trees, bushes, creepers, and so on. This same method applies also to the essence of water. 'Sākhā' means small branches. 'Pasākha' is a bough. 'Rukkhapaveṇi' means the succession of trees. 'Santānayamāne' means connecting successively, one after another.

Maṇḍūkakaṇṭakoti eko macchakaṇṭakoti vadanti. Anupādānoti pahīnacaturupādāno, rūpādīsu vā kiñcipi agaṇhanto.

They say that 'frog's thorn' is a type of fish-thorn. 'Anupādāno' means one who has abandoned the four clingings, or one who does not grasp at anything whatsoever among forms and so on.

837. Idha samudācāro nāma laddhattalābhatāti khaṇattayasamaṅgisamudācāruppannanti āha “vattamānuppannameva samudācāruppanna”nti. Pubbabhāge anuppajjamānampīti tasmiṃ āpāthagate ārammaṇe ādito pavattajavanavāresu anuppajjamānampi. Adhiggahitattāti ayonisomanasikārena abhiruyha gahitattā, daḷhaṃ gahitattāti attho. Aparabhāgeti aparasmiṃ kālabhāge, kālantareti attho. Ekantena uppattitoti paccayasamavāye sati tathā ayonisomanasikārassa tattha nibbattattā niyamena uppajjanato. Kalyāṇigāmeti evaṃnāmake gāme. Rohaṇe kira abhirūpānaṃ itthīnaṃ uppattiṭṭhānatāya so gāmo tathā vuccati. Cittasantatimanāruḷhanti paccuppannataṃ paṭisedheti. “Uppattinivārakassa hetuno abhāvā”ti etena paccaye [V 2.0473] sati paccayasamavāye uppajjanārahatāya avikkhambhitassa uppannatāpariyāyoti dasseti. Nanu ca asamūhatuppannampi paccaye sati uppajjanārahameva? Saccametaṃ, pahānavisesabhāvakato [M 2.0503] pana nesaṃ bhedo. Yathā avikkhambhitāsamūhatabhūmiladdhuppannaṃ sati paccayasamavāye uppajjanārahaṃ, evaṃ ārammaṇādhiggahituppannampīti tividhassāpi bhūmiladdhena ekasaṅgahatā vuttā.

837. Here, samudācāra means the state of having obtained what is obtainable. Thus, that which is endowed with the three moments is called samudācāruppanna. Therefore, he says, 'Only what has arisen in the present is samudācāruppanna.' 'Even if not arising in the initial stage' means even if not arising in the initial javana-courses that occur when that object comes into range. 'Adhiggahitattā' means because of being grasped by overpowering through unwise attention, because of being firmly grasped—this is the meaning. 'Aparabhāge' means in a later period of time; the meaning is at another time. 'Ekantena uppattito' means because when there is a concurrence of conditions, and unwise attention has arisen there in that way, it arises inevitably. 'Kalyāṇigāme' means in a village of that name. It is said that in Rohaṇa, that village is so-called because it is the place of origin for beautiful women. By the words 'not having ascended into the continuity of consciousness,' he denies its state of being present. By this statement, 'due to the absence of a cause that prevents arising,' he shows that because of its capability to arise when a condition is present—when there is a concurrence of conditions—it is a synonym for the 'arisen' state of that which is unsuppressed. Is it not so that even that which has arisen as uneradicated is capable of arising when a condition is present? This is true; however, their distinction is made by the specific nature of the abandonment. Just as the unsuppressed, the uneradicated, and the ground-acquired are capable of arising when there is a concurrence of conditions, so too is that which has arisen through grasping an object. Thus, it is stated that these three types are included as one under the term 'ground-acquired'.

838. Akusalampi bhūtāpagatuppannaṃ atītattā na pahātabbaṃ, tathā ekaccaṃ okāsakatuppannaṃ itaraṃ appahātabbato, sesadvayaṃ khaṇattayasamaṅgibhāvatoti āha “amaggavajjhattā”ti. Kenacīti catūsu maggañāṇesu kenaci. Tassāti yathāvuttassa catubbidhassapi uppannassa. Taṃ uppannabhāvaṃ vināsayamānanti anuppattidhammatāpādanena uppajjanārahataṃ vināsentaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ lokiyañāṇena yathābalaṃ pahīnameva lokuttarañāṇaṃ pajahatīti lokiyaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ.

838. Even the unwholesome that has arisen and passed away is not to be abandoned because it is past. Likewise, one kind of opportunity-made arisen state is not to be abandoned because it is past, while the other kind is not to be abandoned because it is not in the category of things to be abandoned. The remaining two are not to be abandoned because they are endowed with the three moments. Thus, he says, 'because of being excluded from the path.' 'Kenaci' means by any of the four path-knowledges. 'Tassa' means of that fourfold arisen state as previously described. 'Destroying its state of having arisen' means destroying its capability to arise by bringing it to a state of having the nature of non-arising. The inclusion of the term 'mundane' is made because supramundane knowledge abandons only that which has first been abandoned by mundane knowledge according to its strength.

Pariññādikiccakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on the Functions Beginning with Full Understanding

839. Saccābhisamayakālasminti catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ paṭivijjhanakkhaṇe. Vuttānīti “dukkhaṃ pariññeyya”ntiādinā (saṃ. ni. 5.1099), “yo, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ passatī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 5.1100) ca vuttāni. Yathāsabhāvenāti aviparītasabhāvena. “Jānitabbānī”ti vatvā tesaṃ jānanavidhiṃ upamāvasena aṭṭhakathāyaṃ tāva vuttanayena dassetuṃ “vuttaṃ heta”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

839. ‘At the time of the realization of the truths’ means at the moment of penetrating the four Noble Truths. These are stated: ‘Suffering should be fully understood,’ and so on (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1099), and ‘Monks, whoever sees suffering,’ and so on (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1100). ‘According to their true nature’ means according to their undistorted nature. Having stated, ‘They should be known,’ in order to show the method of knowing these functions by way of simile, in the commentary, according to the method already stated, it is said, ‘This has been stated,’ and so on.

Tattha yathā padīpotiādi ekassa ñāṇassa ekakkhaṇe cattāri kiccāni kathaṃ sambhavanti. Na hi tādisaṃ kiñci loke diṭṭhaṃ atthi, na ca vacanaṃ labbhatīti antolīnacodanaṃ manasi katvā vuttaṃ “pariññābhisamayenā”ti. Anavasesato paricchijja jānanasaṅkhātena paṭivijjhanena abhisameti asammohavasena paṭivijjhati. Pahānābhisamayenāti samucchedappahānasaṅkhātena paṭivijjhanena asammohato abhisameti. Maggaṃ bhāvanābhisamayenāti maggañāṇaṃ sammāsaṅkappādisesamaggaṃ sahajātādipaccayatāvasena bhāvanābhisamayena. Abhisameti pubbabhāgabhāvanāsambhūtena ariyamaggabhāvanāsaṅkhātena paṭivijjhanena abhisameti aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ asammohato [V 2.0474] paṭivijjhati. Maggañāṇañhi sampayuttadhammesu sammohaṃ viddhaṃsentaṃ attanipi sammohaṃ viddhaṃsetiyeva. Nirodhanti nibbānaṃ. Sacchikiriyābhisamayenāti paccakkhakaraṇasaṅkhātena paṭivijjhanena. Pāpuṇātīti [M 2.0504] adhigacchati. Svāyaṃ adhigamo dassanapaṭivedhoti āha “passati paṭivijjhatī”ti.

Here, regarding the phrase ‘like a lamp,’ and so on, the question is raised: how can four functions occur for one knowledge in a single moment? Indeed, nothing like this is seen in the world, nor can such a statement be found. Considering this implicit objection, it is said: ‘through understanding as realization.’ It realizes by penetrating, which is knowing by fully comprehending without remainder; it penetrates without delusion. ‘Through abandoning as realization’ means it realizes without delusion by penetrating, which is abandonment by eradication. Regarding ‘the path through development as realization,’ path-knowledge realizes the remaining path factors beginning with right intention by means of realization as development, through its power as a co-nascent condition and so on. It realizes through the penetration defined as the development of the Noble Path, arisen from prior development; it penetrates the eight-factored path without delusion. For path-knowledge, while destroying delusion regarding associated states, also destroys delusion within itself. ‘Cessation’ means Nibbāna. ‘Through direct realization as realization’ means by penetrating, which is making evident. ‘It attains’ means it achieves. This attainment is the penetration that is seeing; therefore, it is said: ‘one sees, one penetrates.’

“Nirodhaṃ…pe… paṭivijjhatī”ti etena nirodhasaccamekaṃ ārammaṇapaṭivedhena cattāripi saccāni asammohapaṭivedhena maggañāṇaṃ paṭivijjhatīti evaṃ yuttivasena vibhāvitaṃ ekapaṭivedhaṃ āgamenapi sādhetuṃ “vuttampi ceta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. “Sabbaṃ veditabba”nti iminā “yo dukkhasamudayaṃ passati, so dukkhampi passatī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 5.1100) āgataṃ samudayaṃ saccādimūlakaṃ yojanaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

By ‘…penetrates cessation…,’ through this it is shown that path-knowledge penetrates the one truth of cessation by way of object-penetration, and all four truths by way of non-delusion-penetration. Thus, to establish this simultaneous penetration, which has been explained by way of reasoning, also by way of scripture, it is said, ‘This has also been stated,’ and so on. By ‘All is to be known,’ it includes the connection originating with the truth of origin and so on, which is found in the text beginning, ‘Whoever sees the origin of suffering also sees suffering,’ and so on (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1100).

Na cetaṃ kālantaradassanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, atha kho ekapaṭivedhamevāti dassentena “maggasamaṅgissa ñāṇaṃ, dukkhepetaṃ ñāṇa”ntiādinā (vibha. 794; paṭi. ma. 1.109) aparaṃ suttapadaṃ ānītaṃ. Tathā hi “yo nu kho, āvuso, dukkhaṃ passati, dukkhasamudayampi so passati…pe… paṭipadampi so passatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1100) ekasaccadassanasamaṅgino aññasaccadassanasamaṅgibhāvavicāraṇāya tamatthaṃ sādhetuṃ āyasmatā gavampatittherena vuttaṃ, paccekañca saccattayadassanayojanā katā. Aññathā kamābhisamaye purimadiṭṭhassa puna adassanato samudayādiṃ passato dukkhādidassanaṃ puna avattabbaṃ siyā, vuccamāne ca sabbadassanaṃ dassanantaraparamanti dassanānuparamo eva siyāti.

And this was not said with reference to seeing at another time; rather, to show that it is a simultaneous penetration, another sutta passage was brought forward: ‘The knowledge of one endowed with the path is knowledge in suffering,’ and so on (Vibh. 794; Paṭi. Ma. 1.109). For indeed, this meaning was established by the Venerable Gavampati Thera when, in the course of examining the state of being endowed with the seeing of another truth for one endowed with the seeing of one truth, he said: ‘Friend, whoever sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering… also sees the path’ (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1100), and the connection of seeing the three truths respectively was made. Otherwise, in a gradual realization, for one who sees the origin and so on, it would be unnecessary to speak again of seeing suffering and so on, which was seen before. And if it were spoken of, since all seeing would have another seeing as its principal, there would only be a non-cessation of seeing.

Nissayabhāvahetutāya dukkhapariññāya vaṭṭijhāpanasadisatā, paṭipakkhaviddhaṃsanatāya samudayappahānassa andhakāravidhamanasadisatā, ñāṇālokaparibrūhanatāya maggabhāvanāya ālokaviddhaṃsanasadisatā, tena tena maggena yathā yathā nirodhassa sacchikiriyā, tathā tathā kilesasnehapariyādānaṃ hotīti nirodhasacchikiriyāya snehapariyādānasadisatā kāraṇūpacārena vuttā.

By reason of its nature as a support, the full understanding of suffering is like the burning away of a wick. By reason of its destruction of opposing factors, the abandoning of the origin is like the dispelling of darkness. By reason of its increase of the light of knowledge, the development of the path is like the shining forth of light. In whatever way the realization of cessation occurs through each respective path, in that same way the exhaustion of the oil of the defilements occurs; thus, the realization of cessation is said to be like the exhaustion of oil, stated by way of causal metaphor.

840. Obhāsetīti pakāseti. Kilesapaṭippassaddhinti sabbakilesadarathapariḷāhavūpasamabhāvato kilesānaṃ paṭippassaddhibhūtaṃ.

840. ‘It illuminates’ means it makes manifest. ‘The subsiding of defilements’ refers to that which has become the subsiding of defilements, due to its nature as the stilling of all defilements, torments, and burning.

841. Appetīti [V 2.0475] pappoti. Dukkhapariññāya sakkāyatīrasamatikkamabhāvato orimatīrappahānasadisatā, maggabhāvanāya sattattiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammāvahanatāya bhaṇḍavahanasadisatā.

841. ‘Appeti’ means it attains. For the full understanding of suffering, by reason of its overcoming the shore of self-identity, there is a likeness to abandoning the near shore. For the development of the path, by reason of its bearing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, there is a likeness to carrying a load.

842. Pavattaṃ [M 2.0505] ñāṇaṃ assāti pavattañāṇo, maggo. Assa maggassa.

842. ‘Arisen knowledge belongs to it,’ thus it is called pavattañāṇa, the path. Of that path.

Tathaṭṭhenāti tathasabhāvena, pīḷanādiaviparītasabhāvenāti attho. Ekapaṭivedhānīti ekajjhaṃ paṭivijjhitabbākārāni.

‘By the true nature’ means by its true intrinsic nature, that is, by its nature not contrary to oppression and so on. ‘Single penetrations’ means aspects that are to be penetrated simultaneously.

Dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭhotiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā buddhānussativaṇṇanāyaṃ (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 1.144) vuttameva. Ekasaṅgahitānīti ekeneva saṅgahitāni. Kena? Tathaṭṭhena, saccaṭṭhenāti attho. Yaṃ ekasaṅgahitantiādi ñāṇassa ekapaṭivedhadassanaṃ. Maggañāṇañhi nirodhameva ārammaṇaṃ karontampi yo so dukkhādīsu tacchāvipallāsabhūtabhāvasaṅkhāto saccaṭṭho, tappaṭicchādakasammohaviddhaṃsanena taṃ yāthāvato paṭivijjhantaṃ paccakkhaṃ karontameva pavattati. Yato aparabhāge pīḷanādayo soḷasapi saccaṭṭhā ariyassa hatthāmalakaṃ viya yāthāvato upaṭṭhahanti.

What is to be said regarding ‘the characteristic of suffering as oppression,’ and so on, has already been stated below in the commentary on the recollection of the Buddha (Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā 1.144). ‘Comprehended by one thing’ means comprehended by one thing alone. By what? By the true nature, that is, by the meaning of truth. The phrase ‘that which is comprehended by one thing,’ and so on, shows the single penetration of knowledge. For path-knowledge, even while taking only cessation as its object, operates by penetrating and directly realizing in accordance with reality that very meaning of truth—the nature of suffering, and so on, which is characterized as the actual, undistorted state—by dispelling the delusion that obscures it. Wherefore, in the subsequent phase, all sixteen aspects of truth, such as oppression, become evident in accordance with reality to the noble one, as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand.

843. Atthāti ñāṇena araṇīyato atthāti laddhasamaññā ākārā. Aññasaccadassanavasenāti samudayādisaccantaradassanavasena. Āvibhāvatoti pakāsabhāvato. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ye ākārā dukkhādīsu sabhāvavasena, saccantaradassanavasena ca āvibhavanti, te pīḷanādayo cattāroyevāti soḷaseva vuttā, na aññeti. Ayamattho idhādhippetoti kathamidaṃ viññāyatīti āha “tattha katamaṃ dukkhe ñāṇa”ntiādi. Tenetaṃ dasseti – yasmā pāḷiyaṃ visuṃ visuṃ ārammaṇakaraṇavasenapi saccañāṇaṃ vuttaṃ kiccanibbattivasenapi, tasmā viññāyati “sabhāvato, saccantaradassanato ca saccānaṃ ākārā āvibhavantī”ti.

843. ‘Atthā’ (realities) are characteristics that have acquired the designation ‘atthā’ because they are to be known by knowledge. ‘By way of seeing other truths’ means by way of seeing other truths such as the origin, and so on. ‘By way of becoming manifest’ means by way of being manifest. This is what is said: those characteristics that become evident in suffering, and so on, by way of their intrinsic nature and by way of seeing other truths, are indeed only four each, such as oppression, and so on, thus sixteen are stated, not others. ‘This meaning is intended here’ – how is this to be understood? He says, beginning with ‘Here, what is knowledge of suffering?’ By this he shows: because in the Pāḷi texts, knowledge of the truths is described both by way of taking objects separately and by way of fulfilling functions, therefore it is understood that ‘the characteristics of the truths become evident both by their intrinsic nature and by way of seeing other truths.’

Kiccanibbattivasena dassanaṃ āvibhāvato dassanasadisanti taṃ anāmasitvā itarameva dassento “tatthā”tiādimāha. Tatthāti tesu dvīsu dassanesu. Āyūhitanti piṇḍavasena nibbattitaṃ. Yañhi kiñci paccayuppannaṃ nāma, sabbaṃ taṃ samuditameva nibbattatīti. Saṅkhatanti paccayantarehi samecca sambhūya kataṃ. Rāsikatanti puñjakataṃ. Anekameva hi paccayuppannaṃ ekajjhaṃ [V 2.0476] nibbattamānaṃ attano paccayehi rāsikataṃ viya hotīti. Tasmāti samudayena āyūhitattā. Assāti dukkhasaccassa. Yasmiṃ santāne uppanno[M 2.0506], tassa kilesasantāpaharo. Sayampi kilesapariḷāhābhāvato susītalo. Santāpaṭṭho āvibhavati uḷāradassanena tadaññassa anuḷārabhāvo viyāti dassento āha “āyasmato”tiādi. Avipariṇāmadhammassa niccasabhāvassa vattabbameva natthi paṭipakkhato āvibhavanākārassa sukhasiddhito.

Seeing by way of the accomplishment of its function is similar to seeing because it becomes manifest; not touching upon that, but showing only the other, he says, beginning with ‘There.’ ‘There’ means among those two seeings. ‘Accumulated’ means produced by way of aggregation. For whatever is called conditionally arisen, all of that is produced only as a collection. ‘Conditioned’ means made by coming together and arising together with other conditions. ‘Massed’ means made into a heap. For many conditionally arisen things, being produced together, are as if massed by their own conditions. ‘Therefore’ means because of being accumulated by the collection. ‘Its’ refers to the truth of suffering. In whichever continuum it has arisen, it is a remover of the torment of defilements of that continuum. Itself is also very cool due to the absence of the burning of defilements. The characteristic of torment becomes manifest, just as through a sublime seeing, the state of not-being-sublime of another becomes manifest. Showing this, he says, beginning with ‘of the venerable one.’ Regarding that which has a nature of non-alteration, a permanent nature, there is indeed nothing to be said, because the characteristic of its manifestation by way of its opposite is easily accomplished.

Nidānaṭṭho āvibhavati idamassa nidadātīti. Saṃyogapalibodhaṭṭhā paṭipakkhavasena āvibhavanākārāti dassento āha “visaṃyogabhūtassā”tiādi. Kilesadukkhehi saṃyojanaṭṭho saṃyogaṭṭho. Saṃsāracārake palibuddhanaṭṭho palibodhaṭṭho.

The characteristic of being a cause becomes manifest thus: 'This [craving] gives that [suffering].' Showing that the characteristics of connection and obstruction are modes of becoming manifest by way of opposition, he says, beginning with 'for one who is free from connection,' and so on. The characteristic of connection is the state of being connected with defilements and suffering. The characteristic of obstruction is the state of obstructing in the prison of saṃsāra.

Kilesasaṅgaṇikādivasena avivekabhūtassa. Vivekaṭṭho upadhivivekatā. Sabbasaṅkhāravivittatā asaṅkhatabhāvoti evaṃ acchariyabbhutasabhāvopi ariyamaggo saṅkhato eva, ayameva ca eko asaṅkhatoti nirodhassa asaṅkhatabhāvo supākaṭo hoti. Dukkhaṃ visaṃ maraṇadhammato tassa agadabhūtaṃ amataṃ nibbānaṃ.

For that which has become a state of non-seclusion by way of having defilements as companions, and so on. The characteristic of seclusion is seclusion from the substrata. The state of being secluded from all formations is the unconditioned state. Thus, although the noble path has a wonderful and marvelous nature, it is indeed conditioned. And only this one [Nibbāna] is unconditioned; thus, the unconditioned nature of cessation becomes very manifest. Suffering is a poison because it has the nature of death; Nibbāna is the deathless, being an antidote for it.

“Maggo”ti sambhāvetabbataṃ patto sukhumasantabhāvena upaṭṭhito nikantibhūtopi nāyaṃ samudayo hetu nibbānassa pattiyā. Ayaṃ ariyamaggo hetūti maggāmaggañāṇadassane vuttanayena maggassa hetuṭṭho āvibhavati. Nirodhadassanenāti ativiya nipuṇassa paramagambhīrassa nirodhasaccassa dassanena. Tenāha “paramasukhumānī”tiādi. Dukkhadassanenāti ativiya ādīnavappattiyā vipulatarādīnavassa dukkhasaccassa dassanena. Tappaṭipakkhato ādhipateyyaṭṭho. Tenāha “anekarogātura…pe… uḷārabhāvo viyā”ti. Evamete yathārahaṃ anvayato, byatirekato ca saccesu āvibhavanākārā vibhāvitā.

Although this origin [craving] is esteemed as 'the path,' appears with a subtle and peaceful nature, and becomes delight-craving, it is not the cause for the attainment of Nibbāna. This noble path is the cause. Thus, by the method stated in the knowledge and vision of path and not-path, the characteristic of the path as a cause becomes manifest. ‘By the vision of cessation’ means: by the vision of the extremely subtle and exceedingly profound truth of cessation. Therefore, he said, 'exceedingly subtle,' and so on. ‘By the vision of suffering’ means: by the vision of the truth of suffering, which has very extensive dangers, because it is a state of extreme danger. By way of opposition to that, the characteristic of dominance becomes manifest. Therefore, he said, 'like one afflicted with many diseases... a great state.' Thus, these modes of becoming manifest in the truths have been explained, as is appropriate, both by direct correspondence and by contrast.

Ekekassāti ekekassa atthassa, pīḷanāyūhananissaraṇaniyyānaṭṭhe sandhāyāha. Tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇanti saṅkhatādiatthe. Ye pana vādino. Nānābhisamayanti nānāñāṇena abhisamayaṃ, catunnaṃ saccānaṃ nānākkhaṇe nānāñāṇena paṭivijjhananti attho. Yadi hi maggañāṇassa catūsu saccesu nānābhisamayo siyā, dukkhadassanādīhi paṭhamamaggādīhi pahātabbānaṃ saṃyojanattayādīnaṃ [M 2.0507] ekadesappahānaṃ āpajjati. Tathā ca sati ekadesasotāpattimaggaṭṭhatādippasaṅgo. Taṃtaṃdassanānantarañca [V 2.0477] taṃtaṃphalena bhavitabbanti taṃtaṃpaheyyakilesapaṭippassaddhibhūtānaṃ phalānaṃ maggānaṃ viya catukkatā siyā. Tathā ca sati ekadesasotāpannatādippasaṅgo. Kiñca bhiyyo – yadi maggañāṇassa nānābhisamayo siyā, aññena ñāṇena dukkhaṃ passati. Aññena samudayaṃ, aññena nirodhaṃ, aññena maggaṃ, evaṃ sati maggakiccaṃ aparipuṇṇameva siyā. Maggadassanena hi dvayagati, teneva vā tassa dassanaṃ, aññena vāti. Tattha paṭhamo tāva pakkho na yujjati attani pavattiyā asambhavato. Na hi teneva aṅgulaggena tameva parāmasituṃ sakkā. Atha aññena anavaṭṭhānappasaṅgo “yena maggaṃ passati, sopi maggo. Tampi yena passati, sopi maggo”ti. Tasmā ekābhisamayato yathāvutto asammohapaṭivedhova yutto. Apica paricchinditabbaṃ, samucchinditabbañca saccadvayaṃ ārabbha pavattamānassa maggañāṇassa paricchindanasamucchindanāni na sambhavanti tato anissaraṇato. Na hi dukkhapariññāsamudayappahānāni dukkhasamudayasaccārammaṇena ñāṇena kātuṃ sakkuṇeyyāni. Nibbānārammaṇena pana tattha, itaradvaye ca sammohaṃ viddhaṃsentena sakkā kātunti ekābhisamayo eva yutto. Ayaṃ pana attho pāḷiyaṃ āgato evāti “tesaṃ uttaraṃ abhidhamme kathāvatthusmiṃ vuttamevā”ti.

Regarding 'for each': He said this referring to the aspects of oppression, exertion, escape, and the means of escape for each and every meaning. Regarding 'of the three, of the three': this refers to the meanings such as 'conditioned', etc. But those who hold other views say: 'Diverse realizations' means realization through diverse knowledges, that is, the penetration of the four truths at different moments by different knowledges. For if the path-knowledge had a diverse realization of the four truths, then through the vision of suffering, etc., the partial abandonment of the three fetters, etc., to be abandoned by the first path, etc., would result. And that being so, the undesirable consequence of being partially established in the path of stream-entry, etc., would arise. And, since immediately after the vision of each respective truth there must be its respective fruit, there would be a fourfoldness of fruits—which are the calming of the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path—just as there is of the paths. And that being so, the undesirable consequence of being a partial stream-enterer, etc., would arise. Furthermore, if the path-knowledge had a diverse realization, one would see suffering with one knowledge, the origin with another, cessation with another, and the path with another. This being so, the function of the path would be incomplete indeed. For with the vision of the path, there are two alternatives: either the vision of it by that very knowledge or by another. Among these, the first alternative is not tenable because of the impossibility of its own activity upon itself. For it is not possible to touch that very fingertip with that same fingertip. Now, if by another, there is the undesirable consequence of an infinite regress: 'That by which one sees the path, that too is a path. And that by which one sees that, that too is a path.' Therefore, because of the single, simultaneous realization, only the penetration without confusion, as stated before, is appropriate. Moreover, for the path-knowledge that arises in relation to the two truths that are to be comprehended and eradicated, the functions of comprehending and eradicating are not possible, because there is no escape from them. For the full understanding of suffering and the abandoning of the origin cannot be accomplished by a knowledge that has the truths of suffering and origin as its object. But it is possible to do so by a knowledge that has Nibbāna as its object, while destroying confusion regarding those two truths and the other two. Therefore, only a single, simultaneous realization is appropriate. But this meaning has indeed come down in the Pāḷi, thus he said: 'Their rebuttal is stated in the Abhidhamma, in the Kathāvatthu.'

Pariññādippabhedakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Classification of Comprehension, etc.

845. Abhiññāpaññātiādīnaṃ attho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Apica sutamayāya, cintāmayāya, ekaccabhāvanāmayāya ca abhivisiṭṭhāya paññāya ñātā abhiññātā. Āveṇikā bhūmi pariññantarānaṃ avisayabhāvato. Na hi nāmarūpaparicchedapaccayapariggahaṇavasena tīraṇapariññādīnaṃ pavatti atthi.

845. The meaning of terms such as 'wisdom of direct knowledge' has already been stated below. Moreover, things known by a wisdom more distinguished than that born of learning, born of reflection, and some born of mental development, are 'directly known'. It is a unique domain because it is not the object of other comprehensions. For indeed, there is no occurrence of comprehension by judgment, etc., by way of discerning name-and-form and grasping conditions.

846. Anulomañāṇampi aniccādivaseneva saṅkhāre ārabbha pavattati, pageva paṭisaṅkhānupassanādayoti āha “yāva anulomā āveṇikā bhūmī”ti. Kāmañcettha tīraṇapariññābhūmiyaṃ ñātappahānapariññāyopi laddhāvasarā, tattha pana yathā tīraṇapariññā sātisayaṃ kiccakārī, na tathā itarāti āveṇikaggahaṇaṃ.

846. Conformity-knowledge also proceeds with formations as its object only by way of impermanence, etc.; how much more so the contemplation of reflection and so on. Therefore, he said: 'up to conformity is a unique domain.' And although here, in the domain of comprehension by judgment, comprehension by knowing and comprehension by abandoning also find their opportunity, the term 'unique' is used because, in that domain, comprehension by judgment is exceptionally functional, whereas the others are not so.

847. Nippariyāyena [M 2.0508] pahānapariññā nāma maggañāṇanti “yāva maggañāṇā bhūmī”ti vuttaṃ[V 2.0478]. Ayaṃ idha adhippetāti idha abhisamayakāle kiccavicāre ayaṃ pahānapariññā adhippetā tadatthattā sesapariññānaṃ. Tenāha “yasmā vā”tiādi.

847. Directly, comprehension by abandoning is path-knowledge; therefore, it is said, 'the domain up to path-knowledge.' 'This is intended here' means: here, at the time of realization, in the examination of the function, this comprehension by abandoning is intended, because the remaining comprehensions have that as their purpose. Therefore, he said, 'Because…' etc.

Tadatthāyevāti pahānapariññatthā eva. Atha vā tadatthāyevāti pahānatthā eva. Atha vā tadatthāyevāti maggatthā eva. Ñātatīraṇapariññā hi yāvadeva maggādhigamatthāya pavattā. Niyamato ñātā ceva tīritā ca honti ñātatīritabhāvehi vinā pahānābhāvato, pahānasiddhiyañca ñātatīritabhāvasiddhito. Maggañāṇañhi dukkhe pariññābhisamayavasena pavattamānaṃ tassa sabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ viya sāmaññalakkhaṇampi paṭivijjhatīti vuccati tappaṭicchādakasammohaviddhaṃsanato. Tenāha “pariññattayampi…pe… veditabba”nti.

'For that very purpose' means solely for the purpose of comprehension by abandoning. Or alternatively, 'for that very purpose' means solely for the purpose of abandoning. Or alternatively, 'for that very purpose' means solely for the purpose of the path. For comprehension by knowing and comprehension by judgment proceed only for the purpose of attaining the path. Necessarily, things are known and judged, for without the state of being known and judged there is no abandoning, and the accomplishment of abandoning depends on the accomplishment of the state of being known and judged. For path-knowledge, while proceeding by way of realization through comprehension in regard to suffering, is said to penetrate its general characteristic as well, just like its specific characteristic, because it destroys the delusion that conceals it. Therefore, he said: 'The threefold comprehension… should be understood…'

848. Pariññā viyāti tividhatāsāmaññaṃ nidasseti, na pariññāpahātabbatāsāmaññaṃ vikkhambhanappahānassa aripaññākiccabhāvato. Kāmacchandādayo yathā na cittaṃ pariyuṭṭhāya tiṭṭhanti, evaṃ pariyuṭṭhānassa nisedhanaṃ appavattikaraṇaṃ vikkhambhanaṃ, vikkhambhanameva pahānaṃ vikkhambhanappahānaṃ. Pākaṭattāti “ayaṃ abyāpannacitto vigatathinamiddho”tiādinā (a. ni. 4.198) paresampi pākaṭattā. “Na sahasā cittaṃ ajjhottharantī”ti idaṃ paṭiladdhamattassa jhānassa vasena vuttaṃ, subhāvite pana paguṇajjhāne yāva carimakacittampi na ajjhottharanteva. Atha vā jhānassa pubbabhāgepīti jhānādhigamatthāya pubbabhāgapaṭipattiyā. Pacchābhāgepīti jhānaṃ labhitvā aññakiccappasutassapi. Vitakkādayoti vitakkavicārapītisukharūpasaññādayo. Dutiyajjhānādīnaṃ paṭipakkhā dutiyādīsu appitesuyeva vikkhambhanti, tato tato vuṭṭhitamattassa pana pavattanti parittacittavaseneva vuṭṭhahanato.

848. The phrase 'like comprehension' indicates a commonality in being threefold, not the commonality of what is to be abandoned by comprehension, because abandoning by suppression does not have the function of comprehension. Just as sensual desire and other defilements do not persist by obsessing the mind, the prevention of obsession, the causing of non-arising, is suppression; suppression itself is abandoning—this is abandoning by suppression. 'Because it is manifest' means that it is manifest to others also, as in the phrase, 'This one has a mind free from ill will, devoid of sloth and torpor.' 'They do not overwhelm the mind suddenly'—this is said with reference to one who has just attained jhāna. But when jhāna is well-developed and proficient, they do not overwhelm it even up to the final moment of consciousness. Alternatively, 'in the preliminary stage of jhāna also' refers to the preliminary practice for the purpose of attaining jhāna; and 'in the subsequent stage also' refers to one who, having attained jhāna, is also engaged in other duties. 'Initial thought and so on' refers to initial thought, sustained thought, joy, happiness, form-perception, and so on. The opposing factors of the second jhāna and so on are suppressed only when one has attained the second jhāna and so on. However, for one who has just emerged from them, they arise again, because of emerging only by the power of a limited mind.

849. “Padīpena andhakārassa viyā”ti idaṃ paṭipakkhena pahīnabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Paṭipakkho hi padīpo andhakārassa, ghaṭappahāro pana sevālassa na paṭipakkho, kevalaṃ pavattinivāraṇamattameva karotīti. Tena asatipi ujuvipaccanīkatāya dutiyajjhānādīnaṃ vitakkādīnaṃ vikkhambhanassa taṃ nidassanaṃ suṭṭhutaraṃ yujjati. “Vipassanāya avayavabhūtenā”ti idaṃ idhādhikatatadaṅgappahānassa [M 2.0509] dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Sīlavisodhanādināpi hi tadaṅgappahānaṃ hotiyevāti. Ñāṇaṅgenāti ñāṇasaṅkhātena kāraṇena. Tadaṅgena tadaṅgassa pahānaṃ tadaṅgappahānaṃ. Sati vijjamāne khandhapañcakasaṅkhāte kāye, sayaṃ vā tattha sati diṭṭhi sakkāyadiṭṭhi, “rūpaṃ attato [V 2.0479] samanupassatī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 3.81; 4.345) nayena vuttā attānudiṭṭhi. Soḷasavatthukā, aṭṭhavatthukā ca kaṅkhāva malaṃ kaṅkhāmalaṃ. Samūhagāhassāti “attā attaniya”nti evaṃ pavattasamūhagahaṇassa pahānaṃ kalāpasammasanena ekādasasu okāsesu pakkhipitvā vikiraṇavasena khandhānaṃ dassanato. Assādasaññāyāti pañcakkhandhe assādanavasena pavattamicchāsaññāya. Appaṭisaṅkhānassāti paṭisaṅkhānapaṭipakkhassa mohassa. Anupekkhanassāti apekkhāya. Saṅkhāresu niccādigāho saccapaṭilomagāho maggasaccādhigamassa vilomanato. Sādīnavesu anādīnavasaññitā, anādīnave ca sādīnavasaññitā saccapaṭilomagāhoti ca vadanti.

849. “Like a lamp dispels darkness,” this is said to show the state of being abandoned by an opposing factor. For a lamp is the opposing factor to darkness, whereas a blow from a pot is not an opposing factor to moss; it merely prevents its occurrence. Therefore, even in the absence of direct opposition, that illustration is most suitable for the suppression of initial thought and so on by the second jhāna and so on. “Through insight as a constituent part,” this is said to show the abandonment-by-substitution that is under discussion here. For abandonment-by-substitution indeed occurs even through the purification of virtue and so on. “By the factor of knowledge” means by the cause called knowledge. The abandonment of a particular factor by that very factor is abandonment-by-substitution. Identity-view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) is the view regarding the existing body designated as the five aggregates, or the view that is present there in oneself; the view of self (attānudiṭṭhi) is that stated in the manner of “one regards form as self” and so on. The defilement of doubt (kaṅkhāmala) is doubt itself, which has sixteen and eight bases. “[The abandonment] of grasping as a whole” refers to the abandonment of grasping a collection that occurs as “self” or “belonging to self,” by seeing the aggregates by way of scattering them after placing them into eleven instances through comprehension of groups. “[The abandonment] of the perception of gratification” refers to the wrong perception that arises by way of gratification regarding the five aggregates. “[The abandonment] of non-reflection” refers to delusion (moha), the opposing factor of reflection. “[The abandonment] of lack of careful regard” refers to longing. Grasping formations as permanent and so on is a grasping contrary to the truth, because it is contrary to the attainment of the path-truth. And they say that the perception of the dangerous as undangerous, and the undangerous as dangerous, is a grasping contrary to the truth.

Evaṃ visuddhikkamena tadaṅgappahānaṃ dassetvā idāni aṭṭhārasamahāvipassanāvasenapi taṃ dassetuṃ “yaṃ vā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yaṃ vā pana pahānanti sambandho.

Having thus shown abandonment-by-substitution by way of the sequence of purification, now, in order to show it also by way of the eighteen great insights, the passage beginning “or whatever abandonment” is stated. Therein, the connection is “or whatever abandonment [there is].”

850. Vuttameva “sabbaṃ saṅkhāragataṃ aniccato anupassatī”tiādinā (visuddhi. 2.742).

850. It has indeed been stated by the passage beginning, “one contemplates all that has come to be a formation as impermanent”.

Santatisamūhakiccārammaṇānaṃ vasena ghanaggahaṇaṃ ghanasaññā, tassā ghanasaññāya.

Grasping as a solid mass by way of continuity, collection, function, and object is the perception of compactness. Of that perception of compactness.

Nirodhe adhimuttatā, tāyāti tiyaddhagatānaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ nirodhameva disvā tattha adhimuccanavasena pavattapaññā, tāya. Āyūhanassāti abhisaṅkharaṇassa.

Intentness on cessation: [This is] the wisdom that has arisen by way of being intent on that [cessation], having seen only the cessation of formations that have traversed the three periods of time. By that [wisdom]. Of constructing: of the act of constructing.

Taṃ taṃ paricchedanti ādānanikkhepādikaṃ taṃ taṃ paricchedaṃ. Aññathāpavattidassananti vuttaparicchedato pubbe, pacchā ca aññākārappavattiyā dassanaṃ, avatthāvisesappavattidassanaṃ vā. Dhuvasaññāyāti thirabhāvaggahaṇassa.

That particular demarcation: that particular demarcation, such as taking up and putting down. Seeing its occurrence as otherwise: the seeing of its occurrence in a different mode before and after the stated demarcation, or the seeing of the occurrence of a distinct state.
