“Vipassatī”ti vuttaṃ, kīdisī panettha vipassanā icchitabbāti taṃ niddhāraṇatthaṃ “vipassanā panesā”tiādinā tameva vipassanaṃ tidhā bhinditvā dasseti. Mandā ce vipassanā, dandhābhiññaṃ maggaṃ sādheti. Tikkhā ce, khippābhiññanti ayaṃ mandatikkhatāya viseso. Lakkhaṇappattā pana vipassanā maggassa paccayo hotiyevāti imamatthaṃ dassento āha “saṅkhāra…pe… hotiyevā”ti. Tikkhāva vaṭṭati saṅkhārārammaṇepi sati sabbasaṅkhārehi vivaṭṭanākāreneva pavattanato, maggo viya visaṅkhāragatassa phalassa [M 2.0527] paccayabhāvato ca. Tenāha “maggabhāvanāsadisā”ti. Yasmā atimandā samathādikā saṅkhārānaṃ nirodhane asamatthā samathaniṭṭhā hoti, atitikkhā ñāṇādikā sātisayaṃ saṅkhāresu dosadassane phalasamāpattiniṭṭhā hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “nātimandanātitikkhā vaṭṭatī”ti. Esa nirodhasamāpajjanako. Te saṅkhāreti te paṭhamajjhānasaṅkhāre.

It is said, 'one sees with insight.' Here, what kind of insight is to be desired? In order to clarify that, with the text beginning 'But this insight...', he shows that very insight by dividing it into three kinds. If insight is weak, it accomplishes the path with slow direct knowledge. If it is sharp, it accomplishes the path with quick direct knowledge. This is the distinction in being weak and sharp. Indeed, insight that has reached the characteristic becomes a condition for the path. Desiring to show this meaning, he said, 'formations…pe… becomes.' Only sharp insight is suitable, because, even though it has formations as its object, it proceeds only in the manner of turning away from all formations, and because, like the path, it is a condition for the fruit which has gone to the unconditioned. Therefore, he said, 'it is similar to the development of the path.' Because insight that is too weak, being predominated by serenity, is incapable of causing the cessation of formations, it culminates in serenity; and insight that is too sharp, being predominated by knowledge, due to seeing faults in formations excessively, culminates in the attainment of fruition. Therefore, it is said, 'It should be neither too weak nor too sharp.' This is the one who enters the attainment of cessation. As for 'those formations', it means those formations of the first jhāna.

“Tathevā”ti iminā “nātimandāya nātitikkhāyā”ti imamatthaṃ ākaḍḍhati. Esa nayo sesesupi. “Ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya tattha saṅkhāre tatheva vipassatī”ti vattabbaṃ, heṭṭhā vuttanayattā pana taṃ avatvā “catubbidhaṃ pubbakiccaṃ karoti”cceva vuttanti keci, taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ. Vipassanācārato hi samādhicāro, tasmā samāpattito vuṭṭhāya pubbakiccaṃ kātabbaṃ. Tathā hi paratopi “ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya imaṃ pubbakiccaṃ katvā”tiādiṃ (visuddhi. 2.879) vakkhati, na pana “tattha saṅkhāre tatheva vipassitvā”ti. Nānābaddhaavikopananti attanā asambaddhassa parikkhārassa avināsanaṃ. Yathā taṃ na vinassati, tathā adhiṭṭhānaṃ. Saṅghapaṭimānananti saṅghassa paṭimānanāvajjanaṃ. Satthupakkosananti satthu pakkosanāvajjanaṃ. Addhānaparicchedanti jīvitaddhānaparicchedaṃ pubbakiccaṃ karotīti sambandho.

By 'just so,' it draws out the meaning 'with insight that is neither too weak nor too sharp.' This is the method in the remaining cases as well. It should be said: 'Having entered and emerged from the base of nothingness, one contemplates the formations therein just so.' However, because the method has been stated before, some say that, without stating that, it is only said, 'one performs the fourfold preliminary duty.' That is merely their opinion. Indeed, the practice of concentration is to be desired over the practice of insight; therefore, having emerged from the attainment, the preliminary duty should be done. For so, later on, he will say: 'Having entered and emerged from the base of nothingness, having performed this preliminary duty...' and so on, but not 'having contemplated the formations therein just so.' 'Non-damage to things not attached' means the non-destruction of requisites not connected with oneself. The determination is made in such a way that they are not destroyed. 'Awaiting the Saṅgha' means adverting to the Saṅgha's waiting. 'The Teacher's summons' means adverting to the Teacher's summons. 'Determining the time-span' means determining the life-span; one performs this preliminary duty—this is the connection.

875. Adhiṭṭhātabbanti cittaṃ uppādetabbaṃ. Tathā cittuppādanameva hettha adhiṭṭhānaṃ.

875. 'To be resolved upon' means the mind should be made to arise. Indeed, here, the very arising of the mind in such a way is the determination.

Cittajarūpādīnaṃ anuppajjanato, pacchājātapaccayādiupatthambhābhāvato ca sattāhameva tathā sarīraṃ [V 2.0496] pavattati, tato paraṃ kilamatīti sattāhameva paricchinditvā nirodhaṃ samāpajjantīti vadanti.

Because mind-produced materiality, and so on, do not arise, and because of the absence of supporting conditions such as post-nascence condition, the body continues in that way for only seven days; after that, it deteriorates. Thus, they say that one enters cessation after determining it to be for only seven days.

Samāpattivasenevāti nirodhasamāpattivaseneva. Naṃ aggiādiantarāyaṃ rakkhati samāpannako adhiṭṭhānavasenāti adhippāyo. Āyasmato sañjīvassātiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā iddhikathāyaṃ (visuddhi. 2.374) vuttameva.

‘By the power of attainment alone’ means by the power of the attainment of cessation alone. The meaning is that the determination of one who has attained protects them from dangers such as fire. As for the Venerable Sañjīva, and so on, what needs to be said has already been stated in the earlier discussion on spiritual powers (Visuddhimagga 2.374).

876. Etassāti [M 2.0528] nirodhaṃ samāpajjantassa, nirodhasamāpajjanassa vā. Tasmiṃ samayeti tasmiṃ tassa bhikkhuno upasaṅkamanasamaye vuṭṭhātiyeva. Kālaparicchedasadisañhetaṃ.

876. ‘Of this’ refers to one who is entering cessation, or of the entering of cessation. ‘At that time’ means at the time when that monk approaches, he emerges indeed. For this is similar to a demarcation of time.

Evaṃ garukāti aggiādīhipi anabhibhavanīyaṃ nirodhaṃ samāpannaṃ samāpattito vuṭṭhāpanato evaṃ garukā hi saṅghassa āṇā nāma, tasmā attano hitasukhaṃ ākaṅkhantena jīvitahetupi saṅghassa āṇā na atikkamitabbāti adhippāyo.

The command of the Saṅgha is indeed so weighty because it causes a person who has entered the attainment of cessation—which cannot be overcome even by fire and so on—to emerge from that attainment. Therefore, one desiring their own welfare and happiness should not transgress the Saṅgha’s command even for the sake of life—this is the meaning.

877. Na pakkosati “satthā taṃ, āvuso, āmantetī”ti. “Vuṭṭhahissāmī”ti āvajjitabbanti sambandho.

877. He does not call out, ‘Friend, the Teacher summons you.’ The connection is that one should advert, ‘I will emerge.’

878. Jīvitaddhānassāti attano jīvitakālassa jīvitappavattiyā. Āyu eva āyusaṅkhārā. “Āyuusmāviññāṇānī”ti ca vadanti, te cassa pakaticittasseva ārammaṇaṃ honti. Antonirodhe maraṇaṃ natthi carimabhavaṅgena mīyanato. Āvajjitvāva samāpajjitabbaṃ “sahasā maraṇaṃ mā ahosī”ti. Sahasā hi maraṇe aññabyākaraṇabhikkhuovādadānasāsanānubhāvadīpanānaṃ anissaro siyā, anāgāmino vā aggamaggānadhigamo siyā. Avasesanti nānābaddhaavikopanāditividhampi pubbakiccaṃ. Vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ.

878. The term `Jīvitaddhānassa` means ‘of one's own lifetime,’ ‘of the continuation of life.’ The life-faculty itself is the life-formation. And they say, ‘Life, heat, and consciousness,’ and these become the object of one's natural mind. During the attainment of cessation, there is no death, because death occurs with the final life-continuum consciousness. One must enter the attainment only after having adverted, thinking, ‘May sudden death not occur.’ For in the case of a sudden death, one might be without mastery over declaring another's final knowledge, giving exhortation to the monks, and illuminating the power of the Dispensation; or, for a non-returner, there might be non-attainment of the highest path. The term `Avasesa` refers to the remaining preliminary duties, which are of three kinds, beginning with not damaging one's various belongings. This is stated in the commentary.

879. Kiñcāpi “ekaṃ vā dve vā”ti aniyametvā viya vuttaṃ, dve vāre eva pana niyamato vadanti. Cittavāreti nevasaññānāsaññāyatanacittavāre. Nirodhaṃ phusatīti acittakabhāvamevāha. Nirodhassa payogattāti cittanirodhāya payogabhāvato, baladvayasambharaṇādipayogassa cittanirodhattāti attho. Samathavipassanābalasamannāgamo, ñāṇasamādhicariyāvasībhāvo cettha [V 2.0497] aññamaññānativattanavaseneva icchitabboti āha “dve samathavipassanādhamme yuganaddhe katvā”ti. Anupubbanirodhassa payogoti paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ, tadanupassanānañca anupubbato nirodhanassāyaṃ payogo. Idaṃ vuttanayena aṭṭhasamāpattiārohanaṃ na nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiyā samāpajjanassa. Tasmā dvinnaṃ cittānaṃ upari cittāni na pavattantīti yojanā.

879. Although it is said as if without specifying, ‘one or two,’ they definitively speak of only two occasions. ‘On the occasion of the mind’ refers to the occasions of the mind of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. ‘Touches cessation’ means only the state of being without mind. ‘Because it is the striving for cessation’ means because it is the effort for the cessation of mind; the meaning is that the effort, such as accumulating the two powers, has the cessation of mind as its purpose. And here, the possession of the powers of serenity and insight, and the mastery in the conduct of knowledge and concentration, should be desired only by way of not transgressing one another. Therefore, he said, ‘having yoked together the two things, serenity and insight.’ ‘The striving for gradual cessation’ means this is the effort for the successive cessation of the first jhāna and so on, and of the insight that contemplates them. This ascent through the eight attainments, in the manner stated, is not for the entering of the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Therefore, the construing is that minds do not arise above these two minds.

Parato [M 2.0529] acittako bhavituṃ na sakkotīti sakalaṃ yathāparicchinnakālaṃ acittako bhavituṃ na sakkoti. Tañca kho saṅghapaṭimānanasatthupakkosanaaddhānaparicchedāvajjanānaṃ akaraṇena, na nānābaddhaavikopanassa. Tassa hi akaraṇena kadāci kevalaṃ tādisassa parikkhārassa avināso na siyā, na nirodhasamāpattivibandho. Ayañca attho mahānāgattheravatthunā vibhāvito eva. Evaṃ sante tīhi ākārehi nirodhasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhānaṃ hotīti āpajjati, tasmā taṃ na sārato paccetabbaṃ. Paṭinivattitvā puna ākiñcaññāyataneyeva patiṭṭhātīti iminā samāpattiyā vibandhe jāte evaṃ hotīti dasseti, avibandheneva pana yathāparicchinnakālavītikkamane phalacittuppattiyā vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Evañca katvā gambhīrakandaroruḷhatattapāsāṇakkantapurisanidassanampi samatthitaṃ hotīti keci vadanti. Apare pana “pubbakiccassa akatattā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samāpannamattova ‘paṭinivattitvā ākiñcaññāyatane patiṭṭhātī’ti vuttattā saṅghapaṭimānanādiekaccapubbakiccākaraṇe aṅgavekallato nirodhasamāpattisamāpajjanaṃ na ijjhatevā”ti vadanti. Vattasadisañhetaṃ nirodhasamāpattiyā, yadidaṃ pubbakiccakaraṇaṃ. Tasmā tattha yaṃ garutaraṃ, tassa akaraṇaṃ samāpajjanaṃ vibandhatīti apare. Vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ. “Ākiñcaññāyatane patiṭṭhātī”ti ca idaṃ puna ākiñcaññāyatanassa samāpajjitabbattā vuttaṃ. Samāpajjitvā hi vuṭṭhāya pubbakiccassa kātabbattā.

The statement ‘one cannot remain without mind beyond that’ means one cannot remain without mind for the entire predetermined time. And indeed, this is due to not performing the preliminary acts of awaiting the Saṅgha, the Teacher's summons, and adverting to the lifespan's limit, not due to the non-performance of the task of protecting the various requisites. For by not performing that, at times merely the destruction of such requisites might occur, but there would not be an obstruction to the attainment of cessation. And this meaning has indeed been clarified by the story of the Elder Mahānāga. This being so, it follows that emergence from the attainment of cessation occurs in three ways; therefore, that statement should not be accepted as authoritative. By the phrase, ‘Having returned, one is re-established in the base of nothingness,’ it is shown that this happens when an obstruction to the attainment has arisen. But when there is no obstruction, emergence occurs with the arising of fruition-consciousness upon the passing of the predetermined time. And for this reason, the example of a man who has descended into a deep chasm and a man who has stepped on a heated stone slab is also supported, thus some say. But others say: ‘Because it is said, “On account of the preliminary duty not having been performed, one who has only just attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception returns and is re-established in the base of nothingness,” it follows that when some preliminary duty, such as awaiting the Saṅgha, is not performed, due to a deficiency in the factors, the entering of the attainment of cessation is not accomplished at all.’ Indeed, this performance of preliminary duties is like an observance for the attainment of cessation. Therefore, among them, the non-performance of whichever is more weighty obstructs the attainment, thus others say. This should be understood after investigation. And this statement, ‘one is established in the base of nothingness,’ is said because the base of nothingness has to be entered again. For, having entered and emerged, the preliminary duties must be performed.

Yathā panātiādi katapubbakiccatāsāmaññena upamāsaṃsandanaṃ.

‘Just as,’ and so on: the analogy connects through the common characteristic of having performed prior duties.

880. Assāti nirodhasamāpattiyā. “Kālaparicchedavasenā”tiādinā catūhi ākārehi nirodhasamāpattiyā ṭhānaṃ dasseti.

880. `Assa` (of this) refers to the attainment of cessation. By the phrase beginning with ‘By way of the time limit,’ it shows the abiding of the attainment of cessation in four ways.

882. Vivekaninnanti [V 2.0498] nissaraṇavivekaninnaṃ, pageva saṅkhāravimukhatāya, phalacittuppattiyā cāti veditabbaṃ.

882. ‘Inclined to seclusion’ should be understood as being inclined towards the seclusion of escape, both because of having turned away from formations from the very beginning and because of the arising of fruition-consciousness.

883. Ūsaṅkhārattayapaṭippassaddhiyā, avasesacetasikaviññāṇābhāvena rūpadhammamattāvasesatāya ca matanirodhasamāpannānaṃ avisesaṃ gahetvā pucchā “matassa ca samāpannassa ca ko viseso”ti. Kāmaṃ nesaṃ saṅkhārattayapaṭippassaddhiādīhi [M 2.0530] aviseso, rūpadhammamattāvasesatāya pana āyuusmāindriyānaṃ apagamānapagamanaṃ visesoti dassetuṃ “yvāya”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

883. Having considered the non-distinction between one who is dead and one who has attained cessation—due to the calming of the three formations, the absence of remaining mental factors and consciousness, and the state of only material phenomena remaining—the question was asked: ‘What is the difference between one who is dead and one who has attained cessation?’ Indeed, for them there is no difference with regard to the calming of the three formations and so on. However, to show that in the state of only material phenomena remaining, the difference is the departure and non-departure of life, heat, and the faculties, it was said: ‘For this one…’ and so on.

884. Sabhāvatoti sabhāvadhammato, paramatthatoti attho. Paramatthato hi vijjamānānaṃ saṅkhatādibhāvena vattabbataṃ labhati, na avijjamānaṃ. Samāpajjantassa vasenāti yasmā samāpajjantassa ariyapuggalassa samathavipassanādhamme yuganaddhe katvā aṭṭha samāpattiyo ārohantassa anukkamena saṅkhārānaṃ paṭippassambhanapayoganibbattiyā nirodhasamāpatti nipphannā nāma hoti, tasmā taṃ payoganibbattiṃ upādāya “nipphannā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

884. 'By its own nature' means by its own essential nature, in the ultimate sense. For, in the ultimate sense, that which truly exists obtains the state of being describable as conditioned and so on, but not that which does not exist. 'By the power of the one attaining' means that because for the noble person attaining—who, having yoked together the qualities of serenity and insight, ascends through the eight attainments in sequence—the attainment of cessation is said to be accomplished by the production of the application of calming the formations, therefore, with reference to that production of the application, it is proper to say 'accomplished'.

Saṅkhāravūpasamato, santadhammasamanvayato ca santaṃ. Ariyehi eva nisevitabbattā ariyanisevitaṃ. Tissannampi dukkhatānaṃ nibbutabhāvato nibbānamiti saṅkhaṃ upāgataṃ. Ariyaṃ paññanti suvisuddhaṃ maggaphalapaññaṃ. Imissāpīti nirodhasamāpattiyā. Samāpattisamatthatāti samāpajjanasamatthatā.

It is peaceful because of the calming of formations and because of conforming to the peaceful Dhamma of the immaterial attainments. It is called 'resorted to by the noble' because it is to be resorted to only by the noble ones. It has come to be designated as 'Nibbāna' because of the state of extinguishment of all three kinds of suffering. 'Noble wisdom' means the thoroughly purified wisdom of the path and fruition. 'Of this also' refers to the attainment of cessation. 'Capability for attainment' means the capability of attaining.

Āhuneyyabhāvādisiddhikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Accomplishment of the State of Being Worthy of Offerings and So Forth

885. Āhuneyyabhāvādisiddhīti āhuneyyapāhuneyyadakkhiṇeyyaañjalikaraṇīyaanuttarapuññakkhettabhāvasiddhi. Avisesenāti dassanamaggapaññādivisesena vinā, etissā lokuttarapaññāya. Ānetvā hunitabbanti āhunaṃ, dūratopi ānetvā dātabbadānaṃ, taṃ paṭiggahetuṃ yuttoti āhuneyyo. Pāhunaṃ vuccati āgantukadānaṃ, taṃ paṭiggahetuṃ yuttoti pāhuneyyo. Dakkhiṇaṃ arahatīti dakkhiṇeyyo, añjalikaraṇaṃ añjalikammaṃ, taṃ arahatīti añjalikaraṇīyo. Anuttaraṃ uttamaṃ sattānaṃ puññaviruhanaṭṭhānanti anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassāti ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana heṭṭhā vuttoyeva.

885. The accomplishment of being worthy of offerings and so forth (āhuneyyabhāvādisiddhi) means the accomplishment of being worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of donations, worthy of reverential salutation, and an unsurpassed field of merit. 'Without distinction' means without the distinction of the wisdom of the path of vision and so forth, with regard to this supramundane wisdom. 'Āhuna' means what should be brought and offered; one who is fit to receive a donation that should be brought even from afar and given is worthy of offerings (āhuneyya). 'Pāhuna' is said to be a gift for a guest; one who is fit to receive it is worthy of hospitality (pāhuneyya). One who deserves a donation (dakkhiṇa) is worthy of donations (dakkhiṇeyya). 'Añjalikaraṇa' is the act of reverential salutation; one who deserves it is worthy of reverential salutation (añjalikaraṇīya). Because it is an unsurpassed, supreme place for the growth of merit for beings, it is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. This is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, has indeed been stated below.

886. Mandāya [V 2.0499] vipassanāya āgatoti atikkhāya vipassanāya vasena paṭhamamaggapaññaṃ bhāvetvā sotāpannabhāvaṃ āgato. Saddhādīnaṃ mudūnaṃ indriyānaṃ vasena mudindriyopi samāno. Sattakkhattuparamoti sattakkhattuṃ paramā bhavūpapatti attabhāvaggahaṇaṃ, tato paraṃ aṭṭhamaṃ bhavaṃ nādiyatīti [M 2.0531] sattakkhattuparamo. Saṃsaritvāti paṭisandhiggahaṇavasena aparāparaṃ gantvā. Dukkhassantaṃ karotīti vaṭṭadukkhassa pariyantaṃ pariyosānaṃ karoti. Ayaṃ kālena devalokassa, kālena manussalokassāti missakassa bhavassa vasena “sattasugatibhave saṃsaritvā”ti vutto. Kulato kulaṃ gacchatīti kolaṃkolo. Sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyato paṭṭhāya hi nīcakule upapatti nāma natthi, mahābhogakulesuyeva nibbattatīti attho. Dve vā tīṇi vā kulānīti devamanussavasena dve vā tayo vā bhave. Iti ayampi missakabhaveneva kathito. Desanāmattameva cetaṃ “dve vā tīṇi vā”ti. Yāva chaṭṭhabhavā saṃsarantopi kolaṃkolova hoti. Attabhāvaggahaṇasaṅkhātaṃ ekaṃyeva khandhabījaṃ etassa atthīti ekabījī. “Mānusakaṃ bhava”nti idampi desanāmattaṃ. “Devabhavaṃ nibbattetī”tipi vattuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Ko panetesaṃ imaṃ pabhedaṃ niyametīti? Tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ vipassanā. Sace hi upari tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ vipassanā balavatī hoti, ekabījī nāma hoti. Tato mandāya kolaṃkolo, tato mandatarāya sattakkhattuparamo.

886. "One who has arrived through weak insight" (Mandāya vipassanāya āgato) means one who has attained the state of a stream-enterer by having developed the wisdom of the first path by means of insight that is not sharp. Being one with tender faculties such as faith and so on. "Seven-times-at-most" (Sattakkhattuparamo) means that the taking of an individual existence, arising in a state of being, is for a maximum of seven times; after that, one does not take up an eighth existence, therefore one is called a 'seven-times-at-most'. "Having wandered on" (saṃsaritvā) means having gone on successively by way of taking rebirth-linking. "Makes an end of suffering" (dukkhassantaṃ karoti) means one makes an end, a conclusion, to the suffering of the round. This one is said to have "wandered on through seven happy states of existence" by way of a mixed existence—at times in the deva world, at times in the human world. "Goes from a noble family to a noble family" (kulato kulaṃ gacchati), therefore one is called a 'family-to-family' one (kolaṃkolo). For indeed, from the realization of the fruit of stream-entry onwards, there is no such thing as rebirth in a low family; the meaning is that one is reborn only in families of great wealth and high station. "Two or three families" (dve vā tīṇi vā kulāni) means two or three existences by way of devas and humans. Thus, this one also is spoken of only by way of a mixed existence. And this, "two or three," is merely a manner of exposition. Even one who wanders on for up to the sixth existence is still a 'family-to-family' one. For this person, there is only one seed of the aggregates, designated as the taking of an individual existence, therefore one is called a 'one-seeder' (ekabījī). This "a human existence" is also merely a manner of exposition. It is indeed fitting to also say, "one brings about a deva existence." But what determines this distinction among them? The insight of the three paths. For if indeed the insight of the three higher paths is strong, one is called a 'one-seeder'. Through insight weaker than that, one is a 'family-to-family' one; through insight even weaker than that, one is a 'seven-times-at-most'.

887. Paṭisandhivasena sakiṃ āgacchatīti sakadāgāmī. Sakidevāti ekavāraṃyeva. “Imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvā”ti iminā pañcasu sakadāgāmīsu cattāro vajjetvā ekova gahito. Ekacco hi idha sakadāgāmiphalaṃ patvā idheva parinibbāti, ekacco idha patvā devaloke parinibbāti, ekacco devaloke patvā tattheva parinibbāti, ekacco devaloke patvā idhūpapajjitvā parinibbāti. Ime cattāropi idha na gahitā. Yo pana idha patvā devaloke yāvatāyukaṃ vasitvā puna idhūpapajjitvā parinibbāti, ayaṃ idha gahito.

887. Because he comes once by means of rebirth-linking, he is called a once-returner (sakadāgāmī). 'Only once' (sakideva) means just one time. By the text, 'Having come to this world' (imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvā), only one among the five kinds of once-returners is taken, excluding the four. For a certain person, having attained the once-returner fruition here, attains final Nibbāna right here; a certain person, having attained it here, attains final Nibbāna in the deva world; a certain person, having attained it in the deva world, attains final Nibbāna right there; a certain person, having attained it in the deva world, is reborn here and attains final Nibbāna. These four are not taken here. But the one who, having attained it here, lives for the full lifespan in the deva world, is reborn here again, and then attains final Nibbāna—this is the one taken here.

888. Paṭisandhivasena idha anāgamanato anāgāmī. Indriyavemattatāvasenāti saddhādīnaṃ vimuttiparipācakaindriyānaṃ paropariyattena. Pañcadhā idha vihāya niṭṭho hotīti so anāgāmī antarāparinibbāyiādibhāvena pañcapakārena imaṃ lokaṃ pajahitvā parinibbāyanako hoti. Āyuvemajjhassa antarāyeva kilesaparinibbānena parinibbāyanato antarāparinibbāyī[M 2.0532]. Upahaccāti vā upagantvā kālakiriyaṃ. Appayogenāti adhimattapayogena vinā appakasireneva tikkhindriyatāya [V 2.0500] sukheneva. Sappayogenāti ettha vuttavipariyāyena attho veditabbo. Uddhaṃ vā hi bhāvena uddhamassa taṇhāsotaṃ, vaṭṭasotaṃ vāti uddhaṃsoto. Uddhaṃ vā gantvā paṭilabhitabbato uddhamassa maggasotanti uddhaṃsoto. Paṭisandhivasena akaniṭṭhabhavaṃ gacchatīti akaniṭṭhagāmī.

888. Because of not coming to this world by means of rebirth-linking, he is called a non-returner (anāgāmī). 'By means of the difference in faculties' (indriyavemattatāvasena) refers to the state of being mature or immature of the faculties, such as faith, which bring liberation to maturity. Regarding 'He is established in five ways, having abandoned this world here' (pañcadhā idha vihāya niṭṭho hoti): that non-returner is one who attains final Nibbāna in five ways—such as being one who attains final Nibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyī)—having abandoned this world. Because of attaining final Nibbāna through the final Nibbāna of defilements right in the interval of half the lifespan, he is called an antarāparinibbāyī. Or, upahacca means having approached death. 'With little effort' (appayogena) means without excessive effort, with little difficulty and with ease, because of having keen faculties. 'With effort' (sappayogenāti): here the meaning should be understood in the opposite way to what was stated. Or indeed, because his stream of craving, or the stream of the round, is by nature upward-flowing, he is called an uddhaṃsoto (one who goes upstream). Or, because for him the stream of the path is upwards, as it is to be obtained by going upwards, he is called an uddhaṃsoto. Because he goes to the Akaniṭṭha existence by means of rebirth-linking, he is called an akaniṭṭhagāmī (one who goes to Akaniṭṭha).

Yatthupapannoti avihādīsu yattha yattha upapanno. Imesaṃ pana anāgāmīnaṃ pabhedajānanatthaṃ uddhaṃsotaakaniṭṭhagāmicatukkaṃ veditabbaṃ – yo hi avihato paṭṭhāya cattāro devaloke sodhetvā akaniṭṭhaṃ gantvā parinibbāti, ayaṃ uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī nāma. Yo pana heṭṭhā tayo devaloke sodhetvā sudassīdevaloke ṭhatvā parinibbāti, ayaṃ uddhaṃsoto naakaniṭṭhagāmī nāma. Yo ito akaniṭṭhameva gantvā parinibbāti, ayaṃ nauddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī nāma. Yo pana heṭṭhā catūsu devalokesu tattha tattheva parinibbāti, ayaṃ nauddhaṃsoto naakaniṭṭhagāmī nāma. Ete pana avihesu upapannasamanantarā āyuvemajjhaṃ appatvā, patvā ca parinibbāyanavasena tayo antarāparinibbāyino, eko upahaccaparinibbāyī, eko uddhaṃsototi pañca. Te asaṅkhārasasaṅkhāraparinibbāyivibhāgena dasa honti. Tathā atappasudassasudassīsūti cattāro dasakā cattālīsaṃ. Akaniṭṭhe pana uddhaṃsoto natthi. Tayo antarāparinibbāyino, eko upahaccaparinibbāyīti cattāro. Te asaṅkhārasasaṅkhāraparinibbāyivibhāgena aṭṭhāti aṭṭhacattālīsaṃ anāgāmino.

Wherever they are reborn: this means wherever one is reborn among the Aviha realms and so on. For the purpose of knowing the distinctions among these non-returners, the tetrad of the upstream-goer bound for Akaniṭṭha should be known: (1) One who, starting from the Aviha realm, traversing the four deva worlds, goes to Akaniṭṭha and attains parinibbāna—this is called an 'upstream-goer bound for Akaniṭṭha.' (2) One who, having traversed the three deva worlds below, attains parinibbāna while established in the Sudassī deva world—this is called an 'upstream-goer not bound for Akaniṭṭha.' (3) One who goes from here only to Akaniṭṭha and attains parinibbāna—this is called a 'non-upstream-goer bound for Akaniṭṭha.' (4) One who attains parinibbāna in that very place among the four deva worlds below—this is called a 'non-upstream-goer not bound for Akaniṭṭha.' Furthermore, these non-returners, by way of attaining parinibbāna in the Aviha realms—either immediately upon rebirth, or before reaching the midpoint of the lifespan, or after having reached it—are of five types: three who attain parinibbāna in the interval, one who attains parinibbāna by reduction, and one upstream-goer. These five, when divided into those who attain parinibbāna without exertion and with exertion, become ten. Likewise in the Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī realms, there are four groups of ten, making forty. In the Akaniṭṭha realm, however, there is no upstream-goer. There are four: three who attain parinibbāna in the interval and one who attains parinibbāna by reduction. When these are divided into those who attain parinibbāna without exertion and with exertion, they become eight. Thus, there are forty-eight non-returners.

Sotāpannā pana paṭipadābhedena cattāro sattakkhattuparamā, cattāro kolaṃkolā, cattāro ekabījinoti saddhādhurena paṭipannā dvādasa, tathā paññādhurenāti catuvīsati.

The stream-enterers, furthermore, by the distinction in their practice, are: four seven-times-at-most-returners, four clan-to-clan-goers, and four one-seeders. Thus, there are twelve who practice with faith as their leading faculty, and likewise with wisdom as their leading faculty, making twenty-four.

Sakadāgāmino suññatavimokkhena vimuttā paṭipadāvasena cattāro, tathā animittaappaṇihitavimokkhehīti dvādasa.

The once-returners liberated through the liberation of emptiness are four, by way of practice; likewise, with the signless and desireless liberations, there are twelve in total.

889. Tathā arahanto. Te pana dvādasa paññāvimuttā, dvādasa ubhatobhāgavimuttā, dvādasa tevijjā, dvādasa chaḷabhiññā, dvādasa paṭisambhidāppattāti [M 2.0533] samasaṭṭhi honti. Evamete saddhiṃ paccekasambuddhasammāsambuddhehi chacattālīsādhikasataṃ ariyā. Yasmā tesaṃ ariyabhāvasiddhi ariyāya paññābhāvanāya, tena vuttaṃ “āhuneyyabhāvādisiddhipi imissā lokuttarapaññābhāvanāya ānisaṃso”ti. Lokiyavijjābhiññāhi vināpi ubhatobhāgavimuttatā hotīti [V 2.0501] ubhatobhāgavimutto visuṃ gahito. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttanti yaṃ catutthamaggapaññābhāvanaṃ sandhāya heṭṭhā saṅkhepato gāthāvaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ pana vuttākāraṃ nigamanavasena dassetuṃ “maggakkhaṇe”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kāmaṃ catūsupi maggakkhaṇesu taṃ jaṭaṃ vijaṭeti nāma, phalakkhaṇesupi yathārahaṃ vijaṭitajaṭo, aggaphalakkhaṇeyeva pana sabbaso vijaṭitajaṭo, tato paraṃ vijaṭetabbāya jaṭāya abhāvato. Tenettha heṭṭhā heṭṭhimamaggapaññābhāvanānisaṃsassa vuttattāva catutthamaggapaññābhāvanāvasena attho vutto.

889. Likewise the Arahants. Further, among them, twelve are liberated by wisdom, twelve are liberated in both ways, twelve possess the three knowledges, twelve possess the six supernormal knowledges, and twelve have attained the analytical knowledges—thus they are sixty in all. In this way, these noble ones, together with the Paccekabuddhas and the Sammāsambuddhas, are one hundred and forty-six noble ones. Because the accomplishment of their state as a noble one is through the development of noble wisdom, it was therefore said: “The accomplishment of the state of being worthy of offerings, etc., is also a benefit of this development of supramundane wisdom.” The state of being liberated in both ways can occur even without the worldly knowledges and supernormal knowledges; hence, the one 'liberated in both ways' is taken up separately. The statement made previously in brief in the commentary on the verse was in reference to the development of the wisdom of the fourth path; further, to show that stated meaning by way of a conclusion, 'at the moment of the path,' etc., was said. Indeed, at the moments of all four paths, one is said to disentangle that tangle of craving. At the moments of fruition, too, one has the tangle of craving disentangled as is appropriate. But it is only at the moment of the highest fruition that one has the tangle of craving completely disentangled, because after that there is no further tangle of craving to be disentangled. Therefore, since the benefit of developing the wisdom of the lower paths has already been stated previously, the meaning here has been explained in terms of the development of the wisdom of the fourth path.

Ratinti abhiratiṃ, abhirucinti attho. Tatthāti ariyāya paññābhāvanāya.

‘Ratiṃ’ means enjoyment, pleasure. ‘Tattha’ means in the development of noble wisdom.

890. Imissā gāthāyāti imissaṃ gāthāyaṃ. Gāthā hi attano atthabhūtassa visuddhimaggassa ādhārabhāvena vuttā, sāmivacanaṃ vā etaṃ atthassa taṃsambandhibhāvato.

890. ‘Imissā gāthāya’ means ‘imissaṃ gāthāyaṃ’ (in this verse). Indeed, the verse is stated as the foundation for the Path of Purification, which is its own essence; or, this is a genitive expression, because the meaning is related to that verse.

Paññābhāvanānisaṃsaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the benefits of developing wisdom is concluded.

Iti tevīsatimaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus, the commentary on the twenty-third chapter.

Nigamanakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Concluding Discourse

891. Imissā [M 2.0534] dāni gāthāyātiādīnaṃ gāthānaṃ attho heṭṭhā vutto eva. Svāyaṃ “visuddhimaggaṃ bhāsissa”nti evaṃ paṭiññāto visuddhimaggo ettāvatā bhāsito hotīti sambandho.

891. The meaning of the verses beginning with 'Imissā dāni gāthāya' has already been stated previously. This Path of Purification, which was undertaken thus, “I shall expound the Path of Purification,” has by this much been expounded; thus is the connection.

892. Tatthātiādīsu ayaṃ padasambandhena saddhiṃ saṅkhepattho – tesaṃ “sīle patiṭṭhāyā”tigāthāyaṃ vuttānaṃ sīlādippabhedānaṃ atthānaṃ pañcannampi mahānikāyānaṃ aṭṭhakathānaye aṭṭhakathātantiyaṃ tattha tattha vutto yo vinicchayo, yebhuyyena taṃ sabbaṃ samāharitvā samānetvā nikāyantarassa nikāyagatavādadosasaṅkarehi mutto so nicchayo yasmā pakāsito, tasmā visuddhikāmehi yogīhi etasmiṃ visuddhimagge ādaro karaṇīyoyevāti.

892. In such passages beginning with 'Tattha,' this is the concise meaning together with the connection of the words: Whatever determination is spoken of here and there in the commentarial method and tradition of all five great Nikāyas regarding the meanings of those divisions such as virtue, etc., which were spoken of in the verse beginning 'Sīle patiṭṭhāya'—having brought together all of that for the most part, because that determination, freed from the corruptions of the intermingling of doctrines established in other Nikāyas and one's own Nikāya, has been explained, therefore, reverence should certainly be shown to this Path of Purification by yogis who desire purity.

Nigamanagāthāyo

Concluding Verses

Ettāvatā [M 2.0535][V 2.0502] ca –

And by this much:

Suvisuddhasamācāro, visuddhanayamaṇḍitaṃ;

Visuddhimaggaṃ lokassa, yadaccantavisuddhiyā.

That Path of Purification, adorned with pure methods, which for the ultimate purification of the world,

Abhāsi karuṇāvega-samussāhitamānaso;

Mahesi vipulodāta-visuddhimatipāṭavo.

the great sage of perfectly pure conduct, with a mind urged on by the force of compassion and possessing vast, noble, and pure, sharp wisdom, has expounded.

Tassa atthaṃ pakāsetuṃ, kathāmaggaṃ purātanaṃ;

Nissāya yā samāraddhā, atthasaṃvaṇṇanā mayā.

In order to explain its meaning, relying on the ancient path of discourse, this exposition of the meaning has been well undertaken by me.

Āyācito siddhagāma-pariveṇanivāsinā;

Therena dāṭhanāgena, suddhācārena dhīmatā.

Having been requested by the wise Elder Dāṭhanāga, of pure conduct, who dwells in the Siddhagāma monastery.

Sā esā paramatthānaṃ, tattha tattha yathārahaṃ;

Nidhānato paramattha-mañjūsā nāma nāmato.

This very commentary, because it is a repository of ultimate meanings fittingly placed here and there, is by name called the Paramatthamañjūsā.

Sampattā pariniṭṭhānaṃ, anākulavinicchayā;

Aṭṭhāsītippamāṇāya, pāḷiyā bhāṇavārato.

This commentary, having unconfused determinations, has reached its final completion with a Pāḷi text measuring eighty-eight recitation sections (bhāṇavāra).

Iti taṃ saṅkharontena, yaṃ taṃ adhigataṃ mayā;

Puññaṃ tassānubhāvena, lokanāthassa sāsane.

Thus, by composing that work, whatever merit has been attained by me, through the power of that merit, in the Dispensation of the Lord of the World,

Ogāhetvā visuddhāya, sīlādipaṭipattiyā;

Sabbepi dehino hontu, vimuttirasabhāgino.

having plunged into the pure practice of virtue and so forth, may all beings become partakers of the taste of liberation.

Ciraṃ [V 2.0503] tiṭṭhatu lokasmiṃ, sammāsambuddhasāsanaṃ;

Tasmiṃ sagāravā niccaṃ, hontu sabbepi pāṇino.

Long may the Dispensation of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One endure in the world; may all living beings always be respectful towards it.

Sammā vassatu kālena, devo rājā mahīpati;

Saddhammanirato lokaṃ, dhammeneva pasāsatūti.

May the rain fall properly in due season; may the king, the lord of the earth, delighting in the True Dhamma, rule the world only in accordance with the Dhamma.

Badaratitthavihāravāsinā ācariyadhammapālena katā

Composed by the teacher Dhammapāla, a resident of the Badaratittha Monastery.

Paramatthamañjūsā nāma visuddhimaggamahāṭīkā samattā.

The Great Sub-commentary on the Visuddhimagga, named the Paramatthamañjūsā, is completed.

Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā samattā.

The Great Sub-commentary on the Visuddhimagga is completed.
